Inadequate space heating / displacement / elderly living alone

diagnostics.rationale: standard digital thermometers do not read below 34 °C — Bristol or oesophageal probes required

management.detail: Rough movement can precipitate VF — log roll only, no chest pounding unless arrest.
Remove wet clothes, warm blankets, warm room (25 °C), sweet warm drinks if alert. Aim 0.5–2 °C/h rewarming.
Forced-air warmer (Bair Hugger) to truncal areas; warm IV fluids 40 °C; warm humidified O₂ 40 °C.
Cardiopulmonary bypass / ECMO if available — best outcome. Pleural / peritoneal / bladder lavage with warm fluid otherwise. Continue CPR + rewarming together — no death declaration until > 32 °C.
Withhold drugs < 30 °C (no clearance); thereafter double dosing intervals. Defibrillation x3 in VF — if no response, continue CPR + warm + retry at 30 °C.

title: Eclampsia
presentation: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure in patient with pre-eclampsia features (hypertension + proteinuria after 20 weeks)
Antepartum (50 %), intrapartum (25 %), postpartum (25 % — up to 6 weeks)
Often preceded by headache, visual disturbance, RUQ pain, hyper-reflexia
redFlags: HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, raised LFTs, low platelets)

diagnostics.rationale: proteinuria ≥ 300 mg/24 h or PCR ≥ 30 mg/mmol

diagnostics.test: FBC + LFTs + creatinine + LDH + urate + clotting

management.detail: Protect airway, oxygen, IV access ×2. Postpartum monitoring continues 24 h after delivery.

Magnesium sulphate 4 g IV over 5 min (or 5 g IM in each buttock) loading + 1 g/h IV maintenance (or 5 g IM every 4 h) — continue for 24 h after last seizure or delivery (whichever later). Monitor reflexes + RR + urine output.
Target 140–150/90–100. Labetalol 10–20 mg IV every 10 min (max 300 mg) OR hydralazine 5 mg IV every 20 min OR nifedipine 10 mg PO every 30 min.
Stabilise mother first; deliver as soon as practicable (vaginal if cervix favourable + no fetal distress; otherwise caesarean). Continue MgSO₄ 24 h postpartum.
Loss of reflexes / RR < 12 / urine < 20 mL/h — stop MgSO₄. Calcium gluconate 1 g IV slow if severe.
Continue antihypertensives postpartum until BP normalises. Multidisciplinary follow-up for cardiovascular risk.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (MOH)

title: Cholera
presentation: Sudden profuse painless rice-water diarrhoea + vomiting
Severe dehydration develops within hours — sunken eyes, washerwoman hands, weak pulse
May be afebrile or low-grade fever
Outbreak setting — refugee camp / flood / contaminated water

management.detail: Severe dehydration (Plan C): Ringer's lactate 100 mL/kg IV — first 30 mL/kg in 30 min (60 min if < 1 yr), then 70 mL/kg in 2.5 h (5 h if < 1 yr). Reassess every 30 min. Add ORS PO 5 mL/kg/h as soon as patient can drink.
ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 h under supervision in cholera treatment centre. Continue zinc 20 mg/day × 10 days for children.
Adults: doxycycline 300 mg single dose OR azithromycin 1 g single dose. Children + pregnant: azithromycin 20 mg/kg single dose (max 1 g). Reserve for severe cases / outbreak control.
Notify district + WHO immediately. Establish cholera treatment centre. Safe water + sanitation + soap. Oral cholera vaccine (OCV) ring vaccination in coordination with district / GAVI.
Urine output target > 1 mL/kg/h; pulse + BP every 15 min; bicarbonate; glucose in children.

references.label: WHO Cholera Outbreak Response Field Manual 2024
Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) Technical Guidelines, 3rd edition (MOH)

title: Typhoid (enteric) fever
presentation: Step-ladder fever rising over 7–10 days
Relative bradycardia (Faget sign)
Hepatosplenomegaly + rose spots on trunk
Constipation early then green pea-soup diarrhoea later
Confusion + 'typhoid state' in 2nd week
redFlags: Intestinal perforation (week 3 — sudden abdominal pain + peritonism)

diagnostics.rationale: highest yield ~90 %, used when blood culture negative + clinical suspicion
low specificity in endemic areas — use only with high titres + clinical pattern

management.step: Empirical antibiotic — fluoroquinolone susceptibility falling in SSA
management.detail: Adults: azithromycin 1 g PO/IV day 1 then 500 mg/day × 6 days OR ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily × 10–14 days. Children: azithromycin 20 mg/kg/day × 7 days OR ceftriaxone 75 mg/kg/day × 10–14 days. Add carbapenem if XDR S. Typhi (Pakistan / spreading).
Paracetamol for fever. Adequate fluids. Soft diet (constipation common — avoid laxatives).
If shock / encephalopathy: dexamethasone 3 mg/kg IV then 1 mg/kg every 6 h × 48 h reduces mortality (Hoffman 1984).
Urgent surgical opinion — resection / repair. Continue broad antibiotic.
Notify. Stool culture clearance × 3 negative before food-handler return to work. Typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV) for outbreaks + endemic infant immunisation (WHO SAGE 2017).

references.label: WHO Typhoid Vaccines: WHO position paper 2018

title: Ebola virus disease (EVD)
presentation: Incubation 2–21 days; presents with abrupt high fever, malaise, myalgia, headache
GI phase (day 3–10): vomiting, profuse diarrhoea, abdominal pain
Late: haemorrhagic features in some — petechiae, conjunctival haemorrhage, GI bleed
Africa endemic foci: DR Congo, Uganda, Sudan, Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia
redFlags: Travel / contact from outbreak zone within 21 days

diagnostics.rationale: single private room + PPE + dedicated equipment; notify national IHR focal point + WHO

diagnostics.test: Ebola RT-PCR on whole blood / oral swab (in ill / deceased)
diagnostics.rationale: definitive; sensitivity rises after day 3 of symptoms

diagnostics.test: Rapid antigen RDT (where PCR not available)

diagnostics.rationale: common alternative diagnoses — never delay isolation while testing

management.detail: Single room with bathroom. Strict PPE per WHO algorithm. Cohort confirmed cases. No needle re-sheathing. Safe waste handling. Dedicated team. Restrict visitors.

Aggressive fluid replacement (oral + IV) — patients lose 5–10 L/day GI fluid. Correct electrolytes (K, Mg, Ca). Empirical antibiotics for septic shock. Antipyretic (paracetamol — AVOID aspirin/NSAIDs).
For Zaire ebolavirus: Inmazeb (atoltivimab/maftivimab/odesivimab) or Ebanga (ansuvimab) — single IV dose, 50 mg/kg per component. Substantial mortality reduction (PALM trial 2019).
rVSV-ZEBOV (Ervebo) ring vaccination of contacts + healthcare workers. Cervarix Ad26/MVA prime-boost in pre-exposure.
WHO + IHR within 24 h. Identify contacts back 21 days; monitor daily for 21 days.
Late sequelae: arthralgia, uveitis (referral), depression. Viral persistence in semen — counsel barrier contraception for ≥ 12 months.

references.label: Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) Technical Guidelines, 3rd edition (MOH)

title: Lassa fever
presentation: Insidious onset fever + malaise over 1–3 days; pharyngitis with exudate
Retrosternal pain, conjunctival injection, oedema of face/neck
Later: hearing loss (25 % of survivors), GI bleed, encephalopathy
West Africa endemic: Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Guinea (rural Mastomys natalensis rodent zones)
redFlags: Travel / contact in endemic West African zone

diagnostics.rationale: ribavirin started empirically; viral load high; transmission via body fluids

diagnostics.test: Lassa RT-PCR on serum / throat swab

management.detail: Single room, PPE, dedicated team. Notify IHR. Less aggressive PPE than Ebola but still strict.
30 mg/kg loading IV then 16 mg/kg every 6 h × 4 days then 8 mg/kg every 8 h × 6 days. Most effective if started within 6 days of illness. Reduces mortality 5× in severe disease (McCormick 1986).
IV fluids + electrolytes. Avoid aspirin / NSAIDs (haemorrhage).
Termination of pregnancy in severe Lassa improves maternal survival (high obstetric mortality).
WHO within 24 h. Monitor contacts daily for fever × 21 days.

references.label: Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) Technical Guidelines, 3rd edition (MOH)

title: Mpox (monkeypox)
presentation: Fever + lymphadenopathy (distinguishing feature from smallpox / VZV) + headache + myalgia
Rash 1–3 days later: deep-seated firm vesiculopustules — face, palms, soles, oropharynx, anogenital
Lesions evolve synchronously through macule → papule → vesicle → pustule → crust over 2–4 weeks
Clade I (Central Africa) — historically more severe than Clade II (West Africa). 2024 SSA outbreak — Clade Ib + Ia
redFlags: Mucosal involvement causing airway / eye complications

diagnostics.rationale: definitive; swab vesicle/pustule fluid or crust
current outbreak transmitted often via close intimate contact

management.detail: Until all lesions crusted + new epithelialised skin (typically 2–4 weeks). Single room / cohort. Standard + contact + droplet PPE; airborne PPE during aerosol-generating procedures.
Analgesia (paracetamol, opioid if severe — rectal lesions painful). Adequate fluids. Topical antiseptic. Manage bacterial superinfection.
Tecovirimat 600 mg BD PO × 14 days (adult) — evidence for severe disease, immunocompromised, paediatric, pregnancy. Brincidofovir as alternative.
MVA-BN (Imvanex / Jynneos) — ring vaccination of contacts. Post-exposure within 4 days for prevention; up to 14 days to modify severity.
WHO + IHR (PHEIC declared August 2024). Contact tracing for 21 days.

references.label: Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) Technical Guidelines, 3rd edition (MOH)

title: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis)
presentation: Children 6 months–6 years, peak 1–2 yr; autumn/winter peak
Coryza for 12–48 h → barking 'seal' cough + inspiratory stridor + hoarse voice
Worse at night + when distressed
Mild — stridor only on exertion / agitation
Moderate — stridor at rest + mild–moderate recession
Severe — marked stridor + recession + RR ↑ + agitation / drowsiness + cyanosis
redFlags: Drooling + leaning forward + toxic appearance → epiglottitis (do NOT examine throat)
Sudden onset without coryza → foreign body aspiration
Failure to respond to nebulised adrenaline in 30 min

diagnostics.rationale: do not perform routine bloods or imaging in mild–moderate croup

diagnostics.test: Lateral neck X-ray (only if epiglottitis differential)
diagnostics.rationale: subglottic narrowing 'steeple sign' in croup; 'thumbprint' in epiglottitis

management.detail: Sit child on parent's lap; minimise distress; do not look in throat unless prepared to manage airway.
Single dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (or 0.6 mg/kg if moderate/severe; max 16 mg). Onset in 1–2 h. Acceptable: prednisolone 1 mg/kg as alternative. Discharge after 4 h observation if improved.
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 (5 mg) via O₂ mask — repeat in 30 min if no response. Onset minutes. Observe ≥ 4 h after (rebound effect).
Call paediatric anaesthetist. Senior airway team — small-bore endotracheal tube (1 size smaller than predicted) in theatre. IV access only AFTER airway secured.
Croup typically resolves over 3–5 days. Return if stridor at rest, working hard to breathe, drowsy, drooling, or new fever.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Bronchiolitis (under 2 years)
presentation: Children under 2 yrs (peak 3–6 months) with coryza progressing to cough + tachypnoea + wheeze + fine crackles
Feeding difficulty (key clinical marker)
Peak severity day 3–5 of illness, lasts 7–10 days
RSV most common; rhinovirus, hMPV, parainfluenza
redFlags: Marked respiratory distress (RR > 70, grunting, severe recession)
High-risk: < 3 months, ex-preterm, congenital heart disease, CLD, neuromuscular disease, immunocompromised

diagnostics.rationale: RSV PCR only for cohorting purposes when admitted

diagnostics.test: CXR + bloods only if uncertain diagnosis or critical
diagnostics.rationale: avoid unnecessary investigations — diffuse hyperinflation + atelectasis on CXR

management.detail: Maintain oxygen saturation ≥ 92 % (consider lower threshold in well-perfused infants per NICE). High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) for moderate-severe. NG / IV fluids if poor feeding (give 2/3 maintenance to avoid SIADH). Avoid sedation.
Routine bronchodilators (salbutamol, ipratropium), corticosteroids, antibiotics, hypertonic saline, ribavirin, chest physiotherapy — NOT recommended in typical bronchiolitis.
Consider HFNC 2 L/kg/min, CPAP, intubation for type 2 RF / exhaustion. RSV monoclonal antibody (nirsevimab) for prevention in high-risk infants.
Safe to discharge when feeding adequately (> 50–75 %), SpO₂ ≥ 92 % on air for several hours, parents confident. Safety-net advice on red flags.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Cervical cancer screening (HPV/VIA/cytology)
presentation: Screening of asymptomatic women — most early lesions silent
Risk amplified by HIV, smoking, multiple partners, lack of prior screening
Cervical cancer leading cause of cancer death in women in SSA
redFlags: Postmenopausal bleeding — refer for colposcopy regardless of screening result

diagnostics.rationale: WHO preferred — every 5 years from age 30 (or 25 if HIV+); higher sensitivity than VIA / cytology
single-visit screen-and-treat — practical in low-resource settings; every 3 years from 25–49
where HPV testing unavailable; every 3 years 25–49 + every 5 years 50–65

management.detail: Recall at 5 yrs (HPV) or 3 yrs (VIA/cytology). HIV+ women — recall at 3 yrs (HPV) or annually (VIA/cytology).

management.step: HPV positive — partial genotyping (16/18 +) or VIA / cytology abnormal
management.detail: Triage with colposcopy + biopsy. If cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN2/3) — excisional treatment (LLETZ / cone biopsy).
VIA-positive + acetowhite lesion eligible for thermal ablation / cryotherapy → same-visit treatment. Refer if lesion > 75 % of cervix, extends into endocervix, or suspicion of invasion.
HPV vaccination programme — single dose for girls 9–14 (WHO SAGE 2022). Address HIV control + smoking cessation.

title: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
presentation: Sudden severe unilateral eye pain + headache + nausea / vomiting
Red eye with cloudy / 'steamy' cornea + fixed mid-dilated pupil
Halos around lights + visual loss
Risk factors: hyperopia, age > 50, Asian ethnicity, dim light, anticholinergic drugs (TCA, antihistamine, atropine)
redFlags: Failure to respond to medical therapy within 1 h

management.detail: Send to eye unit immediately; vision-threatening.
Lie patient supine. Topical drops: timolol 0.5 % one drop + apraclonidine 1 % + pilocarpine 2 % every 5 min × 3. Systemic: acetazolamide 500 mg IV (or 500 mg PO) then 250 mg every 6 h.

management.step: If IOP > 50 or unresponsive at 1 h
management.detail: IV mannitol 1–2 g/kg over 30 min (caution in cardiac / renal disease). Topical steroid (dexamethasone) once IOP starts falling.
Peripheral iridotomy bilaterally (other eye is at risk) within 24–48 h once cornea clears.
Avoid anticholinergic drugs. Counsel re recurrence in untreated fellow eye.

title: Testicular torsion
presentation: Sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain + swelling (often during sleep or sport)
Nausea + vomiting
Peak age — neonatal + adolescent (10–18 yrs)
High-riding testis with horizontal lie + absent cremasteric reflex
redFlags: Time from onset > 6 h — testicular viability dropping rapidly
Bilateral pain (perinatal torsion → both can twist)
Suspected intermittent torsion (recurrent episodes — refer for elective fixation)

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnosis — DO NOT DELAY for imaging
diagnostics.rationale: TWIST score (testicular swelling, hard testis, absent cremasteric reflex, nausea/vomiting, high-riding) — high score → straight to theatre

diagnostics.test: Doppler ultrasound only if equivocal + immediately available
diagnostics.rationale: absent intratesticular flow; never delay surgery > 30 min for imaging

management.detail: Salvage rate ~100 % if explored within 6 h; ~50 % at 6–12 h; ~10 % > 12 h. Bilateral scrotal exploration + detorsion + bilateral orchidopexy (the contralateral testis is at risk of metachronous torsion).

management.step: Manual detorsion (only if surgery > 1 h away)
management.detail: 'Open book' — rotate testis outward toward thigh (relief in 80 % of medial torsions). Still requires emergency orchidopexy after.
Orchidectomy + contralateral fixation. Counsel about future fertility / hormonal effects.
Sperm cryopreservation discussion in adolescents who lose testis. Refer to fertility specialist.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children

title: Acute bacterial meningitis — adult
presentation: Classic triad — fever + neck stiffness + altered mental state (only ~45 %); add headache → 95 % sensitivity for any 2 of 4
Petechiae / purpura → meningococcal
Cranial nerve palsies → consider TB
Recurrent → CSF leak (basal skull fracture) / immunocompromised
SSA meningitis belt (Dec–Apr) — Neisseria meningitidis A, W, C, X
redFlags: Suspected raised ICP (papilloedema, posturing) — do NOT LP first

diagnostics.test: Antibiotics WITHIN 1 hour — do not delay for LP
diagnostics.rationale: every hour delay associated with 30 % increase in mortality

diagnostics.test: Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics if can be done within 10 min
diagnostics.rationale: if not, take cultures after antibiotic but ASAP

diagnostics.test: LP after CT brain if any contraindication
diagnostics.rationale: CT first if: focal neuro, immunocompromised, new seizure, GCS < 13, signs of raised ICP

diagnostics.test: CSF: cell count, protein, glucose (with paired serum), Gram stain, culture, latex / PCR for major pathogens
diagnostics.rationale: typical bacterial: neutrophilic pleocytosis, ↑ protein, ↓ glucose < 50 % serum

management.detail: ABC. Senior support. Notify public health (meningococcal). Strict + droplet precautions until 24 h on effective antibiotics.

Adults 18–50: ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 h. > 50 yrs or immunocompromised: ceftriaxone 2 g BD + amoxicillin 2 g every 4 h (Listeria cover). Penicillin allergy: chloramphenicol + cotrimoxazole. SSA meningitis belt outbreaks: chloramphenicol oily IM single dose 100 mg/kg (max 3 g) for mass campaigns.

0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 h × 4 days, START WITH OR BEFORE first antibiotic dose; reduces mortality + neurological sequelae in pneumococcal disease (developed-world evidence). Avoid in immunocompromised + post-neurosurgical.
Head up 30°, normocapnia, mannitol 1 g/kg if signs of herniation, neurosurgical opinion.

Meningococcal: ceftriaxone 7 days + ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose to close contacts within 24 h. Pneumococcal: ceftriaxone 10–14 days. Listeria: amoxicillin 3 weeks. TB: standard 4-drug regimen + dexamethasone weaning over 8 weeks (Tunkel).
Audiology at discharge + 4 weeks. Developmental + cognitive follow-up. Reinforce vaccination of close contacts.

title: Acute pancreatitis
presentation: Sudden epigastric pain radiating to back, worse on lying flat, eased by leaning forward
Vomiting (often resistant to antiemetics)
Fever
Causes (I-GET-SMASHED): Idiopathic, Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion sting, Hyperlipidaemia/Ca/parathyroid, ERCP, Drugs
redFlags: Cullen sign (periumbilical bruising) / Grey-Turner sign (flank bruising) — necrotising pancreatitis
Tachypnoea + hypoxia — ARDS or pleural effusion
Persistent organ failure > 48 h — high mortality

diagnostics.rationale: diagnostic — combined with abdominal pain / imaging

diagnostics.test: FBC, U+E, glucose, calcium, LDH, LFTs, ABG, CRP
diagnostics.rationale: for severity scoring; CRP > 150 at 48 h → severe

diagnostics.test: CT abdomen with contrast at 72 h
diagnostics.rationale: ONLY if diagnostic uncertainty or to assess for necrosis after 72 h — too early on day 1

management.detail: Lactated Ringer's 5–10 mL/kg/h titrated to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h, MAP > 65 + lactate clearance. Avoid over-resuscitation (worsens ARDS). Reassess at 6 + 12 + 24 h.
IV morphine PRN (does NOT cause sphincter of Oddi spasm in usual doses) + paracetamol 1 g IV every 6 h. PCA if severe.
NG / NJ feeding within 48–72 h reduces infection + mortality vs TPN. Resume PO when nausea resolves and pain improving.

Gallstone + cholangitis / persistent obstruction: ERCP within 24 h. Otherwise gallstone pancreatitis: laparoscopic cholecystectomy SAME admission for mild disease (NEJM). Hypertriglyceridaemia: insulin infusion / plasmapheresis.
Use only for infected necrosis (positive culture / clinical sepsis from day 7+). Imipenem 500 mg IV every 6 h preferred (best pancreatic penetration). Routine prophylaxis does NOT reduce mortality.
Step-up approach: percutaneous drainage → endoscopic/laparoscopic necrosectomy. Avoid open surgery in first 4 weeks.

title: Acute variceal haemorrhage
presentation: Haematemesis + melaena + features of chronic liver disease (jaundice, spider naevi, palmar erythema, ascites, asterixis)
Hypovolaemic shock — often dramatic blood loss
Bleeding aggravated by infection (translocation) + coagulopathy

diagnostics.test: FBC + group + crossmatch + INR + albumin + LFTs + creatinine

management.detail: Two large-bore IV. Transfuse RBC to target Hb 70–80 g/L (HIGHER threshold worsens portal pressure → more bleeding — Villanueva NEJM 2013). Platelets if < 50; FFP if INR > 1.5 + bleeding. Vitamin K 10 mg IV.
Terlipressin 2 mg IV every 4 h × 5 days (preferred) OR octreotide 50 µg bolus + 50 µg/h × 5 days. Both reduce portal pressure + improve haemostasis.
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily × 7 days — reduces mortality + infection rate; start at diagnosis.
Band ligation for oesophageal varices (first-line). Sclerotherapy alternative. Gastric variceal: cyanoacrylate glue injection.
Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken–Blakemore) — short-term bridge only. TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) — definitive rescue, lowers portal pressure.
Non-selective β-blocker (propranolol / carvedilol) titrated to HR < 60 + repeat banding every 2–4 weeks until eradicated. Continue β-blocker indefinitely. Consider TIPS if recurrent.

title: Acute pulmonary embolism
presentation: Sudden dyspnoea + pleuritic chest pain + haemoptysis + tachycardia + tachypnoea
Syncope or shock (massive PE)
Risk factors: recent immobilisation / surgery / pregnancy / OCP / malignancy / prior VTE / inherited thrombophilia
Wells score for risk stratification
redFlags: Right heart strain on ECHO / raised troponin → submassive PE
Pregnancy (V/Q scan preferred to limit fetal radiation)

diagnostics.test: D-dimer in low-probability patients only (NOT in high probability — proceed to imaging)

diagnostics.rationale: preferred in pregnancy + IV contrast allergy + young women (lower breast radiation)

diagnostics.test: Bedside echo — RV dilatation, McConnell sign, septal flattening
diagnostics.rationale: in shock — supports massive PE before CT

management.detail: Systemic thrombolysis: alteplase 10 mg IV bolus + 90 mg over 2 h (max 100 mg). Half-dose in age > 75 yrs / low weight. Catheter-directed thrombolysis if available. ECMO bridge if facility allows.

management.step: Submassive PE — RV strain but no shock
management.detail: Therapeutic anticoagulation; consider thrombolysis in selected younger / good-functional cases (PEITHO). Catheter-directed thrombolysis if available.

management.step: Stable PE — outpatient when low-risk (PESI low / sPESI 0)
management.detail: DOAC apixaban 10 mg BD × 7 days then 5 mg BD (or rivaroxaban 15 mg BD × 21 days then 20 mg OD). LMWH if cancer / pregnancy. Warfarin alternative.
LMWH (NOT DOACs — cross placenta); continue therapeutic dose throughout pregnancy + 6 weeks postpartum. Switch to UFH 36 h before planned delivery.
Provoked: 3 months. Unprovoked: long-term consideration based on bleeding risk vs recurrence (HERDOO2, men 1 yr score).
ONLY for absolute contraindication to anticoagulation (active bleed); retrievable + remove ASAP.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Anaphylaxis — clinical management
presentation: Acute onset (minutes-hours) of skin/mucosal involvement (urticaria, lip/face swelling) PLUS one of: respiratory compromise (dyspnoea, wheeze, stridor, hypoxia), hypotension/shock, GI symptoms (vomiting, diarrhoea), severe disabling abdominal pain
OR sudden hypotension / bronchospasm / laryngeal involvement after exposure to known allergen
Common triggers: foods (peanut, tree nut, shellfish), drugs (β-lactams, NSAID, contrast), venom (bee, wasp, fire ant), latex, exercise-induced

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnosis — treat first, test later
Serum mast cell tryptase — at 1–2 h + 4 h + 24 h + baseline
diagnostics.rationale: supports diagnosis (peaks ~1 h, returns to baseline 24 h)

diagnostics.test: Specific IgE / skin prick allergy testing
diagnostics.rationale: after recovery + by allergist — identify trigger

management.detail: Stop suspected drug / infusion / food. Lie patient flat with legs raised (sitting up if respiratory distress; left lateral if pregnant).

Adult / ≥ 12 yrs: 500 µg (0.5 mL). Child 6–12: 300 µg. Child < 6 yrs: 150 µg. Repeat every 5 min if no improvement. IV adrenaline 50 µg boluses ONLY by experienced clinician with monitoring (cardiac arrest dosing 1 mg if peri-arrest).
15 L/min via reservoir mask. 2 large-bore IV. Fluid bolus 500–1000 mL (10 mL/kg child) IV stat; repeat as needed.

Bronchospasm: nebulised salbutamol 5 mg + ipratropium 500 µg. Stridor: nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000. NB: H1/H2 antihistamines + steroids are NO LONGER recommended in initial management (Resuscitation Council UK 2021 + EAACI 2021 — they do NOT reverse anaphylaxis). Use only for delayed symptomatic relief after adrenaline.
IV adrenaline infusion 0.05–1 µg/kg/min via central line. Add glucagon 1–5 mg IV for patients on β-blocker. Vasopressin / methylene blue if catecholamine-resistant.

Minimum 6 h observation after symptom resolution (12 h if asthma / refractory). Provide 2× adrenaline auto-injector + written emergency plan + allergy clinic referral. AVOID NSAIDs in subsequent episodes.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy
presentation: West Haven grade I — mild confusion, day-night reversal
Grade II — drowsiness, asterixis, inappropriate behaviour
Grade III — somnolent but rousable, gross disorientation
Grade IV — coma
Precipitants: infection (SBP, UTI, chest), GI bleed, constipation, electrolyte (hypokalaemia / alkalosis), sedatives, diuretic overuse, dehydration, dietary protein excess, TIPS
redFlags: Acute liver failure (no chronic disease) — King's College criteria → transplant

diagnostics.test: Clinical assessment + Number Connection Test in early grades
Identify precipitant — septic screen (urine, blood, chest, ascitic tap), endoscopy if GI bleed, U+E, glucose, ABG, drug review
diagnostics.rationale: addressing precipitant is curative in many cases
supports diagnosis if elevated but normal does NOT exclude; do NOT trend in management

diagnostics.test: Brain imaging if focal signs / atypical / coma — exclude bleed, infection, structural

management.detail: Antibiotic for SBP (cefotaxime 2 g IV every 8 h × 5 days). Stop sedatives + diuretics. Correct electrolytes (K, Mg). Manage GI bleed. Treat constipation.
Lactulose 30–45 mL PO/NG/PR every 1–2 h until soft bowel motion, then titrate to 2–3 stools/day. Rifaximin 550 mg twice daily reduces recurrence (specialist; consider in repeat HE).
Normal protein 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day (do NOT restrict — old practice abandoned). Branched-chain amino acid supplement in refractory cases. Enteral feeding if grade III–IV.
GCS-based intubation + ICU. Albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1 + 1 g/kg day 3 in SBP (Sort 1999) — reduces hepatorenal syndrome.
Specialist referral. LOLA (L-ornithine-L-aspartate) controversial. TIPS reversal (rare). Liver transplant assessment if persistent.
Continue lactulose + rifaximin. Patient + family education on signs + driving safety. Avoid sedatives. Monitor for new precipitant.

title: Acute appendicitis
presentation: Periumbilical pain migrating to RIF over 12–24 h
Anorexia, nausea, vomiting (vomit AFTER pain — appendicitis; before — gastroenteritis)
Low-grade fever (high fever suggests perforation)
Tenderness at McBurney's point, Rovsing sign, psoas sign, obturator sign
Atypical in pregnancy (location shifts up + lateral), elderly (often advanced), young children

diagnostics.rationale: guides imaging vs observation; ≥ 7 high risk

diagnostics.test: USS — first-line in children + women + pregnancy
diagnostics.rationale: non-compressible, blind-ended structure > 6 mm, free fluid

diagnostics.test: CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast — adults with equivocal exam / atypical

diagnostics.rationale: leucocytosis + raised CRP support; normal results do not exclude

management.step: IV access, fluids, NBM, analgesia, antiemetic
management.detail: Crystalloid resuscitation. Morphine PRN (does NOT mask diagnosis per RCT evidence). Ondansetron / cyclizine.
Co-amoxiclav 1.2 g IV (or cefuroxime + metronidazole; or piperacillin-tazobactam in severe sepsis / immunocompromised) at decision to operate.
Within 24 h of diagnosis (delayed > 36 h increases perforation). Open if not available / pregnancy 3rd trimester. Specimen to histology.

Antibiotics alone (CODA trial) — IV then oral × 7 days. ~30 % recurrence at 1 year. Reserve for: non-operative candidate / patient choice / phlegmon. Plan interval appendicectomy if mass / suspicion of perforation.
IV antibiotics + percutaneous drainage. Interval appendicectomy 6–8 weeks later.
Lap appendicectomy safe in 1st + 2nd trimester. Open right lower-quadrant approach often used in 3rd trimester. Tocolysis discussion + obstetric input.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children

title: Ascending cholangitis (Tokyo)
presentation: Charcot triad — RUQ pain + fever + jaundice (only 50–70 %)
Reynolds pentad — Charcot + hypotension + confusion (severe / suppurative)
Causes: choledocholithiasis, malignant biliary obstruction, post-ERCP stricture, anastomotic stricture

diagnostics.test: FBC + LFTs (ALP + GGT + bilirubin) + CRP + blood cultures

management.detail: Blood cultures, broad antibiotics, lactate, fluids 30 mL/kg, vasopressor if MAP < 65.
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 8 h (gram negatives + enterococci + anaerobes). Severe: add metronidazole + escalate to carbapenem. Adjust per culture.
ERCP with stent / sphincterotomy — first-line. Percutaneous transhepatic drainage if ERCP fails or anatomical access not feasible. Surgery very rarely indicated acutely.
Same admission if mild + fit; otherwise within 6 weeks. Clear duct stones at ERCP.
Brushings at ERCP + EUS-FNA. Refer for oncology / hepatobiliary input.

title: Acute cholecystitis
presentation: RUQ pain (often > 6 h, post-prandial) + fever + nausea
Murphy sign (arrest of inspiration on RUQ palpation)
Mass palpable in RUQ in 30 %
Acalculous in critically ill / TPN / post-trauma
redFlags: Gangrenous / emphysematous (gas in wall on imaging) — urgent surgery

diagnostics.rationale: gallstones + thickened gallbladder wall > 4 mm + pericholecystic fluid + sonographic Murphy sign

diagnostics.test: HIDA scan / MRI — if USS equivocal

management.detail: Crystalloid resuscitation. Morphine + paracetamol. Antiemetic.
Co-amoxiclav 1.2 g IV every 8 h × 5–7 days OR piperacillin-tazobactam if severe sepsis.
Within 7 days of symptom onset preferred over delayed (CHOCOLATE Lancet 2018 + Tokyo 2018). Lower complications + shorter LOS.
Drainage tube — bridge to interval surgery or definitive in moribund / critical care patient. Antibiotic + observation.
Urgent cholecystectomy or cholecystostomy — high mortality if missed.

title: Postpartum (perinatal) depression
presentation: Onset within 12 months postpartum (most within 6 weeks)
Persistent low mood + anhedonia + sleep disturbance distinct from infant needs
Tearfulness, anxiety, guilt, feelings of inadequacy as mother
Postpartum blues (first 2 weeks, transient — does NOT need treatment) vs depression (persistent + functional impairment)
Postpartum psychosis — separate emergency (delusions, hallucinations, mania) — admit for safety
redFlags: Thoughts of harming baby (intrusive thoughts vs intent)
Inability to care for self / baby

management.detail: Suicide / infanticide risk assessment. Psychosis → urgent psychiatric admission (mother-baby unit if available). Mild-moderate depression → community-based.
Psychoeducation, peer support, exercise, mindfulness, brief psychotherapy. Re-assess at 2–4 weeks.

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) or interpersonal therapy (IPT). Sertraline 50–100 mg OD first-line antidepressant (most evidence in lactation + lowest milk transfer). Citalopram acceptable. AVOID paroxetine + venlafaxine + fluoxetine (longer infant half-life). Treat for ≥ 6 months after recovery.
Most SSRIs compatible with breastfeeding — monitor infant for sedation / poor feeding. Counsel on benefit-risk.
Mother-baby psychiatric unit. Atypical antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine) + lithium if bipolar. Multidisciplinary safety planning.
GP / health visitor follow-up weekly initially; rescreen EPDS. Multidisciplinary input — health visitor, IAPT/psychology, perinatal psychiatry.

references.label: NICE CG192 Antenatal + Postnatal Mental Health
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Hypoglycaemia — acute management
presentation: Sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger (autonomic — BGM 3.0–3.9 mmol/L)
Confusion, behaviour change, drowsiness (neuroglycopenic — BGM < 3.0)
Seizure, coma (severe — < 2.0)
Causes: insulin / SU overdose (most common), inadequate carbohydrate intake, exercise, alcohol, sepsis, addisonian crisis, liver failure, tumour (insulinoma)
Pitfalls: long-acting insulin (glargine) → prolonged hypos; sulfonylurea overdose → days-long hypos
redFlags: Hypoglycaemia in non-diabetic — investigate (insulinoma, Addisonian crisis, factitious)

diagnostics.test: Capillary BGM at point of care
diagnostics.rationale: do not delay treatment for lab confirmation; venous if BGM unreliable

diagnostics.test: Venous glucose, U+E, LFTs, FBC, cortisol, insulin + C-peptide + sulfonylurea screen (when cause unclear)

management.detail: 15–20 g fast-acting carbohydrate (4 glucose tabs / 150 mL fruit juice / 200 mL milk / 2 tsp sugar in water). Recheck BGM at 15 min; repeat if still < 4 mmol/L. Once corrected: long-acting carbohydrate (sandwich, biscuit + milk) unless next meal due soon.
Adult: 100 mL of 20 % dextrose IV over 10 min (or 200 mL of 10 %). Child: 2 mL/kg 10 % dextrose. Recheck BGM at 10 min; repeat if needed.

Glucagon 1 mg IM (0.5 mg if < 25 kg). Place patient in recovery position. Give oral carbohydrate when able to swallow. Glucagon less effective in alcohol / liver disease / sulfonylurea overdose / repeated hypos (depletes glycogen).
Glucose infusion 10–20 % at maintenance rate + frequent BGM × 24–48 h. Octreotide 50 µg SC every 8 h (suppresses pancreatic insulin) for sulfonylurea overdose. Admit.

Review insulin / SU regimen with patient. CGM consideration. Reduce dose. Driver — DVLA notification per local regulations. Patient + family education + glucagon prescription for severe hypoglycaemia-prone patient.

references.label: Kenya National Clinical Guidelines for Management of Diabetes Mellitus, Ministry of Health

title: Toxoplasmic encephalitis (HIV-associated)
presentation: Subacute (days–weeks) onset of focal neurology — hemiparesis, dysarthria, ataxia
Headache + low-grade fever, confusion, seizures
Almost always CD4 < 100 (often < 50)
redFlags: Single deep periventricular lesion → suspect primary CNS lymphoma

diagnostics.rationale: multiple ring-enhancing lesions at grey-white junction + basal ganglia
improvement at 14 days confirms; failure → biopsy

management.detail: Pyrimethamine 200 mg loading then 50–75 mg OD + sulfadiazine 1000–1500 mg every 6 h + leucovorin 10–25 mg/day × ≥ 6 weeks.
Pyrimethamine + clindamycin 600 mg every 6 h. OR cotrimoxazole 5/25 mg/kg every 12 h.
Anticonvulsant for seizures; dexamethasone only for mass effect / herniation.
Pyrimethamine 25–50 mg/day + sulfadiazine 500–1000 mg every 6 h + leucovorin 10 mg/day OR cotrimoxazole 960 mg OD until CD4 > 200 × 6 months on suppressive ART.
WHO 2024 — IRIS risk lower than cryptococcal meningitis.

references.label: Kenya Guidelines on Use of Antiretroviral Drugs for Treating and Preventing HIV Infection (NASCOP)

title: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP)
presentation: Subacute dry cough + exertional dyspnoea + low-grade fever
Hypoxia on exertion (desaturation on 6-min walk)
Immunosuppressed: HIV CD4 < 200, post-transplant, chemo, high-dose steroid
redFlags: PaO₂ < 70 mmHg or A-a gradient ≥ 35 → severe

diagnostics.test: HRCT — ground-glass with mosaic + spared periphery + pneumatoceles
Induced sputum / BAL — Giemsa / silver / PCR

management.detail: Cotrimoxazole 15–20 mg/kg/day (TMP) IV or PO in 3–4 divided doses × 21 days.
Clindamycin 600 mg IV every 6 h + primaquine 30 mg PO/day (check G6PD), OR pentamidine 4 mg/kg IV/day, OR atovaquone 750 mg BD (mild only).
Prednisolone 40 mg BD × 5 days then 40 mg OD × 5 days then 20 mg OD × 11 days — start within 72 h.
O₂ to SpO₂ ≥ 92 %; escalate to HFNC / NIV / IMV.
Start ART within 2 weeks. Cotrimoxazole 960 mg OD until CD4 > 200 × 3 months on ART.

references.label: Kenya Guidelines on Use of Antiretroviral Drugs for Treating and Preventing HIV Infection in Kenya (NASCOP, MOH)

title: CMV retinitis (HIV)
presentation: Floaters, scotomata, blurred vision, photopsia
HIV with CD4 < 50
Fundoscopy: 'pizza pie' — fluffy white opacification + haemorrhage along vascular arcades

management.detail: Valganciclovir 900 mg PO BD × 21 days with food, OR IV ganciclovir 5 mg/kg every 12 h × 14 days.
Intravitreal ganciclovir 2 mg every 2–3 days × 2–4 doses by ophthalmologist.
Valganciclovir 900 mg OD until CD4 > 100 × 3–6 months on ART + resolved retinitis.
Steroid for IRIS uveitis.

references.label: Kenya Guidelines on Use of Antiretroviral Drugs for Treating and Preventing HIV Infection (NASCOP)

title: Post-sexual-assault clinical care
presentation: Recent sexual assault — may present via self, police, safeguarding
Acute injury, distress, dissociation
May present hours / days / weeks later

diagnostics.test: SARC forensic exam within 7 days (12 days vaginal)
diagnostics.rationale: preserve evidence chain — only with consent

diagnostics.test: STI screen — CT/NG NAAT, syphilis, HIV, HBsAg, HCV

management.detail: Private room, chaperone, choice of clinician gender; ISVA referral; safeguarding for children + vulnerable adults.
Wound care, tetanus prophylaxis. Hepatitis B vaccine + HBIG if source HBV+ within 48 h.
TDF/FTC + DTG once daily × 28 days. Repeat HIV test at 6 + 12 weeks.
Copper IUD (> 99 % efficacy) preferred. Alternative: ulipristal 30 mg within 120 h, OR levonorgestrel 1.5 mg within 72 h.
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + azithromycin 1 g PO + metronidazole 2 g PO single dose.
Specialist sexual violence service. PHQ-9 + GAD-7 at follow-up. Repeat STI/HIV tests per schedule.

references.label: WHO Clinical management of rape + IPV 2019
BASHH UK Guidelines on sexual assault
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Septic shock — adult
presentation: Sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥ 65 AND lactate > 2 despite adequate resuscitation
Fever / hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnoea, altered mentation, oliguria, mottling
Sources: pulmonary > UTI > intra-abdominal > skin > catheter > meningitis

diagnostics.test: Sepsis 6 within 1 h — blood cultures + lactate + UO + O₂ + IV fluids + antibiotics
FBC + U+E + LFT + clotting + CRP + procalcitonin
Imaging guided by suspicion (CXR, USS/CT, LP if meningism)

management.detail: Lactate, blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics, broad-spectrum IV antibiotic within 1 h, IV crystalloid 30 mL/kg if hypotensive or lactate > 4 (Ringer's preferred over saline), vasopressor (noradrenaline) if MAP < 65 despite fluids.
Drain abscess, debride necrosis, remove infected line, decompress obstruction within 6–12 h.
Noradrenaline first. Add vasopressin 0.03 units/min when noradrenaline > 0.25 µg/kg/min. Dobutamine if low CO with adequate volume. Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if catecholamine-resistant.
Lung-protective 6 mL/kg IBW + plateau < 30 + PEEP 8–15.
Glycaemic control 6–10 mmol/L. DVT prophylaxis. Stress-ulcer prophylaxis if MV. RRT if KDIGO stage 3 + indication. Early enteral nutrition.
Review at 48–72 h. Procalcitonin to guide duration.

title: Acute kidney injury (KDIGO)
presentation: Rise in creatinine ≥ 26 µmol/L within 48 h OR ≥ 1.5× baseline in 7 days OR urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h × 6 h
Stage 1: 1.5–1.9×; Stage 2: 2.0–2.9×; Stage 3: ≥ 3× or > 354 µmol/L or RRT
Causes: pre-renal (volume / sepsis / low CO), intrinsic (ATN, GN, AIN, contrast, nephrotoxins, rhabdo), post-renal (obstruction)

diagnostics.test: Renal screen if intrinsic suspected (ANCA, anti-GBM, complement, Ig, hepatitis, SPEP)

management.detail: Sepsis treatment, Toxins removed (NSAID, ACEi/ARB, contrast, aminoglycoside), Optimise BP + volume, Prevent further harm.
Balanced crystalloid preferred over saline (SMART). Target MAP ≥ 65 + UO > 0.5 mL/kg/h. Avoid over-resuscitation in established AKI.

management.step: Hyperkalaemia urgent if K > 6.5 / ECG changes
management.detail: Calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 % IV + insulin-dextrose + nebulised salbutamol + NaHCO₃ if acidaemic + calcium resonium / patiromer.
Acidosis (pH < 7.15), Electrolytes (K > 6.5 / phosphate), Intoxications dialysable, Overload, Uraemia. STARRT-AKI 2020 — no benefit from early elective RRT.
Adjust all renally excreted drugs (metformin held, opioids reduced).
Recheck creatinine + urinalysis at 3 months. 5–10 % progress to CKD. Nephrology referral if persistent.

title: Hyperkalaemia — acute management
presentation: Often asymptomatic until severe
Muscle weakness, paraesthesia, palpitations
ECG: peaked T → PR prolongation → loss of P → wide QRS → sinusoidal → asystole / VF
Causes: AKI / CKD, ACEi/ARB/MRA + NSAID, K-sparing diuretic, K supplements, rhabdo, tumour lysis, Addison, DKA, suxamethonium in deafferentation

diagnostics.rationale: treat emergently for any change without waiting for repeat

management.detail: If ECG changes OR K > 6.5: calcium gluconate 10 % 10 mL IV over 5 min, onset 3 min, lasts 30–60 min. Repeat at 5 min if no ECG improvement.
Insulin 10 units in 50 mL 50 % glucose IV over 15 min — onset 15 min, lasts 4–6 h. Monitor BGM hourly × 6 h. Salbutamol nebulised 10–20 mg.
Sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol IV over 15 min only if pH < 7.2.
Calcium resonium 15 g PO/PR every 8 h (slow). Patiromer / SZC. Furosemide if euvolaemic with functioning kidneys.
Refractory hyperkalaemia / dialysis-dependent CKD / AKI → urgent haemodialysis.
Stop ACEi/ARB/MRA/K supplement. Low-K diet. Repeat U+E at 1 + 6 + 24 h.

references.label: ERC Reversible Causes of Cardiac Arrest 2021

title: Status epilepticus — clinical management
presentation: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure > 5 min OR ≥ 2 seizures without recovery (operational definition)
Established > 30 min; refractory if continues > 30 min despite 2 lines; super-refractory > 24 h
Causes: low AED levels, alcohol withdrawal, electrolytes, CNS infection, structural, drugs, eclampsia

diagnostics.test: Capillary glucose at point of care
FBC, U+E, calcium, magnesium, glucose, LFT, lactate, ABG, AED levels, toxicology
EEG if persistent altered consciousness / treatment resistance

management.detail: ABC, position to prevent injury, O₂, IV access, bloods + BGM. Reverse hypoglycaemia (50 mL 50 % glucose). Thiamine 100 mg IV before glucose if alcoholic / malnourished.
Adult: lorazepam 4 mg IV (or 0.1 mg/kg); repeat once at 10 min. Alternatives: diazepam 10 mg IV / midazolam 10 mg IM/IN/buccal (community). Child: lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV / midazolam 0.2 mg/kg IM/IN.

Adult: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4500 mg) over 5–10 min (non-inferior to phenytoin — ESETT). Alternatives: fosphenytoin / phenytoin 20 mg/kg at max 50 mg/min, sodium valproate 40 mg/kg IV (AVOID in pregnancy). Eclampsia: magnesium sulphate 4 g IV + 1 g/h infusion.
ICU + RSI. Midazolam infusion 0.05–2 mg/kg/h OR propofol 1–5 mg/kg/h OR thiopental. Continuous EEG. Burst suppression × 24–48 h then taper.
Restart AEDs. LP if febrile. Imaging for structural lesion.
Continue maintenance AED. EEG + neurology follow-up. Driving advice. Buccal midazolam at home for recurrence.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders (mhGAP adaptation), Ministry of Health

title: Guillain-Barré syndrome
presentation: Ascending symmetric weakness over days–4 weeks; distal sensory symptoms often first
Areflexia / hyporeflexia
Recent infection 1–4 weeks prior (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, Zika, Influenza)
Variants: Miller-Fisher (ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia), pharyngo-cervico-brachial, pure motor, sensory ataxic
redFlags: Respiratory weakness — FVC < 20 mL/kg or falling → intubate

diagnostics.test: LP — albumino-cytological dissociation (high protein, normal WCC)
diagnostics.rationale: may be normal in first week

diagnostics.test: Spirometry FVC + MIP every 4–6 h initially
diagnostics.rationale: intubation timing — do not wait for SpO₂ drop

management.detail: ICU if FVC < 20 mL/kg, MIP < 30, MEP < 40, bulbar weakness, autonomic instability. 20–30 % need ventilation.
IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days, OR plasma exchange 5 sessions of 50 mL/kg over 2 weeks. Equally effective. Steroids NOT effective.
Elective intubation when FVC < 15 mL/kg / rapid decline. Tracheostomy if expected ventilation > 2 weeks.
AVOID suxamethonium (hyperkalaemia from denervation). Continuous ECG. Cautious antihypertensive/vasopressor titration.
DVT prophylaxis (LMWH). Pressure care. Gabapentin/pregabalin for neuropathic pain. NG feeding if bulbar. Early physio + OT. Psychological support.
85 % recover well at 6–12 months; 20 % residual weakness; mortality 3–5 %. Multidisciplinary rehab.

title: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
presentation: Acute onset (< 7 days), bilateral opacities not fully explained by cardiac failure, P/F < 300 on PEEP ≥ 5
Severity: mild (P/F 200–300), moderate (100–200), severe (< 100)
Causes: sepsis (40 %), pneumonia, aspiration, transfusion (TRALI), pancreatitis, trauma, burns, COVID-19

diagnostics.rationale: bilateral airspace shadowing; ground-glass + consolidation in dependent areas

diagnostics.test: Identify cause — septic screen, BAL, lipase, drug review

management.detail: Antibiotics for sepsis, source control, treat aspiration / pancreatitis, stop offending drug.
Vt 4–6 mL/kg IBW, plateau < 30, PEEP titrated to FiO₂ table, permissive hypercapnia (pH ≥ 7.20), driving pressure < 14.
If P/F < 150 despite optimised ventilation: prone ≥ 16 h per session. Mortality reduction.
Cisatracurium 48 h infusion for severe ARDS — consider for dyssynchrony / persistent severe hypoxia.
Conservative after initial resuscitation — net even or negative reduces ventilator days (FACTT).
Inhaled NO (transient improvement). V-V ECMO for severe ARDS P/F < 80 with reversible cause.
Dexamethasone 6 mg/day × 10 days reduces mortality in moderate-severe (DEXA-ARDS 2020). Use in COVID-19 ARDS.

title: Chronic hepatitis B
presentation: HBsAg+ for ≥ 6 months
Most asymptomatic; fatigue, anorexia, RUQ discomfort
Decompensated cirrhosis features in late disease
Endemic in SSA — mostly vertical or early childhood
redFlags: HCC surveillance — Asian/African male > 40, family history
Pregnancy with HBV DNA > 200000 IU/mL — vertical transmission risk

diagnostics.test: HBV serology — HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc (total + IgM), HBeAg, anti-HBe

management.detail: Treatment indicated in immune-active phase (ALT > 2× ULN + DNA > 20000 IU/mL HBeAg+ / > 2000 HBeAg–), all cirrhotics, pregnancy with DNA > 200000.
Tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg PO OD (preferred in pregnancy + young) OR entecavir 0.5 mg PO OD on empty stomach. TAF if available + bone/renal concerns.
Screen all. TDF from week 24–28 if maternal DNA > 200000. Infant: HepB vaccine within 24 h + HBIG for HBsAg+ mothers.
6-monthly USS + AFP: cirrhotics, African ≥ 20 yrs, Asian men ≥ 40 / women ≥ 50, family history.
Alcohol cessation. HepA vaccine. Counsel sexual + household contacts → screen + vaccinate. Avoid hepatotoxic drugs.
HBV DNA + ALT every 3–6 months. Annual fibrosis assessment. Most need indefinite treatment.

title: Chronic hepatitis C
presentation: HCV Ab+ + HCV RNA+ for ≥ 6 months
Asymptomatic in majority; fatigue, depression
Cirrhosis when advanced
Risk: PWID, transfusion before screening, occupational exposure, MSM HIV+ (acute), unsafe tattoo/piercing, vertical (5 %)

diagnostics.test: HCV Ab (screen) + HCV RNA (confirm active infection)
diagnostics.rationale: Ab+ + RNA– = past resolved or false-positive — repeat RNA at 6 months

diagnostics.test: HCV genotype — now optional with pan-genotypic regimens
ALT, bilirubin, INR, albumin, AFP, creatinine

management.detail: Pan-genotypic: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir 400/100 mg OD × 12 weeks. Decompensated cirrhosis: add ribavirin. SVR > 95 % across genotypes.
Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir 300/120 mg OD × 8 weeks (non-cirrhotic) or × 12 weeks (compensated cirrhosis). Avoid in decompensated cirrhosis.
BEFORE starting DAA — check HBsAg + anti-HBc. If HBsAg+, monitor HBV DNA + treat with TDF if rising.
STOP amiodarone (bradycardia). Adjust statins. Avoid rifampicin.
Confirm cure with HCV RNA undetectable at 12 weeks post-treatment. Continue HCC surveillance if cirrhotic. Re-test annually if ongoing risk.
Defer DAA until postpartum. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir + sofosbuvir/velpatasvir approved from 3 yrs.

title: Acute liver failure
presentation: Acute hepatic dysfunction with coagulopathy INR ≥ 1.5 + hepatic encephalopathy in patient without pre-existing chronic liver disease
Hyperacute (< 7 d): paracetamol, ischaemia; Acute (7–28 d): viral, DILI; Subacute (> 28 d): autoimmune, Wilson, Budd-Chiari
SSA contexts: HBV reactivation, HEV in pregnancy, traditional medicine hepatotoxicity, paracetamol overdose
redFlags: King's College paracetamol: pH < 7.30 OR (INR > 6.5 + Cr > 300 + grade III/IV encephalopathy)
King's College non-paracetamol: INR > 6.5 OR any 3 of [age < 11 / > 40, non-A/non-B aetiology, jaundice > 7 d before encephalopathy, INR > 3.5, bilirubin > 300]

diagnostics.test: INR, ALT/AST, bilirubin, ammonia, creatinine, lactate, ABG, glucose, paracetamol level
Viral hepatitis screen (HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HAV IgM, anti-HEV IgM, anti-HCV, HSV)

management.detail: Time-sensitive transfer if meeting criteria. Use King's + clinical judgement.
Paracetamol → NAC. HBV → tenofovir/entecavir. HSV → IV aciclovir. Autoimmune → methylprednisolone. Mushroom → silibinin. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy → deliver.
Grade I–II: lactulose 30–45 mL every 1–2 h + rifaximin 550 mg BD. Grade III–IV: intubate + ICU. Mannitol 0.5 g/kg / hypertonic saline if raised ICP. AVOID sedatives (propofol acceptable).

Glucose infusion (BGM > 4). Avoid routine FFP (confounds INR prognostication) — use PCC for active bleeding. CVVH for AKI + ammonia. Vasopressors for shock. PPI stress-ulcer prophylaxis if ventilated.
Urgent listing via local protocol. Consider also lactate > 3.5 after fluids + multi-organ failure.
Stop hepatotoxic drugs. Hepatology follow-up. Cause-specific management.

title: Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis)
presentation: Severe hyperthyroidism + organ dysfunction precipitated by stress (infection, surgery, trauma, DKA, pregnancy, iodine load, antithyroid withdrawal)
Hyperpyrexia ≥ 39 °C, sweating, tachycardia / AF / heart failure
Agitation, delirium, psychosis, coma, seizure
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, jaundice
Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale ≥ 45 = highly suggestive

diagnostics.test: TSH, free T4, free T3 — DO NOT delay treatment for results
FBC, glucose, U+E, LFT, cortisol, Ca, blood cultures, ABG, ECG

management.detail: Cooling (paracetamol — AVOID aspirin, displaces T4; tepid sponging + fans). IV fluids + electrolytes. Glucose support.
PROPYLTHIOURACIL 200 mg every 4 h PO/NG (also blocks T4→T3). Alternative: carbimazole 20 mg every 4 h.

management.step: Block hormone RELEASE (1 h AFTER thionamide)
management.detail: Lugol iodine 5–10 drops every 8 h OR sodium iodide 1 g IV every 8 h. NEVER before thionamide (Jod-Basedow).
Propranolol 60–80 mg PO every 4 h (avoid in decompensated HF) OR esmolol infusion. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 h.
Antibiotics for sepsis; manage DKA / MI / AF. Avoid aspirin.
Plasmapheresis / TPE. Definitive thyroidectomy after stabilisation.

title: Myxoedema coma
presentation: Severe long-standing hypothyroidism + decompensation (infection, cold, drugs)
Hypothermia < 35 °C (often missed by standard thermometers)
Altered mental state → coma
Bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia
Non-pitting myxoedema, macroglossia, ileus, urinary retention

diagnostics.test: TSH, FT4, FT3 — DO NOT delay treatment for results
FBC, U+E, glucose, cortisol, LFT, CK, ABG, ECG (low voltage, prolonged QT)

management.detail: Intubate if GCS < 8 / hypoventilation. Passive external rewarming (warm blankets, room 25 °C). Cautious IV fluids. Glucose for hypoglycaemia.
Levothyroxine 200–500 µg IV slow bolus then 50–100 µg IV daily. Add liothyronine (T3) 10–20 µg IV then 10 µg every 4–6 h × 24 h then taper. Lower doses in elderly + CVD.
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 h until cortisol excludes adrenal insufficiency. Give BEFORE levothyroxine to avoid adrenal crisis.
Antibiotics; stop sedatives, amiodarone.
Correct hyponatraemia slowly (< 10 mmol/L in 24 h). AVOID rapid rewarming, sedatives, anti-arrhythmics, opioids.
Identify cause. Patient + family education on adherence.

title: Phaeochromocytoma + paraganglioma
presentation: Classic triad — episodic headache + sweating + palpitations + paroxysmal hypertension
Pallor (not flushing — unlike carcinoid)
Triggers: anaesthesia, surgery, contrast, micturition, opioids, β-blocker (unopposed α)
10 % rule — bilateral, extra-adrenal, malignant, paediatric, familial
Genetic syndromes — VHL, MEN2, NF1, SDHx
redFlags: Hypertensive crisis — chest pain, headache, encephalopathy, MI, stroke

diagnostics.test: 24-h urine fractionated metanephrines + normetanephrines (or plasma free metanephrines)
Stop TCAs, β-blockers, decongestants ≥ 1 week pre-test
CT/MRI adrenal + body after biochemistry positive

management.detail: Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BD titrated to 1 mg/kg/day over 2 weeks. Target SBP < 130 + allow tachycardia / postural drop (good α-blockade). Doxazosin alternative.
Add propranolol / bisoprolol if persistent tachycardia. NEVER start β-blocker first → unopposed α-vasoconstriction → crisis.
5 g NaCl + 2 L water daily for 5 days pre-op.

Severe BP swings during tumour manipulation. Magnesium IV infusion + nitroprusside / GTN / phentolamine for surges; noradrenaline / vasopressin for post-resection hypotension. Avoid morphine, metoclopramide (provoke crisis).
Multidisciplinary team. α-blockade. Surgery in 2nd trimester or combined caesarean + tumour removal in 3rd.
Annual biochemistry. Genetic counselling for family.

title: Adrenal (Addisonian) crisis
presentation: Acute severe primary adrenal insufficiency
Hypotension / shock unresponsive to fluids + vasopressors
Severe fatigue, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea
Hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis
Hyperpigmentation in chronic primary
Triggers: missed steroid / abrupt withdrawal, infection, surgery, trauma, MI

diagnostics.test: Random cortisol + ACTH + electrolytes + glucose + renin + aldosterone (retain for later)
diagnostics.rationale: cortisol < 138 nmol/L in acute illness suggests AI

diagnostics.test: Short Synacthen test (once stable, off hydrocortisone × 24 h or on dexamethasone)

management.detail: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus (children 1–4 mg/kg), then 200 mg/24 h continuous IV infusion (or 50 mg every 6 h) until stable then taper. Patient self-injection 100 mg IM for known emergency.
0.9 % saline 1 L over 1 h, then 4–6 L over 24 h. Add 5–10 % glucose if hypoglycaemic.
Antibiotics, MI management, surgical source control.
Not needed acutely (high-dose hydrocortisone provides). Resume fludrocortisone 100 µg/day once IV hydrocortisone < 50 mg/day.

Once stable: oral hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day 2/3 AM 1/3 PM. DOUBLE dose during illness × 3 days; IM 100 mg if vomiting / surgery / trauma. Steroid emergency card + MedicAlert + IM kit + family training.
Lifelong replacement. ACTH + electrolytes annually. Vaccinate (influenza, pneumococcal). Annual endocrine review.

title: Acute pyelonephritis
presentation: Fever + flank / loin pain + lower urinary tract symptoms
Nausea / vomiting + tachycardia
Costovertebral angle tenderness
Bacteraemia in 25 %
Pregnancy: any UTI with fever or systemic features = pyelonephritis

diagnostics.test: USS / CT KUB if persistent fever > 72 h / recurrent / pregnancy with severe disease

management.detail: Outpatient if stable, tolerating PO, no obstruction, not pregnant, immunocompetent.

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD OR co-amoxiclav 1.2 g IV every 8 h. ESBL risk / severe: piperacillin-tazobactam / carbapenem. Pregnancy: ceftriaxone (avoid trimethoprim 1st trimester + nitrofurantoin 3rd trimester).
Co-amoxiclav 625 mg every 8 h × 10–14 days, OR ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD × 7 days (avoid if local resistance > 10 %). Re-assess at 48 + 72 h.
Urgent decompression (nephrostomy / ureteric stent) within 6–12 h.
ALWAYS admit. IV ceftriaxone until afebrile 48 h then oral. 10–14-day course. Suppressive antibiotic until delivery.
Repeat urine culture 1–2 weeks post in pregnancy + complicated cases. Investigate recurrence with imaging.

title: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)
presentation: Fever, abdominal pain, vomiting in patient with ascites (cirrhosis, nephrotic, HF)
Often subtle — encephalopathy, AKI, hypothermia, low albumin
10 % asymptomatic — any cirrhotic admitted should have diagnostic tap

diagnostics.test: Diagnostic paracentesis on ALL cirrhotic patients with ascites at admission / deterioration

diagnostics.rationale: neutrophils > 250/mm³ confirms; culture + Gram stain + albumin + protein

diagnostics.test: U+E, creatinine, LFT, INR, glucose, FBC

management.detail: Cefotaxime 2 g IV every 8 h × 5 days (most evidence). Alternatives: ceftriaxone 2 g OD, co-amoxiclav. Severe / ESBL: piperacillin-tazobactam / carbapenem.
Albumin 1.5 g/kg IV day 1 + 1 g/kg IV day 3 — reduces HRS + mortality. Particularly if creatinine > 80, urea > 10, bilirubin > 70.
Neutrophil count should fall by > 25 %. If not — broaden antibiotic + consider secondary peritonitis (perforation needs surgery).
Stop NSAIDs, ACEi, aminoglycosides, large-volume diuretics. Albumin replacement (6–8 g/L removed) with large-volume paracentesis.
Norfloxacin 400 mg PO OD OR ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO OD OR cotrimoxazole 960 mg PO OD. Lifelong (or until transplant).
SBP marks decompensated cirrhosis — refer.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS)
presentation: Cairo-Bishop — Laboratory TLS: ≥ 2 of (uric acid > 0.476 mmol/L, K > 6.0, phosphate > 1.45, calcium < 1.75) within 3 days before / 7 days after chemo
Clinical TLS: laboratory TLS + AKI / arrhythmia / seizure
High-risk cancers: Burkitt, ALL, AML high-WBC, large tumour bulk, dehydration, CKD

diagnostics.test: Pre-chemo baseline electrolytes + uric acid + creatinine + LDH
Electrolytes 6–8 hourly during high-risk first 7 days

management.detail: Burkitt, ALL WBC > 100, AML WBC > 50, large NHL, bulky disease, CKD, hyperuricaemia.
IV crystalloid 3 L/m²/day (200 mL/kg/day < 10 kg) starting 24–48 h pre-chemo. Target urine 80–100 mL/m²/h. Avoid K-containing fluids. Loop diuretic if needed.
High risk: rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV OD × 5 days (test G6PD first). Moderate risk: allopurinol 300 mg PO OD.
Hyperkalaemia per emergency protocol. Hyperphosphataemia → sevelamer + dialysis. Hypocalcaemia — treat only if symptomatic.
Lower threshold than other AKI. Indications: refractory K / phosphate / symptomatic Ca / oliguric AKI / fluid overload.
Not routine — calcium phosphate crystallisation. Maintain pH 6.5–7.5.

references.label: Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Acute spinal cord compression
presentation: Progressive back / radicular pain (worse at night / cough / Valsalva)
Bilateral lower-limb weakness + sensory level
Bladder + bowel disturbance (LATE)
Causes: malignancy (breast, lung, prostate, myeloma) 70 %; abscess, haematoma, disc, trauma
Cauda equina: bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, retention with overflow, reduced anal tone
redFlags: Time-critical — recovery related to neurology at decompression
Cauda equina with retention — surgical emergency

diagnostics.rationale: definitive imaging; whole spine for surgical planning

diagnostics.test: FBC, U+E, LFT, Ca, tumour markers + immunoglobulins / SPEP

management.detail: Flat bed rest, log-roll only. Discuss with neurosurgery + radiation oncology immediately.
Dexamethasone 16 mg IV stat then 4 mg every 6 h (or 8 mg BD). Reduces oedema + delays progression. PPI cover.
First-line for surgical candidates with single-level disease, deficit < 48 h old, life expectancy > 3 months. Within 24 h.
Single-fraction / short-course if surgery not appropriate. Often combined with surgery.

management.step: Cauda equina — surgical emergency within 48 h
management.detail: Decompression within 48 h (better outcomes within 24 h). Catheterise; bladder rehabilitation post.
Early PT + OT. DVT prophylaxis. Pressure care. Bladder + bowel management. Pain control. Psychological support. Advance care planning.

references.label: NICE NG234 Metastatic Spinal Cord Compression
Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health

title: Migraine — acute + preventive
presentation: Recurrent moderate-severe unilateral throbbing headache lasting 4–72 h
Photophobia + phonophobia + nausea + vomiting
Aura in 30 % — visual scintillations, hemianopia, paraesthesia, dysphasia, < 60 min
Triggers: stress, sleep change, menstruation, alcohol, dehydration, fasting
Female:male 3:1; peak 20–40 years
redFlags: Worse on lying / Valsalva — raised ICP

diagnostics.rationale: Pulsatile, hOurs duration, Unilateral, Nausea, Disabling — 4 of 5 = probable
no routine imaging in classic migraine

management.detail: Regular sleep, meals, hydration, exercise. Reduce caffeine + medication overuse (no analgesic > 10–15 days/month).
MILD: paracetamol 1 g + ibuprofen 400 mg + antiemetic (metoclopramide / domperidone). MODERATE-SEVERE: triptan (sumatriptan 50–100 mg PO; 6 mg SC; nasal 20 mg) + NSAID + antiemetic. AVOID opioids.
IV ketorolac 30 mg + metoclopramide 10 mg + IV fluids + dexamethasone 4–10 mg IV. Greater occipital nerve block. Ubrogepant alternative.

First-line: propranolol 80–160 mg/day (avoid in asthma), topiramate 50–100 mg/day (avoid in pregnancy / fertility planning), amitriptyline 10–75 mg nocte. CGRP monoclonals (erenumab) for refractory. Botulinum toxin A for chronic migraine.
Avoid triptans 1st trimester + ergots throughout. Acute: paracetamol + metoclopramide. Preventive: propranolol acceptable; avoid topiramate. Riboflavin 400 mg/day safe.
Diagnostic uncertainty, status migrainosus > 72 h, refractory to 3 preventive trials, medication overuse, chronic migraine (> 15 days/month).

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Lactational mastitis
presentation: Unilateral painful, warm, erythematous breast in lactating woman
Often wedge-shaped tender area
Fever, flu-like symptoms
Usually 2–6 weeks postpartum
Cause — milk stasis (poor latch, missed feeds, oversupply) ± bacterial infection (Staph aureus)

diagnostics.test: Breast milk culture if treatment failure / hospital-acquired / recurrent
USS breast if fluctuant / not improving at 48 h

management.detail: Frequent effective milk removal is cornerstone — feed affected side first, pump if baby reluctant. Does not harm baby. Lactation consultant for latch + supply issues.
Warm compress before feeding, cold after. Paracetamol + ibuprofen (breastfeeding-compatible). Rest + hydration.

management.step: Antibiotic if no improvement at 24 h / systemic / nipple fissure
management.detail: Flucloxacillin 500 mg every 6 h PO × 10–14 days. Penicillin-allergic: erythromycin 500 mg every 6 h. MRSA risk: clindamycin 300–450 mg every 6 h. Continue breastfeeding.
USS-guided needle aspiration preferred over incision. Culture sent. Surgical drainage only if aspiration fails / large.
Antenatal + postnatal latch support. Avoid abrupt weaning. Address nipple trauma + restrictive clothing.
Investigate inflammatory carcinoma in non-lactating. Specialist breast clinic. Long-term oral antibiotic occasionally.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Otitis externa
presentation: Ear pain + itch + tragal tenderness + otorrhoea
External canal swollen + erythematous ± debris on otoscopy
Hearing loss if canal obstructed
Risk: swimming, humid climate, hearing aid, eczema, diabetes, immunocompromised
Malignant (necrotising) OE in diabetic / immunocompromised — severe pain + cranial nerve palsy + bone involvement (Pseudomonas)
redFlags: Malignant (necrotising) OE — diabetes + severe pain + CN palsy → urgent ENT + IV anti-pseudomonal + CT temporal bone

diagnostics.test: Microsuction by ENT if debris obstructs / not improving
Swab for culture if recurrent / not improving / immunocompromised

management.detail: Microsuction (ideal) or dry-mopping with cotton wool wisps.
Cipro + dexamethasone drops 4 drops BD × 7 days, OR ofloxacin / cipro alone. AVOID aminoglycoside if perforated TM. Acetic acid 2 % spray for mild OE.
Flucloxacillin 500 mg every 6 h × 7 days OR co-amoxiclav 625 mg every 8 h.
Pope / ribbon-gauze wick by ENT soaked in topical antibiotic-steroid; review at 48 h.
Urgent ENT referral. IV ciprofloxacin 400 mg every 8 h × 6–8 weeks. CT temporal bone + MRI. Strict glycaemic control. Mortality 10–20 %.
Dry ears after swimming. Silicone earplugs if recurrent. Treat eczema. Glycaemic control.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Hypothyroidism (chronic management)
presentation: Fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, hair thinning
Bradycardia, hyporeflexia, mild peripheral oedema
Goitre or post-thyroidectomy / radioiodine atrophy
Pregnancy: ↑ TBG → ↑ levothyroxine requirement (30 %)
Causes: Hashimoto autoimmune (most), iodine deficiency (SSA endemic), drug (lithium, amiodarone), post-radioiodine, post-thyroidectomy
redFlags: Ischaemic heart disease — start low, go slow
Subclinical hypothyroidism with TPO+ antibodies + planning pregnancy

diagnostics.rationale: TSH > 10 mU/L = overt primary; TSH 4–10 + low T4 = mild; TSH 4–10 + normal T4 = subclinical
supports autoimmune aetiology + higher progression to overt

management.detail: Overt hypothyroidism (TSH > 10 / TSH 4–10 + low T4): always. Subclinical TSH 4–10: treat if symptomatic, TPO+, planning pregnancy, fertility issues, < 65 yrs. TSH > 10 always treat.

Adult < 65 yrs healthy: 1.6 µg/kg/day (typical 50–125 µg). Elderly / IHD: start 25 µg/day, titrate by 12.5–25 µg every 6 weeks. Take on empty stomach 30 min before food + 4 h apart from iron / calcium / PPI / fibre / soya.
Recheck TSH at 6–8 weeks. Target TSH 0.4–4.0 mU/L (1.0–2.5 if planning pregnancy / pregnant). Once stable, annual TSH. Reassess if dose change, illness, weight change, pregnancy.
TSH target < 2.5 in 1st trimester / < 3.0 in 2nd + 3rd. INCREASE dose by ~30 % on confirmed pregnancy + 4-weekly TSH. Hashimoto antibodies = more likely to need dose increase.
Iodine deficiency goitre: iodised salt + iodine supplement. Drug-induced: review precipitant (lithium, amiodarone, interferon). Post-thyroidectomy: lifelong replacement.
Lifelong therapy. Take on empty stomach + same time daily. Report symptoms of over-replacement (palpitations, weight loss, anxiety). Annual review.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
presentation: Rotterdam criteria — any 2 of 3: oligo/anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, alopecia, raised testosterone), polycystic ovaries on USS
Menstrual irregularity, infertility, weight gain, insulin resistance
Hirsutism, acne, male-pattern hair loss
Acanthosis nigricans, central obesity
Family history of T2DM / metabolic syndrome
redFlags: Severe hyperandrogenism (rapid onset, very high testosterone) — investigate adrenal / ovarian tumour
Endometrial hyperplasia (if amenorrhoea > 90 days → annual progestin withdrawal bleed)

diagnostics.test: FSH + LH + testosterone + SHBG + free androgen index
diagnostics.rationale: raised LH:FSH (often), raised testosterone (mild — > 7 suggests other cause)
rule out other causes of androgen excess + oligomenorrhoea

diagnostics.test: OGTT, lipid profile, BMI, BP, waist circumference
Pelvic USS — polycystic morphology (≥ 20 follicles or ovarian volume > 10 mL)
diagnostics.rationale: supports diagnosis; not required if 2 other criteria met

management.detail: 5–10 % weight loss restores ovulation + improves hyperandrogenism + insulin resistance. Mediterranean / low-GI diet. Aerobic + resistance exercise 150 min/week.

Combined hormonal contraceptive (COC) — also helps acne + hirsutism. Cyproterone-containing pills more effective for hirsutism. If COC contraindicated: progestogen withdrawal every 3 months OR LNG-IUS for endometrial protection.

First-line: COC ± mechanical (shaving, eflornithine cream). Refractory: add spironolactone 50–100 mg/day (anti-androgen) + COC (contraception essential — teratogenic). Topical retinoid / benzoyl peroxide for acne.

Pre-conception: weight loss + folic acid + smoking cessation. Letrozole 2.5–7.5 mg days 2–6 (1st-line per PCOS-2018) OR clomifene 50–100 mg days 2–6. Metformin reduces miscarriage rate. Refer specialist if not pregnant after 6 cycles.
Metformin if IGT / T2DM or insulin resistance — improves metabolic + menstrual outcomes. Annual OGTT if at-risk. BP + lipids annually.
Screen for depression + anxiety + eating disorders + sleep apnoea (high prevalence). Refer for psychological support.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Endometriosis
presentation: Chronic pelvic pain + dysmenorrhoea worsening with age
Deep dyspareunia (rectovaginal disease)
Cyclical bowel / bladder symptoms (dyschezia, dysuria, haematochezia, haematuria — bowel + bladder endometriosis)
Infertility — 30–50 % of women with endometriosis
Diagnostic delay typically 7–10 years
redFlags: Chronic pelvic pain unresponsive to standard treatment

diagnostics.rationale: first-line; identifies endometriomas + deep infiltrating disease in expert hands
deep infiltrating disease + bowel involvement + surgical planning

diagnostics.test: Laparoscopy + biopsy — gold standard but no longer required for diagnosis with adequate imaging

management.step: Empirical first-line — no definitive diagnosis required
management.detail: Pain relief: paracetamol + NSAID + ± COC continuously (no pill-free interval) OR progestogen-only (medroxyprogesterone acetate, norethisterone, dienogest 2 mg OD, LNG-IUS).
GnRH analogue (goserelin / leuprorelin) 3-monthly with add-back tibolone / HRT for ≥ 6 months. Limits to ≤ 12 months due to bone mineral density loss.

Laparoscopic excision (preferred over ablation) for: persistent pain unresponsive to medical therapy, endometrioma > 3 cm, deep infiltrating disease, infertility. Specialist endometriosis centre for severe disease.

Mild-moderate disease — surgical excision improves spontaneous conception. Stage III–IV / failed surgery → IVF (downregulation with GnRH + IVF improves outcomes). DO NOT delay fertility treatment by medical suppression.
Pain management specialist + psychology + pelvic physiotherapy for chronic disease. Patient-led support groups (Endometriosis UK).

Recurrence common after surgery (~30 % at 5 yrs); continue hormonal suppression unless trying to conceive. Annual review. Counsel re menopause — symptoms may improve but extra-pelvic disease can persist.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Menopause + HRT
presentation: Vasomotor (hot flushes + night sweats) — 75–80 % of perimenopausal women
Mood + sleep disturbance
Genitourinary syndrome (vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, recurrent UTI, urgency)
Joint pain, cognitive change, libido reduction
Average age 51 (UK); premature menopause < 40 yrs (1 %); early menopause 40–45 yrs (5 %)
redFlags: Premature menopause (< 40 yrs) — investigate FMR1, karyotype, autoimmune; lifelong HRT until natural age
Postmenopausal bleeding — urgent gynae 2-week wait (endometrial cancer)

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnosis ≥ 45 yrs with typical symptoms — no biochemical test needed
FSH > 30 IU/L (twice, 6 weeks apart) only if < 45 yrs or atypical symptoms
Baseline BP, BMI, cholesterol, glucose, DEXA if risk factors
diagnostics.rationale: cardiovascular + bone risk assessment before HRT

management.detail: Exercise, weight management, cool environment, avoid triggers (alcohol, caffeine, spicy). CBT for vasomotor + mood + sleep.

management.step: HRT — first-line for moderate-severe vasomotor + premature menopause
management.detail: Combined HRT (oestrogen + progestogen) if uterus intact — sequential if perimenopausal, continuous if > 12 months amenorrhoea. Oestrogen-only if hysterectomy. Transdermal oestrogen preferred (lower VTE + stroke risk). Micronised progesterone 100 mg nocte (continuous) — preferred over MPA (better metabolic + breast profile).
Vaginal oestrogen (estriol cream / pessary / ring) — minimal systemic absorption, indefinite use OK including after breast cancer (specialist advice). Vaginal moisturisers (Replens) + lubricants.
Vasomotor: SSRI (citalopram, escitalopram), SNRI (venlafaxine), gabapentin 900 mg/day, clonidine 50 µg BD. Newer: fezolinetant (neurokinin antagonist).

Breast cancer — small increase with combined HRT (1 extra per 1000 women-years; less with micronised progesterone). VTE — transdermal not increased; oral 2× baseline. Stroke — > 60 yrs oral; reduced with transdermal. CHD — start within 10 years of menopause = neutral / protective; later = neutral.
Annual review. No arbitrary upper time limit — individualise based on symptoms + risk. Premature menopause: HRT until natural menopausal age (51) at minimum. Stop gradually.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Osteoporosis + fragility fracture prevention
presentation: Often asymptomatic until fragility fracture — vertebral (loss of height, kyphosis, back pain), hip, wrist (Colles), pelvis

Risk factors: ageing, postmenopausal, low BMI, FH hip fracture, smoking, alcohol > 4 units/day, glucocorticoids ≥ 5 mg prednisolone × 3 months, untreated hyperthyroidism, low calcium / vitamin D intake
Secondary causes: hypogonadism, hyperparathyroidism, malabsorption, CKD, RA, anorexia
redFlags: Sudden severe back pain in elderly — vertebral compression
Glucocorticoid use ≥ 5 mg prednisolone for ≥ 3 months — bisphosphonate from outset

diagnostics.rationale: decide who needs DEXA + treatment threshold

diagnostics.test: DEXA scan — lumbar spine + femoral neck
Secondary cause screen — FBC, Ca, PO₄, ALP, LFT, vitamin D, PTH, TSH, testosterone (men), coeliac antibodies, SPEP / serum free light chains (if MGUS/myeloma suspected)
Vertebral fracture assessment (lateral DXA imaging) — bonus on DEXA scan

management.detail: Calcium 1000–1200 mg/day + vitamin D 800–1000 IU/day. Weight-bearing + resistance exercise. Smoking cessation. Alcohol ≤ 2 units/day. Falls prevention (vision check, home hazards, gait + balance).
TREAT if: prior fragility fracture (any age), T-score ≤ -2.5 (DEXA), FRAX 10-yr major OP fracture > 20 % or hip > 3 %, or glucocorticoid ≥ 7.5 mg prednisolone.

Alendronate 70 mg PO weekly (or risedronate 35 mg PO weekly) — generic, effective. Zoledronate 5 mg IV annually — preferred for non-adherent / oesophageal disease / very high risk. Adequate Ca + vitamin D essential.

Denosumab 60 mg SC every 6 months — alternative if bisphosphonate intolerant. NEVER stop without follow-on bisphosphonate (rebound vertebral fractures). Teriparatide (PTH analogue) 20 µg SC daily × 24 months — anabolic; reserve for very high risk + multiple fractures + post-vertebral fracture; specialist.
Start bisphosphonate (oral alendronate / risedronate) from onset of glucocorticoid course if ≥ 7.5 mg prednisolone equivalent × ≥ 3 months. Calcium + vitamin D + lifestyle.
DEXA every 2–3 yrs. After 5 yrs alendronate (3 yrs zoledronate) — consider drug holiday vs continue based on risk. Annual review of adherence + side effects + new fracture.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Rheumatoid arthritis
presentation: Symmetric polyarthritis of small joints (MCPs, PIPs, MTPs, wrists)
Morning stiffness > 30 min, gelling after rest
Bilateral, with synovitis (swelling, warmth, tenderness)
Constitutional — fatigue, weight loss, low-grade fever
Extra-articular: rheumatoid nodules, vasculitis, episcleritis, ILD, pericarditis
redFlags: Atlanto-axial subluxation (cord compression risk; pre-op cervical X-ray)
Rheumatoid lung disease — caplan, ILD, pleural effusion

diagnostics.rationale: joint count + serology + acute phase + duration
anti-CCP highly specific; both negative in 20 % (seronegative RA)
baseline — periarticular osteopenia, erosions, joint space narrowing

diagnostics.test: USS / MRI of synovitis when clinical exam equivocal

management.step: Early referral to rheumatology — within 3 weeks
management.detail: Early aggressive treatment improves long-term outcome (treat-to-target). Window of opportunity in first 12 weeks.

Methotrexate 7.5–10 mg PO once weekly, titrate to 15–25 mg + folic acid 5 mg weekly (different day). Onset 6–12 weeks. Bridge with prednisolone tapered. Monitor FBC + LFTs + creatinine 2-weekly initially. AVOID in pregnancy + breastfeeding.

management.step: Add second DMARD if response inadequate at 3 months
management.detail: Sulfasalazine 500 mg → 2–3 g/day + hydroxychloroquine 200 mg BD. Triple therapy non-inferior to biologics in some patients (TEAR trial).

If failure of ≥ 2 conventional DMARDs (or methotrexate alone if biologic + methotrexate together planned). Anti-TNF (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab) first-line biologic. Alternatives: tocilizumab (anti-IL6), abatacept (T-cell co-stim), rituximab (anti-CD20), JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib). Pre-treatment: TB IGRA + HBV + HCV + HIV screen + vaccinate (no live vaccines on biologic).
NSAID for breakthrough pain (with PPI in over-65 / GI risk). Intra-articular corticosteroid for individual joint flare. Avoid long-term oral steroid > 6 months — bone + metabolic + infection risks.
