presentation: Bacterial infection of the umbilical stump and surrounding tissue; an important SSA neonatal-sepsis source where cord care is poor
Periumbilical redness, induration, discharge, foul smell
May progress rapidly to sepsis, necrotising fasciitis, or portal pyaemia
redFlags: Spreading erythema/induration, crepitus → necrotising fasciitis — surgical emergency
Signs of sepsis (poor feeding, temperature instability, lethargy)

diagnostics.rationale: measure periumbilical erythema/induration; assess for systemic sepsis

management.detail: Admit and start IV broad-spectrum cover (e.g. ampicillin + gentamicin; add anti-staphylococcal/anaerobic cover for severe/necrotising disease).
Urgent debridement if necrotising fasciitis suspected.
Thermoregulation, feeding/fluids, glucose, monitor for sepsis.
Clean cord care; WHO chlorhexidine 7.1% cord application in high-mortality settings; promote hygienic delivery.

references.label: WHO Newborn cord care / chlorhexidine guidance
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Cerebral palsy
presentation: Permanent, non-progressive disorder of movement and posture from an early brain insult (antenatal, perinatal asphyxia, kernicterus, neonatal infection)
Delayed motor milestones, abnormal tone (spasticity commonest), persistent primitive reflexes
Subtypes: spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic, mixed; often with comorbidities (epilepsy, intellectual disability, feeding/communication problems)
A common SSA childhood disability, frequently linked to preventable perinatal events
redFlags: Regression/loss of skills (suggests a progressive disorder — re-evaluate)
Severe feeding difficulty / aspiration / faltering growth
Hip subluxation, contractures, or severe spasticity affecting function

diagnostics.rationale: identify the underlying lesion / exclude progressive pathology
vision, hearing, feeding, seizures, cognition, hips

management.detail: Physiotherapy, occupational and speech/feeding therapy; positioning, mobility aids and orthoses — the cornerstone of care.
Stretching/splinting, oral agents (baclofen), botulinum toxin to targeted muscles; orthopaedic/neurosurgical input for severe cases.
Antiepileptics for seizures, nutrition support, vision/hearing aids, communication support.
Caregiver training, school inclusion, community-based rehabilitation; prevention through perinatal care and jaundice/infection management.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Clubfoot (congenital talipes equinovarus)
presentation: Congenital foot deformity (equinus, varus, adductus, cavus); common and very treatable if started early
Rigid inward/downward-turned foot from birth, uni- or bilateral
Idiopathic most common; may be syndromic/neurogenic
Untreated clubfoot is a major preventable cause of physical disability in SSA
redFlags: Associated neuromuscular condition (e.g. spina bifida) — assess

management.detail: Serial weekly plaster casts to correct the deformity, usually with a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy — corrects most idiopathic clubfeet without major surgery.
Boots-and-bar bracing after casting (full-time then night-time for years) — essential to prevent recurrence; emphasise adherence.
Start within the first weeks of life for best results; established Ponseti programmes exist across SSA.
Soft-tissue/bony procedures when casting is insufficient or for late presentation.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Intestinal amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery)
presentation: Entamoeba histolytica colitis; faecal-oral, common with poor sanitation in SSA
Gradual-onset bloody, mucoid diarrhoea with cramps and tenesmus; fever often mild/absent
Spectrum from asymptomatic carriage to fulminant colitis
Can disseminate to cause amoebic liver abscess
redFlags: Fulminant/necrotising colitis, toxic megacolon or perforation

diagnostics.rationale: trophozoites with ingested red cells (or cysts); differentiate from Shigella
distinguishes E. histolytica from non-pathogenic E. dispar

management.detail: Metronidazole (or tinidazole) for invasive disease — 7–10 days; faster symptom control with tinidazole.
Follow with diloxanide furoate or paromomycin to eradicate intestinal cysts and prevent relapse/transmission (also treat asymptomatic cyst passers in non-endemic settings).
ORS/IV fluids for fluid losses.
Safe water, sanitation, hand hygiene; investigate for concurrent liver abscess if RUQ symptoms.

title: Taeniasis (intestinal tapeworm)
presentation: Adult Taenia solium (pork) or T. saginata (beef) tapeworm from undercooked meat
Often asymptomatic; mild abdominal discomfort, passage of motile proglottids in stool
T. solium carriers are the source of human cysticercosis/neurocysticercosis — a key public-health link
Eosinophilia may be present
redFlags: T. solium taeniasis (cysticercosis transmission risk to self/others)

diagnostics.rationale: diagnose; species often indistinguishable by eggs

management.detail: Single-dose praziquantel (5–10 mg/kg) or niclosamide eliminates the adult worm.
Speciate where possible; counsel on cysticercosis risk and hygiene to prevent autoinfection/transmission.
Meat inspection, thorough cooking, sanitation, treat carriers; consider neurocysticercosis screening in symptomatic patients.
Confirm clearance.

title: Chikungunya
presentation: Alphavirus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes; outbreaks across SSA
Abrupt high fever with severe, often symmetrical polyarthralgia/arthritis and rash
Arthralgia can persist for weeks–months (chronic phase)
Co-circulates with dengue — distinguish (chikungunya: more joint pain; dengue: more haemorrhage/leakage)
redFlags: Severe disease in neonates (vertical transmission), elderly, comorbidities

diagnostics.rationale: lymphopenia; platelets less reduced than dengue

management.detail: Rest, fluids, paracetamol for fever/pain; no specific antiviral.
Bleeding risk if dengue; then NSAIDs may help arthralgia.
Analgesia, physiotherapy; rheumatology input for persistent arthritis.
Mosquito avoidance, source reduction; notify for outbreak response.

title: Relapsing fever (louse-/tick-borne)
presentation: Borrelia spp.; louse-borne (B. recurrentis — epidemic, crowding/displacement in the Horn of Africa) or tick-borne (endemic)
Recurring episodes of high fever lasting days separated by afebrile intervals
Headache, myalgia, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, bleeding
Spirochaetaemia detectable during febrile episodes
redFlags: Severe disease: myocarditis, hepatic failure, bleeding, splenic rupture
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after the first antibiotic dose (can be life-threatening)

management.detail: Single-dose (louse-borne) or short-course (tick-borne) doxycycline; erythromycin/penicillin alternatives — highly effective.
Observe closely after the first dose; supportive care for rigors/hypotension.
Fluids, manage bleeding/organ dysfunction.
Delousing/hygiene for louse-borne epidemics, tick avoidance for endemic disease; notify.

title: Female genital schistosomiasis
presentation: Schistosoma haematobium egg deposition in the female genital tract; highly prevalent yet under-recognised in endemic SSA
Bloody/abnormal vaginal discharge, post-coital bleeding, pelvic pain, dyspareunia, contact bleeding
Characteristic 'sandy patches'/grainy lesions on the cervix/vagina at speculum exam
Associated with infertility and increased HIV acquisition risk
redFlags: Symptoms mimicking cervical cancer/STI — examine and screen

diagnostics.rationale: sandy patches, grainy/rubbery lesions, abnormal vessels on cervix/vagina

diagnostics.test: Urine microscopy for S. haematobium eggs
diagnostics.rationale: supports diagnosis (may be negative despite genital disease)
VIA/cytology/HPV and STI testing — overlapping presentation

management.detail: Praziquantel 40 mg/kg (single or split dose) treats the schistosome infection; earlier treatment limits irreversible genital damage.
Treat co-infections/STIs; counsel on infertility risk and HIV prevention; established lesions may not fully reverse.

management.step: Integrate with cervical screening + HIV services
management.detail: Examine and screen opportunistically in endemic areas.
Mass drug administration and WASH in endemic communities; treat girls before genital damage develops.

references.label: WHO Female genital schistosomiasis: a pocket atlas

title: Haemorrhoids
presentation: Symptomatic engorgement of the anal vascular cushions; very common, aggravated by constipation, straining, pregnancy
Bright-red rectal bleeding (on the paper/coating stool), pruritus, prolapse, perianal lump
Internal graded I–IV by prolapse; external can thrombose causing acute pain
redFlags: Rectal bleeding with red-flag features (weight loss, change in bowel habit, age >50, anaemia) — exclude colorectal cancer
Acute thrombosed/strangulated haemorrhoid with severe pain

diagnostics.rationale: confirm and grade; visualise internal haemorrhoids
colonoscopy/FBC if red-flags or age >50 — never attribute bleeding to piles without examining

management.detail: High-fibre diet, fluids, stool softeners/laxatives to avoid straining; topical agents for symptom relief; perianal hygiene.
Rubber-band ligation (grade I–III) or sclerotherapy for persistent internal haemorrhoids.
Haemorrhoidectomy for grade III–IV/large external or failed conservative therapy.
Within 48–72 h consider excision for rapid pain relief; otherwise conservative with analgesia and stool softeners.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Anal fissure
presentation: Linear tear of the anoderm, usually posterior midline, often after passing hard stool
Severe sharp pain on defecation with bright-red bleeding; anal spasm
Chronic fissure (>6 weeks) has a sentinel pile/skin tag and exposed internal sphincter fibres
redFlags: Atypical/lateral or multiple fissures — exclude Crohn's, TB, HIV, syphilis, malignancy

diagnostics.rationale: visualise the fissure (often posterior midline); avoid painful PR/proctoscopy acutely

diagnostics.test: Consider underlying disease for atypical fissures

management.detail: High-fibre diet, fluids, laxatives and sitz baths break the pain–spasm cycle — most acute fissures heal.
Topical GTN or diltiazem to lower sphincter tone and promote healing (headache common with GTN).
Chemical sphincterotomy for chronic fissures failing topical therapy.
Lateral internal sphincterotomy for refractory chronic fissures (small incontinence risk).

references.label: ASCRS Practice Parameters for anal fissures
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Perianal abscess and fistula-in-ano
presentation: Infection of the anal glands forming a perianal/ischiorectal abscess; may evolve into a fistula-in-ano
Throbbing perianal pain, swelling, redness, fever; fluctuant tender mass
Recurrent discharge from an external opening suggests a fistula
Consider Crohn's, TB and HIV in recurrent/complex disease
redFlags: Spreading sepsis / necrotising perineal infection (Fournier's gangrene) — emergency

diagnostics.rationale: locate and define the abscess; examination under anaesthesia for deep/complex collections
delineate complex fistula tracks before surgery
Crohn's/TB/HIV in recurrent or complex cases

management.detail: Definitive treatment for an abscess — drain without waiting for 'pointing'; antibiotics alone are insufficient.
Add antibiotics for cellulitis, sepsis, immunocompromise or diabetes.
Lay open simple low fistulae; seton/staged procedures for complex/high tracks to protect continence.
Crohn's-related disease needs combined medical–surgical care; urgent debridement for Fournier's gangrene.

references.label: ASCRS anorectal abscess and fistula guidance

title: Perforated appendicitis with peritonitis
presentation: Progression of appendicitis to perforation, more common with late presentation (typical in SSA)
Migratory RIF pain becoming generalised, high fever, vomiting, generalised peritonism
May form an appendix mass/abscess; sepsis/shock in advanced cases
redFlags: Generalised peritonitis, sepsis or shock — emergency laparotomy
Extremes of age with diagnostic delay

management.detail: IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone + metronidazole) before theatre.
Open or laparoscopic with peritoneal lavage for perforation/peritonitis.
Consider antibiotics ± image-guided drainage with interval appendicectomy in selected stable patients.
Continue antibiotics per severity, monitor for collection/ileus, sepsis source control.

references.label: WSES Jerusalem guidelines for acute appendicitis

title: Perforated peptic ulcer
presentation: Full-thickness perforation of a gastric/duodenal ulcer causing chemical then bacterial peritonitis
Sudden severe epigastric pain becoming generalised, board-like rigidity
Risk factors: H. pylori, NSAIDs, smoking; free air under the diaphragm on erect film
redFlags: Generalised peritonitis, sepsis, shock — surgical emergency

management.detail: IV fluids, NG decompression, analgesia, broad-spectrum antibiotics, PPI.
Omental (Graham) patch repair and peritoneal lavage; open or laparoscopic.
Eradicate H. pylori, stop NSAIDs, acid suppression; biopsy gastric ulcers to exclude malignancy.
Sepsis monitoring, nutrition, confirm H. pylori eradication.

title: Kwashiorkor (oedematous severe acute malnutrition)
presentation: Oedematous severe acute malnutrition from inadequate protein/energy intake, often with infection
Bilateral pitting oedema (feet→legs→face), apathy/irritability, 'flaky-paint' dermatosis, sparse depigmented hair, hepatomegaly
Weight may be masked by oedema; appetite poor
High mortality without careful, phased re-feeding
redFlags: Hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration/shock, severe anaemia, infection (often hidden)
Failed appetite test / complications → inpatient care

diagnostics.rationale: diagnose and grade SAM; oedema defines kwashiorkor

diagnostics.test: Blood glucose, infection screen, electrolytes, Hb

management.detail: Stabilisation: treat/prevent hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration (ReSoMal, NOT standard ORS), electrolytes, infection; cautious feeding (F-75).
Start low-energy F-75 then transition to catch-up F-100/RUTF only after oedema resolves and appetite returns — avoid refeeding syndrome and fluid overload.
Vitamin A, folate, zinc and a multivitamin; withhold iron until the recovery (catch-up) phase.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics routinely in complicated SAM; sensory stimulation; transition to outpatient therapeutic feeding and monitor.

references.label: WHO Management of severe acute malnutrition guidance
Kenya National Guideline for Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM), Ministry of Health

title: Nutritional rickets
presentation: Defective bone mineralisation in growing children from vitamin D and/or calcium deficiency
Bowing of legs, widened wrists/ankles, rachitic rosary, frontal bossing, delayed fontanelle closure/dentition
Growth faltering, bone pain, hypotonia; risk factors include exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation and limited sun exposure
redFlags: Consider renal/hepatic or genetic causes if refractory

diagnostics.test: Serum calcium, phosphate, ALP, 25-OH vitamin D, PTH

diagnostics.rationale: exclude renal causes in refractory cases

management.detail: Treatment-dose vitamin D (cholecalciferol/ergocalciferol) with adequate dietary/supplemental calcium per age — corrects biochemistry and heals bone.
IV/oral calcium for symptomatic hypocalcaemia (seizures/tetany).
Continue maintenance vitamin D and calcium; promote sunlight and dietary sources.
Routine infant vitamin D supplementation, especially exclusively breastfed infants; follow-up biochemistry/radiology and orthopaedic review for residual deformity.

references.label: Global Consensus on Prevention and Management of Nutritional Rickets
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
presentation: Spectrum of abnormal hip development from dysplasia to dislocation; better outcomes with early detection
Neonate: positive Barlow/Ortolani, asymmetric thigh creases, limited abduction
Older infant/child: leg-length discrepancy, painless limp, toe-walking
Risk factors: breech, female, family history, oligohydramnios
redFlags: Late diagnosis (walking age) — worse outcomes, may need surgery

diagnostics.rationale: imaging of choice before ossification; for risk factors/abnormal exam

management.detail: Abduction harness for infants <6 months maintains reduction and promotes normal acetabular development — high success when started early.
For later presentation/failed harness, under anaesthetic with arthrogram.
For irreducible or late-presenting dislocations.
Targeted screening of at-risk infants; monitor acetabular development radiologically.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children

title: Trigeminal neuralgia
presentation: Paroxysmal, severe, electric-shock-like unilateral facial pain in trigeminal nerve territory
Triggered by light touch, chewing, talking, cold air; brief stabs with refractory periods
Usually idiopathic (neurovascular compression); secondary causes include MS and tumours
redFlags: Sensory loss, bilateral symptoms, deafness or other neurology — suspect a secondary cause (MS/tumour) → image
Severe weight loss from inability to eat

diagnostics.rationale: characteristic paroxysmal trigeminal pain with triggers and normal exam
for atypical features/young patients/sensory signs — exclude secondary causes and assess neurovascular compression

management.detail: Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine) titrated to effect markedly reduces attacks; monitor for rash/hyponatraemia/blood dyscrasia.
Add/switch to lamotrigine, baclofen or gabapentin for inadequate response/intolerance.
Neurosurgery — microvascular decompression (durable) or ablative procedures (radiofrequency, balloon, gamma knife).
Nutrition support during severe flares; treat any identified secondary cause.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Ascariasis (roundworm)
presentation: Ascaris lumbricoides, the largest and one of the commonest soil-transmitted helminths in SSA
Often asymptomatic; heavy load causes abdominal pain, malnutrition, growth faltering in children
Larval lung migration → Loeffler syndrome (cough, wheeze, transient infiltrates, eosinophilia)
Worms may be passed/vomited
redFlags: Intestinal obstruction from a worm bolus (children)
Severe respiratory symptoms in Loeffler syndrome

management.detail: Albendazole 400 mg single dose (or mebendazole) clears the infection; pyrantel is an alternative.
Conservative management ± piperazine for partial obstruction; surgery/endoscopy for complete obstruction or biliary ascariasis.
Nutritional support, iron as needed.
WHO preventive chemotherapy (deworming) of at-risk groups, sanitation and hygiene.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Hookworm disease
presentation: Necator americanus / Ancylostoma duodenale; major cause of iron-deficiency anaemia in SSA
Larvae penetrate skin (ground itch) → lung migration → intestinal attachment with chronic blood loss
Fatigue, pallor, breathlessness from anaemia; epigastric pain; growth/cognitive impact in children
Eosinophilia, hypoproteinaemia in heavy infection
redFlags: Faltering growth / cognitive impairment in children

management.detail: Albendazole 400 mg single dose (or mebendazole) — high cure rates.
Treat iron-deficiency anaemia with oral (or IV) iron; transfuse only for severe symptomatic anaemia.
Deworm after the first trimester per WHO and treat anaemia.
WHO preventive chemotherapy, footwear, sanitation and hygiene to interrupt transmission.

title: Acute otitis media (childhood)
presentation: Acute middle-ear infection, very common in young children, often after a viral URTI
Ear pain, fever, irritability, ear-tugging in infants; bulging/red tympanic membrane
Otorrhoea if the drum perforates; usually self-limiting
Recurrent/persistent disease can cause hearing loss and CSOM
redFlags: <6 months, or bilateral with significant illness

diagnostics.rationale: bulging, erythematous, immobile tympanic membrane ± effusion/perforation

management.detail: Paracetamol/ibuprofen for pain and fever — the priority for comfort.
Many cases resolve without antibiotics; offer delayed/no antibiotic for mild disease in older children.
Amoxicillin first-line (high-dose) for <6 months, bilateral in <2 years, otorrhoea, or severe/persistent illness; co-amoxiclav for failure.
Review persistent effusion/hearing; pneumococcal vaccination; manage recurrent disease/refer for grommets if needed.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
presentation: Immune-complex nephritis 1–3 weeks after streptococcal throat or skin infection; common in SSA children
Nephritic syndrome: haematuria (cola-coloured urine), oedema (periorbital), hypertension, oliguria
Usually self-limiting in children with good recovery
Low complement (C3) that normalises by ~8 weeks
redFlags: Acute kidney injury / fluid overload / pulmonary oedema

diagnostics.rationale: renal function; low C3 supports diagnosis

diagnostics.test: Evidence of streptococcal infection (ASOT/anti-DNase B, throat/skin swab)

management.detail: Salt and fluid restriction; treat the streptococcal infection (penicillin) to limit spread (does not alter the nephritis course).
Loop diuretics (furosemide) for oedema/hypertension; antihypertensives for severe hypertension.
Treat hyperkalaemia/acidosis; dialysis rarely needed for severe AKI.
Monitor BP, renal function and urinalysis until C3 and urine normalise; most children recover fully.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: African tick-bite fever (rickettsiosis)
presentation: Rickettsia africae from Amblyomma tick bites; common in rural/savannah SSA and travellers
Fever, headache, myalgia with one or more inoculation eschars (tache noire) and regional lymphadenopathy
Maculopapular/vesicular rash variable; usually milder than Mediterranean spotted fever
Often multiple eschars (clustered tick bites)

diagnostics.rationale: characteristic tache noire is a strong clue

diagnostics.test: Serology / PCR of eschar where available

management.detail: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for ~7 days (or until afebrile several days) — rapid response; first-line.
Macrolide (azithromycin) in pregnancy/children where doxycycline is avoided.
Antipyretics, hydration; most cases are self-limiting and respond quickly.
Tick avoidance, protective clothing, repellents and prompt tick removal.

title: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis
presentation: Most acute sinusitis is viral; bacterial infection suggested by persistence/worsening
Facial pain/pressure, nasal obstruction, purulent discharge, hyposmia, worse on bending forward
Bacterial features: symptoms >10 days, 'double-sickening', high fever with purulence
Maxillary sinus most often involved
redFlags: Orbital cellulitis/abscess (eye swelling, proptosis, painful/restricted eye movement, visual change) — emergency

diagnostics.rationale: duration and pattern distinguish bacterial from viral; examine for complications
only if complications suspected or recurrent/refractory

management.detail: Analgesia, saline irrigation, intranasal corticosteroid, decongestants short-term — sufficient for most (viral) cases.
Reserve amoxicillin (or co-amoxiclav) for persistent >10 days, worsening, or severe disease; doxycycline/macrolide if penicillin-allergic.
IV antibiotics + ENT/ophthalmology/neurosurgery for orbital or intracranial complications.
ENT referral and assessment for underlying allergy/anatomy.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Allergic / vernal keratoconjunctivitis
presentation: Chronic, often seasonal, bilateral ocular allergy; vernal form severe in children in hot dry climates (common in SSA)
Intense itching, redness, watering, photophobia, ropy mucoid discharge
Giant 'cobblestone' papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva; limbal Horner-Trantas dots in vernal disease
Risk of vision-threatening corneal involvement (shield ulcers) in severe vernal disease
redFlags: Corneal involvement / shield ulcer — vision-threatening, refer

diagnostics.rationale: tarsal papillae, limbal changes, corneal involvement

management.detail: Reduce triggers (dust, pollen), lubricants and cold compresses for symptom relief.
Dual-action agents (e.g. olopatadine) or mast-cell stabilisers for maintenance control.

management.step: Topical steroids / immunomodulators for severe disease
management.detail: Short steroid pulses (specialist, monitor IOP) and topical ciclosporin/tacrolimus for vernal disease to spare steroids.
Manage shield ulcers and prevent scarring with ophthalmology input.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children

title: Acute bacterial parotitis
presentation: Ascending Staphylococcus aureus infection of the parotid gland, classically in dehydrated/elderly/post-operative patients
Acute painful swelling over the parotid, worse with eating; fever
Pus expressible from Stensen's duct on gland massage
Dehydration and poor oral hygiene are key risk factors
redFlags: Spreading infection / abscess, airway compromise from neck swelling

diagnostics.rationale: purulent discharge from Stensen's duct confirms

diagnostics.test: Pus culture + blood culture if septic

management.detail: Correct dehydration, oral care, sialogogues (sour sweets) and gland massage to promote salivary flow.
Empirical anti-staphylococcal therapy (e.g. flucloxacillin; cover MRSA where prevalent) adjusted to culture.
Incision and drainage/aspiration for an abscess not responding to antibiotics.
Hydration and oral hygiene, especially peri-operatively and in the elderly.

references.label: ENT/IDSA head and neck infection guidance

title: Tension pneumothorax
presentation: Severe respiratory distress and tachypnoea, often after chest trauma or positive-pressure ventilation.
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side, absent breath sounds and hyper-resonance on that side.
Distended neck veins, hypotension and tachycardia (obstructive shock).
redFlags: Cardiovascular collapse / cardiac arrest — needle decompression must not wait for imaging.
Rapidly rising ventilation pressures in an intubated patient.

diagnostics.rationale: Decompress on clinical grounds; do NOT delay for a chest X-ray in an unstable patient.
Absent lung sliding supports the diagnosis when available and time permits.
Confirmatory only AFTER decompression in a stabilised patient.

management.detail: Large-bore cannula in the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line OR 4th/5th space anterior axillary line; a hiss of air confirms.
Insert an intercostal drain (5th space, anterior axillary line) after decompression and connect to an underwater seal.
Treat shock, give oxygen, and address the underlying cause (trauma, barotrauma).

references.label: ATLS Advanced Trauma Life Support — thoracic trauma
WHO Integrated Management for Emergency & Essential Surgical Care (IMEESC)

title: Open (compound) fracture
presentation: Fracture with an overlying wound communicating with the bone or fracture haematoma.
Visible bone, exposed fat, or bleeding consistent with a deep wound over a fracture.
High-energy mechanism with significant soft-tissue injury.
redFlags: Absent distal pulses or signs of vascular injury — surgical emergency.
Gross contamination, devitalised tissue or established infection.

diagnostics.rationale: Document distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation and motor function before and after any manipulation.
Define fracture configuration and joint involvement.
Guides antibiotic choice, debridement urgency and prognosis.

management.detail: Give IV antibiotics within 1 hour (e.g. a first-generation cephalosporin; add gentamicin and metronidazole for higher-grade/contaminated wounds).
Assess immunisation status; give tetanus toxoid +/- immunoglobulin per wound risk.
Remove gross contamination, cover with a saline-soaked sterile dressing, photograph once, then splint and analgese; do not repeatedly expose.
Refer for theatre debridement and skeletal stabilisation; timing depends on contamination and limb viability.

title: Acute compartment syndrome
presentation: Pain out of proportion to the injury, worsening despite analgesia.
Pain on passive stretch of the muscles in the affected compartment.
Tense, swollen compartment, often after fracture, crush, reperfusion or tight casting.
redFlags: Paraesthesia, paralysis and pulselessness are LATE signs — do not wait for them.
A tight cast or dressing — split/remove immediately.
Rising creatine kinase / myoglobinuria suggesting muscle necrosis.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; the earliest reliable sign is escalating pain and pain on passive stretch.
A delta pressure (diastolic BP − compartment pressure) < 30 mmHg supports the diagnosis where monitoring is available.
Detect rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury.

management.detail: Split or remove any cast/dressing down to skin; keep the limb at heart level (not elevated).
Definitive treatment is urgent surgical fasciotomy of all involved compartments — do not delay for investigations.
Oxygen, analgesia, IV fluids to protect kidneys from myoglobinuria; correct hyperkalaemia.

references.label: BOAST Diagnosis & Management of Compartment Syndrome of the Limbs

title: Blunt splenic injury
presentation: Left upper quadrant pain and tenderness after blunt abdominal trauma; left lower rib fractures raise suspicion.
Referred left shoulder-tip pain (Kehr sign).
Signs of hypovolaemia: tachycardia, hypotension after a high-energy mechanism.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability not responding to resuscitation — needs immediate laparotomy.

diagnostics.rationale: Detects free intraperitoneal fluid at the bedside in the unstable patient.
Grades injury and identifies active extravasation in the stable patient.
Monitors for delayed bleeding during non-operative management.

management.detail: Two large-bore cannulae, balanced resuscitation, activate major haemorrhage protocol and crossmatch.
Haemodynamic instability → laparotomy (splenectomy/repair). Stable patients with lower-grade injury → non-operative management +/- angioembolisation.
If splenectomy performed, vaccinate against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Hib, meningococcus) and counsel on overwhelming post-splenectomy infection.

references.label: WSES classification & guidelines for splenic trauma

title: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
presentation: Lower abdominal/pelvic pain, often bilateral, in a sexually active woman.
Abnormal vaginal/cervical discharge, deep dyspareunia, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.
Cervical motion, adnexal or uterine tenderness on bimanual examination.
redFlags: Fever, rigors, severe pain or signs of pelvic peritonitis (possible tubo-ovarian abscess).
Pregnancy — exclude ectopic, and treat as complicated.
Failure to improve at 72 hours on oral therapy.

diagnostics.rationale: Always exclude ectopic pregnancy in a woman with pelvic pain.

diagnostics.test: NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis
diagnostics.rationale: Identifies the commonest causative organisms; do not delay treatment for results.
Indicated if a tubo-ovarian abscess is suspected or the patient is severely unwell.

management.detail: Treat on clinical suspicion to preserve fertility, e.g. IM ceftriaxone plus oral doxycycline and metronidazole; tailor to local guidance.
Admit for IV therapy if pregnant, severely unwell, tubo-ovarian abscess, or failed oral therapy.
Treat sexual partners, advise abstinence until both treated, offer HIV/syphilis screening and contraception review.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the management of STIs

title: Puerperal (postpartum) sepsis
presentation: Fever, lower abdominal pain and offensive lochia within 6 weeks of delivery or abortion.
Uterine tenderness, sub-involution of the uterus.
Tachycardia, malaise, may progress to septic shock.
redFlags: Hypotension, altered mental state, lactate ≥ 2 — manage as septic shock (sepsis six).
Severe abdominal pain or peritonism (retained products, uterine perforation, abscess).
Group A streptococcal infection — rapidly progressive, high mortality.

diagnostics.rationale: Take before antibiotics where possible; lactate guides resuscitation.
Detects retained products of conception or pelvic collection.

management.detail: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, IV fluids, oxygen; take cultures, lactate and monitor urine output.
Evacuate retained products, drain collections; consider hysterectomy in life-threatening uterine infection.
Cover Gram-negative, anaerobes and streptococci (e.g. broad-spectrum beta-lactam + metronidazole; add clindamycin if invasive GAS suspected for toxin suppression).

references.label: WHO recommendations for prevention and treatment of maternal peripartum infections
RCOG Green-top Guideline — sepsis in pregnancy/puerperium
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (MOH)

title: Obstructed labour
presentation: Failure of labour to progress despite good contractions; prolonged labour.
Maternal exhaustion, dehydration, maternal tachycardia and pyrexia.
Excessive moulding, caput, a Bandl ring, or oedematous vulva/cervix.
redFlags: Continuous lower abdominal pain with cessation of contractions and a tender abdomen — impending/actual uterine rupture.
Foetal distress or absent foetal heart.
Haematuria or signs suggesting fistula formation from prolonged pressure.

diagnostics.rationale: Crossing the action line signals obstruction needing intervention.
Assess descent, presentation, moulding, caput and a possible Bandl ring.
Identifies foetal compromise requiring expedited delivery.

management.detail: IV fluids, correct dehydration, analgesia, antibiotics; insert a urinary catheter.
Caesarean section is usually required; symphysiotomy or assisted delivery only where appropriate and CS is unavailable.
Active management of the third stage (PPH risk), monitor for fistula, sepsis and uterine rupture.

references.label: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (MCPC)
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (MOH)

title: Umbilical cord prolapse
presentation: Cord palpable or visible below the presenting part after rupture of membranes.
Sudden foetal bradycardia or variable decelerations after membrane rupture.
Risk factors: malpresentation, prematurity, polyhydramnios, high presenting part.
redFlags: Foetal bradycardia — obstetric emergency requiring immediate delivery.
Cord compression / vasospasm with deteriorating foetal heart trace.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms cord presentation and assesses cervical dilatation for mode of delivery.

management.detail: Elevate the presenting part manually; place the mother knee-chest or in steep head-down/left-lateral position; consider bladder filling. Minimise cord handling and keep it warm.
Category-1 caesarean section unless vaginal delivery is imminent and faster.
Summon obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams immediately.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 50 — Umbilical Cord Prolapse
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Placental abruption
presentation: Sudden constant abdominal pain with or without vaginal bleeding after 20 weeks.
A tense, tender, 'woody-hard' uterus; uterine hypertonus.
Bleeding may be concealed — shock may be out of proportion to visible blood loss.
redFlags: Maternal shock, foetal distress or absent foetal heart.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; ultrasound is insensitive and must not delay management.
Detect anaemia and DIC; prepare for transfusion.
Quantifies feto-maternal haemorrhage to guide anti-D dosing.

management.detail: Large-bore IV access, balanced transfusion, activate major haemorrhage protocol, monitor closely.
Foetal distress or maternal compromise → emergency caesarean. If foetus dead and mother stable, aim for vaginal delivery with close monitoring.
Correct coagulopathy, give anti-D to Rh-negative women, watch for PPH and renal failure.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 63 — Antepartum Haemorrhage
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Placenta praevia
presentation: Painless bright-red vaginal bleeding after 20 weeks of gestation.
A soft, non-tender uterus; the presenting part is high or malpresenting.
Often diagnosed on a routine anomaly scan before bleeding occurs.
redFlags: Heavy bleeding with maternal compromise or foetal distress.
Do NOT perform a digital vaginal examination until praevia is excluded — it can provoke torrential haemorrhage.

diagnostics.rationale: Localises the placenta relative to the internal os; transvaginal is safe and more accurate.

management.detail: Manage with speculum only after praevia excluded; admit symptomatic women.
Stable, preterm → conservative with steroids for foetal lung maturity. Heavy bleeding or term → caesarean section.
Plan delivery in a facility with blood and surgical support; give anti-D if Rh-negative.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 27a — Placenta Praevia
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Hyperemesis gravidarum
presentation: Persistent severe nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy with weight loss (>5% of pre-pregnancy weight).
Dehydration, ketonuria and electrolyte disturbance.
Inability to maintain adequate oral intake.
redFlags: Confusion, ataxia or ophthalmoplegia — Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency.
Severe electrolyte derangement or unremitting symptoms.

diagnostics.rationale: Quantifies severity; ketonuria indicates significant dehydration.

diagnostics.test: U&E, FBC, and assess for other causes
diagnostics.rationale: Identify hypokalaemia/hyponatraemia; exclude UTI, thyroid disease, molar pregnancy.
Standardised severity scoring to guide management.

management.detail: IV normal saline with potassium as needed; avoid dextrose-only fluids before thiamine.
Give thiamine to prevent Wernicke; first-line antiemetics include antihistamines (cyclizine) / doxylamine-pyridoxine, then metoclopramide or ondansetron per local guidance.
Consider thromboprophylaxis during admission; review nutrition; escalate refractory cases.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 69 — Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Ovarian (adnexal) torsion
presentation: Sudden severe unilateral lower abdominal/pelvic pain, often with nausea and vomiting.
May be intermittent (torsion-detorsion); often a palpable adnexal mass.
Frequently associated with an ovarian cyst or mass acting as a lead point.
redFlags: Peritonism or signs of ovarian necrosis.
Haemodynamic instability suggesting an alternative diagnosis (ruptured ectopic).

diagnostics.rationale: Shows an enlarged oedematous ovary; absent flow supports torsion but present flow does NOT exclude it.

management.detail: Diagnosis is surgical — laparoscopy for detorsion to preserve the ovary; delay risks necrosis.
Adequate analgesia, antiemetics, keep nil by mouth pending theatre.
Detorse and conserve where possible; cystectomy if a lead-point cyst; oophorectomy only if clearly necrotic.

references.label: RCOG / ESHRE guidance on management of ovarian torsion

title: Typhoid intestinal perforation
presentation: Worsening abdominal pain and distension in the 2nd–3rd week of untreated/partially treated typhoid fever.
Generalised peritonitis: guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness.
Often a terminal-ileum perforation; may present with sepsis.
redFlags: Septic shock and peritonitis — surgical emergency.

diagnostics.rationale: Free air under the diaphragm confirms perforation.
Confirms Salmonella Typhi and assesses severity.

management.detail: IV fluids, correct electrolytes, nasogastric decompression, urinary catheter; treat sepsis.
Cover Salmonella and enteric flora (e.g. ceftriaxone plus metronidazole; tailor to local resistance).
Identify and repair/resect perforation(s), peritoneal lavage; consider stoma if heavy contamination.

references.label: WHO Background document: the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of typhoid fever

title: Neonatal tetanus
presentation: A neonate who fed and cried normally for the first 2 days, then develops difficulty feeding (inability to suck) from days 3–28.
Generalised stiffness, spasms, trismus and opisthotonus.
History of unclean cord care or non-sterile delivery; mother not fully tetanus-immunised.
redFlags: Apnoea during spasms, laryngospasm, autonomic instability.

diagnostics.rationale: Based on the characteristic history and spasms; no confirmatory test should delay treatment.
Identifies the portal of entry and prevention failures.

management.step: Neutralise toxin and treat the wound
management.detail: Give human tetanus immunoglobulin (or antitoxin), antibiotics (metronidazole), and clean the umbilical stump.
Benzodiazepines (diazepam) titrated to control spasms; nurse in a quiet, dark environment; secure the airway and support ventilation as needed.
Nasogastric feeding, fluids; immunise the infant on recovery and the mother; promote maternal TT vaccination and clean delivery/cord care to prevent recurrence.

references.label: WHO Maternal and neonatal tetanus elimination (MNTE)
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Congenital syphilis
presentation: Early (<2 yrs): hepatosplenomegaly, rash (palms/soles), snuffles (rhinitis), jaundice, anaemia, bone lesions, failure to thrive.
Many infants are asymptomatic at birth — maternal serology drives detection.
Late stigmata: Hutchinson teeth, saddle nose, sabre shins, interstitial keratitis, deafness.

diagnostics.test: Maternal and infant treponemal + non-treponemal serology (RPR/VDRL)
diagnostics.rationale: Infant RPR ≥ 4× the maternal titre suggests infection; compare paired sera.

management.detail: Treat proven/probable cases with IV benzylpenicillin (or procaine penicillin) for 10 days; single-dose benzathine penicillin only for low-risk infants with adequately treated mothers per protocol.
Screen and treat all pregnant women for syphilis early; treat partners — the key intervention to eliminate congenital syphilis.
Serial serology, ophthalmology, audiology and developmental follow-up.

references.label: WHO Guideline on syphilis screening and treatment for pregnant women
CDC STI Treatment Guidelines — Congenital Syphilis
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Leptospirosis
presentation: Acute febrile illness with severe myalgia (especially calves), headache and conjunctival suffusion.
Exposure to fresh water, soil, rodents, or animals (farming, flooding, sewage).
Biphasic course; may progress to Weil disease (jaundice, renal failure, haemorrhage).
redFlags: Jaundice with acute kidney injury (Weil disease).

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms infection; PCR is useful early, serology later (paired titres).
Treat empirically on suspicion in endemic settings — do not wait for confirmation.

management.detail: Mild: oral doxycycline (or azithromycin). Severe: IV penicillin (benzylpenicillin) or ceftriaxone.
Fluids, renal support/dialysis for AKI, respiratory support for pulmonary haemorrhage.
Avoid contaminated water, rodent control, protective clothing; doxycycline chemoprophylaxis for high-risk short-term exposure.

references.label: WHO Human Leptospirosis: guidance for diagnosis, surveillance and control
Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) Technical Guidelines, 3rd ed, Ministry of Health

title: Mumps
presentation: Painful swelling of one or both parotid glands, fever and malaise.
Earache and pain on chewing; angle-of-jaw swelling obscuring the mandibular angle.
Often a prodrome of low-grade fever and headache.
redFlags: Severe headache, neck stiffness or photophobia (mumps meningitis/encephalitis).

diagnostics.rationale: Typical parotitis in an unvaccinated person is usually sufficient.

diagnostics.test: Mumps IgM serology or RT-PCR (saliva/buccal swab)
diagnostics.rationale: Confirms in atypical cases and for surveillance.

management.detail: Analgesia/antipyretics, hydration, soft diet; mumps is self-limiting in most cases.
Scrotal support and analgesia for orchitis; assess for meningitis/pancreatitis as needed.
MMR vaccination is the key preventive measure; isolate for 5 days after parotid swelling onset; notify per local policy.

references.label: Kenya National Immunization Programme (KEPI/NVIP) Schedule, Ministry of Health

title: Rubella (German measles)
presentation: Mild fever with a fine pink maculopapular rash spreading from the face downward.
Tender post-auricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy.
Arthralgia, especially in adult women; often subclinical.
redFlags: Infection in early pregnancy — high risk of congenital rubella syndrome (deafness, cataracts, cardiac defects).

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms acute infection; essential when a pregnant woman is exposed.
Identifies susceptible pregnant women for postpartum vaccination.

management.detail: Antipyretics and rest; rubella is self-limiting in children and most adults.
Avoid contact with pregnant women; counsel and test exposed pregnant women — vaccine cannot be given in pregnancy.
MMR vaccination; offer to non-immune women postpartum; notify per local policy.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Varicella (chickenpox)
presentation: Generalised pruritic vesicular rash in successive crops (macule → papule → vesicle → crust) with lesions at different stages.
Fever and malaise, often a mild prodrome.
Centripetal distribution; mucosal involvement.
redFlags: Immunocompromise, pregnancy, or neonatal exposure — high complication risk.
Secondary bacterial skin infection / necrotising fasciitis.

diagnostics.rationale: The polymorphic rash with lesions at different stages is characteristic.
For atypical or severe cases and in the immunocompromised.

management.detail: Antipruritics, antipyretics (avoid aspirin in children — Reye syndrome), keep nails short, prevent scratching.
Oral/IV aciclovir for adults, immunocompromised, pregnant women and severe disease, ideally within 24 hours of rash.
Varicella vaccine; varicella-zoster immunoglobulin for susceptible high-risk contacts (pregnant, immunocompromised, neonates).

references.label: WHO Varicella and herpes zoster vaccines: position paper
Kenya National Immunization Programme (KEPI/NVIP) Schedule, Ministry of Health

title: Enterobiasis (pinworm / threadworm)
presentation: Perianal itching, worse at night, in a child (and often household members).
Disturbed sleep, irritability; sometimes vulvovaginitis in girls.
Visible thread-like white worms around the anus or in stool.

diagnostics.rationale: Applied to the perianal skin in the morning to collect eggs for microscopy.
Typical nocturnal pruritus often warrants empirical treatment, especially in households.

management.detail: Single dose of mebendazole, albendazole or pyrantel pamoate, repeated after 2 weeks to catch reinfection.
Treat all household members simultaneously to break the reinfection cycle.
Hand-washing, short nails, wash bed linen and underwear in hot water, morning showering.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Dental (odontogenic) abscess
presentation: Severe, throbbing, localised tooth pain with sensitivity to percussion.
Facial/gingival swelling, a tender fluctuant mass, possible discharge.
Fever and regional lymphadenopathy.
redFlags: Difficulty breathing or swallowing, drooling, trismus, floor-of-mouth swelling — spreading deep-space infection (Ludwig angina) is a airway emergency.
Peri-orbital/orbital involvement, or signs of cavernous sinus thrombosis.

diagnostics.rationale: Identify the causative tooth, fluctuance, and spread to fascial spaces.

management.detail: Definitive treatment is drainage and dental treatment (extraction or root-canal); refer to dental services.
Paracetamol and/or NSAIDs for pain.
Amoxicillin (add metronidazole) or amoxicillin-clavulanate when there is spreading infection, systemic upset or immunocompromise; antibiotics are not a substitute for drainage.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Maxillofacial trauma
presentation: Facial pain, swelling, deformity, malocclusion or trismus after facial trauma.
Epistaxis, periorbital bruising, diplopia, or numbness over the cheek (infraorbital nerve).
Mobile facial segments (Le Fort fractures), step deformities, or a flattened cheek.
redFlags: Airway compromise from bleeding, displaced fractures or oedema — secure the airway first.
Visual loss / retrobulbar haemorrhage — needs urgent decompression.

diagnostics.rationale: Airway and concurrent life-threatening injuries take priority over the facial injury.
Defines fracture pattern (orbital, zygoma, mandible, Le Fort) for surgical planning.
Detects globe injury, diplopia and entrapment requiring urgent intervention.

management.detail: Secure the airway (anticipate difficulty); control bleeding with packing/pressure; immobilise the C-spine.
Provide analgesia; antibiotics for open/compound fractures and contaminated wounds; tetanus prophylaxis.
Refer to maxillofacial/ophthalmology for definitive fixation; urgent referral for orbital compartment syndrome.

title: Flail chest and pulmonary contusion
presentation: Paradoxical chest-wall movement after blunt chest trauma (a segment moving in on inspiration).
Severe chest pain, splinting and shallow breathing.
Hypoxia, often worsening over 24–48 hours as underlying lung contusion evolves.
redFlags: Worsening hypoxia despite oxygen — evolving contusion/ARDS.

diagnostics.rationale: Identifies multiple rib fractures, contusion, pneumothorax and haemothorax.
Tracks oxygenation and ventilation in evolving contusion.

management.detail: Effective analgesia (including regional/epidural) is central — it allows deep breathing and coughing, preventing atelectasis.
Physiotherapy and, where needed, non-invasive or invasive ventilation; judicious fluids to avoid worsening contusion.
Rib fixation may benefit selected patients with significant flail; treat associated injuries.

references.label: EAST guidelines on rib fracture management

title: Blunt hepatic (liver) injury
presentation: Right upper quadrant pain/tenderness after blunt abdominal trauma; right lower rib fractures raise suspicion.
Signs of hypovolaemia (tachycardia, hypotension) after a high-energy mechanism.
Referred right shoulder pain; abdominal distension.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability unresponsive to resuscitation — immediate laparotomy.

diagnostics.rationale: Detects free intraperitoneal fluid at the bedside in unstable patients.
Grades injury and identifies active arterial extravasation (stable patients).
Monitors for delayed bleeding during non-operative management.

management.detail: Large-bore access, balanced transfusion, activate major haemorrhage protocol, crossmatch, tranexamic acid early in trauma.
Instability -> laparotomy (packing, repair). Stable -> non-operative management +/- angioembolisation of active bleeding.
Watch for biliary leak, hepatic abscess, delayed haemorrhage and abdominal compartment syndrome.

title: Traumatic haemothorax
presentation: Respiratory distress and reduced breath sounds with dullness to percussion on the affected side after chest trauma.
Signs of blood loss: tachycardia, hypotension.
Often with rib fractures or penetrating injury.
redFlags: Massive haemothorax (>1.5 L initial drainage or ongoing >200 mL/h) — needs thoracotomy.

diagnostics.rationale: Detects pleural fluid; ultrasound is rapid at the bedside.

management.detail: Oxygen, IV access, balanced transfusion; insert a large-bore intercostal chest drain and measure output.
Urgent thoracotomy/VATS for massive initial loss or persistent high output.
Manage rib fractures, pneumothorax and analgesia to enable ventilation.

title: Extradural (epidural) haematoma
presentation: Head trauma (often temporal) with a 'lucid interval' followed by rapid deterioration.
Headache, vomiting, declining GCS.
Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil and contralateral weakness (late, herniation).
redFlags: Falling GCS, unequal pupils, Cushing response (hypertension + bradycardia) — impending herniation.

diagnostics.rationale: Shows a biconvex (lentiform) hyperdense collection, classically from a middle meningeal artery tear.

management.detail: Secure airway, maintain oxygenation and normal CO2, avoid hypotension, head up 30 degrees; treat raised ICP (hypertonic saline/mannitol).
Urgent craniotomy and evacuation — outcomes are excellent if decompressed early.
Immediate referral/transfer to a neurosurgical unit; reverse any anticoagulation.

references.label: NICE Head injury: assessment and early management

title: Acute subdural haematoma
presentation: Head trauma (often elderly, anticoagulated, or alcohol use) with depressed or fluctuating consciousness.
Headache, confusion, focal neurology.
May present insidiously (chronic subdural) with gradual cognitive decline.

diagnostics.rationale: Shows a crescentic collection over the convexity, crossing suture lines.
Identifies and guides reversal of anticoagulation.

management.detail: Airway/oxygenation, avoid hypotension/hypoxia; urgently reverse anticoagulation (e.g. PCC for warfarin).
Evacuation for significant acute haematoma with mass effect; burr holes for symptomatic chronic subdural.
Manage raised ICP, seizures, and monitor neuro-observations.

title: Traumatic spinal cord injury
presentation: Limb weakness, sensory loss or paralysis after trauma; a sensory level.
Neck/back pain, bony tenderness or deformity.
Priapism, urinary retention, loss of anal tone.
redFlags: High cervical injury with respiratory compromise (diaphragmatic failure).

diagnostics.rationale: Document motor/sensory level and sphincter function (ASIA assessment).
Defines bony injury and cord/ligamentous damage.

management.detail: Maintain in-line immobilisation, log-roll; airway with C-spine control; avoid secondary injury.
Treat neurogenic shock (fluids then vasopressors, atropine for bradycardia); maintain MAP for cord perfusion; ventilatory support for high lesions.
Urgent spinal surgery referral; prevent pressure sores, VTE, bladder/bowel complications.

references.label: ATLS — spine and spinal cord trauma

title: Pelvic fracture with haemorrhage
presentation: Pelvic pain and instability after a high-energy mechanism.
Hypovolaemic shock out of proportion to other injuries (massive retroperitoneal bleeding).
Perineal/scrotal bruising, leg-length discrepancy, blood at the urethral meatus.
redFlags: Open pelvic fracture / associated bowel or urogenital injury.

diagnostics.rationale: Identifies fracture pattern and excludes intraperitoneal bleeding.

management.detail: Bind at the level of the greater trochanters early to reduce volume and tamponade venous bleeding.
Balanced transfusion, major haemorrhage protocol, tranexamic acid, crossmatch.
Angioembolisation, preperitoneal packing or external fixation per local pathway; urgent referral.

title: Crush syndrome / rhabdomyolysis
presentation: Muscle pain, weakness and swelling after prolonged compression, immobilisation, seizures or extreme exertion.
Dark (tea-coloured) urine from myoglobinuria.
Often after entrapment or a prolonged 'long lie'.
redFlags: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes / arrhythmia — life-threatening on reperfusion.

diagnostics.rationale: Detect hyperkalaemia and AKI requiring urgent treatment.

management.detail: Early generous isotonic fluid resuscitation to maintain urine output and protect the kidneys; start before extrication where possible.
Calcium gluconate for cardioprotection, insulin-dextrose, and other measures; monitor ECG continuously.
Watch for compartment syndrome, correct acidosis, renal replacement therapy for refractory hyperkalaemia/AKI.

references.label: Disaster medicine guidance on crush injury (WHO/ISN)

title: Open globe (penetrating eye) injury
presentation: Eye pain and visual loss after penetrating or blunt trauma.
A teardrop/peaked pupil, prolapsed uveal tissue, shallow anterior chamber, or visible laceration.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage with reduced vision.
redFlags: Any suspected open globe — do NOT apply pressure or topical drops.

diagnostics.rationale: Avoid manipulating the globe; document vision in each eye.

diagnostics.test: CT orbit (avoid MRI if metallic FB)
diagnostics.rationale: Identifies globe rupture and intraocular foreign bodies.

management.detail: Apply a rigid eye shield (not a pad), keep nil by mouth, antiemetics to prevent Valsalva, avoid any pressure or drops.
Analgesia, antiemetics, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis.
Emergency referral for surgical repair; avoid delays to reduce endophthalmitis and vision loss.

references.label: Royal College of Ophthalmologists — ocular trauma guidance

title: Drowning and submersion injury
presentation: Respiratory distress, cough, hypoxia after a submersion event; may be asymptomatic initially.
Altered consciousness, vomiting, hypothermia.
Possible cardiac arrest.
redFlags: Worsening respiratory failure over hours (delayed deterioration).
Hypothermia and associated trauma (e.g. cervical spine in diving).

diagnostics.rationale: Detect hypothermia; observe symptomatic patients for delayed deterioration.

management.detail: Drowning is primarily a hypoxic insult — early rescue breaths and high-flow oxygen; ventilatory support/PEEP for respiratory failure.
Standard ALS with attention to rewarming in hypothermia ('not dead until warm and dead'); protect the cervical spine if mechanism suggests.
Admit symptomatic patients; manage ARDS supportively; antibiotics only for established infection.

title: Uterine rupture
presentation: Sudden severe abdominal pain, often with cessation of contractions, in labour (especially with a previous caesarean scar).
Maternal tachycardia/shock, abnormal foetal heart rate, vaginal bleeding.
Loss of station of the presenting part; palpable foetal parts abdominally.
redFlags: Maternal collapse and foetal bradycardia/death — immediate laparotomy.
Scar dehiscence in a labouring VBAC.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical and time-critical; do not delay for imaging.

management.detail: Major haemorrhage protocol, large-bore access, balanced transfusion, summon obstetric/anaesthetic teams.
Deliver the foetus and repair the uterus; hysterectomy if repair impossible or bleeding uncontrolled.
Monitor for ongoing bleeding, sepsis; counsel on future pregnancies and delivery mode.

references.label: RCOG guidance — birth after previous caesarean
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Shoulder dystocia
presentation: Failure of the shoulders to deliver after the head, with gentle downward traction (the 'turtle sign').
Head retracts against the perineum.
Risk factors: macrosomia, diabetes, previous dystocia, prolonged labour.
redFlags: Delay to delivery — risk of hypoxic injury and death.
Brachial plexus injury / fracture from excessive traction.

diagnostics.rationale: Recognise immediately; call for help and start manoeuvres without delay.

management.detail: Summon help, hyperflex maternal hips (McRoberts), apply suprapubic pressure; discourage fundal pressure and excessive traction.
Internal rotational manoeuvres (Rubin/Woods), deliver the posterior arm; consider all-fours position.
Record times and manoeuvres; assess neonate for injury and mother for haemorrhage/trauma; debrief.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 42 — Shoulder Dystocia
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Retained placenta
presentation: Failure to deliver the placenta within 30 minutes of birth despite active management.
Ongoing or intermittent vaginal bleeding.
Risk of postpartum haemorrhage and infection.
redFlags: Signs of placenta accreta (morbidly adherent placenta).

diagnostics.rationale: Assess uterine tone, bleeding and whether the placenta is separated.

management.detail: IV access, fluids; controlled cord traction with oxytocin; empty the bladder.
If not delivered or bleeding, perform manual removal under analgesia/anaesthesia with antibiotic cover.
Treat PPH, give antibiotics; suspect accreta if the plane cannot be developed — stop and seek senior/surgical help.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage
presentation: Abnormal/excessive vaginal bleeding from 24 hours to 6 weeks postpartum.
Often with offensive lochia, fever and uterine tenderness (endometritis).
Sub-involuted uterus.

management.detail: IV access, fluids/transfusion if bleeding heavily; uterotonics and tranexamic acid.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected endometritis.
Surgical evacuation of retained products if present; senior obstetric input.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 52 — Postpartum Haemorrhage
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (MOH)

title: Molar pregnancy (hydatidiform mole)
presentation: Irregular vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy, often with a uterus large for dates.
Hyperemesis, exaggerated pregnancy symptoms; passage of grape-like vesicles.
Very high beta-hCG; absent foetal heart in a complete mole.
redFlags: Heavy haemorrhage; signs of metastatic gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

diagnostics.rationale: Shows a 'snowstorm'/cluster-of-grapes appearance with no foetus (complete mole).
Markedly elevated; used for diagnosis and post-evacuation monitoring.

management.detail: Suction curettage; send tissue for histology; give anti-D if Rh-negative.
Serial beta-hCG monitoring to detect persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia; register with a trophoblastic disease centre.
Avoid pregnancy until hCG normalises; reliable contraception during follow-up.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 38 — Gestational Trophoblastic Disease
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Amniotic fluid embolism
presentation: Sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxia and seizures during labour, delivery or immediately postpartum.
Profound hypotension and respiratory failure.
Followed by disseminated intravascular coagulation and haemorrhage.

diagnostics.rationale: Recognise the sudden triad of hypoxia, hypotension and coagulopathy; no confirmatory test should delay treatment.
Detect and guide treatment of DIC.

management.detail: Call for help, ALS with left uterine displacement / perimortem caesarean within 5 minutes if arrest; oxygenation and circulatory support.
Massive transfusion protocol, fibrinogen/cryoprecipitate, tranexamic acid; correct DIC.
ICU support, vasopressors/inotropes, consider advanced therapies (e.g. ECMO) where available.

references.label: RCOG / UKOSS guidance on amniotic fluid embolism
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Carbon monoxide poisoning
presentation: Headache, nausea, dizziness and confusion, often with multiple household members or co-exposed individuals affected.
Exposure to faulty heaters, smoke, or fumes in an enclosed space.
Normal SpO2 on pulse oximetry despite hypoxia (falsely reassuring).
redFlags: Loss of consciousness, seizures, chest pain or arrhythmia.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms exposure; standard pulse oximetry is unreliable and reads falsely normal.
Detect myocardial ischaemia and assess severity.

management.detail: Give high-concentration oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask immediately to displace CO and shorten its half-life; continue until symptoms resolve and COHb normalises.
Monitor cardiac status, treat seizures and acidosis; remove from the source and assess co-exposed individuals.
Discuss hyperbaric oxygen for severe poisoning (loss of consciousness, neurological signs, pregnancy, ischaemia) where available.

references.label: TOXBASE / national poisons guidance — carbon monoxide

title: Toxic alcohol poisoning (methanol / ethylene glycol)
presentation: Inebriation followed by a latent period, then deterioration; history of ingesting non-beverage alcohol/antifreeze.
Methanol: visual disturbance ('snowstorm'/blindness). Ethylene glycol: flank pain, oxalate crystalluria, AKI.
Severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
redFlags: Severe metabolic acidosis with raised osmolar gap.
Visual loss (methanol) or acute kidney injury (ethylene glycol).

diagnostics.test: ABG/venous gas with anion and osmolar gap
diagnostics.rationale: High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with a raised osmolar gap supports toxic alcohol ingestion.

diagnostics.test: Serum methanol/ethylene glycol levels and renal function
diagnostics.rationale: Confirm and quantify where available; assess AKI.

management.detail: Give fomepizole (preferred) or ethanol to inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase and prevent toxic metabolite formation — start early on suspicion.
Sodium bicarbonate for severe acidosis; folinic acid/folate (methanol) and thiamine/pyridoxine (ethylene glycol) as adjuncts.
Indicated for severe acidosis, high levels, visual symptoms or renal failure to remove toxin and metabolites.

references.label: TOXBASE / national poisons guidance — toxic alcohols

title: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose
presentation: Drowsiness, anticholinergic features (dry, dilated, tachycardic, agitated/confused) after TCA ingestion.
Seizures and rapid deterioration.
Hypotension and broad-complex arrhythmia.
redFlags: QRS widening >100 ms — predicts seizures and arrhythmia.

diagnostics.rationale: QRS prolongation and a tall terminal R wave in aVR indicate cardiotoxicity and guide bicarbonate therapy.
Assess acidosis and potassium; guide treatment.

management.detail: Give IV sodium bicarbonate boluses for QRS widening, arrhythmia or hypotension, targeting serum pH ~7.45–7.55.
Secure the airway; treat seizures with benzodiazepines; activated charcoal if early and airway protected.
IV fluids and vasopressors for hypotension; avoid class Ia/Ic and III antiarrhythmics; magnesium/lipid emulsion in refractory cases per toxicology advice.

references.label: TOXBASE / national poisons guidance — tricyclic antidepressants

title: Salicylate (aspirin) poisoning
presentation: Tinnitus, deafness, nausea/vomiting, sweating and hyperventilation after aspirin overdose.
Mixed acid-base picture: early respiratory alkalosis then high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
Agitation, confusion in severe cases.
redFlags: Altered mental status, seizures, coma (CNS salicylate — needs dialysis).
High or rising salicylate level with acidosis.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirm and trend; levels can keep rising with delayed-release preparations.
Characterise the mixed acid-base disturbance and guide alkalinisation.

management.detail: IV fluids and sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise the urine (target urine pH 7.5–8.5), enhancing salicylate elimination; replace potassium.
Give if presenting early with a protected airway; consider repeat doses for large/sustained-release ingestions.
For severe poisoning: altered mental state, very high levels, acidosis refractory to treatment, renal failure or pulmonary oedema.

title: Hyponatraemia
presentation: Often asymptomatic; nausea, headache, lethargy and confusion as sodium falls.
Severe/rapid falls: seizures, reduced consciousness, coma.
Assess volume status (hypo-, eu- or hypervolaemic).
redFlags: Seizures or reduced GCS — severe symptomatic hyponatraemia needs hypertonic saline.
Very rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination — limit the daily rise.
Acute (<48 h) drops are higher risk.

diagnostics.test: Serum and urine sodium and osmolality
diagnostics.rationale: Classifies the cause (e.g. SIADH, hypovolaemia, hypervolaemia) and guides treatment.
Distinguishes hypovolaemic, euvolaemic and hypervolaemic hyponatraemia.

management.detail: For seizures/coma, give boluses of hypertonic (3%) saline to raise sodium by a few mmol/L until symptoms abate.

management.step: Correct the cause and control the rate
management.detail: Fluid restriction for SIADH/hypervolaemia, saline for hypovolaemia; limit correction to ~8–10 mmol/L in 24 h to avoid osmotic demyelination.
Frequent sodium checks; re-lower with dextrose/desmopressin if over-correcting.

title: Hypocalcaemia
presentation: Perioral and peripheral paraesthesia, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm.
Chvostek and Trousseau signs.
Causes: hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, CKD, post-thyroidectomy, hyperventilation.

diagnostics.test: Magnesium, phosphate, PTH, vitamin D, ECG
diagnostics.rationale: Identify the cause; magnesium must be corrected for calcium to respond; check QT.

management.detail: Give IV calcium gluconate (with cardiac monitoring) for tetany, seizures, laryngospasm or ECG changes.
Replace magnesium — hypocalcaemia is refractory until hypomagnesaemia is corrected.
Oral calcium and vitamin D (alfacalcidol/calcitriol if hypoparathyroid or CKD) for ongoing replacement.

references.label: Society for Endocrinology — acute hypocalcaemia guidance

title: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)
presentation: Isolated thrombocytopenia with mucocutaneous bleeding: petechiae, purpura, easy bruising, epistaxis.
Often follows a viral illness in children; more chronic in adults.
Otherwise well, with no anaemia or leucopenia.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms isolated thrombocytopenia with otherwise normal counts and film (large platelets).
Consider HIV, hepatitis C, drugs, SLE and other causes of low platelets.

management.detail: Many children and asymptomatic adults with platelets >20–30 x10^9/L can be observed.
Corticosteroids (prednisolone) +/- IV immunoglobulin for bleeding or very low counts; IVIG gives a faster rise.
Combine IVIG, high-dose steroids and platelet transfusion for life-threatening haemorrhage; refer to haematology; consider second-line agents (e.g. TPO agonists, rituximab) for chronic ITP.

references.label: ASH / international consensus guidelines on ITP

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
presentation: Bleeding from multiple sites (venepuncture, mucosa, surgical wounds) and/or microvascular thrombosis.
Occurs secondary to sepsis, obstetric emergencies, trauma, malignancy or severe inflammation.
Organ dysfunction from microthrombi.
redFlags: Severe haemorrhage or widespread thrombosis with organ failure.

diagnostics.rationale: Prolonged PT/APTT, low platelets and fibrinogen with high D-dimer support DIC; trend serially.

management.detail: The priority is aggressive treatment of the trigger (e.g. sepsis, evacuation of abruption) — DIC will not resolve otherwise.
Platelets, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen guided by counts and bleeding; tranexamic acid is generally avoided unless directed by specialists.
Involve haematology/critical care; consider anticoagulation only in predominantly thrombotic DIC under specialist guidance.

references.label: ISTH / BSH guidelines on the diagnosis and management of DIC

title: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)
presentation: Severe unilateral sore throat with worsening odynophagia and trismus.
Muffled 'hot potato' voice, drooling, fever.
Uvular deviation away from a swollen, displaced tonsil with peritonsillar bulging.
redFlags: Spread to deep neck spaces / mediastinitis.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is usually clinical from the characteristic asymmetric peritonsillar swelling.

diagnostics.test: Needle aspiration / CT for deep extension
diagnostics.rationale: Aspiration is diagnostic and therapeutic; CT if deep-space spread is suspected.

management.detail: Needle aspiration or incision and drainage of the abscess — the key therapeutic step; ENT referral.
IV antibiotics covering streptococci and oral anaerobes (e.g. benzylpenicillin + metronidazole, or amoxicillin-clavulanate); a single dose of corticosteroid may reduce symptoms.
Analgesia, IV fluids for dehydration; monitor the airway.

references.label: ENT UK guidance on peritonsillar abscess

title: Acute epiglottitis (supraglottitis)
presentation: Rapid-onset severe sore throat, odynophagia, drooling and fever.
Muffled voice, tripod/sniffing posture, stridor; the patient looks toxic.
Often Haemophilus influenzae type b in unimmunised individuals.
redFlags: Impending airway obstruction — do NOT examine the throat or distress the patient (especially children).

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; definitive examination (laryngoscopy) is done in a controlled setting prepared to secure the airway.
Only if the patient is stable and it will not delay airway management.

management.detail: Keep the patient calm and upright; summon senior anaesthetic/ENT help; secure the airway in theatre with surgical airway backup before other interventions.
IV third-generation cephalosporin (e.g. ceftriaxone) once the airway is safe; humidified oxygen.
ICU monitoring; treat close contacts/prophylaxis per local Hib guidance; promote Hib vaccination.

references.label: Difficult Airway Society / ENT UK guidance on epiglottitis

title: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis
presentation: Prodrome of fever and malaise, then a painful erythematous/dusky rash with blistering and skin detachment.
Mucosal involvement (eyes, mouth, genitals) with erosions; positive Nikolsky sign.
Usually 1–3 weeks after a culprit drug (e.g. sulfonamides, antiepileptics, allopurinol, NSAIDs).
redFlags: Extensive skin detachment (TEN >30% body surface area) — high mortality.
Ocular, airway or genitourinary mucosal involvement.
Sepsis, fluid loss and organ dysfunction.

diagnostics.rationale: Recognise the pattern; biopsy confirms full-thickness epidermal necrosis.
Estimates prognosis and guides level of care.

management.detail: Withdrawing the offending drug early is the single most important intervention; review all medications.
Manage in a burns/ICU setting: fluid and electrolyte replacement, temperature control, wound care, analgesia, nutrition, infection surveillance.
Early ophthalmology, dermatology and intensive care; immunomodulation (e.g. ciclosporin/IVIG) is used in some centres.

references.label: UK guidelines for the management of SJS/TEN in adults

title: Orbital cellulitis
presentation: Painful red swollen eye with proptosis, in a patient who is systemically unwell.
Painful and restricted eye movements (ophthalmoplegia), often with reduced vision.
Frequently complicates sinusitis, especially in children.
redFlags: Reduced visual acuity, proptosis, painful ophthalmoplegia or a relative afferent pupillary defect — sight- and life-threatening.
Signs of intracranial spread (cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, abscess).

diagnostics.test: CT orbits and sinuses with contrast
diagnostics.rationale: Distinguishes orbital (post-septal) from preseptal cellulitis and detects abscess/sinus source.

diagnostics.test: Visual acuity, pupils and colour vision
diagnostics.rationale: Monitor optic nerve function; deterioration prompts urgent surgery.

management.detail: Admit and start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering streptococci, staphylococci and anaerobes without delay.
Involve ophthalmology and ENT; serial visual assessments.
Drain orbital/subperiosteal abscess or sinus disease if there is an abscess, visual compromise or failure to improve.

references.label: RCOphth / ENT UK guidance on orbital cellulitis

title: Central retinal artery occlusion
presentation: Sudden, painless, profound loss of vision in one eye.
A relative afferent pupillary defect; pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula.
Often older patients with vascular risk factors; consider giant cell arteritis.
redFlags: This is a stroke of the eye — assess as a time-critical event.
Jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, headache (giant cell arteritis) — needs urgent steroids.

diagnostics.rationale: Shows retinal pallor and a cherry-red spot.
Screen for giant cell arteritis, which requires immediate high-dose steroids to protect the other eye.

management.detail: Refer emergently; ocular massage and measures to lower intraocular pressure may be attempted within the first hours, though evidence of benefit is limited.
If GCA is suspected, start high-dose corticosteroids immediately to protect the fellow eye — do not wait for biopsy.
Investigate as for a TIA/stroke (carotids, heart, risk factors) and refer to the stroke/TIA pathway.

references.label: RCOphth guidance on retinal artery occlusion

title: Intussusception (paediatric)
presentation: Intermittent severe colicky abdominal pain with drawing-up of the legs, in an infant (typically 3 months–3 years).
Vomiting, lethargy between episodes, and 'redcurrant jelly' stool (late).
A sausage-shaped abdominal mass.
redFlags: Bilious vomiting, peritonitis, shock — signs of bowel ischaemia/perforation.
Lethargy out of proportion (can mimic sepsis/encephalopathy).

management.detail: IV fluids, nasogastric decompression, analgesia; involve paediatric surgery.
Air (pneumatic) or contrast enema reduction in the stable child without peritonitis or perforation.
Operative reduction/resection if enema fails, or if there is perforation, peritonitis or a pathological lead point.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Kawasaki disease
presentation: Fever ≥5 days in a young child plus: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, mucosal changes (red cracked lips, strawberry tongue), polymorphous rash, extremity changes (oedema/desquamation), and cervical lymphadenopathy.
Marked irritability.
Incomplete forms occur, especially in infants.
redFlags: Coronary artery aneurysms — the major complication.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; raised CRP/ESR, thrombocytosis (2nd week) support it.
Assess coronary arteries at diagnosis and on follow-up.

management.detail: Give IVIG, ideally within 10 days of fever onset, to reduce the risk of coronary aneurysms.
Aspirin (anti-inflammatory then antiplatelet dose) per protocol — one of the few paediatric indications for aspirin.
Cardiology follow-up with echocardiography; consider additional therapy (e.g. steroids) for IVIG-resistant or high-risk cases.

references.label: AHA scientific statement on Kawasaki disease
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Hypertensive emergency
presentation: Severely raised blood pressure (often >180/120 mmHg) WITH acute target-organ damage.
Encephalopathy (headache, confusion, seizures), chest pain, breathlessness, focal neurology or visual change.
