Distinguish from hypertensive urgency (high BP without acute organ damage).
redFlags: Encephalopathy, stroke, acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary oedema, aortic dissection or AKI.

diagnostics.rationale: ECG, troponin, renal function, urinalysis, fundoscopy, and imaging guided by symptoms (CT head, CT aorta).
Confirm with an appropriate cuff in both arms.

management.detail: Use titratable IV agents (e.g. labetalol, GTN, nicardipine/sodium nitroprusside) in a monitored setting; lower MAP by ~20–25% in the first hour (not to normal) to avoid hypoperfusion.
Aortic dissection needs rapid HR/BP control (beta-blocker first); stroke and pregnancy have specific targets — avoid abrupt drops in ischaemic stroke.
Identify precipitants; switch to oral agents and arrange follow-up once stable.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block
presentation: Bradycardia with syncope, presyncope, fatigue, breathlessness or chest pain.
ECG shows AV dissociation — P waves and QRS independent, with a slow escape rhythm.
May follow MI, drugs, fibrosis or electrolyte disturbance.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability: hypotension, reduced consciousness, ischaemia or heart failure.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms AV dissociation and the escape rate.

management.detail: Atropine (often limited benefit in infranodal block), then transcutaneous pacing and/or chronotropic infusions (adrenaline/isoprenaline) as a bridge.
Stop offending drugs, correct electrolytes, treat ischaemia.
Urgent temporary pacing if unstable; refer for permanent pacemaker in persistent/symptomatic high-grade block.

title: Cardiac tamponade
presentation: Breathlessness, tachycardia and hypotension with raised JVP and muffled heart sounds (Beck triad).
Pulsus paradoxus.
Causes: pericarditis, malignancy, uraemia, trauma, aortic dissection.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms effusion with diastolic chamber collapse and respiratory variation in flows.
Low voltages/electrical alternans; enlarged globular heart.

management.detail: Urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis (or surgical drainage) is the definitive treatment for unstable tamponade.
Cautious IV fluids may briefly support filling; avoid measures that reduce preload.
Manage the underlying aetiology; surgery for traumatic/aortic causes.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Acute myocarditis
presentation: Chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations, often after a viral illness.
May mimic acute coronary syndrome; can present with heart failure or arrhythmia.
Raised troponin with non-obstructed coronaries.

diagnostics.rationale: Detect dysfunction, arrhythmia and raised biomarkers.
Supports the diagnosis; exclude an ischaemic cause.

management.detail: Treat heart failure and arrhythmia; haemodynamic/ICU support (including mechanical support) for fulminant cases.
Restrict strenuous activity during recovery; avoid NSAIDs.
Address identifiable causes; immunosuppression only for specific aetiologies under specialist care.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Spontaneous pneumothorax
presentation: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness, classically in a tall thin young person (primary) or with underlying lung disease (secondary).
Reduced breath sounds and hyper-resonance on the affected side.
Often sudden onset at rest.
redFlags: Features of tension (severe distress, hypotension, tracheal deviation) — decompress immediately.
Secondary pneumothorax in COPD — poorly tolerated.

diagnostics.rationale: Clarifies complex, loculated or uncertain cases.

management.detail: Give oxygen; decide management by size, symptoms and primary vs secondary type per guideline.
Needle aspiration for many primary cases; intercostal chest drain for large/secondary/failed aspiration or breathless patients.
Smoking cessation; refer for pleurodesis/surgery after recurrence or persistent air leak.

title: Pleural effusion
presentation: Progressive breathlessness with reduced breath sounds and stony dullness to percussion.
Reduced chest expansion on the affected side.
May have features of the underlying cause (heart failure, infection, malignancy).
redFlags: Empyema/complicated parapneumonic effusion (sepsis, pus) — needs drainage.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirm, size and guide safe aspiration.
Distinguishes transudate from exudate; send for biochemistry, microbiology, cytology and pH.

management.detail: Transudates (e.g. heart failure) — treat the underlying condition; diuresis often suffices.
Therapeutic aspiration for symptoms; chest drain for empyema/complicated parapneumonic effusion (pH <7.2 or pus) with antibiotics.
Pursue malignancy/TB workup; consider thoracoscopy for undiagnosed exudates.

title: Acute mesenteric ischaemia
presentation: Sudden severe abdominal pain that is OUT OF PROPORTION to examination findings.
Risk factors: atrial fibrillation, atherosclerosis, hypercoagulability, low-flow states.
Later: peritonism, bloody diarrhoea and shock as bowel infarcts.
redFlags: Rising lactate with severe pain — impending bowel infarction.

diagnostics.test: CT angiography of the mesenteric vessels
diagnostics.rationale: First-line to identify arterial/venous occlusion and bowel ischaemia.
Raised lactate and metabolic acidosis indicate ischaemia; normal values do not exclude it early.

management.detail: Aggressive fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, analgesia; systemic anticoagulation (heparin) for embolic/thrombotic disease.
Urgent revascularisation (embolectomy, endovascular or bypass) and surgical resection of non-viable bowel.
ICU support; second-look laparotomy as needed; treat AF and other sources.

references.label: WSES guidelines on acute mesenteric ischaemia

title: Acute diverticulitis
presentation: Left lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever and altered bowel habit, typically in older adults.
Localised tenderness; possible palpable mass.
Nausea; urinary symptoms if adjacent inflammation.
redFlags: Generalised peritonitis (perforation), abscess, fistula or obstruction.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms diverticulitis and grades complications (abscess, perforation).

management.detail: Many mild cases are managed with analgesia and observation; antibiotics selectively (e.g. systemic upset, comorbidity, immunosuppression).
IV antibiotics and admission; radiological drainage of abscesses; surgery for perforation/peritonitis or failure to improve.
Colonic evaluation after recovery to exclude malignancy; dietary advice.

title: Nephrotic syndrome
presentation: Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and peripheral/periorbital oedema.
Frothy urine, weight gain, ascites.
Common in children (minimal change disease); diverse causes in adults.
redFlags: Acute kidney injury or severe hypovolaemia.

diagnostics.test: Urine protein quantification and serum albumin
Renal function, lipids and cause-specific tests
diagnostics.rationale: Assess severity and identify secondary causes; renal biopsy in adults / atypical children.

management.detail: Salt and fluid restriction, loop diuretics for oedema; ACE inhibitor/ARB to reduce proteinuria (mainly in adults).
Corticosteroids for steroid-sensitive minimal change disease (most children); immunosuppression guided by biopsy in others.
Address thrombosis risk, infection prophylaxis/vaccination, and manage hyperlipidaemia.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Fournier gangrene
presentation: Rapidly progressive necrotising infection of the perineal, genital or perianal region.
Severe pain (often out of proportion), swelling, erythema, crepitus and foul odour.
Systemic toxicity; diabetes and immunocompromise are risk factors.
redFlags: Septic shock and rapid spread — surgical emergency.

diagnostics.rationale: Do not delay surgery for imaging in a toxic patient; CT may delineate extent if stable.
Assess sepsis severity and guide antibiotics.

management.detail: Sepsis six, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (cover Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobes; consider clindamycin for toxin suppression).
Urgent and aggressive debridement of all necrotic tissue is the definitive treatment; repeat as needed.
ICU support, diversion if needed, later reconstruction; control diabetes and comorbidity.

references.label: WSES guidelines on necrotising soft-tissue infections

title: Priapism
presentation: Persistent painful erection lasting >4 hours, unrelated to sexual stimulation.
Ischaemic (low-flow) priapism is painful and rigid — a compartment-syndrome-like emergency.
Causes: sickle cell disease, drugs (including intracavernosal/erectile agents), malignancy.
redFlags: Ischaemic priapism >4 hours — risk of permanent erectile dysfunction.

diagnostics.rationale: Distinguishes ischaemic (hypoxic, acidotic) from non-ischaemic priapism.
Identifies sickle cell disease as a precipitant.

management.detail: Aspirate cavernosal blood and inject a diluted alpha-agonist (e.g. phenylephrine) with monitoring; treat sickle cell crisis concurrently.
Surgical shunt if aspiration/injection fails.
Often managed conservatively or with selective embolisation; refer to urology.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
presentation: Sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache, maximal within seconds ('worst headache of life').
Neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, reduced consciousness.
May follow exertion; often from a ruptured berry aneurysm.

diagnostics.rationale: Highly sensitive within 6 hours; shows blood in the subarachnoid space.

diagnostics.test: Lumbar puncture (if CT negative and clinical suspicion remains)
diagnostics.rationale: Xanthochromia after ~12 hours supports the diagnosis.

management.detail: ABC, analgesia, control BP, bed rest; urgent neurosurgical/neuro-interventional referral.
Nimodipine to reduce delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm; manage hydrocephalus and seizures.
Early endovascular coiling or surgical clipping to prevent re-bleeding.

references.label: AHA/ASA guidelines for aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Transient ischaemic attack (TIA)
presentation: Transient focal neurological deficit (e.g. unilateral weakness, speech disturbance, amaurosis fugax) that fully resolves, usually within an hour.
No acute infarction on imaging by definition.
A warning of high short-term stroke risk.
redFlags: Crescendo TIAs or AF — high stroke risk.
Carotid territory symptoms with a tight stenosis.

diagnostics.test: Urgent specialist assessment and brain imaging
diagnostics.rationale: Confirm the diagnosis and exclude mimics/haemorrhage.
Identify carotid stenosis and atrial fibrillation as treatable causes.

management.detail: Give aspirin at once (unless contraindicated) and arrange urgent TIA-clinic review; short-term dual antiplatelet therapy in selected high-risk patients.
Anticoagulate for AF; refer for carotid endarterectomy for significant symptomatic stenosis.
Statin, blood-pressure control, diabetes management, smoking cessation; driving advice.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Myasthenia gravis (and myasthenic crisis)
presentation: Fatigable muscle weakness worsening with activity and improving with rest.
Ptosis, diplopia, bulbar symptoms (dysphagia, dysarthria) and limb weakness.
Crisis: respiratory muscle weakness with ventilatory failure.
redFlags: Myasthenic crisis: breathlessness, weak cough, falling vital capacity — needs ventilatory support.

diagnostics.rationale: Monitors respiratory function in crisis (not SpO2, which falls late).

management.detail: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (pyridostigmine) for symptom control.
Corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression; consider thymectomy in selected patients.
Monitor respiration closely; IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange and ventilatory support for crisis; treat precipitants and avoid offending drugs.

references.label: International consensus guidance for management of myasthenia gravis

title: Multiple sclerosis
presentation: Episodes of CNS dysfunction separated in time and space: optic neuritis, sensory disturbance, weakness, ataxia, bladder symptoms.
Relapsing-remitting course most commonly; fatigue is prominent.
Symptoms may worsen with heat (Uhthoff phenomenon).

diagnostics.test: MRI brain and spinal cord with contrast
diagnostics.rationale: Demonstrates lesions disseminated in time and space (McDonald criteria).
Supports the diagnosis and helps exclude mimics.

management.detail: High-dose corticosteroids shorten relapse duration; plasma exchange for severe steroid-refractory relapses.
Start a disease-modifying therapy in relapsing disease to reduce relapse rate and disability progression (specialist-led).
Manage spasticity, bladder dysfunction, fatigue, pain and mood; multidisciplinary rehabilitation.

references.label: ECTRIMS/EAN guideline on the treatment of multiple sclerosis

title: Mammalian bite wound (dog/cat/human)
presentation: A puncture, laceration or crush wound from an animal or human bite.
Cat bites cause deep puncture wounds with high infection risk (Pasteurella); human bites risk Eikenella and viral transmission.
Signs of infection (redness, swelling, discharge) may develop over 24–72 hours.
redFlags: Spreading cellulitis, abscess, tenosynovitis or joint/bone involvement.
Rabies risk (assess exposure and need for post-exposure prophylaxis).
Clenched-fist 'fight-bite' injuries over the knuckles (joint penetration).

diagnostics.rationale: Assess depth, structures involved (tendon, joint, nerve) and contamination.
Detect fractures, retained teeth or joint involvement.

management.detail: Copious irrigation and debridement; generally leave high-risk bite wounds open or delay primary closure (especially cat/human bites and hands).
Co-amoxiclav is first-line prophylaxis/treatment; assess tetanus status and rabies post-exposure prophylaxis based on the animal and region; consider hepatitis B/HIV risk for human bites.
Review for infection; refer hand/joint involvement to surgery.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Iron poisoning
presentation: Stages: early GI toxicity (vomiting, diarrhoea, GI bleeding), an apparent latent period, then shock and metabolic acidosis, hepatic failure and late strictures.
Common in young children ingesting iron tablets/supplements.
Severity relates to elemental iron dose (mg/kg).
redFlags: Shock, coma, severe metabolic acidosis or persistent vomiting.
High serum iron level or radio-opaque tablets on X-ray.

diagnostics.rationale: Guides severity and need for chelation.
Radio-opaque tablets confirm ingestion; assess acidosis and organ injury.

management.detail: Aggressive IV fluids; whole-bowel irrigation for significant ingestions or visible tablets (activated charcoal does NOT bind iron).
IV desferrioxamine for severe toxicity (shock, acidosis, high iron level, significant symptoms).
Manage acidosis, coagulopathy and hepatic failure; monitor for late GI strictures.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children

title: Digoxin toxicity
presentation: Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, confusion and visual disturbance (yellow-green halos).
Bradyarrhythmias and almost any tachy/brady-arrhythmia (classically with AV block).
Acute overdose vs chronic toxicity (often older patients with renal impairment).
redFlags: Hyperkalaemia in acute toxicity (marker of severity).

diagnostics.test: Serum digoxin level, potassium and renal function
diagnostics.rationale: Confirm toxicity; potassium guides prognosis/treatment in acute overdose.
Detect characteristic arrhythmias and conduction block.

management.detail: Give digoxin immune Fab for life-threatening arrhythmia, significant hyperkalaemia, or haemodynamic instability.
Correct hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia; atropine and temporary pacing for bradycardia; treat ventricular arrhythmia (avoid calcium in hyperkalaemia from digoxin).
Activated charcoal if early after acute ingestion with a protected airway.

title: Beta-blocker / calcium-channel-blocker overdose
presentation: Bradycardia and hypotension after overdose of a beta-blocker or calcium-channel blocker.
Beta-blockers: bronchospasm, hypoglycaemia, seizures (especially lipophilic agents). CCBs: hyperglycaemia, preserved consciousness despite shock.
Conduction block and cardiogenic shock.

diagnostics.rationale: Detect bradycardia, conduction block and QRS/QT changes.
Hyperglycaemia suggests CCB toxicity; guides high-dose insulin therapy.

management.detail: IV fluids, atropine, calcium (for CCB), and glucagon (for beta-blockers); decontamination/whole-bowel irrigation for sustained-release ingestions.
High-dose insulin with glucose is a key inotropic therapy for significant CCB (and beta-blocker) toxicity; monitor glucose and potassium.
Vasopressors, IV lipid emulsion for lipophilic agents, transvenous pacing and mechanical circulatory support for refractory shock.

references.label: TOXBASE / national poisons guidance — beta-blockers and calcium-channel blockers

title: High-altitude illness (AMS, HACE, HAPE)
presentation: Acute mountain sickness: headache, nausea, fatigue and poor sleep after rapid ascent above ~2500 m.
High-altitude cerebral oedema (HACE): ataxia, confusion, reduced consciousness.
High-altitude pulmonary oedema (HAPE): breathlessness at rest, cough, reduced exercise tolerance, frothy sputum.
redFlags: Failure to improve or worsening despite rest.

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnosis based on altitude and symptoms
diagnostics.rationale: History of recent ascent with typical features is sufficient.

management.detail: Immediate descent is the definitive treatment for HACE and HAPE; stop further ascent for AMS.
Oxygen/portable hyperbaric chamber; acetazolamide for AMS prevention/treatment, dexamethasone for HACE, nifedipine for HAPE.
Gradual ascent, acclimatisation, and prophylaxis (acetazolamide) for susceptible individuals.

references.label: Wilderness Medical Society guidelines for acute altitude illness

title: Electrical injury
presentation: Burns at entry and exit points after contact with an electrical source; deep tissue damage may exceed surface findings.
Cardiac arrhythmia, especially after high-voltage or lightning injury.
Possible loss of consciousness, falls and associated trauma.
redFlags: Compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis from deep muscle injury.

diagnostics.rationale: Identify rhabdomyolysis and risk of pigment nephropathy.

management.detail: Isolate the power source before contact; ALS for arrest (prolonged resuscitation may be warranted in lightning).
Generous IV fluids if significant tissue injury/rhabdomyolysis to maintain urine output.
Treat burns, watch for compartment syndrome, assess for occult deep injury and associated trauma; tetanus prophylaxis.

references.label: Burns and trauma guidance on electrical injuries

title: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIADH)
presentation: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and inappropriately high urine sodium.
Often asymptomatic; nausea, confusion or seizures if severe/rapid.
Causes: CNS disease, lung pathology, malignancy, drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine).

diagnostics.test: Paired serum/urine osmolality and urine sodium
diagnostics.rationale: Inappropriately concentrated urine with high urine sodium in a euvolaemic, hyponatraemic patient supports SIADH after excluding other causes.
Exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency, which mimic SIADH.

management.detail: Hypertonic (3%) saline for seizures/coma, with strict limits on correction rate.
First-line for chronic SIADH; treat the underlying cause and stop offending drugs.
Consider vasopressin-receptor antagonists (vaptans) or other agents under specialist guidance if restriction fails.

title: Diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency/resistance)
presentation: Polyuria with dilute urine and polydipsia; nocturia.
Central (AVP deficiency, e.g. post-pituitary surgery/trauma) or nephrogenic (AVP resistance, e.g. lithium, hypercalcaemia).
Risk of hypernatraemia if access to water is limited.
redFlags: Hypernatraemia and dehydration, especially if unable to drink.

diagnostics.test: Paired serum/urine osmolality (+/- water deprivation test)
diagnostics.rationale: Demonstrates inability to concentrate urine; copeptin/desmopressin response distinguishes central from nephrogenic.

diagnostics.test: Calcium, potassium, glucose and drug review
diagnostics.rationale: Identify reversible causes of nephrogenic DI and exclude osmotic diuresis.

management.detail: Allow free access to fluids; in acute/inpatient settings replace water deficit and monitor sodium closely.
Desmopressin replacement, titrated to symptoms and sodium.
Remove the cause (e.g. lithium), correct calcium/potassium; low-salt diet and thiazide +/- amiloride to reduce urine output.

references.label: Society for Endocrinology guidance on diabetes insipidus
Kenya National Clinical Guidelines for Management of Diabetes Mellitus, Ministry of Health
WHO Package of Essential NCD Interventions (WHO PEN) — Diabetes

title: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome)
presentation: Hypertension that is resistant to treatment, often with hypokalaemia.
May be normokalaemic; muscle weakness, cramps and polyuria when potassium is low.
An under-recognised, treatable cause of secondary hypertension.

diagnostics.rationale: Screening test (raised aldosterone with suppressed renin); withdraw interfering drugs where possible.

diagnostics.test: Confirmatory testing and adrenal imaging +/- vein sampling
diagnostics.rationale: Confirm autonomous secretion and distinguish unilateral adenoma from bilateral hyperplasia.

management.detail: Spironolactone (or eplerenone) controls blood pressure and corrects hypokalaemia, especially in bilateral disease.
Laparoscopic adrenalectomy can cure or improve hypertension from a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma.
Track blood pressure, potassium and renal function; manage cardiovascular risk.

references.label: Endocrine Society guideline on primary aldosteronism
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health
WHO Package of Essential NCD Interventions (WHO PEN) — Cardiovascular disease

title: Cushing syndrome
presentation: Weight gain with central obesity, moon face, dorsocervical fat pad and proximal myopathy.
Purple striae, easy bruising, hypertension, glucose intolerance and mood change.
Commonest cause is exogenous corticosteroids; endogenous causes include pituitary (Cushing disease), adrenal and ectopic ACTH.
redFlags: Severe hypokalaemia and very high cortisol (ectopic ACTH/malignancy).

diagnostics.rationale: Overnight dexamethasone suppression test, late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urinary free cortisol.
Distinguishes ACTH-dependent from independent causes and localises the source.

management.detail: Taper exogenous steroids where possible; surgery (transsphenoidal for pituitary, adrenalectomy for adrenal) for endogenous disease.
Steroidogenesis inhibitors to lower cortisol while awaiting/if unsuitable for surgery (specialist-led).
Treat hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis, thromboprophylaxis and infection risk.

references.label: Endocrine Society guideline on Cushing syndrome

title: Acromegaly
presentation: Insidious enlargement of the hands, feet and facial features (coarsening, prognathism); ring/shoe size increase.
Headache, visual field defects, sweating, arthralgia and obstructive sleep apnoea.
Usually from a growth-hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma.
redFlags: Visual field loss from chiasmal compression.

diagnostics.test: Serum IGF-1 and oral glucose tolerance test with GH
diagnostics.rationale: Raised IGF-1 and failure of GH to suppress confirm the diagnosis.
Localises the adenoma and assesses chiasmal compression.

management.detail: Transsphenoidal resection is first-line for most adenomas.
Somatostatin analogues (e.g. octreotide/lanreotide), GH-receptor antagonist or dopamine agonists when surgery is incomplete or unsuitable.
Monitor for residual disease, hypopituitarism, cardiovascular risk, sleep apnoea and colonoscopy surveillance.

title: COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2 infection)
presentation: Fever, cough, fatigue, sore throat, anosmia/ageusia, myalgia; ranges from asymptomatic to severe pneumonia.
Breathlessness typically from day 5–7 in those who deteriorate.
Higher risk of severe disease in older adults and those with comorbidities.
redFlags: Hypoxia (SpO2 <94% on air), severe breathlessness, confusion.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms infection; PCR is more sensitive.
Identifies hypoxia and need for oxygen/admission.

management.detail: Antipyretics, fluids and self-isolation for mild disease; safety-net advice on red flags.

management.step: Oxygen and steroids for severe disease
management.detail: Target oxygen saturation; dexamethasone for patients needing oxygen; thromboprophylaxis on admission.
Consider antivirals (e.g. nirmatrelvir-ritonavir) early in high-risk outpatients per local eligibility; vaccinate to prevent.

references.label: WHO Clinical management of COVID-19 living guideline
Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) Technical Guidelines, 3rd edition (MOH)

title: Seasonal influenza
presentation: Abrupt onset of fever, myalgia, headache, dry cough and malaise.
Sore throat and rhinitis; prostration more marked than the common cold.
Self-limiting in most healthy adults over about a week.
redFlags: Exacerbation of chronic disease; dehydration in the elderly.

diagnostics.rationale: Often sufficient; PCR/antigen testing for severe, hospitalised or high-risk cases.

management.detail: Rest, fluids, antipyretics; most cases need no antivirals.
Neuraminidase inhibitor (oseltamivir) within 48 hours for severe disease or high-risk groups.
Annual influenza vaccination for at-risk groups; respiratory hygiene.

references.label: Kenya National Immunization Programme (KEPI/NVIP) Schedule, Ministry of Health

title: Hepatitis A
presentation: Acute onset of fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea and right-upper-quadrant discomfort, followed by jaundice and dark urine.
Faeco-oral transmission; outbreaks linked to contaminated food/water.
Usually self-limiting; does not cause chronic infection.
redFlags: Features of acute liver failure (encephalopathy, coagulopathy) — rare but serious.

diagnostics.rationale: Assess hepatitis severity and detect liver failure.

management.detail: Rest, hydration, antiemetics; avoid hepatotoxins and alcohol; most recover fully.
Watch for encephalopathy/coagulopathy; refer if signs of acute liver failure.
Hand hygiene, safe water/food; hepatitis A vaccine and post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts.

references.label: Kenya National Immunization Programme (KEPI/NVIP) Schedule, Ministry of Health

title: Scarlet fever
presentation: Fever and sore throat followed by a fine, sandpaper-like erythematous rash sparing the perioral area.
Strawberry tongue, flushed cheeks, and rash accentuated in skin folds (Pastia lines).
Caused by toxin-producing group A streptococcus; mainly affects children.

diagnostics.test: Throat swab / rapid antigen test for group A strep

diagnostics.rationale: Characteristic rash and pharyngitis usually suffice to start treatment.

management.detail: Penicillin V (or amoxicillin; macrolide if penicillin-allergic) for 10 days to shorten illness and prevent complications.
Antipyretics, fluids; exclude from school until 24 hours of antibiotics.
Notifiable in many settings; watch for complications.

references.label: National guidance on group A streptococcal infection
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children

title: Toxic shock syndrome
presentation: Sudden high fever, diffuse macular erythroderma, hypotension and multi-organ involvement.
Associated with staphylococcal (tampon/wound) or streptococcal (soft-tissue) toxins.
Later desquamation, especially of palms and soles.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; take blood and site cultures but do not delay treatment.

diagnostics.test: Bloods for organ function and lactate

management.detail: Aggressive fluids and vasopressors; ICU support; sepsis six.
Remove tampon/packing, debride infected tissue; combination antibiotics including a protein-synthesis inhibitor (clindamycin) to suppress toxin.
Consider IV immunoglobulin in severe streptococcal TSS; supportive multi-organ care.

references.label: IDSA guidelines on skin and soft-tissue infections

title: Urticaria and angioedema
presentation: Transient itchy weals (hives) that come and go within 24 hours, with or without deeper swelling (angioedema).
Acute (<6 weeks) often post-infective or allergic; chronic when recurring >6 weeks.
Angioedema affects lips, eyelids, tongue and sometimes the airway.
redFlags: Airway involvement (tongue/throat swelling, stridor) or anaphylaxis — emergency.
Angioedema without weals on ACE inhibitors or with C1-inhibitor deficiency.

diagnostics.rationale: History and examination are usually sufficient; identify and avoid triggers.
Consider FBC, inflammatory markers and specific allergy testing where indicated.

management.detail: Manage anaphylaxis/airway angioedema with adrenaline and resuscitation; stop ACE inhibitors in ACE-induced angioedema.
Regular non-sedating H1 antihistamines, up-titrated as needed, are first-line for urticaria.
Add short corticosteroid courses for severe flares; refer chronic refractory urticaria for omalizumab/specialist care.

title: Dermatophytosis (tinea / ringworm)
presentation: Itchy, scaly, annular plaques with central clearing and an active scaly edge (tinea corporis).
Site variants: tinea pedis (athlete's foot), cruris (groin), capitis (scalp, with hair loss), unguium (nails).
Spread by contact with people, animals or soil.
redFlags: Tinea capitis with kerion (boggy inflamed mass) needing oral therapy.

diagnostics.test: Skin scraping for microscopy and culture
diagnostics.rationale: Confirms dermatophyte, especially before oral therapy or in nail/scalp disease.
Typical morphology often suffices for skin infection.

management.detail: Topical azole or terbinafine for localised skin infection.
Oral terbinafine or itraconazole/griseofulvin for scalp, nail or extensive disease; scalp infection always needs oral treatment.
Treat fomites, keep skin dry, treat infected contacts/animals.

references.label: WHO/national dermatology guidance on superficial fungal infections
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Allergic rhinitis
presentation: Sneezing, nasal itch, watery rhinorrhoea and nasal congestion, often with itchy watery eyes.
Seasonal (pollen) or perennial (dust mite, animals); allergic 'shiners' and a nasal crease in children.
Frequently coexists with asthma.
redFlags: Unilateral symptoms, bleeding or facial pain (suggest other pathology).

diagnostics.rationale: History of typical symptoms and triggers is usually sufficient.
Identifies triggers when diagnosis is unclear or immunotherapy is considered.

management.detail: Reduce exposure to identified triggers.
Intranasal corticosteroids (most effective for persistent symptoms) and non-sedating oral/intranasal antihistamines; saline rinses.
Consider leukotriene antagonists or allergen immunotherapy for refractory disease; treat coexisting asthma.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
presentation: Brief (seconds) episodes of rotatory vertigo triggered by head-position changes (rolling over, looking up).
No persistent hearing loss or tinnitus.
Most commonly affects the posterior semicircular canal.
redFlags: Central features: persistent vertigo, focal neurology, vertical/direction-changing nystagmus.
New severe headache or other posterior-circulation stroke signs.

diagnostics.rationale: Provokes characteristic torsional/up-beating nystagmus, confirming posterior-canal BPPV.
Excludes central causes of positional vertigo.

management.detail: Epley manoeuvre is highly effective first-line treatment for posterior-canal BPPV.
Explain the benign nature; repeat manoeuvres if symptoms persist.
Vestibular sedatives are generally unhelpful and may delay recovery; avoid prolonged use.

references.label: AAO-HNS clinical practice guideline on BPPV
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Ménière disease
presentation: Recurrent spontaneous episodes of vertigo lasting minutes to hours.
Fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and a sensation of aural fullness.
Usually unilateral initially.
redFlags: Neurological signs suggesting a central cause.

diagnostics.rationale: Documents fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss.

diagnostics.test: MRI of the internal auditory meatus
diagnostics.rationale: Excludes a vestibular schwannoma or central pathology.

management.detail: Vestibular sedatives/antiemetics for severe acute vertigo, used short-term.
Low-salt diet, reduce caffeine/alcohol; betahistine and/or diuretics to reduce attack frequency.
Refer to ENT for intratympanic therapy or surgery; provide vestibular rehabilitation and hearing support.

title: Tension-type headache
presentation: Bilateral, pressing/tightening (band-like) headache of mild-to-moderate intensity.
Not aggravated by routine activity; no nausea (or only mild), and not both photophobia and phonophobia.
Often associated with stress, poor posture or fatigue.
redFlags: Thunderclap onset, progressive headache, focal neurology, fever or features of raised intracranial pressure.
New headache in older adults (consider giant cell arteritis).

diagnostics.rationale: Based on typical features and a normal examination; no imaging needed without red flags.
Distinguishes from migraine and identifies medication-overuse headache.

management.detail: Simple analgesia (paracetamol or NSAID); limit use to avoid medication-overuse headache.
Manage stress, sleep, posture and hydration; physiotherapy where relevant.
Consider amitriptyline for frequent chronic tension-type headache.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Cluster headache
presentation: Attacks of severe strictly unilateral orbital/temporal pain lasting 15–180 minutes.
Ipsilateral autonomic features: lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, ptosis/miosis.
Restlessness/agitation during attacks; clustering over weeks with remissions.
redFlags: First or atypical presentation — exclude secondary causes with imaging.
Horner syndrome that persists between attacks.

diagnostics.rationale: Characteristic attacks with autonomic features; MRI brain to exclude structural causes at first presentation.
Identify autonomic signs and exclude persistent deficits.

management.detail: High-flow 100% oxygen and subcutaneous/intranasal sumatriptan abort attacks; simple analgesia is ineffective.
Short corticosteroid course or greater occipital nerve block to bridge until prophylaxis works.
Verapamil is first-line preventive; refer to neurology for refractory cases.

references.label: NICE headaches guideline; international cluster headache guidance

title: Polymyalgia rheumatica
presentation: New bilateral shoulder and/or pelvic girdle pain and morning stiffness (>45 minutes) in a patient over 50.
Difficulty rising from a chair or raising arms; systemic symptoms (fatigue, low-grade fever).
Marked, rapid response to low-dose corticosteroids.
redFlags: Symptoms of giant cell arteritis (headache, jaw claudication, visual loss) — urgent high-dose steroids.
Features of inflammatory arthritis or malignancy.

diagnostics.rationale: Usually raised inflammatory markers support the diagnosis.
Check for RA, myositis (CK), thyroid disease and malignancy where atypical.

management.detail: Low-dose oral prednisolone with a dramatic response; taper slowly over months guided by symptoms and markers.
Educate the patient to report cranial symptoms urgently.
Calcium/vitamin D and bisphosphonate to prevent steroid-induced osteoporosis.

title: Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis)
presentation: New temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication in a patient over 50.
Visual symptoms (amaurosis fugax, diplopia) — a medical emergency.
Often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica and raised inflammatory markers.
redFlags: Any visual symptoms — risk of irreversible blindness; start steroids immediately.

diagnostics.rationale: Markedly raised in most cases; do not delay steroids awaiting results.

diagnostics.test: Temporal artery biopsy or vascular ultrasound
diagnostics.rationale: Confirms the diagnosis; biopsy can remain positive for ~2 weeks after starting steroids.

management.detail: Start high-dose prednisolone at once (IV methylprednisolone if visual loss) — do NOT wait for biopsy.
Arrange biopsy/ultrasound promptly; taper steroids slowly over 1–2 years guided by symptoms/markers.
Low-dose aspirin in selected patients, bone and gastric protection; consider tocilizumab as a steroid-sparing agent.

references.label: BSR guideline on giant cell arteritis

title: Axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis)
presentation: Chronic inflammatory back pain in a young adult: insidious onset, morning stiffness >30 minutes, improvement with exercise not rest, night pain.
Reduced spinal mobility and chest expansion over time.
Associated enthesitis, peripheral arthritis, uveitis, psoriasis or IBD.
redFlags: Acute anterior uveitis (painful red eye) needing urgent ophthalmology.
Spinal fracture in a fused, rigid spine after minor trauma.

diagnostics.rationale: Detects early sacroiliitis before radiographic changes.
Support the diagnosis in the right clinical context.

management.detail: Regular exercise and physiotherapy are the cornerstone to maintain mobility and posture.
First-line pharmacotherapy for pain and stiffness.
TNF or IL-17 inhibitors for active disease refractory to NSAIDs (specialist-led); treat extra-articular manifestations.

title: Primary hyperparathyroidism
presentation: Often asymptomatic, found on finding hypercalcaemia on routine bloods.
Symptomatic: 'stones, bones, abdominal groans and psychic moans' — renal stones, bone pain, constipation, low mood.
Usually due to a parathyroid adenoma.
redFlags: Severe hypercalcaemia / hypercalcaemic crisis (confusion, dehydration, arrhythmia).

diagnostics.test: Calcium, PTH, phosphate and vitamin D
diagnostics.rationale: Raised calcium with an inappropriately normal/high PTH confirms the diagnosis.
Assess end-organ effects and localise an adenoma for surgery; exclude FHH.

management.detail: IV fluids and, if severe, bisphosphonate/calcitonin.
Surgery is curative and indicated for symptomatic disease or end-organ damage.
Monitor mild asymptomatic disease; ensure hydration, adequate vitamin D; cinacalcet if surgery unsuitable.

references.label: International workshop guidelines on asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism

title: Hypercalcaemia
presentation: Polyuria, polydipsia, constipation, nausea, fatigue and confusion.
Severity-dependent; commonest causes are primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy.
Short QT interval on ECG.
redFlags: Severe hypercalcaemia (corrected calcium high) with confusion, dehydration or arrhythmia — emergency.

diagnostics.test: Renal function, phosphate, vitamin D, ECG
diagnostics.rationale: Assess severity, cause and cardiac effect.

management.detail: Aggressive IV isotonic saline is the cornerstone of acute treatment.
IV bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronic acid) for malignancy; calcitonin for rapid short-term reduction; treat the underlying cause.
Track calcium, renal function and fluid balance; avoid thiazides and calcium/vitamin D supplements.

references.label: Society for Endocrinology guidance on acute hypercalcaemia

title: Hypokalaemia
presentation: Often asymptomatic; muscle weakness, cramps, fatigue and constipation as potassium falls.
Causes: diuretics, GI losses (vomiting/diarrhoea), hyperaldosteronism, refeeding.
Severe: arrhythmia and paralysis.
redFlags: ECG changes (U waves, flattened T waves) and arrhythmia — life-threatening.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms hypokalaemia, detects cardiac effects; magnesium must be corrected for potassium to respond.

management.detail: Oral replacement for mild cases; cautious IV potassium with cardiac monitoring for severe/symptomatic hypokalaemia.
Replace magnesium concurrently — hypokalaemia is refractory until this is corrected.
Adjust diuretics, treat GI losses or hyperaldosteronism; recheck levels.

title: Biliary colic / symptomatic gallstones
presentation: Episodic severe right-upper-quadrant/epigastric pain, often after fatty meals, lasting up to a few hours.
Pain may radiate to the right scapula; associated nausea.
Between episodes the patient is well; no fever (distinguishes from cholecystitis).
redFlags: Fever and persistent RUQ pain (acute cholecystitis).
Jaundice with pain and fever (ascending cholangitis).
Epigastric pain radiating to the back (gallstone pancreatitis).

diagnostics.rationale: First-line to detect gallstones and assess the gallbladder wall and bile ducts.

management.detail: Analgesia for acute pain; advise a low-fat diet.
Refer for laparoscopic cholecystectomy for recurrent symptomatic stones.
Escalate promptly if features of cholecystitis, cholangitis or pancreatitis develop.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
presentation: Re-experiencing a traumatic event (flashbacks, nightmares, intrusive memories).
Avoidance of reminders, hyperarousal (hypervigilance, startle, sleep disturbance) and negative mood/cognitions.
Symptoms persisting beyond a month after trauma.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; screening tools support case finding.

management.detail: Trauma-focused CBT or EMDR is first-line treatment.
An SSRI (or SNRI) where psychological therapy is declined, ineffective, or for comorbid depression.
Address sleep, substance use and social support; manage suicide risk.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders (mhGAP adaptation), Ministry of Health

title: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)
presentation: Recurrent intrusive obsessions (thoughts, images, urges) causing anxiety.
Compulsions (repetitive behaviours/mental acts) performed to reduce distress.
Time-consuming (>1 hour/day) and impairing; insight is usually retained.
redFlags: Severe functional impairment or suicide risk.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; assess severity and impact (e.g. Y-BOCS).
Screen for depression and suicide risk.

management.detail: CBT with exposure and response prevention is first-line.
An SSRI (often at higher doses and longer trials than for depression); clomipramine as an alternative.
Combine therapy and medication for moderate-severe disease; refer refractory cases for specialist augmentation.

references.label: NICE OCD and body dysmorphic disorder guideline
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders (mhGAP adaptation), Ministry of Health

title: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura)
presentation: Palpable purpura over the buttocks and extensor surfaces of the legs in a child.
Arthralgia/arthritis, colicky abdominal pain, and renal involvement (haematuria/proteinuria).
Often follows an upper respiratory infection.

diagnostics.rationale: Characteristic purpura with normal platelets in a well child usually suffices.
Detect and monitor renal involvement (the main determinant of long-term outcome).

management.detail: Most cases are self-limiting; rest, hydration and simple analgesia.
Serial urinalysis and BP for weeks–months; refer significant nephritis to nephrology.
Corticosteroids for severe abdominal pain or significant renal/other organ involvement (specialist-guided).

references.label: EULAR/PRINTO/PRES criteria and management guidance for IgA vasculitis
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children

title: Abnormal uterine bleeding (heavy menstrual bleeding)
presentation: Excessive menstrual blood loss affecting quality of life, with or without irregular bleeding.
Possible symptoms of anaemia (fatigue, breathlessness).
Causes structured by PALM-COEIN (structural vs non-structural).
redFlags: Risk factors for endometrial cancer (obesity, unopposed oestrogen, age).

diagnostics.rationale: Assess anaemia and exclude pregnancy-related bleeding.
Identify structural causes and exclude malignancy in at-risk women.

management.step: Treat anaemia and exclude red flags
management.detail: Iron for anaemia; investigate/refer postmenopausal or high-risk bleeding.
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first-line; tranexamic acid/NSAIDs for acute heavy bleeding; hormonal options as alternatives.
Endometrial ablation or surgery (myomectomy/hysterectomy) for refractory disease or structural causes.

references.label: NICE heavy menstrual bleeding guideline; FIGO PALM-COEIN
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia
presentation: Rapid onset of fatigue, pallor and breathlessness (anaemia), bleeding/bruising (thrombocytopenia) and infections (neutropenia).
Bone pain, gum infiltration; usually older adults.
Often blasts on the peripheral blood film.
redFlags: Severe bleeding / DIC (especially acute promyelocytic leukaemia).
Leukostasis (very high blast count) with breathlessness/confusion.

diagnostics.rationale: Cytopenias with circulating blasts suggest acute leukaemia.
Confirms diagnosis, subtype and risk for treatment planning.

management.detail: Refer immediately; treat neutropenic sepsis and DIC as emergencies.
Transfusion, infection prophylaxis/treatment, tumour-lysis prevention with hydration and allopurinol/rasburicase.
Intensive chemotherapy +/- stem cell transplant; all-trans retinoic acid for acute promyelocytic leukaemia (specialist-led).

references.label: Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
presentation: Fatigue, pallor, bleeding/bruising, recurrent infection and bone pain, most commonly in children.
Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly; sometimes a mediastinal mass (T-cell).
Circulating blasts on the film.

diagnostics.test: FBC, film and bone marrow with immunophenotyping

diagnostics.rationale: Assess CNS disease and risk stratification.

management.detail: Immediate haematology/oncology referral; manage sepsis and tumour lysis.
Prolonged risk-adapted chemotherapy with CNS-directed therapy; excellent cure rates in children.
Stem cell transplant or targeted agents in high-risk/relapsed disease (specialist-led).

references.label: Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Chronic myeloid leukaemia
presentation: Often incidental leucocytosis; fatigue, weight loss, sweats and abdominal fullness from splenomegaly.
Massive splenomegaly is characteristic.
Defined by the Philadelphia chromosome / BCR-ABL1 fusion.
redFlags: Very high white count with leukostasis.

diagnostics.rationale: Leucocytosis with the full spectrum of myeloid cells; basophilia.
Confirms the diagnosis and provides a marker for monitoring response.

management.detail: A BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase inhibitor (e.g. imatinib) is the cornerstone, giving excellent long-term control.
Serial BCR-ABL1 PCR to track molecular response and detect resistance.
Switch TKI or consider transplant for resistance/blast crisis (specialist-led).

references.label: Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
presentation: Often asymptomatic lymphocytosis found incidentally in older adults.
Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, fatigue and recurrent infections as it progresses.
Smear cells on the blood film.
redFlags: Richter transformation (rapid nodal growth, B symptoms).
Recurrent severe infection from immune dysfunction.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms a clonal B-cell lymphocytosis with the characteristic phenotype.
Clinical staging (Rai/Binet) and genetics guide management timing.

management.detail: Many early-stage asymptomatic patients are simply monitored ('watch and wait').
Targeted therapy (BTK/BCL-2 inhibitors) +/- anti-CD20 antibody for progressive/symptomatic disease (specialist-led).
Vaccination and prompt treatment of infections; manage autoimmune cytopenias.

references.label: Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Hodgkin lymphoma
presentation: Painless, often cervical, lymphadenopathy in a young adult (bimodal age distribution).
B symptoms: fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss; pruritus; alcohol-induced node pain.
Reed-Sternberg cells on biopsy.

diagnostics.rationale: Determines stage and guides treatment and response assessment.

management.detail: Refer for staging and combined-modality treatment.
Curable in most with combination chemotherapy, with radiotherapy in selected cases.
Monitor for late effects (second cancers, cardiac, fertility) given the young population and high cure rate.

references.label: Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
presentation: Painless lymphadenopathy, which may be widespread; extranodal disease is common.
B symptoms, fatigue; presentation varies from indolent to aggressive.
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the commonest aggressive type.
redFlags: Aggressive lymphoma with rapid growth, organ compromise or tumour lysis.

diagnostics.rationale: Histology and immunophenotyping define the subtype, which drives treatment.

management.detail: Indolent lymphomas may be observed; aggressive types treated with immunochemotherapy (e.g. R-CHOP) — specialist-led.
Tumour-lysis prevention, infection management, growth-factor support.
Restaging by PET-CT; manage relapse with further lines/transplant/CAR-T as appropriate.

references.label: Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Multiple myeloma
presentation: The CRAB features: hyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia and Bone lesions/pain.
Bone pain (especially back), pathological fractures, recurrent infections.
Older adults; monoclonal paraprotein on electrophoresis.
redFlags: Spinal cord compression from vertebral disease.
Hypercalcaemic crisis and acute kidney injury.

diagnostics.test: Serum/urine protein electrophoresis and free light chains
diagnostics.rationale: Detects and quantifies the monoclonal protein.

diagnostics.test: Bone marrow, calcium, renal function and skeletal imaging
diagnostics.rationale: Confirms plasma-cell infiltration and end-organ (CRAB) damage.

management.detail: Treat hypercalcaemia, AKI and cord compression urgently.
Combination therapy (proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulators, anti-CD38, steroids) +/- autologous transplant (specialist-led).
Bisphosphonates for bone disease, infection prophylaxis/vaccination, thromboprophylaxis with immunomodulators, analgesia.

references.label: Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Beta-thalassaemia
presentation: Thalassaemia major: severe transfusion-dependent anaemia from infancy, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly and skeletal changes.
Thalassaemia minor (trait): mild microcytic anaemia, often asymptomatic.
Common in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South and Southeast Asian populations.
redFlags: Iron overload from transfusions (cardiac, hepatic, endocrine).

diagnostics.rationale: Microcytic anaemia with raised HbA2/HbF confirms beta-thalassaemia.
Distinguish from iron deficiency and monitor transfusional iron overload.

management.detail: Regular transfusion to maintain haemoglobin and suppress ineffective erythropoiesis.
Chelation (e.g. desferrioxamine or oral chelators) to prevent and treat iron overload.
Folic acid, manage endocrine/cardiac complications, genetic counselling; consider transplant in selected children.

title: Haemophilia A and B
presentation: Excessive or spontaneous bleeding: haemarthroses, deep muscle haematomas, prolonged bleeding after trauma/surgery.
X-linked recessive — affects males; factor VIII (A) or IX (B) deficiency.
Severity correlates with factor level.

diagnostics.rationale: Prolonged APTT with reduced factor VIII or IX confirms the type and severity.
Detects antibodies that neutralise replacement factor.

management.detail: Replace the deficient factor for bleeds and around procedures; prophylaxis in severe disease.
Desmopressin for mild haemophilia A; tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding; avoid IM injections and antiplatelet/anticoagulant drugs.
Manage through a haemophilia centre; address inhibitors and joint health.

references.label: WFH guidelines for the management of haemophilia

title: Von Willebrand disease
presentation: Mucocutaneous bleeding: epistaxis, easy bruising, heavy menstrual bleeding, bleeding after dental work/surgery.
The commonest inherited bleeding disorder; usually autosomal dominant.
Family history of bleeding is common.

diagnostics.test: von Willebrand factor antigen and activity, factor VIII

diagnostics.rationale: Assess overall haemostasis; platelets are usually normal.

management.detail: Raises vWF/factor VIII in type 1 disease for minor bleeds/procedures (test responsiveness first).
For type 3, severe bleeding, or major surgery.
Tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding; hormonal control of heavy menstrual bleeding; avoid antiplatelet drugs.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
presentation: Fatigue, pallor and jaundice with dark urine from haemolysis.
Warm (IgG, commonest) or cold (IgM) types; may be idiopathic or secondary (CLL, lupus, infection, drugs).
Splenomegaly may be present.

diagnostics.rationale: Positive DAT confirms immune-mediated haemolysis and the antibody type.

diagnostics.test: Haemolysis markers (reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin) and film
diagnostics.rationale: Confirm active haemolysis; spherocytes/agglutination on film.

management.detail: Warm AIHA: corticosteroids first-line +/- rituximab; cold AIHA: keep warm, treat the underlying cause, rituximab; address secondary causes.
Transfuse for severe anaemia (with specialist guidance on cross-matching difficulties).
Folic acid; thromboprophylaxis in active haemolysis; second-line therapy/splenectomy for refractory warm AIHA.

references.label: BSH guideline on the management of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia

title: Alcohol-related hepatitis
presentation: Recent heavy alcohol use with rapid-onset jaundice, tender hepatomegaly and malaise.
Fever, anorexia; may have features of decompensated liver disease (ascites, encephalopathy).
Often a background of chronic liver disease.

diagnostics.rationale: Characteristic pattern; bilirubin and INR drive severity scores.
Exclude infection and biliary obstruction; assess the liver.

management.detail: Alcohol cessation with withdrawal management, nutrition (including thiamine), and treat infection/AKI.
Use Maddrey discriminant function/MELD to identify severe disease.
Consider corticosteroids for severe alcoholic hepatitis without contraindication; monitor response (Lille score).

references.label: EASL/AASLD guidance on alcohol-related liver disease

title: Autoimmune hepatitis
presentation: Fatigue, jaundice and abnormal liver enzymes, often in women.
May present acutely or as chronic hepatitis/cirrhosis; associated with other autoimmune diseases.
Raised IgG and autoantibodies.

diagnostics.rationale: Support the diagnosis when other causes are excluded.
Confirms interface hepatitis and assesses fibrosis.

management.detail: Corticosteroids to induce remission, with azathioprine as a steroid-sparing maintenance agent.
Track LFTs and IgG to guide therapy; bone protection on steroids.
Screen for varices and hepatocellular carcinoma; consider transplant for end-stage disease.

title: Primary biliary cholangitis
presentation: Fatigue and pruritus, often in middle-aged women.
Cholestatic liver enzymes (raised ALP); may be asymptomatic at diagnosis.
Associated with other autoimmune conditions; later jaundice and cirrhosis.
redFlags: Features of overlap with autoimmune hepatitis.

diagnostics.rationale: AMA positivity with cholestatic LFTs is highly suggestive.
Exclude biliary obstruction; biopsy if diagnosis unclear or overlap suspected.

management.detail: First-line therapy that improves liver biochemistry and outcomes; assess biochemical response.
Add obeticholic acid or fibrates for inadequate response (specialist-led).
Treat pruritus (e.g. colestyramine), fatigue and osteoporosis; surveillance for cirrhosis complications.

title: Hereditary haemochromatosis
presentation: Fatigue, arthralgia, and 'bronze' skin pigmentation from iron overload.
May present with diabetes, liver disease, cardiomyopathy or hypogonadism.
Usually due to HFE gene mutations; often detected on raised ferritin/transferrin saturation.

diagnostics.rationale: Raised values prompt evaluation for iron overload.
Confirms the diagnosis; assess hepatic iron/fibrosis (MRI, sometimes biopsy).

management.detail: Regular venesection to deplete iron stores is the mainstay, then maintenance phlebotomy.
Chelation where venesection is not tolerated/feasible.
Treat diabetes/cardiac/endocrine effects; surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis; family screening.

title: Wilson disease
presentation: Hepatic (hepatitis, cirrhosis, acute liver failure) and/or neuropsychiatric features (tremor, dystonia, dysarthria, mood/behaviour change) in a young person.
Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp examination.
Autosomal recessive copper accumulation (ATP7B mutations).
redFlags: Acute liver failure with Coombs-negative haemolysis (often needs transplant).

diagnostics.rationale: Low caeruloplasmin with high urinary copper supports the diagnosis.
Kayser-Fleischer rings, ATP7B testing and hepatic copper confirm.

management.detail: Lifelong chelation (penicillamine or trientine) to remove copper; introduce carefully (neurological worsening can occur).
Zinc to block intestinal copper absorption (maintenance); avoid copper-rich foods.
Liver transplant for acute liver failure/decompensation; screen relatives.

title: Achalasia
presentation: Progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids.
Regurgitation of undigested food, chest pain and weight loss.
Caused by failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation and absent peristalsis.
redFlags: Rapidly progressive symptoms in older adults (exclude pseudoachalasia/malignancy).

diagnostics.rationale: Gold standard — shows absent peristalsis and impaired LES relaxation.

management.detail: Pneumatic dilatation or laparoscopic Heller myotomy (or POEM) relieve obstruction durably.
Botulinum toxin injection or nitrates/calcium-channel blockers for poor surgical candidates.
Monitor symptoms and nutrition; surveillance for the small long-term cancer risk.

title: Chronic pancreatitis
presentation: Recurrent or persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back, often relieved by sitting forward.
Features of exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhoea, weight loss) and endocrine insufficiency (diabetes).
Most commonly related to alcohol; pancreatic calcification may be seen.
redFlags: New pancreatic mass / weight loss (exclude pancreatic cancer).
Complications: pseudocyst, biliary/duodenal obstruction, GI bleeding.

diagnostics.rationale: Shows ductal changes, calcification and complications.

management.detail: Alcohol and smoking cessation; analgesia (step-wise), addressing neuropathic component.
Pancreatic enzyme replacement and fat-soluble vitamins for exocrine insufficiency; manage diabetes.
Endoscopic/surgical therapy for obstructing ductal disease, pseudocysts or refractory pain.

title: Acute anterior uveitis (iritis)
presentation: Painful red eye with photophobia and blurred vision, usually unilateral.
Circumcorneal (ciliary) redness, a small or irregular pupil, and cells/flare in the anterior chamber.
May be idiopathic or associated with HLA-B27 conditions, sarcoidosis or infection.
redFlags: Marked visual loss, hypopyon, or raised intraocular pressure.
Features suggesting infective or posterior uveitis.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms anterior-chamber inflammation (cells and flare) and complications.

diagnostics.test: Targeted systemic workup for recurrent cases

management.detail: Refer for slit-lamp assessment and treatment.
Topical corticosteroids reduce inflammation; a cycloplegic (e.g. cyclopentolate) relieves pain and prevents synechiae.
Address systemic associations; monitor intraocular pressure on steroids.

references.label: Royal College of Ophthalmologists — uveitis guidance

title: Retinal detachment
presentation: Sudden onset of floaters and flashes (photopsia), followed by a 'curtain' or shadow across the visual field.
Painless progressive visual field loss; reduced acuity if the macula is involved.
Risk factors: myopia, prior cataract surgery, trauma, family history.
redFlags: Macula-threatening or macula-off detachment — sight-threatening, needs urgent surgery.
Sudden shower of floaters with flashes.

diagnostics.rationale: Visualises the detached retina and any tears.
Detects detachment when the fundus cannot be seen.

management.detail: Refer immediately; macula-on detachment is a surgical emergency to preserve central vision.
Positioning advice per ophthalmology while awaiting surgery.
Vitrectomy, scleral buckle or pneumatic retinopexy depending on type; laser/cryotherapy for tears without detachment.

references.label: Royal College of Ophthalmologists — retinal detachment guidance

title: Chemical eye injury (ocular burn)
presentation: Pain, redness, tearing and blurred vision after a chemical splash.
Alkali burns (e.g. cement, ammonia) penetrate deeply and are more dangerous than acids.
Corneal haze and conjunctival/limbal blanching indicate severity.

diagnostics.rationale: Guides duration of irrigation; continue until pH normalises (~7).

diagnostics.test: Visual acuity and slit-lamp after irrigation

management.detail: Irrigate the eye with water/saline for at least 15–30 minutes BEFORE anything else — do not delay for examination; remove particulate matter.

management.step: Check and re-irrigate to neutral pH
management.detail: Recheck pH and continue irrigation until normalised.
Refer urgently; treat with lubricants, topical steroids/antibiotics and IOP control per specialist.

references.label: Royal College of Ophthalmologists — chemical eye injury guidance

title: Age-related macular degeneration
presentation: Gradual central vision loss and distortion (straight lines appear wavy) in an older adult (dry AMD).
Sudden central visual loss/distortion suggests neovascular (wet) AMD.
Drusen and pigmentary changes at the macula.
redFlags: Sudden distortion/central scotoma — possible wet AMD needing urgent anti-VEGF.

diagnostics.rationale: Identifies drusen/macular changes; Amsler detects distortion.
Detects fluid/neovascular membrane and guides treatment.

management.detail: Suspected wet AMD needs rapid referral for intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy to preserve vision.
Smoking cessation, dietary advice and AREDS-type supplements for intermediate disease.
Visual aids and rehabilitation; monitor with Amsler grid for conversion to wet AMD.

references.label: Royal College of Ophthalmologists — AMD guidance

title: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
presentation: Progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting in an infant, typically 2–8 weeks old.
Hungry after vomiting; weight loss and dehydration.
A palpable 'olive' mass and visible gastric peristalsis.

diagnostics.rationale: Detect the characteristic hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis to correct before surgery.

management.detail: Pyloric stenosis is a MEDICAL emergency before a surgical one — rehydrate and correct alkalosis/electrolytes first.
Ramstedt pyloromyotomy once the infant is biochemically stable.
Reintroduce feeds and monitor; excellent prognosis.

references.label: Paediatric surgical guidance on pyloric stenosis
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children

title: Hepatocellular carcinoma
presentation: Often arises in chronic liver disease/cirrhosis (hepatitis B/C, alcohol, NAFLD).
Weight loss, RUQ pain, decompensation of previously stable cirrhosis, or detected on surveillance.
Raised alpha-fetoprotein in some cases.

diagnostics.test: Multiphase CT or MRI of the liver
diagnostics.rationale: Characteristic arterial enhancement with washout can be diagnostic in cirrhosis without biopsy.
Supports diagnosis and assesses hepatic reserve.

management.detail: 6-monthly ultrasound (+/- AFP) in at-risk cirrhosis enables curative treatment.
Resection, ablation or transplantation for early-stage disease with adequate liver function.
TACE for intermediate disease; systemic therapy (e.g. immunotherapy combinations) for advanced disease (MDT-led).

references.label: Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health

title: Aortic stenosis
presentation: Exertional dyspnoea, angina and syncope (the classic triad) as stenosis becomes severe.
An ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, with a slow-rising pulse.
Often degenerative (elderly) or from a bicuspid valve (younger).
redFlags: Syncope, heart failure or angina — symptomatic severe AS has a poor prognosis without intervention.
Severe stenosis with low gradient and reduced ejection fraction.

diagnostics.rationale: Grades severity (valve area, gradient) and assesses LV function.
Detects LV hypertrophy and guides timing of referral.

management.detail: Refer symptomatic or severe AS to cardiology; avoid vasodilators that can cause hypotension.
Surgical (SAVR) or transcatheter (TAVI) aortic valve replacement is the definitive treatment for severe symptomatic disease.
Serial echocardiography; manage cardiovascular risk factors.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Mitral regurgitation
presentation: Exertional dyspnoea, fatigue and palpitations; may be asymptomatic for years.
A pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.
Causes: degenerative (prolapse), functional, rheumatic, ischaemic, endocarditis.
redFlags: Acute severe MR (e.g. papillary muscle rupture) with pulmonary oedema/shock — surgical emergency.

diagnostics.rationale: Defines mechanism and severity and assesses LV size/function.

management.detail: Standard heart-failure therapy and rate/rhythm and anticoagulation for AF.
Refer severe primary MR (especially with symptoms or LV dysfunction) for valve repair/replacement; transcatheter options in selected patients.
Serial echocardiography to time intervention before irreversible LV damage.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Dilated cardiomyopathy
presentation: Heart failure symptoms: breathlessness, orthopnoea, oedema and fatigue.
Left ventricular dilatation and systolic dysfunction not explained by loading/coronary disease.
Causes: genetic, viral, alcohol, peripartum, toxins.
redFlags: Ventricular arrhythmia or syncope (sudden death risk).

diagnostics.rationale: Shows a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle.
Identify reversible causes; cardiac MRI for aetiology.

management.detail: ACE inhibitor/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor improve outcomes; diuretics for congestion.
Consider ICD/CRT for selected patients; treat arrhythmia and thromboembolism risk.
Abstinence in alcoholic/peripartum types; manage reversible causes; advanced therapies for refractory disease.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
presentation: Exertional breathlessness, chest pain, palpitations or syncope; may be asymptomatic.
An ejection murmur that increases with Valsalva (dynamic LV outflow obstruction).
Commonest cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes; often autosomal dominant.
redFlags: Exertional syncope or family history of sudden death.

diagnostics.rationale: Demonstrates asymmetric LV hypertrophy and outflow obstruction.
Detect arrhythmia and assess sudden-death risk; cardiac MRI and genetics as indicated.

management.detail: Beta-blockers or rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers; avoid dehydration and vasodilators that worsen obstruction.
ICD for high-risk patients; activity advice; family screening.
Septal reduction (myectomy or alcohol ablation) for severe symptomatic obstruction; cardiac myosin inhibitors in selected patients.

title: Atrial flutter
presentation: Palpitations, breathlessness, chest discomfort or fatigue; may be asymptomatic.
Regular tachycardia, classically around 150 bpm (2:1 block) with sawtooth flutter waves.
Shares thromboembolic risk with atrial fibrillation.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability — needs urgent synchronised cardioversion.

diagnostics.rationale: Sawtooth flutter waves, especially in the inferior leads.
Assess structural disease and stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc).

management.detail: Rate control (beta-blocker/diltiazem) or cardioversion; flutter often responds well to DC cardioversion.
Stroke prevention per CHA2DS2-VASc, as for atrial fibrillation.
Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is highly effective and curative for typical flutter.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Ventricular tachycardia
presentation: Palpitations, presyncope, syncope, chest pain or cardiac arrest.
A broad-complex tachycardia; assume VT in any broad-complex tachycardia until proven otherwise, especially with structural heart disease.
May be monomorphic (scar-related) or polymorphic (ischaemia, long QT).
redFlags: Pulseless VT — cardiac arrest, defibrillate immediately.

diagnostics.test: Electrolytes, troponin and assessment for structural/ischaemic cause

management.detail: Pulseless VT → defibrillation and CPR. Unstable VT with a pulse → synchronised cardioversion.
Antiarrhythmic (e.g. amiodarone) and correct electrolytes/ischaemia; magnesium for torsades.
Treat underlying disease; ICD and/or ablation for recurrent VT (specialist-led).

references.label: Resuscitation Council ALS; ESC ventricular arrhythmia guidelines
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Bronchiectasis
presentation: Chronic productive cough with large volumes of purulent sputum.
Recurrent chest infections, breathlessness and sometimes haemoptysis.
Causes: post-infective, cystic fibrosis, immune deficiency, ABPA, idiopathic.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnostic — shows dilated, thick-walled bronchi (signet-ring sign).

management.detail: Daily chest physiotherapy and mucoactive measures are the cornerstone.
Prolonged antibiotic courses targeted to sputum organisms; consider long-term macrolide for frequent exacerbations.
Address underlying cause, vaccinate, pulmonary rehabilitation; manage haemoptysis.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea
presentation: Loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas and daytime sleepiness.
Morning headaches, poor concentration, and refractory hypertension.
Risk factors: obesity, large neck circumference, retrognathia.

diagnostics.rationale: Quantifies apnoea-hypopnoea index to confirm and grade severity.
Assesses daytime sleepiness and treatment need.

management.detail: Weight loss, reduce alcohol/sedatives, sleep position; treat nasal obstruction.
Continuous positive airway pressure is first-line for moderate-severe disease and improves symptoms and cardiovascular risk.
Mandibular advancement devices for milder disease; advise on driving safety per regulations.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
presentation: Progressive exertional breathlessness and a persistent dry cough in an older adult.
Fine bibasal end-inspiratory 'velcro' crackles and finger clubbing.
A diagnosis of exclusion among the interstitial lung diseases.
redFlags: Acute exacerbation with rapid respiratory deterioration (high mortality).

diagnostics.rationale: A usual interstitial pneumonia pattern (subpleural reticulation, honeycombing) supports the diagnosis.
Restrictive pattern with reduced transfer factor; track progression.

management.detail: Pirfenidone or nintedanib slow decline in lung function (specialist-initiated).
Oxygen for hypoxia, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination, and treat reflux/comorbidities.
Lung transplantation in suitable patients; early palliative input for symptom control.

title: Sarcoidosis
presentation: Often asymptomatic bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on imaging; cough and breathlessness.
Extrapulmonary features: erythema nodosum, uveitis, arthralgia, skin lesions, hypercalcaemia.
Löfgren syndrome (fever, hilar nodes, erythema nodosum, arthralgia) has a good prognosis.
redFlags: Severe hypercalcaemia or progressive pulmonary fibrosis.

diagnostics.rationale: Non-caseating granulomas confirm; exclude TB and lymphoma.

management.detail: Many cases (e.g. Löfgren) resolve spontaneously and need only monitoring.
For significant pulmonary, cardiac, neurological, ocular or hypercalcaemic disease; steroid-sparing agents for chronic disease.
Cardiology/ophthalmology/neurology input for those organ involvements; monitor for relapse.

title: Lower gastrointestinal bleeding
presentation: Fresh red or maroon blood per rectum, or clots.
Causes: diverticular disease, angiodysplasia, haemorrhoids, colitis, malignancy.
Brisk upper GI bleeding can also present as rectal bleeding.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability or ongoing heavy bleeding.
Features suggesting malignancy or ischaemic colitis.

diagnostics.rationale: FBC, coagulation, group & save/crossmatch; assess severity.
Localises and may treat the source; CT angiography for active brisk bleeding.

management.detail: IV access, fluids/transfusion as needed, correct coagulopathy; most lower GI bleeds settle spontaneously.
Endoscopic therapy, angiographic embolisation, or surgery for refractory bleeding; exclude upper GI source if unstable.
Colonic evaluation to exclude malignancy; review antithrombotic drugs.

title: Gastric cancer (diagnostic pathway)
presentation: Dyspepsia, early satiety, weight loss, anorexia and epigastric pain.
Iron-deficiency anaemia, dysphagia, or a palpable mass in advanced disease.
Risk factors: H. pylori, smoking, diet, atrophic gastritis.
redFlags: Alarm features: weight loss, dysphagia, GI bleeding, vomiting, anaemia, mass — urgent referral.

diagnostics.rationale: Direct visualisation and histology for diagnosis.

management.detail: Refer alarm symptoms on a suspected-cancer pathway for prompt endoscopy.
Surgery with perioperative chemotherapy for resectable disease; chemotherapy/targeted therapy for advanced disease (MDT-led).
Nutrition, manage obstruction/bleeding, palliative care as needed.

references.label: Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Pancreatic cancer (diagnostic pathway)
presentation: Painless obstructive jaundice (head of pancreas), or epigastric/back pain and weight loss (body/tail).
New-onset diabetes, steatorrhoea, and non-specific symptoms causing late presentation.
Often advanced at diagnosis.
redFlags: New diabetes with weight loss in an older adult.

diagnostics.rationale: Assesses the primary tumour, vascular involvement and metastases.
Supports diagnosis and provides tissue; ERCP for biliary obstruction.

management.detail: Refer suspected cases promptly; relieve biliary obstruction (stenting) as needed.
Surgical resection (Whipple) for the minority with resectable disease; chemotherapy for advanced disease (MDT-led).
Pancreatic enzyme replacement, pain control, nutrition and early palliative care.

references.label: Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Bladder cancer (diagnostic pathway)
presentation: Painless visible haematuria is the hallmark presentation.
Irritative urinary symptoms; risk factors include smoking and occupational exposures.
Usually urothelial carcinoma.
redFlags: Visible haematuria at any age (urgent referral).

diagnostics.rationale: Direct visualisation and biopsy of bladder lesions.
Assess the upper tracts and stage disease.

management.detail: Refer visible (and unexplained non-visible) haematuria on a suspected-cancer pathway.
Transurethral resection +/- intravesical BCG/chemotherapy with surveillance.
Radical cystectomy or radiotherapy +/- chemotherapy; systemic therapy for metastatic disease (MDT-led).

references.label: Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Renal cell carcinoma
presentation: Often incidental on imaging; the classic triad (flank pain, haematuria, mass) is uncommon and late.
Constitutional symptoms, anaemia or paraneoplastic features (hypercalcaemia, polycythaemia).
A left varicocele may indicate renal vein involvement.

diagnostics.rationale: Characterises the renal mass and stages disease.

management.detail: Partial or radical nephrectomy for localised disease; active surveillance for small tumours in selected patients.
Targeted therapy (TKIs) and immunotherapy for metastatic disease (MDT-led).
Surveillance imaging; monitor renal function.

references.label: Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: IgA nephropathy
presentation: Episodic visible haematuria, classically within days of an upper respiratory infection ('synpharyngitic').
Often persistent microscopic haematuria and proteinuria found incidentally.
The commonest primary glomerulonephritis worldwide.
