management.detail: Oestrogen (with progestogen if uterus present) until natural menopause age - bone/cardiovascular protection.
Discuss reduced fertility and oocyte donation options.
Bone density and autoimmune screening.

references.label: ESHRE guideline on the management of premature ovarian insufficiency

title: Asherman syndrome
presentation: Intrauterine adhesions causing light/absent periods after uterine instrumentation.
Subfertility or recurrent pregnancy loss.
Often follows dilatation and curettage, especially postpartum.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnostic gold standard; visualises and treats adhesions.

management.detail: Surgical division of adhesions.
Oestrogen therapy +/- intrauterine barrier post-operatively.
Minimise aggressive uterine instrumentation.

references.label: Guidance on the management of intrauterine adhesions

title: Primary dysmenorrhoea
presentation: Crampy lower abdominal pain with menstruation, no underlying pathology.
Onset soon after menarche; pain at or just before onset of bleeding.
May radiate to back/thighs with nausea.
redFlags: Onset later in life or progressively worsening (consider secondary causes: endometriosis, fibroids, PID).

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; exclude secondary causes if red flags.

management.detail: First-line analgesia, started at symptom onset.
Combined pill or LNG-IUS to reduce pain.
Heat, exercise; reassess if not responding.

title: Bartholin cyst and abscess
presentation: Unilateral labial swelling; painless cyst or painful abscess.
Abscess: hot, tender, fluctuant mass at the posterior vestibule.
Difficulty sitting/walking when large.
redFlags: Recurrent or solid mass in women over 40 (consider biopsy to exclude carcinoma).

management.detail: No treatment needed.
Incision and drainage with Word catheter or marsupialisation to reduce recurrence.
For surrounding cellulitis or systemic features; treat STI if identified.

references.label: Gynaecology guidance on Bartholin gland cyst and abscess

title: Pelvic organ prolapse
presentation: Sensation of a vaginal bulge or 'something coming down'.
Pelvic pressure, urinary, bowel or sexual dysfunction.
Worse on standing/straining; risk factors parity, ageing, obesity.

diagnostics.rationale: Quantifies the compartment and degree of prolapse.

management.detail: Pelvic floor muscle training, weight loss, treat constipation.
Vaginal pessary for support, especially if surgery unsuitable.
Reconstructive or obliterative surgery for symptomatic prolapse.

references.label: NICE guideline NG123: urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women

title: Dystonia (cervical/focal)
presentation: Sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing abnormal postures/twisting.
Cervical dystonia (torticollis) is the commonest focal form.
Sensory 'geste antagoniste' may transiently relieve it.
redFlags: Acute dystonia after dopamine-blocking drugs (treat as drug reaction).
Rapid progression or additional neurological signs (secondary cause).

management.detail: IV procyclidine/benzatropine and stop the offending drug.
First-line for cervical/focal dystonia.
Anticholinergics, physiotherapy; deep brain stimulation for refractory generalised dystonia.

references.label: Movement Disorder Society guidance on dystonia

title: Huntington disease
presentation: Progressive chorea, cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms.
Autosomal dominant; CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in HTT.
Positive family history; onset usually 30-50 years.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms diagnosis; pre-test genetic counselling essential.

management.detail: Neurology, psychiatry, genetics, therapy and palliative support.
Tetrabenazine/antipsychotics for chorea; treat depression/psychosis; manage swallowing.
For the patient and at-risk relatives.

title: Narcolepsy
presentation: Excessive daytime sleepiness with irresistible sleep attacks.
Cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone with emotion) in type 1.
Sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations.

diagnostics.test: Polysomnography and multiple sleep latency test
diagnostics.rationale: Shows reduced sleep latency and sleep-onset REM.

management.detail: Behavioural foundation; advise on driving safety.
Modafinil or methylphenidate for sleepiness.
Sodium oxybate or antidepressants (SNRI/SSRI).

references.label: AASM clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence

title: Enteropathic arthritis
presentation: Inflammatory arthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease.
Peripheral (often large joints, parallels bowel activity) or axial (independent).
May have enthesitis, dactylitis, uveitis.
redFlags: Active IBD flare with systemic upset.

management.detail: Peripheral arthritis often improves with bowel disease control.
Cautious NSAIDs (may flare IBD), intra-articular steroids; sulfasalazine for peripheral disease.
Anti-TNF for axial disease or refractory arthritis with active IBD.

references.label: Guidance on the management of enteropathic spondyloarthritis

title: Primary sclerosing cholangitis
presentation: Fatigue, pruritus and cholestatic LFTs, often in men with IBD.
Recurrent cholangitis; progressive bile duct strictures.
Strong association with ulcerative colitis.

diagnostics.rationale: Shows multifocal strictures and beading of bile ducts.
Screen for associated IBD and colorectal cancer.

management.detail: Treat pruritus, fat-soluble vitamins; no proven disease-modifying drug.
ERCP for dominant strictures; antibiotics for cholangitis.
Cholangiocarcinoma, colorectal and HCC surveillance; liver transplant for end-stage disease.

references.label: EASL clinical practice guidelines on sclerosing cholangitis

title: Hereditary haemochromatosis
presentation: Fatigue, arthralgia, skin pigmentation ('bronze diabetes').
Hepatomegaly, diabetes, hypogonadism, cardiomyopathy.
Iron overload, usually HFE-related (C282Y).

diagnostics.test: HFE genotyping; MRI for liver iron

management.detail: Regular phlebotomy to deplete iron, then maintenance.
For those unable to tolerate venesection.
Treat diabetes/cardiac disease; HCC surveillance if cirrhotic; screen relatives.

references.label: EASL clinical practice guidelines for HFE haemochromatosis

title: Polycythaemia vera
presentation: Raised haemoglobin/haematocrit with thrombotic risk.
Aquagenic pruritus, plethora, erythromelalgia, headache.
Splenomegaly; usually JAK2 V617F positive.
redFlags: Transformation to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia.

diagnostics.rationale: Low in PV; excludes secondary causes.

management.detail: Target haematocrit <0.45.
Low-dose aspirin to reduce thrombosis (unless contraindicated).
Hydroxycarbamide for high-risk disease; manage cardiovascular risk.

references.label: BSH guideline for the management of polycythaemia vera

title: Essential thrombocythaemia
presentation: Persistently raised platelet count, often incidental.
Vasomotor symptoms (headache, erythromelalgia), thrombosis or bleeding.
Driver mutations JAK2, CALR or MPL.

management.detail: Age, prior thrombosis and mutation guide therapy.
For vasomotor symptoms and thrombotic risk.
Hydroxycarbamide for high-risk disease; manage cardiovascular risk.

references.label: BSH guideline for the management of essential thrombocythaemia

title: Myelofibrosis
presentation: Fatigue, weight loss and night sweats with massive splenomegaly.
Anaemia and a leucoerythroblastic blood film with teardrop cells.
Primary or following PV/ET.

diagnostics.test: Blood film and bone marrow trephine

management.detail: Observation for low-risk disease.
JAK inhibitor (ruxolitinib) for splenomegaly/symptoms; transfusion support.
Allogeneic stem cell transplant for eligible high-risk patients.

references.label: BSH guideline for the management of myelofibrosis

title: Aplastic anaemia
presentation: Pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow.
Fatigue (anaemia), infections (neutropenia), bleeding (thrombocytopenia).
Often immune-mediated; may follow drugs, viruses or be inherited.

management.detail: Transfusions and prompt management of neutropenic sepsis.
Allogeneic transplant for younger patients; immunosuppression (ATG + ciclosporin) +/- eltrombopag otherwise.
Stop causative drugs.

references.label: BSH guidelines for the diagnosis and management of aplastic anaemia

title: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
presentation: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia.
Neurological signs, fever and renal impairment (classic pentad).
Caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency; a medical emergency.
redFlags: Any suspected TTP is an emergency (untreated mortality is high).

diagnostics.rationale: MAHA with thrombocytopenia and normal coagulation.
Severely reduced; do not delay treatment for the result.

management.detail: Life-saving; start immediately on clinical suspicion.
Corticosteroids and rituximab; caplacizumab where available.
Unless life-threatening bleeding (may worsen thrombosis).

references.label: BSH guideline on the diagnosis and management of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

title: Hereditary spherocytosis
presentation: Chronic haemolytic anaemia with jaundice and splenomegaly.
Spherocytes on blood film; usually autosomal dominant.
Gallstones and aplastic crises (parvovirus).

management.detail: Supplement to support erythropoiesis.
For crises.
For severe disease (with prior vaccination and prophylaxis); cholecystectomy for gallstones.

references.label: BSH guidelines for the diagnosis and management of hereditary spherocytosis

title: Antiphospholipid syndrome
presentation: Arterial/venous thrombosis and/or pregnancy morbidity with persistent antiphospholipid antibodies.
Recurrent miscarriage, late fetal loss.
May be primary or secondary to lupus.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirm on two occasions 12 weeks apart.

management.detail: Long-term warfarin (avoid DOACs in triple-positive/arterial disease).
Aspirin plus LMWH in pregnancy.
Anticoagulation, steroids, plasma exchange/IVIG.

management.detail: Treat plasma cell clone in AL (chemotherapy); treat underlying inflammation in AA; ATTR-specific drugs for ATTR.
Heart failure and renal management.
National amyloidosis centre.

diagnostics.rationale: Screen for optic glioma and complications.

Excise symptomatic/suspicious lesions; manage hypertension.
For the patient and family.

Everolimus for SEGA and renal angiomyolipoma.
Multidisciplinary monitoring of brain, kidneys, heart, lungs and skin.

Double oral steroid in illness; emergency IM hydrocortisone and steroid card.
IV hydrocortisone and fluids for adrenal crisis.

title: Acute psychosis (mhGAP primary-care pathway)
presentation: Recent onset (days to weeks) of disorganised speech or behaviour.
Delusions (fixed false beliefs) or hallucinations.
Marked agitation, aggression or social withdrawal.
Loss of insight; impaired self-care.
redFlags: Suicidal or homicidal ideation with plan or intent.
Severe agitation endangering self or others.
Catatonia, mutism, or refusal to eat / drink.

diagnostics.test: Brief structured mental state exam (mhGAP-IG MNS quick assessment)
diagnostics.rationale: Differentiate acute psychosis from delirium and substance-induced state.

diagnostics.test: Random blood glucose, urea + electrolytes, urinalysis
diagnostics.rationale: Rule out hypoglycaemia, uraemia, UTI-precipitated delirium.

management.step: Safety first — calm environment, remove harmful objects
management.detail: 1 person at a time; reassure; do NOT physically restrain except as last resort. If transport needed, accompany the patient.

management.step: Rapid tranquillisation only if agitation endangers patient or others
management.detail: First line: oral haloperidol 2–5 mg + lorazepam 1–2 mg (or diazepam 5–10 mg) IM if oral refused. Re-assess after 30–60 min.
Oral haloperidol 1.5–5 mg twice daily, OR risperidone 1–2 mg twice daily. Start LOW in older adults. Avoid in dementia (stroke risk; if essential, lowest dose, shortest duration).
Correct hypoglycaemia, electrolytes, infection. Treat substance withdrawal per CIWA-Ar / COWS protocol.
Explain that psychosis is a treatable illness; counter stigma; involve family in monitoring.
Review at 24–72 h, then weekly. Refer to mental-health specialist within 1 week. Continue antipsychotic 6–12 months minimum after first episode.

title: Self-harm / suicide risk (mhGAP SUI pathway)
presentation: Recent act of self-harm (cutting, overdose, hanging attempt).
Expressed suicidal ideation, plan or intent.
Withdrawal, hopelessness, giving away possessions.
Persistent severe depression, psychosis, alcohol/drug intoxication, recent major loss.
redFlags: Active suicidal plan with means and intent → emergency.
Recent serious self-harm act (overdose, hanging, drowning).
Severe agitation; refusal to discuss safety.
Acute toxicity (paracetamol > 7.5 g, organophosphate ingestion, TCA, anything haemodynamically unstable).

diagnostics.test: Direct clinical interview using mhGAP SUI assessment
diagnostics.rationale: Ask DIRECTLY about suicidal thoughts — asking does not increase risk.

diagnostics.test: Medical assessment of any injury / overdose
diagnostics.rationale: Treat the medical sequelae first (e.g. paracetamol → NAC per nomogram; organophosphate → atropine + PAM; benzodiazepine → supportive).

management.detail: Do NOT leave the patient alone. Remove access to means (medications, sharps, firearms, ropes, pesticides). Move to a safe space.
Resuscitate per ABCDE. Apply antidote protocols (see antidote registry: paracetamol-nac, organophosphate-atropine, tca-sodium-bicarbonate, opioid-naloxone, etc.).
Listen non-judgementally; do not minimise. Identify supports. Validate distress.
Initiate / optimise antidepressant for moderate–severe depression (SSRI first line); antipsychotic for command hallucinations; benzodiazepine SHORT term for severe agitation.

Co-create a written safety plan: warning signs, internal coping, social contacts, professionals, crisis hotline. Schedule follow-up within 24–72 h after discharge. Engage family or trusted person to monitor.
Refer to mental-health specialist for ALL who self-harmed or have suicide plan. Where unavailable, weekly primary-care review.

Pervasive sadness, anhedonia, somatic complaints, school avoidance.
Excessive worry, separation anxiety, social withdrawal.
Developmental difficulties: delay in language, social communication or learning.
redFlags: Suicidal ideation or self-harm — assess urgently.
Acute behavioural change with fever, headache or focal neurology — exclude organic cause.

diagnostics.rationale: Differentiate developmentally appropriate vs disordered behaviour.

diagnostics.rationale: Cross-setting symptom confirmation; required for ADHD per DSM/ICD criteria.

management.detail: Explain normal child development, behaviour-modification basics (praise positive, ignore minor negative, time-out for severe). First-line for most behavioural problems in low-resource settings.

Where available, parent training programmes; CBT for anxiety/depression in adolescents.

management.step: Engage families compassionately and review regularly
management.detail: Monthly review during titration; quarterly when stable.

title: Disorders due to substance use (mhGAP SUB pathway, excluding alcohol & opioids)
presentation: Recurrent substance use despite harm (work, relationships, health).
Tolerance or withdrawal symptoms.
Failed attempts to cut down or stop.
Substantial time spent obtaining or using the substance.

redFlags: Acute intoxication with reduced GCS / respiratory depression — resuscitate.
Stimulant chest pain → ACS workup; hypertensive emergency.
Severe benzodiazepine withdrawal — risk of seizures (treat as alcohol withdrawal: long-acting benzodiazepine taper).
Suicidal ideation, command hallucinations (stimulant or hallucinogen).
Pregnancy with substance use — refer urgently.

diagnostics.rationale: Standardised brief screening for non-alcohol substances.
Identify substances when patient denies use or in acute presentations.
Rule out cardiac toxicity and QT prolongation.

diagnostics.test: BBV screen (HIV, hep B, hep C)
diagnostics.rationale: Especially for any injecting drug use.

management.step: Brief intervention based on FRAMES / motivational interviewing
management.detail: Feedback on risk, emphasise personal Responsibility, give Advice to cut down/stop, offer a Menu of options, Empathy, support Self-efficacy. Effective even in single 10–15 min primary-care visit for at-risk use.
Supportive; treat agitation with low-dose benzodiazepine (avoid antipsychotic alone in stimulant toxicity). Refer if respiratory depression.

Benzodiazepine taper for sedative-hypnotic and benzodiazepine withdrawal (diazepam 20–40 mg/day initially, reducing by 10% every 1–2 weeks). Symptomatic for cannabis/stimulant withdrawal (no specific pharmacotherapy proven).
Stimulant use disorder: no consistently effective pharmacotherapy; intensive psychosocial intervention is mainstay. Cannabis use disorder: psychological intervention first line.
Refer to community-based recovery programmes; assess and treat comorbid mental health conditions; consider harm reduction (needle exchange, naloxone training for any injecting user).
Weekly to monthly with progress monitoring; treat as a chronic relapsing condition — relapse is part of recovery, not failure.

title: Acute mania (mhGAP-aligned)
presentation: Elevated, expansive or irritable mood for ≥1 week.
Decreased need for sleep, increased energy.
Pressured speech, flight of ideas, racing thoughts.
Grandiosity, distractibility, risk-taking behaviour (spending, sexual, driving).
Psychotic features may be mood-congruent (grandiose delusions, hallucinations).
redFlags: Severe agitation or aggression; harm to self/others.
Comorbid substance / stimulant use precipitating mania.

diagnostics.test: Brief mental state exam ± Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS)
diagnostics.rationale: Differentiate mania from schizophrenia / stimulant intoxication.

diagnostics.test: TSH, FBC, U&E, urine drug screen
ECG if antipsychotic / mood stabiliser planned

management.step: Reduce stimulation; provide safe quiet environment
management.detail: Limit visitors; remove valuables / car keys to protect from impulsive harm.
Continuation of antidepressant may sustain mania; specialist may continue if mood stabiliser cover is robust.

Lithium 600–1200 mg/day (target trough 0.6–1.0 mmol/L; titrate by level) OR sodium valproate 500–1000 mg/day in divided doses (NOT in women of childbearing potential without PPP). OR olanzapine 10–20 mg/day, risperidone 2–4 mg/day, or haloperidol 5–10 mg/day for rapid effect.
Lorazepam 1–2 mg PRN for severe agitation / insomnia; restrict to short courses.
All first-episode mania needs psychiatric assessment; consider inpatient admission for severe mania, psychotic features, or harm risk.
Daily mental state, weight, food/fluid intake. Lithium level on day 5 of stable dose; renal function and thyroid 6-monthly long term.

references.label: NICE CG185 — Bipolar disorder: assessment and management

title: Generalised anxiety disorder (mhGAP / GAD pathway)
presentation: Excessive worry on most days for ≥6 months across multiple domains.
Difficulty controlling the worry.
Restlessness, easily fatigued, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance.
GAD-7 score ≥10.
redFlags: Severe functional impairment (cannot work or care for self).
Symptoms suggesting alternative diagnosis (panic disorder, OCD, PTSD, depression, hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma).

diagnostics.rationale: Comorbid depression is common; treatment may need to address both.

management.detail: Explain GAD as a treatable condition; sleep hygiene, regular exercise, reduce caffeine/alcohol/cannabis.

management.step: Low-intensity psychological intervention (first line for mild)
management.detail: Self-help CBT materials, applied relaxation, or guided self-help where available.
12–16 sessions of cognitive-behavioural therapy is first-line evidence-based treatment.

management.step: Pharmacotherapy when psychological therapy unavailable / declined or in moderate–severe
management.detail: First line: SSRI (sertraline 50–200 mg, escitalopram 10–20 mg, paroxetine 20–50 mg). Second line: SNRI (venlafaxine, duloxetine). Avoid benzodiazepines except for short-term crisis (≤2–4 weeks).
Review at 1–2 weeks (warn about initial worsening), then every 2–4 weeks. Continue effective antidepressant ≥12 months after remission to reduce relapse.

references.label: WHO mhGAP Intervention Guide — Other Significant Mental Health Complaints (OTH)

title: Acute stress reaction and adjustment disorder (mhGAP-aligned)
presentation: Onset within days of a clearly identifiable major stressor (assault, accident, disaster, bereavement, displacement).
Anxiety, irritability, intrusive thoughts of the event, difficulty sleeping.
Acute stress reaction resolves within days–weeks; adjustment disorder up to 6 months (longer if chronic stressor).
redFlags: Symptoms persisting > 1 month with re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal → consider PTSD.
Inability to care for self / children.

diagnostics.test: Clinical interview focused on the precipitant and current symptoms.
diagnostics.rationale: Differentiate acute stress vs PTSD vs adjustment disorder vs depression.

management.detail: Listen — Look — Link. Provide a safe environment, validate distress, connect to family / social support, address basic needs (food, shelter, security).
Encourage normal activities, sleep, social contact. Avoid alcohol/sedatives. Explain that distress is a normal reaction and usually subsides within weeks.
Benzodiazepines may impair natural recovery and risk dependence; reserve for short-term crisis.
Problem-solving counselling (4–6 sessions) for adjustment disorder.
Refer if symptoms persist, suicidal ideation emerges, or PTSD develops.

references.label: WHO Psychological first aid: guide for field workers (2011)
WHO mhGAP — Other significant mental health complaints (OTH)

title: Dementia (mhGAP DEM pathway, primary-care management)
presentation: Progressive (≥6 months) decline in memory, language, executive function or visuospatial skills.
Functional decline: instrumental ADLs (finance, cooking, medication) then basic ADLs.
Behavioural and psychological symptoms (apathy, irritability, wandering, hallucinations) common as the disease progresses.
Insight often reduced; informant history is essential.
redFlags: Sudden onset / stepwise progression → vascular dementia or stroke.
Rapidly progressive cognitive decline → consider Creutzfeldt-Jakob, autoimmune encephalitis, normal pressure hydrocephalus, B12 deficiency.
Acute confusion in known dementia → delirium (treat reversible cause).
Suicide risk or severe behavioural disturbance.

diagnostics.test: TSH, B12, folate, U&E, calcium, glucose, syphilis serology where indicated

diagnostics.rationale: Detect vascular disease, tumours, hydrocephalus; not always available in LMIC.

management.step: Explain the diagnosis sensitively to patient and family
management.detail: Plan for the future: advance directives, lasting power of attorney, driving safety, financial planning.
B12 / folate / thyroid replacement, optimise vascular risk factors (BP, glycaemia, lipids, smoking).

management.step: Non-pharmacological first line for behavioural symptoms
management.detail: Structured routines, orientation cues, addressing pain/discomfort, music therapy, social stimulation.

Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) for mild–moderate Alzheimer's where available; memantine for moderate–severe. Antipsychotics ONLY for severe distress / risk; lowest dose, shortest duration — high stroke and death risk in dementia.
Psychoeducation, respite, peer-support groups; assess for carer depression.
Palliative approach in advanced dementia; avoid hospital admissions, focus on comfort.

references.label: WHO mhGAP Intervention Guide v2.0 — Dementia (DEM)

title: WHO HEARTS — stepwise blood-pressure-lowering protocol
presentation: Adult with confirmed hypertension (mean BP ≥140/90 mmHg on two visits, or ≥135/85 mmHg on home/ambulatory readings).
Asymptomatic in most; symptoms (headache, vision change, chest pain) occur with severe hypertension or end-organ damage.
redFlags: BP ≥180/120 mmHg with new symptoms (chest pain, neurological deficit, severe headache, breathlessness) → hypertensive emergency, refer urgently.
BP ≥180/120 mmHg without symptoms but with new end-organ damage on tests → hypertensive urgency.
Suspected secondary hypertension: young patient (<30) with severe HT, very high resistant BP, hypokalaemia (consider Conn's), abdominal bruit (renal artery stenosis), paroxysms (phaeochromocytoma).

diagnostics.test: Confirm BP with calibrated upper-arm device, 2 readings 1 min apart, on 2 separate visits.
diagnostics.rationale: Avoid white-coat hypertension and isolated readings.

diagnostics.test: Urine dipstick (protein, blood) and urine albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR).
Serum creatinine + eGFR, electrolytes, fasting lipids, fasting glucose / HbA1c.
diagnostics.rationale: Baseline organ function, comorbid risk, baseline before ACEi/ARB and diuretic.

diagnostics.test: Total CVD risk (WHO/ISH chart or HEARTS app) — see pen-cvd-risk rule.

management.step: Lifestyle for ALL (and continue alongside medication)
management.detail: Reduce salt to <5 g/day; DASH-style diet rich in fruit, vegetables, whole grain; weight loss to BMI 20–25; ≥150 min/week moderate activity; smoking cessation; alcohol ≤2 standard drinks/day men, ≤1 women.

management.step: Initiate pharmacotherapy in fixed-dose combination where available
management.detail: STEP 1: Either (a) ACE inhibitor / ARB at standard dose (enalapril 10 mg or losartan 50 mg) OR (b) dihydropyridine CCB (amlodipine 5 mg). Many guidelines now recommend STARTING with a low-dose combination (ACEi/ARB + CCB) for faster control.

management.step: STEP 2 at 4 weeks if BP not at target
management.detail: Combine ACEi/ARB + CCB (if not already).

management.step: STEP 3 at 4–8 weeks if still uncontrolled
management.detail: Add thiazide-like diuretic (hydrochlorothiazide 12.5–25 mg, or indapamide 1.5 mg).
Add spironolactone 25 mg (check potassium and eGFR first; avoid if K >5.0 or eGFR <30). Consider referral for secondary hypertension workup.
General adult: <140/90; <130/80 in diabetes, CKD, post-stroke if tolerated; aim for <130/80 if high CV risk.
Every 4 weeks during titration; every 3–6 months once at target. Annual review of CV risk, ACR, lipids, renal function.

title: WHO HEARTS — statin therapy for primary CVD prevention
presentation: Adult ≥40 years undergoing total cardiovascular-risk assessment (WHO/ISH or other validated tool).
Adult with diabetes mellitus ≥40 years.
Adult with established CKD (eGFR <60) or albuminuria.
redFlags: Active liver disease (ALT > 3×ULN, decompensated cirrhosis) — defer statin.
Statin-related severe muscle pain or rhabdomyolysis history.

diagnostics.test: Total CVD risk via HEARTS / WHO-ISH chart.
diagnostics.rationale: Decide eligibility — primary prevention if 10-year CVD risk ≥20% (some programmes ≥10% with diabetes / CKD).

diagnostics.test: Baseline ALT, creatinine, CK if symptoms.

diagnostics.rationale: Baseline cholesterol; non-fasting acceptable for risk estimation.

management.detail: Statin reduces 10-year CV event risk by ~25–30%; over 5 years, treating ~50–100 high-risk people prevents 1 major event.
Atorvastatin 10–20 mg daily OR simvastatin 20–40 mg daily (avoid simvastatin > 20 mg with SLCO1B1 risk allele or strong CYP3A4 inhibitor).

management.step: Counsel on muscle symptoms and persist
management.detail: Most muscle symptoms are not true intolerance — try a dose reduction or different statin before abandoning therapy.
Lipid response and ALT at 8–12 weeks; tolerability annually. CK only if symptoms (do not screen).

management.step: Combine with HEARTS lifestyle intervention and BP control
management.detail: Statin is one prong; reinforce smoking cessation, BP target, glycaemic control.

title: WHO HEARTS — aspirin for primary prevention (RESTRICTED indications)
presentation: Adult 40–70 with high CVD risk being considered for primary-prevention aspirin.
redFlags: Age > 70 years — bleeding risk outweighs benefit (do NOT routinely initiate).
Active or recent peptic ulcer, GI bleeding, intracranial bleeding.

diagnostics.test: Total CVD risk via WHO/ISH HEARTS chart.
Bleeding risk assessment (history of GI bleed, PUD, anticoagulant use, BP control).
diagnostics.rationale: Aspirin's net benefit hinges on bleeding risk being low.

management.detail: Recent evidence (ASPREE, ASCEND, ARRIVE) shows little net benefit in primary prevention. Most current guidance now advises AGAINST routine primary-prevention aspirin in older adults. Discuss carefully with patient if 10-year CV risk ≥10% AND bleeding risk low AND age 40–70.

Lowest effective dose 75–100 mg daily; co-prescribe PPI if any GI risk; eradicate H. pylori where indicated.
Especially as patient ages or develops bleeding-risk factors — stop if balance shifts.

title: WHO HEARTS — healthy-lifestyle counselling for NCD prevention
presentation: Any adult attending primary care, regardless of presenting complaint, with at least one modifiable CV risk factor (smoking, low physical activity, unhealthy diet, harmful alcohol use, overweight/obesity).

diagnostics.test: Brief lifestyle assessment (4 questions: tobacco, alcohol, diet, activity).
diagnostics.rationale: Identify modifiable risks at every encounter.

diagnostics.test: Anthropometry: weight, height, BMI, waist circumference.
Blood pressure at every visit ≥40 years.

management.detail: Brief advice (1–3 min) doubles quit rates. Offer nicotine-replacement therapy (NRT), bupropion or varenicline where available; refer to quitline.
≥5 servings fruit + vegetables/day; whole grains; reduce ultra-processed foods, salt to <5 g/day, free sugar to <10% energy; emphasise locally available healthy foods.
≥150 min/week moderate-intensity OR ≥75 min/week vigorous, plus muscle-strengthening on 2 days. Older adults add balance training.
Reduce to ≤2 standard drinks/day (men) or ≤1 (women); 2 alcohol-free days/week. AUDIT-C ≥4 men or ≥3 women — offer brief intervention.

Screen for depression (PHQ-9) and anxiety (GAD-7); address sleep apnoea risk (STOP-BANG).
Brief intervention at every visit; reinforce small wins; team-based care multiplies impact.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis (adult)
presentation: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, vomiting, abdominal pain.
Kussmaul breathing (deep sighing) with ketotic (acetone) breath.
Dehydration (dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, hypotension).
Altered mental state from drowsiness to coma in severe disease.
Common precipitants: infection, insulin omission, new-onset T1DM, MI, pancreatitis, drugs (SGLT2i — euDKA, steroids, antipsychotics).
redFlags: Severe acidosis pH < 7.0 or HCO3 < 5 mmol/L.
Hypokalaemia (K+ < 3.5 mmol/L) BEFORE insulin — must replace potassium first.
Suspected cerebral oedema (paediatric > adult, but possible — headache, focal signs, falling GCS in first 24h).
Pregnancy with DKA → maternal/fetal high-risk, urgent obstetric input.

diagnostics.test: Capillary blood glucose + capillary ketones (β-hydroxybutyrate ≥ 3.0 mmol/L diagnostic) or urine ketones (≥ 2+).
diagnostics.rationale: Bedside confirmation of ketosis with hyperglycaemia.

diagnostics.test: Venous blood gas — pH, bicarbonate, anion gap.
diagnostics.rationale: Confirm metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.30 or HCO3 < 15 with raised anion gap).
Guide IV fluid and potassium replacement; identify AKI.

diagnostics.test: FBC, CRP, urine dip, blood and urine culture; CXR; ECG; troponin where indicated.

diagnostics.rationale: Exclude pancreatitis as both precipitant and mimic.

management.step: ABCDE; high-flow O2 if hypoxic; large-bore IV access; cardiac monitoring
management.detail: Catheterise if reduced consciousness, oliguria, or hourly urine output needed.

0.9% NaCl 1 L over the first hour (give faster if shocked). Then 1 L over 2 h, 1 L over 2 h, 1 L over 4 h, 1 L over 4 h, 1 L over 6 h (adjust for elderly / cardiac/renal disease — slower). Switch to 0.45% NaCl if corrected sodium rises.

0.1 unit/kg/hour of soluble (regular) insulin. Continue patient's long-acting insulin at usual dose. Target: capillary ketones falling by ≥ 0.5 mmol/L/h AND bicarbonate rising by ≥ 3 mmol/L/h AND glucose falling by ≥ 3 mmol/L/h. If not on target, increase FRII by 1 unit/h.
Withhold IV K+ in 1st L (and ALL insulin) if K+ < 3.5 mmol/L until K+ replaced. K+ 3.5–5.5: add 40 mmol KCl per L. K+ > 5.5: no K+ in fluids and recheck hourly. Re-check K+ at 1 h then 2-hourly.
Run 10% dextrose 125 mL/h alongside saline to allow continued insulin (to clear ketones) without hypoglycaemia.
Antibiotics if infection suspected; antiplatelet/troponin pathway if MI; obstetric input if pregnant.

pH > 7.30, bicarbonate > 18, ketones < 0.6, patient eating/drinking. Switch to subcutaneous insulin (give short-acting 30 min BEFORE stopping infusion to avoid rebound DKA). Diabetes specialist nurse / endocrine review.
Hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, fluid overload (especially elderly), cerebral oedema (rare but devastating).

references.label: JBDS-IP The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults (2023)

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis (paediatric / adolescent)
presentation: Polyuria (often as new-onset bedwetting), polydipsia, weight loss.
Vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy, deep sighing (Kussmaul) breathing.
First presentation of type 1 diabetes in ~25 % of children.
May be precipitated by infection, insulin omission, insulin-pump failure.
redFlags: Severe DKA: pH < 7.1, drowsiness, severe dehydration ≥ 10%.
Cerebral oedema warning signs: headache, agitation/irritability, falling GCS, focal neurology, bradycardia with hypertension, abnormal posturing — RAPID action required.

diagnostics.test: Capillary glucose (> 11 mmol/L) + capillary ketones ≥ 3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones ≥ 2+.
Venous blood gas (pH and bicarbonate) for severity.
diagnostics.rationale: Mild DKA: pH 7.20–7.29 or HCO3 10–17. Moderate: pH 7.1–7.19 or HCO3 5–9. Severe: pH < 7.1 or HCO3 < 5.

diagnostics.test: Weight (essential — guides fluid + insulin dose) and clinical dehydration estimate.
diagnostics.rationale: Use 5% deficit for moderate, 7% for severe — DO NOT exceed 8% deficit assumption (cerebral oedema risk).

diagnostics.test: U&E, FBC, glucose, blood/urine culture, CXR if respiratory signs.

management.detail: 0.9% NaCl 10 mL/kg bolus over 15 min, repeat once if still shocked. Do NOT subtract from deficit. AVOID large bolus volumes — cerebral oedema risk.

management.step: Calculate fluids: maintenance + deficit over 48 h
management.detail: Use 0.9% NaCl. Maintenance: 100/50/20 mL/kg/day rule (or Holliday-Segar). Deficit: assume 5% in mild–moderate DKA, 7% in severe; replace evenly over 48 h. Total hourly rate = (maintenance + deficit − any bolus given) ÷ 48.

management.step: Insulin infusion 1–2 h AFTER fluids started
management.detail: 0.05–0.1 unit/kg/h soluble insulin. Do NOT bolus. Lower-end 0.05 in young children, post-cardiac-arrest, or already drowsy. Continue any long-acting insulin (glargine, degludec) at usual dose.
Add KCl 40 mmol/L to fluids once urinating, K+ < 5.5, and not anuric. Continuous ECG if K+ abnormal.

management.step: Add glucose when blood glucose < 14 mmol/L
management.detail: Switch to 0.9% NaCl + 5% dextrose ± 0.45% NaCl + 5% dextrose. Continue insulin to clear ketones.

management.step: Cerebral oedema — RECOGNISE EARLY, treat IMMEDIATELY
management.detail: If signs (headache, drowsiness, bradycardia + hypertension): 3% NaCl 5 mL/kg over 10–15 min OR mannitol 1 g/kg over 10 min. Reduce fluids by 1/3, head up 30°, intubate if needed. Urgent transfer to PICU; CT head AFTER treatment.
When ketones < 1.0, pH > 7.30, child eating: SC short-acting before stopping infusion (give 30 min overlap). Educate family on diabetes and sick-day rules.

references.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022 — DKA in children
Kenya National Clinical Guidelines for Management of Diabetes Mellitus, Ministry of Health
WHO Package of Essential NCD Interventions (WHO PEN) — Diabetes

title: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS)
presentation: Profound dehydration (often days of polyuria + reduced intake).
Altered consciousness, confusion, focal seizures.
Marked hyperglycaemia (usually > 30 mmol/L), serum osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg.
Minimal or absent ketosis (pH > 7.30, HCO3 > 15, ketones < 3 mmol/L) — distinguishes from DKA.
Older adults with T2DM; often precipitated by infection, MI, CVA, or steroid therapy.
redFlags: Acute kidney injury, MI, sepsis as precipitant.
Lower-limb venous thromboembolism (HHS is highly prothrombotic — VTE prophylaxis essential).

diagnostics.test: Calculate osmolality: 2×(Na+) + glucose + urea (all in mmol/L).
diagnostics.rationale: Guides severity; HHS osmolality usually > 320; aim to fall by < 5 mOsm/kg/h.

diagnostics.test: Capillary glucose + ketones; venous blood gas; U&E.
diagnostics.rationale: Distinguish HHS from DKA and monitor.

diagnostics.test: FBC, CRP, blood + urine culture, ECG, troponin, CXR.
CT head if persistent neurology after correction.

management.step: IV fluids — SLOWER and more cautious than DKA
management.detail: 0.9% NaCl, aim for 3–6 L positive balance over the first 12 h. Avoid rapid osmolality changes (target < 5 mOsm/kg/h fall, < 10 mmol/L Na+ fall per 24 h) — central pontine myelinolysis and cerebral oedema risk.
Withhold insulin until glucose stops falling with fluids alone, OR if ketones > 1 mmol/L (mixed picture). Then 0.05 unit/kg/h. Target glucose fall 4–6 mmol/L/h.
Often less depleted than DKA but still replace as needed (40 mmol/L if K+ 3.5–5.5).
LMWH at prophylactic dose unless contraindicated — HHS confers very high thrombotic risk.
Antibiotics for infection, reperfusion for MI, stroke pathway, manage cause of insulin discontinuation.
Often immobile elderly with neuropathy and dehydration — pressure ulcer prevention from admission.
Switch to SC insulin once eating; many HHS patients can subsequently be controlled on oral agents but insulin often continued. Diabetes education + structured follow-up.

references.label: JBDS-IP The management of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in adults (2022)
ADA Standards of Care — Hyperglycaemic crises
Kenya National Clinical Guidelines for Management of Diabetes Mellitus, Ministry of Health

title: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM)
presentation: Mostly asymptomatic — detected by routine screening.
Risk factors: BMI ≥ 30, previous GDM, previous large-for-gestational-age baby (≥ 4.5 kg), 1st-degree relative with diabetes, ethnic background (South Asian, African Caribbean, Middle Eastern), PCOS.
Polyhydramnios, fetal macrosomia or accelerated growth on antenatal scan.
redFlags: Pre-existing (overt) diabetes detected in early pregnancy (HbA1c ≥ 6.5% before 20 weeks) — manage as type 2 diabetes in pregnancy.
DKA in pregnancy — emergency, maternal + fetal mortality high.
Pre-eclampsia, sustained hypertension, fetal distress on monitoring.

diagnostics.test: Screening: 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) at 24–28 weeks for at-risk women (WHO / IADPSG criteria).
diagnostics.rationale: Diagnostic if any of: FPG ≥ 5.1, 1-h ≥ 10.0, 2-h ≥ 8.5 mmol/L.

diagnostics.test: Early OGTT or HbA1c at booking if high risk.
Self-monitoring of blood glucose 4 times daily after diagnosis (fasting + 1 h postprandial).
Fetal growth + amniotic fluid scan every 4 weeks from 28 weeks.

management.detail: Dietitian referral; low-glycaemic-index diet, regular physical activity (30 min walking daily), weight management within pregnancy recommendations.

management.step: Pharmacotherapy if targets not met in 1–2 weeks
management.detail: Metformin first line (start 500 mg with evening meal, titrate weekly to max 2 g/day) — well-tolerated and safe in pregnancy. Add or substitute insulin if metformin insufficient or contraindicated. Glibenclamide is a second-line option in some guidelines but less preferred.
Isophane (NPH) at bedtime for raised fasting; rapid-acting (aspart, lispro) with meals for postprandial. Detemir is also accepted in pregnancy.
Joint diabetes-antenatal clinic. Fortnightly visits from 28 weeks. Aspirin 75–150 mg/day from 12 weeks for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis.
Plan delivery by 40+6 weeks; offer induction or LSCS by 37–38+6 weeks if macrosomia or other risk. Continue glucose monitoring intrapartum; insulin sliding scale if glucose > 7 mmol/L.

Stop GDM-specific therapy after delivery. Encourage breastfeeding (reduces type 2 risk for mother and infant). Repeat fasting glucose or HbA1c at 6–13 weeks postpartum, then annually — 50% develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years.
Plan future pregnancies preconceptually; lifestyle modification reduces type 2 incidence.

references.label: WHO Diagnostic criteria and classification of hyperglycaemia first detected in pregnancy (2013)
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: WHO HEARTS-D — stepwise type 2 diabetes management protocol (adult)
presentation: Adult with confirmed type 2 diabetes (FPG ≥ 7.0, 2-h PG ≥ 11.1 on OGTT, HbA1c ≥ 6.5%, or random PG ≥ 11.1 with classic symptoms).
Initial assessment: symptoms, complications (eye, foot, renal, cardiovascular), comorbid cardiovascular risk factors.
redFlags: DKA / HHS at presentation → admit and treat as emergency.
HbA1c > 10% or fasting glucose > 16 → consider starting insulin immediately.
Severe hypoglycaemia (any episode requiring third-party assistance) — review regimen.
Symptomatic infection (especially foot, urinary, dental) — treat early.

diagnostics.test: Baseline + annual HbA1c, fasting lipids, U&E + eGFR, urine ACR, ALT.
diagnostics.rationale: Track glycaemic control, lipid status, kidney function, hepatic steatosis.

diagnostics.test: Annual foot examination (monofilament, pulses, deformities) + annual retinal screening.

diagnostics.rationale: Decide on statin and aspirin per HEARTS protocol.

management.detail: Most: < 7.0% (53 mmol/mol). Frail elderly or limited life expectancy: 7.5–8.5%. Recent diagnosis, motivated, no comorbidity: < 6.5% if achievable without hypoglycaemia.

Diet (low refined carbohydrate, weight loss 5–10%), 150 min/week activity. Start metformin 500 mg with meal, titrate to 1 g twice daily over 4 weeks. Reduce dose if eGFR 30–44; stop if eGFR < 30. Continue lifelong if tolerated.

management.step: STEP 2 — Add second agent at 3 months if HbA1c above target
management.detail: Choose based on comorbidity: SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) if heart failure or CKD; GLP-1 agonist (liraglutide, semaglutide) if obesity / atherosclerotic CVD; sulfonylurea (gliclazide) if cost-limited and no hypo concern; DPP-4 inhibitor (sitagliptin) if hypo concern and no CVD/CKD indication.

management.step: STEP 3 — Add third agent at 3–6 months if still above target
management.detail: Combine classes; avoid duplicating mechanism. Consider basal insulin (NPH bedtime or analogue) when oral options exhausted.
Add prandial insulin (basal-plus then basal-bolus); or switch to premixed BID. Continue metformin lifelong.
Statin (atorvastatin 20 mg) for primary prevention if ≥ 40 years. ACEi/ARB if hypertension, albuminuria, or CKD. Aspirin ONLY for secondary prevention.

Structured group education at diagnosis. Sick-day rules (continue medication, hydrate, check glucose more often, seek help if vomiting or ketones positive). Smoking cessation. Annual review of complications and goals.

references.label: WHO HEARTS-D: Diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes (HEARTS-D module, 2020)
ADA / EASD Consensus Report 2022 — Management of hyperglycaemia in type 2 diabetes
Kenya National Clinical Guidelines for Management of Diabetes Mellitus, Ministry of Health

title: IMCI — very severe febrile disease (child 2–59 months)
presentation: Child 2–59 months with fever (axillary ≥ 37.5°C or history of fever in past 3 days).
WITH any general danger sign: unable to drink/breastfeed, vomiting everything, recent or current convulsions, lethargic or unconscious.
OR stiff neck.
OR bulging fontanelle in infants.
redFlags: Shock (cold peripheries, weak pulse, capillary refill > 3 s).
Petechial / purpuric rash with fever — suspect meningococcal disease.
Severe pallor with fever (suspect severe malaria).

diagnostics.test: Malaria RDT and thick + thin blood smear if endemic area.
diagnostics.rationale: Severe malaria common cause; needs IV artesunate.

diagnostics.test: Haemoglobin (severe anaemia in severe malaria common).
Blood culture, FBC, CRP where available; lumbar puncture if signs of meningitis (and no contraindication).

management.step: Pre-referral treatment (any setting — start within minutes)
management.detail: Give a single dose of: (a) IM/IV ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg (or IM benzylpenicillin + IM gentamicin if ceftriaxone unavailable), AND (b) for suspected severe malaria: IM/IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg (preferred) or IM artemether 3.2 mg/kg, AND (c) treat hypoglycaemia (10% dextrose 5 mL/kg IV), AND (d) treat convulsion (rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg or IV/IM midazolam 0.2 mg/kg).
Oxygen if SpO2 < 90 % or severe respiratory distress. Recovery position if unconscious; suction secretions.

management.step: IV fluids only for shock or severe dehydration
management.detail: FEAST trial showed routine bolus harmful in non-shocked African children. Give 10–20 mL/kg crystalloid ONLY if shocked, then reassess; otherwise maintenance only via NG or oral if tolerating.
Continue pre-referral antibiotic + antimalarial. Keep warm; check glucose en route.

Continue IV ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg/day. IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 h then daily for severe malaria, transitioning to oral ACT for 3 days once tolerating. Manage convulsions with phenobarbital/phenytoin if recurrent. Treat anaemia (transfuse if Hb < 4 g/dL or 4–6 with respiratory distress).

references.label: WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children (2nd ed.)
WHO Guidelines for the treatment of malaria (3rd ed., 2015)

title: IMCI — severe pneumonia (child 2–59 months, chest indrawing or general danger sign)
presentation: Cough or difficulty breathing for any duration.
AND lower chest-wall indrawing (severe pneumonia) OR any IMCI general danger sign (very severe pneumonia).
Fast breathing thresholds (count for 60 s): age 2–11 m ≥ 50/min; age 12–59 m ≥ 40/min.
redFlags: Grunting, head nodding, severe chest indrawing.
Stridor at rest, severe acute malnutrition.

diagnostics.test: Pulse oximetry — SpO2 essential bedside test.
diagnostics.rationale: Hypoxaemia is a key marker of severity and need for oxygen.

diagnostics.test: Respiratory rate count over 60 s when child quiet.
Where available: CXR, FBC, blood culture, HIV test if status unknown.

management.detail: Nasal prongs 0.5–2 L/min for infants, up to 4 L/min for older children. Target SpO2 ≥ 90 %. Escalate to CPAP / HFNC if available for impending failure.
IV ampicillin 50 mg/kg every 6 h + IM/IV gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg once daily for 5 days. Add cloxacillin if Staph aureus suspected (post-measles, abscess, pneumatocoele, empyema).

management.step: Alternative — IV ceftriaxone for severe presentation or in high-resistance settings
management.detail: Ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg IM/IV once daily, especially if meningitis cannot be excluded clinically.
Maintain hydration (oral preferred, NG if cannot drink, IV at 75% maintenance if cannot tolerate). Antipyretic (paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 6 h). Continue feeding.
Severe malaria, severe acute malnutrition, anaemia, HIV — coordinate management.

management.step: Switch to oral and discharge planning
management.detail: Once afebrile 48 h, eating/drinking, SpO2 ≥ 90 %, RR returning to normal — switch to oral amoxicillin 40 mg/kg twice daily to complete 5–7 days total.

management.step: Counsel caregiver on danger signs for re-presentation
management.detail: Fast breathing, indrawing, inability to drink, fever > 3 days, convulsion, child becomes sicker.

references.label: WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children, 2nd ed. — Pneumonia chapters
WHO Revised classification and treatment of pneumonia in children (2014)

title: IMCI — possible serious bacterial infection (PSBI) in young infant < 2 months
presentation: Infant < 60 days with ANY of: fast breathing (RR ≥ 60/min), severe chest indrawing, fever (≥ 37.5°C axillary), hypothermia (< 35.5°C), no movement on stimulation, not feeding well, convulsions, umbilical redness extending to skin, or pus draining from ear.
Critical illness (clinical severe infection):  any sign of CSI — not feeding, lethargic/unconscious, convulsions, severe chest indrawing.
redFlags: ALL young infants with any PSBI sign are at high risk — neonatal sepsis carries mortality > 20 % if untreated.
Critical illness (CSI) — refer ALWAYS to hospital.

diagnostics.test: Vital signs (RR, HR, temperature axillary, SpO2 if available).
At hospital: blood culture, FBC, CRP, LP (if no contraindication), urine culture (clean catch or SPA).

management.step: Refer to hospital ALWAYS if critical illness, OR home referral declined PSBI sign
management.detail: Begin pre-referral antibiotic immediately.

management.step: Pre-referral antibiotic (single dose) at health facility
management.detail: IM ampicillin 50 mg/kg + IM gentamicin (age < 7 days: 5 mg/kg if ≥ 2 kg; 3 mg/kg if < 2 kg; age 7 days–2 m: 7.5 mg/kg). Give vitamin K 1 mg IM if not given at birth. Treat hypoglycaemia with 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg IV bolus then maintenance.

management.step: Hospital-based treatment — first 7 days IV antibiotics
management.detail: IV ampicillin + gentamicin for 7 days (extend to 10–14 days if meningitis confirmed). Reassess at 48–72 h based on cultures and clinical response. Add cefotaxime if late-onset meningitis suspected.

management.step: Outpatient simplified regimen — for non-critical PSBI when referral not possible
management.detail: WHO simplified regimens (research-supported): IM gentamicin once daily for 7 days + oral amoxicillin twice daily for 7 days (PSBI with fast breathing alone in 7–59-day-olds may use oral amoxicillin alone in some programmes). Use only in supervised home-management programmes where referral truly impossible.

Maintain warmth (kangaroo mother care, especially preterm/low birthweight). Encourage exclusive breastfeeding; expressed breast-milk via NG/cup if cannot suckle. Treat seizures (phenobarbital 20 mg/kg loading). Oxygen if hypoxic.
Counsel mother on danger signs, exclusive breastfeeding, immunisation. Schedule community follow-up at 2–3 days then weekly until 8 weeks.

references.label: WHO IMCI Chart booklet for young infants 0–2 months
WHO Managing possible serious bacterial infection in young infants when referral is not feasible (2015)
WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children — Newborn chapter

title: ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) — adult
presentation: Sudden central or left-sided crushing chest pain ≥ 20 min duration, often radiating to jaw, neck or left arm.
Associated diaphoresis, dyspnoea, nausea, syncope.
Anterior infarct: LAD territory — risk of cardiogenic shock, large area at risk.
Inferior infarct: RCA / LCx territory — bradycardia, hypotension, possible RV involvement.
Atypical presentations more common in elderly, women, diabetics: dyspnoea, fatigue, epigastric pain, syncope.
redFlags: Cardiogenic shock (SBP < 90, cold peripheries, pulmonary oedema).
Mechanical complications: acute mitral regurgitation, VSD, free-wall rupture.
Sustained ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, complete heart block.
Aortic dissection mimics — sudden tearing pain to the back, BP discrepancy, widened mediastinum on CXR.

diagnostics.test: 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact — and repeat every 15 min if non-diagnostic but ongoing pain.
diagnostics.rationale: STEMI criteria: ≥ 1 mm ST elevation in ≥ 2 contiguous limb leads, or ≥ 2 mm in V1–V3 men (≥ 1.5 mm women); new LBBB; posterior infarct (ST depression V1–V3 with tall R).
Confirm myocardial injury; not required to commence reperfusion.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, glucose, lipids, coagulation, CXR (mediastinum).
diagnostics.rationale: Baseline + exclude dissection and other mimics.
Identify regional wall-motion abnormality, mechanical complications.

management.detail: ABCDE; supplemental O2 ONLY if SpO2 < 90 %; large-bore IV access; cardiac monitor; aspirin 300 mg chewed; sublingual GTN if SBP > 90 (NOT in inferior MI with RV involvement). Analgesia: morphine 2–4 mg IV (or fentanyl) titrated to pain.
Primary PCI (preferred): if PCI-capable centre and door-to-balloon time can be < 90 min (or < 120 min if transferred). Otherwise fibrinolysis within 30 min of arrival ('door-to-needle').

management.step: Fibrinolytic therapy (if PCI not available within 120 min)
management.detail: Tenecteplase weight-banded IV bolus (preferred), OR alteplase (15 mg bolus + 0.75 mg/kg over 30 min + 0.5 mg/kg over 60 min, max 100 mg), OR streptokinase 1.5 MU over 60 min. Co-administer enoxaparin (or unfractionated heparin), aspirin + clopidogrel 300 mg loading (75 mg if > 75 y). Plan rescue PCI if no resolution at 60–90 min or any deterioration.
Aspirin 75 mg daily + ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily (or prasugrel) — preferred over clopidogrel post-PCI; clopidogrel 75 mg daily if fibrinolysis given or bleeding risk.
Unfractionated heparin or enoxaparin during PCI; bivalirudin alternative.

High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg). ACE inhibitor (or ARB) — within 24 h. β-blocker (oral within 24 h if no shock / CHF / heart block). Aldosterone antagonist (eplerenone) if EF ≤ 40% with HF or diabetes.
Refer to cardiac rehab; smoking cessation, structured exercise, weight control, dietitian, mental health screen.

management.step: Long-term DAPT, statin, ACEi, β-blocker indefinitely (statin and antiplatelet)
management.detail: DAPT 12 months post-ACS standard (longer if very high ischaemic risk). Annual review of LV function and risk factors.

references.label: ESC 2023 Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes
ACC/AHA Guideline for the management of patients with STEMI (2013, with updates)
WHO Package of essential noncommunicable disease interventions (PEN) — Acute coronary events
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS / NSTEMI / unstable angina) — adult
presentation: New-onset, crescendo, or rest angina (unstable angina) — pain at rest > 20 min, or accelerating exertional angina.
Chest discomfort with autonomic symptoms; may be atypical in elderly / women / diabetic.
Often preserved LV function; risk-stratify based on troponin trajectory and ischaemic ECG changes.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability, ongoing chest pain despite therapy, malignant arrhythmia, mechanical complication.
Refractory ischaemic ECG changes (dynamic ST depression or T inversion).

diagnostics.test: Serial 12-lead ECG (admission + at 3 and 6 h, or with any pain change).
diagnostics.rationale: Look for ST depression, T inversion, transient ST elevation.

diagnostics.test: High-sensitivity troponin at 0 + 1–3 h (use ESC 0/1-h algorithm if available).
diagnostics.rationale: Rule-in / rule-out NSTEMI; troponin rise + fall pattern.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, glucose, lipids, coagulation, CXR.
diagnostics.rationale: Identify comorbidity; rule out alternative diagnoses.
Stratify low / intermediate / high risk → timing of invasive coronary angiography.

management.detail: ABCDE; O2 only if SpO2 < 90 %; aspirin 300 mg loading; analgesia (morphine 2–4 mg IV titrated); sublingual GTN; cardiac monitor; large-bore IV access.

Aspirin 75 mg daily indefinitely + a P2Y12 inhibitor: ticagrelor 180 mg load then 90 mg twice daily (preferred), OR prasugrel (only post-known coronary anatomy), OR clopidogrel 300 mg load then 75 mg daily (if ticagrelor/prasugrel contraindicated).
Fondaparinux 2.5 mg SC daily (preferred — best safety profile) OR enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC twice daily OR unfractionated heparin.
β-blocker (start oral within 24 h if no shock / acute HF / heart block). High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg). ACE inhibitor if HTN, HF, LV dysfunction, diabetes.

management.step: Timing of invasive coronary angiography (per risk)
management.detail: Very high risk (haemodynamic instability, life-threatening arrhythmia, mechanical complication, refractory ischaemia): IMMEDIATE (< 2 h). High risk (rise/fall troponin consistent with NSTEMI, dynamic ECG changes, GRACE > 140): EARLY (< 24 h). Intermediate (diabetes, CKD, prior MI, LVEF < 40, GRACE 109–140): within 72 h. Low risk: non-invasive testing first.
Aspirin + P2Y12 (DAPT) for 12 months; aspirin indefinitely. High-intensity statin. ACEi/ARB. β-blocker. Cardiac rehabilitation. Smoking cessation, BP and diabetes control.

references.label: ESC 2023 Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Anaphylaxis — adult emergency pathway (adrenaline-first)
presentation: Sudden (minutes–hours) onset of life-threatening Airway, Breathing or Circulation problem in the presence of likely allergen exposure.
Airway: throat tightness, stridor, hoarseness, tongue swelling.
Breathing: severe shortness of breath, wheeze, SpO2 < 92%, cyanosis, exhaustion.
Circulation: hypotension (SBP < 90), tachycardia, syncope, pale clammy.
Skin/mucosa (in 80–90% but absence does NOT exclude anaphylaxis): urticaria, angioedema, flushing, pruritus.
GI: cramping abdominal pain, vomiting, incontinence.
redFlags: Severe bronchospasm not responding to adrenaline.
Hypotension refractory to fluids and adrenaline (consider biphasic reaction, beta-blocker effect → use glucagon).
Pregnancy — left lateral tilt, lower threshold for early delivery if maternal compromise.

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnosis — do NOT delay adrenaline for tests.
Serum tryptase: baseline + 1–2 h + 24 h post-event.
diagnostics.rationale: Confirm mast-cell activation retrospectively; helps clarify uncertain cases.

diagnostics.test: Allergen-specific IgE / skin prick testing in allergy clinic later.

management.detail: Stop any IV drug / blood product. Remove insect sting (scrape, do not squeeze). Lie flat with legs elevated (pregnant: left lateral). Do NOT stand or sit if hypotensive — risk of empty-ventricle arrest.

management.step: IM ADRENALINE — first-line drug, give without delay
management.detail: Adult: 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) IM into anterolateral thigh. Repeat every 5 min as needed. ALWAYS use IM (not subcut, not first-line IV). IV adrenaline ONLY in critical-care setting with cardiac monitoring (50–100 microgram IV bolus or 1–10 microgram/min infusion).
100% O2 via non-rebreather mask. Position by ABCs: lay flat if hypotensive, sit up if respiratory distress dominates.
1–2 L 0.9% NaCl or balanced crystalloid wide-open if hypotensive; repeat as needed (often 4–6 L required).
Salbutamol 5 mg nebulised (+ ipratropium 0.5 mg) — adjunct only; does NOT replace adrenaline.

Chlorphenamine 10 mg IV (or oral if mild) — for cutaneous symptoms. Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV — no proven benefit in acute event but commonly given; do NOT delay adrenaline. Glucagon 1–2 mg IV if on β-blocker and refractory hypotension.
20% recur within 1–72 h (most within 8 h). Monitor at least 6 h after symptom resolution if uncomplicated; 12–24 h if severe / hypotension / >1 dose adrenaline / asthma / known biphasic history.

Prescribe 2 adrenaline auto-injectors (e.g. EpiPen 0.3 mg) and demonstrate use. Action plan + medic-alert ID. Refer to allergy clinic. Counsel on trigger avoidance. Document the event clearly. Continue any oral antihistamine + steroid 3 days.

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK — Emergency treatment of anaphylactic reactions (2021)

title: Status asthmaticus / life-threatening acute asthma — adult
presentation: Severe asthma exacerbation not responding to initial bronchodilator therapy.
Inability to complete sentences, RR > 25, HR > 110, PEF 33–50% best/predicted (acute severe).
Life-threatening features: SpO2 < 92%, PEF < 33%, silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, exhaustion, arrhythmia, hypotension, altered consciousness.
Near-fatal: rising PaCO2 or need for IMV.
redFlags: Rising PaCO2 on ABG (asthmatics normally hyperventilate; normal/high CO2 = pre-arrest).
Previous near-fatal asthma, ICU admission, intubation, or rapid deterioration.

diagnostics.test: PEF before and after each treatment.
ABG if SpO2 < 92% or life-threatening features.
CXR if suspect pneumothorax, pneumonia, lobar collapse, or no improvement.

management.detail: High-flow via non-rebreather initially; titrate down as SpO2 stabilises.

management.step: Inhaled β2-agonist + ipratropium continuously or every 15 min
management.detail: Salbutamol 5 mg nebulised driven by oxygen, every 15 min or continuous. Add ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulised every 4–6 h.

management.step: Systemic corticosteroid — give early to ALL
management.detail: Oral prednisolone 40–50 mg (continue 5–7 days) OR IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 h if cannot swallow. No taper needed unless > 14 days.

management.step: IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 20 min — life-threatening or no response
management.detail: Bronchodilator effect; consider in severe / life-threatening asthma not responding to nebulised therapy.

management.step: IV salbutamol or aminophylline — specialist only
management.detail: Consider IV salbutamol or IV aminophylline (loading 5 mg/kg over 20 min) under specialist supervision if not responding.

Indications: exhaustion, rising CO2, falling SpO2 despite treatment, altered consciousness, cardiorespiratory arrest. Use ketamine for induction (bronchodilator). Permissive hypercapnia ventilation — long expiratory time, low rate, careful for breath-stacking and pneumothorax.
Infection (often viral), allergen, NSAID/β-blocker exposure, smoking, non-adherence.

Continue oral prednisolone 5–7 days. Step-up controller therapy (inhaled corticosteroid + LABA). Inhaler-technique check. Written personalised asthma action plan. Smoking cessation. Follow-up within 2 working days.

references.label: GINA — Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention (2024)
BTS/SIGN British guideline on the management of asthma

title: Severe acute exacerbation of COPD — adult
presentation: Acute increase in dyspnoea, sputum volume or purulence beyond day-to-day variation.
Severe: SpO2 < 88% or worsening type-II respiratory failure (pH < 7.35, PaCO2 > 6.0 kPa).
Often precipitated by infection (viral or bacterial) or air pollution.
redFlags: Respiratory acidosis on ABG (pH < 7.35) — needs NIV.
Pneumothorax, large effusion, pulmonary embolism — exclude on CXR ± imaging.

diagnostics.test: ABG on room air or controlled oxygen (target SpO2 88–92%).
diagnostics.rationale: Detect hypercapnia + acidosis; decide NIV need.
Exclude pneumonia, pneumothorax, effusion, heart failure.

diagnostics.test: Sputum culture if purulent / not responding.

management.step: Controlled oxygen — target SpO2 88–92% via Venturi mask
management.detail: Excess O2 → worsened hypercapnia. Start 24–28% O2 and titrate via SpO2; check ABG within 30–60 min.
Salbutamol 5 mg + ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulised every 4–6 h (more frequent if severe).
Oral prednisolone 30–40 mg for 5 days (IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 h only if cannot swallow).

management.step: Antibiotic for purulent sputum / consolidation / NIV need
management.detail: Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS or doxycycline 200 mg loading then 100 mg daily for 5 days. Co-amoxiclav or per local guidelines if severe / inpatient.

management.step: Non-invasive ventilation (NIV — BiPAP) for type II respiratory failure
management.detail: Indications: pH < 7.35 with PaCO2 > 6 kPa after 1 h of optimal medical therapy. Start IPAP 12 cmH2O, EPAP 4 cmH2O; titrate IPAP up by 2–5 cmH2O every 10 min to target. Plan ceiling of care BEFORE escalation (NIV may be the ceiling for severe COPD without intubation candidacy).
If NIV fails, severe acidosis (pH < 7.25), exhaustion, agitation precluding NIV, or coexistent acute pulmonary oedema/sepsis with appropriate goals of care.
Antibiotics for infection, diuretic for fluid overload, anticoagulation for PE, drain pneumothorax.

Optimise inhalers (technique check + step up to triple therapy if frequent exacerbations). Pulmonary rehab referral. Smoking cessation. Vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal). Long-term oxygen assessment if persistent hypoxaemia.

references.label: GOLD 2024 — Global Strategy for Prevention, Diagnosis and Management of COPD
BTS/ICS guideline for the ventilatory management of acute hypercapnic respiratory failure

title: Severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
presentation: Pregnancy ≥ 20 weeks (or post-partum) with BP ≥ 160/110 mmHg on two occasions ≥ 4 h apart, OR severe features at lower BP.
Severe features: severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric / RUQ pain, vomiting, hyperreflexia, clonus, oliguria, pulmonary oedema.
Laboratory: proteinuria ≥ 5 g/24 h or +++ dipstick; platelets < 100; AST/ALT > 2× ULN; creatinine > 90; haemolysis.
Eclampsia: tonic-clonic seizure not attributable to other cause in pre-eclampsia.
redFlags: Pulmonary oedema, oliguria (<30 mL/h), HELLP syndrome.
Severe headache unresponsive to paracetamol, visual disturbance.

diagnostics.test: BP repeated 4 h apart (or immediately if severe features).
Urinalysis (dipstick + protein-creatinine ratio or 24 h urine).
FBC, U&E, LFT, LDH, blood film, coagulation, group + save.
diagnostics.rationale: Identify HELLP and DIC; prepare for transfusion.

diagnostics.test: Fetal CTG, umbilical artery Doppler, growth assessment.

management.step: Magnesium sulphate — for ALL severe pre-eclampsia and ALL eclampsia
management.detail: Loading: 4 g IV over 5–15 min (or 5 g IM each buttock — Pritchard regimen). Maintenance: 1 g/h IV (or 5 g IM every 4 h). Continue 24 h after last seizure or delivery. Monitor reflexes (lost reflexes = toxicity), respiratory rate (> 12), urine output (> 100 mL in 4 h).

management.step: Treat magnesium toxicity with calcium gluconate
management.detail: 1 g IV slowly if respiratory depression or absent reflexes; stop magnesium.

management.step: Antihypertensive — first line: oral nifedipine OR IV labetalol
management.detail: Oral nifedipine 10 mg, may repeat after 30 min × 3; OR IV labetalol 20 mg bolus, double every 10 min (max 300 mg total); OR IV hydralazine 5 mg bolus (10 min onset, repeat every 20 min). Target BP < 160/110 acutely, < 150/100 sustained — avoid sudden drop.

management.step: Delivery is the only definitive treatment
management.detail: Eclampsia or severe pre-eclampsia at ≥ 34 weeks: deliver after maternal stabilisation. < 34 weeks: corticosteroid course (betamethasone 12 mg × 2 doses 24 h apart) for fetal lung maturity; deliver if maternal/fetal compromise.
Vaginal birth often achievable; expedited via induction or LSCS as clinically indicated. Avoid prolonged labour.

Continue magnesium 24 h after delivery / last seizure. BP can WORSEN postpartum — review BP every 4 h × 24 h, then daily for 5–7 days. Antihypertensives may be needed for weeks. Counsel about future cardiovascular risk.
Aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks for prophylaxis; high-risk planning. Recurrence risk ~15–25%.

references.label: WHO Recommendations for prevention and treatment of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia (2011)
NICE NG133 — Hypertension in pregnancy: diagnosis and management
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (MOH)

title: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) — emergency management
presentation: Primary PPH: blood loss ≥ 500 mL after vaginal birth or ≥ 1000 mL after LSCS within 24 h of delivery (major if ≥ 1000 mL or any haemodynamic compromise).
Secondary PPH: abnormal bleeding from 24 h to 12 weeks postpartum.
Causes — '4 Ts': Tone (uterine atony, 70%), Trauma (laceration, rupture), Tissue (retained products), Thrombin (coagulopathy).
redFlags: Estimated blood loss > 1500 mL or ongoing brisk bleeding.
Maternal shock — SBP < 90, HR > 120, oliguria, altered consciousness.
Uterine rupture (sudden cessation of contractions, fetal distress before delivery, presenting part recedes).
Concealed bleeding (placental abruption, broad ligament haematoma).
Suspected amniotic fluid embolism (sudden collapse, cyanosis, coagulopathy).

diagnostics.test: Estimated and measured blood loss (weigh swabs, calibrated drape).
FBC, group + crossmatch 4 units, coagulation, fibrinogen, U&E, LFT.
diagnostics.rationale: Guide transfusion; fibrinogen < 2 g/L is independent predictor of severity.

management.step: Call for help; ABCDE; high-flow O2
management.detail: Activate massive haemorrhage protocol if > 1500 mL or ongoing brisk loss. Two large-bore IVs. Crystalloid bolus.
Empty the uterus and bladder. Continuous bimanual compression if atony — buys time.

1) Oxytocin 5–10 IU slow IV bolus + 40 IU in 500 mL crystalloid infusion. 2) Ergometrine 0.5 mg IM (avoid in hypertension / pre-eclampsia / cardiac disease). 3) Carboprost (PGF2α) 250 microgram IM every 15 min (max 8 doses; avoid in asthma). 4) Misoprostol 800 microgram sublingual / rectal (especially where injectables unavailable).

management.step: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 h of bleeding onset
management.detail: WOMAN trial — reduces maternal mortality from PPH; repeat 1 g if continued bleeding at 30 min.
Genital tract inspection under anaesthesia if active bleeding despite uterotonics. Repair laceration. Manual removal of placenta / curettage for retained tissue.

Intrauterine balloon tamponade (Bakri or condom catheter). If still bleeding → laparotomy: B-Lynch suture, bilateral uterine artery ligation, internal iliac artery ligation, or hysterectomy. Interventional radiology if available.
Activate protocol: PRBC : FFP : platelets in 1:1:1. Cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen < 2 g/L. Replace calcium (every 4 units PRBC). Keep warm. Recombinant factor VIIa specialist last resort.
ICU/HDU monitoring. Watch for further bleeding, postpartum eclampsia, AKI, Sheehan syndrome, DVT (LMWH once bleeding controlled). Iron replacement; debrief and counsel.

references.label: WHO Recommendations for the prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage (2012, updated)
FIGO PPH initiative — non-pneumatic anti-shock garment; misoprostol
RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 52 — Prevention and management of PPH
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (MOH)

title: Severe falciparum malaria — adult complete management pathway
presentation: Falciparum parasitaemia (any density in non-immune; > 2% may suggest severity in semi-immune) with one or more of:

Impaired consciousness (GCS < 11), prostration, multiple seizures, severe anaemia (Hb < 7 g/dL adult), jaundice, respiratory distress (ARDS), shock, AKI (creatinine > 265 micromol/L), hypoglycaemia (< 2.2 mmol/L), acidosis (HCO3 < 15), abnormal bleeding, parasitaemia > 10%.
redFlags: Coma (cerebral malaria) — high mortality even with treatment.
Pulmonary oedema / ARDS — can develop after starting treatment.
Severe acidosis, hypoglycaemia (especially in pregnant women, children, on quinine).
Acute renal failure — common; may require dialysis.
Co-infection with bacterial sepsis (Salmonella in particular) — broad-spectrum antibiotic.

diagnostics.rationale: Bedside; HRP-2 may be falsely negative if deletion.
Hypoglycaemia common, especially on quinine, in children, in pregnancy.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, creatinine, glucose, lactate, ABG, coag, LFT, blood culture.
diagnostics.rationale: Quantify organ dysfunction; rule out bacterial co-infection.

diagnostics.test: Daily monitoring of haematocrit, parasitaemia, lactate.

management.detail: 2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12, 24 h then daily for at least 24 h and until oral therapy possible (minimum 3 doses). Switch to a full 3-day course of oral artemisinin-based combination therapy (AL, AS-AQ, DHA-PPQ) once tolerating.

management.step: If artesunate unavailable — IM artemether (second line) or IV quinine (third line)
management.detail: Artemether 3.2 mg/kg IM loading then 1.6 mg/kg daily. Quinine: loading 20 mg/kg IV over 4 h, then 10 mg/kg every 8 h (cardiac monitor; hypoglycaemia risk). Switch to oral when able.

management.step: Empirical antibiotic for adult with severe malaria + shock/AKI/severe disease
management.detail: IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily — Salmonella bacteraemia in 5–10% of severe malaria adults.
Avoid aggressive fluid resuscitation in non-shocked patients (FEAST in children, similar adult concerns) — risk of pulmonary oedema. Maintenance only with cautious assessment of perfusion.

Hypoglycaemia: 10% dextrose 5 mL/kg bolus then maintenance. Severe anaemia: transfuse if Hb < 7 g/dL or symptomatic. AKI: avoid nephrotoxins; haemodialysis if uraemic, fluid-overloaded, K+ > 6.5. Seizures: benzodiazepine + phenytoin/phenobarbital. ARDS: low-tidal-volume ventilation.
Artesunate safe in all trimesters in severe malaria. Children: weight-based dosing; minimum 3 mg/kg artesunate if < 20 kg. Strict glucose and Hb monitoring.

Post-artesunate delayed haemolytic anaemia: monitor Hb weekly for 4 weeks. Cognitive sequelae in children — neurodevelopmental follow-up after cerebral malaria. Vector control + chemoprophylaxis counselling.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the treatment of malaria, 3rd ed. (2015) and 2021 update
WHO Severe malaria (Trop Med Int Health supplement, 2014)
Kenya National Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Malaria (MOH, Division of National Malaria Programme)

title: Pulmonary tuberculosis — drug-sensitive, adult treatment
presentation: Cough ≥ 2 weeks (often productive ± haemoptysis), fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue.
Risk factors: HIV, prior TB, household TB contact, prison, healthcare worker, malnutrition, diabetes, smoking, alcohol use.
Extrapulmonary involvement in up to 20% — lymph node, pleural, miliary, CNS, spinal (Pott's), abdominal, genitourinary.
redFlags: Suspected TB meningitis (headache, neck stiffness, cranial nerve palsies, altered consciousness).
Pre-existing liver disease (modified regimen, increased hepatotoxicity risk).
Suspected drug-resistant TB (history of treatment failure, contact with known DR-TB).

diagnostics.test: Sputum molecular test (Xpert MTB/RIF or Ultra) — preferred first test.
diagnostics.rationale: Rapid (2 h) detection of M. tuberculosis with rifampicin resistance.
Where molecular unavailable; culture for DST.
Pattern suggests TB (upper-lobe cavities, miliary nodules, hilar lymphadenopathy).

diagnostics.test: HIV test, blood glucose, hepatitis B + C, baseline LFT, creatinine, FBC.

management.detail: Intensive phase: 2 months of isoniazid (H) + rifampicin (R) + pyrazinamide (Z) + ethambutol (E), weight-banded daily. Continuation phase: 4 months of HR daily.
Standardised FDC tablets simplify adherence; use weight-banded per WHO.

management.step: Add pyridoxine 25 mg daily for all (50 mg if HIV / pregnancy / alcohol use)
management.detail: Prevents INH-induced peripheral neuropathy.

management.step: DOT or video-DOT and adherence support
management.detail: Directly-observed therapy or video DOT for patients at risk of non-adherence; education + patient-centred support package.

Clinical review, sputum smear/Xpert at month 2 (and month 5 if positive at month 2 → assess for failure). Monitor weight; adjust dose if weight band changes. LFT if symptoms (anorexia, jaundice) — stop drugs if ALT > 5× ULN.
Start ART within 2 weeks of TB treatment if CD4 < 50; within 8 weeks otherwise. Preferred ART: dolutegravir-based (efavirenz alternative if interaction issues with rifampicin).
Stop all hepatotoxic anti-TB drugs (HRZ); use ethambutol + streptomycin/levofloxacin temporarily. Re-challenge sequentially with R, then H, then Z; permanent withdrawal of Z if recurrent.
Screen household and close contacts; offer TB preventive therapy (3HP, 6H, 4R) to eligible contacts.

references.label: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis — Module 4: Drug-susceptible TB treatment (2022)
WHO Operational handbook on tuberculosis — Module 5: Management of TB in children and adolescents
Kenya National Tuberculosis, Leprosy and Lung Disease Program (NTLD-P) — Management of Tuberculosis Guidelines

title: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) — adult, WHO BPaLM/BPaL pathway
presentation: TB with resistance to at least rifampicin (RR-TB), with or without isoniazid resistance.
Risk factors: prior TB treatment failure, default, relapse, contact with known DR-TB, residence in high-MDR settings.
Often more advanced disease at diagnosis; longer infectivity.
redFlags: XDR-TB (rifampicin + fluoroquinolone resistance ± other Group A) — limited options, specialist management.
Concurrent advanced HIV, liver disease, pregnancy, paediatric age — specialist regimen modifications.
QT prolongation risk (baseline ECG + monthly QTc; many DR-TB drugs prolong QT).
Hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, optic neuritis (linezolid), psychiatric symptoms (cycloserine).

diagnostics.test: Drug-susceptibility testing — molecular (Xpert MTB/XDR) for fluoroquinolone + injectable resistance; phenotypic DST for all Group A + B drugs.
Baseline ECG, LFT, U&E, FBC, TSH, visual acuity + colour vision, audiometry.
diagnostics.rationale: Establish baseline before nephrotoxic / ototoxic / hepatotoxic drugs.

diagnostics.test: HIV, hepatitis B + C, pregnancy test, diabetes screen.

management.step: All-oral BPaL or BPaLM regimen (WHO 2022) — 6 months for most RR-TB / MDR-TB
management.detail: BPaLM: bedaquiline 400 mg daily × 2 weeks then 200 mg 3× weekly + pretomanid 200 mg daily + linezolid 600 mg daily + moxifloxacin 400 mg daily — for 6 months (extend to 9 if culture not converted by month 4). BPaL (without moxifloxacin) for pre-XDR/XDR or moxifloxacin contraindicated.

management.step: Longer (9–20 month) individualised regimens — when BPaLM unsuitable
management.detail: Use Group A (bedaquiline, linezolid, levofloxacin/moxifloxacin) + Group B (clofazimine, cycloserine) ± Group C drugs (ethambutol, delamanid, pyrazinamide, imipenem, amikacin, ethionamide, p-aminosalicylic acid) per resistance profile.
Monthly: clinical review, weight, ECG (QTc), FBC, LFT, U&E, glucose; every 2 months: TSH (ethionamide), visual acuity (linezolid). Daily symptom check by patient + DOT supporter.
Daily DOT or video-DOT; psychosocial counselling; nutritional support; transport vouchers; treatment of mental health and substance use comorbidity.

Linezolid: stop if peripheral neuropathy / optic neuritis / cytopenia; dose reduce 300 mg if early. Clofazimine: skin pigmentation, QT. Cycloserine: psychiatric — coadminister pyridoxine 100 mg/day. Bedaquiline + delamanid: QT monitoring (ECG monthly).
Single-room isolation with N95 respirator (HCW) until 2 negative smears; airborne precautions; counsel patient and household.
Sputum culture monthly. Post-treatment follow-up every 6 months for 2 years to detect relapse.

references.label: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis — Module 4: Drug-resistant TB treatment (2022 update)
WHO Operational handbook on TB — MDR/RR-TB Treatment regimens
Kenya National Tuberculosis, Leprosy and Lung Disease Program (NTLD-P) — Management of Tuberculosis Guidelines

title: Advanced HIV disease (AHD) — adult care package
presentation: Adult living with HIV with CD4 < 200 cells/microL OR WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 disease.

Often presents with weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, oral candidiasis, recurrent infections, or AIDS-defining illness (PCP, cryptococcal meningitis, TB, oesophageal candidiasis, Kaposi sarcoma, severe wasting).
