Newly diagnosed, re-engaging after treatment interruption, or experiencing virological failure.
redFlags: Suspected cryptococcal meningitis (headache, fever, vomiting, neck stiffness, altered consciousness).
Suspected TB (cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss).
Severe wasting (BMI < 18.5 with progressive weight loss).
Disseminated Kaposi sarcoma with visceral involvement.
IRIS within first 6 months of starting ART.

diagnostics.test: Cryptococcal antigen (serum or LP CSF if symptoms).
diagnostics.rationale: Routine CrAg screening when CD4 < 200; pre-empt cryptococcal meningitis.
TB screening; LAM has high yield in AHD.
Confirm treatment failure if on ART; baseline if new.

diagnostics.test: FBC, creatinine, LFT, hepatitis B + C screen, syphilis serology.

management.step: WHO AHD package — screen, treat, prevent
management.detail: Systematic implementation of: rapid ART initiation, OI screening (CrAg, TB-LAM), OI prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole, isoniazid preventive therapy or 3HP), pre-emptive treatment for CrAg-positive.

First line: tenofovir + lamivudine (or emtricitabine) + dolutegravir (TLD). Start within 7 days of HIV diagnosis (same-day initiation) UNLESS untreated cryptococcal meningitis or TB meningitis (defer ART 4–8 weeks).

960 mg daily for ALL with CD4 < 350 (or all in high TB/malaria settings regardless of CD4) — prevents PCP, toxoplasmosis, bacterial pneumonia, malaria, isosporiasis. Continue until CD4 > 350 sustained for ≥ 6 months.
After active TB excluded: 3HP (isoniazid + rifapentine weekly × 12 weeks) preferred; 6H or 9H alternatives. Strongly recommended for ALL PLHIV regardless of CD4.

If serum CrAg positive without symptoms: fluconazole 800 mg/day × 2 weeks → 400 mg/day × 8 weeks → 200 mg/day maintenance until CD4 > 200 × 6 months. If symptomatic (LP needed) — full cryptococcal meningitis induction (amphotericin B + flucytosine or oral fluconazole high-dose per WHO 2022 guidance).
Nutritional assessment; therapeutic feeds if BMI < 18.5. Disclosure support, peer counsellors, mental health screen.
Paradoxical worsening of existing OI within 4–8 weeks of ART — continue ART; treat the unmasked / paradoxical OI; corticosteroids (prednisolone 1 mg/kg) for severe TB-IRIS / KS-IRIS.
Visit at 2 weeks, 4 weeks, then monthly until stable. Viral load at 6 months and annually.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for managing advanced HIV disease and rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy (2017, 2022 update)
WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring (2021)
Kenya Guidelines on Use of Antiretroviral Drugs for Treating and Preventing HIV Infection in Kenya (NASCOP, MOH)

title: Cholera — severe dehydration management (adult and child)
presentation: Profuse painless watery ("rice water") diarrhoea of sudden onset, often with vomiting.
Rapid dehydration; loss of skin turgor, sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, weak pulse, hypotension, oliguria.
Outbreak context — strong epidemiological link in endemic / outbreak areas.
redFlags: Severe dehydration: lethargy, sunken eyes, drinks poorly or not at all, very slow skin pinch retraction → IV fluids urgently.
Children, elderly, pregnant — higher mortality; closer monitoring.

diagnostics.rationale: Plan A — no signs; Plan B — some signs (ORS); Plan C — severe signs (IV).

diagnostics.test: Stool dark-field microscopy or RDT during outbreak.
diagnostics.rationale: Confirm Vibrio cholerae — supports public-health response.

diagnostics.test: Capillary glucose; serum electrolytes if severe / atypical / elderly.

management.detail: Increased fluids and continued feeding at home. Give ORS after each loose stool: children < 2 y 50–100 mL; 2–10 y 100–200 mL; ≥ 10 y as much as wants. Zinc 20 mg daily × 10–14 days for children 2 months–5 years.
Oral rehydration in health facility: 75 mL/kg ORS over 4 h. Reassess at 4 h; switch to Plan C if not improving; or Plan A continuation.

Ringer's lactate (or Hartmann's) IV immediately. Child < 12 m: 30 mL/kg in 1 h then 70 mL/kg over 5 h. Older + adult: 30 mL/kg over 30 min then 70 mL/kg over 2.5 h. Reassess every 15–30 min; insert NG tube and give ORS 20 mL/kg/h while establishing IV if available.
Single-dose doxycycline 300 mg PO adults (or azithromycin 1 g if pregnant or paediatric). Reduces stool volume, duration, and bacterial shedding. NOT a substitute for rehydration.
Once able to drink, start ORS and reduce IV rate. Match losses with ORS.
Children especially: 10% dextrose 5 mL/kg if hypoglycaemic. Hypokalaemia after rehydration — bananas, ORS contains K+; rarely need IV KCl.
Strict hand hygiene; chlorinated water; safe disposal of vomit / stool; barrier nursing if cluster. Notify public-health authorities (notifiable disease).
Oral cholera vaccine for outbreak control and high-risk populations; WASH interventions; community engagement.

references.label: WHO Cholera technical guidance + WHO/UNICEF Diarrhoea treatment Plans A/B/C
Global Task Force on Cholera Control — Ending Cholera roadmap
Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) Technical Guidelines, 3rd ed, Ministry of Health

title: Venomous snakebite — initial and antivenom management (adult and child)
presentation: Recent bite, sometimes unwitnessed (early morning, sleeping on floor in endemic areas).
Local: pain, swelling, ecchymosis, blistering, necrosis (cytotoxic vipers — common in Africa, Asia, Americas).
Haematotoxic (vipers, some elapids): coagulopathy with epistaxis, gum bleeding, haematuria, intracerebral haemorrhage.
Neurotoxic (elapids — cobra, krait, mamba, sea snake): ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, dysarthria, descending paralysis, respiratory failure.
Myotoxic (sea snake, some Australian elapids): muscle pain, dark urine (myoglobinuria), AKI, hyperkalaemia.
redFlags: Drowsiness or paralysis — neurotoxic envenomation, risk of respiratory failure.
Whole-blood clotting test (20WBCT) ≥ 20 min — abnormal coagulation, indication for antivenom.
Children — higher venom dose per kg, more severe outcomes.

diagnostics.rationale: Sensitive marker of systemic envenomation needing antivenom.

diagnostics.test: FBC, INR/PT, fibrinogen, U&E, creatine kinase, urine for blood/myoglobin, ECG.
Identify snake if safe and possible (photo, description).
diagnostics.rationale: Helps select monovalent vs polyvalent antivenom.

management.step: First aid — what NOT to do
management.detail: Do NOT: apply tourniquet, cut, suck, apply ice, use traditional remedies. DO: reassure, immobilise bitten limb with splint at heart level, remove rings/watches, transport rapidly to hospital. Pressure immobilisation (crepe bandage from bite up the limb) IF a clearly neurotoxic Australasian elapid; otherwise discouraged.
Intubate early if neurotoxic paralysis (do not wait for SpO2 fall). Two large-bore IVs; mark progress of swelling; observe for at least 24 h even if asymptomatic.

Indications: 20WBCT abnormal, systemic bleeding, neurotoxicity, shock, severe local swelling extending fast. Give species-appropriate polyvalent or monovalent antivenom per region. Start dose 5–10 vials (paediatric same as adult — venom is not weight-based). Premedicate with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV + chlorphenamine 10 mg IV ONLY where pyrogenic reactions common; have adrenaline ready for anaphylaxis.
Repeat 20WBCT at 6 h; if still > 20 min give a second dose. Continue every 6 h until coagulation normalises or clinical improvement.
If ptosis / weakness from postsynaptic elapid (cobra, sea snake) — test dose neostigmine 0.04 mg/kg IV (children 0.04 mg/kg) preceded by atropine 0.6 mg IV; if improvement, repeat 2–4-hourly.
Tetanus prophylaxis (after coagulopathy controlled). Wound care; debride necrosis at 5–7 days when demarcation complete. Antibiotics ONLY if obvious infection. Renal replacement if AKI.
Prevention: protective footwear, sleep above ground level, vector control, community education. Snake-bite is a WHO neglected tropical disease — link to programme reporting.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the management of snakebites, 2nd ed. (SEARO 2016)
WHO Snakebite envenoming — A strategy for prevention and control (2019)
Kenya National Guidelines for the Prevention, Diagnosis and Management of Snakebite Envenoming, Ministry of Health

title: Neutropenic sepsis — oncology emergency
presentation: Patient receiving cancer treatment (typically 7–10 days post-chemotherapy) with neutrophil count < 0.5 × 10⁹/L (or < 1.0 and predicted to fall).
Fever ≥ 38°C (single) or ≥ 37.5°C sustained for 1 h.
May be afebrile but unwell — high index of suspicion.
redFlags: Sepsis or septic shock (raised lactate, hypotension, organ dysfunction).
Anaerobic infection signs — necrotising perineal infection, typhlitis (abdominal pain, fever, neutropenia).
Central venous catheter infection — line removal often needed.
Mucositis with bleeding / inability to swallow.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, LFT, lactate, glucose, CRP, blood cultures (peripheral + each lumen of CVC) — within 1 h.
Urinalysis + culture, sputum culture, CXR, stool culture if diarrhoea.
Skin examination of all sites including perineum + IV/CVC sites.
CT chest/abdomen/pelvis if persistent fever > 96 h on broad-spectrum therapy.

management.detail: Give: high-flow O2 if hypoxic, blood cultures + lactate, IV fluid 30 mL/kg crystalloid, BROAD-SPECTRUM IV antibiotic, measure urine output, repeat lactate.

IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 h (or meropenem 1 g every 8 h if penicillin-anaphylaxis or local pattern). Add IV vancomycin or teicoplanin if MRSA risk / suspected line infection / severe mucositis / shock.
Remove infected IV catheters if persistent positive cultures or unstable; drain abscesses; surgical consult for typhlitis or necrotising soft-tissue infection.
Score ≥ 21 = low risk: may step down to oral therapy (co-amoxiclav + ciprofloxacin) after 48 h if stable and afebrile. Score < 21 = high risk: continue IV broad-spectrum.
Reassess: add empirical antifungal (fluconazole if low risk for mould, voriconazole / liposomal amphotericin for mould risk). CT chest for fungal pneumonia.
Not routine in established neutropenic sepsis; consider in severe infection, prolonged neutropenia, sepsis with comorbidity (per local protocols).

De-escalate at 48–72 h based on culture results. Continue until afebrile + neutrophil count > 0.5 × 10⁹/L. Refer to oncology for chemotherapy dose modification or addition of prophylactic G-CSF for next cycle.

references.label: NICE CG151 — Neutropenic sepsis: prevention and management
ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines: management of febrile neutropenia (2016)
IDSA Clinical Practice Guideline for Use of Antimicrobial Agents in Febrile Neutropenic Cancer Patients
Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health

title: Acute ischaemic stroke — thrombolysis / thrombectomy pathway
presentation: Sudden focal neurological deficit (limb weakness, dysphasia, dysarthria, facial droop, hemianopia, cerebellar signs).
FAST recognition (Face, Arm, Speech, Time) — pre-hospital triage.
Time-window critical: thrombolysis ≤ 4.5 h (with strict criteria up to 9 h for wake-up stroke + perfusion imaging); thrombectomy ≤ 24 h for large-vessel occlusion with favourable imaging.
redFlags: Suspected intracerebral haemorrhage (sudden severe headache, vomiting, very high BP, reduced consciousness) — CT mandatory before thrombolysis.
Posterior circulation stroke — basilar occlusion can present with vertigo, dysarthria, ataxia, then coma; thrombectomy time window often longer (specialist).
Stroke mimics: hypoglycaemia, seizure with Todd paresis, migraine.
Active bleeding, recent major surgery, recent intracranial / spinal surgery — thrombolysis contraindicated.
Anticoagulant use (INR > 1.7, or DOAC within 48 h) — thrombolysis usually contraindicated.

diagnostics.test: Non-contrast CT head WITHIN 25 minutes of arrival.
diagnostics.rationale: Exclude haemorrhage; identify early ischaemic changes (ASPECTS); identify hyperdense vessel sign.
Identify large-vessel occlusion eligible for thrombectomy.

diagnostics.test: CT perfusion (where available) for late-window (4.5–9 h, or wake-up).
Capillary glucose, BP, ECG, FBC, U&E, coag, troponin.
diagnostics.rationale: Exclude hypoglycaemia mimic; identify atrial fibrillation; baseline.

management.detail: ABCDE; manage airway; supplemental O2 only if SpO2 < 94%; large-bore IV; treat hypoglycaemia; do not aggressively lower BP unless > 185/110 (thrombolysis) or > 220/120 (no thrombolysis) — use labetalol IV.
10% bolus over 1 min then 90% infusion over 60 min (max 90 mg total). Within 4.5 h of symptom onset. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg single bolus is non-inferior alternative becoming more common.
≤ 6 h symptom onset for all LVO; 6–24 h with favourable CT perfusion (DEFUSE-3, DAWN criteria). Specialist comprehensive stroke centre.

Stroke unit; neurological observations every 15 min × 2 h, then every 30 min × 6 h, then hourly. BP < 180/105. No antiplatelet / anticoagulant for 24 h. Repeat CT at 24 h before starting antiplatelet.

Antiplatelet: aspirin 300 mg × 2 weeks then 75 mg lifelong (or clopidogrel 75 mg). DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 21 days for minor stroke / high-risk TIA, then single agent. Anticoagulant for AF: DOAC after 5–14 days (sooner for small infarct, later for large). Statin (atorvastatin 80 mg). BP control < 130/80 (start within 24 h if BP > 140/90 and stable). Diabetes management. Carotid endarterectomy if symptomatic stenosis 50–99%.
Multidisciplinary team (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy) within 24 h. Swallow assessment before oral intake. Mood screen at 4–6 weeks.

references.label: ESO Guidelines on intravenous thrombolysis for acute ischaemic stroke (2021)
AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke (2019, with updates)
WHO Package of essential noncommunicable disease interventions (PEN) — Stroke
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Acute intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH)
presentation: Sudden severe headache, vomiting, focal neurology and rapid deterioration in level of consciousness (more so than ischaemic stroke).
Often known hypertension; or anticoagulant / antiplatelet use.
Pupillary changes, posturing, Cushing reflex (bradycardia + hypertension) signal raised ICP.
redFlags: GCS ≤ 8, fixed dilated pupil — impending tentorial herniation.
Cerebellar haematoma > 3 cm — surgical emergency, risk of brainstem compression.
Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (suspect if 'thunderclap' headache; mostly subarachnoid blood pattern on CT).

diagnostics.rationale: Volume and location predict outcome; ICH score.
Identify aneurysm, AVM, dural sinus thrombosis underlying.

diagnostics.test: FBC, coag (INR, APTT), platelet count, U&E, glucose, group + save.
diagnostics.rationale: Identify reversible coagulopathy; prepare for surgery.

management.detail: Intubate for GCS ≤ 8, depressed gag, vomiting. Elevate head of bed 30°. Avoid hypotonic fluids.

Acute lowering to systolic 130–140 mmHg within first hour — IV labetalol 10–20 mg bolus, then infusion 1–2 mg/min OR nicardipine. INTERACT-2 + ATACH-2 trials: SBP target 140 mmHg safe + may reduce haematoma expansion.

Warfarin: vitamin K 10 mg IV + 4-factor PCC 50 IU/kg. Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV. Factor Xa DOAC: andexanet alfa OR 4-factor PCC 50 IU/kg. Heparin: protamine 1 mg per 100 IU heparin given in past 2–3 h. Antiplatelet: platelet transfusion ONLY if neurosurgery imminent (PATCH trial — harmful otherwise).
Elevation, hypertonic saline (3% 5 mL/kg bolus) or mannitol 1 g/kg IV; reverse hypotonic states; sedate and target normocapnia. Avoid steroids.

management.step: Seizure prophylaxis ONLY if seizure occurs
management.detail: Not routine. Treat seizures with IV levetiracetam or phenytoin.

Indications for surgery: cerebellar haematoma > 3 cm with deterioration or brainstem compression; superficial lobar haematoma > 30 mL with mass effect; hydrocephalus from IVH (EVD); selected supratentorial cases (STITCH II, MISTIE III for minimally-invasive evacuation).
Glucose control, fever management, DVT prophylaxis (mechanical immediately; LMWH after 24–48 h if haematoma stable), aspiration precautions, nutritional support.

Aggressive BP control < 130/80 (most important intervention). Address underlying cause (CAA, hypertensive vasculopathy, anticoagulant indication review). Statin generally continued — no clear benefit but withholding not justified.

references.label: AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage (2022)
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Diabetic foot ulcer and infection — IWGDF integrated management
presentation: Ulcer or wound on foot of person with diabetes.
Often painless (sensory neuropathy); may have surrounding cellulitis, sloughy base, exposed deep structures.
Risk factors: peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease (PAD), foot deformity (Charcot, hammer toes), prior ulcer/amputation, smoking, poor glycaemic control.
redFlags: Severe infection: systemic features (fever, tachycardia, raised WBC/CRP), extensive cellulitis (> 2 cm beyond ulcer), abscess, gangrene, deep tissue involvement.
Acute Charcot foot: red, warm, swollen foot without obvious infection in a neuropathic patient (skin temp > 2°C contralateral; rocker-bottom deformity if untreated).
Critical limb ischaemia (rest pain, gangrene, non-healing wound, ABI < 0.4 or absent pedal pulses).
Necrotising fasciitis (rapid progression, pain disproportionate, crepitus, dusky skin) — surgical emergency.

diagnostics.test: Wagner / UT classification + IDSA infection severity grading.

diagnostics.rationale: Detect osteomyelitis (positive PTB or X-ray changes after 2 weeks).

diagnostics.test: MRI foot if deep infection / osteomyelitis suspected and X-ray equivocal.
Deep tissue swab or curettage after debridement (NOT superficial swab).
ABI / toe-brachial index; arterial duplex if PAD suspected.
diagnostics.rationale: Identify ischaemia; revascularisation may be needed.

management.detail: Diabetes specialist, vascular, orthopaedic, infectious disease, podiatry, microbiology, nursing — diabetic foot clinic significantly reduces amputation.

management.step: Offloading is essential — non-removable total-contact cast or removable knee-high walker
management.detail: Plantar ulcers will not heal without effective pressure relief. Offloading is the most-evidence-based intervention after revascularisation.
Sharp surgical debridement of necrotic tissue and callus at each visit; gentle saline cleansing; appropriate dressing (foam, hydrocolloid, alginate per exudate).

management.step: Antibiotic for infected ulcer (DON'T treat colonised but non-infected)
management.detail: Mild (IDSA 2 — local cellulitis < 2 cm): oral flucloxacillin or co-amoxiclav 7–14 days. Moderate (IDSA 3 — deeper / systemic mild): IV co-amoxiclav OR ceftriaxone + metronidazole 14–21 days. Severe (IDSA 4 — sepsis): IV broad-spectrum (piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem) + cover MRSA with vancomycin in high-risk areas. Adjust to deep tissue culture results.
4–6 weeks of bone-active antibiotic following surgical debridement; longer if residual bone infection. Some chronic cases require resection.
Endovascular or surgical bypass for PAD with non-healing ulcer or critical limb ischaemia.
Strict immobilisation in total-contact cast for 8–12 weeks until temperature normalises; bisphosphonate role debated. Bracing after.
Aim HbA1c 7–8% during healing. Smoking cessation. Statin, ACEi/ARB per CVD risk. Daily foot inspection + protective footwear lifelong.
Spare limb where possible. If amputation needed, plan optimal level for prosthetic rehabilitation; psychological support.

references.label: IWGDF Guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetic foot disease (2023)
IDSA Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Diabetic Foot Infections
Kenya National Clinical Guidelines for Management of Diabetes Mellitus, Ministry of Health

title: Sepsis and septic shock — adult (Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
presentation: Suspected or confirmed infection PLUS organ dysfunction (Sepsis-3: SOFA increase ≥ 2).
Septic shock: persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor to maintain MAP ≥ 65 mmHg AND lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate volume resuscitation.
Common foci: chest, urinary, intra-abdominal, skin/soft tissue, CNS, line.
redFlags: Suspected necrotising soft-tissue infection (urgent surgical debridement).
Pregnancy / immediate postpartum — maternal sepsis pathway.

diagnostics.test: Lactate, FBC, U&E, LFT, coagulation, CRP, blood gas, glucose, blood cultures × 2 from different sites.
Urine + sputum + wound + CSF / drain fluid cultures per suspected focus.
Imaging per suspected source (CXR, CT abdomen, USS abscess).
Continuous monitoring: BP, HR, SpO2, RR, urine output, mental state.

management.detail: Measure lactate; obtain blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics (do not delay > 45 min); broad-spectrum IV antibiotic; begin 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 within 3 h; vasopressor if hypotension persists during/after resuscitation to keep MAP ≥ 65.
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV (or meropenem 1 g if Pen-anaphylaxis / known ESBL); add vancomycin if MRSA risk; add clindamycin for necrotising soft tissue. De-escalate at 48–72 h per cultures.
Drain abscess, remove infected line, debride necrotic tissue, decompress urinary obstruction, surgical washout of intra-abdominal source — ideally within 6–12 h of recognition.

Noradrenaline 0.05–0.5 microgram/kg/min via central line (peripheral acceptable < 6 h while CVC sourced). Add vasopressin 0.03 unit/min if persistent. Add adrenaline if myocardial dysfunction. Target MAP ≥ 65 mmHg.
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV (continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 h) for septic shock requiring noradrenaline > 0.25 microgram/kg/min for > 4 h.
Low tidal volume 6 mL/kg IBW, plateau pressure < 30 cmH2O, prone positioning for PaO2/FiO2 < 150.

management.step: Glucose 7.8–10 mmol/L; VTE prophylaxis; stress-ulcer prophylaxis selectively
management.detail: Avoid tight glycaemic control; LMWH unless contraindicated; PPI for high-risk patients only (ventilated > 48 h, coagulopathy).
De-escalate antibiotics; assess for de-resuscitation (negative fluid balance after 48 h); spontaneous breathing trial daily; rehabilitation.

title: Acute adrenal crisis (Addisonian crisis)
presentation: Hypotension/shock disproportionate to clinical picture.
Severe vomiting, abdominal pain, fever.
Hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, prerenal AKI.
Background of known Addison's, hypopituitarism, recent steroid withdrawal, or steroid stress in chronic glucocorticoid therapy.
Precipitants: infection, surgery, trauma, MI, missed doses, vomiting unable to take oral hydrocortisone.
redFlags: Shock unresponsive to fluid + vasopressor — give empiric hydrocortisone.
Concurrent severe infection (sepsis pathway as well).

diagnostics.test: Random cortisol + ACTH at presentation BEFORE first steroid dose (if rapidly available).
diagnostics.rationale: Diagnostic confirmation later; do NOT delay treatment.
Identify hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis.

management.detail: Do NOT delay for confirmatory tests. Repeat 100 mg IV every 6 h for first 24 h (or continuous infusion 200 mg/24 h).
1 L 0.9% NaCl over the first hour, then titrate to volume status. Add dextrose if hypoglycaemic. Avoid hypotonic fluids — risk worsening hyponatraemia.
Calcium gluconate for cardiac protection if K+ > 6.5 with ECG changes; insulin/dextrose; β2-agonist; will improve with hydrocortisone + saline.
10% dextrose IV; monitor glucose every 1–2 h initially.
Antibiotics for infection; analgesia + surgical input if trauma/abdomen.
After 24–48 h stability, reduce hydrocortisone to 50 mg every 6 h IV, then 20 mg morning / 10 mg evening oral (or pre-illness dose if known).

management.step: Add fludrocortisone once on oral hydrocortisone ≤ 50 mg/day
management.detail: Fludrocortisone 0.05–0.1 mg daily (for Addison's; not needed in secondary adrenal insufficiency).

All patients with adrenal insufficiency need a medic-alert bracelet, hydrocortisone emergency injection kit, sick-day rules (double oral steroid dose for febrile illness; switch to IM/IV hydrocortisone if vomiting).

references.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline — Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (2016)

title: Severe hyperkalaemia — emergency management
presentation: Serum K+ > 6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes (peaked T, widened QRS, loss of P wave, sine wave) OR K+ > 6.5 regardless of ECG.
Often asymptomatic; muscle weakness, paraesthesia, palpitations at higher levels; cardiac arrest at very high levels.
Causes: AKI / CKD, drugs (ACEi/ARB, NSAID, spironolactone, K-sparing diuretic, trimethoprim, heparin), rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, haemolysis, Addison's, acidosis.
redFlags: Peaked T waves, widened QRS, loss of P, sine wave on ECG — IMMEDIATE calcium.
Bradycardia or any arrhythmia with hyperkalaemia.

diagnostics.test: U&E, creatinine, glucose, blood gas, CK if rhabdomyolysis suspected.

management.step: Cardiac protection — calcium FIRST if any ECG change
management.detail: 10% calcium gluconate 10 mL IV over 5–10 min (or 10% calcium chloride 5 mL via central line). Onset within 1–3 min; lasts 30–60 min. Repeat if ECG changes persist after 10 min.

management.step: Shift K+ intracellularly (lowers serum K+ over 15–30 min)
management.detail: Insulin-dextrose: 10 units soluble insulin in 250 mL 10% dextrose IV over 30 min (or 50 mL 50% dextrose + 10 units actrapid push). Check glucose hourly × 6 h — hypoglycaemia risk. Nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg additive effect. Sodium bicarbonate ONLY in severe metabolic acidosis (additive to insulin in some protocols).

management.step: Remove K+ from the body (slower onset)
management.detail: Potassium binders: patiromer 8.4 g or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g (faster onset, 1 h). Diuresis if euvolaemic (IV furosemide 40–80 mg). Polystyrene sulfonate (Resonium / Kayexalate) — slower, GI side effects.

management.step: Haemodialysis — definitive treatment when other measures inadequate or in established renal failure
management.detail: Indications: K+ > 6.5 unresponsive, AKI/CKD with oliguria, severe acidosis, fluid overload. Most effective single intervention; arrange urgently.
ACEi/ARB, spironolactone, NSAID, trimethoprim, K supplements; review other contributors.

management.step: Restrict dietary K+; identify and treat cause
management.detail: Treat AKI; address rhabdomyolysis (IV fluids + alkalinisation); address acidosis.

management.step: Re-measure K+ every 30–60 min until stable
management.detail: Continuous cardiac monitoring; expect K+ fall over 30–60 min with insulin/dextrose.

references.label: UK Renal Association — Treatment of acute hyperkalaemia in adults (2020)
KDIGO + ASN consensus on potassium management

title: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia
presentation: Serum Na+ < 125 mmol/L with severe symptoms — seizures, coma, respiratory arrest, vomiting.
Moderate symptoms: headache, nausea, confusion, falls.

Common causes: SIADH, thiazide diuretic, hypovolaemic (vomiting, diarrhoea, Addison's), hypervolaemic (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic), psychogenic polydipsia, MDMA, exercise-associated hyponatraemia.
redFlags: Seizure / coma / brainstem herniation signs → urgent hypertonic saline.
Acute onset (< 48 h) hyponatraemia — higher risk of cerebral oedema.
Chronic hyponatraemia (> 48 h or unknown duration) — risk of osmotic demyelination if corrected too fast.
Concurrent hypokalaemia — replacing K+ raises Na+, increases ODS risk.
Hypothyroidism / adrenal insufficiency — treat the cause.

diagnostics.test: Repeat serum Na+ + plasma osmolality + paired urine Na+ and osmolality.
diagnostics.rationale: Classify as hypotonic (true) vs pseudo / translocational; identify SIADH (urine osmolality > 100, urine Na+ > 30 in euvolaemic patient).

diagnostics.test: Clinical volume assessment — JVP, skin turgor, oedema, BP, postural drop.
Glucose; calculate corrected Na+ in hyperglycaemia.

management.detail: 3% NaCl 150 mL IV over 10 min (or 2 mL/kg). Repeat × 2 if symptoms persist (max 3 doses). Target Na+ rise of 5 mmol/L acutely. STOP hypertonic saline once symptoms resolve.
Total rise: max 10 mmol/L in 24 h (8 mmol/L if high ODS risk: chronic, hypokalaemia, malnutrition, alcoholism, liver disease). Re-check Na+ every 2–4 h.
Give 5% dextrose 10 mL/kg over 1 h or DDAVP 2 microgram SC every 8 h to drop Na+ back to target rate. This prevents osmotic demyelination.

Stop thiazide / SSRI / carbamazepine. SIADH: fluid restriction 500–1000 mL/day; consider tolvaptan (vaptan) or oral urea. Hypovolaemic: 0.9% NaCl cautiously. Hypervolaemic: salt + fluid restrict + loop diuretic; treat underlying HF/cirrhosis.
K+ replacement raises Na+; combine carefully into the daily correction target.
Identify malignancy, CNS / pulmonary disease, drugs.

references.label: European Society of Endocrinology / ERA-EDTA / ESICM clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia (2014)
Spasovski G et al. EJE 2014 — Hyponatraemia diagnosis and treatment

title: Refractory / super-refractory status epilepticus
presentation: Continuous seizure activity (clinical or electrographic) > 5 min, or repeated seizures without recovery between, that fails two adequately-dosed antiseizure drugs (refractory) or persists > 24 h on anaesthetic infusion (super-refractory).
redFlags: Non-convulsive status epilepticus in altered consciousness — EEG essential.
Hypoxia, severe acidosis, hyperthermia from prolonged convulsion.
Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, autoimmune encephalitis, CNS infection — treatable underlying cause.
New-onset refractory status epilepticus (NORSE) — autoimmune workup.
Pregnancy: maternal + fetal compromise; consider eclampsia (Mg + delivery planning).

diagnostics.test: Capillary glucose; venous blood gas; U&E; calcium; magnesium; FBC; LFT; CK; toxicology screen.
LP if encephalitis / meningitis suspected and no contraindication.
diagnostics.rationale: HSV PCR + autoimmune workup (NMDAR Ab, LGI1, GABA-B).

diagnostics.test: Continuous EEG monitoring once on anaesthetic.

management.detail: ABC; protect airway; high-flow O2; check glucose (give 10% dextrose if hypoglycaemic). IV/IM/buccal: lorazepam 4 mg IV, OR midazolam 10 mg IM/buccal, OR diazepam 10 mg IV. Give thiamine 200 mg IV if alcohol use suspected (before glucose).
If still seizing at 5 min, repeat benzodiazepine once.

management.step: Stage 3 (20–40 min) — second-line antiseizure drug (established status)
management.detail: ONE of (per ESETT trial — equivalent efficacy): IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4.5 g) over 5 min; IV valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3 g) over 10 min — AVOID in young women + pregnancy + valproate-naive without PPP; IV fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (max 1.5 g) over 10 min, OR phenytoin 20 mg/kg (max 1 g) at ≤ 50 mg/min with cardiac monitor.

Intubate. ICU. IV propofol bolus 2 mg/kg then infusion 5–10 mg/kg/h titrated to EEG burst-suppression. OR midazolam loading 0.2 mg/kg then 0.1–0.5 mg/kg/h. OR thiopental / ketamine combinations. Continue for 24–48 h then attempt wean.

Specialist neurology + ICU. Consider: ketamine infusion, magnesium infusion (pre-eclampsia), high-dose pyridoxine (INH toxicity), corticosteroids + IVIG / plasma exchange (autoimmune NORSE), ketogenic diet, hypothermia, surgery.
Antiviral (aciclovir) for HSV; antibiotics for bacterial meningitis; magnesium for eclampsia; pyridoxine for INH; correct electrolytes; immunotherapy for autoimmune.
Continue at least 2 antiseizure drugs (e.g. levetiracetam + valproate); aim for 24 h seizure-free on EEG before weaning anaesthetic.

references.label: Neurocritical Care Society Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Status Epilepticus (2012, with updates)
ESETT trial NEJM 2019 — levetiracetam, valproate, fosphenytoin equivalent
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders (mhGAP adaptation), Ministry of Health

title: Acute viral encephalitis (focus HSV)
presentation: Fever + acute or subacute alteration of mental status / personality change / confusion.
New-onset seizures, especially focal.
Focal neurological deficits — dysphasia, hemiparesis (HSV often temporal).
Headache, nausea, vomiting; signs of meningeal irritation may be subtle.
redFlags: Focal neurology with raised ICP — neurosurgery review, defer LP until imaging.
Immunocompromised — consider CMV, VZV, JC virus, toxoplasma, cryptococcus.
Pregnant — risk to fetus (VZV, HSV); manage with obstetric input.

diagnostics.test: MRI brain (T2/FLAIR + DWI) — preferred; CT if MRI unavailable.
diagnostics.rationale: Temporal lobe oedema highly suggestive of HSV encephalitis.

diagnostics.test: LP — opening pressure, cell count, protein, glucose, HSV-1/2 + VZV + enterovirus PCR; bacterial cultures; oligoclonal bands.
diagnostics.rationale: Definitive diagnosis; lymphocytic pleocytosis + raised protein typical.

diagnostics.test: EEG — temporal periodic discharges support HSV.
Blood cultures, HIV test, autoimmune encephalitis panel if PCR negative.
Pregnancy test in women of childbearing potential.

management.detail: IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg (lean body weight) every 8 h for 14–21 days. Start empirically while waiting for LP / PCR if clinical suspicion — early treatment dramatically reduces mortality and morbidity for HSV encephalitis.

management.step: Cover empirical bacterial meningitis as well
management.detail: IV ceftriaxone 2 g BID + amoxicillin 2 g 4-hourly (≥ 50 yrs / immunocompromised — Listeria cover). Stop when bacterial cultures negative.
Benzodiazepine then second-line per status epilepticus pathway. Consider prophylactic levetiracetam in acute encephalitis with focal MRI changes.
Head elevation 30°; control fever (paracetamol, cooling); avoid hypotonic fluids; mannitol or 3% NaCl for impending herniation; monitor ICP if available.
Airway protection if GCS ≤ 8; DVT prophylaxis; nutritional support; pressure-area care.
Aciclovir crystal nephropathy risk — keep well hydrated, monitor U&E daily, adjust dose for renal impairment.

management.step: Treat alternative diagnoses based on PCR/serology
management.detail: VZV: continue aciclovir + steroid if vasculitis. CMV: ganciclovir. JC: reduce immunosuppression. Autoimmune (NMDAR Ab): high-dose steroids + IVIG / plasma exchange + tumour search (ovarian teratoma).
Post-encephalitis cognitive deficits, behavioural change, epilepsy common; multidisciplinary rehabilitation.

references.label: BIA + ABN — UK national guidelines for the management of viral encephalitis in adults (2012)

title: Myasthenic crisis (acute neuromuscular respiratory failure)
presentation: Severe weakness with respiratory failure in known or suspected myasthenia gravis.

Often precipitated by infection, surgery, medication change, missed pyridostigmine, certain drugs (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, beta-blockers, magnesium, neuromuscular blockers, ICI immunotherapy).
Bulbar weakness (dysphagia, dysarthria), dyspnoea worse on exertion / lying flat, reduced FVC < 1 L or 20 mL/kg, single-breath count < 25.
redFlags: FVC < 15 mL/kg or falling rapidly → intubate.
Severe bulbar weakness with secretion pooling → high aspiration risk.
Cholinergic crisis (over-treatment with anticholinesterase) — pinpoint pupils, salivation, lacrimation, fasciculation, diarrhoea — distinguish carefully.

diagnostics.test: FVC, single-breath count (count to 25 on one breath in English ≈ FVC 2 L), negative inspiratory force.
diagnostics.rationale: Quantify respiratory muscle strength and trend.
Hypercapnia is a LATE sign — do NOT wait for it before intubating.

management.detail: Sit upright; monitor FVC and SpO2; nasal cannula O2 to keep SpO2 ≥ 94%. Intubate ELECTIVELY (don't wait for crash) for FVC < 15 mL/kg, hypoxia, bulbar weakness with aspiration, or rapid trajectory decline. Avoid succinylcholine and aminoglycoside-class neuromuscular relaxants — use rocuronium with reduced dose under careful TOF monitoring.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, beta-blockers, magnesium IV, iodinated contrast, statins (review), ICI immunotherapy.
Plasma exchange (PLEX) 5 sessions over 7–14 days OR IVIG 2 g/kg over 2–5 days. Both equivalent in efficacy; PLEX may be slightly faster. Specialist input.
Prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily can transiently worsen weakness in first 1–2 weeks (treatment-induced exacerbation); start AFTER PLEX/IVIG given to prevent worsening crisis.

management.step: Continue / restart pyridostigmine — but recognise cholinergic crisis
management.detail: Resume pyridostigmine 60 mg 4–6-hourly once oral feeding safe. If history suggests over-treatment (recent dose escalation, cholinergic symptoms): WITHDRAW pyridostigmine for 48 h and reassess.
Azathioprine, mycophenolate, rituximab, eculizumab (refractory), efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab — specialist outpatient plan.
Thymectomy indicated for thymoma; consider for non-thymomatous generalised AChR-positive MG age < 65 (MGTX trial).
Educate patient on drugs to avoid (printed list), early symptoms of crisis, emergency contact pathway, vaccination (especially pneumococcal, influenza).

references.label: International Consensus Guidance for Management of Myasthenia Gravis (Sanders et al. Neurology 2016, 2020 update)

title: Severe acute pancreatitis — adult
presentation: Severe constant epigastric pain radiating to back, nausea, vomiting.
Diagnosis (2 of 3): characteristic pain, amylase / lipase ≥ 3× ULN, characteristic imaging.
Severity: Atlanta classification — mild (no organ failure), moderately severe (transient OF < 48 h, local complications), severe (persistent organ failure > 48 h).
Causes: gallstones, alcohol (top 2), hypertriglyceridaemia, ERCP, drugs (azathioprine, valproate, GLP-1, oestrogens), trauma, idiopathic.
redFlags: Persistent SIRS / organ failure (SBP < 90, RR > 20, AKI, ARDS).
Necrotising pancreatitis with infection (often after first week — fever, sepsis, deterioration).

diagnostics.test: Serum lipase (more specific than amylase); ALT > 150 supports gallstone aetiology.
Contrast CT abdomen at 72–96 h if severe / no improvement — modified CT severity index.
diagnostics.rationale: Identify necrosis + collections; do NOT do CT in first 24 h (underestimates necrosis).

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, calcium, glucose, triglycerides, blood gas, lactate, CRP at 48 h.
diagnostics.rationale: Severity scoring (Glasgow-Imrie, BISAP, APACHE-II); calcium / triglyceride aetiology.

diagnostics.test: MRCP / EUS if biliary cause + jaundice / cholangitis.

management.step: Early aggressive fluid resuscitation — but goal-directed, not blanket large volumes
management.detail: Lactated Ringer's 5–10 mL/kg/h for the first 12–24 h, reassessing every 4–6 h to euvolaemia (HR < 120, MAP > 65, urine output 0.5–1 mL/kg/h, lactate falling). Avoid OVER-resuscitation (WATERFALL trial — moderate volume superior to aggressive).
IV opioid (morphine, fentanyl); avoid pethidine (poorly evidenced 'Oddi sphincter' claim is outdated). Epidural analgesia in severe cases.
NG or NJ feeding is preferred to NPO if patient can tolerate. Reduces infectious complications and bacterial translocation. TPN only if enteral truly impossible.

Gallstone + cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction → urgent ERCP within 24–48 h. Alcohol → IV thiamine, treat withdrawal, brief intervention. Hypertriglyceridaemia → insulin infusion ± plasmapheresis. Drug-induced → stop drug. Cholecystectomy during the same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis; after recovery for severe.

management.step: Antibiotics ONLY for suspected infected necrosis
management.detail: Do NOT routinely prophylactically antibiotic. If clinical deterioration > 7–10 days with fever / sepsis: CT-guided FNA + start meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam. Image-guided drainage / minimally-invasive necrosectomy (step-up) preferred over open.
Respiratory support (NIV / IMV with lung-protective ventilation for ARDS); renal replacement therapy for AKI; vasopressors for septic / distributive shock; monitor intra-abdominal pressure.

Alcohol cessation. Cholecystectomy. Manage diabetes (often new onset after severe pancreatitis). Pseudocyst surveillance / drainage if symptomatic > 6 weeks. Pancreatic exocrine replacement if steatorrhoea.

references.label: AGA Institute Guideline for the Initial Management of Acute Pancreatitis (2018, updated)
IAP/APA evidence-based guidelines for the management of acute pancreatitis
WATERFALL trial NEJM 2022 — moderate vs aggressive fluid

title: Acute variceal haemorrhage (oesophageal / gastric)
presentation: Haematemesis (bright red) / melaena in patient with cirrhosis / portal hypertension.
Often haemodynamically unstable; encephalopathy may worsen.
Mortality remains 15–25% in first episode despite modern care.
redFlags: Concurrent infection (SBP, cellulitis) — drives rebleeding and mortality.

diagnostics.test: FBC, urgent crossmatch 4 units, coagulation, fibrinogen, U&E, LFT, lactate, blood gas.
Lactate / Glasgow-Blatchford score, AIMS65 — risk stratification.
Urgent upper GI endoscopy within 12 hours.

management.detail: Intubate for GCS ≤ 8, ongoing massive haematemesis, or for safe endoscopy. Two large-bore IVs, monitoring.
Aim Hb 70–80 g/L — over-transfusion increases portal pressure and rebleeding (Villanueva et al. NEJM 2013). Use platelet > 50, fibrinogen > 1.5, INR target < 2.5 (avoid over-correction).
Terlipressin 2 mg IV every 4 h (preferred where available — reduces mortality), OR octreotide 50 microgram IV bolus + 25–50 microgram/h infusion × 2–5 days, OR somatostatin. Continue for 2–5 days.
IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily for 5–7 days — reduces mortality, rebleeding, SBP, and bacterial infection. Give to ALL patients with cirrhosis and upper GI bleed regardless of ascites.
Variceal band ligation for oesophageal varices; tissue adhesive (cyanoacrylate glue) for gastric varices. Pre-procedural IV erythromycin 250 mg 30 min before improves view.

Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore / Minnesota tube) as bridge — protect airway; max 24 h. Self-expanding metal stent (SX-Ella Danis). TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) — definitive for refractory bleeding.
Lactulose 30 mL every 1–2 h to 3–4 soft stools/day; rifaximin 550 mg BD adjunct. Treat precipitants (infection, electrolyte, sedatives, GI bleed itself).

Non-selective β-blocker (carvedilol 6.25 mg BD or propranolol 20–40 mg BD titrated to HR 55) + repeat endoscopic band ligation every 2–4 weeks until eradication, then surveillance every 6–12 months. Consider TIPS if rebleeding despite combination therapy.

references.label: Baveno VII Consensus Workshop on Portal Hypertension (2022)
AASLD Practice Guidance on Portal Hypertensive Bleeding in Cirrhosis

title: Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI)
presentation: Acute kidney injury in cirrhosis with ascites, without other identifiable cause after volume challenge.

Updated 2015 ICA criteria: AKI in cirrhosis + no improvement after 2 days off diuretics and with albumin 1 g/kg, no shock, no nephrotoxin, no parenchymal kidney disease (proteinuria < 0.5 g/day, no haematuria, normal USS).
HRS-AKI replaces older 'HRS type 1'; HRS-NAKI replaces 'type 2'.
redFlags: Acute-on-chronic liver failure with multi-organ failure.

diagnostics.test: Urine albumin / sodium / sediment + USS kidneys.
diagnostics.rationale: Exclude parenchymal renal disease and obstruction; urine Na often < 10 mmol/L in HRS.
Identify and treat SBP / other infection (common precipitant).

management.step: Withhold nephrotoxins, diuretics, NSAID, lactulose adjustment
management.detail: Stop ACEi/ARB, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, IV contrast. Pause diuretics.
Human albumin 20% 1 g/kg/day (max 100 g) × 2 days. If creatinine improves, HRS excluded; treat as pre-renal.

Terlipressin 0.5–1 mg IV every 4–6 h (titrate to MAP rise + diuresis; max 12 mg/day) × up to 14 days OR continuous infusion 2 mg/24 h escalating to 12 mg/24 h. Combine with albumin 20–40 g/day. Alternative: noradrenaline infusion (ICU only) targeting MAP rise 10 mmHg; or midodrine + octreotide + albumin (less effective).
Stop if respiratory failure (terlipressin can cause acute respiratory distress — CONFIRM trial signal), severe ischaemia (digital, mesenteric, cardiac), or hyponatraemia.
SBP: IV cefotaxime + albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1 + 1 g/kg day 3. Variceal bleed treatment per variceal pathway. Avoid further hits.
RRT as bridge to liver transplantation; not for HRS without transplant prospect (poor outcomes). Continuous modalities preferred for haemodynamic stability.

management.step: Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment
management.detail: Refer urgently to transplant centre. Combined liver-kidney transplant considered for prolonged HRS or pre-existing CKD.

references.label: International Club of Ascites consensus criteria (2015, updated 2019)
EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines for management of decompensated cirrhosis (2018)
AASLD Practice Guidance on hepatorenal syndrome

title: Massive pulmonary embolism (high-risk PE)
presentation: Sudden cardiovascular collapse / shock / cardiac arrest in patient with PE risk factors (immobility, malignancy, recent surgery, OCP/pregnancy, prior VTE).
Dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, syncope, haemoptysis.
ECG: sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3, right heart strain (T inversion V1–V3); raised troponin / BNP.
Echo: right ventricular dilatation / hypokinesis, McConnell sign, septal flattening.
redFlags: Persistent hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg or drop > 40) — massive PE, immediate thrombolysis indication.
Cardiac arrest with suspected PE — consider intra-arrest thrombolysis.
Pregnant — increased PE risk; careful imaging choice (V/Q vs CTPA).
Active bleeding — contraindication to thrombolysis; consider catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy.

diagnostics.test: CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) — first-line if stable.
Bedside echo if too unstable for CT.
diagnostics.rationale: RV strain supports diagnosis in collapsed patient.

diagnostics.test: D-dimer NOT useful when high pre-test probability + instability — proceed direct to imaging.
V/Q scan if CTPA contraindicated (severe renal impairment, contrast allergy, pregnancy).

management.detail: High-flow O2; cautious IV fluid (500 mL bolus then reassess — RV failure worsens with excess fluid); central + arterial line.
Noradrenaline first-line; add dobutamine 2.5–10 microgram/kg/min if RV dysfunction with adequate MAP. AVOID inhaled NO without ICU experience.

management.step: Systemic thrombolysis — first-line for massive PE without bleeding contraindications
management.detail: IV alteplase 100 mg over 2 h (or 50 mg over 1–2 h if higher bleed risk); follow with unfractionated heparin once aPTT < 2× normal post-lysis.
For high-risk PE with relative contraindication to systemic lysis, or post-lysis failure. Specialist interventional radiology / cardiology centres.
Massive PE with absolute lysis contraindication or failure; specialist cardiothoracic centre.
Unfractionated heparin infusion during resuscitation / lysis; transition to LMWH then DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban) for at least 3 months — lifelong if unprovoked, malignancy, persistent risk factor.
Consider intra-arrest 50 mg alteplase bolus; continue CPR ≥ 60 min after lysis.
Echocardiography at 3–6 months for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) screen; if persistent dyspnoea, V/Q scan; specialist PH referral.

references.label: ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism (2019, updated 2024)
AHA Scientific Statement on Management of Massive and Submassive Pulmonary Embolism
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis)
presentation: Severe thyrotoxicosis precipitated by infection, surgery, trauma, RAI, iodine load (contrast), childbirth, withdrawal of antithyroid drug, DKA.
Hyperpyrexia > 38.5°C, agitation / delirium / coma, tachycardia > 130, AF, heart failure, vomiting / diarrhoea, jaundice.
Burch-Wartofsky score ≥ 45 supports diagnosis; ≥ 25–44 impending.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirm thyrotoxicosis; treatment urgency does not wait for results.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, glucose, LFT, calcium, blood culture, CXR, ECG.

management.detail: Cooling (sponging, cold IV fluids, paracetamol). AVOID aspirin (displaces T4 from binding proteins). IV fluids; correct electrolytes.
Propylthiouracil (PTU) 500–1000 mg PO/NG loading then 200 mg every 4 h (preferred — also blocks T4→T3); OR carbimazole 60–80 mg/day. Both via NG if unable to swallow.

management.step: Block release — wait at least 1 hour after thionamide
management.detail: Lugol's iodine 8 drops every 6 h (or potassium iodide 5 drops every 6 h) — at least 1 h after thionamide to avoid further hormone synthesis.

Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 6 h (also covers possible adrenal insufficiency). Propranolol 60–80 mg every 4 h PO/NG OR esmolol infusion 50–200 microgram/kg/min IV — controls tachycardia and conversion. AVOID propranolol in decompensated HF — use digoxin / cautious esmolol.
Antibiotics if infection, treat DKA, obstetric input for pregnancy.
Removes circulating thyroid hormone; consider in failure of medical therapy.
Total thyroidectomy or RAI ablation after euthyroid state achieved. Continue antithyroid therapy in meantime.

references.label: American Thyroid Association Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Hyperthyroidism (2016)
Burch HB, Wartofsky L — Life-threatening thyrotoxicosis: thyroid storm (1993)

title: Paracetamol overdose — adult emergency management
presentation: Single acute overdose (within 1 h ingestion) or staggered (multiple doses > 1 h apart).
First 24 h: often asymptomatic; nausea, vomiting, pallor, lethargy.
24–72 h: hepatic damage emerges — RUQ pain, deranged LFT, INR rise, encephalopathy.
72–96 h: fulminant hepatic failure peak; jaundice, encephalopathy, AKI, lactic acidosis.
≥ 7.5 g (or > 150 mg/kg, whichever is lower) acute is potentially hepatotoxic; staggered > 4 g/24 h needs treatment if symptomatic.
redFlags: Late presentation (> 8 h post-ingestion) — start NAC empirically.
King's College criteria (pH < 7.3 at 24 h OR INR > 6.5 / creatinine > 300 / encephalopathy grade III/IV) — transplant referral.
Co-ingestion of other hepatotoxins or staggered overdose — higher risk regardless of nomogram.
Pregnancy — maternal + fetal NAC is safe and effective.
Suicidal ideation — mental health pathway after medical stabilisation.

diagnostics.test: Serum paracetamol level at 4 hours post-ingestion (no earlier) — plot on Rumack-Matthew nomogram (UK 100 mg/L line; some countries use 150 line).
diagnostics.rationale: Determines whether NAC is needed for acute overdose.

diagnostics.test: LFT (ALT), INR, creatinine, venous blood gas + lactate, glucose.

management.step: If presented within 1 h of acute ingestion → consider activated charcoal
management.detail: Charcoal 50 g PO if airway protected and ingestion < 1 h. Do NOT delay NAC for this.

management.step: Acute single ingestion < 8 h: take level at ≥ 4 h, treat based on nomogram
management.detail: If above treatment line → IV N-acetylcysteine. If below → no treatment but observe.

management.step: Acute single ingestion 8–24 h post: START NAC IMMEDIATELY, await level (treat unless clearly below line + ALT normal)
management.detail: Time-criticalness rises sharply after 8 h.

management.step: Staggered ingestion / unknown timing: START NAC EMPIRICALLY if dose > 75 mg/kg (or > 150 mg/kg / 24 h)
management.detail: Nomogram not valid; treat regardless.

STANDARD: bag 1 — 150 mg/kg in 200 mL 5% dextrose over 1 h; bag 2 — 50 mg/kg in 500 mL over 4 h; bag 3 — 100 mg/kg in 1000 mL over 16 h. Max body weight 110 kg for dose calculation. SNAP 12-hour alternative: 100 mg/kg over 2 h then 200 mg/kg over 10 h (less reaction, equivalent efficacy).
Common (10–15%) — flushing, urticaria, wheeze; usually first hour. Pause infusion, give chlorphenamine ± nebulised salbutamol, then RESTART at slower rate.

management.step: Re-check ALT, INR, creatinine at end of NAC (21 h) — continue NAC if abnormal
management.detail: Continue NAC if ALT > 2× ULN, INR > 1.3, paracetamol still detectable, or symptomatic. King's College criteria → liver transplant referral.

management.step: Mental health assessment ALWAYS for intentional self-poisoning
management.detail: See mhgap-self-harm pathway; do not discharge without psychiatric review and safety plan.

references.label: MHRA / UK Toxbase paracetamol overdose treatment nomogram and protocol
American Association of Poison Control Centres consensus

title: Opioid overdose — emergency management
presentation: Reduced consciousness, respiratory depression (RR < 12, often slow shallow), pinpoint pupils (miosis).
Cyanosis, bradycardia, hypotension.
Suggestive history / setting (paraphernalia, methadone, fentanyl patches), or known opioid prescription / use.
Pulmonary oedema can occur (especially with heroin / fentanyl).
redFlags: Apnoea, no spontaneous breathing — immediate naloxone + bag-mask ventilation.
Cardiac arrest — full ACLS with naloxone push.
Body-packer (drug mule) — risk of catastrophic OD if package ruptures; surgical opinion.
Fentanyl / carfentanil — much higher doses of naloxone needed; risk of recurrent toxicity.
Sympathomimetic features (mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension) — consider co-ingestion (cocaine, stimulant).

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnosis from triad of reduced consciousness + miosis + respiratory depression.
Capillary glucose, ECG (QT prolongation methadone), ABG.

diagnostics.rationale: Identify opioid + co-ingestants (will not identify fentanyl on standard panel).

diagnostics.test: CXR if hypoxia / persistent symptoms (non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema).
Acetaminophen + salicylate level in unknown overdose.

management.step: Airway + breathing — bag-mask ventilation if apnoeic / hypoventilation
management.detail: Position, jaw thrust, OPA / NPA. Pre-oxygenate before naloxone.

management.step: Naloxone — titrate to ventilation, not to consciousness
management.detail: IV naloxone 0.04–0.4 mg (start low — 40–100 microgram in suspected opioid-dependent patient to avoid precipitated withdrawal), repeat every 2–3 min up to 2 mg or until adequate ventilation. IM 0.4–2 mg if no IV access. Intranasal 2–4 mg via atomiser. Higher doses (up to 10 mg) for fentanyl / carfentanil.

management.step: Naloxone infusion if long-acting opioid (methadone, sustained-release, fentanyl patch)
management.detail: Hourly infusion at 2/3 of the bolus dose that restored breathing. Continue at least 12–24 h. Watch for resedation.

management.step: Remove fentanyl patches; gastric decontamination only for body-packers
management.detail: Whole-bowel irrigation with PEG for body-packers; surgical removal if package rupture suspected.
Supportive O2 / CPAP / IMV; usually resolves over 12–24 h without specific therapy.

management.step: Observe at least 4–6 h after last naloxone dose
management.detail: Discharge only when fully alert, ambulating, normal vital signs sustained without further naloxone. Longer observation (24 h) for long-acting opioids (methadone).

Take-home naloxone training for patient + household; refer to opioid agonist therapy (methadone / buprenorphine — see opioid-use-disorder-treatment); HIV / HCV testing; safe injection counselling; mental health referral if intentional.

references.label: WHO Community management of opioid overdose (2014)
ACMT position statement on opioid overdose management

title: Benzodiazepine overdose
presentation: Reduced consciousness, ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus.
Pure benzodiazepine OD rarely causes severe respiratory depression unless co-ingested with opioid, alcohol, TCA, antihistamine.
Onset: ~30 min oral; minutes IV.
redFlags: Co-ingestion suspected (mixed OD is the norm).
Hypotension, bradycardia, hypothermia (severe or combined OD).

diagnostics.test: Urine drug screen — note false negatives common (clonazepam, alprazolam, lorazepam, midazolam often not detected on basic panels).
Paracetamol + salicylate level if intentional / unknown.

management.detail: Most pure benzodiazepine OD recover with observation only. Position for airway, supplemental O2, IV access, monitoring.

0.2 mg IV over 30 sec, repeat 0.3 mg then 0.5 mg at 1-min intervals (max 3 mg). ONLY consider for: iatrogenic procedural sedation reversal, OR isolated benzodiazepine OD in a non-dependent patient with severe respiratory depression. CONTRAINDICATED in chronic benzodiazepine use (seizure precipitation), TCA / pro-convulsant co-ingestion, status epilepticus / seizure history, raised ICP. Effects last 30–60 min, may need re-dosing.

management.step: Activated charcoal only if presented < 1 h and airway protected
management.detail: Not routinely indicated for isolated benzodiazepine OD due to airway risk.
Discharge home when alert, ambulatory, hemodynamically stable.
Follow specific antidote pathways.
Intentional OD → psychiatric assessment. Iatrogenic dependence → controlled tapering plan (10% per 1–2 weeks).

title: Cyanide poisoning (smoke inhalation, occupational, intentional)
presentation: Rapid onset (minutes) after inhalation of fire smoke (closed-space fire), occupational exposure (mining, electroplating), or intentional ingestion.
Headache, dizziness, anxiety, dyspnoea, seizures, loss of consciousness, cardiovascular collapse.
Cherry-red skin classical but unreliable; venous blood may appear bright red (high venous PaO2 — tissues cannot use O2).
Severe lactic acidosis (lactate > 8 mmol/L in smoke-inhalation victim is virtually diagnostic).
redFlags: Loss of consciousness, seizure, cardiac arrest in smoke-inhalation context.
Severe metabolic acidosis with elevated venous O2 saturation (narrowed AV oxygen gap).
Concurrent CO poisoning (often coexists) — treat both.

diagnostics.test: Lactate (> 8 mmol/L in smoke-inhalation 90% sensitive for cyanide toxicity).
Arterial + venous blood gas (narrowed AV oxygen gap, severe metabolic acidosis).
COHb (carboxyhaemoglobin) — usually co-occurs with cyanide in fire victims.
Cyanide blood level (specialist, results too slow for acute management).

management.detail: High-flow O2 via non-rebreather. Intubate if reduced consciousness, severe acidosis, airway burns.

management.step: Empirical antidote IMMEDIATELY for severe presentation
management.detail: Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) 5 g IV over 15 min — preferred (safer, can give while waiting confirmation). Paediatric: 70 mg/kg up to 5 g. Repeat dose if persistent / re-deterioration.
Sodium thiosulfate 12.5 g IV (paediatric 400 mg/kg, max 12.5 g) over 10 min — can combine with hydroxocobalamin or use alone in resource-limited setting.

management.step: Sodium nitrite + amyl nitrite — older regimen
management.detail: AVOID in smoke-inhalation victim with concurrent CO poisoning (induces methaemoglobinaemia, worsens O2 delivery). Reserve for isolated cyanide ingestion when hydroxocobalamin unavailable.
100% O2 ± hyperbaric per CO-poisoning pathway.
Aggressive resuscitation; vasopressor for hypotension; bicarbonate for severe acidosis.
Skin: remove clothing, irrigate. Ingestion: activated charcoal if < 1 h ingestion AND airway protected.

references.label: American Association of Poison Control Centres / ACMT consensus on cyanide poisoning

title: Toxic alcohol (methanol / ethylene glycol) poisoning
presentation: Suspect in any unexplained severe metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap AND raised osmolal gap.
Methanol: 12–24 h latent period then nausea, abdominal pain, visual symptoms (blurred vision, scotomata, blindness from optic nerve damage); 'snowstorm' visual disturbance.

Ethylene glycol: stage 1 (0–12 h) intoxication 'drunk' without alcohol; stage 2 (12–24 h) cardiopulmonary (tachycardia, hypertension, pulmonary oedema); stage 3 (24–72 h) AKI with calcium oxalate crystalluria.
Sources: methanol — fortified moonshine, antifreeze, windscreen wash; ethylene glycol — antifreeze, brake fluid.
redFlags: Visual changes — methanol-induced blindness can be permanent if delayed treatment.
Anuria — ethylene glycol AKI; needs urgent dialysis.
Concurrent ethanol — affects timing of toxicity (ethanol competes for ADH; symptoms delayed but eventually appear).

diagnostics.test: Blood gas, lactate, glucose, U&E, calcium, anion gap, osmolal gap.
diagnostics.rationale: Raised anion gap acidosis (HAGMA) + raised osmolal gap (> 10 mOsm/kg) classical.
Confirmatory but slow — treat empirically while awaiting.

diagnostics.test: Urinalysis (calcium oxalate crystals in ethylene glycol — variable).
Fluorescein examination under Wood's lamp (ethylene glycol antifreeze contains fluorescein).

management.detail: Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV loading over 30 min then 10 mg/kg every 12 h × 4 doses, then 15 mg/kg every 12 h until level < 3.2 mmol/L AND no acidosis. Continue throughout dialysis.

management.step: Alternative — IV ethanol if fomepizole unavailable
management.detail: Loading 0.8 g/kg as 10% ethanol IV over 30 min, then 100 mg/kg/h infusion. Target serum ethanol 1–1.5 g/L (100–150 mg/dL). Frequent level monitoring; high complication rate; not preferred where fomepizole exists.

Indications: severe acidosis (pH < 7.25 or HCO3 < 15), visual symptoms (methanol), AKI / oliguria, level > 50 mg/dL (15 mmol/L methanol; 50 mg/dL = 8 mmol/L ethylene glycol), failure to respond to fomepizole. Continue until level < 20 mg/dL and no acidosis.

Methanol: folinic acid 1 mg/kg IV every 4 h (max 50 mg) — accelerates formate metabolism. Ethylene glycol: pyridoxine 50 mg IV every 6 h + thiamine 100 mg IV every 6 h — co-factors that convert glycolate to non-toxic metabolites.
IV fluids; bicarbonate for severe acidosis; calcium replacement (ethylene glycol chelates calcium); vasopressor; intubation if severe.
Poisons centre + nephrology / ICU. Ophthalmology for methanol visual changes (urgent fundoscopy).

references.label: AACT / EAPCCT position statement on fomepizole
EXTRIP recommendations for methanol + ethylene glycol

title: Lithium toxicity — acute, acute-on-chronic, chronic
presentation: Acute (large overdose, naive patient): early GI predominant — vomiting, diarrhoea; neurological symptoms develop over hours-days.
Acute-on-chronic (overdose on chronic therapy): combined GI + neuro from the outset; higher morbidity.

Chronic (excess dosing, drug interaction, dehydration, AKI): neurological predominates — tremor, hyperreflexia, ataxia, confusion, dysarthria, seizures, coma. Permanent cerebellar damage possible (SILENT syndrome).
Lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia.
redFlags: Lithium level > 4.0 mmol/L — almost always need haemodialysis.
Persistent neurological signs after correction — SILENT syndrome.
Concurrent NSAID, ACEi/ARB, thiazide, dehydration — accentuate toxicity.

diagnostics.test: Serum lithium level (immediate + 4 h + every 4 h until falling).
U&E, creatinine, calcium, TSH, glucose, ECG (QT prolongation).
Review medications (concurrent NSAID, ACEi, ARB, thiazide, fluconazole).

management.detail: And any nephrotoxic / interacting drug (NSAID, ACEi, ARB, thiazide).
Restore intravascular volume; target urine output 100–300 mL/h. AVOID inducing diuresis with loop / thiazide — these worsen toxicity.
Activated charcoal NOT effective (does not bind lithium). Whole-bowel irrigation (PEG 1–2 L/h) for sustained-release ingestion within 1–2 h.

EXTRIP indications: lithium > 4.0 mmol/L; level 2.5–4.0 + severe symptoms (seizures, coma, life-threatening arrhythmia, renal failure); chronic toxicity with neurological symptoms; impaired renal function. Continue until lithium < 1.0 mmol/L AND no rebound after 6 h off dialysis.
Seizures: benzodiazepine then second-line. Cardiac arrhythmia: avoid additional QT-prolonging drugs. Diabetes insipidus: cautious correction of sodium; consider amiloride.

Consider alternative mood stabiliser (valproate, lamotrigine) especially after severe / SILENT presentation. If continuing lithium, lower dose + closer monitoring + lithium-safe co-prescription review.

title: Beta-blocker overdose
presentation: Hypotension, bradycardia, decreased cardiac output.
Conduction abnormalities — AV block, prolonged QRS (especially with propranolol, sotalol).
Bronchospasm, hypoglycaemia (lipophilic agents — propranolol).
Seizures, coma (lipophilic agents).
Sotalol overdose — torsades de pointes (potassium channel blockade).
redFlags: Co-ingestion of calcium channel blocker, digoxin, TCA — additive cardiotoxicity.

diagnostics.test: Echo if shock (assess LV function for inotrope choice).

management.detail: Atropine 0.5–1 mg IV first-line for bradycardia. Glucose for hypoglycaemia.

management.step: Activated charcoal if < 1 h ingestion + airway protected
management.detail: Consider whole-bowel irrigation for sustained-release.
5–10 mg IV bolus over 1–2 min, repeat once if no response, then infusion 1–10 mg/h (warning: vomiting — protect airway). Acts via cAMP independently of β-receptors.

management.step: High-dose insulin euglycaemia (HIE) therapy — for refractory shock
management.detail: Insulin 1 unit/kg bolus then 0.5–1 unit/kg/h infusion; co-infuse dextrose 0.5 g/kg/h to maintain glucose 5–11 mmol/L; replace potassium. Onset 20–30 min; superior inotropy + insulin resistance in cardiogenic shock.

management.step: IV lipid emulsion for severely lipophilic agent + cardiac arrest / refractory shock
management.detail: 20% Intralipid 1.5 mL/kg bolus then 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion for 30–60 min. Acts as 'lipid sink'.
Noradrenaline / adrenaline / dopamine for shock; isoproterenol if available. Transcutaneous or transvenous pacing for refractory bradycardia.
Specialist centre; bridges through the toxin metabolism window.
Treat torsades with magnesium sulphate 2 g IV; consider isoprenaline + overdrive pacing. Haemodialysis effective for sotalol (water-soluble).

references.label: AACT / ACMT consensus on β-blocker / CCB overdose

title: Calcium channel blocker overdose
presentation: Non-dihydropyridine (verapamil, diltiazem): bradycardia, AV block, hypotension, cardiogenic shock — typically more severe.
Dihydropyridine (amlodipine, nifedipine): pronounced peripheral vasodilation, reflex tachycardia (lost in severe OD), hypotension.
Hyperglycaemia (CCBs impair insulin release), metabolic acidosis (poor perfusion).
Sustained-release preparations cause delayed (4–18 h) presentation.
redFlags: Cardiogenic shock unresponsive to fluid + atropine.
Refractory hyperglycaemia despite insulin (severe poisoning marker).
Sustained-release preparation — delayed peak; admit even if asymptomatic.

diagnostics.test: ECG, glucose (often elevated), U&E, lactate, blood gas, calcium.

diagnostics.rationale: Assess LV function for inotrope selection.

management.detail: Atropine 0.5–1 mg IV first-line for bradycardia (often ineffective). Fluid resuscitation (10–20 mL/kg crystalloid) for hypotension.

management.step: Activated charcoal + whole-bowel irrigation for sustained-release within 1–2 h
management.detail: PEG 1–2 L/h for up to 24 h if sustained-release.
Calcium chloride 10% 10–20 mL via CVC OR calcium gluconate 10% 30–60 mL peripheral; repeat every 10–20 min × 3; then infusion of calcium gluconate 0.2–0.4 mL/kg/h. Aim for ionised Ca 1.5–2× normal.

management.step: Glucagon — adjunct (less effective than for β-blocker)
management.detail: 5–10 mg IV bolus, repeat once.

management.step: High-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy (HIE) — first-line for shock
management.detail: Insulin 1 unit/kg bolus then 0.5–10 units/kg/h infusion (can escalate higher in CCB OD than β-blocker), dextrose 0.5 g/kg/h titrated to glucose 5–11 mmol/L; replace K+. ICU monitoring. Improves inotropy + reverses metabolic effects.
Noradrenaline first; add adrenaline / dobutamine if needed.

management.step: Methylene blue / lipid emulsion for refractory cases
management.detail: Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV for vasoplegic shock (dihydropyridines). Lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus + 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion for severe refractory toxicity.
Specialist centre — bridges through metabolism (24–48 h).

management.step: Transvenous pacing for symptomatic bradyarrhythmia not responsive to drugs
management.detail: Capture often difficult; mechanical support more reliable.

references.label: AACT / ACMT consensus on CCB overdose

title: Iron overdose (severe) — adult / paediatric
presentation: Stage 1 (0–6 h): GI — vomiting, diarrhoea, haematemesis, abdominal pain.
Stage 2 (6–24 h): apparent improvement (latent stage — may falsely reassure).
Stage 3 (12–24 h): systemic toxicity — metabolic acidosis, shock, hepatic failure, coagulopathy, AKI.
Stage 4 (2–4 days): hepatic necrosis.
Stage 5 (4–6 weeks): late GI strictures (gastric outlet obstruction).
Toxic ingested elemental iron > 20 mg/kg; severe > 60 mg/kg.
redFlags: Serum iron > 90 micromol/L (500 microgram/dL) — severe toxicity likely.

diagnostics.test: Serum iron level at 4 h post-ingestion (peak).
diagnostics.rationale: Severity assessment; > 90 micromol/L (500 microgram/dL) needs chelation.
Guides decontamination (whole-bowel irrigation if tablets visible).

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, LFT, coag, blood gas, glucose, lactate.
Group + crossmatch in active GI bleeding.

management.step: Supportive ABCDE + aggressive IV fluid resuscitation
management.detail: Crystalloid 20 mL/kg bolus; treat hypotension; correct acidosis with bicarbonate if severe.

management.step: Whole-bowel irrigation if radiopaque tablets visible / large ingestion within 1–2 h
management.detail: PEG 25 mL/kg/h via NG for paediatric (1–2 L/h adult) until rectal effluent clear. AVOID activated charcoal — does not bind iron.

Indications: serum iron > 90 micromol/L (500 microgram/dL), severe symptoms (shock, severe acidosis, coma), or ingested > 60 mg/kg elemental iron. Dose: 15 mg/kg/h IV infusion (max 6 g/day; some sources allow more in life-threatening). Continue until: serum iron < 90, urine clear (no 'vin rose' colour), patient asymptomatic, acidosis resolved. Limit ≤ 24 h to avoid ARDS / yersiniosis.
Pulmonary toxicity if > 24 h — stop earlier when criteria met.
RRT for AKI; vitamin K + FFP for coagulopathy; NAC for hepatic injury; supportive ICU care.
Outpatient follow-up at 4–6 weeks for gastric outlet symptoms.

management.step: Mental health pathway for intentional overdose
management.detail: Psychiatric assessment before discharge.

references.label: AACT / EAPCCT position paper on iron overdose

title: Lead poisoning (adult and paediatric)
presentation: Children: developmental delay, behavioural / cognitive impairment, anaemia, abdominal pain, anorexia, irritability. Severe: encephalopathy (vomiting, ataxia, seizures, coma).
Adults: fatigue, anaemia, abdominal pain, peripheral motor neuropathy (wrist drop), hypertension, renal impairment, infertility, gingival lead line (Burton's line).

Common exposures: leaded paint, soil, water (lead pipes / solder), cosmetics (kohl, surma, sindoor), traditional remedies, occupational (battery, smelter, demolition), pottery glaze, leaded gasoline (historical).
redFlags: Encephalopathy (seizures, coma, altered consciousness) — medical emergency, chelation IMMEDIATELY.
Blood lead > 70 microgram/dL child / > 100 adult — severe.
Persistent occupational / environmental exposure — public-health notification.

diagnostics.test: Whole-blood lead level (venous, NOT capillary — capillary often false elevated from contamination).
FBC + blood film (basophilic stippling, microcytic anaemia).
X-ray abdomen if recent ingestion suspected (lead chips / paint).
diagnostics.rationale: Identify retained lead in GI tract.

diagnostics.test: X-ray long bones in children (lead lines at metaphysis).

management.detail: Without removal from exposure, chelation is futile. Engage public health, occupational health, environmental services.

management.step: Decontaminate gut if recent ingestion / lead visible on X-ray
management.detail: Whole-bowel irrigation (PEG) to remove retained lead. Consider endoscopy if large foreign body.

Children: blood lead ≥ 45 microgram/dL — DMSA (succimer) 10 mg/kg PO every 8 h × 5 days then every 12 h × 14 days. Blood lead ≥ 70 OR encephalopathy: dimercaprol (BAL) 3–5 mg/kg IM every 4 h + CaNa2EDTA 1500 mg/m²/day IV. Adults: blood lead > 80 (or > 50 with symptoms) — DMSA or CaNa2EDTA.
Dimercaprol (BAL) IM 4–6-hourly + CaNa2EDTA infusion; ICU monitoring; treat seizures (benzodiazepine), cerebral oedema.

management.step: Supportive — anaemia correction (iron deficiency commonly coexists)
management.detail: Iron + folate replacement; transfusion if severe symptomatic anaemia.

management.step: Long-term follow-up + cognitive assessment in children
management.detail: Repeat blood lead level 2 weeks after chelation, then monthly until < 10 microgram/dL. Educational support, behavioural intervention for children with cognitive deficits.
Notify (notifiable disease in many jurisdictions). Workplace exposure assessment + control; home + soil testing; secondary prevention for siblings / coworkers.

references.label: WHO Lead poisoning guidance + Global elimination of leaded paint
CDC Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention Program
AAP Policy Statement on Prevention of Childhood Lead Toxicity
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Maternal sepsis (antepartum, intrapartum, postpartum)
presentation: Fever (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C) with suspected/confirmed infection during pregnancy or up to 42 days postpartum.
Tachycardia, tachypnoea, raised WBC, lactate ≥ 2.
Common foci: chorioamnionitis, endometritis, septic abortion, UTI/pyelonephritis, mastitis, wound infection (LSCS, episiotomy), pneumonia.
redFlags: Group A streptococcal sepsis — rapid deterioration.
Necrotising fasciitis of perineum / abdominal wound.
Suspected septic abortion (recent termination, retained products).

diagnostics.test: Vital signs incl temperature; modified obstetric early warning score.
Lactate, blood cultures × 2, FBC, CRP, U&E, LFT, coag, group + save.
Urine + high vaginal/cervical swabs + placenta culture; CXR; USS pelvis if retained products suspected.
Fetal heart monitoring if antepartum / intrapartum.

management.step: Surviving Sepsis Hour-1 bundle PLUS obstetric considerations
management.detail: Cultures BEFORE antibiotics (don't delay > 45 min); lactate; broad-spectrum IV antibiotic; 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension; noradrenaline for MAP < 65.

IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 6-hourly + IV clindamycin 600–900 mg 8-hourly (clindamycin covers GAS toxin + anaerobes) ± gentamicin for severe sepsis. Avoid tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones in pregnancy.
Septic abortion / chorioamnionitis / retained products → expedite delivery + ERPC. Endometritis postpartum → uterine evacuation if retained POC.
Wound debridement; drain abscess; hysterectomy if life-threatening sepsis from uterine source unresponsive to antibiotics.

management.step: Treat group A streptococcal sepsis specifically
management.detail: Add clindamycin to penicillin (toxin suppression); consider IVIG 1–2 g/kg if toxic shock features.
DIC management; AKI / RRT; ARDS support; neonatal team if delivered preterm. Discuss with anaesthetics, obstetrics, neonatology, microbiology, ICU.
Identify and treat sequelae (DVT/PE risk high — give LMWH prophylaxis); psychological support; debrief; future pregnancy plan.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 64a + 64b — Bacterial sepsis in pregnancy and following pregnancy
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (MOH)

title: Tetralogy of Fallot — hypercyanotic 'Tet' spell
presentation: Infant or young child with known TOF (or undiagnosed cyanotic CHD) develops sudden cyanosis, hyperpnoea, distress.
Triggered by crying, feeding, defaecation, dehydration, infection, anaesthesia.
Loss of murmur (right-to-left shunt increased; less flow across RVOT).
redFlags: Loss of consciousness / seizure / cardiac arrest.
Persistent cyanosis after positioning and oxygen.
Recurrent spells — accelerated need for definitive repair.

management.detail: Increases systemic vascular resistance, reduces R→L shunt; comfort parent holding infant in knee-chest position.
Minimal handling; oxygen via mask (caution — too much may close PDA in ductal-dependent lesions; in pure TOF the duct usually not relied upon).

management.step: Morphine 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IM or SC (or fentanyl IN 1–2 microgram/kg)
management.detail: Reduces hyperpnoea + agitation, breaking the spell cycle.
Reverses dehydration + raises preload + reduces R→L shunt magnitude.

management.step: Phenylephrine 5–20 microgram/kg IV bolus or 0.1–0.5 microgram/kg/min infusion
management.detail: Raises SVR, reduces R→L shunt — only if other measures fail.

management.step: Propranolol 0.05–0.1 mg/kg IV (or 1–4 mg/kg/day PO maintenance)
management.detail: Reduces infundibular spasm; long-term prophylaxis between spells while awaiting surgery.

management.step: Sodium bicarbonate if severe metabolic acidosis
management.detail: 1–2 mmol/kg IV for pH < 7.2.

management.step: AVOID inotropes that increase contractility (digoxin, dopamine, adrenaline)
management.detail: Worsen RVOT obstruction by increasing infundibular spasm.

management.step: Refer urgently to paediatric cardiology for definitive repair
management.detail: Recurrent spells are an indication to accelerate surgical correction.

references.label: AHA Guidelines for the Management of Congenital Heart Disease
Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners — Cyanotic spell management
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Ductal-dependent congenital heart disease — newborn presentation
presentation: Newborn 1–14 days old presenting with cyanosis, tachypnoea, poor feeding, shock as ductus arteriosus closes.

Two patterns: (a) ductal-dependent pulmonary blood flow (pulmonary atresia, severe pulmonary stenosis, tricuspid atresia) — cyanosis predominant; (b) ductal-dependent systemic blood flow (hypoplastic left heart, critical aortic stenosis, coarctation, interrupted arch) — shock, weak femoral pulses, lactic acidosis.
SpO2 differential (right arm vs lower limb) suggests coarctation.
redFlags: Shock with poor femoral pulses — ductal-dependent systemic circulation.
Severe cyanosis with normal lung exam — cyanotic CHD until proven otherwise.
Heart failure with hepatomegaly + tachycardia + cool peripheries.
Acidosis with normal SpO2 but lactate > 4 — suggests inadequate systemic flow.

diagnostics.test: Pulse oximetry pre-ductal (right arm) + post-ductal (any foot) — 'critical CHD screen'.
Hyperoxia test (10 min 100% O2) — PaO2 rise < 100 mmHg suggests cyanotic CHD.
CXR, ECG, blood gas, lactate, glucose, FBC, U&E.

management.step: OPEN THE DUCT — prostaglandin E1 IMMEDIATELY
management.detail: Alprostadil (PGE1) IV 0.05–0.1 microgram/kg/min via central or large peripheral line, starting as soon as ductal-dependent lesion suspected — DO NOT wait for echo. Reduce to 0.01–0.02 microgram/kg/min once ductus open. Side effects: apnoea (be ready to intubate), fever, hypotension, hyperexcitability.

Most newborns on prostaglandin need intubation electively for transport (apnoea risk). Lung-protective ventilation. Avoid hyperoxia in ductal-dependent SYSTEMIC circulation (excessive PVR drop diverts flow from systemic).
Avoid large fluid boluses (may worsen pulmonary overcirculation). Inotrope (dopamine 5–10 microgram/kg/min OR low-dose adrenaline) for shock. Correct metabolic acidosis.
