For HLHS / single ventricle, target SpO2 75–85% — too high SpO2 = pulmonary overcirculation + systemic underperfusion. Aim for balanced flow.
Routine high FiO2 in pre-operative ductal-dependent SYSTEMIC lesions. Sudden ductal closure (e.g. stopping PGE1).

management.step: Transfer to tertiary paediatric cardiac centre
management.detail: Specialist neonatal cardiac transport team. Continue PGE1, ventilation, glucose monitoring en route.
Surgical or catheter-based palliation / repair — Norwood (HLHS), arch repair (coarctation/IAA), BT shunt (cyanotic with low pulmonary flow), septostomy (TGA).

references.label: AHA/AAP Pulse Oximetry Critical CHD Screening Guidelines
WHO Care of the newborn — congenital heart disease module
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Paediatric supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)
presentation: Infant: poor feeding, irritability, pallor, sweating, tachypnoea — heart failure can develop within 24–48 h.
Older child: palpitations, chest discomfort, lightheadedness, syncope.
Heart rate: infant typically > 220/min; child > 180/min; adolescent > 150/min, NARROW QRS, regular, minimal beat-to-beat variability.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability — hypotension, altered consciousness, severe heart failure.
Wide-complex tachycardia — assume VT until proven otherwise.
Pre-excitation (WPW) on baseline ECG — avoid AV-nodal-blocking agents long-term unless specialist guided.

diagnostics.rationale: Distinguish SVT from VT and sinus tachycardia; identify accessory pathway.

diagnostics.test: Continuous cardiac monitoring; print rhythm strip during interventions.

management.step: Unstable (shock, severe heart failure) — synchronised DC cardioversion
management.detail: 0.5–1 J/kg synchronised, escalate to 2 J/kg. Sedate if conscious; do NOT delay if peri-arrest.
Infant: ice/water bag to face for 15 sec (Diving reflex). Child: Valsalva (blow into syringe for 15 sec). Modified Valsalva (postural change after Valsalva) superior in older child.

management.step: IV adenosine if vagal manoeuvres fail
management.detail: 0.1 mg/kg IV rapid push (close to heart) followed by 5 mL saline flush; escalate to 0.2 mg/kg, max 12 mg single dose. Record rhythm strip during administration. Effects last seconds — very short half-life.
IV amiodarone 5 mg/kg over 30–60 min (consider cardiology consult), OR procainamide 15 mg/kg over 30 min, OR flecainide (under specialist guidance), OR overdrive pacing (transoesophageal in infant).
Severe hypotension / cardiac arrest reported. Use only in older children under specialist guidance.
Fever, electrolytes, drugs, congenital accessory pathway (WPW). Echo for structural disease.
Catheter ablation curative for accessory pathway (preferred ≥ 5 years). Beta-blocker or flecainide prophylaxis for recurrent SVT. Refer paediatric electrophysiology.

references.label: European Heart Rhythm Association consensus on paediatric arrhythmia management
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health
WHO Package of Essential NCD Interventions (WHO PEN) — Cardiovascular disease

title: Severe bronchiolitis — infant (RSV + non-RSV)
presentation: Infant < 1 year (peak 2–6 months) with 1–3 days of coryzal symptoms followed by cough, tachypnoea, wheeze, crackles, increased work of breathing.
Feeding difficulty, apnoea (especially preterm and < 2 months).
Risk factors for severe disease: < 3 months, preterm, congenital heart disease, immunosuppression, chronic lung disease.
redFlags: Severe respiratory distress (head-bobbing, grunting, severe recession, RR > 70).

diagnostics.test: Pulse oximetry; capillary blood gas if respiratory failure.
Respiratory virus PCR (RSV + others) — selectively for cohorting.
CXR ONLY if focal signs / no improvement / suspected complication.
diagnostics.rationale: Routine CXR not indicated; can be misleading.

diagnostics.test: FBC + CRP — only if suspected superinfection.

management.detail: Minimal handling; quiet environment; head elevation.
Nasal prong 1–4 L/min; target 92–96%. Avoid hyperoxia.
Small frequent feeds; NG feed if cannot maintain oral intake; IV maintenance fluid (2/3 maintenance to avoid SIADH-related hyponatraemia).

management.step: High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) for moderate-severe distress
management.detail: 1–2 L/kg/min humidified heated O2 + air mix. Reduces work of breathing and intubation rate. CPAP or BiPAP for further escalation.

management.step: Intubation + IMV for respiratory failure / apnoea / exhaustion
management.detail: PICU level. Permissive hypercapnia; PEEP; bronchodilator NOT routinely beneficial.

Antibiotics (no benefit unless documented bacterial superinfection — secondary AOM, pneumonia). Bronchodilators (no proven benefit; trial then stop if no response). Inhaled or systemic corticosteroids (no benefit in bronchiolitis — distinct from asthma). Hypertonic saline routinely (modest evidence, not currently recommended in UK / Australasia).
Continuous monitoring; consider CPAP / intubation if apnoeic episodes.
SpO2 ≥ 94% room air sustained; feeding > 75% normal; no significant distress for 4 h. Safety-net for re-presentation. RSV vaccination/nirsevimab consideration for at-risk siblings + next season.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Severe viral croup (laryngotracheobronchitis)
presentation: Child 6 months–5 years with sudden onset of barking cough, hoarse voice, stridor, often worse at night.

Mild: occasional cough, no stridor at rest. Moderate: stridor at rest, recession, normal mental state. Severe: marked stridor at rest, severe recession, agitated / drowsy, cyanosis, exhaustion. Impending respiratory failure: silence, sternal indrawing, drowsiness, falling SpO2.
redFlags: Drooling, dysphagia, tripod position — consider epiglottitis instead.
Toxic appearance, high fever — consider bacterial tracheitis.
Failure to respond to nebulised adrenaline within 30 min.
Recurrent or atypical croup — anatomical abnormality.

diagnostics.test: DO NOT examine throat with tongue depressor if epiglottitis possible.
Avoid distressing investigations; SpO2 may underestimate severity.

management.step: Minimal handling; parent in arms; calm environment
management.detail: Agitation worsens upper airway obstruction. Avoid IV cannulation, throat examination, NG tube unless essential.

management.step: Single dose dexamethasone for ALL except mildest
management.detail: 0.15 mg/kg PO (max 10 mg). Higher dose 0.6 mg/kg if cannot tolerate oral / vomiting / severe. Onset 6 h; duration 24–48 h. IV or IM same dose if cannot swallow. Prednisolone 1 mg/kg less evidence.

management.step: Nebulised adrenaline for moderate-severe stridor at rest
management.detail: 5 mL of 1:1000 (5 mg) nebulised, can repeat every 20–30 min. Effects: rapid onset (~10 min), duration 1–2 h — observe ≥ 2–4 h after for 'rebound' before discharge.
Blow-by mask in arms; avoid mask trauma. CAUTION: oxygen can mask deterioration; use clinical scoring alongside.

management.step: Refer to ICU / consider intubation if
management.detail: Recurrent / no response to adrenaline + steroid; exhaustion; falling consciousness; severe air entry reduction. Senior anaesthetic / ENT involvement. Use smaller-than-usual ETT (1 size below age-predicted).
Mixed 70:30 helium:oxygen reduces work of breathing; specialist centre.
Improvement sustained ≥ 2–4 h after last adrenaline; no stridor at rest; normal feeding; carers can return if worse. Safety-netting essential.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Kawasaki disease — diagnosis + IVIG treatment
presentation: Fever > 38°C for ≥ 5 days AND at least 4 of: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis; polymorphous rash; mucositis (strawberry tongue, cracked lips, pharyngeal injection); extremity changes (palmar/sole erythema, induration, peri-ungual desquamation); cervical lymphadenopathy ≥ 1.5 cm (often unilateral).
Incomplete KD: fewer criteria but echocardiographic features (coronary artery dilatation).
Atypical: < 6 m and > 9 y often present incompletely; very high coronary aneurysm risk.
redFlags: Coronary artery aneurysm on echo — Z-score ≥ 2.5 dilation.
Macrophage activation syndrome (cytopenias, very high ferritin, hepatitis, splenomegaly).
Shock state (Kawasaki disease shock syndrome — rare, more severe outcomes).
Refractory disease (persistent fever 36 h after first IVIG).

diagnostics.test: FBC, CRP, ESR, ALT, sodium, urinalysis.
Exclude alternatives (viral, scarlet fever, drug reaction, JIA-SoJIA).

management.detail: IVIG 2 g/kg single dose over 8–12 h. PLUS aspirin 30–50 mg/kg/day (American 80–100 mg/kg/day) divided 6-hourly until afebrile 48 h, then 3–5 mg/kg/day antiplatelet × 6–8 weeks (longer if coronary aneurysm).

management.step: High-risk patients — add adjunctive steroids upfront
management.detail: Infants < 1 year, severe coronary dilatation, KDSS, RAISE / Kobayashi high score: IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg/day × 3 days OR oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day with taper.

management.step: Refractory KD (fever > 36 h after first IVIG)
management.detail: Second IVIG dose 2 g/kg OR pulsed steroid OR infliximab 5 mg/kg IV OR ciclosporin OR anakinra — under paediatric rheumatology / cardiology guidance.
Echo at 6 weeks, then per coronary status. Large or giant aneurysm: dual antiplatelet + warfarin; lifelong cardiology follow-up; stress testing in adulthood.

management.step: Avoid live vaccines × 11 months after IVIG
management.detail: MMR + varicella delay due to passive antibody interference.
Recurrence risk ~1–3%; lifelong cardiovascular monitoring even if normal coronaries (subclinical endothelial dysfunction).

references.label: AHA Scientific Statement: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease (2017)
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C)
presentation: Child / adolescent < 21 years with persistent fever ≥ 3 days, raised inflammatory markers, multi-organ involvement (≥ 2 systems), and recent SARS-CoV-2 infection or exposure (positive PCR / antigen / antibody, or known contact 4–6 weeks prior).

Common features: GI (severe abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea — may mimic appendicitis), mucocutaneous (rash, conjunctivitis, swollen lips — overlap with KD), cardiac (myocarditis, coronary dilation, shock), neurological (irritability, headache), haematological.
redFlags: Macrophage activation features (very high ferritin, cytopenias).

diagnostics.test: SARS-CoV-2 PCR + antibody, FBC, CRP, ferritin, troponin, BNP, D-dimer, fibrinogen, LFT, U&E, urinalysis.
diagnostics.rationale: Confirm post-COVID-19 inflammatory state + identify organ involvement.
Detect myocarditis, coronary dilation, ventricular dysfunction.

diagnostics.test: Imaging (CXR, abdominal USS) per organ involvement.
Exclude alternative diagnoses (sepsis, KD, JIA-SoJIA, toxic shock).

management.detail: Manage shock (fluids cautiously; vasopressor noradrenaline first; inotrope if myocardial dysfunction). Lung-protective ventilation if ARDS.
Reduces inflammation + cardiac involvement (overlap with Kawasaki regimen). Single dose; may repeat in refractory cases.

management.step: Methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day (or pulsed 10–30 mg/kg for severe)
management.detail: Added to IVIG in moderate-severe MIS-C; combination superior to IVIG alone in outcomes (RECOVERY-MISC, Best Available Treatment Study).
Anakinra 2–10 mg/kg/day (IL-1 antagonist) OR infliximab 5–10 mg/kg OR tocilizumab — under paediatric rheumatology guidance.
Prophylactic enoxaparin for ALL admitted MIS-C; therapeutic dosing if confirmed thrombosis, large coronary aneurysm, or significant LV dysfunction.

management.step: Aspirin 3–5 mg/kg/day until coronary normal + platelets normal × 4 weeks
management.detail: Antiplatelet for coronary protection.
Echo at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, 6 months. Long-term cardiology if coronary involvement. Vaccination guidance + return-to-sport screening.

references.label: WHO Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children and adolescents temporally related to COVID-19 (2020)
ACR Clinical Guidance for the Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children Associated With SARS-CoV-2
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Severe accidental hypothermia (core temperature < 28°C)
presentation: Core temperature < 28°C (severe), 28–32°C (moderate), 32–35°C (mild).
Severe: coma, fixed pupils, severe bradycardia / asystole, no detectable signs of life.
Increased risk: elderly, alcohol intoxication, drugs (sedatives), hypothyroidism, sepsis, immersion, exposure, homelessness.
redFlags: Cardiac arrhythmia (J wave, AF, bradycardia, VF) at low temperatures.
Apparent death — 'NOT DEAD UNTIL WARM AND DEAD' — continue resuscitation until core temp > 32°C.
Concurrent trauma — secondary survey when stable.

diagnostics.test: Core temperature (oesophageal, rectal, bladder — not tympanic if peripheral).
ECG, ABG, glucose, electrolytes, FBC, coag, CK, ethanol level.
CXR, FAST scan if trauma suspected.
TSH if elderly / no obvious exposure history.

management.detail: Rough handling can precipitate VF in cold heart. Remove wet clothing; insulate; horizontal position. Avoid hot baths / vigorous rubbing.

management.step: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation if no signs of life
management.detail: Continuous chest compressions; intubate cautiously (laryngeal stimulation may trigger VF). Withhold drugs and defibrillation initially if core temp < 30°C — generally ineffective.

Mild (32–35°C): passive — remove wet clothing + blankets in warm environment. Moderate (28–32°C): active external — forced-air warming (Bair Hugger), warmed IV fluids 40–42°C, warmed humidified O2 42°C. Severe (< 28°C): active internal — body cavity lavage, haemodialysis, OR extracorporeal life support (ECLS, ECMO) which is the standard of care for haemodynamically unstable hypothermic patients.

management.step: Defibrillation — single shock then resume CPR
management.detail: If VF persists despite rewarming to 30°C, single shock then continue rewarming + CPR. Multiple shocks generally ineffective < 30°C.
Withhold adrenaline, lidocaine, amiodarone < 30°C. > 30°C give standard ACLS doses but consider doubling interval (every 6–10 min instead of 3–5).

Rewarming shock (peripheral vasodilation): fluid bolus. Afterdrop: monitor for paradoxical cooling from peripheral cold blood return. Acidosis, hyperkalaemia — predict outcome; K+ > 12 in adults / > 20 in children suggests irreversibility.
Sepsis (hypothermia may be sepsis); hypoglycaemia (give 10% dextrose); hypothyroidism (T4 + steroid); alcohol / drug toxicity; underlying trauma.
ICU monitoring; rewarming injury surveillance; psychological / social support if homeless / addiction; family debrief especially after prolonged resuscitation.

references.label: Wilderness Medical Society Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia

title: Severe heat stroke (classical and exertional)
presentation: Core temperature > 40°C with CNS dysfunction (altered consciousness, seizure, coma, ataxia).
Classical: elderly / chronically ill in heat wave; minimal sweating, hot dry skin.
Exertional: young athlete / military / labourer during exertion in heat; usually sweating, lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis.
Multi-organ failure: AKI, DIC, hepatic failure, ARDS.
redFlags: Children, elderly, comorbid cardiac/renal — higher mortality.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, glucose, LFT (ALT often 5000+), CK, coag, lactate, ABG.

management.step: Rapid cooling — 'cool first, transport second' for exertional heat stroke
management.detail: Cold-water immersion (2–14°C tub) — gold standard for exertional; cool by ~0.2°C/min, stop at 38.5–39.0°C. Alternative for classical / unstable: evaporative cooling (mist + fan), ice packs to groin / axillae / neck, cold IV fluids. Avoid antipyretics (paracetamol / NSAID) — ineffective + hepatic / renal toxicity.
Intubate if unconscious / convulsing. IV fluid resuscitation (caution — avoid overload; goal urine output 0.5–1 mL/kg/h). Vasopressor if hypotensive after fluids.
Benzodiazepine for seizures; treat rhabdomyolysis (IV fluid, maintain urine output, alkalinise urine if myoglobinuric); RRT for severe AKI / hyperkalaemia.
FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets per coag; NAC for hepatic injury; lung-protective ventilation.
Continue cooling causes hypothermia; reassess every 5 min.
Dantrolene (proven not effective — different mechanism to malignant hyperthermia). Antibiotics (unless co-existing sepsis). Antipyretics.
Many patients have persistent thermoregulatory dysfunction for months; avoid heat exposure × 6–12 months; gradual return to activity under guidance.

references.label: Korey Stringer Institute Best Practice on Exertional Heat Stroke
Wilderness Medical Society Practice Guidelines for Heat-Related Illness
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health
WHO Package of Essential NCD Interventions (WHO PEN) — Cardiovascular disease

title: Drowning and submersion injury
presentation: Submersion in water (fresh or salt) with associated hypoxia and aspiration.
Spectrum: minimal aspiration (transient hypoxia) → severe hypoxic injury → cardiac arrest.
Often hypothermic concurrently; cervical injury if diving.
redFlags: Cardiac arrest at scene — start resuscitation; outcomes can be excellent with prompt high-quality CPR.
Suspected cervical spine injury (dive into shallow water, surf).
Children in lukewarm water (bathtub) — child protection screen.

diagnostics.test: ABG, lactate, glucose, electrolytes, FBC, coag.
diagnostics.rationale: Quantify hypoxia + identify aspiration / electrolyte changes.

diagnostics.test: CXR (initial often normal; aspirate evolves over 24 h); CT head + C-spine if dive / trauma.

diagnostics.rationale: Identify primary cause (e.g. LQTS triggering drowning in swimmers).

management.detail: Rescuer safety FIRST. Standard BLS — emphasise 5 initial rescue breaths (hypoxia is the driving injury). Cervical-spine precautions ONLY if diving / surf or clear signs of injury.
Intubate if GCS ≤ 8, severe hypoxia, exhaustion. Lung-protective ventilation; PEEP for hypoxaemia (often need higher PEEP). HFNC / CPAP for milder cases.
Avoid hyper / hypocapnia, maintain normoxia, head elevation, treat seizures. Targeted temperature management 32–36°C × 24 h for post-arrest CPR — beneficial in cardiac-arrest drowning.
Per hypothermia pathway; rewarm to 36°C; avoid hyperthermia.
No prophylactic antibiotics or steroids. Treat aspiration pneumonia later if infection develops (CXR change + clinical). ARDS supportive.
Asymptomatic, normal CXR, normal SpO2 — observe 4–8 h then discharge with safety-netting. ANY symptomatic patient — admit for at least 24 h.
Swimming education; pool fencing; supervision of children; CPR training for caregivers; alcohol-and-water counselling.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (rAAA)
presentation: Sudden severe abdominal / back / flank pain, often with collapse / hypotension.
Pulsatile abdominal mass; sometimes Cullen / Grey-Turner sign.
Risk factors: male, age > 65, smoking, hypertension, family history, atherosclerotic disease.
Classic triad (pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass) in ~50%.
redFlags: Ureteric colic / 'renal stone' in older male — consider rAAA mimic.

diagnostics.test: Bedside USS (FAST) — first line; identifies aneurysm + free fluid.
diagnostics.rationale: Rapid bedside diagnosis; sensitive for aneurysm but less for rupture.

diagnostics.test: CT angiogram if haemodynamically stable enough.
Group + crossmatch ≥ 10 units; activate massive transfusion protocol.
FBC, U&E, coag, blood gas, lactate, troponin.

management.detail: Target SBP 70–90 mmHg / palpable radial pulse (mental status preserved) — over-resuscitation worsens bleeding by raising intraluminal pressure and disrupting clot.

management.step: Two large-bore IVs + central + arterial line in theatre
management.detail: Massive transfusion 1:1:1 ratio. Avoid crystalloid where possible — use blood + FFP + platelets.

EVAR — first-line where anatomy suitable + centre experienced; lower 30-day mortality. Open repair for hostile neck anatomy / EVAR unsuitable. IMPROVE trial: EVAR-first strategy associated with better long-term outcome.
Permissive hypotension until aortic clamp; rapid sequence induction; have surgeon ready to clamp BEFORE induction in unstable patient. Cell salvage.
Manage compartment syndrome (abdominal — IAP monitoring), MI, AKI (often pre-existing + ischaemia/reperfusion), bowel ischaemia (look for lactic acidosis day 1–3).
Smoking cessation; BP control; statin; aspirin; AAA surveillance for contralateral aneurysm. Family screening of first-degree relatives.

references.label: ESVS Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Abdominal Aorto-Iliac Artery Aneurysms (2024)
IMPROVE trial Lancet 2014 — endovascular vs open
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health
WHO Package of Essential NCD Interventions (WHO PEN) — Cardiovascular disease

title: Acute limb ischaemia
presentation: Sudden onset of '6 Ps': Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paraesthesia, Paralysis, Perishing cold.
Causes: embolus (60% — cardiac AF, mural thrombus, endocarditis), in-situ thrombosis (40% — on PAD), trauma, dissection, graft occlusion.

Rutherford classification: I viable; IIa marginally threatened (rest pain, mild sensory loss); IIb immediately threatened (paralysis, severe pain); III irreversible (anaesthesia, paralysis, mottling).
redFlags: Rutherford IIb — surgical emergency within 4–6 hours to save limb.
Rutherford III (irreversible) — primary amputation; revascularisation futile.
Compartment syndrome post-revascularisation — prophylactic fasciotomy if > 6 h ischaemia.
Reperfusion injury — rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, lactic acidosis, AKI.

diagnostics.test: CT angiogram (or MRA, conventional angiogram) if stable.
FBC, U&E, CK, coagulation, group + save.
diagnostics.rationale: Baseline + screen for thrombophilia / prepare for surgery.

management.detail: Bolus 80 units/kg (max 5000) IV then infusion targeting aPTT 1.5–2.5× control. Reduces propagation of thrombus.
IV opioid; keep limb at heart level (NOT elevated — increases ischaemia); warmth without direct heat.

Embolic: surgical embolectomy with Fogarty catheter (most embolectomies done < 12 h ischaemia). Thrombotic in-situ: catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) over 12–24 h, then treat underlying lesion (angioplasty / bypass). Combined surgical + endovascular common.
Consider prophylactic four-compartment fasciotomy when revascularising > 6 h ischaemia, or for clinical compartment syndrome.
Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation; alkalinise urine if myoglobinuric; correct hyperkalaemia; RRT if AKI.
Cardiac embolism: anticoagulate (DOAC / warfarin); manage AF. PAD: statin, antiplatelet, smoking cessation, structured exercise, future surveillance.
Rutherford III; ongoing necrosis with sepsis; functional outcome poor with delayed revascularisation. Multidisciplinary decision with patient + family.

references.label: ESVS Clinical Practice Guideline on Acute Limb Ischaemia (2020)
Society for Vascular Surgery clinical guideline

title: Cerebral malaria — child + adult
presentation: Confirmed P. falciparum parasitaemia (RDT or microscopy) WITH unrousable coma (GCS < 11 / Blantyre coma score < 3 in children) not attributable to other cause.
Often preceded by fever, headache, vomiting, repeated seizures.
Children: rapid progression to coma over hours-days; mortality 15–25%.
Adults: typically slower onset, more multi-organ failure.
redFlags: Severe anaemia (Hb < 5), shock, ARDS, AKI, jaundice, lactic acidosis (lactate > 5 mmol/L), hypoglycaemia, hyperparasitaemia (> 10%).
Co-infection (bacterial sepsis — Salmonella common in Africa).
Long-term neurodevelopmental sequelae in surviving children (25–35%).

diagnostics.test: Capillary glucose hourly (hypoglycaemia very common, especially on quinine + in children).
FBC, U&E, blood gas, lactate, glucose, LFT, coag, urine output.
LP if no contraindication — exclude bacterial meningitis as concurrent.
Blood culture — Salmonella co-bacteraemia common in African children with severe malaria.

management.step: IV artesunate IMMEDIATELY — first-line parenteral antimalarial
management.detail: 2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12, 24 h then daily until oral therapy possible (minimum 3 doses + once eating). Paediatric < 20 kg: 3 mg/kg per dose. Switch to full 3-day course of oral ACT once tolerating.

management.step: If artesunate unavailable — IM artemether or IV quinine
management.detail: Artemether 3.2 mg/kg IM loading then 1.6 mg/kg daily. Quinine loading 20 mg/kg IV over 4 h then 10 mg/kg every 8 h with cardiac monitor — hypoglycaemia risk.

management.step: Empirical antibiotic for severe paediatric malaria
management.detail: IV ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg/day — Salmonella co-bacteraemia. Adults with severe disease + shock / AKI: also cover empirically.
10% dextrose 5 mL/kg bolus then maintenance — recheck glucose hourly.
Benzodiazepine then phenobarbital / levetiracetam. AVOID prophylactic phenobarbital (PEMC trial — increased mortality).
Transfuse if Hb < 5 g/dL OR Hb 5–6 with respiratory distress / cardiac failure / parasitaemia > 10%. Use whole blood or packed cells.
Avoid aggressive boluses (FEAST trial in non-shocked African children showed harm). Cautious maintenance only; specific small boluses if truly shocked.
AKI common in adults; haemodialysis indicated for uraemia / hyperkalaemia / fluid overload.
Watch for post-artesunate delayed haemolytic anaemia (check Hb weekly × 4 weeks). Neurodevelopmental follow-up for child survivors. Vector control + chemoprophylaxis counselling.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the treatment of malaria 3rd ed. (2015, 2021 update)
WHO Severe malaria (Trop Med Int Health supplement)
Kenya National Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Malaria (MOH, Division of National Malaria Programme)

title: Severe dengue (dengue with severe plasma leak / haemorrhage / organ involvement)
presentation: Day 4–7 of febrile illness in dengue-endemic area: 'critical phase' begins as fever defervesces; plasma leak peaks.
Severe plasma leak: rapid pulse pressure narrowing < 20 mmHg, hypotension, ascites, pleural effusion.
Severe bleeding: GI, intracerebral; thrombocytopenia (typically < 50, often < 20).
Severe organ impairment: liver (AST/ALT > 1000), CNS (encephalopathy), heart (myocarditis), AKI.
redFlags: Warning signs (WHO): abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleed, lethargy / restlessness, liver > 2 cm, rising HCT with rapid platelet fall.

diagnostics.test: Dengue NS1 antigen (day 1–5), IgM/IgG (day 5+), dengue PCR (day 0–4).
Daily FBC — track HCT + platelet trend.
diagnostics.rationale: Rising HCT + falling platelets predict plasma leak.

diagnostics.test: U&E, LFT, blood gas, lactate, coagulation.
USS chest + abdomen for plasma leak signs.

management.detail: Febrile phase: paracetamol (AVOID aspirin, NSAID, IM injections, steroids). Critical phase (day 4–7): close monitoring of HCT + vital signs every 2–4 h. Recovery phase (day 7+): reabsorption of leaked fluid — restrict fluids to avoid overload.

management.step: Group A (no warning signs): outpatient ORS + monitoring
management.detail: Encourage oral fluids; daily FBC; safety-net for warning signs.

management.step: Group B (warning signs): IV isotonic fluid in hospital
management.detail: 0.9% NaCl OR Hartmann's 5–7 mL/kg/h × 1–2 h, reduce to 3–5 then 2–3 mL/kg/h, titrate to HCT + vital signs + urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h. Reassess every 2 h.

management.step: Group C (severe dengue with shock): aggressive resuscitation
management.detail: Compensated shock: 10–20 mL/kg isotonic over 1 h, reassess; if responding reduce rate as above. Decompensated: 20 mL/kg over 15 min, repeat; if still in shock consider colloid (gelofusin / albumin) and search for occult bleed.
Packed red cells 5–10 mL/kg (don't wait for low Hb if active bleed + shock). FFP / cryoprecipitate / platelet only for actively bleeding patient — NOT prophylactic at any platelet level.
Prophylactic platelet transfusion (no evidence benefit; cost + transfusion reaction). Aspirin / NSAIDs (bleeding). IM injections (haematoma). Routine steroids (no benefit; may worsen).
Reabsorption of leaked fluid → risk pulmonary oedema. Reduce IV fluids when HCT drops to baseline; consider furosemide for overload.
Vector control (Aedes aegypti); community education; outbreak surveillance; notifiable disease.

references.label: WHO Dengue: Guidelines for diagnosis, treatment, prevention and control (2009)
WHO Handbook for clinical management of dengue (2012)
Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) Technical Guidelines, 3rd ed, Ministry of Health

title: Acute rheumatic fever
presentation: Onset 2–4 weeks after group A streptococcal pharyngitis (or skin infection in some regions).
Jones criteria (revised 2015) — moderate-high-risk populations:
Major: carditis (clinical OR subclinical on echo), polyarthritis or aseptic monoarthritis or polyarthralgia (in high-risk), chorea (Sydenham), erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.
Minor: monoarthralgia, fever ≥ 38°C, ESR ≥ 30 / CRP ≥ 30, prolonged PR.
Diagnosis: 2 major + evidence of preceding GAS OR 1 major + 2 minor + evidence of preceding GAS.
redFlags: Heart failure from carditis — admit, treat with diuretic / ACEi / steroid for severe.
Pregnancy with rheumatic heart disease — high maternal mortality, multidisciplinary plan.

diagnostics.test: ASO + anti-DNase B titres (rising or high).
Throat swab for GAS culture / rapid antigen.
diagnostics.rationale: Often negative by the time ARF presents but worth attempting.

diagnostics.test: ECG (prolonged PR, AV block); CXR (cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion).

diagnostics.rationale: Even when clinical exam unremarkable; especially required by revised Jones criteria.

management.detail: Single IM benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units (600 000 if < 27 kg). Alternative: oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg BID × 10 days. Macrolide if penicillin allergy.

Aspirin 80–100 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses (max 4 g/day) — taper over 6 weeks; OR naproxen 10–20 mg/kg/day. For severe carditis with heart failure: prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg) for 2 weeks then taper.
Bed rest + reassurance; pharmacotherapy only for severe (carbamazepine 7–20 mg/kg/day or sodium valproate 15–20 mg/kg/day); IVIG / steroid for refractory.
Diuretic, ACEi, beta-blocker per HF guidelines; valve surgery for severe regurgitation.

IM benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units every 21–28 days (or 4-weekly). Duration: 5 years OR until age 21 (no carditis); 10 years OR until age 21 (carditis without persistent valve disease); LIFELONG (persistent valve disease, valve surgery).
Annual echo for those with subclinical or clinical carditis. Specialist cardiology + cardiothoracic for valve surgery.
Register patient with rheumatic heart disease control programme; community health worker delivery of benzathine; family screening.

references.label: AHA Revision of the Jones Criteria for the Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever (2015)
WHO Rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease — Technical report series
Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)
presentation: Classic triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia + AKI.
Typical (STEC-HUS): preceded by bloody diarrhoea from Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 (or non-O157), Shigella, Salmonella — peak 1–10 days after onset of diarrhoea.
Atypical HUS (aHUS): complement-mediated, no preceding diarrhoea, often familial / recurrent — eculizumab treatable.
Children typically 6 months – 5 years.
redFlags: Anuria — severe AKI; may need RRT.
aHUS suspected (no diarrhoea, recurrence, family history) — specialist evaluation for eculizumab.

diagnostics.test: FBC + blood film (schistocytes, low platelets, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia).
LDH (high), bilirubin (indirect raised), haptoglobin (low), direct antiglobulin (negative — distinguishes from autoimmune).
Stool culture for STEC + Shiga-toxin EIA + PCR; stool for Shigella.
Complement testing (CH50, C3, C4, ADAMTS13 activity) — distinguish aHUS from TTP.

management.detail: Strict fluid balance; correct electrolytes (especially K+); pain control; antiemetic; bowel rest if severe colitis.
Indications: uraemia, fluid overload, severe metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia, anuria > 24 h. Peritoneal dialysis often used in children.
Packed red cells for Hb < 6 g/dL or symptomatic. Platelet transfusion ONLY for active bleeding or invasive procedure (may worsen thrombosis).

Antibiotics for STEC enteric infection (may worsen HUS risk by increasing Shiga-toxin release — controversial but generally avoided in O157:H7). Antimotility agents. Routine prophylactic platelet transfusion.

management.step: Eculizumab — for atypical HUS or severe / refractory STEC-HUS with CNS involvement
management.detail: Anti-C5 monoclonal antibody — give meningococcal vaccine 2 weeks before (or peri-administration with prophylactic antibiotics). Continued lifelong in aHUS unless transplant + complement-uninvolved donor.
All STEC-HUS survivors need nephrology follow-up — chronic CKD develops in 25–30% over years (proteinuria, hypertension, declining GFR). Annual BP, urinalysis, eGFR.
Notifiable disease. Trace E. coli outbreak source; food safety; hand hygiene. Family / nursery contact screening.

references.label: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases (2021) — Thrombotic microangiopathy
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Botulism (foodborne, wound, infant) — clinical recognition + antitoxin
presentation: Symmetric descending flaccid paralysis — cranial nerves first (diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, ptosis) → respiratory → limb.
PRESERVED sensation, no fever (unless wound infection), pupils may be fixed dilated.
Foodborne: 12–36 h after home-canned vegetables, fermented fish, honey (infant).
Wound: IV drug users (black tar heroin), trauma.
Infant (< 12 months): constipation, weak cry, poor feeding, floppy ('floppy infant'); often honey or environmental spores.
redFlags: Severe bulbar weakness with secretion pooling — aspiration.
Differential: Guillain-Barré (ascending; preserved cranial nerves often), myasthenia gravis (asymmetric / fatigue), Lambert-Eaton, stroke.

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnosis — DO NOT delay antitoxin for tests.
Serum + stool + wound + food samples to public-health laboratory for toxin detection (mouse bioassay).
Stool culture for C. botulinum + Shiga toxin (infant botulism).

management.detail: Botulism is a public-health emergency in most jurisdictions — outbreak investigation + antitoxin sourced via public-health laboratory.

management.step: Equine heptavalent antitoxin (foodborne / wound) — adult + children > 1 year
management.detail: Single vial IV — neutralises circulating toxin (does NOT reverse paralysis already established). Skin test for hypersensitivity per local protocol. Give as soon as suspected — do not wait for lab confirmation.

management.step: Human botulism immune globulin (BabyBIG) — infant botulism
management.detail: Specific human-derived; rapid IV. Reduces hospitalisation duration significantly. Source through national infant botulism programme.
Intubate ELECTIVELY for FVC < 30%, declining trajectory, or bulbar weakness. May need ventilation weeks-months. Tracheostomy when prolonged.
Wound botulism: surgical debridement + IV penicillin G or metronidazole (NOT aminoglycoside — worsens NM blockade).
Worsen neuromuscular blockade. If antibiotic needed, use β-lactams or metronidazole.

DVT prophylaxis; nutritional support; pressure-area care; eye lubricants for fixed eye opening; psychological support. Slow recovery (weeks-months); near-full neurological recovery typical with supportive care.
Avoid honey < 12 months. Safe home-canning (pressure cook at 116°C × 30 min). Address IV drug-use harm reduction. Outbreak response: trace source, recall food, identify other exposed.

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Acute cholangitis (Tokyo criteria) — adult
presentation: Charcot triad: RUQ pain + fever + jaundice (in 50–70%).
Reynolds pentad: triad + hypotension + altered consciousness — severe form.
Risk: gallstones (most common), biliary stricture, post-ERCP, malignancy obstruction, indwelling biliary stent.
redFlags: Severe (Tokyo Grade III): organ dysfunction (cardiovascular, neurological, respiratory, hepatic, renal, haematological).

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, LFT (high ALP + GGT + bilirubin), lactate, blood culture, CRP.
USS abdomen — first-line bedside (dilated CBD, stones).
MRCP or EUS for non-conclusive USS.
CT abdomen if perforation / abscess / atypical.

management.detail: IV fluids; vasopressor for shock; cultures BEFORE antibiotics; lactate.

Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 6-hourly OR ceftriaxone 2 g + metronidazole 500 mg 8-hourly (community-acquired); meropenem + vancomycin for healthcare-associated. Cover Enterococcus in healthcare-associated.

management.step: Biliary drainage — definitive treatment, timing per severity
management.detail: Grade I (mild): early ERCP within 48 h. Grade II (moderate): ERCP within 24 h. Grade III (severe): URGENT ERCP within 12 h after stabilisation. If ERCP fails: percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage (PTBD) or surgery.
Stone: ERCP + sphincterotomy + stone extraction; cholecystectomy after resolution. Malignant stricture: stent (plastic or metal). Benign stricture: balloon dilatation.
Mechanical ventilation, vasopressor, RRT as needed.
Cholecystectomy within same admission for gallstone cholangitis (delaying increases recurrence). Surveillance for stent occlusion if malignant.

references.label: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 for acute cholangitis and cholecystitis

title: Perforated viscus (acute abdomen with free intraperitoneal air)
presentation: Sudden onset severe diffuse abdominal pain ± peritonism (rigidity, rebound, guarding, percussion tenderness).
Often preceded by pre-existing peptic ulcer, diverticulitis, malignancy, IBD, foreign body, trauma.
Tachycardia, fever, hypotension as peritonitis evolves.
Iatrogenic: post-colonoscopy, post-ERCP, post-laparoscopy.
redFlags: Elderly + frailty + multiple comorbidities — careful goals-of-care discussion.
Free air on erect CXR / CT — surgical emergency.

diagnostics.test: Erect CXR (free sub-diaphragmatic air, may miss small perforations).
CT abdomen + pelvis with contrast (or non-contrast if AKI) — gold standard.
FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, lactate, blood gas, group + crossmatch.

management.detail: ABCDE; IV fluid 30 mL/kg; vasopressor if shocked; oxygen; analgesia (morphine titrated); NG decompression.
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g + metronidazole if not already; OR meropenem in severely ill / healthcare-associated. Cover gut anaerobes.

Most perforations need surgery within 6 h (Hartmann's procedure for diverticular perforation, omental patch for duodenal ulcer perforation, primary repair / resection per cause). Non-operative management of contained / sealed perforation in selected stable patients.
Optimise resuscitation but do not delay > 6 h for stable perforation; cross-match blood; antibiotics; analgesia; NG; catheter; consent including stoma possibility.
Source control + temporary closure; planned return for definitive surgery after physiological stabilisation.
Antibiotics 5–7 days (longer if abscess); enteral nutrition early; DVT prophylaxis; surveillance for anastomotic leak / collection.

references.label: WSES Consensus Conferences on management of complicated intra-abdominal infections

title: Toxic megacolon / severe acute ulcerative colitis flare
presentation: Acute severe UC: ≥ 6 bloody stools/day + at least one systemic sign (HR > 90, temp > 37.8°C, Hb < 105, ESR > 30) — Truelove-Witts severe criteria.
Toxic megacolon: transverse colon diameter > 6 cm on imaging + systemic toxicity.
Risk factors: opioid / anticholinergic use, hypokalaemia, antimotility agents, C. difficile co-infection, CMV in immunocompromised.
redFlags: Failure to improve on day 3 of IV steroid — escalate / surgical input.

diagnostics.test: AXR daily — measure transverse colon diameter; mucosal islands / thumbprinting.
FBC, CRP, ESR, U&E, albumin, ferritin.
Avoid total colonoscopy — perforation risk; flexible sigmoidoscopy minimum.

management.step: Admit to gastroenterology + surgery joint care
management.detail: Daily ward round with both teams; consent for colectomy from day 1.
Opioids, anticholinergics, antimotility agents (loperamide), NSAIDs.
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 6 h OR methylprednisolone 60 mg/day.
LMWH — UC carries very high VTE risk during flare, even with bleeding (paradoxical).

management.step: Antibiotics — only if perforation / sepsis / megacolon
management.detail: Routine antibiotics not indicated. Cover with piperacillin-tazobactam + metronidazole if toxic megacolon, perforation, or septic.

management.step: Rescue therapy at day 3 if not responding
management.detail: Choose ciclosporin 2 mg/kg/day IV OR infliximab 5 mg/kg IV. Failure of rescue at day 5–7 — colectomy. Surgery should not be delayed for failed second-line.

Indications: perforation, massive haemorrhage, toxic megacolon not improving in 24 h, failed medical therapy. Operation: subtotal colectomy + end ileostomy + preserved rectum (definitive proctectomy + IPAA later).
Maintain steroid taper + start steroid-sparing immunomodulator (azathioprine, biologic). Outpatient gastroenterology within 2 weeks; colonoscopy in 3–6 months.

references.label: ECCO Guidelines on UC; Truelove SC, Witts LJ. BMJ 1955

title: Pyogenic liver abscess
presentation: Fever + RUQ pain + hepatomegaly; raised inflammatory markers, deranged LFTs.
Often subacute (weeks); 50% diabetic; biliary tract, portal pyaemia, or haematogenous spread.
Common organisms: E. coli, Klebsiella (especially in SE Asia + diabetes), Streptococcus anginosus group, anaerobes.
redFlags: Ruptured abscess into peritoneum / pleural cavity / pericardium.
Klebsiella pneumoniae invasive syndrome — endophthalmitis, meningitis, septic emboli.
Amoebic abscess differential — serology mandatory in endemic / travel.

diagnostics.test: Contrast CT abdomen (preferred) or USS abdomen.
FBC, CRP, LFT, blood culture × 2, lactate.
Aspiration / drainage of pus — Gram + culture.
Amoebic serology + stool E. histolytica antigen in endemic / travel.
diagnostics.rationale: Distinguish amoebic (drainage usually unnecessary) from pyogenic.

management.detail: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 6-hourly OR ceftriaxone 2 g daily + metronidazole 500 mg 8-hourly × 4–6 weeks total. Streamline to culture-directed.

management.step: Drainage — image-guided percutaneous catheter for abscess > 3–5 cm
management.detail: USS or CT-guided drain; leave in until output minimal + clinical improvement. Aspiration alone for smaller (< 5 cm); repeat aspiration if needed.

management.step: Surgical drainage for failed percutaneous / multiple / ruptured abscess
management.detail: Laparotomy or laparoscopic drainage.
Biliary tract obstruction → ERCP. Diabetes optimisation. Colonoscopy in cryptogenic abscess (often Streptococcus anginosus colorectal source). Exclude immunocompromise.
Ophthalmology assessment (endophthalmitis), CT head, urinalysis, blood cultures — antibiotics extended duration; serotype K1/K2 hypervirulence.
Often need long oral course (4–6 weeks total) — co-amoxiclav, ciprofloxacin + metronidazole; OPAT for IV continuation.

references.label: IDSA / WSES guidance on liver abscess

title: Retropharyngeal abscess (children + adults)
presentation: Children (peak 2–4 years): fever, drooling, neck stiffness, refusal to feed, hot-potato voice, hyperextension of neck, torticollis.
Adults: fever, neck pain, dysphagia, often post-instrumentation / fishbone foreign body / IV drug user.
Stridor + airway compromise in advanced.
redFlags: Airway compromise — early intubation in operating theatre with ENT.

diagnostics.test: Lateral neck X-ray (widened prevertebral soft tissue > 7 mm at C2 / > 14 mm at C6 in adult).
CT neck with contrast — diagnostic + delineates abscess + mediastinal extension.
FBC, CRP, blood culture, throat / pus cultures.

management.detail: Senior anaesthetist + ENT immediately. Avoid distressing examination in children. Plan intubation in theatre with surgical airway backup.
Cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 8 h + clindamycin 10 mg/kg every 6 h (adults: ceftriaxone 2 g + metronidazole + IV vancomycin if MRSA suspected). Cover polymicrobial + anaerobes.

Indications: abscess > 2 cm, airway compromise, failed conservative trial 24–48 h, suspected gas-forming infection. Transoral incision and drainage; external approach for large / mediastinal extension.
Analgesia; antipyretic; IV fluids; nutritional support; consider NG / parenteral feeding if dysphagia.
Continue IV antibiotics 2–4 weeks total; switch to oral once afebrile + improving; ENT follow-up. Surveillance for complications (mediastinitis, Lemierre).

references.label: AAO-HNS Clinical Indicators on Deep Neck Infections
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children

title: Ludwig angina (submandibular fascial space infection)
presentation: Rapidly progressive bilateral submandibular + sublingual + submental swelling.
Floor of mouth oedema with tongue elevation; trismus; drooling; muffled 'hot potato' voice.
Usually odontogenic (2nd / 3rd molar root abscess); also post-extraction, mandibular fracture, sialadenitis.
redFlags: Stridor / impending airway obstruction — IMMEDIATE secured airway.

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnosis primarily; do NOT delay airway management.
CT neck with contrast once airway secured.
diagnostics.rationale: Defines extent, gas-forming infection, mediastinal extension.

diagnostics.test: FBC, CRP, blood culture, intraoperative cultures.
diagnostics.rationale: Polymicrobial: Streptococcus viridans, Staph aureus, Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium.

management.step: AIRWAY FIRST — awake fibre-optic intubation OR surgical airway
management.detail: Conventional laryngoscopy + supraglottic devices often impossible due to floor-of-mouth oedema and trismus. Surgical airway (tracheostomy) below the suprasternal notch is the safest in severe Ludwig's. Avoid succinylcholine + RSI — high failure rate.
Penicillin G 4 MU IV every 4 h + metronidazole 500 mg every 8 h OR ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g every 6 h OR clindamycin 600 mg every 6 h (if penicillin allergic). Add vancomycin if MRSA risk.
Extra-oral incision and drainage of all involved fascial spaces; dental extraction / endodontic treatment of source tooth. Avoid intra-oral drainage in unsecured airway.
Maintain secured airway; analgesia; nutrition (likely NG / parenteral × days); DVT prophylaxis.
Decannulate tracheostomy when oedema resolved + swallowing safe. Continue IV antibiotics 2–4 weeks total; oral 6 weeks. Maxillofacial / ENT follow-up.

references.label: AAO-HNS guidance on deep neck infection management
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health
WHO Package of Essential NCD Interventions (WHO PEN) — Cardiovascular disease

title: Acute supraglottitis / epiglottitis in adults
presentation: Rapid-onset severe sore throat with disproportionate pain on swallowing, dysphagia, drooling, muffled / hot-potato voice.
Tripod position, fever, tachycardia, stridor, respiratory distress at presentation.
Decline of Hib vaccination has shifted demographics to adults; Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, atypicals also common.
redFlags: Stridor at rest / drooling — airway obstruction imminent.
Posterior pharyngeal abscess / supraglottic abscess complication.
Pregnancy + epiglottitis — maternal + fetal high risk.

diagnostics.test: Do NOT examine throat with tongue depressor — risk laryngospasm.
diagnostics.rationale: Safety; rely on history + visual inspection.

diagnostics.test: Lateral neck X-ray — 'thumbprint sign' on swollen epiglottis.
diagnostics.rationale: Supportive but not always available; delay must not occur.

diagnostics.test: Flexible nasendoscopy by ENT — definitive bedside diagnosis.
FBC, CRP, blood culture, throat swab.

management.detail: Avoid agitation; keep patient sitting; senior anaesthetic + ENT activation.

management.step: Secure the airway PROACTIVELY — operating theatre
management.detail: Awake fibre-optic OR gas induction with spontaneous breathing; ENT scrubbed for surgical airway backup. AVOID muscle relaxant induction in suspected supraglottic obstruction.
Ceftriaxone 2 g daily + (clindamycin OR vancomycin if MRSA risk) for 7–14 days. Adjust to cultures.
Dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 h × 24 h reduces airway oedema. Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg can temporise.
Sedation; ventilator support; daily ENT assessment of supraglottic swelling before extubation.
Antibiotic course; ENT review; consider Hib vaccination if not done.

references.label: AAO-HNS Clinical Indicators; UpToDate adult epiglottitis

title: Central retinal artery occlusion — sudden painless vision loss emergency
presentation: Sudden painless monocular vision loss (count fingers or worse).
Pale retina with cherry-red spot (preserved choroidal flow); relative afferent pupillary defect.
Often atherosclerotic / embolic — TIA / stroke / carotid stenosis equivalent.
Giant cell arteritis must be excluded (age > 50, headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, raised ESR).
redFlags: Time < 4–6 h from onset — potential window for intervention.
Concurrent stroke symptoms — same workup as ischaemic stroke.

diagnostics.test: Urgent ESR + CRP (rule out GCA) + FBC.
diagnostics.rationale: If GCA suspected: high-dose steroid pending biopsy.

diagnostics.test: Carotid Doppler + cardiac assessment (ECG, echo) + CT/MR angiography brain + neck.
diagnostics.rationale: Same workup as TIA / stroke — identify source.

management.step: Treat as stroke equivalent — admit to stroke unit
management.detail: Vision recovery rare regardless of intervention, but stroke risk in following days substantially elevated — same secondary prevention as TIA.

management.step: Consider ocular massage + AC paracentesis if within 4 h
management.detail: Ocular digital massage; anterior chamber paracentesis to lower IOP; carbogen inhalation (5% CO2 / 95% O2); IV acetazolamide 500 mg — evidence weak but minimally invasive.

management.step: Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) — only in clinical trial or stroke pathway < 4.5 h
management.detail: Limited evidence; risk of haemorrhage. Some centres use stroke fibrinolysis pathway for CRAO < 4.5 h with similar contraindications.

management.step: IF GCA suspected — high-dose IV methylprednisolone IMMEDIATELY
management.detail: 1 g IV daily × 3 days then oral prednisolone 60–80 mg/day. DO NOT wait for biopsy; protects second eye + stroke risk. Refer rheumatology + temporal artery biopsy within 2 weeks.
Antiplatelet (aspirin / clopidogrel), statin, BP control, smoking cessation. Anticoagulant if AF identified. Carotid endarterectomy if symptomatic stenosis 50–99%.
Vision loss usually permanent; focus on second-eye protection + stroke prevention. Driving + work implications. Low-vision support.

references.label: AAO Preferred Practice Pattern — CRAO; American Heart Association scientific statement on CRAO as a stroke equivalent (2021)
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health
WHO Package of Essential NCD Interventions (WHO PEN) — Cardiovascular disease

title: Cauda equina syndrome
presentation: Bilateral or unilateral lower-limb radicular pain + sensory disturbance.
Saddle (perineal) anaesthesia / paraesthesia.
Bladder dysfunction — retention with overflow, painless retention, reduced anal sphincter tone.
Bowel dysfunction — faecal incontinence, reduced sensation.
Sexual dysfunction — erectile dysfunction, reduced vaginal sensation.
Causes: large central disc herniation (most common), tumour (primary or metastatic), epidural abscess, haematoma, spinal stenosis, trauma.
redFlags: Urinary retention with post-void residual > 200 mL — sensitive for CES.
Suspected epidural abscess (fever, focal back tenderness, IVDU, immunocompromise).

diagnostics.test: Urgent MRI lumbar spine — within hours.
Neurological + per-rectal examination (anal tone + perianal sensation).
FBC, CRP, blood culture if abscess suspected.

management.detail: Bladder retention is harmful; catheterise. Refer urgently to spinal / neurosurgery — surgical decompression within 24–48 h of CES onset preserves function.

Microdiscectomy for disc; laminectomy + drainage for abscess (also IV antibiotic); resection for tumour; haematoma evacuation. Timing — within 48 h of CES symptoms (some advocate < 24 h for incomplete CES with retention).
Empirical IV vancomycin + ceftriaxone 6 weeks (longer if vertebral osteomyelitis); blood + abscess cultures.
Dexamethasone 16 mg IV/PO loading then 4–8 mg every 6 h pending radiotherapy / surgery.
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, urology / continence specialist (intermittent self-catheterisation), psychological support. Sexual / fertility counselling. Bladder + bowel programmes.
Time of CES symptoms onset + investigations + intervention is critical evidence; document exhaustively as CES is a frequent litigation source.

references.label: British Association of Spine Surgeons consensus on CES (2018, with updates)

title: Spinal epidural abscess
presentation: Classic triad (40%): back pain + fever + neurological deficit.
Local back tenderness with progressive neurology over hours-days (radiculopathy → weakness → paralysis).
Risk: IVDU, immunocompromise (diabetes, HIV, steroid), prior spinal surgery / instrumentation, distant infection (skin, UTI, endocarditis).
Most common organism: Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA / MRSA); also Streptococcus, gram-negatives, anaerobes, mycobacteria.
redFlags: Bilateral leg weakness or progressive deficit — neurosurgical emergency.
Suspected cervical level — risk of rapid quadriparesis + respiratory compromise.

diagnostics.test: Urgent MRI whole spine with contrast.
diagnostics.rationale: Definitive imaging; defines level + skip lesions.

diagnostics.test: Blood cultures × 2; CT-guided aspiration for culture.
Echocardiography (endocarditis source); search for primary source.

management.step: Surgical decompression + drainage — for ANY neurological deficit
management.detail: Laminectomy + decompression within 24–48 h of neurological deficit. Sample for culture. Non-surgical management only in patients without deficit AND organism + susceptibility known + clinical stability.
Vancomycin + ceftriaxone or piperacillin-tazobactam pending cultures; tailor to organism. Duration: 4 weeks minimum after source control, 6–8 weeks if vertebral osteomyelitis.
IVDU harm reduction; endocarditis workup; skin / soft tissue infection.
Orthosis if instability post-laminectomy or due to vertebral involvement.
Multidisciplinary spinal rehabilitation; psychological support; addressing IVDU / chronic illness.

references.label: Darouiche RO. Spinal epidural abscess. NEJM 2006; IDSA guidelines on native vertebral osteomyelitis

title: Acute traumatic spinal cord injury
presentation: High-energy mechanism: RTA, fall from height, diving injury, gunshot.
Acute neurological deficit — sensory + motor — at and below level of injury.
Neurogenic shock: bradycardia + hypotension (loss of sympathetic outflow, especially T6 and above).
Spinal shock: temporary loss of all reflexes (including bulbocavernosus) below injury — recovers over days-weeks.
redFlags: Penetrating injury — risk vascular + infective complications.
Pregnancy — ATLS in left lateral tilt.

diagnostics.test: ATLS primary survey + ASIA neurological exam.
MRI spine — definitive for cord injury + ligamentous injury.
diagnostics.rationale: Soft tissue + cord oedema; surgical planning.

diagnostics.test: Pan-CT for polytrauma if mechanism + GCS impaired.

management.detail: Cervical collar + log roll until imaging cleared. Maintain in-line immobilisation during airway management.
High-cervical: intubate early (respiratory failure imminent). Use manual in-line stabilisation, video laryngoscopy, awake fibre-optic for unstable injury.

Distinguish neurogenic (bradycardia + hypotension) from hypovolaemic (tachycardia + hypotension). Neurogenic: noradrenaline or low-dose adrenaline to target MAP 85–90 mmHg × 7 days (improves spinal cord perfusion + outcomes per ASIA / Consortium for Spinal Cord Medicine).

NASCIS II / III high-dose methylprednisolone showed marginal benefit at cost of complications; current consensus: NOT recommended routinely; discuss carefully if within 8 h penetrating injury without contraindications.
STASCIS trial: surgical decompression < 24 h improves neurological outcome. Closed reduction for cervical facet dislocations; surgical fusion for unstable injuries.

Maintain SpO2 > 92%, normocapnia, normothermia, normoglycaemia, MAP 85–90 mmHg × 7 days. DVT prophylaxis (LMWH from 72 h post-injury once haemodynamically stable). Pressure-area care; bladder programme; bowel programme.

Specialist spinal centre — multidisciplinary rehabilitation (physio, OT, neuropsychology, social work, peer support). Long-term: bladder, bowel, skin, sexual, vocational programmes. Mental-health screening (depression + PTSD common).

references.label: ATLS Manual; ASIA International Standards; AANS/CNS Spine Section guidelines

title: Severe traumatic brain injury (GCS ≤ 8)
presentation: Head trauma with GCS ≤ 8 (severe), 9–12 (moderate), 13–15 (mild).
Mechanisms: RTA, fall, assault, sports, blast.
Primary injury: contusion, diffuse axonal injury, haematoma (extradural, subdural, intracerebral).
Secondary injury: hypoxia, hypotension, ICP rise, seizure, hyperthermia.
redFlags: Pupillary asymmetry / fixed dilated — impending herniation.
Focal neurology, vomiting > 3 episodes, seizure post-TBI, anticoagulation.
Polytrauma with concurrent hypovolaemia / chest / abdominal injury.

diagnostics.test: GCS + pupil exam serial; FOUR score in intubated.
Non-contrast CT head + cervical spine within 30 min.
ABG, glucose, electrolytes, coag, FBC, group + crossmatch.

diagnostics.rationale: Distinguish intoxication vs TBI; both common.

management.detail: SpO2 > 92% (intubate if GCS ≤ 8); MAP ≥ 80 mmHg / CPP ≥ 60 mmHg; normocapnia (PaCO2 35–40 mmHg); avoid hypotension; head-up 30°. Hypotonic fluids contraindicated.

management.step: Intubation for GCS ≤ 8 / impending respiratory failure
management.detail: RSI with cervical immobilisation; ketamine 1.5 mg/kg + rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg preferred (ketamine no longer contraindicated in TBI). Avoid succinylcholine in established TBI with hyperkalaemia risk.

management.step: Reverse anticoagulation immediately if on warfarin / DOAC / antiplatelet
management.detail: Per ICH pathway: vit K + 4F-PCC for warfarin; idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet/4F-PCC for FXa; tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 h per CRASH-3.

Hyperosmolar therapy: hypertonic saline 3% 5 mL/kg or 23.4% bolus; or mannitol 1 g/kg. Drain CSF via EVD. Cooling to 35°C (avoid prophylactic hypothermia). Maintain CPP ≥ 60. Surgical decompression for haematoma or refractory ICP (decompressive craniectomy).
Levetiracetam 1 g BD × 7 days reduces early post-traumatic seizure incidence; no benefit beyond 7 days.
Normothermia (treat fever aggressively), normoglycaemia, no hyponatraemia, DVT prophylaxis with mechanical immediately + LMWH after 24–48 h once haematoma stable, nutritional support.
Extradural / acute subdural / large intracerebral with mass effect / midline shift > 5 mm. Decompressive craniectomy for refractory ICP per RESCUEicp.
Early specialist rehabilitation; cognitive + behavioural support; family + psychological care; vocational rehabilitation; return-to-driving + return-to-work assessments.

references.label: Brain Trauma Foundation Guidelines for the Management of Severe TBI (4th edition); CRASH-3 trial Lancet 2019

title: Unstable pelvic fracture with haemorrhage
presentation: High-energy mechanism (RTA, fall from height, crush).
Pelvic pain, deformity, instability on examination (assess once during ATLS, not repeatedly).
Haemodynamic instability — retroperitoneal haemorrhage from venous plexus + arterial branches.
Open pelvic fracture (vaginal, rectal, perineal wound) — high mortality.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability with confirmed pelvic fracture — pelvic binder + theatre / IR.
Urogenital injury — blood at meatus, scrotal haematoma, high-riding prostate (consult before catheterising).

diagnostics.test: Pelvic X-ray AP during primary survey.
FAST scan / DPL for concurrent abdominal source.
CT angiogram pelvis once stable (or going to IR).
FBC, lactate, coag, group + crossmatch ≥ 10 units.
Retrograde urethrogram + cystogram before catheter if urogenital injury.

management.step: Pelvic binder at the level of greater trochanters
management.detail: Reduces pelvic volume + venous bleeding; apply early during primary survey for any suspected unstable fracture. Do NOT remove for X-ray.
PRBC:FFP:platelets 1:1:1; tranexamic acid 1 g IV (CRASH-2) within 3 h; warmed products; cell salvage if available; permissive hypotension target SBP 80–90.

management.step: Haemorrhage control — IR-first or surgical packing
management.detail: Hybrid theatre / dedicated IR — angiography + embolisation for arterial bleeding. Pre-peritoneal pelvic packing as alternative or adjunct in centres without IR. REBOA in highly selected cases.
After resuscitation: external fixation immediate; definitive plate / screw fixation as physiology allows.
Defunctioning colostomy for perineal contamination; debridement; antibiotics; tetanus.
Suprapubic catheter for urethral injury; urology consult; cystogram for bladder rupture (intraperitoneal → surgical; extraperitoneal → conservative).
DVT very high risk — mechanical immediately, LMWH from 24–48 h once stable. Early mobilisation; orthopaedic + physiotherapy rehabilitation. Mental-health screen.

references.label: WSES guidelines on pelvic fracture trauma; ATLS Manual; AAST classification

title: Acute endophthalmitis — post-procedural or endogenous
presentation: Sudden severe pain, vision loss, hypopyon, conjunctival injection within days-weeks of intraocular procedure (cataract surgery, intravitreal injection, trauma).
Endogenous: bloodstream seeding (IVDU, hospital, immunocompromised) — often bilateral.
Acute (< 6 weeks post-op) most commonly bacterial (coagulase-negative Staph, Strep, gram-negative); chronic — Propionibacterium acnes, fungal.
redFlags: Complete loss of red reflex, severe pain.
Filtering bleb-related — high virulence Streptococcus, gram-negatives.

diagnostics.test: Vitreous + aqueous tap for culture / PCR — preferably at time of intervention.
Blood cultures + septic workup if endogenous.

management.detail: Vancomycin 1 mg + ceftazidime 2.25 mg (or amikacin 0.4 mg) in 0.1 mL each — covers Gram-positive + Gram-negative. Within hours of presentation.

EVS criteria: vision ≤ light perception or worse → consider vitrectomy (improves outcome). For better vision, vitrectomy not consistently better than tap alone in EVS but practice trending toward early vitrectomy.
Topical vancomycin + ceftazidime hourly; oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily (penetrates intraocular fluid).
Intravitreal dexamethasone 400 microgram considered to reduce inflammation but may worsen if undiagnosed fungal; topical / oral steroid typically given after antibiotic established.
IV antibiotics for bacteraemia; endocarditis workup; remove infected line; treat candidaemia (echinocandin).
Daily review until improving; repeat tap / vitrectomy if no improvement at 48 h. Long-term: cataract / IOL retention vs explantation; visual rehabilitation; counselling on guarded prognosis.

references.label: Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS); ESCRS / AAO guidance

title: Necrotising soft tissue infection (Fournier, fasciitis, myositis)
presentation: Pain out of proportion to clinical signs; rapidly progressing erythema, skin discolouration, blistering, bullae, crepitus (gas-forming).
Systemic toxicity disproportionate to local appearance: fever, tachycardia, hypotension.
Subtype Fournier gangrene: perineal / scrotal — diabetic + immunocompromised men commonly.
Polymicrobial (type I) vs monomicrobial (type II — group A strep, Staph aureus).
redFlags: Pain out of proportion + rapid spread (cm/h).
Streptococcal / staphylococcal toxic shock — DIC, multi-organ failure.
Delay to surgical debridement > 12 h significantly worsens mortality.

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnosis takes priority — DO NOT delay surgery for imaging if classical features.
LRINEC score (CRP, WBC, Hb, Na, creatinine, glucose) ≥ 6 suggests NSTI.
CT / MRI — gas, fascial involvement (use if diagnosis uncertain + patient stable).
FBC, U&E, lactate, creatinine, CK, coag, blood culture, intra-operative tissue culture.

management.step: URGENT surgical debridement — within hours of recognition
management.detail: Wide excision of all non-viable tissue beyond visible margin; repeat 'second look' at 24 h. Mortality directly correlates with surgical delay. Defunctioning colostomy for Fournier with perineal contamination.
Meropenem 1 g 8-hourly + clindamycin 1.2 g 6-hourly (clindamycin suppresses streptococcal toxin) ± vancomycin (MRSA). Tailor to cultures. Continue 48 h after last debridement + sepsis resolution.
Aggressive IV fluid; vasopressor noradrenaline; blood products; correct coagulopathy.
IVIG 1–2 g/kg if confirmed group A strep with TSS features.
Adjunctive role in centres with rapid access (mainly for clostridial myonecrosis); should never delay surgery.
Skin grafting / flap reconstruction once disease controlled. Wound care nurse; physiotherapy; psychological + functional rehabilitation.
Long-term surveillance for adhesions, hernia, sexual + urinary dysfunction (Fournier); colostomy reversal in selected patients.

references.label: WSES Guidelines on NSTI (2018); IDSA Diagnosis and Management of Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

title: Cavernous sinus thrombosis
presentation: Headache + fever + cranial nerve palsies (III, IV, V1+V2, VI) + proptosis + chemosis.
Often spread from facial infection (mid-face triangle: 'danger zone' — nasal furuncle, sinusitis, dental, orbital cellulitis).
Pre-thrombotic / septic state.
redFlags: Rapid progression to bilateral cranial nerve involvement.

diagnostics.test: MRI brain + MR venography (or CT venography).
diagnostics.rationale: Definitive imaging — cavernous sinus filling defect.

diagnostics.test: FBC, CRP, blood culture, coag, lactate.
Identify primary source — facial / dental / sinus.

management.detail: Cover Staph aureus (including MRSA), Streptococcus, anaerobes, gram-negatives: vancomycin + ceftriaxone 2 g BD + metronidazole 500 mg 8-hourly × 3–4 weeks (longer if abscess).
LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD) or unfractionated heparin — reduces clot propagation; case series suggest mortality benefit despite haemorrhagic risk. Continue 3–6 months.
Dexamethasone 4 mg every 6 h may reduce inflammation + cranial nerve injury — limited evidence.
Surgical drainage of sphenoid sinus / sinusitis / dental abscess; nasal / dental specialty consultation.
Airway protection if reduced consciousness; manage seizures; ICP monitoring if needed; eye care for proptosis (lubrication, tarsorrhaphy).
Endocrine evaluation for pituitary function 6 weeks later; ophthalmology for residual deficits; long-term anticoagulation review based on thrombophilia screen.

references.label: Plewa MC, Tadi P. Cavernous sinus thrombosis (StatPearls)

title: Acute aortic dissection (Stanford A + B)
presentation: Sudden severe ('tearing', 'ripping') chest / back / abdominal pain — pain location migrates with dissection progression.
BP discrepancy between arms (≥ 20 mmHg systolic); pulse deficit; new aortic regurgitation murmur.
Neurology (stroke, syncope, paraplegia), abdominal pain (mesenteric), AKI, leg ischaemia depending on branch involvement.
Risk: hypertension (>70%), connective-tissue disorders (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos), bicuspid aortic valve, pregnancy, cocaine.
redFlags: Cardiac tamponade — beck triad, pulsus paradoxus, distended JVP.

diagnostics.rationale: Identify intimal flap (Type A); aortic regurg; effusion; tamponade.

diagnostics.test: CT angiography aorta — first-line if stable.
ECG — exclude STEMI; may show inferior changes if coronary involvement.

diagnostics.rationale: Not specific; do not delay imaging.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, lactate, troponin, group + crossmatch.

management.detail: Target HR 60–80, SBP 100–120 mmHg. IV labetalol or esmolol infusion (esmolol preferred — titratable). Add IV nitroprusside / GTN if BP still high AFTER β-blocker (vasodilator-first risks reflex tachycardia worsening dissection). Pain control with morphine.
Open cardiothoracic surgical repair (replacement of ascending aorta + aortic root / valve as needed) — mortality 1–2% per hour untreated. Arrange immediate cardiothoracic transfer.
BP + HR control as above × at least 3 days in HDU/ICU. Endovascular repair (TEVAR) for complicated Type B: malperfusion, refractory pain, expansion, rupture. Open surgery rarely needed.
Stroke — supportive (no thrombolysis — propagates dissection). Mesenteric ischaemia — fenestration / branch stenting. Acute renal failure — RRT. Aortic regurg / tamponade — emergency repair.

Lifelong CT angiography every 3, 6, 12 months then annually. Strict BP control < 120/80. Connective-tissue disorder genetic screening + family screen. Avoid heavy isometric exercise. Pregnancy counselling in Marfan + dissection history.
Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, vascular Ehlers-Danlos, bicuspid aortic valve. First-degree relatives — screening echocardiography.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS)
presentation: Facial / neck / arm swelling, plethora, distended neck veins, dyspnoea, cough, hoarseness.
Worsening over weeks; often presenting feature of mediastinal malignancy (lung cancer, lymphoma, mediastinal germ cell tumour, thymic).
Less commonly thrombosis around central venous catheter / pacemaker lead, or fibrosing mediastinitis.
redFlags: Imminent superior orbital fissure syndrome (severe head swelling).

diagnostics.test: Tissue biopsy — bronchoscopy, mediastinoscopy, percutaneous — BEFORE empirical steroid where feasible.
FBC, LDH, beta-HCG, AFP, uric acid, urate.

management.detail: Head-up positioning, supplemental O2. Avoid lying flat. Avoid upper-limb IV cannulation (use femoral). Anaesthetic input if airway compromise — careful with sedation.

management.step: Endovascular stenting — definitive symptom relief in 24–48 h
management.detail: First-line for severe / rapidly progressive symptoms regardless of cause; interventional radiology. Allows time for tissue diagnosis without delay in oncology workup.
Steroids alter lymphoma pathology — get diagnostic biopsy first if patient stable. If true emergency airway threat: empirical dexamethasone 4–8 mg IV every 6 h until biopsy.

Lymphoma: chemotherapy (R-CHOP / ABVD) urgently; usually rapid response. Small-cell lung cancer: chemotherapy. NSCLC: stenting + radiotherapy + targeted therapy / immunotherapy per molecular profile. Germ cell tumour: BEP chemotherapy. Catheter-related thrombosis: anticoagulate + consider catheter removal.
Furosemide — modest relief of facial / arm oedema. Dexamethasone — reduces tumour oedema (especially lymphoma). Analgesia for headache.
LMWH then DOAC (DOAC well-evidenced in cancer-associated thrombosis), with consideration for thrombolysis if recent (< 14 d) extensive thrombus.

references.label: ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines for management of cancer-related emergencies; NCCN Distress Management / Supportive Care
Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Malignant hypercalcaemia
presentation: Adjusted calcium > 2.8 mmol/L with malignancy.
'Stones, bones, abdominal moans, psychic groans': renal stones, bone pain / pathological fracture, abdominal pain / constipation / pancreatitis, confusion / depression.
Severe (Ca > 3.5): vomiting, polyuria-polydipsia, dehydration, AKI, lethargy, coma, arrhythmia.
Mechanisms: PTHrP (squamous lung, head + neck, renal), osteolytic metastases (myeloma, breast), vitamin D production (lymphoma), ectopic PTH (rare).

diagnostics.test: Adjusted (corrected) calcium = total Ca + 0.02 × (40 – albumin g/L); OR ionised Ca preferred.
U&E, creatinine, phosphate, magnesium, PTH (low in malignant), PTHrP, vitamin D, urine Ca:Cr.
diagnostics.rationale: Identify mechanism; PTH suppression confirms malignant or non-PTH cause.

diagnostics.test: Imaging for primary malignancy if unknown (CXR, mammography, CT chest/abdomen, myeloma screen).

management.detail: 0.9% NaCl 200–500 mL/h titrated to euvolaemia + urine output 100–150 mL/h. Total 3–6 L over first 24 h. AVOID thiazide diuretic (reduces Ca excretion); furosemide ONLY after volume restored if hypervolaemic.

management.step: IV bisphosphonate — mainstay for malignant hypercalcaemia
management.detail: Zoledronate 4 mg IV over 15 min (reduce dose if eGFR < 60); pamidronate 60–90 mg IV over 2–4 h alternative. Onset 24–48 h; peak effect 4–7 days; duration 2–4 weeks. Renal adjustment essential.
Calcitonin 4 IU/kg SC every 12 h for 24–48 h — onset 2–4 h. Used as adjunct while waiting for bisphosphonate effect. Tachyphylaxis limits to short course.

management.step: Denosumab for bisphosphonate-refractory or renal failure
management.detail: 120 mg SC for refractory cases or when bisphosphonate contraindicated (eGFR < 30). Onset slower; risk of severe rebound hypocalcaemia.
Prednisolone 40–60 mg/day for myeloma, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, lymphoma-associated calcitriol; ineffective for solid-tumour bone metastasis.
Definitive oncological treatment is the best long-term control.

management.step: Haemodialysis for life-threatening level / renal failure
management.detail: Low-calcium dialysate; for Ca > 4 with severe symptoms / cardiac arrhythmia / AKI not responding to medical therapy.

references.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Hypercalcemia (2020)
Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) toxicity — immune-related adverse events
presentation: Patient on anti-PD-1 (nivolumab, pembrolizumab), anti-PD-L1 (atezolizumab, durvalumab), anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab), or combination.
Onset usually 4–12 weeks but can occur ANY TIME during or after therapy (months).
Common irAEs by system:
Skin: rash, pruritus, vitiligo, severe SJS/TEN.
GI: diarrhoea, colitis, hepatitis (transaminitis).
Endocrine: thyroiditis (transient thyrotoxicosis → hypothyroidism), hypophysitis, adrenalitis (adrenal insufficiency), type 1 diabetes (often DKA at presentation).
Pulmonary: pneumonitis (dyspnoea, cough, hypoxia).
Neurologic: myasthenia gravis-like, encephalitis, Guillain-Barré, transverse myelitis.
Cardiac: myocarditis (high mortality, rare).
Renal: interstitial nephritis.
redFlags: Grade 3–4 toxicity in any system — admit, hold ICI, urgent steroid.
Myocarditis (raised troponin, ECG changes, dyspnoea) — high mortality; multidisciplinary urgent management.
Suspected adrenal crisis (often hyperpigmentation absent — secondary).

diagnostics.test: Routine baseline before each cycle: FBC, U&E, LFT, TSH, glucose, cortisol if symptomatic.
Symptomatic-specific: CT chest pneumonitis; troponin + ECG + echo myocarditis; flexible sigmoidoscopy + biopsy colitis; cortisol + ACTH adrenal; pituitary MRI + hormone panel hypophysitis.
Auto-antibodies for differential (NMDAR, AChR, anti-striated, etc.).

management.step: Grade by CTCAE; hold ICI for ≥ grade 2
management.detail: Grade 1 (mild): observe; continue ICI. Grade 2 (moderate): hold ICI; corticosteroid 0.5–1 mg/kg/day. Grade 3 (severe): hold + admit + prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day or IV methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day. Grade 4 (life-threatening): IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily × 3 days.
Taper over 4–8 weeks once symptoms grade ≤ 1. Faster taper risks relapse.
Infliximab 5 mg/kg for colitis / IO arthritis; mycophenolate mofetil for hepatitis; rituximab; tocilizumab; tacrolimus — under specialist multidisciplinary (oncology + organ specialist) guidance.

Pneumonitis: oxygen + steroid; severe → infliximab / MMF. Colitis: IV steroid then infliximab if no response 72 h. Hepatitis: hold ICI; AST/ALT > 5x ULN → steroid. Endocrine: usually permanent — replace hormone (levothyroxine, hydrocortisone, insulin). Myocarditis: high-dose steroid + early mycophenolate / ATG / abatacept. T1DM with DKA: standard DKA management.
Hypothyroidism, hypocortisolism, hypogonadism, T1DM — do not stop replacement; counsel sick-day rules for hypocortisolism.

Possible for grade 1–2 toxicity once resolved with low-dose steroid; AVOID re-challenge for grade 3 cardiac, neurological, pulmonary. Re-challenge with different class (anti-PD-1 if Grade 3 anti-CTLA-4).
Symptoms requiring urgent review; medic-alert; sick-day rules; immunisation review (avoid live vaccines).

references.label: ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines: Management of toxicities from immunotherapy

title: Head and neck cancer — diagnosis and treatment pathway
presentation: Persistent (≥ 3 weeks): non-healing oral ulcer, neck mass, hoarseness, dysphagia, otalgia (referred), epistaxis, nasal obstruction.
Risk factors: tobacco (smoke + chew), alcohol, HPV (oropharyngeal — rising incidence), poor oral hygiene, EBV (nasopharyngeal — endemic SE Asia, North Africa), betel nut, immunosuppression.
Specific anatomical sites: oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx, larynx, nasopharynx, nasal cavity + paranasal sinuses, salivary gland.
redFlags: Hot potato voice, drooling, dysphagia, fixed neck mass.
Massive haemoptysis (rare); pre-emptive risk in advanced laryngeal.

diagnostics.test: Biopsy (panendoscopy + EUA) for histology + HPV (p16) + EBV testing.

diagnostics.rationale: Identify SCC; HPV / EBV testing of FNA.

management.detail: ENT surgery + oncology + radiation oncology + dental + speech-language therapy + dietitian + clinical nurse specialist + palliative care.
Single-modality: surgery (selective neck dissection + primary excision) OR radiotherapy. Choose based on functional outcome + location.
Concurrent chemoradiotherapy (cisplatin 100 mg/m² × 3 cycles + 70 Gy radiation in 35 fractions) OR surgery + adjuvant chemoradiotherapy. HPV+ oropharyngeal — may de-escalate (active research).
Platinum-based chemotherapy + cetuximab (EXTREME); pembrolizumab single-agent or combination (KEYNOTE-048) for PD-L1 high; nivolumab for platinum-refractory.
Dental assessment + pre-radiotherapy extractions; PEG / NG feeding tube; speech + swallow therapy; xerostomia management; trismus prevention exercises; smoking + alcohol cessation.
Years 1–2: every 1–3 months. Years 3–5: every 3–6 months. After 5 years: annually. PET-CT at 12 weeks post-treatment + as clinically indicated.
