Manage long-term toxicities: dysphagia, xerostomia, dental decay, hearing loss (cisplatin), neuropathy, hypothyroidism. Psychological support; vocational + cosmetic rehabilitation.

references.label: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Head and Neck Cancers
Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health

title: Oesophageal cancer — diagnosis and management pathway
presentation: Progressive dysphagia (solids → liquids), weight loss, retrosternal pain, regurgitation.
Adenocarcinoma (rising — lower 1/3, GOJ, Barrett's, GORD, obesity) vs squamous cell carcinoma (upper 2/3, smoking, alcohol, hot beverages, achalasia).
Late: hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal), haematemesis, pneumonia (fistula), supraclavicular node, hepatomegaly.
redFlags: Dysphagia + weight loss in any adult ≥ 40 — urgent OGD.

diagnostics.test: Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy — first-line diagnostic.
CT chest + abdomen + pelvis with contrast.
Laparoscopy + peritoneal washings for adenocarcinoma GOJ.
MDT discussion; nutritional assessment; cardiopulmonary fitness.

management.detail: Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) or endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) for selected T1a; high-grade dysplasia in Barrett's: ablation + EMR. Surveillance ± completion oesophagectomy if high-risk features.
Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (CROSS regimen — carboplatin + paclitaxel + 41.4 Gy) → oesophagectomy at 6–8 weeks. OR perioperative chemotherapy (FLOT or MAGIC for adenocarcinoma).
For surgically unfit / squamous cell with good response. Cisplatin + 5-FU + 50.4 Gy.

Stenting (self-expanding metal stent) for dysphagia in irresectable / metastatic. Palliative chemotherapy (oxaliplatin + capecitabine for adenocarcinoma; chemoradiotherapy for SCC). Trastuzumab for HER2+ adenocarcinoma. Pembrolizumab + chemotherapy for PD-L1 CPS ≥ 10.
Nutritional support — pre-op feeding via jejunostomy or NG; post-op enteral nutrition. Smoking + alcohol cessation. Pain management. Palliative care input from diagnosis in advanced disease.
Annual surveillance (CT 6-monthly × 2 years then annually). Long-term: anastomotic stricture (endoscopic dilatation), reflux, dumping syndrome, vitamin B12 / iron deficiency.

references.label: ESMO oesophageal cancer guidelines; NCCN Esophageal and Esophagogastric Junction Cancers
Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)
presentation: Persistent cytopenia (Hb < 10, neutrophils < 1.8, platelets < 100) in older adult.
Often asymptomatic — discovered on routine FBC.
Symptoms: fatigue, dyspnoea, infections, bruising.
Spectrum: refractory cytopenia → MDS with excess blasts (5–19%) → AML (blasts ≥ 20%).
Risk factors: age, prior chemotherapy / radiotherapy (therapy-related MDS), benzene exposure.
redFlags: Iron overload from chronic transfusion (ferritin > 1000) — start chelation.

diagnostics.test: Bone marrow aspirate + biopsy + cytogenetics + FISH + molecular (SF3B1, TP53, ASXL1, U2AF1).
B12, folate, iron studies, thyroid, EPO, viral hepatitis.

management.detail: Low / very low risk: focus on symptom relief. Intermediate-high: disease-modifying therapy.

Erythropoietin-stimulating agent (epoetin or darbepoetin) for anaemia with EPO < 500. Lenalidomide for del(5q). Luspatercept for ring-sideroblast subtypes. Transfusion + iron chelation when ferritin > 1000.
Azacitidine 75 mg/m² SC daily × 7 days every 4 weeks OR decitabine 20 mg/m² IV × 5 days every 4 weeks. Continue until progression / toxicity. Median overall survival improved vs supportive care.

management.step: Allogeneic stem cell transplant — only curative option
management.detail: Higher-risk patients, age < 70 (selected up to 75), good performance status, matched donor available. Conditioning intensity adjusted for age + comorbidity.

Red cell transfusion for symptomatic anaemia (target Hb > 80, individualised). Platelet transfusion for active bleeding or prophylaxis < 10. Antibiotic prophylaxis selectively in neutropenic patients. Iron chelation (deferasirox) when transfusion-dependent.
Standard AML chemotherapy if fit; venetoclax + azacitidine for unfit; allogeneic transplant if responding.
Symptom management (fatigue, infection, bleeding); shared decision-making; advance care planning.

references.label: IPSS-M Bernard E et al. NEJM Evid 2022
Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)
presentation: Platelet drop ≥ 30–50% from baseline, typically 5–10 days after heparin exposure (faster in re-exposure within last 100 days).
PARADOXICAL thrombosis: limb, mesenteric, pulmonary, intracardiac, adrenal — venous AND arterial.
Skin necrosis at injection site, anaphylactoid reaction with IV bolus.
Risk: post-cardiac surgery (3%), orthopaedic surgery (1%), medical (<0.5%); unfractionated > LMWH risk.
redFlags: Any new thrombosis on heparin — assume HIT until disproved.
Acute limb ischaemia / mesenteric ischaemia / pulmonary embolism on heparin.
Severe thrombocytopenia (< 20) with active bleeding (rare but reported).
Atypical: < 4 days from heparin (re-exposure within 100 days).

diagnostics.rationale: Pre-test probability; score 0–3 low (rule out without serology), 4–5 intermediate, 6–8 high.
Sensitive but not specific (positive in many without clinical HIT).

diagnostics.test: Confirmatory functional assay — SRA (serotonin release assay) or HIPA.
Imaging for thrombosis based on symptoms (Doppler, CTPA, abdominal imaging).

management.detail: Including unfractionated heparin (bolus, infusion, flushes), LMWH, heparin-coated catheters. Replace with non-heparin anticoagulant.

Direct thrombin inhibitor: argatroban (preferred — renal-independent) infusion adjusted to aPTT 1.5–3× control. OR fondaparinux 7.5 mg SC daily (off-label but well-evidenced). OR DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban) for stable patients without active major bleeding. Bivalirudin in cardiac surgery.

Warfarin alone — risk of microvascular thrombosis (skin necrosis, venous limb gangrene) when initiated during acute HIT. Wait until platelet count > 150 × 10⁹/L before adding warfarin to argatroban / fondaparinux.
Risk of further thrombosis; reserve only for active major bleeding.
Therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulation × at least 3 months (longer if persistent risk). Surgical embolectomy / thrombectomy if limb-threatening.

Document HIT in medical record + allergy alert; avoid heparin lifelong (rare exception: cardiac surgery > 100 days after HIT when antibodies negative — bolus heparin during bypass only, with bivalirudin pre/post). Counsel patient + medic-alert.

references.label: ASH 2018 Guidelines on management of HIT

title: Acute sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis — adult
presentation: Severe pain — typically bone, back, chest, abdomen.
Often preceded by dehydration, infection, cold, altitude, stress.
May progress to chest crisis (cough, hypoxia, infiltrate), splenic sequestration, stroke, priapism, AKI.
redFlags: Acute chest syndrome (new infiltrate + hypoxia + fever + chest pain).
Severe pre-existing pulmonary hypertension / heart failure.

diagnostics.test: U&E, LFT, LDH, bilirubin, blood culture, urinalysis.
Reticulocyte (low in aplastic crisis — parvovirus B19).

management.step: Aggressive pain control within 30 min of presentation
management.detail: IV opioid (morphine 0.1 mg/kg or hydromorphone) titrated to pain score; patient-controlled analgesia early. Paracetamol + NSAID adjunct (caution NSAID in AKI). Reassess every 15–30 min until pain controlled.
Maintenance + correct deficit; avoid over-hydration (heart failure, pulmonary oedema risk). 0.9% NaCl or balanced crystalloid.
Maintain SpO2 ≥ 95% — hypoxia worsens sickling.

management.step: Antibiotics if febrile / signs of infection
management.detail: IV ceftriaxone 2 g + macrolide (covers atypical pneumonia in chest crisis); add vancomycin if MRSA risk.

Oxygen + ceftriaxone + macrolide + incentive spirometry; simple or exchange transfusion if hypoxia / multi-lobar disease; bronchodilator if wheeze. Avoid over-transfusion (target Hb 100 g/L max in non-emergency).
Target HbS < 30% via red cell exchange; tPA for ischaemic stroke per stroke pathway (caveat: case-by-case).
IV hydration + analgesia; aspiration / phenylephrine injection by urology; exchange transfusion.

Hydroxyurea 15–35 mg/kg/day — reduces crisis frequency, mortality. L-glutamine, voxelotor, crizanlizumab for additional control. Allogeneic stem cell transplant — curative option for selected. Vaccinations (pneumococcal, meningococcal, influenza); penicillin prophylaxis in children.

references.label: ASH Pocket Guide on Sickle Cell Disease (2020)
BSH guideline for the management of acute painful crisis in sickle cell disease

title: Systemic lupus erythematosus — severe acute flare (lupus nephritis, CNS, haematological, cardiopulmonary)
presentation: Lupus nephritis: proteinuria > 0.5 g/24 h, active urinary sediment, AKI, hypertension — class III/IV needs aggressive therapy.
Neuropsychiatric: seizure, psychosis, stroke, transverse myelitis, demyelination, severe headache.
Haematological: severe autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (Hb < 7), severe thrombocytopenia (< 20).
Cardiopulmonary: severe pleuropericarditis with tamponade, pulmonary haemorrhage, severe Libman-Sacks endocarditis.
Triggers: infection, sun exposure, drug withdrawal, pregnancy, stress.
redFlags: Rapidly progressive AKI / nephritic syndrome → urgent renal biopsy.
Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (haemoptysis + hypoxia + falling Hb).
Macrophage activation syndrome (cytopenias + very high ferritin + hepatitis + splenomegaly).
Pregnancy with active SLE — high-risk maternal + fetal outcomes.

diagnostics.test: ANA, anti-dsDNA, complement (C3/C4 — falling in flare), anti-Smith, anti-Ro/La, antiphospholipid antibodies.
FBC, U&E, creatinine, urinalysis (UPCR or 24 h protein), CRP (usually low; high suggests infection), ESR, ferritin, LDH, complement.
Renal biopsy for lupus nephritis class (III/IV proliferative needs aggressive Rx).
Septic workup — flares and infection cause similar presentation.

management.detail: Stop offending drugs (procainamide, hydralazine drug-induced lupus); treat infection; UV protection.

Lupus nephritis class III/IV: IV cyclophosphamide (NIH 750 mg/m² monthly × 6, OR Euro-Lupus 500 mg every 2 weeks × 6) OR mycophenolate mofetil 2–3 g/day × 6 months. ADD IV methylprednisolone 250–1000 mg daily × 3 days then oral prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day tapered over 6 months. ADD belimumab 200 mg SC weekly for moderate-severe.
400 mg/day (200 mg if low weight or eGFR < 60) — reduces flares, mortality, thromboembolism, organ damage. Annual ophthalmology screen for retinal toxicity.

MMF 1–2 g/day OR azathioprine 1–2 mg/kg/day × ≥ 3 years; consider belimumab as add-on; voclosporin or anifrolumab for refractory class III/IV (LN); rituximab for refractory haematological / mucocutaneous.

Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage: IVMP + plasma exchange + cyclophosphamide. CAPS: anticoagulation + steroid + plasma exchange + IVIG. Severe AIHA: IVMP + rituximab. Severe NPSLE: IVMP + cyclophosphamide; anticoagulate for thrombotic events.

Aggressive CV risk-factor management (statin, BP), antiplatelet for aPL+, contraception counselling (avoid oestrogen-containing in aPL+; copper IUD or progesterone only), pregnancy planning at SLE remission only.

Stable SLE × 6 months before conception; continue hydroxychloroquine; switch to pregnancy-compatible immunosuppression (azathioprine, tacrolimus); aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks; specialist obstetric MDT.

references.label: EULAR/ACR criteria for SLE; KDIGO Lupus Nephritis 2024
BSR/BHPR Guideline for the management of SLE

title: ANCA-associated vasculitis — acute / active disease
presentation: Constitutional: fever, weight loss, malaise.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA): upper + lower respiratory + renal; saddle nose, sinusitis, hearing loss, subglottic stenosis, nodules + cavities.
Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA): glomerulonephritis + alveolar haemorrhage; less granulomatous / ENT.
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA): asthma + eosinophilia + small-vessel vasculitis; cardiomyopathy.
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis: crescentic GN; AKI.
Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage: haemoptysis + hypoxia + bilateral infiltrates + falling Hb.
redFlags: Sinusitis / subglottic stenosis with airway compromise.

diagnostics.test: ANCA: c-ANCA / PR3 (GPA), p-ANCA / MPO (MPA, EGPA, also drug-induced).
Urinalysis (haematuria + RBC casts + proteinuria), UPCR, creatinine.
Renal biopsy — gold standard (pauci-immune crescentic GN).
CT chest (nodules, cavities, infiltrates, alveolar haemorrhage).

management.detail: Organ-threatening / severe: high-dose IV methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg daily × 3 days + oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day tapered + (cyclophosphamide 15 mg/kg every 2–3 weeks × 6 doses OR rituximab 375 mg/m²/week × 4 doses).

PEXIVAS trial: PLEX no longer routine in all AAV. Reserve for severe alveolar haemorrhage (selective) and dialysis-dependent AKI (creatinine > 350 with crescentic GN). Adjunctive immunosuppression remains essential.
Co-trimoxazole 480 mg daily during induction + first 6 months of maintenance — prevents PJP in cyclophosphamide / high-dose steroid.
Rituximab 1 g every 6 months × 4–5 years (MAINRITSAN) OR azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day OR methotrexate 20–25 mg/week — for ≥ 2–4 years.
Mepolizumab 300 mg SC every 4 weeks for steroid-dependent / refractory eosinophilic disease.
Switch class (rituximab → cyclophosphamide or vice versa); IVIG; emerging — avacopan oral C5a receptor inhibitor reduces steroid exposure (ADVOCATE trial).

Monthly review during induction; quarterly maintenance. Bone protection (DEXA, bisphosphonate). Cardiovascular risk. Vaccinations (avoid live; influenza + pneumococcal). Cancer surveillance (cyclophosphamide cumulative dose < 25 g lifetime — bladder + haematological).

references.label: EULAR/ERA-EDTA recommendations for the management of ANCA-associated vasculitis (2024 update); PEXIVAS trial NEJM 2020

title: Dermatomyositis / polymyositis — diagnosis + acute management
presentation: Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness over weeks-months — difficulty rising from chair / climbing stairs / lifting arms.
Dermatomyositis: heliotrope rash, Gottron papules over MCP/PIP knuckles, shawl sign, mechanic's hands, calcinosis (juvenile).
Constitutional: fatigue, fever, weight loss, dysphagia, dysphonia.
Lung involvement (anti-MDA5, anti-Jo-1): rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease.
Cardiac: arrhythmia, myocarditis.
Cancer association in adult-onset (especially anti-TIF1γ, anti-NXP2) — workup mandatory.
redFlags: Rapidly progressive ILD (anti-MDA5+) — high mortality, urgent immunosuppression.
Respiratory failure from muscle weakness / aspiration.

diagnostics.test: Creatine kinase (markedly raised typically); ALT, AST, LDH, aldolase.
Myositis-specific antibodies (Jo-1, MDA5, NXP2, TIF1γ, Mi-2, SAE, HMGCR, SRP).
EMG (myopathic features), MRI muscle (oedema), muscle biopsy.
CT chest / HRCT — ILD screening for all.
Cancer screen — age-appropriate (mammogram, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, OGD/colonoscopy, gynae/urology) in adult DM.

management.detail: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (max 80 mg) until CK improves + clinical improvement; taper over 6–12 months. IV methylprednisolone 1 g × 3 days for severe / rapidly progressive ILD.
Methotrexate 15–25 mg/week (caution if ILD) OR azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day OR mycophenolate 2–3 g/day. Add early for rapid steroid taper.
Aggressive combination: high-dose pulsed steroid + cyclophosphamide + calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus); plasma exchange + tofacitinib emerging. Specialist ILD-rheumatology MDT.

management.step: IVIG for refractory disease or severe dysphagia
management.detail: IVIG 2 g/kg over 2–5 days; can repeat monthly. Useful adjunct, especially with skin / dysphagia / pregnancy.
375 mg/m² weekly × 4 or 1 g every 6 months — RIM trial; benefit emerges over 6 months.
Physiotherapy + occupational therapy; SALT for dysphagia; sun protection (DM rash); calcium / vitamin D + bisphosphonate. Dietary intervention; gentle resistance exercise once stable.
Adult-onset DM: cancer screen at diagnosis + every 1–2 years × 3 years (ovarian, breast, lung, colon, lymphoma). Treat occult cancer rather than DM in paraneoplastic cases — myositis often improves.

references.label: EULAR/ACR Classification Criteria for Adult and Juvenile Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathies

title: Paediatric osteosarcoma
presentation: Persistent localised bone pain at site of long-bone metaphysis (distal femur > proximal tibia > proximal humerus); often worse at night.
Soft-tissue mass over the bone; pathological fracture rarely first presentation.
Adolescent growth-spurt age peak.
Risk: prior radiotherapy, Li-Fraumeni, hereditary retinoblastoma, Paget's disease (older).
redFlags: Pathological fracture — must not delay biopsy.
Suspected joint involvement → limb salvage planning critical.
Tumour lysis at start of chemotherapy.

diagnostics.test: Plain X-ray of affected bone (sunburst, Codman triangle, mixed lytic / sclerotic).
MRI primary tumour (defines soft-tissue + intramedullary extent).
CT chest (pulmonary metastases) + bone scan / PET-CT for skip lesions.
Biopsy by specialist sarcoma surgeon along planned resection tract.
FBC, U&E, LFT, LDH, ALP, CRP, echo (baseline before doxorubicin).

management.step: Specialist paediatric / sarcoma centre referral immediately
management.detail: Outcomes correlate with high-volume centre treatment + adherence to international protocols (EURAMOS, MAP).
Methotrexate (high-dose with folinic acid rescue) + Adriamycin (doxorubicin) + Platinum (cisplatin) — 2–3 cycles before surgery.
Wide margins; limb salvage with endoprosthesis / allograft / rotation plasty; amputation for unsalvageable / invading vessels / nerves. Specialist orthopaedic surgeon.
Continue MAP × 3–4 more cycles after surgery (total 6 months); intensify regimen for poor histological response (< 90% necrosis).
Pulmonary metastasectomy + chemotherapy. Outcomes much better than other paediatric sarcomas with pulmonary mets.
Salvage chemotherapy (ifosfamide + etoposide); MAPK / mTOR / multi-kinase inhibitors in clinical trials; reTreatment of metastases.

Years 1–2 every 3 months CXR + clinical; years 3–5 every 6 months; then annual × 10 years. Surveillance for late-effects: cardiotoxicity (doxorubicin), nephrotoxicity (platinum), hearing loss (cisplatin), infertility, secondary malignancy. Psychosocial support; rehabilitation.

references.label: EURAMOS-1 trial; NCCN Bone Cancer Guidelines

title: Paediatric Ewing sarcoma
presentation: Bone or soft-tissue mass in children / adolescents — pelvis, femur, chest wall, humerus common.
Pain (often nocturnal), swelling, systemic features (fever, weight loss — distinguishes from osteosarcoma).
Characteristic EWSR1-FLI1 fusion (or variant) on molecular testing.
Metastatic at diagnosis in 25% (lungs > bone > marrow).
redFlags: Spinal cord compression from vertebral / paraspinal Ewing.
Tumour lysis at start of chemotherapy.

diagnostics.test: MRI primary tumour + whole-body MRI / bone scan / PET-CT for staging.
Biopsy with molecular confirmation (EWSR1 rearrangement by FISH or sequencing).
Baseline echo + GFR + audiometry + reproductive counselling.

management.detail: Outcomes substantially better at specialist centres with international protocols (Euro Ewing 2012 / AEWS1031).
Vincristine + Doxorubicin + Cyclophosphamide alternating with Ifosfamide + Etoposide, given every 2 weeks (interval-compressed) for 6 cycles.
Surgery for resectable lesions (preferred); radiation alone for unresectable; combined for close margins or large unresectable primary. Specialist sarcoma surgical + radiation expertise.
Additional 8 cycles VDC/IE → total ~11 months therapy.
Lung metastasectomy + whole-lung radiation 15–18 Gy; bone metastases — local radiotherapy; intensification chemotherapy / high-dose with stem cell rescue in selected.
Hyperhydration + rasburicase / allopurinol from start of chemo — high tumour burden + responsive.

Cardiotoxicity (doxorubicin), nephrotoxicity (ifosfamide — also encephalopathy + Fanconi), infertility (ifosfamide / cyclophosphamide — fertility preservation BEFORE), second malignancy (radiotherapy + alkylating), hearing, neuropathy. Lifelong surveillance.

references.label: Euro Ewing 2012 trial; AEWS1031; ESMO Bone Sarcoma Guidelines

title: Paediatric rhabdomyosarcoma
presentation: Painless soft-tissue mass — head + neck (incl orbit, parameningeal), genitourinary (bladder, prostate, vagina), extremity, trunk.
Orbit RMS: proptosis, eyelid swelling, painless.
Parameningeal: cranial-nerve palsies, headache.
GU: haematuria, urinary retention, vaginal mass (sarcoma botryoides — 'grape-like').
Subtypes: embryonal (favourable; younger), alveolar (PAX-FOXO1 fusion+ — adverse), pleomorphic (adult).
redFlags: Tumour lysis at start of chemotherapy.

diagnostics.test: Biopsy with histology + immunohistochemistry (desmin, myogenin, MyoD1) + PAX3/7-FOXO1 fusion testing.
CT chest + bone scan + bone marrow biopsy + LP (parameningeal sites).
Echo, GFR, audiometry, fertility counselling (older adolescent).

management.detail: International protocols (COG / EpSSG).
Risk-adapted: chemotherapy (VAC — vincristine + actinomycin-D + cyclophosphamide standard backbone) + local control (surgery and/or radiation).

Low risk (embryonal, completely resected): VA × 22 weeks. Intermediate: VAC + RT × 42 weeks. High (metastatic): intensified VAC ± ivosidenib / vinorelbine / temsirolimus / temozolomide; consider HDC + stem cell rescue in selected.

Surgery first if function-preserving; otherwise after chemotherapy. Radiotherapy at week 13 if needed (avoid in orbital RMS where possible). Brachytherapy for vaginal / bladder RMS — preserves function.
Intrathecal chemotherapy + whole-brain RT for meningeal involvement; aggressive systemic chemo.
Hyperhydration + allopurinol or rasburicase.
Growth, endocrine (especially orbital / parameningeal RT), cardiotoxicity, infertility, secondary malignancy. Long-term multidisciplinary follow-up.

references.label: COG / IRSG protocols; EpSSG Soft Tissue Sarcoma Guidelines

title: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
presentation: Woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain ± vaginal bleeding ± positive pregnancy test + shock.
Often history of amenorrhea 6–8 weeks; sometimes assumed period.
Shoulder tip pain (referred from diaphragmatic irritation).
Risk: prior ectopic, tubal surgery / damage (PID, salpingitis), IVF, IUD failure, smoking, pregnancy of unknown location (PUL).
redFlags: Persistent severe pain even without confirmed bleeding.

diagnostics.test: Transvaginal ultrasound — empty uterus, adnexal mass / sac, free fluid in pouch of Douglas.
FBC, group + crossmatch ≥ 4 units, lactate, coagulation.
Bedside FAST scan in unstable patient.

management.step: Resuscitation + activate massive transfusion if shocked
management.detail: ABCDE; two large-bore IV; permissive hypotension SBP 80–90 until source control; PRBC/FFP/platelet 1:1:1; tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 h.
Laparotomy if unstable; laparoscopy if stable. Salpingectomy preferred over salpingostomy unless contralateral tube damaged + fertility desired. Treat haemoperitoneum.

management.step: Anti-D 250 IU IM for RhD-negative women
management.detail: Within 72 h of bleeding event.
Monitor recovery; psychological support for pregnancy loss; counsel future-pregnancy risk (recurrence 10%); next pregnancy early scan at 6 weeks.

management.step: Methotrexate medical management — only stable, asymptomatic, hCG < 5000
management.detail: Single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m² IM with strict follow-up; not appropriate in ruptured presentation.
Pre-conception fertility assessment; IVF consideration if both tubes affected; avoid IUD-failure scenarios with discussion.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 21 Ectopic pregnancy
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Severe pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) / tubo-ovarian abscess
presentation: Lower abdominal pain + cervical motion tenderness + fever ± vaginal discharge ± dyspareunia.
Risk: chlamydia, gonorrhoea, mixed anaerobic (especially with IUD); bacterial vaginosis; recent termination / instrumentation; multiple partners.
Severe: high fever, peritonism, tubo-ovarian abscess on imaging.

diagnostics.test: Endocervical NAAT for chlamydia + gonorrhoea; high vaginal swab.
FBC, CRP, lactate, blood culture if febrile.

management.step: Outpatient (mild PID, no TOA, can take oral)
management.detail: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose + doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days + metronidazole 400 mg BD × 14 days. Avoid intercourse + treat partner.

management.step: Inpatient (severe / TOA / pregnancy / failed outpatient / immunocompromise)
management.detail: IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily + doxycycline 100 mg IV/PO BD + metronidazole 500 mg IV TDS. Switch to oral when afebrile 24 h + improving (continue total 14 days).
Image-guided drainage (USS or CT) for TOA > 4–8 cm or failing antibiotics 48–72 h. Salpingectomy + drainage if rupture / septic shock.
Modern evidence: do NOT routinely remove IUD if mild-moderate PID; remove if severe / not improving by 48 h / TOA / actinomyces.
Sexual contacts in past 6 months treated for chlamydia + gonorrhoea; partner notification per public-health pathway.
Review at 72 h then 2 weeks; counsel future-fertility risk (ectopic, infertility, chronic pelvic pain). Long-term contraception planning.

references.label: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021; WHO STI guidelines

title: Severe hyperemesis gravidarum (HG)
presentation: Persistent vomiting in pregnancy with ≥ 5% pre-pregnancy weight loss + ketonuria + electrolyte disturbance.
PUQE score ≥ 13 (Pregnancy-Unique Quantification of Emesis) = severe.
Peak first trimester (8–12 weeks); usually resolves by 20 weeks.
Risk: previous HG, multiple pregnancy, molar pregnancy, female fetus, family history.
redFlags: Wernicke encephalopathy — confusion + ataxia + ophthalmoplegia (give thiamine BEFORE dextrose).
Persistent vomiting beyond 20 weeks — exclude alternative cause.

diagnostics.test: Urinalysis (ketonuria), U&E, glucose, FBC, LFT, TFT, calcium, phosphate, magnesium.

management.detail: IV 0.9% NaCl + KCl per deficit (typically 1 L over 1 h then maintenance + replacement). AVOID dextrose-containing fluids until thiamine given (Wernicke risk).

management.step: Thiamine — give BEFORE any glucose-containing fluid
management.detail: IV thiamine 100–200 mg before dextrose. Pabrinex IV pairs ampoules I + II daily × 3 days when refeeding.

First-line: cyclizine 50 mg or promethazine 25 mg or doxylamine + pyridoxine (B6) — well-evidenced and safe. Second: prochlorperazine, metoclopramide, ondansetron (use after 10 weeks where possible — modest cleft-palate signal but benefit usually outweighs). Third: methylprednisolone 16 mg TDS for 3 days then taper (only refractory, after 10 weeks).
Oral diet as tolerated; multivitamin (avoid retinol > 8000 IU); NG / NJ enteral feeding if not improving; parenteral nutrition only for severe + refractory.
LMWH for hospitalised HG with dehydration (high VTE risk during pregnancy + immobilisation).
HG is associated with depression / PTSD; offer counselling; address concerns about pregnancy termination decision.
Symptom review weekly; usually resolves 2nd trimester. Plan with obstetric team for pre-labour and postpartum (recurrence risk 75% next pregnancy).

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 69 — Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and HG
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Urosepsis with obstructive uropathy
presentation: Urinary tract infection (UTI) with systemic inflammation + sepsis criteria.
Obstruction by ureteric stone, malignancy, retroperitoneal fibrosis, post-op stricture, BPH retention.
Severe: high fever, rigors, flank pain, AKI, septic shock.
Risk: diabetes, immunosuppression, recurrent UTI, indwelling catheter, recent urological instrumentation.
redFlags: Pyonephrosis (pus in obstructed renal pelvis) — needs urgent drainage.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, creatinine, lactate, blood culture × 2, CRP.
USS renal tract — hydronephrosis from obstruction.
Non-contrast CT KUB — gold standard for stones + obstruction.

management.detail: Cultures BEFORE antibiotics; lactate; IV antibiotic; 30 mL/kg crystalloid; vasopressor for shock.
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 6-hourly OR meropenem 1 g 8-hourly (severe / known ESBL). Add aminoglycoside (gentamicin 5–7 mg/kg) for first 48 h in septic shock. Adjust per culture.

Percutaneous nephrostomy (preferred for proximal obstruction / unstable patient) OR retrograde ureteric stent (preferred for distal obstruction / stable). Definitive stone management (lithotripsy / ureteroscopy) AFTER sepsis resolved.
Vasopressor; renal replacement therapy for severe AKI / hyperkalaemia; respiratory support.
De-escalate at 48–72 h based on cultures; total 7–14 days for complicated UTI with sepsis.
Repeat imaging at 6–12 weeks; definitive stone management; nephrology follow-up if persistent CKD; investigate underlying cause + recurrence prevention.

references.label: EAU Guidelines on Urological Infections; IDSA UTI guidelines

title: Acute urinary retention — male
presentation: Sudden inability to void with painful palpable suprapubic bladder.
Often elderly; precipitants: BPH, constipation, anticholinergic / decongestant / opioid medications, alcohol intoxication, urinary tract infection, post-operative.
Less commonly: prostate cancer, urethral stricture, neurological causes (cauda equina), bladder calculus.
redFlags: Suspected cauda equina (bilateral leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia, painless retention).
Concurrent AKI from obstructive uropathy + uraemia.
Post-obstructive diuresis after catheterisation — replace fluid + electrolytes.

diagnostics.test: Bedside bladder ultrasound for retention volume.
U&E, creatinine + USS renal tract if creatinine raised.
PR exam (BPH size; prostate cancer signs).

management.step: Urethral catheter — slow drainage (clamp every 500 mL × 5 min)
management.detail: Standard 14–16 Fr; bigger if blood clots. Avoid haematuria + hypotension from rapid decompression in chronic-on-acute. Suprapubic catheter if urethral access difficult / contraindicated.
Stop offending medications; treat UTI; treat constipation. Tamsulosin 400 microgram daily helps trial without catheter (TWOC) in BPH.
Hourly urine output; if > 200 mL/h, replace IV fluid with 0.45% NaCl ~75% of urine output; monitor electrolytes (K+, Na+, Mg, phosphate).
TWOC success rate higher if pre-treated with tamsulosin × 48 h + treat underlying cause. Failed TWOC: re-catheterise + urology follow-up.
BPH: medical therapy (alpha-blocker + 5-ARI), TURP if recurrent / large prostate / complications. Prostate cancer pathway. Bladder calculus management.

references.label: EAU Guidelines on Non-neurogenic Male LUTS
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN)
presentation: Painful rapidly evolving skin pain + erythema → atypical targets / macular eruption → bullae → epidermal detachment.
Mucosal involvement (≥ 2 sites): oral, ocular, genital, anal.
SJS < 10% BSA detachment; SJS/TEN overlap 10–30%; TEN > 30%.

Drug cause in 90% — onset typically 1–4 weeks after starting: sulphonamides, allopurinol (HLA-B*58:01), aromatic anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine — HLA-B*15:02 / A*31:01), NSAIDs, nevirapine, antiretrovirals.
Infection (Mycoplasma) more common SJS cause in children.
redFlags: Severe mucosal involvement (oral feeding impaired, ocular surface damage).
Septic shock from skin barrier loss.
Pneumonia from mucosal sloughing of airway.

diagnostics.test: Skin biopsy (frozen section + paraffin) for histology.
diagnostics.rationale: Differentiate from autoimmune bullous + erythema multiforme.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, glucose, LFT, blood gas, lactate.
Drug history — onset within 4 weeks of starting culprit; HLA testing in some populations.

management.detail: Most important intervention — improves outcome. Document on chart and patient record forever.
Multidisciplinary care: dermatology + intensive care + ophthalmology + dietetics + plastics. Mortality lower in specialist centres.
Warm environment; non-adherent dressings; minimal handling. Fluid resuscitation per Parkland-style (less than thermal burn typically). Nutritional support — high calorie + protein; NG feeding.
Specialist dressings (e.g. mepilex, biological); avoid silver sulfadiazine (sulfa cross-reactivity); analgesia.
Eye drops (lubricant, antibiotic, steroid); amniotic membrane transplantation for severe ocular surface disease (prevents long-term blindness).

Ciclosporin 3–5 mg/kg/day (most evidence; START EARLY); IVIG 2–3 g/kg (mixed evidence); systemic steroid (controversial — may increase mortality); etanercept / infliximab (emerging). Withhold all if active infection.
Routine prophylactic antibiotic NOT recommended; treat documented infection.
LMWH; PPI.
Ophthalmology lifelong; dermatology long-term skin care; psychological support; document medication allergy + cross-reactivities (e.g. all aromatic anticonvulsants after one).

references.label: British Association of Dermatologists guideline on management of SJS/TEN

title: Erythroderma / exfoliative dermatitis
presentation: Generalised erythema involving ≥ 90% BSA + scaling, often with pruritus, heat / fluid loss, lymphadenopathy, peripheral oedema.
Aetiology: drug reaction (most common), pre-existing dermatosis flare (atopic eczema, psoriasis, contact dermatitis), cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Sezary syndrome), idiopathic.
Systemic: hypothermia (heat loss), hypoalbuminaemia, high-output cardiac failure, AKI from dehydration.
redFlags: Suspected Sezary syndrome — abnormal lymphocyte count, lymphadenopathy → urgent dermatology biopsy + flow cytometry.

diagnostics.test: Skin biopsy (× 2–3 sites) — distinguish drug, dermatosis, lymphoma.
FBC + film, U&E, LFT, albumin, glucose, calcium, ferritin.
Peripheral flow cytometry for Sezary cells.
Drug history — meticulous review of all new drugs over preceding 1–8 weeks.

management.detail: Warm environment, fluid + electrolyte correction, nutritional support, gentle skin care with emollients, monitoring for sepsis.
Many cases drug-induced; rationalise medication list.
Liberal greasy emollient hourly; topical moderate-potency steroid; wet wraps (cool / tepid) for relief.
Eczema / psoriasis flare: systemic therapy (methotrexate, ciclosporin, biologic). Drug: stop + supportive. CTCL: refer haematology / dermatology oncology — specific staging + therapy.

Severe / atopic background: ciclosporin 3–5 mg/kg/day OR methotrexate 7.5–15 mg/week. Psoriasis: avoid sudden steroid withdrawal (precipitates pustular form); use methotrexate or ciclosporin. Biologic (dupilumab, secukinumab) as indicated.
Routine antibiotic NOT recommended; treat sepsis when present.
Dermatology long-term care; document trigger + avoidance; psychological support.

references.label: British Association of Dermatologists guideline on erythroderma

title: Generalised pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch) flare
presentation: Acute onset of widespread sterile pustules on erythematous background — generalised distribution.
Fever, malaise, leukocytosis, severe systemic illness.
Triggers: abrupt withdrawal of systemic / topical steroids, infection, hypocalcaemia, pregnancy (impetigo herpetiformis), drugs (lithium, beta-blockers, terbinafine, NSAIDs, ICI).
redFlags: Pregnancy form (impetigo herpetiformis) — high fetal mortality.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, LFT, calcium, magnesium, blood culture, swab pustules.
Identify trigger (recent steroid taper, new drug, infection).

management.detail: Reinstate systemic steroid if abrupt withdrawal trigger (slow taper). Correct calcium. Treat infection.
Cyclosporine 3–5 mg/kg/day (fast onset) OR acitretin 0.5–1 mg/kg/day OR infliximab 5 mg/kg (fastest onset — preferred severe). Methotrexate 15–25 mg/week (slower).

management.step: Targeted IL-36 receptor antagonist for von Zumbusch
management.detail: Spesolimab 900 mg IV single dose — rapid resolution (within 1 week) per EFFISAYIL trial; dramatic effect for GPP flare; specialist initiation.
Liberal emollient; mild topical steroid (potent topical agents can rebound).
IV fluids; nutrition; calcium replacement; analgesia; sepsis surveillance.
Maintenance biologic (IL-17, IL-23) for chronic psoriasis prevention; avoid known triggers (oral steroids unless absolutely necessary); pregnancy planning under specialist care.

references.label: British Association of Dermatologists guidelines on psoriasis; ERASURE / EFFISAYIL trials

title: Disseminated herpes zoster — immunocompromised host
presentation: ≥ 20 vesicles outside primary + adjacent dermatomes, OR multidermatomal involvement, OR visceral involvement (CNS, lung, liver) in an immunocompromised patient.
Risk: HIV, haematological malignancy, transplant, immunosuppressive drugs.
Visceral: encephalitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, myelitis.
Trigeminal herpes zoster ophthalmicus + ear (Ramsay Hunt) — special considerations.
redFlags: Trigeminal (V1) involvement + Hutchinson sign (nose tip) → ophthalmology urgent.
Ramsay Hunt syndrome (geniculate ganglion) → facial palsy + ear vesicles.
Acute pain with later post-herpetic neuralgia.

diagnostics.test: PCR of vesicle fluid (preferred) OR direct fluorescent antibody.
LP if neurological involvement; CXR if respiratory; LFT.
FBC, CD4 count if HIV+, immune status review.
Ophthalmology slit-lamp + fundoscopy if V1 / suspected eye involvement.

management.step: IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 h — IMMEDIATELY
management.detail: Within 72 h of rash onset for best outcome (but treat after 72 h if new lesions, complications). Renal-adjusted dose; ensure hydration to avoid crystal nephropathy. Duration 7–14 days (longer for visceral / CNS).
Aciclovir-resistant VZV (TK-deficient strains in advanced HIV / transplant) — foscarnet 60 mg/kg IV 8-hourly with renal monitoring.

Ramsay Hunt + Bell-like facial palsy: oral prednisolone 60 mg/day × 5 days then taper. Acute retinal necrosis: high-dose steroid after aciclovir. Pneumonitis: consider steroid. Avoid in immunocompromised generally — case-by-case.
Acute: paracetamol + opioid + gabapentin or pregabalin. PHN prevention: amitriptyline 10–25 mg nocte + gabapentin titration.
Encephalitis: IV aciclovir 14–21 days + supportive. Pneumonitis: aciclovir + supportive O2. Acute retinal necrosis: IV aciclovir + intravitreal foscarnet + later oral valaciclovir.
HIV: start / optimise ART after acute infection controlled. Transplant: reduce immunosuppression if possible. Malignancy: balance chemo with infection control.
Post-recovery + immune reconstitution: recombinant zoster vaccine recommended ≥ 18 in immunocompromised; live vaccine NOT to be given.

references.label: IDSA Guidelines for the Management of VZV in HIV; AAO ophthalmic herpes zoster

title: Severe cellulitis / complicated soft-tissue infection
presentation: Erythema, warmth, swelling, tenderness — usually lower limb in adults.
Severe: systemic features (fever, tachycardia, hypotension), rapid spread, blistering, lymphangitis, lymphadenopathy.

Distinguish: erysipelas (well-demarcated, more streptococcal, raised), cellulitis (less defined, can be staph), necrotising fasciitis (pain disproportionate, crepitus, anaesthesia — see NSTI pathway).
Predisposing: lymphoedema, diabetes, IV drug use, venous insufficiency, immunocompromise, fungal interdigital infection (tinea pedis).
redFlags: Pain disproportionate to clinical signs — consider necrotising fasciitis.
Crepitus, anaesthesia over lesion, rapid spread (cm/h) — NSTI.
Periorbital / orbital — see orbital cellulitis pathway.
Penetrating injury / animal / human bite + immunocompromise.

diagnostics.test: Mark and date the erythema border.
Wound swab + blood cultures if febrile.

management.detail: Class I: oral antibiotic + outpatient. Class II: oral / IV + observed outpatient. Class III/IV: IV inpatient — sepsis or organ dysfunction.
Oral: flucloxacillin 500 mg–1 g 6-hourly × 7 days. Clarithromycin / doxycycline if penicillin allergy. Add metronidazole if anaerobic suspected.

IV flucloxacillin 1–2 g 6-hourly + IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 4-hourly. OR co-amoxiclav 1.2 g 8-hourly. OR clindamycin if penicillin-anaphylactic. ADD IV vancomycin / teicoplanin if MRSA risk. Switch oral when afebrile + improving (CRP falling, demarcation clear).

management.step: Source control — drainage of any abscess; debridement of necrotic tissue
management.detail: Image-guided or surgical.
Elevation of affected limb; analgesia; cool compress; identify + treat tinea pedis (terbinafine cream) as a portal of entry.
Consider resistant organism, deeper infection, NSTI, alternative diagnosis (DVT, erysipeloid, pyoderma gangrenosum, lipodermatosclerosis, contact dermatitis).
Skin care of affected limb; treat lymphoedema (compression); antifungal of toe-webs; benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU monthly for ≥ 3 episodes recurrent cellulitis (PATCH trials).

references.label: IDSA Diagnosis and Management of Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

title: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) — diagnosis + chronic management
presentation: Rotterdam criteria (2/3): oligo/anovulation; clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism; polycystic ovaries on USS — after exclusion of other causes.
Common features: oligomenorrhoea / amenorrhoea; hirsutism (Ferriman-Gallwey ≥ 8); acne; alopecia; subfertility; weight gain; insulin resistance; metabolic syndrome.
Long-term risks: T2DM (40% by age 40), CVD, endometrial hyperplasia / cancer, OSA, NAFLD, depression.
redFlags: Virilisation (clitoromegaly, voice deepening, severe hirsutism) — exclude androgen-secreting tumour.
Severe insulin resistance with acanthosis nigricans + obesity — HAIR-AN syndrome.

diagnostics.test: Day 2–5 cycle: LH, FSH, oestradiol, free testosterone, SHBG (calculate FAI), DHEAS, 17-OHP, prolactin, TSH.
Transvaginal USS — antral follicle count ≥ 20 per ovary OR ovarian volume > 10 mL.
Metabolic screen: fasting glucose / OGTT / HbA1c, lipid profile, ALT, BP, waist circumference.

management.detail: Weight reduction 5–10% restores ovulation in many. Mediterranean / low-glycaemic diet + 150 min/week activity. Smoking cessation.

Combined oral contraceptive (preferred — also reduces hyperandrogenism), OR progesterone (cyclical or continuous: micronised progesterone, levonorgestrel IUS, MPA). Avoid amenorrhoea > 3 months (endometrial hyperplasia risk).

COC first-line (combined oestrogen + progestin reduces ovarian + adrenal androgens). Add anti-androgen (spironolactone 100–200 mg/day; cyproterone acetate) for refractory hirsutism + acne. Topical eflornithine for facial hirsutism. Laser / electrolysis for definitive.

Letrozole 2.5 mg days 2–6 cycle (now first-line — superior to clomiphene). Metformin 500 mg TDS adjunct, especially in obese / glucose intolerant. Gonadotropins for letrozole-resistant; IVF if needed.
Metformin 500 mg–2 g daily for insulin resistance / IGT (off-label outside diabetes). Annual fasting glucose / HbA1c. GLP-1 agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor if T2DM.
Annual BMI, BP, lipid, glucose; biennial OSA screen (STOP-BANG); endometrial USS if amenorrhoea + obesity; PHQ-9 + GAD-7. Address body image + fertility distress.

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Erectile dysfunction — evaluation and treatment
presentation: Persistent or recurrent inability to achieve or maintain erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual performance.

Common causes: vasculogenic (most), endocrine (hypogonadism, diabetes, thyroid), neurogenic, drug-induced (antihypertensives, SSRIs, antiandrogens, opioids, alcohol, cannabis), psychogenic, post-prostatectomy.
Indicator of cardiovascular disease in many men — often precedes overt CAD by 3–5 years.
redFlags: Sudden onset / persistent priapism (> 4 h — emergency).
Concurrent angina / unstable cardiovascular disease — assess cardiovascular fitness for sex.
Bilateral perineal trauma / pelvic fracture history.
Pituitary symptoms (visual change, headache, galactorrhoea — exclude prolactinoma).

diagnostics.test: Sexual + medication + psychological history; IIEF-5 questionnaire.
Fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid profile, BP, waist circumference.
Morning total testosterone × 2 (confirmatory + repeat if low); LH, prolactin, TSH, SHBG (calculate free testosterone).
Cardiovascular risk score; consider further cardiac testing in high-risk.
Penile Doppler / nocturnal tumescence ONLY in selected cases (e.g. medico-legal, vascular surgery candidate).

management.detail: Smoking cessation (single most useful lifestyle change), weight loss, regular exercise, reduce alcohol, treat OSA. Review and adjust offending medications (switch SSRI / antihypertensive class).

Sildenafil 25–100 mg, tadalafil 5–20 mg (or 2.5–5 mg daily for chronic + concomitant BPH symptoms), vardenafil, avanafil. Counsel on timing, fat-meal interaction (sildenafil), nitrate contraindication. Try 4–6 doses at maximum dose before declaring failure.

Replace testosterone (gel, IM injection, oral undecanoate) if symptomatic + repeated low morning testosterone < 8 nmol/L. Monitor PSA + haematocrit + lipids; do NOT replace in prostate cancer / severe LUTS / haematocrit > 0.50.

management.step: Second-line — vacuum erection device, intracavernosal alprostadil, intraurethral alprostadil
management.detail: Combination therapy for PDE5i failure or contraindication.
For refractory ED; high satisfaction. Specialist andrology centre.
Particularly for psychogenic ED, performance anxiety, relationship issues.
ED often early sign of CAD — full cardiovascular risk assessment + management.

references.label: EAU Guidelines on Male Sexual + Reproductive Health 2024
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis)
presentation: Acute: 7–14 days post-exposure; Romaña sign (unilateral painless palpebral oedema at vector inoculation site), chagoma at skin entry, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, mild myocarditis.
Indeterminate (latent): asymptomatic, positive serology, normal cardiac + GI tests; lifelong risk of progression.

Chronic (after years-decades): chagasic cardiomyopathy (cardiomegaly, conduction defects, arrhythmia, heart failure, sudden death), megaoesophagus (dysphagia, regurgitation), megacolon (chronic constipation).
Transmission: triatomine vector (Latin America), congenital, transfusion, organ transplant, oral (food contamination).
redFlags: Severe chagasic cardiomyopathy with LV dysfunction or ventricular arrhythmia.
Pregnancy + Chagas — congenital transmission risk; treat after delivery + breastfeeding.

diagnostics.test: Acute: PCR / direct microscopy of blood / Strout method.
Chronic / indeterminate: 2 serology tests (ELISA + IFA, different antigens).
Barium studies / manometry for GI form.
Newborn of seropositive mother: serial PCR + serology to 9 months.

management.detail: Benznidazole 5–7 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses × 60 days (adult); paediatric 5–10 mg/kg/day. Nifurtimox 8–10 mg/kg/day × 60–90 days (adult). Indications: acute infection, congenital, reactivation (immunosuppression), children + adolescents with chronic infection, women of childbearing age before pregnancy, indeterminate-form adults < 50.
Benznidazole: rash, peripheral neuropathy, bone marrow suppression — monthly FBC, LFT. Nifurtimox: anorexia, weight loss, peripheral neuropathy, psychiatric symptoms. Discontinue if severe.

ACEi / ARB + β-blocker (cautious — bradycardia common) + spironolactone + diuretic per HF guidelines. ICD for sustained VT / aborted sudden death. Pacemaker for symptomatic bradycardia / heart block. Amiodarone for arrhythmia. Cardiac transplantation for end-stage.
Megaoesophagus: pneumatic dilation; Heller myotomy + Dor fundoplication. Megacolon: bowel rest, manual disimpaction, sigmoidectomy for severe.

Do NOT treat in pregnancy (teratogenic — benznidazole pregnancy category C; nifurtimox D). Plan treatment between pregnancies + before next conception. Screen all newborns of seropositive mothers; treat congenital infection promptly (excellent cure rate in infants).

Vector control (insecticide spraying, housing improvement). Universal blood + organ donor screening in endemic + non-endemic regions with immigrant populations. Education + screening of immigrants from endemic regions.

references.label: PAHO/WHO Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of Chagas disease (2018)

title: Viral haemorrhagic fever (Marburg, CCHF, Lassa, yellow fever) — recognition + containment
presentation: Fever > 38°C with travel from / residence in endemic area (incubation 2–21 days).
Initial nonspecific: fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue, sore throat.
Day 4–7: nausea/vomiting/diarrhoea/abdominal pain.
Late: petechiae, gum bleeding, GI bleed, conjunctival injection, hypotension, DIC, ARDS, multi-organ failure.

Specific clues: Crimean-Congo (tick bite, severe haemorrhage + thrombocytopenia), Marburg (Ugandan / Angolan outbreak; bat exposure cave), Lassa (West Africa; rodent contact; pharyngitis), Yellow fever (jaundice + Faget sign + black vomit).
redFlags: Cluster of cases / healthcare worker exposure.
Pregnancy + VHF — very high maternal + fetal mortality.
ANY suspected VHF — IMMEDIATE infection control + public health notification.

diagnostics.test: ISOLATE patient + alert public health BEFORE any sample taken (BSL-4 lab handling).
diagnostics.rationale: Healthcare worker infection control is paramount.

diagnostics.test: RT-PCR for specific virus at reference laboratory (CDC, PHE, BNITM).
FBC, U&E, coag, LFT — thrombocytopenia, transaminitis, AKI common.

diagnostics.rationale: Differential — typhoid, leptospirosis, severe malaria, severe dengue can mimic.

management.detail: Single negative-pressure room (or isolated area). PPE: hood, N95/FFP3 or PAPR, double gloves, gown, eye protection. Trained dedicated staff; minimise number of staff + procedures. Aerosol-generating procedures avoid unless essential.
Mandatory notification (notifiable disease). Contact tracing + monitoring of contacts × 21 days.
Aggressive fluid resuscitation, electrolyte correction, blood products for bleeding, ICU support for organ failure. Avoid IM injections + sharps where possible.

Lassa: ribavirin IV 30 mg/kg loading then 16 mg/kg every 6 h × 4 days then 8 mg/kg every 8 h × 6 days. Effective if started within 6 days. Crimean-Congo: ribavirin (controversial; meta-analyses uncertain — give where local protocol). Marburg / Ebola: REGN-EB3 / mAb114 monoclonal antibodies — Marburg now has approved monoclonals.
Supportive — no specific antiviral. Vaccination is the cornerstone of prevention.
VERY high mortality + fetal loss. Avoid termination unless maternal life-threatening; supportive care. Specialist input.
Long-term sequelae (joint pain, fatigue, ocular — uveitis common in Ebola survivors). Sexual transmission persistence (Ebola, Marburg in semen for months) — counsel + sexual-health follow-up.
Per WHO + local protocol; ribavirin for Lassa exposure; vaccination consideration for Marburg / Ebola exposure (rVSV).

references.label: WHO Clinical management of patients with viral haemorrhagic fever
Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) Technical Guidelines, 3rd edition (MOH)

title: Severe leptospirosis (Weil disease)
presentation: Biphasic illness: initial septicaemic phase (3–7 days) — fever, headache, myalgia (calf pain), conjunctival suffusion, GI symptoms.
Severe (Weil): high fever, jaundice, AKI, haemorrhage (pulmonary, GI), myocarditis.
Exposure: contact with water / soil contaminated by rodent urine (farmers, sewer workers, soldiers, triathletes, post-flood, plantation workers).
Pulmonary haemorrhage syndrome — high mortality.
redFlags: Suspected co-infection with malaria / dengue / typhoid.

diagnostics.test: Microagglutination test (MAT) — gold standard; ELISA IgM for early.
diagnostics.rationale: Serology; takes 7–10 days for IgM rise.

diagnostics.test: PCR (early phase < 7 days) — blood / urine / CSF.
FBC (thrombocytopenia common), U&E, LFT (elevated bilirubin disproportionate to transaminases), CK (rhabdomyolysis), urinalysis.

management.detail: Mild: doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days OR azithromycin 500 mg daily × 3 days. Severe: IV penicillin G 1.5 MU 6-hourly × 7 days OR IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily × 7 days OR IV doxycycline.
IV fluid; vasopressor for shock; respiratory support for pulmonary haemorrhage / ARDS.
Early haemodialysis improves outcomes in oliguric AKI.

Pulmonary haemorrhage: protective ventilation, transfusion, methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily × 3 days (controversial — some evidence in severe pulmonary haemorrhage). DIC / coagulopathy: FFP, platelets.
Fever + hypotension on antibiotic initiation — supportive; brief; antibiotic should not be stopped.
Notifiable in many jurisdictions. Occupational exposure prophylaxis (doxycycline 200 mg weekly for known exposure). Rodent control, protective footwear, water-source treatment.

references.label: WHO Leptospirosis Burden Epidemiology Reference Group

title: Rickettsial disease (typhus + spotted fever group)
presentation: Spotted fever group: tick-borne (Rocky Mountain spotted fever, African tick-bite fever, Mediterranean spotted fever).
Typhus group: louse-borne (epidemic typhus), flea-borne (murine typhus), mite-borne (scrub typhus).
Triad: fever + headache + rash. Eschar at tick / mite bite (esp. African + scrub).
Severe: encephalopathy, ARDS, AKI, vasculitic complications, multi-organ failure.
redFlags: Delay > 5 days from symptom onset to antibiotic — significantly worse outcome.
Suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever — high mortality without treatment.
Pregnancy — alternative antibiotic (azithromycin) for second / third trimester.
Children < 8 years — short doxycycline course now considered acceptable in severe rickettsial.

diagnostics.test: Clinical recognition + epidemiological history is key — DO NOT delay treatment for confirmation.
Indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) — gold standard; paired acute + convalescent (3–6 weeks).

management.detail: Adult: 100 mg PO/IV BD × 7–10 days (continue until afebrile + 3 days). Children: 2.2 mg/kg BD (max 100 mg BD) — short courses now considered acceptable even in < 8 years for severe rickettsial. Pregnancy second / third trimester: azithromycin 500 mg daily × 7 days alternative (chloramphenicol historically used).
Antipyretic, IV fluids, organ support as needed. Vasculitic / encephalopathic complications may need ICU.
Often co-infection or differential — malaria, dengue, typhoid, leptospirosis.
Insecticide-treated clothing (permethrin); DEET repellent; tick checks; rodent + arthropod control. Travel-medicine counselling.

references.label: CDC Rickettsial Diseases Guideline; WHO scrub typhus

title: Candidaemia and invasive candidiasis
presentation: Fever + sepsis in patient with central venous catheter, broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, abdominal surgery, parenteral nutrition, immunocompromise.
Hospital-acquired candidaemia (3rd-5th most common bloodstream infection in ICU).
Species shift to non-albicans Candida (C. glabrata fluconazole-resistant; C. auris emerging globally with multi-drug resistance).
Complications: endocarditis, endophthalmitis, hepatosplenic, CNS, vertebral osteomyelitis.
redFlags: Septic shock — empirical antifungal in high-risk.
Candida auris — strict isolation + infection control.
Endophthalmitis (vision loss) — all candidaemia need ophthalmology screen.
Endocarditis with prosthetic valve — surgical removal often needed.

diagnostics.test: Blood culture × 2 sets from different sites + each lumen of CVC.
MALDI-TOF or molecular for rapid species identification.
diagnostics.rationale: Treatment choice — C. glabrata / C. krusei often fluconazole-resistant.
Endophthalmitis screening — recommended for ALL candidaemia.

diagnostics.test: Repeat blood cultures every 24–48 h until 2 consecutive negative.

management.step: Empirical antifungal in suspected candidaemia + septic shock
management.detail: Echinocandin (caspofungin 70 mg loading then 50 mg daily; anidulafungin 200 mg loading then 100 mg daily; micafungin 100 mg daily) — first-line for any critically ill / azole-exposed / unknown species.

C. albicans (susceptible): switch to fluconazole 800 mg loading then 400 mg daily. C. glabrata: continue echinocandin or voriconazole. C. krusei (intrinsically fluconazole-R): echinocandin / voriconazole / liposomal amphotericin. C. auris: echinocandin first; isavuconazole / posaconazole / amphotericin per susceptibility.
Catheter removal reduces mortality + accelerates clearance. Insert new line on opposite side once cultures negative.
Ophthalmology screen, echocardiography for endocarditis, abdominal imaging for hepatosplenic, MRI brain / spine if focal.
14 days from first negative blood culture for uncomplicated candidaemia. 6–12 weeks for endocarditis, osteomyelitis, CNS.
Antibiotic stewardship; bundle for CVC care; selective fluconazole prophylaxis (high-risk ICU, neutropenic). Active surveillance for C. auris in outbreak settings.

references.label: IDSA Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Candidiasis (2016)

title: Acute / primary HIV infection (HIV seroconversion illness)
presentation: Within 2–4 weeks of HIV exposure: 'flu-like' or 'mononucleosis-like' illness in 40–90%.
Fever (96%), lymphadenopathy (75%), pharyngitis (70%), rash (50% — maculopapular trunk/face), myalgia / arthralgia, headache, oral / genital ulcers (mucocutaneous).
Less commonly: severe presentations with opportunistic infection (PJP, Candida, oesophageal ulceration), meningoencephalitis.
High viral load + extreme infectivity during seroconversion — public-health priority.
redFlags: Severe OI at seroconversion (rare but indicates severe immunosuppression — often progresses rapidly).
Pregnancy + acute HIV — very high mother-to-child transmission risk.
Suspected post-exposure scenario — calculate window + offer PEP if within 72 h.

diagnostics.test: 4th-generation HIV antigen / antibody combination test (Ab + p24 antigen).
diagnostics.rationale: Window 2–4 weeks (vs 6–12 weeks for 3rd generation Ab-only).

diagnostics.test: HIV RNA viral load — positive within 1–2 weeks (very high level, often > 10⁶).
Co-infection screen: hepatitis B + C, syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia.

management.detail: Disclose privately + with adequate time. Provide written information + signposting to peer support. Confidentiality, partner-notification process explained.

management.step: Start ART rapidly (test-and-treat — same-day where possible)
management.detail: Preferred regimen: dolutegravir + (tenofovir alafenamide OR tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) + emtricitabine OR lamivudine (DTG + TAF/F or DTG + TDF/3TC — formulated as TLD or B/F/TAF). Bictegravir / TAF / FTC also first-line. Continue lifelong.
Antipyretic, analgesia, oral care for ulcers, antiemetic. Most seroconversion symptoms resolve in 2–4 weeks.

management.step: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis if CD4 < 350 at presentation
management.detail: 480 mg daily — covers PJP / toxoplasmosis / bacterial.
TB symptom screen + LAM if available; CrAg in advanced HIV; viral hepatitis treatment if co-infected; syphilis treatment.
Encourage disclosure to current + recent (3–6 months) partners; partner testing + PEP within 72 h of exposure; counsel on U=U (undetectable = untransmittable) once viral load suppressed.
Depression / suicide risk screen at diagnosis; counselling; peer-support referral. ART adherence is critical; treat as chronic-disease management.

references.label: Kenya Guidelines on Use of Antiretroviral Drugs for Treating and Preventing HIV Infection in Kenya (NASCOP, MOH)

title: Postpartum psychosis (puerperal psychosis)
presentation: Acute onset within 2 weeks of childbirth (usually 1–4 days postpartum).
Severe mood disturbance (mania or depression), psychotic symptoms (delusions often baby-related, hallucinations), confusion, perplexity.
Risk: history of bipolar disorder (recurrence ~50%), prior puerperal psychosis (recurrence ~50%), first pregnancy, family history.
redFlags: Severe agitation / unable to care for baby.
Confusion + altered consciousness — exclude delirium (infection, electrolyte, medication, eclampsia).
Baby's safety paramount — do NOT leave baby alone with severely unwell mother.

diagnostics.test: Urgent psychiatric assessment; suicide + infanticide risk.
Septic workup, U&E, glucose, calcium, TSH, urinalysis, neurological exam.
diagnostics.rationale: Exclude organic causes (delirium, eclampsia, thyroid storm, vitamin deficiency).

diagnostics.test: CT head if focal neurology / suspicion of CVA / cortical venous sinus thrombosis.

management.step: Safety + admission to specialist mother + baby unit if available
management.detail: Ideally joint admission with infant in mother-baby psychiatric unit. Otherwise mother admission with arranged infant care + access for breastfeeding.

Olanzapine 5–20 mg/day OR risperidone 2–6 mg/day OR haloperidol 5–10 mg/day. Add valproate / lithium for prominent manic features (lithium preferred in absence of breastfeeding; valproate avoid in childbearing without PPP). Benzodiazepine adjunct for severe agitation / sleep.

management.step: ECT for severe / refractory / catatonic / suicidal
management.detail: Very effective in postpartum psychosis — rapid response, safe in breastfeeding mother.

Most antipsychotics compatible with breastfeeding (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone — moderate evidence). Lithium typically AVOIDED in breastfeeding (infant toxicity reported). Plan with specialist + counsel mother.
Risk-assess infant safety + arrange care + safeguarding referral if indicated. Multidisciplinary involvement (health visitor, social work, perinatal psychiatry, obstetrics).
Perinatal psychiatry follow-up minimum 12 months. Bipolar disorder follow-up if confirmed. Prenatal prophylaxis (lithium or other mood stabiliser) in future pregnancies — high recurrence.

references.label: RCPsych perinatal psychiatry guidance; NICE CG192 antenatal + postnatal mental health
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Severe eating disorder — medical emergency (anorexia / bulimia)
presentation: Severe restriction / purging: BMI < 14 (or rapid weight loss > 1 kg/week), bradycardia HR < 40, hypotension SBP < 90, hypothermia < 35°C, electrolyte derangement, cardiac arrhythmia.
Bulimia: severe electrolyte / metabolic disturbance from vomiting / laxative / diuretic abuse.
Refeeding syndrome risk: hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, thiamine deficiency.
Children + adolescents: growth retardation, delayed puberty, osteoporosis.
redFlags: Inability to maintain weight / nutritional intake at home.

diagnostics.test: Vital signs + weight + height + BMI percentile (peads).
FBC, U&E (including phosphate + magnesium), glucose, LFT, calcium, TFT, ECG.
diagnostics.rationale: Identify electrolyte / cardiac / liver / endocrine complications.

management.step: Specialist eating-disorder unit admission for severe
management.detail: Multi-disciplinary team: psychiatry + dietitian + nursing + physician. Outpatient family-based therapy for children where not severe.

Start at 20–30 kcal/kg/day (or 1000 kcal/day) and increase by 200 kcal every 24–48 h. Watch for refeeding syndrome FIRST 7–10 DAYS. Monitor phosphate, K+, Mg, glucose 2-times daily initially. Replace electrolytes proactively. Thiamine 200–300 mg/day IV / PO before refeeding.
ECG monitoring during refeeding for high-risk; cardiac rhythm monitoring if severe bradycardia or QTc prolongation.
Family-based therapy (FBT) for adolescents with anorexia (preferred). Cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT-E) for bulimia + adults. Specialist treatment — Maudsley, FREED, MANTRA, SSCM.
Depression, anxiety, OCD, PTSD common. SSRI for bulimia (fluoxetine 60 mg). Cautious psychotropic use in low-BMI patients (cardiac effects).
Calcium 1500 mg + vitamin D 800 IU daily; consider transdermal oestrogen (NOT oral COC — does not protect bone) in adolescents with amenorrhoea > 6 months.
Mental Health Act / Mental Capacity Act when life-threatening + patient refuses; senior psychiatric + legal review.
Treatment-resistance + relapsing course common; persistence + multidisciplinary outpatient follow-up. Mortality ~5% (anorexia).

references.label: MARSIPAN + Junior MARSIPAN guidance; NICE NG69 Eating disorders
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Acute delirium in older adults
presentation: Acute onset (hours-days) + fluctuating course + inattention + disorganised thinking / altered consciousness.
Hyperactive: agitation, hallucinations, restlessness, removing lines.
Hypoactive: lethargy, withdrawal — often missed; worse prognosis.
Mixed: alternating.

Common precipitants: infection (UTI, chest), pain, drug side-effects (anticholinergic, opioid, benzodiazepine, steroid), constipation, urinary retention, electrolyte / glucose disturbance, hypoxia, post-operative, stroke, alcohol withdrawal, dementia / Parkinson disease.
redFlags: Reduced consciousness — exclude stroke, intracranial event, hypoglycaemia.

diagnostics.test: 4AT or CAM-ICU bedside screen for delirium.
FBC, U&E, glucose, calcium, CRP, urinalysis, blood culture, CXR if respiratory signs.
ECG, glucose, oxygen saturation, capillary glucose.
CT head if focal neurology, head trauma, persistent unexplained.

management.detail: Address PINCH-ME (Pain, Infection, Nutrition / dehydration, Constipation, Hydration, Medications, Environment).

Re-orientation, familiar objects + family presence, day-night cycle (window, clock, sleep hygiene), single-occupancy room, hearing aids + glasses on, ambulation when safe, hydration, nutrition. Avoid restraints + multiple bed moves.
Untreated pain is common cause; regular paracetamol; cautious opioid; avoid NSAID in renal failure / older.

ONLY for severe agitation endangering self / others / interfering with essential care; or for distressing psychotic symptoms. Haloperidol 0.5–1 mg PO/IM (peak 4–6 h); olanzapine 2.5–5 mg; risperidone 0.25–0.5 mg. AVOID in Parkinson disease / dementia with Lewy bodies (use quetiapine 12.5–25 mg). AVOID benzodiazepines except for alcohol / benzodiazepine withdrawal or specific indications (catatonia, NMS).
IV thiamine 200–500 mg TDS × 3 days then 100 mg TDS oral; treat hypoglycaemia AFTER giving thiamine.

Delirium often persists weeks–months. Cognitive screen (MMSE / MoCA) at 4–6 weeks (delirium associated with new diagnosis of dementia in many). Education for family on recognising recurrence. Avoid further inpatient stays where possible.

references.label: NICE CG103 Delirium; BGS / ESCMID delirium guidance
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders (mhGAP adaptation), Ministry of Health

title: Frailty — Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment + tailored intervention
presentation: Clinical syndrome with reduced physiological reserve + vulnerability to stressors.
Phenotype (Fried): weight loss, exhaustion, weakness (low grip), slow gait, low activity (≥ 3 of 5 = frail; 1–2 = pre-frail).
Accumulation (Rockwood): clinical frailty scale 1–9 (1 very fit, 9 terminally ill); ≥ 5 = mild frailty.
Functional decline; falls; incontinence; delirium on minor illness; polypharmacy harm; hospitalisation cascade.
redFlags: Severe / advanced frailty (CFS ≥ 7) — consider end-of-life planning.
Falls with fracture, head injury, recurrent.

diagnostics.test: Clinical Frailty Scale (Rockwood); grip strength; Timed Up and Go; gait speed.
Comprehensive geriatric assessment domains: medical, mental health, functional (ADL/IADL), social, environmental, medication.
FBC, U&E, glucose, TFT, B12, folate, vitamin D, calcium, ferritin, CRP, urinalysis.
MMSE / MoCA cognitive screen + PHQ-9 / GAD-7 / GDS-15.
DEXA if osteoporosis risk; falls assessment.

management.step: Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment + multidisciplinary care plan
management.detail: Geriatrician + GP + nurse + physio + OT + dietitian + pharmacist + social work + carer.
Polypharmacy review (STOPP/START, Beers, OncoBeers); correct anaemia, B12, vitamin D, thyroid, depression; optimise comorbidities; pain management.
Resistance + balance training (e.g. Otago programme) 3 times/week; improves muscle mass + falls + functional capacity. Tai chi reduces falls.
1.2 g/kg/day protein (higher than non-frail); calorie supplementation if undernutrition; treat dental issues + swallowing problems; vitamin D 800 IU + calcium 1000 mg daily if deficient.
Identify fall risk (Timed Up and Go > 12 s, recent falls); home assessment for hazards; vision + hearing review; medication review; falls clinic + balance training; alarm system.
Pelvic floor exercises; bladder retraining; treat UTI; review anticholinergic burden; consider mirabegron over oxybutynin.

management.step: Advance care planning + cessation of futile intervention
management.detail: Discuss goals of care, ceiling of treatment, ReSPECT / POLST equivalent. Consider de-prescribing of preventive medications with low remaining benefit (e.g. statin in last 6–12 months of life). Hospice / palliative care referral when appropriate.
Carer assessment + respite + financial benefits; befriending / day-centre; technology-enabled care (telecare).

references.label: British Geriatrics Society Fit for Frailty; WHO Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE)
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Severe obstructive sleep apnoea — CPAP + co-morbidity pathway
presentation: Severe OSA: apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) ≥ 30/h on polysomnography or home sleep study.
Symptoms: excessive daytime sleepiness (Epworth ≥ 15), witnessed apnoea / loud snoring, choking at night, morning headache, unrefreshing sleep.
Risk: obesity (BMI > 30), male, age, neck circumference > 43 cm, retrognathia, alcohol / sedative use, hypothyroidism, menopause.
Complications: hypertension, arrhythmia, MI, stroke, T2DM, MVA, cognitive impairment.
redFlags: Severe sleepiness in driver / safety-critical occupation — driving counselling + restriction.
Pulmonary hypertension / right heart failure (overlap with COPD / obesity hypoventilation syndrome).
Pregnancy + severe OSA — maternal + fetal compromise.

diagnostics.test: Polysomnography (PSG) — gold standard; home sleep test (HST) acceptable for high-pretest probability.
Epworth Sleepiness Scale ≥ 15 = severe daytime sleepiness.
TSH, ECG, echo (if heart failure / arrhythmia), HbA1c.

management.detail: Auto-CPAP titration (4–20 cmH2O) or fixed CPAP after laboratory titration. Heated humidification. Mask fitting + education vital. Improves daytime sleepiness, BP, cardiovascular outcomes.

management.step: Bilevel (BiPAP) for CPAP intolerance / obesity hypoventilation
management.detail: Switch if CPAP not tolerated or coexistent hypoventilation (BMI > 40, daytime hypercapnia).
Custom-made for adequately dentate patients with mild-moderate OSA; less effective than CPAP for severe.
Weight loss (10% reduction reduces AHI by 20–30%); avoid alcohol / sedatives; positional therapy if supine-only; smoking cessation; sleep hygiene.
Sustained weight loss substantially improves / resolves OSA in many morbidly obese.
Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (modest effect); maxillomandibular advancement (effective in selected); hypoglossal-nerve stimulator (Inspire) for CPAP-intolerant moderate-severe.
BP control (CPAP itself reduces BP); diabetes optimisation; CV-risk modification; treat reflux. Driving restriction until adequate CPAP adherence (4 h/night minimum > 70% nights).
Specialist obstetric input; CPAP safe in pregnancy.
CPAP compliance reviewed at 1 month + 3 months + annually; download data; adjust pressure + mask + education for non-adherence.

references.label: AASM Clinical Practice Guideline on Diagnosis + Treatment of OSA
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) — diagnosis and treatment
presentation: Progressive exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, chest discomfort, syncope, palpitations.
Signs: loud P2, RV heave, pansystolic murmur (TR), raised JVP, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly.

Groups (WHO classification): Group 1 PAH (idiopathic, heritable, drug-induced, connective tissue, HIV, portal hypertension, congenital heart), Group 2 (left heart disease), Group 3 (lung disease + hypoxia), Group 4 (CTEPH — chronic thromboembolic), Group 5 (multifactorial).
redFlags: Functional class III/IV (WHO FC III: symptoms with less than ordinary activity; IV: at rest).
Right heart failure (peripheral oedema, ascites, raised JVP).
Syncope on exertion — high mortality marker.
Pregnancy + PAH — 30–50% mortality; pregnancy is contraindicated.
Suspected pulmonary veno-occlusive disease (poor response to vasodilators, pulmonary oedema on therapy).

diagnostics.test: Transthoracic echocardiography — estimate PA systolic pressure + RV size/function.
Right heart catheterisation — gold standard for diagnosis. PAH = mean PAP > 20 mmHg + PCWP ≤ 15 + PVR > 2 WU.
Pulmonary function tests + DLCO; HRCT chest (Group 3 vs 4).
V/Q scan — to exclude CTEPH (Group 4); pulmonary angiography if positive.
Autoimmune screen (ANA, anti-dsDNA, scleroderma antibodies); HIV; liver biochemistry + USS.

management.step: Refer all suspected PAH to specialist PH centre
management.detail: Phenotyping + risk stratification (REVEAL 2.0, ESC/ERS 4-strata) drive therapy.
Diuretics for congestion. Oxygen for hypoxia. Anticoagulation: routine for CTEPH; selected for idiopathic PAH. Avoid pregnancy (contraception counselling). Vaccinations. Cardiac rehabilitation.
Positive responders (< 10% of idiopathic): high-dose calcium-channel blocker (nifedipine, diltiazem); long-term survival benefit. Most do NOT respond.

Combination therapy increasingly used UP-FRONT: ERA (ambrisentan, bosentan, macitentan) + PDE-5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil) ± soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator (riociguat). Add prostacyclin pathway (selexipag oral, treprostinil IV/SC/inhaled, epoprostenol IV) for severe / high-risk. Goal-directed therapy by risk strata.
Pulmonary endarterectomy — potentially curative; refer specialist centre. Riociguat + balloon pulmonary angioplasty for inoperable / persistent.
For functional class III/IV with worsening despite triple therapy.
Pregnancy contraindicated; effective contraception (not oestrogen — thrombosis); termination considered if pregnant; specialist multidisciplinary care.
3-monthly review with WHO FC, 6MWT, BNP, echo; right heart catheter at 12 months + as needed.

references.label: ESC/ERS Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension (2022)

title: Severe Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI)
presentation: Watery diarrhoea (≥ 3 stools / 24 h) after recent (within 12 weeks) antibiotic exposure, hospitalisation, or PPI.
Severe: WBC > 15, albumin < 30, creatinine > 1.5× baseline.
Fulminant: hypotension, ileus, megacolon, perforation, multi-organ failure.
Recurrence common (15–30% after first episode; 40–60% after recurrence).
redFlags: Fulminant CDI — hypotension / shock, ileus, megacolon — surgical assessment.

diagnostics.test: Stool C. difficile testing: enzyme immunoassay (EIA) for toxin A/B + GDH antigen + nucleic-acid amplification (NAAT).
diagnostics.rationale: Multi-step algorithm preferred to avoid over-diagnosis (colonised carriers).

diagnostics.test: Abdominal X-ray + CT if suspected ileus / megacolon / perforation.
Flexible sigmoidoscopy — pseudomembranes diagnostic (not routinely needed).

management.detail: Where clinically possible, switch / stop offending broad-spectrum antibiotic. Single-room isolation with strict hand hygiene (soap + water — alcohol gel ineffective for spores).
Fidaxomicin 200 mg BD × 10 days OR vancomycin 125 mg QDS × 10 days (oral; not IV). Avoid metronidazole as first-line (less effective, more recurrence).
Vancomycin 500 mg QDS PO/NG + vancomycin 500 mg in 100 mL saline rectal every 6 h (if ileus) + IV metronidazole 500 mg every 8 h. Surgical consult for colectomy / loop ileostomy + vancomycin lavage.

First recurrence: fidaxomicin 10-day course OR vancomycin tapered/pulsed regimen (125 mg QDS × 14 days → BD × 7 → daily × 7 → every 2 days × 8 → every 3 days × 15). Second + further: faecal microbiota transplant (FMT) — 90% cure rate.
Monoclonal anti-toxin B antibody — 10 mg/kg IV single dose; reduces recurrence by ~10% in high-risk.
IV fluids; electrolyte correction; antipyretic; AVOID antimotility (loperamide). Stop PPI if not strictly indicated.
Contact precautions + dedicated equipment for duration of diarrhoea + 48 h afterwards. Bleach-based environmental cleaning. Antimicrobial stewardship.

references.label: IDSA/SHEA Clinical Practice Guidelines for C. difficile (2021)

title: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) — C1 inhibitor deficiency
presentation: Recurrent episodes of non-pruritic, non-pitting subcutaneous OR submucosal swelling lasting 2–5 days.
Common sites: face, extremities, GI tract (severe colicky pain, vomiting — often mistaken for surgical abdomen), genitals, AIRWAY (laryngeal — life-threatening).
No urticaria (distinguishes from histamine-mediated).
Triggers: trauma, surgery / dental work, infection, oestrogens (OCP, pregnancy, menstruation), stress, ACE inhibitors.
Family history (autosomal dominant — SERPING1 gene); but 25% de novo.
redFlags: Laryngeal oedema — airway compromise; death within hours.
Severe abdominal attack — mistaken for surgical abdomen, can lead to unnecessary laparotomy.
ACE inhibitor co-administration — adds bradykinin pathway burden.

diagnostics.test: C4 level (low between + during attacks — sensitive screening).

diagnostics.rationale: Type I (low quantity), Type II (normal quantity, low function), Type III (normal — XII gene).

diagnostics.test: SERPING1 / F12 / PLG / ANGPT1 / KNG1 genetic testing.

management.detail: C1 inhibitor concentrate (Berinert, Cinryze) 20 IU/kg IV (preferred). OR icatibant 30 mg SC (bradykinin B2 antagonist). OR ecallantide 30 mg SC (kallikrein inhibitor). All effective within 1–4 h. AVOID antihistamines, steroids, adrenaline — these target histamine pathway, ineffective for bradykinin-mediated HAE.
Laryngeal attack: SECURE AIRWAY proactively — awake fibre-optic OR surgical airway; cancellable in time once C1-INH given. Adrenaline IM may provide brief temporising effect (not curative).

management.step: Long-term prophylaxis — indicated for severe / frequent attacks
management.detail: Berotralstat (oral plasma kallikrein inhibitor — newer); OR lanadelumab SC every 2 weeks; OR C1-INH concentrate IV twice-weekly; OR attenuated androgens (danazol 200 mg/day — less preferred long-term due to androgenic + hepatic effects).
C1-INH 1000 IU IV 1–6 h before dental / surgical procedure. Have rescue C1-INH available.
STOP ACE inhibitors. Avoid oestrogen-containing contraception (use copper IUD, progesterone-only, levonorgestrel IUS). Counsel on pregnancy planning + delivery (C1-INH cover).
First-degree relatives — C4 + C1-INH testing; affected individuals need rescue therapy available + emergency action plan.
