Patient + family training to inject C1-INH / icatibant at home. Medic-alert bracelet. Emergency-department alert card.

references.label: WAO/EAACI International Guideline for the Management of HAE (2021 update)

title: Severe asthma — eosinophilic phenotype + biologic pathway
presentation: Persistent symptoms / frequent exacerbations / dependence on systemic corticosteroids despite high-dose inhaled steroid + LABA + adherence + technique optimised.
Phenotyping critical: eosinophilic (blood eosinophils ≥ 300, FeNO ≥ 25), T2-high vs T2-low.
Common in severe asthma: nasal polyps, AERD (Samter triad), allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.
redFlags: Frequent oral corticosteroid courses (≥ 2 per year) — cumulative toxicity.

diagnostics.test: Confirm asthma diagnosis (spirometry, reversibility, peak flow variability, methacholine challenge).
Trigger investigation: skin-prick / IgE for aeroallergens; specific Aspergillus IgE / IgG for ABPA; eosinophilic vasculitis (EGPA) workup.
Biomarkers: blood eosinophils, FeNO, total IgE, sputum eosinophils.
CT chest if recurrent infection / bronchiectasis suspected.

management.detail: High-dose ICS + LABA + add LAMA (tiotropium) ± LTRA (montelukast — counsel on neuropsychiatric warnings).
Smoking cessation; allergen avoidance; obesity; OSA; GERD; chronic rhinosinusitis / nasal polyps (intranasal steroid; FESS in selected); anxiety / depression.

Anti-IL-5 / anti-IL-5R (mepolizumab 100 mg SC every 4 weeks; reslizumab 3 mg/kg IV every 4 weeks; benralizumab 30 mg SC every 4 weeks × 3 then every 8 weeks). Eligibility typically eosinophils ≥ 300 + exacerbations / OCS dependence.
Omalizumab SC every 2–4 weeks (weight + IgE-dose calculated); eligibility allergic + IgE 30–1500 + sensitisation.

Tezepelumab 210 mg SC every 4 weeks — works for both T2-high + T2-low (broader). Dupilumab 200/300 mg SC every 2 weeks — eosinophils ≥ 150 OR FeNO ≥ 25; also covers atopic dermatitis, CRS with nasal polyps, EGPA.
Selected severe non-eosinophilic / biologic-failure cases at specialist centre.
Confirmed ABPA (raised IgE + Aspergillus-specific): oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day × 2 weeks then taper + itraconazole 200 mg BD × 16 weeks (monitor LFT + level).
Multidisciplinary clinic; structured patient education; written personalised asthma action plan.

references.label: ERS / ATS task force statements on biologics

title: Wilson disease — acute liver failure / neurological presentation
presentation: Autosomal recessive copper-accumulation disorder (ATP7B mutations).
Hepatic: childhood-adolescent age — acute hepatitis, chronic cirrhosis, acute-on-chronic liver failure (highest copper + bilirubin / ALP < 4 ratio + Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia).
Neurological: adolescent-young adult — tremor (wing-beating), dysarthria, dystonia, ataxia, parkinsonism, dysphagia.
Psychiatric: personality change, depression, psychosis, cognitive decline.
Kayser-Fleischer rings (slit-lamp) in 95% with neurological + 50% hepatic.
redFlags: Acute liver failure (Wilson type) — HIGH MORTALITY without urgent transplantation.
Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia + acute liver failure pattern — classical Wilson ALF.
Pregnancy + Wilson — continue therapy with zinc / trientine (avoid penicillamine doses > 1 g).
Suspected ESRD with copper accumulation — adjust chelator dosing.

diagnostics.test: Serum ceruloplasmin (low < 20 mg/dL) + 24-h urinary copper (high > 100 microgram).
Liver biopsy with copper quantification > 250 microgram/g dry weight.
Brain MRI — basal ganglia + thalamus + brainstem T2 hyperintensities.

management.detail: Penicillamine 1–1.5 g/day in 4 divided doses (with pyridoxine 25 mg/day); titrate to urinary copper. Trientine 1–1.6 g/day in 3 divided doses — better tolerated, especially neurological worsening risk (10–25% on penicillamine). Both during pregnancy at reduced dose.

Zinc acetate 50 mg TDS (separate from food + chelator by 1 h); blocks intestinal copper absorption + induces metallothionein. Once stable + asymptomatic; preferred for asymptomatic / pre-symptomatic siblings.
Avoid shellfish, organ meats, nuts, chocolate, mushrooms, dried fruit. Demineralised water if copper plumbing.

New Wilson index score ≥ 11 (bilirubin + INR + ALT + WBC + albumin) — high mortality without transplant; urgent listing. Outcomes excellent post-transplant (cures Wilson; no need for further chelation).
Switch to trientine + zinc. Symptomatic treatment of movement disorders (anticholinergic, dopaminergic per Parkinsonian features).

Quarterly: LFT, FBC, U&E, urinary copper (target 200–500 microgram on therapy). 6-monthly: ceruloplasmin, free copper, slit-lamp. Annual neurological + psychiatric review. Compliance is critical — non-adherence relapse risk.
First-degree relatives — biochemical + genetic; pre-symptomatic siblings benefit greatly from prophylactic zinc.

references.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Wilson disease (2012, updated)

title: Pemphigus vulgaris — severe / acute
presentation: Painful flaccid intra-epidermal blisters + erosions on skin + mucous membranes (oral 50% as presenting feature).
Nikolsky sign positive (lateral pressure produces blister).
Autoimmune — anti-desmoglein 3 (mucosal) + 1 (cutaneous) IgG antibodies.
Severe: > 10% BSA involvement, mucosal involvement preventing eating, secondary infection, electrolyte / fluid loss.
redFlags: Severe mucosal involvement — impaired feeding + hydration.

diagnostics.test: Skin biopsy — perilesional for histology (suprabasal acantholysis); H&E.
Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) — intercellular IgG + C3 staining in epidermis.
Indirect IF + ELISA for anti-desmoglein 1 + 3 antibodies.
diagnostics.rationale: Distinguish PV (Dsg3 ± Dsg1) from foliaceus (Dsg1 only).

diagnostics.test: Baseline + serial: FBC, U&E, glucose, lipid, vitamin D, DEXA, hepatitis B + TB screen before immunosuppression.

management.detail: Rituximab 1 g IV every 2 weeks × 2 doses, then maintenance every 6 months (PEMPHIX trial: superior to mycophenolate for sustained remission). Concomitant prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day with planned rapid taper 4–6 months.
Azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day OR mycophenolate 2–3 g/day (TPMT testing before azathioprine). Steroid taper depends on disease control.
Specialist dressings; oral hygiene + topical analgesia (lidocaine viscous, sucralfate suspension); pain management.
Bath / shower with antiseptic; topical antibiotic; PJP prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole if on rituximab + steroid (480 mg daily). Treat documented infection — staphylococcal common.
Soft / liquid diet; NG / parenteral if severe oral involvement; vitamin / mineral supplementation.
Calcium + vitamin D + bisphosphonate during prolonged steroid; diabetes screening + management.
Quarterly clinical + serial antibody titres (anti-Dsg correlate with activity); CD19 monitoring on rituximab; relapse with antibody rise often precedes clinical.

references.label: International Pemphigus Foundation / EADV / BAD guidelines on pemphigus management; PEMPHIX trial Lancet 2017

title: Prosthetic joint infection (periprosthetic joint infection)
presentation: Pain at site of prosthetic joint with one of: sinus / fistula communicating with joint, purulence on aspiration, raised inflammatory markers + 2 positive cultures, raised synovial WBC + neutrophil %.
Early (< 3 months post-op): often Staph aureus, gram-negatives, polymicrobial.
Delayed (3–12 months): coagulase-negative Staph, P. acnes — indolent.
Late (> 12 months): haematogenous — Staph aureus, Strep, dental / GU source.
Increasing problem with multi-drug resistant organisms.
redFlags: Synovial fluid cell count > 4200 with > 70% neutrophils — specific.
Loosening of prosthesis on imaging — chronic infection.
Co-existing native joint infection or osteomyelitis.

diagnostics.test: Synovial fluid aspiration: cell count + differential + Gram + culture + alpha-defensin.
diagnostics.rationale: Mainstay of diagnosis; aspirate BEFORE antibiotic.

diagnostics.test: FBC, CRP, ESR (chronic indolent often elevated only modestly).
Multiple intraoperative tissue samples (≥ 3–5) at debridement / revision.
Sonication of explanted prosthesis (mechanically removes biofilm).
Imaging: X-ray (loosening); CT / MRI; bone scan; PET-CT.

management.step: Multidisciplinary team — orthopaedics + infection + plastics + microbiology
management.detail: Specialist centre with joint-revision capability.

management.step: Surgical strategy depends on chronicity + prosthesis stability + organism
management.detail: DAIR (debridement + antibiotics + implant retention) — early infection < 3 weeks duration, stable prosthesis, susceptible organism. One-stage exchange — chronic with known sensitive organism. Two-stage exchange — chronic with unknown / resistant organism (gold standard for complex).

management.step: Empirical antibiotic — broad-spectrum WHILE awaiting cultures
management.detail: IV vancomycin + ceftriaxone (or piperacillin-tazobactam if pseudomonas risk). Hold empirical antibiotic UNTIL after intraoperative samples wherever feasible.

After culture: 4–6 weeks IV (or oral with high bioavailability) + 2–3 months oral. DAIR retention requires longer (12 months minimum + lifelong suppression in some). Add rifampicin for Staph (biofilm-active) — never as monotherapy.
MRSA: vancomycin / daptomycin. Pseudomonas: ceftazidime / ciprofloxacin. Mycobacterium: prolonged combination per ATB sensitivity. Fungal: amphotericin B / azole.
Multidisciplinary physiotherapy + occupational therapy; revision surgery + prosthesis design; pain management; psychological support.
Eradication rates DAIR 50–80%, one-stage 80–90%, two-stage 85–95%. Suppressive antibiotic therapy (oral) for selected (elderly / unfit / poor revision candidates).

references.label: IDSA Diagnosis and Management of Prosthetic Joint Infection (2013); MSIS Diagnostic Criteria for PJI

title: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH)
presentation: Sudden severe ('thunderclap') headache — worst-ever in life; often peaks within seconds.
± Loss of consciousness, vomiting, photophobia, neck stiffness (meningism develops over hours).
Focal neurology depending on aneurysm location.
Sentinel headache in 30–50% (preceding rupture days-weeks earlier) — missed diagnosis common.
Risk: hypertension, smoking, alcohol, family history, polycystic kidney disease, connective-tissue disorders.
redFlags: Hunt-Hess / WFNS grades IV-V — high mortality.
Rebleeding (15% in first 24 h, peak risk) — secure aneurysm urgently.
Cardiogenic shock from neurogenic stunned myocardium / Takotsubo.
Hyponatraemia from cerebral salt wasting / SIADH.

diagnostics.test: Non-contrast CT head — sensitive > 99% within first 6 h.
LP if CT negative + clinical suspicion + > 12 h symptom onset (xanthochromia in CSF supernatant).
diagnostics.rationale: Detects late presentation when CT may be negative.

diagnostics.test: CT angiogram (CTA) or digital subtraction angiogram (DSA).
diagnostics.rationale: Identify aneurysm location + size for planning.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, coag, glucose, troponin, ECG.

management.detail: Intubate if GCS ≤ 8. Head-up 30°. Stool softener (avoid Valsalva). Severe pain control.
Labetalol / nicardipine IV. Avoid over-treatment (cerebral perfusion). Treat acute hypertensive surge.
Endovascular coiling (preferred where anatomy suitable per ISAT trial) OR neurosurgical clipping. Decision in specialist neurovascular centre.

management.step: Nimodipine 60 mg PO/NG every 4 h × 21 days
management.detail: Calcium-channel blocker — reduces vasospasm-related ischaemia + improves outcomes. Hypotension can be limiting — reduce dose / frequency rather than stop.

Maintain euvolaemia + normo-tension (avoid hypovolaemia). 'Triple-H' (hypertension + hypervolaemia + haemodilution) — superseded by simple induced hypertension when DCI develops. Endovascular intra-arterial nimodipine / angioplasty for refractory vasospasm.
EVD for acute hydrocephalus; ICP monitoring; CSF drainage. VP shunt for persistent (15–20%).

Seizures: levetiracetam prophylaxis × 7 days for poor-grade or aneurysm at risk areas. Hyponatraemia: fluid + salt replacement (cerebral salt wasting > SIADH in SAH context). Cardiac dysfunction: supportive; usually reversible. DVT prophylaxis with mechanical immediately + LMWH from 24 h post-securing.

Multidisciplinary rehab; cognitive screening; psychological care (anxiety / depression common). Annual surveillance for recurrent aneurysm in selected; first-degree relative screening (> 2 affected first-degree).

references.label: AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (2023)
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Acute gout flare — severe / refractory
presentation: Sudden onset severe monoarticular arthritis (often 1st MTP joint — podagra; ankle, knee, wrist, finger).
Joint exquisitely tender, red, warm, swollen.
Polyarticular in chronic tophaceous + transplant + diuretic patients.
Risk: men, age, hyperuricaemia, diuretic, alcohol, purine-rich diet, renal impairment, metabolic syndrome.
Triggers: trauma, surgery, dehydration, alcohol, starting / changing urate-lowering therapy.
redFlags: Septic arthritis differential — aspirate + culture + microscopy MANDATORY in any acute monoarthritis.
Polyarticular gout — often missed; mistaken for RA / cellulitis.
Renal impairment limiting NSAID + colchicine use.
Pregnancy — gout very rare; consider underlying cause.

diagnostics.test: Joint aspiration with Gram stain + culture + crystal microscopy.
diagnostics.rationale: Negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals = MSU; rule out sepsis.

diagnostics.test: Serum urate — variable in acute flare (can be normal); recheck at 4–6 weeks.
Dual-energy CT (DECT) — visualises tophi without aspiration.
diagnostics.rationale: Alternative imaging when aspiration not feasible.

management.detail: NSAID: naproxen 500 mg BD × 5 days (or alternative). Colchicine: 1 mg loading then 500 microgram 1 h later, then 500 microgram BD until improvement (lower dose if eGFR 30–60). Glucocorticoid: prednisolone 30–40 mg/day × 5 days. Intra-articular steroid for monoarticular.
IL-1 antagonist: canakinumab 150 mg SC single dose (high cost; reserve for refractory / multiple comorbidity). Anakinra 100 mg SC daily × 3 days alternative.
Do NOT stop allopurinol / febuxostat during flare — increases flare duration. If newly starting urate-lowering: pre-treat with NSAID / colchicine / low-dose steroid prophylaxis for 3–6 months.

Target serum urate < 360 micromol/L (< 300 if tophi). Allopurinol 100 mg start, titrate by 100 mg every 4 weeks to target (max 900 mg). HLA-B*58:01 screening in Han Chinese / Korean / Thai before allopurinol. Febuxostat 80 mg daily for allopurinol-intolerant / failure (cardiovascular caution). Pegloticase IV every 2 weeks for refractory tophaceous.

Weight reduction; reduce alcohol (especially beer); reduce sugary drinks; Mediterranean diet; avoid offal / shellfish. Treat hypertension (losartan or amlodipine — modestly uricosuric). Treat metabolic syndrome.
Quarterly during titration of urate-lowering; then annually. Recheck urate + tophi shrinkage. Stop colchicine prophylaxis after 3–6 months once urate at target + no flares.

references.label: EULAR Recommendations for management of gout (2016, with updates)
ACR Guideline for the Management of Gout (2020)
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Phaeochromocytoma crisis (catecholamine storm)
presentation: Paroxysmal severe hypertension (often > 200/110), throbbing headache, sweating, palpitations, anxiety.
Triggers: anaesthesia / surgery, IV contrast, glucagon, beta-blocker WITHOUT prior alpha-blockade, tyramine foods, opioids.
Severe: end-organ damage (cardiomyopathy, ARDS, MI, stroke, AKI), multi-organ failure.
Often missed: familial syndromes (MEN2, VHL, NF1), bladder phaeochromocytoma (paroxysms with micturition).
redFlags: Pregnancy + phaeochromocytoma — maternal + fetal mortality 50% if undiagnosed.
Suspected unstable phaeo at intubation / induction — refractory hypertension.
Concurrent bowel ischaemia from severe vasoconstriction.

diagnostics.test: Plasma metanephrines + normetanephrines (preferred — fasting + supine 30 min).
CT / MRI abdomen + neck + chest + pelvis (whole-body MIBG for metastatic / extra-adrenal).

management.detail: Phenoxybenzamine (irreversible, preferred) 10–20 mg BD titrated to symptom control + supine BP < 130/80 (or postural hypotension). Doxazosin 1–8 mg/day alternative. Start 7–14 days before surgery.

management.step: Add beta-blocker ONLY after adequate alpha-blockade (3–5 days)
management.detail: Beta-blocker first causes UNOPPOSED alpha-vasoconstriction → severe hypertensive crisis + heart failure. Propranolol, atenolol, or labetalol used to control tachycardia after alpha-blockade established.
Liberal salt diet + IV fluids — most patients are chronically vasoconstricted + volume-depleted; pre-operative volume expansion prevents post-tumour-removal hypotension.
IV phentolamine 1–5 mg boluses every 10 min. IV sodium nitroprusside infusion. IV magnesium sulphate 2 g (especially in pregnancy).

Laparoscopic adrenalectomy (or open for large / malignant). Optimise alpha-blockade + volume + beta-blockade pre-op. Anaesthetist + surgeon experienced in phaeo cases. Plan post-tumour-removal hypotension management.
Phenoxybenzamine safe; control BP + remove in second trimester ideally; LSCS preferred at term. Specialist multidisciplinary team.
Chemotherapy (CVD = cyclophosphamide + vincristine + dacarbazine); MIBG-radioisotope therapy; surgical debulking. Specialist endocrine oncology.
Annual biochemistry + imaging × 10 years (recurrence in 10–15%); first-degree relatives — biochemistry + genetic screen.

references.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Pheochromocytoma + Paraganglioma (2014)

title: Pituitary apoplexy (acute haemorrhage / infarction of pituitary)
presentation: Sudden severe headache (often retro-orbital), vomiting, visual disturbance (visual field defect / cranial nerve palsies III, IV, VI), reduced consciousness.
Most patients have undiagnosed pituitary adenoma; ~25% present as apoplexy as first manifestation.
Adrenal crisis + hypopituitarism develops over hours-days.
Triggers: anticoagulation, surgery, head trauma, contrast study, dopamine agonist, pregnancy, oestrogen.
redFlags: Reduced consciousness / cranial-nerve palsies — neurosurgical emergency.
Pregnancy with pituitary apoplexy — fetal compromise + Sheehan-like postpartum.

diagnostics.test: MRI pituitary with contrast (preferred) — haemorrhage or infarction within pituitary, often with sellar / suprasellar mass.
Hormonal: cortisol (random + ACTH), TFT (free T4 + TSH), prolactin, LH/FSH, testosterone (men) / oestradiol (women), IGF-1 + GH.

diagnostics.rationale: Electrolyte disturbance from hypocortisolism + diabetes insipidus.

management.detail: 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg / 24 h infusion (or 50 mg every 6 h). Do NOT wait for cortisol result — secondary adrenal insufficiency near-universal.
Saline + correct hyponatraemia + glucose; treat diabetes insipidus with desmopressin if polyuria > 200 mL/h + hypernatraemia (test fluid intake / urine osmolality differential).
Trans-sphenoidal decompression for: visual deterioration, reduced consciousness, severe visual field defect, expanding mass. Conservative if minimal symptoms + stable vision.

management.step: Conservative management for stable / mild cases
management.detail: Hydrocortisone replacement + close monitoring; serial visual + neurological assessments; MRI at 3 months to assess pituitary residuum.

Hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in 2–3 divided doses; thyroxine 50–125 microgram/day (titrate to free T4 mid-range); testosterone replacement for men; oestrogen for premenopausal women (HRT vs COC); DDAVP if diabetes insipidus; growth hormone if proven adult GH deficiency.
Pituitary endocrinology team; annual MRI for residual / recurrent adenoma; lifetime hormone replacement + sick-day rule education.
Triple-dose hydrocortisone before surgery / infection / stress, in all patients with hypopituitarism. Emergency hydrocortisone kit + medic-alert bracelet.

references.label: Society for Endocrinology Clinical Guideline on Pituitary Apoplexy (2011)

title: Severe alcohol withdrawal / delirium tremens
presentation: Stage 1 (6–12 h): tremor, anxiety, GI upset, headache, sweating, palpitations.
Stage 2 (24–48 h): alcoholic hallucinosis (auditory > visual), seizures (typically 24–48 h, usually generalised tonic-clonic).
Stage 3 (48–72 h, sometimes up to day 5): delirium tremens — global confusion + autonomic instability (HR > 100, BP > 160, T > 38.5, sweating) + visual / tactile hallucinations.
Mortality DT 5–15% even with treatment; > 35% without.
Wernicke encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency): triad — ataxia + ophthalmoplegia + confusion (often incomplete).
redFlags: DT with severe autonomic instability — ICU.
Concomitant medical complication (pneumonia, head injury, GI bleed, pancreatitis, sepsis, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia).
Pregnancy + alcohol withdrawal — fetal alcohol exposure + maternal complications.

diagnostics.test: FBC (anaemia, macrocytosis), U&E, LFT (raised AST > ALT, GGT), glucose, magnesium, phosphate, INR, calcium.
ECG (atrial fibrillation, prolonged QT, holiday heart syndrome).

diagnostics.rationale: Identify hypoglycaemia (especially in chronic alcohol-use + malnourished).

diagnostics.test: CT head if focal neurology / persistent confusion / suspected subdural.

management.step: Thiamine FIRST — IV pabrinex BEFORE any glucose
management.detail: Pabrinex IV pairs ampoules I + II three-times daily × 3 days, then 100 mg oral daily long-term. Wernicke encephalopathy: 500 mg IV thiamine TDS × 3 days then 250 mg daily × 5 days. Do NOT give dextrose before thiamine.

Long-acting (chlordiazepoxide 10–50 mg every 1–4 h titrated to CIWA-Ar) OR diazepam 10–20 mg every 1–4 h. Hepatic impairment: switch to short-acting (lorazepam 1–4 mg every 1–4 h) — not glucuronide-conjugated.
IV diazepam 10 mg every 5–10 min until calm (often very high doses needed — 200–800 mg total). Lorazepam infusion. Add propofol or dexmedetomidine for refractory / intubated.

Phenobarbital 10 mg/kg IV slow loading then titrated for resistant cases (synergistic with benzodiazepine). Beta-blocker for autonomic features (after established benzo dosing). Antipsychotic (haloperidol 2.5 mg IM) ONLY for hallucinations / severe agitation despite benzo — NOT seizure prevention.
Magnesium 2 g IV (most alcohol-dependent patients deficient — predisposes to seizures + arrhythmia). Replace K+, phosphate, calcium.
Benzodiazepine + magnesium; if status epilepticus — per status epilepticus pathway. Long-term antiseizure drug NOT needed after isolated withdrawal seizures.

management.step: Brief intervention + relapse prevention before discharge
management.detail: Motivational interviewing; alcohol cessation pharmacotherapy: naltrexone 50 mg/day (oral) OR vivitrol IM monthly; acamprosate 666 mg TDS; disulfiram (selected). Refer to community alcohol services / mutual support (AA / SMART).
Continue oral thiamine 100 mg daily indefinitely; multivitamin; address malnutrition; safeguard against silent progression to Korsakoff dementia.

references.label: NICE CG100 Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis and clinical management of alcohol-related physical complications; SAMHSA TIP 45
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders (mhGAP adaptation), Ministry of Health

title: Opioid use disorder — buprenorphine / methadone induction + maintenance
presentation: Chronic opioid use disorder (heroin, prescription opioid, fentanyl, etc.) seeking treatment or after overdose.
Diagnostic features (DSM-5): ≥ 2 of 11 criteria including loss of control, withdrawal, tolerance, social impairment, risky use.
Co-occurring: depression, anxiety, PTSD, HIV, HCV, HBV; high mortality from overdose without treatment.
redFlags: Pregnancy + OUD — continue MAT (do NOT detoxify mid-pregnancy; risk of preterm birth / fetal distress).
Concurrent benzodiazepine / alcohol dependence — combined treatment risk-stratification.
Methadone QT prolongation risk — ECG before + during treatment.
Recent overdose — high re-overdose risk; immediate MAT initiation is protective.

diagnostics.test: Urine drug screen + observed naltrexone challenge (only after opioid-free 7+ days for naltrexone option).
ECG (baseline QTc) before methadone; LFT, U&E.

management.detail: Buprenorphine-naloxone (preferred — partial agonist, ceiling effect, safer in overdose), OR methadone (full agonist — for high tolerance, structured clinic), OR extended-release naltrexone (only after 7–10 days opioid-free; no risk of misuse but lower retention).

Begin when patient in moderate withdrawal (COWS ≥ 12). Start 2–4 mg SL, titrate by 2–4 mg every 1–4 h to symptom relief (typically day 1 8–16 mg). Days 2–7: titrate to 16–24 mg daily. Avoid precipitated withdrawal (do NOT give if recent full-agonist use). Long-acting (Sublocade SC monthly) for stabilised patients.
Start 10–30 mg daily; titrate slowly (by 5 mg every 3–5 days) to 60–120 mg target. ECG before + after dose titration; risk of overdose during initiation (peak day 3–4).
ALL patients + household members trained in naloxone use; intranasal (4 mg) easiest. Reduces overdose mortality > 50%.

Continue methadone or buprenorphine (do NOT switch agents mid-pregnancy unless essential). Adjust dose to address physiological changes. Neonatal abstinence syndrome management at birth (Finnegan scoring; morphine titration). Breastfeeding compatible.
Counselling (CBT, contingency management, motivational enhancement); peer support; vocational + housing support; treat co-occurring mental illness (SSRIs, mood stabilisers as needed).
Needle / syringe exchange; safer-injection education; fentanyl test strips; supervised consumption services (where available); naloxone distribution; HIV PrEP for at-risk patients.

MAT is chronic-disease management — no fixed end-date; relapse is part of recovery, not failure. Random urine + addiction-medicine follow-up; gradual taper only if patient stable + motivated (often years on MAT).

references.label: SAMHSA TIP 63 Medications for Opioid Use Disorder; WHO Guidelines for the Management of Substance Use
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders (mhGAP adaptation), Ministry of Health

title: High altitude illness — AMS / HACE / HAPE
presentation: Acute mountain sickness (AMS): headache + nausea / vomiting / fatigue / dizziness / sleep disturbance, > 6 h after arrival > 2500 m.
High-altitude cerebral oedema (HACE): AMS + ataxia + altered consciousness (rare but life-threatening).
High-altitude pulmonary oedema (HAPE): exertional dyspnoea > resting, cough, frothy / blood-tinged sputum, crackles, hypoxia — usually > 3000 m, 2–4 days after arrival.
Risk: rapid ascent, individual susceptibility, prior episode, viral infection, dehydration, alcohol, sleeping pills.
redFlags: Resting tachycardia + dyspnoea + frothy sputum — HAPE.
Children + pregnant — increased risk of severe altitude illness.
Sea-level return delayed by terrain — anticipate need for evacuation.

diagnostics.test: Lake Louise Score for AMS (headache + GI / fatigue / dizziness / sleep — 3+ supports AMS).
Pulse oximetry — usually low at altitude; serial measurement tracks deterioration.
diagnostics.rationale: Trend matters more than absolute number.

diagnostics.test: Chest examination + auscultation — crackles in HAPE.
Neurological exam (truncal ataxia heel-to-toe walking — sensitive for HACE).

management.detail: STOP ascent until symptoms resolve. Hydration + paracetamol / ibuprofen / aspirin for headache; antiemetic. Acetazolamide 250 mg BD accelerates acclimatisation.

Lose ≥ 500–1000 m of altitude IMMEDIATELY (do NOT wait for daylight / helicopter). Dexamethasone 8 mg PO/IM/IV loading then 4 mg every 6 h. Oxygen if available. Portable hyperbaric chamber (Gamow bag) as bridge. Continue dexamethasone at lower altitude × 24 h.

Descend ≥ 500–1000 m. Oxygen to target SpO2 > 90%. Nifedipine 30 mg slow-release PO BD OR sildenafil 50 mg every 8 h OR tadalafil 10 mg BD — pulmonary vasodilators. Avoid exertion. Portable hyperbaric chamber if descent delayed.

Graded ascent (climb high, sleep low; max 300 m / day above 2500 m + rest day every 1000 m). Acetazolamide 125–250 mg BD starting 24 h before ascent + 2 days at altitude for known susceptibility. Avoid alcohol + sedatives during first 24 h.

More susceptible to AMS than adults; cannot articulate symptoms — irritable / off-feeding / lethargic; descend on any concern. Avoid high altitude in infants < 6 weeks; specialist advice for chronic conditions.
Limit to < 2500 m for sleeping. Avoid above 3500 m in pregnancy; if high-altitude residents — monitor for IUGR + pre-eclampsia.
Recovery typically within 24–72 h of descent + supportive care. Future trips: acetazolamide prophylaxis + slower ascent.

references.label: Wilderness Medical Society Practice Guidelines for the Prevention, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Acute Altitude Illness

title: Severe haemophilia A / B — acute bleed emergency
presentation: Known haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) or B (IX deficiency) — severe < 1% activity; moderate 1–5%; mild 5–40%.
Bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis) — 80% of bleeds; recurrent → chronic arthropathy.
Muscle haematomas — iliopsoas, calf, forearm (compartment syndrome).
Mucocutaneous, GI, urinary, retroperitoneal, intracranial (highest mortality).
Female carriers — usually mild but can bleed; haemophilia A heterozygotes with skewed X-inactivation.
redFlags: Intracranial bleed — highest mortality emergency; CT IMMEDIATELY.
Inhibitor (alloantibody to factor) — first-line factor concentrate ineffective; rapid escalation.

diagnostics.test: FBC, APTT (prolonged), PT (normal), fibrinogen, factor VIII / IX activity, von Willebrand factor antigen + activity.
Inhibitor screen (Bethesda assay) — especially in non-responding to factor.
Imaging per suspected bleed: CT head (low threshold), USS / MRI of muscle / joint, CT abdomen for retroperitoneal.

management.step: ACT EARLY — give factor concentrate IMMEDIATELY before any imaging if suspected major bleed
management.detail: Most family / patient knows their concentrate type + dose. 'When in doubt, treat'. Delay → permanent damage.

Recombinant or plasma-derived FVIII: 1 unit/kg raises factor by 2%. Target: 30–40% for mild bleeds (joint, muscle, mucosal); 80–100% for major bleeds (intracranial, retroperitoneal, abdominal); 50–80% for surgery. Half-life ~12 h; repeat every 12 h or as continuous infusion 2–4 units/kg/h.

Recombinant FIX: 1 unit/kg raises factor by 1%. Same targets as above but doses ~50% higher (lower recovery). Half-life ~24 h; repeat every 24 h. Extended half-life recombinant FIX (nonacog beta pegol, eftrenonacog alfa) — longer dosing intervals.

management.step: Emicizumab (anti-FIXa / FX bispecific antibody) — preventive AND emergency
management.detail: Patients on emicizumab prophylaxis: standard factor concentrate doses for bleed but factor levels not measured by routine APTT. Avoid activated PCC (aPCC) in emicizumab patients — thrombotic microangiopathy risk.
Activated prothrombin complex concentrate (FEIBA / aPCC) OR recombinant factor VIIa (NovoSeven) — if inhibitor present. Long-term: emicizumab + immune-tolerance induction.

Tranexamic acid 25 mg/kg every 8 h for mucocutaneous + dental + minor surgery (NOT in haematuria — clot in ureter). Desmopressin 0.3 microgram/kg IV in mild-moderate haemophilia A (raises VIII transiently).

RICE (rest + ice + compression + elevation). Factor replacement + physiotherapy. Joint aspiration only by specialist in selected cases. Long-term: prophylactic factor 2–3× per week to prevent arthropathy.
X-linked recessive; counsel carriers + screen newborn boys; genetic testing for family. Comprehensive haemophilia centre for shared care.

references.label: WFH Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia (3rd edition, 2020)

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) — induction emergency + chemotherapy
presentation: Children (2–5 years peak) or older adults; pancytopenia / blasts on FBC.
Fatigue, pallor (anaemia), bleeding (thrombocytopenia), infection (neutropenia).
Bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, mediastinal mass (T-cell), CNS involvement.
Severe risk at presentation: hyperleukocytosis (WBC > 100), tumour lysis, sepsis from neutropenia.
redFlags: Hyperleukocytosis with leukostasis — pulmonary, CNS, ocular leukostasis; urgent leukapheresis.
Tumour lysis syndrome — hyperuricaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, AKI.
CNS involvement (cranial nerve palsy, headache, vomiting) — CSF cytology mandatory.

diagnostics.test: FBC + blood film (blasts), bone marrow aspirate + biopsy + flow cytometry + cytogenetics + molecular (BCR-ABL1 for Ph+ ALL, MLL rearrangement infant, IKZF1 deletion adverse).
LP with intrathecal chemotherapy at induction (CSF cytology + flow).
FBC, U&E, urate, phosphate, LDH, calcium for TLS monitoring.
Echo (baseline before anthracycline), CXR, abdominal USS, HBV/HCV/HIV.

management.detail: Treat infection (broad-spectrum + empirical antifungal in neutropenic + persistent fever), transfusion (PRBC for Hb < 80, platelets for < 10 or active bleeding), correct coagulopathy.
IV hydration 3 L/m²/day, rasburicase (after G6PD screening) for high-risk; allopurinol for intermediate / low risk. K+, phosphate, calcium monitoring 4–6-hourly; RRT if severe.
Hydration + low-dose chemotherapy (steroid + cyclophosphamide); leukapheresis for symptomatic leukostasis (WBC > 100 with pulmonary / CNS symptoms).

Paediatric ALL (BFM-style): prednisolone + vincristine + asparaginase + daunorubicin + intrathecal methotrexate × 4 weeks. Adult ALL: hyper-CVAD (cyclophosphamide + vincristine + doxorubicin + dexamethasone) alternating with methotrexate + cytarabine. Ph+: add tyrosine kinase inhibitor (imatinib / dasatinib / ponatinib).
Intrathecal methotrexate (and cytarabine for high-risk) at induction + consolidation phases. Avoid cranial radiotherapy except very high-risk.

Pegaspargase / E. coli asparaginase causes pancreatitis, thrombosis (CNS sinus), coagulopathy, anaphylaxis, hyperglycaemia. Monitor amylase + coagulation; treat with FFP / antithrombin for severe coagulopathy.

Consolidation, maintenance (mercaptopurine + methotrexate × 2–3 years). High-risk / relapsed: allogeneic stem cell transplant; CAR-T cell therapy (tisagenlecleucel for refractory paediatric / young adult).
PJP prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole 3× weekly during therapy). Antifungal prophylaxis. Anti-emetic. Mucositis care. Nutritional support. Psychosocial support — specialist paediatric / AYA oncology team.

references.label: BFM protocols; UKALL paediatric; ECOG / GMALL adult; NCCN ALL Guidelines
Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) — emergency
presentation: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia (often < 30 × 10⁹/L) + new neurological symptoms / fever / AKI / abdominal pain.
Acquired (auto-Ab against ADAMTS13) is most common; congenital (Upshaw-Schulman) is rare.
Triggers: pregnancy, infection, malignancy, drugs (clopidogrel, ticlopidine, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, gemcitabine, mitomycin C, quinine, interferon).
Classic pentad: MAHA + thrombocytopenia + neurological + AKI + fever — only 40%; do not wait for full pentad.
redFlags: Severe AKI (less common in TTP — more in HUS).

diagnostics.test: FBC + blood film (schistocytes ≥ 1% — diagnostic) + LDH (high) + bilirubin + haptoglobin + Coombs (negative — distinguishes from autoimmune).
ADAMTS13 activity < 10% confirms TTP; ADAMTS13 inhibitor (acquired).
diagnostics.rationale: Distinguish from HUS / DIC. Results may not be immediate — START treatment empirically.

diagnostics.test: Pregnancy test, stool culture (HUS differential), viral screen (HIV, hepatitis).
Direct antiglobulin test, autoimmune screen (SLE), drug history.

management.step: URGENT plasma exchange (PEX) — within 4–8 h of suspicion
management.detail: Daily PEX (1.5× plasma volume initially, then 1.0× volume) using FFP / cryoprecipitate-poor plasma until platelet count > 150 × 10⁹/L × 2 consecutive days + LDH normalising. Mortality drops from 90% to 10% with PEX.
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily × 3 days then oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day tapered. Reduces ADAMTS13-inhibitor activity.
10 mg IV bolus then 10 mg SC daily until ADAMTS13 activity ≥ 20%. Accelerates platelet recovery + reduces refractory / relapse rates per HERCULES trial. Combine with PEX + steroid.
375 mg/m² weekly × 4 doses — particularly for ADAMTS13 inhibitor-positive disease. Reduces relapse.
Risk of progressive thrombosis; reserve only for life-threatening bleeding.
Stop offending drug; treat underlying infection / malignancy / pregnancy management.
Folate supplementation (rapid red cell turnover); transfusion of red cells for severe anaemia; cardiac + renal monitoring; seizure management; thromboprophylaxis once platelets > 50.
ADAMTS13 monitoring quarterly; relapse 30–40% in 10 years — pre-emptive rituximab in ADAMTS13 < 10% even without active disease. Pregnancy planning + monitoring.

references.label: ISTH Guidelines on the Treatment of TTP (2020); BSH guidelines on diagnosis + management of TTP

title: Dental trauma — avulsed permanent tooth + maxillofacial emergencies
presentation: Avulsion: complete displacement of tooth from socket — most commonly maxillary central incisor in children / adolescents.
Other dental injuries: luxation (intrusion, extrusion, lateral), crown fracture, root fracture, alveolar fracture.
Soft-tissue injury: lacerations to lip, gingiva, tongue.
Maxillofacial fracture: midface (Le Fort I/II/III), mandible, orbital floor 'blow-out', zygoma.
redFlags: Airway compromise (mandibular fracture, severe haemorrhage, tongue swelling).
Severe maxillofacial injury — exclude head + cervical-spine + intracranial injury.
Intracranial signs (CSF rhinorrhoea, raccoon eyes, Battle sign) — base of skull fracture.
Tooth replantation timing — outcome strongly depends on time out of socket + storage medium.

diagnostics.test: Clinical exam (intra + extra-oral); identify all injured teeth + status; soft-tissue + bony injury.

diagnostics.rationale: Identify root fracture, alveolar fracture, retained fragment.

diagnostics.test: Maxillofacial CT for suspected facial / orbital fracture.

management.step: Avulsed permanent tooth — REPLANT WITHIN MINUTES
management.detail: If found and on scene: rinse with saline / milk (NOT scrub or wipe — preserves periodontal ligament cells); reinsert into socket; have patient bite on gauze; seek dental help within hours. Avoid storing in water (osmotic damage).

management.step: If avulsed tooth cannot be replanted immediately — storage medium priority
management.detail: Best to worst: Hank's Balanced Salt Solution (HBSS / Save-A-Tooth) > cold milk > saliva (between cheek + gums in conscious patient) > saline > water (last resort). Replant within 60 minutes for best outcome.

Reposition + flexible splint × 2 weeks (rigid splint for alveolar fracture + 4 weeks). Endodontic treatment 7–14 days post-replantation (pulp necrosis common). Tetanus prophylaxis; oral antibiotic (amoxicillin / doxycycline > 12 y) × 7 days; chlorhexidine mouthwash.

management.step: Avulsed primary (deciduous) tooth — DO NOT REPLANT
management.detail: Risk of damage to developing permanent tooth bud. Refer paediatric dentist for monitoring.
Reposition + splint × 2 weeks for extrusion / lateral; 4 weeks for intrusion; clinical / radiographic follow-up. Endodontic intervention if pulp necrosis.
Crown fracture: dental restoration / pulp capping / RCT per pulp exposure. Root fracture: splint × 4 weeks (cervical-mid) or 4 months (apical). Replantation of fragment if available.
Maxillofacial / ENT / ophthalmology / neurosurgery as required. Open reduction + internal fixation for displaced fractures. Antibiotics + tetanus.
Clinical + radiographic follow-up at 1, 3, 6, 12 months + annually for any traumatised tooth. Watch for resorption + pulp necrosis. Orthodontic / restorative needs.

references.label: International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) Guidelines (2020)
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children

title: Chronic neuropathic pain — diagnosis + tiered management
presentation: Pain in distribution of identifiable nerve / neuroanatomical area following neurological injury (peripheral neuropathy, post-herpetic, trigeminal, post-stroke, post-surgical, radiculopathy, MS-related, CRPS).
Burning / shooting / stabbing / electric quality; allodynia (pain from non-painful stimuli); hyperalgesia.
Often associated with sleep disturbance, depression, anxiety, functional impairment.
redFlags: Suspected new compressive lesion (spinal cord, root) — escalate urgent imaging.
Constitutional features (weight loss, night sweats) — exclude malignancy.
New neurology — exclude evolving cord / nerve lesion.
Suicidal ideation — depression with chronic pain.
Pregnancy + chronic pain — limited pharmacotherapy options.

diagnostics.test: DN4 / LANSS / PainDETECT screening — distinguish neuropathic from nociceptive.
Targeted investigation per cause: nerve conduction studies / EMG, MRI spine, blood glucose / HbA1c, B12, thyroid, paraproteinaemia, HIV serology.

management.detail: Optimise glycaemic control (diabetic neuropathy); vitamin B12 replacement; treat infection; decompression surgery for compressive.

Choose ONE of: amitriptyline 10–25 mg nocte titrate to 75 mg; OR duloxetine 30 mg → 60 mg; OR gabapentin 300 mg → 1200 mg TDS (slow titration); OR pregabalin 75 mg BD → 300 mg BD. Reassess at 4 weeks; if inadequate response after dose optimisation, switch class.
Combine first-line classes (e.g. duloxetine + gabapentin); evidence supports additive effect.
Capsaicin 0.075% cream OR 8% patch (PHN, focal); lidocaine 5% patch (PHN, focal — well tolerated, low systemic absorption).
Tramadol may have role; strong opioid only for refractory severe — risk-benefit + addiction risk; specialist input. Avoid long-term opioids.

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-CP), mindfulness-based stress reduction, graded exercise / activity pacing, pain education (Explain Pain framework), physiotherapy, TENS, acupuncture. Multidisciplinary pain clinic for complex cases.

Trigeminal neuralgia: carbamazepine 100 mg BD titrate up; oxcarbazepine alternative; microvascular decompression for refractory. PHN: pregabalin / gabapentin / lidocaine patch / capsaicin. CRPS: physiotherapy + mirror therapy + early multidisciplinary clinic + bisphosphonate for bone loss.
Nerve block, spinal cord stimulation, intrathecal drug delivery — for refractory + specialist centre. Botulinum toxin for selected (PHN, plantar pain).

references.label: NICE CG173 Neuropathic pain in adults (2019 update); IASP Neuropathic Pain Special Interest Group recommendations
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Diabetic retinopathy — screening + sight-threatening management
presentation: Background diabetic retinopathy: microaneurysms, dot/blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots (mild non-proliferative DR).
Pre-proliferative / severe NPDR: venous beading, IRMA, multiple haemorrhages — high risk of progression.
Proliferative DR: neovascularisation of disc / elsewhere — vitreous haemorrhage + traction retinal detachment + neovascular glaucoma.
Diabetic macular oedema (DMO) — leading cause of vision loss in DM; can occur at any stage.
Risk factors: duration of diabetes, HbA1c, BP, lipids, pregnancy, renal disease.
redFlags: Sudden vision loss — vitreous haemorrhage / retinal detachment / neovascular glaucoma.
New floaters + flashes — posterior vitreous detachment / retinal tear.
Pre-proliferative or proliferative DR — urgent ophthalmology assessment.
Diabetes + pregnancy — DR can worsen rapidly.

diagnostics.test: Annual dilated retinal screening: digital photography + grading.
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) for macular oedema.
HbA1c, lipids, BP, U&E (renal function affects DR progression).

management.detail: HbA1c target < 7% (avoid rapid drop in advanced DR — worsens transiently). BP < 130/80. Lipid lowering. Smoking cessation. Renal protection.

management.step: Annual screening — first 5 years if onset > age 30 then annual; from puberty onwards in type 1; from diagnosis in type 2
management.detail: Pregnant: screening at first antenatal visit, repeat 16–24 + 28 weeks. Pre-pregnancy planning for optimal control.
Laser causes regression of neovascular vessels — gold standard for PDR. Multiple sessions; mild peripheral vision loss + night-vision impairment as side effects.

management.step: Diabetic macular oedema — anti-VEGF intravitreal injection
management.detail: Ranibizumab / aflibercept / faricimab monthly × 3–5 then PRN. Bevacizumab off-label alternative (cost-effective). Improves vision in most. Add focal laser for selected residual leakage. Intravitreal dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) for refractory.
For non-resolving vitreous haemorrhage > 3 months, traction retinal detachment, combined traction-rhegmatogenous. Specialist vitreoretinal centre.
Intravitreal anti-VEGF + PRP + IOP-lowering medication + glaucoma drainage device. Pain control.
Severe vision loss: low-vision aids, social services, occupational rehabilitation, driving certification, family support.

references.label: AAO Diabetic Retinopathy Preferred Practice Pattern (2019)
Kenya National Clinical Guidelines for Management of Diabetes Mellitus, Ministry of Health

title: Acute anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury — adult
presentation: Sports injury — pivoting / cutting / landing from jump with audible 'pop'; immediate inability to continue + rapid swelling within hours (haemarthrosis).
Anterior instability + 'giving way' with subsequent activity.
Often coexistent injuries: medial collateral ligament (50%), meniscus (50–75% acute), articular cartilage.
redFlags: Locked knee with displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear.
Concurrent posterior cruciate / multi-ligament knee injury — high-energy mechanism + dislocation; rule out vascular injury (popliteal artery).

diagnostics.test: Lachman test (most sensitive), anterior drawer, pivot shift.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirm ACL tear + identify associated injuries (meniscal, MCL, articular cartilage).
Exclude Segond fracture (avulsion at lateral tibial plateau — pathognomonic) + tibial plateau fracture.

management.detail: Rest + ice + compression + elevation; non-weight-bearing initially with crutches. Aspirate large haemarthrosis if very painful (consider FAT droplets — osteochondral fracture / cruciate ligament fracture).

management.step: Physiotherapy first — restore range of motion + quadriceps strength
management.detail: Pre-operative rehabilitation improves post-surgical outcomes. Start within days of injury — early gentle range of motion + isometric quadriceps + open-chain hamstring.
Older / lower-demand / less unstable patients — bracing + physiotherapy + activity modification can avoid surgery. Counsel risk of cartilage / meniscus damage with recurrent instability.

Indicated for: athletes / pivoting-sport returnees, recurrent giving way, additional repairable meniscal damage, multi-ligament knee injury, paediatric patients. Autograft (hamstring or patellar tendon) — gold standard; allograft for revisions / multi-ligament. Timing: usually 4–6 weeks post-injury (allow swelling to resolve + range of motion improve).

Multi-phase 9–12 months: range of motion, quadriceps + hamstring strengthening, neuromuscular control, return-to-running (3–4 months), return-to-sport (9–12 months). ACL re-rupture rate 5–10% on graft + 5–10% contralateral — neuromuscular training reduces.
Meniscal repair preferred over meniscectomy when feasible (sparing meniscus delays osteoarthritis). Osteochondral fragment fixation / microfracture / OAT / ACI.
Even after successful ACL reconstruction, 20–30% develop OA in 10–15 years; emphasise neuromuscular training, weight management.

references.label: AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline on Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries; British Orthopaedic Sports Trauma + Arthroscopy Society

title: Achilles tendon rupture
presentation: Sudden severe pain in posterior calf during sport / sudden exertion ('felt as if kicked from behind').
Often middle-aged 'weekend warrior'; men > women 5:1.
Risk factors: prior calf injury, fluoroquinolone (especially with steroid), local corticosteroid injection, chronic Achilles tendinopathy, diabetes.
Inability to plantarflex effectively; gap palpable along tendon.
redFlags: Open injury — requires urgent surgical debridement + repair.
Vascular / neurological deficit (rare with isolated Achilles).
Bilateral / spontaneous — suspect systemic cause (fluoroquinolone, immunosuppression).

diagnostics.test: Thompson (Simmonds) test — squeeze calf with patient prone; lack of plantarflexion = positive (sensitive + specific).
USS calf — confirm rupture + measure tendon gap.
MRI — gold standard but rarely needed for diagnosis; useful for partial / chronic tears.

management.detail: Equinus splint / cast (foot plantarflexed) reduces tendon gap. Refer orthopaedics within days. Crutches non-weight-bearing initially.

Modern evidence: equally good outcomes for active / mobile patients in functional rehabilitation programmes (UKSTAR / ARTERY trials). Surgery preferred for: tendon gap > 1 cm at neutral position with USS, very active patients, elite athletes. Conservative preferred for: older / less active / surgical risk + adequate gap closure in plantarflexion.
Equinus cast / boot × 8–10 weeks with progressive plantarflexion reduction; full weight-bearing in boot from 4 weeks; physiotherapy from week 6; return-to-sport 4–6 months.
Open or percutaneous (smaller incision, lower wound complications, similar functional outcome). Followed by same functional rehabilitation as conservative.

Multi-phase: range of motion → strengthening → return-to-running → return-to-sport. Eccentric calf strengthening (Alfredson protocol) reduces re-rupture. Return-to-running ~4 months; return-to-pivoting / cutting 6 months.

Conservative: 7–13% re-rupture (vs 2–4% surgical). Surgical: wound infection (especially with prior steroid injection / open injury), sural nerve injury, DVT (incidence 35% subclinical — consider LMWH prophylaxis 6 weeks).
Avoid fluoroquinolones in those with prior tendinopathy. Pre-exercise warm-up + eccentric strengthening for those at risk.

references.label: AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline on Management of Acute Achilles Tendon Rupture; UKSTAR + ARTERY trials

title: Congenital hypothyroidism — neonatal screening + management
presentation: Most identified by national newborn screening (heel-prick blood spot — TSH ≥ 20 mIU/L).
Clinically: prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, lethargy, constipation, hypothermia, large posterior fontanelle, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, hoarse cry, hypotonia.
Often clinically subtle in first weeks — early detection essential to prevent cretinism + intellectual disability.
Causes: thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis, ectopia — 80%), dyshormonogenesis (recessive — 20%); transient (maternal antibody, iodine deficiency / excess, drug-induced).
redFlags: Severe presentation (TSH > 60 + low T4 + clinical features).
Family history of dyshormonogenesis — recessive screening important.
Iodine-deficient region — endemic cretinism prevention via salt iodisation.
Symptomatic / clinical hypothyroidism not detected by screen (rare false-negative or no screening programme).

diagnostics.test: Newborn screen TSH (or T4 in some programmes).
diagnostics.rationale: Mandatory in most countries; identifies most cases.

diagnostics.test: Confirmatory venous TSH + free T4 within 48 h of positive screen.
Thyroid ultrasound + nuclear scan (Tc-99m or I-123) within first 1–2 weeks of treatment.
diagnostics.rationale: Identify aetiology (agenesis vs ectopia vs dyshormonogenesis).

diagnostics.test: Maternal TSH + thyroid antibodies if transient suspected.

management.step: Start levothyroxine WITHIN 14 DAYS of birth
management.detail: Levothyroxine 10–15 microgram/kg/day PO once daily (full dose from start, NOT titrate up). Higher dose 12–15 microgram/kg/day for severe (low T4 < 5 pmol/L).
Crush tablet + mix with small amount of water / breast milk / formula; AVOID giving with soya / iron / calcium / fibre (interferes absorption). Daily at same time.
Every 2 weeks until TSH normalises (target < 5 mIU/L); then every 1–3 months in first year; every 2–4 months ages 1–3 years; every 6–12 months thereafter. Free T4 in upper half of normal range.
Dose increases proportionally with body weight. Aim levothyroxine within recommended range; over-replacement causes craniosynostosis + behavioural problems.
Trial off treatment for 30 days; if TSH stays normal, transient; if rises, permanent congenital hypothyroidism — restart + lifelong.
Routine developmental screening at 6, 12, 18, 24 months. Early intervention if any delay. Properly treated children have normal IQ + development.
Recurrence risk depends on aetiology — dyshormonogenesis 25% (autosomal recessive); dysgenesis < 5%. Maternal hypothyroidism management in future pregnancies + thyroid antibody screening.
Specialist paediatric endocrine team — lifetime levothyroxine. Adult-care transition + adherence support; pregnancy counselling for affected women (dose increases 25–50% in pregnancy).

references.label: ESPE / ATA Guidelines on Congenital Hypothyroidism (2014, updated)
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Newborn screening — heel-prick programme (PKU, congenital hypothyroidism, CF, SCID, etc.)
presentation: Heel-prick blood sample 48–72 hours after birth.

Programme content varies by country — typical: phenylketonuria, congenital hypothyroidism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell + thalassaemia, MCAD deficiency + other inherited metabolic disorders, severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
Additional newborn checks: NIPE (Newborn Infant Physical Examination — within 72 h + at 6–8 weeks), pulse oximetry for critical CHD, hearing screen.
redFlags: Positive screen — requires urgent confirmation + treatment within days.
False-positive results — distress to family; arrange rapid confirmatory testing.
Early discharge / home birth — ensure heel prick is performed.
Pre-term infant — repeat heel prick at term-equivalent age may be needed.
Maternal drug history affects interpretation (e.g. maternal levothyroxine).

diagnostics.test: Heel-prick (blood-spot) sample on filter paper at 48–72 h (after milk feeds established).
Repeat heel prick at 7–10 days for borderline / specific conditions per local protocol.
Targeted confirmatory tests: tandem mass spectrometry, immunoreactive trypsinogen, T-cell receptor excision circles (SCID), TSH, plasma phenylalanine, etc.

diagnostics.rationale: Inherited disorder management + future pregnancy planning.

management.detail: Positive screen → infant recalled within 24–48 h → confirmatory venous sample → specialist referral within days → initiate treatment ASAP.

Phenylketonuria (PKU): low-phenylalanine diet + protein substitute lifelong; sapropterin for selected. Congenital hypothyroidism: levothyroxine 10–15 microgram/kg/day. CAH: hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone; mineralocorticoid replacement. Cystic fibrosis: specialist multidisciplinary CF centre. Sickle cell: penicillin prophylaxis + pneumococcal vaccination + family education + comprehensive sickle cell programme. MCAD: avoid fasting, frequent feeds, glucose for illness. SCID: protective isolation + stem-cell transplant (curative).
Sensitive disclosure of positive screen + treatment plan; written information; genetic counselling for inherited disorders. Address parental anxiety + distress.
Genetic counselling + carrier testing; pre-natal diagnosis options; counselling on recurrence risk.
Track positive predictive value; false-positive rate; time-to-treatment. Public-health monitoring.
Coordinated transition for chronic conditions (PKU, CF, SCD, CAH); shared transition clinic; education on self-management.

references.label: WHO Newborn screening recommendations; ACMG Recommended Uniform Newborn Screening Panel (USA)

title: Congenital TORCH infections (toxoplasma, rubella, CMV, herpes, syphilis, parvovirus, Zika)
presentation: Common: small for gestational age, microcephaly, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, rash, chorioretinitis, intracranial calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss.
Toxoplasma: chorioretinitis + hydrocephalus + intracranial calcifications.
Rubella: cataracts + congenital heart disease (PDA) + sensorineural hearing loss.
CMV: 90% asymptomatic at birth; sensorineural hearing loss is most common late presentation; petechiae + thrombocytopenia + jaundice severe at birth.
Herpes: vesicular skin lesions + encephalitis; usually neonatal acquisition.
Syphilis: rhinitis + maculopapular rash + bony lesions + hepatosplenomegaly (early); Hutchinson teeth + saddle nose + interstitial keratitis (late).
Parvovirus B19: hydrops fetalis + severe anaemia.
Zika: microcephaly + brain calcifications + ocular abnormalities.
redFlags: Severe congenital symptoms (encephalopathy, severe hydrops, multi-organ involvement).
Suspected herpes encephalitis — urgent IV aciclovir.
Bilateral cataracts / hearing loss — early intervention saves vision / hearing.
Maternal seroconversion during pregnancy — antenatal management + neonatal follow-up.

diagnostics.test: Maternal serology / PCR for individual pathogens at first antenatal visit + retest if seroconversion suspected.
Neonatal serology + PCR (saliva / urine for CMV; serum for others); IgM + IgA support congenital.
Ophthalmology examination, hearing test (otoacoustic emissions + auditory brainstem response), neuroimaging (MRI / cranial US).
FBC, LFT, U&E, syphilis serology (mother + baby), bone radiographs if syphilis suspected.

management.detail: Oral valganciclovir 16 mg/kg BD × 6 months — reduces hearing deterioration + improves developmental outcomes for symptomatic congenital CMV. Monitor FBC + LFT (neutropenia + hepatotoxicity).

management.step: Toxoplasma — pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid × 12 months
management.detail: First-year intensive treatment improves long-term ocular + neurological outcomes.
Supportive; no specific antiviral. Cataract surgery; cochlear implant for hearing loss; cardiology follow-up for CHD; developmental services.

IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 h × 14 days (skin / eye / mouth) or × 21 days (CNS / disseminated). Long-term oral aciclovir prophylaxis × 6 months reduces recurrence + improves neurodevelopmental outcome.
IV penicillin G 50 000 units/kg every 12 h × 7 days then every 8 h to complete 10 days, OR IM procaine penicillin 50 000 units/kg daily × 10 days. Maternal treatment essential to prevent.
Intrauterine transfusion for fetal anaemia; supportive postnatally.
Supportive; specialist neurodevelopmental + ophthalmological follow-up; prevention via vector control + travel advisory.
Paediatric infectious disease + neurology + ophthalmology + audiology + developmental pediatrics + family genetic counselling. Lifelong neurodevelopmental support.

references.label: CDC / AAP Red Book Pediatric Infectious Disease; WHO congenital syphilis elimination guidance
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Tobacco use cessation — comprehensive pharmacotherapy + behavioural pathway
presentation: Current tobacco use (cigarette, e-cigarette, smokeless / chewing tobacco, hookah, cigar).
Heaviness of smoking index: cigarettes/day + time-to-first-cigarette in morning < 30 min predicts severe nicotine dependence.
Withdrawal symptoms: irritability, anxiety, low mood, increased appetite, sleep disturbance, restlessness, cravings — peak 1–3 days, resolve over 4–6 weeks.
Comorbid: depression, anxiety, alcohol use, schizophrenia — quit attempts often coincide with mental health.
redFlags: Severe psychiatric comorbidity — coordinate with mental health team.
Cardiovascular disease + planning surgery — counsel benefit-risk of quitting within 4 weeks of major surgery (delayed wound healing initially but better overall outcome).
Recent MI / stroke — quitting reduces re-event but pharmacotherapy choice considered.

diagnostics.test: Brief 5A intervention (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange) at every clinical encounter.
Carbon monoxide breath test (ppm) for verification + motivation.
Cardiovascular + respiratory assessment in long-term smokers.

management.detail: Doubling brief intervention effectiveness. Group counselling, telephone quitline, text-message support, smartphone apps. Combined behavioural + pharmacotherapy approach is most effective.

Patches (slow release) + short-acting (gum, lozenge, inhaler, nasal spray) for breakthrough cravings. Patches: 21 mg / 24 h for > 10 cigarettes/day; 14 mg for 5–10; 7 mg taper. Use combination NRT (patch + short-acting) — superior to single. Continue × 8–12 weeks then taper.

Partial nicotinic agonist; reduces both withdrawal AND reward. 0.5 mg daily × 3 days → 0.5 mg BD × 4 days → 1 mg BD × 12 weeks; continue 12 weeks if successful. Counsel re: neuropsychiatric warnings (now lifted from black box per EAGLES trial); rare cardiovascular events; nausea + abnormal dreams common.
150 mg daily × 3 days then 150 mg BD × 7–12 weeks. AVOID in seizure disorder, eating disorder, alcohol withdrawal. Useful in patients with concurrent depression.
Partial nicotinic agonist (plant-derived); 25-day course; lower cost than varenicline; non-inferior efficacy per RAUORA + RANGUE trials.
Combining varenicline + NRT may be more effective than either alone (especially for heavy smokers). Extended duration (3–6 months) of NRT or varenicline if relapse risk.

Behavioural support FIRST. NRT preferred over varenicline / bupropion (limited safety data); intermittent dose (gum, lozenge) to reduce sustained nicotine exposure; quit completely if possible. Specialist support important.

Smokers unable to quit with NRT / varenicline may benefit from e-cigarettes as harm-reduction (lower risk than continued smoking but not without risk). Avoid in never-smokers + adolescents. Eventually plan complete cessation.
Review at 1, 4, 12, 24 weeks. Address relapse compassionately — multiple quit attempts often required. Adapt pharmacotherapy + behavioural strategies.

references.label: USPSTF Tobacco Smoking Cessation Recommendation (2021); UK NICE Tobacco — preventing uptake, promoting quitting (NG209)
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders (mhGAP adaptation), Ministry of Health

title: Leprosy reactions — type 1 (reversal) + type 2 (ENL) emergency
presentation: Patient with leprosy (Hansen disease) on multidrug therapy or recently completed.

Type 1 (reversal reaction): acute inflammation of existing skin lesions + nerve trunks (ulnar > median > radial > tibial > peroneal); neuritis — pain + tenderness + new motor / sensory deficit (claw hand, foot drop, ophthalmoplegia, facial palsy).
Type 2 (erythema nodosum leprosum, ENL): new crops of tender erythematous nodules + fever + systemic features + arthritis + iritis + orchitis + neuritis; usually multibacillary leprosy.
Triggers: starting MDT, completing MDT (relapse), pregnancy, infection, stress.
redFlags: Neuritis with new nerve function impairment — risk of permanent disability; emergency steroid.
Severe systemic ENL with organ involvement.
Pregnancy + leprosy reaction — treat reaction; continue MDT.

diagnostics.test: Clinical recognition + assessment of nerve function (sensory + motor + reflexes).

diagnostics.rationale: Identify renal / hepatic involvement (ENL); baseline for steroid.

diagnostics.test: Skin smear for AFB if uncertain (relapse vs reaction).

management.detail: Do NOT stop MDT (rifampicin + dapsone ± clofazimine) during reaction — reactions are immune phenomena, not treatment failure.

Prednisolone 40–60 mg/day with TAPER over 4–6 months. Onset of motor / sensory deficit within last 6 months has best chance of recovery. Combine with physiotherapy + neural splints to prevent contracture.

Mild (skin only): NSAID + analgesia. Severe (with neuritis / orchitis / iridocyclitis / arthritis / systemic): prednisolone 40–60 mg/day + thalidomide 100–400 mg/day (where available; contraceptive counselling MANDATORY).

Thalidomide is most effective. Clofazimine 300 mg/day × 3 months + steroid for thalidomide-restricted (women of childbearing potential without contraception). Methotrexate / ciclosporin / TNF inhibitor under specialist.

management.step: Manage neuritis — surgical decompression for refractory
management.detail: If nerve abscess on imaging or no improvement despite 4 weeks high-dose steroid, surgical decompression of nerve trunk.
Atropine 1% drops + topical steroid; ophthalmology urgent. Wear sunglasses + lubricate.
Routine sensory + motor assessment; protective footwear / gloves; ulcer care; physiotherapy; occupational therapy; community programmes; counselling. Address stigma.
Household contacts screened annually × 5 years. Single-dose rifampicin prophylaxis (per WHO 2018) reduces incidence in contacts.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of leprosy (2018, updated)
Kenya National Tuberculosis, Leprosy and Lung Disease Program (NTLD-P) Guidelines, Ministry of Health

title: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) — severe
presentation: Fever > 2 weeks + splenomegaly + hepatomegaly + pancytopenia + weight loss.
Endemic: India / Bangladesh / Nepal / Sudan / Brazil; sandfly vector.
Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL): hypopigmented macules / papules after VL treatment.
HIV co-infection — atypical + relapsing + more severe; AIDS-defining illness in endemic regions.
Severe: secondary infection (pneumonia, sepsis), severe anaemia, bleeding (DIC), AKI, hepatic failure.
redFlags: Pregnancy + VL — fetal loss + maternal complications.
HIV co-infection — relapsing + difficult to treat.

diagnostics.test: Bone marrow aspirate / spleen aspirate microscopy + culture + PCR.
FBC (pancytopenia), reticulocytes, LFT, U&E, coag, ferritin, LDH.
HIV test (mandatory in endemic + atypical / relapsing cases).
Septic screen if febrile / clinical deterioration on treatment.

management.step: Liposomal amphotericin B (preferred — single or short course)
management.detail: AmBisome 5 mg/kg/day × 1 day in India (single 10 mg/kg dose); 3 mg/kg/day × 6 doses on alternate days for East Africa (total 30 mg/kg). HIV co-infected — extended course (total 40 mg/kg). Renal + electrolyte monitoring.

Miltefosine 100 mg/day × 28 days (oral; teratogenic — pregnancy contraindicated); paromomycin 11 mg/kg IM × 21 days; combination regimens for East Africa (sodium stibogluconate + paromomycin per WHO).
20 mg/kg/day × 30 days IM/IV; now used selectively due to toxicity (cardiac arrhythmia, pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity). Increasingly replaced by AmBisome where available.
AmBisome (extended course) + ART. Relapse common; secondary prophylaxis with AmBisome 4 mg/kg every 2–4 weeks until CD4 > 200.
Miltefosine 100 mg/day × 28 days OR AmBisome 5 mg/kg every other day to total 30 mg/kg. PKDL infectious — public health implications.
Transfusion for severe anaemia; treat secondary infections; nutritional support; thromboprophylaxis. Severe disease — ICU care.
Notifiable disease in endemic countries. Indoor residual spraying; bed nets; reservoir control (especially L. infantum dog reservoir). Elimination programmes in South Asia (rK39 + AmBisome rollout).

title: Japanese encephalitis (JE) — acute
presentation: Sudden fever + headache + vomiting + altered consciousness over 1–6 days.
Children + young adults most affected; endemic Asia + Western Pacific.
Severe: seizures, parkinsonism, coma, brainstem dysfunction, raised ICP.
Mortality 20–30%; long-term neurological sequelae in 30–50% of survivors.
Vector: Culex mosquito; pigs + waterbirds amplification host; rural / agricultural transmission.

diagnostics.test: JE IgM in CSF (preferred) and / or serum — confirms in clinical context.
MRI brain — bilateral thalamic + substantia nigra + basal ganglia involvement characteristic.
LP: lymphocytic pleocytosis + raised protein + normal glucose.
Exclude alternative encephalitides: HSV, rabies, enterovirus, dengue, scrub typhus, cerebral malaria, TBE.
FBC, U&E, glucose, blood culture, malaria smear (in endemic).

management.detail: ICU-level supportive care; airway protection if GCS ≤ 8; mechanical ventilation; manage seizures (per status epilepticus pathway); ICP management; correct electrolytes; antipyretic; nutrition.

management.step: Empirical antiviral pending PCR — IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 h
management.detail: Continue until HSV PCR negative (HSV encephalitis would be tragic to miss).
Levetiracetam / phenytoin / phenobarbital for seizures; head elevation, normoxia, normocapnia, normothermia; hyperosmolar therapy for raised ICP.
Physiotherapy + occupational therapy + speech / swallow therapy + neuropsychology; long-term often required.
Notifiable in most jurisdictions. Vector control; vaccination of at-risk populations; surveillance of pigs (amplifying host).

Inactivated Vero-cell vaccine OR live attenuated SA 14-14-2 — routine in endemic countries (single dose primary + booster). Travellers to endemic regions for > 30 days — JE vaccine. Lifelong immunity expected from booster.
Cognitive screening; epilepsy management (50% develop post-encephalitic epilepsy); movement-disorder management; social + educational support; family support.

references.label: WHO Japanese encephalitis vaccines: WHO position paper (2015)
Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) Technical Guidelines, 3rd ed, Ministry of Health

title: Parkinson disease — comprehensive long-term management
presentation: Motor: asymmetric resting tremor + bradykinesia + rigidity + postural instability (late).
Non-motor: REM sleep behaviour disorder (prodromal), hyposmia, constipation, anxiety, depression, cognitive impairment, autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic hypotension, urinary, sexual).
Levodopa-induced complications: motor fluctuations + dyskinesia after 5–10 years; impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexual).
Differential: vascular parkinsonism, drug-induced (antipsychotics, metoclopramide), atypical (PSP, MSA, CBD, DLB).
redFlags: Acute confusion / psychosis — exclude trigger (infection, drug); manage carefully (clozapine, quetiapine).
Acute akinesia / hyperthermia — neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome from dopaminergic withdrawal (e.g. patient nil-by-mouth).
Pregnancy + Parkinson disease — limited safety data; specialist input.

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnosis (MDS criteria) — asymmetric onset + bradykinesia + tremor / rigidity + sustained response to levodopa.
DAT-SPECT scan if uncertain (distinguishes idiopathic / atypical PD from essential tremor / drug-induced / functional).
MRI brain — exclude structural / vascular cause.
Cognitive + mood screen (MoCA, PHQ-9), sleep history (RBD screen), autonomic testing.

management.detail: Specialist movement disorder clinic + nurse specialist + physiotherapy + occupational therapy + speech + language therapy (swallow + voice) + dietitian + neuropsychology + social work.

Younger / motor: levodopa-carbidopa OR dopamine agonist (pramipexole, ropinirole) OR MAO-B inhibitor (rasagiline, selegiline). Older / cognitive impairment: levodopa first (less neuropsychiatric). Combination as needed.

Add COMT inhibitor (entacapone, opicapone) extends levodopa effect; amantadine reduces dyskinesia. Apomorphine (subcut PRN or pump); continuous duodenal levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (Duodopa); deep brain stimulation (subthalamic / globus pallidus) for selected. Specialist input.

Orthostatic hypotension: fludrocortisone, midodrine, droxidopa, compression stockings, salt + fluid. Constipation: lactulose / macrogol. Sleep: melatonin / clonazepam for RBD. Pain: paracetamol + neuropathic / musculoskeletal targeted. Mood: SSRI / SNRI (avoid in serotonin syndrome with MAOI). Cognitive: rivastigmine for dementia.

Psychosis: reduce dopaminergic drugs; quetiapine 12.5–50 mg OR clozapine (specialist with monitoring); AVOID typical antipsychotics + olanzapine + risperidone (worsen PD). Impulse control disorder: reduce / stop dopamine agonist.
STN or GPi targets; selected patients with motor fluctuations + dyskinesia + good cognitive function + good levodopa response. Pre-surgical multidisciplinary assessment.
Falls clinic; balance training (LSVT BIG); gait training; cueing strategies; home assessment for hazards; bone health (DEXA, calcium, vit D, bisphosphonate).
Advanced PD: high symptom burden + carer strain; palliative care input from moderate-stage; advance care planning; do-not-resuscitate; medication review for de-prescribing of low-yield drugs.

references.label: NICE NG71 Parkinson's disease in adults; MDS criteria for PD

title: Alzheimer disease — diagnosis + comprehensive management
presentation: Insidious + progressive memory loss + executive dysfunction + visuospatial deficit + language difficulty + behavioural change.
Functional decline: instrumental ADLs (finance, cooking, medication) → basic ADLs.
Late: incontinence, gait disturbance, swallowing difficulty, total dependence.
Early-onset (< 65) — often genetic (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) or atypical (posterior cortical atrophy, logopenic primary progressive aphasia, behavioural / dysexecutive).
Risk factors: APOE ε4 allele, age, family history, cardiovascular risk factors, traumatic brain injury, hearing loss, depression, social isolation, poor education, alcohol.
redFlags: Rapidly progressive cognitive decline — consider Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, autoimmune encephalitis, paraneoplastic, normal pressure hydrocephalus.
Suspected delirium superimposed on dementia — exclude infection / metabolic / drug effect.
Behavioural + psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) — agitation, aggression, psychosis, depression.
Suicide risk during depression / early diagnosis.
Severe caregiver burnout / suspected elder abuse.

diagnostics.test: Blood tests for reversible causes: TSH, B12, folate, U&E, glucose, calcium, syphilis (if risk), HIV (if risk).
Neuroimaging: MRI (medial temporal lobe atrophy) preferred; CT alternative.
Specialist tests in research / selected: CSF biomarkers (amyloid β, tau, p-tau), amyloid + tau PET, blood-based biomarkers (emerging).
diagnostics.rationale: Increasing role for biological diagnosis + targeted therapy.

management.detail: Memory clinic; nurse specialist; OT / physio; social work; palliative care; family support. Dementia-friendly design at home + community.

Donepezil 5 mg daily titrate to 10 mg; rivastigmine 1.5 mg BD titrate to 6 mg BD (transdermal alternative); galantamine. Modest benefit on cognition + function + behaviour. Common adverse: GI upset, bradycardia, weight loss. ECG before / during if cardiac risk.
NMDA receptor antagonist; 5 mg daily titrate to 10 mg BD over 4 weeks. Can combine with cholinesterase inhibitor.

Lecanemab + donanemab (anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies) — approved in some jurisdictions for early symptomatic AD with confirmed amyloid pathology. Slow cognitive decline ~30% over 18 months. Side-effect: ARIA (amyloid-related imaging abnormalities — oedema + microhaemorrhage); APOE ε4 homozygotes — highest ARIA risk. Specialist centre with MRI surveillance.

Identify trigger (pain, infection, hunger, environment), structured routine, music therapy, animal-assisted therapy. Only if severe distress / safety risk → atypical antipsychotic (risperidone 0.25–0.5 mg BD — short-course; documented increased stroke + mortality; avoid in dementia with Lewy bodies).
SSRI (citalopram, sertraline). Avoid TCA (anticholinergic) + benzodiazepine.
Carer well-being is critical. Education, training, peer support, respite care, financial benefits, occupational therapy assessment of home.

Early discussion when capacity preserved: lasting power of attorney; advance directives; care preferences; place of care. Palliative care in advanced dementia — comfort-focused; avoid hospital admissions where possible.

Lancet Commission 12 modifiable factors — hearing aids, BP, smoking, depression, social engagement, exercise, alcohol moderation, sleep, education / brain training, diabetes, obesity, air pollution. Even in established AD.

references.label: NICE NG97 Dementia; Lancet Commission Dementia 2024; FDA / EMA labels for anti-amyloid mAbs
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders (mhGAP adaptation), Ministry of Health

title: Multiple sclerosis — relapse management + disease-modifying therapy
presentation: Relapse: new / worsening neurological deficit > 24 hours without infection / fever (pseudo-relapse from fever or infection).
Common: optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, brainstem syndrome, cerebellar, hemispheric.
Background: relapsing-remitting (most common); secondary progressive (after RR); primary progressive (~10%).
Co-morbid: depression, fatigue, neuropathic pain, sphincter / sexual dysfunction, spasticity, cognitive impairment, gait + balance impairment.
redFlags: Suspected first acute attack — confirm with MRI + LP before starting DMT (NMOSD + MOGAD differentials).
Aggressive MS (high lesion burden + frequent severe relapses) — early high-efficacy DMT.
Pregnancy + relapse — most DMTs contraindicated; supportive management.
Suspected progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) — particularly natalizumab-treated; JC virus.
PROGRESSIVE neurology + no clear relapse — disease progression vs alternative diagnosis.

diagnostics.test: MRI brain + spine with gadolinium — McDonald 2017 criteria for dissemination in space + time.
LP: oligoclonal bands, IgG index — supportive.
Differential: AQP4 + MOG antibodies (NMOSD / MOGAD), HIV / HTLV-1 / Lyme / B12, paraneoplastic, sarcoid.
JC virus antibody status (natalizumab risk stratification).

management.detail: 1 g IV daily × 3–5 days; OR oral 500 mg–1 g daily × 5 days (non-inferior to IV per COPOUSEP). Counsel on side effects (mood, hyperglycaemia, insomnia, infection). Treat infection / fever first (pseudo-relapse).
5–7 sessions over 14 days for steroid-refractory acute severe disabling relapses, especially optic neuritis.

Moderate efficacy: interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide. Higher efficacy: fingolimod (S1P modulator), ozanimod / siponimod / ponesimod; ocrelizumab / ofatumumab (anti-CD20); cladribine; natalizumab. Aggressive MS — start with higher-efficacy upfront. Recent shift toward 'flip the pyramid' (higher efficacy first).
Ocrelizumab approved for primary progressive MS. Siponimod for active secondary progressive MS. Supportive care + symptom management dominant for non-active progressive MS.

Spasticity: baclofen, tizanidine, gabapentin, intrathecal baclofen, botulinum toxin. Bladder: anticholinergic, mirabegron, intermittent self-catheterisation. Fatigue: amantadine, modafinil, exercise. Mood: SSRI. Pain: gabapentin, amitriptyline. Mobility: dalfampridine.
