redFlags: Cardiac sarcoidosis with arrhythmia / heart block / sudden death risk — urgent EP + cardiac MRI / FDG-PET + ICD consideration.
Severe neurosarcoidosis — cranial mass, meningitis, hydrocephalus, focal neurology.
Pregnancy — disease often improves; some immunosuppressants contraindicated.

diagnostics.test: HRCT chest with characteristic perilymphatic nodules + LN + fibrosis pattern.
Tissue biopsy demonstrating non-caseating granulomas — bronchoscopy + EBUS-TBNA (preferred over mediastinoscopy); skin / lymph node; consider biopsy of accessible site.

Comprehensive systemic workup: ECG + echo + cardiac MRI / FDG-PET (cardiac involvement); ophthalmology (slit-lamp + fundoscopy); calcium + 24-h urinary Ca + vitamin D; renal function + urinalysis; LFT; cranial MRI if neuro features.
ACE level — supportive (not diagnostic; raised in 50–60%); soluble IL-2 receptor — adjunct.
Exclude TB, fungal, berylliosis, lymphoma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
diagnostics.rationale: Critical differential — TB especially in endemic areas.

management.detail: Many cases (especially Lofgren) self-limit. NSAIDs / paracetamol for arthralgia. Topical / inhaled steroid for skin or airway. Follow at 3–6 month intervals.

management.step: Systemic glucocorticoid — first-line for active organ disease
management.detail: Indications: progressive pulmonary disease / symptomatic deterioration, hypercalcaemia, cardiac involvement, neurosarcoidosis, posterior uveitis, severe skin / liver / spleen / renal. Prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day (max 40 mg) × 4–6 weeks then taper over 6–12 months. Most relapse if too rapid taper.
Methotrexate 10–25 mg/week (preferred — most evidence). Azathioprine 1.5–2.5 mg/kg/day; mycophenolate 2–3 g/day; hydroxychloroquine 200–400 mg/day for skin / mild pulmonary / hypercalcaemia.
Infliximab — TNF inhibitor; effective for steroid-refractory pulmonary + neurosarcoidosis + skin (lupus pernio). Adalimumab alternative. Rituximab + abatacept emerging.

Cardiac: cardiac MRI / FDG-PET + biopsy; immunosuppression + amiodarone for arrhythmia + ICD if VT / aborted SCD / advanced AV block. Neuro: high-dose steroid + immunosuppression + infliximab. Eye: topical + systemic per ophthalmology. Hypercalcaemia: avoid sun + vitamin D + dietary calcium; steroid; ketoconazole (anti-vitamin D activation).
Specialist PHT centre — distinct from idiopathic PAH; cautious use of PAH-targeted therapy + treat sarcoidosis.
Lung transplant for refractory severe pulmonary fibrosis or pulmonary hypertension.
Disease often improves; continue hydroxychloroquine + low-dose steroid. Avoid methotrexate + leflunomide. Specialist obstetric care.
Annual PFTs + chest imaging + ophthalmology + ECG; vitamin D + calcium surveillance. Vaccinations + cardiovascular risk management.

references.label: ATS / ERS / WASOG Sarcoidosis Guidelines (2020); ATS / ERS / JRS / ALAT IPF + ILD

title: Autoimmune hepatitis — diagnosis + immunosuppression
presentation: Subacute / chronic hepatitis: fatigue, jaundice, raised transaminases (AST/ALT > 5–10× ULN often), hypergammaglobulinaemia (IgG), autoantibodies.
Type 1 (most common): ANA + smooth muscle antibody (anti-SMA / actin); any age, female predominant.
Type 2: anti-LKM-1 + anti-LC1; usually paediatric / younger.
Type 3: anti-SLA/LP.
Acute presentation can mimic acute liver failure (10%).
Overlap syndromes with PBC + PSC.
Often associated with other autoimmune disease — thyroid, T1D, coeliac, IBD, vitiligo.
redFlags: Acute severe / fulminant hepatic failure (INR > 1.5, encephalopathy) — emergency hepatology + transplant evaluation.
Pregnancy + AIH — usually improves but flare postpartum.

diagnostics.test: ALT, AST, bilirubin, ALP, albumin, INR (severity).
Autoantibodies: ANA, anti-SMA, anti-LKM-1, anti-SLA/LP, anti-ANCA (PSC overlap).
IgG (raised); IgM if PBC overlap; IgA mild.
Liver biopsy — interface hepatitis + lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate + rosetting.
Simplified or Revised IAIHG diagnostic criteria.
Exclude viral (HBV / HCV / HEV / HSV / EBV / CMV), drug-induced hepatotoxicity, Wilson, NAFLD, alpha-1 antitrypsin, haemochromatosis.
Cholangiogram (MRCP) if cholestatic features — overlap PSC.

management.detail: Prednisolone 40–60 mg/day monotherapy OR prednisolone 30 mg/day + azathioprine 50 mg → 1–2 mg/kg/day (combination preferred — less steroid). Budesonide alternative for non-cirrhotic (first-pass metabolism).
Azathioprine 1–2 mg/kg/day monotherapy OR low-dose prednisolone + AZA. Continue ≥ 2–4 years after biochemical remission; relapse common on cessation. Lifelong therapy for many.
Mycophenolate 1–3 g/day; tacrolimus 0.5–6 mg/day (trough 5–8 ng/mL); rituximab (specialist); ciclosporin.
IV methylprednisolone 60–100 mg/day; assess for liver transplant if no response in 7 days. AIH-related liver failure has high mortality without transplant.
For fulminant failure or end-stage cirrhosis. AIH can recur in graft (15–40%) — continue immunosuppression.
USS + AFP every 6 months in cirrhosis.

TPMT testing before azathioprine. Monthly FBC + LFT initially → 3-monthly when stable. Vaccinations (pneumococcal, influenza, hepatitis A + B); avoid live vaccines on immunosuppression. PJP prophylaxis with high-dose steroid + immunosuppression.
Continue azathioprine + low-dose prednisolone (safer than disease flare). Avoid mycophenolate (teratogenic). Multidisciplinary obstetric + hepatology. Postpartum flare common — monitor closely.
Screen for + manage co-occurring autoimmune disease. Alcohol abstinence. Vaccinations. Long-term biochemical + clinical follow-up.

references.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Autoimmune Hepatitis (2024 update); AASLD AIH Guidance

title: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) — diagnosis + management
presentation: Chronic progressive cholestatic liver disease — multifocal strictures + segmental dilations of intra + extra-hepatic bile ducts.
Asymptomatic — detected on raised ALP + GGT + abnormal LFT screening.
Symptomatic: fatigue, pruritus, jaundice, abdominal pain, recurrent cholangitis (fever + RUQ pain + jaundice).
Strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (~70% with PSC have IBD, mostly UC).
Progression: cirrhosis + portal hypertension + variceal bleeding + ascites.
Increased cancer risk: cholangiocarcinoma (lifetime 10–15%), gallbladder cancer, colorectal (with concurrent IBD).
redFlags: Acute ascending cholangitis — emergency antibiotics + ERCP drainage.
Rapid clinical / biochemical deterioration — exclude dominant stricture (CCA suspicion).
Suspected cholangiocarcinoma (rising CA 19-9, dominant stricture on MRCP).
Concurrent IBD flare with PSC requires careful immunosuppression choice.

diagnostics.test: MRCP — first-line imaging (characteristic beaded appearance of bile ducts).
ERCP — diagnostic only if MRCP non-diagnostic OR for therapeutic dilatation of dominant stricture; carries pancreatitis + cholangitis risk.
Liver biopsy in selected — small-duct PSC, overlap syndrome.
diagnostics.rationale: Confirm small-duct disease or autoimmune overlap.

diagnostics.test: Annual colonoscopy from diagnosis (CRC surveillance — PSC + UC has very high CRC risk).
MRCP + CA 19-9 + brushings during ERCP if CCA suspected.
Annual abdominal USS for gallbladder polyp / cancer surveillance.
Annual MRCP for early CCA detection (some centres).

management.detail: Ursodeoxycholic acid 13–17 mg/kg/day commonly used (improves biochemistry; uncertain long-term outcome benefit; AVOID high doses > 28 mg/kg). Vancomycin oral 50 mg/kg/day for paediatric PSC (limited adult evidence). Trials ongoing: norUDCA, vedolizumab, simtuzumab, FXR agonists.
Pruritus: cholestyramine, rifampicin, naltrexone, sertraline. Fatigue. Steatorrhoea — fat-soluble vitamin (ADEK) replacement. Bone disease — calcium + vitamin D + DEXA.
ERCP + balloon dilatation ± stenting; brush cytology for cholangiocarcinoma. Antibiotic cover for ERCP.
IV antibiotic (piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone + metronidazole); urgent biliary drainage if obstructive (ERCP).
Avoid mesalamine alone (often inadequate in PSC-IBD); biologics often needed; CRC surveillance from diagnosis annually (not just 8 years like other UC).

Annual MRCP + CA 19-9 increasingly used. Suspected CCA: brush cytology + cross-sectional imaging + multidisciplinary. Some early CCA in PSC — consider transplant per local protocol (Mayo neoadjuvant + transplant for selected hilar).

Indications: decompensated cirrhosis, intractable pruritus, recurrent cholangitis, early CCA per protocol. Best survival outcomes among transplant indications. PSC can recur post-transplant (20%); colon cancer risk continues.

management.step: Colonoscopy surveillance — annual in PSC + IBD
management.detail: Earlier + more frequent than non-PSC IBD due to dramatically elevated CRC risk.

management.step: Specialist hepatology + IBD + transplant + colorectal team
management.detail: Multidisciplinary clinic; cascade care + family education.

references.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on PSC (2022); AASLD PSC Guidance

title: Age-related macular degeneration — early to advanced management
presentation: Most common cause of irreversible vision loss in adults > 65 in developed countries.
Dry AMD (80–90%): drusen + retinal pigment epithelium atrophy + geographic atrophy; gradual central vision loss.
Wet (exudative) AMD: choroidal neovascularisation + sub-retinal fluid / haemorrhage / exudate; sudden / rapid central vision loss + metamorphopsia (lines wavy on Amsler grid).
Risk: age, smoking, family history (CFH + ARMS2 variants), white ethnicity, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, low-fish-diet, sunlight exposure.
redFlags: Acute / sub-acute vision distortion (metamorphopsia, scotoma) — urgent ophthalmology for possible wet AMD or rapid deterioration.
Falls + injuries from central vision loss.
Depression / social isolation from vision loss.

diagnostics.test: Slit-lamp + dilated fundoscopy for drusen, RPE changes, sub-retinal fluid / haemorrhage.
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) — sub-retinal fluid + drusen + RPE changes.
diagnostics.rationale: Sensitive diagnosis + monitoring; gold standard for treatment decisions.

diagnostics.test: Fluorescein angiography for confirming neovascularisation / classifying.
OCT angiography — alternative for assessing neovascularisation without dye.

management.step: Smoking cessation + risk factor modification — FOUNDATION
management.detail: Single most important — smoking 2–3× risk; quitting reduces. Mediterranean / leafy-green / fish-rich diet. UV protection (sunglasses). BP + lipid control.

management.step: AREDS-2 vitamin supplementation for intermediate / advanced dry AMD
management.detail: Vitamin C + E + zinc + copper + lutein + zeaxanthin. Reduces progression to advanced disease by ~25%. NOT for early AMD or no AMD. AVOID beta-carotene in smokers (lung cancer risk).

management.step: Wet AMD — anti-VEGF intravitreal injection (PARADIGM CHANGE)
management.detail: Aflibercept (every 8 weeks after loading; 8 mg high-dose Eylea-HD or faricimab can extend interval), ranibizumab, brolucizumab. Faricimab (anti-Ang-2/anti-VEGF) — extended interval. Initial monthly × 3 then treat-and-extend OR PRN regimens. Lifelong therapy in most. Bevacizumab off-label affordable alternative.
Pegcetacoplan (complement C3 inhibitor) intravitreal every 25–60 days; avacincaptad pegol (anti-C5) — slow GA progression (15–22%). FDA-approved 2023. Specialist initiation.
Magnifiers, telescopic glasses, lighting, contrast enhancement, eccentric viewing training, audio-books, screen readers, smartphone apps. Occupational therapy + social services.
Notify driving authority per local rules (may need to surrender licence). Falls prevention; home assessment; medication review for hypotensives.
Depression + anxiety + social isolation common. Screen + treat. Peer support groups + counselling. Independence support.
Amsler grid daily — sudden distortion / new scotoma → urgent ophthalmology. Empower for early treatment.
OCT + visual acuity every 1–3 months on anti-VEGF; less frequent for stable dry AMD.

references.label: AAO Preferred Practice Pattern Age-Related Macular Degeneration (2024); AREDS + AREDS-2; HAWK + HARRIER + TENAYA / LUCERNE + OAKS / DERBY
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Primary open-angle glaucoma — diagnosis + IOP-lowering therapy
presentation: Progressive optic neuropathy — cupping (vertical cup-to-disc ratio increase) + retinal nerve fibre layer thinning + visual field loss (peripheral first, central preserved late).
Most common type — open anterior chamber angle; raised IOP usually but normal-tension glaucoma also.
Risk: age > 40, African / Caribbean ancestry, family history, high myopia, diabetes, chronic steroid use.
Asymptomatic until very late — leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide.
Normal-tension glaucoma: glaucomatous damage despite IOP < 21 mmHg.
redFlags: Acute angle-closure (severe pain + red eye + halos + nausea) — distinct entity; emergency.
Pregnancy + glaucoma — limit some topical agents.

diagnostics.test: Intraocular pressure (IOP) — Goldmann applanation gold standard.
diagnostics.rationale: Baseline + monitor; aim individualised target reduction.

diagnostics.test: Optic disc examination + photograph (cup-to-disc ratio + disc haemorrhage + RNFL).
Optical coherence tomography (RNFL + ganglion cell complex).

diagnostics.rationale: Confirm open angle + exclude angle closure / secondary.

diagnostics.test: Central corneal thickness (CCT) — affects IOP measurement.

management.step: Target IOP reduction individualised (20–40% from baseline)
management.detail: Aggressive target for advanced disease / continued progression / younger patient. Set + adjust based on progression.

Latanoprost / travoprost / bimatoprost / tafluprost once daily. Highly effective (~25–30% IOP reduction); side effects: iris pigmentation, eyelash growth, periorbital fat atrophy, mild conjunctival hyperaemia.
Recent LiGHT trial — SLT effective as primary therapy; many patients can avoid drops. Painless, repeatable.

Beta-blocker (timolol — caution asthma, bradyarrhythmia). Alpha-2 agonist (brimonidine — fatigue, allergic conjunctivitis). Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (dorzolamide, brinzolamide). Rho kinase inhibitor (netarsudil — newer).
For inadequate IOP control on maximum medical therapy. Gold standard surgical. MMC adjunct for high-risk.
iStent + Hydrus microstent + Xen gel stent + ECP + Trabectome + KDB goniotomy. Better safety profile but less IOP reduction; often combined with cataract surgery.
For refractory glaucoma / failed trabeculectomy / specific secondary glaucomas.
End-stage; eyes with poor visual potential. Trans-scleral or endoscopic.
Drop instruction + nasolacrimal occlusion (reduce systemic absorption). Reminder systems. Combination drops to simplify regimen. Address cost barriers.
Stable disease: every 6–12 months. Progressing: more frequent. OCT + visual field tracking; intensify if progressing.

references.label: European Glaucoma Society Guidelines (2020); AAO Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma PPP; LiGHT trial
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Couple infertility — investigation + assisted reproductive technology
presentation: Inability to achieve pregnancy after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse (6 months if female ≥ 35).
Causes: female (ovulatory ~25%, tubal / pelvic ~20%, endometriosis 10%, uterine 5%); male (~30% — oligospermia / azoospermia / motility / morphology); combined; unexplained 15–20%.
Risk factors: age (especially female > 35), smoking, alcohol, obesity, prior STIs / PID, prior surgery, chemotherapy / radiotherapy, medication, occupational exposure, genetic / chromosomal.
redFlags: Azoospermia — chromosome / Y-microdeletion + cystic fibrosis workup.
Endometriosis severe / deep / endometrioma — specialist surgical.
Cancer in either partner — fertility preservation BEFORE chemotherapy / radiotherapy / hormone therapy.

diagnostics.test: Female: cycle history, FSH + LH + oestradiol + AMH + prolactin + TSH + androgens day 2–5; mid-luteal progesterone confirms ovulation; pelvic USS (antral follicle count + structural); hysterosalpingography or HyCoSy for tubal patency; laparoscopy for endometriosis.

Male: semen analysis × 2 (WHO 2021 criteria — concentration ≥ 16 × 10⁶/mL; total motility ≥ 42%; morphology ≥ 4%); testicular examination; FSH + LH + testosterone + prolactin; scrotal USS if abnormal exam.
Both: hepatitis B + C + HIV + syphilis + immunity status (rubella + varicella).
Specialist referral after 1 year (or 6 months if ≥ 35) of trying.

management.detail: Smoking + alcohol + recreational drug cessation. BMI 20–30 (under- + over-weight both reduce fertility). Reduce stress + adequate sleep + balanced diet. Folic acid 400 microgram (5 mg if epilepsy or family history NTD) pre-conception. Avoid hot baths / saunas for male. Timed intercourse around ovulation.

Hyperprolactinaemia: dopamine agonist (cabergoline). Hypothyroidism: levothyroxine. PCOS: weight loss + metformin + letrozole / clomiphene for ovulation induction. Endometriosis: surgical resection + assisted reproductive technology. Male hypogonadism: testosterone (note — testosterone reduces fertility; not appropriate if seeking pregnancy); pulsatile GnRH or gonadotropins for hypogonadotropic. Surgical varicocele repair selectively.

First-line: letrozole 2.5–7.5 mg days 2–6 (preferred over clomiphene per evidence). Clomiphene 50–150 mg days 2–6 if letrozole unavailable. Gonadotropin (FSH) for clomiphene-resistant. Cycle monitoring + trigger + intercourse-timing.
Indications: mild male factor, unexplained infertility, cervical factor, donor sperm. With or without ovulation induction. Less expensive than IVF; success per cycle ~10–15%.

Indications: tubal disease, severe male factor (IVF + ICSI), endometriosis, failed IUI, advanced maternal age, unexplained infertility > 2 years. Controlled ovarian stimulation + egg retrieval + fertilisation + embryo culture + transfer. Single embryo transfer increasingly standard (reduce multiple). Frozen embryo transfer for selected (PCOS, OHSS risk, PGT).Success per cycle live birth rate ~30% (under 35), declining with age.
For severe male factor — direct injection of single sperm into oocyte. Surgical sperm retrieval (PESA / TESE / micro-TESE) for azoospermia.
PGT-A for aneuploidy (advanced age, recurrent loss); PGT-M for monogenic (Marfan, BRCA, Huntington, CF, SCD); PGT-SR for structural rearrangements.
Donor egg / sperm / embryo + gestational surrogacy. Counselling + legal + ethical considerations.
Pre-chemotherapy / radiotherapy / hormone therapy: egg + embryo + sperm + ovarian / testicular tissue freezing. Cancer-related pre-treatment freezing increasingly standard of care.
Infertility distress + treatment burden is substantial; counselling + peer support throughout. Address relationship + body image + grief.

references.label: NICE CG156 Fertility Problems; ESHRE / ASRM Guidelines; WHO 2021 semen analysis

title: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) — lifelong care
presentation: Autosomal recessive — CYP21A2 mutations cause cortisol deficiency + androgen excess.

Classical salt-wasting (75%): newborn salt-losing crisis (vomiting, dehydration, shock, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia) + virilisation (female ambiguous genitalia; male hyperpigmentation + macrogenitosomia).
Classical simple virilising (25%): female ambiguous genitalia; male early virilisation.
Non-classical (NCCAH): adolescent / adult onset — hirsutism, irregular menses, infertility (often mistaken for PCOS), early pubarche in children.
Newborn screening for 17-OHP captures most classical cases.
redFlags: Salt-wasting crisis in newborn — life-threatening; IV hydrocortisone + saline + glucose immediately.
Adrenal crisis at any age — physiological stress, illness, missed dose, surgery.
Ambiguous genitalia at birth — emergency multidisciplinary assessment + delay sex assignment.
Maternal CAH planning pregnancy — fetal management considerations.

diagnostics.test: Confirmatory: serum 17-OHP (very high in classical; mildly raised in NCCAH); ACTH stimulation test for borderline / NCCAH (post-stimulation 17-OHP > 30 nmol/L).
Sodium, potassium, glucose, ACTH, cortisol, renin.
Karyotype + pelvic ultrasound for ambiguous genitalia.

management.detail: IV hydrocortisone 50–100 mg/m² stat then 50 mg/m²/day. IV 0.9% NaCl + 10% dextrose for hypoglycaemia. Treat hyperkalaemia. Newborn — early diagnosis from newborn screen prevents.

Children: hydrocortisone 10–15 mg/m²/day in 2–3 divided doses (preferred over longer-acting because of growth effects). Adult: hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in divided doses OR longer-acting (prednisolone, dexamethasone) — but worse growth + metabolic profile in younger. Recent: hydrocortisone-modified-release (Plenadren) once daily; mineralocorticoid mimicking circadian (Chronocort).
Fludrocortisone 0.05–0.2 mg/day. Salt supplement in infants. Monitor BP + electrolytes + renin (target 4–8 ng/mL/h).

Double or triple glucocorticoid dose for fever / illness / dental procedure / minor surgery. IM hydrocortisone (Solu-Cortef Act-O-Vial) kit for vomiting / unable to take oral. Major surgery: 50–100 mg IV every 6 h until eating + recovered.

Multidisciplinary team (paediatric endocrine + urology + psychology + genetics + ethics). Delayed sex assignment + minimal surgery; preserve fertility + sexual function. Family + ethical counselling + support.
Monitor growth carefully — both over-treatment (suppress growth) + under-treatment (rapid advance of bone age + reduced final height). Pubertal monitoring.
Low-dose hydrocortisone or prednisolone if symptomatic (hirsutism, infertility, early puberty); not required if asymptomatic. Sometimes only intermittent during stress.

Pre-conception planning. Glucocorticoid dose review. Fetal CAH risk if both parents carriers — pre-implantation genetic diagnosis option. Maternal CAH + classic — IVF + careful monitoring; consider prenatal dexamethasone (in classic) to prevent female fetal virilisation (controversial — long-term safety concerns).

Cardiovascular risk (over-treatment leads to obesity + insulin resistance + dyslipidaemia + hypertension; under-treatment leads to androgen excess + adrenal hyperplasia + adrenal rest tumours in testis / ovary). Annual cardiovascular + bone + fertility + tumour surveillance.

management.step: Patient + family education + transition + emergency kit
management.detail: Medic-alert bracelet; emergency hydrocortisone IM kit; sick-day rules education for family + school + workplace; lifelong specialist follow-up; structured paediatric — adult transition.

references.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (2018)
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health
WHO Recommendations on Maternal and Newborn Care

title: Phenylketonuria — lifelong dietary management + sapropterin
presentation: Autosomal recessive PAH gene mutations causing phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency.
Newborn screen (heel-prick) detects elevated phenylalanine.
Untreated: profound intellectual disability + microcephaly + seizures + behavioural problems + musty body odour + eczema + hypopigmentation.
Treated from birth: normal IQ + function.
Sub-classifications by Phe level + BH4 responsiveness.
Maternal PKU syndrome: maternal Phe > 6 mg/dL in pregnancy causes fetal microcephaly + congenital heart disease + intellectual disability — DEVASTATING.
redFlags: Untreated / poorly-treated newborn — emergency dietary intervention.
Pregnant woman with PKU — Phe must be < 6 mg/dL (preferred < 4) BEFORE conception + throughout pregnancy.
Adolescent / adult discontinuation of diet — cognitive decline + executive function impairment + mood disturbance + anxiety.

diagnostics.test: Newborn screen (heel-prick Phe). Confirmatory: plasma Phe + tyrosine + DHPR + biopterin.

diagnostics.rationale: Severity classification + sapropterin responsiveness prediction + family screening.

diagnostics.test: BH4 (sapropterin) loading test — identifies responsive subset.
Blood Phe monitoring (target < 360 micromol/L children; < 360–600 adults — though adult targets less strict in some guidelines).

management.detail: Strict low-protein diet (avoid meat, fish, eggs, milk, nuts, legumes, ordinary bread/pasta). Phe-free medical food + amino acid formulae provide protein. Tailored to BLOOD PHE LEVELS rather than weight-based. Frequent dietitian + specialist contact. Children: blood Phe weekly initially → monthly when stable.
Synthetic BH4 cofactor; identifies ~30% responsiveness. Reduces Phe → allows liberalised diet (still restricted). Higher cost; specialist initiation.
Pegylated enzyme substitute — degrades Phe extracorporally. Subcutaneous injection. Anaphylaxis risk (carry epinephrine; REMS programme). Allows substantial diet liberation.

PRE-CONCEPTION: achieve blood Phe < 6 mg/dL (preferred < 4) × 3 months before. CONTINUE throughout pregnancy + breastfeeding. High-risk obstetric care. Counsel partner / fetus risk. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis option for affected couples wanting unaffected child.
Annual neurodevelopmental + cognitive assessment in children; periodic in adults. Treat depression / anxiety / ADHD — common in PKU especially when poorly controlled.
Diet adherence often falters in adolescence; long-term consequences become apparent in adulthood. Structured transition + ongoing support. Address adult-specific issues (cardiovascular, bone).
Cascade testing of siblings + extended family. Reproductive counselling for affected + carriers. Pre-implantation diagnosis for at-risk couples.
Catabolic illness can raise Phe rapidly. Continue Phe-free formula; hydrate; treat illness; monitor Phe closely; contact specialist for severe / refractory.

references.label: ACMG Practice Guideline on Diagnosis + Management of PKU; National PKU Alliance

title: Uveitis — anterior + intermediate + posterior + panuveitis
presentation: Anterior uveitis (iritis / iridocyclitis): painful red eye + photophobia + reduced vision + circumlimbal injection + miosis + slit-lamp keratic precipitates / hypopyon / posterior synechiae.
Intermediate uveitis (pars planitis): floaters + vision reduction; vitreous cells / snowballs / snowbanking on indirect ophthalmoscopy.
Posterior uveitis (chorioretinitis): variable vision loss; retinal / choroidal lesions on fundoscopy / OCT / fluorescein angiography.
Panuveitis: all chambers involved.

Aetiology: idiopathic (~50%); HLA-B27 (acute anterior — especially with axial spondyloarthritis, IBD, psoriasis, reactive); juvenile idiopathic arthritis (chronic anterior — often asymptomatic in children, blindness risk); sarcoidosis; Behçet; toxoplasmosis; CMV (HIV); syphilis; TB; herpes (HSV / VZV); idiopathic Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada; multiple sclerosis.
redFlags: Acute angle-closure secondary to uveitis — raised IOP, pain, vision loss.
Vitritis with retinal lesion — exclude infection (CMV, toxoplasmosis, syphilis, TB).
Hypopyon — Behçet, endogenous endophthalmitis, severe HLA-B27.
Bilateral panuveitis with neurological — Behçet, sarcoidosis, VKH, multiple sclerosis.
Asymptomatic uveitis in child with JIA — blindness risk; routine ophthalmology screen.

diagnostics.rationale: Cystoid macular oedema — most vision-threatening complication.

diagnostics.test: Systemic workup based on pattern: FBC + ESR + ANA + HLA-B27 + ACE + lysozyme + syphilis serology + HIV + IGRA TB + CXR; toxoplasmosis IgG + PCR; HSV / VZV PCR vitreous; consider chest CT for sarcoid.
Diagnostic anterior chamber tap or vitreous sample for atypical / refractory / suspected infection.

management.detail: Topical corticosteroid (prednisolone 1% / dexamethasone) hourly initially then taper. Cycloplegic (cyclopentolate / atropine) for pain + posterior synechiae prevention. Treat underlying systemic disease.

Periocular / intravitreal triamcinolone or dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex 0.7 mg lasting 4–6 months); fluocinolone implant (Iluvien 0.19 mg lasting 3 years; Yutiq 0.18 mg lasting 3 years; Retisert 0.59 mg lasting 2.5 years). Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for severe + taper.
Antimetabolites (methotrexate, mycophenolate, azathioprine) first-line second tier. Calcineurin inhibitors (ciclosporin, tacrolimus). Alkylating (cyclophosphamide for severe / vasculitic).
Anti-TNF (adalimumab — FDA-approved for non-infectious uveitis based on VISUAL trials; infliximab) for refractory non-infectious uveitis. Tocilizumab + rituximab in selected. JAK inhibitor emerging.

Toxoplasmosis: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid OR co-trimoxazole + steroid for vision-threatening macular lesion. CMV retinitis (HIV): ganciclovir / foscarnet IV + intravitreal. HSV / VZV: oral / IV aciclovir + topical steroid (under cover). Syphilis: high-dose IV penicillin G × 2 weeks (treat as neurosyphilis). TB: standard TB therapy + topical / systemic steroid.
Topical NSAID + periocular / intravitreal steroid + systemic immunosuppression + anti-VEGF in selected.
Uveitic glaucoma: IOP-lowering + minimise steroid where possible; trabeculectomy / drainage device. Cataract: surgery once inflammation controlled × 3 months pre-op. Retinal detachment: vitrectomy.
Asymptomatic — slit-lamp screening every 3–6 months; topical + systemic methotrexate + adalimumab early to prevent blindness.
Ophthalmology + rheumatology + ID + paediatrics + specialist uveitis clinic. Patient education + medication adherence + long-term follow-up.

references.label: AAO Preferred Practice Pattern on Uveitis (2020); IUSG / SUN nomenclature; ESCRS

title: Medulloblastoma — paediatric posterior fossa tumour
presentation: Most common malignant paediatric brain tumour (peak 5–9 years).
Cerebellar / brainstem signs: ataxia, gait disturbance, intention tremor, cranial neuropathies.
Raised ICP: morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema, lethargy, behavioural change.
Macrocephaly in infants.
Drop metastases (leptomeningeal spread — ~30% at diagnosis): back pain, focal neuro.
Molecular subgroups (WHO 2021): WNT (best prognosis), SHH (intermediate, infant subtype), Group 3 (high-risk metastatic), Group 4 (most common, intermediate).
redFlags: Severe obstructive hydrocephalus (4th ventricle compression) — EVD.
Spinal cord drop metastasis with cord compression.
Posterior fossa syndrome post-resection (mutism + irritability + emotional dysregulation — 25%).
Infants — radiotherapy avoided (devastating long-term effects); chemotherapy-only approaches.

diagnostics.test: MRI brain + entire neuraxis (spine) with contrast.
diagnostics.rationale: Posterior fossa tumour location + size + hydrocephalus + drop metastasis.

diagnostics.test: CSF cytology (lumbar puncture after surgical decompression of hydrocephalus).
Tissue biopsy / resection specimen — histology + molecular: methylation profiling, WNT (CTNNB1 mutation, monosomy 6), SHH (PTCH1, SUFU, MYCN amplification), Group 3 (MYC amplification), Group 4.
Baseline endocrine + audiology + neurocognitive + dental + ophthalmology + cardiac.
Genetic counselling — predisposition syndromes (Li-Fraumeni, Gorlin, familial adenomatous polyposis with Turcot, Fanconi anaemia).

management.detail: Multidisciplinary team (neurosurgery + paediatric oncology + radiation oncology + neuropsychology + endocrinology + audiology). Outcomes substantially better at high-volume centres + clinical trial enrolment encouraged.
Gross total / near-total resection improves outcomes. EVD for hydrocephalus + posterior fossa craniotomy. Posterior fossa syndrome counselling pre-op.

Standard-risk (gross-total resected, no metastases, > 3 years, no MYC/MYCN amplification): craniospinal RT 23.4 Gy + boost to tumour bed 54 Gy + maintenance chemotherapy (cisplatin + lomustine + vincristine OR cyclophosphamide + cisplatin + vincristine). High-risk (metastases / sub-total resection / MYC amplification): intensified chemoradiotherapy ± high-dose chemo + stem-cell rescue. Infants (< 3 years): radiotherapy AVOIDED — chemotherapy-only approaches (head-saving infant protocols).
Excellent prognosis (~90% 5-year survival); current trials reducing radiation dose + chemotherapy intensity to mitigate late effects (SJYC07, COG ACNS1422).
Vismodegib (smoothened inhibitor) for adult / older paediatric refractory; cautious in growing children — premature epiphyseal closure.

Neurocognitive (IQ decline ~2 points/year radiation), endocrine (panhypopituitarism, growth hormone, hypothyroidism, gonadal failure, ACTH deficiency), audiology (cisplatin ototoxicity), secondary malignancy (radiation + alkylator), cardiotoxicity, vascular (Moyamoya post-radiation).
Multidisciplinary rehabilitation; school re-integration + IEP; family support + counselling; siblings.
Salvage chemotherapy ± high-dose with stem cell rescue + re-irradiation in selected. Targeted therapy per molecular subgroup (clinical trials).

references.label: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System (2021); COG / SIOPE / HIT protocols
Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health

title: Retinoblastoma — paediatric intraocular malignancy
presentation: Most common paediatric intraocular cancer — median diagnosis 18 months (unilateral) / 12 months (bilateral).
Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex — 'cat eye reflex'): most common presenting sign.
Strabismus, vision loss, red eye, glaucoma, hyphaema, proptosis (advanced).
Hereditary (40%) — germline RB1 mutation (autosomal dominant; bilateral / multifocal / younger; trilateral with pineoblastoma).
Sporadic (60%) — somatic mutation; unilateral.
Survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma at lifetime risk of second cancers (osteosarcoma + soft-tissue sarcoma + melanoma + brain tumours).
redFlags: Suspected bilateral / multifocal disease — likely hereditary; genetic counselling.
Pregnant carrier — prenatal counselling + early postnatal screening of newborn.

diagnostics.test: Detailed ophthalmological examination under anaesthesia (EUA) with indirect ophthalmoscopy + RetCam imaging.
diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis + staging (International Classification of Retinoblastoma); definitive (no biopsy — seeding risk).

diagnostics.test: Ocular ultrasound + MRI orbit + brain (for trilateral disease).

diagnostics.rationale: Hereditary vs sporadic; family counselling + screening of siblings.

diagnostics.test: Bone marrow + CSF + bone scan for advanced / extraocular suspicion.
Examination of parents + siblings + offspring of survivors.

management.detail: Multidisciplinary: ophthalmic oncologist + paediatric oncologist + geneticist + interventional radiologist + radiation oncologist. Goals: life > eye > vision.

management.step: Eye-salvaging treatment (groups A-D per International Classification)
management.detail: Group A: laser photocoagulation OR cryotherapy. Groups B-D: systemic intravenous chemotherapy (vincristine + etoposide + carboplatin) + focal consolidation (laser / cryo). Intra-arterial chemotherapy (super-selective ophthalmic artery infusion of melphalan / topotecan / carboplatin) — preferred at experienced centres. Intravitreal melphalan / topotecan for vitreous seeds.
Surgical removal of eye when not salvageable / vision unrecoverable / optic-nerve involvement / glaucoma + buphthalmos. Long optic-nerve stump for staging. Prosthesis fitting.
High-dose chemotherapy + stem-cell rescue. Intrathecal chemotherapy for CNS. Radiotherapy (focal + craniospinal for trilateral).

management.step: External beam radiotherapy — limit due to long-term risks
management.detail: Increases second-cancer risk substantially in hereditary RB. Reserved for salvage / extraocular disease.
Genetic testing of all newborn siblings of affected child + offspring of survivors. EUA from neonatal period if hereditary suspected — early treatment maximises eye / vision preservation.

management.step: Surveillance for second malignancy in hereditary RB survivors
management.detail: Lifetime risk ~50% for second cancer. Avoid radiation where possible (treatment + diagnostic — minimize CT, prefer MRI). Annual surveillance + early symptomatic investigation. Sun protection. Educate patient + family.
Prosthesis adjustment + visual rehabilitation for residual vision. Low-vision aids. School + occupational support.
Hereditary carriers — pre-implantation genetic diagnosis option; prenatal testing; postnatal early ophthalmology.

references.label: International Society of Ocular Oncology / ICRB criteria; American Brain Tumor Association

title: Neurofibromatosis type 1 — comprehensive lifelong care
presentation: Autosomal dominant — NF1 (neurofibromin) gene; 50% de novo.

Diagnostic criteria (NIH revised 2021): ≥ 2 of café-au-lait macules (≥ 6 lesions > 5 mm pre-pubertal / > 15 mm post-pubertal); freckling axillary / inguinal; Lisch nodules (iris hamartoma); optic pathway glioma; first-degree relative; characteristic bone lesion (sphenoid dysplasia, tibial pseudarthrosis); ≥ 2 cutaneous / subcutaneous neurofibromas OR plexiform neurofibroma.

Multi-system manifestations: cutaneous neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas (risk of MPNST), optic pathway glioma, low-grade glioma, intellectual difficulty + ADHD + learning disability, scoliosis, sphenoid dysplasia, pseudarthrosis, hypertension (often secondary — phaeochromocytoma 0.1–5%; renal artery stenosis), GIST, breast cancer (women 30–50 → 5× background risk), juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia.
redFlags: New / rapidly growing / painful neurofibroma — exclude MPNST (malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour — 8–13% lifetime in NF1).
Visual disturbance — optic pathway glioma (most common ~15% — particularly age 1–7).
Spinal cord compression from plexiform neurofibroma.
Hypertension — secondary cause workup (phaeochromocytoma / renal artery stenosis).
Pregnancy + NF1 — increased growth of neurofibromas + hypertension risk.
Acute deterioration in adolescent / young adult — MPNST.

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnostic criteria + careful skin / eye / musculoskeletal examination.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirmation + family cascade + sporadic vs familial.

diagnostics.test: Annual / 6-monthly ophthalmology + visual acuity / fields in childhood (peak optic glioma risk age 1–7).
Annual blood pressure + secondary HT workup if HTN.
Whole-body MRI baseline + symptom-driven for plexiform / MPNST surveillance.
Annual breast screen from age 30 in females + early mammography.

management.detail: Geneticist + neurologist + neurosurgeon + dermatologist + ophthalmologist + orthopaedic + endocrinologist + oncologist + psychologist + paediatrician + family + specialist nurse.

management.step: Plexiform neurofibroma — selumetinib (MEK inhibitor) for symptomatic / progressive paediatric
management.detail: FDA-approved (SPRINT trial). Adolescent + adult — surgical resection if accessible + symptomatic; large / inoperable — surveillance + MEK inhibitor.
Excision / laser ablation for symptomatic / cosmetic / pre-malignant. Emerging targeted therapies (MEK inhibitor selumetinib topical formulations in trial).

MOST do NOT need treatment. Treatment indications: visual decline / radiographic progression. Carboplatin + vincristine OR vinblastine OR MEK inhibitor (selumetinib) increasingly first-line. AVOID radiotherapy in NF1 (very high secondary cancer + moyamoya + cognitive decline risk).
Wide local excision + adjuvant chemotherapy (ifosfamide + doxorubicin) + radiotherapy if margins close. Aggressive disease — high mortality.
Plasma + urinary metanephrines (phaeochromocytoma); MRA for renal artery stenosis; standard ACE inhibitor (renal artery stenosis caveats).
Bracing / surgery for progressive curves. Tibial pseudarthrosis — orthopaedic + bisphosphonate + bracing + surgery.
Educational support (IEP); ADHD treatment (stimulant / non-stimulant); cognitive rehabilitation; family counselling.
50% offspring inheritance. Pre-implantation diagnosis option. Pregnancy may accelerate neurofibroma growth + BP monitoring intensified.
Annual MRI + mammography from age 30 (5× background risk); consider risk-reducing mastectomy in selected after counselling.
First-degree relatives — clinical + genetic; explain 50% inheritance.

references.label: Revised NF1 Diagnostic Criteria (Legius et al. 2021); SPRINT trial; ESCO + AAP NF1 surveillance

title: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) — multisystem management
presentation: Autosomal dominant — TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin) mutations; ~70% de novo. 50% inheritance.

CNS: cortical tubers, subependymal nodules (SENs), subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (SEGAs), epilepsy (80–90% — onset infantile spasms common; LGS / focal / drug-resistant), TAND (TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders — intellectual disability, ASD, ADHD, anxiety, depression).
Skin: facial angiofibroma (post-pubertal), forehead plaque, ash-leaf macules (early), shagreen patch, ungual fibroma.
Cardiac: rhabdomyoma — often detected antenatally / infancy; usually regress.
Renal: angiomyolipoma (AML — large > 3 cm risk of bleeding), polycystic kidneys, RCC.
Pulmonary: lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) — women 20–40; cystic lung disease + pneumothorax.
Ophthalmology: retinal hamartoma.
Endocrine: subclinical hypothyroidism, growth hormone effects, parathyroid adenoma.
redFlags: Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA) with growth / hydrocephalus — surgical / mTOR inhibitor.
Drug-resistant epilepsy — surgical + dietary + mTOR inhibitor.
AML > 3 cm with vascular pattern — bleeding risk; mTOR inhibitor + embolisation.
LAM with progressive lung function decline.

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnostic criteria (TSC International Consensus 2012, updated 2021).
diagnostics.rationale: Definite diagnosis with 2 major OR 1 major + 2 minor criteria.

diagnostics.test: Baseline + surveillance MRI brain every 1–3 years until age 25 (SEGA screening).
Renal MRI / USS — baseline + every 1–3 years lifelong.
HRCT chest baseline at age 18 in women + every 5–10 years (LAM screening).
Echocardiogram if cardiac symptoms / antenatally detected rhabdomyoma.
Annual skin / dental / ophthalmology / cognitive / behavioural assessment.

management.detail: Neurology + neurosurgery + nephrology + respiratory + dermatology + cardiology + endocrinology + psychology + paediatrician / adult medicine + family support.

Everolimus 4.5 mg/m² daily (paediatric) or 10 mg daily (adult) — approved for SEGA (when surgery not feasible), AML (renal), LAM, drug-resistant epilepsy (EXIST + EXIST-2 + EXIST-3 trials). Sirolimus topical for facial angiofibroma. Monitor: trough levels, lipids, glucose, oral ulcers, infection.

Infantile spasms: vigabatrin first-line (PARTICULARLY EFFECTIVE in TSC — ARDIE trial). Other seizure types: standard antiepileptic. Refractory: ketogenic diet, VNS, mTOR inhibitor, epilepsy surgery (high yield in TSC; specialist multidisciplinary).
Growing / symptomatic SEGA: surgical resection (preferred) OR everolimus. Hydrocephalus emergency — EVD + surgical decompression.
AML > 3 cm: everolimus to shrink + selective embolisation. Acute bleeding: emergency embolisation. Active surveillance for smaller / stable.

Sirolimus / everolimus — slows lung function decline + reduces chylothorax (MILES trial). Pulmonary function monitoring + smoking cessation. Pleurodesis / lung transplant for end-stage. Oestrogen-containing contraception cautious.
Most regress without intervention. Symptomatic / obstructive — surgery or everolimus.
Topical sirolimus 0.1% twice daily for facial angiofibroma (FDA-approved Hyftor / Vitos). Laser therapy alternative. Surgical excision for shagreen / forehead plaque.
Annual TAND-checklist assessment. Educational support; behavioural therapy; SSRI / methylphenidate / atomoxetine; intensive support for severe ID.
50% inheritance. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis option. Newborns of affected parents: serial echocardiogram + skin examination.

references.label: TSC International Consensus Diagnostic Criteria (Northrup et al. 2021); EXIST + MILES + ARDIE trials; TSC Alliance

title: Turner syndrome (45,X / mosaic) — lifelong multidisciplinary care
presentation: Chromosomal abnormality — complete or partial monosomy X (45,X most common; mosaic 45,X/46,XX; structural X abnormalities).
Newborn / infant: lymphoedema, redundant nuchal skin, low birthweight.
Childhood: short stature, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, low hairline, low-set ears, cubitus valgus, neck webbing, short fourth metacarpal, Madelung deformity.
Adolescence / adult: delayed / absent puberty, primary amenorrhoea, infertility.
Cardiovascular: bicuspid aortic valve (30%), coarctation (10%), aortic dilation + dissection — leading cause of mortality.
Endocrine: hypothyroidism (Hashimoto, 25%), type 2 diabetes, ovarian failure (primary), GH responsive growth.
Renal: horseshoe kidney (10%), collecting system anomaly.
Hearing: conductive + sensorineural loss (50%).
Cognitive: NORMAL IQ; specific visuospatial + math difficulties; ADHD risk.
Skeletal: osteoporosis risk (oestrogen deficiency + secondary).
redFlags: Aortic dissection — rare but devastating; surveillance critical.
Aortic root > 2.0 cm/m² ascending diameter — prophylactic surgery consideration.
Pregnancy in Turner — high maternal cardiac mortality from aortic dissection; specialist counselling pre-conception MANDATORY.

diagnostics.test: Karyotype on peripheral blood (30 metaphase cells for mosaicism detection).
Comprehensive newborn / childhood assessment: echocardiography + renal USS + thyroid + DEXA + skeletal survey.
Annual / 2-yearly cardiac MRI / CT angiography (aortic root surveillance).

management.detail: Paediatric / adult endocrinology + cardiology + gynaecology + audiology + ENT + orthopaedics + psychology + nephrology + dental.

rGH from age 4–6 (or earlier if growth failure) until adult height attained; achieves ~7 cm additional adult height. Add oxandrolone (anabolic) age 9+ for further height. Monitor: growth velocity, glucose, lipids.

Start low-dose 17β-oestradiol from age 11–12 (transdermal preferred); titrate over 2–3 years; add progestogen once breakthrough bleeding or 2 years after starting; mimics normal pubertal development. CONTINUE oestrogen + progestogen until age of expected menopause (~50).

Aortic root size for body surface area (Z-score). Annual / 2-yearly MRI / CT angio. Beta-blocker (atenolol / metoprolol) OR losartan for aortic protection. Prophylactic root replacement at ascending aortic diameter > 2.5 cm/m² OR > 2.0 cm/m² with risk factors (bicuspid valve, coarctation, hypertension). Aortic dissection emergency — per dissection pathway.

Spontaneous fertility rare (mostly mosaic 45,X/46,XX). Donor egg + IVF pregnancy possible. PRE-CONCEPTION cardiac assessment MANDATORY — pregnancy contraindicated if aortic root > 2.0 cm/m² OR significant valve / coarctation / aortic dissection. Specialist obstetric care. Fertility preservation (ovarian tissue / oocyte cryopreservation) emerging in selected adolescents.
Hypothyroidism: levothyroxine. Type 2 diabetes: standard management. Hypertension: target < 130/80; ACEi / ARB / beta-blocker.
Calcium + vitamin D + bisphosphonate for osteoporosis. Weight-bearing exercise. Continue HRT through reproductive age.
Hearing aids for sensorineural loss. Grommets for childhood serous otitis media. Annual ENT review.
IQ usually normal; specific math + visuospatial support. School-based IEP. ADHD treatment if indicated. Social + body-image counselling.

management.step: Transition to adult care + lifelong follow-up
management.detail: Structured adolescent → adult Turner clinic. Continuous multidisciplinary care; cardiovascular + endocrine + bone + psychological.

references.label: International Turner Syndrome Consensus (Gravholt et al. 2017); ENDO Society Turner; Turner Syndrome Society

title: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) — lifelong management
presentation: Chromosomal disorder — extra X chromosome (47,XXY most common; variants 48,XXXY; mosaic).
Childhood: often unrecognised — language delay; learning + behavioural difficulties; delayed speech; tall stature.
Adolescent / adult: small firm testes (< 6 mL), incomplete virilisation, gynaecomastia, sparse facial / body hair, eunuchoidal proportions (long limbs).
Infertility (95%) — non-obstructive azoospermia.
Hypogonadism: low testosterone + raised LH + FSH from adolescence.

Comorbidities: type 2 diabetes + metabolic syndrome (3–5×), cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, autoimmune (thyroid, SLE, RA, vasculitis), breast cancer (50× background — small absolute), germ-cell tumours, mental health (depression, anxiety, autism spectrum overlap).
redFlags: Severe psychiatric presentation — increased mental health burden.
Pregnancy planning — reproductive technology + fertility preservation timing critical.

diagnostics.test: Karyotype on peripheral blood (50 cells for mosaicism).
Morning total + free testosterone + LH + FSH + oestradiol + SHBG.
Semen analysis (azoospermia in 95% — but rare sperm sometimes; cryptozoospermia).
TSH + autoimmune screen + lipids + glucose / HbA1c + cardiovascular risk assessment.
Mental health screening (PHQ-9 + GAD-7 + autism spectrum).
Annual breast examination + low-threshold imaging (mammography / ultrasound).

management.detail: Endocrinology + reproductive medicine + psychology + cardiology + bone-specialist + family / partner support.

IM testosterone enanthate / cypionate (250 mg every 2–4 weeks) OR transdermal gel (50–100 mg daily) OR long-acting IM testosterone undecanoate (1000 mg every 10–14 weeks). Target morning total testosterone in mid-normal range. Monitor: haematocrit (polycythaemia), PSA, lipids, BP, mood, libido. Counsel on infertility (suppresses spermatogenesis).

management.step: Fertility — sperm retrieval BEFORE testosterone OR with washout
management.detail: Micro-TESE (microsurgical testicular sperm extraction) yields sperm in 40–60% of KS adolescents / young men. EARLIER (adolescent) may improve outcomes — best window before testosterone. Cryopreservation for future ART (IVF + ICSI). Withhold testosterone if attempting fertility ± transition with HCG / clomiphene.
Calcium 1000 mg + vitamin D 800 IU daily. DEXA every 2–5 years. Bisphosphonate for osteoporosis.
Standard CVD risk reduction; BP < 130/80; statin per risk; diabetes screening; weight management. Higher MI risk; CVD leading cause of death.
Higher rates of depression, anxiety, learning difficulty, autism spectrum, ADHD. Mental health screening + treatment. Educational support + IEP.

Annual breast self-examination + clinical exam. Low-threshold imaging for breast lump; mammography per local risk-adapted protocols. Mediastinal germ cell tumour — exclude with imaging if symptoms (rare).
Reassurance for mild. Aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole) limited evidence. Reduction mammoplasty for severe / psychologically distressing.
Paediatric → adult; complete medical + reproductive workup; long-term endocrinology + lifestyle + psychological care.

management.step: Pre-implantation genetic counselling for partners considering pregnancy
management.detail: Pregnancy from KS man with cryopreserved sperm via IVF + ICSI; recurrence risk in offspring slightly elevated but usually low.

references.label: European Academy of Andrology Clinical Practice Guideline on Klinefelter; Endocrine Society male hypogonadism

title: Severe intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) — monitoring + delivery timing
presentation: Fetus failing to reach growth potential — estimated fetal weight < 10th centile (small for gestational age) OR < 3rd centile (severe SGA / IUGR), with abnormal Doppler / amniotic fluid / fetal monitoring.

Causes: placental insufficiency (most common — pre-eclampsia, maternal vascular disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, smoking, drug use), maternal (severe medical illness, malnutrition), fetal (congenital infection — TORCH, chromosomal abnormality, structural anomaly), genetic (Russell-Silver syndrome, IGF-1 mutations).
Early-onset (< 32 weeks): more severe; placental insufficiency dominant; high perinatal mortality + long-term morbidity.
Late-onset (≥ 32 weeks): more common; less severe; better short-term outcomes.
redFlags: Absent / reversed end-diastolic flow in umbilical artery — critical placental insufficiency; consider delivery.
Abnormal ductus venosus Doppler (a-wave reversal) — fetal cardiac compromise; delivery indicated.

diagnostics.test: Serial growth scans (every 2 weeks) — estimated fetal weight + abdominal circumference + amniotic fluid.
Umbilical artery Doppler (UA) every 1–2 weeks; weekly if abnormal.
Middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler + cerebroplacental ratio (CPR).
Ductus venosus Doppler if UA absent / reversed end-diastolic flow.
CTG biophysical profile (BPP) — fetal heart rate + amniotic fluid + breathing + movement + tone.
Maternal: BP + urinalysis + bloods for pre-eclampsia; PIGF + sFlt-1 (where available).
Fetal echocardiography + invasive testing (CVS / amniocentesis) for suspected genetic / structural.
TORCH serology + CMV PCR if congenital infection suspected.

management.detail: Obstetrician + sonographer + neonatologist + paediatric + genetic counsellor + maternal-fetal medicine specialist.
Stop smoking + recreational drugs; optimise nutrition; treat severe maternal illness; manage diabetes; aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks for placental disease.
Betamethasone 12 mg × 2 doses 24 hours apart if delivery anticipated 24–34 weeks (some up to 36+6). Repeat course if delivery delayed > 7 days + still < 34 weeks.
MgSO4 4 g IV loading + 1 g/h infusion for 4 g total — given for at-risk preterm < 30 (some up to 32) weeks; reduces cerebral palsy + severe motor dysfunction.

TRUFFLE + DIGITAT trials guide. Early IUGR (< 32 weeks) with absent / reversed end-diastolic flow OR ductus venosus a-wave reversal: deliver. Pulsatility index > 95th centile + CPR < 1: deliver at 36–37 weeks. Severe oligohydramnios / abnormal CTG / maternal pre-eclampsia: deliver.
EFW < 3rd centile: 36 weeks. EFW 3-10th + abnormal Doppler / CPR: 37 weeks. Isolated SGA (no Doppler change): 38–39 weeks.

Vaginal acceptable if other obstetric reasons not contraindicating — continuous CTG. LSCS for: severe IUGR with abnormal Doppler / CTG / oligohydramnios; breech / malpresentation; severe maternal disease.
Specialist neonatology team present at delivery. Prepare for hypothermia + hypoglycaemia + polycythaemia + thrombocytopenia. Cord blood sampling + paediatric review + parental counselling.
Growth monitoring; metabolic + cardiovascular surveillance long-term (Barker hypothesis — fetal programming of adult disease).
Increased risk of recurrent IUGR + pre-eclampsia. Pre-conception counselling; aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks; specialist obstetric care.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 31 SGA / IUGR; ISUOG Practice Guideline; TRUFFLE + DIGITAT trials
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: Severe nodulocystic acne — isotretinoin pathway
presentation: Severe acne vulgaris — Grade IV (nodulocystic with scarring) OR severe Grade III with psychological / scarring impact OR moderate refractory to 6 months of conventional therapy.
Common: face, chest, back; nodules + cysts + scarring; post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; psychological distress + body image + depression + suicidality.
Female: often hormonal pattern (jawline, chin); PCOS overlap; pre-menstrual exacerbation.
Acne fulminans — sudden severe ulcerative + systemic (fever, polyarthritis) — emergency.
redFlags: Acne fulminans — emergency systemic steroid + isotretinoin.
Severe acne with PCOS / hyperandrogenism workup.
Depression / suicidal ideation — careful isotretinoin discussion + monitoring.
Female of childbearing potential considering isotretinoin — Pregnancy Prevention Programme essential.
Inflammatory bowel disease history — small but acknowledged signal with isotretinoin.

diagnostics.test: Hormonal workup for female adolescent / adult with hyperandrogenism: free testosterone, DHEAS, 17-OHP, prolactin, TSH.
Pre-isotretinoin: LFT + lipids + FBC + pregnancy test in females (× 2 — confirm not pregnant + monthly throughout).
Mental health screen (PHQ-9) pre + during therapy.

management.detail: Topical: retinoid + benzoyl peroxide + topical antibiotic (clindamycin / erythromycin only with BPO to prevent resistance). Systemic: doxycycline 100 mg daily × 3–6 months (lymecycline / minocycline alternatives — watch hyperpigmentation + autoimmune); hormonal therapy in women (COC + spironolactone 50–200 mg).

management.step: Isotretinoin — severe / refractory / scarring / psychological impact
management.detail: 0.5–1 mg/kg/day (or 0.25–0.5 with low-dose protocol — emerging — extended duration; same cumulative dose). Target cumulative 120–150 mg/kg total. Specialist dermatology initiation. Duration typically 5–7 months. Cure rate ~75–80%; second course in ~30%.

MANDATORY for all females of childbearing potential. 2 reliable contraceptive methods OR strict abstinence × 1 month before + during + 1 month after. Monthly negative pregnancy test before each prescription. Counsel on TERATOGENICITY — severe craniofacial, cardiac, CNS, thymus malformations.

Mucocutaneous (universal): lip balm, emollient, eye drops, sunscreen. Hypertriglyceridaemia: monitor month 2 + 4; reduce dose / hold if > 5 mmol/L. Hepatotoxicity: monitor LFT month 2 + 4. Acne flare in first month — start prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg × 2–4 weeks if severe (especially acne fulminans). Photosensitivity. Reduced night vision.
Depression + anxiety + suicidal ideation can occur on isotretinoin — counsel + monitor monthly + emergency contact information. Discontinue if significant psychiatric event.
Small signal of new IBD on isotretinoin; discuss + careful screening.
Combined oral contraceptive + spironolactone 50–200 mg/day — effective for hormonal acne; PCOS-overlap. Anti-androgen monotherapy with mandatory contraception.
Once active disease controlled: chemical peel, microneedling, fractional laser, dermal filler, subcision, punch excision, dermabrasion. Acne keloids — intralesional triamcinolone + silicone.
Address body image + relationships + mental health throughout treatment. Refer counsellor / CBT as needed.

Systemic prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg × 4 weeks + isotretinoin started at 0.1–0.5 mg/kg (gradual increase). Continue overlap × 2–4 weeks then taper steroid. Avoid initial isotretinoin alone (risk of severe flare).

references.label: European Dermatology Forum Acne Guideline (2024); American Academy of Dermatology Acne Guidelines; BAD
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Narcolepsy type 1 + type 2 — diagnosis + treatment
presentation: Type 1 (cataplectic): excessive daytime sleepiness + cataplexy (sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion); hypnagogic hallucinations; sleep paralysis; disrupted nocturnal sleep.
Type 2: excessive daytime sleepiness WITHOUT cataplexy.
Onset: bimodal (adolescent / young adult most common; secondary peak ~35 years).
Autoimmune destruction of hypocretin (orexin) neurons — strongly HLA-DQB1*06:02 associated.
Comorbid: depression, obesity, type 2 diabetes, OSA, parasomnias.
redFlags: Sudden onset cataplexy + sleepiness post-infection (especially post-H1N1 vaccination — historical; post-strep / EBV).
Suspected narcolepsy in driver / safety-critical job — driving cessation pending evaluation.

diagnostics.test: Detailed sleep history + sleep diary + Epworth Sleepiness Scale.
Polysomnography (PSG) overnight + multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) next day — gold standard.
diagnostics.rationale: Mean sleep latency ≤ 8 min + ≥ 2 sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs) — diagnostic.

diagnostics.test: Cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1 < 110 pg/mL — confirms type 1 (replaces need for cataplexy criterion in some).
Rule out: other sleep disorders (OSA, periodic limb movement, idiopathic hypersomnia), shift work, medication-related, depression.

management.detail: 20-minute scheduled naps (1–3 times daily) reduce sleepiness + medication burden. Regular sleep schedule + good sleep hygiene. Avoid caffeine close to bedtime.

Modafinil 100–400 mg/day OR armodafinil 150–250 mg. Onset 1–2 hours. Side effects: headache, anxiety, nausea, reduced COC efficacy (counsel alternative contraception). Solriamfetol 75–150 mg as alternative.
Effective for sleepiness; abuse potential; cardiovascular caution. Reserve for inadequate response to first-line.
8.9–35.6 mg/day; non-stimulant; effective for sleepiness + cataplexy; better tolerated. QTc monitoring.

management.step: Sodium oxybate (Xyrem) / low-sodium oxybate (Xywav) — for cataplexy + sleepiness
management.detail: Taken nocturnally in two doses 3 hours apart. Highly effective for cataplexy + improves sleep quality + reduces daytime sleepiness. Schedule III (US) — abuse risk. Pregnancy + breastfeeding caution. Monitor breathing + dependence.
SSRI (venlafaxine, fluoxetine) — modest; TCA (clomipramine 25–75 mg) — effective but anticholinergic; sodium oxybate.
Counsel re: driving — varies by jurisdiction; many require notification + treatment + assessment. Safety-critical occupations require accommodation / role change.
Screen + treat depression + anxiety. Address obesity + diabetes + sleep apnoea (often coexist).
Stop sodium oxybate (limited data). Modafinil moderate risk — discuss alternatives. Specialist neurology + obstetric. Postpartum risk of cataplexy + sleepiness — support.
Narcolepsy support groups; school / workplace accommodations; emergency contact information; safety planning around cataplexy triggers.

references.label: American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline on Narcolepsy (2021); ESRS European Sleep Research Society

title: Chronic insomnia disorder — CBT-I + pharmacotherapy
presentation: Difficulty initiating + maintaining sleep ≥ 3 nights/week for ≥ 3 months with daytime impairment (fatigue, mood, concentration, work / school performance).
Often comorbid: depression / anxiety (40–60%), chronic pain, OSA, restless legs syndrome.
Behavioural / cognitive contributors: poor sleep hygiene, conditioned arousal, paradoxical insomnia.
redFlags: Suspected OSA — particularly snoring + witnessed apnoeas + obesity + STOP-BANG ≥ 5.
Severe daytime sleepiness — narcolepsy / OSA / circadian rhythm disorder.
Substance / medication contributing — caffeine, alcohol, recreational drugs, beta-blocker, stimulants, antidepressants (some).
Restless legs syndrome — iron deficiency check.

diagnostics.test: Detailed sleep history + sleep diary × 2 weeks.
Validated questionnaires (Insomnia Severity Index — ISI; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index — PSQI).
Iron studies + ferritin for restless legs / periodic limb movements.

management.step: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) — FIRST-LINE
management.detail: Components: sleep restriction therapy; stimulus control; cognitive restructuring; relaxation; sleep hygiene. Delivered face-to-face / group / digital (effective). Lasting effect > pharmacological without dependence. 5–8 sessions over 6–8 weeks.

Z-drugs (zolpidem 5–10 mg, zopiclone 3.75–7.5 mg, eszopiclone) OR benzodiazepine receptor agonist — short-term (< 4 weeks) due to tolerance + dependence + falls in elderly + cognitive impact. Suvorexant / lemborexant / daridorexant (orexin receptor antagonists) — newer, less dependence, longer-term use considered. Sedating antidepressant (mirtazapine 15–30 mg, trazodone 25–100 mg, doxepin 3–6 mg) for insomnia + depression. AVOID over-the-counter antihistamine (poor evidence + side effects, especially elderly).
Prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg (Circadin) — approved for adults > 55 short-term. Modest effect; useful for circadian rhythm disorders + jet lag. Off-label paediatric use (selective).

Depression: SSRI + CBT (combined depression + insomnia treatment improves both). Chronic pain: gabapentinoids + sleep-promoting agent. OSA: CPAP. RLS: dopamine agonist OR alpha-2-delta ligand. Hot flushes: HRT or SSRI.

Regular sleep schedule; no naps > 30 min after 3 pm; avoid bright light 2 h before bed; no caffeine 6 h before bed; no alcohol 3 h before bed; relaxing pre-sleep routine; cool dark quiet bedroom; bed for sleep / sex only; aerobic exercise (not within 3 h of bed).
CBT-I particularly important; avoid sedative-hypnotics (falls + dementia association). Sleep restriction approach. Address comorbidities.
Non-pharmacological first. Magnesium glycinate, glycine, sleep hygiene. Avoid sedative-hypnotics — risk-benefit; antihistamines (doxylamine — safer; diphenhydramine), tricyclics in some. Specialist.
Sleep clinic referral for inadequate response, suspected OSA / RLS / narcolepsy, polysomnography needed, persistent severe insomnia despite optimised treatment.

references.label: AASM Insomnia 2021; NICE NG219 Insomnia; ESRS
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Hepatocellular carcinoma — BCLC staging + stage-adapted treatment
presentation: Most common primary liver cancer; 80% on background of cirrhosis (HBV / HCV / NAFLD / alcohol / haemochromatosis).
Often asymptomatic — detected on surveillance imaging in known cirrhosis.
Symptomatic: RUQ pain, weight loss, jaundice, ascites, hepatic decompensation, paraneoplastic (hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, polycythaemia).

BCLC staging: stage 0 (very early — single < 2 cm + Child-Pugh A); stage A (early — single or up to 3 ≤ 3 cm + Child-Pugh A/B); stage B (intermediate — multinodular without vascular invasion / metastases); stage C (advanced — portal invasion / metastases / N1); stage D (terminal — Child-Pugh C / ECOG > 2).
Diagnosis: tumour ≥ 1 cm in cirrhosis + characteristic CT / MRI hallmarks (arterial enhancement + portal washout) → diagnostic without biopsy.
redFlags: Rapidly rising AFP > 200 + lesion in cirrhosis — likely HCC.
Decompensated cirrhosis with new lesion — advanced disease.
Portal vein thrombosis — bland vs tumour thrombus distinction critical for treatment.
Suspected ruptured HCC (sudden severe abdominal pain + shock + haemoperitoneum) — emergency.

diagnostics.test: Surveillance for at-risk: USS + AFP every 6 months in compensated cirrhosis + chronic HBV with risk factors.
diagnostics.rationale: Early detection; cures possible at very-early / early stages.

diagnostics.test: Multiphase contrast CT or MRI liver — characteristic enhancement pattern.
diagnostics.rationale: Diagnostic without biopsy if hallmarks present in cirrhosis.

diagnostics.test: AFP + AFP-L3 + DCP (PIVKA-II) — markers; not diagnostic alone.
Biopsy — selected (atypical imaging, no cirrhosis, planning systemic therapy).
Staging: CT chest + bone scan if symptoms.
Liver function (Child-Pugh + MELD) + ECOG performance status.

management.detail: Hepatologist + interventional radiologist + transplant + surgical oncologist + medical oncologist + radiation oncologist + nuclear medicine + nurse.

Liver transplantation (Milan criteria: 1 ≤ 5 cm OR 3 ≤ 3 cm, no vascular invasion / metastases) — best long-term outcomes. Resection for Child-Pugh A with preserved function + no portal hypertension + no significant cirrhosis. Ablation (radiofrequency / microwave / cryoablation) for small tumours / unfit for surgery — comparable to resection for small lesions.
Transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE) — bead / conventional. Selective internal radiation therapy (SIRT / yttrium-90) — alternative. Multiple sessions per response. Bridge to transplant in some.

First-line: atezolizumab + bevacizumab (IMbrave150 — gold standard if no varices / GI bleeding risk; endoscopy first). Durvalumab + tremelimumab (STRIDE / HIMALAYA). Second-line: sorafenib OR lenvatinib (TKIs); regorafenib / cabozantinib / ramucirumab (second-line).
Symptom-directed only; palliative care; best supportive care.

Antiviral therapy (HBV: entecavir / tenofovir; HCV: direct-acting antivirals — SVR essential before / during HCC treatment). Alcohol cessation. NASH management. Hepatitis B prophylaxis during chemoembolisation / immunotherapy.
Pre-treatment endoscopy; eradicate / prophylax varices before atezolizumab + bevacizumab (bevacizumab bleeding risk).
Triphasic CT / MRI 3-monthly initially; AFP. Recurrence common — early detection essential.
Long-term hepatology follow-up; cirrhosis complications surveillance; family member screening for HBV / HCV; lifestyle modification.

references.label: EASL CPG on HCC (2018, updated); AASLD HCC (2023); IMbrave150 + HIMALAYA trials; BCLC 2022 update
Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health

title: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma — diagnosis + treatment pathway
presentation: Insidious onset — often advanced at diagnosis. Persistent epigastric / back pain, weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, painless obstructive jaundice (head of pancreas — Courvoisier sign), new-onset diabetes / change in pre-existing diabetes, steatorrhoea, depression.
Less common: thromboembolism (Trousseau syndrome), acute pancreatitis, paraneoplastic dermatosis.
Risk factors: smoking (2-3×), chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, family history, hereditary (BRCA1/2, PALB2, ATM, Lynch — 10%), obesity, alcohol, occupational chemical exposure.
Histology: ductal adenocarcinoma (90%), neuroendocrine tumour (5%, different biology + treatment), cystic, intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN).
redFlags: Painless obstructive jaundice — high suspicion for pancreatic head cancer.
Cholangitis from biliary obstruction — emergency drainage + antibiotics.
Severe abdominal pain — may indicate locally advanced / nerve invasion / acute pancreatitis.
Venous thromboembolism in middle-age + weight loss — paraneoplastic.
Performance-status decline + cachexia — modify treatment intensity.

diagnostics.test: Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) + FNA — most sensitive; tissue diagnosis + better than CT for small lesions.
MRI + MRCP for biliary anatomy / biliary obstruction / cyst characterisation.
PET-CT for selected — detect distant disease pre-resection.
CA 19-9 — baseline + monitoring; can be false-positive (jaundice / inflammation) or false-negative (Lewis antigen negative).
Genetic testing for hereditary syndromes (BRCA1/2 + PALB2 + ATM + Lynch + p16) — all PDAC for treatment-defining + family.
Multidisciplinary review of resectability + neoadjuvant candidacy.

management.detail: Hepatobiliary surgeon + oncologist + radiation oncologist + interventional radiologist + endoscopist + pathologist + dietitian + palliative care.

management.step: Resectable disease (~15% at diagnosis) — neoadjuvant + surgery
management.detail: Increasingly neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX (modified) OR gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel × 4 cycles → surgical re-staging → Whipple procedure (head) OR distal pancreatectomy (body / tail) → adjuvant chemotherapy. Modified FOLFIRINOX as adjuvant standard (PRODIGE 24).
Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX × 6 months ± radiotherapy → re-stage → surgery if responsive (20–40%). Improves R0 resection rates.

Performance-status driven: ECOG 0–1: FOLFIRINOX (oxaliplatin + irinotecan + 5-FU + leucovorin). ECOG 2: gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel (less toxic). ECOG 3+: gemcitabine monotherapy or best supportive care.
Germline BRCA1/2-mutated metastatic PDAC: olaparib maintenance after platinum-based response (POLO trial).

Biliary obstruction — endoscopic stent (preferred) OR percutaneous biliary drainage. Duodenal obstruction — duodenal stent / gastrojejunostomy. Pain — celiac plexus block / neurolysis + opioids + adjuvants (gabapentin). Pancreatic enzyme replacement (Creon) for steatorrhoea. Diabetes management. Thromboprophylaxis (high-risk LMWH).
Dietitian + high-calorie diet + pancreatic enzyme replacement + nutritional supplements; consider feeding tube for severe.

Cascade BRCA / PALB2 / ATM / Lynch testing. High-risk family (≥ 2 affected first-degree relatives, BRCA carrier with FH) — annual MRI / EUS surveillance starting age 50 (or 10 years before youngest affected).

Median survival metastatic 6–11 months; resected 25–30 months; 5-year survival ~10% overall. Early palliative involvement improves outcomes. Address goals of care, symptom control, advance directives.
CT + CA 19-9 every 3 months × 2 years then every 6 months × 3 years.

references.label: ESMO + NCCN Pancreatic Cancer Guidelines; PRODIGE 24 + POLO + PRINTO trials
Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary + follicular) — risk-stratified treatment
presentation: Most common endocrine malignancy. Female:male 3:1; peak 30-50 years.
Papillary (80–85%) — better prognosis; lymph node spread; multifocal common; BRAF V600E mutation in 50%.
Follicular (10–15%) — vascular invasion; haematogenous (lung, bone); not lymph node typically; better prognosis if minimally invasive.
Presentation: asymptomatic thyroid nodule (incidental on imaging); palpable neck mass; hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve compression); dysphagia / dyspnoea (large); cervical lymphadenopathy.
Anaplastic (1%) — extremely aggressive; rapid growth + airway compromise; median survival 6 months.
Medullary (parafollicular C-cell, MEN-2 association — separate biology + treatment).
redFlags: Rapidly growing thyroid mass — exclude anaplastic / lymphoma.
Vocal cord paralysis — recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement.
Family history of MEN-2 — RET gene testing; medullary thyroid cancer.
Distant metastases at diagnosis (lung + bone) — modify treatment intensity.
Pregnancy + thyroid cancer — usually delay treatment but surgery sometimes needed.

diagnostics.test: Thyroid ultrasound — TIRADS / ATA risk categorisation; suspicious nodules > 1 cm (some 0.5 cm if high-risk features) → FNA.
Molecular testing of indeterminate / non-diagnostic FNA (Bethesda III / IV) — Afirma / ThyroSeq / Veracyte — molecular panels.
diagnostics.rationale: Risk-stratify indeterminate nodules; avoid unnecessary surgery.

diagnostics.test: Pre-operative neck USS + vocal cord assessment.
TSH, free T4, calcium (parathyroid baseline), calcitonin (if medullary suspected), thyroglobulin baseline.
BRAF V600E + RET + NTRK + TERT mutation testing — high-risk + recurrent / refractory.

management.detail: Endocrine surgeon + endocrinologist + nuclear medicine physician + oncologist + pathologist + ENT + radiologist.

management.step: Low-risk papillary microcarcinoma (< 1 cm, intrathyroidal, no nodes) — active surveillance OR lobectomy
management.detail: Active surveillance increasingly accepted for very low-risk papillary microcarcinoma. Lobectomy for definitive treatment + smaller scar + no thyroid hormone replacement needed.

management.step: Standard low-risk (T1-T2 N0) — lobectomy + selective central nodes
management.detail: Hemithyroidectomy. Levothyroxine selectively (not always needed).

management.step: Intermediate / high-risk — total thyroidectomy ± central neck dissection
management.detail: Multifocal / large tumour / nodal disease / extrathyroidal extension / distant metastases. Lateral neck dissection for clinical / radiological lateral nodal disease.

Low-risk: usually NOT needed. Intermediate-risk: selective per individual factors. High-risk: standard adjuvant after total thyroidectomy. Recombinant TSH (rhTSH) for stimulation (avoids hypothyroid state).

Levothyroxine to suppress TSH: high-risk TSH < 0.1; intermediate TSH 0.1–0.5; low-risk TSH 0.5–2.0 (normal range). Monitor bone + cardiac for over-suppression. De-escalate as evidence of remission grows.
TSH + thyroglobulin + neck USS every 6–12 months. Stimulated thyroglobulin (TSH-stimulated or rhTSH) for ablated patients to monitor recurrence.

Surgical resection of resectable recurrences. RAI for iodine-avid metastases. Radiotherapy for symptomatic / brain / bone. Sorafenib / lenvatinib (multikinase TKI) for RAI-refractory progressive disease. Selpercatinib (RET-positive); dabrafenib + trametinib (BRAF V600E + anaplastic — recently approved). NTRK / ALK inhibitors for fusion-positive.

Airway management priority (tracheostomy if needed); dabrafenib + trametinib for BRAF V600E (~25% — neoadjuvant + then surgery in selected; RECOVER study); pembrolizumab + chemotherapy + radiotherapy. Mortality high; palliative care early.
Surgery preferably delayed to 2nd trimester or postpartum. RAI contraindicated (avoid pregnancy × 6–12 months post-RAI). Thyroxine dose increases in pregnancy.
MEN-2 (medullary) — RET gene testing. Familial papillary — less established.

references.label: ATA Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules + Differentiated Thyroid Cancer (2015, with updates); ESMO Thyroid Cancer
Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health
WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) — KIT-targeted treatment
presentation: Most common mesenchymal GI tumour. Stomach (60%), small bowel (30%), colorectal / oesophagus / extra-GI (10%).
Variable presentation: incidental on imaging / endoscopy; GI bleeding (haematemesis / melaena); abdominal mass; abdominal pain; obstruction; perforation.

Driver mutations: KIT (75%, particularly exon 11 — best imatinib response) and PDGFRA (10% — exon 18 D842V resistant to imatinib). Wild-type GIST (15% — SDH-deficient pediatric / Carney triad; NF1-associated; BRAF / NTRK).
Risk-stratification: tumour size, mitotic count, location, mutation status.
redFlags: Metastatic at diagnosis (15% — liver predominantly; lung / bone rarer than other GI tumours).
Suspected paediatric GIST — different biology (SDH-deficient); refer specialist.

diagnostics.test: Endoscopic ultrasound + biopsy (EUS-FNA) — better than blind biopsy for risk of bleeding / seeding.
Histology + IHC (CD117 / KIT positive; DOG1 positive; CD34 variable; SMA / desmin negative).
Molecular: KIT (exons 9, 11, 13, 17), PDGFRA (exons 12, 14, 18 — D842V), SDH (paediatric / wild-type), BRAF, NTRK, NF1 association.

management.detail: Pathologist + surgical / medical / radiation oncologist + interventional radiologist. Outcomes superior at high-volume centres.
Wide local excision with negative margins; no routine lymphadenectomy (uncommon nodal spread). Laparoscopic acceptable for selected. Avoid tumour rupture (peritoneal seeding catastrophic).

Imatinib 400 mg daily × 3 years for high-risk (size > 5 cm + mitotic count > 5/50 HPF OR > 10 cm any mitotic OR ruptured). KIT exon 11 — best response; exon 9 — needs higher dose (800 mg); D842V PDGFRA — imatinib RESISTANT (use avapritinib).
Imatinib × 6–12 months to downsize before surgery; preserve function (rectal / oesophageal / duodenal GIST).
400 mg daily (800 mg for KIT exon 9). Continuous indefinite therapy. Median PFS ~30 months.

Second-line: sunitinib 50 mg × 4 weeks on / 2 off. Third-line: regorafenib 160 mg daily 3 weeks on / 1 off. Fourth-line: ripretinib 150 mg daily. PDGFRA D842V: avapritinib 300 mg daily (first-line for this mutation). NTRK fusion: larotrectinib / entrectinib. BRAF V600E: dabrafenib + trametinib. Wild-type / SDH-deficient: less responsive to imatinib; tipiraciclib / sunitinib / regorafenib + clinical trials.
Adjuvant imatinib: CT + clinical every 3 months × first year then every 6 months for 5 years. Metastatic on TKI: every 3 months CT.
Imatinib: oedema, GI, muscle cramp, rash, hepatic. Sunitinib: cardiovascular, hypertension, hand-foot syndrome, hypothyroidism. Regorafenib: hand-foot, hypertension, fatigue. Monitor + dose-modify.
