NF1, Carney triad (GIST + paraganglioma + pulmonary chondroma — paediatric), Carney-Stratakis syndrome — SDH-deficient. Genetic counselling.

references.label: ESMO + NCCN GIST Guidelines; INTRIGUE + INVICTUS + VOYAGER trials

title: Cervical cancer — screening + stage-based treatment
presentation: HPV-driven (>95% — high-risk types 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58).
Early: often asymptomatic, screen-detected. Symptomatic — abnormal vaginal bleeding (post-coital, intermenstrual, post-menopausal), watery discharge, pelvic pain.
Advanced: hydronephrosis (ureteric obstruction), pelvic pain, bowel symptoms, leg oedema, fistula (vesicovaginal, rectovaginal).
Histology: squamous cell carcinoma (75%), adenocarcinoma (20%), adenosquamous, small cell (poor prognosis), neuroendocrine.
Risk: HPV, smoking, immunosuppression, multiple partners, early sexual debut, lack of screening, COCP long-term (mild).
redFlags: Massive bleeding from advanced cervical cancer — radiation / embolisation / vaginal packing.
Acute renal failure from bilateral ureteric obstruction — nephrostomy.
DVT / PE — high cancer + pelvic mass risk.
Pregnancy + cervical cancer — multidisciplinary (oncology + obstetrics + neonatal); fertility-sparing approach possible for early disease.

diagnostics.test: Cervical screening (HPV testing primary; cytology if available).
Pelvic MRI — gold standard for tumour size + parametrial / nodal involvement.
PET-CT or CT chest / abdomen — nodal + distant disease.
Examination under anaesthesia + cystoscopy + sigmoidoscopy if locally advanced.

management.detail: Gynaecological oncologist + radiation oncologist + medical oncologist + pathologist + radiologist + clinical nurse specialist + fertility specialist + psychology.
Loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP / LLETZ) OR cold knife conisation. Cervical follow-up at 6 months post-treatment + return to routine screening per protocol.
For fertility-sparing in young women + selected pathology (no LVSI). Hysterectomy for definitive.

management.step: Stage IA2-IB1 (small tumour) — radical hysterectomy + pelvic lymphadenectomy
management.detail: Or fertility-sparing radical trachelectomy + cerclage for early-stage + desired pregnancy. Sentinel lymph node mapping increasingly accepted.
External beam radiotherapy + brachytherapy + concurrent weekly cisplatin (40 mg/m²). Equivalent / better outcomes than radical surgery for larger tumours.
Definitive curative-intent. Pembrolizumab added for PD-L1+ FIGO III-IVA (KEYNOTE-A18). Adjuvant pembrolizumab for high-risk post-CRT (KEYNOTE-A18).

Cisplatin + paclitaxel + bevacizumab (BEV — improves OS in GOG-240). Pembrolizumab + chemotherapy + bevacizumab (KEYNOTE-826) — new first-line for PD-L1+ metastatic. Cemiplimab second-line (EMPOWER-Cervical 1).

Multidisciplinary decision: gestational age, stage, patient preference. Delay treatment until fetal viability where stage allows (early disease); some early disease can be managed with conisation + close monitoring. Locally advanced / metastatic — discussion of pregnancy termination + treatment OR delayed treatment until fetal viability + Caesarean + treatment. Refer specialist.

Sexual dysfunction (vaginal shortening / dryness — vaginal dilator, lubricant, oestrogen if possible); bowel + bladder dysfunction; lymphoedema; psychological / body image. Vaginal moisturisers + dilators.
HPV vaccine eligible age (9-26 typically; up to 45 in some); essential for primary prevention. Cervical screening continued in vaccinated.

references.label: ESMO + NCCN Cervical Cancer Guidelines; FIGO 2018 staging; KEYNOTE-A18 + KEYNOTE-826
Kenya National Cancer Treatment Guidelines (National Cancer Control Programme), Ministry of Health

title: Moderate-severe ulcerative colitis — biologic + treat-to-target
presentation: Chronic relapsing inflammation of colonic mucosa — contiguous from rectum; varying extent (proctitis 30%, left-sided 30%, extensive / pancolitis 30%).
Bloody diarrhoea + urgency + tenesmus + abdominal pain + fatigue + extra-intestinal manifestations.
Severity (Truelove-Witts): mild < 4 stools / day; moderate 4–6; severe ≥ 6 + systemic signs (HR > 90, T > 37.8, Hb < 105, ESR > 30).
Comorbidities: PSC (~5% of UC; 70% of PSC has UC), spondyloarthropathy, ocular (uveitis, episcleritis), skin (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum), AIH, oral aphthous.
redFlags: Acute severe colitis (ASUC; see toxic-megacolon pathway).
Suspected CRC in long-standing extensive disease.
Pregnancy + active UC — treat actively; flare worse than therapy.
C. difficile + CMV superinfection in steroid-refractory.
VTE risk extremely elevated during flare — even with bleeding.

diagnostics.test: Ileocolonoscopy + biopsies — diagnosis + extent + activity (Mayo endoscopic subscore).
Faecal calprotectin — disease activity monitoring; non-invasive.
FBC + CRP + albumin + ferritin + B12 + vitamin D + nutrition assessment.
C. difficile + CMV PCR + stool cultures.
Pre-biologic: hepatitis B + C + HIV + TB (IGRA + CXR) + varicella; vaccinations.
CRC surveillance — colonoscopy at 8 years then every 1–3 years.

management.detail: Mesalamine (5-ASA) suppositories 1 g / enemas 1 g daily for proctitis; foam / enema for left-sided. Combine with oral mesalamine 2.4-4.8 g/day for extensive. Cochrane: combined oral + topical superior.
Oral prednisolone 40 mg/day taper over 8 weeks. Add steroid-sparing thiopurine (azathioprine 2 mg/kg, TPMT testing) for relapsing / steroid-dependent.

Anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab) first-line. Vedolizumab (anti-α4β7 integrin) — gut-selective; safer profile. Ustekinumab (IL-12/23). JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib — oral, fast onset, caution VTE + cardiovascular). Ozanimod (S1P modulator).

management.step: Acute severe UC — hospital admission + IV steroid
management.detail: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 h × 3 days assessment; if inadequate response (Travis criteria — > 8 stools or CRP > 45 at day 3) → rescue with infliximab OR ciclosporin; failure of rescue at day 5–7 → colectomy.
Symptomatic remission + endoscopic healing (Mayo 0–1) + histological healing. Therapeutic drug monitoring (anti-TNF trough levels + anti-drug antibodies).
Continue mesalamine + thiopurine + anti-TNF; certolizumab no placental transfer. Active disease worse than medication for mother + baby. Tofacitinib / JAK inhibitor avoid in pregnancy.
Pancolitis: from 8 years post-diagnosis. Left-sided: from 15 years. Chromoendoscopy + targeted biopsy preferred. Annual in high-risk (PSC + UC, family history). Dysplasia → colectomy.

Indications: refractory severe disease, dysplasia / cancer, complications (perforation, haemorrhage, fistula). Subtotal colectomy + ileostomy + planned restorative proctocolectomy + IPAA (J-pouch) — cures UC; some long-term pouchitis.
LMWH for ALL hospitalised flares — even with rectal bleeding. UC + flare carries extreme VTE risk.

Pneumococcal + flu + COVID + zoster (live avoided on biologic); hepatitis B before biologic. Smoking cessation (paradoxically can worsen UC after quitting). Bone protection (calcium + vitamin D). Mental health support.

references.label: ECCO UC Guidelines 2022 (update); AGA Practice Guidelines; True UCDS

title: Severe / chronic migraine — CGRP-targeted prevention + acute therapy
presentation: Migraine: recurrent unilateral pulsating headache + photophobia + phonophobia + nausea ± vomiting ± aura, 4–72 h duration, female predominant 3:1.
Episodic (< 15 headache days / month) vs chronic (≥ 15 days / month for > 3 months with ≥ 8 migraine days).
Aura (25%): visual scotoma + scintillating + sensory + motor / dysphasic / brainstem aura (migraine with aura subtype).
Triggers: stress, sleep disturbance, hormonal (menstrual), food (chocolate, cheese, alcohol, MSG), caffeine withdrawal, weather, missed meals, dehydration.
Comorbid: depression, anxiety, PTSD, sleep disorder, obesity, cardiovascular disease, stroke (especially migraine with aura), epilepsy.
redFlags: Thunderclap headache (peak intensity within 1 minute) — SAH / cerebral venous sinus thrombosis / RCVS.
New-onset > 50 — temporal arteritis; brain tumour; subdural haematoma.
New focal neurology / persistent aura > 1 h — investigate.
Headache with fever + neck stiffness — meningitis.
Postpartum severe headache — eclampsia / cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
Medication overuse headache (MOH) — > 10 days / month opioid / triptan / combination analgesic.

diagnostics.test: Clinical (ICHD-3 criteria) — no investigation for typical episodic migraine.
Imaging (MRI brain) — atypical features, red flags, > 50 new onset, change in pattern.
Headache diary — frequency + triggers + treatment response.
Cardiovascular risk assessment for women > 35 with aura + smoking (avoid oestrogen-containing contraception).
Pregnancy test before pharmacotherapy in women of childbearing potential.

management.detail: Regular sleep + meals + hydration + exercise + stress management. Identify + avoid individual triggers. Mediterranean diet. Limit caffeine 2 cups/day. Riboflavin 400 mg + coenzyme Q10 + magnesium 600 mg supplementation modest evidence.

Mild: paracetamol 1 g + ibuprofen 400-600 mg + antiemetic (metoclopramide / domperidone). Moderate-severe: triptan (sumatriptan 50-100 mg PO OR 6 mg SC; rizatriptan, zolmitriptan, almotriptan, eletriptan). AVOID triptan in cardiovascular disease, uncontrolled HTN, pregnancy, migraine with brainstem / hemiplegic aura. CGRP receptor antagonist (gepants — ubrogepant, rimegepant) — no vasoconstriction, safer in cardiovascular. Lasmiditan (selective 5-HT1F agonist) — no vasoconstriction; driving caution. AVOID opioids + butalbital + barbiturate (medication overuse + tolerance).

management.step: Preventive therapy — indicated for ≥ 4 days / month OR debilitating attacks
management.detail: First-line: propranolol 80-240 mg/day (heart disease, asthma caveat). Topiramate 50-100 mg/day (cognitive, kidney stones, pregnancy avoid). Amitriptyline 10-50 mg nocte (depression overlap, anticholinergic). Sodium valproate (NOT women of childbearing potential). Candesartan 8-16 mg. Flunarizine.

Erenumab 70-140 mg SC monthly OR fremanezumab 225 mg SC monthly / 675 mg quarterly OR galcanezumab 240 mg loading + 120 mg monthly OR eptinezumab IV every 3 months. Generally indicated after ≥ 2 first-line preventives fail. Effective for both episodic + chronic migraine. Constipation, injection site reactions, rare cardiovascular events (relative monitoring).
Rimegepant 75 mg every other day OR atogepant 60 mg daily — oral CGRP antagonist; alternative to mAbs.
Onabotulinum toxin A 155 units (PREEMPT protocol) every 12 weeks — FDA-approved for chronic migraine. Withdraw overused medication (often worsens before improving).

Paracetamol first-line. Sumatriptan limited safety data — avoid where possible (use in severe / refractory only). Propranolol acceptable for prevention. Most preventives avoided (topiramate, valproate, ergot). Magnesium + riboflavin. Specialist neurology.
Withdraw overused medication (cold turkey OR taper); bridging therapy (steroid prednisolone 60 mg taper, or naproxen, or DHE if specialist); start preventive simultaneously; counsel patient + family.

Greater occipital nerve block; sphenopalatine ganglion block; ablation; neurostimulation (transcutaneous supraorbital — Cefaly; remote electrical neuromodulation — Nerivio; vagus nerve stimulation). Refer specialist headache clinic.
Treat depression / anxiety + sleep disorders + obesity + chronic pain. Aerobic exercise. Mindfulness-based CBT.

references.label: AHS Consensus on CGRP for Migraine (2021 update); EHF Migraine; ICHD-3
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Sport-related concussion / mild traumatic brain injury
presentation: Sport / occupational head injury — biomechanical force directly to head OR transmitted to head.

Clinical features: somatic (headache, dizziness, balance problems, photophobia, phonophobia, vision changes); cognitive (confusion, memory disturbance, slowed reaction time, difficulty concentrating); emotional (irritability, anxiety, low mood); sleep (insomnia, hypersomnia).
GCS 13–15 + LOC ≤ 30 min + post-traumatic amnesia ≤ 24 h.
Most resolve within 1-4 weeks (children may take longer); persistent symptoms > 4 weeks = persistent post-concussion symptoms.
Repetitive sub-concussive impacts may cause long-term chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) — particularly in contact sports.
redFlags: Worsening headache + vomiting + confusion + LOC > 30 min — exclude bleed (CT head).
Anticoagulation / antiplatelet — lower threshold for imaging.
Skull fracture (basal — raccoon eyes, Battle sign, CSF rhinorrhoea / otorrhoea).
Same-day return to play after concussion — second-impact syndrome (catastrophic in adolescents).

diagnostics.test: Clinical assessment — Sport Concussion Assessment Tool 6 (SCAT6) for adults / Child SCAT6 for paediatric.
Glasgow Coma Scale + neurological examination + cervical-spine assessment.

CT head per Canadian CT Head Rule / NICE criteria — NOT routinely; selectively for red flags + GCS < 15 + LOC > 5 min + amnesia > 30 min + age > 65 + anticoagulation + intoxication + concerning mechanism.
Symptom inventory (PCS scale) + neurocognitive testing (ImPACT, SCAT 6).

management.detail: Any suspected concussion = removal from play same day. 'When in doubt, sit them out'. NEVER return same day in adolescents / children.
BRIEF physical + cognitive rest (24-48 hours) — not prolonged. Recent evidence: prolonged rest worsens outcomes.

management.step: Active rehabilitation — gradual return to function
management.detail: Sub-symptom threshold aerobic exercise after 24-48 h (improves recovery — Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test informed). Vestibular rehabilitation for vestibular symptoms. Cognitive rehabilitation for persistent cognitive symptoms. Vision therapy for ocular motor.

Step 1: daily activity at home with no symptoms. Step 2: school activities (light cognitive). Step 3: return to school part-time. Step 4: full days. Step 5: full activities. Each step 24 h apart; if symptoms — step back.

management.step: Graduated return-to-sport (RTSp) — Concussion in Sport Group 2017
management.detail: Step 1: symptom-limited activity. Step 2: light aerobic. Step 3: sport-specific exercise. Step 4: non-contact training. Step 5: full contact practice (medical clearance). Step 6: return to competitive play. Minimum 24 h per step → minimum 6 days. Children + adolescents: more conservative.
Analgesia: paracetamol (avoid NSAIDs in first 24-48 h — bleeding risk in rare missed bleed). Antiemetic. Sleep hygiene + low-dose melatonin. Address mood + anxiety.

Multidisciplinary clinic — neurology + sports medicine + physiotherapy + psychology + occupational therapy. Vestibular + vision rehabilitation. CBT for mood / anxiety. Sleep optimisation. Headache management. Education + reassurance.

management.step: Repeat concussions + chronic traumatic encephalopathy concerns
management.detail: Higher risk after first concussion. Multiple concussions especially close together — increased risk of complications. Permanent retirement from contact sport considered after multiple severe / prolonged recoveries / persistent symptoms. CTE — long-term cognitive + behavioural changes; only diagnosable post-mortem currently.
Slower recovery; more conservative return-to-play; greater academic accommodations. Family + school + sport coordinator involvement.
Helmet use; rule changes in sport (no head contact); coaching education; baseline testing (controversial).

references.label: Concussion in Sport Group Consensus Statement (Amsterdam 2022); CDC HEADS UP; American Academy of Neurology
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children

title: Maternal cardiac arrest — resuscitation + peri-mortem caesarean
presentation: Cardiac arrest in pregnant patient ≥ 20 weeks gestation OR fundal height at / above umbilicus.

Causes: amniotic fluid embolism, pulmonary embolism, haemorrhage (PPH, abruption, ectopic, rupture), pre-eclampsia / eclampsia, sepsis, cardiac (peripartum cardiomyopathy, ACS, dissection), trauma, drug-related (Mg toxicity, anaesthesia, illicit).
Maternal physiology challenges: aortocaval compression by gravid uterus reduces CPR effectiveness; increased oxygen consumption + decreased reserve; airway changes (more difficult intubation).
Dual patient — mother + fetus.
redFlags: ALL pregnant cardiac arrests — peri-mortem caesarean section (PMCS) within 4–5 minutes if no ROSC.
Massive haemorrhage — massive transfusion protocol + surgical control.

diagnostics.test: ABCDE during ongoing CPR — minimise interruption.

diagnostics.rationale: Identify free fluid (ruptured ectopic, abruption), PE, tamponade.

diagnostics.test: FBC + crossmatch + coagulation + fibrinogen + lactate + ABG + electrolytes (Mg+ glucose).

management.step: Call for help — maternal cardiac arrest team
management.detail: Multidisciplinary: obstetrics + anaesthetics + neonatology + ICU + emergency. Prepare for PMCS.

management.step: Standard adult ALS — modified for pregnancy
management.detail: Standard chest compressions (slightly higher position on sternum). Standard defibrillation. Standard drug doses + ventilation.
Manual displacement of uterus to LEFT by assistant pushing from right side — improves CPR effectiveness more than tilt. Critical from 20 weeks.

management.step: Peri-mortem caesarean section (PMCS) within 4-5 MINUTES if no ROSC
management.detail: PRIMARILY for MATERNAL benefit — emptying uterus improves return of circulation by reducing aortocaval compression. Secondarily for fetus. Decision at 4 min; delivery by 5 min. Done at site of arrest — DO NOT transfer to theatre. Make midline vertical incision. Continue CPR throughout. Neonatology present.

Amniotic fluid embolism: supportive — DIC management. Massive haemorrhage: massive transfusion + tranexamic acid + uterotonic + surgical / IR control. Eclampsia: MgSO4 4 g IV. PE: alteplase considered. Local anaesthetic toxicity: 20% intralipid 1.5 mL/kg bolus + 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion. Cardiac: PCI / surgery. Sepsis: hour-1 bundle.
Anticipate difficult intubation; senior anaesthetist; smaller ETT; ramped position; consider video laryngoscopy + cricoid pressure controversial.
Targeted temperature management 32-36°C as per non-pregnant. Identify + treat underlying cause. ICU level care.
Neonatology prepared for delivery. Family + bereavement support if poor outcome. Debrief team.
Mandatory case review (MBRRACE-UK or local equivalent). Learn from each case.

references.label: AHA Maternal Cardiac Arrest Scientific Statement (2015 + 2021 update); ERC ALS pregnancy; MBRRACE-UK
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health

title: WHO PEN — total cardiovascular risk screening + management (Kenya primary care)
presentation: Adult ≥ 40 years (or younger if symptomatic) attending primary care for opportunistic screening (or with established risk factor).
WHO/ISH CVD risk prediction charts — age, sex, smoking, BP, total cholesterol (or no-cholesterol option for low-resource), diabetes.
Categorise: < 10% (low), 10–20% (moderate), 20–30% (high), ≥ 30% (very high) 10-year risk of fatal + non-fatal CVD.
Kenya national NCD policy aligns with WHO PEN package — prioritises hypertension, diabetes, CVD risk, asthma / COPD basic care in primary facility.
redFlags: Established CVD (prior MI, stroke, PAD) — treat as very-high-risk regardless of score.
Diabetes with target-organ damage — high-risk threshold.
Familial hypercholesterolaemia (LDL ≥ 5 mmol/L, family history premature CVD) — treat without scoring + specialist.

diagnostics.test: BP × 2 readings (different visits if not severe). Use calibrated upper-arm device.
Capillary blood glucose / fasting glucose / HbA1c.
Total cholesterol (optional if no laboratory — WHO/ISH no-cholesterol chart usable).
Smoking + alcohol + physical activity + diet questions.

management.step: Apply WHO/ISH CVD risk chart for region — Africa AFR-D / E table
management.detail: Generate 10-year risk category using age, sex, BP, smoking, diabetes, total cholesterol (if available).

management.step: Universal lifestyle counselling (5As: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange)
management.detail: Tobacco cessation; reduce salt < 5 g/day; reduce sugar; ≥ 5 fruit + vegetable servings/day; ≥ 150 min/week physical activity; alcohol moderation; weight loss to BMI 20–25.

management.step: Treat individual risk factors regardless of total score
management.detail: BP ≥ 140/90 sustained: lifestyle + medication if persists. HbA1c ≥ 6.5%: diabetes treatment per WHO HEARTS-D pathway. LDL above target: lifestyle + statin per CVD risk.

management.step: Add statin therapy by CVD risk band
management.detail: < 10% risk: lifestyle only. 10–20%: lifestyle + statin if cholesterol/risk factors not improving. ≥ 20%: lifestyle + statin (atorvastatin 10–20 mg or simvastatin 20–40 mg) + BP medication if BP elevated. ≥ 30% OR established CVD: aggressive statin + BP + antiplatelet for secondary prevention only (no routine aspirin primary prevention per modern evidence).

management.step: Antihypertensive therapy per WHO HEARTS protocol
management.detail: Step 1: ACEi/ARB OR DHP-CCB (amlodipine 5 mg). Step 2: combination ACEi/ARB + CCB. Step 3: add thiazide. Step 4: spironolactone for resistant. Target < 140/90 (< 130/80 in diabetes/CKD/post-stroke if tolerated).

management.step: Diabetes per WHO HEARTS-D / Kenya NCD program
management.detail: Metformin first-line; titrate to HbA1c target; add second / third agent. Insulin for HbA1c > 10% or new presentation with marked symptoms. Annual eye + foot + renal screening.
Brief intervention + NRT / bupropion / varenicline / cytisine where available. Counsel re: cardiovascular benefit (50% reduction in 1 year).
Annual cardiovascular risk reassessment. Adjust therapy per response. Multidisciplinary (community health worker + nurse + clinical officer + GP) supported in Kenya primary care setting.
Resistant hypertension; suspected secondary HTN; established CVD; symptomatic angina / heart failure; severe diabetes; complications (retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy).
Engage community health workers + village health teams; structural support for accessing essential medicines (Kenya Essential Medicines List); HEARTS technical package implementation.

references.label: WHO Package of essential noncommunicable disease interventions (PEN) for primary health care (2020); WHO HEARTS technical package; Kenya National NCD Strategic Plan 2021-2025

title: WHO 2016 antenatal care — 8-contact model + Kenya MOH protocol
presentation: Pregnant woman (any gestation) presenting for antenatal care.
WHO 2016 recommends EIGHT contacts (replaced previous four-visit model) to reduce perinatal mortality + improve maternal experience.
Kenya MOH protocol (Linda Mama free maternity care): aligns with WHO; prioritises early booking + multi-visit care + community engagement.
First contact: by 12 weeks; subsequent contacts at 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38, 40 weeks.
redFlags: Severe pre-eclampsia / eclampsia features at any contact — emergency.
Decreased fetal movement / IUGR / abnormal Doppler.
Suspected ectopic / molar pregnancy at early contact.

diagnostics.test: First contact (≤ 12 weeks): dating scan (USS), confirm pregnancy, gestational age, dating; obstetric + medical + family + social history; physical examination; BP, weight, height; blood group + Rh + irregular antibodies; FBC; HIV + syphilis + hepatitis B (Kenya: also malaria + TB symptom screen).
Routine bloods + screening at each visit per protocol: urinalysis for proteinuria + glucose; symphysis-fundal height; fetal heart sounds (Doppler from 12 weeks; pinard 24+ weeks).
OGTT 24-28 weeks for gestational diabetes screening.
Anti-D for RhD-negative women at 28-30 weeks + after sensitising events.
Anomaly USS at 20-24 weeks where available.

management.detail: Comprehensive history + physical; routine bloods; pregnancy + birth-plan counselling; lifestyle (smoking + alcohol + nutrition + folic acid 400 microgram + iron); intimate partner violence routine enquiry; vaccination review (Tdap, influenza, COVID); maternal mental health PHQ-2 screen.

management.step: Contact 2 (20 weeks) — fetal anomaly scan + growth
management.detail: Detailed anomaly USS where available; OGTT planning; review blood results; continue iron + folic acid; reinforce education.
BP + urine + SFH + FHS; FBC repeat; OGTT result review; address concerns; movement counselling.
BP + urine + SFH + FHS; preterm birth risk assessment; anti-D for RhD-neg at 28-30; pertussis vaccination 16-32 weeks; birth-plan discussion.
BP + urine + SFH + FHS; GBS screening (selected); breastfeeding education; postnatal contraception planning; birthing plan finalise.
BP + urine + SFH + FHS; presentation assessment; ECV consideration for breech; finalise birth plan; postnatal mental health planning.
BP + urine + SFH + FHS; induction of labour discussion (41 weeks if no spontaneous); membrane sweeping considered.

Iron + folic acid 400 microgram daily (5 mg if epilepsy / previous NTD / sickle cell disease); calcium 1.5–2 g/day in low-calcium populations; aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks for pre-eclampsia high-risk; tetanus vaccination per protocol; ITN distribution in malaria-endemic Kenya; HIV monitoring + ART continuation; malaria intermittent preventive treatment (IPTp with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine in endemic Kenya regions); nutrition counselling; intimate partner violence screening + support; mental health screening.

Multiple pregnancy; previous LSCS; previous PPH; previous stillbirth / IUFD; gestational diabetes; gestational hypertension; chronic medical conditions; suspected fetal anomaly / IUGR; advanced maternal age; significant social vulnerability.
Free maternity care + transport voucher + community follow-up. Engage community health worker + village health team.

references.label: WHO Recommendations on Antenatal Care for a Positive Pregnancy Experience (2016); Kenya MOH National ANC Guidelines + Linda Mama; FIGO + ACOG

title: WHO postnatal care — mother + newborn
presentation: Postnatal period — first 6 weeks after delivery for mother + newborn.
WHO recommends FOUR postnatal contacts in first 6 weeks: within 24 hours, day 3 (48-72 h), 7-14 days, 6 weeks.
Kenya MOH integrates WHO recommendations with community-level follow-up by trained CHWs.
Highest-mortality period for mother (40% maternal deaths within first day) + newborn (40% neonatal deaths within first day).
redFlags: Maternal: severe haemorrhage, severe headache + vision changes (postpartum eclampsia / cerebral venous sinus thrombosis), fever + offensive lochia (sepsis), severe abdominal pain (uterine atony / retained placenta), respiratory distress (PE / amniotic fluid embolism), severe depression / suicidal ideation, deep vein thrombosis, breast abscess, urinary retention / incontinence.

Newborn: not feeding well, lethargy / floppiness, fast breathing > 60/min, severe chest indrawing, jaundice (especially day 1), fever / hypothermia, convulsions, umbilical infection, low birthweight < 2.5 kg, weight loss > 7%, persistent vomiting.

diagnostics.test: Maternal — BP + temperature + pulse at every contact; weight; pain; lochia colour + amount; uterine involution (height); breast examination; perineal / wound check.

Newborn — temperature + respiratory rate + colour + activity + feeding; weight (track for 7-10% loss + recovery by day 14); umbilical stump; jaundice; reflexes; cardiac auscultation (CCHD pulse-oximetry screen day 1).
diagnostics.rationale: Identify neonatal sepsis / jaundice / heart disease.

diagnostics.test: PHQ-2 / Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale at 6-8 weeks.
Newborn screen heel-prick (PKU, CH, MCAD, CF, SCD, SCID where included).
Maternal FBC if anaemic ANC / postpartum.

management.detail: Maternal: BP + uterus + bleeding + perineum + breast + voiding + mood + breastfeeding success. Newborn: vital signs + feeding + warmth + skin-to-skin (delayed cord clamping + early breastfeeding within 1 h essential). Vitamin K 1 mg IM to newborn. Erythromycin / tetracycline eye prophylaxis. Hepatitis B vaccination (within 24 h). BCG + OPV birth dose per Kenya schedule.

Track 5-10% weight loss in newborn (recovers by day 10-14); check breastfeeding latch + frequency; jaundice (clinical + bilirubin if elevated); fever / hypothermia; maternal bleeding + breastfeeding pain; mental health observation.

Weight recovered to birthweight; routine vaccinations; cord care; maternal recovery + mood (postpartum 'blues' usually peak day 3-5); contraception counselling (LAM, COC after 6 weeks, progesterone-only sooner, copper IUD post-placental, vasectomy + tubal ligation discussion); breast care; resuming activities.

Comprehensive maternal — cardiovascular (BP, postpartum eclampsia surveillance), perineum, urinary + bowel function, pelvic floor, contraception initiation, mental health (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). Newborn — growth + development + feeding + immunisations (Kenya: 6-week visit gets DPT-HepB-Hib + OPV + PCV + Rotavirus).

WHO recommendation: exclusive breastfeeding 6 months + continued breastfeeding to 2 years with complementary feeds. Address common problems: poor latch, sore nipples, mastitis (manage early), perceived insufficient milk, return to work (express + store).

Postpartum 'blues' (day 3-7, self-limiting) → distinguish from postpartum depression (persistent symptoms ≥ 2 weeks). PHQ-2 / Edinburgh PDS screen. Treat depression + anxiety; severe — postpartum psychosis emergency (mother-baby unit).

WHO recommends at least 24-month interval between pregnancies. Postnatal contraception: LAM if exclusively breastfeeding < 6 months + amenorrhoeic + < 6 m postpartum (98% effective). Progestin-only pill / implant / DMPA injection (breastfeeding compatible). Combined OCP > 6 weeks postpartum (not in breastfeeding women < 6 weeks). LARC: copper IUD post-placental; LNG-IUS 6 weeks postpartum; implant any time. Permanent: tubal ligation (postpartum or interval) + vasectomy.
CHW (community health worker) home visits day 1, 3, 7, 28 + 6 weeks. Linkage to Linda Mama free maternity. ITN distribution in malaria-endemic. PMTCT continuation. Birth registration.
Any red flag; severe postpartum depression; ongoing severe pain; significant retained placenta / haemorrhage; suspected sepsis; postpartum eclampsia; newborn dangerous signs.
Newborn: DTP-HepB-Hib + IPV/OPV + PCV + Rotavirus per Kenya schedule. Mother: routine adult vaccinations; HIV testing if not done; family planning initiation.

references.label: WHO Recommendations on Postnatal Care of the Mother + Newborn (2022 update); Kenya MOH Postnatal Care Guidelines

title: Family planning + contraception — comprehensive method-mix counselling
presentation: Patient seeking contraception OR postpartum / post-abortion family planning.
WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) — risk categorisation for each method per medical condition: Category 1 (no restriction) → Category 4 (unacceptable risk).
Kenya MOH family planning: comprehensive method mix, free in public facilities, community-based distribution of pills + condoms by CHWs.
redFlags: Postpartum first 6 weeks — limit oestrogen-containing (VTE risk).
Migraine WITH aura — avoid combined oestrogen-progestogen contraception (stroke risk).
Suspected IPV — discuss covert / undetectable methods (implant, IUD).
Religious / cultural considerations — respect + offer all options.

diagnostics.test: Detailed history — current sexual activity, parity, plans, previous contraception, medical history, BP, BMI, smoking, headaches, breast exam, pelvic exam selective.
Pregnancy exclusion before starting method (LMP > 4 weeks or other reliable exclusion).
STI screen as appropriate (especially adolescent + new partner + symptoms).
Counselling on STI prevention — dual protection (contraception + condom).

management.detail: Most effective (Tier 1, < 1% pregnancy/year typical use): implant (Implanon NXT — 3 years; Jadelle — 5 years), IUD (copper TCu380A — 10-12 years; LNG-IUS Mirena/Kyleena — 6-8 years), sterilisation (female tubal occlusion / vasectomy). Tier 2 (6-9% typical use): DMPA injectable 3-monthly; combined oral contraceptive; progestogen-only pill; combined patch; combined vaginal ring. Tier 3 (12-28%): male / female condom, diaphragm, withdrawal, fertility awareness, lactational amenorrhoea (LAM).

management.step: Long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) — FIRST-LINE for most
management.detail: Implant + IUD: 'fit-and-forget'; highest continuation + lowest unintended pregnancy. Implanon NXT (etonogestrel) — most popular in Kenya; insertion / removal trained provider. Jadelle — 5-year alternative. Copper IUD — non-hormonal; insertion any time including immediate postpartum. LNG-IUS — reduces bleeding; emerging role for menorrhagia + HRT-progestogen.

COC: 21-day or 24-day active; common low-dose 30 microgram ethinyl oestradiol + levonorgestrel / norethisterone. Patch (weekly) + ring (monthly) alternatives. Start any time if reasonably certain not pregnant (quick-start). Counsel re: VTE + ischaemic stroke + breast cancer (small increased) vs benefit. AVOID: migraine with aura, VTE history, smoking > 35 years, BP > 160/100, recent peripartum, breast cancer.

Progestogen-only pill (POP / 'mini-pill') — strict timing; useful where oestrogen contraindicated. Desogestrel-POP (Cerazette) — 12-hour window (more forgiving). DMPA injectable — 3-monthly; convenient; bone density caution (reversible). Subdermal implant Implanon — 3 years; first-line LARC in Kenya.

Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose — within 72 h (less effective 72-120 h). Ulipristal acetate 30 mg — within 120 h, more effective for later use. Copper IUD insertion within 120 h — most effective; can be retained for ongoing contraception.

Tubal ligation (female) — laparoscopic / mini-laparotomy / hysteroscopic (some). Vasectomy (male) — simpler + safer + more cost-effective; counsel 12-week semen test post-op for sterility. Both nearly 100% effective; technically reversible but assume permanent.

Immediate postpartum (within 48 h) IUD + implant. LAM if exclusively breastfeeding + amenorrhoeic + < 6 months. COC after 6 weeks postpartum (NOT in breastfeeding women in first 6 weeks). Post-abortion: contraception can be initiated immediately; addresses unmet need.
Confidential counselling + non-judgmental approach + STI dual protection + Tier 1 LARC offered first. Education + skill-building. Consent considerations + Gillick-competence.

Counsel realistic side-effect expectations (breakthrough bleeding, amenorrhoea, breast tenderness, mood). Switch if intolerable. Address misconceptions (e.g. weight gain less than perceived). Continuation counselling.

management.step: Kenya CBP / CBD + free public-facility provision
management.detail: Community-based pill + condom distribution; integrated post-pregnancy + post-abortion FP; free in public facilities including LARC insertion.

references.label: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use 5th edition (2015); FSRH UK MEC; Kenya MOH National Family Planning Guidelines

title: WHO ETAT — paediatric emergency triage assessment + treatment (Kenya outpatient + hospital)
presentation: Sick child arriving at outpatient department / emergency / health facility — triage decision needed.
ETAT (Emergency Triage Assessment + Treatment) framework: identify emergency signs (need treatment immediately), priority signs (need expedited assessment), non-urgent (queue).
Validated in Kenya + multiple LMIC settings — reduces under-5 mortality in busy outpatient.
redFlags: Circulation — shock, severe pallor + cold extremities.
Severe acute malnutrition with danger signs.

diagnostics.test: Quick visual triage — emergency signs (ABCD + dehydration / convulsion).

Priority signs: tiny baby (< 2 months), temperature (very hot — fever > 39 / very cold), trauma, pallor, poisoning, pain, respiratory distress, restless / continuously irritable / lethargic, referral, urgent (under-nutrition, oedema).
Full IMCI assessment for non-emergency / non-priority — see IMCI pathway.

management.detail: Airway: position, suction, oxygen. Breathing: support, oxygen if SpO2 < 90 (or central cyanosis without saturometer). Circulation: IV / IO access + 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus if shocked (caution in severe febrile illness without shock — FEAST). Disability: glucose for convulsion + treat hypoglycaemia (10% dextrose 5 mL/kg IV). Diarrhoea / severe dehydration: Plan C IV rehydration (per IMCI Plan C). Severe malnutrition: F-75 + cautious resuscitation (different fluid protocols).
Move to front of queue; full IMCI / IMAI assessment within 15-30 minutes.
Full IMCI assessment in turn.
30 seconds per child to identify emergency / priority. Standardised algorithm. Trained staff at entry point. Necessary equipment (oxygen + IV fluids + emergency drugs) immediately available.
Record triage category + intervention + outcomes. Identify systemic issues + training needs.
Children with emergency signs requiring inpatient care, persistent priority signs, social vulnerability.
ETAT incorporated into outpatient department of every level-2 + level-3 facility. CHWs trained for community-level recognition + referral. ETAT-Africa + ETAT+ regional adaptations.

references.label: WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children + ETAT module; Kenya MOH Standard Treatment Guidelines for Paediatrics

title: Kenya malaria policy — diagnosis + treatment + prevention
presentation: Malaria endemic in lake region + coast + parts of western Kenya; epidemic-prone in highlands; low in arid / semi-arid; very low in urban areas.
Predominantly P. falciparum (90%+); P. malariae + P. ovale less common.
All ages affected — under-5 + pregnant women highest morbidity / mortality.
Presents with fever — uncomplicated (asymptomatic — mild) or severe (see severe malaria pathway).
redFlags: Severe malaria features — see severe falciparum malaria pathway.
Pregnant woman with malaria — high risk.
Returning traveller from endemic area within 6 weeks.
Severe anaemia + cerebral malaria + multi-organ failure.

diagnostics.test: RDT — first-line in Kenya. HRP-2 (P. falciparum) + pLDH (pan-malaria) — different commercial kits available.
Thick + thin blood smear (microscopy) — gold standard for confirmation + species + parasitaemia + monitoring.
DO NOT TREAT empirically without confirmation — WHO + Kenya policy.
diagnostics.rationale: Prevents over-treatment + antimalarial pressure for resistance + identifies alternative diagnoses.

management.step: Uncomplicated P. falciparum — artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT)
management.detail: Kenya first-line: Artemether-lumefantrine (AL — 'Coartem') — 6-dose regimen over 3 days. Weight-banded: 5–14 kg 1 tablet; 15–24 kg 2 tablets; 25–34 kg 3 tablets; ≥ 35 kg 4 tablets — each dose × 6 doses at 0, 8, 24, 36, 48, 60 hours. Take with fatty food / milk to improve absorption.
DHA-PPQ alternative. 3-day course. Both AL + DHA-PPQ available in Kenya.

management.step: Severe malaria — IV artesunate (per severe malaria pathway)
management.detail: IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 h then daily until oral. Switch to oral ACT for 3-day course once tolerating. IV artemether OR IV quinine if artesunate unavailable. See severe falciparum malaria pathway.

management.step: P. malariae / P. ovale / P. vivax
management.detail: AL effective for blood-stage. P. ovale + P. vivax also need primaquine 0.25 mg/kg/day × 14 days for hypnozoite clearance (after G6PD screening); P. vivax very rare in Kenya.

1st trimester: quinine + clindamycin for uncomplicated. 2nd + 3rd trimester: ACT (AL) acceptable. Intermittent preventive therapy in pregnancy (IPTp): sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine 3 doses each at least 4 weeks apart starting 2nd trimester (Kenya endemic regions).

Insecticide-treated bednets (ITNs / LLINs) — universal coverage; free distribution + community-based education. Indoor residual spraying (IRS) — targeted high-transmission areas. Larval source management. Vector control. Community health volunteer engagement.

Travellers to endemic areas: atovaquone-proguanil OR mefloquine OR doxycycline. Kenya residents in endemic areas: routine prophylaxis not given (rather ITNs + early case management); pregnant women IPTp.
Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) for under-5 in highly seasonal epidemic regions. School-based malaria control programmes.
RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine — being rolled out in Kenya pilot + scale-up. R21/Matrix-M — recently licensed; complementary to vector + treatment measures.
Notifiable disease in Kenya. Active case detection in epidemic-prone areas. CHV-supported test-treat-track approach.

references.label: Kenya MOH National Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment + Prevention of Malaria; WHO Guidelines for Malaria

title: Kenya National Tuberculosis Programme — diagnosis + treatment
presentation: Kenya has high TB burden — 7th highest in Africa; estimated 558 per 100,000 population; high HIV + TB co-infection.
Common presentation: cough > 2 weeks + fever + night sweats + weight loss + anorexia.
Extra-pulmonary common: lymph node, pleural, miliary, abdominal, CNS, spinal (Pott's), genitourinary.
Paediatric TB: contact history + chronic illness + failure to thrive + chronic cough.
Kenya focus on case-finding + DOT + adherence + outcome tracking.
redFlags: Suspected drug-resistant TB — prior treatment failure / contact with known DR-TB / treatment default.
TB meningitis / disseminated / miliary — high mortality.
Concurrent HIV + TB — see advanced HIV pathway.

diagnostics.test: Cough ≥ 2 weeks — collect 2 sputum samples (spot + early morning) for Xpert MTB/RIF + microscopy + culture.
Xpert MTB/RIF as primary diagnostic — rapid (~2 hours) + rifampicin resistance detection. Kenya rollout extensive.
Sputum microscopy (Ziehl-Neelsen) — where Xpert not available; serial samples.

diagnostics.rationale: Pattern supports TB (upper-lobe cavities, miliary, hilar adenopathy).

diagnostics.test: HIV testing — mandatory for ALL TB patients in Kenya.
FBC + U&E + LFT + creatinine + diabetes screen.
Paediatric: Mantoux + contact tracing + paediatric Xpert + chest X-ray + (often empirical given diagnostic difficulty).

management.detail: Intensive phase: 2 months HRZE (isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol) daily. Continuation phase: 4 months HR daily. Weight-banded FDC (fixed-dose combination) tablets per Kenya formulary.
Family / community-based DOT — Kenya emphasis. CHV-supported daily observation. Treatment supporter selected by patient + community.

management.step: Pyridoxine 25-50 mg daily for all on isoniazid
management.detail: Prevent peripheral neuropathy; especially HIV + diabetic + malnourished + pregnant.
Clinical + weight + adherence + side effects. Sputum smear at end of intensive phase (month 2) — if positive, repeat at month 3 + 5; if month 5 positive — treatment failure → DR-TB workup.

Hepatotoxicity: stop all hepatotoxic (HRZ); ethambutol + streptomycin / fluoroquinolone bridge; rechallenge sequentially (rifampicin first, then isoniazid, then pyrazinamide); permanent withdrawal of agent triggering ALT > 5× ULN. Optic neuritis: stop ethambutol. Visual changes — ophthalmology. Skin rash: antihistamine; severe (SJS/TEN) — stop.

Start ART within 2 weeks if CD4 < 50; within 8 weeks if higher. Preferred regimen: TLD (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir) — adjust dolutegravir to 50 mg BD with rifampicin. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. PJP screen. ART continuation after TB cure.

Kenya National DR-TB Programme — specialist centres. BPaL or BPaLM 6-month regimen per WHO 2022 / Kenya adaptation: bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid ± moxifloxacin × 6 months. Longer individualised regimens for complex resistance. Strict adherence + monthly QTc + LFT + visual + audiometric monitoring.

Outcome categories: cured (negative culture + symptoms gone), treatment completed, treatment failure, died, lost to follow-up, transferred out. Cohort analysis 6 + 12 months. Target > 90% treatment success.

Household + close contacts screened — < 5 years + HIV-positive contacts: TPT (3HP — isoniazid + rifapentine weekly × 12 weeks; OR 6 months daily isoniazid). Universal TPT for PLHIV regardless of contact (Kenya policy). Symptomatic contacts: full TB workup.

Pregnancy: standard regimen; pyridoxine + vitamin K (prevent neonatal bleeding). Children: weight-banded paediatric formulations + 6-month regimen; BPaLM increasingly considered. Severe drug-resistant TB: specialist management.

National Tuberculosis, Leprosy + Lung Disease Program oversight. Free TB diagnosis + treatment in public facilities. Community DOTS + adherence support. Patient tracing for default. Drug supply chain + quality assurance.

references.label: WHO consolidated TB guidelines (multiple modules); Kenya National TB Programme guidelines; Kenya NTLD Strategic Plan

title: Kenya HIV testing services + PrEP + treatment access
presentation: Patient seeking HIV testing — provider-initiated testing + counselling (PITC), voluntary counselling + testing (VCT), index testing of contacts, self-testing, ART entry point.

Kenya context: ~1.4 million people living with HIV; mature programme — high coverage of testing + ART + PrEP; concentrated epidemic in key populations (FSW, MSM, IDU); generalised in coastal + lake regions.
PrEP available in Kenya since 2017 — adolescent girls + young women, key populations, serodiscordant couples.
redFlags: Acute HIV / seroconversion illness — Ag/Ab combo testing + viral load.
Pregnant woman with positive HIV — PMTCT pathway + ART within 7 days.
Advanced HIV (CD4 < 200 or WHO stage 3/4) — AHD package.
TB + HIV co-infection — concurrent treatment timing.
PrEP candidate not eligible (active HIV / hepatitis B / renal insufficiency).
Suspected sexual / gender-based violence — post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) within 72 h.

diagnostics.test: First test: rapid test (HIV1/2 antibody — Determine + KHB / Trinity / Unigold per Kenya algorithm).
Confirmatory: second rapid test (different antigen / format) per Kenya algorithm. Tiebreaker if needed.
Acute HIV / window-period: 4th-generation Ag/Ab combo + viral load.
HIV self-test (HIVST) — oral fluid or fingerprick; community-distributed in Kenya.
diagnostics.rationale: Expand access; high sensitivity + specificity but needs confirmation.

diagnostics.test: Post-test: CD4 + HIV viral load + hepatitis B / C / syphilis + TB symptom screen + ART resistance testing if clinically indicated.
Kenya: integration with antenatal care + sexual + reproductive health + outpatient department + community.

management.step: Positive test — immediate linkage to care
management.detail: Pre-ART preparation: comprehensive counselling + disclosure support + adherence counselling + partner / family contact tracing. ART initiation: same-day OR within 7 days (Kenya same-day initiation since 2018). Preferred first-line: TLD (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir).

First-line: TLD. Alternatives for intolerance / interactions: TDF/FTC/EFV → TLD switch; TAF/FTC/DTG. Children: paediatric weight-banded formulations. Monitoring: viral load at 6 months + then annually. CD4 monitoring routinely at baseline; less frequent on suppressed ART. Suspect failure: VL > 1000 copies/mL — adherence counselling + re-check at 3 months; if still > 1000 + second-line.

Co-trimoxazole 960 mg daily for ALL adults + children CD4 < 350 (or all in high TB-malaria burden settings). TB preventive therapy (3HP / 6H) for ALL PLHIV after active TB excluded. Cryptococcal antigen screen for CD4 < 200 — pre-emptive fluconazole if positive.
See advanced-hiv-disease-adult pathway — full WHO AHD package.

Kenya PrEP eligibility: high-risk negative individuals — adolescent girls + young women in high prevalence settings, sex workers, MSM, PWID, serodiscordant couples (with positive partner not virally suppressed), recent STI / multiple partners. Regimens: oral TDF/FTC (Truvada) daily — Kenya first-line. Long-acting cabotegravir injection (CAB-LA) IM every 2 months — emerging access. Dapivirine vaginal ring — alternative for women. On-demand 2-1-1 PrEP for MSM (specific context).
Within 72 hours of exposure (occupational, sexual, sexual assault). TDF/FTC/DTG × 28 days. HIV test baseline + 6 weeks + 12 weeks + 6 months. Counsel + adherence support.

All HIV-positive pregnant women: lifelong ART (TLD or TLE per regimen). Infant prophylaxis: nevirapine (high-risk infant) OR AZT depending on maternal status + viral load + breastfeeding decision. Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months OR exclusive formula feeding (mother's decision with counselling). Postpartum maternal continuation + infant follow-up.
Active contact tracing + testing of sexual + needle-sharing partners of newly diagnosed people; assisted partner notification supported by Kenya MOH.
WHO + Kenya scale-up: 60% reduction in female-to-male HIV transmission. Free in public facilities + community campaigns. Integration with HIV testing + STI screening + condom counselling.

management.step: Kenya National HIV/STI Programme + DREAMS partnership
management.detail: Free HIV testing + ART + PrEP. DREAMS programme for adolescent girls + young women (HIV prevention + economic empowerment + education). KEPHIA Kenya population-based surveys monitor progress.

references.label: Kenya MOH National AIDS + STI Control Programme (NASCOP) Guidelines (latest); WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services + ART + PrEP

title: STI syndromic management — WHO + Kenya detailed pathway
presentation: Patient presenting with sexual / reproductive symptoms — syndromic approach used widely in primary care + low-resource settings where lab confirmation unavailable.
Syndromes: urethral discharge (male), vaginal discharge, lower abdominal pain (female), genital ulcer, scrotal swelling, inguinal bubo, neonatal conjunctivitis.
WHO + Kenya STI syndromic management — covers common bacterial + protozoal causes with empirical antibiotic combinations.
redFlags: Pelvic inflammatory disease severity — abscess, sepsis, peritonitis.
Suspected sexual abuse / violence — see specific pathway + PEP + emergency contraception.
Pregnancy + STI — fetal risk; adjust regimen.
Suspected HIV + STI co-infection — testing offered.
Recurrent infection — confirm partner treatment + drug resistance + behavioural risk.
Suspected disseminated gonorrhoea / syphilis — systemic features.

diagnostics.test: History — symptoms onset, sexual history, prior infection, partner notification, allergy.
Physical examination — genitalia + bimanual / speculum (female) + lymph nodes + skin.
Where lab available: urine NAAT for gonorrhoea + chlamydia; urethral / cervical / vaginal / rectal swabs; syphilis serology (RPR / VDRL + treponemal); HIV test; hepatitis B + C; HSV PCR.
Where lab unavailable: syndromic approach per WHO algorithm.

management.detail: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose + doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days. Pregnancy: ceftriaxone + azithromycin 1 g single dose (replace doxycycline).

management.step: Vaginal discharge — broader cover (gonorrhoea, chlamydia, trichomonas, candida, BV)
management.detail: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days + metronidazole 2 g single dose + clotrimazole intravaginal 500 mg single dose. Risk-assess for gonorrhoea / chlamydia inclusion.

EXCLUDE: ectopic pregnancy, surgical abdomen, abscess. Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days + metronidazole 400 mg BD × 14 days. Severe / pregnant / refractory: hospital admission + IV therapy. See severe PID pathway.

management.step: Genital ulcer — syphilis + chancroid + HSV cover
management.detail: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose (primary / secondary / early latent syphilis) + ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose for chancroid + aciclovir 400 mg TDS × 7 days (or specific HSV-related regimen). Pregnancy: erythromycin / azithromycin alternative for chancroid; penicillin desensitisation for severe penicillin allergy + syphilis.
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days. Exclude torsion (urgent surgical consult if young + acute onset).

management.step: Inguinal bubo (with / without ulcer) — lymphogranuloma venereum + chancroid
management.detail: Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 21 days (LGV) + treat associated ulcer.

Newborn with discharge: ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM single dose (max 125 mg) — gonococcal cover; erythromycin syrup 12.5 mg/kg QID × 14 days (chlamydial cover). Prophylaxis at birth: 1% tetracycline / erythromycin eye ointment OR povidone-iodine 2.5% drops universally.

Treat all sexual contacts in past 3-6 months — even if asymptomatic — to prevent reinfection + onward transmission. Anonymous notification options (Kenya: provider-assisted referral). Counselling + condom education.
All STI presentations — opportunity to offer comprehensive sexual + reproductive health screen. Repeat at 3 + 6 months for high-risk.
Condom use education + demonstration. Vaccination (hepatitis B, HPV, varicella). Brief intervention for risk reduction. PrEP discussion for high-risk.

Gonorrhoea: monitor for cephalosporin + azithromycin resistance — surveillance via Kenya MOH. Update protocols if resistance emerges. Treatment failure → repeat testing + culture / NAAT + susceptibility.

Test of cure at 1-4 weeks for gonorrhoea / chlamydia (selective). Syphilis: RPR / VDRL titres at 3 + 6 + 12 months. HIV / hepatitis screening at 3 + 6 months. Behavioural / risk-reduction reinforcement.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Management of STIs (2021); Kenya MOH National Guidelines for STI Care + Management (2018, updated 2021)

title: Intimate partner violence — screening + response in primary care
presentation: Patient at risk of / experiencing intimate partner violence — physical, sexual, emotional / psychological, financial, controlling, stalking, technology-facilitated.
Pregnant women particularly affected — escalates often during pregnancy.
Lifetime prevalence in Kenya — ~40% women experience IPV.
Often-missed presentations: chronic pelvic / abdominal pain, depression, anxiety, PTSD, somatic symptoms, suicide attempt, repeated injury, repeated STI, recurrent pregnancy loss.
WHO + Kenya MOH recommend universal screening in antenatal + sexual + reproductive health + emergency + mental health.
redFlags: Immediate safety risk — child / partner threatening; weapon present; recent escalation; strangulation history (high risk of homicide).
Child also at risk — child protection notification.
Severe mental health — suicide ideation; severe PTSD; substance use.
Geographical isolation / migration / refugee — limited support access.
Disclosure should NOT trigger forced reporting (varies by jurisdiction); patient-led + consent-based.

diagnostics.test: Routine enquiry — non-judgmental + private + during established trust.
Validated screen — HITS, WAST, AAS, Composite Abuse Scale.
Asses ImmediateRisk: weapon access, strangulation, escalation, control, jealousy, threats, financial control, social isolation.
STI screen + pregnancy test + contraception review.
Injury documentation (drawings + photos + descriptions) if requested.

management.detail: Listen — actively + empathetically. Inquire about needs + concerns. Validate experience. Enhance safety. Support follow-up.
Use affirming language: 'You did not cause this' + 'You are not to blame' + 'This was not your fault' + 'Many people experience this'.

Discuss safe place to go in emergency; pack 'go bag' (documents, money, medications, phone, children's needs); identify emergency contact + safe word; review household weapons; technology safety (different password, location tracking off, separate email).

Treat injuries; emergency contraception + STI prophylaxis + HIV PEP within 72 h if sexual assault; document carefully; offer forensic examination + medico-legal documentation (no forced reporting unless mandated). Pregnancy + IPV — augmented antenatal care + safety + neonatal.
Treat depression / anxiety / PTSD. Trauma-focused CBT once safe. Cognitive processing therapy. Avoid encouraging premature return to relationship. Substance use co-treatment.

Refer to IPV-specialist services: domestic violence shelter / refuge; legal aid; counselling; social work; police (with patient consent). Kenya: National Council for Gender + Development; Gender-Based Violence Recovery Centres at major hospitals; Polysensitive Recovery Centres.
Children witnessing IPV — psychological harm; child protection notification per jurisdiction. Kenya: Children Officer + Department of Children Services.
Multidisciplinary antenatal care + augmented monitoring + safety. IPV increases pre-eclampsia + preterm birth + LBW + postpartum depression.
Community-based women's groups + economic empowerment + skill-building. Kenya: SAUTI ya Wanawake; HAKI Africa; AMHF; FIDA Kenya legal aid.
Vicarious trauma in providers; supervision + debrief. IPV-response training for all primary care providers (Kenya MOH guidelines).
Schedule follow-up; do not pressure for decisions; respect autonomy; non-judgmental approach throughout.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Health Sector Response to IPV + Sexual Violence Against Women (2014); Kenya National Policy + Plan of Action on Elimination of Gender-Based Violence

title: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis — Kenya MOH protocol
presentation: Patient with potential rabies exposure — bite, scratch, or mucous-membrane / open-wound contact with saliva from suspect / known rabid animal (dog most common in Kenya; cats, bats, jackals, hyenas, mongooses).
Kenya context: dog rabies endemic; ~2000 human deaths annually estimated; rural + peri-urban exposure common.
Once clinical signs appear — 100% fatal; prevention via post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) critical.

WHO categories: I (touch / lick on intact skin) — no PEP; II (minor scratch / abrasion without bleeding) — vaccine; III (bite / scratch with bleeding / mucosa / multiple wounds / immunocompromised) — vaccine + rabies immunoglobulin (RIG).
redFlags: Category III exposure — RIG essential + vaccine.
Severe wound — bleeding, deep, multiple bites, face, neck, hands.
Vaccination already started elsewhere — continue with appropriate schedule.
Suspected rabid animal — quarantine / observe (dogs / cats) per protocol; humane testing if available.
Pregnancy is NOT a contraindication to PEP.

diagnostics.test: Detailed exposure history — animal species, vaccination status, behaviour (provoked vs unprovoked attack), suspect rabies signs (foaming, aggression, paralysis), location, type of contact.
Wound assessment — type, depth, location, severity.
Animal observation / quarantine (10 days for dogs + cats in Kenya).
diagnostics.rationale: If animal remains healthy, suspect rabies excluded.

diagnostics.test: Animal testing (laboratory confirmation) — if available; dRIT / FAT.

management.step: Immediate wound care — paramount FIRST step
management.detail: Wash wound thoroughly with soap + water for 15 MINUTES; rinse with normal saline. Apply povidone-iodine OR 70% alcohol. Do NOT suture wound primarily (delayed primary closure); leave open for drainage. Avoid suturing where possible (especially in cat / category III); irrigate copiously.

Tetanus toxoid OR Td if last dose > 5 years OR uncertain. Antibiotic for cat bites (50% infection) — co-amoxiclav 625 mg TDS × 5-7 days OR doxycycline 100 mg BD. Dog bite if deep / contaminated / immunocompromised — co-amoxiclav.

management.step: Category I exposure (no broken skin / saliva on intact skin)
management.detail: No PEP required. Reassurance + wound care + observation.

management.step: Category II exposure (minor scratch / nibble without bleeding / lick on broken skin)
management.detail: VACCINE only. Kenya WHO updated 2-dose intradermal protocol: 0.1 mL × 2 sites days 0 + 3 + 7 (Essen IM regimen 1 mL into deltoid days 0, 3, 7, 14 / 28 alternative). Verocell-derived purified rabies vaccine commonly available.

management.step: Category III exposure (bite / scratch with bleeding / mucosa / immunocompromised)
management.detail: VACCINE + RABIES IMMUNOGLOBULIN (RIG). Vaccine: same schedule as Category II. RIG: 20 IU/kg HUMAN rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG) OR 40 IU/kg EQUINE (ERIG, more available in Kenya — skin test for hypersensitivity). Infiltrate AROUND wound + surrounding tissue — as much as wound permits; ANY REMAINDER given IM at site distant from vaccine.

management.step: Previously vaccinated patient (pre-exposure prophylaxis OR previous full PEP)
management.detail: VACCINE booster: 2 doses days 0 + 3 (no RIG needed).

Dogs / cats — quarantine 10 days. If animal remains healthy at 10 days — exposure unlikely rabid + can STOP vaccination (or complete short course). If animal develops illness OR dies — continue full PEP + test brain. Wild / unidentifiable / stray — treat as if rabid + complete PEP.
All doses essential — vaccine has very high efficacy when completed timely. Counsel patient on importance of adherence.
Pregnancy: PEP safe + effective. Immunocompromised: complete IM Essen regimen + RIG essential. Infants: same dosing; gentle wound care.

Recommended for: laboratory workers + animal handlers + cavers + travellers to highly endemic areas with limited PEP access + children in rabies-endemic regions. WHO 2-dose intradermal schedule days 0 + 7. Periodic serological monitoring + boosters for ongoing risk.

Free PEP in public health facilities. Community education on dog vaccination + dog population management. National rabies elimination strategy targeting 'zero by 30' (zero human rabies deaths by 2030).

references.label: WHO Rabies Vaccines + Immunoglobulins Position Paper (2018, updated); Kenya MOH National Rabies Control Programme; Kenya Veterinary Vaccines Production Institute

title: Kenya Essential Medicines List + WHO Model EML — primary care formulary
presentation: Kenya Essential Medicines List (KEML) — official formulary; aligned with WHO Model EML (2023, 23rd list); updated periodically.
Categorised by level of care: primary care + sub-county / county hospital + tertiary.
Free / subsidised access via public health facilities + community-based services (CHV-distributed).
Underpins universal health coverage (UHC) + Linda Mama + Beyond Zero campaign + national hospital insurance fund (NHIF).
redFlags: Medicine stockout — critical for emergency / chronic disease control.
Substandard / falsified medicines — Kenya MOH quality assurance through Pharmacy + Poisons Board.
Off-formulary medications — require justification + special procurement.
Antimicrobial resistance — irrational use of unrestricted prescription.
Patient unable to afford non-formulary alternative — adjust to formulary.

diagnostics.test: Knowledge of EML for level of care + age (adult / paediatric).
Renal + hepatic function for dose adjustment.

management.step: Essential medicines by therapeutic class — high-impact + cost-effective
management.detail: Cardiovascular: amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril, atenolol, atorvastatin, aspirin, furosemide. Diabetes: metformin, glibenclamide, gliclazide, insulin (NPH + soluble + premixed). Respiratory: salbutamol + ipratropium + beclomethasone inhalers, prednisolone. Infectious disease: amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, doxycycline, azithromycin, ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, artemether-lumefantrine, tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir. Mental health: amitriptyline, fluoxetine, haloperidol, olanzapine, diazepam, carbamazepine, valproate, phenytoin, lithium. Pain: paracetamol, ibuprofen, morphine, codeine + paracetamol. Cancer: vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, cisplatin, paclitaxel, tamoxifen, imatinib. Endocrine: levothyroxine, hydrocortisone, prednisolone, dexamethasone, oestradiol patch, levonorgestrel implant, copper IUD. Other: oral rehydration salts, zinc tablets, vitamin K (newborn), iron + folic acid, calcium, magnesium, salbutamol nebules.

Right drug, right dose, right duration, right indication, right cost. Generic prescribing where applicable. Avoid polypharmacy + over-prescribing antibiotics. Patient counselling on adherence + adverse effects.
Kenya National Action Plan on AMR — restricted antibiotic prescribing. Use of guidelines + reserved antibiotics requiring approval. Surveillance of resistance patterns.
KEMSA (Kenya Medical Supplies Authority) — central procurement + distribution. Track stockouts; emergency procurement when needed.
Pharmacy + Poisons Board — quality, safety, efficacy monitoring. Report adverse drug reactions through Kenya Pharmacovigilance Centre.
NHIF coverage for essential medicines. Linda Mama + Beyond Zero campaigns address maternal + child health medicines. UHC expansion.
Vigilance — patient-empowerment + provider education + supply-chain integrity + community awareness.
MOH-supported training + clinical audit of prescribing practices + feedback loops.
Paediatric formulations (suspensions, scored tablets, weight-banded). Pregnancy + breastfeeding considerations. Renal + hepatic dosing.

references.label: Kenya National Medicines Policy + Kenya Essential Medicines List (most recent update); WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (23rd 2023); KEMSA

title: WHO AWaRe antibiotic stewardship — primary care + hospital
presentation: Clinical decision involving antibiotic prescribing across all settings.
AWaRe (Access, Watch, Reserve) framework launched WHO 2017; embedded in WHO Essential Medicines List + Kenya AMR National Action Plan + Kenya EML.

ACCESS antibiotics (first-choice): amoxicillin, ampicillin, benzylpenicillin, phenoxymethylpenicillin, flucloxacillin, cefalexin, cefazolin, doxycycline, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, metronidazole, gentamicin, nitrofurantoin, clindamycin (selected).

WATCH antibiotics (broader spectrum, more resistance concern): macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin), fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin), 3rd / 4th-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone, cefepime), carbapenems (meropenem, ertapenem), piperacillin-tazobactam, vancomycin (IV), linezolid.

RESERVE antibiotics (last-resort, multidrug-resistant infections): ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, colistin, daptomycin, fosfomycin IV, plazomicin, polymyxin B, tigecycline, fidaxomicin.
redFlags: Sepsis requiring empirical broad-spectrum — escalate then de-escalate.
Antibiotic-resistant infection — culture-driven; reserved antibiotics only with susceptibility.

diagnostics.test: Confirm infection — clinical + investigation (CRP, WBC, urinalysis, cultures, imaging) before antibiotic where possible.
Culture + sensitivities BEFORE antibiotic where feasible.

diagnostics.rationale: Empirical choice based on local resistance data.

diagnostics.test: Allergy history clarification (true allergy vs intolerance).
Renal / hepatic / weight + height for dose adjustment.

management.step: First-line Access antibiotic for community-acquired infection
management.detail: WHO target: ≥ 60% of antibiotic use should be from ACCESS category. Examples: community-acquired pneumonia — amoxicillin; uncomplicated UTI — nitrofurantoin / trimethoprim; cellulitis — flucloxacillin; pharyngitis (group A strep) — phenoxymethylpenicillin; chlamydia — doxycycline; helicobacter eradication — amoxicillin + clarithromycin + PPI.

management.step: Watch antibiotic — reserve for specific indications
management.detail: Ceftriaxone: hospital-acquired pneumonia, gonorrhoea, meningitis, severe community infection. Azithromycin: chlamydia, atypical pneumonia, trachoma MDA. Ciprofloxacin: complicated UTI, traveller's diarrhoea, bone / joint, severe shigella. Restrict + audit; not first-line for ambulatory infection.

management.step: Reserve antibiotic — strict criteria + senior approval
management.detail: Multidrug-resistant organisms confirmed on susceptibility (carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae, MRSA, VRE, ESBL); failure of conventional + culture-defined; ID consultant approval. NOT empirical.

management.step: Duration — shorter is better (where evidence supports)
management.detail: Community-acquired pneumonia: 5 days (often previously 7-10). Uncomplicated UTI: 3 days (nitrofurantoin) or 5 days (trimethoprim). Cellulitis: 5-7 days. Sinusitis: 5-7 days. Tonsillitis (GAS): 10 days (full course). Endocarditis: 4-6 weeks. Osteomyelitis: 6 weeks.
Once culture + susceptibility known, narrow spectrum; switch to oral when stable; complete course.

Hand hygiene (most important infection prevention); vaccination (reduce infection burden); avoid antibiotic in viral / self-limiting illness; non-antibiotic alternatives (saline nasal irrigation for sinusitis, fluids + rest for viral); patient education on prudent use; consider delayed prescriptions in select cases.

Kenya AMR National Action Plan + KEMSA + Antimicrobial Stewardship Programme — facility-level monitoring + audit. Local + national antibiogram dissemination. Continuing medical education + prescribing audit.

Multidisciplinary antimicrobial stewardship team (pharmacist + ID + microbiology + infection control); restricted formulary; pre-prescription authorisation; post-prescription review; clinical guidelines + protocols; education + behaviour change.

Kenya Antimicrobial Resistance Containment Committee (KARCC); routine resistance reporting (GLASS — Global Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance); facility AMR / consumption monitoring; outbreak detection.

references.label: WHO AWaRe Classification (2021 update); WHO Essential Medicines List 2023; Kenya National AMR Policy + AMR Action Plan; GLASS reports

title: WHO Triple elimination of mother-to-child transmission — HIV + syphilis + hepatitis B (Kenya pathway)
presentation: Pregnant woman receiving antenatal care — universal testing for HIV + syphilis + hepatitis B as part of WHO + Kenya MOH triple elimination strategy.
WHO targets ≥ 95% antenatal testing + ≥ 90% treatment coverage for elimination of MTCT — paths to validation for individual diseases + combined.
Kenya MOH implementing through PMTCT programme + Linda Mama + integration with antenatal care.
redFlags: Late-presentation / unbooked HIV-positive pregnancy — urgent ART + neonatal prophylaxis.
Active maternal syphilis with raised RPR + symptoms — emergency treatment to prevent congenital syphilis (stillbirth, neonatal death, congenital syphilis).
HBeAg-positive / high viral load HBV mother — tenofovir from 28 weeks + neonatal HBIG + accelerated immunisation.
Co-infection (HIV + syphilis; HIV + hepatitis B) — combined management.
Failed PMTCT (HIV transmission in infant despite intervention) — pediatric ART + investigation.

diagnostics.test: HIV: rapid test as part of routine ANC; if positive — confirmatory test + viral load + CD4.
Syphilis: rapid plasma reagin (RPR) / venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) + treponemal antibody test.
Hepatitis B: HBsAg testing; if positive — HBeAg + viral load + LFTs.
diagnostics.rationale: Identify active HBV + assess transmission risk.

diagnostics.test: Re-test in 3rd trimester if initial negative + high-risk.
Postnatal infant testing per protocol: HIV PCR at 6 weeks + 6 months + 12 months OR 18 months; syphilis serology + RPR; HBsAg + anti-HBc at 9-12 months.

management.detail: Opt-out testing for HIV + syphilis + hepatitis B at first ANC contact (per Kenya MOH protocol). Confidential + voluntary + with informed consent. Pre + post-test counselling. Repeat in 3rd trimester for high-risk.

management.step: HIV-positive pregnancy — Option B+ lifelong ART
management.detail: Start ART within 7 days of diagnosis (same-day if possible). Kenya first-line: TLD (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir). Continue lifelong. Viral load at 36 weeks ideally < 50 copies/mL. Infant antiretroviral prophylaxis per WHO + Kenya 2021 — nevirapine for high-risk infants ± dual prophylaxis with zidovudine.

Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose for primary, secondary, early-latent (< 1 year). Late-latent + unknown duration: 3 weekly doses. Allergic + pregnant: DESENSITISATION + penicillin (no alternative as effective for congenital syphilis prevention; doxycycline contraindicated in pregnancy). Repeat RPR at delivery + monitor titres to assess response.

management.step: Hepatitis B-positive pregnancy — tenofovir + neonatal interventions
management.detail: HBeAg-positive OR HBV DNA > 200,000 IU/mL: start tenofovir from week 28 to reduce viral load + transmission. ALL HBsAg-positive pregnancies: neonatal hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth + hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) within 12 hours (where available); continue routine HBV vaccination at 6 + 10 + 14 weeks per Kenya schedule.

HIV + syphilis: prioritise treatment of both — penicillin G + ART. HIV + HBV: TLD (tenofovir-containing) covers both. Triple-positive: lifelong ART + benzathine penicillin + HBV treatment + neonatal-specific prophylaxis.

HIV: vaginal delivery preferred if viral suppressed; LSCS if VL > 1000 at 36 weeks or detectable. AVOID prolonged labour + invasive obstetric procedures (FBS, instrumental). Antiretroviral cover during labour. Continue ART postpartum lifelong. Syphilis: vaginal delivery; manage as usual. HBV: vaginal delivery acceptable; ensure neonatal vaccine + HBIG.

HIV-exposed infant: prophylaxis 6-12 weeks (nevirapine + zidovudine), PCR at 6 weeks + 6 months + 12 months; breastfeeding with continued mother ART (preferred over formula in resource-limited where formula not safely possible); co-trimoxazole from 6 weeks. Syphilis-exposed: examine + investigate; treat if confirmed (penicillin per congenital syphilis protocol). HBV-exposed: vaccine within 24 hours + HBIG + complete schedule.
Lifelong ART. Lifelong hepatitis B antiviral if indicated. Repeat syphilis serology at 6, 12, 24 months to monitor response. Family planning + future-pregnancy planning.

WHO triple elimination criteria: low / declining incidence of MTCT for each disease; ≥ 95% antenatal coverage; ≥ 90% treatment coverage; data quality + monitoring. Kenya progressing toward validation.
Linda Mama coverage + CHV-supported testing + adherence + follow-up. Reduce stigma + improve retention in care. Integration of HIV + syphilis + HBV testing into routine ANC.

references.label: WHO Triple Elimination of MTCT framework (2017, with updates); Kenya MOH PMTCT National Guidelines; CDC + UNICEF dual elimination guidance

title: Mass drug administration — preventive chemotherapy + vitamin A campaigns
presentation: Mass drug administration (MDA) campaigns for: soil-transmitted helminths (Ascaris, Trichuris, hookworm); schistosomiasis; trachoma (azithromycin); lymphatic filariasis (DEC + albendazole); onchocerciasis (ivermectin); vitamin A supplementation for children 6-59 months.
Kenya: NTD national programme + school-based deworming + community-based; integrated into immunisation + nutrition campaigns + Vitamin A days.
Target populations: children + women of reproductive age + endemic-area residents.
redFlags: Suspected severe acute malnutrition in MDA recipient — treat malnutrition first.
Concurrent acute illness — defer routine MDA.
Suspected Loa loa endemic + ivermectin — encephalopathy risk; pre-MDA screening.
Pregnancy + MDA — albendazole + mebendazole + DEC + praziquantel safety + dose modifications per WHO.
Adverse drug reaction — Mazzotti for filaria / itch / fever; manage symptomatically.

diagnostics.test: Sentinel site monitoring — stool parasitology for STH + S. mansoni; urine for S. haematobium; nodule + skin snip for onchocerciasis.
diagnostics.rationale: Track MDA impact + transition to elimination.

diagnostics.test: Vitamin A coverage monitoring + child age + height + weight.

management.detail: Albendazole 400 mg (children 12-24 months: 200 mg) single dose OR mebendazole 500 mg single dose, twice yearly in high-prevalence areas (≥ 50%) — annually for moderate (20-49%). Target: preschool (1-4 years) + school-age (5-14 years) + women of childbearing age. Kenya school-based deworming days integrated with WASH education.

Praziquantel 40 mg/kg single dose. Frequency depends on prevalence: ≥ 50% — annually in all school-age + adults at risk; 10-49% — annually for school-age + adults at risk; < 10% — selective treatment. Kenya endemic regions (lake + western).

Albendazole 400 mg + diethylcarbamazine (DEC) 6 mg/kg OR ivermectin 200 microgram/kg + albendazole 400 mg, annually × 5-7 years in endemic areas. Kenya: targeted MDA + transmission assessment surveys. Severe cases — lymphoedema + hydrocele management.

Ivermectin 150 microgram/kg single dose annually (twice yearly in some areas) for ≥ 15 years to interrupt transmission. AVOID in Loa loa co-endemic without screening (encephalopathy risk). Kenya: low onchocerciasis burden but neighbouring regions affected.

Surgery for trichiasis + Antibiotics (azithromycin 20 mg/kg single dose OR tetracycline eye ointment, annual MDA in endemic communities) + Facial cleanliness + Environmental improvement (water + latrines). Kenya: targeted areas (Kajiado, Narok, etc.) + integrated with WASH.

Children 6-11 months: 100,000 IU oral single dose every 6 months. Children 12-59 months: 200,000 IU oral single dose every 6 months. Postpartum women in deficient areas: 200,000 IU within 6 weeks. Kenya: Maternal + Child Health Week + Vitamin A days + integration with immunisation. Reduces under-5 mortality 24% + measles mortality 50% + diarrhoea mortality.

Pregnant women: iron 30-60 mg + folic acid 0.4 mg daily throughout pregnancy. Children 6-23 months in high-prevalence anaemia: iron-fortified MNP (micronutrient powders) OR iron 10-12.5 mg daily × 3 months/year. Adolescent girls: 60 mg iron + 0.4 mg folic acid weekly. Kenya: nutritional programme integration.

management.step: Combined MDA campaigns — Maternal + Child Health Week
management.detail: Integrated delivery: vitamin A + deworming albendazole + immunisation catch-up + growth monitoring + nutrition education + WASH messaging. Community health worker delivery + outreach. Twice-yearly campaigns in Kenya. School-based delivery for school-age.
Coverage targets ≥ 75%. Sentinel site evaluation. Transmission assessment surveys (LF). Trachoma + onchocerciasis impact assessments. Post-MDA surveillance for re-emergence.

Albendazole / mebendazole: well-tolerated; rare abdominal pain. Praziquantel: nausea + abdominal pain + dizziness (more in heavily-infected). Ivermectin: Mazzotti reaction in onchocerciasis (pruritus, rash, fever); Loa loa encephalopathy in co-endemic. DEC: systemic + ocular reactions in onchocerciasis (so AVOID DEC in oncho-endemic). Vitamin A: very high doses can cause hypervitaminosis A; counsel.
Drug delivery alone insufficient — combine with: latrine construction + use + handwashing + safe water + footwear + behavioural change communication for sustained impact + breaking transmission.

references.label: WHO Guideline: Preventive chemotherapy to control STH (2017); WHO Schistosomiasis preventive chemotherapy (2022); WHO Vitamin A supplementation in infants + children 6-59 months (2011); Kenya MOH NTD Strategic Plan

title: WHO ICOPE — integrated care for older people + healthy aging
presentation: Older adult (≥ 60) attending primary care for health maintenance / chronic disease management.
WHO Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) framework: shift from disease-by-disease to function-centred care.
Six domains of intrinsic capacity: cognition, mobility, vitality (malnutrition), vision, hearing, psychological (depression + mood).
ICOPE Step 1: screen all 6 domains in primary care. Step 2: detailed assessment for identified concerns. Step 3: personalised care plan. Step 4: monitor. Step 5: engage community + caregiver.
