redFlags: Recent falls + recurrent fracture — falls clinic + bone health.
Suspected delirium superimposed on dementia — investigate underlying cause.
Severe weight loss > 5% in 3 months — investigate (malnutrition / cancer / depression / cognitive).
Acute cognitive change — exclude reversible cause.
Suspected elder abuse / neglect / financial exploitation.

diagnostics.test: ICOPE 6-domain screen at each primary care contact.
Cognition: 'remember 3 words + draw clock at 5 min' OR MoCA / MMSE for fuller assessment.
Mobility: chair-stand test (≥ 14 sec abnormal); gait speed; Timed Up + Go (> 12 sec abnormal).
Vitality / nutrition: weight loss > 3 kg in 3 months; appetite loss; SNAQ; mini-nutritional assessment.
Vision: read a small text; near + distance acuity; pinhole if reduced.
Hearing: whisper test + audiometry where available.
Comprehensive geriatric assessment for positive screen — medical / mental / functional / social / environmental / medication.

management.detail: Address each affected domain. Person-centred. Community + caregiver involvement. Multidisciplinary as needed.

Comprehensive workup for cognitive decline; treat reversible causes; cognitive stimulation + physical activity + social engagement; address vision + hearing + sleep; treat depression / anxiety; address polypharmacy (Beers criteria, STOPP/START). Refer dementia care pathway if appropriate.

Structured exercise (resistance + balance + Tai Chi + Otago programme); home modification + hazard reduction; medication review (anticholinergic burden); vision optimisation; calcium + vitamin D + DEXA + bisphosphonate / denosumab for osteoporosis.

Address malnutrition: dietary advice + protein 1.2 g/kg/day + ONS (oral nutritional supplements) if intake inadequate + treat reversible causes (dental, dysphagia, depression, drugs). Vitamin D + B12 + folate replacement. Smoking cessation.

Cataract surgery (often access-limited in LMIC — Kenya CCBRT outreach); glasses; macular degeneration anti-VEGF; glaucoma management. Hearing aids; auditory rehabilitation; remove cerumen. Address communication.
Treat depression + anxiety (preferred non-pharmacological first: CBT, exercise, social engagement; SSRI if needed). Address social isolation. Bereavement support.
Identify potentially inappropriate medication; de-prescribe when benefit / risk shifts; involve patient + family + pharmacist + GP. Anticholinergic burden — particularly important.
Clinical Frailty Scale or other; engage in advance care planning; ReSPECT / DNACPR equivalent; goals of care discussion. Living wills + lasting power of attorney.
Identify caregiver burden + risk of burnout; respite care; carer education; financial benefits; community resources. Address own physical + mental health.
Annual influenza; pneumococcal (PCV + PPV per schedule); COVID; zoster (recombinant Shingrix from 50+); pertussis boosters; tetanus.

Hypertension + diabetes + lipids per age-adapted targets. Cancer screening based on life expectancy + preferences (mammography, colonoscopy, prostate). Dementia screening every 1-2 years; cognitive assessment if concerns. Frailty-adapted prescribing.

Recognise heterogeneous older population — rural + urban + family-based + community + institutional. Engage CHVs + community health committee + faith-based organisations. Kenya National Policy for Older Persons + Aging (under development). Integrate with existing services (NCD clinic + ART + nutrition).

references.label: WHO ICOPE Guidelines (2017) + handbook (2019); WHO Decade of Healthy Ageing 2021-2030; Kenya MOH Health Sector Older Persons + Aging Strategic Plan

title: Outbreak investigation + integrated disease surveillance response
presentation: Cluster of unusual illness in defined population / geographical area exceeding expected baseline.
Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance + Response (IDSR) framework — strengthened post-COVID, post-Ebola, post-cholera outbreaks.
Priority diseases include: cholera, measles, polio (any AFP), Ebola / VHF, meningococcal, viral haemorrhagic fevers, COVID-19, mpox, neonatal tetanus, yellow fever, plague, rabies (any human case).
Includes any unusual cluster: respiratory, gastrointestinal, neurological, dermatological, maternal mortality.
redFlags: Suspected VHF / Ebola — strict infection control + immediate reporting.
Cholera outbreak with rapid case escalation.
Acute flaccid paralysis (any case requiring polio investigation).
Bioterrorism suspicion (smallpox, plague, botulism, tularemia, anthrax).
Resource-limited setting with inadequate isolation / PPE.

diagnostics.test: Line list — patient demographics + onset + symptoms + exposure + outcome.
Specimens for laboratory: blood + serum + stool + CSF + nasopharyngeal swab + tissue biopsy.
Environmental investigation (water + food + sanitation + animal source).

management.detail: Surveillance system identifies signal — confirm with laboratory + clinical case definition + exclude artifact (reporting changes, diagnostic test changes). Apply case definition + classify (suspected + probable + confirmed).

Multidisciplinary: epidemiology + clinical + laboratory + WASH + risk communication + community engagement + logistics + leadership / political. Kenya: National Public Health Institute (NPHI) leads, Sub-County + County Rapid Response Teams.

management.step: Implement control measures — case management + isolation + transmission control
management.detail: Treat cases per disease-specific protocol. Isolation + cohort + droplet / airborne / contact precautions per pathogen. WASH for waterborne + foodborne. Vector control for arbovirus / VHF. Animal source control for zoonosis.

Outbreak response immunisation: measles MR / yellow fever / OCV (oral cholera vaccine) / meningococcal / pneumococcal / hepatitis E. Stockpile activation. Ring vaccination (Ebola / smallpox). Reactive campaigns + catch-up.

Standardised case management protocols. Drug stockpiles (rabies vaccine + RIG; cholera ORS + antibiotics; Ebola monoclonal antibodies; tamiflu). Treatment centres established + staffed for severe cases.

Identify + trace + monitor contacts (variable per disease — 21 days for Ebola; 14 days for cholera + meningococcal). CHV-supported in Kenya — community-based surveillance. Risk-categorised contact follow-up.

Trustworthy + transparent + culturally-appropriate messaging. Engage community leaders + faith-based + traditional healers. Address rumour + misinformation. Multi-language + multi-channel. Empower community participation.
Specimen referral system to reference / KEMRI; rapid diagnostics deployment; supply chain for PPE + therapeutics + vaccines. Quality assurance.

management.step: Notify WHO + IHR — International Health Regulations
management.detail: Notifiable disease per IHR 2005 — Kenya is signatory. Public health emergency of international concern (PHEIC) reporting for severe / unusual events. Cross-border coordination for transboundary risk.
Universal precautions + appropriate PPE + training + post-exposure protocols + mental health support. Vaccination where available.
Document outbreak + response. Identify gaps + strengthen surveillance + readiness. Update protocols. Capacity-building + training. Stockpile replenishment.

references.label: WHO IHR 2005; Africa CDC + WHO AFRO IDSR Framework; Kenya MOH IDSR Guidelines + National Public Health Institute

title: WHO surgical care at the district hospital — essential surgery + safety checklist
presentation: Patient requiring surgical intervention at district hospital level — emergency + elective.
WHO Surgical Care at the District Hospital framework: defines essential surgical capacity at first-referral level.
Kenya: county hospitals provide district-level surgery; referral pathway to teaching / national hospital for complex.
Lancet Commission on Global Surgery — universal access to safe surgery as part of UHC.
redFlags: Patient instability — ABC stabilisation BEFORE surgery.
Inadequate facility resources — refer rather than attempt.
Patient not consented / unable to consent — assess capacity.

diagnostics.test: Comprehensive pre-operative assessment — history + examination + investigations.
FBC + U&E + glucose + cross-match (if blood likely needed).
ECG + CXR + further imaging per indication.
Pregnancy test for female of childbearing potential.
WHO Surgical Safety Checklist completion before, during, and after.

management.step: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist — IMPLEMENT FOR EVERY SURGERY
management.detail: Sign-in (before anaesthesia): patient ID + procedure + consent + site marking + anaesthetic safety + pulse oximetry + allergy + difficult airway + blood loss risk. Time-out (before incision): team introduction + patient + procedure + critical events + antibiotic prophylaxis given. Sign-out (before patient leaves OR): procedure recorded + instruments + sponges + specimen + equipment problems + post-op concerns. Reduces mortality + morbidity 30%.

EMERGENCY: airway management + thoracostomy + abdominal exploration for trauma / perforation / obstruction + appendicectomy + groin / inguinal hernia repair + emergency C-section + ectopic pregnancy + caesarean hysterectomy + PPH surgical management + ruptured ectopic + bowel resection + perforated viscus + hydrocele aspiration + abscess drainage + wound debridement + circumcision (medical) + neonatal pyloric stenosis + paediatric appendicectomy + intussusception. ELECTIVE: hernia repair + hydrocele + appendicectomy + cholecystectomy + tubal ligation + vasectomy + minor procedures.

Within 60 minutes of incision (vancomycin / fluoroquinolone: 120 min). Choice + duration per surgery type: clean (no antibiotic), clean-contaminated (1-3 doses cephalosporin), contaminated (extended), dirty (therapeutic). Single dose for most. Kenya formulary aligned with Kenya AMR Action Plan.
Risk-stratified: mechanical (intermittent pneumatic compression + graduated stockings) + chemoprophylaxis (LMWH) per surgery type + patient risk. Continue postoperatively until mobile.
Adequate analgesia (WHO ladder + multimodal); thromboprophylaxis; early mobilisation; nutrition; wound care; infection surveillance; pain assessment + management.

Spinal anaesthesia for caesarean + lower extremity surgery — safe + cost-effective. General anaesthesia with ketamine + halothane / isoflurane (or TIVA propofol where available). Regional blocks. Local with sedation. Trained anaesthesia provider essential.
Cross-matched blood ready; emergency O-negative + group-specific. Kenya National Blood Transfusion Service. Cell salvage for selected. Tranexamic acid for haemorrhage.

Wound infection (superficial vs deep); anastomotic leak; bleeding; ileus + obstruction; respiratory complications (atelectasis, pneumonia); thromboembolism; AKI; delirium; sepsis. Early diagnosis + intervention.

Complex / specialist surgery beyond district capacity: cardiac surgery; neurosurgery (head injury > minor); paediatric specialty (newborn surgery); complex oncology resection; transplant; complex vascular; major reconstructive. Pre-arranged + accompanied transfer.
Kenya CCBRT + free surgical camps + Smile Train (cleft) + Operation Smile + Mercy Ships + Faith-based hospitals — extend access to under-served. Coordinate with MOH.
Local infection control + audit + morbidity + mortality reviews + continuous improvement. Surgical safety culture + checklist compliance audit.

references.label: WHO Surgical Care at the District Hospital (2003 + updates); WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (2009 update); Lancet Commission on Global Surgery 2030; Kenya MOH Standard Operating Procedures

title: Occupational needlestick injury / blood-borne pathogen exposure — healthcare worker
presentation: Healthcare worker / community worker / lab worker / first responder with percutaneous or mucocutaneous exposure to blood / body fluid.
Risk per exposure: HIV ~0.3% (percutaneous); 0.09% (mucocutaneous). HBV: up to 30% if source HBeAg+. HCV: ~1.8%.
Most preventable; WHO + Kenya MOH have policies for prevention + post-exposure management.
redFlags: Deep injury + hollow-needle + source viral load high — high HIV + HBV + HCV risk.
Source unknown / source HIV-positive — full PEP.
Pregnancy of exposed worker — adjust PEP regimen.
Delayed presentation > 72 hours — no PEP for HIV (still HBV + HCV testing + follow-up).

diagnostics.test: Source + recipient HIV + HBV (HBsAg + anti-HBs) + HCV testing.
Baseline FBC + U&E + LFT for PEP monitoring.
Risk assessment — type of injury + source status + time since exposure.

management.detail: Encourage bleeding (do NOT scrub or apply caustic); wash with soap + running water; do NOT use bleach / antiseptic directly. Mucosa: irrigate with water / saline. Eye: irrigate with sterile water / saline ≥ 5 minutes (remove contact lens after first irrigation).

Within hours of exposure. Document: type of injury (percutaneous / mucocutaneous), depth, fluid type, source patient status, time since exposure. Provide written information + post-exposure counselling.

Indications: any percutaneous / mucocutaneous exposure to HIV-positive source OR source-unknown high-risk situation. Kenya first-line: TDF/3TC + DTG (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir) × 28 days. Alternative: TDF/FTC + raltegravir. Counselling on adherence + side effects. HIV testing at baseline + 6 weeks + 12 weeks + 6 months.

Source HBsAg-positive: assess recipient HBV status. Vaccinated + protective (anti-HBs ≥ 10 mIU/mL): no action. Vaccinated + non-responder: HBIG + start vaccination series. Unvaccinated: HBIG within 24-48 hours + start hepatitis B vaccination 0/1/6 month schedule. HBIG dose: 0.06 mL/kg IM within 24 hours.
No PEP available. Baseline + 12-week + 24-week HCV antibody + HCV RNA at 6 weeks. If seroconversion → direct-acting antiviral treatment per Kenya HCV guidelines (sofosbuvir-based regimens).
PEP not contraindicated; TDF/3TC + DTG considered safe. Counsel + monitor. Continue ART beyond pregnancy if HIV-positive.
Tetanus immunisation status check + booster if last dose > 5 years. Rabies PEP if animal-source exposure (see rabies pathway).

HIV: 6 weeks + 12 weeks + 6 months. HBV: 1 + 6 months. HCV: 6 weeks + 12 weeks + 6 months. Stop PEP if confirmed source HIV-negative. Counsel re: sexual + bloodborne transmission avoidance during follow-up period.
Acute stress response common. Psychological counselling. Employer support + workplace return planning. Workplace incident investigation.

Universal precautions; appropriate PPE; safety-engineered devices (retractable / shielded needles); no needle recapping; sharps disposal containers at point-of-use; vaccinations (HBV mandatory; HPV + influenza + COVID + pneumococcal + zoster recommended); training + audit + culture of safety.
Occupational Safety + Health Act; workplace incident reporting; PEP availability + free access; HBV vaccination programme for healthcare workers; psychological support integration.

references.label: WHO Post-Exposure Prophylaxis to Prevent HIV Infection (2014, updated); CDC Updated Recommendations on PEP; Kenya NASCOP PEP Guidelines

title: Adolescent pregnancy — comprehensive care + sexual + reproductive health
presentation: Pregnant adolescent — 10-19 years; often first contact with healthcare.
Kenya: ~15% of girls give birth before age 18; ~5% before 15; geographic + socioeconomic disparities; substantial unmet need for contraception.

Heightened risk: preterm birth, low birth weight, neonatal mortality (girls < 15 — 5× higher), maternal mortality (15-19: 2× higher), prolonged + obstructed labour, postpartum haemorrhage, eclampsia, anaemia, school dropout, social vulnerability.
WHO + Kenya MOH adolescent-friendly services + Kenya National Adolescent Sexual + Reproductive Health Policy.
redFlags: Adolescent < 14 years — child protection notification; statutory rape consideration per jurisdiction.
Suspected sexual assault — emergency contraception + PEP.
School dropout — educational continuity support needed.

diagnostics.test: Comprehensive history with adolescent-friendly approach — pregnancy duration, support, schooling, partner age + relationship, intimate partner violence / abuse / coercion, mental health, substance use, contraception history, prior pregnancies.
Routine ANC tests — Hb, blood group + Rh, HIV + syphilis + hepatitis B, urinalysis, dating ultrasound, BP, weight + height.

diagnostics.rationale: Common in adolescents; treat to reduce preterm + neonatal complications.

diagnostics.test: Mental health screen (PHQ-9 + GAD-7; suicide assessment).

management.detail: Private + welcoming + age-appropriate. Adolescent + caregiver in care (where consent + appropriate). Respect autonomy + decision-making capacity. Non-judgmental + empathetic approach essential.

More frequent contacts than standard adult; close monitoring of growth + BP + signs of pre-eclampsia. Iron + folic acid (often higher dose 5 mg folic acid); calcium; nutritional supplementation. Tetanus + flu + pertussis + COVID vaccination. ANC contact + Linda Mama enrolment.

Continue pregnancy + parenting; adoption; safe + legal termination (where available + indicated). Kenya: termination for life-threatening conditions per Penal Code + Constitution Article 26(4). Non-judgmental options counselling. Refer specialist if uncertain.

management.step: Safe abortion / post-abortion care (where legally indicated + accessible)
management.detail: Medication: misoprostol ± mifepristone per gestation. Surgical: manual vacuum aspiration. Post-abortion care: contraception + STI + mental health + counselling. Kenya legal context cautious — consult specialist + ethics.

Antenatal initiation of contraception planning. LARC (implant, IUD) — first-line postpartum for adolescents (high continuation + low pregnancy rate). Counsel re: dual protection (condom + LARC for STI). Encourage school continuation.

Treat depression + anxiety (SSRI + counselling). Identify + address abuse (per IPV pathway). Connect to social services + community supports. Educational continuity — work with school + Ministry of Education. Family support engagement.
Adolescent still growing — dual nutritional demands. Iron + calcium + adequate protein + calories. Weight gain monitoring.

Skilled birth attendant + facility delivery. Continuous companion. Adolescent + young primigravida — close monitoring (prolonged labour + obstructed labour + need for assisted / Caesarean). Cervical pre-ripening / induction per protocol.

Routine postnatal care + mental health screening at 6-8 weeks (postpartum depression more common). Lactation support — exclusive breastfeeding 6 months. Routine infant care + immunisations. Family planning at 6 weeks postpartum.

Encourage return to school post-delivery. Vocational training where school not feasible. Cash transfer programs (Kenya: Hunger Safety Net). DREAMS programme for adolescent girls + young women — comprehensive package.
Midwife + obstetrician + paediatrician + GP + social worker + psychologist + nutritionist + community health worker + adolescent peer support.

Adolescent < 14 + sexual activity / pregnancy: statutory rape per Kenya Sexual Offences Act + report to Children's Officer + child protection. Even if 14-17 — consider coercion + abuse. Confidentiality balanced with protection.

references.label: WHO Adolescent Pregnancy fact sheet + guidelines; Kenya National Adolescent SRH Policy; DREAMS Partnership

title: Childhood immunisation catch-up + WHO + Kenya EPI schedule
presentation: Child with incomplete immunisation history — newly arrived migrant, displacement, defaulted, unknown history.
Kenya Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI) schedule from birth to age 18 months for routine; plus campaigns + boosters.
WHO recommends catch-up for any incomplete child up to age 18 — never too late.
redFlags: Suspected severe allergy / anaphylaxis to vaccine component — alternative vaccine / specialist.
Immunocompromised — modified schedule + avoid live vaccines (where possible).
Recent IVIG / blood product — delay live vaccines.
Pregnancy in adolescent — avoid live (MMR + varicella + yellow fever).
Outbreak situation — additional doses + accelerated schedule.

diagnostics.test: Vaccine history — written records preferred; verbal acceptable if no doubt; assume unvaccinated if uncertain.
Age + medical history + immune status + allergies + previous adverse events.
Document new doses in vaccine card + national registry.

management.detail: AT BIRTH: BCG + OPV (zero dose) + Hepatitis B birth dose. 6 WEEKS: DTwP-HepB-Hib (Penta1) + OPV1 + PCV1 + Rota1. 10 WEEKS: Penta2 + OPV2 + PCV2 + Rota2. 14 WEEKS: Penta3 + OPV3 (or IPV in some) + PCV3. 9 MONTHS: Measles-Rubella (MR1) + Yellow Fever (endemic regions). 18 MONTHS: MR2 + DTP booster. School entry / adolescent: HPV (girls 10 + 14 — increasingly boys), Td booster, COVID.

management.step: WHO catch-up schedule for unvaccinated / incomplete child
management.detail: Apply minimum age + minimum interval rules. Live vaccines (BCG + MMR + varicella + yellow fever + rotavirus) need ≥ 4 weeks between if not given on same day. Inactivated vaccines: any spacing ≥ 4 weeks between doses.

Child < 1 year: 3 doses 4 weeks apart. Child 1-5 years: 3 doses 4 weeks apart. Child > 5 years: Td (tetanus + reduced diphtheria) + acellular pertussis where available. HepB: 3 doses 0/1/6 months (4 weeks minimum + 2 months minimum) for those missed.

Measles-rubella: 2 doses minimum 4 weeks apart from age 9 months (anywhere) or 12 months (some); apply minimum age cut-off; ensure dose at ≥ 12 months (children given < 9 months need extra dose). Yellow fever (endemic regions): one dose for life from age 9 months.
WHO catch-up: ensure complete primary OPV / IPV series. Kenya: 3-4 doses OPV with IPV at 14 weeks. WHO recommendation for at least one dose IPV in routine schedule (combined IPV/OPV approach).

Girls 10-14 (Kenya 10 + 14 years): 2-dose schedule 6-12 months apart. Boys increasingly added (Kenya: gender-neutral programme). Age 15-26: 3-dose schedule 0/1-2/6 months. Single-dose schedule for low-income settings emerging.
Limited age window for rotavirus — first dose 6-15 weeks; last by 8 months. After 8 months, no rotavirus.

Tdap (or Td if pertussis vaccine unavailable) every 10 years. MMR if unvaccinated (2 doses 4 weeks apart). Varicella if susceptible. HPV. Hepatitis B if unvaccinated. Meningococcal (selected). Influenza annually.

Immunocompromised: inactivated vaccines safe + given normally. AVOID LIVE (BCG, OPV, MMR, varicella, yellow fever, rotavirus, intranasal flu, LAIV) — unless specific specialist indication. Pregnant adolescent: avoid LIVE; give inactivated (influenza + tetanus + pertussis + COVID); HPV completed pre-conception or postpartum.
Critical — vaccine potency depends on cold chain (2-8°C for most). VVM (vaccine vial monitor) check. Document + report breaches. Kenya KEMSA cold chain monitoring.

Provide accurate information + address concerns. Build trust + rapport. Address misinformation. Community engagement + religious / traditional leaders. WHO 3Cs of vaccine hesitancy: Complacency, Confidence, Convenience.
Kenya MOSI (Mtoto Salama Imara) digital immunisation tracking system. Vaccine card to caregiver. Mark every visit. Schedule reminders. CHV-supported community follow-up.

references.label: WHO Immunization Schedules + WHO Practical Guide to Vaccine Catch-up; Kenya Expanded Programme on Immunisation Standard Operating Procedures; Kenya National Immunisation Policy + Comprehensive Multi-year Plan

title: Refugee + migrant health — comprehensive assessment + care
presentation: Refugee + asylum seeker + migrant patient — new arrival, in transit, or settled.
Kenya hosts ~520,000 refugees (UNHCR 2024) — predominantly from Somalia, South Sudan, DRC, Ethiopia, Burundi.

Common health needs: infectious disease (TB, HIV, malaria), mental health (PTSD, depression), reproductive health, chronic disease, malnutrition, occupational + interpersonal violence, vaccine catch-up, social vulnerability.
WHO Global Action Plan on the Health of Refugees + Migrants (2019-2023).
Kenya MOH integrated refugee health within national health system since 2017 transition.
redFlags: Acute infectious disease in cluster (TB / cholera / measles outbreak in camp).
Severe mental health crisis — suicide / psychosis.
Severe chronic disease (HIV / hepatitis / TB / DM / cancer) — continuation of treatment.

diagnostics.test: Comprehensive arrival health assessment — physical + mental + social + nutritional + dental + vision + hearing.
Tuberculosis screening — symptom + CXR + sputum / GeneXpert; latent TB testing if appropriate.
HIV + syphilis + hepatitis B + C + malaria screening per country of origin / risk.
Routine bloods + nutrition assessment + B12 + vitamin D + iron.
Mental health screening (PTSD checklist + PHQ-9 + GAD-7).
Female genital mutilation (FGM) assessment if from prevalent region.
Reproductive health + contraception + pregnancy testing as appropriate.

management.step: Comprehensive first-arrival health screen + integration into Kenya health system
management.detail: Within 30 days of arrival — comprehensive screen at refugee health centre or county facility. Issue refugee health card. Linkage to NHIF + Linda Mama + free TB/HIV programmes. Continuity of any ongoing treatment (HIV ART, TB treatment, NCD medication).

TB: per Kenya National TB Programme — same regimens + DOT + cohort monitoring. HIV: linkage to ART (free public sector); continuation across borders + facilities. Malaria: free in public facilities. Hepatitis B + C: vaccination + treatment per Kenya hepatitis policy.

Recognise trauma sequelae (PTSD, depression, anxiety, complex grief, somatisation). Psychological first aid → counselling → mental health specialist if severe. Avoid re-traumatisation — trauma-informed care. Address torture survivors with specialist services (Kenya: IRCT-affiliated centres). Peer support + community engagement + cultural mediators.
Antenatal care + Linda Mama enrolment. Childhood immunisation catch-up per Kenya EPI. Growth monitoring + nutrition for under-5 (SAM treatment per WHO + Kenya protocols). Adolescent SRH services.

Targeted screening — severe acute malnutrition (SAM) treatment per Kenya CMAM (Community-based Management of Acute Malnutrition). Therapeutic feeding programmes. Iron + folate + multivitamin. Address food insecurity.

Sensitive enquiry + non-judgmental care. Address physical complications (urinary, sexual, obstetric). Avoid re-traumatisation. Specialist deinfibulation surgery (Kenya — selected centres). Multidisciplinary care (gynaecology + psychology + cultural).
Sensitive enquiry. Care per WHO LIVES framework + Kenya GBV pathway. Emergency contraception + PEP + STI prophylaxis + medico-legal support.
Identify + continue medication for HIV, TB, NCDs. Build into routine care. Counsel re: medication adherence + side effects.
Per Kenya EPI schedule + WHO catch-up guidelines. Document + integrate with Kenya national registry.
Translation services + cultural mediators (Kakuma + Dadaab refugee health centres). Religious + cultural sensitivity. Engage community leaders + health workers.
Issue health records portable + transferable. Refer for refugee status determination + legal support. Address social determinants (housing, schooling, employment, family reunification).

management.step: Integration with UNHCR + IOM + non-governmental partners
management.detail: Coordinated approach via UNHCR Refugee Coordination Model. IOM for migrants. Kenya partners: IRC, Kenya Red Cross, MSF, faith-based organisations. Avoid parallel systems — integrate into Kenya national health programmes.

references.label: WHO Global Action Plan: Health of Refugees + Migrants 2019-2023; UNHCR + WHO Public Health Guidance Note; Kenya MOH Refugee Health Strategy + Integration

title: Community health volunteer (CHV) — integrated community case management (Kenya + WHO)
presentation: Kenya community health strategy: every community has trained CHVs (typically one per ~100 households) providing first-contact care + linking to formal facility.
iCCM (Integrated Community Case Management): trained CHVs identify + treat childhood illness (pneumonia + diarrhoea + malaria + malnutrition) at community level.
Wider CHV roles: pregnancy registration + ANC referrals + postnatal follow-up + immunisation defaulter tracing + TB / HIV adherence + chronic disease support + health education + referral.
redFlags: Danger signs in any age — refer immediately to facility (cannot drink / breastfeed, vomiting everything, convulsions, lethargic / unconscious, severe respiratory distress, severe dehydration, severe anaemia, suspected serious infection).
Newborn danger signs — IMCI young infant pathway.
Pregnant woman with danger signs — antenatal red flags.
Adult with severe symptoms — sepsis / heart attack / stroke / severe trauma.
Suspected outbreak / cluster — alert district health team.
CHV safety in conflict / disease outbreak — PPE + training.

diagnostics.test: CHV uses standardised algorithms (e.g. WHO IMCI Community Pictorial Algorithm) — danger signs + symptoms + simple measurements.
Respiratory rate counting; temperature (sometimes mid-upper arm circumference - MUAC for malnutrition screening); RDT for malaria; bedside glucose where available.
Refer to facility for further investigation / management if criteria met.

management.detail: Level 1 — community health units (CHU) of ~5,000 population, with CHV (~10 per CHU) + Community Health Extension Worker (CHEW) supervising. Links to level 2/3 health facility. Recently formalised + remunerated.

CHV with iCCM training treats: simple childhood pneumonia (fast breathing without chest indrawing) with amoxicillin dispersible tablets; uncomplicated malaria with AL after positive RDT; diarrhoea with ORS + zinc supplementation; severe acute malnutrition referral (with appetite test + outpatient therapeutic care community follow-up). Refer all severe illness.

Pregnancy registration + Linda Mama enrolment. ANC defaulter tracing + visit reminders. Birth preparedness + complication readiness counselling. Postnatal home visits days 1, 3, 7, 28. Newborn danger sign recognition + referral. Exclusive breastfeeding promotion. Family planning referral / commodity distribution.

Adherence support (DOT — direct observation of TB treatment; ART adherence). Defaulter tracing. NCD education (HEARTS, healthy lifestyle, hypertension + diabetes monitoring where equipped). Mental health awareness + linkage.
Identify under-immunised children + bring to facility / outreach. Support catch-up + campaign delivery. Trust + community engagement.

WASH (hand washing, latrine use, safe water), nutrition (breastfeeding, complementary feeding), sexual + reproductive health, family planning, malaria prevention (ITN use), TB symptom awareness, HIV testing promotion, vaccination promotion, NCD risk factor reduction.
Recognise outbreak signs + report to CHEW + health facility — measles, cholera, polio (AFP), neonatal tetanus, maternal mortality. Strengthens IDSR system.

Pre-positioned commodities at community: ORS + zinc + albendazole + Vitamin A + chlorhexidine for cord care + iron-folate + chlorhexidine + condoms + family planning pills. Stock managed by CHV with CHEW supervision.

Standardised forms — household register + sick child register + maternal register + immunisation defaulter list. Monthly reports to CHEW + sub-county health team. Increasingly electronic (Kenya Community Health Information System).

Initial training (~3-6 weeks) + refresher training annually. Monthly supervisor meetings. Continuous learning. Performance feedback. Recognition + motivation. Recent Kenya reforms — recognition + stipend / payment of CHVs (Kshs 2,500/month nationally + county supplements).
Supportive supervision + commodity availability + functional referral + community engagement. Quality of care monitoring (case-mix + treatment adherence + outcomes).
CHVs not substitutes for trained health workers. Avoid task-overload. Clear referral criteria + facility back-up essential.

references.label: WHO iCCM (2014 + updates); Kenya Community Health Strategy 2021-2025; Kenya MOH Community Health Information System

title: Hand hygiene + infection prevention + control (WHO 5 moments)
presentation: Single most important intervention for prevention of healthcare-associated infection (HAI).

WHO 5 moments for hand hygiene: 1) Before touching patient. 2) Before clean / aseptic procedure. 3) After body fluid exposure / risk. 4) After touching patient. 5) After touching patient surroundings.
Kenya MOH IPC strategy aligned with WHO; widespread implementation post-COVID + Ebola threats.
redFlags: Outbreak / cluster of HAI — review IPC practices.
MDRO emergence (MRSA / VRE / CRE / C. difficile) in facility — heightened IPC.
Norovirus / cholera / rotavirus cluster — alcohol gel inadequate; use soap + water.
C. difficile — soap + water (alcohol gel does not kill spores).
Severe diarrhoeal outbreak — strict barrier precautions.
Suspected high-consequence pathogen (Ebola, Marburg, Lassa, MPOX, smallpox, plague, anthrax) — escalate precautions + isolation.

diagnostics.test: Hand hygiene compliance audit — observational measurement.
MDRO surveillance — facility antibiogram + screening on admission for high-risk.
HAI rates — bloodstream / urinary / pneumonia / surgical site infections.

management.detail: Alcohol-based hand rub 20-30 seconds preferred for routine (faster, more effective, less skin irritation). Soap + water 40-60 seconds for visibly soiled hands, C. difficile, norovirus, anthrax spores. Both — WHO 6-step / 7-step technique covering all surfaces.

Assume all body fluids potentially infectious. Hand hygiene; PPE based on task; safe injection practice; respiratory hygiene; safe handling of patient equipment + linen; cleaning + disinfection of environment + medical equipment.

Contact precautions: MRSA, VRE, C. difficile, scabies, MDROs. Droplet precautions: influenza, meningococcal meningitis, mumps, pertussis. Airborne precautions: TB, measles, varicella, MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2 (in aerosol-generating procedures), MPOX. Strict barrier precautions for VHFs.
Gloves (single-use); gown / apron; surgical mask / N95 (FFP3) respirator; eye protection (goggles / face shield). Donning + doffing order critical. Reusable equipment cleaned + disinfected.
Hand hygiene + sterile gloves + drapes + skin preparation (chlorhexidine 2% in alcohol — superior to povidone iodine) + barrier precautions. Surgical site preparation + antibiotic prophylaxis timing.

Central venous catheter: insertion bundle (hand hygiene + maximal barrier precaution + chlorhexidine skin antisepsis + optimal site selection + daily review of necessity). Urinary catheter: indication-based + remove early + drainage bag below bladder + closed drainage system.
Per AWaRe pathway — appropriate selection + duration. Right indication, right drug, right dose. Antimicrobial stewardship programme + audit + feedback.

High-touch surfaces cleaned + disinfected (sodium hypochlorite 1000 ppm for general; 10,000 ppm for blood spills; H2O2 vapor / UV for terminal). Trained cleaners + standardised protocols. Frequent cleaning of patient zones.
Hepatitis B (mandatory in Kenya MOH); influenza annually; MMR + varicella + Tdap + COVID. Pre-employment + ongoing. Screening + post-exposure as per pathway.
IPC committee + outbreak response team + emergency procurement (PPE + disinfectants + isolation supplies) + isolation rooms + training. Annual drill. Surge capacity planning.

Regular training + competency assessment. Cultural shift to 'IPC as everyone's responsibility'. Champion programmes. Monitoring + feedback. Just culture + non-punitive incident reporting. Kenya MOH IPC training rolled out post-Ebola + post-COVID.
Reliable water + sanitation + waste management essential foundation. Kenya many facilities still lack basic WASH — programmatic priority. JMP WASH in healthcare facilities indicators.

WHO 5-pillar approach: 1) System change (infrastructure, supplies). 2) Training. 3) Monitoring + feedback. 4) Reminders + communication. 5) Institutional safety climate. Combined approach more effective than single.

references.label: WHO Guidelines on Hand Hygiene in Health Care (2009); WHO Core Components of IPC (2016); Kenya National IPC Guidelines + IPC Strategy

title: Snakebite envenomation (Kenya WHO snakebite roadmap)
population: All ages, peak in rural agricultural workers, herders, children walking at dusk; high burden in Baringo, Kilifi, Kwale, Kajiado, Turkana, West Pokot
presentation: Fang marks (may be absent with elapids), local swelling/blistering/necrosis (vipers — puff adder, saw-scaled), neurotoxicity (cobras, black mamba — ptosis, dysphagia, paralysis, respiratory failure), haematotoxicity (vipers — bleeding gums/urine/GI, 20-minute whole blood clotting test failure), cardiotoxicity, AKI, compartment syndrome
redFlags: Neurotoxic signs: ptosis, dysphagia, respiratory failure (intubate)
20-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT) failure = systemic envenomation
diagnostics: 20-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT) — bedside, repeat every 6h
CBC, platelets, INR/PT, fibrinogen, creatinine, urinalysis (hematuria, proteinuria)
ECG for cardiotoxicity
Identify snake if possible (photograph at safe distance — do NOT bring live snake)
management: First aid: immobilise limb in neutral position, remove rings/tight clothing; do NOT cut, suck, apply tourniquet, ice, or electric shock
Pressure immobilisation bandage ONLY for neurotoxic elapids (mambas, cobras) — not for vipers
Transport urgently to facility with antivenom
Polyvalent antivenom (SAIMR or Inoserp PanAfrica per Kenya MOH) for systemic envenomation: neurotoxicity, coagulopathy (20WBCT failure), shock, severe local swelling crossing joint
Premedicate with adrenaline 0.25 mg SC + hydrocortisone + chlorphenamine to reduce anaphylactoid reactions
Initial dose 10 vials IV over 1 hour; repeat at 6h if 20WBCT still failed or neurotoxicity persists
Neostigmine + atropine for cobra neurotoxicity (response confirms diagnosis)
Respiratory support: intubation + ventilation for paralysis
Tetanus prophylaxis; antibiotics ONLY if abscess/necrosis (not prophylactic)
Surgical: fasciotomy only if compartment pressures documented elevated (rare — most swelling is subcutaneous)
Avoid IM injections (bleeding risk)

references.label: WHO Guidelines for Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010, updated 2024)
Kenya MOH National Guidelines for Prevention, Diagnosis and Management of Snakebite (2019)

title: Severe acute malnutrition — IMAM (WHO + Kenya IMAM guidelines)
population: Children 6–59 months with MUAC < 11.5 cm or WHZ < −3 or bilateral pitting oedema; Kenya ASAL counties highest burden
presentation: Marasmus (severe wasting, old-man face, prominent ribs, baggy-pants buttocks), kwashiorkor (bilateral pitting oedema, hair changes, dermatosis, hepatomegaly), or marasmic-kwashiorkor; appetite test outcome determines inpatient vs OTP
redFlags: Bilateral pitting oedema grade 3 (face + legs + arms)
Medical complications: hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, severe dehydration, shock, severe anaemia, LRTI, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargy
diagnostics: Anthropometry: MUAC, weight-for-height z-score, height, oedema grading
Appetite test with RUTF (Plumpy'Nut)
Blood glucose, malaria RDT, Hb, HIV test (per Kenya HTS guidelines)
Stool for parasites, urine dipstick
management: Stabilisation phase (Phase 1, inpatient) for complicated SAM: F-75 therapeutic milk 130 ml/kg/day in 8–12 feeds (lower osmolality), correct hypoglycaemia (10% dextrose 5 ml/kg), hypothermia (skin-to-skin), electrolytes (no iron in phase 1)

Routine medicines: amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day × 5–7 days (or ceftriaxone if complicated), vitamin A on day 1 (only if no oedema and not given in last 1 month), folic acid 5 mg day 1 then 1 mg daily, measles vaccine on day of admission if eligible
Transition phase: change F-75 to F-100 or RUTF when appetite returns and oedema reducing

Rehabilitation (OTP — outpatient therapeutic programme) for uncomplicated SAM: RUTF 200 kcal/kg/day, weekly review × 6–8 weeks until discharge criteria (WHZ ≥ −2 or MUAC ≥ 12.5 cm × 2 visits, no oedema × 2 weeks)
Caregiver counselling: continue breastfeeding, exclusive RUTF (no sharing), safe water, hygiene
HIV-positive children: start ART per Kenya HIV ART guidelines once stabilised
Prevent refeeding syndrome: low-volume slow start, monitor electrolytes
Do NOT give IV fluids unless shock (then ReSoMal oral preferred; if IV essential, use half-strength Darrow's with 5% dextrose 15 ml/kg over 1h, reassess)

references.label: WHO Updates on the management of SAM in infants and children (2023)
Kenya National Guideline for Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM, 2023)

title: Postpartum hemorrhage — WHO active management + E-MOTIVE bundle
population: All women postpartum — leading direct cause of maternal mortality globally and in Kenya (Linda Mama programme)
presentation: Blood loss > 500 ml after vaginal delivery or > 1000 ml after caesarean, OR any blood loss with hemodynamic instability; primary (< 24h) most common from uterine atony (70%), trauma, retained products, coagulopathy (4Ts)
redFlags: Estimated blood loss > 1000 ml or ongoing brisk bleeding
Calibrated drape blood loss > 500 ml triggers E-MOTIVE bundle
Genital tract laceration extending into vault
diagnostics: Calibrated under-buttock drape for objective blood loss measurement
Vital signs every 5 minutes, shock index
Hb, group and crossmatch, coagulation, fibrinogen
Speculum exam for trauma; bimanual for tone and retained products
management: PREVENTION — Active management of third stage labour (AMTSL) for ALL births: oxytocin 10 IU IM within 1 minute of birth, controlled cord traction, uterine massage post-delivery (or carbetocin 100 mcg IM where heat-stable preparation available — preferred where cold chain unreliable per WHO 2018)
TREATMENT — WHO E-MOTIVE bundle (early detection + bundle of first-response treatments): triggered by calibrated drape > 500 ml or clinical concern
E — Early detection (calibrated drape)
M — Massage (uterine fundal)
O — Oxytocic drugs (oxytocin 10 IU IM/slow IV + 20 IU in 1L saline at 60 drops/min)
T — Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 min within 3 hours of bleeding onset (WOMAN trial)
I — IV fluids (crystalloid 1–2 L)
V — Vaginal/genital tract examination for trauma + bladder catheterisation
E — Escalation if not controlled in 30 min
Second-line: misoprostol 800 mcg sublingual, ergometrine 0.5 mg IM (avoid if hypertension), carboprost 250 mcg IM (avoid if asthma)
Mechanical: bimanual uterine compression, aortic compression, balloon tamponade (Bakri or condom catheter), non-pneumatic anti-shock garment (NASG) for transport
Surgical: B-Lynch suture, uterine artery ligation, hysterectomy as last resort
Blood transfusion per massive transfusion protocol; activate emergency obstetric referral
Retained placenta: manual removal under anesthesia + antibiotics

references.label: WHO Recommendations on Prevention and Treatment of Postpartum Haemorrhage (2022)
Kenya MOH National Guidelines on Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (Linda Mama)
WOMAN trial — tranexamic acid in PPH (Lancet 2017)

title: Sepsis Hour-1 bundle (Surviving Sepsis + WHO)
population: Adults with suspected infection + organ dysfunction (qSOFA ≥ 2 or NEWS2 ≥ 5 or SOFA increase ≥ 2)
presentation: Infection source (pneumonia, UTI, abdominal, soft tissue, meningitis) plus organ dysfunction: altered mental state, tachypnoea ≥ 22, SBP ≤ 100, hypoxaemia, oliguria, mottling, ↑ lactate; septic shock = vasopressor needed + lactate > 2 despite fluids
redFlags: SBP < 90 or MAP < 65 not responding to fluids
Respiratory rate > 30, SpO2 < 90% on room air
diagnostics: Lactate (point-of-care preferred)
Blood cultures × 2 (different sites) BEFORE antibiotics — do not delay > 45 min
FBC, U&E, creatinine, LFTs, CRP, procalcitonin, coagulation, glucose
Urinalysis + urine culture, chest X-ray, source-specific cultures
ABG if available
qSOFA / NEWS2 / SOFA scoring
Imaging for source: CT abdomen if suspected intra-abdominal source
management: HOUR-1 BUNDLE (start within 1 hour of recognition):
1. Measure lactate, remeasure in 2–4h if initial > 2
2. Obtain blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics

3. Broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour: ceftriaxone 2 g IV + amikacin (community-acquired); piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem if hospital-acquired/immunocompromised; add vancomycin if MRSA risk
4. Crystalloid 30 ml/kg IV over first 3 hours for hypotension or lactate > 4 — reassess fluid responsiveness (passive leg raise, dynamic measures); avoid hydroxyethyl starches
5. Vasopressors (noradrenaline first-line, target MAP ≥ 65) if hypotension persists despite fluids; add vasopressin 0.03 U/min if escalating noradrenaline
Source control within 6–12 hours: drain abscess, remove infected line, debride necrotic tissue
Antibiotic stewardship: de-escalate based on cultures within 48–72h, total duration usually 7 days (longer for endocarditis, osteomyelitis)
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for septic shock requiring vasopressors
Glucose control: target 140–180 mg/dL
VTE prophylaxis, stress ulcer prophylaxis, head-up 30°
Steroids do NOT replace antibiotics in malaria-endemic settings (test for malaria with RDT in febrile sepsis)
WHO IMAI severe acute illness algorithm + escalation pathway

references.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines 2021 + Hour-1 Bundle Update 2024
WHO Resolution WHA70.7 on Sepsis (2017) + WHO Global Report on Sepsis (2020)
WHO IMAI District Clinician Manual (severe illness)
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Cholera outbreak case management + outbreak response (Kenya IDSR + GTFCC)
population: All ages; outbreak-prone in Kenya counties with WASH gaps — Tana River, Garissa, Mandera, Wajir, Turkana, Migori, Kisumu, informal urban settlements
presentation: Acute profuse watery 'rice water' diarrhoea ± vomiting, rapid dehydration within hours; case definition (outbreak setting): any person ≥ 2 years with acute watery diarrhoea (and severe dehydration or death from acute watery diarrhoea); confirm by stool culture or Vibrio cholerae RDT
redFlags: Severe dehydration: lethargy/unconscious, sunken eyes, unable to drink, skin pinch goes back very slowly, weak/absent pulse
Pregnant women, children < 5, elderly — higher mortality
Cluster of ≥ 2 cases in same household/village within 1 week — notify within 24h
diagnostics: Clinical case definition sufficient in outbreak (no lab needed for treatment)
Stool RDT (Crystal VC) at sentinel sites for outbreak confirmation
Stool culture (Cary-Blair transport) for first 10–20 cases for confirmation + AMR
Notification: IDSR immediately reportable (within 24h to County Health → MOH → WHO under IHR)
management: PLAN C (severe dehydration): Ringer's lactate IV — adults 100 ml/kg over 3h (30 ml/kg in first 30 min, then 70 ml/kg in next 2.5h); children < 1 year 30 ml/kg in first 1h then 70 ml/kg in next 5h; reassess every 15–30 min, continue ORS as soon as able to drink
PLAN B (some dehydration): ORS 75 ml/kg over 4h
PLAN A (no dehydration): ORS after each loose stool, continue feeding
Antibiotics for severe cases / high-output: doxycycline 300 mg single dose (adults); azithromycin 20 mg/kg single dose (children, pregnant women)
Zinc 20 mg daily × 10 days for children < 5 years (10 mg if < 6 months)
Cholera Treatment Centre (CTC) setup: dedicated cots with hole + bucket, ORS corner, chlorine 0.05% hand wash, 0.2% for surfaces, 2% for excreta
Oral cholera vaccine (OCV) — reactive campaign in outbreak per Kenya MOH and GTFCC; pre-emptive in high-risk areas; 2 doses 14 days apart for long-term, single dose for outbreak
Case investigation: line list, chlorination of water source, identify common exposure, promote handwashing, safe water (Aquatabs), food hygiene
Burial: safe and dignified burial protocol
WHO IHR notification + Kenya MOH IDSR weekly reporting

references.label: Global Task Force on Cholera Control (GTFCC) Ending Cholera Roadmap 2030
Kenya MOH National Plan for Multisectoral Prevention and Control of Cholera 2022–2030
WHO Cholera Outbreak Response Field Manual
Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) Technical Guidelines 3rd edition

title: Gender-based violence clinical care (WHO LIVES + Kenya National GBV Guidelines)
population: All ages and genders presenting with disclosed or suspected sexual violence, intimate partner violence, child abuse, or FGM complications
presentation: Survivors may present with physical injuries, sexual assault, pregnancy concerns, STI symptoms, mental health crises, or non-specific somatic complaints; presentations within 72h (HIV PEP window) or 120h (EC window) urgent
redFlags: Acute sexual assault within 72 hours (HIV PEP window)
Acute sexual assault within 120 hours (emergency contraception window)
Pediatric sexual abuse (child protection mandatory reporting)
FGM with complications (haemorrhage, sepsis, obstructed labour)
diagnostics: Comprehensive medical history + injury documentation with body map + photographs (with consent)
Forensic specimen collection where indicated AND survivor consents (PRC1 form per Kenya guidelines, chain of custody)
HIV rapid test (baseline), syphilis, hepatitis B, pregnancy test
STI screening: gonorrhoea, chlamydia per syndromic management
Mental health screening (PHQ-9, GAD-7, PTSD checklist)
management: FIRST-LINE psychological support — WHO LIVES approach:
L — Listen with empathy, without judgement
I — Inquire about needs and concerns
V — Validate (believe + non-blaming)
E — Enhance safety (safety planning)
S — Support (refer to services)
Sexual assault clinical package (within 72h):
HIV PEP: TLD (tenofovir-lamivudine-dolutegravir) × 28 days per Kenya NASCOP
Emergency contraception: levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose (within 120h, more effective earlier) OR Cu-IUD (within 120h, most effective)
STI prophylaxis: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + azithromycin 1 g PO + metronidazole 2 g PO
Hepatitis B vaccine + HBIG if unvaccinated
Tetanus booster
Wound care, suturing as needed
Documentation: PRC1 / P3 form (Kenya police medical examination form) completed by trained provider
Referral to SGBV recovery centre (where available — Kenya has SGBV one-stop centres in major hospitals), psychosocial counsellor, police (with consent unless child)
Child sexual abuse: MANDATORY reporting per Kenya Children Act + Sexual Offences Act; involve child protection officer
Safety planning for IPV: code word, go-bag, safe location, escape route, GBV hotline 1195 (Kenya) or 1199
Follow-up at 1 week, 2 weeks, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months for HIV, syphilis, mental health
Address FGM complications + counsel against medicalisation per WHO + Kenya Anti-FGM Act 2011

references.label: WHO Clinical Handbook on Health Care for Women Subjected to Intimate Partner Violence or Sexual Violence (2014)
Kenya National Guidelines on Management of Sexual Violence (3rd edition, 2014, updated)
Kenya National Policy for the Prevention and Response to Gender Based Violence
WHO RESPECT framework for preventing violence against women

title: WHO Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative + breastfeeding support (Kenya BFHI)
population: All mothers and newborns; Kenya MOH endorses exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months then continued with complementary feeding to 24 months
presentation: Routine postnatal contact for breastfeeding initiation, established feeding review, or concerns: poor latch, sore nipples, mastitis, perceived low supply, infant weight loss, jaundice, refusal to feed
redFlags: Newborn weight loss > 10% birth weight or not regained by day 14
Mastitis with abscess (fluctuant, fever, systemic toxicity)
Mother HIV positive — counsel per Kenya PMTCT (ART + EBF then continued BF with ART)
diagnostics: Latch assessment (LATCH score)
Feeding observation — positioning, attachment, swallowing
Weight, output diary (wets/stools)
Maternal nipple/breast examination
Infant oral exam for ankyloglossia (tongue-tie)
management: WHO/UNICEF Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding (BFHI revised 2018):
1. Hospital policy compliance with International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes
2. Staff competence training
3. Antenatal counselling on importance and management
4. Skin-to-skin within 1 hour of birth + first feed
5. Show mothers how to breastfeed and maintain lactation even if separated
6. NO food or drink other than breastmilk unless medically indicated
7. Rooming-in 24 hours/day
8. Responsive feeding (on demand, cues, not schedule)
9. NO artificial teats or pacifiers
10. Discharge with referral to community breastfeeding support
Position + attachment (CHIN: Chin to breast, Head free, In line, Nose to nipple): wide mouth, more areola visible above than below, slow deep sucks
Sore nipples: correct latch, air-dry, lanolin or expressed milk, treat candida (nystatin) if persistent
Engorgement: frequent feeding, cool compress between, warm before feed, hand expression
Blocked duct: massage during feed, vary positions, warm compress
Mastitis: continue breastfeeding (safe + accelerates recovery), rest, NSAID, dicloxacillin/flucloxacillin 500 mg QID × 10 days; ultrasound + drainage if abscess
Low milk supply (true is rare): increase feeding frequency, ensure transfer, skin-to-skin, galactagogues last resort (domperidone where licensed)
Working mothers: hand expression / pump, safe storage (4h room, 24h fridge, 3 months freezer), Kenya Employment Act guarantees lactation breaks
Complementary feeding from 6 months: continue BF, introduce iron-rich foods, responsive feeding
WHO Code: NO formula advertising, free samples, or promotion in health facilities

references.label: WHO/UNICEF Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative — Revised, Updated and Expanded (2018)
WHO Guideline: Protecting, promoting and supporting breastfeeding in facilities providing maternity and newborn services (2017)
Kenya MOH Baby Friendly Community Initiative + National Nutrition Action Plan 2018–2022
Kenya Breast Milk Substitutes (Regulation and Control) Act 2012

title: Road traffic injury — WHO trauma primary survey + Kenya pre-hospital
population: All ages — Kenya has one of the highest road traffic fatality rates in Africa; boda-boda (motorcycle) injuries a leading cause of admissions
presentation: Multiple injury patterns — head injury, blunt chest/abdomen, long bone fractures, spinal injury, polytrauma; pre-hospital scoop-and-run common in Kenya; helmet/seatbelt status often poor
redFlags: Signs of base of skull fracture (raccoon eyes, Battle sign, CSF rhinorrhoea)
diagnostics: Primary survey: cABCDE (catastrophic haemorrhage, Airway+C-spine, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure)
Secondary survey: head-to-toe + AMPLE history
FAST scan if available
FBC, group + crossmatch, lactate, base excess
Imaging: CT head/c-spine/chest/abdo-pelvis per indication (NEXUS / Canadian C-spine rules); plain films for long bones
Trauma scoring: GCS, RTS, ISS
management: Pre-hospital: bystander call 1195 (or county dispatch), scene safety, control external haemorrhage with direct pressure / tourniquet, in-line c-spine immobilisation if mechanism suggestive, recovery position if unconscious, do NOT remove helmet unless airway compromised + trained
Primary survey (resuscitation):
c — Catastrophic haemorrhage: tourniquet, pressure dressing, pelvic binder
A — Airway: chin lift/jaw thrust, suction, OPA/NPA, definitive airway if GCS ≤ 8; in-line c-spine
B — Breathing: high-flow O2, treat tension pneumothorax (needle decompression 2nd ICS MCL or 4th–5th ICS AAL), chest drain for haemothorax
C — Circulation: 2 large-bore IVs, permissive hypotension (target SBP 80–90 until haemorrhage controlled), warmed crystalloid then blood, tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3h of injury (CRASH-2)
D — Disability: GCS, pupils, glucose, BE-FAST
E — Exposure: log roll, prevent hypothermia
Massive transfusion protocol 1:1:1 (RBC:plasma:platelets) if shock + active bleeding
Head injury: maintain SBP > 110, SpO2 > 94%, head-up 30°, mannitol or hypertonic saline for raised ICP signs, urgent CT, neurosurgical referral
C-spine: rigid collar + log roll until cleared clinically (NEXUS / Canadian) or radiologically
Pelvic fracture: pelvic binder at level of greater trochanters, do NOT spring pelvis
Long bone fracture: splint + analgesia, reduce if vascular compromise
Open fracture: IV cefazolin + tetanus, irrigation, debridement within 6h
Damage control surgery for unstable patients (stop bleed + contamination, return for definitive)
Disposition: trauma centre activation per Kenya National Emergency Medical Care Strategy
Helmet/seatbelt education + WHO Decade of Action for Road Safety

references.label: WHO Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023
WHO Decade of Action for Road Safety 2021–2030
Kenya National Emergency Medical Care Strategy 2020–2025
CRASH-2 trial — tranexamic acid in trauma (Lancet 2010)

title: Pediatric HIV — diagnosis + ART (Kenya NASCOP + WHO)
population: HIV-exposed infants (born to mothers living with HIV) and children/adolescents living with HIV; Kenya PMTCT cascade
presentation: HIV-exposed infants on prophylaxis + early infant diagnosis schedule; symptomatic disease: failure to thrive, recurrent infections, oral candida, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, encephalopathy, severe pneumonia (Pneumocystis), TB
redFlags: Positive infant HIV DNA PCR at any age
diagnostics: HIV-exposed infant testing (Kenya schedule): HIV DNA PCR at 6 weeks, 6 months, 12 months, and 18 months OR 6 weeks after cessation of breastfeeding (whichever later); rapid antibody test at 18+ months
Confirmatory PCR on any positive result
Baseline CD4, viral load, FBC, ALT, creatinine, hepatitis B sAg
TB screening (symptom + IGRA/CXR), cryptococcal antigen if ≥ 5 yrs and CD4 < 100
Routine viral load: 6 months after ART start, 12 months, then annually (Kenya algorithm); enhanced adherence counselling if VL > 1000
management: PMTCT: maternal ART (lifelong TLD) + infant NVP/AZT prophylaxis per Kenya NASCOP (6 weeks if low-risk, 12 weeks high-risk + cotrimoxazole)
Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis from 6 weeks of age in all HIV-exposed infants until HIV definitively excluded; lifelong in HIV-positive < 5 yrs and CD4 < 350 or stage 2–4 in older
Start ART in ALL children with confirmed HIV regardless of CD4 (Test + Start)
First-line ART per Kenya 2022 guidelines:
< 4 weeks: AZT + 3TC + NVP (or RAL where available)
4 weeks–< 20 kg: ABC + 3TC + DTG (paediatric dispersible)
≥ 20 kg: TDF (or TAF) + 3TC + DTG
Avoid EFV in young children (neuropsychiatric, dosing); avoid PI-boosted regimens unless second-line
Adherence support: paediatric formulations (DTG 10 mg dispersible, ABC/3TC dispersible), caregiver counselling, pill boxes, family-based approach
Disclosure: WHO recommends progressive disclosure from age 6, full disclosure by age 12 with caregiver support
Adolescent-friendly services: Operation Triple Zero (zero missed appointments, zero missed doses, zero viral load) per Kenya
Co-infection: TB preventive therapy (TPT) for all eligible (isoniazid + rifapentine 3HP or 6-month INH); ART within 2–8 weeks of TB treatment start
Routine immunisations including BCG ONLY if asymptomatic and CD4 ≥ 25% (avoid BCG in symptomatic infants); give measles + rotavirus per schedule
Nutrition: assess at every visit, manage SAM per IMAM
Monitor for ART side effects: DTG weight gain, ABC HSR (HLA-B*5701), TDF renal (less in children)
Transition to adult clinic by age 19–24 with structured handover
Linkage to OVC services + Linda Mama if mother postpartum

references.label: Kenya ARV Guidelines for Treatment and Prevention of HIV in Kenya (NASCOP, 2022 edition)
WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring (2021, 2024 update)
Kenya Operation Triple Zero adolescent strategy

title: Drowning prevention + clinical management (WHO Global Report on Drowning)
population: All ages; highest burden in children under 5 and adolescent males; Kenya — Lake Victoria, Indian Ocean coast, rural water bodies; flood-related during long rains
presentation: Submersion incident with respiratory impairment; classified by outcome — death, survival with morbidity, survival without morbidity; spectrum from cough/dyspnoea to cardiac arrest; cold water immersion — hypothermia
redFlags: Cardiac arrest — start CPR with 5 rescue breaths first (different from cardiac arrest)
Co-existing trauma, alcohol, illicit drug, seizure trigger
diagnostics: Vital signs, SpO2, core temperature, mental status
ABG, electrolytes, glucose, lactate
ECG (QT prolongation in hypothermia)
Chest X-ray (may be delayed)
C-spine imaging if mechanism + signs
Toxicology if suspected
management: PREVENTION (WHO 10 evidence-based interventions):
Install barriers (fencing around water)
Provide safe places away from water for pre-school children
Teach school-age children swimming, water safety, safe rescue
Train bystanders in safe rescue + resuscitation
Set + enforce safe boating, shipping, and ferry regulations
Build resilience to flooding
Coordinate national water safety plan
Reduce alcohol use around water
Improve resuscitation in event of drowning
Strengthen public awareness

Pre-hospital: safe rescue ('reach, throw, row, go' — don't enter water without flotation + training), start in-water rescue breathing if trained, get to land, BLS with FIVE rescue breaths first then chest compressions (hypoxia is primary problem), oxygen high-flow
ED: ABCDE, oxygen titrated to SpO2 ≥ 94%, NIV (CPAP) or intubation if respiratory failure
Cervical spine: only immobilise if mechanism (diving) or signs
Active rewarming if hypothermic (T < 32°C — invasive); 'not dead until warm and dead' but stop after 30 min if no rhythm > 32°C
Routine antibiotics + steroids NOT recommended
Observation: asymptomatic with normal exam after 4–6h can be discharged; any symptoms admit
Avoid abdominal thrusts (no benefit, aspiration risk)
Mental health screening + safety planning (suicide attempts a cause)

references.label: WHO Global Report on Drowning: Preventing a Leading Killer (2014) + Status Report 2024
WHO Preventing Drowning: an implementation guide (2017)
UN Resolution A/RES/75/273 on Global Drowning Prevention
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Neonatal resuscitation — Helping Babies Breathe + WHO Essential Newborn Care
population: All newborns at birth; approximately 10% require some assistance, 1% require extensive resuscitation
presentation: Newborn at delivery — assess crying / breathing / tone within first 30 seconds; non-vigorous, apnoea, gasping, cyanosis, bradycardia (HR < 100)
redFlags: Apnoea / gasping / not crying at birth
Antepartum haemorrhage / fetal distress / cord prolapse
diagnostics: Apgar score at 1 and 5 minutes (and 10 min if depressed)
Heart rate by auscultation or umbilical pulse (most accurate)
Respiratory effort, tone, colour, response to stimulation
Pulse oximetry on right hand (preductal) — target SpO2 by minutes after birth (1 min 60–65%, 5 min 80–85%, 10 min 85–95%)
Glucose if persistent depression
management: Helping Babies Breathe (WHO + AAP) Action Plan:
Preparation: bag-and-mask (size 0 or 1), suction, warm clean cloth × 2, ties + razor blade, ambient temperature 25–28°C, identify helper
THE GOLDEN MINUTE — first 60 seconds:
0–30 sec: dry thoroughly, keep warm (skin-to-skin if crying), clear airway only if needed
If crying: routine care — skin-to-skin, delayed cord clamping ≥ 1 min, initiate breastfeeding within 1 hour
If not crying: stimulate (rub back/feet) and clear airway
If still not breathing by 60 seconds: cut cord and move to resuscitation area
Bag-mask ventilation 40–60 breaths/min, room air for term (21% O2); supplemental O2 only if SpO2 below target after effective ventilation
Ensure chest rise — reposition head (neutral), reapply mask, suction, open mouth, increase pressure
Continued evaluation:
HR ≥ 100 + breathing: post-resuscitation care, monitor
HR < 100: continue ventilation
HR < 60 after 30 sec of effective ventilation: chest compressions 3:1 with ventilation (90 compressions + 30 breaths per minute), 100% O2, IV/UVC access, adrenaline 0.01–0.03 mg/kg IV
Meconium: routine intubation + suctioning NO LONGER recommended; only if airway obstruction with non-vigorous infant
Preterm < 32 weeks: plastic wrap, exothermic mattress, CPAP 5 cmH2O, start at 30% O2 titrated, surfactant if intubated
Post-resuscitation: maintain temperature (skin-to-skin or warmer), glucose ≥ 47 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L), monitor breathing, refer to NBU if persistent depression / GCS / seizures
Therapeutic hypothermia (33.5°C × 72h) for HIE in facilities with capability — start within 6h

WHO Essential Newborn Care: keep warm (skin-to-skin), early initiation of breastfeeding within 1 hour, delayed cord clamping ≥ 1 min, eye prophylaxis (1% tetracycline or povidone-iodine), vitamin K 1 mg IM, BCG + OPV0 + hepatitis B birth dose
Discontinue resuscitation if no HR after 20 minutes of complete and adequate resuscitation

references.label: WHO Guidelines on Basic Newborn Resuscitation (2012, updated 2024)
Helping Babies Breathe 2nd Edition (AAP + Laerdal Global Health)
Kenya MOH Basic Paediatric Protocols + Newborn Resuscitation Algorithm

title: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis — Kenya rabies elimination strategy + WHO
population: All persons with potential rabies exposure (dog/cat/bat/wildlife bite/scratch/mucosal contact); Kenya — dog-mediated rabies endemic, target zero human dog-mediated rabies deaths by 2030
presentation: Exposure history: bite, scratch, lick on mucous membrane / broken skin, by suspected rabid mammal (especially dog in Kenya); WHO Category I (touching/feeding — no PEP), II (nibbling/minor scratch no bleeding — vaccine), III (transdermal bite/scratch/mucosal/bat — vaccine + RIG)
redFlags: Category III exposure (bleeding bite, mucosal contact, bat exposure) — needs RIG
Bite to head, face, neck, hand, genital — proximity to CNS
Immunocompromised (HIV, transplant) — needs full vaccine + RIG regardless of category
Animal escaped or unable to observe × 10 days
Bat in room (even without obvious bite — treat as Category III)
Established rabies (hydrophobia, aerophobia) — uniformly fatal, palliative care only
diagnostics: Clinical exposure assessment (category + site)
Identify animal: domestic dog with known owner — observe 10 days; if dog healthy at day 10, can stop PEP
Wild animal or unknown / stray dog — assume rabid, complete PEP
No diagnostic test changes clinical decision pre-symptom
Established disease: post-mortem brain DFA / PCR (public health)
management: IMMEDIATE WOUND CARE (single most important intervention):
Wash wound thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes
Apply virucidal — 70% alcohol or povidone-iodine
Do NOT suture (or delayed suturing after RIG infiltration)
Tetanus prophylaxis per status
Antibiotic prophylaxis (amoxicillin-clavulanate) for deep/contaminated bites
RABIES VACCINE — Kenya uses WHO-prequalified cell-culture vaccine:
Intramuscular regimen (Essen, 5-dose): days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28 — deltoid (anterolateral thigh in children)
Intradermal regimen (Updated Thai Red Cross, dose-sparing per WHO 2018): days 0, 3, 7, 28 — 0.1 ml at 2 sites each visit (4 visits, 2 sites = 8 doses total)
WHO 2018 abridged IM: days 0, 3, 7 — 1 site each (total 3 visits) for previously unvaccinated AND IPC available
Previously vaccinated: 2 doses days 0 + 3 only (no RIG needed)
RABIES IMMUNOGLOBULIN (RIG) — for Category III + immunocompromised:
Human RIG 20 IU/kg or Equine RIG 40 IU/kg
Infiltrate AS MUCH AS POSSIBLE into and around the wound(s); any remaining IM at distant site
Give only at day 0 with first vaccine dose (or up to day 7 if delayed)
Do NOT exceed calculated dose (suppresses vaccine response)
Pre-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk groups (vets, animal handlers, lab workers, travellers to remote endemic areas): 2 doses days 0 + 7 (WHO 2018 abridged)
One Health: notify county veterinary, mass dog vaccination + sterilisation (target 70% dog vaccination coverage), community education, report under Kenya Rabies Elimination Strategy 2014–2030
Counsel: complete schedule essential, do not interrupt; report adverse events

references.label: WHO Rabies vaccines: WHO position paper (2018, updated)
WHO Expert Consultation on Rabies, third report (TRS 1012, 2018)
Zero by 30: Global Strategic Plan to End Human Deaths from Dog-Mediated Rabies by 2030 (WHO/OIE/FAO/GARC)

title: Anthrax — cutaneous, gastrointestinal, inhalational (SSA outbreak-prone)
population: Pastoralists, livestock handlers, abattoir workers, hide processors across SSA — Kenya, Ethiopia, Uganda, Tanzania, Zambia. Outbreak-prone after livestock deaths in rangelands.
presentation: Cutaneous (95%): painless papule → vesicle → black eschar with surrounding non-pitting oedema, often on hands/face/neck after contact with infected animal/hide. Gastrointestinal: fever, severe abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea after eating undercooked infected meat. Inhalational: biphasic — flu-like prodrome then mediastinitis with widened mediastinum, shock, meningitis (50% develop meningoencephalitis).
redFlags: Massive non-pitting oedema around eschar (toxin-mediated, can compromise airway if neck/face)
Cluster of cases / livestock deaths in same locality (notify under IDSR)
Bioterrorism concern (multiple inhalational cases without exposure)
diagnostics: Gram stain of vesicle fluid or eschar edge — large gram-positive rods in chains
Blood culture (systemic), CSF if meningism
PCR for B. anthracis at reference lab
Chest X-ray / CT — mediastinal widening, pleural effusion
Notify county veterinary + IDSR within 24h (Kenya immediately reportable)
management: Cutaneous, uncomplicated, no systemic signs: ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BD × 7–10 days (or doxycycline 100 mg BD); 60 days if associated with intentional release

Systemic (GI / inhalational / severe cutaneous with extensive oedema or head/neck): combination therapy IV ciprofloxacin 400 mg q8h + clindamycin 900 mg q8h (antitoxin effect) + meropenem 2 g q8h if meningitis or severe
Antitoxin: raxibacumab or obiltoxaximab IV single dose for systemic / inhalational (where available; anthrax immune globulin in some countries)
Supportive: airway protection if facial/cervical oedema (early intubation), drain pleural effusion, vasopressors, steroids for severe oedema or meningitis
Do NOT excise cutaneous lesion — wound dressing + systemic antibiotic only
Post-exposure prophylaxis (after confirmed B. anthracis exposure): ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD × 60 days + 3-dose anthrax vaccine series
Public health: notify under IDSR, livestock vaccination campaign, safe disposal of carcasses (DO NOT slaughter/skin), community education on not consuming sick animals, decontaminate hides
Personal protective equipment for slaughter workers; livestock anthrax vaccination annually in endemic areas

references.label: WHO Anthrax in humans and animals 4th edition (FAO/OIE/WHO)
Kenya IDSR Technical Guidelines — Anthrax case definition

title: Brucellosis — Malta fever (SSA pastoralist communities)
population: Pastoralists, livestock owners, herders, abattoir workers, dairy workers, consumers of raw milk/cheese in SSA — common in Kenya, Ethiopia, Uganda, Somalia, Sudan
presentation: Insidious onset undulant fever, drenching night sweats with characteristic 'wet straw' odour, malaise, weight loss, arthralgia (large joints — hips, knees, sacroiliac), back pain, hepatosplenomegaly. Often misdiagnosed as malaria or TB.
redFlags: Endocarditis (1–2%, leading cause of brucellosis death)
Spondylitis with epidural abscess (severe back pain, neurological deficit)
diagnostics: Blood culture (Castaneda bottles, prolonged incubation up to 6 weeks — inform lab of suspicion + biosafety)
Serum agglutination test (SAT) titre ≥ 1:160 or 4-fold rise; 2-ME test for chronic disease; Rose Bengal for screening
PCR (reference lab)
FBC (cytopaenias), ESR/CRP, LFT (mild transaminitis), blood smear (rule out malaria + relapsing fever)
Imaging if focal — MRI spine for spondylitis, echo for endocarditis
Notify under IDSR; investigate exposure history (raw milk, parturition assistance, abortion materials)
management: Uncomplicated adult: doxycycline 100 mg PO BD × 6 weeks + rifampicin 600–900 mg PO daily × 6 weeks (WHO regimen) OR doxycycline 6 weeks + streptomycin 1 g IM × 14–21 days (more efficacious, less relapse — preferred when available)
Children > 8 years: same as adult
Children ≤ 8 years: rifampicin + cotrimoxazole × 6 weeks (avoid doxycycline tooth staining)
Pregnancy: rifampicin monotherapy × 6 weeks or rifampicin + cotrimoxazole (avoid doxycycline + streptomycin)
Neurobrucellosis: triple therapy doxycycline + rifampicin + ceftriaxone × 3–6 months minimum
Spondylitis: triple therapy × 3 months, surgical drainage if abscess + neurological deficit
Endocarditis: triple therapy + valve replacement usually required, 6+ months treatment
Counsel: complete full course (relapse risk), avoid raw milk/cheese, occupational protective equipment, livestock vaccination
Public health: report under IDSR, county veterinary collaboration for herd test + slaughter, milk pasteurisation campaign, S19 / Rev1 livestock vaccination

references.label: WHO Brucellosis in humans and animals (WHO/CDS/EPR/2006.7)
Corbel MJ. Brucellosis: an overview. Emerg Infect Dis 1997
Kenya MOH One Health strategic plan for control of brucellosis

title: Rift Valley Fever — outbreak response (SSA)
population: Livestock keepers, abattoir workers, veterinarians during epizootics — Kenya (Garissa, Wajir, Mandera, Tana River, Baringo, Kilifi), Tanzania, Sudan, Somalia, Madagascar; flooding/El Niño-associated mosquito-driven outbreaks
presentation: Most infections asymptomatic or self-limiting febrile illness (90%). Severe forms (1–10%): haemorrhagic fever (jaundice, petechiae, GI bleeding, DIC — 50% mortality), encephalitis (1–4 weeks after onset), ocular disease (retinitis with macular scarring, permanent vision loss in 1–10%). Livestock: 'abortion storms' — mass abortions and high neonatal mortality in sheep/goats/cattle precede human cases.
redFlags: Haemorrhagic signs: petechiae, ecchymoses, GI/gum bleeding
Jaundice with raised transaminases > 1000 IU/L (predicts severe disease)
Cluster of cases + reports of livestock abortions / deaths (notify within 24h)
diagnostics: RT-PCR (KEMRI / reference lab — BSL3)
RVF IgM ELISA (paired sera)
FBC (thrombocytopaenia, leucopaenia), LFT (markedly raised AST/ALT), coagulation, creatinine
Blood smear and malaria RDT (rule out other febrile illness)
Notify IDSR within 24h; WHO IHR notification (potentially PHEIC)
Coordinate with county veterinary services on livestock investigation
management: No specific antiviral therapy; supportive care
Severe / haemorrhagic: ICU admission, blood product support (FFP, platelets, cryoprecipitate guided by DIC), AKI dialysis, vasopressor support
Ribavirin has been used in compassionate situations but evidence weak; consider in encephalitis at specialist centre
Vaccination NOT yet available for humans (Smithburn vaccine for livestock — used in outbreak ring vaccination per county veterinary)
Strict barrier nursing — body fluid precautions; standard precautions sufficient (no human-to-human transmission documented)

PUBLIC HEALTH: enhanced surveillance, vector control (mosquito source reduction, ITNs), ban on slaughter/movement of animals from affected areas, safe disposal of aborted material, livestock vaccination (high-risk areas after El Niño rainfall warning)
Community risk communication: PPE for handling livestock, no consumption of meat from sick animals
Ophthalmology follow-up for survivors with visual symptoms

references.label: WHO Rift Valley Fever Fact Sheet + Outbreak Response
FAO Decision-Support Tool for RVF (FAO Animal Production and Health Manual No. 19)

title: Leptospirosis — flood-associated + occupational (SSA)
population: Sewer workers, rice farmers, sugarcane cutters, abattoir staff, fishermen, flood-exposed populations across SSA; rising incidence with urban floods (Nairobi, Mombasa, Dar es Salaam, Lagos)
presentation: Biphasic: 5–14 days incubation; phase 1 (4–7 days) — abrupt fever, intense myalgia (especially calves), severe headache, conjunctival suffusion (without exudate — diagnostic clue). Defervescence, then phase 2 — immune phase with meningism, uveitis. Severe (5–10%) — Weil's disease: jaundice, AKI, pulmonary haemorrhage (high mortality).
redFlags: Exposure to floodwater, sewers, livestock, or rodents
diagnostics: Microscopic agglutination test (MAT) — paired sera (acute + 7–10 days later)
Leptospira IgM ELISA (earliest at day 5–7)
PCR on blood (first 10 days) or urine (after day 10) at reference lab
Dark-field microscopy of blood/urine (low sensitivity)
FBC (leucocytosis, thrombocytopaenia), LFT (hyperbilirubinaemia disproportionate to transaminitis), CK (rhabdomyolysis), creatinine, urinalysis (proteinuria, haematuria)
CXR if respiratory — bilateral infiltrates suggest pulmonary haemorrhage
Differential: dengue, malaria, viral hepatitis, scrub typhus
management: Mild / uncomplicated: doxycycline 100 mg PO BD × 7 days (adults, non-pregnant) OR amoxicillin 500 mg TDS × 7 days (children, pregnancy)
Severe: IV penicillin G 1.5 MU q6h × 7 days OR ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily × 7 days OR doxycycline IV (where available)
Watch for Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction within hours of starting antibiotic — supportive only
ICU care for severe: ventilation for pulmonary haemorrhage (lung-protective strategy), dialysis for AKI (often reversible), blood products
Methylprednisolone has been used for pulmonary haemorrhage / severe disease — evidence limited but considered in refractory cases
Plasma exchange for severe / refractory pulmonary haemorrhage
Prophylaxis: doxycycline 200 mg weekly for high-risk occupational exposure or short-term deployment (military, disaster response)
Public health: notify under IDSR; vector control (rodent), source identification (flooded water source), community PPE for sewer/agricultural workers, drainage improvement

references.label: WHO Leptospirosis Reference Group — Human Leptospirosis: Guidance for Diagnosis, Surveillance and Control (2003, updated)
PAHO Leptospirosis Surveillance and Response Manual
Kenya MOH Leptospirosis case definition in IDSR

title: Organophosphate (OP) poisoning — agricultural exposure (SSA)
population: Agricultural workers, smallholder farmers across SSA — Kenya tea/coffee/horticulture sector, Ethiopia, Uganda. Also intentional self-poisoning (one of the most common methods of suicide in rural SSA — high lethality).
presentation: Cholinergic toxidrome — DUMBELS (Defecation, Urination, Miosis, Bronchorrhoea/Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation) and SLUDGE (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI upset, Emesis); nicotinic — muscle fasciculations, weakness, hypertension, tachycardia; CNS — confusion, seizures, coma. Severity by Peradeniya OP poisoning scale. Distinctive garlic/petrochemical odour.
redFlags: Intermediate syndrome (24–96h) — proximal muscle weakness, neck flexor weakness, respiratory paralysis (often missed)
Delayed neuropathy (OP-induced delayed polyneuropathy, weeks later)
Intentional ingestion of pesticide (high lethality — paraquat especially)
diagnostics: Plasma cholinesterase activity (pseudocholinesterase) — diagnostic + prognostic; RBC cholinesterase preferred but less available
ABG, lactate, electrolytes, glucose, creatinine
ECG (QT prolongation, AV block, tachy/bradyarrhythmias)
Try to identify specific compound (bring container) — paraquat vs OP carries very different prognosis
