management: RESUSCITATION first: A — protect airway (early intubation if GCS drop or severe secretions), suction copiously; B — ventilate, treat bronchospasm; C — IV access, fluids (cautious — pulmonary oedema risk)
DECONTAMINATION: remove contaminated clothes, wash skin with soap/water; activated charcoal 1 g/kg if < 1h since ingestion AND airway protected

ATROPINE — titrate to atropinisation (clear chest, HR > 80, SBP > 90, dry axillae, pupils mid-position): initial 2–5 mg IV in adults, double every 5 min until atropinised; then infusion 10–20% of cumulative dose per hour. Do NOT use pupil size alone as endpoint (miosis may persist).

PRALIDOXIME (oxime) — 2-PAM 30 mg/kg IV bolus over 30 min then 8 mg/kg/h infusion × 7 days or until weaning ventilator (WHO recommended dose — controversial; evidence mixed); most effective if given within 24h
Diazepam 10–20 mg IV for seizures or agitation (avoid suxamethonium for intubation — prolonged paralysis)
Watch for INTERMEDIATE SYNDROME: monitor respiratory function (NIF, FVC), keep intubated/ventilated 5–7 days if severe poisoning
Avoid: hyoscine (no central action), succinylcholine (prolonged block), aminophylline, theophylline

Paraquat: NO antidote, fatal in most adults — gastric lavage, multiple-dose activated charcoal or Fuller's earth, AVOID supplemental oxygen (worsens lung fibrosis — use lowest FiO2 to maintain SpO2 ≥ 88%), immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide + methylprednisolone) controversial
Mental health assessment for intentional poisoning + safety planning

Public health: WHO/FAO Code on Pesticide Management, restrict highly hazardous pesticides (Kenya banned several HHPs 2022), promote integrated pest management, community storage safety, suicide prevention via means restriction

references.label: WHO Clinical management of acute pesticide intoxication: prevention of suicidal behaviours (2008)
Eddleston M et al. Management of acute organophosphorus pesticide poisoning. Lancet 2008
Kenya Pest Control Products Board — list of restricted/banned pesticides
WHO/FAO International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management (2014)

title: Adolescent-friendly health services (Kenya AYP / WHO AA-HA!)
population: 10–19 year olds (early 10–14, late 15–19); Kenya — DREAMS partnership counties prioritise adolescent girls and young women (AGYW) 10–24
presentation: Routine adolescent contact (HEEADSSS-screened), problem-focused (mental health crisis, contraception, STI, GBV disclosure, substance use, school refusal), or programmatic (HIV testing, HPV vaccine, school health visit)
redFlags: Sexual violence disclosure (apply Kenya GBV pathway)
Pregnancy in adolescent < 16 years (defilement — mandatory reporting Sexual Offences Act)
Newly diagnosed HIV (start ART + Operation Triple Zero)
diagnostics: HEEADSSS confidential interview: Home, Education/Employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/depression, Safety
PHQ-A or PHQ-9 for depression, GAD-7 for anxiety, CRAFFT for substance use
Pregnancy test + STI screen (per syndromic or risk-based), HIV testing per NASCOP (opt-out at 15+ with maturity assessment, parental consent < 15)
Anthropometry, blood pressure
School performance discussion
management: PRINCIPLES (WHO AA-HA! Global Standards for Quality of Health Care for Adolescents):
Accessible: youth-friendly hours / location, no/low cost, adolescent-only or dedicated corner
Acceptable: confidentiality, non-judgement, peer staff training
Appropriate: clinical staff trained in adolescent development
Effective: evidence-based protocols
Equitable: reach marginalised (out-of-school, key populations, disabled, rural)
CONFIDENTIALITY: explain limits (suicide, abuse, defilement). Apply Kenya Children Act + maturity assessment for capacity.
MENTAL HEALTH: WHO mhGAP IG-2 adolescent module; depression — psychosocial first then SSRI (fluoxetine) if moderate-severe; anxiety — CBT; refer for self-harm risk

SEXUAL + REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH: full method mix contraception (LARC including implants and Cu-IUD per WHO MEC), condoms for dual protection, EC (levonorgestrel up to 120h or Cu-IUD); STI syndromic; HIV testing + PrEP eligibility (AGYW 15+, MSM, sex workers); HPV vaccine for 10-year-old girls (Kenya catch-up to 14 yrs)
PREGNANCY in adolescent — comprehensive ANC + Linda Mama, screen for IPV, depression; defilement reporting if < 18 yrs and partner > 18 (Sexual Offences Act)
SUBSTANCE USE: CRAFFT screen, brief intervention, refer to NACADA-affiliated services for SUD
EDUCATION continuity: re-entry policy after pregnancy/parenting (Kenya school re-entry guidelines 2020)
SCHOOL HEALTH: deworming (annual albendazole), iron-folate for adolescent girls, menstrual health (sanitary towels), comprehensive sexuality education
NUTRITION: counselling on iron-rich foods + supplementation
DREAMS bundle for AGYW: ART for HIV+, PrEP, gender-norms transformation, economic strengthening, parenting/caregiver, school subsidies
Refer for GBV per Kenya National GBV Guidelines (one-stop SGBV centres)

references.label: WHO Global Accelerated Action for the Health of Adolescents (AA-HA!) 2nd edition 2023
WHO Global Standards for Quality Health-Care Services for Adolescents (2015)
Kenya National Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health Policy 2015
Kenya Ministry of Education Re-entry policy 2020
DREAMS partnership — Determined, Resilient, Empowered, AIDS-free, Mentored, Safe

title: Burns — comprehensive care + Parkland resuscitation (SSA primary care to district)
population: All ages; high burden in SSA — paraffin / kerosene stove burns common in informal settlements, scald burns in young children, electrical burns in informal sector, women cooking on open fires (IPV-associated burns also a flag)
presentation: Assess: mechanism (scald, flame, contact, chemical, electrical), depth (superficial / superficial partial / deep partial / full thickness), total body surface area (Lund-Browder for children, rule of 9s for adults, palmar method 1% for small/scattered), inhalational injury, associated trauma
redFlags: Inhalational injury (facial burns, singed eyebrows/nostril hair, soot in sputum, hoarse voice, stridor)
Burns > 10% TBSA in children or > 15% in adults (referral threshold)
Burns to face, hands, feet, perineum, major joints (refer regardless of size)
Electrical burns (high-voltage — myoglobinuria, arrhythmia, hidden tissue damage)
diagnostics: ABCDE with C-spine consideration in explosion
Calculate TBSA (exclude erythema only — Lund-Browder paediatric chart)
FBC, U&E, creatinine, glucose, ABG with carboxyhaemoglobin (CO), lactate, CK (electrical), group + crossmatch
Chest X-ray, ECG (electrical), bronchoscopy if inhalational suspected
management: PRIMARY SURVEY: stop the burning process (irrigate chemical with copious water 20+ min), high-flow O2 100%, intubate early if inhalational suspected (oedema develops over hours — gets harder), c-spine if mechanism

FLUID RESUSCITATION — Parkland formula for adults + adolescents: 4 ml/kg × %TBSA Ringer's lactate over 24h from time of burn; HALF in first 8h, half over next 16h; titrate to urine output 0.5 ml/kg/h adults, 1 ml/kg/h children (1.5–2 ml/kg/h if electrical with myoglobinuria)
PAEDIATRIC fluid: Modified Parkland (3 ml/kg × %TBSA) + maintenance (Holliday-Segar) using D5/0.9% saline or D5/Ringer's; monitor glucose
ANALGESIA: IV opioid (morphine 0.1 mg/kg) — avoid IM/SC (unpredictable absorption with shock)

WOUND CARE: cool with running tap water for 20 min (within 3h of injury); cover with cling film initially; in facility — clean with chlorhexidine, debride blisters > 2 cm or thick, apply silver sulfadiazine (1% — but avoid on face/eyes, sulpha allergy, < 2 months, pregnancy near term) or honey-impregnated dressings; non-adherent dressing; change every 1–3 days or per exudate
Honey-based wound dressings — evidence supports use in low-resource settings, faster healing of superficial partial
Tetanus prophylaxis; antibiotics ONLY for clinical infection (not prophylactic)
Nasogastric feeding within 6h for major burns (preserves gut, reduces translocation)
Escharotomy for circumferential full-thickness limb/torso burns with compromise
Fasciotomy for high-voltage electrical with compartment syndrome
Skin grafting at 2–3 weeks for deep partial / full thickness not healing
Inhalational injury: bronchoscopy, ventilation with PEEP, salbutamol, mucolytics; CO poisoning — 100% O2 until COHb < 5%; cyanide (closed-space fire) — hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV
REHABILITATION: early mobilisation, splinting in position of function, pressure garments to prevent hypertrophic scar (6 months), psychosocial support, scar massage
REFERRAL criteria (American Burn Association adapted): partial > 10% TBSA, full thickness > 5%, face/hands/feet/perineum, inhalational, electrical, chemical, comorbidity, suspected NAI
PREVENTION: paraffin stove safety, child-supervised cooking, smoke alarms, hot tap thermostat ≤ 49°C, fire-safe candles, IPV screening for women with burns

references.label: ISBI Practice Guidelines for Burn Care (Part 2 — 2018)
Kenya National Burn Care Guidelines (Kenyatta National Hospital)
WHO Plan for Burn Prevention and Care (2008)
Cochrane Honey for wounds and burns (2015)

title: Tungiasis (jiggers) — Tunga penetrans (SSA NTD)
population: Poor rural communities in SSA with bare ground / sandy soil — Kenya (Murang'a, Kiambu, Nyandarua, coastal), Uganda, Tanzania, Madagascar, Brazil; children + elderly disproportionately affected; school absenteeism + stigma
presentation: Painful itchy nodule on feet (toes especially periungual, sole), with central black dot (gravid female flea), expanding white halo (egg sac). Stages — Fortaleza Classification I-V. Heavy infestation: hundreds of lesions, ulceration, deformity, gait disturbance, secondary bacterial infection.
redFlags: Gangrene / toe autoamputation in heavy chronic disease
diagnostics: Clinical diagnosis from characteristic lesion
Wound swab if secondary infection suspected
Tetanus immunisation status
management: TREATMENT (per WHO/ Kenya National NTD Programme + Ahadi Kenya Trust):
Mild: dimeticone (NYDA) two-oil mixture topical — covers flea, immobilises and kills within 7 days; repeat at 7 days

Alternatives: 95% pure dimeticone, surgical removal with sterile needle (only with proper training + sterilisation — risk of infection if not done well; AVOID 'unsterile thorn removal' traditional practice which spreads infection)
Wound care after extraction: chlorhexidine wash, topical antibiotic if infected, tetanus booster
Avoid kerosene/petrol home remedies (cause chemical burns)
Heavy infestation / cellulitis: oral antibiotic (flucloxacillin or cephalexin); admit if systemic toxicity
Tetanus immunisation per status (booster or full course)
PREVENTION (community-level required for sustained control):
Close-toed shoes (cement floors in schools / homes)
Concrete/screeded floors (replace earth floors)
Daily inspection of feet in endemic areas
Animal reservoirs — treat dogs / pigs / livestock with topical insecticide (key — fleas reinfest from animals)
Community health volunteers (CHV) for case-finding + treatment
School health programmes + footwear support
Kenya National Policy on Prevention and Control of Jigger Infestation (2014)

references.label: Kenya National Policy on Prevention and Control of Jigger Infestation 2014
Heukelbach J et al. Tungiasis treatment with dimeticone two-oil mixture. Lancet Infect Dis 2006

title: Podoconiosis — non-filarial elephantiasis (SSA highland NTD)
population: Barefoot agricultural workers in highland volcanic soil areas — Ethiopia (most affected), Rwanda, Burundi, Cameroon, Uganda highlands, Kenya highlands (limited foci). Genetically susceptible individuals exposed to silica/aluminosilicate clay.
presentation: Bilateral asymmetric ascending lymphoedema, starting in feet (forefoot mossy / nodular), itching, burning, hyperkeratosis, then progressive elephantiasis below the knee. Distinguishable from lymphatic filariasis (LF) by: bilateral, ascending from feet, NO inguinal involvement, NO microfilariae, highland (LF lowland).
redFlags: Acute adenolymphangitis (ADL) attack — fever, redness, swelling, lymphangitis (treat as cellulitis + manage long-term)
diagnostics: Clinical diagnosis based on presentation + barefoot history in endemic area
Negative night blood film for microfilariae (rules out LF)
Staging (Tekola 0–5)
management: WHO simple lymphoedema management package (same as LF morbidity management):
Daily foot hygiene — wash with soap + water at room temperature, dry thoroughly between toes
Skin care — emollient (vaseline), treat fissures + fungal infection (clotrimazole)
Elevation when seated/sleeping
Exercise — toe wiggling, ankle rotation, calf pumps
Compression — bandaging or stockings when available
Always wear shoes — closed footwear
Treat ADL attacks with rest, elevation, paracetamol, antibiotic if cellulitis (penicillin V or flucloxacillin) × 7 days; severe — IV penicillin
Surgical management (nodulectomy) for severe nodular disease in selected patients (refer to specialised centre)
PREVENTION (primary): close-toed shoes from childhood in endemic areas, cement floors, sock/footwear provision in schools
Psychosocial support — patient support groups (Mossy Foot Initiative model), inclusion in NTD programmes per WHO Roadmap 2030
Community-led footwear and floor improvement

references.label: WHO Podoconiosis is a Neglected Tropical Disease 2011
Davey G et al. Podoconiosis: non-infectious geochemical elephantiasis. Trans R Soc Trop Med Hyg 2007
International Podoconiosis Initiative + Mossy Foot Project
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Sickle cell disease — comprehensive care (SSA)
population: Highest global burden in SSA (Nigeria, DRC, Tanzania, Kenya coast, Uganda) — ~75% of cases worldwide; carrier rate 25–30% in Lake Victoria region, coastal Kenya. Diagnosed at newborn screen or after first vaso-occlusive crisis.
presentation: Vaso-occlusive crisis (pain — bones, chest, abdomen, dactylitis in infants), acute chest syndrome (chest pain, hypoxia, infiltrate), splenic sequestration (rapid splenomegaly, anaemia — child), aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19), stroke, priapism, leg ulcer, gallstones, retinopathy, AVN femoral head, recurrent infections (functional asplenia)
redFlags: Acute chest syndrome (new infiltrate + chest pain + hypoxia ± fever) — mortality 1–10%
Stroke — sudden focal deficit (use TCD screening for primary prevention in children)
Splenic sequestration in child (rapid Hb drop, splenomegaly, shock)
Aplastic crisis (reticulocyte count near zero, severe anaemia)
Sepsis — fever in SCD = sepsis until proven otherwise (functional asplenia, pneumococcal risk)
diagnostics: Newborn screening with HPLC / IEF (Kenya pilot in high-prevalence counties) or point-of-care (Sickle SCAN)
Hb electrophoresis or HPLC for diagnosis (HbSS, HbSC, HbSβ-thal)
FBC + reticulocyte, blood film (sickled cells, Howell-Jolly bodies — functional asplenia)
Baseline LDH, bilirubin, ferritin, U&E, creatinine, urinalysis
Annual TCD (transcranial Doppler) ages 2–16 — primary stroke prevention (transfuse if TCD > 200 cm/s)
Acute crisis: CXR if chest symptoms, blood culture if febrile, Hb + reticulocyte (vs baseline)
management: PROPHYLAXIS (initiate at diagnosis):
Penicillin V 125 mg BD (< 3 yrs) / 250 mg BD (3–5 yrs) — at least until age 5; longer if past pneumococcal sepsis
Pneumococcal vaccination — PCV13 routine + PPSV23 at 2 + 5 yrs
Meningococcal (ACWY + B), Hib, annual influenza, hepatitis B, COVID
Folic acid 5 mg daily lifelong
Insecticide-treated bed nets in malaria-endemic areas + chemoprophylaxis (where indicated per Kenya MNCH)

Hydroxyurea — disease-modifying — start in ALL children ≥ 9 months with HbSS regardless of severity (WHO + NHLBI 2014 + REACH trial 2019), start dose 20 mg/kg/day, titrate to MTD 35 mg/kg/day; monitor FBC every 4–8 weeks
ACUTE PAIN CRISIS:
Pain assessment (NRS/Wong-Baker)
IV/SC opioid within 30 min of arrival (morphine 0.1 mg/kg or hydromorphone) — DO NOT delay; supplement with NSAID + paracetamol
IV fluids 1.5× maintenance (avoid over-hydration — pulmonary oedema)
O2 only if SpO2 < 94% on room air
Warm packs, distraction, avoid cold
Incentive spirometry every 2h while in bed (prevents ACS)
Empirical antibiotics (ceftriaxone + macrolide) if fever / suspected ACS
ACUTE CHEST SYNDROME:
Antibiotics (ceftriaxone + azithromycin/clarithromycin)
Oxygen, bronchodilators
Simple transfusion if Hb < 90% baseline + worsening
EXCHANGE transfusion if severe / multilobar (target HbS < 30%)
Incentive spirometry, sit up
STROKE:
Acute — urgent exchange transfusion (target HbS < 30%, Hb 100)
Primary prevention — chronic transfusion if TCD high; alternative hydroxyurea (TWiTCH trial)
PRIAPISM:
> 4 hours — urology aspiration + α-agonist (etilefrine)

PREGNANCY: high-risk; folate 5 mg; transfusion threshold individualised (prophylactic transfusion in selected high-risk); aspirin 75 mg from 12 weeks (preeclampsia prevention); deliver in tertiary centre
ALLOGENEIC HSCT — curative — for severe disease with HLA-matched sibling donor (limited in SSA)
Newer: gene therapy (Casgevy, Lyfgenia — high cost, advocacy needed for SSA access)
Family planning + genetic counselling (carrier testing for spouse)
Pediatric to adult transition clinic from age 16
Newborn screening expansion (Kenya pilot programmes — advocacy for national rollout)

references.label: WHO Sickle Cell Disease — A regional priority in Africa (AFR/RC60/8)
WHO Strategy for the Prevention and Control of Sickle Cell Disease in the African Region
REACH trial — Hydroxyurea for children with SCA in SSA. NEJM 2019
Kenya MOH National Sickle Cell Disease Policy + draft strategic plan
BSH Standards for the Clinical Care of Adults with SCD in the UK (2018)

title: Obstetric fistula — comprehensive care + Kenya fistula strategy
population: Women who suffered prolonged obstructed labour, mostly in SSA (Kenya, Ethiopia, Uganda, Nigeria, DRC); often young, rural, primiparous; profound stigma + abandonment
presentation: Continuous urinary +/- faecal incontinence after obstructed labour, often with stillborn baby; ammoniacal dermatitis, foot drop (from prolonged squat), depression, social isolation, divorce
redFlags: Foot drop / lower limb neurological deficit
diagnostics: Pelvic examination + dye test (methylene blue / phenazopyridine PO) — differentiates VVF vs uterocervical vs ureteric fistula
Cystoscopy + IVU at specialist centre
Urinalysis + culture, creatinine
Depression screening (PHQ-9)
management: Initial care: catheter (Foley + leg bag) — early continuous catheterisation may close some recent fistulae (within 6 weeks of delivery) without surgery (15–20%)
Skin care: barrier cream, regular bathing, absorbent pads
Treat infection, depression (mhGAP)
Refer to fistula surgical centre — Kenya: KNH, Jamaa Mission, Beyond Zero campaigns + Fistula Foundation network
Surgical repair — most via vaginal approach by trained fistula surgeon; success rate 85–90% first attempt; complex cases need abdominal / combined
Post-op: catheter 14–21 days, no PV intercourse 3 months, plan delivery by elective C-section in future pregnancy
Holistic rehabilitation: counselling, livelihood/vocational training, community reintegration (Beyond Zero campaign in Kenya)
PREVENTION (most important):
Education of girls + delay first pregnancy
Skilled birth attendance + Linda Mama
Early identification of obstructed labour via partograph
Emergency obstetric and newborn care (EmONC) access
Comprehensive family planning
End child marriage (Kenya legal age 18 under Marriage Act 2014)
Address obstetric VVF root causes per UNFPA Campaign to End Fistula by 2030

references.label: WHO Obstetric Fistula: Guiding Principles for Clinical Management and Programme Development (2006)
FIGO + UNFPA Campaign to End Fistula by 2030
Kenya National Strategic Framework for the Elimination of Obstetric Fistula 2014–2019 (extended)
International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) Global Competency-Based Fistula Surgery Training Manual

title: School health programme — deworming + vitamin A + adolescent iron-folate (SSA)
population: Pre-school + school-age children + adolescent girls in SSA; Kenya National School-Based Deworming Programme (NSBDP) covers >6 million children
presentation: Programmatic — community campaign + school-based delivery, not symptomatic presentations; addresses STH (Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris), schistosomiasis (where prevalent), vitamin A deficiency (subclinical), iron-deficiency anaemia in adolescent girls
redFlags: Heavy STH infection — wasting, growth failure, intellectual stunting
Severe vitamin A deficiency — night blindness, Bitot spots, corneal xerosis (refer urgently)
Severe iron-deficiency anaemia in adolescent girl (impacts pregnancy outcomes)
diagnostics: School-based campaigns — no individual diagnostic required for mass treatment (per WHO criteria when prevalence ≥ 20% for STH or schisto)
Sentinel surveillance with Kato-Katz / urine filtration
Hb for adolescent girls (where capacity)
Mid-arm circumference / BMI screening
management: PRE-SCHOOL CHILDREN (12–59 months):
Vitamin A 100,000 IU (6–11 months) / 200,000 IU (12–59 months) every 6 months
Albendazole 200 mg (12–23 months) / 400 mg (24–59 months) every 6 months in high-burden areas
Routine measles + Vitamin A combined campaigns
SCHOOL-AGE CHILDREN (5–14 years):
Albendazole 400 mg or mebendazole 500 mg PO single dose annually (twice yearly if STH prevalence > 50%)
Praziquantel 40 mg/kg PO single dose annually in schistosomiasis-endemic areas (prevalence > 10%)
ADOLESCENT GIRLS (10–19 years):
Weekly iron-folic acid 60 mg elemental iron + 2.8 mg folic acid in moderate-severe anaemia prevalence (Kenya — many counties)
Comprehensive sexuality education
HPV vaccine (10-year-olds, Kenya catch-up to 14)
Menstrual hygiene management — Kenya Sanitary Towels Programme
Tetanus-diphtheria booster
ALL SCHOOL CHILDREN:
Eye + hearing screening, refractive error referral (vision screening, glasses)
Oral health — fluoride varnish, atraumatic restorative treatment (ART), counsel on tooth brushing
WASH — handwashing with soap, latrine use, school feeding programme
Mental health awareness + school counsellor pathway (Kenya counsellor cadre)
Insecticide-treated bed nets + malaria intermittent preventive treatment in school (IPTsc) per WHO 2022 in moderate-high transmission areas
Anti-jigger interventions in endemic areas (shoes + concrete floors)
MONITORING: coverage > 75% target, drug coverage validation, MDA campaign reporting
PARTNERSHIPS: KEMRI, Evidence Action, Ministry of Education + MOH joint NSBDP

references.label: WHO Preventive Chemotherapy guidelines for STH + Schistosomiasis (2022)
WHO Guideline: Vitamin A supplementation in infants and children 6–59 months 2011
WHO Guideline: Intermittent iron and folic acid supplementation in menstruating women 2011
WHO 2022 IPT for schoolchildren in malaria moderate-high transmission settings
WHO NTD Roadmap 2021–2030 STH elimination as public health problem

title: Noma (cancrum oris) — gangrenous stomatitis (SSA + child poverty)
population: Children 2–6 years living in extreme poverty + malnutrition in the 'Noma Belt' (sub-Saharan Africa from Senegal to Ethiopia, especially Niger, Nigeria, Burkina Faso, Mali, Sudan, Ethiopia, parts of Kenya); added to WHO NTD list in 2023
presentation: Acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis → rapid progression to gangrenous necrosis of orofacial tissues (cheek, lips, jaw bone, nose) within days; without treatment, 90% mortality within 2–3 weeks; survivors left with severe facial disfigurement, trismus, eating/speech difficulty, stigma
redFlags: Foul mouth odour, foul-smelling oral discharge
Black tissue / sloughing on cheek or gum
Cheek swelling with bluish-black skin discoloration (stage 3 — gangrene)
Coexisting measles, malaria, HIV, immune suppression
diagnostics: Clinical staging (Enwonwu et al — 0 simple gingivitis, 1 acute necrotising gingivitis, 2 oedema, 3 gangrene, 4 scarring, 5 sequelae)
FBC, malaria RDT, HIV test, blood culture if septic
Nutritional assessment (MUAC, WHZ — almost always SAM)
Wound swab if possible (mixed anaerobic + Fusobacterium + Prevotella + spirochaetes)
management: URGENT — acute noma is a medical emergency:
IV antibiotics: amoxicillin-clavulanate OR ampicillin + metronidazole + gentamicin (cover anaerobes + gram-positive + gram-negative) × 7–14 days
Aggressive nutritional rehabilitation (IMAM SAM protocol — F-75/F-100/RUTF)
Treat malaria, measles, dehydration, HIV per protocols
Wound care: chlorhexidine/saline rinses 4× daily, gentle debridement of frankly necrotic tissue only after antibiotic response
Pain relief, mouth care
Vitamin A 200,000 IU stat (if not given recently)
Folate, multivitamin, zinc supplementation
Refer to reconstructive surgery centre after stabilisation (3–6 months later) — Kenya can refer to International Noma Hospital / Hilfsaktion Noma network
PREVENTION (priority — noma is a poverty-driven preventable disease):
Address malnutrition (IMAM, RUTF, vitamin A campaigns)
Routine immunisation (measles especially)
Oral health — toothbrushing education, ANUG recognition
Early breastfeeding, safe water, sanitation
Train community health workers on stage 1–2 recognition (window for cure)
Address poverty + food insecurity at policy level
WHO Resolution adding noma to NTD list (2023) — advocate for resource mobilisation

references.label: WHO Noma is a Neglected Tropical Disease 2023 (added to NTD roadmap)
WHO Information Brochure for Early Detection and Management of Noma
Enwonwu CO et al. Pathogenesis of cancrum oris. Lancet Infect Dis 2006
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) — SSA endemic
population: Endemic in eastern Africa (Sudan, South Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya — Baringo, Turkana, West Pokot, Wajir; Uganda — Karamoja). Children + young men with HIV co-infection.
presentation: Insidious fever (often > 1 month), massive splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, weight loss, pancytopaenia, dark skin pigmentation (kala-azar = 'black sickness'). HIV co-infection — atypical, recurrent. Post kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) months/years after treatment in 50% of African cases.
redFlags: Concurrent TB / amoebic abscess / haematological malignancy in differential
diagnostics: rK39 rapid antigen test (sensitive in primary cases; less reliable in HIV co-infection or relapse)
Spleen / bone marrow / lymph node aspirate for amastigotes (microscopy + culture)
Direct agglutination test (DAT) at reference lab
FBC (pancytopaenia), LFT, U&E, HIV test (essential), TB screen
Notify under IDSR; Kenya NTD Programme + KEMRI reference lab
management: FIRST-LINE eastern Africa (per WHO 2010, MSF, Kenya MOH): paromomycin 15 mg/kg/day IM × 17 days + sodium stibogluconate (SSG) 20 mg/kg/day IV/IM × 17 days — combination shorter + reduces toxicity vs SSG monotherapy
ALTERNATIVE: liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome) 3–5 mg/kg/day × 6 doses (days 1–5 and 10) — total dose 30 mg/kg; preferred in pregnancy, severe disease, age > 45, HIV co-infection
Miltefosine 2.5 mg/kg/day PO × 28 days (oral option — but lower efficacy in Africa, teratogenic)
HIV co-infection: AmBisome 40 mg/kg total + miltefosine combination; secondary prophylaxis monthly AmBisome 4 mg/kg until CD4 > 200
Supportive: transfuse if severe anaemia, treat concurrent infections, nutritional rehabilitation
Monitor SSG ECG QT prolongation, LFT, amylase; AmBisome — nephrotoxicity, hypokalaemia, infusion reactions
PKDL — treat if severe / disseminated (AmBisome or miltefosine)
Public health: indoor residual spraying for sandfly control, treated bednets, case-finding in endemic foci, advocacy for AmBisome access

references.label: WHO Control of the leishmaniases (TRS 949, 2010, updated)
Kenya MOH National Visceral Leishmaniasis Strategic Plan

title: Human African trypanosomiasis (HAT) — sleeping sickness
population: T.b. gambiense — chronic, western/central Africa (DRC, CAR, South Sudan, Uganda focus). T.b. rhodesiense — acute, eastern/southern Africa (Uganda, Tanzania, Malawi, Zimbabwe, Kenya — Lambwe Valley). Tsetse fly bite exposure.
presentation: Stage 1 (haemolymphatic): chancre at bite, intermittent fever, lymphadenopathy (posterior cervical — Winterbottom sign in gambiense), hepatosplenomegaly. Stage 2 (meningoencephalitic): sleep disturbance (reversed circadian rhythm, daytime somnolence), psychiatric symptoms, movement disorder, seizures, coma, death. Rhodesiense progresses in weeks; gambiense over months-years.
redFlags: CNS involvement (CSF WBC > 5 or trypanosomes in CSF)
diagnostics: Card Agglutination Test for Trypanosomiasis (CATT) screening for T.b. gambiense
Microscopy: chancre aspirate, blood (thick film + concentrated buffy coat), lymph node aspirate, CSF
CSF examination: WBC count + trypanosomes — staging defines treatment
Notify WHO HAT surveillance + ESPEN
management: T.b. GAMBIENSE — Fexinidazole PO × 10 days (NEW WHO 2019 first-line for stage 1 and stage 2 with CSF WBC ≤ 100); alternative — Nifurtimox-Eflornithine Combination Therapy (NECT) for severe stage 2 (eflornithine 200 mg/kg IV q6h × 7 days + nifurtimox PO × 10 days)
T.b. RHODESIENSE — stage 1: suramin (slow IV, premed); stage 2: melarsoprol (highly toxic — reactive encephalopathy in 10%, fatal in 5%); melarsoprol-protected schedule with prednisolone
Newer: acoziborole oral single dose (in trials for gambiense)
Supportive: anticonvulsants, nutritional support, treat concurrent infections
Lumbar puncture follow-up at 6, 12, 24 months to confirm cure
Public health: vector control (insecticide-impregnated traps + targets, sterile insect technique), active case-finding in foci, elimination as public health problem (WHO target 2030 for gambiense)

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the treatment of human African trypanosomiasis 2019

title: Cutaneous leishmaniasis (Old World) — SSA
population: L. major (zoonotic, rural), L. tropica (anthroponotic, urban) — Ethiopia, Sudan, Somalia, Kenya (foci), Algeria. Children commonly affected.
presentation: Painless papule at sandfly bite site → ulcerates over weeks with raised indurated border + crusted base ('Aleppo boil', 'oriental sore'). Usually self-healing 3–18 months leaving scar. Disseminated cutaneous in immunocompromised. Mucosal involvement uncommon in Old World.
diagnostics: Clinical recognition + endemic exposure
Skin slit smear from lesion edge — Giemsa staining for amastigotes
PCR (most sensitive)
Culture in Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle media (specialised)
management: Small / few uncomplicated lesions on body: physiological saline + monitor (self-healing); intralesional antimonial (SSG 1–3 ml per lesion weekly × 2–6 weeks); cryotherapy; thermotherapy (50°C × 30 sec × 1–2 sessions)
Multiple / facial / large / chronic: systemic SSG 20 mg/kg/day IV/IM × 20 days; miltefosine 2.5 mg/kg/day × 28 days (avoid pregnancy); amphotericin B for refractory
Wound care + analgesia
Cosmetic counselling — scarring usually permanent
Public health: sandfly bite avoidance (DEET, ITN), insecticide spraying, reservoir control

references.label: Aronson NE et al. Diagnosis and treatment of leishmaniasis. CID 2017
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Lymphatic filariasis — Wuchereria bancrofti (SSA elimination)
population: Coastal Kenya (historically), coastal Tanzania, Mozambique, Madagascar, Nigeria, Ghana. WHO Global Programme to Eliminate LF — many SSA countries on path or achieved elimination (Kenya 2023 elimination as public health problem).
presentation: Most asymptomatic with microfilaraemia. Acute: filarial fever, acute lymphangitis (ascending limb redness/heat), funiculitis, epididymitis. Chronic: lymphoedema (legs > arms > genitals), elephantiasis, hydrocele (very common in men in endemic areas).
redFlags: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (asthma + raised IgE + microfilariae)
diagnostics: Filariasis Test Strip (FTS) — W. bancrofti antigen (now preferred over night blood film)
Night blood smear (22:00–02:00) for microfilariae
Ultrasound for filarial dance sign (scrotal) — pathognomonic
management: PREVENTIVE CHEMOTHERAPY (MDA) — triple drug therapy IDA (ivermectin 200 mcg/kg + DEC 6 mg/kg + albendazole 400 mg) where loa loa NOT co-endemic; DA (DEC + albendazole) elsewhere
Endemic in loa loa co-endemic area: avoid ivermectin/DEC (encephalopathy); use albendazole twice yearly + vector control
Individual chronic management — WHO morbidity package: daily hygiene, skin care, elevation, exercise, compression, footwear, treat ADL with antibiotic + paracetamol
Hydrocele: surgical hydrocelectomy at district hospital
Public health: MDA × 5–7 rounds + transmission assessment surveys; ITNs + insecticide spraying

references.label: WHO Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis

title: Onchocerciasis (river blindness) — SSA
population: Highly endemic in West + Central Africa (DRC, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Uganda, South Sudan). Black fly (Simulium) breeding rivers — riparian communities. African Programme for Onchocerciasis Control (APOC) → ESPEN.
presentation: Pruritus (severe — 'troublesome itching'), filarial skin disease (sowda, lichenified onchodermatitis, leopard skin depigmentation, atrophic skin), subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomas — bony prominences), lymphadenopathy, ocular involvement progressing to visual impairment and blindness.
redFlags: Children with eye signs (sclerosing keratitis, anterior uveitis)
Co-endemic Loa loa (encephalopathy risk with ivermectin)
diagnostics: Skin snip from buttock / iliac crest microscopy for microfilariae
Slit-lamp for ocular microfilariae
Ov16 rapid antibody test
OEPA / ESPEN community survey methods
management: Ivermectin 150 mcg/kg PO single dose annually (preferred biannually 6-monthly in active transmission per WHO 2023) × 10–15 years — kills microfilariae but not adult worms
In Loa loa-co-endemic area with mLOA > 8,000/ml: alternative doxycycline 100–200 mg/day × 4–6 weeks (kills Wolbachia, sterilises adult worms) — avoid ivermectin
Symptomatic: antihistamine for pruritus, low-dose prednisolone for severe inflammation
Nodulectomy for accessible onchocercomas
Eye care + cataract surgery as needed
Public health: MDA via ESPEN, vector control (Simulium larvicide), entomological + parasitological surveillance

title: Buruli ulcer — Mycobacterium ulcerans (SSA NTD)
population: Rural communities near slow-moving water — Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Benin, Cameroon, DRC, Uganda. Children most affected. Kenya rare cases.
presentation: Stage 1: painless subcutaneous nodule / papule / plaque / oedema → stage 2: necrotising ulcer with characteristic undermined edges (large, painless, slow). Stage 3: long-term complications — contractures, amputation. Bones in 5–10%.
redFlags: Cosmetic / functional impact on growing child
diagnostics: Clinical recognition by trained personnel + endemic area
PCR for IS2404 on swab / fine-needle aspirate / biopsy
Ziehl-Neelsen — acid-fast bacilli
Culture (specialised lab, slow growth)
management: WHO RECOMMENDED REGIMEN (2017+): rifampicin 10 mg/kg PO daily + clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg PO BD × 8 weeks (replaced streptomycin in 2017)
Wound care daily — gentle cleansing with normal saline, non-adherent dressing
Surgery for limited disease — minimal debridement only; AVOID extensive early surgery (poor results)
Skin grafting after antibiotic completion for large ulcers
Physiotherapy + splinting to prevent contractures
Manage paradoxical reaction (worsening during/after treatment) — supportive
Public health: case finding via CHV, school surveys, education, BCG vaccination may provide partial protection

references.label: WHO Treatment of Mycobacterium ulcerans disease (Buruli ulcer) 2012/2017
WHO BU global health programme + Stop Buruli initiative

title: Hydatid disease (cystic echinococcosis) — Echinococcus granulosus
population: Pastoralists across SSA with dog–sheep cycle — Kenya (Turkana — highest reported global prevalence historically), Ethiopia, Sudan, Mongolia, central Asia. Children + adults with chronic exposure.
presentation: Slow-growing cysts most commonly in liver (70%) or lung (20%), sometimes spleen, brain, bone. Asymptomatic for years. Symptoms by compression or rupture: hepatic mass, biliary obstruction, cough/haemoptysis (lung), seizures (brain), bone pain/fracture. Rupture — anaphylaxis + dissemination.
diagnostics: Ultrasound (WHO classification CE1-CE5) — primary imaging modality
CT / MRI for lung, brain, deep cysts
Serology (ELISA / Western blot) — useful for diagnosis + post-treatment monitoring
Eosinophilia (variable)
DO NOT aspirate without preparation (anaphylaxis + dissemination risk)
management: Treatment by WHO cyst stage:
CE1 + CE3a small (< 5 cm): albendazole 10–15 mg/kg/day PO × 3–6 months OR PAIR (Puncture-Aspiration-Injection of scolicide-Re-aspiration)
CE2, CE3b active complex: surgery (cystectomy / pericystectomy / liver resection) + albendazole pre/post
CE4 + CE5 inactive: watch and wait — usually no treatment
Albendazole: pre-surgical 4 days before + post 1 month minimum; for inoperable disease months-years; monitor LFT + WCC monthly
PAIR — preferred non-surgical when accessible; covers needle in 1-2% hypertonic saline / 95% alcohol; albendazole cover 4 d pre + 1 month post
Surgery: open or laparoscopic; protect surgical field with hypertonic saline-soaked gauze (anti-spill)
Anaphylaxis from rupture: adrenaline IM + supportive
Lung cyst: surgery preferred (cyst evacuation + capitonnage)
Public health: dog deworming (praziquantel every 6 weeks), restrict dog access to abattoir / sheep carcasses, safe slaughter practices, community education (Kenya — particularly Turkana programme)

references.label: WHO IWGE Expert consensus on diagnosis + treatment of cystic + alveolar echinococcosis 2010
Kenya MOH Hydatid Disease Control Programme (Turkana)

title: Neurocysticercosis — Taenia solium
population: Communities with pig-raising + poor sanitation across SSA, Latin America, South Asia. Leading cause of adult-onset epilepsy in endemic areas — > 30% of new epilepsy cases in SSA endemic regions.
presentation: Most common: late-onset focal-onset seizures (often the only presentation). Headache, raised ICP (hydrocephalus from ventricular cysts), focal deficit, encephalopathy. Cysts may be parenchymal (most), subarachnoid (giant racemose), intraventricular, ocular, spinal.
redFlags: Spinal cord cyst with cord compression
diagnostics: CT or MRI brain — staged cysts (vesicular, colloidal, granular, calcified) — Del Brutto criteria
Serology: enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (EITB) most specific; ELISA
Stool ova + parasite (concurrent tapeworm in 10%)
ECG before albendazole + praziquantel co-administration (interaction)
management: Antiepileptic for seizures (carbamazepine, levetiracetam) — duration depends on lesion type, calcified persists with seizures so AED long-term

PARENCHYMAL VIABLE cysts: albendazole 15 mg/kg/day PO BD × 10–14 days (≤ 800 mg/day) + dexamethasone 6 mg/day BEFORE + during (reduce reactive inflammation); for 2 or more cysts add praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day × 10 days (combination per RCT 2014)
SINGLE viable cyst + seizures: albendazole monotherapy + steroid
INTRAVENTRICULAR / SUBARACHNOID giant: neurosurgical removal / endoscopic; prolonged albendazole + high-dose steroid
Hydrocephalus: VP shunt; sometimes resect cyst causing block
Calcified lesions only: NO cysticidal therapy needed; just AED
Ocular cyst: surgical removal — never give cysticidal (inflammatory blindness)
Treat concurrent tapeworm carrier with single-dose praziquantel 5–10 mg/kg
Public health: improved sanitation, pig confinement, meat inspection, community education — WHO seven-step framework for cysticercosis control

references.label: Garcia HH et al. NEJM 2014 — Combination cysticidal therapy
IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines for Neurocysticercosis 2017

title: Schistosomiasis comprehensive — intestinal + urinary (SSA)
population: S. haematobium (urinary — coastal Kenya, Lake Victoria region, Nile valley), S. mansoni (intestinal — Lake Victoria + Tana River). 90% of global cases in SSA. Children + fishing communities highest burden.
presentation: Acute: swimmer's itch (cercarial dermatitis), Katayama syndrome (4–8 wk post exposure — fever, urticaria, hepatomegaly, eosinophilia). Chronic: urinary (haematuria — especially terminal, dysuria, bladder cancer late), intestinal (chronic diarrhoea, blood in stool, hepatosplenomegaly), hepatic fibrosis (Symmer's clay-pipe-stem), portal hypertension, pulmonary hypertension, neurological (rare, mass lesion).
redFlags: Massive haematemesis from oesophageal varices (hepatosplenic schisto)
Bladder cancer (squamous — 5–10 fold risk in chronic urinary)
Female genital schistosomiasis (HIV acquisition risk + infertility — under-recognised)
diagnostics: S. mansoni: stool Kato-Katz × 2 (eggs); CCA urine cassette (point-of-care)
S. haematobium: urine filtration / centrifugation for eggs (midday sample, after exercise)
Serology (ELISA) for ectopic / Katayama / non-endemic traveller
Ultrasound liver (Symmer's), bladder, kidneys
FBC (eosinophilia), LFT, urinalysis
Bladder cystoscopy if long-standing haematuria (squamous cell carcinoma surveillance)
management: Praziquantel 40 mg/kg PO single dose (S. haematobium, S. mansoni, S. japonicum 60 mg/kg in 2 doses)
MDA: school-based annual praziquantel 40 mg/kg in endemic schools when prevalence > 10% (WHO 2022 expanded recommendation includes pre-school children + non-school age)
Katayama syndrome: praziquantel + steroid (prednisolone)
Female genital schistosomiasis: praziquantel + symptomatic; treat partner; counsel on HIV / fertility risk
Hepatosplenic: praziquantel; manage varices (banding); never cures fibrosis
Neuroschistosomiasis: praziquantel + dexamethasone + neurosurgical decompression if needed

Public health: snail control (mollusciciding focal hot spots), safe water, sanitation, behaviour change (avoid bathing/washing in infested waters), MDA via Kenya NSBDP + ESPEN, WHO NTD Roadmap target — elimination as public health problem by 2030

title: Soil-transmitted helminths — Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris (SSA MDA)
population: Ubiquitous across SSA primary care — pre-school + school-age children + women of reproductive age. Hookworm major cause of iron-deficiency anaemia in adolescents + pregnant women.
presentation: Often asymptomatic. Heavy: failure to thrive, IDA (hookworm — Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus), abdominal pain, diarrhoea, rectal prolapse (heavy Trichuris), Loeffler syndrome (Ascaris larval migration — cough, wheeze, eosinophilia), bowel obstruction (massive Ascaris).
diagnostics: Kato-Katz stool microscopy (egg count quantitative)
FBC (anaemia + eosinophilia)
Stool for occult blood if hookworm + anaemia
management: INDIVIDUAL:
Albendazole 400 mg PO single dose (adults + children > 24 mo) covers all three; 200 mg if 12–24 mo
Mebendazole 500 mg single dose (alternative; less effective for hookworm)
Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg for Strongyloides (which mebendazole misses)
Iron supplementation if anaemic (60 mg elemental adult; 3 mg/kg/day paediatric × 3 months)
Treat concurrent malaria, malnutrition
PREVENTIVE CHEMOTHERAPY (MDA):
Pre-school: albendazole 400 mg (≥ 24 mo) or 200 mg (12–24 mo) every 6 months
School: albendazole 400 mg or mebendazole 500 mg annually; biannually if STH prevalence > 50%
WRA: WHO 2017 recommendation — albendazole 400 mg twice yearly where prevalence > 20%; safe after 1st trimester in pregnancy
Pregnant women: 1 dose in 2nd / 3rd trimester (WHO safe)
Public health: WASH improvements, latrine use, handwashing, footwear (hookworm), Kenya National School-Based Deworming Programme — > 6 million children annually

title: Lassa fever (viral haemorrhagic fever) — West African
population: Endemic in West Africa — Nigeria (major), Sierra Leone, Liberia, Guinea, Benin. Imported cases possible elsewhere. Healthcare workers high-risk (nosocomial). Rodent reservoir Mastomys natalensis.
presentation: Insidious onset (vs other VHFs): fever, malaise, sore throat, retrosternal pain, conjunctivitis, vomiting, diarrhoea over 1–3 weeks. Severe (20%): facial oedema, mucosal bleeding, hypotension, encephalopathy, sensorineural deafness (33% of survivors — characteristic).
redFlags: Pregnancy (very high maternal + fetal mortality, especially 3rd trimester — deliver / evacuate uterus may improve maternal survival)
diagnostics: RT-PCR at BSL3 reference lab (Kenya — KEMRI; refer per IDSR)
Lassa IgM ELISA
FBC (thrombocytopaenia, lymphopaenia), LFT (very raised AST > ALT classically), creatinine, coagulation
Notify IDSR + WHO IHR — PHEIC eligible
management: Strict barrier nursing in dedicated isolation unit — full PPE per WHO Lassa PPE protocol
Ribavirin IV 30 mg/kg loading + 16 mg/kg q6h × 4 days then 8 mg/kg q8h × 6 days — most effective within first 6 days of illness
Supportive: IV fluids, blood products, AKI dialysis, electrolyte correction
Pregnancy: ribavirin teratogenic but balance vs maternal mortality — IDLO emergency use
Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for high-risk exposed contacts: oral ribavirin × 10 days
Public health: ring contact-tracing (21-day quarantine), rodent control (food storage, traps, secure housing), funeral practice safety, healthcare worker training + PPE supply
WHO Coordination — Africa CDC + WHO AFRO outbreak response

references.label: WHO Clinical management of Lassa fever interim guidelines
Nigeria CDC Lassa Fever National Guidelines
Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) Technical Guidelines, 3rd ed, Ministry of Health

title: Mpox (monkeypox) clade I + clade II — SSA
population: Clade I — DRC, Central African Republic, Burundi, Uganda, Rwanda, Kenya (sporadic since 2024). Clade II spread globally 2022. Children + immunocompromised + MSM with high-risk sexual networks at risk. WHO PHEIC declared 2022 + 2024.
presentation: Incubation 5–21 days. Prodrome — fever, lymphadenopathy (characteristic — distinguishes from smallpox), headache, malaise. Rash — papular/vesicular/pustular → crusts; uniform stage per lesion; can be limited to anogenital area in sexual transmission. Painful proctitis common in 2022+ outbreak.
redFlags: Severe disease in HIV (CD4 < 200) — necrotising lesions, sepsis
Cluster of cases — notify IDSR within 24h
diagnostics: PCR from lesion swab (vesicle / pustule / crust) — most reliable; oropharyngeal swab if lesions absent
Serology not routinely used
HIV testing offered to all (high co-infection)
STI screen (syphilis, chlamydia, gonorrhoea, HSV — co-infection common)
Notify IDSR + WHO IHR
management: Most cases self-limiting — supportive: analgesia (oral pain often severe), fluids, antiemetic, wound care (saline cleansing), pruritus (antihistamine), bacterial secondary infection (flucloxacillin if cellulitis)

Severe disease / immunocompromised / paediatric / pregnancy: tecovirimat (oral or IV — limited availability in SSA but expanding via ACT-A / WHO PCH; STOMP trial showed no benefit in mild clade II but evidence for severe + clade I ongoing)
VIGIV (vaccinia immune globulin) for very severe cases / vaccine adverse events
Antiviral choice + access via WHO MEURI protocol in outbreaks
Isolation: standard + contact + droplet until all lesions crusted + new epithelium
VACCINATION — MVA-BN (Jynneos) 2-dose pre-exposure for high-risk + post-exposure within 4 days; SSA access via WHO + Africa CDC outbreak response
Public health: contact tracing, case isolation 21 days, sexual health partner notification, community education on transmission, reduce stigma (sexual networks, MSM)
Kenya MOH issued screening + management protocol 2024 after first cases

references.label: WHO Mpox interim clinical management guidelines 2024
Africa CDC Mpox Continental Preparedness Plan 2024
Kenya MOH Mpox Preparedness + Response Plan 2024
STOMP trial — tecovirimat in mpox NEJM 2024

title: Trachoma — SAFE strategy (SSA elimination)
population: Dry rural communities across Sahel + Horn of Africa — Ethiopia (highest global burden), Sudan, South Sudan, Chad, Niger, Mali, Kenya (formerly endemic in northern arid counties; now eliminated as PHP).
presentation: Chlamydia trachomatis recurrent infection from childhood → conjunctival scarring → trichiasis (in-turned lashes) → corneal opacity → blindness. WHO classification: TF (follicular), TI (intense), TS (scarring), TT (trichiasis), CO (corneal opacity).
redFlags: Child with TF in dry-eyed community — community-wide intervention
diagnostics: Clinical WHO grading by trained examiner (community surveys)
PCR or NAAT for C. trachomatis in research / monitoring
Slit lamp for trichiasis + cornea
management: SAFE strategy (WHO 4-pillar):
Surgery for trichiasis (TT) — bilamellar tarsal rotation; conducted in community campaigns by trained ophthalmic clinical officers
Antibiotic — azithromycin 20 mg/kg PO single dose (adults 1 g) annually × 3–5 years in communities with TF prevalence ≥ 5% in children 1–9 yrs; MDA
Facial cleanliness — community education on daily face washing
Environmental improvement — latrines (reduce flies — Musca sorbens vector), water access
TT individual: surgery (BTR) — refer to ophthalmic clinical officer; epilation only short-term temporising
CO blindness: low vision aids + rehabilitation; corneal graft rarely available
Pfizer International Trachoma Initiative — donated azithromycin
Kenya MOH validated trachoma elimination as PHP 2024
Continued surveillance after elimination to prevent recrudescence

title: Preoperative cardiac risk assessment — ASA + RCRI + NSQIP
population: All adults undergoing non-cardiac surgery — outpatient pre-anaesthetic clinic, day-of-surgery review.
presentation: Routine pre-op contact. Risk-stratify: functional capacity (METs), cardiac risk indices, frailty, comorbidity.
redFlags: Active ACS, decompensated HF, severe valve disease (AS aortic), arrhythmia uncontrolled
Recent stent (DES < 6 mo, BMS < 1 mo) on DAPT — postpone elective
Poor functional capacity (< 4 METs) + intermediate-high risk surgery
diagnostics: ASA physical status I–VI
RCRI (high-risk surgery, IHD, HF, CVD, insulin-DM, Cr > 177)
ACS-NSQIP risk calculator (MICA, surgical risk)
Functional capacity — Duke Activity Status Index / 4-METs
Targeted ECG, echo, troponin only if indicated (NOT routine)
FBC, U&E, glucose, coagulation per surgery + comorbidity
Frailty: Clinical Frailty Scale; nutrition: MNA
management: Optimise comorbidity: BP < 140/90, glycaemic (HbA1c < 64), Hb correction, smoking cessation 4 weeks pre-op
Continue β-blockers, statins, ACE-i (or hold morning of surgery), aspirin (most surgeries continue; stop only for high bleeding risk specific procedures)
Bridge anticoagulation per CHA2DS2-VASc + procedural bleeding risk; DOACs hold 24–48h (renal function dependent)
Diabetes: variable rate insulin infusion for major; stop SGLT2 inhibitor 3 days pre (ketoacidosis risk)
Cardiac stress testing only if 4 METs poor + intermediate-high risk + would change management
Echo only if known/suspected severe valve disease or PHT or HF
Frailty: prehabilitation, multidisciplinary geriatric input, anaesthesia plan
Postpone elective if active medical issue uncontrolled; document risk-benefit if proceeding
Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocol where available

title: Rapid sequence induction (RSI) — emergency airway
population: Patients needing emergency intubation at risk of aspiration: full stomach, GI bleed, bowel obstruction, pregnancy, trauma, severe sepsis, depressed conscious level.
presentation: Airway emergency — failure to maintain / protect airway / oxygenate / ventilate. Pre-intubation hypoxaemia, hypotension, acidosis predict peri-intubation cardiac arrest.
diagnostics: Airway assessment LEMON (Look-Evaluate 3-3-2-Mallampati-Obstruction-Neck mobility)
Plan A/B/C/D (DAS difficult airway algorithm)
Vital signs, SpO2, capnography mandatory
ECG, IV access × 2, bloods including K+
management: PRE-INTUBATION CHECKLIST (7 P's): Preparation (equipment + drugs + suction + back-up), Preoxygenation, Pretreatment (lidocaine / fentanyl in selected — debated), Paralysis with induction, Placement, Postintubation
Position: 30° head-up; ramped if obese (ear-sternal notch); reverse Trendelenburg for pregnancy
Preoxygenation: 3 min tidal volume or 8 vital capacity breaths via tight-fitting mask + NIV if SpO2 < 93%; nasal cannula at 15 L for apnoeic oxygenation
Optimise haemodynamics BEFORE: fluid bolus, push-dose pressor (phenylephrine 50–100 mcg, adrenaline 5–20 mcg), shock-index < 0.9 target
INDUCTION + PARALYSIS (push simultaneously, no bag-mask if not desaturating):
Ketamine 1–2 mg/kg (haemodynamic-stable, asthma, sepsis — preferred) OR etomidate 0.3 mg/kg (preserves BP but adrenal suppression — single-dose acceptable) OR propofol 1–2 mg/kg (avoid in shock)

+ Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg IV (preferred — neutral haemodynamics, fast onset, sugammadex reversal available) OR suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg (faster but K+ release; AVOID if hyperK+, burns > 48h, prolonged immobility, NMS, denervation)
Cricoid pressure: routinely applied (Sellick) — but release if difficult; emerging evidence against universal use
Direct or video laryngoscope (video preferred for first-pass success per multiple RCTs)
Capnography to confirm — required for ALL intubations
Post-intubation: secure tube, OG/NG decompression, lung-protective ventilation (Vt 6–8 ml/kg IBW), analgesia + sedation, recheck haemodynamics
Failed intubation: DAS algorithm — Plan B (alternative blade / VL / bougie), Plan C (LMA / supraglottic), Plan D (emergency front-of-neck access — cricothyroidotomy)
Avoid 'physiologically difficult airway' assumption — fix shock + acidosis + hypoxia FIRST where possible

title: Spinal anaesthesia — technique, contraindications, complications
population: Lower abdominal, pelvic, perineal, lower limb surgery; caesarean delivery — most common anaesthesia method for elective + many emergency C-sections.
presentation: Single-shot intrathecal injection (typically L3-L4 or L4-L5 below conus). Onset 5–10 min, duration 2–4 h depending on agent. Sensory + motor + sympathetic block.
redFlags: Hypotension (very common — sympathectomy) — pre-load + co-load + vasopressor
Total spinal (high block — bradycardia + hypotension + apnoea + arm paralysis)
Cauda equina (rare — toxic agent or pressure)
diagnostics: Pre-op assessment: anticoag history, spine examination, allergies, infection
Coagulation (FBC, INR) if relevant
Document neurological baseline
management: CONTRAINDICATIONS — absolute: patient refusal, infection at site, raised ICP, severe coagulopathy (platelets < 50 or therapeutic anticoag), severe aortic stenosis (relative); relative: fixed CO state, lumbar spine disease, neurological disease

Anticoag timing (ESRA): therapeutic LMWH withhold 24h; prophylactic LMWH 12h; warfarin INR < 1.5; DOAC withhold 48–72h depending on agent + renal; aspirin OK; clopidogrel 7 d; ticagrelor 5 d; bridge if high thrombotic risk
Position: sitting (easier, useful for hyperbaric in obstetric) or lateral
L3-L4 / L4-L5 interspace (line between iliac crests = L4 spinous process)
Aseptic technique — chlorhexidine, sterile gown + gloves + drape
25–27G pencil-point needle (Whitacre / Sprotte) — reduces PDPH vs cutting Quincke
Hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% 2–3 ml for C-section (with fentanyl 15 mcg ± morphine 100 mcg for analgesia); plain 0.5% bupivacaine for orthopaedic
BLOCK ASSESSMENT: cold sensation (ethyl chloride) to T4 (nipple) for C-section, T6–T10 for lower abdo, T10 for lower limb

HYPOTENSION management: phenylephrine infusion 50–100 mcg/min as needed (or 100 mcg boluses); CO-LOAD with crystalloid 10–15 ml/kg starting at intrathecal injection (pre-load not effective); maintain MAP > 65 (obstetric > 90 mmHg for fetal welfare)
Avoid ephedrine in obstetric — fetal acidosis (phenylephrine preferred)
PDPH treatment: hydration, caffeine, analgesia; epidural blood patch if > 48h persistent + severe (gold standard)
EMERGENCY: spinal haematoma — neurological deficit + back pain + recent neuraxial → urgent MRI + neurosurgical decompression within 8h (irreversible cord damage)

title: Acute postoperative pain — multimodal analgesia
population: All postoperative patients; chronic pain patients undergoing surgery especially challenging.
presentation: Pain assessment using NRS (0–10), behavioural pain scale in non-verbal, FLACC paediatric. Quality-of-recovery 15 (QoR-15) outcome measure.
redFlags: New severe pain after stable period (complication: bleeding, ischaemia, compartment, anastomotic)
Opioid-induced respiratory depression (RR < 8, SpO2 < 92%, sedation score ≥ 3) — naloxone
Persistent post-surgical pain > 3 months — refer chronic pain service
diagnostics: Pain trajectory + sleep + mood + function
Side effects: nausea, constipation, sedation, urinary retention
Local: signs of complication or wound infection
management: MULTIMODAL ANALGESIA (cornerstone — reduces opioid + improves outcomes):
Baseline: paracetamol 1 g IV/PO q6h (max 4 g/d, less in liver disease / low weight) — always unless contraindicated

NSAID: ibuprofen 400 mg q8h or ketorolac 10 mg q6h ± diclofenac 50 mg q8h — avoid in renal impairment / GI bleed / asthma / pregnancy 3rd trimester / cardiac high risk; consider COX-2 (celecoxib) if GI risk
Opioid: short-acting for severe — morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV (titrate), oxycodone 5 mg PO q4h prn; PCA morphine for major (1 mg bolus, 5 min lockout, no background unless opioid-tolerant)
Regional anaesthesia where possible — TAP block (abdo), fascia iliaca (hip), femoral / popliteal (lower limb), interscalene (shoulder), serratus anterior (thoracic / breast)
Adjuvants:
Gabapentinoid (gabapentin 300 mg or pregabalin 75 mg pre-op + post) — opioid-sparing but caution sedation + falls in elderly; off-label
Ketamine low-dose 0.1–0.25 mg/kg bolus + 0.1 mg/kg/h infusion — opioid-sparing especially opioid-tolerant
IV lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg bolus then 1.5–2 mg/kg/h intra-op (laparotomy)
Dexamethasone 4–8 mg pre-op — analgesia + PONV prevention
α2-agonist (dexmedetomidine, clonidine) — opioid-sparing, sedation
ENHANCED RECOVERY (ERAS): pre-op education, no prolonged fasting, carbohydrate drink, normothermia, goal-directed fluid, multimodal analgesia, early oral, early mobilisation
OPIOID-RELATED ADVERSE EVENTS prevention: stool softener + senna routine; ondansetron 4 mg if PONV; pulse oximetry continuous in high-risk
NALOXONE 40 mcg IV every 2 min if respiratory depression; 100 mcg IM if no IV; expect re-sedation (repeated dosing or infusion)
PERSISTENT POST-SURGICAL PAIN: identify high-risk pre-op (chronic pain, anxiety, catastrophising, female, young); refer chronic pain at 6 weeks if NRS > 4
OPIOID-TOLERANT: continue baseline opioid + multimodal; PCA backgrounds appropriate; methadone rotation specialist input
DISCHARGE: minimise opioid quantity (< 3 days for most), counsel safe storage + disposal; tapering plan

title: Malignant hyperthermia — anaesthetic emergency
population: Genetically susceptible (RYR1, CACNA1S mutations — autosomal dominant) — incidence ~1:50,000 adults, higher in children. Family history of anaesthetic death / complications a key clue.
presentation: Hypermetabolic crisis triggered by volatile anaesthetic (sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, halothane) or suxamethonium. Earliest: rising end-tidal CO2 unresponsive to ventilation, tachycardia, muscle rigidity (especially masseter spasm after suxamethonium). Later: hyperthermia (rises 1°C every 5 min), arrhythmia, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, DIC, AKI. Mortality 1–5% with prompt dantrolene.
redFlags: Unexplained ETCO2 rise + tachycardia during anaesthesia
diagnostics: Clinical recognition + Clinical Grading Scale
ABG (severe acidosis), serum K+ (hyperK+), CK (markedly raised, peak at 24h), myoglobin (urine + serum), coag, LFT
ECG (arrhythmia, peaked T)
Core temperature (oesophageal / bladder)
Definitive diagnosis post-recovery: caffeine-halothane contracture test (CHCT) on muscle biopsy; genetic testing for RYR1 / CACNA1S
management: EMERGENCY — call for help + MH cart:
1. STOP triggering agent (volatile, sux). Continue surgery on IV anaesthesia (propofol, opioid, ketamine, non-depolarising NMBA)
2. Switch ventilator to 100% O2 at high flows (10 L/min) — hyperventilate to lower ETCO2

3. DANTROLENE 2.5 mg/kg IV bolus (reconstitute 20 mg vials with 60 ml sterile water — need many vials; new ryanodex formulation 250 mg vial = 1 patient dose 2.5 mg/kg avg adult) — repeat every 5 min until ETCO2 + HR + rigidity reverse, up to 10 mg/kg total
4. ACTIVE COOLING: cold IV fluids, ice packs to axillae/groin/neck, gastric/bladder lavage with cold saline, surface cooling; STOP at 38°C to prevent shivering
5. Treat hyperkalaemia: calcium gluconate 1 g, insulin + glucose, salbutamol, sodium bicarbonate, dialysis if refractory
6. Treat arrhythmia: amiodarone (NOT calcium channel blockers — interact with dantrolene)
7. Maintain urine output > 2 ml/kg/h (forced alkaline diuresis, mannitol); manage rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI
8. ICU admission post-event for at least 24h — recrudescence in 25%
9. Continue dantrolene 1 mg/kg q4–6h × 24h post-acute event
10. Inform family — counsel, refer for testing, MedicAlert bracelet, MH safe anaesthesia in future (TIVA, regional)
POST: report to MH Registry (UK, NA-MHAUS) and refer index case for confirmatory testing

title: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) — recognition + lipid rescue
population: Any patient receiving regional anaesthesia (peripheral nerve block, epidural, infiltration) — accidental intravascular injection OR systemic absorption. Higher risk: extremes of age, pregnancy, low body weight, cardiac/hepatic/renal disease.
presentation: EARLY (excitation): perioral tingling, metallic taste, tinnitus, agitation, confusion. LATE (depression): seizures, LOC, hypotension, bradycardia, ventricular arrhythmia, asystole. Symptoms may be DELAYED up to 30+ min after injection. Bupivacaine the worst (cardiotoxic > CNS); ropivacaine less cardiotoxic; lidocaine mostly CNS.
redFlags: Bradycardia + hypotension after epidural / IVRA tourniquet release
ANY neurological symptom after block — STOP injection
diagnostics: Clinical recognition — high index of suspicion is key
Total dose calculation: maximum safe dose by weight
Continuous monitoring during + after regional anaesthesia ≥ 30 min
ECG, ABG
Plasma LA level (research / forensic only)
management: PREVENTION (key — outcome poor once cardiac arrest):
Calculate + don't exceed max dose (lignocaine 4.5 mg/kg, with adrenaline 7 mg/kg; bupivacaine 2 mg/kg; ropivacaine 3 mg/kg)
Incremental dose with aspiration every 3–5 ml
Use ultrasound guidance
Add adrenaline 1:200,000 as intravascular marker (HR rise)
Continuous ECG + SpO2 during + after
TREATMENT — at first sign of LAST:
1. STOP LA injection immediately, call for help, prepare lipid emulsion
2. Airway — 100% O2, intubate if seizing / unconscious
3. SEIZURES: benzodiazepine first-line (midazolam 1–2 mg IV; lorazepam 4 mg) — avoid propofol if haemodynamically unstable
4. LIPID EMULSION RESCUE (Intralipid 20%):
Bolus 1.5 ml/kg over 1 min (≈100 ml in 70 kg adult)
Infusion 0.25 ml/kg/min
Repeat bolus × 2 if persistent collapse
Double infusion if BP drops
Max 12 ml/kg cumulative
5. Cardiac arrest: standard ACLS with MODIFICATIONS:
AVOID vasopressin
REDUCE adrenaline dose to < 1 mcg/kg
AVOID calcium channel blockers, β-blockers, lidocaine antiarrhythmic
AMIODARONE for VT/VF
PROLONGED CPR if needed (> 60 min) — may eventually respond to lipid
Consider cardiopulmonary bypass / ECMO
6. Lipid emulsion mechanism: lipid sink + metabolic effect + ion channel modulation
7. Post-event: ICU 12+ h; report to local + national LAST registry

title: Postoperative nausea + vomiting (PONV) — prevention + treatment
population: All postoperative patients — particularly Apfel high-risk (female, non-smoker, prior PONV / motion sickness, post-op opioid).
presentation: Common: 20–30% routinely, 70–80% high-risk. Distressing, delays discharge, dehydration, aspiration, wound dehiscence.
redFlags: Persistent vomiting despite multi-drug therapy — consider surgical complication (bowel obstruction, intracranial)
diagnostics: ECG before ondansetron (QT prolongation in long-QT)
U&E if persistent (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia)
management: PREVENTION (multi-modal — use N agents based on risk):
Low risk (0–1 factors): one agent or none
Mod (2 factors): 2 agents from different classes
High (3–4 factors): 3+ agents + TIVA + minimise opioids
DRUG CLASSES (different sites of action — combine):
5-HT3 antagonist: ondansetron 4 mg IV at induction or end of surgery (longer effect end of surgery); granisetron 1 mg
Corticosteroid: dexamethasone 4–8 mg IV at induction
D2 antagonist: droperidol 0.625 mg IV (low-dose, black box warning); metoclopramide 10–20 mg (less effective)
NK1 antagonist: aprepitant 40 mg PO (longer prophylaxis, expensive)
Anticholinergic: scopolamine transdermal patch (extra-strong for motion sickness)
Antihistamine: cyclizine 50 mg (less in elderly), promethazine
ANAESTHESIA TECHNIQUE:
TIVA propofol > volatile (lower PONV)
Avoid N2O (especially > 1h)
Regional > GA where appropriate
Minimise opioids — multimodal analgesia
Adequate hydration (10–15 ml/kg crystalloid)
TREATMENT (established PONV) — use DIFFERENT class from prophylaxis (don't repeat ondansetron in 6h):
Ondansetron 1 mg (lower dose for rescue, max 16 mg cumulative)
Droperidol 0.625 mg (with ECG check)
Promethazine 6.25 mg
Dexamethasone if not already given
Acupressure P6 (sea-bands) adjunctive
AVOID metoclopramide in young women (extrapyramidal); avoid droperidol in long QT

title: Perioperative blood management — Patient Blood Management
population: All surgical patients — preoperative anaemia in 25–40% major surgery patients.
presentation: Pre-op anaemia (Hb < 130 men, < 120 women) doubles morbidity + mortality. Intraoperative blood loss requires transparent decision-making for transfusion vs conservation.
redFlags: Massive haemorrhage (≥ 4 RBC units in 1h or ≥ 10 units in 24h)
diagnostics: Pre-op FBC + ferritin + B12 + folate at least 4 weeks pre-op for elective major surgery
Type + screen / crossmatch as needed
Intra-op: estimated blood loss, urine output, lactate, ABG, Hb (point-of-care)
Viscoelastic testing (ROTEM / TEG) for major / cardiac / liver surgery
Standard coag (PT, INR, APTT, fibrinogen, platelet count)
management: Patient Blood Management (PBM) 3 pillars:
1. OPTIMISE pre-op haemoglobin:
Identify + treat anaemia 4 weeks before elective surgery
IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg single dose or iron sucrose 200 mg × 5) for iron deficiency
B12 / folate if deficient
Erythropoietin if Hb < 130 men / < 120 women + no malignancy / vascular contraindication
Defer elective surgery if Hb < 100 + correctable
2. MINIMISE intra-op blood loss:
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction + repeat at 3h (or 15–30 mg/kg) — all major surgery, trauma, post-partum (CRASH-2, WOMAN, HALT-IT trials)
Cell salvage (intraoperative autotransfusion) — orthopaedic, cardiac, OB
Acute normovolaemic haemodilution (ANH)
Permissive hypotension where appropriate
Minimally invasive surgical technique
Reverse anticoagulants pre-op (Idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet for Xa inhibitors, 4F-PCC for warfarin)
3. RESTRICTIVE transfusion threshold:
Hb < 70 (or < 80 if cardiovascular disease, symptomatic, ICU) — multiple RCTs support restrictive (TRICC, TRISS, TITRe2)
Single-unit transfusion + reassess (don't transfuse 2 units automatically)
Platelets: < 10 (no bleeding), < 20 (procedure), < 50 (active bleeding / major surgery), < 100 (CNS / cardiac)
FFP: only with active bleeding + INR > 1.5 or fibrinogen < 1.5–2 g/L; do NOT use prophylactically
Fibrinogen concentrate / cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen < 1.5 (< 2 obstetric)
MASSIVE HAEMORRHAGE PROTOCOL: 1:1:1 RBC:FFP:platelets ratio (or whole blood where available), TXA, calcium, viscoelastic-guided
JEHOVAH'S WITNESS / refused transfusion: optimise pre-op aggressively, IV iron, EPO, cell salvage, minimise sampling, tolerate lower Hb threshold (50–60), discuss respectfully
Post-op: continue iron, monitor Hb trajectory, restart anticoagulant per bleeding risk

title: Chronic non-cancer pain — biopsychosocial + WHO ladder + opioid stewardship
population: Adults with pain > 3 months — 20% of adults globally; rising opioid crisis in HICs + emerging in LMICs.
presentation: Pain types: nociceptive (somatic, visceral), neuropathic (burning, electric, allodynia, hyperalgesia), nociplastic (central sensitisation — fibromyalgia, CRPS). Often multifactorial. Comorbid depression, anxiety, sleep, occupational impact.
redFlags: Pain with B symptoms (weight loss, fever — malignancy)
Pain after trauma not improving (compartment / non-union)
diagnostics: Comprehensive pain assessment: location, character, severity, triggers, function
DN4 / painDETECT for neuropathic component
Mental health: PHQ-9, GAD-7
Functional capacity, sleep, work
Imaging only if red flags or planned intervention (avoid in non-specific LBP)
Opioid risk: ORT (Opioid Risk Tool), SOAPP-R; baseline urine drug screen for opioid-naive on chronic; check Prescription Drug Monitoring Program if available
management: BIOPSYCHOSOCIAL FRAMEWORK — pharm + non-pharm + psychological + social
NON-PHARM (first-line, continuous):
Exercise — graded activity, pacing, physiotherapy
Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) ± acceptance + commitment (ACT)
Mindfulness, MBSR (Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction)
Sleep hygiene, weight management
Heat / cold, TENS
Multidisciplinary pain rehabilitation
PHARMACOLOGICAL (WHO modified ladder):
Step 1 (mild): paracetamol + NSAID (with PPI if GI risk; avoid in CKD, GIB, CV high risk)
Step 2 (moderate): add weak opioid — tramadol (caution serotonin syndrome with SSRI), codeine; OR shift to neuropathic agent if neuropathic
Step 3 (severe): strong opioid (morphine, oxycodone) — careful patient selection, time-limited trial, max 50 morphine equivalents/day in chronic non-cancer; reassess

Adjuvants for neuropathic: TCA (amitriptyline 10–75 mg nocte — caution elderly anticholinergic), SNRI (duloxetine 60 mg), gabapentinoid (gabapentin 900–3600 mg/d or pregabalin 75–600 mg/d) — slow titration
Adjuvants for nociplastic (fibromyalgia): SNRI duloxetine, pregabalin, low-dose amitriptyline
Topical: capsaicin, lidocaine patch 5%
Cannabinoids — limited evidence, regulatory varies; for neuropathic / palliative
OPIOID STEWARDSHIP (CDC 2022 + WHO):
Reserve for severe pain when benefit > risk + non-opioid inadequate
START low + slow; reassess at 4 weeks, then every 3 months
Time-limited trial — taper if no functional improvement at 12 weeks
Naloxone co-prescribed for those on > 50 MME or with risk factors
Avoid concurrent benzodiazepines + opioids
Tapering: 10% per month for long-term; never stop abruptly (withdrawal — buprenorphine bridge if OUD)
Suspected opioid use disorder (OUD): refer for medication-assisted treatment (methadone or buprenorphine)
INTERVENTIONS (selected): trigger point injection, epidural steroid, radiofrequency ablation, spinal cord stimulator (refractory), intrathecal pump (refractory cancer pain)
Set FUNCTIONAL goals — not pain-free, but improved function + QoL

title: Opioid overdose — recognition + naloxone
population: Anyone using opioids — illicit (heroin, fentanyl-adulterated), prescription (oxycodone, morphine, methadone, tramadol), or therapeutic over-sedation. Lay rescuer naloxone increasingly available. Kenya — emerging issue with rising prescription opioid use.
presentation: Opioid toxidrome triad: pinpoint pupils (miosis) + respiratory depression (< 12) + reduced consciousness. Also: bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia. Look for needle marks, fentanyl patch, pills.
redFlags: Methadone / sustained-release oxycodone — prolonged toxicity (24h+ obs)
diagnostics: Clinical recognition
POC glucose (rule out hypoglycaemia)
ABG, ECG (QT prolongation methadone), CK if down for hours (rhabdomyolysis), CXR (aspiration pneumonia, ARDS noncardiogenic)
Urine toxicology — supportive but slow; specific testing for fentanyl + xylazine
management: RESUSCITATION:
Open airway, jaw thrust, OPA
Bag-valve-mask 10 L O2 — focus on VENTILATION (most deaths from hypoxic respiratory failure, not arrest)
IV access
NALOXONE:
Lay rescuer: 4 mg intranasal (Narcan nasal) — repeat every 2–3 min if no response
IV: 0.4 mg IV (or IM if no IV) — TITRATE to respiratory rate, NOT consciousness
Repeat every 2–3 min; total up to 10 mg for fentanyl-adulterated
IM 0.4 mg if no IV access (slower onset)
Infusion: 0.4 mg/h titrated (longer-acting opioids — methadone, oxycodone SR)
Aim: RR > 12, adequate ventilation — NOT full reversal (precipitates withdrawal + agitation)
OBSERVE:
Heroin: 4–6h after last naloxone dose minimum (resedation common as naloxone half-life ≈ 30 min, heroin much longer)
Methadone / SR oxycodone / fentanyl patch: 24+ h
Fentanyl-laced: prolonged observation
POST-OVERDOSE:
Treat aspiration pneumonia, ARDS, rhabdo, AKI as needed
Screen for OUD; refer to medication-assisted treatment (methadone / buprenorphine — even initiate in ED with linkage)
Take-home naloxone (THN) + bystander training for the patient + family
Mental health: depression, suicide risk assessment
Safer-use counselling: not using alone, fentanyl test strips, supervised consumption sites if available
PREVENTION:
Co-prescribe naloxone with high-MME prescriptions
Tapering chronic opioids carefully
Opioid stewardship — avoid concurrent benzodiazepines
Community naloxone distribution to family of OUD patients

title: Procedural sedation and analgesia (PSA) — emergency department
population: Patients requiring short painful or anxiety-provoking procedures (fracture reduction, joint relocation, abscess drainage, cardioversion, endoscopy, dental).
presentation: Spectrum: minimal sedation (anxiolysis) → moderate (responsive to voice) → deep (responsive only to painful stimuli, may need airway support) → general anaesthesia. Goal: efficient, safe, with rapid recovery.
redFlags: High aspiration risk (recent meal, GI obstruction, pregnancy, opioid)
diagnostics: Pre-sedation assessment: AMPLE, fasting, ASA status, allergies, airway (LEMON), comorbidity
Consent + agree level of sedation needed
Monitoring requirements: continuous SpO2 + capnography + ECG + NIBP + observer dedicated to patient
management: PRE-PROCEDURE CHECKLIST:
Confirm fasting (NPO 2h clear fluids, 4h breast milk, 6h light meal — but in emergency may proceed with full stomach + aspiration precautions)
IV access + crash trolley + advanced airway equipment ready
Reversal agents (naloxone, flumazenil) drawn up
Dedicated observer (cannot be person doing procedure)
Pre-oxygenate with nasal O2 throughout
Baseline vitals + EWS
DRUG CHOICES (titrate to effect):

Ketamine 1 mg/kg IV slow over 1 min (or 4 mg/kg IM) — analgesia + sedation + dissociation; preserves airway + respiratory drive; ideal for paeds, asthma, hypotensive. Re-dose 0.5 mg/kg q5–10 min. Co-administer ondansetron 4 mg (emergence vomiting).
Propofol 0.5–1 mg/kg IV bolus titrated, 20–30 mg q1–3 min for prolonged — rapid onset/offset; care with apnoea + hypotension
Ketofol — mix ketamine + propofol 1:1 — smoother, less PONV, less apnoea than propofol alone
Midazolam 0.02 mg/kg IV (1–2 mg adult) — anxiolytic; not analgesic; reverse with flumazenil
Fentanyl 0.5–1 mcg/kg IV — analgesic; reverse with naloxone
Dexmedetomidine 1 mcg/kg IV over 10 min, then 0.2–0.7 mcg/kg/h — sedation without resp depression
Nitrous oxide 50:50 with O2 inhaled — analgesia + anxiolysis for minor procedures
PAEDIATRIC: ketamine + atropine (less secretions); intranasal midazolam / fentanyl for minor pain
INTRA-PROCEDURE:
Continuous monitoring; document vital signs every 5 min
ETCO2 (capnography) — most sensitive for apnoea / hypoventilation
Stop procedure if airway / breathing / circulatory compromise
COMPLICATIONS:
Hypoxia (SpO2 < 92%) — chin lift, jaw thrust, BVM, decrease sedative
Apnoea — BVM until breathing returns; consider reversal
Hypotension — fluid bolus; vasopressor if severe
Vomiting / aspiration — suction, lateral position, intubate if compromised
Emergence reaction (ketamine, in adults — < 5%) — quiet environment, midazolam 1 mg
RECOVERY:
Monitor until pre-sedation level (Modified Aldrete Score ≥ 9)
Discharge criteria: stable vitals, ambulating, tolerating PO, no NV, with responsible adult
Do NOT drive / sign legal docs / care for child × 24h
