title: Postpartum depression — Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)
population: Women in the year after childbirth — prevalence 10–20% globally, higher in LMICs + SSA (15–25%). Father / partner / non-birthing parent also at risk (~10%). Universal screening at 6-week postnatal visit + 3, 6, 12 months.
presentation: Persistent low mood / anhedonia / hopelessness > 2 weeks postpartum (DSM-5 within 4 weeks; ICD-11 within 6 months). Differs from 'baby blues' (resolves within 2 weeks, no functional impairment). May present with anxiety, intrusive thoughts of harming infant, fatigue beyond expected, withdrawal from baby. Postpartum psychosis (rare ~1:1000) — emergency.
redFlags: Suicidal ideation / plan / intent — emergency referral
Thoughts of harming infant — child protection + emergency mental health
Psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions about infant, bizarre behaviour) — postpartum psychosis admit
Severe functional impairment (not caring for self / infant)
Recurrent severe pre-existing mood disorder (high relapse)
diagnostics: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) — 10-item, score 0–30, ≥ 10 likely depression, ≥ 13 probable; positive item 10 = suicidal ideation → assess immediately
PHQ-9 alternative
Whooley 2-question case-finder for primary care
Risk factors: previous depression / anxiety, traumatic birth, lack of social support, partner violence, low SES, infant illness, breastfeeding difficulty, hormonal changes
Differential: hypothyroidism (TSH), anaemia (FBC), B12, sleep deprivation
management: STEPPED CARE (WHO mhGAP-IG2 + NICE CG192):
Mild–moderate:
Active listening + psychoeducation
Increase social support, baby-care relief, sleep hygiene
Structured CBT or interpersonal therapy (IPT) — first-line
Group therapy / peer support (mothers' groups)
Physical activity (walking with baby)
Moderate–severe / failed psychotherapy:
SSRI first-line — sertraline 50–100 mg daily (lowest infant exposure if breastfeeding); paroxetine alternative (caution — short half-life)
AVOID fluoxetine first-line (long half-life accumulates in infant); avoid citalopram > 20 mg if breastfeeding
Continue antidepressant 6–12 months minimum if effective
Refer for CBT in parallel
TCA alternatives if needed (nortriptyline)
Severe / suicidal / psychotic — URGENT psychiatric referral, consider admission:
Postpartum psychosis: antipsychotic (olanzapine, risperidone) + mood stabiliser (lithium — careful breastfeeding) + admit to mother-baby unit if available
ECT for severe refractory / catatonia
Brexanolone IV (neurosteroid GABA-A modulator) approved for severe PPD where available — single infusion 60h, expensive
BREASTFEEDING compatibility:
Sertraline + paroxetine — low infant levels, generally compatible
Avoid fluoxetine + citalopram (high dose) + lithium with breastfeeding
Educate patient — most antidepressants compatible per LactMed
INFANT: assess attachment, refer to paediatrics + early childhood services; risk of developmental delay if maternal PPD untreated
PARTNER: screen partner too; couple counselling
Kenya MOH integrating maternal mental health into MNCH services + community health worker training (mhGAP, WHO Thinking Healthy programme)
WHO Thinking Healthy Programme — CHV-delivered CBT-based intervention shown effective in LMIC

title: Maternal sepsis — recognition + Sepsis-Six (peripartum specific)
population: Pregnant women (antepartum, intrapartum, postpartum to 42 days). Globally 5th leading cause of maternal mortality; SSA disproportionate. Chorioamnionitis, endometritis, UTI, mastitis, wound infection, post-abortal sepsis common sources.
presentation: Pregnancy alters physiology — masks sepsis (relative tachycardia + tachypnoea normal; WCC normally elevated). Use obstetric-specific scores (omqSOFA, SIRS-O). Specific sources: chorioamnionitis (fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, foul liquor), endometritis (boggy uterus, foul lochia 24h+), septic abortion, wound + episiotomy infection, mastitis, pyelonephritis (very common in pregnancy).
redFlags: Fetal tachycardia / fetal distress (in utero source)
Group A Strep recognition (especially postpartum — necrotising fasciitis risk)
diagnostics: omqSOFA: GCS < 15, RR > 25, SBP < 90 (≥ 2 = sepsis)
Source examination: abdomen (uterine tenderness, peritonism, wound), perineum, breasts, urine, CXR (pneumonia), LP if meningism
FBC, CRP, lactate, U&E, LFT, coagulation, blood culture × 2 BEFORE antibiotics, urine culture, high vaginal swab, placenta swab if recently delivered, breast milk if mastitis
Fetal assessment if undelivered (CTG)
USS if retained products / abscess suspected
management: MATERNAL SEPSIS-SIX (within 1 hour of recognition):
1. Senior obstetric + anaesthetic + critical care alert
2. High-flow oxygen (target SpO2 ≥ 94%)
3. Blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics

4. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotic within 1h: pip-tazo 4.5 g q8h OR ceftriaxone 2 g + metronidazole 500 mg q8h (covers anaerobes — endometritis); add gentamicin 5 mg/kg or amikacin if shock; add clindamycin 600 mg q6h if Group A Strep / TSS suspected (anti-toxin)
5. IV crystalloid 30 ml/kg over 3h for hypotension or lactate > 4
6. Measure lactate + urine output (catheterise)
SOURCE CONTROL within 6–12 hours:
Septic abortion: evacuate retained products (MVA) — definitive control
Endometritis: antibiotics; D&C if retained products
Chorioamnionitis (undelivered): expedite delivery (vaginal preferred, C-section for obstetric indication); antibiotics during labour
Wound: open + debride + drain pus
Mastitis: drain abscess
Necrotising fasciitis: URGENT surgical debridement
Vasopressor: noradrenaline first-line if hypotension despite fluids (target MAP ≥ 65)
ICU admission for severe / septic shock
Anti-coagulation: VTE prophylaxis with LMWH (pregnancy + sepsis very high risk)
Delivery considerations: maternal stabilisation priority; expedite if intrauterine source
Postpartum considerations: continue breastfeeding if mother able + antibiotics compatible (most are)
Watch for HELLP / pre-eclampsia overlap
Notify MDR / maternal death review if death

RCOG Green-top 64a + 64b Bacterial Sepsis in Pregnancy 2012

title: Eclampsia + severe pre-eclampsia — magnesium sulphate (MAGPIE)
population: Pregnant + postpartum women (up to 6 weeks). Highest cause of maternal mortality globally; SSA disproportionate. Severe pre-eclampsia BP ≥ 160/110 + proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction; eclampsia = seizure on background.
presentation: Pre-eclampsia severe features: BP ≥ 160/110, severe headache, visual disturbance, RUQ/epigastric pain, hyperreflexia / clonus, oliguria, pulmonary oedema. Eclampsia: tonic-clonic seizure. HELLP: haemolysis + raised LFTs + low platelets.
diagnostics: BP measurement standardised + repeated 4 hours apart for diagnosis
Urine dipstick proteinuria; spot urine PCR > 30 mg/mmol or 24h > 300 mg
FBC, U&E, LFT, urate, LDH, coag
CTG / biophysical profile
Reflexes + clonus check during magnesium infusion
management: ECLAMPTIC SEIZURE:
ABC, lateral position, suction, high-flow O2
MAGNESIUM SULPHATE — drug of choice (MAGPIE 2002 — reduced eclampsia 58%):
Loading: 4 g IV slowly over 5–10 min (mix 4 g in 20 ml saline)
Maintenance: 1 g/h IV infusion × 24h after delivery / last seizure
Alternative IM: 5 g each buttock + 5 g q4h × 24h (used where IV not available; pain at injection)
Recurrent seizure: further 2 g IV bolus
Watch toxicity: loss of patellar reflex (give Ca gluconate), RR < 12 (hypocalcaemia, paralysis), oliguria (reduce dose)
Calcium gluconate 1 g IV antidote available bedside
SEVERE HYPERTENSION (≥ 160/110) — treat within 30–60 min:
Labetalol 20 mg IV; double q10 min up to 80 mg (max 220 mg cumulative); or 200 mg PO
Hydralazine 5 mg IV q20 min (avoid in CV disease)
Nifedipine 10 mg PO (NOT sublingual — uncontrolled drop)
Target SBP 140–155, DBP 90–105 (avoid sudden drop — placental hypoperfusion)
FLUID management: CAUTIOUS — pulmonary oedema risk; maintenance 80 ml/h crystalloid; fluid challenge only if oliguria + invasive monitoring
DELIVERY:
Definitive treatment of pre-eclampsia / eclampsia is delivery
After maternal stabilisation
Vaginal delivery preferred unless obstetric indication for C-section
At ≥ 34 weeks: deliver; 24–33+6: stabilise + corticosteroids + deliver per maternal/fetal status; < 24: counsel termination if severe
POSTPARTUM:
Continue magnesium 24h post-delivery / last seizure
Monitor BP for 6 weeks (hypertension may persist or worsen)
VTE prophylaxis (high risk)
HELLP usually resolves within 48h of delivery
Future pregnancy counselling: 15% recurrence pre-eclampsia, aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks in next pregnancy (USPSTF/ACOG)
RECURRENCE PREVENTION: low-dose aspirin from 12–16 weeks in subsequent pregnancy + calcium 1.5–2 g/d in calcium-deficient diets (LMIC including most of SSA — WHO recommendation)
Notify MDR if death

references.label: WHO Recommendations for Prevention and Treatment of Pre-eclampsia and Eclampsia 2011
RCOG Green-top 10A The Management of Severe Pre-eclampsia/Eclampsia
Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (Linda Mama)

title: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) — screening + management
population: Pregnant women — global prevalence rising (10–25% depending on criteria); higher in SSA + South Asian populations. Universal screening 24–28 weeks vs risk-based varies by guideline.
presentation: Usually asymptomatic (screen-detected). Risk factors: obesity (BMI > 30), age > 35, family history T2DM, previous GDM / macrosomia, PCOS, ethnicity, glycosuria. Complications: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycaemia, RDS, pre-eclampsia, polyhydramnios, future T2DM (50% at 10 years).
redFlags: Suspected congenital anomaly (in poorly controlled overt diabetes mistaken for GDM)
Poor glycaemic control (fasting > 5.3, postprandial > 7.8 mmol/L) despite diet
diagnostics: WHO 2013 + IADPSG criteria: 75 g OGTT at 24–28 weeks — fasting ≥ 5.1, 1h ≥ 10.0, 2h ≥ 8.5 mmol/L (any one diagnoses GDM)
NICE alternative: 75 g OGTT — fasting ≥ 5.6, 2h ≥ 7.8
Pre-existing diabetes if fasting ≥ 7.0 or random ≥ 11.1 or HbA1c ≥ 48 at booking
FBG only screening — used in LMIC programmes including Kenya MOH
Risk-based vs universal — Kenya MOH risk-based plus universal in tertiary
Fundoscopy + urinary ACR + ECG in overt diabetes (T1/T2 not GDM)
management: DIET + LIFESTYLE (1st-line; many controlled by this alone):
Low-glycaemic-index carbohydrate, portion control, regular meals + snacks
Weight gain limits (IOM): underweight 12.5–18 kg, normal 11.5–16, overweight 7–11.5, obese 5–9
Exercise — 30 min walking daily after meals (lowers postprandial)
Self-monitor blood glucose 4× daily — fasting + 1h postprandial after each meal
Target: fasting < 5.3, 1h post < 7.8 (or 2h post < 6.7) mmol/L
PHARMACOLOGICAL (if targets not met in 1–2 weeks):
Metformin 500 mg BD (titrate to 2 g/d max) — first-line PO; safe in pregnancy, infant + maternal outcomes equivalent to insulin (MiG trial); WHO + ADA + NICE endorse; about 30–50% need insulin added
Insulin — gold standard; NPH bedtime + rapid acting prandial; doses titrated; required for tighter control / when metformin contraindicated / type 1 / overt T2
Glibenclamide — second-line; falling out of favour (crosses placenta, neonatal hypoglycaemia)
ANTENATAL MONITORING:
Growth scans every 4 weeks from 28 weeks
Fetal surveillance (CTG, BPP) weekly from 36 weeks
Aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks (pre-eclampsia prevention)
DELIVERY:
Diet-controlled GDM: deliver by 40+6
Insulin-controlled: deliver by 38–39 weeks
Suspected macrosomia (> 4.5 kg): offer C-section (reduce shoulder dystocia)
Intrapartum: variable rate insulin infusion to maintain glucose 4–7 mmol/L; CTG monitoring
POSTPARTUM:
Stop insulin / metformin immediately at delivery
Encourage breastfeeding (reduces future maternal T2DM + childhood obesity)
Fasting glucose or 75g OGTT at 6–12 weeks postpartum (T2DM screen)
Annual diabetes screening lifelong (50% develop T2DM in 10 years)
Lifestyle counselling + weight management
Future pregnancy: pre-conception counselling, optimise weight + glucose, aspirin
NEONATAL: glucose monitoring within 30 min + 2h + pre-feeds × 24h; treat hypoglycaemia per neonatal protocol

title: VTE in pregnancy + postpartum — risk-stratify + LMWH
population: All pregnant + postpartum women. Pregnancy is hypercoagulable; VTE 5× more common than non-pregnant; postpartum highest risk especially first 6 weeks. Leading direct cause of maternal mortality in many HICs.
presentation: DVT — leg swelling/pain (predominantly LEFT-sided in pregnancy 80% — iliac vein compression by gravid uterus); PE — dyspnoea, chest pain, tachycardia, syncope, haemoptysis; subtle presentations common.
redFlags: Sudden dyspnoea / chest pain — exclude PE urgently
Massive PE with haemodynamic instability — thrombolysis consideration
diagnostics: RCOG VTE risk score: assess at booking, antenatal admission, postpartum
DVT: compression ultrasound (whole leg)
PE: chest X-ray, ECG (sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3, RBBB), ABG (low O2 + low CO2 + raised gradient); definitive — CTPA preferred; V/Q if young + normal CXR (radiation comparable; ventilation half-dose)
D-dimer NOT reliable in pregnancy (physiologically raised); use clinical probability + imaging
Thrombophilia screen — usually defer to postpartum 6+ weeks
management: RISK STRATIFICATION (RCOG Green-top 37a):
ANTENATAL:
≥ 4 risk factors: LMWH from 1st trimester to 6 weeks postpartum
3 risk factors: LMWH from 28 weeks
2 risk factors: ?from 28 weeks (intermediate decision)
Major risk factors: previous VTE, thrombophilia (lupus anticoagulant, antiphospholipid, factor V Leiden homozygous, AT deficiency), antiphospholipid syndrome
POSTPARTUM (highest risk):
≥ 2 risk factors / any major: LMWH × 6 weeks
Caesarean section: at least 10 days (longer if other RFs)
Routine antenatal hospital admission: 7 days LMWH
DOSING (RCOG):
Prophylactic enoxaparin: 40 mg SC OD (50–90 kg); 60 mg OD (91–130 kg); higher per weight
AT < 50 kg: 20 mg OD
Treatment dose for confirmed VTE: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC BD (or 1.5 mg/kg OD)
AVOID warfarin in pregnancy (teratogenic 6–12 weeks, fetal bleeding); LMWH is mainstay throughout pregnancy
Stop LMWH 24h before planned induction / C-section / regional anaesthesia (more conservative — 24h for prophylactic, 24h for treatment dose); restart 6–12h postpartum if no bleeding
Avoid DOACs in pregnancy / breastfeeding (insufficient safety data)
MASSIVE PE: thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2h) for haemodynamic collapse — risks high but justified; surgical embolectomy alternative
Mechanical: TED stockings, IPC during admission, early mobilisation
Aspirin alone insufficient for VTE prophylaxis in pregnancy
Patient education: warning signs, seek help urgently
Document risk assessment at every contact + after any admission / surgery

title: Shoulder dystocia — HELPERR algorithm
population: Vaginal delivery — incidence 0.6–1.4% of all vaginal births. Risk factors: macrosomia, GDM, prior shoulder dystocia, prolonged second stage, instrumental delivery — but most occur without RFs.
presentation: After delivery of head — failure to deliver shoulders with normal traction; 'turtle sign' — head retracts against perineum. Need delivery within 5 min (after that fetal hypoxia + brachial plexus injury rise).
redFlags: Failure to deliver in 5 minutes — escalate
Brachial plexus injury (Erb-Klumpke) — most common complication
Maternal: PPH, 3rd/4th degree tear, symphysis pubis separation
Fetal: hypoxic injury, fracture clavicle/humerus, death
diagnostics: Clinical recognition — turtle sign + failure to deliver
Document: time of head delivery, manoeuvres + order + duration, who performed, fetal condition, cord blood gas
Postpartum: examine neonate for brachial plexus + fractures
management: HELPERR mnemonic — sequential, escalating manoeuvres (each 30 sec):
H — Call for HELP (senior obstetric, paediatric, anaesthetic + scribe + clock)
E — EVALUATE for Episiotomy (not always needed — bony obstruction not soft tissue; cut if needed for room for hands)
L — LEGS — McROBERT'S manoeuvre: hyperflex thighs onto abdomen (one assistant each side); resolves 40% by rotating symphysis upwards
P — PRESSURE — suprapubic (NOT fundal — fundal worsens impaction) — assistant applies CPR-like pressure downwards + laterally on impacted anterior shoulder for 30 seconds; resolves additional 20%
E — ENTER pelvis (internal manoeuvres):
Rubin II: pressure on posterior aspect of anterior shoulder to adduct + rotate to oblique
Wood's screw: pressure on anterior aspect of posterior shoulder to rotate 180°
Reverse Wood's screw: reverse rotation
R — REMOVE posterior arm: insert hand along posterior vaginal wall, sweep posterior arm across chest, deliver
R — ROLL onto all fours (Gaskin manoeuvre) — gravity may help
LAST RESORT (rarely used in routine practice — usually for catastrophic dystocia):
Deliberate fracture of clavicle (cleidotomy)
Symphysiotomy (in low-resource settings without C-section access — Kenya MOH protocol includes for catastrophic shoulder dystocia where C-section not possible)
Zavanelli manoeuvre (push head back into pelvis, deliver by C-section) — last resort
POST-DELIVERY:
Cord blood gases (umbilical artery + vein)
Examine baby — Erb's palsy (waiter's tip — most common), Klumpke (claw hand), clavicle/humerus fracture
Refer paediatric for assessment + physiotherapy
Maternal: examine for tears, atony, PPH (high risk after dystocia)
Debrief team + family (informed disclosure if injury)
Skill drills (PROMPT) — train regularly; reduces brachial plexus injury

title: Antenatal care — WHO 8-contact model + Linda Mama (Kenya)
population: All pregnant women — Kenya Linda Mama programme provides free MNH services. WHO 2016 recommended 8 contacts (replacing FANC 4-visit model).
presentation: Routine ANC contact at: 1 (< 12 wk booking), 2 (20 wk), 3 (26 wk), 4 (30 wk), 5 (34 wk), 6 (36 wk), 7 (38 wk), 8 (40 wk). Booking visit most comprehensive.
redFlags: Symptoms of UTI (pyelonephritis — prevent with screening)
diagnostics: Booking: history + examination + dating ultrasound + bloods (FBC, blood group + Rh, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B sAg, hepatitis C, rubella, varicella, sickle cell + thalassaemia screen where indicated), MSU, urinalysis
Each visit: BP, urinalysis, fundal height, fetal HR ≥ 12 weeks (Doppler), fetal movements ≥ 24 wk, presentation 36+ wk
Recommended ultrasound: dating (booking), anomaly (18–22 weeks), growth (28, 32, 36 weeks) where access
Screening: GDM 24–28 wk, anaemia each trimester, GBS swab 35–37 wk (where policy)
Aspirin risk assessment at 12 wk: USPSTF criteria → low-dose 75–150 mg pre-eclampsia prevention from 12 wk
Mental health: EPDS / Whooley booking + 28 wk
VTE risk at booking + each admission
management: BOOKING (< 12 weeks):
Comprehensive history (medical, obstetric, family, social, mental health, IPV, FGM)
Folic acid 5 mg daily (preferably from pre-conception) — higher dose if epilepsy, diabetes, BMI > 30, twins, prior NTD
Iron + folic acid (60 mg + 0.4 mg) daily — WHO + Kenya MOH
Calcium 1.5–2 g daily in low-calcium populations (WHO 2018 — most SSA, including Kenya — pre-eclampsia prevention)
Aspirin 75–150 mg from 12–16 weeks for pre-eclampsia high-risk
Diet + lifestyle: balanced diet, weight gain, avoid alcohol, smoking, recreational drugs, traditional herbs

Insecticide-treated bed nets + intermittent preventive treatment for malaria (IPTp): sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine 3 doses ≥ 1 month apart in moderate-high transmission counties (Kenya endemic areas) — Kenya MOH National Malaria in Pregnancy guidelines
Tetanus-diphtheria (Td) booster per WHO schedule (2 doses minimum in first pregnancy)
Hepatitis B vaccine + tdap (pertussis maternal) where available
Counsel on danger signs + birth preparedness
Skilled birth attendance + Linda Mama enrolment (Kenya)
HIV testing (opt-out) + treat with ART for PMTCT
Syphilis test + treat (single dose benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM if positive)
Hepatitis B sAg + manage per protocol (infant immunoprophylaxis at birth)
Family planning counselling for post-partum contraception
ONGOING (visits 2–8):
BP + urinalysis each visit
Fetal monitoring (fundal height, fetal movements, FHR)
Continued IFA + IPTp + nutrition counselling
Anomaly scan 18–22 weeks
GDM screen 24–28 weeks
Anti-D 28 + 34 weeks (Rh-negative women, where available)
Birth plan refinement
Breastfeeding preparation
Postpartum contraception choice (LARC same day as delivery possible)
Pertussis-containing vaccine (Tdap) 28–36 weeks (UK, US recommendations; Kenya catchup if not yet given)
External cephalic version offered for breech ≥ 36 weeks
DANGER SIGNS counselling — return immediately for:
Bleeding, severe headache/visual changes, reduced fetal movements, severe abdominal pain, fever, severe vomiting, dyspnoea, water breaking, labour pain < 37 wk
BIRTH PREPAREDNESS — facility delivery (skilled birth attendant), transport plan, emergency funds, blood donor, companion, supplies

title: Intrapartum fetal monitoring + WHO Labour Care Guide (partogram)
population: All women in labour. WHO Labour Care Guide (2020) updated the previous partogram — emphasises woman-centred decisions.
presentation: Labour assessment + ongoing monitoring of maternal + fetal wellbeing. Triggers for action based on time + fetal heart rate + cervix + contractions.
redFlags: Late decelerations / persistent bradycardia < 110 / persistent tachycardia > 160
Failure to progress (no cervical change × 4 hours in active labour, or no descent in 2nd stage)
diagnostics: Pinard / Doppler intermittent for low-risk (every 15 min in 1st stage, every 5 min in 2nd; for 60 sec after contraction)
Continuous CTG for high-risk (oxytocin, meconium, pyrexia, suspected fetal compromise) — DR C BRaVADO interpretation
DR — Define Risk
C — Contractions
BRa — Baseline Rate
V — Variability
A — Accelerations
D — Decelerations
O — Overall impression
Fetal blood sampling pH at fully dilated if continuous CTG concerning (where available)
Vaginal examination 4-hourly in active 1st stage (cervix + station + caput + moulding)
Maternal: BP, pulse, temperature, urinalysis hourly
management: WHO Labour Care Guide (2020) — replaces older partogram:
Decision-points + woman-centred care
Cervical dilatation MONITORING (no longer a strict 1 cm/h alert/action line)
Recognition that 4 cm is not the onset of active labour; active phase typically from 5 cm
Avoid amniotomy + oxytocin augmentation routinely (was over-used)
Discourage routine episiotomy
Respectful + companion-of-choice care
Hydration + oral intake during low-risk labour
Mobility + birth position of choice
Pain relief options offered (epidural, non-pharm — water, mobility, massage)
FETAL MONITORING:
Low-risk: intermittent every 15 min stage 1, every 5 min stage 2
High-risk: continuous CTG
Suspected fetal compromise: CTG; if concerning — fetal scalp pH or expedited delivery
MANAGEMENT OF DECELERATIONS:
Position change (left lateral)
IV fluid bolus
Stop oxytocin if running
Maternal O2 (debated efficacy; consider for hypoxia)
Tocolysis (terbutaline 250 mcg SC) if hyperstimulation
Vaginal exam — exclude cord prolapse
Expedite delivery if persistent (instrumental or C-section)
PROLONGED LABOUR:
Latent phase prolonged: review, hydration, mobility, often progresses
Active phase arrest > 4h: review (CPD? malposition?); cautious oxytocin if no contraindication
2nd stage arrest: review presentation + maternal effort; instrumental or C-section
INTRAPARTUM ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS for GBS:
Penicillin G 5 MU IV then 2.5 MU q4h until delivery (where GBS screening done; or risk-based — preterm, PROM > 18h, intrapartum pyrexia, previous GBS-affected infant)
ACTIVE MANAGEMENT 3rd STAGE (AMTSL):
Oxytocin 10 IU IM within 1 min of birth (or carbetocin 100 mcg if heat-stable available)
Controlled cord traction
Uterine massage after delivery of placenta
DELAYED CORD CLAMPING ≥ 1 minute (preterm + term)
Skin-to-skin within 1 hour + early breastfeeding
BIRTH companion of choice (WHO + Respectful Maternity Care)

title: PROM + preterm PROM (PPROM) — management
population: Term PROM 8–10% pregnancies; preterm PROM (< 37 weeks) 3% — major cause of preterm birth. Risk factors: smoking, low SES, prior PROM, polyhydramnios, twins, ascending infection (BV, GBS, chlamydia).
presentation: Sudden gush or continuous trickle of fluid per vagina. Distinguish from urinary leakage, vaginal discharge. Confirm with sterile speculum (pooling, valsalva), nitrazine, ferning, AmnioSure / Actim-PROM if uncertain.
redFlags: Chorioamnionitis (maternal pyrexia, tachycardia, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia, foul liquor)
Placental abruption (vaginal bleeding + pain + hard uterus)
diagnostics: Sterile speculum (NO digital exam — increases infection risk)
Pooling of liquor, valsalva test, nitrazine (alkaline — yellow→blue), ferning microscopy
AmnioSure (PAMG-1) / Actim-PROM if equivocal
Ultrasound — oligohydramnios supportive
Vaginal/cervical culture for GBS
FBC, CRP, urine MSU
CTG / fetal HR
Gestational age + estimated fetal weight
management: TERM PROM (≥ 37 weeks):
Offer induction (immediate or expectant up to 24h)
Active = lower chorioamnionitis + earlier delivery
Expectant: 50% in labour within 12h, 90% within 48h
Antibiotics: if not delivered within 18h (penicillin GBS prophylaxis or per local culture)
Discuss + shared decision
PRETERM PROM (< 37 weeks):
Goal: maximise gestation (lung maturity) while monitoring for infection
ADMIT to facility with neonatal capacity
Confirm diagnosis + gestational age
AVOID digital exam unless in active labour
CORTICOSTEROIDS for fetal lung maturity 24–34+6 weeks: betamethasone 12 mg IM × 2 (24h apart) or dexamethasone 6 mg IM × 4 (12h apart); single course — reduces RDS + IVH + neonatal death
ANTIBIOTICS PROM PPROM (latency): erythromycin 250 mg QDS × 10 days (ORACLE I — extends latency, reduces neonatal morbidity); AVOID amoxicillin-clavulanate (NEC association in ORACLE)
MAGNESIUM SULPHATE for neuroprotection if < 32 weeks + imminent delivery: 4 g IV loading + 1 g/h × up to 24h (reduces CP)
Tocolysis NOT routine in PPROM (no benefit); consider short-term to allow steroids / transfer
Surveillance: maternal temperature 4-hourly, FBC + CRP regularly, CTG / BPP
Deliver if: 34+0 weeks (or 36+0 weeks per some guidelines — debate; PPROMT trial 34–36 weeks expectant equivalent), chorioamnionitis suspected, fetal distress, abruption, cord prolapse
Delivery mode: vaginal preferred unless obstetric indication
NEONATAL: cord blood gases, observation for sepsis × 48h (PPROM, prolonged ROM, intrapartum pyrexia), empirical antibiotics if clinical signs
Counsel parents: prognosis by gestation, neonatal involvement, breastfeeding plan, kangaroo mother care if preterm
Kenya Linda Mama covers admission + delivery + neonatal care

title: Postpartum mental health spectrum — baby blues, PPD, psychosis, OCD, PTSD
population: All women postpartum; partners/co-parents also at risk. Significant under-recognition in SSA primary care.
presentation: Spectrum: baby blues (50–80%, day 3–5, resolves 2 wk), PPD (10–20%, > 2 wk, screen with EPDS), postpartum anxiety + OCD (intrusive thoughts of harm), postpartum psychosis (1:1000, emergency, days 2–14), birth trauma + PTSD (3–6%).
redFlags: Postpartum psychosis (rapid onset, mood lability, hallucinations, delusions, suicide/infanticide ideation)
Thoughts of harming infant (intrusive vs psychotic — assess insight)
Bipolar disorder history (high relapse risk peripartum — 50–70%)
diagnostics: EPDS at 6 wk postnatal contact + 3, 6, 12 mo
Whooley 2-question case-find
Assess for psychosis: hallucinations, delusions, thought disorder, rapid cycling, lability
Assess for OCD: ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts vs ego-syntonic psychotic
Assess for PTSD: re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal of birth-related
Suicide + infanticide risk assessment
Substance use screen
management: BABY BLUES: education + reassurance + sleep + social support; rescreen at 2 weeks; refer if persistent
POSTPARTUM DEPRESSION (mod–severe): stepped care per separate condition (postpartum-depression-edinburgh-pnd):
CBT / IPT first-line
SSRI (sertraline preferred for breastfeeding) for mod–severe
Brexanolone IV (where available) — single 60h infusion for severe
Zuranolone (oral neurosteroid GABA-A) — FDA-approved 2023 for severe PPD
POSTPARTUM ANXIETY / OCD: CBT + SSRI; common but under-recognised
POSTPARTUM PSYCHOSIS (EMERGENCY):
Admit (ideally mother-baby unit; refer to tertiary)
Antipsychotic — olanzapine, risperidone (compatible with breastfeeding mostly)
Mood stabiliser if bipolar — lithium (monitor levels; infant exposure significant — discuss alternatives or formula feeding); valproate AVOID in women of reproductive potential
ECT for severe / refractory / catatonia / suicidal
Long-term: identify bipolar diathesis, plan for next pregnancy (prophylactic mood stabiliser, close monitoring)
PTSD POST-BIRTH: trauma-focused CBT, EMDR; debrief in immediate aftermath NOT recommended (may worsen); offer in following weeks; SSRI if persistent
BIPOLAR + PREGNANCY/POSTPARTUM:
Pre-conception: optimise mood stabiliser balancing teratogenicity (avoid valproate, carbamazepine if possible — lamotrigine + olanzapine preferred)
Postpartum prophylaxis CRITICAL — restart mood stabiliser if stopped
Risk of postpartum psychosis 50–70% in bipolar I
PARTNER mental health: 10% paternal PPD; screen, refer
BREASTFEEDING + medication: most antidepressants + antipsychotics compatible (LactMed); risk-benefit conversation
INFANT: attachment, developmental assessment, parenting support
Kenya: integrate into Linda Mama postnatal care + CHV training, WHO Thinking Healthy programme

references.label: NICE CG192 Antenatal + Postnatal Mental Health 2014/2018
ACOG Committee Opinion 757 Screening for Perinatal Depression 2018

title: HFrEF — guideline-directed medical therapy (4 pillars + ARNI)
population: HFrEF (LVEF ≤ 40%) — symptomatic NYHA II–IV. Substantial reduction in mortality + hospitalisation with 4-pillar GDMT.
presentation: Dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND, fatigue, exercise intolerance, lower limb oedema. Acute decompensation: pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock.
redFlags: NYHA IV at rest / advanced HF — refer specialist (transplant / LVAD / palliation)
Renal dysfunction worsening on RAAS / SGLT2i
diagnostics: Echo for LVEF (key for treatment classification HFrEF ≤ 40, HFmrEF 41–49, HFpEF ≥ 50)
BNP / NT-proBNP
ECG (LBBB, QRS > 130 — CRT consideration)
FBC, U&E, LFT, ferritin (iron deficiency — IV iron benefits)
TSH (thyroid as reversible cause), HIV, HbA1c
Cardiac MRI / coronary angio for aetiology workup
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing if transplant candidate
management: GDMT 4 PILLARS (start ALL simultaneously / sequentially within weeks; all reduce mortality):
1. ARNI / ACE-i / ARB:
ARNI preferred (sacubitril/valsartan 24/26 → 49/51 → 97/103 mg BD per tolerance — PARADIGM-HF NEJM 2014)
If ARNI not available: ACE-i (enalapril, ramipril, lisinopril) or ARB (losartan, candesartan, valsartan)
Switch from ACE-i to ARNI: 36h washout to avoid angioedema
2. β-BLOCKER (HF-specific): bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, nebivolol — start LOW + uptitrate weekly to target
3. MRA (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist): spironolactone 25 mg or eplerenone — RALES + EMPHASIS-HF; monitor K+ + Cr
4. SGLT2 INHIBITOR: dapagliflozin 10 mg / empagliflozin 10 mg — DAPA-HF + EMPEROR-Reduced — benefit IRRESPECTIVE of diabetes
ADD-ON THERAPIES:
Loop diuretic for symptom control (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide)
Ivabradine — for HR > 70 on max β-blocker + sinus rhythm (SHIFT)
Hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate — African ancestry (A-HeFT) OR ACE/ARB intolerant
Digoxin — symptom relief in AF + HF (DIG trial — no mortality benefit)
Vericiguat — guanylate cyclase stimulator for worsening HF (VICTORIA)
IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose) if ferritin < 100 or TSAT < 20% (CONFIRM-HF + AFFIRM-AHF)
DEVICE THERAPY:
CRT: LBBB + QRS ≥ 130 ms + LVEF ≤ 35% + NYHA II–IV on optimal therapy
ICD: LVEF ≤ 35% + NYHA II–III + life expectancy > 1 yr (post-MI ≥ 40 days)
ICD + CRT (CRT-D) if both indicated
ADVANCED HF (NYHA IIIb–IV despite optimal):
IV inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone) — palliative or bridge
LVAD as destination therapy or bridge to transplant
Heart transplant — < 65 yr, no contraindications
Palliative care + advance care planning
MONITORING: weight daily, U&E + K+ every 1–2 wk during titration then 3-monthly

HEART FAILURE EDUCATION: salt < 2 g/day, fluid restriction 1.5–2 L/day if hyponatraemia, weight monitor + flexible diuretic, smoking cessation, ETOH limit, vaccinations (flu + pneumococcal + COVID), exercise programme (cardiac rehab)
Atrial fibrillation in HFrEF: anticoagulate per CHA2DS2-VASc; rhythm control — catheter ablation (CASTLE-AF) or amiodarone; rate control β-blocker (NOT non-DHP CCB in HFrEF)

title: HFpEF — heart failure preserved ejection fraction
population: LVEF ≥ 50% with HF symptoms + objective evidence raised filling pressures. Predominantly older women, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, atrial fibrillation. 50% of HF prevalence; treatment options historically limited.
presentation: Dyspnoea on exertion, fatigue, oedema, hospital admission for HF; often confused with deconditioning, COPD, anaemia.
diagnostics: Echo: LVEF ≥ 50%, LV mass index raised, LA enlargement (LAVI > 34), diastolic dysfunction (E/e' > 14), pulmonary HT
BNP / NT-proBNP raised
HFA-PEFF or H2FPEF score for diagnostic certainty
Cardiac MRI for amyloid (suspected if LV mass+, low voltage on ECG)
Bone scintigraphy (Tc-PYP) for ATTR amyloid
Iron studies (HF + iron deficiency)
Workup for cause: HTN, ischaemic, valvular, restrictive (amyloid, sarcoid, hypereosinophilic), constrictive pericarditis
management: AETIOLOGY-DIRECTED:
Hypertension: aggressive BP control (target < 130/80)
Diabetes: tight HbA1c + SGLT2 inhibitor
AF: rhythm + rate control + anticoagulation
Obesity: weight loss (semaglutide / tirzepatide — STEP-HFpEF trial showed improved QOL + 6MWD)
Sleep apnoea: CPAP
Amyloid: tafamidis (ATTR-ACT) — disease-modifying for ATTR-CM
GDMT (lifesaving evidence growing):
SGLT2 INHIBITOR — dapagliflozin / empagliflozin: reduces HF hospitalisation across full EF spectrum (DELIVER + EMPEROR-Preserved)
MRA: spironolactone (TOPCAT — modest signal especially LVEF 50–55%, lower potassium); finerenone (FIDELIO-DKD adjacent; FINEARTS-HF positive 2024)
ARNI: marginal benefit (PARAGON-HF — subset LVEF 50–57% benefited)
Loop diuretic for volume
AVOID nitrate routinely (NEAT trial — no benefit + worse exercise)
Exercise training — cardiac rehabilitation evidence in HFpEF
CARDIAC AMYLOID specifically:
Tafamidis 61 mg daily — ATTR-CM (ATTR-ACT)
Patisiran / vutrisiran — hereditary ATTR with polyneuropathy
AL amyloid — chemotherapy + bortezomib + autoHSCT
Atrial fibrillation strategy IMPORTANT in HFpEF — rhythm control often preferred
AVOID β-blocker without specific indication (loss of chronotropic reserve worsens HFpEF exercise capacity, although mortality similar)
Patient education + multidisciplinary HF team referral if multiple admissions

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Atrial fibrillation — CHA2DS2-VASc + DOAC + rhythm/rate (2024)
population: Adults — prevalence 1–4% rising with age; 25% lifetime risk over 40. Atrial fibrillation prevalence rising in SSA (often missed). Major cause of preventable stroke.
presentation: Palpitations, fatigue, dyspnoea, syncope; often asymptomatic and detected on incidental ECG / opportunistic screening. Pulse — irregularly irregular. Stroke as first presentation (cardioembolic 4–5×).
redFlags: Pre-excitation (WPW + AF — narrow + wide QRS) — AVOID AV-nodal blockers
Suspected MI / acute coronary syndrome triggering AF
Stroke / TIA with AF — urgent anticoagulation start
diagnostics: 12-lead ECG: irregular RR + absent P waves + fibrillatory waves
Implantable loop recorder / wearable (smart watch) for paroxysmal
FBC, U&E, LFT, TSH, glucose, NT-proBNP
Echocardiogram (left atrial size, LV function, valves)
CHA2DS2-VASc score: Congestive HF (1), Hypertension (1), Age ≥ 75 (2) / 65–74 (1), Diabetes (1), Stroke/TIA (2), Vascular disease (1), Female (1)
HAS-BLED bleeding risk: HTN, Abnormal renal/liver, Stroke, Bleeding, Labile INR, Elderly, Drugs/alcohol
TOE / 4-week anticoag before cardioversion if AF duration > 48h or unknown
management: ANTICOAGULATION (stroke prevention):
CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 2 (or ≥ 1 in men, ≥ 2 in women): anticoagulate
DOAC PREFERRED over warfarin (apixaban 5 mg BD, rivaroxaban 20 mg OD, dabigatran 150 mg BD, edoxaban 60 mg OD) — equivalent / superior efficacy + safer bleeding profile
Apixaban best safety profile in elderly + CKD (eGFR ≥ 25)
Renal dose adjustment per drug (apixaban 2.5 BD if 2 of: age ≥ 80, Cr ≥ 133, weight ≤ 60)
Warfarin if: severe CKD (eGFR < 15), mechanical valve, mitral stenosis
Avoid antiplatelet for AF stroke prevention (less effective + similar bleeding)
Left atrial appendage closure (Watchman) — high stroke risk + contraindication to anticoag
Bridging only for very high stroke risk (mechanical valve, recent stroke, CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 7) — DOACs do not need bridging
RATE CONTROL:
β-blocker (bisoprolol, metoprolol) or non-DHP CCB (diltiazem, verapamil — AVOID in HFrEF)
Digoxin add-on if needed (especially HF or sedentary)
Target resting HR < 110 (lenient — RACE II) or < 80 (strict symptoms)
RHYTHM CONTROL:
Electrical cardioversion: synchronised DC 100–200 J (biphasic); rate-controlled + anticoag 3 wk pre + 4 wk post (or TOE-guided immediate)
Pharmacological cardioversion: amiodarone 300 mg IV over 30 min then 900 mg/24h, or 600–800 mg/d PO loading; flecainide 'pill in pocket' for paroxysmal no structural HD
Catheter ablation (PVI) — increasing first-line for symptomatic paroxysmal AF, HF-AF (CASTLE-AF), young; EAST-AFNET 4 — early rhythm control reduces CV events
Rhythm control preferred in HF, young, persistent symptoms despite rate control, recent onset
ACUTE AF unstable: synchronised cardioversion 100–200 J + anticoagulation
Lifestyle: weight loss, ETOH reduction, OSA treatment, BP control, exercise — modify risk factors
AF + HFrEF: catheter ablation superior (CASTLE-AF) when feasible
AF + recent MI / PCI: triple therapy → dual (DOAC + clopidogrel) → monotherapy DOAC per AUGUSTUS / ENTRUST-AF PCI
Pregnancy: prefer rate control + LMWH (warfarin teratogenic 1st trim; DOACs avoid)

title: Stable angina + chronic coronary syndrome — anti-anginal + secondary prevention
population: Adults with stable angina, known CAD, post-MI / PCI / CABG; major cause of mortality worldwide.
presentation: Exertional chest tightness/pain radiating to arm/jaw/back, relieved by rest or GTN < 5 min; Canadian CV Society class I–IV. Atypical in women, diabetics, elderly.
redFlags: Crescendo / rest angina (unstable angina — treat as ACS)
Left main / 3-vessel CAD — surgical revascularisation discussion
Refractory angina despite max medical therapy
diagnostics: ECG (often normal at rest)
Functional test: exercise tolerance test, stress echo, cardiac MRI, SPECT, PET
Anatomic: CT coronary angiogram (1st-line per NICE 2016 for typical angina); invasive coronary angio for high-risk / pre-revasc
FBC, U&E, LFT, lipid profile, HbA1c, TSH
management: LIFESTYLE + RISK FACTOR (foundation):
Smoking cessation (largest risk reduction)
Diet — Mediterranean / DASH
Exercise — 150 min moderate weekly + resistance
Weight loss (target BMI < 25 / waist < 102 men, < 88 women)
ETOH moderation, sleep, stress
Vaccinations: flu annually (reduces CV events), pneumococcal
ANTI-ANGINAL FIRST-LINE:
β-blocker (bisoprolol, atenolol, metoprolol) — symptom + post-MI mortality
OR non-DHP CCB (diltiazem, verapamil) if β-blocker contraindicated (avoid combo with β-blocker — bradycardia / AV block)
GTN sublingual for acute angina + prophylaxis before known trigger
ANTI-ANGINAL SECOND-LINE (if symptomatic despite first-line):
Long-acting nitrate (isosorbide mononitrate) with nitrate-free interval
DHP CCB (amlodipine) if β-blocker insufficient
Ivabradine — sinus rhythm + HR > 70
Nicorandil (K-channel opener)
Ranolazine (late Na current inhibitor)
Trimetazidine (metabolic — limited evidence)
SECONDARY PREVENTION (all CAD):
Aspirin 75–100 mg daily (clopidogrel 75 mg if aspirin intolerant)
STATIN HIGH-INTENSITY: atorvastatin 80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg — target LDL < 1.4 mmol/L (ESC 2019) or > 50% reduction
Add ezetimibe + PCSK9 inhibitor (alirocumab, evolocumab) if LDL target not met
Inclisiran (siRNA) 2× yearly — adjunct or alternative
Icosapent ethyl (REDUCE-IT) 4 g/day if persistent triglycerides 1.5–5.6 mmol/L despite statin + CV disease
ACE-I or ARB (especially if HF, DM, CKD, HTN, post-MI)
Tight BP control < 130/80
HbA1c target individualised (< 53 / 7% generally)
DAPT post-PCI: aspirin + P2Y12 (clopidogrel 75 mg / ticagrelor 90 mg BD / prasugrel) for 6–12 mo (3 mo if high bleeding) — extended to 12–24 mo if high ischaemic risk + low bleeding
REVASCULARISATION:
PCI for refractory symptoms, large area ischaemia, left main, proximal LAD
CABG for left main, 3VD with diabetes / LV dysfunction, complex anatomy (SYNTAX score)
Heart team discussion
Cardiac rehabilitation — universally recommended (mortality benefit)
Long-term aspirin + statin + ACE-i + β-blocker post-MI (A-B-C-S)
Patient education: angina trigger avoidance, GTN use, when to call emergency

NICE CG95 Chest Pain of Recent Onset 2016
Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Resistant hypertension — PATHWAY-2 + secondary causes
population: BP > 140/90 (or > 130/80 if diabetes / CKD) despite 3+ antihypertensives at optimal doses including a diuretic. Adherence + lifestyle confirmed. ~5–15% of hypertensives.
presentation: Routine review of poorly controlled BP. Look for white-coat (24h ABPM) vs true resistant.
redFlags: Drug-induced (NSAID, OCP, steroid, decongestant, cocaine, ETOH)
diagnostics: 24h ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM) — confirm true resistant vs white coat
Adherence: directly observed dose, urine drug measurement, electronic pill bottle

Secondary HT workup: aldosterone/renin ratio (4 weeks off mineralocorticoid antagonist + ACE/ARB), 24h urinary metanephrines, plasma cortisol / late-night salivary, renal Doppler / CTA, OSA screening (STOP-Bang, polysomnography), TSH
End-organ damage: UA, ACR, eGFR, ECG, echo, fundoscopy
FBC, lipid, glucose, U&E, eGFR
management: OPTIMISE existing:
Confirm adherence + lifestyle (Na < 5 g/day, alcohol, exercise, weight)
Stop interfering drugs (NSAIDs, OCP, decongestant)
Confirm best classes — ACE/ARB + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic at maximum tolerated dose
ADD 4th-line agent:
SPIRONOLACTONE 25 mg → 50 mg (PATHWAY-2 trial — superior to bisoprolol + doxazosin); monitor K+ + Cr (especially CKD)
If K+ > 5.5: switch to bisoprolol (β-blocker), doxazosin (α-blocker), or clonidine
Eplerenone alternative (less gynaecomastia)
TREAT SECONDARY CAUSES:
Primary aldosteronism: spironolactone + adrenal CT + venous sampling + adrenalectomy if unilateral adenoma
RAS: medical management + statin + smoking cessation; angioplasty selected (FH ARAS uncommon — ASTRAL/CORAL negative for routine PTRA)
Phaeo: phenoxybenzamine then β-blocker then surgery
Cushing: refer endocrine
OSA: CPAP
REFRACTORY HT (despite all):
Centrally acting (clonidine, moxonidine)
Hydralazine + nitrate (mainly HF)
Endothelin antagonist (aprocitentan — PRECISION trial 2023 — newly approved for resistant HT)
Renal denervation — radiofrequency / ultrasound percutaneous (SPYRAL HTN-OFF MED + RADIANCE-HTN — modest BP reduction; option for refractory)
Specialist referral — tertiary hypertension clinic
End-organ protection: SGLT2 inhibitor in CKD/DM, finerenone if albuminuria + DM2

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Acute ischaemic stroke — IV thrombolysis + mechanical thrombectomy
population: Adults with acute focal neurological deficit. Onset-to-treatment time critical — 'Time is brain': ~1.9 million neurons lost per minute.
presentation: Sudden onset focal deficit: hemiparesis, dysphasia, dysarthria, hemianopia, ataxia, vertigo + diplopia (posterior); BE FAST screen.
redFlags: Posterior circulation (basilar — high mortality without recanalisation, atypical signs — coma, locked-in)
Large hemispheric stroke (malignant — risk of decompressive craniectomy)
AF with new stroke — anticoagulate after window
Carotid bruit / known carotid disease — endarterectomy / stenting
diagnostics: URGENT non-contrast CT brain — exclude haemorrhage; early ischaemic changes (ASPECTS score)
CT angiography head + neck — large vessel occlusion (LVO — ICA, M1, basilar)
CT perfusion or MRI for late window (6–24h) — penumbra estimation
FBC, U&E, glucose, INR, troponin, ECG, LFT
Door-to-CT < 25 min, door-to-needle < 60 min targets
management: ACUTE PRESENTATION:
BE FAST recognition + EMS activation
Stroke unit pathway — best evidence-based intervention overall
ABCs, O2 if SpO2 < 94%, glucose 7–10 mmol/L, BP per protocol
BP MANAGEMENT:
Pre-thrombolysis: target < 185/110 (use labetalol 10–20 mg IV q10 min, hydralazine, nicardipine)
Post-thrombolysis: target < 180/105 × 24h
Non-thrombolysis: permissive hypertension up to 220/120 unless end-organ damage
IV THROMBOLYSIS (alteplase 0.9 mg/kg max 90 mg, 10% bolus then 90% over 60 min):
Standard window 0–4.5h from onset
Extended window 4.5–9h with imaging selection (penumbra on perfusion) — EXTEND trial
Wake-up stroke / unknown onset — MRI DWI-FLAIR mismatch selection (WAKE-UP, EXTEND)
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg single bolus — emerging alternative (EXTEND-IA TNK + AcT trials non-inferior)

CONTRAINDICATIONS: recent surgery, bleeding, INR > 1.7, BP > 185/110 uncorrected, recent ICH, large infarct (ASPECTS < 6), recent ischaemic stroke (3 mo), pregnancy (relative), DOAC within 48h (or specific reversal first)
MECHANICAL THROMBECTOMY (most important advance):
Large vessel occlusion (ICA, M1, basilar, sometimes M2 / vertebral)
Within 6h of onset standard (multiple trials MR CLEAN, EXTEND-IA, SWIFT-PRIME, REVASCAT, ESCAPE)
EXTENDED window 6–24h with perfusion mismatch (DAWN, DEFUSE 3)
Combine with IV thrombolysis if eligible (DIRECT-MT — non-inferiority debated, but combine standard)
Basilar occlusion — thrombectomy up to 24h (BAOCHE, ATTENTION 2022) — game-changer
ANCILLARY:
Glucose 7.8–10, avoid hyperthermia
Aspirin 300 mg PO/PR within 48h (not within 24h of thrombolysis)
Statin (high-intensity) early
VTE prophylaxis (mechanical IPC initially; LMWH after 24h)
Swallow screen before oral intake
Decompressive hemicraniectomy for malignant MCA stroke < 60 yr (HAMLET, DESTINY, DECIMAL)
SECONDARY PREVENTION (start before discharge):
Antiplatelet: aspirin 75 mg + clopidogrel 75 mg × 21 days (CHANCE / POINT — minor stroke / high-risk TIA), then aspirin or clopidogrel mono
Anticoagulant for AF (DOAC preferred) — restart timing per HARMONI / 1-3-6-12 day rule by severity
Statin high-intensity LDL < 1.4 (SPARCL — atorvastatin 80 mg)
BP control target < 130/80
Carotid: endarterectomy / stenting for symptomatic > 50% stenosis within 2 wk
Smoking cessation, exercise, diet, weight, ETOH limit, OSA
REHABILITATION: early mobilisation, SLT for dysphasia, OT, physio, mental health (post-stroke depression common)

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Adult cardiac arrest — ACLS + post-ROSC care
population: Adults in cardiac arrest (out-of-hospital + in-hospital). Survival depends on early recognition + bystander CPR + early defibrillation + advanced care.
presentation: Unresponsive, not breathing normally, no pulse. VF/VT shockable vs PEA/asystole non-shockable.
redFlags: Witnessed collapse with shockable rhythm — best survival
Asystole as initial rhythm — poor prognosis
Pregnancy — perimortem C-section within 4 min if no ROSC at 4 min ≥ 20 weeks GA
Drowning, electrocution, hypothermia, anaphylaxis, tox — specific reversible causes
diagnostics: During arrest: rhythm check every 2 min, capnography (ETCO2 — < 10 = poor; sudden rise suggests ROSC)
Post-ROSC: 12-lead ECG (STEMI), ABG, glucose, electrolytes, troponin, lactate, FBC, coag, CT brain (post-anoxic)
Coronary angiography for STEMI post-ROSC
management: BLS: chest compressions 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm adult, full recoil, < 10 sec interruptions, ratio 30:2 if no advanced airway; once advanced airway: continuous compressions + 10 breaths/min
EARLY DEFIBRILLATION: 150–200 J biphasic ASAP for VF/pulseless VT — every 2 min if persists
ACLS:
Adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 min (give ASAP in non-shockable; after 2nd shock in shockable)
Amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus after 3rd shock (lidocaine alternative)
Magnesium 2 g IV for torsades / hypoMg
Reverse causes — 4 Hs (Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo-/hyperkalaemia + electrolytes, Hypothermia) + 4 Ts (Thrombosis cardiac/pulmonary, Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins)
Calcium for hyperK+ / hyperMg+ / CCB / β-blocker tox
Sodium bicarb only for hyperK+ / tox (TCA, ASA)
Lipid emulsion for LA toxicity
Naloxone for opioid
Empiric thrombolysis (tPA 50 mg IV bolus then 50 mg/2h) for suspected PE
TXA + massive transfusion for haemorrhage
Bicarbonate / hyperventilation for TCA / ASA toxicity
AIRWAY: bag-mask first; supraglottic (LMA) or ETT once trained — do NOT interrupt compressions for advanced airway
WAVEFORM CAPNOGRAPHY mandatory once advanced airway
ECMO (eCPR) — selected patients in trial centres (refractory VF + witnessed + bystander CPR < 60 min)
POST-ROSC (FOCUS — equally important as resuscitation):
Target SpO2 92–98% (AVOID hyperoxia)
Target PaCO2 35–45 (normocapnia)
Target MAP ≥ 65 (vasopressor as needed)
Target glucose 7.8–10
Target temperature management (TTM): 32–36°C × 24h (controversial — TTM2 trial showed no benefit of 33° vs 36°/normothermia; current most centres do normothermia with active fever prevention)
EEG monitoring for seizures (10–20% post-anoxic) — treat with levetiracetam
Urgent coronary angiography if STEMI / strong suspicion ACS
CT brain for prognostication / cause
Neurological prognostication NOT BEFORE 72 hours (multimodal — clinical, EEG, NSE, MRI, somatosensory evoked potentials)
PEDIATRIC modifications: 2:1 compressions (newborns 3:1), 4 J/kg defibrillation, drug doses weight-based
OBSTETRIC: pillow under right hip (left lateral tilt) for venous return; perimortem C-section within 4 min if not ROSC at 4 min + ≥ 20 weeks GA
Post-resuscitation debrief team + family + survivor

title: Pulmonary embolism — PESI / sPESI risk stratification + treatment
population: Adults presenting with dyspnoea, chest pain, syncope, or with venous thromboembolism risk factors. Incidence 1–2 per 1000/year; mortality 5–25%.
presentation: Dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, cough, haemoptysis, syncope, hypotension, hypoxia, tachycardia, tachypnoea, raised JVP, accentuated P2. DVT signs (unilateral leg swelling).
redFlags: Right ventricular dysfunction on echo / CT — intermediate-high risk
Recent surgery / immobility / cancer / pregnancy / OCP / known thrombophilia
diagnostics: Wells / Geneva score → low/intermediate/high probability
D-dimer if low/intermediate probability (age-adjusted threshold > 50 yr: age × 10 µg/L)
CTPA — gold standard imaging (if elevated D-dimer or high probability)
V/Q if CT contraindicated (pregnancy, contrast allergy, severe CKD)
ECG (S1Q3T3, RBBB, T inversion V1-V4)
ABG (raised A-a gradient)
Troponin + NT-proBNP for risk stratification
Echo — RV dysfunction (intermediate-high risk PE)
Compression US legs if PE confirmed (DVT)
sPESI / PESI score for mortality risk:
PESI class I/II (low) — outpatient consideration
PESI class III–V — admit
Hestia criteria — alternative for outpatient candidate
management: INITIAL: oxygen, IV access, fluids cautious (RV preload-dependent — over-resuscitation worsens)
ANTICOAGULATION (start while investigating if high suspicion + no high bleeding risk):
DOAC PREFERRED (apixaban 10 mg BD × 7 d then 5 mg BD; rivaroxaban 15 mg BD × 21 d then 20 mg OD; dabigatran/edoxaban after 5–10 d LMWH lead-in)
LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD) — cancer-associated PE (CLOT, Hokusai-VTE Cancer), pregnancy, awaiting decision
Warfarin — bridged with LMWH × 5 days + INR > 2 × 24h (less common now)
UFH infusion — when haemodynamically unstable, severe renal failure, planned thrombolysis / surgery
DURATION:
Provoked (transient RF) — 3 months
Unprovoked / persistent RF — extended indefinitely (with risk-benefit reassessment) — DOAC reduced dose (apixaban 2.5 mg BD or rivaroxaban 10 mg OD) for extended phase (AMPLIFY-EXT, EINSTEIN-CHOICE)
Cancer-associated — at least 6 months, often indefinite
MASSIVE / HIGH-RISK PE (haemodynamic instability):
SYSTEMIC THROMBOLYSIS — alteplase 100 mg IV over 2h (or 10 mg bolus + 90 mg/2h) for shock / refractory hypoxia
Contraindications: recent surgery (10 days), recent stroke (3 mo), bleeding diathesis, severe HTN, recent CPR — relative
Surgical embolectomy / catheter-directed thrombolysis if systemic contraindicated
ECMO as bridge in selected centres
INTERMEDIATE-HIGH risk (RV dysfunction + troponin raised, BP normal):
Anticoagulate + close monitor in HDU
Half-dose thrombolysis controversial (PEITHO trial — increased bleeding, no mortality benefit; further trials ongoing)
Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) emerging — lower dose, less bleeding (selected centres)
IVC filter — only if anticoagulation contraindicated + active VTE; retrievable + remove ASAP
OUTPATIENT TREATMENT: low-risk PE (sPESI 0, Hestia all negative, social support, no bleeding) — start DOAC + discharge same day with follow-up (HoT-PE)
Pregnancy: LMWH (1 mg/kg BD treatment dose); thrombolysis only if life-threatening; CTPA with shielding or V/Q

Post-PE care: 3-month review for residual symptoms, persistent pulmonary HT (chronic thromboembolic pulmonary HT — CTEPH; refer specialist if symptomatic + raised PASP), thrombophilia workup if unprovoked + young / family history

title: Hypertensive emergency vs urgency — pathway
population: Adults with markedly elevated BP — emergency (BP usually > 180/120 with end-organ damage) vs urgency (high BP, no acute end-organ damage). Common ED presentation; only emergency needs IV/parenteral.
presentation: End-organ damage signs:
redFlags: Aortic dissection (tearing chest/back pain, asymmetric pulses)
Hypertensive encephalopathy (papilloedema + headache + seizure + altered mental state)
diagnostics: BP both arms (asymmetry > 20 mmHg in dissection)
ECG (LVH, ischaemia)
Fundoscopy (papilloedema, haemorrhages, exudates — grade III/IV retinopathy = emergency)
FBC, U&E, creatinine, urinalysis (proteinuria + RBC casts — acute kidney injury)
Troponin
CXR (pulmonary oedema, mediastinal widening)
CT chest with contrast (dissection)
CT brain if neurological signs
Echo (acute MR, LV dysfunction, dissection)
Urinary metanephrines / drug screen if suspected secondary cause
management: HYPERTENSIVE EMERGENCY (end-organ damage):
Admit ICU/HDU, arterial line, continuous monitoring
CAUTIOUS BP REDUCTION — avoid > 25% in 1h (cerebral autoregulation impaired — risk of watershed infarct)
Target: MAP reduction 10–20% in 1h, then to 160/100 over 2–6h, then gradually to baseline over 24–48h
EXCEPTIONS to gradual reduction:
Aortic dissection: target SBP < 120 in 5–10 min + HR < 60 (start with β-blocker before vasodilator)
Acute ischaemic stroke pre-thrombolysis: target < 185/110
Acute ischaemic stroke not thrombolysed: lenient permissive (< 220/120)
Eclampsia: target SBP 140–155, DBP 90–105
IV AGENTS:
Labetalol IV 20 mg over 2 min then double q10 min up to 80 mg (max 220 mg cumulative); infusion 0.5–2 mg/min
Nicardipine IV 5 mg/h up to 15 mg/h
Hydralazine 5 mg IV q15 min (used in pregnancy)
Sodium nitroprusside 0.25–10 mcg/kg/min — rapid, titratable; risk of cyanide toxicity > 24h
GTN infusion — preferred in pulmonary oedema / ACS (preload + afterload)
Esmolol — short-acting β-blocker for dissection / phaeo
Phentolamine — phaeo / cocaine (α-blocker)
Magnesium sulphate — eclampsia
URGENCY (no end-organ damage):
Oral therapy — restart / increase usual antihypertensives
Amlodipine 5–10 mg, lisinopril 10–20 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, labetalol 200 mg PO
Goal: gradual reduction over 24–48h to safer range (< 160/100), full target over weeks
AVOID rapid SL nifedipine, hydralazine boluses — uncontrolled hypotension
Outpatient follow-up within 1 week
INVESTIGATE secondary cause (RAS, primary aldo, phaeo, OSA, CKD, Cushing) once stable
Long-term: optimise per resistant HT pathway

title: Type 2 diabetes — modern algorithm (GLP-1 RA + SGLT2i first-line)
population: Adults with T2DM — global burden 537 million; Africa rising fastest. Cardiovascular + renal disease major causes of mortality.
presentation: Asymptomatic in screening / polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, blurred vision, recurrent infections, neuropathy, retinopathy, nephropathy. Diabetic ketoacidosis or HHS as presentation in 10–30% in LMIC.
diagnostics: HbA1c ≥ 48 mmol/mol (6.5%), fasting glucose ≥ 7.0, 2h OGTT ≥ 11.1, random ≥ 11.1 + symptoms
Annual review: HbA1c, BP, lipids, eGFR + ACR, fundoscopy / retinal photo, foot exam, weight + BMI
DPN screen: monofilament + reflexes + tuning fork
Mental health screen (depression 2× more common); injection technique
management: MODERN ALGORITHM (ADA 2024, EASD 2022 — paradigm shift):
GLYCAEMIC TARGET INDIVIDUALISED: HbA1c < 53 mmol/mol (7%) most; 48 (6.5%) young + healthy; 58 (7.5%) elderly + comorbid; 64 (8%) frail
CHOICE OF FIRST-LINE NOW EVIDENCE-DRIVEN BY COMORBIDITY (not just A1c):
ASCVD or high CV risk: GLP-1 RA (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide) ± SGLT2i — first-line even before metformin if affordable
Heart failure / CKD with albuminuria: SGLT2i first-line (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin)
No comorbidity + cost barrier: metformin first-line; add GLP-1RA / SGLT2i when accessible
COMBINATIONS based on goals — most patients need 2–3 agents
AGENTS:
Metformin 500 mg BD → 2 g/day (split if GI; XR formulation); contraindicated eGFR < 30; hold for IV contrast + sepsis
GLP-1 RA: semaglutide SC weekly 0.25 → 1 → 2 mg (or oral 7–14 mg/d Rybelsus); liraglutide SC 0.6 → 1.8 mg/day; dulaglutide weekly 0.75 → 4.5 mg
Benefits: weight loss 5–15%, HbA1c −1.5%, CV protection (LEADER, SUSTAIN-6, REWIND), renal benefit (FLOW), low hypoglycaemia
Side effects: GI (nausea, vomiting), pancreatitis (rare), gallbladder, contraindicated MEN2 / medullary thyroid Ca
TIRZEPATIDE (dual GIP/GLP-1) weekly: 2.5 → 15 mg — most potent for weight loss + A1c
SGLT2i: dapagliflozin 10 mg, empagliflozin 10–25 mg, canagliflozin 100–300 mg
Benefits: HF (EMPA-REG, DECLARE), CKD (DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY), weight loss modest
Side effects: genital mycotic, UTI, euglycaemic DKA, Fournier gangrene rare, volume depletion; STOP for surgery 3 d
DPP-4 inhibitor: sitagliptin, linagliptin (renal-friendly) — neutral CV; for elderly + cost-sensitive
SU: gliclazide MR (preferred — lower hypo than glibenclamide); reserve due to hypoglycaemia, weight gain
Pioglitazone — HF risk, fluid retention, fracture (women); useful for insulin resistance, NAFLD
Acarbose — postprandial, GI side effects
Insulin: basal (glargine, detemir, degludec) then basal-bolus; aspart, glulisine prandial
EQUITY: GLP-1 + SGLT2 cost barrier in SSA — advocate for inclusion in EML (Kenya KEML 2023 added some); MOH price negotiation; generic where available
BP TARGET < 130/80 (ACE-i / ARB first if ACR > 3); statin (atorva 20 mg) for ASCVD primary prevention if age > 40 + DM
ASPIRIN 75 mg for secondary prevention; primary only if high CV risk + low bleed (individualised)
ANNUAL: HbA1c 3-monthly until target, then 6-monthly; UEC + ACR + lipids + retinal screen + foot exam + dental annually
Education: SMBG (frequency tailored), DAFNE for T1DM, carb counting, hypoglycaemia management, sick day rules, structured education (DESMOND, X-PERT)
REMISSION: T2DM remission possible with weight loss > 10–15% (DiRECT — bariatric, low-cal diet, GLP-1)
BARIATRIC SURGERY (metabolic): BMI ≥ 35 + DM, or BMI ≥ 32.5 SE Asian; superior to medical for remission

title: Obesity — comprehensive care + GLP-1 RA + bariatric (2024)
population: Adults with BMI ≥ 30 (or ≥ 27.5 SE Asian) or with weight-related comorbidity. Now treated as chronic relapsing disease, not lifestyle failure.
presentation: Routine measurement + comorbidity assessment: T2DM, HTN, dyslipidaemia, OSA, NAFLD, OA, cancer risk, mental health, infertility.
diagnostics: BMI + waist circumference + waist-to-hip ratio + visceral adiposity
Edmonton Obesity Staging System (EOSS) — function + comorbidity guides intensity
Comorbidity workup: HbA1c, lipids, LFTs, FibroScan/FibroSure for NAFLD, polysomnography if OSA suspected, TSH, cortisol if Cushing features
Mental health: depression + binge eating disorder screening
management: FOUNDATION (all):
Lifestyle — nutrition (Mediterranean, DASH, very low-calorie diet for short-term ~ 800 kcal/d), exercise (≥ 200 min/week), sleep, stress
Behavioural therapy / CBT — sustained engagement key
Treat reversible causes (Cushing, hypothyroidism, OSA, depression, weight-promoting meds)
Weight loss 5–10% improves comorbidity meaningfully
PHARMACOTHERAPY (BMI ≥ 30 or ≥ 27 with comorbidity):
GLP-1 RA — paradigm-shifting weight loss
SEMAGLUTIDE 2.4 mg weekly (Wegovy) — STEP trials avg 15% weight loss
LIRAGLUTIDE 3 mg daily (Saxenda) — 5–10%
GIP/GLP-1 dual TIRZEPATIDE 5/10/15 mg weekly (Mounjaro/Zepbound) — SURMOUNT-1 avg 22% weight loss at high dose; superior to semaglutide head-to-head (SURMOUNT-5)
Combo phentermine/topiramate ER (Qsymia) — moderate efficacy
Naltrexone/bupropion (Contrave) — modest, useful with binge eating / depression
Orlistat — GI side effects, fat malabsorption
EMERGING: retatrutide (triple agonist GLP-1/GIP/glucagon — phase 3); cagrilintide+semaglutide combo
BARIATRIC / METABOLIC SURGERY:
Indications: BMI ≥ 35 (or ≥ 32.5 SE Asian) + comorbidity, BMI ≥ 40 without
Sleeve gastrectomy (most common — restrictive)
Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) — restrictive + malabsorptive, best for T2DM remission
Biliopancreatic diversion / duodenal switch — most powerful, more nutritional concerns
Mini-gastric bypass alternative
Multidisciplinary preparation: dietician, psychology, fitness, behavioural
Outcomes: 25–35% total weight loss, T2DM remission 50–70%, HTN improvement, OSA, NAFLD
Risks: surgical complications, nutritional deficiencies (B12, iron, Ca, vit D, thiamine), dumping syndrome, hypoglycaemia (post-RYGB), psychological adjustment
Lifelong micronutrient supplementation + monitoring
PAEDIATRIC obesity:
Lifestyle family-based
Pharmacotherapy approved age 12+: liraglutide (Saxenda) — SCALE Teens; semaglutide (Wegovy) ≥ 12 yr — STEP TEENS 16% weight loss
Bariatric in adolescents with severe obesity + comorbidity
Address WEIGHT STIGMA — chronic disease framing; person-first language; trauma-informed care
OBESITY AS CHRONIC DISEASE: relapse expected after stopping pharmacotherapy → long-term treatment paradigm
Kenya MOH NCD Strategic Plan includes obesity; advocate for affordable GLP-1 access

title: CKD — modern care (SGLT2i + finerenone + ACE-i/ARB + GLP-1 RA)
population: Adults with CKD — eGFR < 60 / albuminuria > 30 mg/g for > 3 months. Major SSA burden; growing diabetes prevalence driving CKD epidemic.
presentation: Often asymptomatic until CKD 4–5. Look for: albuminuria, hypertension, anaemia, bone disease, electrolyte abnormalities, uraemia (late).
diagnostics: eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021 without race coefficient) + ACR (KDIGO heat map G1–G5 + A1–A3)
Albumin/creatinine ratio on early-morning urine (or PCR alternative)
Urinalysis + microscopy (RBC casts → glomerular)
FBC + ferritin + B12/folate; U&E + Ca + PO4 + bicarb
PTH + vitamin D for bone-mineral disease assessment from G3
Renal US (size, obstruction, polycystic)
Cause workup: ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, immunoglobulins, hepatitis serology, HIV, complement, urine M-band, light chains; renal biopsy if cause unclear / nephritic / nephrotic
management: RISK FACTOR MODIFICATION (all CKD):
BP target < 130/80 (SPRINT < 120 for selected)
Smoking cessation
Weight management
Reduce salt < 5 g/d
Avoid NSAIDs
Statin (atorva 20 mg) for primary prevention adults ≥ 50
FOUR PILLARS OF CKD CARE (paradigm shift, 2024):
1. RAS BLOCKADE (ACE-i / ARB) — for ACR > 30 or HTN; max tolerated dose; monitor K+ + Cr (allow ≤ 30% Cr rise + K+ < 5.5)
2. SGLT2 INHIBITOR — dapagliflozin / empagliflozin for ACR > 200 + eGFR > 20 (DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY) — works WITHOUT diabetes; cardio-renal protection
3. FINERENONE (non-steroidal MRA) 10–20 mg — T2DM + CKD with albuminuria (FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO-DKD); reduce CV + renal events on top of ACE/SGLT2
4. GLP-1 RA — semaglutide for T2DM + CKD (FLOW NEJM 2024 — renal protection); + weight loss
ANAEMIA:
Iron repletion first (ferritin > 100, TSAT > 20%) — oral iron struggles in CKD; IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose, iron sucrose) often needed
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA — darbepoetin, epoetin) if Hb < 100 + symptoms; target Hb 100–115 (avoid > 130 — CV risk)
Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors (roxadustat, daprodustat) — oral, emerging
BONE-MINERAL DISEASE:
Phosphate binder (calcium carbonate, sevelamer, lanthanum) if PO4 raised
Active vitamin D (calcitriol) if PTH > target
Cinacalcet for severe secondary hyperparathyroidism
Avoid bisphosphonates if eGFR < 30
ACIDOSIS: sodium bicarbonate 600 mg BD to TID if HCO3 < 22 — slows progression (UBI trial)
ELECTROLYTES: hyperkalaemia — diet K+ < 2 g/d, low-K substitute, patiromer / SZC if persistent
DIET: protein 0.8 g/kg/d (lower 0.6 g/kg in non-dialysed; protein-energy wasting in advanced)
REFER NEPHROLOGY:
eGFR < 30 (G4)
ACR > 700
Rapidly progressive
Resistant HTN / electrolyte / anaemia
Genetic / suspected glomerular disease
Plan for KRT (haemodialysis, peritoneal, transplant, conservative)
Vascular access (AV fistula) at eGFR 15–20 for HD planning
TRANSPLANT — pre-emptive ideal; living donor preferred outcomes
Education: structured CKD education (e.g. CKD checkpoint) + co-management with PCP
Kenya: scaling up haemodialysis access (NHIF coverage); KDIGO 2024 alignment

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis — comprehensive protocol
population: T1DM most common but increasing T2DM (especially with SGLT2i — euglycaemic DKA). Children: ketosis-prone diabetes presentation common in SSA.
presentation: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul respiration, fruity breath, dehydration, altered mental state. Pregnancy + DKA: lower threshold (BG 12 mmol/L may be DKA).
redFlags: Cerebral oedema (paeds especially) — headache, GCS drop
diagnostics: Diagnostic triad: hyperglycaemia (> 11; or any in known T1DM), ketonaemia/uria (> 3 mmol/L β-hydroxybutyrate or moderate–large urine ketones), acidosis (pH < 7.3 or HCO3 < 15)
Severity: mild pH 7.25–7.3, mod 7.0–7.25, severe < 7.0
Hourly: capillary glucose + ketones, GCS, vitals; 2-hourly: U&E + glucose + ketones venous; 4-hourly: ABG/VBG
Identify trigger: infection (CRP, cultures, CXR), missed insulin, MI (ECG, troponin), pancreatitis (amylase), pregnancy
management: FLUID:
0.9% NaCl 1L over 1h (slower if elderly / cardiac); next 1L/2h; 1L/4h; 1L/8h
Switch to 0.45% NaCl + 5% dextrose when glucose < 14 mmol/L
AVOID large volume Hartmann/RL — lactate metabolism issues (debated, but most use 0.9% saline)
Volume considerations: paeds — slower rate (mild dehydration), avoid bolus > 10 ml/kg unless shock (cerebral oedema risk in paeds)
INSULIN:
Fixed-rate IV infusion (FRIII) 0.1 U/kg/h (max 50 kg = 5 U/h)
Continue patient's long-acting basal insulin from start (NEW UK guidance — reduces rebound hyperglycaemia)
Target: ketones fall by 0.5 mmol/L/h, HCO3 rise by 3 mmol/L/h, glucose fall by 3 mmol/L/h
Increase rate by 1 U/h if not falling adequately
Switch to subcutaneous when ketones < 0.3, pH > 7.3, HCO3 > 18, eating + drinking — overlap 1 h
POTASSIUM:
Crucial — insulin drives K+ intracellular
Initial K+ > 5.5: no replacement, recheck 2h
K+ 3.5–5.5: add 40 mmol KCl per litre
K+ < 3.5: HOLD insulin until K+ replaced (! — gives time for replacement) + 20 mmol/h via central line
BICARBONATE: NOT routinely (no outcome benefit) — only if pH < 7.0 with shock / hyperkalaemia (small dose 50 mmol)
PHOSPHATE: only if < 0.3 — phosphate sandoz or IV potassium phosphate
TRIGGER MANAGEMENT: treat infection (sepsis-six if septic), continue analgesia, treat MI, treat pancreatitis
EUGLYCAEMIC DKA (especially SGLT2i):
Glucose may be < 14 — same protocol, start dextrose-containing fluid earlier
Stop SGLT2i + maintain insulin + dextrose
Common triggers: low carb intake + SGLT2i, surgery, sepsis, alcohol
PAEDIATRIC:
AVOID rapid fluid bolus (cerebral oedema)
Slower rehydration over 48h
Twice-maintenance fluid
0.05–0.1 U/kg/h insulin
Monitor GCS hourly; mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg if cerebral oedema suspected
POST-DKA:
Identify precipitant + address
Diabetes specialist nurse education — DAFNE / structured education
Insulin pump consideration for recurrent
CGM (continuous glucose monitor) — improved outcomes
Psychological support — chronic disease, eating disorders + insulin omission for weight (diabulimia)
Sick day rules education

title: Thyroid storm — life-threatening thyrotoxicosis
population: Decompensated thyrotoxicosis — usually Graves' disease; precipitants: infection, surgery, trauma, parturition, contrast (iodine), thyroid hormone overdose. Mortality 10–30%.
presentation: Hyperthermia (often > 39°C), severe tachycardia, AF, heart failure, agitation, delirium, seizures, jaundice. Burch–Wartofsky score ≥ 45 = highly suggestive.
diagnostics: Free T4, free T3 (markedly raised) + TSH (suppressed)
TSI / TRAb (Graves' diagnosis)
Burch–Wartofsky Point Scale (BWPS)
Identify precipitant: cultures, CXR, ECG, troponin, β-hCG if female
FBC + LFT + glucose + U&E + Ca
ABG, lactate
management: ICU admission + supportive care
FLUIDS: aggressive — high insensible losses + dehydration; 200–300 ml/h initially (cardiac function permitting); add dextrose (hyperthyroid hypoglycaemia)
COOLING: cool sponging, ice packs, paracetamol; AVOID aspirin (displaces T4 from binding protein, worsens)
SEDATION: BZD (lorazepam 2–4 mg) for agitation
MULTIDRUG THYROID-SPECIFIC THERAPY (in this sequence — critical):

1. β-BLOCKER: propranolol 60–120 mg q4–6h PO (or 0.5–1 mg slow IV q15 min) — blocks adrenergic + inhibits T4→T3; esmolol IV in HF; calcium channel blocker (diltiazem) if β-blocker contraindicated (severe asthma)
2. THIONAMIDE: PROPYLTHIOURACIL (PTU) preferred over methimazole in storm (blocks T4→T3 conversion peripherally) — 600 mg PO loading then 200–300 mg q4–6h; methimazole 20–40 mg q4–6h alternative
3. IODINE (BLOCKS RELEASE) — give ≥ 1 HOUR AFTER thionamide (otherwise organifies and worsens): SSKI 5 drops q6h, Lugol's iodine 8 drops q6h, or sodium iodide 1 g IV q12h
4. CORTICOSTEROID: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h — blocks T4→T3 conversion + treats potential adrenal insufficiency
5. CHOLESTYRAMINE 4 g QDS — binds T4/T3 in gut, prevents enterohepatic recirculation
TREAT precipitant: antibiotics if sepsis, deliver if pregnancy precipitant
Plasmapheresis or therapeutic plasma exchange for refractory cases
Definitive treatment AFTER acute resolution:
Radioactive iodine ablation (RAI) — preferred adult
Thyroidectomy — pregnancy 2nd trimester, large goitre, opthalmopathy, refractory
Long-term thionamide (12–18 months remission attempt in mild)
Beta-blocker propranolol continued until euthyroid (relieves adrenergic + reduces T4→T3)
PREGNANCY: PTU preferred in 1st trimester (teratogenicity methimazole), methimazole in 2nd/3rd
Iodine contrast: avoid in known Graves' / autonomous nodule; if essential, give methimazole + steroid pre-procedure

title: Addisonian crisis — adrenal insufficiency emergency
population: Patients with primary (Addison's), secondary (pituitary), or tertiary (chronic glucocorticoid then abrupt withdrawal — most common cause globally) adrenal insufficiency under stress (infection, surgery, trauma, dose missed).
presentation: Hypotension (often shock — vasopressor-refractory), nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, hyperpigmentation (primary), hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia (primary), hypoglycaemia, fatigue, mental state changes. Mortality if delayed treatment.
redFlags: Hypotension unresponsive to fluids — give hydrocortisone WITHOUT waiting for cortisol result
diagnostics: Plasma cortisol + ACTH PRE-treatment (interpret later — do NOT delay hydrocortisone)
U&E (Na low, K+ high in primary), glucose (low), bicarbonate (low)
Random cortisol < 138 nmol/L (5 µg/dL) in severely ill suggests AI
Short Synacthen test (250 mcg IM/IV — measure cortisol at 0 + 30 + 60 min; peak < 500 nmol/L abnormal) — AFTER acute treatment
Identify cause: long-term glucocorticoid, Addison's (autoimmune, TB, HIV, mets, infiltrative), pituitary (mass, surgery, head trauma)
Look for adrenal autoantibodies (21-hydroxylase) if primary
management: DO NOT WAIT for cortisol result if suspecting crisis:
1. HYDROCORTISONE 100 mg IV bolus IMMEDIATELY
Continue 50 mg IV q6h or 200 mg/24h infusion × 24h
Switch to oral when stable
2. AGGRESSIVE IV FLUID — 0.9% saline 1L over 1h, then guided by haemodynamics; add 5% dextrose if hypoglycaemic
3. TREAT precipitant — antibiotics for sepsis, surgery for source
4. ELECTROLYTES — K+ usually corrects with fluid + steroid; treat hyperK+ if > 6.5 (Ca, insulin/glucose, salbutamol)
5. Glucose — D10 or D50 bolus + maintenance dextrose
FLUDROCORTISONE not needed acutely (hydrocortisone has enough mineralocorticoid at high doses); start oral 50–200 mcg/d when on lower hydrocortisone replacement
TRANSITION:
Day 2: hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h
Day 3: 20–40 mg PO total + start fludrocortisone (primary AI only)
Maintenance: hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/d split (morning + early afternoon), fludrocortisone 50–200 mcg/d morning (primary only)
Investigate cause when stable
EDUCATION (chronic AI — CRITICAL):
Sick day rules: double hydrocortisone dose for fever / infection
Carry emergency injectable hydrocortisone (Solu-Cortef)
MedicAlert bracelet
Surgical / dental procedure stress dosing
Glucocorticoid taper rules — must withdraw slowly if > 3 weeks treatment
Adrenal crisis card
Iatrogenic AI: tapered withdrawal of exogenous glucocorticoid; concurrent stress dosing during illness

title: Pituitary apoplexy — endocrine + neurosurgical emergency
population: Patients with usually undiagnosed pituitary adenoma — sudden haemorrhage / infarction. Precipitants: hypertension, diabetes, anticoagulation, head trauma, pregnancy (Sheehan in postpartum hypotension), surgery.
presentation: Sudden severe retro-orbital headache + visual deficit (chiasm compression — bitemporal hemianopia) ± cavernous sinus signs (CN III, IV, VI palsies + diplopia) ± reduced consciousness + adrenal crisis features.
redFlags: Sudden severe headache + visual symptoms (think pituitary, SAH, dissection, meningitis)
Visual acuity dropping rapidly — emergency decompression
diagnostics: MRI pituitary urgently (or CT if MRI unavailable — less sensitive but detects haemorrhage)
Hormonal panel: cortisol, ACTH, TSH, free T4, prolactin, LH, FSH, testosterone/estradiol, IGF-1, GH
Electrolytes (Na, K, glucose), FBC, coag
Visual fields (Goldmann or automated perimetry) — formal
LP if SAH suspected (do AFTER MRI to exclude haemorrhage / hydrocephalus)
management: IMMEDIATE (do not await neuroimaging if suspected — adrenal cover):
1. HYDROCORTISONE 100 mg IV bolus + 50 mg IV q6h (treats secondary adrenal insufficiency — common in pituitary apoplexy)
2. IV fluids for hypotension
3. Glucose if hypoglycaemic
4. Treat hyponatraemia / hypothyroidism carefully (slow correction)
NEUROSURGICAL DECOMPRESSION:
Trans-sphenoidal surgery for: deteriorating vision, ophthalmoplegia not improving, GCS reduction, severe + persistent symptoms
Conservative if: stable vision, mild symptoms, good response to steroid
Decision in MDT — endocrinology + neurosurgery + ophthalmology
HORMONE REPLACEMENT (definitive):
Hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/d split for life if cortisol deficient
Levothyroxine 50–125 mcg/d if hypothyroid (start AFTER cortisol replaced — precipitates crisis if reverse)
Sex hormone replacement: testosterone for men, estrogen + progesterone (or HRT) for premenopausal women
GH replacement (specialist)
DDAVP for diabetes insipidus (less common in apoplexy)
FOLLOW-UP:
Visual field assessment + imaging follow-up
Lifelong endocrine review
MedicAlert + emergency steroid
Sheehan syndrome: postpartum hypotension causes pituitary infarction; presentation may be delayed (months-years) — failure to lactate, amenorrhoea, AI symptoms

title: Hyponatraemia — acute + chronic algorithm
population: Most common electrolyte abnormality in hospital (15–30% inpatients). Often iatrogenic (hypotonic fluids, thiazide, SSRI). High morbidity if mismanaged (osmotic demyelination from rapid correction).
presentation: Asymptomatic mild often. Severe (Na < 125) — nausea, confusion, headache, seizure, coma. Chronic better tolerated than acute. SIADH from drugs (carbamazepine, SSRI, opioid, thiazide), malignancy (small-cell lung), CNS pathology, pulmonary disease, idiopathic.
redFlags: Acute severe (Na < 125 with seizure / coma / brainstem signs) — emergency hypertonic saline
Rhabdomyolysis / rapid correction → osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis)
Liver / cardiac failure with hyponatraemia (poor prognosis)
diagnostics: Volume status: hypovolaemic vs euvolaemic vs hypervolaemic (clinical)
Serum osmolality (hypotonic < 275, isotonic 275–295 = pseudo, hypertonic > 295 = hyperglycaemia/mannitol)
Urine osmolality + Na concentration:
Urine osm < 100 = primary polydipsia or beer potomania
Urine osm > 100 + low urine Na (< 20) = hypovolaemic (vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretic remote, third-space loss)
Urine osm > 100 + urine Na > 30 = SIADH (euvolaemic), Addison's, diuretic recent, salt-losing nephropathy
TSH, cortisol (8 am or random + Synacthen), urinary Na, serum + urine ketones, glucose
If SIADH: CT chest/brain looking for cause
management: STEP 1 — RECOGNISE SEVERITY:
Severe symptoms (seizure, coma, brainstem) — EMERGENCY regardless of Na level
Moderate symptoms (vomiting, confusion, headache) — urgent
Asymptomatic mild (Na 130–134) — investigate cause + treat slowly
EMERGENCY (severe symptoms):
Hypertonic saline 3% 150 ml IV bolus over 20 min; reassess; repeat × 2 if needed
Aim: rise Na 5 mmol/L within 1h → resolve neurological symptoms
Then SLOW down → target rise NO MORE than 8–10 mmol/L in first 24h (some say 6 mmol/L in first 6h, 8 in 24h) — to prevent osmotic demyelination
ICU/HDU management
Investigate cause + treat
BY VOLUME STATUS (chronic / non-emergency):
HYPOVOLAEMIC: 0.9% saline; treat losses
EUVOLAEMIC (SIADH most common):
Fluid restriction 800–1000 ml/d (1st line)
Salt + protein (urea 15 g/d adjuvant)
Loop diuretic + salt tablets
Vaptan (tolvaptan 15 mg) — V2 antagonist; specialist supervision (rapid correction risk); for moderate-severe SIADH refractory
Treat underlying cause (stop drug, malignancy)
HYPERVOLAEMIC (CCF, cirrhosis, nephrotic):
Fluid + Na restriction
Loop diuretic
Tolvaptan for selected refractory (cirrhosis avoid — hepatotoxicity)
Treat underlying disease
PSEUDOHYPONATRAEMIA: severe hyperlipidaemia / hyperproteinaemia — no specific treatment for sodium
HYPERTONIC: severe hyperglycaemia (each 5.5 mmol/L glucose ↑ → Na falls 2.4); correct glucose
PROPHYLAXIS in inpatients: AVOID hypotonic IV fluid in adults; use 0.9% saline / balanced solutions; vigilance with thiazide, SSRI; cancer patient SIADH education
Watch for OVERCORRECTION: if Na rises > 10 mmol/L in 24h, give 5% dextrose IV + DDAVP to bring Na back down (re-lowering protocol)
