title: Diabetic foot ulcer + Charcot — comprehensive care
population: Patients with T1DM or T2DM. Lifetime DFU risk 19–34%. Globally diabetes is leading cause of non-traumatic lower limb amputation; SSA — late presentation common.
presentation: Neuropathic (painless), ischaemic (painful), or neuro-ischaemic ulcer; site (plantar pressure points, toes, dorsum); depth + signs of infection (cellulitis, deep abscess, osteomyelitis); presence of gangrene; Charcot neuroarthropathy (acute hot swollen non-painful foot with deformity).
redFlags: Deep wound with bone exposed / probe-to-bone positive (osteomyelitis)
Acute Charcot (often misdiagnosed as DVT / cellulitis)
Critical limb ischaemia (rest pain, gangrene) — revascularisation urgent
diagnostics: Wagner / IDSA + IWGDF classification (PEDIS, SINBAD)
Vascular: ABI (>1.3 unreliable in calcified vessels — common in DM; toe pressures + TBI), Doppler waveform, CT/MR angio if revasc planned
Neuropathy: 10g monofilament + Ipswich Touch Test + vibration + reflexes + temp
Probe-to-bone test (PTB) + plain X-ray (osteomyelitis — 4-week sensitivity); MRI gold standard
Swab from depth + tissue / bone biopsy for culture (NOT superficial swab)
FBC, ESR, CRP, glucose, HbA1c, U&E
Charcot: serial X-ray, MRI, bone scan
management: 5 PILLARS (IWGDF):
1. CONTROL infection
2. CONTROL ischaemia
3. CONTROL pressure (offloading)
4. WOUND care
5. Glucose / risk factor control
INFECTION:
Mild (no systemic, < 2 cm cellulitis): oral antibiotic 7–14 d — flucloxacillin 500 mg QDS or cephalexin 500 mg QDS
Moderate (severe cellulitis, deep, no systemic): broader oral or IV — co-amoxiclav, ciprofloxacin + clindamycin, IDSA / IWGDF guidance
Severe (systemic toxicity / necrotising / wet gangrene): IV broad-spectrum — pip-tazo, meropenem, vanc + cefepime; surgical urgent
Osteomyelitis: prolonged 6 weeks IV/oral antibiotic + surgical debridement; resection if persistent
Cover anaerobes if necrotic / fetid
Avoid tetracycline / fluoroquinolone in monotherapy (Pseudomonas + MRSA need targeted)
ISCHAEMIA:
ABI / waveform / CT angiogram
Revascularisation (angioplasty / stent / bypass) if critical limb ischaemia
Vascular team early
Smoking cessation
Antiplatelet + statin
OFFLOADING:
Total Contact Cast (TCC) — gold standard for plantar ulcer in non-infected, non-ischaemic foot
Removable cast walker (rendered irremovable preferable)
Heel relief / felted foam
Crutches / wheelchair if forefoot
Bed rest acceptable if intolerant of cast
Patient education on adherence — critical
WOUND CARE:
Sharp debridement of callus + necrotic tissue at every visit
Dressing — moist wound healing, alginate for exudate, foam, hydrogel; honey-based dressings useful in LMIC
Negative pressure wound therapy for selected cavitating wounds
Skin substitutes / growth factors / hyperbaric oxygen — selected cases
AVOID hydrogen peroxide, iodine for routine cleansing (cytotoxic)
GLUCOSE CONTROL: optimise per separate condition
CHARCOT NEUROARTHROPATHY:
Suspect in any hot swollen foot in person with diabetic neuropathy — even without DVT signs
IMMEDIATE offloading (total contact cast) + non-weight-bearing × 8–12 weeks minimum
Imaging: X-ray (Stage I–III Eichenholtz); MRI early; bone scan
Bisphosphonate role uncertain (specialist)
Reconstruction surgery (specialist) for chronic deformity
PREVENTION (foot care education):
Annual foot screen with risk stratification
Daily self-inspection (mirror), hygiene, moisturise (NOT between toes)
Custom footwear / orthotic for high-risk
Never barefoot — especially Kenya MOH targeting jiggers + diabetic foot
Smoking cessation, glucose, BP, lipids
Podiatry early referral
Multidisciplinary foot clinic (diabetologist + vascular + ortho + microbio + tissue viability) — reduces amputation

references.label: IWGDF Guidelines 2023 (PEDIS, classification, prevention, infection, peripheral artery disease, offloading)
NICE NG19 Diabetic Foot Problems 2015 + updates
Kenya MOH Diabetes Guidelines + KEML insulin / antibiotics

title: COPD — GOLD 2024 framework + exacerbation management
population: Adults — smoking + biomass smoke + occupational exposure; rising SSA burden from indoor cooking smoke. Global 4th leading cause of death; underdiagnosed.
presentation: Chronic productive cough, dyspnoea, exercise intolerance, wheeze; exacerbation = increased dyspnoea/cough/sputum/purulence. GOLD ABE classification: A (low symptoms low risk), B (high symptoms low risk), E (exacerbator regardless symptoms — simplified 2023+).
redFlags: Severe exacerbation — sats < 88%, RR > 30, accessory muscles, cyanosis
diagnostics: Spirometry — post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.7 confirms (GOLD 1–4 by FEV1% predicted)
CAT / mMRC symptom score
Eosinophil count (blood) — > 300 = ICS responder; > 100 = consider ICS
Alpha-1 antitrypsin in all (especially young / non-smoker / lower-lobe predominance / family hx)
CXR / CT for emphysema + bronchiectasis + cancer screen
ABG if severe / hypercapnia suspected
Pulse oximetry; consider home oximetry monitoring
Echocardiogram for pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale assessment
management: FOUNDATION:
Smoking cessation — single most important intervention (NRT, varenicline, bupropion, behavioural)
Pulmonary rehabilitation — 6–12 weeks programme
Vaccinations: annual flu, pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), pertussis Tdap, COVID, RSV (60+, NEW 2023)
Reduce biomass exposure (improved cookstoves) — major SSA priority
Nutritional support for cachexia
PHARMACOTHERAPY (GOLD 2024 — by ABE):
A (low symptoms, low exacerbations): SABA or SAMA prn; LABA or LAMA if persistent
B (high symptoms, low exacerbations): LABA + LAMA (e.g. indacaterol/glycopyrronium, vilanterol/umeclidinium)
E (exacerbator): LABA + LAMA; ADD ICS if blood eosinophils ≥ 300 (LABA + LAMA + ICS — TRILOGY/IMPACT/ETHOS triple therapy)
Roflumilast for chronic bronchitis + severe + frequent exacerbations + FEV1 < 50%
Azithromycin 250–500 mg 3×/wk for selected frequent exacerbators (anti-inflammatory)
Mucolytic (carbocisteine) for chronic productive cough
Alpha-1 antitrypsin augmentation if deficient
SGLT2i and other novel agents in trial for COPD
OXYGEN THERAPY:
Long-term oxygen (LTOT) ≥ 15h/day for resting PaO2 ≤ 7.3 kPa (or ≤ 8 kPa with cor pulmonale / polycythaemia / nocturnal desat)
Ambulatory O2 for exertional desat
Target sats 88–92% (avoid hyperoxia — worsens hypercapnia)
ADVANCED:
Lung volume reduction (surgery / endobronchial valves Zephyr) for severe emphysema
Lung transplant for selected severe
Palliative care + advance care planning
EXACERBATION MANAGEMENT:
Bronchodilator nebulisation (salbutamol 5 mg + ipratropium 500 mcg q4–6h)
Prednisolone 30 mg PO × 5 days (REDUCE trial — 5 vs 14 days non-inferior, less side effect)
Antibiotics if 2+ Anthonisen criteria (more dyspnoea, more sputum, more purulence) — amoxicillin / doxy / co-amox / macrolide 5 days; pip-tazo if Pseudomonas risk
Controlled oxygen (target 88–92% sats) — Venturi mask 24–28%
NIV (BiPAP) for type 2 respiratory failure (pH < 7.35 + pCO2 > 6) — first-line, before intubation
Intubation if NIV failing / agitation / inability to protect airway
Treat trigger: bacterial, viral, PE (consider in COPD), pneumothorax (avoid bag-valve if suspected)
Post-exacerbation: review, optimise inhaler technique, action plan, refer pulmonary rehab

references.label: GOLD Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease Strategy 2024
ERS / ATS Management of COPD Exacerbations 2023
REDUCE trial JAMA 2013 — 5 vs 14 days steroid
Kenya MOH NCD Strategic Plan + NCD Service Package

title: Asthma — GINA 2024 framework + severe asthma biologics
population: Children + adults — global 300 million; rising SSA burden including paediatric, often misdiagnosed as recurrent bronchitis.
presentation: Variable wheeze, cough, dyspnoea, chest tightness — episodic + variable + triggered. Atopic vs non-atopic phenotypes. Severe asthma: requires high-dose ICS-LABA + additional therapy (5%).
redFlags: Severe asthma attack — unable to complete sentences, RR > 30, SpO2 < 92%, peak flow < 50%, silent chest, exhaustion, bradycardia, cyanosis
Near-fatal asthma — pCO2 raised (normal/raised in severe attack is concerning — fatigue)
Status asthmaticus — refractory to initial treatment
Refractory severe asthma despite triple therapy — refer biologic
diagnostics: Spirometry: FEV1/FVC < 0.75/0.8 + bronchodilator reversibility ≥ 12% and ≥ 200 ml (preferably ≥ 400 ml + 15% in adults)
Peak expiratory flow variability > 10% adults / > 13% children over 1–2 weeks
FeNO (exhaled NO) — T2 inflammation marker; > 50 ppb suggests eosinophilic; aids ICS responsiveness prediction
Eosinophil count (blood)
Total + specific IgE for allergens, skin prick if atopy suspected
Bronchial provocation (methacholine, mannitol) if uncertain
Chest X-ray to exclude alternatives (hyperinflation expected)
management: GINA 2024 STEPS — central change: ICS-formoterol both reliever + controller (eliminates SABA-only treatment):
Step 1 (mild intermittent): as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (e.g. budesonide-formoterol 200/6 prn) — MART approach; alternative: SABA + ICS taken when SABA
Step 2: as-needed ICS-formoterol OR daily low-dose ICS + SABA prn
Step 3: low-dose ICS-LABA daily + as-needed ICS-formoterol (MART) OR low-dose ICS-LABA + SABA
Step 4: medium-dose ICS-LABA daily + ICS-formoterol prn
Step 5: high-dose ICS-LABA ± LAMA (triple therapy) + assess for biologics + specialist referral
DEFINITION OF SAFER PRESCRIBING:
AVOID SABA-only treatment (associated with increased mortality SABINA + SABA budget — every additional 3 canisters/yr increases mortality + exacerbation)
No reliever should be used > 2× weekly
Annual review of inhaler technique + adherence + asthma action plan + spacer
SEVERE ASTHMA BIOLOGICS (5% of asthma — refer specialist):
Anti-IgE (omalizumab) — atopic / IgE 30–700
Anti-IL-5 / IL-5R (mepolizumab, benralizumab, reslizumab) — eosinophilic (≥ 300)
Anti-IL-4/IL-13 (dupilumab) — T2 high (eos + FeNO + steroid-dependent)
Anti-TSLP (tezepelumab) — broader Th2-low + high — NAVIGATOR 2021
Macrolide chronic (azithromycin 500 mg 3×/wk — AMAZES) for severe + frequent exacerbations
Bronchial thermoplasty for selected severe
ACUTE EXACERBATION (asthma attack):
Mild–moderate: salbutamol 4–10 puffs spacer q20 min × 1h + prednisolone 50 mg (children 1 mg/kg max 40 mg) × 5 days

Severe (RR > 30, sats < 92%, PEF < 50%): nebulised salbutamol 5 mg + ipratropium 500 mcg q20 min × 3 then q1–4h, oxygen titrated to sats 93–95% (NOT hyperoxia — worsens hypercapnia), IV hydrocortisone 100 mg or oral prednisolone 50 mg
Life-threatening: IV MgSO4 2 g over 20 min (especially severe in children), IV salbutamol infusion if not improving (caution arrhythmia), ICU; IV aminophylline rarely (narrow therapeutic, arrhythmia)
Refractory: IV ketamine, heliox, ECMO; intubation only if absolutely needed (asthma + ETT — pneumothorax / dynamic hyperinflation high)
Antibiotics ONLY if clear bacterial infection
Discharge: tapering prednisolone NOT needed for short courses < 14 d; restart/optimise controller; PEF improvement; action plan
TRIGGERS: viral URTI, allergens, exercise, NSAID (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease — separate entity), GERD, occupational
OCCUPATIONAL asthma: identify + remove exposure
Pregnancy: continue inhalers (uncontrolled asthma worse for fetus than controlled with steroid); ICS budesonide best evidence
Paediatric: spacer + face mask for < 6 yr; viral wheeze vs atopic asthma distinction; preschool wheeze low-dose ICS or LTRA trial
CHILDHOOD ASTHMA SSA: under-treated; education, free generics, spacer access; primary care training

references.label: GINA Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention 2024
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) — CURB-65 / CRB-65 + antibiotics
population: All ages — leading cause of infectious death globally + in SSA. Children < 5 + elderly + immunocompromised highest mortality.
presentation: Cough, sputum, dyspnoea, fever, pleuritic chest pain, focal crackles, bronchial breath sounds. Atypical (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydia) — extrapulmonary features prominent.
redFlags: Severe — CURB-65 ≥ 3 / CRB-65 ≥ 2; sats < 92%, RR > 30, SBP < 90, multilobar, confusion, sepsis
HIV / immunocompromised — atypical pathogens (PCP, fungal, TB)
diagnostics: CURB-65: Confusion, Urea > 7, Resp rate ≥ 30, SBP < 90 / DBP ≤ 60, age ≥ 65
CRB-65 (primary care): same minus urea
Score 0–1 outpatient; 2 admit consideration; ≥ 3 admit + IV antibiotic; ≥ 4 ICU
CXR — consolidation
Pulse oximetry, ABG if severe
FBC, U&E, CRP, glucose, LFT
Blood culture × 2 if severe / before antibiotic
Sputum culture + Gram + AFB (TB common SSA)
Urinary antigen Legionella + pneumococcus (severe / high risk)
Influenza + COVID + RSV PCR seasonally
HIV test in all (especially LMIC)
PCR for atypicals if severe / not responding
CT chest for complications / cavitation / non-resolving
management: TREATMENT BY SEVERITY:
CURB-65 0–1: outpatient — amoxicillin 1 g TDS × 5 days (UK BTS) OR co-amoxiclav OR doxycycline (atypical cover) ± macrolide
CURB-65 2: amoxicillin 1 g TDS + clarithromycin 500 mg BD × 5–7 days
CURB-65 3–5 / severe: IV co-amoxiclav 1.2 g TDS + clarithromycin 500 mg BD; or ceftriaxone 2 g + azithromycin/clarithromycin; vancomycin/linezolid if MRSA risk; carbapenem if HCAP/RFs
Duration: 5 days for non-severe (PRECISE trial — 5 d non-inferior); 7–10 days severe; 10–14 days for complicated (empyema, abscess)
Switch IV to oral when stable + tolerating
Antiviral: oseltamivir if influenza suspected, paxlovid for COVID if eligible
Atypical specific:
Mycoplasma: macrolide / doxycycline / fluoroquinolone
Legionella: macrolide / fluoroquinolone (azithromycin preferred)
Aspiration: anaerobic cover (co-amoxiclav, metronidazole + ceftriaxone)
SSA / RESOURCE considerations:
Kenya MOH essential — amoxicillin + macrolide; consider TB (sputum AFB / GeneXpert) in any pneumonia with weight loss / chronic cough / immunocompromised
HIV patient — cover for PCP (cotrimoxazole 1920 mg TID × 21 days + steroid if pO2 < 9.3 / saturation < 92%); rule out cryptococcal / TB
SUPPORTIVE: O2 titrated to sats 94–98% (88–92% if COPD/Type 2 RF), antipyretic, hydration, VTE prophylaxis if admitted
EMPYEMA / parapneumonic effusion:
Diagnostic tap (pH < 7.2, glucose < 2.2, LDH > 1000, frank pus = empyema)
Chest drain insertion + antibiotic 4–6 weeks
Intrapleural fibrinolytic (alteplase + DNase — MIST2 trial) for locu-lated empyema
Surgical decortication for failure
POST-DISCHARGE: repeat CXR at 6 weeks if smoker / > 50 yr (exclude lung cancer / persistent abnormality); vaccinate against pneumococcal + flu
PREVENTION: pneumococcal vaccine (PCV13 + PPSV23 sequence in high-risk), annual flu, COVID, RSV (60+), Hib in children (routine EPI), smoking cessation, oral hygiene

references.label: Kenya MOH National Pneumonia Treatment Guidelines

title: Hospital-acquired + ventilator-associated pneumonia (HAP/VAP)
population: Hospitalised patients > 48h (HAP) or ventilated > 48h (VAP). High mortality 15–50%. Multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens common.
presentation: New / progressive infiltrate + at least 2 of: fever, leukocytosis, purulent secretions / sputum.
redFlags: Antibiotic failure at 48–72h (consider MDR, fungal, viral, non-infective)
diagnostics: CXR (often non-specific in ICU — atelectasis, oedema, ARDS look similar)
Quantitative or semi-quantitative respiratory culture:
Endotracheal aspirate (semi-quantitative ≥ 10^5 CFU/ml)
Mini-BAL or BAL (10^4 CFU/ml threshold)
Protected specimen brush (10^3 CFU/ml)
PCR multiplex (rapid 1–2h turnaround) — guides empirical therapy
Blood cultures
Procalcitonin (de-escalation guide)
ABG, FBC, lactate, U&E
CT thorax for empyema / abscess / non-resolving
management: EMPIRICAL — local antibiogram crucial; risk-stratify:
Low risk for MDR (no recent antibiotic / hospitalisation < 5 d / not septic):
Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily OR co-amoxiclav 1.2 g q6h IV ± azithromycin (atypical cover)
Cover Pseudomonas if ICU / recent antibiotic / structural lung disease
High risk for MDR:
Anti-pseudomonal β-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g q6h OR cefepime 2 g q8h OR meropenem 1 g q8h)
PLUS second anti-pseudomonal (ciprofloxacin / aminoglycoside) if septic / high mortality risk
PLUS vancomycin OR linezolid if MRSA risk (recent admission / known carrier / dialysis / IVDU)
Consider ceftaroline, ceftolozane-tazobactam, ceftazidime-avibactam for ESBL / CRE per local resistance
DURATION: 7 days (most cases — IDSA / ATS / ERS 2017 — non-inferior to 10–14); 14 days if Staph aureus / Pseudomonas / non-responsive / immunocompromised; bone/joint complications longer
DE-ESCALATE based on culture + procalcitonin guidance
VAP PREVENTION BUNDLE:
Head of bed 30–45°
Sedation interruption + spontaneous breathing trial daily
DVT prophylaxis
Stress ulcer prophylaxis (PPI or H2 blocker)
Chlorhexidine oral care (controversial — 2024 some guidelines pulling back)
Subglottic secretion drainage ETT
Endotracheal cuff pressure maintenance 20–30 cmH2O
Avoid routine ventilator circuit changes
Hand hygiene + chlorhexidine bathing in ICU
Probiotics — evidence-based reduce VAP
Early enteral nutrition
HAP NON-VAP:
Aspiration risk reduction — sit upright for feeds, swallow assessment, oral care
Mobilise + chest physiotherapy
Avoid unnecessary stress ulcer prophylaxis (PPI = bacterial overgrowth)
FAILURE TO IMPROVE: review culture / sensitivity, repeat imaging (abscess, empyema, ARDS), consider non-bacterial (TB, viral COVID, fungal Aspergillus, PCP if immunocompromised), atypicals
Antimicrobial stewardship — review at 48–72h with culture results

references.label: IDSA/ATS Management of Adults with HAP/VAP 2016

title: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) — Berlin + lung-protective ventilation
population: Critically ill patients with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Triggers: pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration, trauma, pancreatitis, transfusion, drowning, near-drowning. COVID-19 caused massive global ARDS surge 2020–2022.
presentation: Acute onset (within 1 week) hypoxaemia + bilateral infiltrates not explained by cardiac / hydrostatic.
redFlags: P/F < 100 (severe ARDS) — prone positioning + ECMO consideration
diagnostics: Berlin criteria: onset ≤ 1 week, bilateral chest infiltrates, not explained by cardiogenic oedema (objective by echo if needed), P/F ratio on PEEP ≥ 5:
Moderate: 100–200
Severe: ≤ 100
Identify trigger: cultures, lipase (pancreatitis), trauma evaluation
Echo (exclude cardiogenic + assess RV)
Lung ultrasound (B-lines, consolidation, pleural effusion)
CT thorax (if cause unclear / non-resolving)
management: LUNG-PROTECTIVE VENTILATION (cornerstone — ARDSNet 2000):
Tidal volume 4–6 ml/kg PREDICTED body weight
Plateau pressure ≤ 30 cmH2O
Driving pressure (plateau − PEEP) < 15 cmH2O ideal
PEEP — ARDSNet table or oesophageal pressure-guided; higher PEEP for moderate-severe ARDS (ALVEOLI / LOV / ART trials — controversial; selective higher PEEP for moderate)
Permissive hypercapnia (pH ≥ 7.15 acceptable)
Target SpO2 88–95%, PaO2 55–80 mmHg
FiO2 lowest to achieve target
PRONE POSITIONING:
P/F < 150 — prone for 16+ h/day (PROSEVA NEJM 2013 — mortality benefit)
Daily reassessment, return supine if response, prone again if deteriorating
NEUROMUSCULAR BLOCKADE:
Early (within 48h) cisatracurium infusion × 48h for severe ARDS (ACURASYS 2010 — benefit; ROSE 2019 — no benefit with light sedation strategy; reserve for refractory + dyssynchrony)
CONSERVATIVE FLUID strategy (FACTT trial) — net even or negative balance once stable
STEROIDS:
Dexamethasone 6 mg daily × 10 days (RECOVERY — COVID + moderate-severe ARDS in COVID)
Hydrocortisone for early ARDS (Meduri 2007 + 2016 + multiple trials — small benefit)
Dexamethasone 20 mg × 5 d then 10 mg × 5 d (DEXA-ARDS 2020 — mortality reduction in non-COVID ARDS)
ECMO (V-V):
P/F < 80 despite optimised ventilation
Refractory hypoxaemia despite prone + NMBA
Severe respiratory acidosis < 7.25 + dynamic hyperinflation
Specialist centre (CESAR + EOLIA trials)
TREAT TRIGGER:
Antibiotics for pneumonia / sepsis
Source control
Antifungal if Aspergillus / Candida (severe ARDS in immunocompromised)
Antiviral for influenza (oseltamivir) / RSV / COVID
Pancreatitis supportive
PREVENTION OF SECONDARY INJURY:
VAP bundle
Stress ulcer prophylaxis
VTE prophylaxis (if not bleeding)
Nutritional — early enteral
Avoid sedation if possible (light sedation strategy — RASS −1 to 0); SAT + SBT daily; mobilise early
Delirium prevention (ABCDEF bundle)
INHALED VASODILATORS (iNO, prostacyclin) — rescue, no mortality benefit
EXTUBATION: SBT pressure support 5 + PEEP 5 × 30–120 min; cuff leak test; secretion management; reassess daily
POST-ICU: rehabilitation programmes, mental health screening (post-traumatic stress + cognitive dysfunction — ICU recovery syndrome)

references.label: ATS/ESICM/SCCM Clinical Practice Guideline: Mechanical Ventilation in Adult Patients with ARDS 2017 + 2024 update
Berlin Definition of ARDS 2012 + revised 2024 (oxygenation index, HFNO)

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea — STOP-Bang + CPAP
population: Adults — prevalence 10–35% (varies by criteria); under-diagnosed; rising with obesity. Children: adenotonsillar hypertrophy most common cause. SSA: emerging awareness.
presentation: Snoring (loud, witnessed apnoea), excessive daytime sleepiness (ESS), morning headache, nocturia, mood / cognitive change, decreased libido. CV risk: HTN (especially resistant), stroke, AF, HF, MACE, T2DM.
redFlags: Sleepy driving — counsel + report to DVLA per local rules
Children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy + behavioural / academic decline
diagnostics: STOP-Bang ≥ 3 high probability: Snoring, Tired, Observed apnoea, BP raised, BMI > 35, Age > 50, Neck > 40 cm, Gender male
Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) > 10 abnormal
Berlin Questionnaire alternative
POLYSOMNOGRAPHY (in-lab type I) — gold standard; type III home (HSAT) acceptable for high-pretest probability without comorbidity
AHI: 5–15 mild, 15–30 moderate, > 30 severe
Oxygen desat index, lowest SpO2
Echo if cor pulmonale / cardiac symptoms
management: LIFESTYLE:
Weight loss — single most effective intervention if BMI > 30 (10% weight loss reduces AHI ~ 26%)
ETOH reduction (especially evening), smoking cessation
Lateral position (avoid supine)
Treat nasal obstruction (allergic rhinitis, deviated septum)
POSITIVE AIRWAY PRESSURE:
CPAP — first-line for moderate-severe + symptomatic mild
Auto-CPAP (APAP) for home titration
Optimal pressure typically 8–12 cmH2O
Heated humidification, nasal pillow/mask choice
Adherence target ≥ 4 h/night × 70% nights
BiPAP for OSA + COPD overlap / OHS / pressure intolerance
ASV for treatment-emergent central / Cheyne-Stokes (avoid in HFrEF — SERVE-HF excess mortality)
MANDIBULAR ADVANCEMENT DEVICE (MAD):
Mild-moderate OSA; CPAP intolerant
Custom-fit by sleep dentist
Monitor TMJ side effects
SURGERY:
Adenotonsillectomy — first-line for children
UPPP, maxillomandibular advancement, hypoglossal nerve stimulator (Inspire) — selected adults
Bariatric surgery — improves/resolves OSA in obesity
PHARMACOLOGICAL:
Tirzepatide for OSA + obesity (SURMOUNT-OSA 2024 — significant AHI reduction with weight loss)
Solriamfetol / pitolisant for residual daytime sleepiness despite treated OSA
AVOID hypnotics + opioids (worsen apnoea)
FOLLOW-UP:
Compliance review (download data from CPAP machine)
Re-PSG if symptoms recur / treatment failure
Cardiovascular risk modification — improved BP control, AF burden, HF symptoms with treatment
Public health: drowsy driving education

references.label: AASM Treatment of Adult OSA with PAP 2019
ATS Clinical Practice Guideline Diagnosis OSA 2022
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) — antifibrotic + comprehensive care
population: Adults > 50 yr (mostly > 65); slightly male predominance; smokers + GERD + occupational dust exposure. Median survival 3–5 years untreated; antifibrotics extend survival.
presentation: Progressive exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, fine end-inspiratory crackles ('Velcro'), clubbing in 50%. Acute exacerbations cause rapid deterioration.
redFlags: Acute exacerbation IPF (worsening dyspnoea < 1 month, new infiltrates, hypoxaemia) — high mortality 50%+
Lung cancer (10–15× increased risk in IPF)
Failure to respond to antifibrotic — refer transplant
diagnostics: HRCT chest — usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern: subpleural + basal predominance + honeycombing + traction bronchiectasis + reticulation (no ground-glass)
Pulmonary function tests: restrictive (FVC < 80% predicted) + reduced DLCO
6-minute walk test (baseline + monitoring)
Blood: exclude connective tissue disease (ANA, RF, anti-CCP, MPO/PR3 ANCA, anti-Scl70, etc.); hypersensitivity pneumonitis precipitins
Bronchoscopy + BAL not routinely needed if HRCT UIP definitive; if needed — TBLB / cryobiopsy / surgical biopsy
Echo for pulmonary HT
Sleep study (OSA common comorbidity)
Discuss at MDT (radiology + pulmonology + pathology if biopsy)
management: ANTIFIBROTICS (first-line — slow progression):
PIRFENIDONE 267 mg TID → 801 mg TID (CAPACITY + ASCEND trials)
Side effects: photosensitivity (sun protection), GI, LFT derangement
NINTEDANIB 150 mg BD (INPULSIS + INBUILD)
Side effects: diarrhoea (common, manage), LFT, bleeding (anticoag caution)
Both: slow FVC decline; do NOT improve symptoms or definitively prolong life
Indications: IPF + other progressive fibrosing ILDs (PF-ILD — including HP, NSIP) per INBUILD
SYMPTOM MANAGEMENT:
Pulmonary rehabilitation — improves exercise capacity + QOL
Supplemental oxygen for resting / exertional hypoxaemia (sats < 88%)
Treat GERD (PPI + lifestyle; some evidence improves IPF outcomes)
Cough — opiate (low-dose morphine), gabapentin, thalidomide (specialist)
Treat anxiety + depression
VACCINATIONS: annual flu, pneumococcal, COVID, pertussis
REFER LUNG TRANSPLANT:
Early — DLCO < 40%, FVC < 80%, ≥ 5% FVC decline in 6 months, oxygen-dependent
Age < 65–70 typically (centre-dependent)
Best post-transplant survival of any indication
ACUTE EXACERBATION:
Exclude infection (cultures, BAL if accessible), PE, cardiac failure
High-dose corticosteroid 500–1000 mg methylprednisolone × 3 days then taper (modest evidence)
Supportive care
High mortality 50–80%; consider palliation
PALLIATIVE CARE: early referral (within months of diagnosis); advance care planning; opioid for dyspnoea; symptom control
Avoid traditional 'pulmonary rehab' approach of bronchodilator + ICS (no benefit, side effects)
Comorbidities: pulmonary HT, OSA, GERD, lung cancer, depression, frailty
Family / genetic counselling — familial PF (TERT, SFTPC, MUC5B variants)

title: Status epilepticus — emergency management algorithm
population: Children + adults — convulsive status epilepticus = continuous seizure > 5 min or recurrent without recovery. Established (10 min), refractory (30 min), super-refractory (> 24h despite anaesthesia).
presentation: Generalised tonic-clonic activity; or focal-onset (motor / non-motor); or non-convulsive (mental state change with subtle motor / EEG-only). High mortality 10–20% acute; permanent neurological damage if prolonged.
redFlags: Refractory status (after benzo + 2nd-line agent) — anaesthesia + ICU
Identified cause requiring specific treatment: meningitis, intracranial bleed, drugs, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, eclampsia
diagnostics: Bedside glucose, electrolytes (Na, Ca, Mg), ABG, lactate
FBC, U&E, LFT, ammonia, AED levels (if on)
Toxicology screen, ETOH
CT brain after stabilised (haemorrhage, mass, oedema)
MRI if focal / atypical
EEG — particularly if not waking after benzo (rule out NCSE)
Lumbar puncture if meningitis suspected (after CT)
management: STEP 1 (0–5 min) — STABILISE:
ABC, position lateral / recovery, suction, high-flow O2
IV access × 2
Bedside glucose — give 50 ml D50 if hypoglycaemic + thiamine 100 mg if any chronic alcohol / malnutrition
Vital signs, temperature monitor
STEP 2 (5–20 min) — FIRST-LINE BENZODIAZEPINE:
IV: lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (4 mg adult, max 8 mg) — preferred (longer duration)
IM: midazolam 10 mg (5 mg if < 40 kg, 10 mg if ≥ 40 kg) — preferred if no IV (RAMPART)
Buccal/intranasal midazolam 10 mg (paediatric prn)
Rectal diazepam 0.2–0.5 mg/kg (community / no IV)
Repeat × 1 after 5 min if continuing
STEP 3 (20–40 min) — SECOND-LINE if benzo failed (ESETT NEJM 2019 — all equally effective ~50% conversion):
LEVETIRACETAM 60 mg/kg IV over 5 min (max 4500 mg) — least drug interactions / sedation
PHENYTOIN 20 mg/kg IV (max 1500 mg, rate ≤ 50 mg/min — cardiotoxic; use fosphenytoin if available faster + safer)
VALPROIC ACID 40 mg/kg IV (max 3000 mg) — avoid in mitochondrial / pregnancy / liver disease
Choose based on patient + drug-drug interactions + availability
STEP 4 (40–60 min) — REFRACTORY: try second 2nd-line agent if first failed
STEP 5 (> 60 min) — ANAESTHESIA + ICU + INTUBATE:
Midazolam infusion 0.05–2 mg/kg/h
Propofol 1–10 mg/kg/h (caution propofol infusion syndrome > 24h or > 4 mg/kg/h)
Pentobarbital / thiopentone — burst suppression on EEG
Ketamine adjunct (NMDA antagonist)
Continuous EEG monitoring
Treat underlying cause aggressively
Wean anaesthesia after 24h seizure-free; reload AED before withdrawal
SPECIFIC CAUSES:
Hypoglycaemia: D50 + thiamine
Hyponatraemia: 3% NaCl
Eclampsia: MgSO4 (NOT phenytoin first)
Toxic: pyridoxine 5 g IV for INH, lipid for LA, naloxone for opioid
Encephalitis (HSV, autoimmune): aciclovir + steroid empiric while awaiting CSF
Bacterial meningitis: ceftriaxone + amoxicillin + dexamethasone
Subdural / SAH: neurosurgical
Alcohol withdrawal: thiamine + BZD (not phenytoin — ineffective)
POST-STATUS:
Long-term AED therapy
Identify + treat cause
Education + driving / occupation advice
Refer epilepsy specialist
Counsel family on rescue benzodiazepine (buccal midazolam) for future event
NON-CONVULSIVE STATUS EPILEPTICUS (NCSE):
Often missed — EEG required
Same algorithm
PAEDIATRIC: weight-based dosing; avoid phenytoin in absence/myoclonic; aggressive temperature management

title: Paediatric sepsis + septic shock — Surviving Sepsis Paediatric 2020
population: Children — sepsis still major killer in SSA (especially < 5 yr — malaria, pneumonia, diarrhoea complicated by sepsis). WHO Sepsis Resolution highlights paediatric priority.
presentation: Tachycardia, tachypnoea, fever (or hypothermia in infants), altered consciousness, mottling, poor capillary refill, hypotension (LATE — children compensate). Phoenix Sepsis Score (2024) replaces SIRS-based criteria for sepsis definition in children.
redFlags: Cold peripheries with normal core temp
Tachycardia not explained by fever / pain (above age-specific norms)
Neonate < 3 mo with any fever ≥ 38°C — immediate workup
diagnostics: Phoenix Sepsis Criteria (2024): respiratory + cardiovascular + coagulation + neurological dysfunction across age bands
Vital signs (heart rate, RR, BP, temperature, capillary refill) — interpret per age norms
Blood cultures × 1 (paeds — single sample if difficult); urine, CSF if meningism, stool, respiratory cultures
FBC + CRP + lactate + glucose + electrolytes + LFT + coagulation
Malaria RDT in endemic area (Kenya, all SSA fever)
HIV test in unknown status
Imaging guided by suspicion (CXR, abdo US)
management: Surviving Sepsis Paediatric Bundle (2020):
FIRST HOUR:
1. Obtain blood culture before antibiotic (do NOT delay beyond 45 min)
2. Administer broad-spectrum antibiotic — ceftriaxone 50–80 mg/kg/day; add vancomycin if MRSA risk / line associated; add anti-pseudomonal if neutropenic / hospital-acquired
3. Fluid resuscitation:
Initial 10–20 ml/kg balanced crystalloid (Hartmann/PlasmaLyte) bolus over 5–10 min
Reassess each bolus — signs of overload (rales, hepatomegaly, gallop) STOP
FEAST trial (Kenya/Tanzania/Uganda) showed harm with bolus in African children with febrile illness without shock — only resus bolus for SHOCK (impaired perfusion); maintenance fluids for compensated
Maintenance fluid for non-shock dehydration
4. Vasopressor (peripheral acceptable initially if no central line):
Adrenaline (epinephrine) 0.05–0.3 mcg/kg/min first-line in paediatric septic shock (vs noradrenaline adult)
Noradrenaline 0.05–0.3 mcg/kg/min alternative
Add vasopressin if escalating dose
5. Measure lactate, recheck at 2–4 h
WITHIN 3 HOURS:
6. Steroids: hydrocortisone 50 mg/m² × 4 doses IV/IM if fluid-refractory shock requiring vasopressor (Adrenal insufficiency common in critically ill child)
7. Adjust antibiotic per culture + clinical course; treat malaria with IV artesunate (Kenya endemic) if positive RDT
8. Source control within 6–12 h (drain abscess, remove infected catheter, debride necrosis)
SUPPORTIVE:
Oxygen titrated to sats 94–98% (88–92% if cyanotic CHD)
Intubate + ventilate for respiratory failure / persistent shock
Glucose 4–8 mmol/L (avoid hypoglycaemia, especially malaria)
Treat hypothermia (skin-to-skin neonate)
Avoid routine HRT (no benefit)
Lung-protective ventilation per ARDS strategy

MENINGOCOCCAEMIA: same as above + dexamethasone before/with antibiotic (controversial in meningococcal — beneficial for pneumococcal), notify public health, contact PEP (ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose or rifampicin 600 mg BD × 2 days adults)
NEONATAL SEPSIS:
< 72h (early): GBS, E. coli — ampicillin + gentamicin or cefotaxime
> 72h (late): nosocomial — vancomycin + cefepime / gentamicin
Lumbar puncture in all (meningitis up to 25%)
Acyclovir for HSV suspicion
WHO IMCI severe disease classification
MALARIA-ASSOCIATED SEPSIS (SSA):
IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24h then daily (AQUAMAT 2010 — superior to quinine)
Treat anaemia, hypoglycaemia, hyperlactataemia, AKI
Antibiotic co-administration (bacterial co-infection common)
PREVENTION:
Immunisation (pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal, BCG, rotavirus, measles)
Breastfeeding promotion
Maternal screening + treatment (intrapartum antibiotic for GBS)
WASH
ITNs + IPTp / IPTi for malaria
Vitamin A campaigns

title: Pulmonary hypertension — WHO classification + group-specific treatment
population: Mean pulmonary artery pressure > 20 mmHg at rest (ESC 2022 — previously 25). 5 WHO groups by aetiology: 1 PAH, 2 left heart, 3 lung disease/hypoxia, 4 chronic thromboembolic (CTEPH), 5 multifactorial. SSA: schistosomiasis-associated PAH globally significant cause.
presentation: Progressive exertional dyspnoea, syncope, chest pain, fatigue, peripheral oedema. Late: right heart failure, cyanosis. RV heave, loud P2, tricuspid regurgitation murmur, raised JVP.
redFlags: WHO functional class IV (symptoms at rest, RV failure)
Acute decompensation triggered by infection / surgery / pregnancy
Pregnancy in known PAH — high mortality
diagnostics: Echocardiogram — screening (TR jet velocity → estimated PASP); RV dimensions; RA size; TAPSE
ECG (RAD, RBBB, RV strain, P pulmonale)
CXR (enlarged pulmonary arteries, RV enlargement)
Right heart catheterisation — DEFINITIVE (mean PAP > 20, PCWP, PVR)
V/Q scan — exclude CTEPH (chronic thromboembolic — must rule out)
CT pulmonary angiogram
Pulmonary function tests + 6MWT
Sleep study (OSA + obesity hypoventilation)
HIV test (PAH increased), schistosomiasis serology (PCR / Kato-Katz / urine in SSA)
ANA, RF, anti-centromere, anti-Scl70 (CTD-associated)
Liver disease workup (portopulmonary)
Genetic counselling for BMPR2 mutation in idiopathic / familial
management: GROUP-SPECIFIC:
GROUP 1 (PAH — idiopathic, heritable, CTD, HIV, portal, schisto, drugs):
General: oxygen if hypoxic, diuretic for RV failure, anticoagulation in IPAH/HPAH (controversial — bleed risk)
Specific therapy by risk stratification:
Low/intermediate risk: dual oral combination — ERA (ambrisentan, macitentan, bosentan) + PDE5i (sildenafil 20 mg TID, tadalafil 40 mg OD) — AMBITION trial
High risk: triple combination including parenteral prostacyclin (epoprostenol IV, treprostinil SC/IV)
Selexipag oral prostacyclin receptor agonist
Riociguat — sGC stimulator (group 1 + 4)
AVOID: ERA + riociguat combination (hypotension)
PAH-specific therapy NEVER given to group 2 / 3 (pulmonary oedema worsens left heart disease + V/Q mismatch)
SOTATERCEPT (activin receptor IIA fusion protein — STELLAR 2023 NEJM) — new disease-modifying for PAH
Lung transplant for refractory
GROUP 2 (left heart disease):
Treat underlying LHD — diuretic, GDMT for HFrEF / HFpEF, valve repair
PAH-specific therapy contraindicated
GROUP 3 (lung disease / hypoxia):
Optimise underlying disease + supplemental O2
CPAP for OSA
Pulmonary rehabilitation
Selected referral for inhaled treprostinil (INCREASE trial — ILD-PAH)
GROUP 4 (CTEPH — chronic thromboembolic):
Lifelong anticoagulation
PULMONARY ENDARTERECTOMY (PEA) — surgical CURE — refer specialised centre
Inoperable: riociguat or balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA)
GROUP 5 (multifactorial):
Treat specific cause (sickle cell, sarcoidosis, glycogen storage, etc.)
Generally avoid PAH-specific therapy
GENERAL MEASURES:
Avoid pregnancy — strong contraception (avoid combined OCP — DVT risk)
Influenza + pneumococcal + COVID vaccination
Pulmonary rehabilitation
Avoid high altitude > 2000 m
Surgery + anaesthesia — high risk; specialist team
Mental health support
Schistosoma-related PAH (most common globally in SSA): praziquantel + PAH-specific therapy

title: Ulcerative colitis — biologics + small molecules (2024)
population: Adults + children — bimodal peak 15–30, 50–80; SSA emerging incidence with urbanisation.
presentation: Bloody diarrhoea, urgency, tenesmus, abdominal pain; Mayo score 0–12 (clinical + endoscopic). Extraintestinal — arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, PSC, ankylosing spondylitis.
redFlags: Severe UC — Truelove + Witts criteria (≥ 6 BO/day + blood + 1 of: pulse > 90, T > 37.8, Hb < 105, ESR > 30) — admit for IV steroids
Acute severe UC failing 3 days IV steroid — colectomy or rescue therapy (infliximab/ciclosporin)
PSC-UC — high colon cancer risk + bile duct cancer
diagnostics: Colonoscopy + biopsies — extent + activity (Mayo endoscopic, UCEIS)
Faecal calprotectin (monitoring + flare assessment)
FBC, ESR, CRP, U&E, LFT, albumin
Stool culture + C. difficile (rule out infection mimicking flare)
TB / hepatitis B / hepatitis C / HIV / VZV screening BEFORE biologic / immunosuppression
Vaccinations status (live vaccines BEFORE biologics)
management: INDUCTION + MAINTENANCE BY SEVERITY:
MILD-MODERATE PROCTITIS / LEFT-SIDED:
Topical: 5-ASA suppositories (proctitis) / enemas (left-sided)
Add oral 5-ASA (mesalazine 2.4–4.8 g/d) if not responding
Topical corticosteroid (budesonide MMX 9 mg) for refractory
MODERATE-SEVERE EXTENSIVE:
Oral 5-ASA 4.8 g/d + topical
Add oral corticosteroid (prednisolone 40 mg taper × 8 weeks) if not responding
AZATHIOPRINE 2–2.5 mg/kg (after TPMT check) — steroid-sparing maintenance
Methotrexate alternative
BIOLOGICS / SMALL MOLECULES (moderate-severe, failed conventional):
Anti-TNF: infliximab IV (5 mg/kg weeks 0, 2, 6 then q8w), adalimumab SC, golimumab SC
Anti-integrin: vedolizumab IV (gut-selective)
Anti-IL-12/23: ustekinumab IV induction + SC maintenance
Anti-IL-23: risankizumab, mirikizumab (NEW 2023-2024 UC)
JAK INHIBITOR: tofacitinib 10 mg BD (induction) → 5 mg BD; upadacitinib 45 mg → 15 mg (boxed warnings — VTE, MACE, malignancy; reserve for failure / consider after age 65 / risk factors)
Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) modulators: ozanimod, etrasimod (NEW 2023 UC)
Treat-to-target paradigm: clinical + endoscopic + histologic + biomarker remission
ACUTE SEVERE UC:
Admit, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg q6h × 3 days
VTE prophylaxis (high VTE risk in active IBD)
Rule out infection (stool culture, C. diff PCR, CMV biopsy)
Day 3 reassessment: failed steroid (≥ 8 BO + CRP > 45) → infliximab IV 5 mg/kg rescue OR ciclosporin OR colectomy
Failed rescue at day 5–7 → COLECTOMY (subtotal with end ileostomy; J-pouch IPAA later)
MAINTENANCE:
5-ASA for mild-moderate maintenance
Thiopurine / biologic / small molecule per induction agent
Combination immunomod + biologic for selected (SONIC strategy)
SURVEILLANCE:
Surveillance colonoscopy from 8–10 years disease duration (or earlier for PSC-UC) annually-2-yearly
Chromoendoscopy / high-definition; targeted biopsies
Refer for prophylactic colectomy if high-grade dysplasia
EXTRAINTESTINAL: refer specialty; treat with IBD therapy if controls disease
Pregnancy: most therapies continued (mesalazine, AZA, anti-TNF — last dose 28-30 wk for some); JAK inhibitor + small molecules AVOID pregnancy
BONE health, mental health, anaemia (IV iron), nutrition support
PSC-UC: ursodeoxycholic acid, MRCP surveillance, refer hepatology

title: Crohn's disease — comprehensive + biologic (2024)
population: Bimodal peak 15–30, 60–70. Transmural inflammation, anywhere mouth-to-anus, skip lesions, granulomas. Phenotypes: inflammatory, stricturing, fistulising, perianal.
presentation: Abdominal pain (RLQ — terminal ileitis), diarrhoea, weight loss, fatigue, fevers, perianal disease, malabsorption. Extraintestinal as in UC.
diagnostics: Colonoscopy + ileoscopy + biopsies (transmural granulomas pathognomonic)
MRI / CT enterography — small bowel (skip lesions, strictures, fistulae)
Capsule endoscopy for small bowel (caution if stricture — use patency capsule first)
EUA + MRI pelvis for perianal disease
Faecal calprotectin
Vitamin B12 (terminal ileal disease)
Iron studies, ferritin (iron + chronic disease)
Pre-biologic screen as UC
management: PRINCIPLES: treat-to-target (clinical + biomarker + endoscopic) — STRIDE-II 2021
INDUCTION:
Mild: budesonide 9 mg/d (ileocaecal) or prednisolone 40 mg
Moderate–severe: corticosteroid + start steroid-sparing immunomodulator (AZA 2 mg/kg or methotrexate 25 mg/week SC) and/or biologic
Severe / fistulising / steroid-dependent: BIOLOGIC EARLY (top-down)
MAINTENANCE BIOLOGIC OPTIONS:
Anti-TNF: infliximab (best evidence for fistulising), adalimumab, certolizumab — combo with thiopurine more effective (SONIC)
Anti-integrin: vedolizumab (less mucosal healing than anti-TNF, slower onset but excellent safety)
Anti-IL-12/23: ustekinumab
Anti-IL-23: risankizumab (ADVANCE / MOTIVATE / FORTIFY)
JAK inhibitor: upadacitinib (U-EXCEL / U-EXCEED / U-ENDURE) — for CD ≥ 18 yr
Avoid JAK in elderly / cardiovascular / VTE risk per pharmacovigilance
PERIANAL DISEASE:
MRI pelvis to map fistula tracts
Examination under anaesthesia + setons + abscess drainage by colorectal surgeon
Anti-TNF (infliximab particularly — ACCENT II)
Combination antibiotic (ciprofloxacin + metronidazole) for adjunct
Mesenchymal stem cell therapy (darvadstrocel) for refractory perianal
STRICTURE:
Mature fibrotic — endoscopic balloon dilation or surgical strictureplasty
Inflammatory — biologic / steroid (some reversibility)
Avoid biologic-induced delay if obstruction imminent
FISTULA:
Surgical + medical combination
Anti-TNF first-line medical
ABSCESS: drain (percutaneous / surgical) BEFORE starting immunosuppression
SURGERY:
Not curative (unlike UC) — recurrence high
Indications: failure of medical, complications (obstruction, fistula, abscess, perforation, cancer)
Limited resection preserve length
Post-op biologic prophylaxis for high-risk (POCER trial)
NUTRITIONAL: B12 supplementation if terminal ileum diseased / resected; iron (IV if oral intolerance); zinc, vit D; short bowel syndrome management
Smoking cessation IMPORTANT — accelerates CD
Bone, mental health, vaccinations, dysplasia surveillance, fertility + pregnancy planning
Pregnancy: continue biologic per UC guidance

title: Chronic hepatitis B — modern antiviral therapy + WHO
population: SSA highest prevalence globally (5–10%); leading cause of HCC. Kenya endemic. Vertical + horizontal transmission. WHO target: elimination as PH problem by 2030 (95% reduction incidence, 65% reduction mortality).
presentation: Asymptomatic chronic carriage common; HBeAg-positive / negative chronic hepatitis; cirrhosis; HCC.
redFlags: HBeAg positive + raised ALT — active replication
HBV DNA > 2000 (or > 20,000 if HBeAg+) + ALT abnormal — treat
HIV / HCV / HDV coinfection — different management
Pregnancy with high VL — prevent vertical transmission
diagnostics: HBsAg (chronic infection > 6 mo)
HBeAg + anti-HBe, anti-HBc IgG / IgM, HBV DNA quantitative
ALT, AST, GGT, bilirubin, albumin, INR, platelets
Liver imaging — US 6-monthly + AFP (HCC surveillance for cirrhotic + non-cirrhotic high-risk: African male > 20, Asian male > 40 / female > 50, family history HCC)
Fibrosis: FibroScan (transient elastography), Fib-4, APRI, Hepascore; liver biopsy if uncertain
Coinfections: HIV, HCV, HDV (HDV common in some regions; test if HBsAg+)
management: WHO 2024 EXPANDED ELIGIBILITY (simplified for LMIC):
TREAT if any of:
Cirrhosis (any HBV DNA)
Significant fibrosis (≥ F2)
ALT > ULN persistent + HBV DNA > 2000
HBeAg+ with significant disease
Pregnant women with HBV DNA > 200,000 IU/ml (PMTCT)
Children > 12 yr with eligibility per individual assessment
FIRST-LINE: TENOFOVIR (TDF 300 mg / TAF 25 mg) daily — high genetic barrier, potent
Entecavir 0.5 mg alternative
Continue indefinitely / lifelong in most (especially cirrhotic)
Stop possible only with HBsAg seroclearance + careful monitoring (uncommon)
AVOID lamivudine monotherapy (high resistance), interferon (Africa availability + tolerance)
PEG-IFN alpha alternative for selected (HBeAg+ younger high ALT) — finite course 48 weeks
MONITORING ON TREATMENT:
ALT + HBV DNA 3-monthly first year, then 6-monthly
HBeAg → anti-HBe seroconversion goal
HBsAg loss = functional cure (rare)
Bone density + renal function (TDF — TAF safer)
HCC surveillance 6-monthly US ± AFP per indication
CIRRHOSIS care: variceal screening + prophylaxis (β-blocker / band ligation), VTE prophylaxis hospital admissions, vaccinate hepatitis A / pneumococcal / flu, screen + treat ascites + encephalopathy
HCC TREATMENT (separate condition):
Resection / ablation early-stage
Transplant (Milan criteria)
TACE (transarterial chemoembolisation)
Systemic — atezolizumab+bevacizumab (IMbrave-150), sorafenib, lenvatinib
PREGNANCY:
HBV DNA > 200,000 IU/ml → tenofovir from 28 weeks until 4 weeks post-partum
Infant: HBIG + HBV vaccine within 12h of birth + complete schedule
Breastfeeding safe on tenofovir
HIV-HBV CO-INFECTION: ART must include 2 anti-HBV agents (TDF + 3TC / FTC); do NOT stop without coverage (HBV flare)
HDV CO-INFECTION:
Bulevirtide (entry inhibitor — NEW for HDV)
PEG-IFN historical
VACCINATION (cornerstone of elimination):
Universal infant vaccination (Kenya — birth dose + 3-dose pentavalent schedule)
Catch-up + high-risk groups
Healthcare workers, household contacts, MSM, sex workers, dialysis patients
Heplisav-B 2-dose adult vaccine alternative
Public health: HBV testing scale-up, linkage to care, simplified treatment per WHO, advocacy for affordable TDF/TAF
Kenya MOH: Hepatitis B included in essential package, NHIF coverage expanding

title: Hepatitis C — direct-acting antivirals (cure ≥ 95%)
population: Global 58 million; SSA prevalence 1–3% in many countries. Now CURABLE with 8–12 week oral therapy; WHO 2030 elimination target.
presentation: Asymptomatic chronic infection; 20% develop cirrhosis at 20 years; HCC, decompensation, extrahepatic (cryoglobulinaemia, MPGN, lichen planus, lymphoma).
redFlags: Re-infection risk after cure (PWID, MSM with high-risk practices)
diagnostics: Anti-HCV (screening) + HCV RNA (confirmation, viral load)
Genotype historically — pan-genotypic DAAs eliminate need (most regimens)
ALT + Fib-4 + APRI + FibroScan (cirrhosis assessment — critical for regimen + duration choice)
Pre-treatment workup: HBV (reactivation risk on DAA), HIV, eGFR, FBC, drug interactions
Pregnancy test (DAAs not studied)
management: PAN-GENOTYPIC DAAs (WHO + most guidelines first-line):
GLECAPREVIR/PIBRENTASVIR 8 weeks (no cirrhosis) / 12 weeks (compensated cirrhosis)
SOFOSBUVIR/VELPATASVIR 12 weeks (with ribavirin if decompensated cirrhosis or NS5A failure)
Cure rate (SVR12) ≥ 95% with 8–12 weeks oral therapy
GENOTYPE-SPECIFIC (older — less used now):
Genotype 1: ledipasvir/sofosbuvir, elbasvir/grazoprevir
Specific to genotype + cirrhosis status
DRUG INTERACTIONS — CHECK ALL BEFORE PRESCRIBING:
Amiodarone + sofosbuvir = bradycardia
PPIs reduce ledipasvir absorption
Statins (consult interaction checker)
Phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin contraindicated
DECOMPENSATED CIRRHOSIS:
Avoid protease inhibitor-containing regimens (glecaprevir, grazoprevir, voxilaprevir)
Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir + ribavirin × 12 weeks
Refer hepatology / transplant centre
HIV-HCV CO-INFECTION:
Same DAAs as mono-infected
Check ART interactions
HBV CO-INFECTION:
HBV reactivation possible on DAA — boxed warning
Check HBsAg pre-DAA; if positive, start anti-HBV therapy (TDF) concurrently
POST-TREATMENT:
HCV RNA 12 weeks after treatment end = SVR12 = cure
Cirrhotic — continue HCC surveillance for life (oncogenic potential persists)
Counsel re-infection prevention (PWID — needle exchange, OAT; MSM safer practices)
Reverse extrahepatic manifestations
Risk reduction: avoid alcohol, hepatotoxins; treat NAFLD if coexists
PROGRAMMATIC ASPECTS:
Test-and-treat models simplified for primary care (WHO 2024 — pan-genotypic, no genotype testing, simplified algorithms)
HCV elimination programmes in Egypt — example of national rollout
Cost barrier in SSA — generic glecaprevir/pibrentasvir + sofosbuvir/velpatasvir access advocacy
Kenya National Viral Hepatitis Strategic Plan

title: MASLD/MASH (formerly NAFLD/NASH) — modern care
population: Global 25–30% adult prevalence; rising worldwide including SSA with metabolic syndrome epidemic. Now leading cause of liver transplant in HICs.
presentation: Mostly asymptomatic; incidental fatty liver on US; raised ALT; metabolic syndrome (T2DM, obesity, dyslipidaemia, HTN). MASH = with inflammation + hepatocyte injury → fibrosis → cirrhosis → HCC.
diagnostics: TERMINOLOGY UPDATE 2023 — Multi-Society:
MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease) replaces NAFLD
MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis) replaces NASH
MetALD — combined metabolic + alcohol
Diagnostic criteria: steatosis + ≥ 1 cardiometabolic risk factor
Step 1: Calculate FIB-4 (age, AST, ALT, platelets) — < 1.3 low risk, > 2.67 high risk
Step 2 if FIB-4 intermediate / high: FibroScan or proprietary test (ELF, FIB-4)
Step 3: refer hepatology if F2+ on FibroScan (≥ 8 kPa)
Liver biopsy gold standard but rarely needed (reserve for unclear cases)
Workup: HbA1c, fasting lipid panel, BMI, blood pressure, ferritin (excess in MASLD/MASH), iron studies, autoimmune (ANA, SMA, AMA — rule out PBC/AIH), hepatitis B/C, alcohol history
MRI / MRI-PDFF — quantitative fat
HCC surveillance — US ± AFP 6-monthly for cirrhotic
management: LIFESTYLE (foundation — 7–10% weight loss reverses MASH):
Mediterranean diet, reduce ultra-processed, fructose, alcohol
Exercise 150–300 min/week aerobic + resistance
Avoid hepatotoxins, alcohol
Coffee 2–3 cups/day (protective)
Smoking cessation
WEIGHT LOSS interventions:
Behavioural / dietitian + structured programme
Pharmacotherapy: semaglutide (NN1148 / GLP-1 RA — improves liver biology), tirzepatide; resmetirom (thyroid hormone receptor β agonist — FIRST FDA-approved 2024 for MASH F2-F3, Madrigal pharm)
Bariatric surgery — improves/reverses MASH; consider BMI ≥ 35 + metabolic syndrome
DRUG SPECIFIC (emerging — formerly no FDA-approved):
RESMETIROM 80 mg daily (MAESTRO-NASH 2024) — MASH F2-F3 — first specific MASH approval
Vitamin E 800 IU/d for non-diabetic biopsy-proven NASH (PIVENS) — some evidence, caution prostate cancer risk
Pioglitazone — improves MASH in T2DM (small RCTs)
GLP-1 RA — improving MASH biology + weight + DM (semaglutide in MASH trials)
TREAT COMORBIDITIES (high CV mortality risk — main cause of death in MASLD):
HTN: ACE-i / ARB (RAAS may help fibrosis)
DM: SGLT2i (also reduces hepatic fat) + GLP-1 RA / tirzepatide
Dyslipidaemia: statin SAFE in NAFLD (not contraindicated despite raised ALT — improves outcomes); ezetimibe; PCSK9i for high-risk
Obesity: GLP-1 RA / tirzepatide / bariatric
OSA: CPAP
AVOID:
Alcohol (especially binge)
Excess paracetamol
Hepatotoxic drugs / supplements
CIRRHOSIS:
HCC surveillance
Variceal screening
Treat decompensation per standard
Refer transplant — MASH-cirrhosis leading indication
PAEDIATRIC: lifestyle first-line; obesity + DM management

title: Acute pancreatitis — modern care (Atlanta 2012 + 2024 update)
population: Adults — gallstones + alcohol account for 70%. Mortality 1–3% mild, 20–30% severe. Hypertriglyceridaemia + hypercalcaemia + drug-induced + post-ERCP + idiopathic.
presentation: Severe epigastric pain radiating to back, nausea, vomiting. Tenderness, guarding. Grey Turner / Cullen sign in haemorrhagic (late + uncommon). SIRS / sepsis / shock in severe.
redFlags: Infected necrosis (clinical + imaging features after week 1)
diagnostics: Diagnosis (2 of 3):
Typical pain
Lipase > 3× ULN (more specific than amylase)
Imaging (US, CT, MRI)
Severity assessment within 48h:
Atlanta 2012: mild (no failure), moderately severe (transient < 48h), severe (persistent > 48h organ failure)
BISAP (5-item — bedside)
SIRS criteria
CT severity score (CTSI) — reserve CT for 72–96h (overestimates early)
Aetiology: US abdomen (gallstones), triglycerides, calcium, IgG4 (autoimmune), drug history (azathioprine, valproate, GLP-1 RA suspected, mesalazine, diuretics)
FBC, U&E, LFT, glucose, Ca, Mg, lipid panel, CRP, ABG
management: EARLY MANAGEMENT (cornerstone):
IV FLUIDS — Hartmann/Ringer's lactate; goal-directed (urine output > 0.5 ml/kg/h, MAP, lactate); NOT excessive (WATERFALL trial 2022 — moderate not aggressive better)
Pain control: opioid (morphine OK historically thought to worsen sphincter — no good evidence)
Antiemetic
Early oral / enteral feeding within 24–72h (NJ NG if not tolerating PO) — improves outcomes vs NPO
Antibiotics ONLY if infected (not prophylactic — PROPATRIA showed harm)
AETIOLOGY-SPECIFIC:
GALLSTONE pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction: ERCP within 24–48h + sphincterotomy
Cholecystectomy DURING same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis (PONCHO trial — reduces recurrence)
ALCOHOL: alcohol cessation + brief intervention; thiamine; manage withdrawal
HYPERTRIGLYCERIDAEMIA: insulin infusion + heparin + plasmapheresis (TG > 1000); fibrate / omega-3 long-term
AUTOIMMUNE (type 1 IgG4-related): corticosteroid
Hypercalcaemia: bisphosphonate after pancreatitis treated
MODERATELY SEVERE / SEVERE:
HDU/ICU
Continuous monitoring, frequent reassessment
Early enteral nutrition via NJ tube (preserves gut, less infection vs TPN)
TPN only if enteral fails
Treat organ failure per standard
CT at 72–96h if not improving — characterise necrosis
NECROTISING PANCREATITIS:
Most necrosis is sterile — supportive only
Infected necrosis: clinical deterioration after week 1 + gas in necrosis on CT or positive FNA
Antibiotics: meropenem 1 g q8h (penetration) or pip-tazo
Drainage: STEP-UP approach (PANTER trial) — percutaneous drainage first → endoscopic necrosectomy → minimally invasive surgical if needed; AVOID early open surgery
Delayed intervention (> 4 weeks) preferred (encapsulated walled-off necrosis easier to drain)
COMPLICATIONS:
Pseudocyst — drain if symptomatic / infected / > 6 cm > 6 weeks
Splenic vein thrombosis → gastric varices → splenectomy
Diabetes mellitus (Type 3c — exocrine + endocrine failure)
Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency — pancreatic enzyme replacement (Creon)
Chronic pancreatitis if recurrent
DISCHARGE: prevent recurrence — cholecystectomy if gallstone, alcohol cessation, lipid control

title: Upper GI bleeding — Glasgow-Blatchford + Forrest + endoscopy
population: Adults with haematemesis / coffee-ground vomit / melaena / haematochezia (massive UGIB). Peptic ulcer + variceal + Mallory-Weiss + cancer + AVMs most common.
presentation: Haematemesis, melaena (most common), haemodynamic instability (shock if massive), anaemia symptoms, syncope, mental state change.
diagnostics: Glasgow-Blatchford score (BUN, Hb, SBP, HR, melaena, syncope, hepatic failure, cardiac failure) — 0 outpatient acceptable
Rockall score — pre-endoscopic + complete (post-endoscopic) for mortality risk
FBC (Hb may be normal acutely — falls with fluid resuscitation), U&E (urea raised — protein meal of blood), LFT (cirrhosis), coag, group + crossmatch
ECG, troponin if elderly / cardiovascular history
Lactate
Urgent endoscopy within 24h (more urgent if unstable / variceal)
Forrest classification (peptic ulcer): Ia spurting, Ib oozing, IIa visible vessel, IIb clot, IIc pigmented, III clean base
management: RESUSCITATION:
Two large-bore IVs (16G+)
Type + crossmatch ≥ 4 units packed cells
Restrictive transfusion target Hb 70–80 (TRICC + Villanueva — restrictive better in UGIB, especially variceal)
Massive transfusion 1:1:1 if shock + active bleeding
TXA — historically used; HALT-IT trial 2020 — no benefit in UGIB + slight increase VTE — abandoned routine use
Reverse anticoagulants: idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet for apixaban/rivaroxaban; 4F-PCC for warfarin (vit K 5–10 mg IV slow + 25–50 IU/kg PCC); FFP if PCC unavailable
Platelet transfusion if < 50 with bleeding
Restart anticoagulant within 7 days if low rebleed + high thrombotic risk (DOAC preferred)
PRE-ENDOSCOPIC PHARMACOTHERAPY:
IV PPI: omeprazole / pantoprazole 80 mg bolus then 8 mg/h infusion × 72h (post-endoscopic for high-risk lesions) — UK guidance
Empirical IV PPI pre-endoscopy NOT supported by recent evidence — UK NICE; but commonly given
VARICEAL suspicion (cirrhosis, signs): terlipressin 2 mg IV q4h (or octreotide 50 mcg bolus + 50 mcg/h infusion) + ceftriaxone 1 g daily × 7 d (reduces SBP + mortality)
ENDOSCOPY (within 24h):
PEPTIC ULCER — Forrest Ia/b/IIa: dual modality — adrenaline injection + thermal/clip; high-risk lesions get IV PPI infusion × 72h post; H. pylori test + eradication after
ULCER Forrest IIc/III: PO PPI, early discharge
VARICES: variceal band ligation (oesophageal); cyanoacrylate glue (gastric); TIPSS for refractory / high-risk (Garcia-Pagán NEJM 2010 early TIPSS)
MALLORY-WEISS: usually self-limits; endoscopic if active
ANGIODYSPLASIA: argon plasma coagulation
TUMOUR: biopsy + oncology referral
REFRACTORY:
Repeat endoscopy
Interventional radiology embolisation
Surgical (rare now)
TIPSS for variceal
POST-ENDOSCOPIC:
Continue PPI for ulcer 4–8 weeks
H. pylori eradication for all ulcer patients (test + treat)
Re-look endoscopy at 6–8 weeks for gastric ulcer (rule out cancer)
Stop NSAIDs/aspirin if causative; if needed, give PPI cover + COX-2
Variceal: secondary prevention β-blocker + EVL; transplant assessment
Cardio-renal restart anticoag/antiplatelet per shared decision
LOWER GI BLEED (haematochezia + stable): CT angio if active + unstable; colonoscopy after stabilisation; usually self-limits; diverticular + angioectasia most common

title: H. pylori — test + treat algorithm (2024 resistance-aware)
population: Global > 50% prevalence; > 70% in many SSA + LMIC. Risk: peptic ulcer (most), gastric cancer (carcinogen — IARC group 1), MALT lymphoma, dyspepsia.
presentation: Dyspepsia, peptic ulcer, gastric cancer, MALT lymphoma, iron deficiency anaemia (unexplained), ITP.
redFlags: Alarm dyspepsia features (ALARMS — Age > 55 new, Loss of weight, Anaemia, Recent onset, Melaena, Swallowing difficulty) — URGENT endoscopy
Treatment failure after 2 rounds — refer specialist / culture for sensitivities
diagnostics: Non-invasive (preferred for diagnosis):
UREA BREATH TEST (UBT) — most accurate; off PPI 2 weeks, antibiotic 4 weeks pre-test
STOOL ANTIGEN — alternative, off PPI 2 weeks
Serology (IgG) — historical, less useful (cannot distinguish past vs current)
Invasive (during endoscopy if indicated):
Rapid urease test (CLO) on biopsy
Histology
Culture + sensitivity (consider if 2+ treatment failures)
TEST INDICATIONS (Maastricht VI/Florence 2022 + ACG):
Active or past peptic ulcer
Uninvestigated dyspepsia in patients < 55 without alarm (test-and-treat)
MALT lymphoma
After gastric cancer / dysplasia
Iron deficiency anaemia unexplained
ITP
Long-term NSAID / aspirin user with risk
First-degree relative of gastric cancer
management: RESISTANCE LANDSCAPE 2024 — clarithromycin resistance > 15% in most regions; metronidazole varies; levofloxacin rising
FIRST-LINE REGIMENS:
BISMUTH QUADRUPLE (preferred in high clarithromycin resistance — Africa, S Asia, S Europe):
Bismuth subcitrate 240 mg QDS + tetracycline 500 mg QDS + metronidazole 500 mg QDS + PPI BD × 14 days
CLARITHROMYCIN TRIPLE (only where local resistance < 15%):
PPI BD + clarithromycin 500 mg BD + amoxicillin 1 g BD × 14 days
CONCOMITANT (alternative non-bismuth quadruple):
PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin + metronidazole × 14 days
Vonoprazan-based: vonoprazan 20 mg BD + amoxicillin 1 g TID (dual) or + clarithromycin (triple) × 14 days — emerging high-efficacy regimen
SECOND-LINE (if first failed):
Bismuth quadruple (if not used first)
Levofloxacin triple: PPI + amoxicillin 1 g BD + levofloxacin 500 mg OD × 14 d (boxed warnings)
Different regimen avoiding antibiotics used in first treatment
THIRD-LINE / RESCUE:
Refer for endoscopy + culture-guided therapy
Rifabutin-based triple (specialist)
DURATION: prefer 14 days (vs 10 — slightly better eradication; trade against adherence)
VERIFY ERADICATION at 4 weeks post-treatment (UBT or stool antigen — off PPI 2 weeks)
PENICILLIN ALLERGY:
Bismuth quadruple (no amox)
Clarithromycin + metronidazole + PPI
Consider penicillin re-challenge (most labelled allergic are not)
AFTER ERADICATION:
Continue PPI 4–8 weeks if active ulcer
Gastric ulcer: repeat endoscopy 6–8 weeks to confirm healing + exclude malignancy
MALT lymphoma: most regress with eradication; oncology if not at 12 months
Family member testing in selected (gastric cancer family)
PREVENTION OF RECURRENCE:
Avoid NSAIDs / aspirin or use COX-2 + PPI
Smoking cessation
Treat GERD
Stress reduction
PUBLIC HEALTH SSA:
High burden + drug resistance challenge
Affordable diagnostics (stool antigen rapid kits)
Kenya MOH gastroenterology services scaling

title: Cirrhosis — comprehensive care + decompensation management
population: Adults with end-stage liver fibrosis from any cause — alcohol, viral, MASLD/MASH, autoimmune. Compensated → decompensated (ascites, variceal bleed, encephalopathy, jaundice).
presentation: Compensated — incidental, FibroScan; decompensated — ascites, oedema, variceal bleed, hepatic encephalopathy, jaundice, coagulopathy, malnutrition.
redFlags: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP — ascites + fever / abdominal pain / encephalopathy + > 250 PMN)
Hepatorenal syndrome (rapidly rising creatinine + volume unresponsive)
diagnostics: Diagnose: imaging (US — heterogeneous + nodular + portal HT signs, splenomegaly, ascites; CT/MRI further detail), FibroScan ≥ 12.5 kPa
Severity: Child-Pugh A 5–6, B 7–9, C 10–15; MELD-Na score (≥ 15 — transplant assessment)
Aetiology: alcohol, hepatitis B/C, MASH, autoimmune (AIH/PBC/PSC), haemochromatosis, Wilson's, α1AT, congestive
Variceal screening: endoscopy at diagnosis + every 1–3 years (extend if non-cirrhotic / no varices)
HCC surveillance: US + AFP every 6 months for all cirrhosis + non-cirrhotic HBV high-risk
Baseline + monitor: FBC + platelets + LFT + INR + albumin + electrolytes + glucose + ammonia (encephalopathy)
Ascites tap: PMN count, culture, albumin (SAAG > 11 portal HT vs < 11 non-portal), cytology
Renal function (HRS workup): creatinine + sodium
management: AETIOLOGY-DIRECTED TREATMENT (key to halt progression):
Alcohol cessation (relapse common — refer addiction, naltrexone, baclofen, acamprosate, mutual support)
Hepatitis B antiviral lifelong (TDF/TAF)
Hepatitis C DAA cure
MASH: weight loss + resmetirom (F2-F3), tirzepatide, statins
Autoimmune: prednisolone + AZA
Haemochromatosis: phlebotomy
Wilson's: zinc + chelation (penicillamine, trientine)
PRIMARY PROPHYLAXIS:
Variceal: non-selective β-blocker (NSBB — propranolol 80 mg/d or carvedilol 12.5 mg/d) for medium/large varices OR EVL; carvedilol superior — Garcia-Tsao 2024
Vaccinations: hep A + B if not immune, pneumococcal, annual flu, COVID
ASCITES:
Sodium restriction (2 g/d max)
Spironolactone 100 mg/d ± furosemide 40 mg/d (ratio 100:40 — natriuresis without K+ disturbance)
Titrate to target weight loss 0.5–1 kg/day; ALBUMIN 25% supplement debated for prophylaxis
Diagnostic paracentesis with each admission (rule out SBP)
Therapeutic LARGE-VOLUME paracentesis with albumin (8 g/L removed)
Refractory: TIPSS, peritoneo-venous shunt, transplant assessment
Avoid PPIs without indication (SBP risk increase)
SBP:
Diagnostic + therapeutic IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily × 5–7 days; quinolone alternative
Albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1 + 1 g/kg day 3 (reduces hepatorenal + mortality — Sort NEJM 1999)
Secondary prophylaxis: norfloxacin 400 mg daily for life until transplant / resolution
Primary prophylaxis for high-risk: low protein ascites + Child C / GI bleed
HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY:
Identify + treat precipitant (infection, GIB, constipation, drugs — opioid/BZD, dehydration, hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia)
Lactulose 30 mL TID titrate to 2–3 soft BO/day
Rifaximin 550 mg BD (added to lactulose for recurrent — Bass NEJM 2010)
L-ornithine L-aspartate alternative
Treat precipitants
VARICEAL BLEED:
Resuscitation + transfusion (restrictive Hb target 70)
Terlipressin / octreotide infusion
Ceftriaxone 1 g/day × 7 d (reduces SBP + mortality)
EVL (band ligation) ± glue for gastric varices
TIPSS for refractory / high-risk (early TIPSS — Garcia-Pagán)
Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore) bridge
HEPATORENAL SYNDROME:
Albumin + terlipressin (or noradrenaline)
Treat precipitant
Refer transplant urgently — HRS type 1 high mortality
Avoid NSAIDs / aminoglycosides / nephrotoxin
ACUTE-ON-CHRONIC LIVER FAILURE: critical care + organ support + transplant priority
HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA (HCC):
Curative: resection (preserved liver function) / ablation (RFA/MWA < 3 cm) / transplant (Milan criteria — 1 lesion < 5 cm or 3 lesions each < 3 cm)
Intermediate: TACE
Advanced: atezolizumab + bevacizumab (IMbrave-150 — first-line systemic), sorafenib, lenvatinib
Terminal: best supportive care
TRANSPLANT REFERRAL:
MELD ≥ 15, decompensation, refractory ascites, recurrent HE, HRS, HCC within Milan, hepatopulmonary syndrome
Exclusions: ongoing alcohol, advanced malignancy, severe extrahepatic disease
Sobriety usually 6 months for alcoholic liver disease (controversial; selected early transplant for severe alcoholic hepatitis — DIALCOHOL trial)
PALLIATIVE CARE: incurable advanced liver disease — symptom + psychological + family support
DRUGS TO AVOID/CAUTION: paracetamol max 2 g/d, NSAIDs, opioids (slow), benzodiazepines, statins safe but caution
MALNUTRITION (very common): refer dietetics; bed time snack; high protein 1.2–1.5 g/kg; supplement

title: IBS — Rome IV + low FODMAP + targeted therapy
population: Adults — prevalence 10–15% globally; female predominant; significant disability + healthcare use. Subtypes IBS-D, IBS-C, IBS-M, IBS-U.
presentation: Recurrent abdominal pain ≥ 1 day/week × 3 months associated with defaecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form. Bloating, urgency, mucus, incomplete evacuation common.
redFlags: Weight loss, blood in stool, nocturnal symptoms — exclude IBD/cancer
Family history bowel cancer / IBD / coeliac
Persistent symptoms despite treatment — escalate workup
diagnostics: Rome IV symptom-based diagnosis (no biomarker)
Limited workup if typical + no red flags: FBC, CRP, faecal calprotectin (< 50 normal — rules out IBD), coeliac serology (anti-tTG IgA + total IgA), TSH
Colonoscopy NOT routine; reserve for red flags / > 50 / failure to respond
Stool MC&S if recent travel / acute onset
Lactose / fructose breath test if specific intolerance suspected
H. pylori test if dyspepsia overlap
management: POSITIVE DIAGNOSIS + EDUCATION:
Explain biopsychosocial — brain-gut axis
Disorder of gut-brain interaction (formerly 'functional')
Validate symptoms — not 'in their head'
Set realistic expectations
DIETARY:
General: regular meals, hydration, limit fatty / spicy / caffeine / alcohol, reduce gas-producing foods
LOW FODMAP — 6–8 week elimination then structured reintroduction; ideally with dietitian
Fermentable Oligo-, Di-, Mono-saccharides + Polyols
Garlic, onion, wheat, beans, apples, pears, lactose, sweeteners
NICE first-line dietary advice; FODMAP second-line if persists
Soluble fibre (psyllium) — IBS-C predominantly
AVOID insoluble fibre (bran) — worsens
Gluten-free — modest benefit subset (non-coeliac wheat sensitivity overlap)
PSYCHOLOGICAL:
Stress + sleep hygiene
CBT (face-to-face or digital — Mahana 2021 RCT — durable improvement)
Gut-directed hypnotherapy — strong evidence
Mindfulness-based stress reduction
PHARMACOLOGICAL (symptom-targeted):
IBS-C:
Soluble fibre (psyllium) — first-line
Osmotic laxative (PEG)
Linaclotide (PRESS trial)
Plecanatide, prucalopride
Avoid stimulant laxatives long-term
IBS-D:
Loperamide as needed
Bile acid binders (colestyramine) — bile acid diarrhoea subset
Eluxadoline
Rifaximin 550 mg TID × 14 d (TARGET trial — reduces bloating + global symptoms)
Antispasmodics: mebeverine, hyoscine, peppermint oil
TCA low-dose (amitriptyline 10–25 mg nocte) — IBS-D + abdominal pain; ATLANTIS trial 2023 confirmed efficacy
SSRI — IBS-C (fluoxetine, paroxetine)
Probiotics — mixed evidence; specific strains for bloating (LP299v, Bifidobacterium infantis)
EMERGING:
Faecal microbiota transplant — research
Mast cell stabilisers (cromoglicate)
REFER GASTROENTEROLOGY:
Refractory symptoms despite optimisation
Diagnostic uncertainty
Severe psychological comorbidity

title: Major depressive disorder — stepped care + treatment-resistant pathway
population: Adults — lifetime prevalence 15–20%; under-detected SSA primary care. WHO mhGAP critical scaling-up framework.
presentation: Persistent low mood / anhedonia + ≥ 4 of (DSM-5 / ICD-11): sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, self-worth, agitation/retardation, suicidal ideation × ≥ 2 weeks. Functional impairment.
redFlags: Active suicidal ideation with plan / intent / access to means — urgent psychiatric review / admit
Bipolar mixed features missed (avoid antidepressant monotherapy)
Suspected serotonin syndrome / NMS on therapy
diagnostics: PHQ-9 (sensitivity, severity, suicide item 9)
GAD-7 (anxiety overlap)
Rule out medical: TSH, FBC, B12/folate, ferritin, U&E, glucose, vit D, calcium
MDQ / HCL-32 to rule out bipolar before antidepressant
Substance use screen (AUDIT, ASSIST, CRAFFT adolescent)
Suicide risk assessment — ideation + intent + plan + access + protective factors + history
Domestic violence + IPV screening
Sleep + diet + exercise + social history
Trauma history
management: STEPPED CARE (WHO mhGAP + NICE NG222):
Step 1 — Recognition + diagnosis + active monitoring; psychoeducation
Step 2 — Mild-moderate: brief psychological intervention
Low-intensity CBT (digital CBT, guided self-help, group CBT)
Behavioural activation
Sleep hygiene, exercise (150 min/week aerobic — meta-analytically as effective as antidepressant for mild)
Mindfulness-based stress reduction
In LMIC: WHO Problem Management Plus (PM+) lay-delivered, EMPOWER / Step-by-Step digital
Step 3 — Moderate-severe: combine medication + psychological
ANTIDEPRESSANT first-line:

SSRI: sertraline 50 mg (preferred — fewer interactions, breastfeeding-safe), citalopram (QT caution > 40 mg), escitalopram, fluoxetine (long half-life — useful for poor adherence), paroxetine (avoid pregnancy + withdrawal)
SNRI: venlafaxine (BP rise > 150 mg), duloxetine (also pain)
Atypical: mirtazapine (sedation + appetite — useful low BMI / insomnia), bupropion (no sexual SE, smoking cessation)
Vortioxetine — multimodal, may have cognitive benefit
Trazodone for insomnia component
Allow 4–6 weeks therapeutic dose before declaring non-response
Continue 6–12 months after remission (longer for recurrent)
Taper slowly to avoid discontinuation
HIGH-INTENSITY PSYCHOLOGICAL THERAPY:
CBT (gold standard)
IPT (interpersonal therapy)
Behavioural activation (BA — STREAM trial — effective + scalable in LMIC)
Counselling for moderate cases
Step 4 — Severe / treatment-resistant:
Specialist psychiatry
Switching antidepressant (different class)
Augmentation: lithium (suicide protective), atypical antipsychotic (aripiprazole, quetiapine), thyroid (T3), bupropion combo, mirtazapine combo
ECT — severe (psychotic, catatonia, suicidal, food refusal, pregnancy)
ESKETAMINE nasal (Spravato) — treatment-resistant
rTMS — repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation
Vagus nerve stimulation (highly refractory)
Psilocybin / MDMA-assisted therapy — research / approved in some jurisdictions
Step 5 — Acute high-risk: admit, intensive treatment + 1:1 if suicide risk
SUICIDE PREVENTION:
Means restriction (firearms, paracetamol > 32 g — packaging legislation, pesticides — Sri Lanka model)
Safety planning (Stanley-Brown)
Lithium for chronic suicidal in mood disorder (NEJM RCT)
Ketamine acute for suicide ideation
Crisis line, follow-up within 7 days post-discharge
PREGNANCY: continue SSRI (sertraline preferred) for mod-severe; balance teratogenic + relapse risk; risk of untreated MDD in pregnancy > medication risk; CBT/IPT first-line mild
BREASTFEEDING: sertraline, paroxetine compatible (low infant levels)
PAEDIATRIC: fluoxetine first-line (only SSRI with adequate evidence); CBT/IPT first-line; risk of suicidal ideation increase short-term — monitor closely
ELDERLY: start low go slow; sertraline / mirtazapine well-tolerated; avoid TCA (anticholinergic + falls); HypoNa risk SSRI/SNRI — monitor
BIPOLAR DEPRESSION (different — do NOT antidepressant alone — switch to mania): quetiapine, lurasidone, lithium, lamotrigine, olanzapine+fluoxetine
PHYSICAL HEALTH: depression doubles CV mortality — address smoking, exercise, weight, diabetes
Kenya / SSA: integrate into primary care per mhGAP; counsellor cadre; community-delivered Friendship Bench (Zimbabwe — Lancet trial); Thinking Healthy peripartum; Empower digital
