title: Bipolar disorder — comprehensive management
population: Adults — lifetime prevalence ~1–2% bipolar I, 2% bipolar II. High suicide mortality (15–20× general). Bimodal onset.
presentation: Bipolar I — mania ± depression; bipolar II — hypomania ± depression. Mixed features. Rapid cycling (≥ 4 episodes/year). Mania: elevated/irritable mood + ↑ activity + decreased sleep + grandiosity + racing thoughts + risk-taking. Depression: as MDD but recognition critical — antidepressant monotherapy contraindicated.
redFlags: Acute mania with psychosis / aggression / suicide risk — admit
Rapid cycling (poor prognosis, requires mood stabiliser optimisation)
Antidepressant-induced mania — stop antidepressant, mood stabiliser
Pregnancy planning on teratogenic mood stabiliser (valproate AVOID WCBP)
diagnostics: Mood Disorder Questionnaire (MDQ), HCL-32 for hypomania case-finding
Comprehensive psychiatric history (essential — first-episode depression in young / family history bipolar = high risk; do not antidepressant alone)
Family history (highly heritable)
TSH, glucose, FBC, U&E, LFT, Mg, Ca (lithium / valproate baseline)
Pregnancy test in WCBP before valproate (BLACK BOX warning)
Substance + alcohol use
Brain imaging if first episode, atypical, neurological signs
management: ACUTE MANIA:
Stop antidepressant if on
Mood stabiliser + antipsychotic:
Lithium 600–1200 mg/day (target 0.6–1.0 mmol/L acute, 0.4–0.8 maintenance)
Valproate (sodium valproate 600–2000 mg/day, target 50–125 mcg/mL) — AVOID WCBP
Carbamazepine alternative
Antipsychotic: olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole, asenapine, cariprazine, lurasidone
Benzodiazepine short-term for agitation / sleep
ECT for severe / refractory / pregnancy
BIPOLAR DEPRESSION:
AVOID antidepressant monotherapy
Quetiapine 300 mg/day (good evidence)
Lurasidone 20–120 mg/day
Olanzapine + fluoxetine (Symbyax)
Lithium
Lamotrigine (slow titration — SJS risk; better for maintenance than acute)
Cariprazine (BIPOLAR-1, BIPOLAR-2 trials)
Pramipexole emerging
Antidepressant only ADJUNCTIVELY to mood stabiliser, careful monitor
MAINTENANCE:
Lithium first-line (suicide-protective + most robust evidence; monitor renal/thyroid/Ca every 6 months)
Valproate (NOT WCBP)
Quetiapine, olanzapine, lurasidone, aripiprazole
Lamotrigine (better for depression prevention)
Long-term — most need lifelong
PSYCHOSOCIAL:
Psychoeducation
Interpersonal social rhythm therapy (IPSRT)
Family-focused therapy
CBT for depression
Mood charting + sleep regulation
PREGNANCY:
AVOID valproate (PRECAUTIONS — National Pregnancy Prevention Programme; contraception confirmed before each dispense)
Lithium — small risk Ebstein's (debated); withdraw 24h pre-delivery + restart immediately postpartum
Lamotrigine — safer; monitor levels (clearance changes pregnancy)
Olanzapine, quetiapine — preferred antipsychotics
ECT safe + effective
Postpartum prophylaxis CRITICAL (50–70% recurrence)
LITHIUM TOXICITY (level > 1.2):
Mild (1.2–1.5): GI, tremor, drowsiness — hold lithium, hydrate
Moderate (1.5–2.5): confusion, ataxia, dysarthria, hyperreflexia
Severe (> 2.5): coma, seizure, arrhythmia — dialysis
Causes: dehydration, NSAID, ACE-i, diuretic, low-salt diet, fever — review drug interactions
PHYSICAL HEALTH: high CV mortality, metabolic syndrome on antipsychotic; annual screening (BP, HbA1c, lipids, weight); manage tobacco, ETOH (very common comorbidity)
SUBSTANCE USE comorbidity high — integrate addiction treatment
Kenya / SSA: under-diagnosed; mhGAP psychosis-bipolar module for primary care; carbamazepine and chlorpromazine widely available; lithium less so but on KEML

title: Schizophrenia + first-episode psychosis — EIP teams
population: Lifetime prevalence ~ 1%; first episode adolescent / young adult (mostly < 30). Duration of untreated psychosis (DUP) inversely correlates with outcome.
presentation: Positive (hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech/behaviour), negative (avolition, alogia, anhedonia, social withdrawal), cognitive (attention, working memory, processing speed), affective.
redFlags: First-episode psychosis — refer Early Intervention Psychosis (EIP) team within 2 weeks
Acute severe psychosis with risk to self / others — admit
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rigidity + hyperthermia + altered mental state + autonomic) — STOP antipsychotic
Clozapine: agranulocytosis (FBC monitoring), myocarditis, ileus, hypersalivation
Suspected organic / drug-induced (cannabis, methamphetamine, cocaine, anti-NMDA encephalitis)
diagnostics: Mental state examination — full psychiatric
Risk assessment (self + others)
Substance use (toxicology screen, urine drug)
Rule out medical: FBC, U&E, LFT, TSH, glucose, B12, Ca, syphilis (especially HIV+), HIV, vitamin D
Brain MRI if first episode, atypical, neuro signs
EEG if seizure / encephalopathy suspected
Anti-NMDA receptor + paraneoplastic antibodies if encephalopathy / women / new
ECG before antipsychotic (QTc, baseline + on therapy)
Family history
management: EARLY INTERVENTION PSYCHOSIS (EIP) — best outcomes:
Multidisciplinary team (psychiatrist, CPN, psychologist, OT, care coordinator)
3-year intensive follow-up post first episode (OPUS trial — better outcomes)
Family education + support
Vocational + educational rehabilitation (supported employment / education)
CBT for psychosis (CBTp)
Cognitive remediation
ANTIPSYCHOTIC (start LOW, go SLOW for first episode):
Atypical first-line: risperidone 0.5–1 mg titrate to 2–6 mg; aripiprazole 5–15 mg; olanzapine 5–20 mg (metabolic concerns); quetiapine; paliperidone; ziprasidone
Avoid haloperidol high-dose first-line (EPS in naïve patient)
Discuss long-acting injectable (LAI) early — improves adherence, reduces relapse + mortality (Tiihonen et al)
Switch if no response by 4–6 weeks at therapeutic dose; trial 2–3 antipsychotics before deeming treatment-resistant
TREATMENT-RESISTANT SCHIZOPHRENIA (failed 2+ adequate trials):
CLOZAPINE — only evidence-based treatment for TRS
Start 12.5 mg, titrate over 2–3 weeks to 300–450 mg/d
Mandatory FBC monitoring: weekly × 18 weeks, then 2-weekly × 1 year, then monthly

Side effects: agranulocytosis (rare 1%), myocarditis (months 1–3 — high mortality if missed; monitor troponin/CRP/ECG weekly first 6 weeks), hypersalivation, sedation, weight gain, seizure (lower threshold), constipation/ileus (BLACK BOX), DKA / metabolic
Augmentation if partial response: amisulpride, aripiprazole, ECT
PSYCHOSOCIAL (always combine):
CBTp
Family intervention
Vocational rehabilitation
Lifestyle / metabolic monitoring
Smoking cessation (very high prevalence — bupropion / NRT)
Substance use treatment
Housing + financial support
PHYSICAL HEALTH (huge mortality gap 15-20 yr — mostly CV):
Annual: BMI, BP, HbA1c, lipids, ECG, FBC (clozapine)
Address tobacco (60%), obesity, DM, dyslipidaemia, OSA
Move metabolic care to primary care with shared protocols
ACUTE MANAGEMENT (agitation / aggression):
De-escalation first (verbal, environment)
Oral medication preferred: olanzapine 10 mg, risperidone 2 mg, lorazepam 1–2 mg
IM if refusing PO: olanzapine 10 mg IM (NOT with IV benzodiazepine — respiratory arrest risk), aripiprazole 9.75 mg IM, haloperidol 5 mg + lorazepam 2 mg IM
AVOID PRN polypharmacy
Watch akathisia (often mistaken for worsening psychosis — propranolol / benzodiazepine)
RELAPSE PREVENTION:
Long-acting injectable (LAI) — every 2–4 weeks (paliperidone, risperidone, aripiprazole long-acting); LAI = 3-month and 6-month formulations available (Invega Trinza / Hafyera)
Adherence support
Identify early warning signs
Manage stress
PREGNANCY / breastfeeding: olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole preferred; avoid carbamazepine + valproate; balance teratogen + maternal stability

Kenya / SSA: mhGAP psychosis-bipolar module, chlorpromazine + haloperidol on KEML (escalation to atypicals needed); LAI access expanding; mental health investment per Kenya Mental Health Policy 2015 + Kenya Mental Health Action Plan

title: Alcohol use disorder — withdrawal + medication-assisted treatment
population: Adults — third leading cause of preventable death globally; growing SSA burden including paediatric/adolescent (chang'aa, illicit brews). Kenya prevalence high; NACADA national agency.
presentation: Use disorder (DSM-5 / ICD-11) — 11 criteria, mild 2-3 / moderate 4-5 / severe ≥ 6. Acute intoxication, withdrawal, complications (gastritis, hepatitis, pancreatitis, neuropathy, Wernicke's-Korsakoff, FAS).
redFlags: Severe withdrawal (CIWA-Ar ≥ 15) — admit + IV benzodiazepine + thiamine
Delirium tremens (24–72h withdrawal — confusion + autonomic + hallucinations + mortality 1–5%)
Withdrawal seizures (12–48h, first time presents in acute withdrawal usually)
Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion + ataxia + ophthalmoplegia — emergency IV thiamine)
diagnostics: AUDIT-C (screening — ≥ 4 men / ≥ 3 women positive) / AUDIT-10 (full screen)
CAGE / TWEAK questionnaire
GGT, AST/ALT (AST:ALT > 2), MCV (raised), carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT)
Severity scoring withdrawal — CIWA-Ar
Comprehensive history: pattern, last drink, withdrawal history, complications, family, social, comorbidity
Pregnancy test
FBC, LFT, glucose, U&E, Mg, PO4 (refeeding), B12, folate
Urine toxicology (concomitant substance use)
Echo if cardiomyopathy suspected
management: BRIEF INTERVENTION + MOTIVATIONAL INTERVIEWING (primary care):
AUDIT-positive — assess motivation + provide structured advice
Effective in primary care for hazardous drinking
FRAMES (Feedback, Responsibility, Advice, Menu, Empathy, Self-efficacy)
DETOXIFICATION (medically supervised):
CIWA-Ar guided benzodiazepine: chlordiazepoxide 20–40 mg q6h tapering over 5–7 days (long half-life; lower hepatotoxicity)
OR diazepam 10–20 mg q6h taper
Lorazepam in hepatic impairment (shorter half-life, no active metabolites)
THIAMINE 100 mg IV / IM × 3 days then PO 100 mg TDS — ALL patients (prevents Wernicke; high-dose Pabrinex IV in malnourished / severe withdrawal)
IV THIAMINE BEFORE glucose (giving glucose first depletes residual thiamine — precipitates Wernicke)
Folate 5 mg, multivitamin, Mg + PO4 (refeeding risk in malnourished)
Hydration + electrolyte correction
DELIRIUM TREMENS — emergency:
HDU/ICU
IV diazepam 10 mg q5–10 min titrate to sedation; may need very large doses
Severe / refractory: phenobarbital, propofol, dexmedetomidine
Continuous monitoring (HR, BP, temperature)
Hydration, electrolytes
Identify triggers (infection, GIB, intracranial pathology)
WITHDRAWAL SEIZURES:
Benzodiazepine (treats withdrawal — prevents further)
Phenytoin NOT effective for alcohol withdrawal seizure
AED only if persistent / status / underlying epilepsy
WERNICKE'S ENCEPHALOPATHY:
IV thiamine 500 mg TDS × 2-3 days then 250 mg daily × 5 days then oral
In ANY alcoholic patient with confusion / cognitive change — empirically give before workup
Refeeding hyperglycaemia worsens — be cautious with glucose
MAINTENANCE / MEDICATION-ASSISTED TREATMENT (MAT) — post-detox:
NALTREXONE oral 50 mg/d or LAI 380 mg/month (Vivitrol) — opioid receptor antagonist, reduces craving + relapse (COMBINE trial)
ACAMPROSATE 333 mg × 2 TDS — modulates glutamate, reduces craving (especially abstinence-oriented)
DISULFIRAM (Antabuse) 250 mg/d — aversive (alcohol-induced reaction); only for highly motivated supervised
Topiramate, gabapentin — off-label evidence
Baclofen — emerging, especially cirrhosis (safer than benzodiazepine maintenance)
Combine with psychosocial — Alcoholics Anonymous (12-step), CBT, motivational enhancement therapy, contingency management
PSYCHOSOCIAL:
CBT, motivational interviewing, 12-step facilitation
Family therapy
Treat comorbidity (depression, anxiety, PTSD, ADHD — often co-existing)
Address social determinants
ALCOHOLIC LIVER DISEASE:
Cessation
Severe alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey > 32, MELD > 21): prednisolone 40 mg × 28 d (response by Lille score day 7); pentoxifylline alternative; consider early liver transplant for selected (DIALCOHOL)
HCC surveillance
Nutrition support — high protein 1.2–1.5 g/kg
POPULATION + PUBLIC HEALTH:

WHO SAFER framework: Strengthen alcohol availability restrictions, Advance + enforce drink-driving counter-measures, Facilitate access to screening + treatment, Enforce bans on alcohol marketing, Raise prices through taxation
Kenya: NACADA (National Authority for the Campaign Against Alcohol and Drug Abuse), Alcoholic Drinks Control Act 2010
FETAL ALCOHOL SPECTRUM DISORDERS prevention: counsel WCBP, no safe amount in pregnancy
Adolescent: CRAFFT screen, parental + school engagement
Driving: legal — counsel; mandatory reporting in some jurisdictions

references.label: WHO Brief Interventions Alcohol Use Disorders (AUDIT, brief intervention)
Kenya NACADA + Alcoholic Drinks Control Act 2010

title: Opioid use disorder (OUD) — medication-assisted treatment (MAT)
population: Adults using opioids — heroin / fentanyl / prescription. SSA emerging including Kenya coast (heroin), urban areas. Strong link to HIV / hepatitis C transmission via IDU.
presentation: Opioid use despite harms; tolerance; withdrawal on stopping (myalgia, sweating, GI, anxiety, insomnia, piloerection, mydriasis); overdose risk.
redFlags: Pregnancy with OUD — methadone or buprenorphine treatment (NOT abrupt withdrawal)
Comorbid HIV / hepatitis C — link to care
Recent release from incarceration / overdose / drug-free period (rapid loss of tolerance, high overdose risk)
diagnostics: DSM-5 / ICD-11 11 criteria — moderate-severe OUD requires medical treatment
Urine drug screen (UDS) — opioid panel + fentanyl + xylazine; methadone metabolite (EDDP) for adherence
Withdrawal: COWS (Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale) for buprenorphine induction
HIV, hepatitis B + C, syphilis, TB (testing essential)
Pregnancy test
FBC, LFT, U&E, ECG (methadone QTc)
management: MEDICATION-ASSISTED TREATMENT (MAT) — first-line, evidence-based, reduces mortality, infection, crime, family disruption:
METHADONE — full mu-opioid agonist:
Daily supervised dispensing (DOT) at clinic / pharmacy initially
Start 30 mg, titrate over weeks to 60–120 mg (target ↓ withdrawal + ↓ use + ↓ cravings without sedation)
Long half-life — accumulates first week (avoid rapid escalation — overdose risk)
QTc monitoring (especially > 100 mg/d, on QT-prolonging drugs)
Drug interactions — CYP3A4 (rifampicin, antiretrovirals — dose adjustment)
Cardiac, sedative interaction with benzodiazepines
BUPRENORPHINE — partial mu-opioid agonist (ceiling effect — safer):
Sublingual (Subutex 0.4–32 mg) or combination with naloxone (Suboxone — abuse-deterrent)
INDUCTION: COWS ≥ 8 (sufficient withdrawal) — give 2–4 mg → repeat q1–2h up to 8 mg day 1, then titrate to 8–24 mg/d
Precipitated withdrawal if given too early (still on full agonist) — wait until COWS ≥ 12
Microinduction / low-dose approach for fentanyl users (Bernese method) — avoids precipitated withdrawal
Long-acting injectable buprenorphine (Sublocade monthly, Brixadi weekly/monthly)
Office-based / primary care prescribing — increased access
Safer overdose profile than methadone (ceiling effect)
EXTENDED-RELEASE NALTREXONE (Vivitrol) 380 mg IM monthly:
Mu-opioid antagonist
Requires 7–10 days opioid-free first (induction barrier)
Useful for highly motivated, post-incarceration, post-treatment
Adherence concern
Avoid abrupt withdrawal alone — high relapse + overdose
OVERDOSE PREVENTION:
Take-home naloxone for all OUD + family
Co-prescribed naloxone with prescription opioids > 50 MME
Bystander training
Fentanyl test strips
Supervised consumption sites (where legal)
PSYCHOSOCIAL:
CBT, motivational interviewing, contingency management
Narcotics Anonymous, SMART Recovery
Trauma-informed care (PTSD common in OUD)
Treat comorbid mental illness
PREGNANCY:
Methadone OR buprenorphine — both first-line
Do NOT withdraw abruptly (fetal distress, miscarriage)
Neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS) — supportive, morphine taper if severe; reduced by maternal buprenorphine vs methadone (MOTHER trial)
Breastfeeding compatible with both (low transfer)
Coordinated obstetric + addiction + paediatric care
INFECTIOUS DISEASE:
HIV testing + linkage to ART; PrEP for HIV-negative high-risk
Hepatitis C: pan-genotypic DAA 8–12 weeks (cure — separate condition); link to treatment regardless of active use (REACH HCV)
Hepatitis B testing + vaccination
Soft tissue infection management (abscess drainage, cellulitis, endocarditis — high risk)
Safer use education: never alone, sterile equipment, needle exchange, syringe service programmes (SSPs)
POST-INCARCERATION:
Continue MAT through transitions (jail health programmes)
Linkage on release CRITICAL (high overdose mortality first 2 weeks)
Naloxone on release
SSA / Kenya specifically:
MAT programmes expanding — Kenya started 2014, Mombasa + Nairobi clinics; methadone + buprenorphine
NACADA + harm reduction services
Address stigma — chronic relapsing disease, not moral failure
Link with HIV / TB / hepatitis services (integrated model)
Needle exchange + outreach

references.label: WHO Community Management of Opioid Overdose 2014
WHO Guidelines for Pharmacological Treatment of OUD 2009 + 2024 update
NIDA Principles of Drug Addiction Treatment 2018
REACH HCV (treat regardless of active use)
Kenya MOH + NACADA Medication-Assisted Therapy Programme

title: PTSD — trauma-focused therapy + first-line treatments
population: Lifetime prevalence ~ 7%; conflict-affected populations + IPV survivors + first responders + refugees substantially higher. Kenya / SSA: post-election violence, IPV, refugee populations.
presentation: After traumatic exposure: re-experiencing (flashbacks, nightmares, intrusive memories), avoidance, hyperarousal (startle, vigilance, insomnia), negative cognitions/mood — symptoms > 1 month with functional impairment. Complex PTSD (ICD-11) adds disturbed self-organisation, emotion regulation, relational difficulties.
redFlags: Acute stress disorder evolving to PTSD (3 d–1 mo post-trauma — opportunity for early intervention)
diagnostics: PCL-5 (PTSD Checklist for DSM-5) — screening + monitoring
CAPS-5 (Clinician-Administered) — diagnostic gold standard
Trauma history + assessment of cognitive + emotional impact
PHQ-9 (depression), GAD-7 (anxiety), AUDIT (alcohol), substance use screen
Suicide + safety assessment
Sleep assessment
management: PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST-LINE (preferred over medication):
TRAUMA-FOCUSED CBT (TF-CBT) — gold standard
Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT)
Prolonged Exposure (PE)
EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitisation + Reprocessing)
Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET) — efficacious in conflict-affected populations
WHO Self-Help+ (PM+, GPM+) — task-shifted LMIC interventions
PHARMACOTHERAPY (second-line OR adjunct OR if therapy unavailable):
SSRI: sertraline 50–200 mg, paroxetine 20–60 mg (FDA-approved for PTSD)
SNRI: venlafaxine 75–225 mg
Allow 8–12 weeks therapeutic dose before declaring non-response
Continue 6–12 months minimum after response
Mirtazapine for sleep + appetite component
Prazosin for nightmares (1–10 mg nocte — α1 antagonist, mixed evidence)
EMERGING:
MDMA-assisted psychotherapy (Phase 3 — approval pending FDA)
Psilocybin-assisted therapy (research)
Ketamine — emerging evidence for PTSD
Stellate ganglion block — case series
AVOID:
Benzodiazepines (worsen PTSD long-term; increase risk dependence)
Single-session debriefing immediately after trauma (no benefit; may worsen — psychological debriefing meta-analysis)
Polypharmacy
ADJUNCTS:
Sleep hygiene + CBT-I for insomnia
Exercise, mindfulness, yoga
Group / peer support (especially veterans, refugees)
Substance use treatment (comorbid)
ACUTE STRESS DISORDER (within 1 month):
Watchful waiting + supportive — many recover spontaneously
Early TF-CBT for moderate-severe (5 sessions reduces PTSD development — Bryant)
Avoid pharmacotherapy + debriefing routinely
COMPLEX PTSD:
STAIR + NST (Skills Training in Affective and Interpersonal Regulation + Narrative Story Telling)
Mentalisation-based therapy
DBT skills training
Longer-duration trauma-focused therapy
Emotion regulation + self-care focus initial phase
REFUGEE / CONFLICT-AFFECTED (LMIC + SSA):
WHO Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP)
Lay-counsellor delivered (Friendship Bench Zimbabwe, Problem Management Plus, NET)
Address social determinants (housing, legal status, family reunification)
Cultural adaptation of interventions
Kenya — Dadaab + Kakuma refugee mental health programmes
PAEDIATRIC PTSD:
TF-CBT (developmentally adapted)
Caregiver involvement
School-based interventions
Avoid pharmacotherapy first-line

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Management of Conditions Specifically Related to Stress 2013/2024
Bryant et al. Early TF-CBT for ASD/PTSD
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders (mhGAP adaptation), Ministry of Health

title: Anxiety disorders — generalised + panic + social, stepped care
population: Common — lifetime prevalence GAD 5%, panic 4%, SAD 12%. Often comorbid with depression + substance use.
presentation: GAD: persistent excessive worry, restlessness, muscle tension, irritability, sleep disturbance, fatigue. Panic: discrete attacks of intense fear + somatic symptoms + agoraphobia. SAD: fear of social judgement.
redFlags: Medical mimics: hyperthyroidism, phaeo, arrhythmia, cardiac, asthma, drugs (caffeine, decongestant, stimulant, withdrawal)
diagnostics: GAD-7 (generalised anxiety severity)
PHQ-9 (depression comorbidity)
Panic Disorder Severity Scale
Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale
Rule out medical: TSH, glucose, ECG (palpitations), urinary metanephrines if phaeo features, FBC
Substance / caffeine / alcohol screen
Sleep, exercise, diet, stressors
management: STEPPED CARE (NICE CG113 GAD, NICE CG113 panic):
Step 1 — Identify + assess + provide education
Step 2 — Low-intensity intervention:
Guided self-help (CBT-based)
Digital CBT (e.g. SilverCloud, Big White Wall)
Psychoeducation groups
Behavioural activation, breathing techniques, progressive muscle relaxation
Step 3 — High-intensity psychological OR medication:
CBT (individual face-to-face, 12–20 sessions; best evidence)
Applied relaxation
ACT (Acceptance + Commitment Therapy)
MEDICATION (when patient prefers / severe / failed psych):
SSRI first-line — sertraline (preferred — fewer interactions), escitalopram, citalopram
SNRI — venlafaxine, duloxetine
PRN benzodiazepine NOT recommended (dependence) — but selected short-course for acute crisis
Pregabalin for GAD (alternative; abuse potential)
Buspirone for GAD (mild)
Propranolol for performance anxiety (situational)
Avoid TCA / MAOI first-line (side effects)
Step 4 — Specialist + complex care:
Combination CBT + SSRI
Augmentation (atypical antipsychotic adjunct, if very refractory)
Treat comorbidity
SPECIFIC:
PANIC DISORDER: CBT (panic-focused — interoceptive exposure + cognitive restructuring); SSRI; AVOID benzodiazepine maintenance
AGORAPHOBIA: exposure-based CBT, SSRI
SOCIAL ANXIETY DISORDER: CBT (group-based), SSRI, performance anxiety — propranolol PRN
SPECIFIC PHOBIA: graded exposure
OCD (related): CBT with ERP (exposure + response prevention), SSRI higher doses
HEALTH ANXIETY: CBT, mindfulness
BENZODIAZEPINES:
AVOID long-term (dependence, falls in elderly, cognitive impairment, road traffic accidents)
Short-term (< 4 weeks) for severe acute crisis only
Lorazepam, diazepam, alprazolam
Taper carefully (10–25% q1–2 weeks) if dependent — never stop abruptly (withdrawal seizures, anxiety rebound)
PREGNANCY: sertraline preferred SSRI; CBT first-line for mild-moderate
PAEDIATRIC: CBT first-line; fluoxetine + sertraline approved
ELDERLY: SSRI start low; avoid benzodiazepine (falls); CBT effective; treat comorbid depression
LIFESTYLE: exercise (anxiolytic effect), reduce caffeine + ETOH + recreational drugs, sleep hygiene, mindfulness
MAINTENANCE: continue medication ≥ 6–12 months after response

references.label: NICE CG113 Generalised Anxiety Disorder + Panic Disorder 2011 + 2024 update

title: Eating disorders — anorexia, bulimia, binge eating disorder
population: AN lifetime prevalence ~ 1% women; BN 1–2%; BED 3–5%; rising in adolescent, men, LMIC. Highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder (AN).
presentation: AN: restricted intake → low BMI + intense fear of weight gain + body image distortion. BN: binge + compensatory (vomiting, laxative, exercise, fasting). BED: binge without compensatory. ARFID, OSFED.
redFlags: Refeeding syndrome (PO4, K, Mg, thiamine deficiency)
Pregnancy with eating disorder (relapse risk, perinatal complications)
diagnostics: Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q), SCOFF, EAT-26
Comprehensive assessment: history, eating pattern, exercise, compensatory behaviours, body image, comorbidity
MEDICAL: weight + height + BMI; HR + BP (lying + standing — orthostasis); temperature; ECG (QTc, bradycardia)
Blood: FBC + U&E + LFT + glucose + Mg + PO4 + Ca + bone profile + albumin + thyroid + B12 + folate
Urinalysis (ketones), pregnancy
DEXA bone density (AN with > 6 months amenorrhoea / low BMI)
Mental health: PHQ-9 + GAD-7 + self-harm history
Family + social assessment
management: ANOREXIA NERVOSA:
Multidisciplinary team (eating disorder specialist + dietitian + psychiatrist + GP)
Adolescents: FAMILY-BASED TREATMENT (FBT, 'Maudsley') — first-line, evidence-based
Adults: CBT-ED (eating disorder-focused CBT), MANTRA, SSCM
Nutritional rehabilitation — START LOW (1200–1400 kcal/day initially), increase gradually to prevent REFEEDING SYNDROME (cardiac failure, hypophosphataemia)
Refeeding electrolyte monitoring daily — PO4 + K + Mg + glucose; replace BEFORE starting feeding if low; thiamine 200 mg/day
Weight target — restore to healthy BMI (≥ 18.5 adult; for child — appropriate centile)
Medication NOT first-line for AN itself; olanzapine low-dose may help weight + anxiety in some; SSRI for comorbid depression/anxiety AFTER weight restored (less effective in starved state)
Bone health: DEXA, vitamin D + calcium; oestrogen replacement controversial
Admission criteria: BMI < 13, rapid weight loss, severe electrolyte disturbance, cardiovascular instability, severe self-harm / suicide
BULIMIA NERVOSA:
CBT-ED first-line (NICE / guideline-recommended)
Interpersonal therapy (IPT) alternative
Medication: fluoxetine 60 mg/d (higher than typical depression dose) — FDA-approved
Address electrolyte (hypoK from vomiting); IV K replacement if severe
Dental + oesophageal review
BINGE EATING DISORDER (BED):
CBT-ED (guided self-help) first-line
IPT alternative
Medication: lisdexamfetamine FDA-approved (caution stimulant abuse); SSRI; topiramate
Address obesity + comorbidity (separate)
Bariatric surgery + BED: treat BED first; risk of relapse post-op
ARFID (Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder):
Multidisciplinary including dietitian + OT + psychology
Family-based intervention
Address sensory issues + autism comorbidity
MEDICAL EMERGENCIES:
Cardiovascular instability — IV fluids cautiously
Refeeding hypophosphataemia — IV phosphate
Bradyarrhythmia — atropine, pacing if needed
Suicide / self-harm — psychiatric admission
INPATIENT vs OUTPATIENT:
Most can be treated outpatient with intensive support
Specialist eating disorder unit for severe (lower mortality than general psych)
Avoid prolonged hospitalisation (institutionalisation; learn coping in real-life setting)
FOLLOW-UP: long-term — relapse common; integrate physical + mental health monitoring
FAMILY support + education
Comorbidity (depression, anxiety, OCD, substance use, BPD) — integrate treatment
Pregnancy: relapse common; specialist multi-D care; nutritional support
Athletes / weight-class sports: high prevalence — screening + education
SSA emerging awareness — under-recognised, often presents late

references.label: AED Critical Points for Early Recognition 2024
APA Guideline for Treatment of Eating Disorders 2023
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: ADHD — child + adult comprehensive management
population: Children: prevalence 5–7%; ~ 60% persist into adulthood. Adults: prevalence 2.5%; high under-diagnosis especially women + minorities + LMIC.
presentation: Triad: inattention + hyperactivity + impulsivity. Subtypes: predominantly inattentive (more women + adults), hyperactive-impulsive, combined. Chronic, pervasive (≥ 2 settings), onset before age 12, functional impairment.
redFlags: Comorbid (very common — > 50%): ODD/CD, mood, anxiety, learning disability, autism, tic disorder, substance use
Cardiovascular RFs / family sudden cardiac death — caution stimulants
Pregnancy with ADHD on stimulants — risk-benefit
Substance misuse / diversion potential with stimulants
diagnostics: Comprehensive history — symptoms + onset + duration + pervasiveness + impairment
Multiple informants (parent + teacher + self)
Rating scales: SNAP-IV (parent + teacher), Conners, ASRS-v1.1 (adult)
DSM-5 / ICD-11 criteria — ≥ 6 inattention OR ≥ 6 hyperactivity-impulsivity (≥ 5 if ≥ 17 yr)
Rule out: hearing/vision, sleep disorder, anxiety, depression, learning disability, autism, substance use, medical (thyroid, anaemia, lead)
Cardiovascular screen: family history sudden death / cardiac, ECG if abnormal screening
Educational + psychological assessment for learning + IQ
Comorbidity screening
management: BEHAVIOURAL + EDUCATIONAL (foundation):
CHILDREN (preschool first-line): parent training, behaviour management, school accommodations (IEP, 504 plans), structured routines
Adults: CBT for adult ADHD (skills, organisation, planning); coaching
Family + couple therapy
Educational support — extra time, organisational support, skills training
Sleep hygiene + exercise + nutrition (omega-3 modest evidence)
Mindfulness — emerging evidence
PHARMACOTHERAPY:
CHILDREN ≥ 6 + ADULTS — STIMULANTS FIRST-LINE (most effective):
METHYLPHENIDATE (Ritalin, Concerta, Medikinet, Equasym) — first-line by many
LISDEXAMFETAMINE (Vyvanse / Elvanse) — prodrug, smoother profile
AMPHETAMINE / DEXAMPHETAMINE (Adderall — combination)
Long-acting preferred for adherence + abuse-deterrent
Titrate slowly, monitor response + side effects (appetite suppression, sleep, mood, weight + height in children, BP, HR)
Annual screening: BP, HR, weight, height (children), mental state
Stimulant holiday during weekends / holidays — child-individualised (growth + appetite balance)
PRE-SCHOOL (< 6 yr): behavioural first; methylphenidate only if severe + behavioural failed
NON-STIMULANTS (second-line OR comorbid tic, anxiety, substance abuse):
Atomoxetine (Strattera) — SNRI; suicidal ideation black box
Guanfacine ER (Intuniv), clonidine XR — α2 agonist; tic + sleep helpful
Bupropion off-label adult
Viloxazine (Qelbree) NEW
COMBINATION stimulant + α2 agonist for partial response
AVOID stimulants if: severe CV disease, structural heart abnormality, hyperthyroidism, glaucoma, acute psychosis, severe substance abuse
TRANSITION: child → adult care; many drop out at 18 (high-risk period)
PREGNANCY: limited safety data; risk-benefit; methylphenidate / dexamphetamine if benefits outweigh
DRIVING / OCCUPATIONAL: counsel — improvement with treatment generally
COMORBIDITY:
Anxiety: SSRI + ADHD med
Depression: SSRI + ADHD med
Substance use: cautious stimulant; lisdexamfetamine (less abuse) or atomoxetine; treat SUD
ODD/CD: parent training, family therapy
Sleep: sleep hygiene + melatonin
Autism: tailored — ADHD treatment can worsen autism core symptoms; careful
ADULT NEW DIAGNOSIS:
Comprehensive history (childhood + adult)
Specialist confirmation usually required
Functional + occupational + relationship assessment
Treatment usually combined CBT + medication
Many women diagnosed in adulthood — recognise inattentive presentation
PUBLIC HEALTH / SCHOOL:
Teacher training
Accommodations + universal design
Anti-stigma
SSA: very under-diagnosed; primary care training; access to medication limited (methylphenidate on KEML Kenya)

title: Dementia + cognitive impairment — diagnosis + management
population: 55 million globally + rising; SSA emerging epidemic with ageing populations + lower awareness; mostly Alzheimer's, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal, mixed.
presentation: Progressive cognitive decline in memory + at least one other domain (executive, language, visuospatial, attention, social cognition) + functional impairment. Behavioural + psychological symptoms (BPSD).
redFlags: Sudden / rapid decline — exclude delirium, stroke, NPH, depression, autoimmune encephalitis
Atypical features (early severe behaviour change, primary visual problems, motor signs) — refer
Hallucinations + visual + fluctuation + parkinsonism — Lewy body (avoid antipsychotics)
diagnostics: MoCA (preferred over MMSE — more sensitive for MCI / Alzheimer)
Detailed cognitive assessment + functional (ADL, IADL)
Caregiver / informant history (Cornell Behavioural Pathology Rating Scale, NPI-Q)
Mood screen (GDS, HADS — depression mimics dementia)
Physical + neurological exam
Reversible causes screen: TSH, B12, folate, FBC, U&E, LFT, glucose, calcium, vit D, HIV (especially LMIC + < 65), syphilis, ammonia, urinary screening, sleep apnoea, drug review
Neuroimaging: MRI (preferred, atrophy pattern + vascular load) or CT (rule out structural / NPH)
Functional imaging if needed: FDG-PET (Alzheimer pattern), DaT scan (Lewy body)
CSF AD biomarkers — amyloid + tau (specialist; emerging plasma assays — pTau217 — promising)
Genetics if young onset / family history
Driving assessment + capacity assessment
management: DISEASE-MODIFYING (NEW for early Alzheimer's):
ANTI-AMYLOID MONOCLONAL ANTIBODIES:
LECANEMAB (Leqembi) — FDA-approved 2023 — for early symptomatic AD with confirmed amyloid
IV infusion biweekly; ARIA-E (oedema) + ARIA-H (haemorrhage) — MRI surveillance
Modest cognitive slowing (CLARITY-AD)
DONANEMAB — FDA-approved 2024 (TRAILBLAZER-ALZ2) — similar profile, can stop when amyloid cleared
APOE genotyping recommended (homozygous E4 — higher ARIA risk)
Cost + access barriers significant (especially SSA)
Aducanumab — controversial, mostly withdrawn
SYMPTOMATIC TREATMENT (still mainstay especially LMIC):
Cholinesterase inhibitors — mild-moderate AD, mixed, DLB, PDD:
Donepezil 5–10 mg/d (most common)
Rivastigmine (oral or patch — useful in nausea, swallowing difficulty)
Galantamine
Common side effects: nausea, diarrhoea, bradycardia (ECG), syncope, nightmares
Memantine — NMDA antagonist; moderate-severe AD; add to ChEI
No good evidence for vascular / FTD specifically
NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL (foundation):
Cognitive stimulation therapy
Physical activity (CV risk reduction + cognitive benefit)
Mediterranean / MIND diet
Hearing + vision optimisation (Lancet Commission modifiable risk factor)
Social engagement
Manage CV risk factors aggressively (HTN, DM, lipids, smoking, obesity)
Sleep hygiene + OSA treatment
Limit alcohol
RISK FACTOR MODIFICATION (Lancet Commission 2024 — 14 modifiable RFs, ~ 45% of dementia attributable):
Lower education, hearing loss, hypertension, smoking, obesity, depression, physical inactivity, diabetes, alcohol, traumatic brain injury, air pollution, social isolation, vision loss, high LDL
FINGER trial (multidomain intervention) — improves cognition
BPSD (behavioural + psychological symptoms):
Non-pharm FIRST — DICE approach (Describe, Investigate, Create, Evaluate)
Identify + treat triggers (pain, infection, constipation, hunger, sleep, environment, fear)
Caregiver education + support
Music therapy + reminiscence + activity
PRN antipsychotic for severe (risperidone, olanzapine) — limit, BLACK BOX increased mortality in dementia
AVOID antipsychotic in LEWY BODY (severe sensitivity)
Trazodone, mirtazapine for sleep / agitation
Cholinesterase inhibitor may help BPSD in DLB
Avoid benzodiazepine (delirium, falls, sedation)
DELIRIUM (commonly overlaid):
Identify + treat cause (infection, drug, dehydration, retention)
Reorientation, family presence, lighting, mobilisation
Pharm only severe behavioural — low-dose haloperidol; AVOID in Lewy/Parkinson dementia
ADVANCE CARE PLANNING:
Early in trajectory while capacity preserved
Lasting power of attorney + advance directive
End-of-life preferences
Palliative care + symptom control
Memory clinic + community dementia care + caregiver respite
SAFETY:
Driving assessment (formal)
Home safety (falls, gas, fire)
Wandering — MedicAlert, GPS
Medication management (dosette)
Financial protection
FAMILY + CAREGIVER SUPPORT:
Education (Alzheimer's Society + similar)
Support groups
Respite care
Burnout + depression in caregivers — screen
PUBLIC HEALTH (LMIC + SSA):
Dementia plan + integration into NCD response
Community awareness — distinguish from 'normal ageing'
Workforce training (CHV-delivered)
Address modifiable RFs population-level
Kenya Dementia Plan emerging

title: Migraine — CGRP era + comprehensive treatment 2024
population: Lifetime prevalence ~15%; women > men 3:1; major disability + workplace cost; chronic migraine (≥ 15 headache days/mo, ≥ 8 migrainous) substantial.
presentation: Episodic: unilateral throbbing pulsating headache + nausea/vomiting + photophobia/phonophobia, 4-72h; ± aura (visual scintillation, scotoma, paraesthesia, dysphasia 20-30 min). Triggers: stress, sleep, hormone, food, weather, exertion.
redFlags: SNOOP/SNOOP10: Systemic (fever/weight loss/cancer), Neurologic (focal/papilloedema/altered MS), Onset sudden (thunderclap — SAH), Older (> 50 new), Pattern change, Positional, Precipitated by exertion/Valsalva, Pregnancy/postpartum, Pulsatile tinnitus, Painkilling overuse — investigate
Pregnancy + headache — exclude PRES, CVT, eclampsia
diagnostics: ICHD-3 criteria — clinical diagnosis
Headache diary (frequency, severity, triggers)
Neurological exam normal in primary migraine
MIDAS / HIT-6 disability scores
Brain imaging ONLY if red flags / atypical / new-onset elderly (NICE)
Bloods rarely needed unless secondary suspicion
Lumbar puncture if thunderclap + normal CT (rule out SAH)
management: ACUTE TREATMENT:
Step 1 — Simple analgesia: paracetamol 1 g + NSAID (ibuprofen 400-600 mg / naproxen 500 mg / aspirin 900 mg) + antiemetic (metoclopramide 10 mg / domperidone)
Step 2 — TRIPTAN if step 1 fails: sumatriptan 50-100 mg PO (or 6 mg SC if severe vomiting), rizatriptan 10 mg ODT, eletriptan, almotriptan, naratriptan (longer half-life)
Contraindications: IHD, uncontrolled HTN, recent vascular event, hemiplegic / brainstem migraine, pregnancy (caution)
Take EARLY in attack
Limit to 10 days/month (medication overuse headache)
GEPANTS (CGRP receptor antagonists) — new oral acute:
Ubrogepant (Ubrelvy) 50-100 mg, rimegepant (Nurtec) 75 mg ODT (also preventive at QOD), zavegepant (Zavzpret) intranasal
Safe in cardiovascular disease, pregnancy data limited
Alternative to triptans
DITANS — lasmiditan 50-200 mg — 5-HT1F selective, no vasoconstriction, sedation
Severe / status migrainosus: IV metoclopramide 10 mg / chlorpromazine 12.5 mg / prochlorperazine 10 mg + IV fluid + IV magnesium 1 g + IV dexamethasone 4-10 mg + greater occipital nerve block
AVOID opioids + barbiturates (worsen, dependence)
PREVENTIVE TREATMENT (≥ 4 days/month or disabling):
CLASSIC ORAL:
β-blocker: propranolol 80-240 mg, metoprolol
Tricyclic: amitriptyline 25-75 mg nocte (also tension-type + sleep)
Antiepileptic: topiramate 25-100 mg (avoid pregnancy — palatoschisis), valproate (avoid WCBP)
Candesartan 16 mg
Pizotifen, flunarizine
Magnesium 400-600 mg, riboflavin 400 mg, coenzyme Q10 (supplements — modest evidence)
Allow 8-12 weeks at therapeutic dose to assess
CGRP MONOCLONAL ANTIBODIES (transformative — first migraine-specific preventives):
Erenumab (Aimovig) — anti-CGRP receptor, 70-140 mg SC monthly
Fremanezumab (Ajovy) — anti-CGRP ligand, 225 mg monthly or 675 mg quarterly
Galcanezumab (Emgality) — 240 mg load then 120 mg monthly
Eptinezumab — IV 100-300 mg quarterly
Use for chronic migraine + frequent episodic + ≥ 2 failed orals; expensive (Kenya access limited)
Rimegepant (gepant) 75 mg every other day — dual acute + preventive
Atogepant 10-60 mg/day preventive gepant
BOTULINUM TOXIN A (Botox) — chronic migraine ≥ 15 days/month, ≥ 8 migrainous; 155-195 units PREEMPT protocol q12 weeks
Galcanezumab + atogepant for cluster headache prevention
NON-PHARM:
Trigger identification + avoidance (sleep, hydration, regular meals, stress)
Aerobic exercise 30 min × 3/week
CBT, biofeedback, relaxation, mindfulness
Neuromodulation devices: transcranial magnetic stimulation (sTMS), Cefaly (TENS), Nerivio (REN)
Acupuncture (modest evidence)
Avoid OCP combined if migraine with aura (stroke risk)
MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE (MOH):
Triptans / opioids / butalbital > 10 days/month OR simple analgesia > 15 days/month
Withdrawal + start preventive + bridge with prednisolone / NSAID
PREGNANCY:
Paracetamol first-line acute; metoclopramide; AVOID NSAIDs after 30 wk
Triptans probably safe (sumatriptan most data) but balance
Preventive: propranolol, amitriptyline; AVOID topiramate (palatoschisis), valproate, ACE/ARB, CGRP mAbs (limited data)
MENSTRUAL MIGRAINE: NSAIDs perimenstrual; long-acting triptan (naratriptan 1 mg BD × 5 days); continuous OCP if non-aura
Refer NEUROLOGY: refractory, chronic, atypical features, suspected secondary, hemiplegic / brainstem aura

title: Multiple sclerosis — modern disease-modifying therapy
population: Young adults 20-40 (median 30); female:male 2:1; geographical gradient; growing SSA awareness but under-diagnosed; vitamin D deficiency + EBV infection major RFs (Bjornevik Science 2022 — EBV near-causal).
presentation: CIS (clinically isolated syndrome), RRMS (relapsing-remitting), SPMS (secondary progressive), PPMS (primary progressive). Common: optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO), transverse myelitis, sensory disturbance, cerebellar (ataxia, tremor), bladder, fatigue, cognitive, Lhermitte sign.
redFlags: Acute severe relapse with significant disability
First demyelinating event — workup MRI + LP + AQP4 + MOG (rule out NMOSD + MOGAD — different treatment)
Progressive (not relapsing) presentation in patient with prior relapses (SPMS conversion)
Atypical features → consider mimics (NMO, MOGAD, infection, neoplasm, vasculitis, ADEM, B12 deficiency, HIV, HTLV-1, neurosarcoidosis)
diagnostics: McDonald 2017 (+ 2024 update) criteria: dissemination in time + space; MRI + CSF oligoclonal bands
Brain + spinal MRI with gadolinium (T2 hyperintense + enhancing lesions for activity)
CSF: oligoclonal bands (unique to CSF — not paired serum), kappa free light chains, raised IgG index
Serum AQP4-IgG (rule out NMOSD), MOG-IgG (MOGAD) — DIFFERENT treatment, ANTI-CD20 may worsen NMO
Vitamin D, vitamin B12, HIV, syphilis, ANA, ANCA, Lyme
Visual evoked potentials (if no clear lesion)
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) — retinal nerve fibre layer thinning
EDSS (Expanded Disability Status Scale) for baseline + monitoring
management: ACUTE RELAPSE:
Disabling relapse: methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily × 3-5 days (or PO equivalent — same efficacy per evidence)
Plasma exchange (PLEX) for steroid-refractory severe relapse
Symptomatic only treatment for mild relapse
DISEASE-MODIFYING THERAPY (DMT) — START EARLY (treat as soon as possible after diagnosis):
TREATMENT PARADIGM SHIFT: 'early high-efficacy' favoured over 'escalation' approach (multiple comparative trials)
Mild-moderate:
INTERFERON-β: IFN-β1a (Avonex IM weekly, Rebif SC), IFN-β1b (Betaferon SC EOD), pegylated
GLATIRAMER ACETATE (Copaxone) 20 mg/d SC or 40 mg 3×/wk
TERIFLUNOMIDE (Aubagio) 14 mg/d PO
DIMETHYL FUMARATE (Tecfidera) 240 mg BD PO — flushing, GI
Diroximel fumarate, monomethyl fumarate variants
High-efficacy (RRMS active or aggressive):
OCRELIZUMAB (Ocrevus) — anti-CD20, 600 mg IV q6 months (also approved PPMS — first proven for primary progressive)
OFATUMUMAB (Kesimpta) — anti-CD20, SC monthly
NATALIZUMAB (Tysabri) — anti-α4 integrin, IV monthly; PML risk in JCV-positive patients (test + risk-stratify; consider extended-interval dosing)
ALEMTUZUMAB (Lemtrada) — anti-CD52, 2-course infusion; autoimmune complications (thyroid, ITP, anti-GBM)
CLADRIBINE (Mavenclad) — oral, 2-year course (induction)
FINGOLIMOD (Gilenya), siponimod (also SPMS), ponesimod, ozanimod — S1P modulators
EMERGING: anti-CD20 ublituximab, tolebrutinib (BTK inhibitor)
CHOICE based on: activity, prognostic factors, comorbidity, pregnancy plans, monitoring requirements, JCV status, vaccination needs, cost
Pre-DMT screening: vaccinations (live vaccines BEFORE start), JCV antibody, TB, hepatitis B/C, HIV, varicella, FBC, LFT, ECG (some), pregnancy test
Monitoring on DMT: FBC, LFT, regular MRI surveillance
SECONDARY PROGRESSIVE MS:
Siponimod (Mayzent — EXPAND trial) — slows disability progression
Cladribine evidence
Limited DMT efficacy once non-active progressive
PRIMARY PROGRESSIVE MS:
Ocrelizumab (ORATORIO) — only approved
SYMPTOMATIC MANAGEMENT:
Spasticity: baclofen, tizanidine, gabapentin, dantrolene; cannabis extract (nabiximols / Sativex); botulinum toxin focal; intrathecal baclofen pump severe
Bladder dysfunction: anticholinergic (oxybutynin / tolterodine / solifenacin), mirabegron, botulinum bladder injection, ISC, indwelling
Fatigue (most common symptom): exercise + sleep + amantadine + modafinil
Cognitive impairment: cognitive rehab, donepezil (variable)
Depression: SSRI
Neuropathic pain: gabapentin, pregabalin, amitriptyline, duloxetine
Sexual dysfunction: PDE5i (men), lubricants, counsel
Walking: dalfampridine (4-AP, Ampyra) 10 mg BD
Trigeminal neuralgia (more common in MS): carbamazepine, microvascular decompression
REHABILITATION: PT, OT, SLT, neurorehabilitation, vocational, psychological
VITAMIN D supplementation 2000-5000 IU (modifiable RF for progression)
Smoking cessation (worsens prognosis)
DIET + exercise + weight management
Vaccinations (NOT live on most DMTs); cover hepatitis B before B-cell depleting; annual flu / COVID
PREGNANCY:
Discontinue most DMTs pre-conception
Glatiramer + IFN may continue per benefit-risk
Natalizumab continue if high active disease (extended interval, washout near delivery)
Ocrelizumab — washout 6 months but emerging evidence safety
Pregnancy itself reduces relapses (T2-3 trimester); postpartum surge — restart DMT or LACTATION-compatible
Breastfeeding: IFN, glatiramer compatible; ocrelizumab emerging data; ofatumumab; natalizumab not

EXPAND siponimod SPMS, ORATORIO ocrelizumab PPMS

title: Epilepsy — modern antiseizure medication + comprehensive care
population: 50 million globally; SSA disproportionate burden + treatment gap > 75%; neurocysticercosis major cause SSA; perinatal injury + head trauma + stroke key.
presentation: Focal-onset (with or without impaired awareness, may evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic); generalised-onset (absence, myoclonic, tonic, atonic, tonic-clonic); unknown onset; epilepsy syndromes (Lennox-Gastaut, Dravet, JME, childhood absence).
redFlags: Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP — main cause of death; identify high-risk)
Pregnancy planning on teratogenic AED (especially valproate AVOID WCBP)
Persistent seizures despite 2 adequate trials (drug-resistant epilepsy — refer surgery)
Suicide risk increase on some AEDs (FDA warning)
diagnostics: Detailed clinical + witness history + video if possible
EEG: standard + sleep-deprived if first non-diagnostic; ambulatory; video-EEG for diagnostic uncertainty + drug-resistant assessment
MRI brain (or CT if MRI unavailable) — structural cause

Bloods (rule out): FBC, U&E, glucose, LFT, Ca, Mg, AED levels, prolactin (immediately post — increases after generalised seizure, may help differential from PNES), HIV, syphilis (especially LMIC), pregnancy
ECG (rule out cardiac syncope)
Investigate aetiology: neurocysticercosis serology + imaging in SSA endemic; TB + HIV brain; autoimmune (anti-NMDA, anti-LGI1)
Genetic for selected (Dravet — SCN1A, epileptic encephalopathies)
management: FIRST SEIZURE:
Diagnose epilepsy if ≥ 2 unprovoked seizures > 24h apart OR 1 seizure + high recurrence risk (epileptic discharge on EEG, structural lesion, ≥ 60% 10-year recurrence)
Provoked seizure (acute symptomatic — fever, electrolyte, withdrawal, hypoglycaemia) — treat cause, NOT chronic AED
Counsel: driving (varies by jurisdiction — UK 6 months + 12 months for some), occupation, swimming alone, heights, photosensitive triggers
AED CHOICE — by seizure type + syndrome + comorbidity + pregnancy potential:
FOCAL-ONSET:
First-line: LAMOTRIGINE (slow titrate SJS), LEVETIRACETAM (behavioural side effect), oxcarbazepine, lacosamide, brivaracetam
Second-line: zonisamide, eslicarbazepine, perampanel, valproate (NOT WCBP), carbamazepine (older)
Cenobamate — NEW for refractory focal
Avoid carbamazepine in HLA-B*1502 (Han Chinese, SE Asian — SJS risk)
GENERALISED:
Tonic-clonic: valproate (most effective but TERATOGENIC — NOT WCBP), lamotrigine, levetiracetam
Absence: ethosuximide (first-line absence), valproate, lamotrigine
Myoclonic: valproate, levetiracetam, topiramate, zonisamide; AVOID carbamazepine + phenytoin + oxcarbazepine + lamotrigine high-dose (may worsen)
Atonic / Lennox-Gastaut / Dravet: clobazam, rufinamide, cannabidiol (Epidiolex — first FDA-approved cannabinoid epilepsy), fenfluramine (Dravet)
JME: valproate / levetiracetam / lamotrigine
GENERAL principles:
Start LOW + go SLOW for tolerability + safety (especially lamotrigine — SJS)
Monotherapy first; combination if monotherapy fails
Trial 2 adequate monotherapies before declaring drug-resistant
Monitor: side effects (mood, weight, cognition, bone, vitamin D), drug-drug interactions (especially enzyme-inducers — phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital reduce contraception + warfarin + DOACs)
Levels: target therapeutic range varies; mostly clinical except phenytoin (narrow therapeutic), carbamazepine, valproate, lamotrigine in pregnancy
PREGNANCY (CRITICAL):
Pre-conception planning ideal
AVOID valproate in WCBP unless absolutely no alternative + NPPP (National Pregnancy Prevention Programme)
Phenobarbital, topiramate, carbamazepine — teratogenic risk
LAMOTRIGINE + LEVETIRACETAM preferred (lowest risk)
Monotherapy lower risk than polypharmacy
Folic acid 5 mg/day pre-conception
Monitor levels through pregnancy (lamotrigine clearance increases substantially — relapse risk)
Vitamin K to mother last month + neonate (enzyme-inducing AEDs)
Breastfeeding: most AEDs compatible (lamotrigine, levetiracetam, valproate — lower transfer; phenobarbital + ethosuximide caution sedation)
DRUG-RESISTANT EPILEPSY (~30%):
REFER EPILEPSY SURGERY CENTRE (where available) — early evaluation important
Temporal lobectomy gold standard for mesial temporal sclerosis (highly successful)
Selective amygdalohippocampectomy, lesionectomy
Functional surgery — corpus callosotomy, hemispherectomy (catastrophic syndromes)
Neurostimulation: vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), responsive neurostimulation (RNS), deep brain stimulation (anterior thalamic nucleus)
KETOGENIC DIET — childhood drug-resistant epilepsy (especially Dravet, Lennox-Gastaut, glucose transporter 1 deficiency); modified Atkins; classic ketogenic
STATUS EPILEPTICUS (separate condition)
SUDEP RISK:
Education for patient + family
Adherence + optimise AED
Nocturnal seizures + supervision
Wearable / bed monitors
PSYCHOSOCIAL: depression + anxiety + stigma + employment + driving
Treat comorbidity (depression — careful AED interactions; SSRI generally safe)
WITHDRAWING AED: consider after 2 years seizure-free; lower if benign childhood epilepsy; high relapse risk for symptomatic; gradual taper
WOMEN'S HEALTH:
Bone health (enzyme-inducing AEDs reduce bone density — vit D + calcium)
Menstrual irregularity
PCOS (valproate)
Contraception (enzyme inducers reduce OCP efficacy; need higher-dose, alternative, IUD)
SSA / Kenya specifically:
Treatment gap > 75% — primary care training + scaling AED access
KEML: phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate, lamotrigine — older agents most affordable
Newer AEDs (levetiracetam) increasingly available
Address neurocysticercosis (cause + leading cause of adult-onset epilepsy SSA endemic)
WHO mhGAP epilepsy module — task-shifted to primary care

WHO mhGAP Epilepsy module + Atlas of Epilepsy

title: Parkinson's disease — comprehensive + advanced therapy
population: Most common neurodegenerative movement disorder; prevalence 1% over 60; SSA emerging awareness with longer life expectancy.
presentation: Cardinal: bradykinesia + at least 1 of: tremor (4-6 Hz pill-rolling rest), rigidity (cogwheel), postural instability. Non-motor: REM sleep behaviour disorder (premotor!), anosmia, constipation, depression, autonomic dysfunction, cognitive decline.
redFlags: Atypical features (early autonomic failure, eye movement, pyramidal, cerebellar, supranuclear gaze palsy, severe symmetric onset, REM sleep behaviour PSP/MSA/DLB) — refer specialist
Hallucinations + cognitive decline (PDD / DLB — avoid antipsychotic, use clozapine/quetiapine)
Sudden withdrawal of levodopa — neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome (continue ALL through illness/surgery)
Pump device problems (DBS, intrajejunal levodopa, apomorphine) — specialist
diagnostics: Clinical diagnosis — MDS Criteria 2015 (UK Brain Bank old)
Levodopa response (good response supports diagnosis)
DaT scan / FP-CIT SPECT — reduced striatal uptake (essential tremor differential)
MRI brain (rule out vascular, NPH, atypical)
Genetic testing for young-onset / family history (LRRK2, GBA, SNCA)
Cognitive screening (MoCA — frequent comorbidity)
Depression screening (PHQ-9 / GDS)
Autonomic function — orthostatic vitals, bladder, bowel
Sleep history (REM sleep behaviour disorder)
management: TIMING of dopaminergic — when symptoms impair quality of life / function (no compelling 'wait' anymore)
EARLY DISEASE:
LEVODOPA / carbidopa (Sinemet / Madopar) — GOLD STANDARD; most effective + safest for older patients

Dopamine AGONIST (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine patch) — less wearing-off + dyskinesia early but: nausea, OEDEMA, somnolence, IMPULSE CONTROL DISORDER (gambling, hypersexuality, eating — counsel + monitor)
MAO-B inhibitor (selegiline, rasagiline, safinamide) — mild benefit, useful adjunct
Anticholinergic (trihexyphenidyl) for tremor in young; AVOID in elderly (cognitive)
Amantadine — mild benefit + reduces dyskinesia in advanced
ADVANCED DISEASE (motor fluctuations + dyskinesia):
Optimise levodopa frequency + dose (smaller more frequent)
Add COMT inhibitor (entacapone, opicapone, tolcapone) — prolong levodopa effect
Add MAO-B inhibitor (rasagiline, safinamide)
Amantadine ER (Gocovri) for levodopa-induced dyskinesia
Apomorphine: SC injections rescue + continuous infusion
Intrajejunal levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (Duopa) — pump
DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION (DBS) — subthalamic nucleus or GPi — for motor fluctuations + dyskinesia + tremor refractory; selected patients (age, cognition, response)
Focused ultrasound thalamotomy/pallidotomy — non-invasive alternative
NON-MOTOR (often more disabling than motor):
Depression: SSRI (paroxetine/sertraline/venlafaxine); avoid TCA (anticholinergic worsens cognition)
Cognitive impairment / dementia (PDD): rivastigmine first-line; donepezil; memantine if severe

Psychosis / hallucinations: REDUCE / stop anticholinergics + amantadine + agonist; use CLOZAPINE or QUETIAPINE (atypical low-risk EPS); avoid haloperidol + risperidone + olanzapine; PIMAVANSERIN (Nuplazid) FDA-approved
Sleep: melatonin for REM sleep behaviour disorder; CBT-I
Constipation: hydration + fibre + laxative (PEG)
Orthostatic hypotension: fludrocortisone, midodrine, droxidopa; compression stockings
Urinary urgency: oxybutynin (cognitive caution) / tolterodine / mirabegron / β3 agonist; botulinum bladder
Drooling: glycopyrronium, atropine SL, botulinum salivary gland
Pain: address musculoskeletal + dystonic + neuropathic; cannabinoid emerging
REHABILITATION (huge benefit):
Physiotherapy (Big + Bold / LSVT BIG)
Speech (LSVT LOUD)
Occupational therapy
Exercise — aerobic, resistance, balance (Tai Chi, dance, boxing)
Multidisciplinary team
ADVANCED CARE PLANNING + PALLIATIVE CARE for end-stage
Driving assessment
Caregiver support
SURGERY + ANAESTHESIA: continue dopaminergic without interruption (NMS-like risk); rotigotine patch / apomorphine for NPO
Hospital admission: ensure dopaminergic timing precise + correct drugs
FALLS PREVENTION + bone health (osteoporosis common)
PREMOTOR diagnosis (research) — REM sleep behaviour disorder + anosmia + constipation → very high lifetime risk

title: Vertigo — BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Ménière's differential
population: Adults — BPPV most common cause (esp > 50); vestibular neuritis next; Ménière's chronic with episodic; central causes (stroke, MS) critical not to miss.
presentation: True vertigo (spinning) — peripheral typically more severe with horizontal/torsional nystagmus + ear/auditory symptoms or positional, central with vertical / direction-changing nystagmus + accompanying neurology. Differential: cardiac syncope (pre-syncope), anaemia, anxiety, drugs.
redFlags: HINTS-plus exam suggestive central (head impulse test normal / direction-changing nystagmus / vertical skew) — stroke/posterior circulation; immediate MRI
Sudden severe vertigo + hearing loss + neurological — stroke
New onset over 50 with vascular risk factors
Recurrent / Ménière's with progressive hearing loss
diagnostics: Detailed history — onset, duration, triggers, associated symptoms (auditory, headache, neurological), drug history
Examination: neuro + cranial nerves + nystagmus characteristics + Romberg + gait + HINTS plus
HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) — peripheral if abnormal head impulse + unidirectional nystagmus + no skew; central concern if HINTS-positive
Dix-Hallpike for posterior canal BPPV (most common — 90%)
Supine roll test for horizontal canal BPPV
Audiometry (Ménière's, vestibular schwannoma, sudden SNHL)
MRI if central concern, persistent, atypical
FBC + glucose if non-vertiginous dizziness
ECG if pre-syncope / cardiac history
management: BPPV (BENIGN PAROXYSMAL POSITIONAL VERTIGO):
Dix-Hallpike — diagnostic (positive = vertigo + characteristic upbeating torsional nystagmus)
EPLEY MANOEUVRE — treatment of posterior canal BPPV; in-office; effective 70-85% first session
Repeat at home or weekly clinic
Semont alternative
Horizontal canal: BBQ roll / Gufoni manoeuvre
Anterior canal: reverse Epley
AVOID prolonged vestibular suppressants (slow recovery)
Brandt-Daroff exercises home maintenance
VESTIBULAR NEURITIS / LABYRINTHITIS:
Acute severe vertigo + nausea + vomiting × days; spontaneous nystagmus (unidirectional fast-phase away from affected ear); intact hearing (neuritis) vs hearing loss (labyrinthitis)
Prednisolone 60 mg/d taper × 3 weeks (modest evidence to improve vestibular recovery)
Antiviral NOT routinely (limited evidence)
Symptom relief 24-72h ONLY: prochlorperazine, promethazine, cyclizine, ondansetron, betahistine
AVOID prolonged suppressants — delay vestibular compensation
Early VESTIBULAR REHABILITATION (Cawthorne-Cooksey, Gaze stabilisation, balance) — accelerates recovery
Most resolve in weeks to months
MÉNIÈRE'S DISEASE:
Episodes lasting 20 min-12h + low-frequency SNHL + tinnitus + aural fullness
Acute: prochlorperazine, betahistine, antiemetic
Maintenance: low-salt diet (< 2 g/d), reduce caffeine + alcohol, betahistine 16 mg TDS
Diuretic (HCTZ + triamterene) — second-line
Intratympanic dexamethasone or gentamicin (refractory + significant disability)
Hearing aid for hearing loss
Endolymphatic sac surgery / vestibular nerve section / labyrinthectomy — last resort
VESTIBULAR MIGRAINE:
Migraine prophylaxis (β-blocker, topiramate, amitriptyline, CGRP)
Acute attack — triptan, antiemetic
Trigger avoidance + lifestyle
CENTRAL VERTIGO:
MRI urgent + neurology referral
Stroke (posterior circulation), TIA, MS, cerebellar tumour, vestibular schwannoma
Treat underlying
PERSISTENT POSTURAL-PERCEPTUAL DIZZINESS (PPPD):
Functional / chronic dizziness — vestibular rehab + SSRI + CBT
REHABILITATION:
Vestibular physiotherapy critical for chronic / unresolved peripheral
Habituation + adaptation + substitution exercises
Driving + occupation counselling
ELDERLY DIZZINESS: multifactorial — review meds (orthostatic, polypharmacy), HR/BP, gait, balance, vision

title: Stroke secondary prevention — DAPT, statin, BP, AF, carotid
population: Patients post-stroke / TIA — at high recurrence risk. Aggressive secondary prevention reduces recurrence + mortality.
presentation: Routine follow-up after stroke / TIA. ABCD2 score / clinical assessment determines acute vs longer-term management.
redFlags: TIA / minor stroke — recent (within 7 days) — high recurrence risk; rapid workup + treatment
Carotid stenosis > 50% symptomatic = consider revascularisation within 2 weeks
Patent foramen ovale + cryptogenic stroke + age < 60 — closure consideration
diagnostics: Brain imaging (MRI preferred for posterior + small lesions; CT initial)
Vessel imaging — CTA / MRA / Doppler carotids + intracranial
Echocardiogram (TTE) — wall motion, EF, valvular, intracardiac mass, septal defect
TOE — atrial appendage, PFO, atrial septum
ECG + 24h Holter monitoring — atrial fibrillation
Extended monitoring (30-day event recorder or implantable loop recorder — CRYSTAL-AF) for cryptogenic stroke
Lipid panel + HbA1c + FBC + U&E + ANA + lupus anticoagulant (cryptogenic stroke + young / atypical)
Stroke aetiology classification (TOAST): large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined
management: ANTITHROMBOTIC THERAPY:
NON-CARDIOEMBOLIC stroke (atherothrombotic, small-vessel, cryptogenic):
DAPT (clopidogrel 75 mg + aspirin 75 mg) × 21 days (CHANCE / POINT — minor stroke / high-risk TIA) → then aspirin OR clopidogrel monotherapy long-term
Aspirin 75 mg or clopidogrel 75 mg monotherapy long-term
Dual antiplatelet beyond 21 days NOT recommended (bleeding > benefit)
Aspirin + dipyridamole MR alternative
Newer: ticagrelor + aspirin (THALES) for selected mild stroke
CARDIOEMBOLIC (atrial fibrillation):
DOAC PREFERRED (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) — better safety/efficacy
Warfarin for mechanical valve, mitral stenosis, severe CKD (eGFR < 15)
Timing post-stroke (1-3-6-12 day rule by severity per RAF):
TIA: start day 1
Small stroke: day 3
Moderate: day 6-7
Large: day 12-14 (haemorrhagic transformation risk)
Bridging usually not needed for DOAC
PFO + cryptogenic stroke < 60 with high-risk features: PFO closure (RESPECT, CLOSE, REDUCE, GORE trials) — reduces recurrence
STATIN — HIGH-INTENSITY:
Atorvastatin 80 mg or rosuvastatin 20-40 mg daily — TARGET LDL < 1.4 mmol/L (SPARCL, ESC 2019)
Add ezetimibe + PCSK9 inhibitor (alirocumab / evolocumab) if LDL target not met
Inclisiran emerging
EVEN if normal LDL — statin reduces stroke recurrence (pleiotropic effect)
BP CONTROL:
Target < 130/80 (most patients) — PROGRESS, SPS3
Gradual reduction (avoid post-stroke acute permissive HTN — first 1-2 weeks)
ACE-i or ARB + thiazide; add CCB for resistant
Especially important for haemorrhagic stroke + small-vessel disease
DIABETES:
Tight HbA1c control < 53 mmol/mol
SGLT2 inhibitor + GLP-1 RA reduce CV events (separate condition)
CAROTID STENOSIS:
Symptomatic > 70% — endarterectomy (CEA) within 2 weeks of event (highest benefit)
Symptomatic 50-69% — CEA in selected (male > female, age > 75)
Asymptomatic > 70% — controversial (CREST-2 + DSP-2 — modern medical therapy may be equivalent)
Carotid stenting alternative; CEA superior in elderly (CREST)
LIFESTYLE:
Smoking cessation (largest modifiable risk reduction)
Mediterranean diet
Exercise 150 min/week aerobic
Weight loss to BMI < 25
Alcohol limit
Sleep + OSA treatment (CPAP)
Stress, depression management
REHABILITATION:
Stroke rehab unit — best evidence
Physio, OT, SLT, neuropsychology
Spasticity — botulinum toxin focal, baclofen
Depression — SSRI (Flame, EFFECTS trials — fluoxetine motor recovery debated)
Mental capacity + driving assessment
DRIVING: 1 month off after TIA (UK DVLA), longer for stroke + based on residual
SECONDARY PREVENTION CLINIC follow-up at 1, 3, 6, 12 months
HAEMORRHAGIC STROKE secondary prevention:
BP control < 130/80 critical
Avoid anticoagulant unless compelling AF (decision after 4-8 weeks with neurology)
Manage source — AVM, aneurysm, amyloid angiopathy
Lobar haemorrhage + ApoE genotype = amyloid angiopathy — avoid anticoag
FAMILY history + young stroke: thrombophilia, hyperhomocysteinaemia, CADASIL, Fabry, vasculitis workup

title: Myasthenia gravis — comprehensive + crisis
population: Bimodal: women 20-40, men > 50. Generalised vs ocular. Acetylcholine receptor antibody (AChR) most common; MuSK antibody minority; LRP4; seronegative.
presentation: Fatigable weakness, worse with use, improves with rest. Ocular (ptosis, diplopia — 50% initial), bulbar (dysphagia, dysarthria, dyspnoea), limb (proximal). Increases through day. Cholinergic crisis from over-treatment (vs myasthenic crisis — under-treatment).
redFlags: Myasthenic crisis — respiratory failure (FVC < 20, MIP < 30) — ICU + IVIG/PLEX + intubation
Thymoma (10% of MG; 30% of thymomas have MG) — chest CT mandatory at diagnosis
Drug-induced exacerbation (avoid: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, β-blockers, magnesium, neuromuscular blockers, statins, lithium, IFN, immune checkpoint inhibitors)
Cholinergic crisis — increased weakness + miosis + fasciculations + GI + sweating (different from myasthenic crisis)
diagnostics: AChR antibody (sensitivity 85% generalised, lower ocular)
MuSK antibody if AChR negative + generalised (limb-bulbar phenotype)
LRP4 + agrin if double-seronegative
Single-fibre EMG (most sensitive) + repetitive nerve stimulation
Edrophonium test (Tensilon) — historical (anaphylaxis + cardiac risk)
Ice pack test for ptosis (cooling improves AChR-mediated weakness)
CT thorax — thymoma screen at diagnosis (all)
Thyroid antibodies + function (associated autoimmune)
FVC + MIP/MEP — respiratory baseline
ECG, cardiac function before β-blocker
management: SYMPTOMATIC:
PYRIDOSTIGMINE 30-60 mg PO every 4-6 hours (max 360 mg/day) — acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; titrate to effect; side effects cholinergic (cramps, diarrhoea, salivation) — atropine can manage
Less effective in MuSK MG
IMMUNOSUPPRESSIVE (for inadequate symptomatic control):
PREDNISOLONE 5-10 mg starting (slow titrate up to 40-60 mg) — DELAY effect 2-4 weeks; initial worsening risk (start LOW + slow)
AZATHIOPRINE — first-line steroid-sparing, takes 6-12 months for effect
Mycophenolate alternative
Methotrexate, tacrolimus, ciclosporin
Rituximab — particularly effective in MuSK MG; AChR + refractory generalised
ECULIZUMAB / RAVULIZUMAB — anti-C5 complement; FDA-approved for AChR+ refractory generalised MG (REGAIN, CHAMPION-MG)
EFGARTIGIMOD (Vyvgart) — neonatal Fc receptor antagonist; FDA-approved 2021 (ADAPT trial)
ROZANOLIXIZUMAB — anti-FcRn, FDA-approved 2023
ZILUCOPLAN — C5 inhibitor SC FDA-approved 2023
Choice depends on antibody, refractoriness, comorbidity, cost, access
THYMECTOMY:
All thymoma patients
Non-thymomatous AChR+ generalised MG age 18-65 — thymectomy improves outcomes (MGTX trial — extends benefit at 5 years follow-up)
Robotic + minimally invasive approaches
MYASTHENIC CRISIS (respiratory failure):
ICU admission, intubate early (don't wait for arrest — neuromuscular blockers difficult to reverse)
IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days OR plasma exchange (PLEX) 5 sessions
Identify + treat trigger (infection, medication, surgery, pregnancy, missed dose)
Continue / restart immunosuppression
AVOID exacerbating drugs (above list)
Optimise nutrition, electrolytes
Wean ventilator carefully
OCULAR MG:
Pyridostigmine first-line
Add prednisolone if inadequate (reduces generalisation risk)
Eye patch for diplopia
PREGNANCY:
Often worsens, especially first trimester + postpartum
Pyridostigmine safe
Prednisolone safe
Azathioprine + cyclosporine considered compatible (risk-benefit)
AVOID mycophenolate + methotrexate + rituximab
IVIG + PLEX safe + effective
Vaginal delivery preferred; uterine smooth muscle not affected
Neonatal MG (transient — maternal antibody transfer) — 10-20%; supportive
ANAESTHESIA / SURGERY:
Continue pyridostigmine + steroid through procedure
AVOID succinylcholine (resistant + prolonged) + non-depolarising NMBA (sensitive)
Use small-dose rocuronium if needed; sugammadex reversal
Regional preferred where possible
MEDICATION ALERT card + bracelet
Address autoimmune comorbidity (thyroid, RA, SLE)
Annual flu, COVID, pneumococcal vaccinations — kill not live; immunosuppressed

title: Headache red flags — SNNOOP10 + secondary differential
population: All headache patients — primary care + emergency. Need to identify 1-5% that are dangerous secondary causes among 95% primary.
presentation: Headache as predominant symptom. Distinguishing primary (migraine, tension, cluster, hemicrania) from secondary (SAH, meningitis, intracranial mass, dissection, venous thrombosis, GCA, idiopathic intracranial HT, sinusitis, dental, glaucoma, drug-induced).
redFlags: SNNOOP10 (one or more = consider secondary): Systemic (fever, weight loss, cancer, HIV), Neoplasm (history), Neurological deficit (focal, papilloedema), Onset sudden (thunderclap < 1 min), Older (> 50 new), Pattern change / Progressive, Positional (Valsalva, postural), Precipitated by exertion / cough / sex, Papilloedema, Painkilling overuse, Postural (worsens lying — IIH; worsens upright — CSF leak), Pregnancy / postpartum
diagnostics: Thunderclap headache (< 1 min to peak) — SAH first; also: CVT, RCVS, pituitary apoplexy, cervical dissection, third ventricle colloid cyst, hypertensive emergency
Urgent non-contrast CT (sensitivity > 95% within 6h, falls after 24h)
Negative CT but high suspicion: LP (xanthochromia, RBC) within 12h post-bleed
CT angiogram for vascular cause
GCA (giant cell arteritis) > 50 yr: temporal tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, ESR/CRP
Start prednisolone 60 mg IMMEDIATELY (don't wait for biopsy — vision loss risk)
Temporal artery biopsy within 1 week
Meningitis / encephalitis: fever + headache + meningism / altered mental state → CT + LP + empiric antibiotics + acyclovir
Intracranial mass: progressive, worse early morning, neurological deficit, papilloedema → MRI
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: obese young woman + papilloedema → LP (raised opening pressure)
Cervical artery dissection: neck pain + Horner's + recent trauma → CT angio / MRA
Cerebral venous thrombosis: pregnancy / postpartum / OCP / thrombophilia → MR venogram
Sinus + dental + ENT — examine
management: FULL HEADACHE HISTORY + EXAMINATION (CNS + cardiovascular + fundoscopy + meningism):
Type, frequency, severity, character, location, duration, associated symptoms, triggers, family history, drug history
Headache diary
DIFFERENTIAL by red flag triage:
No red flags + typical primary: clinical diagnosis, manage
Red flags: targeted workup
PRIMARY HEADACHES:
Migraine (separate condition)
Tension-type headache: bilateral, pressing, mild-moderate, no nausea, may have photo OR phono; analgesia + lifestyle + amitriptyline preventive

Cluster headache: severe unilateral periorbital + autonomic (ptosis, miosis, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, eyelid oedema, facial flushing/sweat); attacks 15 min-3h × clusters; acute — high-flow O2 (12-15 L) for 15-20 min, SC sumatriptan; prevention — verapamil 240-960 mg/d (ECG); galcanezumab (Emgality) FDA-approved 2019
Paroxysmal hemicrania: short attacks, autonomic features, COMPLETE response to indomethacin (diagnostic test)
SUNCT/SUNA: very short (< 1 min) unilateral neuralgia + autonomic; lamotrigine, topiramate
Hemicrania continua: indomethacin-responsive continuous unilateral
TRIGEMINAL NEURALGIA:
Carbamazepine 200-1200 mg/day (BSCEDS warning), oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, baclofen, gabapentin
Microvascular decompression / gamma knife / glycerol rhizotomy
Onabotulinum toxin
MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE: withdrawal + bridge prednisolone / NSAID + start preventive (separate condition)
Persistent post-traumatic headache: similar to migraine — treat as migraine
Cerebrospinal fluid leak (low-pressure headache): epidural blood patch
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension:
Weight loss
Acetazolamide 250-2000 mg/day (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor)
Topiramate alternative
Optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunt for vision threat
SECONDARY HEADACHE:
Treat cause: drain abscess + antibiotics for meningitis; aciclovir for HSV; resect tumour; coil/clip SAH; angioplasty for RCVS / dissection; intracranial pressure management for masses
Refer NEUROLOGY: persistent, atypical, refractory, secondary suspected, hemiplegic/brainstem aura, status migrainosus, new daily persistent headache

title: Distal symmetric polyneuropathy — modern diagnostic + management
population: Common — adults, prevalence 8% > 55; diabetes leading cause (~ 50%), alcohol, B12 deficiency, drugs, hereditary, autoimmune.
presentation: Length-dependent — stocking-and-glove distribution. Sensory loss / paraesthesia / pain (burning, electric, allodynia, hyperalgesia), distal weakness (later), areflexia (ankle), autonomic features (gastroparesis, ED, orthostatic).
redFlags: Rapid onset — workup urgent (autoimmune, vasculitic, paraneoplastic)
Asymmetric — mononeuritis multiplex (vasculitis, leprosy, HIV, diabetes)
Significant motor weakness — CIDP / GBS / paraproteinaemic
Autonomic features prominent — amyloid, GBS, diabetic
Pain refractory — referral for specialist pain
diagnostics: Comprehensive history — diabetes, alcohol, family, occupation, medication, sexually transmitted (HIV / syphilis), nutritional
Examination — pattern, motor + sensory + autonomic, fasciculations, foot exam
INITIAL bloods: HbA1c + fasting glucose (75g OGTT if normal — pre-diabetic neuropathy), FBC + smear, U&E + LFT, vitamin B12 + folate + ferritin, TSH, ANA, ESR/CRP
Extended (no obvious cause): protein electrophoresis + immunofixation (paraproteinaemia — MGUS, multiple myeloma, amyloid), HIV + syphilis serology, ANCA, RF, anti-CCP, HCV
Specific: hereditary screening (CMT — PMP22, MFN2), genetic panel; anti-MAG antibody; sural nerve biopsy (atypical, vasculitis suspected)
Nerve conduction studies + EMG — distinguish axonal vs demyelinating; severity; sub-clinical extent
Skin biopsy for intra-epidermal nerve fibre density (small fibre neuropathy)
Quantitative sensory testing (QST)
Autonomic function tests (HRV, tilt table)
management: TREAT UNDERLYING CAUSE:
Diabetes: tight glucose control (more important T1 than T2 for neuropathy), SGLT2i / GLP-1 RA
Alcohol: cessation + thiamine + B vitamins
B12 deficiency: hydroxocobalamin 1 mg IM weekly × 6 then 3-monthly maintenance (some give PO 1-2 mg/day — adequate in many)
Drug-induced: stop offending agent (chemotherapy — taxanes, platinum, vincristine; isoniazid + pyridoxine; metronidazole; nitrofurantoin; amiodarone; phenytoin)
Hypothyroidism: levothyroxine
HIV: ART + neuropathy-specific management
Leprosy: MDT (rifampicin + clofazimine + dapsone) per WHO; steroids for nerve damage
CIDP: IVIG + steroid + immunosuppression
Vasculitis: steroid + cyclophosphamide / rituximab
Amyloid: chemotherapy + TTR-stabilising (tafamidis), TTR knockdown (patisiran, vutrisiran)
GBS (separate condition): IVIG/PLEX
Paraneoplastic: treat underlying cancer
NEUROPATHIC PAIN MANAGEMENT:
First-line (any of):
Gabapentin 300-3600 mg/day (titrate; CKD adjust)
Pregabalin 75-600 mg/day (similar profile)
Duloxetine 30-120 mg/day (SNRI — also depression / anxiety / pain)
Amitriptyline 10-75 mg nocte (anticholinergic, caution elderly)
Second-line: nortriptyline (better tolerated than amitriptyline elderly), venlafaxine, lamotrigine
Topical: capsaicin 8% patch (Qutenza), lidocaine 5% patch (Lidoderm), compounded creams
Tramadol — short-term moderate pain (avoid with SSRI — serotonin syndrome)
Strong opioid — last resort, time-limited, low-dose, careful selection
Cannabinoid — limited evidence; selected refractory
Combination 2 agents (different class) for partial response
FOOT CARE (diabetic neuropathy) — separate condition:
Annual screen + risk-stratify
Daily inspection
Footwear (avoid barefoot)
Podiatry referral
Detection + treatment of foot ulcer
AUTONOMIC SYMPTOMS:
Gastroparesis: small frequent meals, metoclopramide, erythromycin
Orthostatic hypotension: hydration + salt + compression + fludrocortisone + midodrine
Erectile dysfunction: PDE5i
Urinary symptoms: anticholinergic / α-blocker
PHYSIOTHERAPY: gait + balance + strengthening
Walking aids, AFO for foot drop
Multidisciplinary pain clinic for chronic
TENS, mindfulness, CBT, acceptance for chronic pain
PSYCHOLOGY: depression + anxiety + sleep — common with chronic pain
Patient education on burns / injury risk; protective footwear
