title: Neutropenic sepsis — empirical antibiotics within 1 hour
population: Cancer patients on chemotherapy / haematological malignancy; risk highest 7-14 days post-cytotoxic. Mortality reduces with rapid empirical antibiotics.
presentation: Fever ≥ 38°C (or single ≥ 38.5°C) + neutrophil count < 0.5 × 10⁹/L (or < 1.0 × 10⁹/L expected to fall < 0.5). May lack classical infection signs (no pus + minimal inflammation in neutropenia).
redFlags: Tunnelled line tunnel infection / exit site
Typhlitis / neutropenic enterocolitis (right lower quadrant pain + bloody diarrhoea)
Atypical pneumonia in haematology + prolonged neutropenia (fungal — Aspergillus)
diagnostics: Vital signs (qSOFA / NEWS2)
MASCC score (low risk ≥ 21 — outpatient consideration; high risk < 21)
FBC + differential (confirm neutropenia)
U&E, LFT, glucose, lactate, CRP, procalcitonin
Coagulation
Blood cultures × 2 (peripheral + each lumen of indwelling line — paired for differential time to positivity)
Urine MSU + culture
Stool culture + C. diff PCR if diarrhoea
CXR
Throat swab if respiratory symptoms
Skin lesion biopsy / culture if any
Galactomannan / β-D-glucan for invasive fungal if prolonged / high-risk
CT chest / abdomen if pulmonary / abdominal symptoms not resolving
management: EMPIRICAL ANTIBIOTIC WITHIN 1 HOUR (door-to-needle):
PIPERACILLIN-TAZOBACTAM 4.5 g q8h IV (first-line UK NICE / IDSA — covers gram-positive + Pseudomonas)
OR cefepime 2 g q8h IV
OR meropenem 1 g q8h IV (penicillin allergy / known ESBL / severe / hospital-acquired)
ADD VANCOMYCIN if:
Septic shock
Pneumonia
Cellulitis / SSTI
Tunnelled line tunnel / exit site infection
Severe mucositis
Known MRSA colonisation
ADD aminoglycoside (gentamicin / amikacin) for septic shock
Caspofungin / micafungin if persistent fever > 72h on antibiotics (empirical antifungal)
Antifungal coverage with mould activity (voriconazole / posaconazole) for prolonged severe neutropenia
Antiviral (aciclovir, ganciclovir) if mucositis / cold sores; CMV PCR if HSCT
Cotrimoxazole (PCP) if immunosuppression + lung infiltrate
Local antibiogram + ESBL/CRE prevalence guides choice
RESUSCITATION:
Crystalloid 30 ml/kg over 3h if hypotension / lactate > 4
Oxygen, vasopressor (noradrenaline) if MAP < 65
Source control within 6-12h (drain abscess, line removal, debridement)
ICU admission for septic shock
G-CSF (filgrastim) consideration:
Therapeutic: severe / prolonged neutropenia / sepsis
Prophylactic per chemo regimen risk (> 20% FN risk)
DURATION + DE-ESCALATION:
Continue antibiotics until afebrile + recovering neutrophils (typically 5-7 days minimum)
De-escalate based on culture + clinical course
Consider outpatient oral antibiotic (cipro + amox-clav) for MASCC low-risk + tolerating PO + adherent + support
ANTIFUNGAL THERAPY:
Empirical IV antifungal if fever persists 72-96h on broad-spectrum antibiotics + high-risk for fungal
Caspofungin / micafungin (echinocandin) first-line — broad including Candida + Aspergillus
Voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole — broader mould
Liposomal amphotericin B if azole resistance / multi-organ involvement
TUNNELLED LINE:
Salvage with antibiotic lock if Coag-neg Staph / sensitive gram-negative + clinical improvement + no fungaemia
Remove line: Pseudomonas / mycobacteria / fungaemia / persistent positive cultures / tunnel infection / septic shock
PROPHYLAXIS:
Cotrimoxazole (PCP) for prolonged steroid / ALL / HSCT / transplant
Fluconazole / posaconazole for high-risk haematology / HSCT
Aciclovir for HSCT + ALL + lymphoma
CMV monitoring + pre-emptive therapy
Vaccinations BEFORE chemotherapy if possible
ESCALATE TO ONCOLOGY / HAEMATOLOGY + ICU for septic shock; multi-D

MASCC criteria for outpatient: low risk (≥ 21), age < 60, no chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, no severe medical history, low risk of complications, hypotension absent, ambulatory, no recent hospitalisation, etc.
Recurrent FN: reduce chemo dose intensity, growth factor support, prophylactic antibiotic considerations
EDUCATION: patient + family — thermometer + emergency contact card + know to attend immediately

title: Tumour lysis syndrome — prevention + treatment
population: High-grade lymphoma (Burkitt's, ALL), bulky lymphomas, leukaemias, after initiating cytotoxic chemo / radiation. Risk: WBC > 50, LDH > 2× ULN, baseline urate raised, renal impairment.
presentation: Laboratory TLS (4 criteria — Cairo-Bishop): hyperuricaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia (within 3 days before to 7 days after cytotoxic). Clinical TLS: laboratory + AKI / arrhythmia / seizure.
redFlags: Uric acid > 8 mg/dL (475 µmol/L) — pre-treatment risk
diagnostics: Risk stratification: low / intermediate / high based on histology + tumour bulk + WBC + LDH + renal
Pre-treatment + serial (q6h initially) labs: U&E + uric acid + phosphate + calcium + LDH + lactate
ECG monitor
Urine output strictly
management: PREVENTION (HIGH-RISK):
HIGH RISK (Burkitt, ALL, high WBC AML, bulky lymphoma):
RASBURICASE 0.2 mg/kg IV daily × 1-7 days (recombinant urate oxidase; converts uric acid to allantoin)
Contraindicated G6PD deficiency (haemolysis) — TEST FIRST
Avoid sodium bicarbonate (impairs rasburicase + worsens hypocalcaemia)
INTERMEDIATE RISK:
ALLOPURINOL 300-600 mg/d (xanthine oxidase inhibitor)
Hold methotrexate / azathioprine if on (interaction)
AGGRESSIVE HYDRATION: 3 L/m²/24h normal saline (start 24-48h pre-chemo); maintain UO > 100 ml/m²/h
Avoid potassium-containing fluids (Hartmann) + diuretics initially
Cytoreduction option: gradual dose escalation, pre-phase chemo (especially Burkitt — small doses cyclophosphamide + vincristine + prednisolone × 5 d before full treatment to reduce TLS risk)
TREATMENT (Established TLS):
Aggressive IV fluids
Rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV (even if not given prophylactically)
Hyperkalaemia: calcium gluconate (membrane stabilisation) + insulin/dextrose shift + Resonium / patiromer + dialysis if refractory
Hyperphosphataemia: phosphate binder (Sevelamer, calcium acetate — caution with hyperPO4-Ca product); dialysis if refractory
Hypocalcaemia: replace ONLY if symptomatic (avoid worsening Ca-PO4 product → metastatic calcification); IV calcium gluconate
AKI: dialysis (haemodialysis preferred — most effective phosphate clearance)
Cardiac monitoring + treat arrhythmia
Seizure: benzodiazepine + replace calcium if cause
Continue + treat underlying malignancy + supportive care
Continuous monitoring 24-72h after chemo initiation
Special situations:
CLL: ibrutinib + venetoclax — TLS risk with venetoclax → very slow ramp-up + intensive monitoring + admission for first dose
CAR-T cell therapy: TLS in first 1-2 weeks; same management
Refer NEPHROLOGY for renal replacement
Reassess malignancy response after stabilisation

title: Malignant spinal cord compression — emergency
population: 5-10% of cancer patients — leading to neurological emergency. Common cancers: lung, breast, prostate, myeloma, lymphoma, renal cell.
presentation: Back pain (most common first symptom — > weeks) WORSENED LYING DOWN / Valsalva, motor weakness (subacute / progressive), sensory level, sphincter disturbance (LATE — bladder + bowel), saddle anaesthesia. Suspect in ANY known cancer patient with back pain.
redFlags: Suspected cord compression — back pain in cancer = MRI WITHIN 24 HOURS regardless of neurological signs
Significant motor deficit — better outcome if treated within 24h of onset
diagnostics: URGENT MRI WHOLE SPINE (within 24 hours) — sensitivity > 95%; CT myelogram if MRI contraindicated
Identify primary cancer if not known (clinical + imaging + biopsy)
FBC + U&E + LFT + Ca + bone profile + LDH + tumour markers
CXR + further staging
Bone biopsy / metastatic workup if unknown primary
Neurological assessment + Frankel/ASIA score baseline
VTE risk (immobility + malignancy)
management: IMMEDIATE (do NOT wait for definitive imaging if high suspicion):
Bed rest + log-roll (until spine stability assessed)
DEXAMETHASONE 16 mg IV / PO STAT then 4-8 mg q6h (reduces oedema + may improve outcome)
Adequate analgesia
VTE prophylaxis (LMWH if no contraindication)
Catheter if retention
Coordinated radio-oncology + neurosurgery + spinal MDT — ideally within 24 hours of presentation
DEFINITIVE TREATMENT:

SURGERY for: single-site disease + good performance status + life expectancy > 3 months + radiosensitive tumours (Patchell trial — surgery + RT > RT alone for radio-resistant tumour, surgery within 14 d of paralysis); spinal instability; tissue diagnosis needed; relapse in irradiated area
RADIOTHERAPY for: radiosensitive tumour (lymphoma, myeloma, breast, prostate, lung), multiple levels, poor surgical candidate, post-op consolidation, palliative
STEREOTACTIC BODY RADIATION (SBRT) — for oligometastatic + spinal cord-sparing high-dose
Bisphosphonates / denosumab for myeloma / breast / prostate bone disease (separate)
Chemotherapy / systemic for chemo-responsive (lymphoma, germ cell)
REHABILITATION:
Physiotherapy, OT, SLT as needed
Bladder + bowel management (catheterisation, bowel programme)
Pain management — multimodal
Pressure care
Psychological support
Discharge planning — community rehab + home modification
PALLIATIVE CARE:
Multiple metastases + poor prognosis — palliative RT + supportive care
Pain control: opioid + adjuvant (gabapentin / pregabalin / amitriptyline for neuropathic) + dexamethasone
Address fatigue, mood, end-of-life preferences
PROGNOSIS:
Pre-treatment ambulatory: 75-90% retain ambulation post-treatment
Pre-treatment paraplegic: < 25% regain ambulation
Time to treatment = key prognostic factor
Median survival 3-6 months from MSCC diagnosis (highly variable by primary)
FOLLOW-UP: regular imaging, recurrence, neurology, oncology

title: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy — bisphosphonate + denosumab
population: Cancer patients — breast + lung + myeloma + renal cell + lymphoma; 20-30% of advanced cancer patients. Mechanisms: PTH-related peptide (humoral), osteolysis, 1,25-OH vitamin D production (lymphoma + granulomatous).
presentation: Stones (renal), bones (pain), groans (abdominal), thrones (polyuria), psychic moans (confusion). Severe (Ca > 3.5 mmol/L corrected): nausea, vomiting, dehydration, lethargy, coma, arrhythmia, acute kidney injury.
redFlags: ECG: short QT, J wave, AV block, arrhythmia
diagnostics: Calcium (always interpret as CORRECTED for albumin) — formula: corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin) in mmol/L
Phosphate, PTH (suppressed in malignancy — distinguishes from primary HPT), PTHrP (raised in humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy)
Vitamin D, 1,25-OH vit D
U&E + creatinine + albumin + LFT + LDH
Workup primary if unknown: CXR, mammogram, prostate, SPEP/IFE, urine PEP for Bence Jones
ECG (short QT)
Bone scan, CT staging
management: IMMEDIATE (Ca > 3 mmol/L or symptomatic):
1. IV REHYDRATION:
0.9% saline 3-6 L/24h (cautious in cardiac / renal failure)
Restore intravascular volume + improve renal calcium clearance
Continuous IV until clinically euvolaemic, then maintenance
2. BISPHOSPHONATE (drug of choice — inhibits osteoclast resorption):
ZOLEDRONIC ACID 4 mg IV over 15-30 min — preferred (most effective + fast)
Pamidronate 60-90 mg IV alternative (slower onset)
Renal dose adjustment if eGFR < 30 (skip / reduce)
Onset 24-48h, peak 4-7 days, duration 4 weeks
3. DENOSUMAB 120 mg SC monthly (anti-RANKL):
FDA-approved for hypercalcaemia of malignancy refractory to bisphosphonate
NO renal dose adjustment (safer eGFR < 30 / bisphosphonate intolerant)
Watch for hypocalcaemia + osteonecrosis of jaw + atypical femur fracture
4. CORTICOSTEROIDS for vitamin D-mediated:
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q6h then prednisolone 40-60 mg/d (lymphoma + granulomatous)
5. CALCITONIN 4-8 IU/kg SC/IM q6-12h:
Rapid onset (6-12h), short duration (tachyphylaxis 48h)
Useful bridge until bisphosphonate effect
6. DIALYSIS for refractory + severe AKI / fluid overload
AVOID:
Thiazide diuretics (reduce calcium excretion — worsens)
Lithium (similar)
Continued vitamin D / calcium supplements
Loop diuretics — only after volume repletion (not first-line; older guidance favoured for natriuresis)
Bed rest (immobility worsens — encourage mobilisation)
DEFINITIVE: treat underlying malignancy
PREVENTION:
Bisphosphonate / denosumab prophylaxis for bone metastases (breast / prostate / myeloma)
Adequate hydration
Avoid contributing factors
MONITOR: daily Ca + PO4 + creatinine + U&E; ECG; clinical
Side effects monitor: osteonecrosis of jaw (dental review pre-treatment), atypical femur fracture, hypocalcaemia + tetany (Ca + vit D supplement post-bisphosphonate if cleared but Ca falls), AKI

title: Superior vena cava obstruction (SVCO) — endovascular + tissue diagnosis
population: Mostly malignant (90%) — lung cancer (SCLC most common), lymphoma, germ cell, thymoma, breast met. Benign — thrombus around central line / pacemaker / fibrosing mediastinitis (TB).
presentation: Facial / arm swelling, dilated veins on chest + arms, dyspnoea, headache (worse lying down + Valsalva), visual + cognitive changes, syncope, hoarseness. Pemberton sign — facial plethora on raising arms.
redFlags: Tissue diagnosis NEEDED before non-emergency treatment for new cancer (lymphoma — chemo-curable; SCLC — sensitive; choriocarcinoma — different)
diagnostics: Clinical recognition — characteristic appearance
CT chest with contrast — confirms obstruction + identifies cause + mediastinal mass
Tissue diagnosis BEFORE definitive treatment (unless airway emergency):
Sputum cytology
Bronchoscopy + biopsy
Mediastinoscopy
CT-guided biopsy
Lymph node FNA
Histology guides treatment (lymphoma vs SCLC vs other)
management: STABILISATION:
Head + upper body elevation (45°)
Oxygen if hypoxaemic
DEXAMETHASONE 4-16 mg IV BD-QDS (reduces oedema; controversial — may interfere with lymphoma diagnosis biopsy; if biopsy already done OR clear cancer not lymphoma)
AVOID upper limb IV access (use lower limb)
Furosemide for facial oedema if no haemodynamic compromise
Treat dyspnoea + anxiety
Manage airway emergency if stridor (anaesthesia / ENT involvement; intubate awake if possible — sitting position)
DEFINITIVE TREATMENT BY CAUSE:
LUNG CANCER (SCLC/NSCLC):
Chemotherapy + radiotherapy (SCLC very chemosensitive; NSCLC slower)
Endovascular stent for symptomatic / refractory — rapid symptom relief
LYMPHOMA:
Chemotherapy (R-CHOP, etc) — chemosensitive
Steroid acutely
Radiotherapy for residual / consolidation
GERM CELL TUMOUR:
Cisplatin-based chemotherapy
Highly curable
THYMOMA:
Surgery + radiotherapy + chemotherapy
ENDOVASCULAR STENT (Interventional radiology):
Indication: rapid symptom relief, refractory, palliation
Effective + low morbidity
Anticoagulation post-stent (LMWH then DOAC) — duration depending on residual thrombus + cancer activity
THROMBOLYSIS for clot-predominant (often line-related): TPA local infusion + line removal
Line removal if line-associated thrombus
Anticoagulation for thrombotic component: DOAC or LMWH
FOLLOW-UP: regular CT, treat cancer + restage; symptom monitoring; stent surveillance
Recurrence risk: re-do stent, salvage chemotherapy, palliative
PALLIATIVE: pain + symptom control + advance care planning

title: Immune-related adverse events — checkpoint inhibitor toxicity
population: Patients on immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) — anti-PD1 (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, cemiplimab), anti-PD-L1 (atezolizumab, durvalumab, avelumab), anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab); combinations have higher irAE rates. Used in melanoma, NSCLC, RCC, urothelial, HCC, MSI-H tumours, increasingly many cancers. Any organ system can be affected.
presentation: irAE can occur weeks-months after start; sometimes after stopping. Common: rash (skin) > colitis (GI) > hepatitis > pneumonitis > endocrinopathy > arthritis > others. Severity grading by CTCAE 1-5.
redFlags: Pneumonitis — grade 3-4 (sats < 90, severe symptoms) — admit + high-dose steroid
Myocarditis (chest pain, troponin raise, ECG changes — high mortality)
diagnostics: Baseline (BEFORE ICI): TSH + free T4, ACTH + cortisol, glucose, LFT, FBC, U&E, autoantibodies (TPO, GAD if T1DM family), CXR
On suspected toxicity:
Symptom-specific workup
Skin: examination, dermatology referral, biopsy if severe
GI: stool culture + C. diff + calprotectin; flexible sigmoidoscopy + biopsy for moderate-severe colitis
Liver: LFT, hepatitis B + C, alcohol, autoimmune (ANA, SMA), drug history; imaging
Lung: CT thorax (ground-glass opacity, organising pneumonia, NSIP-like), PFTs + DLCO, BAL
Endocrine: TSH/T4, ACTH/cortisol/short Synacthen, glucose/HbA1c, FSH/LH if pituitary
Cardiac: troponin, ECG, echo, cardiac MRI; endomyocardial biopsy specialist
Neuro: MRI, LP, NCS/EMG, anti-acetylcholine receptor
Renal: urinalysis, eGFR, biopsy if significant
Rheum: ANA, RF, anti-CCP, joint imaging
Haem: FBC + Coombs + retic + LDH + haptoglobin
management: CTCAE GRADING + STEROID ALGORITHM:
GRADE 1 (mild): continue ICI + symptomatic + close monitor
GRADE 2 (moderate): hold ICI + prednisolone 0.5-1 mg/kg/d + resume when ≤ G1
GRADE 3 (severe): hold ICI + prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/d (or IV methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/d) + admit; taper over 4-6 weeks; permanently discontinue ICI for most grade 3 + ALL grade 4
GRADE 4 (life-threatening): IV methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/d + permanent discontinuation + IMMUNOSUPPRESSIVE ESCALATION if not improving within 48-72h:
Colitis: infliximab 5 mg/kg or vedolizumab
Hepatitis: mycophenolate / azathioprine
Pneumonitis: IV ig / mycophenolate / cyclophosphamide / tocilizumab; PCP prophylaxis for prolonged steroid
Myocarditis: high-dose IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day + IVIG / MMF / abatacept / ATG; cardiac MRI + biopsy specialist
Neurological: IVIG + plasma exchange + steroid
Severe skin (SJS/TEN): TEN-equivalent management; ciclosporin / IVIG
ORGAN-SPECIFIC HIGH-YIELD:
THYROIDITIS:
Hyperthyroid phase (early) — usually transient — symptom control β-blocker; NOT thionamide (autoimmune destruction, will become hypo)
Hypothyroid phase (later) — levothyroxine
Continue ICI
HYPOPHYSITIS (esp ipilimumab):
Headache + vision + nausea + adrenal insufficiency features
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat then maintenance
Pituitary panel + MRI pituitary
Often permanent multiple deficits + lifelong replacement
T1 DIABETES (sudden, often DKA presentation):
Insulin therapy + treat DKA
Continue ICI
Lifelong insulin
ADRENAL INSUFFICIENCY:
Hydrocortisone (separate condition)
Continue ICI with replacement
CHECKPOINT INHIBITOR-INDUCED ARTHRITIS:
NSAID, low-dose steroid, methotrexate / tocilizumab if refractory
RECHALLENGE:
After grade 2: usually safe to resume
After grade 3-4: case-by-case; permanent discontinuation for myocarditis / pneumonitis grade 3+ / encephalitis / severe colitis
Different ICI class after toxicity sometimes acceptable
MULTIDISCIPLINARY MANAGEMENT — irAE clinic / committee — oncology + organ specialist
PATIENT EDUCATION:
Carry irAE card + emergency contact
Report new symptoms immediately
Avoid live vaccines on ICI
Pre-existing autoimmune disease — higher irAE risk + specialist input
PCP PROPHYLAXIS (cotrimoxazole) for prolonged high-dose steroid (≥ 20 mg prednisolone × ≥ 4 weeks)

title: Chemotherapy-induced nausea + vomiting (CINV) — modern prophylaxis
population: Patients receiving chemotherapy — major QoL issue; reduces adherence + outcomes. Acute (within 24h), delayed (24-120h), anticipatory, breakthrough, refractory.
presentation: Nausea + vomiting from chemo. Severity by emetogenic potential of regimen + patient factors (female, age < 50, motion sickness history, pregnancy NVP history, anxiety, low ETOH use).
redFlags: Refractory + severe — dehydration / AKI / electrolyte / aspiration / Mallory-Weiss tear / wound dehiscence
Concomitant cause — bowel obstruction / brain mets / hypercalcaemia / GI bleed
Severe constipation from antiemetics (5-HT3, opioid) — bowel obstruction
diagnostics: Categorise chemo emetogenic risk: high (> 90%), moderate (30-90%), low (10-30%), minimal (< 10%)
Patient risk factors
Workup if not typical: U&E + Ca + glucose + abdominal imaging (rule out alternative)
management: PROPHYLAXIS BY EMETOGENIC RISK — give BEFORE chemo + continued days 2-5:
HIGH EMETOGENIC (cisplatin > 50 mg/m², AC, dacarbazine, mechlorethamine, streptozocin, BEACOPP):
Day 1: 5-HT3 antagonist (ondansetron / palonosetron / granisetron) + NK1 antagonist (aprepitant 125 mg / fosaprepitant IV 150 mg / rolapitant) + dexamethasone 12 mg + olanzapine 5-10 mg
Days 2-4: aprepitant 80 mg days 2-3 + dexamethasone 8 mg + olanzapine 10 mg days 2-4
OLANZAPINE-CONTAINING REGIMEN: superior in olanzapine-CINV trial (Navari NEJM 2016) — first-line for HEC now
MODERATE EMETOGENIC (carboplatin AUC ≥ 4, oxaliplatin, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, irinotecan):
Day 1: 5-HT3 + dexamethasone 8-12 mg + add NK1 antagonist for carboplatin AUC ≥ 4 + 4-drug option
Days 2-3: dexamethasone 8 mg
LOW EMETOGENIC:
Day 1: 5-HT3 or dexamethasone or metoclopramide
MINIMAL: no prophylactic; treat if occurs
DRUG SPECIFICS:
5-HT3 antagonists: ondansetron 8 mg PO/IV (max 16 mg single dose PO; max 16 mg/d to limit QT), granisetron 1 mg, palonosetron 0.25 mg IV (long half-life — preferred for delayed)
Constipation + headache + QTc prolongation common
NK1 antagonists: aprepitant 125 mg D1 then 80 mg D2-3; netupitant + palonosetron combination (Akynzeo); rolapitant
Dexamethasone: synergistic; consider impact on diabetes / immunosuppression / steroid-sensitive cancer; lower-dose / shorter for breast cancer (DEX-3 trial — non-inferior)
Olanzapine: 5-10 mg/d 4 days — sedation + metabolic; benzodiazepine alternative for anxiety
Cannabinoid (nabilone, dronabinol) — last-line; psychogenic side effects
Benzodiazepine (lorazepam) for anticipatory; not first-line acute
Promethazine, prochlorperazine — older, useful breakthrough
Antihistamine (cyclizine, hydroxyzine) — adjunct
BREAKTHROUGH:
Add agent from different class
Olanzapine 5-10 mg/d × 3 d
Metoclopramide 10-20 mg q6h
Prochlorperazine 10 mg q6h
Lorazepam 0.5-2 mg q6h for anxiety component
Address cause (constipation, mucositis, brain mets, hyperCa)
REFRACTORY:
Multiple regimens fail
Olanzapine + benzodiazepine + steroid
Consider Mirtazapine 15-30 mg nocte (5-HT2/H1 — efficacy + sedation + appetite)
Cannabinoid
Pre-medication for anticipatory: lorazepam pre-chemo + relaxation / hypnotherapy
Cognitive-behavioural intervention
NON-PHARM ADJUNCTS:
Ginger, acupressure P6 (sea-bands), acupuncture, mindfulness, relaxation
Small frequent meals, bland food, hydration
Avoid strong smells
ELECTROLYTE + HYDRATION:
IV fluid for dehydration
Replace K+ + Mg as needed
ORAL CHEMOTHERAPY: ondansetron PRN; capecitabine, oral targeted therapy — often easier-tolerated
PREGNANCY in cancer patient: ondansetron + metoclopramide + steroid acceptable; avoid NK1 antagonists
PAEDIATRIC: similar approach age-appropriate; aprepitant approved age 6 months+

WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis / WHO Essential Medicines for Cancer

title: Cancer pain — WHO modified ladder + opioid management
population: 30-50% of cancer patients have pain; 70-90% of advanced cancer; under-treated globally, especially SSA (opioid access gap).
presentation: Nociceptive (somatic / visceral), neuropathic (nerve invasion / cord compression / chemo-induced), mixed; bone pain, incident pain (movement-related), breakthrough pain.
redFlags: Spinal cord compression presenting with back pain (separate condition)
Suspected opioid toxicity (sedation, miosis, respiratory depression — naloxone)
Suspected addiction / diversion — manage with respect, MAT links
diagnostics: Pain assessment: location, character, intensity (NRS 0-10), pattern, triggers, function
Mechanism (nociceptive vs neuropathic vs visceral vs mixed)
Identify cause (tumour invasion, metastasis, treatment-related, comorbid)
Imaging if new / changed pain (rule out cord compression, pathological fracture, visceral problem)
Side effects of analgesics
management: WHO MODIFIED LADDER (3-step + adjuvants):
STEP 1 (mild pain NRS 1-3):
Paracetamol 1 g q6h (max 4 g/d; reduce in liver / low weight)
NSAID (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac) + PPI cover; avoid in CKD / GIB / asthma / HF
STEP 2 (mild-moderate persistent NRS 4-6):
Add weak opioid: codeine 30-60 mg q6h, tramadol 50-100 mg q6h (caution serotonin syndrome SSRI)
OR move to step 3 low-dose strong opioid
STEP 3 (moderate-severe NRS ≥ 7):
STRONG OPIOID — modified-release + breakthrough doses:
MORPHINE (gold standard, cheap, available SSA):
Immediate release: 5-10 mg PO q4h
Convert to modified release (MST / Zomorph / Sevredol) BD after 24-48h titration
Breakthrough: 1/6 to 1/10 of total daily dose PRN q1-4h
OXYCODONE: alternative, similar potency 1.5-2× morphine PO
HYDROMORPHONE: 5-7× more potent than morphine; useful when morphine intolerant
FENTANYL transdermal patch (Durogesic) — stable pain, oral route compromised; 12-25 mcg/h start; matrix vs reservoir patches
METHADONE: complex pharmacokinetics, long half-life, NMDA antagonist — useful neuropathic + opioid rotation; specialist
BUPRENORPHINE patch: alternative, partial agonist (ceiling effect — limits maximal dose)
Conversion ratios (oral morphine equivalent — OME):
Codeine 60 mg = morphine 6 mg
Tramadol 50 mg = morphine 5-10 mg
Oxycodone PO 1.5× more potent than morphine PO
Hydromorphone PO 7× morphine PO
Fentanyl 25 mcg/h patch ≈ 60-90 mg morphine PO/24h
OPIOID-INDUCED SIDE EFFECTS (manage proactively):
Constipation: routine laxative (senna + macrogol; methylnaltrexone if refractory) — START WITH OPIOID
Nausea: metoclopramide / haloperidol / ondansetron
Sedation: dose adjust, methylphenidate for refractory daytime sedation
Respiratory depression: naloxone (carefully titrated — avoid precipitating severe pain in tolerant)
Confusion / delirium: rotate opioid (different opioid, different metabolite); reduce dose; treat trigger (infection, hyperCa, brain mets)
Itch: antihistamine, ondansetron, rotation
Myoclonus: rotation, benzodiazepine
Urinary retention: catheterisation, rotation
Hyperalgesia: rotation, ketamine, methadone
OPIOID ROTATION:
Switch to different opioid when intolerable side effects / inadequate analgesia
Reduce calculated dose by 25-50% (incomplete cross-tolerance)
Re-titrate to effect
ADJUVANTS (use parallel with opioid — not replacement):
NEUROPATHIC pain: gabapentin 100-3600 mg/d, pregabalin 75-600 mg/d, amitriptyline 10-75 mg nocte, duloxetine 30-120 mg/d (also depression)
BONE pain: NSAID + bisphosphonate / denosumab + RT + ortho stabilisation if fracture risk
VISCERAL pain: hyoscine butylbromide, octreotide for bowel obstruction
CORTICOSTEROID for liver capsule pain, soft tissue swelling, headache from raised ICP / cord compression
Anaesthetic interventions: nerve block, intrathecal pump, neurolysis, kyphoplasty / vertebroplasty
Ketamine low-dose for refractory pain (specialist)
Methadone rotation for opioid-resistant
NON-PHARM:
Physiotherapy, OT, TENS, acupuncture, massage, heat / cold
CBT, mindfulness, relaxation
Spiritual + psychological support
Address fatigue, mood, sleep, anorexia
BREAKTHROUGH PAIN:
PRN immediate-release opioid (1/6-1/10 of total daily)
Sublingual / nasal fentanyl rapid-onset for predictable incident pain
Pre-emptive dose before movement, dressing change
END-OF-LIFE PAIN:
Continuous SC infusion via syringe driver (CSCI) when oral compromised
Morphine + midazolam + glycopyrronium + cyclizine common
Anticipatory prescribing for SC PRN breakthrough
Family education on managing CSCI
OPIOID ACCESS in SSA (CRITICAL):
Severe global inequity — > 80% of world morphine in HIC
WHO essential medicines list includes oral immediate-release morphine
Kenya MOH National Cancer Control Plan addresses; KEHPRO advocacy
Train clinicians; community-based palliative care (Hospice Kenya, MMUST)
Address regulatory barriers + opioidphobia

ASCO Use of Opioids for Adults With Pain From Cancer 2024

title: End-of-life care — comprehensive comfort + family + bereavement
population: Patients in last weeks-days of life from any incurable disease. Significant SSA palliative care gap.
presentation: Recognition of dying phase: rapid functional decline, decreased oral intake, peripheral cyanosis, mottling, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, altered consciousness, secretions, agitation, cool extremities, urinary output decline, pulse changes.
redFlags: Diagnosis of dying — opportunity to focus on comfort
Place of care + place of death preferences
diagnostics: Recognising dying — multidisciplinary assessment + experienced clinician input
AVOID unnecessary investigations (bloods, imaging) — focus shifts to comfort
Continue meaningful diagnostics (PO checks, glucose for diabetic) if guides comfort
Document goals + preferences + escalation status
management: FRAMEWORK:
Holistic — physical + psychological + social + spiritual + practical
Patient-centred + family-inclusive
Cultural + religious sensitivity
Communication + shared decision-making
Multidisciplinary team (palliative + GP + nurse + chaplain + family)
ANTICIPATORY PRESCRIBING — usually 4 drugs prn SC:
Pain: morphine 2.5-5 mg SC q1-4h prn (or 1/6-1/10 of background)
Distress / breathlessness: midazolam 2.5-5 mg SC q1-4h prn
Nausea: cyclizine 50 mg SC q8h prn or haloperidol 0.5-1.5 mg SC q4h prn
Secretions: hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg SC q4h prn (or hyoscine hydrobromide for combined anti-secretory + sedation)
Have available: prescribed in advance, accessible to family + community team
CONTINUOUS SUBCUTANEOUS INFUSION (CSCI / syringe driver) when oral compromised:
Convert oral opioid to SC (oral morphine to SC morphine 2:1 ratio)
Add anti-emetic (cyclizine 75-150 mg / 24h or haloperidol 1.5-5 mg / 24h)
Add midazolam 10-30 mg / 24h for terminal agitation
Add hyoscine butylbromide 60-120 mg / 24h for noisy secretions
Daily review + titrate
SYMPTOM-SPECIFIC:
PAIN: opioid (separate condition); rotate if tolerance / side effects
BREATHLESSNESS:
Non-pharm: position upright, fan, cool air, calm environment, breathing techniques
Low-dose opioid (morphine 2.5-5 mg PO/SC) — first-line
Benzodiazepine for anxiety component (lorazepam 0.5-1 mg SL)
O2 if hypoxic (not routinely if not)
Treat reversible — thoracentesis, drainage, transfusion (if appropriate stage)
NAUSEA:
Identify mechanism (drugs, raised ICP, bowel obstruction, hypercalcaemia, anxiety, vestibular)
Targeted antiemetic:
Mechanical bowel obstruction: cyclizine + ondansetron + octreotide + dexamethasone; AVOID prokinetic (worsens with full mechanical block)
Raised ICP: cyclizine + dexamethasone
Vestibular: cyclizine, antihistamine
Vagal / GI: metoclopramide (PROKINETIC)
Drug / metabolic: haloperidol low-dose
AGITATION / TERMINAL DELIRIUM:
Identify cause (urinary retention, pain, faecal impaction, drug-induced, hypoxia, hypercalcaemia)
Reorientation + calm environment + family presence
Midazolam 2.5-5 mg SC prn or infusion
Haloperidol 1.5-5 mg / 24h SCI for delirium
Levomepromazine for refractory + need sedation
SECRETIONS (RATTLE):
Reposition + suction if accessible
Hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg SC prn or 60-120 mg / 24h
Glycopyrronium 200-400 mcg SC prn
Family preparation — usually distresses family more than patient
CONSTIPATION:
Routine laxative (senna + macrogol) on opioids
SC methylnaltrexone refractory
Manual evacuation if impacted
Anxiety, depression, spiritual distress — counselling, chaplaincy
ARTIFICIAL HYDRATION + NUTRITION:
Limited benefit in last days; often increases secretions, oedema, breathlessness
Discuss with family — comfort measures + mouth care primary
Continue oral if patient takes
Subcutaneous fluid for hydration only if distress / specific symptom benefit
Withdrawal of CPR + IV fluid + nutrition NOT same as 'withdrawing care' — emphasise to family + clinical team
MEDICATION REVIEW:
Stop unnecessary (lipid-lowering, antihypertensives, antidiabetic, prophylactic — usually)
Continue meaningful (analgesic, anti-emetic, antibiotic if causing comfort, anticonvulsant)
Convert to SC / SL when oral compromised
COMMUNICATION:
Inform patient + family of recognition of dying
Allow questions + concerns + cultural / religious needs
Sit at eye level, allow silence, avoid jargon, prepare for emotion
Address family fears (suffering, choking, oxygen need, opioid concerns)
Spiritual / religious care (chaplain, priest, imam, traditional)
PLACE OF DEATH:
Discuss preferences early
Home / hospice / hospital / care home
Home death requires: family willing + symptom controlled + 24/7 advice + meds available + practical support
Hospice — gold standard for end-of-life care in HIC; Kenya — Nairobi + regional hospices
AFTER DEATH:
Verify death + medical certificate
Inform family with sensitivity
Cultural / religious practices for body care
Pronounce + paperwork sensitively
Bereavement information + follow-up
Notify primary care + community team
BEREAVEMENT:
Acknowledge loss
Support resources
Recognise complicated grief — refer mental health
Children — age-appropriate communication
Anniversary / first events vulnerable
STAFF SUPPORT:
Debrief after challenging deaths
Recognise compassion fatigue + burnout
Self-care
SSA PALLIATIVE CARE:
Major gap — < 10% of need met globally
Hospice Africa (Uganda) model — community-based + oral morphine
WHO Public Health Strategy for Palliative Care (3 pillars — policy / education / drug availability)
Kenya KEHPRO + Kenya National Palliative Care Policy
Train clinicians + community health workers + family caregivers
Address opioidphobia + regulatory barriers
Advocacy for Lancet Commission essentials package

title: Cancer-associated venous thromboembolism — DOAC + LMWH
population: Cancer patients have 4-7× higher VTE risk; chemotherapy + surgery + central lines + immobility further increase. Pancreatic + brain + ovary + lung + lymphoma highest.
presentation: DVT (unilateral leg swelling + pain) / PE (dyspnoea + chest pain + tachycardia) / catheter-related thrombosis / abdominal vein thrombosis (Trousseau syndrome) / cerebral venous thrombosis.
redFlags: Acute massive PE with haemodynamic instability — thrombolysis if no contraindication
Active GI bleeding from luminal cancer (relative contraindication to anticoagulation)
Intracranial metastases / glioma + DOAC bleeding risk
diagnostics: DVT: compression ultrasound; D-dimer often raised in cancer (not specific — use Wells + imaging)
PE: CTPA gold standard; V/Q if contraindicated; D-dimer of limited use; ECG, echo for RV dysfunction
Catheter-related thrombosis: ultrasound

Investigate occult malignancy in unprovoked VTE (5-10% prevalence) — limited screening (age-appropriate screening, breast / pelvic / abdo exam, CXR, abdominal US, urinalysis) — extensive workup low yield (SOME trial)
management: ANTICOAGULATION CHOICE (2024 evidence-driven):
DOAC NOW FIRST-LINE for most cancer-associated VTE (per ITAC, ESMO, NCCN, ASCO):
Apixaban 10 mg BD × 7 d then 5 mg BD (CARAVAGGIO trial — non-inferior to dalteparin + less major bleeding)
Rivaroxaban 15 mg BD × 21 d then 20 mg OD (SELECT-D)
Edoxaban 60 mg OD (Hokusai-VTE Cancer)
LMWH (dalteparin / enoxaparin / tinzaparin) — historical first-line; still preferred for:
Luminal GI malignancy (DOAC GI bleed risk)
Recently diagnosed brain tumour / mets
Drug-drug interactions (CYP3A4 inducers / inhibitors — antifungals, antiepileptics)
Thrombocytopaenia (50-100 — dose-reduce; < 50 — case-by-case)
Renal impairment (DOAC dose-adjust or avoid in severe)
Pregnancy
Patient preference + adherence
Warfarin — falling out of favour (less effective than LMWH/DOAC in cancer-associated VTE, more bleeding)
DURATION:
At least 6 months; consider INDEFINITELY while cancer active + receiving treatment
Reassess at 3-6 months for benefit/bleeding balance
Bridge for procedures (LMWH preferred if interrupting DOAC)
MASSIVE PE:
Thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2h) for haemodynamic instability — careful balance against bleeding risk in cancer (relative contraindication if recent surgery / brain mets / active bleed)
Catheter-directed thrombolysis as alternative
Surgical embolectomy
ECMO bridge
BREAKTHROUGH VTE on anticoagulation:
Switch from DOAC to LMWH (some prefer; evidence limited)
Increase LMWH dose by 25%
Investigate adherence + drug interactions
Heparin-induced thrombocytopaenia (HIT) workup if on UFH/LMWH
Consider IVC filter (retrievable) if anticoagulation contraindicated + active VTE
CATHETER-RELATED THROMBOSIS:
Anticoagulate as standard VTE
Remove line if: line no longer needed, sepsis, persistent symptoms, malposition
Salvage if essential central access — anticoagulate + monitor
PRIMARY PROPHYLAXIS:
HIGH-RISK INPATIENTS (Padua/Khorana score): LMWH or DOAC
HIGH-RISK OUTPATIENTS:
Pancreatic + lung + others Khorana score ≥ 2:
Rivaroxaban 10 mg OD (CASSINI) or apixaban 2.5 mg BD (AVERT)
6 months thromboprophylaxis
Multiple myeloma on lenalidomide / pomalidomide: aspirin (low risk) or LMWH (high risk)
Hospitalised acutely ill: LMWH if no contraindication
Surgical cancer patients: extended LMWH 28 d post-major abdo/pelvic surgery
SPECIAL SITUATIONS:
Central nervous system tumour with VTE: anticoagulate (modest bleeding risk; LMWH preferred over DOAC); careful balance
Thrombocytopaenia: dose-reduce LMWH (50% if plt 25-50); platelet transfusion + standard if < 25
Acute leukaemia + thrombocytopaenia: case-by-case; bridge with reduced anticoag + platelet support
Renal impairment: apixaban + edoxaban OK to eGFR 15; rivaroxaban / dabigatran avoid eGFR < 30
Hepatic impairment: avoid DOAC in Child-Pugh B-C; LMWH
Pregnancy: LMWH (DOAC + warfarin avoid)
Pre-procedure: hold DOAC 24-72h (renal-dependent); bridge if high-risk thrombosis
Trousseau syndrome (migratory superficial thrombophlebitis): suspect occult malignancy
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) in malignancy: treat cause; replace + supportive

title: Paediatric severe pneumonia — WHO IMCI + Kenya MOH protocols
population: Children < 5 years — leading cause of paediatric mortality globally + SSA disproportionate. Kenya: highest under-5 mortality from pneumonia.
presentation: Cough + difficult breathing + age-specific tachypnoea (≥ 60 < 2 mo, ≥ 50 2-11 mo, ≥ 40 12-59 mo). IMCI severe: chest indrawing or any general danger sign (unable to drink/breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargy/unconscious, stridor in calm child).
redFlags: IMCI 'severe pneumonia / very severe disease' — any general danger sign
Severe respiratory distress (head bobbing, grunting, nasal flaring, severe indrawing)
Severe malnutrition (admit per IMAM regardless of pneumonia severity)
diagnostics: Clinical assessment using IMCI chart booklet
Pulse oximetry MANDATORY (key triage tool — WHO 2014)
Respiratory rate (count for full 1 min)
Temperature, weight, MUAC (malnutrition screen)
Glucose (low in severe illness)
Malaria RDT (any febrile child in endemic — Kenya)
HIV test (if status unknown)
FBC (severe), CXR (suspected complication / not improving)
Blood culture if severe / not responding
ABG / VBG if severe
management: WHO IMCI / KENYA MOH PAEDIATRIC PROTOCOLS:
FAST BREATHING / NON-SEVERE PNEUMONIA (no chest indrawing, no danger signs):
Home treatment: amoxicillin DT (dispersible tablet) 40 mg/kg/dose BD × 3 days (WHO 2014 reduced from 5 d)
Treat fever (paracetamol)
Continue feeding + extra fluids
Return immediately if worsening / not improving in 3 days
SEVERE PNEUMONIA (chest indrawing OR danger signs):
ADMIT to facility
OXYGEN if sats < 90% — nasal prongs 0.5-2 L/min (target sats > 90%)
AMOXICILLIN dispersible tablet 40-50 mg/kg BD × 5 days (WHO 2014 — replaces previous penicillin in inpatient mild-moderate)
Severe + danger signs: IV ampicillin 50 mg/kg q6h + gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg OD × 5 days; switch to oral when improving
If failure / very severe: change to ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg/day; add cloxacillin / vancomycin if Staph suspected (empyema, cavitation, post-measles)
Cotrim 8 mg TMP/kg BD × 21 d if HIV-exposed/positive + LRTI (PCP cover) + prednisolone 1 mg/kg if hypoxia
Vitamin A 100,000 IU < 1 yr / 200,000 IU > 1 yr if not given in last month (especially measles)
Zinc 10 mg < 6 mo / 20 mg ≥ 6 mo × 10-14 days for measles / persistent infection
Treat concomitant malaria if RDT+
TB consideration if symptoms > 2 weeks / contact / HIV+ (GeneXpert + sputum/gastric)
VERY SEVERE / IMMINENT FAILURE:
HDU/ICU
CPAP — bubble CPAP for hypoxic infants (proven mortality benefit Kenya/Malawi trials)
Mechanical ventilation if available
IV fluids cautiously — FEAST trial — AVOID bolus in non-shock African children (harmful); use maintenance
Empirical broad-spectrum + cover for atypicals if hospital-acquired
Consider thoracentesis if pleural effusion (empyema management — drain + 4-6 weeks antibiotic)
FOLLOW-UP:
Reassess at 48-72h for response
Discharge when sats > 90% on room air, feeding well, no danger signs
Counsel family on warning signs
Complete vaccination — esp PCV13, Hib, measles, COVID, RSV
PREVENTION:
Immunisation (Hib + PCV13 — Kenya EPI; rotavirus reduces gastro-pneumonia; measles)
Exclusive breastfeeding 6 months
Reduce indoor air pollution (clean cookstoves)
HIV PMTCT + early infant treatment
Vitamin A supplementation campaigns
Address malnutrition (IMAM)
Hand hygiene + WASH
Address overcrowding

title: Neonatal sepsis — early + late onset
population: Newborns < 28 days; major SSA mortality. Early-onset < 72h (vertical — GBS, E. coli, Listeria), late-onset > 72h (nosocomial — coag-neg Staph, Staph aureus, gram-negatives, Candida).
presentation: Subtle + non-specific in neonates — temperature instability (hypo or hyperthermia), feeding poorly, lethargy, irritability, apnoea, grunting, cyanosis, jaundice, abdominal distension, bleeding, seizures, bulging fontanelle (meningitis).
redFlags: Any sick neonate — assume sepsis until proven otherwise
Mother with chorioamnionitis / GBS-positive without IAP
Maternal HSV outbreak / fever near delivery
Inborn errors of metabolism in differential — hypoglycaemia + acidosis + odd odour
diagnostics: Clinical assessment + WHO/IMCI danger signs
ALWAYS perform LUMBAR PUNCTURE — meningitis incidence high + non-specific signs
Blood culture × 1 (paeds — single, careful technique)
FBC + CRP + glucose + electrolytes + bilirubin + coagulation
Urine MSU + culture (suprapubic aspirate if needed)
CXR if respiratory
Surface cultures + gastric aspirate if early-onset
Mother — review GBS status, chorioamnionitis, PROM > 18h, intrapartum fever, antibiotic in labour
HIV test mother + infant if status unknown
Consider HSV PCR if vesicles / maternal genital herpes
Acyclovir empiric if HSV suspected (don't wait for results)
management: EARLY-ONSET SEPSIS (< 72h):
AMPICILLIN 50-100 mg/kg q12h + GENTAMICIN 4-5 mg/kg/day (preterm 3-4 mg/kg q24-36h) — first-line per WHO + Kenya + AAP
Alternative: ampicillin + cefotaxime (some prefer + cover gram-negatives better)
Add acyclovir 60 mg/kg/day in 3 doses if HSV suspected
Treat for 10 days if culture positive (14 days if meningitis 21 days)
Stop antibiotics at 48h if cultures negative + clinical improvement
LATE-ONSET SEPSIS (> 72h):
VANCOMYCIN + GENTAMICIN (or amikacin)
Cefepime / piperacillin-tazobactam / meropenem if hospital-acquired / NICU exposure
Consider antifungal (fluconazole 12 mg/kg IV) for prolonged NICU stay / central line / TPN
Acyclovir if HSV suspected
SUPPORTIVE:
Maintain thermoneutral environment (skin-to-skin/Kangaroo Mother Care)
Glucose 2.6-5 mmol/L (avoid hypoglycaemia — major risk)
Oxygen if sats < 90%
Cautious fluid resuscitation 10-20 ml/kg over 30 min if shock (NOT routine bolus)
Pressor (adrenaline 0.05-0.3 mcg/kg/min) for shock not responsive to fluid
Treat seizures (phenobarbital 20 mg/kg loading)
Vitamin K 1 mg IM (haemorrhagic disease of newborn — give all newborns; some preparations needed if not yet)
Establish enteral feeding when stable (breastmilk preferred; NG if poor suck)
Phototherapy for jaundice (separate)
SPECIFIC PATHOGENS:
GBS: penicillin G 250,000 IU/kg/day; close maternal contacts (other neonate) testing
Listeria: ampicillin + gentamicin × 14-21 days
HSV: acyclovir 60 mg/kg/d × 14-21 days (longer if CNS)
Candida: fluconazole 12 mg/kg/d (or amphotericin B if severe)
Congenital syphilis: penicillin G 50,000 IU/kg q12h × 10 days
Congenital toxoplasmosis: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid × 12 months
Congenital CMV: ganciclovir / valganciclovir
PREVENTION:
INTRAPARTUM ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS for GBS — penicillin G 5 MU then 2.5 MU q4h × delivery
Indications: GBS-positive screen, GBS bacteriuria pregnancy, previous GBS-affected infant, preterm < 37 wk, PROM > 18h, intrapartum fever
Risk-based or universal GBS screening (35-37 weeks)
Skilled birth attendance, clean delivery, cord care, early breastfeeding
Chlorhexidine cord care (low resource — WHO recommendation)
Maternal vaccination (Tdap, RSV — newer)
PMTCT for HIV
Maternal screening + treat syphilis + UTI + bacterial vaginosis
Standard infection control in NICU + hand hygiene + early breast milk
Kenya MOH protocols: standard package per Basic Paediatric Protocols + Newborn Care

title: Paediatric DKA — ISPAD 2022 + slow rehydration
population: T1DM children — initial presentation (especially LMIC late diagnosis), missed insulin, infection, omission. Cerebral oedema (0.5-1%) major preventable mortality cause.
presentation: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, abdominal pain, vomiting, Kussmaul respiration, fruity breath, dehydration, altered mental state. Distinguish from sepsis / appendicitis / gastroenteritis.
redFlags: Cerebral oedema (headache, reduced GCS, papilloedema, abnormal pupillary response, hypertension + bradycardia, change in pattern of respiration, decorticate / decerebrate posturing) — life-threatening
First presentation — risk of cerebral oedema higher
diagnostics: Diagnostic triad: hyperglycaemia > 11 mmol/L (or any in known T1DM) + ketonaemia/uria + acidosis (pH < 7.3, HCO3 < 18)
Severity: mild pH 7.25-7.3, mod 7.0-7.25, severe < 7.0
Hourly: glucose + GCS + vital signs; 2-hourly: U&E + venous gas; 4-hourly: ABG/VBG + ketones
Strict input/output (catheter if obtunded)
Identify trigger: infection (CRP, cultures, CXR), missed insulin, MI rarely paeds, pancreatitis, pregnancy in older adolescents
management: ISPAD 2022 PROTOCOL (different from adult — slower, cerebral oedema risk):
ASSESS:
Mild dehydration (clinical 5%) vs moderate (5-10%) vs severe (> 10% — shock)
Severity by pH
FLUIDS — SLOW REHYDRATION OVER 48 HOURS:
Shock only — 10-20 ml/kg crystalloid bolus over 30-60 min (UK / UK + ISPAD PECARN trials — bolus volume more conservative than older practice)
Maintenance + replace deficit (max 5-10% deficit) over 48h (not bolus, not 24h)
Calculate total: maintenance (Holliday-Segar) + estimated deficit
0.9% NaCl initial; switch to 0.45% NaCl + D5% when glucose < 14-17 mmol/L
AVOID rapid fluid resuscitation (cerebral oedema risk) — PECARN large RCT showed similar outcomes with multiple regimens but ANY excessive fluid harmful
INSULIN:
Start AFTER first hour of fluid (allows partial correction of hypovolaemia)
Fixed-rate IV infusion 0.05-0.1 U/kg/h (ISPAD 0.05 mg/kg/h for younger / less severe — reduces cerebral oedema)
Do NOT bolus insulin (cerebral oedema risk)
Continue LONG-ACTING insulin (basal) if previously on — reduces rebound hyperglycaemia
Target: ketone drop 0.5/h, HCO3 rise 3/h, glucose drop 3-5 mmol/L/h (no faster)
Adjust insulin rate if glucose falling > 5 mmol/L/h
When ketones < 0.5 mmol/L + pH > 7.3 + HCO3 > 18 + eating + drinking — change to SC insulin (overlap 1h to avoid recurrence)
POTASSIUM:
Replace EARLY (insulin shifts K+ intracellular)
K+ > 5.5: no replacement, recheck 2h
K+ 3.5-5.5: add 40 mmol KCl per litre fluid
K+ < 3.5: HOLD INSULIN until K+ replaced; replace K+ + recheck before resuming
BICARBONATE: NOT routine (no benefit + worsens cerebral oedema risk)
PHOSPHATE: replace only if < 0.3
CEREBRAL OEDEMA — emergency (any decline in mental status / pattern of breathing change / focal signs):
IMMEDIATE MANNITOL 0.5-1 g/kg IV over 10-15 min OR 3% NaCl 5 ml/kg over 10-15 min (preferred newer guidance)
Reduce IV fluid rate by 1/3
Elevate head 30°
Intubate + hyperventilate to PaCO2 30-35 if signs of herniation (controversial — avoid excessive hyperventilation)
URGENT CT brain (only after stabilising — do not delay treatment for imaging)
PICU admission
PREVENT CEREBRAL OEDEMA:
Avoid rapid fluid administration
Avoid bicarbonate
Avoid rapid drop in serum glucose (insulin titration to ≤ 5 mmol/L/h drop)
Adequate potassium replacement
Avoid bolus insulin
Maintain serum sodium correction (corrected Na for glucose should rise as glucose falls)
MONITORING:
Hourly: GCS, vital signs, glucose, fluid balance
2-hourly: electrolytes, venous gas, ketones
4-hourly: ABG, full bloods
Cardiac monitoring
TRIGGER MANAGEMENT:
Infection: cultures + appropriate antibiotic
Address missed insulin / psychosocial (insulin omission for weight in adolescents — 'diabulimia')
POST-DKA:
Diabetes specialist nurse education / DAFNE / structured education for family
CGM consideration
Pump consideration recurrent
Psychological support (chronic disease, family burden)
Sick day rules education
Test for celiac + thyroid (associated autoimmune)
Follow-up + community support

title: Severe acute malnutrition — IMAM with hypoglycaemia/hypothermia/dehydration triad
population: Children 6-59 months with MUAC < 11.5 cm OR weight-for-height z-score < −3 OR bilateral pitting oedema. Kenya ASAL counties + drought-affected areas; refugee + IDP populations.
presentation: Marasmus (severe wasting), kwashiorkor (bilateral pitting oedema + dermatosis + hair changes + hepatomegaly), or marasmic-kwashiorkor. WHO criteria: MUAC < 11.5 or WHZ < -3 or oedema.
redFlags: Severe dehydration (cautious — IV fluid bolus harmful per FEAST)
Eye signs of vitamin A deficiency (xerophthalmia, corneal ulceration) — emergency
diagnostics: WHO criteria + clinical staging
Anthropometry: MUAC, weight, height/length, WHZ, oedema grade
Appetite test with RUTF — determines OTP vs inpatient
Blood glucose (always)
Malaria RDT, HIV test
FBC + Hb
Stool for parasites + giardia
Urine dipstick + MSU
Vital signs + temperature
CXR if respiratory signs
TB screening (signs, sputum/gastric, GeneXpert)
management: WHO PROTOCOL — 10 STEPS (STABILISATION → TRANSITION → REHABILITATION):
STABILISATION (PHASE 1 — inpatient if complicated, 1-7 days):
1. HYPOGLYCAEMIA prevention/treatment: glucose every 30 min; F-75 every 2-3h; if BG < 3 — give 50 ml of 10% glucose PO/NG + start F-75
2. HYPOTHERMIA: skin-to-skin / thermal blanket / Kangaroo Mother Care; monitor temp 30 min
3. DEHYDRATION:
AVOID IV resuscitation unless shock (FEAST trial harm)
Use ReSoMal (rehydration solution for malnutrition — low sodium, high potassium) — 5 ml/kg every 30 min × 2h, then 5-10 ml/kg/h for 4-10h
If shock + no IV access: ReSoMal NG or per rectum
If shock + IV essential: half-strength Darrow's with 5% dextrose 15 ml/kg over 1h, reassess
4. ELECTROLYTES: SAM children severely K depleted + Na overloaded — give potassium 3-4 mmol/kg/day + Mg + replenish glucose (in F-75)
5. INFECTION (very common, often subtle):
ALL get prophylactic AMOXICILLIN 50 mg/kg/day × 5-7 days (uncomplicated)
If complicated (signs of severe infection / shock): IV gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg/day + ampicillin 50 mg/kg q6h
Treat malaria if RDT+ (artesunate)
Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis if HIV+
6. MICRONUTRIENTS:
Vitamin A on day 1 IF no oedema and no recent dose (50,000 IU < 6 mo, 100,000 IU 6-11 mo, 200,000 IU > 12 mo)
Vitamin A for ALL children with oedema or eye signs
Folic acid 5 mg day 1 then 1 mg daily
Multivitamin
Zinc (in F-75)
Iron NOT in phase 1 (oxidative stress + worsens infection)
7. F-75 FEEDING (LOW PROTEIN + LACTOSE-FREE):
130 ml/kg/day in 8-12 small feeds (start) — slowly, avoids refeeding
Reduce volume + protein in severe oedema
F-75 = 75 kcal/100 ml, 0.9 g protein/100 ml
NG if not tolerating PO
8. CAUTIOUS REFEEDING + WATCH FOR REFEEDING SYNDROME: hypophosphataemia + hypoK + hypoMg + cardiac failure
TRANSITION (3-5 days):
9. SWITCH from F-75 to F-100 (or RUTF) when:
Appetite returns
Oedema reducing
No medical complication
Slow transition over 2-3 days
REHABILITATION (PHASE 2 — outpatient OTP):
10. RUTF (ready-to-use therapeutic food, Plumpy'Nut):
200 kcal/kg/day OR 175 kcal/kg/day adjusted
Weekly OTP visits — weight, MUAC, MUAC, oedema, appetite, action plan
Continue until 2 visits with WHZ ≥ −2 OR MUAC ≥ 12.5 cm + no oedema × 2 visits
Continue routine medicines per WHO + IMAM
Discharge: nutritional rehab + community support + monitoring
F-75 / F-100 / RUTF — UN and WHO standardised products via UNICEF / WFP procurement; locally produced increasing (Insta in Kenya)
STIMULATION + DEVELOPMENT:
SAM children have neurodevelopmental risks
Play + interaction + responsive caregiving
Care for Child Development (UNICEF)
MONITORING:
Weekly outpatient: weight, MUAC, oedema, appetite, action plan adherence
Inpatient: daily weight, twice-daily oedema, vital signs, appetite
PREVENTION (community + policy):
Maternal nutrition + breastfeeding 6 months exclusive + continued 24 months + complementary feeding
IMCI integrated + growth monitoring (MUAC tape, GMP)
Food security + cash transfer programmes
Address drought + conflict + displacement
Kenya: ASAL counties priority; Cash Transfer + School Feeding + Vitamin A campaigns
Linda Mama + ANC
Address underlying poverty, social determinants
DISCHARGE PLANNING:
Community follow-up by CHV
Linkage to other services (immunisation, social protection, HIV)
Counselling + caregiver education on feeding + hygiene + danger signs
Continued nutritional support for at-risk after discharge
Late mortality (6 months post) higher than discharge — continued follow-up critical

title: Severe paediatric malaria — IV artesunate (AQUAMAT)
population: Children in malaria-endemic areas (SSA — leading cause of child mortality). Highest burden Kenya endemic counties (Lake region, coast, Western, Nyanza).
presentation: Severe complications: cerebral malaria (impaired consciousness, seizures, coma), severe anaemia (Hb < 5 g/dL), respiratory distress (acidotic), hypoglycaemia (very common in children), hyperparasitaemia (> 4%), AKI, jaundice, hyperlactataemia, shock (rare — exclude bacterial co-infection), abnormal bleeding.
redFlags: Hypoglycaemia < 2.2 mmol/L (often profound — give glucose immediately)
Respiratory distress (acidotic breathing — Kussmaul-like) — sign of severe acidosis
Shock — but in African children FEAST showed bolus harm — cautious
Concurrent bacterial sepsis (especially Salmonella in SSA)
diagnostics: MALARIA RDT (HRP2 or pLDH) — first-line (immediate)
MICROSCOPY thick + thin film if available (species + parasitaemia %)
Blood glucose (always — hypoglycaemia very common)
FBC + Hb (severe anaemia)
U&E + creatinine + ABG / VBG + lactate
LFT
Coagulation (DIC risk)
Urinalysis (haemoglobinuria, AKI)
Blood culture (rule out bacterial co-infection — Salmonella common in SSA)
LP if seizure / coma (exclude meningitis — controversial in cerebral malaria due to raised ICP risk; do after stabilising + imaging if possible)
Cross-match for transfusion
management: EMERGENCY MEASURES:
ABCDE
Glucose 25% / 10% 5 ml/kg IV bolus IF BG < 2.2 (CHECK AT PRESENTATION ALWAYS)
Oxygen if sats < 90%
Seizures: phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IM/IV or diazepam 0.5 mg/kg PR (lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV)
Antipyretics for high fever
Cautious fluid (FEAST trial harm with bolus in African children); maintenance 5% dextrose with monitored UO
ANTIMALARIAL — IV ARTESUNATE FIRST-LINE (AQUAMAT, SEAQUAMAT):
2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12, 24h then daily × 24h continuous (minimum 3 doses)
Once tolerating PO + ≥ 24h IV: switch to oral artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) — artemether-lumefantrine 6 doses × 3 days; complete full course
AVOID quinine first-line (inferior — but acceptable second-line if artesunate unavailable: 20 mg/kg IV loading then 10 mg/kg q8h)
Children < 20 kg: artesunate 3 mg/kg/dose (higher dose per kg for small children — pharmacokinetics)
Watch DELAYED HAEMOLYSIS post-artesunate (1-3 weeks — check FBC at follow-up)
SEVERE ANAEMIA:
Transfusion threshold: Hb < 5 g/dL with severe symptoms (respiratory distress, shock, decompensation); Hb < 4 g/dL routine (WHO recommendation; cautious in cardiac child)
Packed cells 10 ml/kg over 3-4h (slow — avoid overload)
Co-administer furosemide if cardiac risk
BACTERIAL CO-INFECTION:
Empirical ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg/day for any severely ill malaria child (especially Salmonella in SSA) — until cultures back
Add vancomycin if severe shock / line
MONITORING:
Vital signs hourly
Glucose 4-hourly (PROFOUND hypoglycaemia common, especially infants + on quinine)
Parasite count + Hb every 12-24h
Urine output
Conscious level + neurological
CEREBRAL MALARIA / SEIZURES:
AVOID phenytoin prophylactically (no benefit)
Seizure management as above
Maintain glucose + electrolytes
Manage raised ICP if signs: head-up 30°, mannitol controversial (no proven benefit); avoid hyperventilation
Corticosteroids — NO benefit, may worsen (older trials)
AKI / BLACKWATER FEVER:
Fluid balance careful
Avoid nephrotoxins
Renal replacement therapy if uraemia / refractory
ACIDOSIS:
Treat underlying (improve perfusion, glucose, transfusion)
Bicarbonate only severe (pH < 7.1) + cautious
FOLLOW-UP:
Complete oral ACT course
Reassess at 7-14 d (post-artesunate haemolysis)
Address ITN use + chemoprophylaxis if applicable
Address concurrent / sequel conditions (anaemia, malnutrition)
PREVENTION:
Insecticide-treated bed nets
Seasonal malaria chemoprophylaxis in Sahel (WHO 2023)
IPTi (intermittent preventive treatment of infants) — pilot in some Kenya counties
RTS,S / R21 malaria VACCINE — RTS,S Mosquirix scaled up Africa; R21 newer + cheaper + similar efficacy
4 doses 6-18 months for children at risk
Kenya pilot RTS,S in Western Kenya — substantial mortality reduction
Maternal IPTp-SP in moderate-high transmission
Vector control (indoor residual spraying, larvicide)
Address environmental — drainage
Public health Kenya MOH: National Malaria Strategy

title: Paediatric trauma resuscitation — ATLS for kids
population: Children with trauma — falls, RTA, drowning, burns, abuse. Anatomic + physiologic differences from adults: larger head, more compliant chest, different airway, less reserve.
presentation: Multiple trauma, polytrauma, head injury, burns, drowning. Mechanism of injury crucial. Non-accidental injury — high index of suspicion.
redFlags: NEXUS criteria for paeds c-spine clearance
Persistent shock despite fluid (consider haemorrhage, tension PTX, tamponade)
Mechanism suggestive of abuse (NAI) — multiple injuries different ages, inconsistent history, social red flags
Suspected spinal injury — log roll + collar (paediatric size)
diagnostics: Primary survey: cABCDE (catastrophic haemorrhage, Airway+c-spine, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure) — age-appropriate norms
Secondary survey: head-to-toe + AMPLE history
Vital signs by age — normal ranges:
Newborn: HR 100-205, RR 30-60, SBP > 60
Infant: HR 100-180, RR 25-50
Toddler: HR 90-150, RR 20-40
Pre-school: HR 80-130
School age: HR 65-110
Adolescent: adult ranges
FAST scan if available
FBC, group + crossmatch, glucose, electrolytes, lactate, base excess, coag
Imaging: CT head/c-spine/chest/abdo per indication (paeds — minimise radiation; targeted)
Trauma scoring: paediatric GCS, paediatric trauma score (PTS), ISS
management: PRE-HOSPITAL:
Scene safety, paediatric-specific equipment
Avoid unnecessary movement
Direct pressure for haemorrhage
In-line c-spine immobilisation
IV access if able, fluid bolus cautious in non-shock (FEAST)
Transport to trauma centre with paediatric capabilities
PRIMARY SURVEY ABCDE:
c (catastrophic): tourniquet + pelvic binder (paediatric size — at level of greater trochanters)
A (airway + c-spine):
Position — neutral (large occiput in young — shoulder roll)
Chin lift / jaw thrust
Suction (small bore Yankauer)
OPA / NPA size-appropriate
Definitive airway: ETT if GCS ≤ 8 — RSI with appropriate dose drugs (ketamine 1-2 mg/kg, rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg, atropine 20 mcg/kg pre-treat in < 1 yr to prevent bradycardia)
ETT size: (age/4) + 4 = mm internal diameter (uncuffed for < 8 traditional but cuffed now acceptable + preferred for trauma due to aspiration)
C-spine: rigid collar + log roll; clear with NEXUS / Canadian paediatric criteria
B (breathing):
High-flow O2
Treat tension pneumothorax — needle decompression 2nd ICS MCL or 4th-5th ICS AAL (alternative children — anterior axillary preferred); chest drain
Haemothorax: chest drain
Flail chest: stabilise, analgesia, may need ventilation
C (circulation):
Hypotension is LATE in children (compensate well; can be near-arrest before BP drops)
Heart rate + perfusion (cap refill, mottling) are earlier signs
IV × 2 large-bore peripheral if possible (16-22G); IO if failed in 90 seconds (proximal tibia)
Crystalloid: 20 ml/kg balanced crystalloid (Hartmann/PlasmaLyte) bolus over 5-10 min
Reassess after each bolus
PERMISSIVE HYPOTENSION in haemorrhage controversial in paeds — typically MAP > 65 (paediatric) target until source controlled
Blood early if ongoing haemorrhage: O-negative emergency, then crossmatched
TRANEXAMIC ACID 15 mg/kg (max 1 g) IV within 3h of injury (CRASH-2 + ENGAGE paediatric)
Massive transfusion protocol 1:1:1 if shock + bleeding
AVOID excessive crystalloid (dilutional coagulopathy, oedema)
D (disability):
GCS (paediatric version for < 4 yr — AVPU acceptable)
Pupils
Glucose (always)
BE-FAST stroke (rare paeds)
Treat hypoglycaemia: 5 ml/kg of 10% glucose
E (exposure):
Log roll
Examine back + perineum + bottom
Prevent hypothermia (children at high risk — large surface area / small body mass)
Warm blankets, warm fluids, warmer environment
SECONDARY SURVEY:
AMPLE + head-to-toe
Document all findings
Look for non-accidental injury signs:
Inconsistent history
Delayed presentation
Multiple injuries different ages
Specific patterns (cigarette burns, immersion lines, bilateral fractures, posterior rib fractures, metaphyseal corner fractures, retinal haemorrhages in shaken baby)
Inappropriate caregiver behaviour
Mandatory reporting per Kenya Children Act + Sexual Offences Act if SA
HEAD INJURY:
Maintain SBP > 110 (or age-appropriate)
Sats > 94%
Head-up 30°
CT head per PECARN criteria (avoid unnecessary radiation in low-risk)
Hypertonic saline 3% 3 ml/kg for raised ICP signs (preferred over mannitol in paeds)
Anticonvulsants if seizing
Neurosurgical referral for significant injuries
C-SPINE:
NEXUS / Canadian paediatric C-spine rule for clinical clearance < 14 yr
CT only if clinical concern + > 14 yr (or specific paeds criteria)
AVOID routine C-spine CT < 8 yr (radiation; MRI preferred where indicated)
SCIWORA (spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality) common in children
PELVIC FRACTURE: binder at greater trochanters (NOT spring pelvis); often associated with massive haemorrhage; angiography embolisation
ABDOMINAL TRAUMA: solid organ injuries managed non-operatively often; FAST + CT; surgical for haemodynamic instability / hollow viscus
LIMB FRACTURES: splint + analgesia + reduce if vascular compromise; open fractures — IV cefazolin + tetanus + irrigation/debridement
OPEN FRACTURE / wound: tetanus prophylaxis + antibiotic (IV cefazolin + gentamicin per BACO)
BURNS (separate condition)
DROWNING (separate condition)
TRAUMA TEAM ACTIVATION CRITERIA per local protocol
DISPOSITION: paediatric trauma centre transfer if local capabilities exceeded
POST-RESUSCITATION:
Damage control surgery for unstable (control bleed + contamination, return for definitive)
ICU + monitoring
Pain control
VTE prophylaxis adolescents
Tetanus prophylaxis
Mental health screening for trauma sequelae
Rehabilitation
Family communication
Mandatory reporting if NAI suspected
PRIMARY PREVENTION:
Child safety education + seat belts + car seats + helmets
Smoke detectors + pool safety + medications safe storage
Address SDOH (poverty, supervision)

PECARN clinical decision rule (head injury, c-spine)
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children — Trauma
Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Child abuse + maltreatment — recognition + mandatory reporting
population: All children — physical, sexual, emotional abuse, neglect. SSA: high prevalence; under-reporting; harmful traditional practices (FGM, child marriage, physical punishment, witchcraft accusations).
presentation: Physical: unexplained / inconsistent injuries, multiple injuries different ages, specific patterns (cigarette burns, immersion lines, hand prints, posterior rib fractures, metaphyseal corner fractures, shaken baby — retinal haemorrhages + subdural). Sexual: STI / pregnancy in child, genital trauma, behavioural change, regression. Neglect: failure to thrive, poor hygiene, untreated medical, missed appointments. Emotional: developmental delay, behavioural disorders, low self-esteem.
redFlags: Domestic violence in home (children at risk too)
diagnostics: Detailed history (separate from caregivers if appropriate age + safe)
Use trained interviewer (child sexual abuse — specialist forensic interview)
AVOID leading questions
Comprehensive examination by trained clinician
Document injuries: body map, photographs (with consent + per protocol), measurements
Investigations as indicated:
Imaging: skeletal survey for non-accidental injury in young child + repeat at 10-14 days; fundoscopy (shaken baby); CT head if neurological
Bloods: FBC, coagulation, LFT, urinalysis, drug screen, alcohol, glucose, calcium (rule out alternative — bleeding disorder, OI, leukaemia)
Pregnancy test, STI screen, HIV test if sexual abuse
Forensic evidence collection within 72-120h (consent + chain of custody) — SAEK kit
Mental health: depression, anxiety, suicidality, behavioural assessment
Developmental + behavioural assessment
Multidisciplinary case review
management: ACUTE — STABILISATION:
Treat injuries per trauma protocols
Sexual assault < 72h: HIV PEP (TLD) × 28 days (Kenya NASCOP)
Sexual assault < 120h: emergency contraception (levonorgestrel 1.5 mg or Cu-IUD)
STI prophylaxis: ceftriaxone + azithromycin + metronidazole
Hepatitis B vaccination + HBIG if unvaccinated
Tetanus prophylaxis
Wound care
Mental health support + psychological first aid
Safety planning
MANDATORY REPORTING (Kenya):
Children Act 2022 + Sexual Offences Act 2006
Required: physical / sexual / emotional abuse, neglect, FGM, defilement (sexual contact with child < 18)
Report to: Children's Department (Children's Officer), Police (Gender Desk), DCI, hospital child protection team
PRC1 / P3 forms for evidence
Inform mother if she is not implicated; involve father if not implicated; sometimes immediate separation needed
Confidentiality limited by mandatory reporting laws
MULTIDISCIPLINARY:
Hospital child protection team (where exists — Kenya KNH + major referrals)
Children's Officer + social worker
Police Gender Desk for sexual abuse
Counsellor + child psychologist
Legal aid (FIDA Kenya, Kituo cha Sheria)
Forensic medical examiner (police surgeon for legal evidence)
Education + housing + protection services
NGO support (e.g. Childline Kenya 116 — toll-free, GBV hotline 1195 / 1199)
SGBV one-stop centre (where available — KNH, GBV Recovery Centre)
SAFETY PLANNING:
Immediate safety — admit if necessary for medical / protection
Place of safety / foster care if extraction needed (children's home, kinship)
Restraining order against perpetrator if needed
School / community awareness for ongoing protection
LONGER-TERM:
Trauma-focused CBT or play therapy
Family therapy if family-based (with caution + safety priority)
Support groups
Educational continuity (especially adolescent pregnancy — Kenya school re-entry policy)
Address developmental + behavioural impact
Long-term mental health follow-up
FGM (specific):
Illegal Kenya Anti-FGM Act 2011 — any procedure on female genital organs not for medical reasons
Acute management: bleeding control, infection, urinary retention, pain
Long-term: defibulation + counselling + obstetric care; do NOT re-infibulate after birth
Public health: prevent — community education, religious leader engagement, alternative rites of passage, prosecution
CHILD MARRIAGE:
Illegal Kenya Marriage Act 2014 — minimum age 18
Address health consequences (obstetric, mental, education)
Public health: girls' education + economic empowerment + community programmes
PROFESSIONAL CONSIDERATIONS:
Document carefully + objectively (medico-legal)
Be prepared for legal proceedings (testify)
Avoid showing emotion that might be misinterpreted
Self-care + supervision (vicarious trauma)
Continuing education on child protection
Multidisciplinary team approach reduces missed cases + improves outcomes
SECONDARY PREVENTION (programmes):
Home visiting programmes for at-risk families
Parenting education
Address parental mental health + substance abuse + IPV
Support for caregivers of children with disability
Early childhood programmes
