title: Kangaroo mother care — preterm + low birthweight newborn
population: Preterm + low birthweight (LBW < 2500g) infants — primarily resource-limited settings where neonatal ICU access limited. WHO Recommendation 2022: ALL preterm + LBW infants, including immediately after birth (paradigm shift from previously 'stabilised infants only').
presentation: Routine intervention from birth or as soon as possible for preterm + LBW. Continuous KMC (24/7 skin-to-skin contact + exclusive breastfeeding + early discharge) reduces neonatal mortality 25-40% in trials.
redFlags: Severe respiratory distress requiring intubation — defer KMC until stable
Massive intracranial haemorrhage requiring intensive care
Severe sepsis with shock — stabilise first then KMC adjunctive
Mother unable to provide KMC — surrogate (father / family member / 'kangaroo dad' / nurse) can provide
diagnostics: Baseline: weight, gestational age, vital signs, temperature
Maternal: postpartum recovery, mental health, social support
Identify any contraindications (rare absolute)
management: WHO 2022 RECOMMENDATIONS (paradigm shift):
INITIATE KMC immediately after birth (not after stabilisation as before)
CONTINUOUS skin-to-skin 24h/day if possible
Includes pre-stabilisation period (immediate KMC trial in NEJM 2021 — 25% mortality reduction)
PRACTICAL POSITIONING:
Infant placed naked (except nappy + cap) between mother's breasts in upright vertical position
Direct skin-to-skin contact
Infant head turned to one side, neck slightly extended, ear over mother's heart
Hips flexed in 'frog' position
Cover with mother's clothing / wrap + warm cloth / blanket
Vital signs monitored regularly
Continuous as much as possible (24h/day if able), with brief breaks for hygiene
FEEDING:
EXCLUSIVE BREASTFEEDING — direct breast where possible
Cup feeding for non-suckling preterm (avoid bottle)
NG tube if very preterm; cup as suckling develops
Frequent small feeds (q2-3h)
Track weight gain (target 15-20 g/kg/day)
Donor breast milk if mother's milk insufficient
ROUTINE NEWBORN CARE:
Vitamin K 1 mg IM at birth (haemorrhagic disease prevention)
Eye prophylaxis (tetracycline 1% or povidone-iodine 2.5%)
Hepatitis B birth dose (within 24h)
BCG + OPV0 if eligible
Cord care (chlorhexidine in low resource — WHO recommendation; or clean + dry)
MONITORING:
Daily weight (target 15-20 g/kg/day after initial loss)
Temperature 6-hourly minimum, more if unstable
Heart rate, respiratory rate, glucose monitoring
Identify danger signs: poor feeding, breathing difficulty, fever, hypothermia, jaundice, lethargy, irritability, vomiting, bloody stool, seizures
ADVANTAGES vs incubator/conventional care:
Thermoregulation (mother adjusts temperature)
Improved breastfeeding rates + duration
Reduced infection (lower nosocomial; protective)
Improved bonding + maternal mental health
Cardiac + respiratory stability
Less hypoglycaemia
Earlier discharge
Cost-effective LMIC
Mortality reduction 25-40% in preterm/LBW (Cochrane + WHO trials including iKMC NEJM 2021)
DISCHARGE CRITERIA:
Weight gain consistent ~ 15 g/kg/day for 3 days
Tolerates feeding well
Mother trained + confident
No medical complication
Community follow-up arranged
Typically discharge at 1800-2000g (some smaller with strong follow-up)
COMMUNITY CONTINUATION:
Continue KMC at home until infant outgrows / unwilling (typically 2-3 months)
Frequent follow-up at clinic (weekly until 2500g)
Community health volunteer support
Kenya MNCH integrated
PROGRAMMATIC EXPANSION (LMIC priority):
Kenya MOH KMC scaling — KMC centres at Level 4+ hospitals + community
Father involvement (father-KMC, 'kangaroo dad')
Address stigma + cultural barriers
Train staff + community
Equip facilities (wraps, beds for mother + infant together)
Allow continuous family presence in NICU (paradigm shift from visitor restrictions)
Lancet Every Newborn Action Plan

references.label: WHO Recommendations for Care of the Preterm or Low-Birth-Weight Infant 2022
Immediate KMC Study Group. NEJM 2021 (iKMC mortality reduction)
Lawn JE et al. Lancet 2016 + Every Newborn Action Plan
Cochrane Kangaroo Mother Care for Low Birth Weight

title: Neonatal jaundice — phototherapy + exchange transfusion thresholds
population: Newborns — physiological jaundice 60%, pathological 5-10%. Kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy) preventable cause of permanent neurodevelopmental disability — major SSA burden due to late presentation.
presentation: Jaundice visible day 2-3 (physiological peak day 3-5, resolves by 1-2 weeks). Pathological: appears in first 24h, rises rapidly, prolonged > 14 days term / 21 days preterm, unwell infant, ABO/Rh incompatibility, family history, conjugated > 20%.
redFlags: Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (hypotonia + retrocollis + opisthotonus + high-pitched cry + drowsy / irritable + poor feeding → escalating to seizures + coma)
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (any) — biliary atresia investigation urgent < 6 weeks
diagnostics: Transcutaneous bilirubin (TcB) for screening; serum bilirubin (SBR) if TcB high or unwell
Direct (conjugated) bilirubin — fractionate
FBC + blood film + reticulocyte count
Blood group + Rh + direct Coombs (DAT) — haemolytic disease of newborn
G6PD test (especially African ancestry — common haemolysis cause; also if poor response to phototherapy)
LFT (raised AST/ALT suggests hepatocellular)
TSH (hypothyroidism)
Septic screen if unwell (FBC + CRP + blood culture + urine)
Stool colour (pale stool suggests biliary atresia)
Galactosaemia screen if prolonged + ill
Newborn screen routine
management: PHYSIOLOGICAL JAUNDICE (most cases):
Watch + reassure
Continue breastfeeding (don't stop — breast milk jaundice usually benign)
Monitor TcB / SBR per nomogram
Daily review until resolving
PHOTOTHERAPY:
THRESHOLD by age, gestation, risk factors (use AAP 2022 + Kenya/WHO nomograms)
Conventional vs intensive (sun + LED + intensive triple-bank LED)
Phototherapy works by converting unconjugated bilirubin to water-soluble isomers excreted in bile + urine
Maximise efficiency: nappy only + eye protection + maximum skin exposure + distance optimised + double-bank for high levels + intensive for very high levels
Continue breastfeeding (interruption rarely needed)
Monitor: SBR every 6-12h depending on level + response
Side effects: dehydration (extra fluids), loose stools, mild rash, retinal damage if no eye protection
Stop when bilirubin > 50 below threshold + falling
REBOUND check 12-24h after stopping
EXCHANGE TRANSFUSION:
THRESHOLD per nomogram (much higher than phototherapy)
Indications: ABO/Rh haemolytic + severe; bilirubin approaching neurotoxic; failed maximal intensive phototherapy
Double-volume exchange (2 × blood volume — 160-200 ml/kg)
Centrifuged O-negative or group-specific compatible blood
ICU/HDU procedure with anaesthetic / neonatal support
Risks: arrhythmia, hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, thrombocytopaenia, infection, NEC
IV IMMUNOGLOBULIN (IVIG):
For isoimmune haemolytic disease (DAT+) reaching exchange threshold
0.5-1 g/kg IV — may avoid exchange
TREAT UNDERLYING CAUSE:
Sepsis: antibiotics
Hypothyroidism: levothyroxine
G6PD deficiency: avoid haemolytic triggers + supportive
Biliary atresia: urgent surgical (Kasai portoenterostomy) BEFORE 8 weeks — best outcomes
ABO/Rh haemolytic: phototherapy + IVIG + exchange if needed; consider EPO + prolonged phototherapy
Cephalohaematoma / extensive bruising: monitor, phototherapy
Breast milk jaundice (prolonged, well infant): continue breastfeeding (interruption diagnostic if needed)
EDUCATION + FOLLOW-UP:
Mother on jaundice signs + when to return
Follow-up 24-72h after discharge if any jaundice or high-risk
Continued monitoring through 2 weeks
PROLONGED JAUNDICE (> 14 days term / 21 days preterm):
Workup: SBR + fractionate + LFT + TFT + G6PD + screen for biliary atresia (stool colour, US) + urine ferric chloride + galactose screen + breast milk jaundice trial
Refer to specialist if conjugated, unwell, evolving
PREVENTION:
Adequate breastfeeding initiation + frequency (8-12 times/day)
Antenatal Rh status + anti-D for Rh-negative mothers (separate management)
Newborn check before discharge
Education for parents on jaundice
Routine bilirubin screening before discharge in high-risk
KERNICTERUS PREVENTION (CRITICAL SSA):
Late presentation common in LMIC + community delivery
Train community health workers on jaundice recognition
Solar phototherapy (innovation for off-grid)
Reduce delays in treatment

references.label: NICE CG98 Jaundice in Newborns 2010 + 2024 update
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children — Neonatal Jaundice
Kenya MOH Basic Paediatric + Newborn Protocols

title: Paediatric asthma — GINA + age-specific management
population: Children + adolescents — prevalence 10-15% rising; SSA under-diagnosis common as 'recurrent bronchitis' / 'wheezy bronchitis'. Asthma deaths preventable.
presentation: Variable wheeze, cough (often dry, worse at night/early morning), dyspnoea, chest tightness — episodic + triggered. < 5 yr: preschool wheeze (viral-induced, episodic) vs atopic asthma (multitrigger, atopic). Acute attack: severity by RR + accessory muscles + sats + ability to speak / feed.
redFlags: Severe attack: unable to speak / feed / cyanosis / silent chest / exhaustion
diagnostics: History: pattern, triggers, family history, atopy (eczema, allergic rhinitis, food allergy)
Examination: wheeze, prolonged expiration, accessory muscles, eczema
Spirometry from age 5: FEV1/FVC < 0.85 + reversibility ≥ 12% post-bronchodilator
FeNO if available — eosinophilic inflammation marker
Peak expiratory flow (PEF) variability > 13% diagnostic in children
Skin prick test or specific IgE for aeroallergens
Asthma control test (cACT / ACQ)
CXR not routine; useful for severe / atypical / not responding
management: GINA 2024 BY AGE GROUP:
≤ 5 YEARS:
Step 1: SABA prn (mild infrequent symptoms)
Step 2: daily low-dose ICS (budesonide 200 mcg, fluticasone 50 mcg) via spacer + face mask (< 4 yr) / mouthpiece (≥ 4 yr) + SABA prn
Step 3: double low-dose ICS or add LTRA (montelukast) — review diagnosis if needed
Step 4: refer specialist; high-dose ICS
Continuous viral-induced wheeze: episodic LTRA / pre-emptive ICS bursts
AVOID LABA in monotherapy in young children (safety + indication concerns)
≥ 6 YEARS (similar to adult GINA):
Step 1: as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (preferred GINA — eliminates SABA-only) OR daily low-dose ICS + SABA
Step 2: as-needed ICS-formoterol OR daily low-dose ICS + SABA
Step 3: daily low-dose ICS-LABA + as-needed ICS-formoterol
Step 4: medium-dose ICS-LABA daily
Step 5: high-dose ICS-LABA + LAMA + refer for biologic + specialist (omalizumab, mepolizumab, dupilumab)
AVOID SABA-only (SABINA mortality)
Annual inhaler technique + adherence + spacer + action plan + asthma education
DELIVERY:
Spacer + face mask < 4 yr
Spacer + mouthpiece 4-7 yr
MDI ± spacer 8+ (most still benefit from spacer)
DPI / breath-actuated if reliably can use (> 8 yr typically)
Avoid neb except acute severe (no benefit + tachycardia)
ACUTE ATTACK MANAGEMENT:
Mild-moderate: salbutamol 4-10 puffs via spacer q20 min × 1h
Severe / inability to use spacer: nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg + ipratropium 250 mcg q20 min
Oral prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg (max 40 mg) × 3-5 days OR dexamethasone 0.3-0.6 mg/kg × 1-2 doses (alternative — better compliance + same efficacy per multiple RCTs)
Oxygen titrated to sats > 94%
Severe: IV MgSO4 40 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 min
Refractory: IV salbutamol infusion (caution arrhythmia + hypokalaemia)
IV aminophylline rarely (narrow therapeutic, arrhythmia, vomiting)
Intubation only if absolutely needed (DYNAMIC HYPERINFLATION + pneumothorax risk)
Watch for hypokalaemia + hypoglycaemia (salbutamol)
ADMISSION CRITERIA:
Severe attack with poor response
Sats < 92% after treatment
Risk factors (previous ICU, near-fatal asthma)
Social: late hour, distance, parental anxiety
DISCHARGE:
Stable on inhaled + oral therapy
Sats > 94% on room air
Reviewed inhaler technique
Action plan
Asthma educator / clinic referral
Restart / step-up preventer
Follow-up in 2-7 days
TRIGGERS:
Viral URTI (most common children)
Allergens (dust mite, pollen, animal dander)
Exercise (pre-treatment SABA or LTRA)
Cold air
Smoking exposure (passive)
Irritants (perfume, cooking smoke — major SSA — improved cookstoves)
Stress
Aspirin/NSAID (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease — AERD, less common in children)
GERD
ALLERGY: comorbid allergic rhinitis (treat with intranasal steroid) + eczema (emollient + steroid) — 'one airway' approach
EXERCISE-INDUCED bronchospasm: SABA pre-exercise; LTRA / ICS-formoterol daily preventer
ATOPIC MARCH: many start as eczema + food allergy → develop allergic rhinitis + asthma; early intervention with peanut introduction (LEAP) + emollient may modify
VACCINATIONS:
Annual influenza
Pneumococcal (PCV13 routine + PPSV23 high-risk)
COVID
Routine EPI
SMOKING EXPOSURE: cessation counselling for caregivers; smoke-free home + car
INDOOR AIR QUALITY: improved cookstoves (major SSA primary care role)
WHO Global Asthma Strategy + Kenya MOH NCD Strategic Plan address paediatric asthma
REFERRAL:
Refractory asthma
Diagnostic uncertainty
Step 4+
Recurrent admissions
Biologic candidate
Workup atypical features

references.label: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols (5th ed, 2022), Ministry of Health

title: Rheumatoid arthritis — treat-to-target + bDMARD/tsDMARD modern
population: Adults — prevalence 0.5-1% globally; women 3× men. Treatment paradigm shift to early aggressive treat-to-target with biologic / JAK inhibitor.
presentation: Symmetric polyarthritis (small joints — MCP, PIP, MTP, wrist), morning stiffness > 30 min, fatigue, extra-articular (nodules, ILD, vasculitis, scleritis, pericarditis, Felty), positive RF / anti-CCP.
redFlags: Severe destructive disease — refer specialist + start DMARD early
Active CV disease (RA doubles CV risk)
diagnostics: ACR/EULAR 2010 classification criteria
RF + anti-CCP (anti-CCP more specific)
ESR, CRP, FBC (anaemia of chronic disease)
X-rays hands + feet at diagnosis (erosions); MRI / ultrasound for early synovitis
Hepatitis B + C + HIV + TB (IGRA + CXR) BEFORE bDMARD
Comorbidity screening: CV risk, lipids, glucose, BP, smoking
Pregnancy test in WCBP before MTX
management: TREAT-TO-TARGET (TTT) paradigm — clinical remission OR low disease activity within 3-6 months; if not, change therapy:
DAS28 < 2.6 remission, < 3.2 low activity
CDAI / SDAI alternative scoring
Boolean-based remission (more stringent)
DISEASE-MODIFYING ANTIRHEUMATIC DRUGS (DMARDs):
CONVENTIONAL synthetic (csDMARDs) — first-line:
METHOTREXATE 7.5-25 mg/week PO/SC — anchor drug; add folic acid 5 mg/wk (NOT on MTX day) reduces side effects
Sulfasalazine 2-3 g/day
Leflunomide 10-20 mg/day
Hydroxychloroquine 200-400 mg/day (mild; lupus combo)
Combination (triple therapy — MTX + SSZ + HCQ) effective alternative to bDMARD
BRIDGE corticosteroid (low-dose prednisolone 5-15 mg + tapering 3-6 months) while csDMARD takes effect
BIOLOGIC DMARDs (bDMARDs) — after inadequate response to MTX optimised:
Anti-TNF: etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab
Anti-IL-6: tocilizumab, sarilumab
Anti-CD20: rituximab
T-cell co-stim: abatacept
Combine with MTX (synergistic, reduces immunogenicity)
TARGETED synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs — JAK inhibitors):
Tofacitinib 5 mg BD, baricitinib 4 mg, upadacitinib 15 mg, filgotinib
BOXED WARNINGS — VTE, MACE, malignancy (especially > 65 + CV risk + active or past smoker); EMA + FDA caution
Reserve for failure of bDMARD or specific indications
STRATEGY:
Diagnosis → MTX (csDMARD) + bridge low-dose pred
If not at target by 3-6 months — add or switch:
Add second csDMARD (triple therapy) OR
Add bDMARD or tsDMARD
Continue + monitor; consider dose tapering bDMARD if sustained remission
ROUTINE MONITORING:
Joint exam + DAS28 every 1-3 months until target, then every 3-6 months
FBC + LFT + creatinine (MTX baseline + every 2-4 weeks until stable + then every 8-12 weeks)
Lipid + BP + glucose (CV risk)
Hepatitis serology pre-treatment + reactivation monitoring
TB screen pre-bDMARD + clinical surveillance
Vaccinations: pneumococcal + annual flu + COVID; NO LIVE vaccines on bDMARDs / JAK / MTX
Lung function + imaging if breathlessness (MTX pneumonitis + ILD)
Annual eye check on HCQ (retinal toxicity > 5 years)
EXTRA-ARTICULAR + COMORBID:
CV risk modification (statin + BP control + DM + smoking cessation)
Osteoporosis: DEXA + bisphosphonate/denosumab if indicated
Infection prevention: vaccinations + PCP prophylaxis high-dose immunosuppression
Mental health: depression + anxiety + fatigue management
Functional: physiotherapy + OT + orthotics
Surgical: joint replacement for severe damage
PREGNANCY:
AVOID methotrexate (teratogen — washout 3 months for both partners) + leflunomide (washout with cholestyramine)
Hydroxychloroquine safe
Sulfasalazine safe (add folate)
Anti-TNF (certolizumab — minimal placental transfer; preferred — CRIB trial); others taper 28-32 wk
Avoid JAK + rituximab
Breastfeeding: HCQ + SSZ + certolizumab compatible
Postpartum often flares — plan
SURGICAL:
Hold MTX week before-after major surgery (controversial)
Hold bDMARD per drug half-life around surgery
Anaesthesia: c-spine assessment (atlanto-axial subluxation in long-standing RA)
Continue HCQ + low-dose steroid

references.label: ORAL Surveillance + Bechman et al JAK safety
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: SLE — modern management + lupus nephritis
population: Women 90% (esp 15-45); African + Caribbean + Asian ancestry higher prevalence + severity. SSA — under-diagnosed; African ancestry — more lupus nephritis + worse outcomes.
presentation: Multisystem: malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthritis, serositis, glomerulonephritis (lupus nephritis), CNS (psychosis, seizure, stroke, transverse myelitis), haematological cytopenias, immunologic abnormalities (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, antiphospholipid), constitutional.
redFlags: Active lupus nephritis (proteinuria, RBC casts, AKI)
CNS lupus (psychosis, seizure, stroke, transverse myelitis)
diagnostics: EULAR/ACR 2019 classification criteria
ANA (sensitive but not specific), anti-dsDNA + anti-Sm (specific), C3 + C4 (active disease — low), antiphospholipid panel (lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin, anti-β2GP1)
Anti-Ro, anti-La (Sjögren / neonatal lupus block)
FBC (cytopaenias, AIHA — direct Coombs), ESR + CRP
U&E + urinalysis + ACR + creatinine (lupus nephritis screening EVERY visit)
LFT, complement C3/C4 (active = low)
Renal biopsy in suspected lupus nephritis (essential — Class I-VI determines treatment)
Brain MRI + LP for CNS lupus
Echo for pericarditis / pulmonary HT
management: GENERAL PRINCIPLES:
Sun protection (broad-spectrum SPF 50+)
Vitamin D supplementation
Smoking cessation (worsens cutaneous + reduces HCQ efficacy)
CV risk modification (lupus is independent CV risk factor)
Vaccinations: pneumococcal, annual flu, COVID, HPV; NO LIVE on immunosuppression
Pregnancy planning (separate)
HYDROXYCHLOROQUINE — backbone for almost ALL patients (200-400 mg/day):
Reduces flares + mortality + organ damage (LUMINA)
Improves pregnancy outcomes (continue through pregnancy)
Annual ophthalmology surveillance (> 5 yr — retinal toxicity)
ORGAN-SPECIFIC:
CUTANEOUS / ARTICULAR / MILD:
HCQ + topical steroid + NSAID
Short-course low-dose prednisolone
Methotrexate or azathioprine if persistent
Belimumab for moderate-severe + standard therapy failure
Anifrolumab (anti-IFN-α/β receptor, FDA 2021) — alternative biologic
LUPUS NEPHRITIS (proliferative — Class III/IV):
Induction (3-6 months):
Mycophenolate mofetil 2-3 g/d OR cyclophosphamide IV (EuroLupus low-dose: 500 mg q2 wk × 6 doses; or NIH high-dose)
+ High-dose corticosteroid: methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg IV pulses × 3 days then prednisolone 0.5-1 mg/kg/d tapering
ALMS + ALMS Maintenance — MMF non-inferior to cyclophosphamide induction + superior maintenance
Maintenance (≥ 2-3 years):
MMF 1-2 g/d OR azathioprine 1.5-2.5 mg/kg/d (HCQ continued)
Voclosporin (calcineurin inhibitor — AURORA trial) — add to MMF for incomplete responders
Newer: belimumab + MMF combination (BLISS-LN 2020)
Rituximab for refractory (but failed primary endpoint in LUNAR trial — used clinically)
Manage HTN (ACE-i / ARB), dyslipidaemia, smoking, anaemia
CLASS V (membranous): MMF + steroid or calcineurin inhibitor
NEUROPSYCHIATRIC SLE:
Treat psychiatric symptoms (antipsychotic, antidepressant)
Immunosuppression for inflammatory NPSLE (steroid + cyclophosphamide / rituximab)
Anticoagulation for thrombotic NPSLE (APS-related)
HAEMATOLOGICAL:
AIHA: steroid + rituximab refractory
Thrombocytopaenia (severe): steroid + IVIG + rituximab
ANTIPHOSPHOLIPID SYNDROME (separate condition)
ACUTE FLARE:
Increased immunosuppression
Identify trigger (infection, sun, drug, pregnancy)
High-dose steroid pulses for severe organ-threatening
PREGNANCY:
HIGH RISK — counsel pre-conception
Optimise — disease quiescent for ≥ 6 months before pregnancy
Continue HCQ throughout (improves outcomes)
Switch teratogenic (CYC, MMF, MTX, JAK) BEFORE conception to safe alternatives (AZA, tacrolimus)
Aspirin from 12 weeks (PE prevention)
Anti-Ro/La: monitor fetal cardiac scans (congenital heart block — 5%, recurrence 15-20%)
Anti-phospholipid: LMWH + aspirin
Flares often 3rd trimester + postpartum
MONITORING:
Disease activity score (SLEDAI / BILAG) every 3-6 months
Anti-dsDNA + complement
Urinalysis + ACR + creatinine EVERY visit
Drug side effects
CV risk + bone health + cancer surveillance
Mental health
Kenya / SSA: African ancestry — more severe + lupus nephritis common; advocate for access to biologics + voclosporin

references.label: EULAR Recommendations Management of SLE 2023 + Lupus Nephritis 2024

title: Gout — treat-to-target serum urate + ULT
population: Most common inflammatory arthritis; men > women; rising globally + SSA with metabolic syndrome epidemic.
presentation: Acute monoarticular arthritis — sudden severe pain + redness + swelling + warmth (1st MTP — podagra classic; ankles, knees, fingers). Tophi in chronic. Triggers: alcohol (beer + spirits), red meat, organ meats, seafood, fructose, diuretics, dehydration, surgery, trauma.
redFlags: Septic arthritis (overlap presentation — must joint aspirate + culture)
Lesch-Nyhan / rare causes in young presentation
diagnostics: Clinical recognition + risk factors (age, male, obesity, alcohol, diuretic, HTN, CKD)
JOINT ASPIRATION for negatively birefringent needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals — diagnostic gold standard (especially first attack / atypical)
Serum urate — but NORMAL in 30% acute attack (drops during attack); recheck 2-4 weeks later
FBC + CRP raised; differential white cells from joint fluid (rule out septic — > 50,000 PMN suggests septic)
Joint culture
Renal function, lipids, glucose, BP (metabolic comorbidity)
X-ray (chronic: punched-out erosions with overhanging edges, tophi)
Ultrasound (double-contour sign — diagnostic in chronic; tophi)
Dual-energy CT (urate-specific)
management: ACUTE ATTACK:
Start within 24h of onset for best results
Multiple effective options (choose based on comorbidity):
NSAID (naproxen 500 mg BD / indomethacin 50 mg q8h / ibuprofen) — first-line if no CKD / GI / CV concern; with PPI
COLCHICINE 1.2 mg STAT then 0.6 mg at 1h then 0.6 mg q12h until attack resolves (max 6 mg/course) — best within 12-36h of onset
Corticosteroid (prednisolone 30-40 mg/d × 5-10 days tapering or IM/IA) — first-line if NSAID/colchicine contraindicated; useful in elderly / CKD / DM
IL-1 inhibitor (canakinumab, anakinra) — refractory / contraindicated
Joint aspiration + intra-articular steroid for monoarticular
Treat for 1-2 weeks until full resolution
URATE-LOWERING THERAPY (ULT) — initiate when:
Tophi present
≥ 2 attacks/year OR even single attack with CKD / urolithiasis / very high urate / young
Imaging-detected urate deposition
Recurrent / disabling
Start during or shortly after acute attack (NOT contraindicated — old myth)
Cover with ANTI-INFLAMMATORY PROPHYLAXIS (colchicine 0.6 mg OD or BD, low-dose NSAID, low-dose pred) × 3-6 months to prevent mobilisation flares
DRUGS:
ALLOPURINOL (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) — first-line:
Start LOW (50-100 mg/d) + titrate to target serum urate < 360 µmol/L (< 300 if tophi)
Renal dose adjust
HLA-B*5801 test before in Han Chinese / Korean / Thai / African ancestry — SJS risk
Drug interactions: azathioprine + 6-MP (reduce doses), warfarin
FEBUXOSTAT 40-80 mg/d (alternative if intolerant/inadequate allopurinol) — CARES trial CV mortality signal — caution CV disease
URICOSURICS: probenecid (avoid in CKD + urolithiasis), benzbromarone, lesinurad (add-on)
PEGLOTICASE IV (recombinant uricase) — refractory; tophi reduction
TREAT-TO-TARGET:
Serum urate < 360 µmol/L (< 6 mg/dL) for most
< 300 µmol/L (< 5 mg/dL) if tophi / severe / erosive
Continue ULT LIFELONG once started
~ 30% of patients need combination ULT to reach target
LIFESTYLE:
Weight loss (10% reduces flares)
Reduce alcohol (especially beer + spirits)
Reduce red meat + organ meats + seafood + fructose-rich (corn syrup beverages)
Increase low-fat dairy + cherries + vitamin C (modest)
Adequate hydration
Avoid crash diets (releases urate)
Skim milk + plant-based protein
COMORBIDITY MANAGEMENT:
HTN — losartan + amlodipine + avoid thiazide + loop where possible (worsen urate)
CKD — dose adjust + close monitor
CV disease — statin + ASA + lifestyle
Metabolic syndrome — SGLT2i (also lower urate)
Switch diuretic if possible
T2DM SGLT2i lowers urate + reduces flares
SURGICAL:
Excision of disabling tophi (cosmetic / mechanical / infection)
Joint replacement for severe destruction
Patient EDUCATION + adherence (chronic disease, target SU, prophylaxis on initiation)

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Axial spondyloarthritis / AS — biologic era + posture
population: Adults — onset usually < 45; men > women 2:1 (historical, but women under-diagnosed). HLA-B27 positive in 90% (variable by ethnicity).
presentation: Inflammatory back pain (worse with rest, better with movement, morning stiffness > 30 min, age < 45, alternating buttock pain), peripheral arthritis, enthesitis (Achilles, plantar fascia), dactylitis, uveitis (anterior — recurrent), psoriasis, IBD, fatigue.
redFlags: Severe restricted spinal mobility / kyphosis — postural rehabilitation
Acute anterior uveitis — refer ophthalmology urgently
Cauda equina (rare, ankylosed spine with fracture)
Spinal fracture (osteoporotic + ankylosed — minor trauma = fracture)
Cervical fracture in fused spine — high mortality
diagnostics: ASAS classification criteria 2009
X-ray sacroiliac joints (bilateral sacroiliitis grade ≥ 2) — definite AS
MRI sacroiliac + spine for non-radiographic axial SpA (active inflammation — bone marrow oedema)
HLA-B27 (high prevalence in axSpA + family history)
CRP, ESR (often mildly raised)
Symptom-based: inflammatory back pain (Calin / Berlin / ASAS criteria)
BASDAI (disease activity), BASMI (mobility), BASFI (function), ASDAS
TB screen + HBV/HCV/HIV before bDMARD
management: FOUNDATION:
EXERCISE — supervised physiotherapy + group exercise + swimming
Postural rehabilitation
Patient education (UK National Axial Spondyloarthritis Society)
Smoking cessation (key — worsens progression + reduces TNFi response)
Mental health support
CV risk modification
PHARMACOLOGICAL:
NSAID — FIRST-LINE long-term — naproxen, indomethacin, etoricoxib — reduces inflammation + may slow radiographic progression (controversial); continuous use higher rate of slow progression
Topical / IA steroid for peripheral arthritis or enthesitis
AVOID systemic steroid (limited efficacy axial)
csDMARDs (sulfasalazine, MTX) — useful for PERIPHERAL arthritis only; INEFFECTIVE for axial disease
BIOLOGIC (failure of ≥ 2 NSAID + BASDAI ≥ 4 + spinal pain ≥ 4):
Anti-TNF: etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab
IL-17 inhibitor: secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab
JAK inhibitor: upadacitinib, tofacitinib (CV / VTE / cancer caution — risk-benefit)
Comorbidity considerations:
Uveitis recurrent — anti-TNF (especially monoclonal antibody — infliximab, adalimumab; etanercept LESS effective for uveitis)
IBD — anti-TNF (monoclonal preferred; etanercept ineffective for IBD); ustekinumab
Psoriasis — IL-17 + TNFi + IL-23 effective
Avoid IL-17 in IBD (may worsen)
Avoid IL-23 (risankizumab) — not effective for axial SpA
Continue for as long as effective; tapering if sustained remission
EXTRA-ARTICULAR:
Anterior uveitis — topical steroid + dilating drops + treat axial disease
IBD — gastroenterology + integrated care
Psoriasis — dermatology
Cardiac — echo for aortic regurgitation + conduction
Pulmonary fibrosis (rare)
OSTEOPOROSIS:
Common in AS
DEXA; treat per fracture risk
Vitamin D + calcium
Bisphosphonate if indicated
SURGICAL:
Total hip / shoulder replacement for severe hip / shoulder involvement
Spinal osteotomy for severe kyphosis (selected)
ANAESTHESIA + spinal fracture:
Ankylosed spine + minor trauma = spine fracture (high mortality cervical)
Awareness in emergency + cautious cervical handling
Difficult intubation (fused cervical spine, atlanto-axial concern)
PREGNANCY:
Often improves during pregnancy
Postpartum flare common
NSAIDs OK first 2 trimesters (avoid 3rd — closure ductus)
Sulfasalazine + HCQ safe (less commonly used in axSpA)
Anti-TNF certolizumab preferred (no placental transfer)
AVOID JAK + secukinumab limited safety data
Vaccinations: as RA (pre-bDMARD; no live)

title: ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA)
population: Rare (5-10/million) but life-threatening. GPA (granulomatosis with polyangiitis), MPA (microscopic polyangiitis), EGPA (eosinophilic GPA — Churg-Strauss).
presentation: Multisystem: ENT (saddle nose, nasal crusting, sinusitis, otitis), respiratory (haemoptysis, cavitating nodules, asthma in EGPA), renal (RPGN with crescents), skin (purpura, ulcer), neuro (mononeuritis multiplex), eye (scleritis, episcleritis, orbital pseudotumour), constitutional.
redFlags: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) — urgent immunosuppression + dialysis if needed
diagnostics: ANCA pattern + specificity: c-ANCA / PR3 → GPA (90% sensitive); p-ANCA / MPO → MPA + EGPA (60% EGPA)
FBC (eosinophilia EGPA), ESR + CRP raised, urinalysis (RBC casts, dysmorphic), creatinine + eGFR
Renal biopsy if suspected glomerulonephritis (pauci-immune crescentic GN — confirms)
Lung biopsy if cavitating nodules (granulomas)
ENT + nasal biopsy for granuloma
Skin biopsy for vasculitis
Imaging: CT chest (cavitating nodules, ground-glass for haemorrhage); CT sinuses
Tissue diagnosis preferred where possible
Hepatitis B/C + HIV + TB before treatment
management: REMISSION INDUCTION (severe, organ-threatening):
CYCLOPHOSPHAMIDE 15 mg/kg IV pulses or 2 mg/kg PO daily × 3-6 months + high-dose corticosteroid (methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg IV pulses × 3 days then prednisolone 1 mg/kg/d tapering)
OR RITUXIMAB 375 mg/m² weekly × 4 doses + steroid (non-inferior to cyclophosphamide — RAVE + RITUXVAS trials; preferred for relapsing disease, PR3+, fertility preservation)
Plasma exchange (PLEX) — pulmonary haemorrhage or severe AKI requiring dialysis (PEXIVAS — modest benefit; reserved for severe renal / pulmonary haemorrhage)
REMISSION MAINTENANCE (after 3-6 months induction):
RITUXIMAB 500 mg every 6 months × 2 years (MAINRITSAN — superior to AZA)
OR azathioprine 1.5-2 mg/kg/d
OR methotrexate 25 mg/week (mild-moderate)
OR mycophenolate mofetil 2 g/d
Continue 2-4 years minimum
Steroid tapered over 6-12 months
AVACOPAN (C5a receptor antagonist — ADVOCATE NEJM 2021):
Newer steroid-SPARING option for severe ANCA-vasculitis
Reduces glucocorticoid exposure
EMA/FDA approved 2021/2022
EGPA specific:
Mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) for non-severe + corticosteroid-dependent EGPA (MIRRA NEJM 2017)
Same induction for severe (steroid + CYC or rituximab)
Asthma management
Five Factors Score for severity
RELAPSE:
Re-induce (rituximab preferred for relapsing)
Check ANCA + biomarkers + clinical
PROPHYLAXIS:
PCP — co-trimoxazole 480-960 mg daily or 3×/week (high-dose immunosuppression)
Antifungal prophylaxis selected
Vaccinations BEFORE biologic where possible (no live on biologic/rituximab)
Pneumococcal + annual flu + COVID; HPV in young women
Antibiotic prophylaxis for sinus + ENT involvement
Bone health: vitamin D + calcium + bisphosphonate (steroid-induced osteoporosis)
FERTILITY:
Cyclophosphamide reduces fertility (egg/sperm banking pre-treatment)
Rituximab preferable in young patients
PREGNANCY:
Plan in remission
Switch teratogenic (CYC, MMF, MTX) before
Azathioprine + steroid safer
High obstetric risk — multidisciplinary
ORGAN-SPECIFIC MANAGEMENT:
Renal: dialysis if needed, renal transplant after sustained remission
Subglottic stenosis (GPA): dilatation + intralesional steroid
Sinus: irrigation + nasal saline + antibiotic for secondary infection
Eye: scleritis treatment + uveitis management
Mononeuritis multiplex: gabapentin/pregabalin + physiotherapy
MONITORING:
Disease activity (BVAS), damage (VDI)
ANCA titre (variable predictor of relapse — clinical primary)
Urinalysis + creatinine EVERY visit
Steroid side effects
CV risk modification
Cancer surveillance (CYC + AZA — bladder + skin)

title: Polymyalgia rheumatica + giant cell arteritis
population: Age > 50 (most > 65); women > men. PMR — common (700/100,000 > 50); GCA more rare (200/100,000 > 50). Often overlap.
presentation: PMR: bilateral shoulder + hip girdle pain + stiffness > 30 min morning, > 2 weeks, normal CK, raised ESR/CRP. GCA: temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms (transient or permanent blindness), polymyalgia, fever, constitutional.
redFlags: VISUAL SYMPTOMS in suspected GCA — START HIGH-DOSE STEROID IMMEDIATELY (don't wait for biopsy — vision loss permanent)
Aortic involvement (aortic aneurysm + aortic regurgitation — chest pain)
Failure to respond to standard steroid — consider GCA hidden or other diagnosis
diagnostics: PMR: clinical + ESR/CRP raised + age ≥ 50 + bilateral shoulder/hip pain + morning stiffness > 30 min + rapid response to low-dose steroid (15-20 mg pred — dramatic response within 1 week is supportive)

GCA: clinical + ACR 1990 / 2022 criteria + TEMPORAL ARTERY BIOPSY (gold standard — within 1 week; some unilateral 2-3 cm; granulomatous arteritis with giant cells + skip lesions; sensitivity 70-90%; CAN BE DONE AFTER STARTING STEROID — don't delay treatment)
Imaging: ultrasound temporal arteries (halo sign — sensitive + non-invasive); FDG-PET / MRA for large-vessel GCA (aorta + branches)
ESR ≥ 50 mm/h, CRP > 100 typical (though normal in 5-10%)
FBC (anaemia of chronic disease), thrombocytosis, LFT (raised ALP)
Ophthalmology assessment if any visual symptoms
management: PMR:
Prednisolone 15-20 mg/day starting dose (NOT 60 mg — that's for GCA)
Rapid response within 1 week (if not — reconsider diagnosis)
Slow taper: 2.5 mg every 2-4 weeks until 10 mg, then 1 mg every 4-8 weeks
Average duration of treatment 12-24 months
Relapse common — increase by 5 mg + re-taper
METHOTREXATE 7.5-15 mg/week as steroid-sparing for relapsing / high-dose dependent
Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6) — alternative steroid-sparing (SEMAPHORE trial 2023 effective in PMR)
Bone protection: vitamin D + calcium + bisphosphonate (steroid-induced osteoporosis)
Glycaemic + BP monitoring + lifestyle
GCA (with or without PMR):
NO VISUAL SYMPTOMS — high-dose prednisolone 40-60 mg/day (1 mg/kg)
VISUAL SYMPTOMS or known large-vessel: IV methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg × 3 days then high-dose prednisolone
START IMMEDIATELY — DO NOT WAIT FOR BIOPSY (visual loss can be permanent + bilateral; biopsy still positive up to 2 weeks after starting steroid)
Slow taper: 60 → 50 → 40 → 35 → 30 mg over weeks; then 2.5 mg every 2-4 weeks until 10 mg; then 1 mg every 4-8 weeks
Average duration of treatment 2-3 years (longer than PMR)
TOCILIZUMAB (anti-IL-6) — first-line steroid-sparing (GiACTA NEJM 2017 — superior remission + reduced steroid exposure); for active disease or relapse
Methotrexate alternative steroid-sparing
Aspirin 75 mg (reduces ischaemic events)
MONITORING:
Clinical relapse (key — labs alone unreliable)
ESR + CRP every 2-4 weeks initially
Steroid side effects: BP, glucose, weight, mood, infection, bone, eye (cataract, glaucoma)
Aortic surveillance in GCA (annual imaging — CT or MR angiogram for aneurysm)
STEROID-INDUCED COMPLICATIONS — proactive management:
Osteoporosis: DEXA + bisphosphonate within 3 months of starting > 7.5 mg pred / day for ≥ 3 months
Vitamin D + calcium
PPI for GI protection
PCP prophylaxis (cotrim) for prolonged > 20 mg / day > 4 weeks
Monitor glucose, BP, weight
Cataract + glaucoma surveillance
Avoid abrupt cessation (adrenal suppression — taper)
TRIGGER MANAGEMENT:
Identify provoking infection / stressor
Treat concomitant conditions
Patient EDUCATION:
Sick day rules (double dose for fever/illness)
Adrenal crisis if abrupt cessation
Steroid card / MedicAlert
Long-term commitment to therapy

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) — thrombosis + obstetric
population: Young adults (typically 20-50); women predominant; primary or secondary to SLE (40-50% with APS have SLE). Major preventable cause of recurrent miscarriage + young stroke.
presentation: Vascular thrombosis (arterial — stroke, MI, limb ischaemia; venous — DVT, PE, cerebral venous, hepatic, mesenteric) AND/OR obstetric morbidity (≥ 1 fetal loss > 10 weeks; ≥ 1 preterm < 34 weeks for PE/IUGR; ≥ 3 unexplained < 10 week miscarriages). Catastrophic APS — multi-organ thrombosis (1%, high mortality).
redFlags: Catastrophic APS — multiple organ thromboses + microthrombi — emergency
Pregnancy with APS — high-risk obstetric care
Lupus anticoagulant + recurrent miscarriage / IUGR / preeclampsia
Triple antibody positivity (LA + ACL + B2GP1) — highest risk
diagnostics: Sydney criteria (2006 + 2023 update):
CLINICAL: vascular thrombosis OR pregnancy morbidity
PLUS LABORATORY (PERSISTENT 12 weeks apart):
Lupus anticoagulant (LA) — DRVVT + APTT-LA
Anti-cardiolipin (aCL) IgG/IgM > 40 GPL/MPL or > 99th percentile
Anti-β2-glycoprotein-1 (anti-β2GP1) IgG/IgM > 99th percentile
All TRIPLE positive = highest thrombosis risk
Exclude other thrombophilias: factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin/protein C/S deficiency, hyperhomocysteinaemia
Workup secondary causes: SLE, malignancy, infection (especially syphilis, HIV), drug-induced (procainamide, hydralazine, chlorpromazine, phenytoin)
management: THROMBOSIS — venous OR arterial:
WARFARIN (target INR 2-3) — first-line for venous; some recommend target 3-4 for arterial / recurrent VTE on standard INR
DOACs were NOT non-inferior in TRAPS + RAPS trials (especially triple-positive arterial thrombosis) — AVOID in:
Triple-positive APS
Arterial thrombosis history
Recurrent thrombosis on warfarin
DOAC ONLY consider in single-positive low-risk VTE patients (after thorough discussion); apixaban / rivaroxaban
Indefinite anticoagulation (lifelong for most)
Add HCQ for SLE-APS
Aspirin 75 mg + statin adjuncts (especially CV)
OBSTETRIC APS:
Aspirin 75-150 mg from positive pregnancy test through delivery
LMWH prophylactic dose throughout pregnancy + 6 weeks postpartum (if history of pregnancy loss OR thrombosis history)
LMWH treatment dose for active VTE / arterial thrombosis history
Continue anticoag postpartum 6 weeks minimum
HCQ (especially SLE-APS)
Multidisciplinary (rheumatology + obstetrics + haematology)
Anti-Ro/La: fetal cardiac monitoring (congenital heart block)
CATASTROPHIC APS (CAPS):
ICU + multi-organ support
TRIPLE THERAPY: anticoagulation (heparin) + corticosteroid + plasma exchange OR IVIG
Add rituximab / eculizumab refractory
Treat trigger (infection, surgery, malignancy, anticoagulation withdrawal)
Mortality 30-50%
ASYMPTOMATIC antiphospholipid + NO thrombosis:
Low-dose aspirin 75-100 mg/day controversial (modest evidence) — consider in high-risk profile (triple-positive, comorbid)
Address CV risk factors aggressively
HCQ if SLE
ADJUNCTS:
Statin for arterial APS
Plaquenil for SLE-APS
Hypertension + diabetes + smoking — address CV risk
Avoid combined OCP (DVT risk) — use progestin-only or IUD
Anti-D considerations Rh-negative pregnancy
PERIOPERATIVE:
Bridge with LMWH (DOAC has shorter half-life — manageable)
Restart anticoagulation post-op early when haemostasis allows
High thrombosis risk in surgery + APS
Mechanical IPC during surgery
MONITORING:
INR 4-weekly when stable on warfarin
Annual APL antibody titre
Pregnancy: monthly antibody titre + LMWH dose adjustment + obstetric monitoring
Renal function (lupus nephritis screening)
CV risk modification
Patient EDUCATION:
Lifelong anticoagulation for most
Carry alert card / MedicAlert
Pregnancy planning (do not stop anticoag without preparation)
Diet + drug interactions for warfarin

Kenya National Guidelines for Quality Obstetrics and Perinatal Care (EmONC), Ministry of Health
WHO Recommendations on Maternal and Newborn Care

title: Fibromyalgia — comprehensive multimodal management
population: Adults — prevalence 2-4%; women 7× men; co-occurs with rheumatologic, IBS, migraine, depression, anxiety.
presentation: Widespread pain + fatigue + sleep disturbance + cognitive (fibro-fog) + somatic symptoms. Modern: nociplastic pain — central sensitisation.
redFlags: Atypical features — exclude alternative (inflammatory arthritis, hypothyroidism, polymyalgia, myositis, sleep apnoea)
diagnostics: Clinical diagnosis using 2010/2016 ACR criteria — Widespread Pain Index (WPI) + Symptom Severity (SS) score; no tender point exam required
Rule out alternative — TSH, CK, ESR/CRP, FBC, vitamin D
Screen for sleep apnoea (STOP-Bang), depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7)
Address comorbid IBS, migraine, TMD, pelvic pain (often co-occur)
management: EDUCATION + VALIDATION (foundation):
Explain nociplastic pain + central sensitisation framework
Validate experience — not 'in their head'
Realistic expectations — manageable, not cured
Set FUNCTIONAL goals (work, family, activity) rather than pain-free
NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL (strongest evidence):
EXERCISE — gradual aerobic + low-impact (water, walking, tai chi, yoga, Pilates) — strongest single intervention
Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) — for pain, sleep, mood
Acceptance + Commitment Therapy (ACT)
Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR)
Sleep hygiene + CBT-I for insomnia
Pacing + activity management
Physiotherapy + multidisciplinary pain rehabilitation
Pool exercise / aquatic therapy
PHARMACOLOGICAL (modest evidence — combine with non-pharm):
TCA: AMITRIPTYLINE 10-50 mg nocte (low-dose; very effective; addresses sleep + pain + mood)
SNRI: DULOXETINE 30-120 mg, milnacipran 50-100 mg BD (FDA-approved for fibromyalgia)
α2δ ligand: PREGABALIN 75-450 mg/d, gabapentin (off-label)
AVOID strong opioids — ineffective + risk of hyperalgesia + addiction
Tramadol low-dose acceptable short-term (caution serotonin syndrome with SNRI / SSRI)
AVOID benzodiazepines (no benefit + dependence)
NSAIDs — ineffective for primary fibromyalgia (use for comorbid OA)
Low-dose naltrexone — emerging evidence
Cannabinoid — limited evidence; selected
Modafinil for fatigue (off-label)
Memantine for fibro-fog (limited evidence)
PSYCHIATRIC COMORBIDITY:
Treat depression / anxiety / PTSD aggressively
Trauma history common — trauma-informed care
Address sleep disorders (OSA, restless legs)
SLEEP:
Non-restorative sleep cardinal feature
CBT-I + melatonin + amitriptyline + pregabalin
Exclude OSA + restless legs
DIET + LIFESTYLE:
No specific 'fibromyalgia diet' but anti-inflammatory pattern (Mediterranean)
Weight management
Avoid caffeine + alcohol excess
Smoking cessation
WORKPLACE:
Often disabling — disability assessment + accommodations
Graded return to work
Reduce work hours / role modification
Vocational rehabilitation
MULTIDISCIPLINARY APPROACH:
Primary care + pain specialist + physiotherapy + OT + psychology + rheumatology (rule out + co-management)
Avoid 'shopping' multiple providers (worsens fragmentation)
Continuity of care critical
ADDRESS SYSTEMIC ISSUES:
Comorbid conditions (IBS, migraine, TMD, pelvic pain, OA) — treat each
Mental health integration
Family education + support
PATIENT EXPECTATIONS:
Improvement gradual
Flares with stress, weather, infection, exertion — anticipate + manage
Lifelong condition with episodic worsening
RED FLAGS to revisit diagnosis:
New focal neurological deficit
Joint swelling / inflammation (vs tenderness)
Constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss)
Significantly elevated inflammatory markers
Significant family history rheumatologic disease

references.label: American Pain Society / ACR Fibromyalgia Guidelines 2018
Cochrane reviews exercise + CBT for fibromyalgia 2023
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Suspected primary immunodeficiency — workup + IVIG
population: Often under-diagnosed — > 450 known PIDs; range from severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID — newborn screen) to common variable immune deficiency (CVID — adult).
presentation: 10 warning signs (Jeffrey Modell Foundation):
redFlags: ≥ 2 months on antibiotics with little effect
Persistent thrush in mouth / fungal skin infection
Need IV antibiotics to clear infections
diagnostics: Full history including: infection frequency / severity / type / location, autoimmune features, family history, growth, complications
FBC + lymphocyte count + smear (lymphopaenia / neutropaenia / thrombocytopaenia)
Immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE)
Specific antibody responses to vaccines (tetanus, pneumococcal) — assess functional immunity
Lymphocyte subsets (CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19, CD56) by flow cytometry
Complement levels (CH50, AH50, C3, C4)
Newborn SCID screening (TREC test)
HIV test (always rule out)
Genetic testing (NGS panels — increasingly accessible)
Imaging for chronic infection sequelae (CT chest for bronchiectasis)
management: REFERRAL to clinical immunologist for diagnosis + management
TREATMENT BY DEFICIENCY TYPE:
ANTIBODY DEFICIENCIES (most common — CVID, XLA, IgA deficiency, transient hypogamma):
IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) 0.4-0.8 g/kg every 3-4 weeks OR
SCIG (subcutaneous) 0.1-0.2 g/kg weekly (home self-administered) OR HyQvia (10% recombinant hyaluronidase facilitated SCIG monthly)
Target IgG trough > 5 g/L (or higher for infection control)
Lifelong replacement for CVID / XLA
Antibiotic prophylaxis (azithromycin / amoxicillin) for chronic respiratory disease

title: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) — comprehensive management
population: Rare (10-30/100,000) but devastating multisystem disease. Women > men 4:1; peak 30-50. African + Native American ancestry — more severe.
presentation: Limited cutaneous (skin sclerosis distal to elbows + face + neck; CREST — Calcinosis + Raynaud + oEsophageal + Sclerodactyly + Telangiectasia; SLOW progression; PAH late) vs Diffuse cutaneous (proximal skin + truncal; rapid progression; ILD + cardiac + renal more common + worse prognosis). Raynaud's universal (preceding skin in 70%).
redFlags: Pulmonary arterial hypertension — major cause of mortality
Renal crisis (sudden severe hypertension + AKI) — emergency
Scleroderma renal crisis — even normotensive ('normotensive renal crisis')
diagnostics: ACR/EULAR 2013 classification criteria
ANA + scleroderma-specific antibodies:
Anti-centromere → limited cutaneous + PAH
Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) → diffuse + ILD
Anti-RNA polymerase III → renal crisis + diffuse
Anti-fibrillarin (U3-RNP), anti-PM-Scl, anti-NOR-90
Pulmonary screening (all patients at baseline + annual):
PFTs + DLCO (FVC + DLCO drop suggest ILD; isolated DLCO drop → PAH)
HRCT chest (ILD — NSIP pattern most common)
Echo + tricuspid regurgitation velocity (PAH screening; RHC if abnormal)
ProBNP
6-minute walk test
Renal: urinalysis + BP (annually + symptoms); creatinine
GI: oesophageal manometry, gastric emptying studies (impaired motility); endoscopy for GERD complications
Cardiac: echo + cardiac MRI + Holter for arrhythmia
Hand: skin score (modified Rodnan)
Nailfold capillaroscopy — useful for Raynaud's differential
management: NO DISEASE-MODIFYING CURE — symptom + organ-specific:
RAYNAUD'S + DIGITAL ULCERS:
Lifestyle: warm clothing, gloves, avoid cold + smoking + stress + beta-blockers
CCB (nifedipine, amlodipine) first-line
PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil) for refractory or digital ulcers
Endothelin antagonist (bosentan) — prevents new digital ulcers (RAPIDS-2)
Iloprost IV (prostacyclin) for severe acute ischaemia / ulcers / refractory
Topical nitrate for individual ulcers
Statin (may improve endothelial)
Digital sympathectomy + amputation for refractory
INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASE:
Mycophenolate mofetil 2-3 g/d — first-line (Scleroderma Lung Study II — non-inferior to cyclophosphamide + safer)
Cyclophosphamide if progressive / severe
NINTEDANIB (antifibrotic) — slows progression (SENSCIS NEJM 2019); add-on or alternative
TOCILIZUMAB (anti-IL-6) — early SSc-ILD with high inflammation (focuSSed NEJM 2020)
Lung transplant for refractory / severe
Anti-fibrotic + immunosuppressive combination emerging
PULMONARY HYPERTENSION (SSc-PAH):
Same as Group 1 PAH (separate condition)
Combination dual oral (ERA + PDE5i) — AMBITION
Add prostacyclin for high-risk
Selexipag, sotatercept (STELLAR), epoprostenol
Lung transplant
SCLERODERMA RENAL CRISIS (emergency):
ACE INHIBITOR — captopril titrated rapidly (start 6.25 mg, titrate q4-8h)
Goal: BP < 140/90 + reverse AKI
Continue ACE-i even with worsening creatinine (paradoxically improves outcomes)
Dialysis if needed (temporary often)
Avoid steroid > 15 mg/d (precipitates renal crisis)
Plasma exchange for refractory
Anti-RNA Pol III + diffuse + recent + skin progressing — highest risk
GI:
PPI for GERD
Promotility (metoclopramide / erythromycin / domperidone) for gastroparesis + intestinal pseudo-obstruction
Rotating antibiotic for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO — rifaximin, tetracycline)
PEG / TPN for severe malnutrition
Anti-emetic + analgesia
Dietitian + dental + speech evaluation
CALCINOSIS:
Diltiazem, sodium thiosulfate (off-label)
Surgical excision for symptomatic
ARTHRITIS / SKIN:
Methotrexate or mycophenolate for skin progression
HCQ + NSAID for arthritis
AUTOLOGOUS HAEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELL TRANSPLANT (HSCT):
Severe diffuse SSc + organ involvement + young + no end-stage disease
ASTIS + SCOT trials — improved long-term survival
Cardiac screening pre-transplant essential
PREGNANCY:
Plan when stable; avoid first 2-3 years after diagnosis
ACE-i contraindicated for routine BP control + RENAL CRISIS PROPHYLAXIS
Postpone if active disease
Multidisciplinary obstetric care
Switch teratogenic before

Body image + functional impact
Depression + anxiety
Support groups
Vocational
Sexual function

Skin score (mRSS)

GI symptoms

title: HIV ART — modern DTG/BIC era (Kenya NASCOP + WHO 2024)
population: Adults + adolescents living with HIV. SSA — 70% of global burden; Kenya 1.4 million PLHIV; treat-all + dolutegravir-based ART standard since 2018.
presentation: Routine HIV care contact OR new diagnosis. Acute HIV — mononucleosis-like (fever, lymphadenopathy, rash, pharyngitis, myalgia 2-4 wks post-exposure). Chronic — asymptomatic until AIDS-defining illness.
redFlags: AIDS-defining illness (cryptococcal meningitis, PCP, KS, lymphoma, oesophageal candidiasis, severe TB) — admit + start ART + opportunistic infection treatment
Treatment failure (viral load > 1000 on 2 occasions) — enhanced adherence then switch to second-line / DRT
Hepatitis B / C co-infection — TDF in regimen + DAA HCV
Acute renal failure on TDF (less with TAF)
diagnostics: HIV diagnosis: rapid test ladder (Determine + First Response + SD Bioline — Kenya NASCOP algorithm; positive on 2 different rapid tests = confirmed)
Pre-treatment: CD4 + viral load + HBsAg + HCV + creatinine + ALT + lipid + glucose + pregnancy + TB symptom screen + cervical cancer screening
Resistance test (genotype) — at baseline (where available; not routine LMIC) + on treatment failure
Tropism (CCR5) test if maraviroc considered
Routine monitoring: VL at 6 months post-ART + annually if undetectable; CD4 not needed if VL undetectable for > 1 year (per WHO simplified monitoring)
Coinfection screen annually: hepatitis B + C + syphilis + STIs + TB
Cardiovascular + metabolic monitoring annually
Cervical cancer screening (HPV-positive) — annual if CD4 < 350 or baseline
Mental health screen
Substance use screen
management: TREAT-ALL — initiate ART for everyone diagnosed HIV+ (regardless of CD4, ARV resistance, age) — WHO 2015 + Kenya NASCOP
RAPID ART INITIATION — within 7 days (or same day if no contraindication) — RAPID trials (CASCADE, TEMPRANO, START)
FIRST-LINE (Kenya NASCOP 2022 + WHO 2024):
TENOFOVIR (TDF 300 mg) + LAMIVUDINE (3TC 300 mg) + DOLUTEGRAVIR (DTG 50 mg) — TLD
Once-daily fixed-dose combination, available generically + Global Fund supported
Highly potent + barrier to resistance + tolerated
DTG superior to EFV (single-tablet, fewer side effects, better CNS profile, fewer drug interactions)
Bictegravir / FTC / TAF (Biktarvy) — alternative; expensive in SSA (advocate generic access)
Switch to dolutegravir-based for those on older regimens (NNRTI-based switch — VISEND, NAMSAL)
Avoid EFV if on rifampicin (TB) — INSTI (DTG) preferred with rifampicin dose-adjusted (50 mg BD with rifampicin)
DTG SAFETY UPDATES:
Neural tube defect signal RESOLVED — recent meta-analyses (Tsepamo) show no significant increased risk vs EFV; DTG safe in pregnancy + WCBP per WHO 2023 (previous concern lifted)
Weight gain (women + Black) — counsel + monitor; address comorbidity (DM, HTN, lipids)
Hyperglycaemia — monitor glucose
Insomnia / mood — switch if persistent
SECOND-LINE (failure on first-line):
Switch INSTI to PI (boosted darunavir + ritonavir) + new NRTI backbone (AZT + 3TC) — if NRTI resistance
OR DTG continue + change NRTI backbone (TAF + emtricitabine or AZT + 3TC) — if no INSTI resistance
Adherence-focused intervention before switch (enhanced adherence counselling × 3 months)
Genotype to guide where available
THIRD-LINE / SALVAGE:
DTG + PI + ETR (etravirine) + ENF (T20)
Newer: LENACAPAVIR (Sunlenca) — capsid inhibitor, q6-monthly SC injection for highly treatment-experienced (FDA 2022)
Cabotegravir + rilpivirine (Cabenuva) — q1-2-monthly IM injection for virologically suppressed
Genotype + tropism testing
Specialist input
OPPORTUNISTIC INFECTION PROPHYLAXIS:
CD4 < 200: cotrim 960 mg daily (PCP, toxo, falciparum malaria)
CD4 < 100: screen for cryptococcal antigen + pre-emptive fluconazole 1200 mg/d × 2 wk if CrAg+ + LP
IGRA + sputum AFB/GeneXpert for TB; TB preventive therapy (3HP — rifapentine + isoniazid 3 months OR 6H — isoniazid 6 months) for all HIV+ without active TB
Annual Pap smear (cervical cancer)
Hepatitis B vaccine (if non-immune)
Pneumococcal + annual flu + COVID vaccines
PrEP for HIV-negative partner / serodiscordant couple
PREGNANCY (PMTCT — Kenya Linda Mama + NASCOP):
TLD lifelong + 3-dose maternal Tdap (separate)
Infant prophylaxis: NVP × 6 wk (low-risk) or 12 wk + cotrim (high-risk per Kenya NASCOP)
Early infant diagnosis (EID) — PCR at 6 wk, 6 mo, 12 mo, 18 mo + 6 wk post-cessation of breastfeeding
Operation Triple Zero (Kenya adolescent strategy — zero missed appointments, zero missed doses, zero viral load)
ADHERENCE + RETENTION:
Multi-month dispensing (3-6 month refills for stable patients) — Differentiated Service Delivery (DSD)
Community ART distribution
Treatment supporters / peer mentors
Mental health + substance abuse integrated treatment
Adolescent-friendly services + transition clinic (16-24)
Address structural barriers (food insecurity, IPV, stigma, transport)
VIRAL LOAD MONITORING:
At 6 months post-ART + annually if undetectable (WHO 2021 simplified)
If VL > 1000: enhanced adherence counselling × 3 months + repeat VL; if still > 1000 → genotype + switch
U=U (Undetectable = Untransmittable) — communicate to patient + partners
DEPRESSION / MENTAL HEALTH: 2× higher in PLHIV; integrate screening + treatment
Address comorbidities: CVD risk (HIV + ART metabolic), bone health (TDF), diabetes, mental health, cancer screening
ELIMINATION (KENYA + UNAIDS 2030 — 95-95-95):
95% diagnosed + 95% on ART + 95% virally suppressed
Index testing + community testing + self-testing (HIVST)
Differentiated service delivery
PrEP scale-up
Address structural drivers (poverty, GBV, stigma)

title: HIV PrEP — comprehensive prevention (cabotegravir LA + lenacapavir + oral)
population: HIV-negative individuals at substantial risk — AGYW (adolescent girls + young women) in HIV burden areas (Kenya DREAMS counties), MSM, transgender, sex workers, serodiscordant couples, PWID. SSA: PrEP scale-up critical for 95-95-95.
presentation: Routine sexual health / prevention contact. PrEP-eligible if substantial HIV exposure risk + HIV-negative + no contraindications.
redFlags: Acute HIV at PrEP initiation (test thoroughly — 4th generation Ag/Ab + RNA if very recent exposure)
Suspected resistance acquisition (PrEP initiated during undiagnosed acute HIV)
Renal impairment (TDF caution; TAF or CAB-LA alternative)
Pregnancy (some PrEP options safe; not all studied)
diagnostics: HIV test (rapid + 4th-gen Ag/Ab; RNA if recent acute exposure suspected)
STI screen (gonorrhoea, chlamydia, syphilis, hepatitis B sAg + sAb + cAb, hepatitis C)
Renal function (creatinine + eGFR — TDF safety)
Pregnancy test (if relevant)
Bone health assessment if long-term TDF planned (osteoporosis risk)
Substance use, mental health, IPV screening (Kenya DREAMS)
management: ORAL PrEP — most accessible globally + SSA scale-up:
TDF/FTC 300/200 mg ONE TABLET DAILY (Truvada / Tenvir-EM)
TDF/3TC alternative (generic; not Truvada-equivalent but used in Kenya)
TAF/FTC (Descovy) — alternative; not approved for cisgender women receptive vaginal sex (DISCOVER trial limitation); useful renal/bone concerns
EFFICACY: > 95% with adherence (PROUD trial near 100%; daily adherence critical)
Side effects: GI start-up symptoms, rare renal, rare bone
On-demand (2-1-1) for MSM: 2 tablets 2-24h before, 1 tablet 24h after first, 1 tablet 48h after first (ipergay) — NOT for women / vaginal sex (long pharmacokinetic lag in cervicovaginal tissue)
Counsel daily adherence + condoms + STI prevention
INJECTABLE LONG-ACTING PrEP (game-changers for SSA + AGYW):
CABOTEGRAVIR-LA (Apretude) — q2-monthly IM injection
HPTN 083 + HPTN 084 — superior to oral TDF/FTC (especially Black MSM + cisgender women)
KENYA approved + scaling 2024 — addresses adherence challenges + stigma
Initial 600 mg IM × 2 (1 month apart) then q8 weeks
Side effects: injection site reactions, weight gain
'Pharmacological tail' — after last dose, oral PrEP / antibody coverage for several months for protection / resistance prevention if HIV occurs
LENACAPAVIR (Sunlenca) — q6-monthly SC injection
PURPOSE-1 + PURPOSE-2 trials 2024 — NEAR 100% EFFICACY (98-100%) — most effective PrEP demonstrated
First-line for high-risk where access — game-changer for HIV elimination
Kenya advocacy for access + generic licensing
Cost barrier — global price negotiations ongoing
DAPIVIRINE VAGINAL RING (PrEPring):
Monthly silicone ring — DREAM + HOPE trials moderate efficacy
Approved EMA + WHO prequalified
Choice for women
Less effective than CAB-LA / lenacapavir but accessible
INITIATION:
Confirm HIV-negative (rapid + 4th-gen Ag/Ab + RNA if suspect acute)
Screen STIs + treat
Hepatitis B vaccine if non-immune (TDF treats hepatitis B — sudden withdrawal of TDF can cause hepatitis flare)
Renal function check
Counsel adherence + dosing + side effects + condoms + STI prevention
Pregnancy counselling (PrEP safe in pregnancy + breastfeeding)
FOLLOW-UP:
Initial visit then 1 month + 3-monthly visits
HIV test every 3 months (or per dosing schedule LA — before each injection)
STI screen 3-monthly
Renal function + adherence + side effects
Acute HIV high suspicion despite negative test: STOP PrEP + RNA testing + resistance + initiate ART
STOP PrEP when:
No longer at substantial risk
Plan to taper / discontinue — continue 28 days after last potential exposure
Side effects intolerable
Renal impairment
PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) — separate condition:
Within 72h of high-risk exposure
TLD (TDF + 3TC + DTG) × 28 days
Same prevention package: STI + hepatitis + counselling
POPULATIONS:
AGYW (Kenya DREAMS counties): integrated SRH + economic empowerment + parenting + safe schools
MSM + transgender: stigma-free clinics, peer outreach
Sex workers: peer-led + comprehensive package
PWID: harm reduction + needle exchange + OAT + PrEP integrated
Serodiscordant couples: PrEP for HIV-negative partner + U=U for positive partner
HIV-exposed infants: ARV prophylaxis per separate condition
BARRIERS + SOLUTIONS:
Stigma — community engagement, peer educators
Adherence (oral) — DSD, multi-month dispensing, LA injections
Cost — Global Fund, PEPFAR, generic licensing
Gender norms — DREAMS, MenStar, men's clinics

title: TB rifampicin-sensitive — 4-month regimen + comprehensive care
population: 10+ million annual TB notifications globally; SSA disproportionate burden; Kenya — 130,000+ notifications/year. HIV co-infection major SSA challenge.
presentation: Cough > 2 weeks, weight loss, night sweats, fever; haemoptysis, dyspnoea, chest pain. Extrapulmonary (lymph node, pleural, spinal, meningeal, abdominal — common in HIV).
redFlags: TB meningitis — high mortality; aggressive treatment + steroids
Severe disseminated TB in HIV/AIDS (CD4 < 100) — IRIS risk
Spinal TB (Pott's) with cord compression — neurosurgical + medical
diagnostics: WHO/Kenya TIBU notification: any presumptive case → workup
Sputum: 2 samples — Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra (rapid, also detects rifampicin resistance) — first-line; sputum smear (Ziehl-Neelsen / fluorescence) historical
Sputum culture (gold standard, slow 4-8 weeks) + drug susceptibility (DST)
Chest X-ray + CT (cavitation, upper lobe predominance, miliary)
Extrapulmonary samples: lymph node FNA + culture; pleural fluid + biopsy; CSF if suspected meningitis; bone/joint aspirate
HIV test ALL (essential — co-management)
Drug-resistance: Xpert MTB/RIF rifampicin; line probe assay (LPA) for fluoroquinolone + 2nd-line injectable; phenotypic DST for full susceptibility
Pre-treatment: FBC, LFT, U&E, glucose, vision (ethambutol), HIV, hepatitis B + C, pregnancy
Contact screening (close contacts — TST/IGRA + symptom screen + CXR if positive)
Children: tuberculin skin test + CXR + history of contact + nutrition assessment + HIV
management: MODERN REGIMEN — WHO 2022 + Kenya updates:
DRUG-SENSITIVE TB (Standard 6-month or new 4-month):
HRZE 2 months (initial): isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol
HR 4 months (continuation): isoniazid + rifampicin
Total 6 months
Fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) — single tablets with all 4 drugs (initial) or 2 (continuation) — improve adherence
NEW 4-MONTH REGIMEN (WHO 2022 — Study 31 / TBTC):
RIPE-LfxRPE 4 months: rifapentine (RPT) + isoniazid + pyrazinamide + moxifloxacin × 17 weeks (8 weeks intensive + 9 weeks continuation)
Higher-dose rifapentine + moxifloxacin
Eligible: drug-sensitive pulmonary TB, age ≥ 12 + ≥ 40 kg
Non-inferior to standard 6-month + shorter
Roll-out variable across LMIC (cost + supply chain)
TB MENINGITIS:
Same drugs but 12 months total + dexamethasone tapering (Thwaites trial — survival benefit)
Higher-dose drugs (isoniazid 10 mg/kg, rifampicin 15 mg/kg) considered for severity
TB-HIV CO-INFECTION:
Start ART early (within 8 weeks of TB treatment start) — within 2 weeks if CD4 < 50 (SAPiT, CAMELIA, STRIDE trials)
DOLUTEGRAVIR-based ART with TB treatment — DTG 50 mg BD when on rifampicin (NAMSAL, INSPIRING)
EFV-based alternatives — but DTG superior
Watch IRIS (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome) — paradoxical worsening; steroid if severe; do NOT stop ART
Cotrim prophylaxis universal (PCP + falciparum)
TB preventive therapy (TPT) post-cure to prevent recurrence
TREATMENT MONITORING:
Monthly clinic visits — adherence (DOT or video DOT), side effects, weight, symptom resolution
Sputum smear / Xpert at 2 + 5 + 6 months (smear conversion key)
Culture at 2 + 6 months
Liver function (especially first 2 months — INH, PZA hepatotoxic): monthly LFTs; hold drugs if AST > 5× ULN or 3× + symptoms
Visual acuity if ethambutol (monthly especially > 15 mg/kg or > 2 months)
Drug interactions — rifampicin major CYP3A4/2C19 inducer (warfarin, OCP, DOAC, antiretrovirals)
Pyridoxine 10-25 mg/day with isoniazid (prevents peripheral neuropathy)
ADHERENCE STRATEGIES:
Directly Observed Treatment (DOT) — community / facility / video / 99DOTS (mobile)
Family treatment supporter
Patient education + counselling
Multi-month dispensing for stable patients
Address structural barriers (food, transport, housing) — patient incentives where possible
Tracing defaulters
Mobile health interventions (Kenya 'Ushauri', SMS reminders)
TREATMENT FAILURE / RECURRENCE:
Repeat workup including DST
Switch to MDR regimen if rifampicin resistance
Specialist referral
PREVENTIVE TREATMENT (TPT):
Indications: HIV+ (all), close contacts (esp children < 5 + immunocompromised), recent TST/IGRA conversion, silicosis, TNFi candidates
Regimens:
3HP: rifapentine 900 mg + INH 900 mg weekly × 12 doses (12 weeks) — preferred where rifapentine available
3HR: rifampicin + INH daily × 3 months
1HP: rifapentine + INH daily × 1 month (newer — ACTG 5279)
6H: INH 300 mg daily × 6 months (classic — more common LMIC)
Pyridoxine 10-25 mg daily with isoniazid
Counsel adherence
PUBLIC HEALTH:
Notify Kenya TIBU within 24h
Contact tracing — household + close contacts
Infection control (cough hygiene + ventilation + N95 healthcare worker + isolation initial)
Address social determinants (poverty + overcrowding + nutrition)
HIV testing in TB patients + reverse
Universal BCG (newborn — Kenya EPI)
WHO End TB Strategy 2035
M72/AS01E TB vaccine candidate — Phase 3 promising
PAEDIATRIC TB:
Weight-based dosing per WHO/Kenya paediatric TB guidelines
Dispersible FDCs (RH 75/50, RHZ 75/50/150) for paeds
ALL HIV+ children household contact of pulmonary TB — 6H TPT
Severe disease (TB meningitis, miliary, disseminated): 12 months + steroid
Nutritional support
PREGNANCY:
Continue treatment — TB worse outcome than treatment toxicity
RIPE (HRZE) safe (except streptomycin → avoid in pregnancy — fetal ototoxicity)
Vitamin K to mother last weeks + neonate
Breastfeeding compatible (low transfer; cover baby with INH if mother smear-positive)

title: MDR/RR-TB + XDR-TB — BPaL / BPaLM modern short regimens
population: Rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) ~ 410,000 cases globally; high-burden countries include India, Russia, China, South Africa, Kenya emerging cases. Treatment historically long (18-24 months) + toxic; revolutionary 6-month all-oral regimens now available.
presentation: Diagnosed by molecular test (Xpert MTB/RIF rifampicin) or DST. May present as treatment failure, contact of MDR patient, or new patient with risk factor.
redFlags: XDR-TB (resistance to any fluoroquinolone + at least one Group A drug — bedaquiline OR linezolid)
QT-prolonging drug combinations (bedaquiline + moxifloxacin/levofloxacin + clofazimine + delamanid — monitor ECG)
Hepatotoxicity / hearing loss / peripheral neuropathy / depression / suicidality from MDR-TB drugs
diagnostics: Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra — first-line (detects rifampicin resistance rapidly)
Line probe assay (LPA) — fluoroquinolone + 2nd-line injectable resistance
Phenotypic DST — comprehensive but slow
Targeted-sequencing / WGS — emerging for full drug susceptibility profile

Baseline + monitoring: FBC + LFT + U&E + glucose + ECG (QTc) + thyroid (capreomycin) + visual acuity (linezolid eye) + colour vision + audiogram (if injectable) + mental health screen + HIV + hepatitis B/C
Sputum culture monthly during treatment
Treatment response: culture conversion by 6 months
management: PARADIGM SHIFT — WHO 2022/2024:
ALL-ORAL 6-MONTH REGIMEN — BPaL / BPaLM (revolutionary, replacing 18-24 month injectable regimens):
BPaL: BEDAQUILINE + PRETOMANID + LINEZOLID
BPaLM: BPaL + MOXIFLOXACIN (for MDR/RR-TB sensitive to fluoroquinolones)
Duration 6 months (can extend to 9 months if needed)
All oral — no injectable
Highly effective (ZeNix, TB-PRACTECAL, NIX-TB)
Linezolid dose: 600 mg/d × 26 weeks (preferred); 1200 mg/d × 9 weeks then 600 mg/d × 17 weeks (alternative if higher initial mycobactericidal needed)
Eligible: pulmonary RR/MDR-TB, age ≥ 14, regardless of HIV status, ALL with QTc baseline acceptable
Pregnancy: avoid pretomanid (limited data); use longer all-oral with bedaquiline + linezolid + clofazimine + cycloserine
Extrapulmonary EXCEPT CNS / pericardial (use longer regimen for these)
EXTENDED ALL-ORAL (9-20 month — for ineligible BPaL/BPaLM or non-responders):
Group A (preferred — must use ALL):
Levofloxacin / moxifloxacin
BEDAQUILINE
LINEZOLID
Group B (preferred):
Clofazimine
Cycloserine / terizidone
Group C (add as needed):
Ethambutol, delamanid, pyrazinamide, imipenem-cilastatin, meropenem, amikacin (when no alternative), ethionamide / prothionamide, p-aminosalicylic acid
DRUG-SPECIFIC MONITORING + COUNSELLING:
BEDAQUILINE — QTc (monthly ECG), LFT, hyperuricaemia
LINEZOLID — peripheral neuropathy + optic neuritis (visual acuity + colour vision monthly), myelosuppression (FBC), lactic acidosis, mitochondrial toxicity; dose-reduce or stop if severe
PRETOMANID — LFT, infertility (testicular toxicity counsel)
CLOFAZIMINE — skin pigmentation (cosmetic), QTc, GI
CYCLOSERINE — neuropsychiatric (depression, psychosis, suicide), neuropathy — pyridoxine 200-300 mg/d
FLUOROQUINOLONE — QTc, tendon rupture, dysglycaemia, peripheral neuropathy, photosensitivity
ETHAMBUTOL — optic neuropathy (colour vision)
AMINOGLYCOSIDE — vestibulotoxicity + nephrotoxicity (audiogram + Cr)
Cumulative QTc on multiple QT-prolonging drugs — careful monitoring + dose adjustment
HIV-MDR-TB:
Concurrent ART (DTG-based)
Watch IRIS
Cotrim prophylaxis
Higher mortality if late
PAEDIATRIC MDR-TB:
Child-friendly formulations (dispersible bedaquiline, dispersible delamanid)
Weight-based dosing per WHO paediatric MDR-TB guidance 2022
3-drug + bedaquiline / delamanid combinations

title: Syphilis — modern staging + treatment (incl Ghon/Doxy-PEP)
population: Resurging globally + SSA + Kenya — MSM disproportionately + congenital from untreated maternal. Major preventable cause of stillbirth + perinatal mortality.
presentation: Primary: painless chancre (3 weeks post-exposure; resolves 3-6 weeks even untreated). Secondary: rash (including palms + soles), condylomata lata, mucous patches, alopecia, constitutional. Latent (no symptoms): early (< 1 year) vs late. Tertiary (10-30 years): gumma, cardiovascular (aortitis), neurosyphilis. Congenital: stillbirth, prematurity, snuffles, hepatosplenomegaly, anaemia, skin lesions, late stigmata (Hutchinson teeth, saddle nose, saber tibia).
redFlags: Neurosyphilis (any stage — visual / hearing / cranial nerve / meningitis / dementia / tabes / general paresis)
Cardiovascular syphilis (aortitis, aortic aneurysm, aortic regurgitation)
Penicillin allergy (delicately re-examine — most are not truly allergic)
Pregnancy + syphilis (treat with benzathine penicillin only — NO alternative effective for fetus)
HIV co-infection (more aggressive, may need extended regimens)
diagnostics: NON-TREPONEMAL: RPR or VDRL — quantitative titre (used to monitor treatment response)
TREPONEMAL: TPPA or FTA-ABS — confirmatory (stays positive lifelong)
Modern (reverse algorithm): start with treponemal EIA/CLIA (cheaper screen), reflex to RPR/VDRL if positive, then TPPA if discordant
Dark-field microscopy of chancre (where available) — direct visualisation
PCR — emerging for direct detection from lesion
LP if NEUROSYPHILIS suspected (any neurological / ophthalmologic / otologic symptom; late latent unknown duration; HIV + ≥ 1:32 RPR; or treatment failure): CSF VDRL + cell count + protein
Echo + CXR for cardiovascular syphilis
HIV + STI screen ALL patients with syphilis (co-infection)
Pregnancy screen / pregnancy test
Maternal serology in any infant with possible congenital syphilis
management: PRIMARY + SECONDARY + EARLY LATENT (< 1 year duration):
BENZATHINE PENICILLIN 2.4 MU IM SINGLE DOSE
Alternative (true penicillin allergy + non-pregnant): doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM/IV daily × 10 days (alternative, less data)
Tetracycline (penicillin allergy)
Azithromycin 2 g PO single dose — RESISTANCE common (do NOT use except where no alternative)
LATE LATENT (> 1 year) + LATENT UNKNOWN DURATION + TERTIARY (except neurosyphilis):
BENZATHINE PENICILLIN 2.4 MU IM WEEKLY × 3 DOSES (week 0, 1, 2)
Alternative: doxycycline 100 mg BD × 28 days
NEUROSYPHILIS (including ocular + otic):
AQUEOUS PENICILLIN G 18-24 MU/day IV (3-4 MU q4h or continuous infusion) × 10-14 days
OR procaine penicillin 2.4 MU IM daily + probenecid 500 mg QDS × 10-14 days
Follow with benzathine penicillin × 3 weekly (some recommend)
Penicillin allergy: ceftriaxone 2 g IV/IM daily × 10-14 days
Repeat LP at 6 + 12 + 24 months — CSF normalisation
CARDIOVASCULAR SYPHILIS:
Same as late latent (3 weekly benzathine)
Cardiac specialist management of valvular / aortic disease
Surgical intervention as needed
PREGNANCY:
BENZATHINE PENICILLIN 2.4 MU IM — NO ALTERNATIVE EFFECTIVE FOR FETUS
If reported penicillin allergy — DESENSITISE (specialist + admission) — do not give alternative; fetal infection persists if mother not on penicillin
Treat at first opportunity in pregnancy
Re-screen at 28 weeks + delivery in high-risk
Infant: examine + dark-field if lesion + RPR (compared to maternal — > 4× higher = congenital probable); congenital infant treatment: aqueous penicillin G IV × 10 days
Triple elimination of MTCT (HIV + syphilis + hepatitis B) per WHO + Kenya
CONGENITAL SYPHILIS:
Aqueous benzylpenicillin 50,000 IU/kg IV q12h × 7 days then q8h × 3 days (10 days total) OR procaine penicillin G 50,000 IU/kg IM daily × 10 days
Stillbirth + early infancy mortality high in untreated
Late stigmata develop without treatment
JARISCH-HERXHEIMER REACTION:
Fever + myalgia + headache + tachycardia within 24h of starting antibiotic (especially primary + secondary, high spirochete load)
Treat supportively (paracetamol + fluids); does NOT require stopping antibiotic
Counsel patient before treatment
Severe in pregnancy — preterm labour risk; observe
FOLLOW-UP:
Clinical + RPR at 6 + 12 + 24 months (some at 3 months for early syphilis)
RPR 4-fold decline by 6 months = treatment response; if not — re-treat (consider neurosyphilis workup)
Long-term titre persistence (serofast) — not treatment failure if otherwise asymptomatic
HIV-positive — follow more closely (slower decline)
Partner notification + treatment (epidemiologic + recent)
Re-screen after treatment + counsel safer sex
PARTNER MANAGEMENT:
All sexual partners 90 days prior (primary), 6 months (secondary), 1 year (early latent) — examine + treat
Late latent + tertiary: partners examined + treated based on clinical / serology
Children of mothers with syphilis screened + treated
Anonymous partner notification services (PartnerSlate / Kenya partner notification)

EMERGING: DOXY-PEP for MSM/TGW at high STI risk — doxycycline 200 mg single dose within 72h after condomless sex (DoxyPEP trial 2023 — significant reduction in syphilis + chlamydia + gonorrhoea) — WHO + many guidelines integrating; antimicrobial resistance concerns balanced
PUBLIC HEALTH:
Notifiable in Kenya — TIBU + STI surveillance
Universal antenatal screening (Kenya Linda Mama)
MSM-focused services + sex worker programmes
Triple elimination MTCT (HIV + syphilis + HBV) per WHO + Kenya MoH
Access to free penicillin

title: Gonorrhoea — ceftriaxone resistance + dual therapy
population: Globally rising incidence; growing antimicrobial resistance — XDR-Neisseria gonorrhoeae a critical priority. Asymptomatic in 50%+ women + 10% men.
presentation: Men: urethritis (purulent discharge, dysuria, 2-7 days post-exposure). Women: cervicitis (often asymptomatic), purulent discharge, dyspareunia, intermenstrual bleeding. Pharyngeal + rectal often asymptomatic. Complications: PID + tubo-ovarian abscess + Fitz-Hugh-Curtis (women), epididymitis + epididymo-orchitis (men), disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI — arthritis-dermatitis), neonatal ophthalmia neonatorum (vertical transmission — vision loss), proctitis.
redFlags: DISSEMINATED GONOCOCCAL INFECTION — fever + migratory polyarthralgia / arthritis + pustular skin rash on extremities + tenosynovitis (admit + IV ceftriaxone)
Ophthalmia neonatorum — within 5 days of birth — purulent conjunctivitis + risk of corneal ulceration + vision loss — emergency IV ceftriaxone + topical + saline irrigation
Septic arthritis (gonococcal — joint aspirate + IV ceftriaxone)
Antimicrobial resistance — increasing cefixime + azithromycin resistance; ceftriaxone resistance emerging
Pregnancy with gonorrhoea (PMTCT + neonatal eye prophylaxis)
diagnostics: NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) — first-line for ANY exposed site; can be self-collected (vaginal swab, urine in men, rectal/pharyngeal swabs)
Culture — for antimicrobial susceptibility testing (essential — surveillance + treatment failures)
Gram stain urethral discharge (men) — gram-negative intracellular diplococci ≈ rapid presumptive diagnosis (sensitivity > 95% symptomatic men)
HIV + syphilis + chlamydia + HBV + HCV testing (co-infection)
Pregnancy test
Joint aspirate if DGI / septic arthritis
Eye discharge swab + Gram (ophthalmia neonatorum)
