UNCOMPLICATED ANOGENITAL + PHARYNGEAL:
CEFTRIAXONE 500 mg IM SINGLE DOSE (CDC 2021 — increased from 250 mg due to resistance trends)
WHO + Kenya: 250-500 mg IM single dose

Plus AZITHROMYCIN 1 g PO single dose (DUAL THERAPY) for chlamydia co-treatment (≥ 30% co-infected) + reduces NG resistance development (CDC 2021 — dual therapy specifically for empiric NG when treating before NAAT result)
CDC 2021 explicitly: ceftriaxone monotherapy adequate IF chlamydia ruled out via NAAT; otherwise dual
Cefixime 800 mg PO — alternative (less effective, less preferred)
Gentamicin 240 mg IM + azithromycin 2 g PO — for true cephalosporin allergy
Spectinomycin where available
TEST OF CURE:
PHARYNGEAL gonorrhoea — NAAT at 14 days (highest failure rate)
Rectal — repeat NAAT at 14 days
Anogenital — symptomatic patients with persistent symptoms
In all treatment failures — culture + susceptibility + report to surveillance
Asymptomatic patient with NAAT-confirmed — no routine test of cure for genital after adequate treatment
DISSEMINATED GONOCOCCAL INFECTION (DGI):
Admit + IV CEFTRIAXONE 1 g daily × 7-14 days
Joint drainage if septic arthritis with effusion
HIV testing
Treat sexual partners
OPHTHALMIA NEONATORUM:
Prevention: 1% tetracycline ophthalmic ointment or povidone-iodine 2.5% at birth (Kenya Linda Mama universal)
Treatment: CEFTRIAXONE 25-50 mg/kg IV/IM single dose (max 125 mg) + saline irrigation + topical erythromycin
Admit + ophthalmology
Treat mother + partner
PID — Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (separate condition):
Outpatient: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days + metronidazole 500 mg BD × 14 days
Inpatient (severe / pregnancy / TOA): IV ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole + drain TOA
EPIDIDYMITIS:
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + doxycycline 100 mg BD × 10 days (sexually active < 35)
PARTNER NOTIFICATION + TREATMENT:
All sexual partners 60 days prior to symptoms / diagnosis — examine + treat
EPT (Expedited Partner Therapy) — provide treatment for partner without seeing if cannot bring partner in (where legal — Kenya MOH framework)
Anonymous partner notification services
SYNDROMIC MANAGEMENT (Kenya MOH for STIs at primary care without lab):
Urethral discharge syndrome (men): ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days
Vaginal discharge syndrome: ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole + fluconazole
GUD (genital ulcer disease): benzathine penicillin + ciprofloxacin (chancroid) + acyclovir (HSV)
PREGNANCY:
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose + azithromycin 1 g (cover for chlamydia)
AVOID doxycycline + tetracyclines + fluoroquinolones
Test partner + treat
Universal antenatal STI screening (Kenya Linda Mama) + treat positive results
Neonatal eye prophylaxis universal
ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE PROGRAMME:
WHO Global Action Plan to Control NG AMR
Kenya NAMRS — NG surveillance sentinel sites
Treatment failures reported + isolate cultured + DST
XDR-NG (resistant to ceftriaxone + azithromycin + other) — limited options: gentamicin + zoliflodacin (NEW oral — Phase 3 — promising) + ertapenem + sitafloxacin
ABSTINENCE × 7 DAYS after treatment + until partner treated
COUNSEL re-infection risk + STI prevention + condom + dual protection
ROUTINE STI SCREENING for high-risk + PrEP candidates (every 3 months)
EMERGING: doxy-PEP for MSM/TGW (separate — significant gonorrhoea reduction)

title: Chlamydia + pelvic inflammatory disease — modern
population: Most common bacterial STI globally; asymptomatic 70%+ women, 50% men; major cause of preventable infertility + ectopic pregnancy + chronic pelvic pain (tubal damage from undetected/untreated PID).
presentation: Chlamydia: asymptomatic mostly. Symptomatic — cervicitis, urethritis (dysuria + discharge), proctitis (MSM), conjunctivitis (vertical or auto-inoculation), reactive arthritis. PID: lower abdominal pain + cervical motion tenderness + adnexal tenderness + fever + abnormal discharge; range mild to severe (TOA — tubo-ovarian abscess) + sequelae (chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy, infertility).

ALSO: pregnancy test (ectopic differential), urinalysis (UTI), gonorrhoea NAAT (co-infection), HIV + syphilis + hepatitis B

Endometrial biopsy if uncertain (endometritis confirmed)
Sexual history + partner contact

Pregnancy: AZITHROMYCIN 1 g PO single dose (doxy contraindicated)

RECTAL CHLAMYDIA: doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days (better than azithromycin)
LGV (lymphogranuloma venereum — chlamydia serovars L1-L3):
More invasive — proctitis, lymphadenopathy, buboes; common MSM + emerging Kenya
DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg BD × 21 DAYS (longer)
Drain fluctuant bubo

OUTPATIENT (mild-moderate, no abscess, tolerating PO, no pregnancy, reliable follow-up):
CEFTRIAXONE 500 mg IM single dose + DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg BD × 14 days + METRONIDAZOLE 500 mg BD × 14 days
Pregnancy: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + azithromycin 1 g + metronidazole (after 1st trimester)
Follow-up at 48-72h — if no improvement, escalate to inpatient
INPATIENT (severe pain / vomiting / sepsis / pregnancy / TOA / fails outpatient / immunocompromised / fertility concerns):
IV CEFTRIAXONE 2 g daily + DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg BD (or IV) + METRONIDAZOLE 500 mg q8h IV
Switch to PO when afebrile + improving (typically 24-48h)
Complete 14 days total
Drain TOA if > 4-6 cm or no improvement (ultrasound-guided percutaneous or laparoscopic)
Pain control + fluid resuscitation as needed
Remove IUD only if no improvement at 48-72h (NOT routinely — leave + treat)
Counsel sexual abstinence × 7 days after treatment + until partner treated
Future pregnancy + IUD discussion (PID elevates ectopic risk)
PARTNER NOTIFICATION + TREATMENT:
All sexual partners 60 days prior — examine + treat empirically (no need to await NAAT)
EPT (expedited partner therapy) — provide treatment for partner if cannot bring partner in (where legal)
Anonymous notification options
TEST OF CURE: NAAT 3 weeks post-treatment for pregnancy + 4 weeks post-treatment for rectal/pharyngeal (where high failure)
Re-screen at 3 months (high re-infection)
PREGNANCY:
Azithromycin 1 g single dose for chlamydia
Test partner + treat
Universal antenatal screening (Kenya Linda Mama)
Vertical transmission: conjunctivitis (5-12 days) + pneumonia (1-3 months); treat infant azithromycin
OPHTHALMIA NEONATORUM (chlamydia): more delayed than gonorrhoea; topical + systemic erythromycin or azithromycin (avoid topical alone)

Cervicitis / urethritis: ceftriaxone + doxycycline (or azithromycin)
Vaginal discharge: + metronidazole + fluconazole

Annual screening for sexually active < 25 women + high-risk populations
Routine antenatal screening (Kenya Linda Mama)
PrEP + Doxy-PEP for MSM/TGW (separate)

title: HPV + cervical cancer — prevention, screening, treatment
population: HPV is universal at some point; cervical cancer is 4th most common cancer in women + leading cause of cancer death in SSA — Kenya 5,236 deaths/year. Highly preventable + curable when caught early.
presentation: HPV: asymptomatic mostly; condyloma acuminata; cervical / vulvar / vaginal / anal / oropharyngeal / penile lesions. Cervical cancer: usually asymptomatic until advanced — irregular vaginal bleeding (post-coital, intermenstrual, post-menopausal), abnormal discharge; advanced — pain, fistula, leg oedema.
redFlags: Suspected cervical cancer — visible lesion / friable cervix / bleeding / urgent referral
Visible warts in child — consider abuse
diagnostics: PRIMARY HPV TESTING (modern preferred — WHO 2021 + many guidelines):
HPV DNA / mRNA test (cervical sample — self-collected vaginal swab acceptable per WHO 2021)
Detects high-risk HPV genotypes (16, 18, 31, 33, 35, etc.)
More sensitive than cytology
Allow longer screening intervals (5-10 years for HPV-negative)
Kenya MOH transitioning
CYTOLOGY (Pap smear) — historic standard:
Conventional Pap or liquid-based
ASCUS, LSIL, ASC-H, HSIL, AGC reporting
Required where HPV testing not available
VISUAL INSPECTION WITH ACETIC ACID (VIA) — for low-resource:
Cervical visualisation 1 minute after 5% acetic acid application; acetowhite lesion = positive
Same-day see + treat with cryotherapy or thermal ablation
WHO-recommended for LMIC with limited cytology capacity
Kenya MOH National Cervical Cancer Prevention + Control Strategy includes VIA
Single-visit screen + treat reduces loss to follow-up
COLPOSCOPY + BIOPSY: positive screen → colposcopy with directed biopsy
Endocervical curettage if no visible lesion or HSIL
STAGING (FIGO 2018): clinical + imaging-based
CT/MRI pelvis + CXR + cystoscopy + sigmoidoscopy
Locally advanced: PET-CT for staging
management: PRIMARY PREVENTION — HPV VACCINATION (TRANSFORMATIVE for SSA + Kenya):
WHO 2022 — ONE-DOSE schedule acceptable for ages 9-20 (single dose efficacy non-inferior; cost + supply optimisation)
Target: girls 9-14 (before sexual debut) — Kenya MoH introduced 2019, catch-up to age 14
Gardasil 9 (9-valent — HPV 6,11,16,18,31,33,45,52,58 — protects against ~ 90% cervical cancers)
Cervarix (2-valent — HPV 16,18)
Gardasil 4 (4-valent)
Boys also benefit (head + neck + anal cancer, condyloma); WHO recommends gender-neutral where possible
Immunocompromised: 3-dose schedule
SECONDARY PREVENTION — SCREENING:
WHO 2021 algorithm:
General population women 30-49 (extended to 25-65): primary HPV testing every 5-10 years
HIV+ women: start age 25 + screen every 3-5 years (more frequent + earlier — increased risk)
Kenya MoH: VIA + HPV testing where available; screen every 3 years; HIV+ every year
Single-visit screen + treat (HPV positive or VIA positive → cryotherapy / thermal ablation same visit)
TREATMENT BY DIAGNOSIS:
CIN 1 (LSIL): observation + repeat in 12 months (most regress)
CIN 2-3 (HSIL): excision (LLETZ / LEEP / cold knife conization) or thermal ablation / cryotherapy (for CIN 2/3 if accessible + small lesion)
Adenocarcinoma in situ: cold knife conization preferred
Pregnancy: defer treatment to postpartum unless invasive cancer
INVASIVE CERVICAL CANCER:
Stage IA1: cone biopsy or simple hysterectomy
Stage IA2-IIA: radical hysterectomy + lymphadenectomy OR chemoradiation
Stage IIB-IVA: chemoradiation (cisplatin + EBRT + brachytherapy) — GOLD STANDARD curative
Stage IVB / metastatic: palliative chemo / radio + checkpoint inhibitor (pembrolizumab — Keynote-826 + cisplatin-paclitaxel combination — practice-changing 2023)
Recurrent: salvage chemo + radio + pembrolizumab
PEDIATRIC / ADOLESCENT: HPV vaccination universal; visible warts in child — assess for abuse
PREGNANCY:
Continue HPV vaccination if pregnancy occurs mid-series — postpone remaining doses until postpartum
HSIL on pregnancy smear: defer to postpartum colposcopy + treatment
Invasive cancer: stage-dependent — may need to deliver early or modify treatment
HIV + CERVICAL CANCER:
Higher incidence + earlier age + more aggressive
ART for HIV (reduces progression)
Screen annually
Treat aggressively
Cervical cancer is AIDS-defining illness in HIV+ women
GENITAL WARTS (Condylomata acuminata):
Patient-applied: imiquimod 5% cream 3×/wk × 16 weeks, podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution / 0.15% cream
Clinic-administered: cryotherapy, TCA / BCA, excision, laser
Recurrence common
Counsel partner + STI screen + HIV test

90% of girls fully HPV vaccinated by 15
70% of women screened with high-performance test by 35 + 45
90% of women with pre-cancer treated + 90% of invasive cancer managed
Kenya National Cervical Cancer Prevention + Control Strategy 2022-2030
Multi-sector + community + religious leaders engagement
Self-sampling expansion (HPV vaginal swab) — addresses access + privacy

title: HSV genital + oral — antiviral suppression + counselling
population: Most common ulcerative STI globally. HSV-2 mostly genital; HSV-1 oral + increasingly genital. Major risk factor for HIV acquisition (3× increased risk). Vertical transmission causes neonatal HSV (rare but devastating).

Neonatal HSV (presenting 1-4 weeks of age — fever, lethargy, vesicles, seizures, sepsis, encephalitis — emergency IV acyclovir)
Severe primary HSV with sepsis / urinary retention / encephalitis

Severe: IV acyclovir 5-10 mg/kg q8h × 5-7 days then PO completion

Valacyclovir 500 mg BD × 3 days (short course)
Famciclovir 1 g BD × 1 day
Self-initiated 'rescue' if patient anticipates outbreaks

Valacyclovir 500 mg-1 g daily

HIV + HSV:
Higher dose suppression (valacyclovir 1 g BD)
Severe chronic ulceration — IV acyclovir then high-dose PO
Acyclovir-resistant HSV — foscarnet IV
Suppression reduces HIV acquisition + transmission
PREGNANCY:
Acyclovir safe in pregnancy (extensive evidence)
Valacyclovir safe

Recurrent HSV with lesions at delivery: C-SECTION (lower risk than primary but still)
Suppression with acyclovir 400 mg TID from 36 weeks reduces lesions at delivery + C-section need
Genital HSV history at delivery (no current lesions): vaginal delivery acceptable; consider suppression

CSF + serum HSV PCR + ALT + ophthalmology + neurology

ACYCLOVIR 10 mg/kg IV q8h × 14-21 days EMPIRICALLY for any suspected encephalitis (low threshold)
Adjust for confirmed pathogen
EEG + MRI + CSF PCR + LP

Atopic dermatitis + HSV — disseminated cutaneous + risk of sepsis + visceral involvement
Admit + IV acyclovir + skin care + antibiotic if secondary bacterial

Lifelong infection (cannot cure)

Asymptomatic shedding — can transmit without lesions
Disclosure to sexual partners — emotional + relational impact

Suppressive therapy + condoms reduce transmission > 90%
Trigger identification (UV, stress, illness, menses, immunosuppression)
Pregnancy planning + delivery considerations

Suppression for affected partner
Condoms
Counsel about risk + asymptomatic shedding

Suppression of affected partner
Avoid sexual activity during outbreak / prodrome

title: Trichomonas + bacterial vaginosis + vulvovaginal candidiasis — workup + treatment
population: Most common causes of vaginal discharge globally. Trichomonas — STI; BV + candida — endogenous (BV polymicrobial; candida fungal). All common SSA + reproductive-age women + pregnant women.
presentation: Trichomonas: yellow-green frothy malodorous discharge + pruritus + dysuria + dyspareunia + strawberry cervix (5-25%); often asymptomatic; men usually asymptomatic carriers. BV: thin grey-white homogeneous discharge + 'fishy' odour (worse after sex / menses) + pH > 4.5; not classically inflammatory. Candida: thick white curdy discharge + intense pruritus + erythema + dyspareunia + dysuria; pH normal.
redFlags: Pregnancy + symptomatic infection — preterm labour + PROM risk; treat
Recurrent (≥ 4/year) — investigate underlying immunosuppression / poor glycaemic / antibiotic exposure
Severe vulvovaginitis in diabetic + uncontrolled — investigate
Pelvic pain / cervical motion tenderness — rule out PID
Mucopurulent discharge with cervicitis — gonorrhoea / chlamydia (syndromic management Kenya)
Persistent / refractory — alternative diagnosis (cervical cancer, allergic reaction, atrophic vaginitis, foreign body)
diagnostics: TRICHOMONAS:
Wet mount microscopy — motile flagellated parasites (sensitivity 60-70%)
NAAT — gold standard (much more sensitive)
Rapid antigen test point-of-care (OSOM, Affirm)
BV (Amsel criteria — 3 of 4):
Thin homogeneous discharge
pH > 4.5 (vaginal pH paper)
Positive 'whiff' test (KOH amine smell)
Clue cells on wet mount (≥ 20% squamous epithelial cells)
OR Nugent score on Gram stain (≥ 7)
CANDIDA:
Wet mount + 10% KOH — hyphae + budding yeast
Culture if recurrent / refractory + species ID (Candida glabrata + krusei resistant to fluconazole)
pH normal (< 4.5)
ALWAYS: HIV + syphilis + STI testing (co-infections)
ALWAYS: GENITAL exam + cervix inspection (rule out PID, malignancy, foreign body)
management: TRICHOMONAS:
METRONIDAZOLE 2 g PO single dose (women)
OR metronidazole 500 mg BD × 7 days (CDC 2021 — preferred for women — superior efficacy)
MEN: metronidazole 2 g PO single dose
Tinidazole 2 g single dose alternative
AVOID alcohol 24h with metronidazole / 72h tinidazole (disulfiram reaction)
TREAT PARTNER (STI — sexual contact transmission)
Abstinence 7 days after treatment + until partner treated
Re-test 3 months (high re-infection)
BV:
METRONIDAZOLE 500 mg PO BD × 7 days — first-line
Metronidazole gel 0.75% intravaginally daily × 5 days
Clindamycin 2% cream intravaginally × 7 days (alternative)
Oral clindamycin 300 mg BD × 7 days
Tinidazole 2 g daily × 2 days
Recurrent: suppression metronidazole gel 2×/week × 4-6 months; oral metronidazole + vaginal boric acid; live cultures probiotic (Lactobacillus)
NOT primarily sexually transmitted but partner treatment in lesbian women may reduce recurrence; men generally not treated
Pregnancy: metronidazole 500 mg BD × 7 days (safe pregnancy) — reduces preterm + PROM risk in symptomatic + high-risk
CANDIDA:
UNCOMPLICATED (sporadic, mild-moderate, immunocompetent, non-pregnant, Candida albicans):
Topical: clotrimazole 1% cream × 7 days OR clotrimazole 500 mg vaginal tablet × 1 OR miconazole 200 mg vaginal × 3 days OR nystatin
Oral: FLUCONAZOLE 150 mg PO single dose
RECURRENT (≥ 4/year) — investigate cause:
Glycaemic control if DM, address antibiotic use, immunosuppression
Induction: fluconazole 150 mg q72h × 3 doses then suppression
Suppression: fluconazole 150 mg weekly × 6 months
COMPLICATED (severe / immunocompromised / pregnancy / non-albicans):
Non-albicans (C. glabrata + krusei) — fluconazole resistant; boric acid 600 mg intravaginally daily × 14 days OR amphotericin B intravaginal OR nystatin
Pregnancy: TOPICAL only (clotrimazole, miconazole) × 7 days; AVOID oral fluconazole (1st trimester teratogenic — cardiac defects per FDA 2016)
Severe: longer course (clotrimazole vaginal 7-14 d + topical hydrocortisone for inflamed vulva)
Counsel: probiotics modest; cotton underwear + avoid douching + reduce sugar; partner unaffected (not sexually transmitted)
Lifestyle: avoid douching + scented products; loose breathable underwear
MIXED / SYNDROMIC (Kenya MOH):
Vaginal discharge syndrome (cervicitis + vaginitis): ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + doxycycline / azithromycin + metronidazole + fluconazole
Treats: gonorrhoea + chlamydia + trichomonas + BV + candida empirically
RECURRENT / REFRACTORY:
Re-examine + culture
Investigate: undiagnosed STI, allergic vaginitis, atrophic vaginitis, retained tampon / foreign body, fistula, lichen planus / sclerosus, malignancy
Test for less common pathogens
Specialist referral (gynaecology + infectious diseases)
PARTNER MANAGEMENT:
Trichomonas: treat
BV: not routinely (men); same-sex female partners may benefit
Candida: not routinely
PREVENTION:
Safer sex + condoms
STI screening + treatment
Avoid douching + scented products + tight synthetic underwear
Probiotics evidence modest
HIV + STI testing + counselling
PEDIATRIC: vaginal discharge / vaginitis in prepubertal — consider sexual abuse

title: Acute appendicitis — Alvarado + AAST + antibiotic-first option
population: Lifetime risk 7-8%; peak 10-30 yr but any age. Most common surgical emergency globally.
presentation: Periumbilical pain migrating to RLQ + anorexia + nausea + vomiting + low-grade fever + RLQ tenderness (McBurney) + guarding + rebound + Rovsing's + psoas + obturator signs. Variable in elderly + children + pregnancy + immunocompromised.
redFlags: Pregnancy with appendicitis (perforation rate higher, fetal loss risk)
Atypical presentation in elderly / children / immunocompromised — delayed diagnosis
Carcinoid / mucocele in appendix at older patients
diagnostics: Alvarado score: Migration + Anorexia + Nausea + Tenderness RLQ + Rebound + Elevated temp + Leucocytosis + Shift to left
FBC (leucocytosis + neutrophil predominance), CRP
Pregnancy test all women of reproductive age
Urinalysis (rule out UTI, kidney stone)
ULTRASOUND first-line in children + pregnancy (no radiation): non-compressible blind-ending tubular structure > 6 mm, target sign, mural thickening, free fluid
CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast — most accurate adults (sensitivity > 95%)
MRI in pregnancy if US equivocal
AAST appendicitis grading 1-5 (uncomplicated → perforated)
management: RESUSCITATION:
IV fluids, NPO, analgesia (does NOT mask diagnosis — Pain Management Trial)
Anti-emetic
Blood for FBC + U&E + crossmatch
ANTIBIOTICS:
Pre-op single dose (uncomplicated) or 4-7 days (complicated)
Pip-tazo 4.5 g q8h or ceftriaxone 2 g + metronidazole 500 mg q8h
Allergy: levofloxacin + metronidazole
SURGICAL (gold standard):
LAPAROSCOPIC APPENDICECTOMY — preferred (shorter recovery, less infection, better cosmesis)
Open via McBurney incision if not laparoscopy
Within 24h (longer delay increases perforation)
Send specimen to histology (rule out carcinoid, lymphoma)
COMPLICATED (perforation / abscess / phlegmon):
IV antibiotics × 4-7 days
CT-guided percutaneous drainage for abscess
Interval appendicectomy 6-12 weeks (controversial — many manage conservatively if no recurrence)
Surgical exploration if peritonitis / failure of conservative
ANTIBIOTIC-FIRST APPROACH (selected uncomplicated):
Adult uncomplicated appendicitis — CODA trial 2020 — antibiotic-first non-inferior at 90 days for major outcomes; ~ 30% appendicectomy by 90 days
Patient preference + shared decision
Not for perforated / abscess / appendicolith
PREGNANCY:
Appendicitis remains the most common surgical condition
US first-line, MRI if uncertain (avoid CT in 1st trimester)
Appendicectomy as needed — laparoscopic safe in pregnancy (2nd trimester ideal)
Antibiotic + early intervention
PAEDIATRIC:
Higher perforation rate (delayed presentation)
US first-line
Conservative + interval appendicectomy for abscess
Antibiotic-only approach increasingly used in selected children (APPY trial)
ELDERLY:
Atypical presentation
Higher perforation + mortality
Lower threshold for imaging + surgery
Investigate for underlying malignancy (occult colorectal cancer)
DISCHARGE + RECOVERY:
Laparoscopic — discharge often day 1-2
Open — 3-5 days
Follow-up histology
Wound care + return to normal activity
Complications: SSI (5%), ileus, intra-abdominal abscess, hernia, infertility (rare)

references.label: WSES Jerusalem Guidelines for Acute Appendicitis 2020 + 2024 update
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Acute cholecystitis — Tokyo Guidelines 18 + early lap-chole
population: Most have gallstones; 10-20% of adults have gallstones; complications include cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis, gallstone ileus.
presentation: RUQ pain (constant > 6h post-meal), fever, Murphy's sign positive, leucocytosis. Severity TG18 (Tokyo Guidelines): Grade I mild, Grade II moderate (leucocytosis + tenderness + symptoms duration), Grade III severe (organ dysfunction).
redFlags: Severe (Grade III) — sepsis / organ dysfunction — ICU + drainage + antibiotics
Emphysematous cholecystitis (gas in wall — high mortality, especially diabetics)
Ascending cholangitis (Charcot triad — fever + jaundice + RUQ pain; Reynolds pentad adds hypotension + altered mental state)
diagnostics: FBC + CRP + LFT (ALT/AST/ALP + bilirubin)
Amylase/lipase (rule out pancreatitis)
U&E + glucose + coag + blood culture if septic
ULTRASOUND first-line: gallbladder wall > 4 mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy positive, gallstones, dilated CBD (suggests choledocholithiasis)
HIDA scan — if US equivocal (non-visualisation of gallbladder = diagnostic for cystic duct obstruction)
CT/MRI for complications / unclear
MRCP if suspected choledocholithiasis or non-diagnostic US
ERCP for both diagnosis + treatment of CBD stones
management: TG18 ALGORITHM:
GRADE I (mild):
Hospital admission, IV fluids, NPO, analgesia
Antibiotics (cefuroxime + metronidazole or pip-tazo)
EARLY LAPAROSCOPIC CHOLECYSTECTOMY (within 72h — recommended over delayed; reduces complications + cost)
GRADE II (moderate):
Same + early lap-chole; if not improving with antibiotics → percutaneous gallbladder drainage (cholecystostomy) bridge
Interval cholecystectomy 6 weeks later if too unwell initially
GRADE III (severe — organ dysfunction):
ICU + sepsis bundle + IV antibiotics + organ support
PERCUTANEOUS CHOLECYSTOSTOMY (radiologically guided) — initial drainage; defer surgery until stable
Cholecystectomy when patient optimised
ANTIBIOTIC CHOICE (Tokyo 18):
Community-acquired mild-moderate: ceftriaxone + metronidazole; or cefuroxime + metronidazole
Severe / hospital-acquired / immunocompromised: piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem ± vancomycin
Duration: 4-7 days post-source control (drainage / surgery); longer if persistent bacteraemia
EARLY vs DELAYED CHOLECYSTECTOMY:
Multiple RCTs + meta-analyses — EARLY (within 72h-1 week of symptom onset) preferred over delayed (6 weeks)
Shorter total hospitalisation, similar conversion rates, fewer complications
Patient counselling + shared decision
CHOLEDOCHOLITHIASIS (CBD stones):
ERCP + sphincterotomy + stone extraction PRE-cholecystectomy (when ALP/bilirubin raised or CBD dilated)
Some prefer intraoperative cholangiogram + laparoscopic CBD exploration if available
ACUTE CHOLANGITIS:
IV antibiotics IMMEDIATELY
ERCP biliary drainage WITHIN 24h (urgent — sepsis source)
ICU if severe
Tokyo 18 severity grading + management
GALLSTONE PANCREATITIS:
Standard pancreatitis management (separate)
ERCP within 24-48h if cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction
SAME-admission cholecystectomy for mild (PONCHO trial)
EMPHYSEMATOUS CHOLECYSTITIS (especially diabetics):
Emergency cholecystectomy (high mortality)
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
ICU support
ACALCULOUS CHOLECYSTITIS (critically ill + no stones):
Drainage (cholecystostomy) — often without cholecystectomy
Treat underlying cause
PAEDIATRIC: less common; biliary atresia consideration in infants
PREGNANCY:
Cholecystectomy as needed — laparoscopic safe (2nd trimester ideal)
Antibiotics + supportive
Avoid CT (US, MRI/MRCP if needed)
POST-OPERATIVE: SSI prevention, mobilisation, return to normal activity

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Intestinal obstruction — small + large bowel
population: Adults — adhesions (post-surgical) account for ~ 60% of SBO; hernias + malignancy; volvulus important SSA (especially sigmoid). Paediatric — intussusception, malrotation, congenital.
presentation: Pain (colicky proximal SBO, more constant distal/large bowel), distension, vomiting (early proximal, faeculent distal), absolute constipation (LBO + complete SBO), high-pitched bowel sounds (early) → silent (late, ischaemia). Signs of strangulation: continuous severe pain + tachycardia + fever + raised lactate + leucocytosis + peritoneal signs.
redFlags: STRANGULATION / ISCHAEMIA — emergency surgery (lactate raised, peritonism, continuous pain, fever, leucocytosis)
Closed-loop obstruction (volvulus, internal hernia, complete LBO with competent ileocaecal valve — at risk of perforation, ischaemia)
Paediatric intussusception (currant jelly stool + sausage mass + colicky)
diagnostics: Vital signs + abdomen + hernia orifices + DRE + previous surgical scars
FBC + U&E (dehydration + AKI) + glucose + lactate (raised = ischaemia) + amylase (rule out pancreatitis)
VBG / ABG (metabolic acidosis = ischaemia)
ERECT CHEST X-RAY (subdiaphragmatic gas = perforation)
SUPINE + ERECT abdominal X-RAY (dilated bowel + air-fluid levels — but limited)
CT ABDOMEN/PELVIS WITH CONTRAST — most accurate (transition point, cause, ischaemia features)
Gastrograffin study — both diagnostic + therapeutic for adhesive SBO (passage to colon within 24h = resolution)
Group + crossmatch if surgery likely
management: INITIAL RESUSCITATION (regardless of cause):
IV fluids (large volume — third space + GI losses) — Hartmann/PlasmaLyte
NPO + NG tube on free drainage (decompression)
Urinary catheter (monitor output)
IV analgesia
Anti-emetic
Correct electrolytes (K+, Na+)
Pressure care + VTE prophylaxis
Early surgical consultation
ADHESIVE SBO (most common SBO — post-surgical):
CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT trial (24-48-72h) if no strangulation features:
NG decompression + IV fluids + correct electrolytes
Gastrograffin oral water-soluble contrast — diagnostic + therapeutic (passage suggests resolution; failure suggests need for surgery)
Resolution in 60-70%
Surgery if: failure of conservative > 72h, complete obstruction, strangulation signs, peritonitis
Laparoscopic adhesiolysis where feasible
HERNIA STRANGULATION:
Attempt manual reduction WITH ANALGESIA + sedation (don't force — strangulated ischaemic bowel cannot be reduced; risk of returning dead bowel)
If reduced — observe + elective repair
If irreducible / strangulated — EMERGENCY SURGERY (hernia repair + bowel resection if necrotic)
LARGE BOWEL OBSTRUCTION:
Most commonly malignancy (60-70%) — particularly left-sided colon cancer
Sigmoid volvulus — endoscopic decompression first attempt; elective sigmoidectomy after
Caecal volvulus — surgery (caecopexy or right hemicolectomy)
Diverticular stricture
Closed-loop obstruction = surgical emergency
CT-confirmed malignant LBO with imminent perforation:
Surgical resection (Hartmann's or anastomosis with stoma)
Self-expanding metal stent (SEMS) — bridge to surgery or palliative
MALIGNANT BOWEL OBSTRUCTION (advanced cancer, peritoneal carcinomatosis):
Surgical bypass / stoma if feasible
Stent for selected
Conservative: NG tube, antiemetic (haloperidol / cyclizine), steroid (dexamethasone), octreotide (reduces secretions)
Palliative care input
VOLVULUS (Sigmoid most common SSA):
Sigmoid — endoscopic detorsion (rigid sigmoidoscope + flatus tube) — successful 60-90%; high recurrence — elective sigmoidectomy
Caecal — surgical (caecopexy or right hemicolectomy)
Mesenteric volvulus (especially infants/children — malrotation) — emergency surgery
PAEDIATRIC:
Intussusception (6 mo - 3 yr): air or hydrostatic enema reduction (US-guided); surgery if fails or peritonism
Malrotation + volvulus — surgical emergency (Ladd's procedure)
Pyloric stenosis — surgical (Ramstedt's)
Hirschsprung's disease — surgical
Hernia (umbilical, inguinal) — incarcerated/strangulated emergency
MECHANICAL vs FUNCTIONAL (ileus):
Ileus — post-op, electrolytes (hypoK), drugs (opioid, anticholinergic), sepsis, intra-abdominal pathology
Treat cause + supportive (NG, fluid, electrolyte correction, mobilisation, prokinetic only if confirmed ileus)
Pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's) — neostigmine 2-2.5 mg IV under cardiac monitoring for refractory colonic dilatation > 10 cm
EARLY MOBILISATION + ENHANCED RECOVERY post-surgery
DISCHARGE + RECOVERY:
Hernia repair education
Adhesive prevention (avoidance of unnecessary surgery; intraoperative anti-adhesion barriers)
Cancer surveillance / oncology + radiotherapy / chemo if malignant
Bowel function review + dietary advice

title: Acute diverticulitis — Hinchey + modern management
population: Common — 50% of adults > 60 have diverticulosis; 10-25% develop diverticulitis. Sigmoid most common Western; right-sided more common Asian + young.
presentation: LLQ pain, fever, leucocytosis, change in bowel habit. Right-sided (Asian / young) mimics appendicitis. Complicated: abscess, perforation, peritonitis, fistula (colovesical, colovaginal, coloenteric), obstruction, stricture, bleeding (separate but related diverticular bleed).
redFlags: Generalised peritonitis (Hinchey III / IV) — emergency surgery
Recurrent diverticulitis (4+ episodes) — consider elective sigmoidectomy
Immunocompromised + diverticulitis — admit, lower threshold for surgery
diagnostics: Clinical: LLQ pain (Asian patients consider right-sided), fever, leucocytosis
FBC + CRP + U&E + lactate
Urinalysis (rule out UTI + fistula investigation)
Pregnancy test
CT ABDOMEN/PELVIS WITH IV + ORAL CONTRAST — gold standard
Hinchey classification: 0 (clinical only) → I (pericolic abscess < 4 cm) → II (pelvic/distant abscess) → III (purulent peritonitis) → IV (faeculent peritonitis)
Identifies abscess, perforation, fistula, stricture
AVOID barium studies in acute (risk of perforation)
After resolution: colonoscopy at 6-8 weeks to exclude malignancy (especially first episode, atypical features)
management: UNCOMPLICATED ACUTE DIVERTICULITIS (CT Hinchey 0 or Ia mild):
ANTIBIOTICS NOT routine in uncomplicated outpatient — recent guideline shift (DIABOLO + AVOD trials):
Selected mild outpatient: no antibiotics + clear fluids + simple analgesia + follow-up
Risk-stratify: immunocompromised, severe pain, leucocytosis, comorbidity, pregnancy, social factors — give antibiotics
Antibiotic (if given): co-amoxiclav 625 mg TDS × 7 days; ciprofloxacin + metronidazole alternative
Clear fluids → low-residue → normal diet as tolerated
Outpatient if mild + tolerating oral + good social support + no immunocompromise
COMPLICATED ACUTE DIVERTICULITIS:
Admit + IV fluids + NPO + IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole, or pip-tazo)
Hinchey I-II (abscess < 4 cm or > 4 cm with image-guided drainage option):
CT-GUIDED PERCUTANEOUS DRAINAGE for abscess > 4 cm
Continue antibiotics until clinical resolution
Elective sigmoidectomy after 6-8 weeks (timing controversial — many guideline now wait + manage future episodes)
Hinchey III (purulent peritonitis):
Surgery — debate between Hartmann's procedure (resection + end colostomy) vs primary anastomosis with diverting loop ileostomy (LADIES trial)
Laparoscopic peritoneal lavage selected (LADIES + DILALA + SCANDIV — Lavage trials — outcomes mixed; reserve for fit selected)
Sigmoidectomy if perforated stable
Hinchey IV (faeculent peritonitis):
HARTMANN'S PROCEDURE — resection + end colostomy + closed rectal stump
Reverse stoma at 3-6 months if able + appropriate
Damage control surgery if unstable
POST-ACUTE FOLLOW-UP:
Colonoscopy 6-8 weeks (rule out underlying CRC — risk 1-2% post-diverticulitis)
Manage risk factors: smoking + obesity + sedentary
Diet: high-fibre, hydration, exercise; avoid red meat excess
Probiotic + mesalazine — limited evidence; not routinely
NSAID + steroid + opioid + immunosuppressive — increase recurrence risk + complications
ELECTIVE SIGMOIDECTOMY:

Recurrent (≥ 4 episodes — controversial), complicated history (fistula, stenosis, persistent symptoms), young (< 50 — historically lower threshold; current less aggressive), immunocompromised (lower threshold)
Laparoscopic preferred
FISTULA:
Most colovesical (men) — TURB-like haematuria + pneumaturia + recurrent UTI; CT + cystoscopy
Elective surgery (resection + closure) when inflammation settled
DIVERTICULAR BLEEDING (separate but related):
Painless brisk LGI bleed; usually self-limits
Resuscitate + colonoscopy + CT angio for localisation + endoscopic / IR embolisation / surgery
PREVENTION (primary + secondary):
High-fibre diet (25-35 g/day)
Avoid red + processed meat excess
Hydration
Exercise + weight management
Smoking cessation
Avoid NSAIDs + steroids where possible
Old advice to avoid nuts/seeds/popcorn — NOT supported

LADIES + DILALA + SCANDIV — laparoscopic lavage for Hinchey III
Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Adult major trauma — ATLS + damage control + ABC
population: Adults with major trauma — RTA, falls, penetrating, blunt, blast. SSA: high road traffic mortality; boda-boda injuries common Kenya. Trauma is leading cause of death age 1-44.
presentation: Multiple injury patterns — head, chest, abdomen, pelvis, limbs, spine. Polytrauma (≥ 2 systems injured). Mechanism + physiology guide management.
redFlags: Cardiac arrest (post-traumatic — manage cause: hypovolaemia, tension PTX, tamponade, hypoxia; thoracotomy for selected penetrating)
Airway compromise (head injury, facial trauma, burns, inhalation)
diagnostics: Primary survey ABCDE (with c-spine + catastrophic haemorrhage)
Secondary survey head-to-toe + AMPLE history
Trauma team activation per local criteria
FAST scan (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma) bedside — pericardial, perihepatic, perisplenic, pelvic
eFAST extended — adds bilateral pneumothorax
FBC + U&E + LFT + glucose + group + crossmatch (large volume) + INR + APTT + fibrinogen + lactate + base excess
ABG / VBG
CT 'pan-scan' (head + neck + chest + abdomen + pelvis) for haemodynamically stable patient with multiple system injury
X-rays: chest, pelvis (if not CT), c-spine (clinical clearance or imaging per NEXUS/Canadian)
ECG + troponin if blunt chest trauma
Trauma scoring: GCS + Revised Trauma Score + ISS
management: PRE-HOSPITAL:
Scene safety + paramedic activation
Catastrophic haemorrhage: tourniquet (windlass-type), pressure dressings, pelvic binder
Airway with c-spine control (jaw thrust + cervical collar)
Breathing — high-flow O2, treat tension PTX (needle decompression / finger thoracostomy)
Circulation — IV access × 2, controlled hypotension if haemorrhage (SBP 80-90), TXA 1 g IV within 3h
Disability — GCS + pupils + glucose
Exposure + hypothermia prevention
Transport to trauma centre with definitive care capability
RECEIVING TEAM:
Pre-arrival information from ambulance
Activate trauma team (anaesthetist + general surgeon + orthopaedic + emergency + radiology + nursing + blood bank)
Massive transfusion protocol pre-activated if expected
PRIMARY SURVEY (cABCDE):
c (catastrophic haemorrhage):
Tourniquet + direct pressure + pelvic binder + haemostatic gauze
A (airway + c-spine):
Look + listen + feel
Open with jaw thrust (avoid head tilt)
Maintain in-line cervical stabilisation
OPA / NPA if needed
Definitive airway if GCS ≤ 8, facial / burn / inhalation, hypoxia despite oxygen — RSI with ketamine (haemodynamic stable in shock) + rocuronium
Video laryngoscope preferred (especially trauma)
Surgical cricothyroidotomy if 'can't intubate, can't oxygenate'
B (breathing):
Look, listen, palpate, percuss, auscultate
High-flow O2 15 L/min
Tension PTX — needle decompression (2nd ICS MCL or 4th-5th ICS AAL) → chest drain (28-32 Fr 5th ICS MAL)
Haemothorax — chest drain; > 1500 ml or > 200 ml/h = thoracotomy
Open PTX — 3-sided dressing → chest drain
Flail chest — analgesia (opioid + regional + paravertebral block) + ventilation if compromise
Cardiac contusion — ECG + troponin + echo
Diaphragmatic rupture
C (circulation):
Pulse + BP + cap refill + skin colour + JVP
IV × 2 large-bore (16G+) — peripheral preferred; IO if failed 90 sec; central if needed
CONTROLLED HYPOTENSION until haemorrhage controlled (SBP 80-90 / MAP 65 in non-head injury; SBP > 110 if head injury)
Crystalloid 1-2 L cautious (avoid over-resuscitation + dilutional coagulopathy)
EARLY BLOOD — O-negative emergency → crossmatched packed cells
MASSIVE TRANSFUSION PROTOCOL: 1:1:1 RBC:FFP:platelets + TXA + calcium + warmth
TXA 1 g IV within 3h then 1 g over 8h (CRASH-2 + CRASH-3 for TBI)
Identify haemorrhage source: external + chest + abdomen + retroperitoneum/pelvis + long bones
Pelvic binder at greater trochanters (NOT spring pelvis); angiographic embolisation
Long bone fractures — splint + reduce
REBOA (resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of aorta) — selected centres for severe non-compressible haemorrhage
D (disability):
GCS + pupils + glucose (treat if low) + neurological exam
Head injury — maintain MAP > 80 + SpO2 > 94% + glucose 7.8-10 + head-up 30°
Raised ICP: hypertonic saline 3% 5 ml/kg or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg
Hypoxia + hypotension WORSE for head injury than uncontrolled bleeding (DAMAGE-CONTROL focus reduces avoidable secondary brain injury)
E (exposure):
Log roll + back + perineum + DRE
Prevent hypothermia (warm room + blankets + warm fluids + warmer)
Trauma triad of death: hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy (treat all simultaneously)
SECONDARY SURVEY:
AMPLE history
Head-to-toe examination + log roll + DRE + perineum + ENT + ophth + odontology
Identify all injuries — 'tertiary survey' on ward review (10-15% injuries missed on initial survey)
Document carefully (forensic + medico-legal)
DAMAGE CONTROL RESUSCITATION + SURGERY:
Permissive hypotension + balanced transfusion (1:1:1) + TXA + warm + early haemorrhage control
Damage control surgery: stop bleed + control contamination + return for definitive after physiology restored (ICU re-warming + correction + 24-48h)
Indications: lactate > 5, pH < 7.2, T < 35, INR > 1.5, BE < -8, massive transfusion > 10 units in 6h
SPECIFIC INJURIES:
Head injury: CT head (per NICE / PECARN / Canadian), neurosurgical referral, mannitol/hypertonic for raised ICP, antibiotic for open / penetrating, antiepileptic for seizure or high-risk
Spinal cord: collar + log roll + maintain MAP > 85 (perfusion); methylprednisolone NOT routinely (NASCIS evidence weak); surgical decompression
Chest: as above
Abdominal: FAST + CT; haemodynamically unstable + positive FAST = laparotomy; stable + positive = CT then management
Pelvic: binder + angio + ortho surgery (pelvic ring fixation)
Solid organ (liver, spleen): non-operative management for stable + AAST low-grade; surgery + angio for high-grade + unstable
Hollow viscus / mesenteric: laparotomy
Limb: tourniquet + reduce + splint + open fracture management (IV antibiotic + tetanus + irrigation + debridement < 6h)
Open fracture Gustilo-Anderson: IV cefazolin + gentamicin + irrigation + debridement within 6h + definitive within 24h
Compartment syndrome — fasciotomy
Burns — separate
Crush injury / rhabdomyolysis — IV fluids + alkaline diuresis + dialysis if severe AKI
POST-RESUSCITATION:
ICU admission for most major trauma
Continued monitoring + organ support
Mental health + family + chaplaincy
Disability + functional recovery focus
PREVENTION (population):
Road safety — helmets, seatbelts, speed limits, enforcement (Kenya emergency medical care strategy)
Workplace safety
Violence prevention
Suicide prevention
WHO Decade of Action for Road Safety 2021-2030

title: Chemical eye injury — irrigation + emergency
population: Workplace + domestic accidents; deliberate assault. SSA: alkali (lime, ammonia, lye, cement, drain cleaner) more devastating than acid (most domestic + commercial industrial); chemical attacks tragically increasing.
presentation: Pain + tearing + blurred vision + redness + chemosis + conjunctival blanching (severe — limbal ischaemia indicates worse prognosis). Roper-Hall grading I-IV.
redFlags: Alkali burn (worse — penetrates deeper) — more emergent than acid
Limbal ischaemia > 1/3 (Roper-Hall III-IV) — poor prognosis + may need stem cell transplant
Periocular skin chemical burns + deep airway burns
diagnostics: IRRIGATE FIRST — do NOT delay for examination or workup
After irrigation: visual acuity, slit lamp, fluorescein (epithelial defect), tonometry (avoid in perforation suspicion)
pH testing after irrigation (continue irrigation until pH 7.0-7.4)
Identify causative chemical (bring container / MSDS)
Roper-Hall grading: I (good prog) → IV (poor)
Photograph for medico-legal documentation
management: IMMEDIATE — IRRIGATE WITHIN SECONDS-MINUTES (every second counts):
1. Remove any solid chemical particles (cement powder, lime) — manually with cotton swab or sterile saline
2. Topical anaesthetic (proparacaine / tetracaine) — facilitates cooperation
3. IRRIGATE COPIOUSLY:
Sterile saline / Ringer's lactate / sterile water — ideal
ANY clean water if at scene — DO NOT DELAY for sterile (especially in field)
Morgan lens / IV tubing into lower fornix
Hold eyelids open + rotate eye to expose all surfaces (irrigate sub-tarsally — evert upper lid + sweep fornix)
MINIMUM 30 MINUTES + check pH (test strip from tear film)
Continue until pH 7.0-7.4 + stable
Alkali — irrigate LONGER (often hours; alkali penetrates deeper + continues to damage)
Total irrigation 1-3 L typical; severe alkali may need 5-10 L
4. Remove foreign body particles after irrigation if remaining
5. Continue irrigation while transferring
POST-IRRIGATION ASSESSMENT + TREATMENT:
Slit lamp + fluorescein
Tonometry (alkali can cause raised IOP)
ANTIBIOTIC topical (chloramphenicol ointment or moxifloxacin drops) — prophylactic
CYCLOPLEGIC (atropine 1% or cyclopentolate 1%) — comfort + reduce uveitis + prevent posterior synechiae
TOPICAL STEROID (prednisolone acetate 1%) — first week to reduce inflammation; AVOID after week 1 (impairs healing) unless ophthalmology specialist
Lubricants — preservative-free
Vitamin C (oral + topical) — collagen synthesis + anti-oxidant
Doxycycline 100 mg BD — MMP inhibitor + anti-inflammatory + slows collagen breakdown (anti-collagenolytic action)
Citrate 10% drops — chelates calcium, reduces alkali-induced damage
Tetanus prophylaxis
Analgesia
Bandage contact lens for healing epithelial defect (specialist)
Symblepharon ring + careful eyelid hygiene
Amniotic membrane transplantation for severe Roper-Hall III-IV (limbal stem cell support + healing)
Limbal stem cell transplantation for total limbal ischaemia
OPHTHALMOLOGY EMERGENCY REFERRAL — all chemical injuries
FOLLOW-UP:
Daily early in severe cases
Watch for: corneal perforation, secondary glaucoma, cataract, symblepharon, dry eye, neurotrophic ulcer, infection
Long-term: corneal transplant for severe scarring (when stable + lid issues addressed); keratoprosthesis (Boston KPro) for end-stage limbal failure
Psychological + occupational support
PROGNOSIS:
Acid: epithelium denatures + sloughs but underlying tissue protected = better
Alkali: penetrates deeper + saponifies cell membranes = worse
Roper-Hall I: good (no scarring); II: scarring + opacity; III: limbal stem cell deficiency, corneal vascularisation; IV: severe ischaemia + perforation
Best predictor of outcome: extent of limbal ischaemia at presentation
PREVENTION (workplace + community):
Eye protection (PPE) — chemical splash goggles
Emergency eye wash stations + 30+ minute capacity
Workplace safety + MSDS access + training
Domestic safe storage of cleaning products
Pesticide safety (especially Kenya agricultural)
Cement workers + agricultural workers + welders + chemical industry — targeted prevention
Public education — irrigate IMMEDIATELY + come to hospital
Kenya National Eye Health Plan

title: Epistaxis — anterior + posterior management
population: Bimodal: children 2-10 + adults > 50; men > women; dry climate + winter higher. Spontaneous + traumatic + medication-related (anticoagulant + antiplatelet + nasal steroid + cocaine). Posterior nosebleeds more severe + need specialist.
presentation: Anterior (90% — Little's area / Kiesselbach's plexus): easily controlled, visible bleeding from anterior septum. Posterior (10% — sphenopalatine artery branch): more severe, bilateral, posterior pharyngeal blood, difficult to visualise, often older patients on anticoagulant.
redFlags: Posterior epistaxis — emergency, need specialist + posterior packing/Foley catheter
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT — Osler-Weber-Rendu — recurrent epistaxis + telangiectasias + AV malformations)
Suspected nasopharyngeal mass / tumour (especially Asian young adult — NPC)
Septal haematoma (post-trauma — drain urgently to prevent septal necrosis + saddle nose)
diagnostics: Vital signs + assess severity + airway + breathing
FBC + coagulation if anticoagulation / severe / bleeding disorder suspected
BP + ECG if HTN suspected as cause
Group + crossmatch if heavy / haemodynamic instability
If suspected mass — nasal endoscopy + imaging (CT)
INR if on warfarin; DOAC levels (apixaban / rivaroxaban) not routine
Identify cause: trauma, dry air, infection (sinusitis), HTN, anticoagulant, drug (cocaine), tumour, HHT, bleeding disorder
management: INITIAL RESUSCITATION (severe / posterior):
Airway protection — suction blood, lateral position to avoid aspiration
IV access + fluids if hypovolaemic
Group + crossmatch + transfuse if needed
Reverse anticoagulation if indicated (vitamin K + 4F-PCC for warfarin; idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet for Xa inhibitors; FFP if PCC unavailable)
FIRST AID (anterior epistaxis):
Sit patient up, lean FORWARD (NOT back — avoid swallowing blood + nausea + aspiration)
Pinch CARTILAGINOUS part of nose (not bony bridge) firmly × 15-20 minutes continuous (do NOT let go to check)
Ice pack on bridge of nose
Spit out blood (do not swallow)
If not stopped — proceed
PROGRESSIVE MEDICAL MANAGEMENT:
1. Topical vasoconstrictor + anaesthetic:
Cophenylcaine (lidocaine + phenylephrine) spray
Oxymetazoline / xylometazoline (Otrivin) — 2-3 sprays each nostril
2. Reapply pressure × 10 min
3. If anterior bleeding identified — CAUTERY:
Topical silver nitrate to bleeding point (only ONE side — bilateral cautery risks septal perforation)
Electrocautery if severe
4. Anterior nasal PACKING if cautery fails / posterior bleed visible:
Rapid Rhino / Merocel (foam-based with hydrocolloid)
Vaseline gauze ribbon (older)
Floseal (haemostatic agent)
Insert + leave 24-48 hours + antibiotic cover (toxic shock syndrome risk — phenoxymethylpenicillin or cephalexin × duration of packing)
5. POSTERIOR PACKING (severe / posterior bleed):
FOLEY CATHETER (16-18 Fr) — through nostril, balloon inflated in nasopharynx, then anterior packing
Specialist double-balloon catheters
ADMIT — risk of hypoxia + vasovagal + arrhythmia from posterior pack
ECG monitoring + O2 + analgesia + antibiotic
6. EMBOLISATION:
Interventional radiology — sphenopalatine + facial artery embolisation
Selected — failure of conservative or recurrent
Risk of facial pain + skin necrosis + stroke
7. SURGICAL LIGATION:
Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation (most effective for posterior)
Anterior + posterior ethmoidal artery ligation
External carotid artery ligation — historical, rarely used
ANTICOAGULATION + ANTIPLATELET:
Continue if possible (CV benefit outweighs)
Reverse only if life-threatening + after consultation
DOAC short half-life — may temporarily hold
Restart after bleeding controlled
RECURRENT EPISTAXIS:
Workup for HHT, bleeding disorder, hypertension, tumour
ENT clinic referral
Saline + emollient (nasal saline + Naseptin / Bactroban + petrolatum) preventive
Humidifier
Avoid nose-picking + nose-blowing
Cautery / coblation of bleeding sites
HHT: tranexamic acid (oral + topical), nasal embolisation, bevacizumab (anti-VEGF — emerging for severe HHT)
PAEDIATRIC:
Most due to digital trauma (nose-picking) + dry air
First aid + prevention (saline + petrolatum)
Avoid cautery routinely
Recurrent — ENT + bleeding disorder workup
SEPTAL HAEMATOMA (after trauma):
Drain urgently (incision + drainage) — prevents septal cartilage necrosis + saddle-nose deformity
Antibiotic + ENT follow-up
SAFETY-NET:
Return immediately if heavy bleeding / unable to control
Apply first aid + come to hospital
Avoid hot drinks, alcohol, spicy food, nose-blowing for 24h after

title: Testicular torsion — urological emergency
population: Adolescents 12-18 most common (bell-clapper deformity); also neonates (extravaginal). 1 in 4000 men < 25. Time-critical — viability declines after 6 hours, < 50% salvage at 12 hours, near 0% at 24 hours.
presentation: Sudden severe testicular pain (often nocturnal), nausea/vomiting, swollen/elevated testis (high-riding), absent cremasteric reflex (most specific sign), horizontal lie (bell-clapper). May have history of similar self-resolving episodes (intermittent torsion).
redFlags: Acute testicular pain with suspicion of torsion — DO NOT DELAY FOR IMAGING — direct to surgery
Suspected appendix testis torsion (less serious but similar presentation — blue dot sign + smaller localised tender area)
Differential includes epididymo-orchitis, hydrocele torsion, hernia, tumour, trauma
diagnostics: CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS — do NOT delay for imaging in classic presentation
TWIST score (clinical scoring): swelling + hard testis + high-riding + nausea/vomiting + absent cremasteric (0-7); ≥ 5 high probability
Colour Doppler ultrasound — sensitivity 89%, specificity 99% for torsion (absent or reduced flow); useful only IF imaging won't delay surgery
Urinalysis (rule out epididymo-orchitis)
STI screen (rule out epididymitis if older + sexually active)
Surgical exploration is BOTH diagnostic + therapeutic
management: EMERGENCY — TIME IS TESTIS:
1. Surgical consultation IMMEDIATELY (within minutes)
2. NPO + IV access + analgesia
3. SURGICAL EXPLORATION as soon as possible (golden window 6 hours):
Bilateral incision (orchiopexy of contralateral testis too — high incidence of contralateral bell-clapper)
Detorsion + assess viability (warm packs, observe for re-perfusion)
Viable testis: bilateral orchiopexy
Non-viable: orchiectomy + contralateral orchiopexy
MANUAL DETORSION (only if surgery delayed):
'Open book' maneuver — rotate affected testis OUTWARD (lateral) from midline (most torsions are inward)
May need 2-3 rotations (often 720°)
Patient comfort + reduced pain = successful detorsion
Still requires definitive orchiopexy (manual detorsion is NOT definitive — risk of re-torsion)
Confirm with Doppler if available
PREOPERATIVE:
Anaesthetic assessment + consent
Discuss possible orchiectomy + counsel patient + family
Antibiotic prophylaxis (cefazolin)
POST-OPERATIVE:
Mobilise early
Analgesia
Discharge same day or next day
Counsel: bilateral orchiopexy prevents future torsion
Future fertility — testis viability + contralateral fertility
If orchiectomy — discuss prosthesis + future psychological + sexual function
ALTERNATIVE DIAGNOSES if torsion ruled out at surgery:
Appendix testis torsion: excision + symptomatic; smaller blue dot near upper pole
Epididymo-orchitis: antibiotics (ceftriaxone + doxycycline for STI; ciprofloxacin if UTI source); scrotal support + NSAID
Hydrocele: drainage if symptomatic
Hernia: surgical repair
Trauma: imaging + supportive
Tumour: workup tumour markers + imaging + urological
NEONATAL TORSION:
Often perinatal extravaginal (entire spermatic cord twists)
Usually not salvageable (occurred in utero)
Surgical exploration + contralateral orchiopexy (prophylactic)
INTERMITTENT TORSION:
Recurrent self-resolving episodes — risk of definitive torsion
Elective bilateral orchiopexy
PATIENT EDUCATION:
Adolescent males — recognise testicular pain + emergency
Importance of rapid presentation (time = testis)
Counsel post-op
MEDICOLEGAL:
Major source of litigation — document clinical exam + timing + decision-making + consent + outcomes

title: Atopic eczema — modern biologic + JAK era
population: Common — 15-20% children + 5-10% adults; rising globally including SSA urban areas. Atopic march: eczema → food allergy → asthma → allergic rhinitis.
presentation: Pruritic + chronic / chronically relapsing dermatitis with characteristic morphology + distribution by age — infant face/extensors; child + adult flexures (antecubital, popliteal). Hanifin + Rajka or UK criteria. Acute (vesicular, weeping), subacute (scaly), chronic (lichenified).
redFlags: Severe atopic eczema with significant impact (SCORAD > 50 / EASI > 21 / IGA 4) — refer dermatology for systemic
Eczema herpeticum (cutaneous HSV — admit + IV aciclovir)
Allergic contact dermatitis overlap — patch test
Suspected DRESS / SJS / contact urticaria in adult
Mental health (significant depression / anxiety / suicidal — chronic itch + appearance)
diagnostics: Hanifin + Rajka or UK Working Party criteria
Severity: SCORAD, EASI, IGA, POEM (patient), DLQI (life impact)
Total + specific IgE (food + aeroallergen — informs if relevant)
Skin prick if specific allergen suspected
Patch test if contact allergen suspected (chronic, treatment-resistant)
Skin swab for bacterial / viral if superinfection
Filaggrin gene (FLG) testing — rarely done clinically but most common genetic factor
Mental health screening
management: PRINCIPLES — chronic management + flare control:
EMOLLIENT (cornerstone — daily lifelong):
Generous + frequent (at least BD; > 250 g/week adult)
Cream / ointment by preference + lesion location
Avoid fragranced / lanolin if sensitised
Apply WITHIN 3 minutes of bath (soak + smear)
TOPICAL CORTICOSTEROID (TCS):
Step-up by potency:
Mild: hydrocortisone 1% — face, flexures, infants
Moderate: clobetasone butyrate, betamethasone valerate 0.025%
Potent: betamethasone valerate 0.1%, mometasone
Very potent: clobetasol propionate — short-term only
Apply BD × 7-14 days for flare then taper
PROACTIVE THERAPY: 2 days/week to recently flared areas during remission — reduces flares
TOPICAL CALCINEURIN INHIBITOR (TCI):
Tacrolimus 0.1% (0.03% in children 2-15)
Pimecrolimus 1%
STEROID-SPARING — useful on face / flexures / long-term maintenance
Slight burning initially (transient)
PHOSPHODIESTERASE-4 INHIBITORS:
Crisaborole 2% topical (age 3+)
Roflumilast — emerging
JAK INHIBITORS — topical:
Ruxolitinib 1.5% (Opzelura) — mild-moderate AD, age 12+ (FDA)
Limited body surface area
ADJUNCTS:
Antihistamine — limited efficacy (sedating at night may help sleep — chlorphenamine, hydroxyzine)
Wet wraps + intensive treatment + topical steroid for severe acute
Bath additives — emerging evidence limited (recent NICE removed routine recommendation)
Bleach baths (0.005% sodium hypochlorite — 1/4 cup household bleach in full bath) × 2/week — reduces colonisation in colonised patients
PHOTOTHERAPY:
Narrowband UVB 3×/week × 2-3 months
Refractory to topical; reduced need with newer biologics
SYSTEMIC (moderate-severe + failed topical):
Conventional immunosuppressants (declining use with biologics):
Ciclosporin 2.5-5 mg/kg/day (fast but renal/BP toxicity; short-term)
Methotrexate 7.5-25 mg/week
Azathioprine 1-3 mg/kg/day (check TPMT)
Mycophenolate mofetil
Oral steroid — only short-course for severe flare (rebound risk)
BIOLOGICS (transformative):
DUPILUMAB (anti-IL-4/IL-13) — adult + paediatric (≥ 6 months — Adore-2 trial 2022 extended); subcutaneous loading then 300 mg q2 weeks; very effective + safe
TRALOKINUMAB (anti-IL-13) — adult; SC q2 weeks
LEBRIKIZUMAB (anti-IL-13) — FDA 2024
NEMOLIZUMAB (anti-IL-31) — significant antipruritic (severe itch); approved 2024
JAK INHIBITORS — oral:
UPADACITINIB 15-30 mg/day — most effective + rapid
BARICITINIB 4 mg/day
ABROCITINIB 100-200 mg/day
BOXED WARNINGS (VTE, MACE, malignancy) — careful with > 65, CV risk, smokers
PEDIATRIC:
Emollient + low-potency TCS — first-line
Tacrolimus 0.03% for age 2-15 face/flexures
Dupilumab from 6 months
Avoid oral steroid + JAK in young children
Food allergy referral if infant + persistent severe
ATOPIC MARCH PREVENTION:
Daily emollient from birth in high-risk (family history) — evidence mixed (BEEP trial 2020 negative; EAT trial earlier positive)
Early peanut introduction at 4-6 months in high-risk (LEAP NEJM 2015) — reduces peanut allergy
Manage food allergies + asthma + allergic rhinitis integrated
ALLERGEN AVOIDANCE — only if documented (skin prick or specific IgE + clinical correlation); blanket dust mite / pet avoidance not evidence-based
ECZEMA HERPETICUM:
Admit + IV aciclovir 5-10 mg/kg q8h
Ophthalmology if peri-orbital
Continue eczema treatment
BACTERIAL SUPERINFECTION (Staph aureus):
Topical antibiotic (mupirocin / fusidic acid) for limited
Oral antibiotic (flucloxacillin) for extensive
Address triggers + emollient
EDUCATION:
Eczema is a chronic condition — manage expectations
Skin care education (eczema schools, demonstration)
Identify + avoid triggers (heat, sweat, soap, fragrance, wool)
Mental health support (especially adolescents — significant impact)
School involvement (eczema action plan)
SSA: emollient access + WHO/IDF advocacy

title: Psoriasis — modern biologic + JAK era
population: Affects 2-3% globally; SSA prevalence under-recognised. Multisystem — skin + nails + joints + scalp + uveitis + IBD + metabolic syndrome + CV risk.
presentation: Plaque (most common) — well-demarcated erythematous scaly plaques (elbows, knees, scalp, lower back); guttate (post-streptococcal); inverse (flexural); pustular; erythrodermic. Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on scale removal), Koebner. Nail pitting + onycholysis. PASI / IGA / BSA for severity.
redFlags: Erythrodermic / generalised pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch) — admit, IV fluid, temperature control, sepsis risk
Severe joint involvement (psoriatic arthritis — early biologic prevents joint damage)
Mental health (depression + anxiety + suicidality — significant impact)
Cardiovascular disease (psoriasis is independent CV risk factor — manage aggressively)
diagnostics: Clinical diagnosis (well-demarcated plaques + scale + Auspitz + classical sites)
Severity: PASI (Psoriasis Area + Severity Index — > 10 severe), IGA, BSA, DLQI (life impact)
Joint examination + GALS — screen for psoriatic arthritis (PsA) at every visit
Mental health screening
Comorbidity: BP + lipids + glucose + HbA1c (metabolic syndrome 2× more common); CV risk assessment
Hepatitis B + C + HIV + TB IGRA + CXR BEFORE biologic
Pregnancy test
Skin biopsy if uncertain (acanthosis + parakeratosis + Munro microabscesses + neutrophils)
management: MILD-MODERATE (BSA < 10%, PASI < 10) — topical:
TOPICAL CORTICOSTEROID — first-line: betamethasone, clobetasol
Limit very potent to 2 weeks then taper
Combination steroid + calcipotriene (Dovobet / Daivobet) — once daily
VITAMIN D ANALOGUE: calcipotriene (calcipotriol), tacalcitol
TAR: coal tar — emollient + anti-inflammatory; cosmetically suboptimal
Salicylic acid 2-5% — keratolytic for thick plaques
Tazarotene (retinoid) — topical
Topical PDE4 inhibitor (roflumilast, tapinarof — newer)
Scalp: tar + steroid; clobetasol shampoo; calcipotriol scalp solution
PHOTOTHERAPY:
Narrowband UVB 3×/week × 30-40 sessions — first-line moderate-severe before biologic
PUVA — less commonly used
MODERATE-SEVERE (BSA > 10% OR PASI > 10 OR DLQI > 10 OR fingernail / face / genital / palmoplantar):
CONVENTIONAL systemic:
Methotrexate 7.5-25 mg/week + folate
Ciclosporin 2.5-5 mg/kg/day (short-term)
Acitretin (retinoid; teratogenic — WCBP avoid)
Fumarates (more common Europe)
BIOLOGICS — paradigm shift (rapid clearance + good safety):
Anti-TNF: etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab, certolizumab
Anti-IL-12/23: ustekinumab
Anti-IL-17: secukinumab, ixekizumab, brodalumab, bimekizumab
Anti-IL-23: guselkumab, risankizumab, tildrakizumab — best for plaque + low immunogenicity
Choice by comorbidity:
PsA — anti-TNF or anti-IL-17 or anti-IL-23 with PsA approval
IBD comorbidity — anti-TNF or anti-IL-23 (avoid IL-17 — may worsen IBD)
Uveitis — anti-TNF mAb
Pregnancy — certolizumab (no placental transfer)
Hepatitis B — anti-IL-23 (lowest reactivation risk)
JAK INHIBITORS — oral:
Deucravacitinib (TYK2 inhibitor — Sotyktu) — psoriasis-specific, FDA-approved 2022, fewer BOXED warnings than other JAK
Apremilast (PDE4 inhibitor — Otezla) — moderate, oral, no specific lab monitoring
ERYTHRODERMIC + GENERALISED PUSTULAR PSORIASIS:
Admit + IV fluid + temperature control
Identify trigger (drug, infection, sudden steroid withdrawal)
Rapid systemic: ciclosporin (most rapid) / infliximab / acitretin
Spesolimab IV (anti-IL-36R — Effisayer FDA 2022) — generalised pustular psoriasis flares
Imsidolimab (anti-IL-36) — emerging
Wound care + nutrition + sepsis prevention
PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS (PsA):
Treat-to-target
csDMARDs: methotrexate, leflunomide, sulfasalazine
bDMARDs as for skin + joint cover (anti-TNF, anti-IL-17, anti-IL-23 with PsA approval)
JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib)
Apremilast (mild)
GRAPPA + EULAR guidelines
COMORBIDITY MANAGEMENT (CRITICAL):
CV risk modification — statin + BP + DM + smoking + weight
Mental health — screen + treat depression / anxiety
Hepatic + NAFLD
Uveitis
IBD
Sleep + obstructive sleep apnoea
VACCINATIONS:
Before biologic — live (varicella, MMR, yellow fever) if needed
Pneumococcal + annual flu + COVID
No live on biologics / JAK
PREGNANCY:
Methotrexate + acitretin teratogenic (acitretin avoid 3 years post-cessation in WCBP)
Certolizumab preferred biologic
Ustekinumab + IL-17 — emerging data acceptable
Pregnancy often improves psoriasis (60%); postpartum flare common
PEDIATRIC:
Topical first-line
Narrowband UVB
Biologics: etanercept (4+), adalimumab (4+), ustekinumab (6+), secukinumab (6+), ixekizumab (6+)
School + psychological support
LIFESTYLE:
Smoking cessation (major)
Alcohol moderation
Weight loss (improves response to therapy)
Mediterranean diet
Stress management
SSA / Kenya:
Under-diagnosed
Limited access to biologics — advocate for KEML + NHIF inclusion
Phototherapy + conventional systemics accessible
Comorbidity management integrated with NCD strategy

title: Renal colic + ureteric stone — modern + MET
population: Lifetime risk 10-20% men, 5-10% women; rising globally. Recurrence 50% within 10 years.
presentation: Sudden severe loin-to-groin pain (colicky, restless patient who cannot lie still — contrast peritonitis where patient is still), nausea/vomiting, haematuria (visible or microscopic), urinary frequency/urgency (if vesicoureteric junction stone). Lower ureteric stone → testicular/labial pain.
redFlags: INFECTED hydronephrosis / obstructive pyelonephritis — pus + obstruction = urological emergency (sepsis + permanent renal damage)
diagnostics: Urinalysis — haematuria (visible 50%, microscopic 90%), nitrites + leucocytes (infection)
Urine MSU + culture
FBC + CRP + U&E + creatinine + calcium + phosphate + urate
Pregnancy test (women)
NON-CONTRAST CT KUB (low-dose) — first-line imaging (sensitivity > 95%); confirms stone + size + location + hydronephrosis
Ultrasound first-line in pregnancy + paediatric (no radiation; less sensitive)
X-ray KUB — useful for stone surveillance if known radio-opaque (calcium oxalate)
MRI/MRU for pregnancy (after US) if needed
Stone analysis — analyse passed/extracted stone (informs prevention)
management: ACUTE:
ANALGESIA — first priority:
NSAID (diclofenac 75 mg IM or 100 mg PR or ibuprofen 600 mg PO) — first-line (reduces ureteric spasm + better than opioid)
Avoid NSAID in CKD / GI bleed / asthma / pregnancy 3rd trimester
Opioid (morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV) for refractory or NSAID contraindicated
IV paracetamol 1 g
Antiemetic
IV fluids if dehydrated / vomiting (do NOT force diuresis — no benefit)
Reassurance + counselling
Urology referral if suspected complication / failure
IMAGING + STONE ASSESSMENT:
CT KUB to confirm + characterise (size, location, density, hydronephrosis)
Stone size:
< 5 mm: 80% pass spontaneously
5-10 mm: 50% pass; consider MET
> 10 mm: low spontaneous passage; intervention
MEDICAL EXPULSIVE THERAPY (MET):
Tamsulosin 0.4 mg/day OR nifedipine 30 mg/day for ureteric stones 5-10 mm in distal ureter — modest benefit (meta-analyses; SUSPEND trial less positive)
Adjunct to spontaneous passage
Up to 4 weeks observation if pain controlled + no complications
NSAIDs PRN + adequate fluids
INFECTED OBSTRUCTED KIDNEY — UROLOGICAL EMERGENCY:
Fever + obstruction (raised creatinine, hydronephrosis, pus in urine) + stone
EMERGENCY DRAINAGE within 6-12 hours: percutaneous nephrostomy OR ureteric stent (JJ stent) — both effective
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole; pip-tazo if septic)
ICU support if septic shock
Stone removal AFTER infection treated (definitive procedure)
DEFINITIVE STONE REMOVAL (when intervention needed):
ESWL (Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy) — non-invasive, day case, less invasive, stones < 2 cm; less effective for hard stones (cystine, calcium oxalate monohydrate)
URS (Ureteroscopy + laser) — first-line for stones 1-2 cm + many distal stones
PCNL (Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy) — > 2 cm, complex, multiple, lower pole > 1 cm
Open / robotic — rarely needed
Stent placement after intervention (relieves swelling, allows urine drainage)
PREGNANCY:
US first-line; MRI if needed
Conservative management preferred
Ureteric stent if intervention needed (general anaesthesia + radiation avoided)
Definitive treatment postpartum
Paracetamol + IV fluids; codeine if needed; avoid NSAID in 3rd trimester
PEDIATRIC:
More likely metabolic cause — extensive workup
US first-line; ultra-low-dose CT if needed
Conservative; pediatric urology involvement
PREVENTION (long-term):
HYDRATION — 2.5-3 L/day urine output (the most important)
Diet:
Reduce salt (< 5 g/day)
Adequate calcium (don't restrict — paradoxically increases stone risk; aim 1000-1200 mg/day)
Reduce animal protein excess (calcium oxalate + uric acid stones)
Reduce oxalate-rich foods if calcium oxalate stones (spinach, rhubarb, nuts)
Reduce fructose (excess sugar)
Citrate-rich (lemonade, oranges)
Identify type from stone analysis + 24h urine:
Calcium oxalate (75-85%) — most common: hydration + diet; thiazide (HCTZ 25-50 mg) for hypercalciuria; potassium citrate; allopurinol if hyperuricosuria
Uric acid stones — alkalinise urine (potassium citrate; bicarbonate); allopurinol if hyperuricaemia
Struvite (Mg-ammonium-phosphate) — infection-related; treat UTI; possible surgical removal
Cystine — rare, genetic; alkalinise + tiopronin / penicillamine
Treat underlying — hyperparathyroidism, RTA, hyperuricaemia, IBD, surgical malabsorption
Tamsulosin / nifedipine MET for ureteric 5-10 mm distal
FOLLOW-UP:
Annual KUB / CT for recurrence monitoring in stone formers
Repeat 24h urine + serum biochemistry
Stone analysis after every passed/extracted stone
Lifestyle + medical prophylaxis

title: BPH — medical + minimally invasive + surgical
population: Histological BPH in > 50% men > 50 + > 80% > 80; symptomatic LUTS in 40-50% men > 60. Significantly impacts quality of life + sleep + work.
presentation: LUTS — storage (frequency, urgency, nocturia, incontinence) + voiding (hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, post-void dribbling, incomplete emptying). Acute urinary retention (medical emergency). Overflow incontinence (chronic retention).
redFlags: Renal impairment from chronic obstruction (post-renal AKI)
Suspected prostate cancer (PSA raised + abnormal DRE — investigate per NICE / EAU pathway)
Neurological cause (cauda equina, MS, Parkinson's) — exclude
diagnostics: International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) — severity (mild 0-7, moderate 8-19, severe 20-35)
Quality of life impact
DRE — enlarged smooth firm prostate (BPH); nodular hard (cancer concern)
Urinalysis + urine culture (rule out UTI, bladder cancer)
PSA — if life expectancy > 10 years + considering treatment (consider shared decision; balance against over-diagnosis)
U&E + creatinine + eGFR
Post-void residual (PVR) bladder scan
Frequency / volume chart for 3 days
Uroflowmetry (peak flow < 10 ml/s suggests obstruction)
Pressure-flow urodynamics if uncertain
TRUS — for surgical planning
Cystoscopy if haematuria / bladder pathology
management: WATCHFUL WAITING / LIFESTYLE — for mild symptoms (IPSS < 8):
Fluid management (less evening intake)
Reduce caffeine + alcohol
Treat constipation
Avoid anticholinergics + sympathomimetics + diuretics (review medication list)
Bladder training
Pelvic floor exercises
Annual review
MEDICAL THERAPY:
α1-BLOCKER (relaxes prostate smooth muscle — rapid symptom relief, weeks):
TAMSULOSIN 0.4 mg/day (preferred — uroselective, less hypotension)
Alfuzosin, doxazosin, terazosin (less selective — hypotension + dizziness; useful if comorbid HTN)
Silodosin (very selective; ejaculatory dysfunction common)
Take at night + slowly stand up
Counsel: floppy iris syndrome — inform cataract surgeon (avoid first-time tamsulosin pre-cataract surgery)
5α-REDUCTASE INHIBITOR (shrinks prostate — slow, months; useful for large prostates > 30-40 g):
FINASTERIDE 5 mg/day OR DUTASTERIDE 0.5 mg/day
Slow onset (3-6 months for full benefit)
Reduces prostate volume 20-30%
Reduces PSA by ~ 50% (double measured PSA for cancer surveillance)
Reduces risk of acute urinary retention + need for surgery (MTOPS trial)
Side effects: ED, decreased libido, gynaecomastia, depression risk
COMBINATION α1-blocker + 5ARI:
Tamsulosin + dutasteride (Combodart / Jalyn)
More effective than monotherapy for moderate-severe + large prostate (MTOPS / CombAT)
Anticholinergic / β3-AGONIST for storage symptoms (urgency, frequency, nocturia):
Solifenacin, oxybutynin, tolterodine, mirabegron (β3 — less anticholinergic SE; preferred elderly)
Combine with α1-blocker for mixed storage + voiding symptoms
Caution PVR > 200 ml (retention risk with anticholinergic)
PDE5 INHIBITOR — DAILY:
Tadalafil 5 mg/day (Cialis) — treats both LUTS + erectile dysfunction
Useful comorbid ED
MINIMALLY INVASIVE (in-office / day case):
UroLift (prostatic urethral lift) — implants pull lateral lobes apart; minimal sexual SE; office
Rezum (water vapour thermal therapy) — heat ablation; office
Aquablation — robotic waterjet
Prostatic artery embolisation (PAE) — IR procedure
SURGICAL (for failed medical or complications):
TURP (Transurethral Resection of Prostate) — gold standard; for prostate 30-80 g
TUIP (incision) — small prostate
HoLEP (Holmium Laser Enucleation) — equivalent to TURP, less bleeding, larger prostates
Open / robotic simple prostatectomy — very large > 80-100 g
Photo-vaporisation (Greenlight)
Complications: retrograde ejaculation, urinary incontinence, ED, urethral stricture, TURP syndrome (hyponatraemia from glycine absorption — managed with bipolar TURP or saline)
ACUTE URINARY RETENTION:
Catheterise (urethral; suprapubic if urethral fails)
Start α1-blocker (improves trial without catheter — TWOC)
TWOC after 1-3 days
If failed TWOC — surgical workup
Watch decompression haematuria + diuresis (admit if significant)
Treat any UTI
FOLLOW-UP:
IPSS + uroflowmetry + PSA + DRE annually if on medical therapy
Cancer surveillance per shared decision
PREVENTION OF PROGRESSION:
Lifestyle
Long-term 5ARI in selected (reduces acute retention)
Mediterranean diet, exercise, weight (modest evidence)

title: Urinary tract infection — comprehensive (uncomplicated → urosepsis)
population: Among most common bacterial infections globally. Women > men. Pregnancy + DM + elderly + catheter + immunocompromised higher risk. Rising resistance especially E. coli (FQ, ESBL).
presentation: Lower UTI (cystitis): dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort, haematuria. Pyelonephritis: loin pain, fever, rigors, nausea/vomiting, systemic. Urosepsis: sepsis features. Asymptomatic bacteriuria (screen + treat only in pregnancy + before invasive urological procedure). Recurrent UTI: ≥ 2 in 6 months / ≥ 3 in 12 months.
redFlags: Pyelonephritis (systemic features) — admit if severe / pregnant / immunocompromised / vomiting / dehydrated / unable to tolerate PO
Recurrent UTI / failure of empirical therapy — culture-directed; investigate (anatomic, stone, immunocompromise)
Catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI) with sepsis — change catheter + treat
Pregnancy + UTI (asymptomatic bacteriuria treat — prevents pyelonephritis + preterm)
Diabetes + emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas in renal parenchyma — emergency)
Suspected STI (urethritis) in young sexually active — chlamydia/gonorrhoea swab
diagnostics: Urinalysis (nitrites — gram-negative converters; leucocytes; haematuria; protein)
Urine MSU + culture (CFU > 10^5 typical; > 10^3 acceptable in symptomatic with dysuria)
FBC + U&E + creatinine + CRP (severity)
Blood cultures if septic / pyelonephritis
Imaging if:
Pyelonephritis not responding 48-72h
Recurrent / atypical pathogen
Suspected stone / obstruction (CT KUB)
Suspected emphysematous pyelonephritis (CT)
Renal abscess
Cystoscopy if recurrent UTI in men + risk factors
Pregnancy: dipstick + culture at booking + every trimester per local protocol
STI screen in young sexually active with persistent UTI symptoms
management: UNCOMPLICATED CYSTITIS (women, non-pregnant, no comorbidity):
FIRST-LINE (per local resistance — WHO + IDSA / EAU):
NITROFURANTOIN 50-100 mg QDS × 5-7 days (avoid if eGFR < 30)
Trimethoprim 200 mg BD × 3 days (resistance > 30% in many areas — check local antibiogram)
Fosfomycin 3 g PO × 1 dose (resistance still low; convenient single dose)
Pivmecillinam 400 mg q8h × 3 days (Scandinavia + UK + emerging)
Alternatives: cephalexin, augmentin (less preferred — more resistance + collateral damage)
AVOID fluoroquinolones for uncomplicated (resistance + AEs: tendon rupture, neuropathy, CDIff, QT)
Reassess at 48-72h
Symptom relief: paracetamol, fluids, urinary alkaliniser (cranberry — modest evidence)
PYELONEPHRITIS (women non-pregnant):

Outpatient (tolerating PO, no sepsis, social support): ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD × 7 days (where FQ resistance < 10%; higher resistance many areas — use parenteral); levofloxacin 750 mg/d × 5-7 days; cotrimoxazole if susceptible
Inpatient (severe / dehydrated / vomiting / pregnancy / sepsis): IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily; IV gentamicin if severe + cover ESBL; pip-tazo if severe / sepsis; meropenem if known ESBL / CRE
Duration: 7-14 days based on severity + organism
CT KUB if not improving 48-72h (rule out obstruction / abscess)
MEN WITH UTI:
Always considered complicated (anatomic factors; possible underlying cause)
Workup urological — DRE + flow + ultrasound + cystoscopy if recurrent
Duration 7-14 days minimum
Treat for prostatitis pathogens if suspected (extended duration ciprofloxacin or cotrimoxazole 4-6 weeks)
PREGNANCY:
Asymptomatic bacteriuria — TREAT (prevent pyelonephritis + preterm labour)
Empirical: nitrofurantoin 50-100 mg QDS × 7 days (avoid 3rd trimester — neonatal haemolytic anaemia), cephalexin 500 mg QDS × 7 days, fosfomycin 3 g single dose
AVOID trimethoprim 1st trimester (folate antagonist) + fluoroquinolones + tetracyclines
Pyelonephritis: IV ceftriaxone 1-2 g/day; admit; multidisciplinary obstetric + ID
Test of cure after pregnancy UTI; re-screen at every visit
Prophylaxis for recurrent: nitrofurantoin 50 mg nocte or cephalexin 250 mg nocte
CATHETER-ASSOCIATED UTI (CAUTI):
Symptomatic — treat (do not treat asymptomatic catheterised bacteriuria — colonisation, not infection, except pregnancy + pre-urological surgery)
Change catheter > 14 days old before culture + treatment
Empirical IV antibiotics covering MDR (pip-tazo or meropenem); de-escalate per culture
Duration 5-10 days
Remove catheter ASAP
CAUTI prevention bundle: aseptic insertion, closed drainage, daily review of need, removal as soon as not needed
ELDERLY:
Asymptomatic bacteriuria common — DO NOT TREAT (only if pregnancy or pre-urological procedure)
Specific symptoms (dysuria, frequency, suprapubic) — treat
Non-specific (confusion, fatigue) alone — investigate for other causes; don't reflex antibiotic
Watch for fluoroquinolone CV / cognitive AEs in elderly
PEDIATRIC:
Lower threshold (sepsis presentation, atypical)
Urgent imaging (US, MCUG, DMSA) per NICE / AAP for first UTI < 3 years or recurrent
Treatment: cotrimoxazole or cephalexin 7-10 days; severe IV ceftriaxone
RECURRENT UTI (≥ 2/6 mo or ≥ 3/12 mo):
Investigate: imaging, cystoscopy (if men or atypical women)
Behavioural: hydration, post-coital voiding, wiping front-to-back, avoid spermicides
Vaginal oestrogen postmenopausal (highly effective)
CRANBERRY juice/extract — modest evidence
D-mannose — limited evidence
Methenamine hippurate — emerging evidence for prophylaxis (ALTAR trial 2022)
Antibiotic prophylaxis: low-dose nitrofurantoin 50 mg nocte or trimethoprim 100 mg nocte × 3-6 months OR post-coital single dose
Self-start treatment for diagnosed pattern
Probiotics — limited evidence
Immunomodulator (Uro-Vaxom — emerging)
ESBL / CRE / MDR — culture-directed; carbapenem if needed; new agents (ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, cefiderocol) for severe CRE
EMPHYSEMATOUS PYELONEPHRITIS (diabetic, gas in renal parenchyma):
EMERGENCY
Aggressive IV antibiotics + tight glycaemic control
Percutaneous drainage + ureteric stent
Nephrectomy for severe non-responsive
ICU support
ANTIMICROBIAL STEWARDSHIP:
Local antibiogram-guided
Avoid quinolones for uncomplicated UTI (collateral damage)
De-escalate per culture
Track + report resistance trends
WHO AWaRe framework (Access vs Watch vs Reserve)
PUBLIC HEALTH SSA:
Address access to clean water + sanitation (prevents UTI)
Vaccinate (Hib + S. pneumoniae reduce some)
Antibiotic stewardship in low-resource settings
