title: Acute otitis media — paediatric + adult
population: Children 6 months - 3 years peak; one of most common reasons for paediatric antibiotic prescription. SSA: under-recognised, complications (mastoiditis, meningitis, hearing loss) more common.
presentation: Acute pain (otalgia), fever, irritability, decreased hearing, ear discharge if TM perforated. Examination: bulging or red tympanic membrane, reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy, otorrhoea if perforated. AOM in children < 2 + bilateral + severe symptoms = antibiotic. Older children + mild = watch-and-wait approach.
redFlags: MASTOIDITIS (post-auricular swelling + protruding pinna + erythema) — admit + IV antibiotics + ENT — emergency
Intracranial complications (meningitis, brain abscess, lateral sinus thrombosis) — neurosurgical emergency
Recurrent AOM (≥ 3 in 6 months or 4 in 12 months) — ENT referral for grommets
Persistent otitis media with effusion (OME) > 3 months bilateral + hearing loss > 25 dB — grommets
Cholesteatoma (chronic discharge + foul smell + hearing loss)
diagnostics: Otoscopy with pneumatic — TM mobility key
Tympanometry if uncertain (flat tracing in OME)
Audiometry (if hearing loss persistent / severe)
Culture of discharge if persistent / atypical / refractory
FBC + CRP only if suspected complication
Imaging (CT temporal bone) for suspected mastoiditis / intracranial complication
management: ACUTE OTITIS MEDIA:
ANALGESIA — first priority (paracetamol, ibuprofen)
Decongestant + antihistamine NOT effective
Topical anaesthetic ear drops (benzocaine) — controversial; not for perforated
ANTIBIOTIC DECISION (watch-and-wait vs antibiotic):
Children < 6 months: ALWAYS antibiotic
Children 6 months - 2 years:
Severe + bilateral + or otorrhoea: antibiotic
Mild + unilateral: watchful waiting acceptable with reliable follow-up at 48-72h; antibiotic if not improving
Children > 2 years + adults:
Mild-moderate: watchful waiting + analgesia first; antibiotic if not improving 48-72h
Severe / immunocompromised: antibiotic
ANTIBIOTIC CHOICE:
AMOXICILLIN 80-90 mg/kg/day in 2 doses × 5-10 days (children); 500-1000 mg q8h adult — first-line
Co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin-clavulanate) if recent antibiotic / treatment failure / day-care attendance / age < 2 with severe / β-lactamase-producing organisms
Cephalosporins (cefuroxime, cefdinir) if penicillin allergy (non-anaphylaxis)
Azithromycin / clarithromycin if severe penicillin allergy
Duration: 5 days (children > 2 years) / 7-10 days (children < 2 / severe / recurrent)
WHO IMCI antibiotics for paediatric OM in LMIC
Resistance: pneumococcal penicillin resistance rising — high-dose amoxicillin (90 mg/kg/d) overcomes most
RECURRENT AOM:
≥ 3 episodes in 6 months OR ≥ 4 in 12 months
GROMMETS (tympanostomy tubes) — ENT referral; reduce recurrences, improve hearing
Adenoidectomy if associated nasal obstruction
Long-term low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis — increasingly avoided (resistance)
Manage risk factors: passive smoke, day-care, pacifier, formula vs breast
Vaccinate (Hib + pneumococcal PCV13 + flu)
OTITIS MEDIA WITH EFFUSION (OME — 'glue ear'):
Hearing loss without acute infection
Watch 3 months — most resolve spontaneously
If persistent bilateral + hearing loss > 25 dB > 3 months — GROMMETS
Hearing aid if not candidate for surgery
Autoinflation (Otovent) — modest evidence
Antibiotic + steroid + decongestant — NOT effective
MASTOIDITIS:
EMERGENCY — admit + IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone + vancomycin or pip-tazo)
CT temporal bone
ENT — cortical mastoidectomy if abscess / complication / fails medical therapy
Intracranial complications neurosurgical
CHOLESTEATOMA:
Surgical (mastoidectomy + tympanoplasty)
Cannot be treated with antibiotics alone
PROPHYLAXIS:
Breastfeeding ≥ 6 months
Avoid passive smoking
Pneumococcal + Hib + influenza vaccination
Treat allergic rhinitis
Adequate nutrition
WHO IMCI: paediatric ear infection module — assess danger signs + treat
Kenya MOH: paediatric protocols include AOM

title: Acute bacterial sinusitis — diagnosis + treatment
population: Common adult; less common children. Major source of antibiotic over-prescription (most sinusitis is viral and self-limiting).
presentation: Bacterial sinusitis = symptoms ≥ 10 days without improvement OR severe (fever > 39, purulent discharge, facial pain × 3 days) OR worsening course after initial improvement ('double sickening'). Symptoms: nasal congestion / discharge, facial pressure / pain, anosmia. Examination: purulent discharge, sinus tenderness.
redFlags: Periorbital cellulitis / orbital cellulitis (infection extends to orbit — admit + IV antibiotics + ophth + ENT)
Cavernous sinus thrombosis (severe headache + bilateral cranial nerve palsies + papilloedema — neurosurgical emergency)
Pott's puffy tumour (frontal sinus abscess + osteomyelitis)
Immunocompromised — invasive fungal (Mucor — diabetic + neutropenic; emergency)
Recurrent / chronic — exclude allergy, structural (nasal polyps), immunodeficiency
diagnostics: Clinical diagnosis (history + symptoms + duration)
NICE / EPOS criteria: bacterial = > 10 days without improvement OR severe / worsening
Examination: nasal endoscopy (specialist), purulence, polyps
Imaging NOT routine (CT only if complication suspected, recurrent, refractory, immunocompromised)
FBC + CRP for severity
Allergic rhinitis assessment (skin prick / specific IgE) if recurrent
Total + specific IgE if immunodeficiency suspected
management: MOST SINUSITIS IS VIRAL — symptom relief:
Intranasal saline irrigation (sinus rinse — high-volume / low-pressure) — strong evidence
Intranasal corticosteroid (mometasone, fluticasone) — reduces symptoms + may avoid antibiotic
Decongestant (oxymetazoline ≤ 3-5 days — rebound rhinitis) + paracetamol / NSAID
Antihistamine (if allergic component)
Hydration + rest
BACTERIAL SINUSITIS (clinical criteria — symptoms ≥ 10 days, severe, or worsening):
FIRST-LINE: AMOXICILLIN 500 mg q8h × 5-10 days (or 90 mg/kg/d if high-resistance area)
Co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin-clavulanate) if recent antibiotic / day-care / high resistance area / fails amoxicillin: 875/125 mg q12h
Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 5-10 days (alternative)
Penicillin allergy: levofloxacin 500 mg/d × 5-7 days; cephalosporin (cefuroxime, cefdinir) if non-severe allergy
AVOID macrolides empirically in many regions (high pneumococcal resistance)
Reassess at 48-72h if not improving
FAILURE OF FIRST-LINE:
Switch to co-amoxiclav or levofloxacin
CT sinuses
ENT referral
ORBITAL / PERIORBITAL CELLULITIS:
Admit + IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone + flucloxacillin or pip-tazo)
Ophthalmology + ENT urgent
Imaging (CT orbits + sinuses)
Surgical drainage of subperiosteal abscess if needed
INTRACRANIAL EXTENSION:
Emergency — admit + IV broad-spectrum (ceftriaxone + metronidazole + vancomycin)
Neurosurgery + ENT urgent
Imaging (CT/MRI)
ICU support
INVASIVE FUNGAL SINUSITIS (immunocompromised, especially diabetic / neutropenic):
EMERGENCY — admit + IV amphotericin B (liposomal preferred — AmBisome)
Urgent surgical debridement
Address underlying immunocompromise (correct DKA, neutropenia)
High mortality
CHRONIC RHINOSINUSITIS (CRS):
> 12 weeks of symptoms
Phenotypes: with polyps (CRSwNP) vs without (CRSsNP)
Saline irrigation + intranasal steroid + treat allergic component
Oral steroid short-course (1-2 weeks)
Antibiotic if acute flare (bacterial)
Doxycycline 100 mg/d × 3 weeks for polyps (mast cell stabilising effect — modest)
Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) — ENT referral if medical failure / structural / polyp surgery
Biologics: dupilumab (CRSwNP — SINUS-24 / SINUS-52), mepolizumab (eosinophilic CRSwNP), omalizumab — for severe + comorbid asthma
ALLERGIC RHINITIS COEXIST:
Intranasal steroid + antihistamine (oral or intranasal)
Allergen avoidance + immunotherapy for severe
FUNGAL BALL (mycetoma — usually maxillary):
Surgical removal (FESS)
Often diabetic / immunocompromised
Not invasive — different from invasive fungal
PEDIATRIC:
Sinusitis rare < 2 years (sinuses not developed)
Symptoms similar to adult
Same diagnostic criteria + treatment
Avoid quinolones
ANTIBIOTIC STEWARDSHIP:
Most acute sinusitis is viral — symptom relief + observation
Reserve antibiotic for clear bacterial features (10+ days, severe, double-sickening)
Local antibiogram + de-escalate
PREVENTION:
Vaccinate (pneumococcal + flu + Hib)
Treat allergic rhinitis aggressively
Smoking cessation
Address dental + gastric reflux (less established triggers)

title: Tonsillitis + pharyngitis — Strep + viral + Centor/FeverPAIN
population: Common all ages; SSA disproportionate rheumatic fever sequelae from untreated GAS (group A strep) pharyngitis. Major source of antibiotic over-prescription.
presentation: Sore throat + fever ± exudate ± lymphadenopathy ± headache ± malaise. Strep more likely if: tonsillar exudate + tender cervical lymphadenopathy + fever > 38 + ABSENCE of cough (Centor / McIsaac criteria) + age 5-15. Viral more likely if: cough + rhinorrhoea + conjunctivitis + diarrhoea.
redFlags: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy — trismus + uvular deviation + 'hot potato' voice + drooling) — admit + drain
Retropharyngeal abscess (children — neck pain, fever, dysphagia, drooling) — admit
Lemierre syndrome (Fusobacterium — necrobacillosis + septic IJV thrombosis + lung emboli)
EBV (infectious mononucleosis) — atypical lymphocytes + heterophile / monospot positive; AVOID amoxicillin (rash)
Diphtheria (rare — vaccination; characteristic grey-white pseudomembrane; toxic appearance — admit + diphtheria antitoxin + antibiotic + isolation)
GAS sequelae: rheumatic fever (especially in SSA) + post-strep glomerulonephritis
Acute laryngitis with stridor — epiglottitis (admit, airway protect)
diagnostics: Centor criteria: fever > 38 + tonsillar exudate + tender cervical nodes + ABSENCE of cough (each 1 point)
0-1: viral likely — no swab, no antibiotic
2-3: rapid antigen detection test (RADT) or throat swab; antibiotic if positive
4: likely strep — antibiotic empirically
McIsaac (modified Centor — adds age points)
FeverPAIN score (UK NICE — Fever + Purulence + Attend rapidly + severe Inflamed tonsils + No cough/coryza) — 0-1 viral; 2-3 RADT/swab; 4-5 empirical antibiotic
Rapid Antigen Detection Test (RADT) — high specificity, lower sensitivity (false negatives need throat culture confirmation in children + young)
Throat culture — gold standard (slow)
Monospot / heterophile antibodies if EBV suspected (atypical lymphocytes on smear)
HIV test if recurrent / severe / risk factors
STI screen if oral sex history
management: MOST PHARYNGITIS IS VIRAL — symptom relief:
Analgesia: paracetamol, ibuprofen
Throat sponge: warm fluids, ice cream, throat lozenges
Hydration + rest
Inform patient of expected course (usually 5-7 days)
GROUP A STREP CONFIRMED OR HIGH PROBABILITY (Centor 4 or RADT/swab positive):
PENICILLIN V (phenoxymethylpenicillin) 500 mg QDS × 10 days (or 250 mg q6h children)
Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS × 10 days alternative (better PO tolerance, similar efficacy; AVOID if EBV suspected — rash)
Penicillin allergy: cephalexin (if non-anaphylaxis) or macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg/d × 5 days or clarithromycin 250 mg BD × 10 days)
Single-dose IM benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU (especially SSA — adherence problem) — also for secondary prophylaxis of rheumatic fever
Duration 10 days CRITICAL (eradicates strep + prevents rheumatic fever + post-strep GN — 5-day courses suboptimal for rheumatic fever prevention in SSA)
NICE: short course 5-day not recommended for confirmed GAS
WHY TREAT STREP PHARYNGITIS:
Modest symptom reduction
Prevent acute rheumatic fever + RHD (SSA priority)
Prevent suppurative complications (peritonsillar abscess, mastoiditis, sinusitis)
Reduce transmission
Post-strep glomerulonephritis (not prevented by antibiotic — but indicated in epidemic / contacts)
PERITONSILLAR ABSCESS (QUINSY):
Trismus + uvular deviation + 'hot potato' voice + drooling
Admit + ENT urgent
IV broad-spectrum (co-amoxiclav or pip-tazo)
Needle aspiration or incision + drainage
Discharge on PO antibiotic × 7-10 days
Recurrent — interval tonsillectomy
EBV (Glandular fever — Infectious mononucleosis):
Supportive (paracetamol, fluids, rest)
AVOID amoxicillin (90% rash)
Avoid contact sport for 4-6 weeks (splenic rupture risk)
Steroid only for severe airway compromise / hepatic / haematological
Counsel — fatigue weeks-months
DIPHTHERIA:
RARE — vaccination success
Pseudomembrane + toxic + bull-neck
Admit isolation + diphtheria antitoxin + penicillin / erythromycin × 14 days
Notify public health + contacts vaccinated + prophylactic erythromycin × 7-10 days for unvaccinated contacts
ACUTE RHEUMATIC FEVER (sequela — SSA priority):
Jones criteria: carditis + arthritis + chorea + erythema marginatum + subcutaneous nodules + supportive (ASOT raised)
Bed rest + aspirin/NSAID + steroid for carditis
Secondary prophylaxis with monthly benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU IM (× 10 years or until age 21 — longer if carditis)
Echocardiography for RHD
Address SSA — Kenya National RHD Programme; awareness + early detection + secondary prophylaxis
RECURRENT TONSILLITIS:
≥ 7 episodes in 1 year OR ≥ 5 in 2 years OR ≥ 3 in 3 years (Paradise criteria)
Tonsillectomy — selected (NICE NG155 / SIGN / AAO-HNS criteria); modest benefit balanced against surgical risk
GONOCOCCAL PHARYNGITIS:
Asymptomatic mostly
Test (NAAT) high-risk + treat
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single + azithromycin 1 g (separate condition — gonorrhoea modern)
HIV: recurrent / severe oropharyngeal infections — test for HIV
ANTIBIOTIC STEWARDSHIP:
Most pharyngitis is viral
Use clinical scoring + RADT/swab to avoid unnecessary antibiotic
WHO AWaRe stewardship
Kenya: balanced — under-treatment in rural primary care + over-treatment in urban — RHD prevention priority
PREVENTION:
Hand hygiene
Cough etiquette
Avoid sharing utensils
Strep vaccine (in development)
SSA / Kenya:
Rheumatic fever + RHD major preventable cardiac disease
Train primary care + community on prevention + secondary prophylaxis
RHD echo screening programmes
Address antibiotic access for primary prevention

title: Venous leg ulcer — compression + comprehensive
population: Most common chronic wound; affects 1-3% of older adults; major burden + cost. Recurrence high (~ 50% at 5 years).
presentation: Painful + chronic wound usually medial gaiter area (above ankle), associated with venous insufficiency (oedema, hyperpigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis, varicose veins, eczema). Typically irregular borders + shallow + exudative.
redFlags: Suspected arterial component (ABPI < 0.8) — caution / contraindicated compression
Sudden enlargement / change — biopsy (Marjolin ulcer — SCC in chronic ulcer)
Failure to heal at 12 weeks — biopsy + specialist
Pyoderma gangrenosum (necrotising autoimmune — different appearance, painful, underlying IBD / RA / haematological)
Atypical / multiple ulcers — vasculitis / malignancy workup
diagnostics: Clinical assessment: ulcer (size, depth, exudate, slough, granulation, infection signs), surrounding skin, peripheral pulses, capillary refill, sensation

ABPI (Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index) — MANDATORY before compression: > 0.8 venous-only (full compression); 0.5-0.8 mixed (modified compression — specialist); < 0.5 arterial-dominant (NO compression — vascular)
Doppler ± duplex for arterial / venous insufficiency
Wound swab if infection signs (NOT routinely)
Wound biopsy if non-healing > 12 weeks or atypical
FBC + albumin + glucose + nutrition assessment
Pain assessment
management: COMPRESSION THERAPY (cornerstone — gold standard):
Four-layer bandaging (Profore) OR short-stretch / inelastic / multi-component
40 mmHg at ankle — maintains compression gradient
Changes weekly (or 2× weekly if heavy exudate)
Continue until ulcer healed
ABPI > 0.8 — full compression; 0.5-0.8 reduced; < 0.5 NO compression
Education + adherence essential
Hosiery (class 2 — 23-32 mmHg at ankle) for healed ulcer maintenance — REDUCES RECURRENCE 50%+
WOUND CARE:
CLEANSING: tap water or saline (don't use hydrogen peroxide / iodine routinely — cytotoxic)
DRESSINGS based on wound bed:
Heavy exudate: alginate or foam
Moderate exudate: hydrocolloid or foam
Dry wound: hydrogel
Sloughy: hydrogel / autolytic debridement
Necrotic: sharp debridement + hydrogel
Infected: silver dressing (short course)
Granulating: non-adherent (Mepitel, Adaptic)
Manage maceration with skin barrier (zinc oxide / Cavilon)
Honey-impregnated dressings — useful in low-resource settings + chronic non-healing
DEBRIDEMENT:
Sharp / surgical for necrotic + slough (specialist)
Autolytic (hydrogel) most common
Enzymatic + biological (maggot) selected
INFECTION:
Critical contamination (delayed healing without classic signs) — topical antimicrobial (silver, iodine — short course)
Cellulitis (spreading erythema + warmth + fever + raised WCC/CRP) — systemic antibiotic (flucloxacillin or co-amoxiclav)
Severe — admit + IV antibiotics
AVOID routine antibiotic for colonisation
AVOID empirical without culture in chronic non-healing
ADJUNCTS:
PENTOXIFYLLINE 400 mg TDS PO — Cochrane evidence improves healing
Skin grafts for large + chronic + non-healing
Negative pressure wound therapy (VAC) — for complex / cavitating
Bilayer skin substitutes (Apligraf)
Hyperbaric oxygen — selected

Paracetamol + NSAID
Neuropathic adjuncts (gabapentin, amitriptyline)
Topical lidocaine before dressing change
Limit opioids
ADDRESS UNDERLYING VENOUS DISEASE:
Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA) or radiofrequency for incompetent superficial veins (EVRA trial — EARLIER ablation improves healing + reduces recurrence)
Sclerotherapy
Open surgery (stripping) — declining
Compression hosiery for maintenance after healing
EDUCATION:
Adherence to compression (single most important)
Elevate legs (heart-level when seated)
Mobilise (calf muscle pump)
Avoid prolonged sitting / standing
Smoking cessation
Weight management
Skin care + emollient
Recurrence prevention with hosiery
PEDIATRIC: venous ulcer rare; investigate venous malformation / hypercoagulability
SPECIALIST REFERRAL:
Mixed arterial-venous (ABPI 0.5-0.8) — vascular
Pure arterial (ABPI < 0.5) — vascular urgent
Suspected malignancy — biopsy
Failure to heal at 12 weeks despite optimal compression — vascular + dermatology + tissue viability
Atypical (vasculitis, autoimmune) — appropriate specialist
Recurrent — endovenous procedure

Tissue viability nurse-led often
GP + community nurse + dietetics + pain + vascular + dermatology + psychology

Honey + simple dressings + compression bandages access
Train primary care + community on compression assessment + delivery
Address co-morbid TB / HIV / lymphoedema + sickle cell ulcers + tropical ulcers

title: Comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) — multidimensional
population: Older adults — increasingly relevant SSA with longer life expectancy + emerging non-communicable disease burden. Multimorbidity (≥ 2 chronic conditions) in 60-80% of > 65 yr.
presentation: Routine assessment of older adult — proactive or reactive (admission, ER visit, functional decline, falls, new diagnosis). Goal: identify treatable problems + maintain function + align care with values.
redFlags: Recurrent falls (≥ 2 in 12 months or 1 with injury) — full falls assessment
End-stage frailty / dying trajectory — palliative care + advance care planning
diagnostics: CGA domains:
1. PHYSICAL HEALTH: chronic conditions, medications, sensory (vision, hearing), continence, weight + nutrition, sleep, pain
2. COGNITIVE: MoCA (preferred over MMSE — more sensitive MCI), 4AT for delirium, depression (GDS-15 / PHQ-9)
3. FUNCTIONAL: ADL (Katz, Barthel), IADL (Lawton), gait + balance (Timed Up and Go, Tinetti, Berg)
4. SOCIAL: living situation, caregiver, finances, social support, isolation, abuse
5. ENVIRONMENTAL: home hazards, accessibility, modifications
6. VALUES + PREFERENCES: advance care planning, goals of care, code status, lasting power of attorney
7. FRAILTY: Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS 1-9), Fried phenotype (weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow gait, low activity)
8. POLYPHARMACY: STOPP/START criteria, deprescribing review, anticholinergic burden
9. NUTRITION: MNA (Mini Nutritional Assessment), unintentional weight loss
10. END-OF-LIFE: surprise question 'would you be surprised if this patient died in the next 12 months?'
management: MULTIDISCIPLINARY TEAM (CGA gold standard):
Geriatrician + primary care + nurse + physio + OT + SLT + dietitian + pharmacist + social worker + palliative care
Coordinated care plan
Patient + family-centred
FOCUS BY DOMAIN:
CHRONIC DISEASE optimisation:
Individualise targets (HbA1c 53-64 instead of 48 for frail; BP 130-140 vs strict 120-130; LDL liberalised)
Continue evidence-based therapy where benefits exceed risks (statins, anticoagulants, GDMT for HF) — but reassess in frail
Deprescribe drugs with diminishing benefit / increasing harm
POLYPHARMACY (≥ 5 medications — common):
STOPP/START criteria — toolkit for prescribing in elderly
Beers Criteria (American Geriatrics Society) — potentially inappropriate medications in older adults
DEPRESCRIBE — systematic review + reduce / stop / switch
Anticholinergic burden (ACB score) — reduce cumulative anticholinergic (cognition + falls)
Polypharmacy reviewed at every contact
FALLS PREVENTION (separate condition)
COGNITIVE: screen + treat reversible + dementia management (separate)
DEPRESSION: SSRI (sertraline, mirtazapine for sleep+appetite), CBT, social engagement
CONTINENCE: bladder diary + treat reversible (UTI, constipation, drugs, prolapse, atrophic) + bladder training + anticholinergic / β3 agonist
NUTRITION: MNA + dietitian referral + ONS (oral nutritional supplements) for malnourished; address sarcopenia + protein 1.0-1.2 g/kg/d + resistance exercise
PHYSICAL ACTIVITY: aerobic + resistance + balance + flexibility (Otago programme — falls reduction)
SOCIAL: address isolation, befriending, community programmes, transport
ENVIRONMENT: home assessment OT, modifications (grab bars, ramps, lighting, removing rugs)
SENSORY: hearing aids (reduce dementia risk — Lancet Commission 2024), vision optimisation
SLEEP: hygiene > hypnotic; CBT-I; treat OSA; avoid benzodiazepine + Z-drug
CARER assessment + respite + support (caregivers also screened — depression, burden)
ADVANCE CARE PLANNING:
Discuss goals, values, treatment limitations EARLY
Lasting power of attorney / advance decision
Resuscitation status (DNACPR)
Place of care preferences
Document + share with family + team
VACCINATIONS: pneumococcal, annual flu, COVID, shingles (Shingrix), RSV (≥ 60), Tdap booster
ABUSE / NEGLECT: screen + safeguarding (Kenya — older persons protection laws)
SETTINGS:
Outpatient CGA — primary care or specialist geriatric clinic
Inpatient CGA — admission for older adult (multiple RCTs show reduced mortality + institutionalisation + better function)
Community CGA — home visiting + integrated care
Emergency department geriatric pathways
MODELS OF CARE:
Geriatric Day Hospital
Hospital at Home
Frailty Hubs / Acute Frailty Units
Integrated care
Telemedicine / remote monitoring
WHO ICOPE (Integrated Care for Older People) — 6 domain assessment (cognition, mobility, malnutrition, vision, hearing, mood) — primary care + community level + LMIC suitable
POPULATION:
Healthy ageing — public health (WHO Decade 2021-2030)
Mid-life prevention (CV, dementia, falls)
Kenya MOH National Policy on Older Persons + emerging geriatric services

title: Falls in older adults — multifactorial assessment + prevention
population: 30% of > 65 + 50% of > 80 fall annually; major cause of disability + fracture (hip) + dependence + death. Multifactorial in elderly.
presentation: Single fall, recurrent falls, fall with injury, fear of falling (limits activity), near-falls, syncope-related (different — separate workup).
redFlags: Hip fracture (Garden / Pauwels) — surgical < 36 hours best outcomes
Head injury on anticoagulant (low threshold CT)
Subdural haematoma (delayed presentation after minor head injury, especially anticoagulated)
Syncope (cardiac, vasovagal, orthostatic, situational) — different workup
Recurrent falls > 1 in 12 months — full multifactorial assessment
diagnostics: FALLS HISTORY: where, when, witnesses, what doing, prodrome, LOC, injury, frequency, environment
Targeted history: medications (especially psychoactive, antihypertensives, hypoglycaemic), comorbidities, alcohol
Examination: gait (Timed Up and Go > 12 sec abnormal), balance (functional reach, Berg), strength (chair rise), neuro, postural BP, cognition (MoCA)
Cardiovascular: ECG, postural BP (lying + standing 1 and 3 min — drop > 20/10 = orthostatic), carotid sinus massage (if appropriate), 24h Holter / loop recorder for syncope
Bone: DEXA (FRAX risk + osteoporosis treatment); vitamin D + Ca + PTH
Cognition: MoCA, GDS
Sensory: visual acuity, audiometry
Environmental: home assessment (OT)
Foot + footwear assessment
Continence
Polypharmacy review
Frailty + sarcopenia assessment
Imaging post-fall: skull (head injury + anticoagulant — low threshold CT), spine (back pain), hip (pain / unable to weight bear), pelvis (elderly + lateral fall + trochanter pain)
management: MULTIFACTORIAL INTERVENTIONS (most effective — Cochrane):
EXERCISE — primary prevention; resistance + balance + tai chi:
Otago Programme (home exercise — physiotherapist-led) — gold standard
Group balance + tai chi — community programmes
> 3 hours/week
Lifelong
HOME MODIFICATION (OT-led):
Grab bars (bathroom, toilet)
Ramps + handrails on stairs
Remove loose rugs, cords
Improve lighting
Bedside commode if nocturia
Stair lift
Pendant alarm / fall detector
MEDICATION REVIEW + DEPRESCRIBING (especially psychoactive):

Withdraw or minimise: benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, opioids, antipsychotics, anticholinergics, antidepressants (especially TCA), antihypertensives causing orthostatic, sedating antihistamines, muscle relaxants, hypoglycaemic + sulfonylureas
Use STOPP/START + Beers + ACB score
Address polypharmacy
VISION:
Optimise (cataract surgery — first eye especially)
Update glasses
Avoid bifocal/varifocals on stairs
FOOTWEAR + FOOT CARE:
Properly fitting closed-toed shoes, low heels, non-slip soles
Avoid walking in socks alone or slippers without backs
Podiatry — corn / nail care + foot deformity
CARDIOVASCULAR:
Postural hypotension: stop offending drugs, hydration, salt liberalise (if no HF), compression stockings, head-up sleeping, fludrocortisone, midodrine, droxidopa
Bradyarrhythmia / heart block / sick sinus → pacemaker
Carotid sinus hypersensitivity → pacemaker
AF + heart failure optimisation
BONE HEALTH:
Vitamin D 800-1000 IU + calcium 1000-1200 mg
DEXA + FRAX
Bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg/wk) for osteoporosis + high fracture risk
Zoledronic acid IV annually if oral not tolerated
Denosumab 60 mg SC q6mo (lifelong — rebound fracture if stopped without bisphosphonate cover)
Romosozumab (anti-sclerostin) — emerging severe osteoporosis
Teriparatide PTH analogue for severe / multiple fractures
Address falls + bone health concurrently (HIP PROTECTORS modest evidence)
COGNITION + MOOD: treat depression, dementia management
CONTINENCE: nocturia + urgency rush to toilet → bedside commode, treat
ALCOHOL + SUBSTANCE USE: address
POSTURAL HYPOTENSION: review medications, slow position change, hydration, fludrocortisone / midodrine if severe
EDUCATION + SAFETY:
Patient + family education
Falls action plan
Recognise prodrome (presyncope)
Pendant alarm
Don't get up in the dark
FALL WITH INJURY:
Trauma protocol — head injury + cervical spine + chest + abdo + pelvis + long bones
Anticoagulated + any head injury — CT head (lower threshold)
Hip fracture: surgical < 36h optimal (NICE NG124); concurrent medical optimisation
Vertebral fracture: pain control + osteoporosis treatment + monitor stability
Pelvic fracture (especially lateral compression in elderly): admit + analgesia + mobilise as able + DVT prophylaxis
FEAR OF FALLING:
Acknowledged + addressed (limits activity → deconditioning → more falls)
CBT + balance training + group activities
POST-FALL ASSESSMENT:
Multifactorial in all who fall ≥ 2× or fall with injury or report fear of falling
Refer falls clinic where available
Multidisciplinary input
POPULATION + PUBLIC HEALTH:
WHO Step Safely 2021
Falls prevention community programmes
Environmental modifications policy

title: Frailty — Clinical Frailty Scale + Fried phenotype + intervention
population: Increasingly recognised geriatric syndrome — affects 10% > 65, 30% > 85; cumulative deficits with age. Distinct from + overlapping with disability + comorbidity.
presentation: Sarcopenia + weakness + slowness + low activity + exhaustion + weight loss. Vulnerability to stressors → adverse outcomes (falls, delirium, hospitalisation, institutionalisation, mortality).
redFlags: CFS 5-6 (mildly to moderately frail) — needs comprehensive support
CFS 7-9 (severely / terminally frail) — palliative + care home / end-of-life pathway
Acute decompensation (delirium, immobility, dependence) from minor stressor
Suspected reversible cause (depression, anaemia, thyroid, hypoxia, infection, polypharmacy)
diagnostics: Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS — Rockwood) 1-9:
1: very fit (active, exercise regularly)
2: well (no active disease but exercise less)
3: managing well (well-controlled medical problems)
4: vulnerable (slowed up, fatigued)
5: mildly frail (more evident slowing, needs help with high-order IADL)
6: moderately frail (needs help with all outside activities + housekeeping)
7: severely frail (completely dependent for personal care)
8: very severely frail (totally dependent, approaching end of life)
9: terminally ill (life expectancy < 6 months)
Fried phenotype (frail = ≥ 3 of 5; pre-frail = 1-2):
1. Unintentional weight loss > 5 kg/year or > 5%
2. Self-reported exhaustion
3. Weakness (grip strength low)
4. Slow walking speed (< 0.8 m/s)
5. Low physical activity
Frailty Index (Rockwood) — counts deficits / total possible
PRISMA-7 / FRAIL scale / Edmonton Frail Scale — alternatives
Sarcopenia: SARC-F + DEXA / handgrip / muscle mass
Investigate underlying reversible: TSH, B12, FBC, U&E, vitamin D, depression, polypharmacy, sensory deficits, social
management: MULTIDIMENSIONAL (CGA approach):
EXERCISE (most evidence — even in advanced frailty):
RESISTANCE + AEROBIC + BALANCE
Strengthening (3×/week) — reverses sarcopenia
Tailored to ability (chair-based for severely frail)
Otago / FaME / Tai Chi / Pilates
Group + individual
Supervised initially → home maintenance
NUTRITION:
Protein 1.0-1.2 g/kg/d (1.2-1.5 in acute illness)
Adequate calories (1500-2000 kcal/d typical)
Address deficiencies — vitamin D 800-1000 IU + calcium, B12, iron
Oral nutritional supplements (ONS) for at-risk + malnourished
Dietitian referral
Address chewing, swallowing, taste, dental, mood, social barriers
Treat sarcopenia (combined exercise + protein)
DEPRESCRIBING + POLYPHARMACY:
Review + simplify regimen
STOPP/START + Beers + ACB
Liberalise targets (HbA1c, BP, lipids) per frailty trajectory
Withdraw drugs with diminishing benefit (statins in CFS 6+ if life expectancy short)
Stop anticholinergics where possible
Re-evaluate benefit:risk regularly
COMORBIDITY OPTIMISATION (individualised):
HF, COPD, DM, CVD — continue evidence-based therapy unless burden > benefit
Pain management
Continence
Sleep + sensory
MOOD + COGNITION:
Screen + treat depression (SSRI sertraline + non-pharm)
Cognitive screening + manage dementia
Social engagement + meaningful activity
FALLS PREVENTION (separate condition — strongly indicated)
ADVANCE CARE PLANNING:
Discuss values, goals of care
Treatment escalation plan (TEP / RESPECT — Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment)
DNACPR + ceilings of care
Lasting power of attorney
Place of care preferences
Document + share
CARER SUPPORT:
Caregiver assessment + needs
Respite care
Support groups
Education on dementia, falls, end-of-life
Address burnout + depression in caregivers
INTEGRATED CARE:
Multidisciplinary team
Care coordination
Hospital-at-home / virtual ward
Frailty hubs
Day hospital
Community services + home care
Avoidance of unnecessary hospitalisation (high risk of delirium + deconditioning + nosocomial)
Telehealth + remote monitoring
Single point of access
END-OF-LIFE CARE (CFS 7-9 or estimated < 12 months):
Surprise question
Symptom-focused
Palliative care input
Hospice referral
Bereavement support
VACCINATIONS: pneumococcal, annual flu, COVID, shingles (Shingrix), RSV (≥ 60), Tdap

title: Delirium — recognition + management (4AT + CAM)
population: 20% of older medical inpatients; 50-80% of ICU patients; 30-50% post-op older surgical patients; under-recognised. Strongly associated with morbidity + mortality + functional decline + dementia onset.
presentation: Acute onset (hours-days) + fluctuating disturbance of attention + awareness + cognition. Hyperactive (agitated, hallucinating — easier to spot), HYPOACTIVE (withdrawn, drowsy — often missed, worse prognosis), mixed. Triggered by stressor (infection, drug, dehydration, pain, hypoxia, electrolyte, retention).
redFlags: Hypoactive delirium — easily missed, worse outcomes than hyperactive
Underlying cause requiring urgent treatment (sepsis, MI, stroke, hyperglycaemia, hypoglycaemia, withdrawal)
Delirium superimposed on dementia (DSD) — high mortality
diagnostics: 4AT (4 'A's test) — bedside, validated, < 2 min:
1. ALERTNESS (normal vs altered)
2. AMT-4 (age, DOB, place, year — 0-4 errors)
3. ATTENTION (months backward Dec → Jul)
4. ACUTE CHANGE / FLUCTUATING COURSE (collateral)
Score: 0 normal, 1-3 possible cognitive impairment, ≥ 4 likely delirium
CAM (Confusion Assessment Method) — alternative, more detailed
Identify TRIGGERS — multifactorial usually:
Drugs (NEW or DOSE CHANGE) — opioid, benzo, anticholinergic, steroid, antibiotic, withdrawal
Infection (UTI, pneumonia, sepsis, meningitis)
Metabolic — Na, glucose, Ca, urea, ammonia
Hypoxia (PaO2 < 60 / sats < 90)
Pain (often undertreated)
Retention urinary or faecal
Sleep deprivation
Sensory deprivation
Hospital environment
Substance withdrawal
Stroke / TIA / seizure (post-ictal)
Subdural haematoma (especially after fall)
Cardiac (MI, arrhythmia, HF)
Wernicke's (thiamine deficiency — alcohol, malnutrition)

Workup: FBC, U&E, glucose, calcium, LFT, ammonia, TSH, B12, urinalysis + culture, blood culture if febrile, CXR, ECG, ABG if hypoxia, drug screen, CT head if focal neurology / suspected SDH / new fall
management: PREVENTION (most effective):
HELP (Hospital Elder Life Program) + multicomponent non-pharmacological:
Frequent reorientation + cognitive stimulation
Sleep hygiene (quiet at night, no waking for non-essential)
Mobilisation early + frequent
Visual + hearing aids on (glasses, hearing aids)
Hydration + nutrition
Pain management
Avoid unnecessary catheters / restraints / lines
Reduces delirium 30%+
MANAGEMENT (established):
IDENTIFY + TREAT CAUSE (essential):
Treat infection + sepsis
Stop / reduce contributing drugs (especially psychoactive)
Correct electrolytes + glucose + hypoxia
Address pain (opioid carefully — paracetamol first; opioid for severe — but morphine itself can worsen)
Treat urinary retention + constipation
Thiamine 100 mg IV/IM × 3 days for any alcohol / malnutrition
Treat withdrawal (benzodiazepine for alcohol; gradual opioid taper)
NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL (first-line):
Quiet, low-stimulus environment
Single room, consistent staff, familiar objects, photos
Family presence
Reorient (clock, calendar, light, reassurance)
Mobilise + sit up + meals + structured day
Sleep hygiene — quiet night, dark, daytime light
Hearing aids + glasses
Hydration + nutrition + pressure care
Address constipation + retention
AVOID restraints (worsens agitation, complications)
PHARMACOLOGICAL (only when essential — severe agitation, danger to self/others, distressing hallucinations):
HALOPERIDOL 0.5-1 mg PO/IM/SC (lower in frail / Lewy / Parkinson — AVOID typical antipsychotic in Lewy body / Parkinson; use clozapine / quetiapine)
Olanzapine 2.5-5 mg PO/IM, risperidone 0.25-0.5 mg PO — atypical alternatives
DEXMEDETOMIDINE for ICU + ventilated (less delirium than benzodiazepine)
AVOID BENZODIAZEPINES (worsen delirium) EXCEPT for alcohol withdrawal, seizures, severe ETOH-naive presentations
QTc check before antipsychotic; minimise dose + duration; reassess daily
Document indication + plan
Avoid polypharmacy + iatrogenic worsening
DELIRIUM SUPERIMPOSED ON DEMENTIA (DSD):
High suspicion in dementia patient with new acute change
Same workup + management
Family + care home staff input on baseline
POST-DELIRIUM:
Follow-up — many have persistent cognitive effects 6-12 months
Reassess dementia (delirium can unmask)
Functional rehabilitation
Family + patient education + counselling (delirium is traumatic — PTSD-like)
Memory clinic referral if persistent
POST-ICU DELIRIUM:
ABCDEF bundle (Awakening + Breathing + Coordination + Delirium monitor + Early mobilise + Family)
PADIS guidelines for sedation + analgesia + delirium
Reduced sedation + earlier mobilise
PERIOPERATIVE:
Pre-op CGA + risk stratification (frailty, cognitive baseline)
Avoid drugs that increase risk (benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, polypharmacy)
Spinal vs general — modest evidence for spinal in hip fracture
Intra-op: maintain BP, glucose, depth of anaesthesia monitoring
Post-op: HELP, early mobilise, pain control, sleep hygiene
Kenya / SSA: under-recognised; train primary care + CHV + ward staff

title: Hip fracture (elderly) — < 36h surgery + ortho-geriatric pathway
population: Elderly osteoporotic fracture — substantial morbidity + mortality (20-30% 1-year mortality). Major SSA burden as ageing population + osteoporosis under-recognised.
presentation: Fall (often from standing height) → hip pain + inability to weight bear + shortened externally rotated leg. Intracapsular (femoral neck — risk avascular necrosis if displaced) vs extracapsular (intertrochanteric, subtrochanteric — DHS / IMN).
redFlags: Hemodynamic instability — internal bleeding (femoral fracture loss up to 1.5 L)
Concurrent injuries (cervical spine, head, chest, abdomen, pelvis)
Heart failure / cardiac instability — optimise but don't delay surgery
Pathological fracture (atypical mechanism / age / cancer history)
diagnostics: Plain hip X-ray AP + lateral (cross-table or frog-leg)
MRI if negative X-ray but high clinical suspicion (occult fracture — common in elderly)
CT alternative if MRI not available
Garden classification (intracapsular): I non-displaced incomplete, II non-displaced complete, III displaced incomplete, IV displaced complete
AO/OTA classification (extracapsular)
Bloods: FBC, group + crossmatch, U&E, glucose, ECG, troponin if cardiac risk
CGA + frailty assessment
DEXA at follow-up (osteoporosis confirmation + treatment)
Vitamin D + Ca + PTH
management: ED + ADMISSION:
Triage as major trauma if mechanism + age suspect
Analgesia: paracetamol + NSAID + opioid; FASCIA ILIACA BLOCK (single-injection ultrasound-guided — strongly recommended; reduces opioid + delirium) — RCEM standard
IV fluid resuscitation
Group + crossmatch + transfuse if Hb < 80 / haemodynamic compromise (restrictive — FOCUS trial)
Reverse anticoagulation per local protocol
Catheter if needed (avoid prolonged)
Pressure care + VTE prophylaxis with LMWH
Admit to dedicated hip fracture unit / ortho-geriatric ward
PRE-OP OPTIMISATION (don't delay surgery for minor abnormalities — overall risk worse with delay):
Anaesthetic + ortho + geriatric assessment
Echo only if cardiac symptoms / signs (not routine)
Optimise within 24-36h max
CONTRAINDICATIONS to surgery (rare): patient choice, active sepsis without source control, dying trajectory
Best Practice Tariff (NICE NG124) — < 36h surgery improves outcomes
SURGICAL MANAGEMENT (within 36 hours):
INTRACAPSULAR — Garden I-II (undisplaced): cannulated hip screws (CHS) — preserves head; high rate of failure if displaced
INTRACAPSULAR — Garden III-IV (displaced) — most cases:
HEMIARTHROPLASTY (cemented) — first-line for elderly + low demand
TOTAL HIP REPLACEMENT (THR) — independent / mobile / younger / pre-existing hip OA (NICE recommends THR over hemi if independent + cognitively fit)
EXTRACAPSULAR (intertrochanteric / subtrochanteric):
DYNAMIC HIP SCREW (DHS) — intertrochanteric stable
INTRAMEDULLARY NAIL (cephalomedullary, e.g. PFN, Gamma) — subtrochanteric, unstable inter, reverse oblique
ANAESTHESIA:
Spinal vs general — modest evidence for spinal benefit (less delirium per recent trials; REGAIN trial 2021 — no difference); shared decision
Avoid sedatives + benzodiazepines
Multimodal analgesia (peripheral blocks + paracetamol + NSAID + opioid)
POST-OP:
ORTHO-GERIATRIC co-management (multidisciplinary — surgeon + geriatrician + nurse + physio + OT)
EARLY MOBILISATION — within 24h post-op (weight-bear as tolerated — critical)
Physiotherapy daily
Pain control (multimodal)
Nutrition + ONS
Pressure care
Bowel + bladder management
VTE prophylaxis (LMWH or DOAC) × 28-35 days (extended prophylaxis post-hip fracture)
Delirium prevention (HELP)
Address polypharmacy + falls + cognitive decline + sensory + bone health
Goals of care discussion
Discharge planning early (rehabilitation pathway)
BONE HEALTH (secondary prevention — DON'T MISS):
All osteoporotic fracture in > 50 = osteoporosis (no need for DEXA confirmation before treatment per FLS — Fracture Liaison Service)
Vitamin D 800-1000 IU + calcium 1000-1200 mg/day

BISPHOSPHONATE (alendronate 70 mg/wk PO or zoledronic acid 5 mg IV annually for first 3-5 years — RECOVERS NEJM ZA after hip fracture) — STARTS within first week post-op (RECOVERY trial — does NOT delay union)
Denosumab if oral intolerant / CKD
Romosozumab for severe / multiple fractures
Teriparatide for severe high-fracture risk
Fracture Liaison Service (FLS) referral — coordinates assessment + treatment
FALLS PREVENTION (separate condition — strongly indicated)
ADVANCE CARE PLANNING + REHABILITATION:
Pre-fracture function (Barthel)
Realistic recovery goals
Discharge — home with rehab vs intermediate care vs care home
Family involvement
Hospice if dying trajectory
OUTCOMES:
20-30% 1-year mortality (highest first 3 months)
50% never regain pre-fracture function
Significant institutionalisation rate
Best outcomes with co-managed pathway

title: Polypharmacy — STOPP/START + Beers + deprescribing systematic
population: Elderly + multimorbidity. Polypharmacy (≥ 5 medications) in 30-40% > 65; ≥ 10 in 20%. Inappropriate prescribing in 20-50% by various criteria.
presentation: Routine medication review trigger: ≥ 5 medications, frailty, falls, delirium, cognitive decline, adverse drug event, transition of care, advance care planning.
redFlags: Adverse drug event / hospital admission attributable
Renal / hepatic impairment + drugs requiring adjustment
diagnostics: MEDICATION RECONCILIATION at every visit / transition (admission, discharge, change in care)
Comprehensive list — prescription + OTC + supplements + herbal + recreational
Identify duplicates, dose discrepancies, interactions
STOPP (Screening Tool of Older People's Potentially inappropriate Prescriptions) — what NOT to prescribe
START (Screening Tool to Alert to Right Treatment) — what SHOULD be prescribed but isn't
Beers Criteria (AGS) — potentially inappropriate medications in older adults
FORTA (Fit fOR The Aged)
PRISCUS list (German)
Anticholinergic burden (ACB score) — cumulative anticholinergic load (cognition + falls)
Renal function (eGFR) — dose adjust
Hepatic function
Allergy + adverse drug reaction history
Adherence: self-report, electronic refill data, pill count, family input
Goals of care + life expectancy (informs treatment burden)
management: SYSTEMATIC REVIEW + DEPRESCRIBING PROCESS:
1. RECONCILE: comprehensive medication list
2. REVIEW: indication, efficacy, safety, adherence, ADRs
3. PRIORITISE: which can be reduced / stopped / switched
4. PLAN: with patient + family + multidisciplinary
5. TAPER: most drugs need gradual taper (especially psychoactive, steroid, antihypertensive — avoid rebound)
6. MONITOR: for benefit + adverse effects post-deprescribe
7. DOCUMENT + COMMUNICATE: between prescribers, in shared records
STOPP CRITERIA — STOP candidates (most evidence-based):
Long-term benzodiazepine (> 4 weeks) — falls + cognitive + dependence
Z-drugs (zolpidem, zopiclone) — similar concerns
Long-term oral steroid for COPD / OA (not RA)
Long-term PPI > 8 weeks at full dose without ongoing indication
Long-term aspirin in primary CV prevention (low risk) — net harm without IHD
TCA (especially amitriptyline) — anticholinergic + falls
First-gen antihistamine (chlorphenamine, diphenhydramine) — anticholinergic
Anticholinergic for OAB without cognitive monitoring
NSAID with significant CV / GI / renal risk
Loop diuretic for ankle oedema without HF
Antipsychotic in dementia (BBW — limit)
Combination of multiple anticholinergics
Sulfonylureas (long-acting glibenclamide) — hypoglycaemia risk
Theophylline (narrow therapeutic + drug interactions)
START CRITERIA — START candidates often missing:
Statin for established ASCVD in patient with > 5 yr life expectancy
ACE-i / ARB for HF, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy
β-blocker for stable angina
Anticoagulant for AF CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 2
Vitamin D + calcium for osteoporosis
Bisphosphonate / denosumab for osteoporosis + fragility fracture
ASA + statin post-MI
PPI for chronic NSAID / antiplatelet with risk factors
Folate + iron in IDA
Influenza + pneumococcal vaccines
INDIVIDUAL CASE: balance benefit vs harm against life expectancy + goals
Statin in 90-year-old with limited life expectancy — usually deprescribe
Tight glycaemic control / BP in frail elderly — liberalise (HbA1c 64 instead of 48; BP 140-150 instead of 130)
Anticoagulant — continue for AF unless very high falls risk with documented benefit < harm calculation
Aspirin in primary prevention — withdraw in elderly (ASPREE)
Statin in primary prevention > 75 yr — individualise (STAREE trial pending)
ANTICHOLINERGIC BURDEN (ACB):
Score each medication (0-3)
Total ACB > 3 = increased dementia + falls + delirium
Cumulative review: anticholinergics for OAB, antihistamine, TCA, antipsychotic, antispasmodic, antiemetic, opioid
Switch to lower-burden alternative (mirabegron β3 instead of anticholinergic; SSRI not TCA; melatonin not benzo)
PRESCRIBING CASCADE:
Adverse effect of one medication treated as new diagnosis with another medication
Examples: anticholinergic constipation → laxative; CCB ankle oedema → diuretic; antipsychotic Parkinson's → levodopa; metoclopramide Parkinson's → dopamine agonist
Recognise + reverse
ADHERENCE OPTIMISATION:
Simplify (once-daily where possible)
Combination tablets
Dosette / blister pack
Smart pillboxes
Carer involvement
Cost (generic, formulary)
Cultural beliefs + traditional medicine
Mental health + cognitive issues addressed
DEPRESCRIBING APPROACH (patient-centred):
Discuss with patient + family
Identify low-priority / high-risk drugs
One at a time taper
Monitor for benefit + adverse effects (withdrawal, recurrence)
Document
Reassess
END-OF-LIFE:
Significantly reduce medication burden
Stop preventive (statin, anti-hypertensive, antidiabetic — many)
Continue symptom-focused (analgesic, antiemetic, antianxiety, antidepressant)
Convert oral to SC infusion when can't swallow (syringe driver)
Anticipatory prescribing
TOOLS + RESOURCES:
Deprescribing.org / Bruyere
STOPP/START app
ACB Calculator
Medstopper
RxRisk-V
Frailty-adjusted prescribing per CGA
MULTIDISCIPLINARY: GP + pharmacist + geriatrician + specialist + patient + family
PHARMACIST review — major value-add (clinical pharmacist embedded in primary care + hospital)
EHR-enabled review + alerts
Kenya / SSA: pharmacy access + cost + traditional medicine + adherence; integrate into NCD chronic care; train primary care + community pharmacy

title: Osteoporosis — DEXA + FRAX + bisphosphonate / denosumab / romosozumab
population: Postmenopausal women + men > 50. SSA: under-diagnosed + under-treated; rising burden as ageing + urbanising population. Lifetime fracture risk 1 in 2 women + 1 in 5 men > 50.
presentation: Asymptomatic until fracture — fragility fracture from low-energy trauma (standing height fall); height loss > 4 cm; kyphosis; back pain (vertebral fracture often silent).
redFlags: Suspected secondary cause (Cushing, hyperparathyroidism, malabsorption, hypogonadism, myeloma, RA, CKD, hyperthyroidism, drug-induced — long-term steroid / aromatase inhibitor / GnRH agonist / SGLT2i bone loss / PPI weak association)
Atypical femur fracture on long-term bisphosphonate (subtrochanteric, transverse — STOP bisphosphonate)
Osteonecrosis of jaw on bisphosphonate / denosumab (dental review pre-treatment)
Severe osteoporosis (T-score < -3.5 / multiple fractures / very high FRAX) — anabolic therapy
diagnostics: DEXA (Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry) — hip + lumbar spine
T-score (vs young adult): normal > -1, osteopenia -1 to -2.5, osteoporosis ≤ -2.5
Z-score (age-matched) — useful younger / men
FRAX — 10-year probability major osteoporotic fracture + hip fracture (validated by country including Kenya)
Treat if FRAX > 20% major / 3% hip (NOF/NICE thresholds — vary by country)
Vertebral fracture assessment (VFA) on DEXA or lateral spine X-ray for height loss
FBC, U&E, calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, 25-OH vitamin D, PTH, TSH, testosterone (men), urinary calcium
Secondary cause workup if young / unexpected / atypical: SPEP/IFE (myeloma), AM cortisol / DST (Cushing), tTG IgA (coeliac), 24h urine free cortisol
Coexistent fragility fracture confirms osteoporosis regardless of DEXA
management: NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL (ALL):
CALCIUM 1000-1200 mg/d (diet preferred — dairy, leafy greens, fortified; supplement if intake low)
VITAMIN D 800-1000 IU/d (or 50,000 IU monthly if deficient)
WEIGHT-BEARING + RESISTANCE EXERCISE 3-5×/week (Tai Chi + balance — also reduces falls)
Smoking cessation
Limit alcohol (< 2 units/day women, < 3 men)
Adequate protein 1.0-1.2 g/kg/d (1.2-1.5 elderly)
Address falls (separate condition)
Adequate sunlight
PHARMACOLOGICAL (T-score ≤ -2.5 OR fragility fracture OR FRAX > threshold OR initiating long-term steroid):
FIRST-LINE — BISPHOSPHONATES (anti-resorptive):
ALENDRONATE 70 mg/week PO — most common, generic, well-tolerated
GI side effects (oesophagitis) — take with full glass water, upright × 30 min, empty stomach
Avoid eGFR < 35
Risedronate 35 mg/week PO
Ibandronate 150 mg/month PO or 3 mg IV q3 mo

ZOLEDRONIC ACID 5 mg IV ANNUALLY — preferred if oral intolerance / adherence concern / hip fracture (RECOVERY ZA after hip fracture); flu-like reaction common with first dose (premedicate paracetamol)
Duration: 5 years oral / 3 years IV initially; reassess for 'drug holiday' if low ongoing risk; longer for high-risk + low T-score + ongoing fractures
Side effects: GI, atypical femur fracture (rare; suspect with thigh pain), osteonecrosis of jaw (rare; dental review pre-treatment + good oral hygiene)
DENOSUMAB 60 mg SC q6 months (anti-RANKL):
Alternative for CKD (eGFR < 35) or bisphosphonate-intolerant
No drug holiday — rebound vertebral fractures if stopped without bisphosphonate cover (DON'T STOP WITHOUT BISPHOSPHONATE TRANSITION)
ONJ + atypical femur fracture risk similar to bisphosphonate
Hypocalcaemia risk in CKD — check Ca + vit D pre-dose
ROMOSOZUMAB (anti-sclerostin Evenity) — anabolic + anti-resorptive:
210 mg SC monthly × 12 months
Severe osteoporosis (T-score < -2.5 + fracture or multiple fractures)
Followed by bisphosphonate / denosumab (gains lost otherwise)
CV warning — recent MI / stroke contraindication (ARCH trial signal)
Expensive — limited access SSA
TERIPARATIDE (PTH 1-34) — anabolic:
20 mcg SC daily × 24 months max (lifetime)
Severe osteoporosis + multiple fragility fractures + failed first-line
Avoid Paget's, history of radiation, hypercalcaemia
Followed by anti-resorptive
ABALOPARATIDE — PTHrP analogue alternative
RALOXIFENE (SERM) — selected post-menopausal:
Reduces vertebral fracture + breast cancer risk
No hip fracture reduction; CV neutral; DVT risk; hot flushes
HRT — postmenopausal symptomatic with osteoporosis (separate consideration)
STRONTIUM RANELATE — limited use due to CV risk
GLUCOCORTICOID-INDUCED OSTEOPOROSIS:
Anyone on > 7.5 mg pred for > 3 months — bone protection
Calcium + vitamin D + bisphosphonate (or denosumab / teriparatide)
Particularly post-menopausal women + men > 50
MALE OSTEOPOROSIS:
Often secondary (hypogonadism, alcohol, glucocorticoid, hypercalciuria, myeloma)
Same medications + treat cause
PREMENOPAUSAL WOMEN:
Investigate secondary cause first
Bisphosphonate avoided unless severe / fractures + secondary cause treated
Lifestyle + cause-directed
PREGNANCY:
Bisphosphonates avoided (skeletal effects on fetus)
Vitamin D + calcium
MONITORING:
DEXA every 1-2 years on treatment
Bone turnover markers (CTX, P1NP) — useful adherence + response check
Adverse effects: dental (osteonecrosis), atypical femur fracture (thigh pain investigate), CV (romosozumab)
VERTEBRAL FRACTURE:
Pain control + activity / mobility
Vertebroplasty / kyphoplasty for severe / persistent pain — VERTOS / VAPOUR trials mixed (modest evidence)
Anti-osteoporotic therapy
Often silent → look for unrecognised on DEXA / VFA
FRACTURE LIAISON SERVICE (FLS) — multidisciplinary post-fracture systematic case-finding + assessment + treatment + adherence support; reduces secondary fractures + mortality
GLOBAL + SSA:
WHO osteoporosis position
Kenya MOH NCD Strategic Plan — emerging recognition
Access to bisphosphonates expanding; advocate for KEML + NHIF
Address vitamin D deficiency (high prevalence even in tropical countries — clothing, indoor lifestyle, dark skin pigmentation, traditional + modern food)
Calcium intake from local sources (kale, traditional vegetables)

title: Advance care planning + end-of-life — goals of care + DNACPR
population: Older adults + serious illness (advanced cancer, end-stage organ failure, advanced dementia, frailty CFS ≥ 7). Critical: discussing EARLY while capacity preserved.
presentation: Routine — best as part of CGA / chronic disease review / on diagnosis of life-limiting illness. Reactive — acute admission / decompensation / dying recognition. Surprise question 'would you be surprised if this patient died in the next 6-12 months?' — trigger.
redFlags: Patient lacks capacity — best-interest decision per Mental Capacity Act / equivalent local legislation
Patient + family disagree about goals of care
Cultural / religious + clinical tension in decision
diagnostics: Trigger: surprise question + frailty assessment + serious illness
Capacity assessment (decision-specific, time-specific)
Identify lasting power of attorney (LPA) / advance directive / health proxy
Values + preferences exploration (Serious Illness Conversation Guide — Ariadne Labs)
Cultural + religious + spiritual context
Prognosis estimation (clinician judgement + tools like PPS / PaP)
Identify family + key decision-makers
management: ADVANCE CARE PLANNING (proactive, while capacity intact):
Discuss EARLY — at diagnosis of serious illness, transitions, routine review
Explore patient values, preferences, goals
What matters most? Quality of life? Specific goals (attend event, see family)? Avoid (intubation, ICU, CPR, prolonged dying)?
Iterative — revisit at intervals + changes
ESSENTIAL QUESTIONS:
What is your understanding of your illness?
What concerns + hopes do you have?
What are you willing / not willing to go through?
What would a good outcome look like?
Who would you want to make decisions if you cannot?
Document — advance directive, LPA, treatment escalation plan (TEP / RESPECT / POLST), DNACPR
Share with family + multidisciplinary team + shared EHR + ambulance / out-of-hours services
DNACPR (Do Not Attempt CPR):
Decision based on clinical futility AND/OR patient wishes
Different from withholding other treatment (treat reversible conditions, palliative care, comfort)
Discuss with patient (if capacity) + family
Document clearly + share with team + ambulance + community + family
Reversible (e.g. acute infection) considerations
Tracey + Winspear judgments — communicate with patient unless evidence of significant harm
TREATMENT ESCALATION PLAN (TEP / RESPECT — Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment):
Broader than DNACPR — includes treatment decisions (admit ICU vs ward; intubate; dialysis; surgery; transfusion; antibiotic IV vs oral; ceilings of care)
Patient + family involved
Anticipate likely deteriorations + plan
GOALS OF CARE CONVERSATIONS (Ariadne Labs Serious Illness Conversation Guide):
Set up: 'I'd like to talk about your future health care'
Assess: 'What is your understanding of your illness? What information would be helpful?'
Share: prognosis (range), expected trajectory
Explore: values, fears, sources of strength
Plan: align treatment with values + document
Affirm + summarise
FAMILY + CAREGIVER:
Often surrogate decision-makers
Education + support
Address conflict / disagreement
Family meeting framework (SPIKES — Set up, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Empathy, Strategy)
Cultural mediators where needed
Spiritual + religious support (chaplain, imam, priest, traditional)
Bereavement preparation + after-death support
PALLIATIVE CARE INTEGRATION:
Early integration (NOT only end-of-life) — improves QoL + survival (Temel NEJM 2010 lung cancer)
Symptom management (separate condition — EoL comprehensive)
Communication + family meetings + spiritual care
Multidisciplinary
PLACE OF CARE / DEATH:
Patient preferences vary
Home — requires family support + 24/7 community + symptom control + anticipatory medications
Hospice — gold standard for dying patient in HIC
Hospital — if no other option / acute decompensation / family unable
Care home — for frail end-stage
Plan for transitions + access
Kenya: hospice movement growing (Hospice Africa Uganda + Kenya hospices); home-based community model
MENTAL CAPACITY:
Decision-specific + time-specific
Presumption of capacity
Test: understand, retain, weigh, communicate
Best-interest decision if lacking capacity (consult family + clinical team)
Kenya Mental Health Act + Children Act (parental responsibility)
ADVOCACY + RIGHTS:
Patient autonomy
Informed consent + refusal
Access to high-quality care + symptom control
Right to die at preferred location
Avoid unnecessary suffering
POPULATION + SSA:
Cultural variation in disclosure (some cultures protect from prognosis information)
Address with sensitivity + cultural mediators
Religious + traditional beliefs (death, afterlife, family obligations)
Limited palliative care + opioid access — advocate (separate condition)
Train primary care + community health workers + traditional leaders
Kenya Hospice + Palliative Care Association + KEHPRO + Kenya National Palliative Care Policy
Multidisciplinary + culturally tailored
STAFF SUPPORT:
Death + dying conversations emotionally demanding
Debrief after challenging deaths
Compassion fatigue + burnout prevention
Self-care + supervision
EDUCATION:
Communication skills training (VitalTalk, Serious Illness Conversation Guide)
Continuing professional development on EoL

title: Elder abuse + neglect — recognition + safeguarding
population: Estimated 10-15% of older adults globally experience some form of abuse — substantially under-reported. SSA: emerging recognition + customary law tensions; witchcraft accusations against older women (Kenya, Tanzania).
presentation: Physical (bruises in unusual locations, fractures, restraint marks); sexual; emotional (humiliation, threats, isolation); financial (unexplained loss of resources, sudden changes to will, prescribed medications missing); neglect (poor hygiene, dehydration, pressure ulcers, untreated medical conditions, weight loss); abandonment; self-neglect (capacity question).
redFlags: Multiple unexplained injuries in different stages of healing
Severe dehydration / malnutrition with caregiver present
Inconsistent history between patient + caregiver / story changes
Sudden financial changes (will, power of attorney, missing assets)
Severely demented patient with no clear caregiver protection
Witchcraft accusation against older woman (SSA cultural-specific)
diagnostics: PRIVATE interview WITHOUT caregiver if possible
Trauma-informed approach + empathy + believe patient
Document carefully (verbatim quotes, body map, photographs with consent + per protocol, witnesses, time)
Physical examination — head-to-toe + genital + skin + pressure points + dentition + hydration + nutrition
Cognitive + mental capacity assessment (separate from suspected abuse)
Depression / anxiety / PTSD screen
FBC, U&E, glucose, calcium, albumin, TFT, B12 — health status
Toxicology if intoxication / medication misuse suspected
Pregnancy + STI test if sexual abuse suspected
Financial review with family / banker / lawyer where appropriate (with consent / capacity)
Home safety + environmental assessment (OT, social work)
Identify support network — who else involved + who is safe
management: SAFETY FIRST:
Immediate safety planning — admit if necessary
Place of safety / respite
Multidisciplinary including social work + geriatric medicine + safeguarding lead + mental health if needed + legal aid
MANDATORY REPORTING (varies by jurisdiction):
UK: safeguarding referral via local authority (adult social care)
US: Adult Protective Services (APS) — mandatory in most states for healthcare professionals
Kenya: Children Act covers minor abuse; older persons protection via National Council for Persons with Disabilities + County Social Services; informal customary mechanisms
Document concerns + escalate per local protocol
ASSESSMENT OF ABUSE TYPE:
Physical: examination + imaging if fractures + photograph
Sexual: forensic examination per protocol + STI / HIV PEP + EC if within window
Emotional / psychological: history + counselling referral
Financial: legal + social work + capacity assessment + protect assets (LPA scrutiny)
Neglect: address basic needs urgently + safeguarding
Self-neglect: capacity assessment + multidisciplinary planning
Institutional: report to regulator (CQC UK; Kenya MOH inspectorate)
MENTAL CAPACITY (CRITICAL):
Decision-specific + time-specific
If capacity intact — respect patient wishes (even if returning to abusive situation; provide resources)
If capacity lacking — best-interest decision + safeguarding + may override autonomy
Court intervention sometimes needed (Court of Protection UK; Guardian / Kadhi in Kenya)
MULTIDISCIPLINARY:
Social work — coordinate care + assessment
Geriatric medicine — health assessment + capacity
Mental health — depression, PTSD, dementia
Legal — financial protection, restraining order
Police — physical / sexual abuse criminal
Family / community — assess if part of solution or problem
NGO support (Age UK, HelpAge International, Mosaic Africa)
Religious + community leaders (sensitively)
PSYCHOLOGICAL SUPPORT:
Counselling — trauma-focused CBT
Support groups
Address depression + anxiety + PTSD
Often complex feelings (love + fear of caregiver) — non-judgemental approach
CAREGIVER ASSESSMENT (perpetrators often family / caregivers — many face their own burdens):
Caregiver burden (Zarit Burden Interview)
Mental health + substance abuse + finance
Respite + support + education — address modifiable factors
Some abuse is intentional; some neglect from inability rather than intent
Separate child / older adult protection from caregiver support
PREVENTION:
Reduce isolation
Multi-generational engagement
Financial safeguards (LPA scrutiny, account monitoring)
Caregiver support + education
Anti-stigma + awareness campaigns
Community programmes for older adults (Kenya — community elders groups)
Address witchcraft accusations (sensitively — community education, religious leader engagement, customary mediation)
Inheritance + property rights protection (especially widows)
Older persons policy + legal framework
POPULATION + SSA:
WHO Toronto Declaration on Global Prevention of Elder Abuse 2002
Increasing recognition with ageing population
Kenya — Constitution Article 57 (protection of older members of society); Older Members of Society Act draft / policy framework
Address customary law + property rights + widows + witchcraft accusation
Community + religious leader engagement
Train healthcare workers + CHV + traditional birth attendants + faith leaders
HelpAge International + Mosaic Africa + national NGOs

title: Urinary incontinence — types + comprehensive management
population: Affects 30-50% of older adults; significantly more common in women + frail. Major impact on QoL + dignity + caregiver burden. Substantially under-reported.
presentation: STRESS (leak on cough / sneeze / exertion — pelvic floor weakness; common postmenopausal), URGE / OAB (sudden urgency + leak — detrusor overactivity; idiopathic or neurological), MIXED, OVERFLOW (chronic retention with overflow — BPH / neurogenic / outlet obstruction), FUNCTIONAL (cognitive / mobility — can't reach toilet in time). Reversible causes (DIPPERS — Delirium, Infection, Pharmaceuticals, Psychological, Endocrine, Restricted mobility, Stool impaction).
redFlags: Suspected cauda equina (back pain + incontinence + saddle anaesthesia + bilateral leg signs) — neurosurgical emergency
Haematuria (rule out bladder cancer — refer urology < 2 weeks)
Suspected fistula (continuous incontinence — vesicovaginal post-obstetric or surgical injury — common SSA)
diagnostics: History: pattern (stress vs urge vs mixed vs overflow), frequency / volume diary 3 days, fluid intake, triggers, quality of life impact, sexual function
DIPPERS reversible cause screen
Examination: abdomen (palpable bladder?), pelvic / DRE (BPH, prolapse, pelvic floor tone, faecal impaction)
Urinalysis + MSU (rule out UTI, glycosuria, haematuria)
Post-void residual bladder scan (PVR — > 100 ml suggests retention)
U&E + creatinine + glucose
Frequency / volume chart 3 days
Cough stress test
Pad test
Urodynamics — only for diagnostic uncertainty / pre-surgery / failed conservative
Cystoscopy if haematuria + risk factors
PSA in men with LUTS overlap
management: REVERSIBLE CAUSES (DIPPERS) — address first:
Delirium
Infection (UTI — treat)
Pharmaceuticals (diuretics, anticholinergics, opioids, alpha-blockers, calcium channel blockers, antipsychotics, alcohol, caffeine excess — review)
Psychological (depression)
Endocrine (diabetes — glycaemic, hypercalcaemia)
Restricted mobility — bedside commode, urinal, accessible toilet
Stool impaction — laxative + disimpaction
STRESS INCONTINENCE:
PELVIC FLOOR MUSCLE TRAINING (PFMT — Kegel exercises) — first-line; supervised by physiotherapist; 3 sets × 10 contractions daily; effective in 60-70%
Lifestyle: weight loss (highly effective), fluid management (avoid excess, especially evening), caffeine reduction, smoking cessation (cough)
Pessaries / continence devices for prolapse / functional incontinence
Topical vaginal oestrogen (postmenopausal — significant benefit for genitourinary syndrome)
Duloxetine (SNRI — modest benefit; nausea + insomnia + suicidality SE — limited use)
SURGICAL: mid-urethral sling (TVT) — gold standard; controversy over mesh complications; selected patients; Burch colposuspension; bulking agents (less effective + temporary)
URGE INCONTINENCE / OAB:
Bladder training (timed voiding + gradual interval extension) — first-line
Lifestyle: avoid bladder irritants (caffeine + alcohol + citrus + carbonated), regulate fluids, PFMT also

ANTIMUSCARINIC: oxybutynin (cheap; SE — dry mouth, constipation, cognitive — caution elderly + dementia), solifenacin (better tolerated), tolterodine, fesoterodine, trospium (no CNS penetration — better elderly)
β3-AGONIST: MIRABEGRON 50 mg/day (preferred elderly + cognitive concerns — less anticholinergic SE; SE — HTN, tachycardia)
Vibegron — newer β3
Combination antimuscarinic + mirabegron for refractory
BOTULINUM TOXIN A intravesical (100 units) — refractory OAB; risk of retention (need ISC) + UTI
Sacral nerve modulation (specialist) for refractory
Posterior tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS) — emerging
Augmentation cystoplasty — last resort
MIXED INCONTINENCE:
PFMT + bladder training + lifestyle
Address predominant component first
Antimuscarinic / β3 if urge predominant
Surgery for stress component
OVERFLOW INCONTINENCE:
Identify cause (BPH, neurogenic, outlet obstruction)
Catheterise initially if severe
Treat BPH (separate condition) — α-blocker + 5ARI
Intermittent self-catheterisation (ISC) for neurogenic
Indwelling catheter (suprapubic preferred) — last resort due to UTI / stone / urethral erosion
FUNCTIONAL INCONTINENCE:
Accessibility — bedside commode, urinal, raised toilet seat, clear path, adequate clothing, urgency cues
Toileting schedule (every 2-3h)
Cognitive support — prompted voiding for dementia
Caregiver education
Mobility aids
Continence products (pads, pants) — supportive only, not solution
SKIN CARE:
Barrier cream (zinc oxide, dimethicone)
Prompt change of incontinence pads
Avoid alkaline soap
Pressure care
Treat fungal / bacterial dermatitis (clotrimazole + hydrocortisone short-term)
FAECAL INCONTINENCE (often coexists):
Treat constipation + impaction
Dietary fibre + adequate fluids
Loperamide for diarrhoea-related
Pelvic floor exercises
Biofeedback
Specialist colorectal referral for refractory (sphincter repair, sacral nerve modulation)
VESICOVAGINAL FISTULA (SSA-specific):
Obstetric injury (prolonged obstructed labour) — continuous incontinence
Surgical repair at fistula centre — Kenya: KNH, Jamaa Mission, Fistula Foundation
Catheterisation early may close some recent < 6 weeks
Address prevention: skilled birth attendance + partogram + EmONC + Linda Mama
URINARY INCONTINENCE ASSOCIATED WITH DEMENTIA / FRAILTY:
Often functional / cognitive cause primarily
Toileting schedule + prompted voiding + caregiver support + accessible toilet
Continence aids
Avoid antimuscarinics if possible (worsen cognition)
Mirabegron preferred if pharmacological needed
Address comorbid sleep + behavioural + medical
POPULATION + SSA:
Major QoL + dignity issue + caregiver burden
Address stigma — many suffer in silence
Train primary care + community + nurse-led continence services
Pessaries + simple devices accessible
Fistula prevention + treatment programmes
Pad access (Kenya — limited NHIF coverage)

title: Hypothyroidism — comprehensive (subclinical, overt, central, congenital)
population: Common — 5% overt, 10-15% subclinical adults; female > male; rising globally including SSA (iodine, autoimmune, post-radiation, post-thyroidectomy).
presentation: Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, depression, hoarse voice, menorrhagia, bradycardia, slow-relaxing reflexes. Severe: myxoedema coma. Subclinical: raised TSH + normal free T4 + minimal symptoms.
redFlags: Myxoedema coma — emergency (hypothermia + altered mental state + hyponatraemia + hypoglycaemia + bradycardia + hypoventilation; mortality 25-60% if missed)
Pregnancy + uncontrolled hypothyroidism (fetal neurodevelopmental damage, miscarriage, pre-eclampsia)
Congenital hypothyroidism — newborn screening + treat within 2 weeks (cretinism prevention)
Suspected central hypothyroidism (low TSH + low free T4 — pituitary cause; investigate pituitary axis)
Coexistent adrenal insufficiency — give hydrocortisone BEFORE thyroxine (avoid adrenal crisis)
Cardiac disease + need rapid replacement — start LOW + slow titrate
diagnostics: TSH (most sensitive) + free T4 (free T3 not routine)
Anti-TPO + anti-Tg antibodies (Hashimoto's confirmation; > 90% chronic autoimmune)
Pregnancy test (women)
FBC (anaemia of chronic disease, B12 / iron deficiency overlap)
U&E + lipid + glucose + LFT (associated abnormalities — hypoNa, dyslipidaemia, raised CK)
Cortisol + ACTH if central / autoimmune polyglandular suspected
Vitamin D + Ca
Coeliac screen (autoimmune association)
Newborn TSH (universal screening — Kenya MOH planned)
Imaging only if nodule on examination (ultrasound) or compressive symptoms
management: OVERT HYPOTHYROIDISM (TSH > 10 OR symptomatic with raised TSH 4-10):
LEVOTHYROXINE (L-T4) — synthetic T4:
Adults < 60 + no cardiac: 1.5-1.7 mcg/kg/d (typical 100-150 mcg/d)
Elderly / cardiac: start 25-50 mcg/d, titrate every 4-6 weeks
Pregnancy: increase dose 25-30% first trimester (LATE trial — start increase as soon as pregnancy confirmed)
Empty stomach, 30-60 min before food / coffee / calcium / iron
Generic + branded — biosimilar levothyroxine acceptable per WHO + Kenya KEML
TARGET: TSH 0.4-2.5 (non-pregnant); 0.1-2.5 (pregnancy, especially first trimester)
RECHECK 6-8 weeks after dose change
Lifelong therapy
SUBCLINICAL HYPOTHYROIDISM (TSH 4-10, normal free T4):
Treat if: TSH > 10, anti-TPO+ + symptoms, pregnancy / fertility, < 65 yr with symptoms / cardiovascular risk, goitre
Observation acceptable in elderly without symptoms (TRUST trial 2017 — no benefit > 65 yr)
Reassess every 6-12 months
CENTRAL HYPOTHYROIDISM (pituitary cause — low TSH + low free T4):
Investigate pituitary axis (cortisol/ACTH first — adrenal insufficiency MUST be treated before thyroxine; otherwise precipitates adrenal crisis)
Imaging — MRI pituitary
Thyroxine titrated by free T4 (TSH is suppressed by hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction; target mid-upper normal range free T4)
Hormone replacement coordinated by endocrinology
Lifelong
PREGNANCY:
Pre-conception: optimise TSH < 2.5
Increase dose 25-30% as soon as pregnancy confirmed (extra 2 tablets/week from existing dose effective initial increase)
Monitor TSH every 4-6 weeks first half + every trimester
Postpartum: return to pre-pregnancy dose
Hypothyroid Hashimoto's — anti-TPO+ — increased miscarriage / preterm risk; selenium not routinely supplemented
Untreated hypothyroidism: fetal neurodevelopmental impact, miscarriage, pre-eclampsia, preterm — TREAT
Postpartum thyroiditis (5-10%): hyper then hypo then resolution; β-blocker symptom relief; some progress to permanent hypo
CONGENITAL HYPOTHYROIDISM:
Newborn screening (TSH heel-prick day 2-5; Kenya MOH planned national rollout)
Start L-T4 10-15 mcg/kg/day within 2 weeks of birth
Prevents cretinism (intellectual disability + growth failure)
Lifelong + endocrinology follow-up
MYXOEDEMA COMA (emergency):
ICU admission
IV L-T4 200-500 mcg loading then 50-100 mcg/d (or alternative IV L-T3 25-50 mcg q8h if available)
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h (BEFORE thyroxine — adrenal cover)
Warm gradually (passive — avoid rapid)
Identify + treat trigger (infection, MI, drugs)
Hydrocortisone, fluids cautious, glucose monitor + replace, treat hyponatraemia carefully
Mortality 25-60% even with treatment
DRUG INTERACTIONS:
Reduce absorption: PPI, calcium, iron, soy, fibre, cholestyramine, sucralfate (separate by 4h)
Increase requirement: oestrogen (OCP, HRT), pregnancy, malabsorption (coeliac, GI surgery)
Reduce requirement: weight loss, ageing, androgen, steroid
Amiodarone — both hyper + hypo possible (monitor TFT)
Lithium — induces hypothyroidism (15-30%)
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (sunitinib) — common
Immune checkpoint inhibitors — immune-related thyroiditis
HASHIMOTO'S THYROIDITIS:
Anti-TPO+ ± anti-Tg+, often female + family history
Often associated with other autoimmune (T1DM, Addison's, vitiligo, coeliac, alopecia)
Goitre often firm + bumpy
Some progress through hyperthyroid phase initially (Hashitoxicosis)
Long-term lymphoma risk (rare, MALT)
T3 + DESICCATED THYROID:
Combination T4/T3 — modest evidence (some patients prefer; physiological argument); not first-line; specialist consideration
Desiccated thyroid (Armour) — older formulation; variable bioavailability
Liothyronine (L-T3) — short half-life, more cardiac effects, mostly for compounded combo
MONITORING:
Stable on therapy: TSH annually
After dose change: 6-8 weeks
Pregnancy + sick day: more frequent
Lifelong + transition of care critical (continue L-T4 always)
POPULATION + SSA:
Iodine sufficiency — Kenya has universal salt iodisation; monitor (some areas deficient)
Newborn screening rollout
Generic L-T4 access via KEML
Awareness — symptoms overlap with anaemia + depression + chronic disease
