title: Hyperthyroidism / Graves — comprehensive management
population: Graves' (autoimmune — TSI/TRAb) most common cause (80%); toxic multinodular goitre + toxic adenoma; thyroiditis (post-partum, painful subacute, silent); iatrogenic (amiodarone, ICI, levothyroxine excess). Women > men 5-10:1.
presentation: Heat intolerance, sweating, weight loss + appetite increase, palpitations, tremor, anxiety / irritability, oligomenorrhoea, hair thinning, frequent stools, lid retraction / lag, tachycardia, AF (especially elderly), proximal muscle weakness, gynaecomastia. Graves'-specific: ophthalmopathy (orbital — protrusion + diplopia + lid retraction + chemosis), dermopathy (pretibial myxoedema), acropachy.
redFlags: Thyroid storm (decompensated thyrotoxicosis — separate condition; Burch-Wartofsky ≥ 45)
Active Graves' ophthalmopathy / severe / sight-threatening — refer urgent (ophth + endo MDT)
Pregnancy + hyperthyroidism (PTU 1st trim then switch to methimazole 2nd/3rd)
Suspected thyroid cancer (cold nodule on scan)
Subacute thyroiditis (painful — viral; supportive; NOT thionamide)
diagnostics: Suppressed TSH + raised free T4 (and / or free T3)
Anti-TSH receptor antibody (TRAb / TSI) — confirms Graves' (very specific)
Anti-TPO + anti-Tg (less specific — Hashitoxicosis transient hyper in Hashimoto's)
Thyroid radioactive iodine uptake scan (I-123 or Tc-99m pertechnetate):
Diffusely raised — Graves'
Patchy / focal — toxic nodular / adenoma
Low / absent — thyroiditis (destructive — leaking pre-formed hormone)
Thyroid ultrasound for nodules / vascularity
FBC + LFT + U&E (baseline before thionamide — agranulocytosis + hepatotoxicity)
ECG (AF + tachycardia)
Pregnancy test (women)
Bone density + DEXA (osteoporosis risk in chronic hyperthyroid)
management: INITIAL SYMPTOM RELIEF:
β-BLOCKER: propranolol 20-40 mg q8h OR atenolol 25-50 mg/d — controls symptoms (tachycardia, tremor, anxiety) within hours-days
Bisoprolol if asthma history (β1-selective)
AVOID in severe HF without optimisation
DEFINITIVE TREATMENT — 3 options (shared decision):
1. THIONAMIDE (anti-thyroid drug):
CARBIMAZOLE (UK) or METHIMAZOLE (US/EU) — preferred (longer half-life, less hepatotoxicity than PTU)
Start 10-40 mg/d titrated to euthyroidism (4-6 wk)
Maintenance 5-10 mg/d for 12-18 months (Graves' — 30-50% remission rate; toxic nodular — lifelong)
Block + replace alternative — high-dose thionamide + levothyroxine
PROPYLTHIOURACIL (PTU) — preferred FIRST TRIMESTER pregnancy (less teratogenic); thyroid storm (blocks T4 → T3 conversion)

Side effects: rash, arthralgia, GI; SERIOUS — AGRANULOCYTOSIS (sudden severe — STOP + FBC + admit if sore throat / fever / mouth ulcer), HEPATOTOXICITY (PTU worse, methimazole cholestatic), pancreatitis, vasculitis (ANCA), aplastic anaemia rare
Pregnancy:
First trimester PTU (carbimazole teratogenic — aplasia cutis, choanal atresia, oesophageal atresia)
Second + third trimesters: switch to methimazole/carbimazole (PTU hepatotoxicity)
Breastfeeding compatible (low transfer)
Target free T4 upper-normal (fetal hypothyroidism risk if maternal hypothyroid)
2. RADIOACTIVE IODINE (I-131):
Definitive for Graves', toxic nodular
Single oral dose → hypothyroidism (most patients) within 3-6 months
CONTRAINDICATED: pregnancy + breastfeeding + Graves' ophthalmopathy (worsens; if needed — steroid cover), severe + child under 5
Pregnancy avoidance × 6 months post; men 4 months
Post-RAI hypothyroidism requires LIFELONG levothyroxine — usually 4-6 months after dose
3. THYROIDECTOMY:
Indications: very large goitre / compressive symptoms; pregnancy 2nd trimester (selected); failed thionamide + RAI; thyroid cancer suspected; ophthalmopathy moderate-severe; patient choice
Total — definitive; hemithyroidectomy for unilateral toxic adenoma
Risks: hypoparathyroidism (transient + permanent), recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (hoarseness), haematoma, post-op hypothyroidism (lifelong LT4)
Pre-op euthyroidism with thionamide + Lugol's iodine 10 d before reduces vascularity
GRAVES' OPHTHALMOPATHY (TED — thyroid eye disease):
Mild: lubricants + cool compresses + selenium 100 mcg BD × 6 mo (CITED trial)
Moderate-severe active: IV methylprednisolone 500 mg/wk × 6 wk then 250 mg/wk × 6 wk (EUGOGO protocol) — cumulative 4.5 g; orbital radiotherapy adjunct
TEPROTUMUMAB (anti-IGF-1R) — TED Phase 3 trials (HZNP); transformative for active moderate-severe; expensive — limited SSA
Mycophenolate, rituximab, tocilizumab — alternatives
AVOID smoking (markedly worsens TED — smoking cessation single most important)
Orbital decompression / strabismus surgery for chronic / sight-threatening
AVOID radioactive iodine in active ophthalmopathy (worsens)
POSTPARTUM THYROIDITIS (5-10% of pregnancies):
Transient hyper phase 1-4 months postpartum → hypo phase → recovery (most)
β-blocker symptom relief in hyper phase
Levothyroxine if symptomatic hypo or persistent hypothyroidism
Anti-TPO+ predicts; higher recurrence subsequent pregnancies + lifetime permanent hypothyroidism
AMIODARONE-INDUCED THYROTOXICOSIS:
Type 1: AIIH — iodine-induced excess synthesis (pre-existing nodular goitre); thionamide effective
Type 2: AIDT — destructive thyroiditis (no underlying disease); steroid (prednisolone 40 mg) effective
Stop amiodarone if possible (long half-life — months)
Thyroidectomy for refractory / severe
ICI-INDUCED THYROIDITIS (immune checkpoint inhibitor):
Often transient hyper (β-blocker — no thionamide as destructive) → hypo (levothyroxine)
CONTINUE ICI (don't stop for thyroid irAE — easily managed)
ATRIAL FIBRILLATION in thyrotoxicosis:
Rate / rhythm control + ANTICOAGULATE per CHA2DS2-VASc
Usually reverts to sinus rhythm after euthyroid 4-6 mo (cardioversion considered then if persistent)
Treat hyperthyroidism definitively
PREGNANCY + GRAVES':
TSAb measurement at 22 + 36 weeks — fetal hyperthyroidism risk (TSAb crosses placenta)
Fetal monitoring (growth, heart rate)
Postnatal — neonatal hyperthyroidism (transient, treated by paediatrician)
BONE HEALTH: chronic hyperthyroidism causes osteoporosis — DEXA + Ca + vit D + bisphosphonate if indicated
Smoking cessation
Iodine excess avoidance (contrast / supplements) during active
Population SSA / Kenya:
Graves' relatively common
Carbimazole + propranolol + RAI + surgery available KEML
Iodine sufficiency check (salt iodisation)
Ophthalmology + endocrinology access expanding

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Thyroid nodule + cancer — ultrasound + FNA + management
population: Thyroid nodules common — palpable 4-7%, ultrasound 19-67% adults; cancer ~ 5%. SSA emerging awareness; rising globally — over-diagnosis tension.
presentation: Most asymptomatic (incidentaloma on imaging). Symptoms suggesting malignancy: hard fixed nodule, rapid growth, hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion), dysphagia, dyspnoea, cervical lymphadenopathy, family history.
redFlags: Hard fixed nodule + cervical lymph nodes — suspected cancer
Family history MEN2 / familial thyroid cancer / DICER1
Young age + nodule (higher cancer risk per nodule)
Suspicious ultrasound features (TI-RADS / EU-TIRADS / ACR-TIRADS — hypoechoic, microcalcifications, irregular margins, taller-than-wide, extrathyroidal extension)
Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (rapidly progressive, hard, fixed — aggressive)
Medullary thyroid cancer in MEN2 family — calcitonin
diagnostics: TSH + free T4 (autonomous functioning adenoma = hot — usually benign; non-functioning = cold — requires FNA)
Anti-TPO + anti-Tg
Calcitonin if family history / MEN2 / suspicious
ULTRASOUND THYROID — sizing + characterisation per TI-RADS:
ACR-TIRADS / EU-TIRADS / Korean — points-based system; TR1-TR5; TR4-5 suggests FNA
Features suggestive of malignancy: hypoechoic, microcalcifications, irregular margins, taller-than-wide, extrathyroidal extension, suspicious cervical nodes
FNA — when indicated by TI-RADS + size:
Bethesda system 1-6:
I: non-diagnostic (repeat FNA)
II: benign (follow-up)
III: AUS/FLUS (5-10% cancer; repeat or molecular)
IV: follicular neoplasm (15-30% cancer; surgery)
V: suspicious for malignancy (60-75% cancer; surgery)
VI: malignant (97% cancer; surgery)
Molecular testing (ThyroSeq, Afirma) for indeterminate (Bethesda III/IV) — reduces unnecessary surgery
Functional scan (radioiodine I-123 or Tc-99m) — hot nodule (autonomous; rarely cancer); cold (FNA)
FBC + LFT + Ca + PO4 baseline if surgery planned
CT/MRI for substernal goitre / extension assessment
Genetic testing: RET (MEN2), DICER1, familial NMTC genes
management: BENIGN NODULES:
Observation — repeat US every 6-12 months initially then every 1-2 years if stable
Repeat FNA if growth (> 50% volume or 2 mm in 2 dimensions)
Suppressive levothyroxine NOT recommended routinely (risks > benefits)
Treat hyperfunctioning hot nodule (RAI / surgery / observation if mild)
Cosmetic / compressive — surgery; thermal ablation (RFA — emerging non-surgical option)
INDETERMINATE (Bethesda III/IV):
Molecular testing where available — reduces unnecessary surgery
Repeat FNA
Surveillance with serial US
Diagnostic surgery (lobectomy) if persistent indeterminate
WELL-DIFFERENTIATED THYROID CANCER (DTC — Papillary + Follicular):
STAGING TNM
RISK STRATIFICATION (ATA risk system + AMES + MACIS): low / intermediate / high
SURGERY:
Lobectomy for small (< 4 cm) low-risk (limited extrathyroidal extension, no lymph nodes, no familial)
Total thyroidectomy for larger / multifocal / high-risk / familial / known nodal disease
Central neck (level VI) lymphadenectomy for known disease
Lateral neck dissection for clinical / imaging-detected lateral disease
POST-OP:
Levothyroxine suppression — TSH target by risk:
High-risk: TSH < 0.1
Intermediate: 0.1-0.5
Radioactive iodine (RAI) ablation — for intermediate / high-risk + select low-risk
Recombinant TSH (Thyrogen) preferred over thyroxine withdrawal
Low-dose 30 mCi vs high-dose 100 mCi (ESTIMABL2, HiLo trials)
Thyroglobulin (Tg) + anti-Tg antibodies + neck US surveillance
SBRT / EBRT for unresectable / locally advanced
ADVANCED / METASTATIC / RAI-REFRACTORY DTC:
Multi-kinase inhibitors: lenvatinib (SELECT trial — first-line), sorafenib
Selective inhibitors: RET inhibitor (selpercatinib for RET-altered), BRAF/MEK (dabrafenib+trametinib for BRAF V600E), NTRK fusion (larotrectinib, entrectinib), ALK (ceritinib)
Redifferentiation strategies (selective inhibitor sensitises RAI uptake) — ASTRA / SELECT-DTC
Immune checkpoint inhibitor — emerging
MEDULLARY THYROID CARCINOMA (MTC):
CALCITONIN + CEA tumour markers
RET mutation (somatic 60% sporadic; germline 100% MEN2)
Always total thyroidectomy + central neck dissection (lateral if positive)
Pre-op screen MEN2 (RET germline test, phaeo screen — plasma metanephrines, calcium for HPT)
Family screening (RET) — prophylactic thyroidectomy in MEN2 carriers (timing by mutation severity)
SELPERCATINIB or pralsetinib for RET-mutated advanced (LIBRETTO-001)
Vandetanib + cabozantinib older multi-kinase inhibitors
ANAPLASTIC THYROID CARCINOMA (ATC):
Aggressive — median survival 6 months untreated
Rapid workup + treat
BRAF V600E mutation in 30% — dabrafenib + trametinib + pembrolizumab (transformative + rapid response in suitable patients)
Standard surgery + chemoradiation
Trial enrolment encouraged
Palliative for poor performance
POOR-DIFFERENTIATED / HÜRTHLE CELL: case-by-case; molecular profiling
THYROID LYMPHOMA:
Suspect rapid goitre + Hashimoto's background
Refer haematology
R-CHOP standard
Surgery usually not required (chemo-curable)
MEN2A + 2B + FMTC:
Germline RET test if MTC / phaeo / HPT family + family screening
Prophylactic thyroidectomy in known carriers (children — timing by mutation)
Multidisciplinary
PREGNANCY:
Cold nodule discovered in pregnancy: US + FNA (acceptable in pregnancy)
Surgery in 2nd trimester if cancer aggressive; otherwise defer to postpartum
Levothyroxine optimisation pre + during
POPULATION + SSA:
Rising incidence (likely partly increased detection)
Address access — US + FNA + thyroid surgery + RAI capacity expanding
Kenya MOH NCD strategy
Multidisciplinary thyroid clinics at tertiary centres

title: Adrenal incidentaloma — characterise + functional workup
population: Common — 4-7% of CT scans, increasing with age. Most benign + non-functioning; small minority functional or malignant.
presentation: Discovered incidentally on imaging done for other reason. Most are non-functioning adrenocortical adenomas (~ 75%); functional minority (Cushing 5-10%, phaeo 3-5%, primary aldosteronism 2-5%); malignant 2-5% (adrenocortical carcinoma 0.5-1%, metastases > 50% in cancer patients).
redFlags: Phaeochromocytoma (any size with episodic features — hypertensive crises, palpitations, sweating, headache, pallor) — risk of catastrophic hypertensive emergency during procedure
Adrenocortical carcinoma — size > 4 cm, heterogeneous, irregular margins, mixed density, rapid growth, high HU on CT (> 20 unenhanced)
Functional with significant comorbidity (refractory HTN, DM, osteoporosis, depression) — Cushing's
Suspected mets (especially lung, melanoma, breast, renal, colon — known cancer)
Bilateral incidentalomas (autonomous cortisol, primary aldo, phaeo, CAH, infection, mets)
Family history MEN, NF1, VHL, hereditary phaeo / paraganglioma
diagnostics: Detailed history + examination (HTN, weight, DM, osteoporosis, mood, hirsutism, virilisation, skin signs of Cushing)
FUNCTIONAL WORKUP — ALL incidentalomas:
Cortisol — overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test (DST); abnormal > 1.8 µg/dL (50 nmol/L) — autonomous cortisol secretion
Phaeo — plasma free metanephrines (or 24h urine fractionated metanephrines)
Primary aldosteronism — ARR (aldosterone/renin ratio) if HTN or hypokalaemia
Adrenocortical carcinoma signs: DHEAS, testosterone (women), oestradiol (men) — sex steroid excess
IMAGING characterisation:
Non-contrast CT: Hounsfield units (HU) — < 10 HU = benign lipid-rich adenoma; > 20 HU + heterogeneous = workup further
Adrenal protocol CT — washout (> 60% absolute washout = benign)
MRI — chemical shift (signal drop on out-of-phase = lipid-rich benign adenoma); useful pregnancy / iodine allergy
PET-CT (FDG) — metastatic / malignant (high SUV)
MIBG / DOTA-octreotate scan for phaeo / paraganglioma
Genetic testing for hereditary phaeo (RET, SDHx, VHL, NF1) — under 50 / bilateral / paraganglioma / family
management: CHARACTERISATION + DECISION (American + European consensus):
Size + imaging + functional + clinical context
Benign features (HU < 10 / washout > 60% / homogeneous / < 4 cm / non-functioning + asymptomatic):
Observation
Repeat imaging at 6-12 months (no growth = benign confirmed)
Annual functional review × 4 years (most autonomous cortisol secretion manifests later)
Discharge if stable + non-functioning at 4 years
FUNCTIONAL TUMOURS:
CUSHING'S syndrome / autonomous cortisol secretion:
Mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS / SAC) — increased CV risk, osteoporosis, DM — consider adrenalectomy + comorbidity workup
Overt Cushing's — surgical adrenalectomy
Pre-op + post-op hydrocortisone cover (adrenal insufficiency)
PHAEOCHROMOCYTOMA:
Pre-op α-BLOCKADE (phenoxybenzamine) 7-14 days BEFORE β-blockade (avoid unopposed α — hypertensive crisis)
Add β-blocker after α (propranolol)
Hydrate well
Anaesthesia consultation
Laparoscopic adrenalectomy (open if large / suspected malignant)
Genetic testing (40% hereditary)
Lifelong follow-up + family screening
PRIMARY ALDOSTERONISM:
Confirmatory testing + adrenal venous sampling (AVS) — lateralises unilateral (adenoma) vs bilateral (hyperplasia)
UNILATERAL adenoma — laparoscopic adrenalectomy (curative)
BILATERAL hyperplasia — mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone 25-100 mg/d or eplerenone 25-50 mg BD)
Adrenal-dependent Cushing's (separate condition)
SUSPECTED MALIGNANT (size > 4 cm / HU > 20 / heterogeneous / rapid growth / functional excess of multiple hormones suggesting ACC):
Surgical adrenalectomy by experienced centre
Adrenocortical carcinoma — staging (CT + PET-CT) + open surgery + adjuvant mitotane
Adjuvant mitotane post-resection
Mitotane + EDP-M (etoposide + doxorubicin + cisplatin + mitotane) for advanced
Multidisciplinary oncology
Trial enrolment encouraged
Metastases — staging + biopsy + treat primary
BILATERAL INCIDENTALOMAS:
Workup carefully (cortisol, aldo, phaeo, CAH)
Infection (TB, fungal — especially HIV / immunocompromised — common SSA)
Adrenal haemorrhage (anticoagulant)
Mets (especially lung, melanoma, breast, renal, colon)
GENETIC:
Hereditary phaeo / paraganglioma — RET, SDHx, VHL, NF1, MAX, FH
Test if < 50 yr / bilateral / paraganglioma / family history / sympathetic
Family cascade screening
Lifelong surveillance
FOLLOW-UP:
Repeat imaging + functional review per guideline
Discharge after 4 years stable + non-functioning
Earlier intervention if growth / functional
PREGNANCY:
Phaeo in pregnancy — high maternal + fetal risk; α-blockade + plan caesarean / surgical timing
Multidisciplinary
POPULATION + SSA:
Emerging recognition with imaging access
TB + fungal infection of adrenals common — endemic areas + HIV
Endocrinology + radiology integration

title: Primary aldosteronism — screen, confirm, lateralise, treat
population: Most common identifiable cause of secondary hypertension — 5-15% of all HTN, > 20% of resistant HTN; under-screened.
presentation: HTN — usually resistant, family history, young onset (< 40); hypokalaemia or normokalaemic; cardiovascular complications + LVH disproportionate to BP; rarely muscle weakness, paraesthesia, polyuria, periodic paralysis.
redFlags: Resistant hypertension (BP > 140/90 on 3 agents including diuretic) — SCREEN
Family history primary aldo / hereditary forms
diagnostics: SCREENING — Aldosterone-to-Renin Ratio (ARR):
Plasma aldosterone (PA) ÷ plasma renin activity (PRA) or direct renin concentration (DRC)
ARR > 20-40 (units vary) + PA > 15 ng/dL suggests primary aldo

Preparation: K+ replete (> 4); cease MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone) × 4-6 weeks before; β-blockers, ACEi/ARB, diuretics can affect (consider switch to non-interfering — verapamil SR + hydralazine + α-blocker — for accurate testing)
Morning sample after 2h upright + 5-15 min seated
CONFIRMATION (if screen positive):
Saline infusion test (failure to suppress aldosterone to < 5 ng/dL after 2L 0.9% saline over 4h)
Captopril challenge (alternative)
Oral salt loading + 24h urine aldosterone
Fludrocortisone suppression
LATERALISATION (essential before surgery):
CT adrenals — may show unilateral adenoma (Conn's), bilateral hyperplasia, or no clear lesion (especially under 35 — small adenoma)
ADRENAL VENOUS SAMPLING (AVS) — gold standard to lateralise; before adrenalectomy in patients > 35 (CT not reliable enough)
Cosyntropin stimulation during AVS to improve accuracy
GENETIC TESTING:
GRA (FH-I) — long arm of chromosome 8 (CYP11B1/CYP11B2 chimeric gene); suppressed by dexamethasone
KCNJ5 (FH-III), CACNA1H, CLCN2 — non-GRA familial forms
Test if family history / early onset
management: UNILATERAL adenoma (Conn's syndrome) — surgical curative:
LAPAROSCOPIC ADRENALECTOMY
Pre-op optimise BP + K+ (spironolactone 50-100 mg/d × 4-6 weeks)
Post-op many normalise BP, some need ongoing antihypertensive
Cure rate (long-term): clinical 50%, biochemical 95%
BILATERAL hyperplasia / non-surgical candidate:
MINERALOCORTICOID RECEPTOR ANTAGONIST:
SPIRONOLACTONE 12.5-100 mg/d (start low; gynaecomastia + reduced libido + menstrual irregularity in 5-30%)
EPLERENONE 25-50 mg BD (selective — less gynaecomastia; less potent than spironolactone)
Esaxerenone (newer, selective, FDA approved 2024 in some regions)
Add amiloride 5-10 mg/d if MRA insufficient
Optimise other antihypertensive (CCB + ACE/ARB)
Monitor K+ (often need additional supplementation in primary aldo + diuretic; opposite in aldo on MRA — hyperK+ risk)
GLUCOCORTICOID-REMEDIABLE ALDOSTERONISM (GRA / FH-I):
Dexamethasone 0.125-0.5 mg/d at bedtime — suppresses chimeric gene
Monitor for steroid side effects + bone health + glucose
GENERAL:
CV risk modification (statin + lifestyle + tobacco cessation)
Heart failure surveillance (LVH from chronic mineralocorticoid excess)
Bone health (osteoporosis risk)
Reassess regularly — BP + K+ + aldosterone targets
FAMILIAL: cascade screening, genetic counselling
PREGNANCY:
Aldosterone physiologically rises in pregnancy
Continue antihypertensive (avoid ACE/ARB + spironolactone — feminisation male fetus)
Use methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine, hydralazine
Delivery + management individualised
POPULATION + SSA:
Major hidden cause of resistant HTN
Train primary care + general medicine on screening
Spironolactone widely available (cheap)
Address barriers to AVS / adrenalectomy (limited centres — refer tertiary)
Kenya MOH NCD Strategic Plan + access to specialist endocrine

title: Cushing's syndrome — workup + treatment
population: Iatrogenic (exogenous steroid — by far most common); endogenous rare. Endogenous Cushing's: pituitary (Cushing's disease — 70%), adrenal (adenoma/carcinoma — 20%), ectopic ACTH (lung small-cell, carcinoid — 10%). Women > men.
presentation: Central obesity + striae (purple, > 1 cm), moon facies, buffalo hump, supraclavicular fullness, thin skin + easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness, HTN, T2DM / glucose intolerance, osteoporosis, depression / psychosis, menstrual irregularity / amenorrhoea / decreased libido / hirsutism, plethora.
redFlags: Suspected ectopic ACTH (rapid onset, severe hypokalaemia, marked weight loss, pigmentation — small-cell lung cancer / carcinoid)
Pituitary apoplexy (acute neurological with sudden vision loss + headache)
Suspected adrenocortical carcinoma (large > 4 cm + heterogeneous + multiple hormone excess)
Cushing in pregnancy (high maternal + fetal risk)
diagnostics: Screening (any 2 abnormal of):
Late-night salivary cortisol — > 4 nmol/L abnormal (most sensitive screen + outpatient)
24h urinary free cortisol — > 3× ULN (3 collections)
Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression — cortisol > 50 nmol/L (1.8 µg/dL) abnormal
2-day low-dose DST (alternative)
If screening abnormal + clinical features — proceed to confirmation + localisation
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS (Cushing confirmed — now where?):
ACTH measurement:
Suppressed (< 5 pg/mL) — adrenal cause; CT/MRI adrenals
Normal-raised (> 10 pg/mL) — ACTH-dependent (pituitary or ectopic); MRI pituitary + 8 mg DST
HIGH-DOSE DST (8 mg overnight) — suppression > 50% suggests pituitary (Cushing's disease); no suppression suggests ectopic
CRH stimulation — pituitary responds; ectopic does not
INFERIOR PETROSAL SINUS SAMPLING (IPSS) — gold standard for pituitary vs ectopic (Cushing's disease: petrosal/peripheral ACTH > 2 basal or > 3 with CRH)
CT chest/abdo/pelvis or PET-CT for ectopic ACTH source
Octreotide scan / PET-DOTATATE for neuroendocrine tumours
MRI pituitary — adenoma (often microadenoma; sensitivity 60-70%; IPSS confirms even if MRI negative)
Bloods: glucose, HbA1c, lipid, electrolytes (hypoK + alkalosis), bone profile, FBC
DEXA (osteoporosis assessment)
Pseudo-Cushing exclusion: dexamethasone-suppressed CRH test or desmopressin test
management: TREAT UNDERLYING CAUSE:
IATROGENIC (most common) — TAPER steroid carefully (avoid abrupt withdrawal — adrenal crisis; gradual reduction depending on duration / dose); consider alternate-day; minimise long-term steroid
PITUITARY (Cushing's disease):
TRANS-SPHENOIDAL SURGERY (TSS) — first-line by experienced neurosurgeon; cure 70-90% microadenoma; lower macroadenoma + invasive
Repeat TSS for residual / recurrence
Pituitary radiotherapy / radiosurgery (gamma knife) — adjuvant; takes months-years
Bilateral adrenalectomy — last resort (cures but Nelson's syndrome — pituitary tumour progression + ACTH-dependent pigmentation)
Medical: pasireotide (somatostatin analogue — SOM230), cabergoline, mifepristone, levoketoconazole, osilodrostat (FDA 2020 — inhibits 11β-hydroxylase — effective)
ECTOPIC ACTH:
Identify + resect source (lung carcinoid, small-cell lung cancer, thymic, pancreatic, medullary thyroid)
Chemotherapy if metastatic (SCLC)
Adrenal blockade with metyrapone / ketoconazole / osilodrostat / etomidate (IV in critically ill)
Bilateral adrenalectomy if no source identified
ADRENAL:
Unilateral adenoma: laparoscopic adrenalectomy + post-op hydrocortisone cover (contralateral adrenal suppressed)
Adrenocortical carcinoma: open adrenalectomy + adjuvant mitotane + EDP-M (separate condition)
MEDICAL THERAPY (adjuvant or for those unfit for / awaiting surgery):
ADRENAL STEROIDOGENESIS INHIBITORS:
Metyrapone 250-1000 mg q6h (11β-hydroxylase inhibitor)
Ketoconazole 200-400 mg TDS (multiple steroidogenesis enzymes; hepatotoxicity)
Levoketoconazole (less hepatotoxic alternative)
Osilodrostat 2-30 mg BD (LINC-3 + LINC-4 trials)
Mitotane (adrenolytic) — for ACC + Cushing's
CENTRAL: pasireotide (Cushing's disease), cabergoline (dopamine agonist)
Glucocorticoid receptor antagonist: mifepristone (Korlym) — for hyperglycaemia in Cushing's; doesn't normalise cortisol
POST-CURE / POST-SURGERY:
Hydrocortisone replacement until HPA recovery (months-year; some require lifelong)
Stress dose for illness / surgery
Sick day rules + MedicAlert + injection
Address comorbidity: DM, HTN, osteoporosis, depression (often persists post-cure)
Bone density + bisphosphonate if indicated
Glycaemic + BP optimisation
Psychiatric assessment + treat
Slow improvement over months
PREGNANCY + CUSHING'S:
Rare + high-risk
Multidisciplinary
Surgical / medical (metyrapone safer than ketoconazole)
Increased risk: pre-eclampsia, GDM, preterm, fetal loss
POPULATION + SSA:
Tertiary centres for definitive treatment
Endocrine + neurosurgery referral
Awareness of iatrogenic Cushing's from over-the-counter steroid
Address skin lightening creams containing topical steroid (Kenya — public health issue)

title: Male hypogonadism — diagnosis + testosterone replacement therapy
population: Primary (testicular failure — Klinefelter, cryptorchidism, mumps, varicocele, chemo/radiation, trauma); Secondary (HPG axis — pituitary, hypothalamic, opioid, steroid, severe systemic illness, obesity, OSA); Age-related decline in older men (function of multimorbidity + obesity + comorbidity rather than pure ageing).
presentation: Sexual: decreased libido + erectile dysfunction + decreased morning erections. Constitutional: fatigue, decreased energy, depressed mood, reduced muscle mass + strength, increased body fat, gynaecomastia, reduced facial / body hair, hot flushes. Bone: osteoporosis. Prepubertal: delayed / absent puberty.
redFlags: Pituitary mass / suspected hypopituitarism (visual symptoms, headache, hypopituitarism features) — workup
Suspected prostate cancer (PSA raised, abnormal DRE) — investigate BEFORE testosterone replacement
Polycythaemia / haematocrit > 54% on TRT — risk of thrombotic events
Severe untreated OSA (testosterone worsens) — treat first
Pregnancy partner exposure to transdermal testosterone (gel) — risk of virilisation
diagnostics: Symptomatic + persistently low morning total testosterone (< 264-280 ng/dL / 9.2-9.7 nmol/L per Endocrine Society) — TWO morning samples on different days needed (high diurnal + day-to-day variability)
FREE testosterone if total borderline or SHBG abnormal
LH + FSH:
Primary: high LH + FSH (testicular failure)
Secondary: low / normal LH + FSH (HPG axis)
Causes workup:
Primary: karyotype (Klinefelter 47,XXY), history (cryptorchidism, mumps, chemo, trauma, infection), examination (testicular size, varicocele)

Secondary: prolactin (prolactinoma), MRI pituitary, full pituitary panel (cortisol, TSH/T4, GH/IGF-1, full sex hormone profile), iron studies (haemochromatosis), opioid history, glucocorticoid history, anabolic steroid abuse, OSA screening, severe systemic illness, obesity (BMI / waist), eating disorder
PSA + DRE before TRT + during
FBC (haematocrit baseline + monitor)
Lipids + HbA1c (metabolic comorbidity)
DEXA (osteoporosis)
If considering ferritin > 1000 / iron > 200 — haemochromatosis (HFE genotype) workup
management: TREAT CAUSE WHERE POSSIBLE:
Obesity: weight loss (modest weight loss often reverses functional secondary hypogonadism)
OSA: CPAP
Opioid: reduce / stop opioid + buprenorphine alternative
Anabolic steroid use: counselling + cessation (HPG axis recovery often months)
Pituitary tumour: surgery / medical (prolactinoma — cabergoline)
Haemochromatosis: phlebotomy
FERTILITY consideration BEFORE TRT (testosterone suppresses spermatogenesis):
If fertility desired: human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) ± FSH (recombinant or hMG) for secondary; not effective for primary (testicular failure)
Selective oestrogen receptor modulator (clomiphene, tamoxifen) — off-label for secondary; preserves fertility
Sperm banking before TRT (especially if young / fertility desired)
TRT suppresses fertility — counsel; reversible with cessation + hCG in months
TESTOSTERONE REPLACEMENT THERAPY (TRT):
Indications: symptomatic + confirmed biochemical hypogonadism + no contraindications

CONTRAINDICATIONS: untreated prostate cancer, active male breast cancer, severe LUTS, haematocrit > 54%, severe HF, untreated OSA, prostate nodule / PSA > 4 without urology workup, planned fertility within 6 months
Formulations:
Intramuscular: testosterone enanthate / cypionate 100-200 mg q1-2 weeks; or testosterone undecanoate 1000 mg q10-14 weeks (long-acting, fewer fluctuations — preferred where available)
Transdermal: testosterone gel 50-100 mg/d (Androgel, Testogel) — daily; avoid skin contact with partners / children (virilisation risk)
Buccal / nasal: less common
Subcutaneous pellets: 6 monthly
Target: mid-range normal total testosterone (350-700 ng/dL)
Monitor: clinical response, total T at 3 + 6 months then annually, haematocrit, PSA + DRE, lipids, glucose, bone density
ADVERSE EFFECTS / MONITORING:
Polycythaemia (haematocrit > 54%) — reduce dose, phlebotomy
Acne, oily skin
Gynaecomastia (aromatisation to oestrogen)
Fluid retention
Sleep apnoea worsening
Prostate enlargement / PSA rise — workup if > 1 ng/mL/yr or > 4
Cardiovascular — TRAVERSE trial 2023 showed no increased MACE in middle-aged + older men + hypogonadism + CV risk (clarifies prior controversy)
Reduced fertility
Mood — usually improves; some worsening
Erythrocytosis monitoring + management
PROSTATE CANCER:
Screen BEFORE TRT (PSA + DRE)
Monitor (q6-12 months on TRT)
Stable prostate cancer (treated curatively, undetectable PSA) — TRT may be considered after thoughtful discussion (recent shift in some guidance — Khera + Morgentaler review)
OLDER MEN / FUNCTIONAL HYPOGONADISM:
Treat reversible (obesity, OSA, opioid, severe illness) FIRST
TRT for symptomatic confirmed older men can improve symptoms (T Trials NEJM 2016)
Individualise risk/benefit
KLINEFELTER:
TRT lifelong
Fertility — micro-TESE + IVF / ICSI for selected (sperm retrieval rate 50-70% young adults)
Address learning + psychosocial issues
Cardiometabolic + bone surveillance
ANABOLIC STEROID ABUSE:
HPG axis recovery: cessation + hCG ± SERM for months
Address mental health + dysmorphia
Monitor for late effects (cardiac, hepatic, mental health)
POPULATION + SSA:
Limited specialist endocrine + andrology access
Recognise + investigate before reflexive TRT
Address obesity epidemic + OSA + diabetes contribution
Counsel + monitor adherence + side effects
Cost — generic depot testosterone enanthate accessible

title: Menopause + HRT — modern individualised therapy
population: All women postmenopausal (median age 51); transition + perimenopause from 40s; significantly affects QoL + bone + CV health. Major paradigm shift from WHI-era restrictive use back to individualised HRT.
presentation: Vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes, night sweats), sleep disturbance, mood (anxiety, depression), cognitive (brain fog), genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM — vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, recurrent UTI, urinary urgency), joint aches, sexual dysfunction. Long-term: osteoporosis + CV risk increase.
redFlags: Postmenopausal bleeding (within 12 months of menstruation cessation) — investigate (endometrial cancer until proven otherwise — TVS + biopsy)
VTE risk + HRT (transdermal preferred; PEACE trial — transdermal estradiol no increased VTE)
Breast cancer history (HRT generally contraindicated — discuss with oncology; vaginal oestrogen acceptable for severe GSM)
Active heart disease / CVA / VTE / liver disease — caution / alternative
Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI < 40 yr) — treat as need oestrogen replacement until natural menopausal age
Migraine with aura (relative contraindication to oral; transdermal safer)
diagnostics: Clinical diagnosis — perimenopause = menstrual irregularity + vasomotor; menopause = 12 months amenorrhoea (over 45 yr)
FSH only useful in younger (< 40 — POI workup) — variable + unreliable in perimenopause
Investigate POI (FSH > 30 × 2 occasions, oestradiol low, amenorrhoea > 4 months in < 40): karyotype, FMR1 (Fragile X), autoimmune (anti-adrenal antibody), thyroid, iron, prolactin
Mood + cognitive screen if predominant symptoms
DEXA at menopause + as risk-stratified
Cardiovascular risk assessment (BP, lipids, glucose)
Mammography per local screening guidelines
TVS if abnormal bleeding (endometrial > 4-5 mm postmenopausal = endometrial biopsy)
management: INDIVIDUALISED HRT:
Paradigm shift — HRT effective + safe in most women within 10 years of menopause / under 60
Symptoms management + bone protection + GSM
Discuss benefits vs risks (CV, breast, VTE, endometrial)
INDICATIONS:
Vasomotor symptoms (most common)
Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM)
Premature ovarian insufficiency (< 40)
Surgical menopause / iatrogenic (BSO, chemo)
Bone protection in selected (consider over bisphosphonate in younger women)
FORMULATIONS:
OESTROGEN:
Oral oestradiol 1-2 mg/d (most common UK)
Transdermal patch (Estradot, Climara, Evorel) 25-100 mcg twice weekly — preferred over oral if VTE risk, migraine with aura, smoking, gallbladder, hepatic, hypertriglyceridaemia
Gel (Sandrena, Oestrogel)
Spray
Conjugated equine oestrogen (older, less used)
Vaginal oestrogen (cream / ring / tablets) — for GSM only; minimal systemic absorption; can be combined with systemic if both indications
PROGESTOGEN (for women with uterus — endometrial protection):
Micronised progesterone 100-200 mg/d nocte (Utrogestan) — most physiological, less metabolic + breast risk; oral cyclical (12 d/month for sequential) or continuous
Synthetic progestins (norethindrone, dydrogesterone)
Mirena IUS — 5 years (off-label endometrial protection; convenient)
NOT NEEDED if hysterectomy
COMBINED PRODUCTS for convenience
TIBOLONE — synthetic with weak oestrogenic / progestogenic / androgenic; alternative for postmenopausal libido + mood
DURATION:
No fixed time limit
Reassess annually
Most use 5-10 years
Younger (POI) — continue until natural menopausal age (51)
Lowest effective dose
Continue if benefit outweighs risk
Tapering not necessary but some prefer
ALTERNATIVES (for women who can't / don't want HRT):
NON-HORMONAL for vasomotor:
SSRI (paroxetine, escitalopram, venlafaxine) — modest benefit
Clonidine 0.05-0.1 mg BD (alpha-2 agonist)
Gabapentin 300-900 mg/d
FEZOLINETANT 45 mg/d (NK3 receptor antagonist — FDA 2023 — first non-hormonal targeted therapy for VMS)
CBT — proven for VMS + sleep
Acupuncture — modest
Lifestyle: layered clothing, cool environment, weight loss, exercise, reduce ETOH/caffeine/spicy
GSM:
Vaginal oestrogen (low-dose — minimal systemic; even in breast cancer with oncology consent — emerging acceptance)
Vaginal moisturiser / lubricant
Ospemifene (oral SERM) — dyspareunia
Vaginal DHEA (prasterone)
Laser / vaginal therapy — caution (FDA warning)
RISK DISCUSSION:
Breast cancer: oestrogen-only HRT (women with hysterectomy) — minimal / no increased risk (WHI re-analysis); combined HRT — modest increased risk after 5 years (1-2 extra cases per 1000 women-years)
Endometrial cancer: oestrogen-only in women with uterus — INCREASED RISK; always combine with progestogen
VTE: oral oestrogen — increased; TRANSDERMAL — no increased (preferred for higher risk)
Stroke: oral — small increased; transdermal — no
CV: HRT < 10 years of menopause / < 60 years — likely cardioprotective (timing hypothesis)
Ovarian cancer: small increase with long-term use
Cognition: probably neutral; younger users may benefit, older may not
MONITORING:
Annual review (symptoms, side effects, breast self-exam + mammography per screening, BP)
Endometrial monitoring not routinely needed if appropriate progestogen + no bleeding
Persistent / unexpected bleeding — TVS + biopsy
BREAST CANCER + MENOPAUSE:
HRT generally contraindicated
Vaginal oestrogen for severe GSM with oncology consent (low absorption; quality of life)
Non-hormonal alternatives (SSRI, gabapentin, fezolinetant, CBT)
Address sexual function (vaginal moisturiser, lubricant)
AVOID phytoestrogens in oestrogen-receptor positive cancer
PREMATURE OVARIAN INSUFFICIENCY (POI < 40):
Higher CV + bone risk if untreated
HRT until natural menopausal age (51) — replacement, not 'just' symptom
Combined oral contraceptive alternative
Address fertility (donor egg / IVF), bone health, CV risk modification, psychological
Karyotype, FMR1, autoimmune workup
POPULATION + SSA:
Limited HRT access + uptake (cost + cultural)
Address misconceptions (WHI mis-interpretation legacy)
Vaginal oestrogen for GSM
Lifestyle + non-pharm
Kenya MOH NCD strategy includes women's midlife health

title: Gender-affirming care — hormone therapy + comprehensive support
population: Trans + non-binary individuals (estimated 0.5-1% of population). Wide range of identities + needs. Mental health + suicide risk significantly higher in non-affirming environments — gender-affirming care reduces these.
presentation: Adolescent / adult presenting with gender incongruence (ICD-11 — depathologised, not disorder). Range of social, hormonal, surgical interventions per individual goals. Mental health (especially anxiety + depression + suicidality + minority stress) common — gender-affirming care is protective.
redFlags: Suicidality / self-harm — common in unaffirmed; affirmation + mental health support critical
Adolescent / minor — parental involvement + capacity + Gillick competency (UK) / mature minor + multidisciplinary
VTE risk on hormone therapy (transdermal preferred for oestrogen)
Suspected gender dysphoria comorbid with mental health (depression, autism, eating disorder) — manage in parallel + don't delay affirmation
Eligibility for surgical procedures — multidisciplinary assessment
Bone health (especially adolescents on GnRH agonists)
diagnostics: Comprehensive assessment by trained provider (multidisciplinary — endocrinology + mental health + primary care + surgery as needed)
Mental health — assess + treat anxiety + depression + suicide + trauma + minority stress
Capacity + informed consent (adolescents — Gillick + family involvement)
Baseline labs: FBC + U&E + LFT + lipids + HbA1c + prolactin + LH + FSH + testosterone + oestradiol + SHBG + PSA (if AMAB)
Sexual + reproductive health: STI screen + cervical screening (if cervix) + breast screening (per current anatomy)
Fertility counselling BEFORE hormone initiation (oocyte / sperm banking — hormones suppress fertility, may be partly reversible)
DEXA (especially adolescents on GnRH agonists + bone-immature)
ECG + cardiovascular risk assessment
Smoking cessation counselling (VTE / CV risk)
Address co-occurring conditions (HIV, depression)
management: CARE MODEL (WPATH 8 + Endocrine Society 2017):
PATIENT-CENTRED + AFFIRMATIVE — gender-affirming care reduces depression + suicide; gatekeeping harmful
Multidisciplinary
INFORMED CONSENT model (adults) increasingly favoured over traditional WPATH letter requirement
SOCIAL GENDER AFFIRMATION:
Name + pronouns
Clothing + presentation
Hair + voice + binding/tucking/packing
Workplace + school accommodation
Legal documentation change
HORMONE THERAPY (MASCULINISING — for trans men + non-binary AMAB-AFAB):
TESTOSTERONE — typical adult target male physiological range (300-700 ng/dL)
IM testosterone enanthate / cypionate 50-100 mg weekly or 100-200 mg q2 weeks
Testosterone undecanoate long-acting IM (Nebido) q10-14 weeks
Transdermal gel 50-100 mg/d (Androgel, Tostran)
EFFECTS — months to years:
Voice deepening (often permanent)
Facial + body hair (permanent)
Acne (transient)
Cessation of menses (3-6 months — many on testosterone alone; some need supplementary norethisterone)
Clitoral enlargement (permanent)
Muscle + redistribution of body fat
Polycythaemia
MONITORING: T level 3-6 mo then annual; FBC for polycythaemia; LFT + lipid; blood pressure
Pregnancy: contraception still needed (testosterone is NOT contraceptive); fertility considerations (suspend hormones for fertility / pregnancy)
HORMONE THERAPY (FEMINISING — for trans women + non-binary AMAB):
OESTRADIOL — target female physiological range (100-200 pg/mL):
Transdermal estradiol (preferred — lower VTE risk; especially > 35 yr / smokers / VTE risk): patches 100-200 mcg twice weekly; gel 2-5 mg/d
Oral estradiol 2-8 mg/d
Sublingual
Conjugated equine oestrogen (older; less used)
NEVER ethinyl estradiol (high VTE) — except certain combined OCP
ANTI-ANDROGEN:
SPIRONOLACTONE 100-200 mg/d (most common — anti-androgen + mineralocorticoid antagonist; monitor K+)
GnRH agonist (leuprolide, triptorelin) — more effective, expensive
Cyproterone acetate 25-100 mg/d (Europe + UK — hepatotoxic + meningioma risk; lower-dose modernly)
Bicalutamide — alternative
5α-reductase inhibitor (finasteride, dutasteride) — for body hair / scalp
EFFECTS — months to years:
Breast development (some, often modest)
Body fat redistribution
Skin softening
Reduced body hair (slow + incomplete; many need electrolysis / laser)
Reduced muscle mass
Reduced libido + erectile function
Decreased testicular size + spermatogenesis
NO voice change (need speech therapy)
NO facial hair removal (need electrolysis / laser)
MONITORING: estradiol + total + free testosterone + LH + FSH + prolactin; K+ if on spironolactone; LFT; lipids; BP
VTE risk: stop hormones before / restart after major surgery; transdermal preferred; smoking cessation; avoid in active VTE / thrombophilia / oestrogen-sensitive cancer
ADOLESCENT CARE:
Multidisciplinary specialist team (Tavistock + GIDS UK; international centres)
Mental health assessment + support
REVERSIBLE GnRH AGONIST puberty suppression (early puberty Tanner 2+):
Buys time + reduces distress
Effects reverse if stopped
Monitor bone density, growth
Cross-hormones from ~ 16 (varies by jurisdiction + assessment)
Surgery (if pursued) typically delayed to adulthood

Recent controversy (Cass Review UK 2024) — calls for cautious + evidence-based approach + research; ongoing debate; international guidelines (WPATH 8) maintain gender-affirming model for adolescents within multidisciplinary specialist setting
SURGICAL OPTIONS (NOT all pursued):
Chest: bilateral mastectomy + chest reconstruction (top surgery — trans men); breast augmentation (trans women)
Genital: phalloplasty / metoidioplasty / vaginectomy (trans men); vaginoplasty / labiaplasty (trans women); both highly specialised
Facial feminisation / masculinisation
Voice surgery (alternative or adjunct to speech therapy)
Adam's apple reduction (chondrolaryngoplasty)
Hysterectomy + oophorectomy / orchiectomy
Eligibility per local + WPATH framework
FERTILITY:
Sperm / oocyte banking before hormone initiation if fertility desired
Testosterone NOT contraceptive (pregnancy can occur)
Discussions with fertility specialist + counselling
MENTAL HEALTH:
Often co-occurring conditions (depression, anxiety, autism, eating disorder)
Address in parallel — do NOT use as reason to delay affirmation
Trans-affirming mental health support
Suicidality monitoring
Family + community support
Address minority stress
SEXUAL HEALTH:
STI screen + cervical / prostate screening per anatomy
Contraception (testosterone not contraceptive)
PrEP (HIV prevention)
Sexual function counselling
PRIMARY CARE:
Routine care per current anatomy (breast screening if breast tissue, cervical if cervix, prostate if prostate)
Address all aspects of health, not just gender-related
Use chosen name + pronouns
POPULATION + SSA / KENYA:
Limited services + legal recognition + significant stigma + criminalisation in some countries
Mental health, HIV prevention, harm reduction
Confidentiality + safety paramount
Increasing advocacy (Galck+ Kenya, GALCK, ISHTAR)
Provide non-judgemental care + referral to safe specialist services where available
Address co-occurring HIV / STI / mental health

title: PCOS — Rotterdam criteria + modern management
population: Most common endocrinopathy in reproductive-age women — 8-13% globally; major cause of anovulatory infertility + metabolic syndrome + endometrial cancer risk; ethnic variation in presentation (South Asian + SSA — more metabolic).
presentation: Hyperandrogenism (hirsutism + acne + male-pattern alopecia + female-pattern body hair); ovulatory dysfunction (oligomenorrhoea / amenorrhoea / anovulatory infertility); polycystic ovary morphology (≥ 12 follicles 2-9 mm or > 10 ml volume per ovary). Metabolic — insulin resistance + obesity + T2DM + dyslipidaemia + NAFLD + OSA + CV risk + depression + anxiety.
redFlags: Suspected secondary cause (Cushing's, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, ovarian / adrenal tumour) — workup
Endometrial hyperplasia / cancer suspected (prolonged amenorrhoea with subsequent bleeding + ultrasound thickened endometrium) — biopsy
Severe insulin resistance + acanthosis nigricans + young + lean — investigate (PCOS-like vs HAIR-AN syndrome)
Pregnancy with PCOS — GDM + pre-eclampsia + preterm risk
diagnostics: ROTTERDAM CRITERIA (2 of 3 required + exclusion of other causes):
Hyperandrogenism (clinical OR biochemical — total/free testosterone, DHEAS, androstenedione)
Ovulatory dysfunction (oligomenorrhoea / amenorrhoea — < 8 cycles/year or > 35 days)
Polycystic ovaries on US (≥ 12 follicles 2-9 mm or > 10 ml volume; high-resolution transducer)
EXCLUDE OTHER CAUSES:
Thyroid (TSH), prolactin, 17-OH-progesterone (CAH), cortisol (Cushing)
Androgen-secreting tumour (rapid virilisation, very high testosterone / DHEAS — workup imaging)
Hyperandrogenic-insulin resistance-acanthosis nigricans (HAIR-AN) syndrome
Premature ovarian insufficiency (FSH > 30)
METABOLIC ASSESSMENT:
Glucose tolerance — 75g OGTT at diagnosis + every 2 years (PCOS T2DM + GDM risk increased)
Lipid panel
BP
Liver function + FibroScan (NAFLD)
Mental health screening (depression / anxiety / eating disorder common)
Sleep apnoea screening (STOP-Bang)
Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) — high in PCOS but not diagnostic alone
management: INDIVIDUALISE — by primary concern (hyperandrogenism / menstrual / fertility / metabolic):
LIFESTYLE — foundation (regardless of BMI):
Healthy diet — Mediterranean / low GI
Regular exercise (150-300 min/wk aerobic + resistance)
Weight loss (5-10% in overweight — significant improvement in metabolic + reproductive)
Sleep hygiene + OSA treatment
Smoking cessation
Mental health support
MENSTRUAL CYCLE REGULATION + ENDOMETRIAL PROTECTION (for women not seeking pregnancy):
Combined oral contraceptive (COC) — first-line
Choose with anti-androgen progestin (drospirenone, cyproterone — Diane-35) for hyperandrogenism
Standard COC for menstrual regularity
Endometrial protection from anovulatory unopposed oestrogen
Cyclical progestin (10-14 days every 1-3 months) — if oestrogen contraindicated
Mirena IUS — endometrial protection + contraception
Avoid prolonged amenorrhoea (> 3-4 months) without endometrial protection (cancer risk)
HYPERANDROGENISM (hirsutism + acne):
COC with anti-androgen progestin
SPIRONOLACTONE 50-200 mg/d (anti-androgen; takes 3-6 months) — combine with COC (women need contraception — teratogen if pregnant)
Cyproterone acetate (Diane-35) — older + effective but VTE + meningioma concerns
Finasteride / dutasteride — for severe hirsutism
Topical eflornithine (Vaniqa) — slows facial hair growth
Cosmetic: shaving, waxing, depilation, electrolysis, laser
Address acne (separate condition)
INSULIN RESISTANCE + METABOLIC:
Lifestyle + weight loss
METFORMIN 500-2000 mg/d — improves insulin resistance + menstrual regularity + modest weight + reduces GDM risk; T2DM prevention
GLP-1 RA / TIRZEPATIDE — emerging for PCOS + obesity (off-label outside obesity indication; very effective for weight + metabolic — increasingly used)
SGLT2i (canagliflozin, empagliflozin) — emerging
Inositol (myo-inositol + D-chiro-inositol 40:1) — modest evidence; insulin-sensitising; well-tolerated
Treat dyslipidaemia + HTN per usual guidelines
Statin for high CV risk
FERTILITY (when pregnancy desired):
Weight optimisation pre-conception
OVULATION INDUCTION first-line:
LETROZOLE 2.5-7.5 mg days 3-7 (Pregnancy in PCOS NEJM 2014 — superior to clomiphene)
Clomiphene 50-150 mg days 3-7 (older first-line; multiple gestation higher than letrozole)
Metformin co-therapy modest benefit
Gonadotrophins (FSH) — second-line, monitoring intense, OHSS + multiple gestation risk
IUI (intrauterine insemination)
IVF — if other measures fail / partner factor / age
Laparoscopic ovarian drilling — selected (clomiphene-resistant)
GLP-1 RA / metabolic surgery — for severe obesity (return to ovulation common after weight loss)
PREGNANCY in PCOS:
Pre-conception: optimise weight + glucose + lifestyle
Monitor: GDM (OGTT 24-28 wk), pre-eclampsia, preterm
Continue metformin (some evidence reduces miscarriage)
Aspirin 75-150 mg from 12 weeks (pre-eclampsia prevention)
MENTAL HEALTH:
Depression, anxiety, body image, eating disorder common — screen + treat
CBT, SSRI, psychological support
ENDOMETRIAL CANCER SURVEILLANCE:
TVS if abnormal bleeding (especially postmenopausal)
Endometrial biopsy if endometrium > 5 mm postmenopausal OR persistent bleeding
Ensure regular endometrial shedding (progestin / COC / MIRENA)
ADOLESCENT PCOS:
Diagnostic challenge — physiological adolescent irregularity + acne first 2 years post-menarche
Defer Rotterdam criteria until 2+ years post-menarche
Lifestyle + COC for menstrual regulation + hyperandrogenism
Metformin if metabolic concerns
Mental health support critical
BARIATRIC SURGERY:
Severe obesity (BMI ≥ 35 + comorbidity)
Improves PCOS substantially (ovulation, metabolic, fertility)
Considered for selected
POPULATION + SSA:
Major emerging burden
South Asian + SSA — more severe metabolic presentation
Often under-diagnosed in primary care
Integrate into NCD + women's health + reproductive health
Kenya MOH NCD Strategic Plan

title: Chronic urticaria — modern algorithm (omalizumab era)
population: Common — affects 1% population at any time. Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) — most. Inducible (cold, heat, pressure, vibration, exercise, cholinergic, solar, aquagenic, dermatographism).
presentation: Recurrent itchy wheals + angioedema for > 6 weeks. Each lesion < 24h. Urticaria activity score (UAS7). May have prodrome (tingling). Angioedema (deep) lasts longer — 2-3 days. Severely impacts QoL.
redFlags: ANAPHYLAXIS — airway / hypotension (separate condition — emergency adrenaline)
Suspected hereditary angioedema (C1-INH deficiency — recurrent angioedema WITHOUT urticaria, NO response to antihistamines; ACE-i-induced different mechanism)
Suspected vasculitis (lesions > 24h + bruising + purpura + raised inflammatory markers) — biopsy
Mast cell disorder (urticaria pigmentosa, mastocytosis) — tryptase + bone marrow
diagnostics: Clinical diagnosis — > 6 weeks of recurrent wheals + angioedema
UAS7 (urticaria activity score) + UCT (urticaria control test) — severity monitoring
Routine bloods only if atypical: FBC + ESR/CRP + TSH + tryptase
Trigger workup ONLY if specific suspicion (food challenge for true food allergy — rare in CSU)
Skin biopsy if vasculitis suspected (lesions > 24h + pigmentation residual)
Hereditary angioedema workup: C1-INH level + function + C4 (low) — for recurrent angioedema without urticaria, family history, ACE-i-resistant
Avoid extensive 'allergy testing' — chronic urticaria is rarely allergic
management: EAACI/WAO/GA²LEN STEP-WISE (international):
Step 1 — H1-ANTIHISTAMINE non-sedating standard dose:
Cetirizine 10 mg OD, loratadine 10 mg OD, fexofenadine 180 mg OD, desloratadine 5 mg OD, bilastine 20 mg OD, levocetirizine 5 mg OD
Avoid 1st-gen sedating (chlorpheniramine, hydroxyzine) — limited; sedation, cognitive, anticholinergic
Step 2 — Up-dose H1 antihistamine UP TO 4× STANDARD (off-label but evidence-based):
E.g. cetirizine 10 mg QDS, fexofenadine 180 mg BD-QDS
Allow 2-4 weeks at each step
Step 3 — ADD OMALIZUMAB 300 mg SC q4 weeks (anti-IgE — Xolair):
Strong evidence in CSU (XCUISITE, ASTERIA-1/2, GLACIAL)
Response 60-70%; injection at clinic; safe in pregnancy
Continue 6-12 months then trial cessation
Alternative: ciclosporin 3-5 mg/kg/d (effective but renal/BP toxicity, short-term — third-line)
Step 4 — REFRACTORY: cyclosporine, methotrexate, mycophenolate; emerging — ligelizumab, dupilumab, BTK inhibitors (remibrutinib — Phase 3)
RESCUE for severe flare: short oral prednisolone 30-40 mg × 3-7 days (not for chronic use)
AVOID NSAIDs (worsen urticaria in 30%) + opioids (mast cell activator) where possible
Lifestyle: identify triggers (heat, alcohol, stress, infection — most are non-allergic); cool environment, loose clothing
Mental health support (chronic itch + appearance + sleep impact — high depression rate)
INDUCIBLE URTICARIA:
Cold: H1 + cold tolerance training; rupatadine, omalizumab
Cholinergic (exercise/sweat): H1 high-dose; refractory: omalizumab
Pressure: H1, montelukast adjunct
Solar: photoprotection + H1; phototherapy desensitisation
Dermatographism: H1, often spontaneous resolution
Avoid trigger primary management
PREGNANCY:
Loratadine, cetirizine, levocetirizine — first-line (most data)
Omalizumab — emerging acceptance (large registries)
AVOID 1st-gen + ciclosporin (risk-benefit)
Hereditary angioedema: C1-INH replacement
ANGIOEDEMA WITHOUT URTICARIA:
ACE-i induced — STOP ACE-i; resolve in days-months; alternative antihypertensive (ARB usually OK; if severe — switch class)

Hereditary angioedema (C1-INH deficiency): icatibant (Firazyr — bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist) acute; lanadelumab (anti-kallikrein) prophylaxis; C1-INH replacement (Berinert acute; Cinryze prophylaxis); androgens (danazol — limited now); fresh frozen plasma if specific therapy unavailable
Acquired C1-INH deficiency — workup malignancy + autoimmune
OPTIMISE control: UAS7 / UCT + objective response; advance step at 2-4 weeks if inadequate

references.label: Kenya Clinical Guidelines for Management and Referral of Common Conditions (Levels 4–6 Hospitals), Ministry of Health

title: Anaphylaxis — recognition + adrenaline first + biphasic care
population: Increasing prevalence — food (peanut, tree nut, shellfish, milk, egg, sesame, wheat), drug (penicillin, NSAID, contrast, NMBA), insect sting, latex, exercise + idiopathic. Children + adolescents food-triggered most common.
presentation: Acute onset (minutes-hours after exposure) of mucocutaneous (urticaria, angioedema, flushing) + respiratory (wheeze, stridor, dyspnoea, hypoxia) + cardiovascular (hypotension, tachycardia, collapse, arrhythmia) + GI (cramps, vomiting, diarrhoea). Two or more system involvement + likely exposure = anaphylaxis.
redFlags: ANY suspected anaphylaxis — IM ADRENALINE FIRST (delays in adrenaline = preventable death)
Airway compromise (stridor, hoarseness, drooling, severe oedema)
Refractory to first dose adrenaline — escalate
Biphasic reaction (returns 1-72h after initial — typically 8-12h; some advocate observation 6-12h)
Beta-blocker use (refractory to adrenaline — give glucagon)
diagnostics: CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS — DO NOT WAIT FOR INVESTIGATIONS
World Allergy Organization criteria — exposure to likely allergen + two of: skin, respiratory, CV, GI
Tryptase (acute + 4-12h post + baseline 24h after) — confirms anaphylaxis if rises > 11.4 ng/mL OR 20% increase + 2 ng/mL above baseline
Identify trigger — history is gold standard; allergy testing 4-6 weeks after (specialist) — skin prick + specific IgE + supervised challenge
After recovery: assess + provide adrenaline auto-injector + action plan + medical alert + allergy specialist follow-up + risk stratify for biphasic
management: IMMEDIATE — DO NOT DELAY for any reason:
1. ADRENALINE (epinephrine) IM ANTERIOR-LATERAL THIGH — most important intervention:
Adult: 0.5 mg (500 mcg) IM = 0.5 mL of 1:1000
Adolescent > 30 kg / 12-17 yr: 0.5 mg IM
Child 6-12 yr: 0.3 mg (300 mcg)
Child 6 mo-6 yr: 0.15 mg (150 mcg)
Infant < 6 mo: 0.1-0.15 mg (limited evidence — use IM device)
REPEAT every 5 minutes if no improvement
Auto-injectors: EpiPen / Jext / Anapen 300 mcg (adult) + 150 mcg (junior < 30 kg)
IM thigh — NOT subcutaneous (slower), NOT deltoid (less effective), NOT IV unless cardiac arrest
2. AIRWAY:
Position supine with legs elevated (cardiovascular); upright if respiratory distress; left lateral if pregnant
High-flow O2 via non-rebreather
Intubation early if upper airway compromise (don't wait — oedema progresses; surgical airway preparation)
3. CIRCULATION:
Large-bore IV access × 2 (don't delay adrenaline for IV)
Crystalloid 20 mL/kg paeds / 1-2 L adult bolus over 10-20 min for hypotension
Repeat boluses
4. REFRACTORY ANAPHYLAXIS (after 2+ doses IM adrenaline + fluid):
ICU-monitored ADRENALINE IV INFUSION — 0.1-1 mcg/kg/min titrated to BP (start 0.1, titrate)
Or noradrenaline / vasopressin / metaraminol
Glucagon 1-2 mg IV if on β-blocker (overcomes β-blockade)
Methylene blue for refractory vasodilatory shock
Adjunctive medications (NOT primary):
Hydrocortisone IV 200 mg adult / 4 mg/kg child (no acute benefit; controversial; may reduce biphasic — not first-line)
Chlorphenamine IV/IM 10 mg adult (does NOT treat anaphylaxis — symptom relief only; do not delay adrenaline)
Salbutamol nebulised for bronchospasm
OBSERVATION + DISCHARGE:
Observe minimum 4-6 hours; longer for severe / refractory / biphasic risk (β-blocker user, asthmatic, late presentation, severe / fluid + adrenaline dependent)
Biphasic reaction risk 5-20% (often within 8-12h)
Prior to discharge:
PROVIDE 2 ADRENALINE AUTO-INJECTORS (carry at all times)
Train patient + family on use (when + how)
Anaphylaxis action plan (BSACI / WAO template)
Medic-alert bracelet
Refer ALLERGY specialist within 4-6 weeks for trigger identification + management plan + venom immunotherapy (if sting) + food allergy specialist + education
Avoid known trigger
Address asthma + cardiovascular comorbidity
Adrenaline auto-injector prescription + repeat
School / workplace plan if child
Discharge medication: 3-5 days oral antihistamine ± oral steroid (does NOT prevent biphasic but controls cutaneous symptoms; controversial)
PREGNANCY:
Same adrenaline doses
Left lateral tilt to relieve IVC compression
Address fetal monitoring (CTG)
Anaesthetic / obstetric / NICU input
BETA-BLOCKER USE:
Adrenaline often less effective
Give GLUCAGON 1-2 mg IV (bypasses β-receptor) — repeat q5 min
Higher adrenaline doses + supportive
PROTRACTED / IDIOPATHIC:
Investigate mastocytosis (baseline tryptase + bone marrow if elevated)
Long-term H1 antihistamine + cromoglycate + omalizumab + leukotriene receptor antagonist for prophylaxis
Specialist allergy / immunology
FOOD-INDUCED EXERCISE-INDUCED ANAPHYLAXIS:
Specific trigger (often wheat — omega-5 gliadin); exercise within hours of food
Avoid combination
POPULATION + EDUCATION:
Schools + workplaces — train on adrenaline auto-injector use
Allergy education (label reading, restaurant ordering)
Hospital / EMS - protocols for community + pre-hospital
SSA: counterfeit / unregulated adrenaline a concern — quality + access advocacy

title: Skin cancer — melanoma + non-melanoma (BCC + SCC) workup
population: Risk: fair skin + sun exposure + immunosuppression + family history + multiple naevi. SSA: less common but more aggressive at presentation due to delayed diagnosis + skin pigmentation masking; albinism populations very high SCC risk.
presentation: MELANOMA — ABCDE (Asymmetry, Border irregular, Colour variegation, Diameter > 6 mm, Evolution). Ugly duckling sign. Subtypes: superficial spreading (commonest), nodular (worst prognosis), lentigo maligna (chronic sun damage), acral lentiginous (palms/soles/nails — most common in SSA + Asian); BCC — pearly papule, telangiectasia, central ulceration ('rodent ulcer'); SCC — keratotic firm nodule, induration, ulceration on sun-exposed skin or chronic wound (Marjolin ulcer).
redFlags: Pigmented lesion + ABCDE features — refer dermatology 2 weeks
Sub-ungual pigmentation (acral melanoma — common SSA + Asian)
SCC arising in chronic ulcer / scar / sinus (Marjolin ulcer)
Multiple BCC / SCC in young / immunocompromised (Gorlin syndrome, XP)
Suspected melanoma in albinism (extremely high risk)
diagnostics: Full-body skin examination + dermoscopy (specialist)
Excisional biopsy with 2-3 mm margin (suspected melanoma — do NOT shave biopsy melanoma if depth important; shave acceptable for clearly benign / BCC)
Punch biopsy for diagnostic uncertainty (if too large to excise)
Breslow thickness + Clark level (melanoma) + AJCC staging (8th edition)
Mitotic rate + ulceration + ulceration + lymphovascular invasion
BRAF V600E mutation testing for stage III/IV melanoma (targeted therapy eligibility)
Lymph node ultrasound + sentinel lymph node biopsy for melanoma > 1 mm or 0.8-1 mm with adverse features
Staging imaging (CT chest/abdo/pelvis + brain MRI ± PET-CT) for stage III/IV
LDH (prognostic — melanoma)
management: PRIMARY EXCISION:
BCC: 4-5 mm margin (low-risk superficial), 5-10 mm (high-risk infiltrative / morphoeic), Mohs surgery for face / high-risk / recurrent
SCC: 4-6 mm low-risk, 6-10 mm high-risk; Mohs for face / high-risk / recurrent
Melanoma: 0.5 cm for in-situ, 1 cm for ≤ 1 mm Breslow, 1-2 cm for 1-2 mm, 2 cm for > 2 mm (UK/AAD)
BCC (most curable):
Surgical excision for most
Mohs micrographic surgery for high-risk + face + recurrent
Cryotherapy / curettage + electrodessication for low-risk superficial
Topical imiquimod 5% / 5-FU for superficial
Photodynamic therapy
Radiotherapy for unresectable / elderly
Vismodegib (Hedgehog pathway) for advanced / metastatic — locally advanced or metastatic BCC (ERIVANCE)
SCC:
Surgical excision (Mohs for face / high-risk / recurrent / immunocompromised)
Field treatment for actinic damage (topical 5-FU, imiquimod, photodynamic)
Radiotherapy alternative
Advanced / metastatic SCC: CEMIPLIMAB (anti-PD1; FDA 2018 EMPOWER-CSCC-1), pembrolizumab; cetuximab + chemoradiation
Mohs for invasive / high-risk
MELANOMA — paradigm shift with immunotherapy:
Stage I-II: wide local excision
Stage III: WLE + SLNB / lymphadenectomy + adjuvant therapy
Adjuvant for high-risk resected: pembrolizumab / nivolumab (anti-PD1) — CHECKMATE-238 / KEYNOTE-054; dabrafenib + trametinib (BRAF V600E mutant — COMBI-AD)
Stage IV: IMMUNOTHERAPY FIRST-LINE: ipilimumab + nivolumab combination (CHECKMATE-067 — 50% 5-yr survival); or anti-PD1 monotherapy; or relatlimab + nivolumab (anti-LAG3 — RELATIVITY-047)
BRAF V600E + V600K (50% melanomas): targeted therapy dabrafenib + trametinib / vemurafenib + cobimetinib / encorafenib + binimetinib
ACRAL MELANOMA (common SSA): less BRAF mutation; immunotherapy + KIT-targeted (imatinib for KIT-mutated)
Brain metastases: ipilimumab + nivolumab effective; stereotactic radiosurgery
Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) — intratumoural
Tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy — LIFILEUCEL FDA 2024 (Amtagvi) for advanced refractory melanoma
PRECISION ONCOLOGY:
BRAF V600E/K — kinase inhibitor
Tumour mutational burden — immunotherapy benefit
PD-L1 status
Microsatellite instability
FOLLOW-UP:
Stage I-II: clinical exam q3-6 mo × 2 yr, q6-12 mo × 5 yr, annual lifetime
Stage III-IV: more intensive imaging + clinical
Patient self-examination education
Second primary risk + family screening (FAMMM, CDKN2A)
PREVENTION:
Primary: sun avoidance + sunscreen SPF 30-50 + protective clothing + sunglasses + avoid tanning beds
Albinism populations (Tanzania + Malawi + Kenya) — sun protection + early intervention essential
Vitamin D adequate intake balanced
Immunosuppressed (transplant, HIV) — vigilant surveillance + sun protection
Sunscreen culturally appropriate + accessible SSA
POPULATION SSA:
Lower incidence overall in darker skin
But often more advanced at presentation + worse outcomes
ACRAL melanoma most common subtype
ALBINISM extremely high SCC rate — public health priority (Standing Voice + Under the Same Sun + Tanzanian albinism programmes)
Address access to dermatology + biopsy + treatment + immunotherapy
Kenya MOH NCD strategy

title: Diabetic retinopathy — screening + treatment (anti-VEGF era)
population: Common chronic complication of diabetes — leading cause of preventable blindness in working-age adults. SSA: rapidly rising with diabetes epidemic; screening + access limited; major preventable blindness.
presentation: Mostly asymptomatic until advanced (sudden vision loss, floaters, distortion). Stages: non-proliferative (mild → moderate → severe) → proliferative (neovascularisation, vitreous haemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment) → diabetic macular oedema (DMO) at any stage.
redFlags: Sudden vision loss / curtain falling (vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment, central retinal vein occlusion) — urgent ophth
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (neovascularisation) — refer ophth urgent for PRP / anti-VEGF
Diabetic macular oedema with vision impact — anti-VEGF or laser focal
Neovascular glaucoma (advanced) — pain + IOP raised — urgent ophth
diagnostics: SCREENING (NICE / ICOPE / WHO):
T1DM: from age 12 OR 5 years post-diagnosis (whichever later)
T2DM: at diagnosis, annually thereafter
Pregnancy + DM: each trimester + post-delivery
Adults with diabetes screened annually with fundus photography (dilated) or slit-lamp ophthalmoscopy
STAGING (ETDRS / ICDR):
NPDR mild (microaneurysms)
NPDR moderate (more microaneurysms + dot/blot haemorrhages + cotton-wool spots + IRMA)
NPDR severe (4-2-1 rule — extensive in 4 quadrants or 2 quadrants venous beading or 1 quadrant IRMA)
PDR (neovascularisation of disc / elsewhere + vitreous haemorrhage + preretinal haemorrhage)
DMO (diabetic macular oedema — fluid in macula; CSDMO clinically significant)
DIAGNOSIS:
Dilated fundus photography / ophthalmoscopy
OPTICAL COHERENCE TOMOGRAPHY (OCT) — macular oedema + structural detail
Fluorescein angiography for selected
OCT angiography — newer
AI screening — emerging (FDA-approved IDx-DR; deployable in primary care + remote SSA — useful for screening gap)
Visual acuity
Comprehensive eye exam including IOP (rule out glaucoma)
management: GLYCAEMIC + BP + LIPID CONTROL (foundation — UKPDS, ACCORD-Eye):
Tight HbA1c (individualised — target ~ 53 mmol/mol for most; avoid hypoglycaemia)
Statin per CV risk + dyslipidaemia
Smoking cessation
Address comorbid renal disease
Avoid rapid HbA1c lowering (paradoxical early worsening of retinopathy — gradual)
MILD-MODERATE NPDR:
Observation + glycaemic / BP / lipid optimisation
Annual screening continued
SEVERE NPDR / PROLIFERATIVE:
PAN-RETINAL PHOTOCOAGULATION (PRP) — laser; reduces severe vision loss

ANTI-VEGF (intravitreal injection) — paradigm shift: ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab (off-label cheaper) — equivalent to PRP for PDR (Protocol S NEJM 2015) — preferred where macular oedema co-exists
Faricimab (Vabysmo — anti-VEGF + anti-Ang2) — newer + longer duration
Vitrectomy for vitreous haemorrhage / tractional retinal detachment
DIABETIC MACULAR OEDEMA (DMO):
Centre-involving with vision impact: ANTI-VEGF intravitreal (aflibercept first-line per DRCR Protocol T — superior at lower vision; ranibizumab + bevacizumab options) monthly initially then PRN
Faricimab longer duration
STEROID intravitreal (triamcinolone, dexamethasone implant Ozurdex, fluocinolone implant Iluvien) — second-line; cataract + IOP rise concerns
Focal/grid laser — for non-centre-involving
Combination strategies
ADVANCED:
Vitrectomy for refractory haemorrhage, fibrotic membrane, traction detachment
Cataract surgery — appropriate timing (worsens DMO if not stabilised first)
Glaucoma management (especially neovascular)
EMERGING THERAPIES:
Anti-VEGF longer-duration (faricimab, brolucizumab)
Port delivery system (PDS — refillable ranibizumab) — Susvimo
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (axitinib intravitreal)
Gene therapy in trials
Anti-inflammatory targeting
POPULATION + SSA:
Major preventable blindness
Limited ophthalmologists in many countries
AI-assisted screening could close gap (deployable at primary care + community)
Anti-VEGF cost barrier — bevacizumab (off-label compounded) much cheaper alternative (Lucentis vs Avastin — equivalent in CATT + IVAN trials; widely used SSA)
Integrated diabetes + eye care
Kenya National Eye Health Plan + Kenya Diabetes Strategy
Cataract + DM common combination — comprehensive eye care

title: Cataract — diagnosis + modern phacoemulsification + IOL
population: Leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide; especially SSA — affordable surgery scale-up has transformed eye health. Age-related (most), congenital, traumatic, metabolic (diabetes), drug-induced (steroid), radiation.
presentation: Gradual painless vision loss — blurry vision, glare, halos around lights at night, faded colours, decreased contrast sensitivity, frequent prescription changes. Examination: opacity in lens (visible at slit-lamp). Mature white cataract late presentation.
redFlags: Acute angle-closure glaucoma in patient with mature cataract — surgical removal urgent
Diabetic with mature cataract — preceding workup
Trauma + cataract + suspected globe perforation — emergency
Posterior subcapsular cataract progression (steroid / DM / radiation — different aetiology workup)
Congenital cataract in newborn (red reflex screening — early surgery before age 6-12 weeks for amblyopia prevention)
diagnostics: Visual acuity (Snellen + pinhole — pinhole improvement suggests refractive component still correctable)
Slit-lamp examination (lens opacity location + density — nuclear, cortical, posterior subcapsular)
Fundoscopy (rule out coexisting macular / retinal / optic nerve disease)
Tonometry (rule out glaucoma)
Biometry pre-surgical (axial length + keratometry — calculate IOL power)
B-scan if dense cataract obscures fundus
Diabetes screen (cataract earlier age in diabetics)
Newborn red reflex screening (congenital cataract — urgent surgery referral)
management: INDICATIONS for surgery:
Visual acuity affecting QoL / occupation / driving / reading
Anisometropia
Phacomorphic glaucoma
Concurrent with retina / glaucoma surgery
Congenital (urgent — amblyopia prevention)
Mature lens-induced complications
MODERN CATARACT SURGERY:
PHACOEMULSIFICATION (phaco) — small-incision (2.2-3 mm), foldable IOL through small incision — gold standard developed world; rapid recovery
Manual small-incision cataract surgery (MSICS) — cost-effective high-volume SSA + India model (Aravind, KCCO Kenya, Kilimanjaro Centre); excellent outcomes
Femtosecond laser-assisted — newer, expensive, marginal benefit
Intraocular lens (IOL):
Monofocal — distance focus (most common; reading glasses needed)
Toric — correct astigmatism
Multifocal / extended depth of focus — reduce need for glasses (trade-offs: night vision halos, expense)
Light-adjustable lens — newer, customise post-op
Cataract surgery improves vision AND reduces falls (Cochrane) + improves cognition + mood + QoL
Out-patient typical (local anaesthesia — topical / subtenon)
PRE-OP:
Biometry for IOL calculation
Optimise systemic conditions (DM, HTN, anticoagulation review)
Address tear film + blepharitis (treat preoperatively)
Topical antibiotic + dilating drops pre-op
INTRA-OP:
Topical / subtenon anaesthesia (general for selected)
Aseptic technique critical (endophthalmitis prevention — pre-op povidone-iodine 5%, intra-cameral cefuroxime / moxifloxacin at end)
POST-OP:
Topical antibiotic + steroid (or NSAID) × 4 weeks tapering
Review at 1 day + 1 week + 4 weeks
Avoid heavy lifting / swimming / eye rubbing × 2 weeks
Visual recovery within days-weeks
Glasses prescription stable at 4-6 weeks
COMPLICATIONS (rare with modern technique):
Endophthalmitis (0.05-0.1%; intra-cameral cefuroxime reduces 80%)
Posterior capsule rupture + vitreous loss
Cystoid macular oedema
Posterior capsule opacification (PCO — 'after cataract') — YAG laser capsulotomy in-office
Toxic anterior segment syndrome (TASS)
Refractive surprise — IOL exchange / refractive surgery
Retinal detachment (increased post-cataract; especially high myopes)
CONGENITAL CATARACT:
Urgent surgery in first 6-12 weeks (amblyopia prevention)
Optical rehabilitation (contact lens initially, IOL later)
Patching therapy for amblyopia
DIABETIC CATARACT:
Earlier age + faster progression
Often coexists with retinopathy — comprehensive eye care
Pre-op stabilise DR + DMO (anti-VEGF if needed; cataract surgery can worsen DMO)
Continue diabetes optimisation
STEROID-INDUCED:
Posterior subcapsular pattern
Topical + systemic + inhaled (high-dose) — all contribute
Reduce steroid dose where possible
Cataract surgery as needed
POPULATION + SSA:
Cataract is LEADING cause of blindness in SSA
Cost-effective interventions (MSICS — < $40 per surgery)
Kenya, Kilimanjaro Centre for Community Ophthalmology (KCCO), Sightsavers, Operation Eyesight Universal — scale-up models
Outreach + tele-ophthalmology + community case-finding
WHO VISION 2020 + IAPB Eye Health Plan
Train cataract surgical team + ophthalmic clinical officers
Kenya National Eye Health Plan

title: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) — screening + medical + surgical
population: Leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. SSA + African ancestry — earlier onset + faster progression + worse outcomes. Family history + age > 40 + IOP > 21 + thin cornea + myopia + diabetes + sleep apnoea.
presentation: Asymptomatic until advanced peripheral vision loss (tunnel vision); patient often unaware until ~ 40% optic nerve damage. Painless progressive optic neuropathy + glaucomatous visual field defects.
redFlags: African ancestry — earlier onset + more aggressive — lower threshold to screen / treat
Rapid progression despite treatment — secondary cause / non-adherence
Suspected pigment dispersion / pseudoexfoliation (different secondary glaucomas)
Normal-tension glaucoma (vascular + neurodegenerative — managed similarly but lower IOP target)
Suspected end-stage / blindness imminent — urgent specialist
diagnostics: SCREENING:
African ancestry + family history > 35 yr — annual screening
General > 40 yr — every 2-3 years
Comprehensive eye exam with IOP + optic nerve + visual field
DIAGNOSIS:
TONOMETRY — IOP > 21 (but not diagnostic alone; 40% of POAG have normal IOP)
GONIOSCOPY — open angle (vs angle-closure)
OPTIC NERVE — cup-to-disc ratio, neuroretinal rim, splinter haemorrhages, NFL defects
VISUAL FIELD (Humphrey 24-2 or similar) — paracentral / arcuate / nasal step defects
OCT optic nerve + RNFL — early structural damage
CORNEAL THICKNESS (pachymetry) — thin cornea = greater real risk + IOP underestimated
Compare to fellow eye + serial monitoring
OCULAR HYPERTENSION (high IOP without optic nerve damage) — risk-stratify per Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS): age, IOP, central corneal thickness, vertical CDR, pattern standard deviation
management: TARGET IOP — individualised, typically:
Mild POAG: 25-30% reduction from baseline
Moderate: 30-40% reduction
Severe / advanced: > 40% + lower absolute (< 14)
Normal-tension: < 12-14
FIRST-LINE:
PROSTAGLANDIN ANALOGUE — once-daily evening:
LATANOPROST 0.005% — generic, most common
Travoprost, bimatoprost, tafluprost
Reduce IOP 25-35%
Side effects: iris pigmentation darkening, eyelash growth, periorbital hyperpigmentation, conjunctival hyperaemia, prostaglandin-associated periorbitopathy
Preservative-free preferred long-term (ocular surface)
SLT — SELECTIVE LASER TRABECULOPLASTY:
LiGHT trial NEJM 2019 — SLT non-inferior + cost-effective as first-line vs drops
Outpatient, low-side-effect, repeatable
Reduces drops + adherence issues
First-line in many guidelines (especially primary care SSA — low cost + access)
SECOND-LINE (add or switch):
β-BLOCKER (timolol 0.5% BD) — cautions asthma + COPD + HF + bradyarrhythmia + systemic interaction
α2-AGONIST (brimonidine BD-TID) — fatigue + allergic conjunctivitis common; avoid in children < 2 (severe sedation/apnoea)
CARBONIC ANHYDRASE INHIBITOR (dorzolamide BD-TID, brinzolamide BD) — burning + bitter taste + sulpha allergy caution
COMBINATIONS (latanoprost + timolol, dorzolamide + timolol — fixed combos improve adherence)
RHO-KINASE INHIBITOR (netarsudil) — newer; conjunctival hyperaemia common
ORAL CARBONIC ANHYDRASE INHIBITOR (acetazolamide) — short-term; systemic SE
THIRD-LINE / REFRACTORY:
TRABECULECTOMY — gold standard surgical; bleb-based; risks: hypotony, infection, bleb leak
TUBE SHUNT (Baerveldt, Ahmed, Molteno valve) — increasingly first-choice surgical alternative
MIGS (minimally invasive glaucoma surgery): iStent, Hydrus, XEN gel stent, Kahook — combined with cataract surgery
Cyclophotocoagulation (laser ablation of ciliary body) — refractory + end-stage
Cataract surgery alone (phacoemulsification) lowers IOP modestly + may stabilise mild glaucoma
ADHERENCE:
Adherence < 50% with drops chronic — key challenge
Punctal occlusion technique training
Simplify regimen (combos, once-daily)
SLT as alternative (one procedure, repeatable)
Reminder systems
Cost (especially SSA) — generic latanoprost + timolol affordable; Kenya KEML
FOLLOW-UP:
Every 3-6 months stable
Visual field + OCT every 6-12 months
More frequent if progression / unstable
PROGRESSION MANAGEMENT:
Identify cause (non-adherence + non-IOP factors)
Reduce target IOP further
Add drug class or switch / surgical intervention
PREGNANCY:
Latanoprost limited data — usually continue if needed
Avoid carbonic anhydrase + acetazolamide (teratogenic 1st trim)
β-blocker — caution; brimonidine — avoid late pregnancy / breastfeeding (infant CNS depression)
POPULATION + SSA:
Major preventable blindness
African ancestry — younger onset + worse outcomes
Train primary care + ophthalmic clinical officers
Telemedicine + tele-ophthalmology + community screening (Glaucoma Eye Health initiatives)
Generic latanoprost + timolol KEML access
SLT as one-stop intervention reducing adherence burden
Kenya National Eye Health Plan + IAPB regional initiatives
