title: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) — observe / steroid / TPO-RA / rituximab
population: All ages; female predominance adult chronic; children — often post-viral self-limiting.
presentation: Petechiae + purpura + mucosal bleeding (gums, epistaxis, menorrhagia) + isolated thrombocytopenia (platelets often < 30 with bleeding). May be incidental finding. Children — sudden onset post-viral; adults — gradual.
redFlags: Splenectomy candidate — vaccinations + lifelong infection risk
diagnostics: Diagnosis of exclusion — FBC + film (isolated low platelets, no abnormalities)
Coagulation normal; UEC + LFT + LDH
HIV + HCV + HBV (treatable causes mimicking ITP)
ANA + APL antibodies (SLE/APS)
Helicobacter pylori (treatment-responsive ITP, esp. Japan)
TSH, immunoglobulins, peripheral blood film for review
Bone marrow biopsy — selected (atypical features, age > 60, before splenectomy, refractory)
Pregnancy test
management: ASH 2019 + International ITP Working Group 2019 + BSH 2003 (update):
OBSERVE if no bleeding + platelets > 30 (adult) or > 20 (child) — most spontaneous remission
FIRST-LINE (need treatment — bleeding or platelets < 30 + bleeding risk):
PREDNISOLONE 1 mg/kg/d × 1-2 wk taper over 6-8 wk (response 60-80%, sustained 20-30%)
OR DEXAMETHASONE 40 mg/d × 4 d (high-dose pulse — equivalent or faster response — preferred newer guidelines)
Or IV IMMUNOGLOBULIN 1 g/kg × 1-2 doses (rapid + temporary; bleeding emergencies, pregnancy, surgery)
Anti-D in Rh+ non-splenectomised (less commonly used)
SECOND-LINE (no sustained response — most adults need it):
TPO RECEPTOR AGONISTS — first-line non-steroid in chronic ITP — preferred over splenectomy first (ASH 2019):
Eltrombopag (Revolade/Promacta) 50 mg PO OD (race-adjust East Asian start 25); food interactions (cation/dairy)
Romiplostim (Nplate) SC weekly titrated
Avatrombopag (Doptelet) oral
Response 80%; thrombosis risk + hepatic + marrow fibrosis (rare)
RITUXIMAB 375 mg/m² × 4 wk — durable remission 20-30%; HBV reactivation screen
FOSTAMATINIB (Syk inhibitor) — refractory
THIRD-LINE / refractory:
Splenectomy — durable remission 60% — VACCINATE pre-op (pneumococcal + Hib + meningococcal) + penicillin prophylaxis lifelong + counsel sepsis risk
Mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, dapsone, danazol
EMERGENCY BLEEDING / surgery / critical thrombocytopenia:
Platelet transfusion + IVIG 1 g/kg + IV methylpred 1 g + TXA + control bleeding source
ICH — neurosurgery consult
PAEDIATRIC ITP:
Most self-limit — observe if mild + no bleeding (watchful waiting BSH/ASH)
Treat only if bleeding or major risk — IVIG / pred / anti-D
Chronic ITP child — same second-line
PREGNANCY:
Mild — observe; severe — pred + IVIG (avoid second-line agents)
Delivery — platelets > 50 for vaginal, > 80 for caesarean / epidural
Neonatal ITP — check platelets in baby (transient — maternal antibody crosses)
HELICOBACTER PYLORI eradication if positive (response variable, esp. Japan + Italy)
AVOID: aspirin / NSAID / antiplatelet; IM injections; rectal exam if platelets < 20
Lifestyle — soft toothbrush + electric razor + avoid contact sport during low platelet phase
Vaccine schedule (no live during immunosuppression)
SSA: pred + IVIG + dexamethasone widely available; rituximab + TPO-RA access advocacy; splenectomy with vaccination + prophylaxis option; integrate with HIV/HCV/HBV treatment.

title: Thalassaemia (α + β) and G6PD deficiency — comprehensive management
population: THALASSAEMIA: Mediterranean + Middle East + South Asia + SE Asia + sub-Saharan + diaspora; α more in Asia/Africa, β more Mediterranean/MENA. G6PD: 400 million globally — sub-Saharan Africa + Mediterranean + Middle East + Asia high; X-linked (males predominantly).
presentation: β-thalassaemia major — transfusion-dependent from 6-24 mo (failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, frontal bossing if untreated, iron overload sequelae); β-intermedia — variable; trait — microcytic asymptomatic. α-thalassaemia — silent carrier → trait → HbH disease → Hb Bart's hydrops (incompatible with life). G6PD — neonatal jaundice + acute haemolytic anaemia after oxidant exposure (fava beans, primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, sulfa, naphthalene, ciprofloxacin, methylene blue).
redFlags: Iron overload sequelae thalassaemia — cardiomyopathy (top mortality cause) + endocrinopathies + hepatic
G6PD favism — severe haemolysis + AKI + DIC + cardiovascular collapse + death
Pregnancy + thalassaemia carrier — antenatal screen partner; genetic counselling
diagnostics: FBC + film + reticulocyte + iron studies + ferritin + Hb electrophoresis / HPLC (HbA2 + HbF + variants)
α-thalassaemia DNA studies (electrophoresis often normal trait — needs molecular)
G6PD enzyme assay — DEFERRED during acute haemolysis (false-normal due to high reticulocytes — repeat in 3 mo); quantitative + qualitative
Neonatal screen — bilirubin + check G6PD before primaquine in malaria-endemic areas
Antenatal + carrier screen (Mediterranean / SSA / Asian populations)
Cardiac T2* MRI + liver MRI/FerriScan for iron overload (transfusion-dependent)
Endocrinopathy screen (transfusion-dependent) — TSH, glucose, calcium, gonadotrophin, GH, vitamin D
management: TIF (Thalassaemia International Federation) 2023 + WHO + BSH:
β-THALASSAEMIA MAJOR (transfusion-dependent):
REGULAR TRANSFUSION (q3-4 wk) maintain pre-transfusion Hb 95-105 g/L — prevents complications
IRON CHELATION mandatory (ferritin > 1000 or after 10-20 transfusions):
Deferasirox (Exjade/Jadenu) PO OD 20-40 mg/kg — first-line modern
Deferiprone PO TDS 75-100 mg/kg/d — cardiac iron chelation good; agranulocytosis risk (FBC monitor)
Deferoxamine SC infusion 8-12h × 5-7 nights/wk — gold standard but burden — pumps
Combination therapy (deferiprone + deferoxamine) for severe cardiac iron
Monitor — ferritin q3 mo, T2* cardiac + liver MRI annual
FOLIC ACID 5 mg/d; vit D + calcium
Splenectomy — selected (hypersplenism + transfusion ↑) — vaccinations + lifelong penicillin
Endocrine surveillance + treat hypogonadism / DM / hypothyroidism / osteoporosis
Cardiac echo + ECG annual; hepatitis surveillance
LUSPATERCEPT (Reblozyl) SC q3 wk — BELIEVE NEJM 2020 — reduces transfusion burden in non-curative β-thal (FDA 2019)
ALLOGENEIC HSCT — matched sibling donor curative in young patient — best outcomes

GENE THERAPY: betibeglogene autotemcel (Zynteglo) lentiviral β-globin — FDA 2022; exa-cel (Casgevy) BCL11A CRISPR FDA 2024 — both curative for transfusion-dependent β-thal (eligible severe; cost + access)
β-INTERMEDIA: intermittent transfusion + chelation; hydroxyurea trial; luspatercept

α-THALASSAEMIA: HbH disease — folate + intermittent transfusion if symptomatic; Bart's hydrops — intrauterine transfusion + planning (some survive with intensive care + chronic transfusion + curative HSCT)
ANTENATAL SCREEN + GENETIC COUNSELLING — prevent severe forms (couple at risk → PGD, antenatal diagnosis, planned pregnancy)
G6PD DEFICIENCY:

Lifelong AVOIDANCE of triggers — fava beans, primaquine (TEST before in malaria-endemic — Kenya MoH), dapsone, sulfa, naphthalene, nitrofurantoin, methylene blue, certain ciprofloxacin/quinolones, rasburicase, henna; certain herbal supplements
Provide medical alert card + family screen
Acute haemolysis: STOP trigger + supportive (hydration to prevent AKI from haemoglobinuria + transfusion if Hb < 60 + symptomatic) + avoid further oxidants; methylene blue contraindicated (worsens)
Neonatal jaundice — phototherapy + exchange if severe — kernicterus prevention
Favism: severe — admit + transfuse + hydrate

Malaria: use ACT (not primaquine) for P. falciparum; for P. vivax radical cure — primaquine 0.25-0.75 mg/kg × 14 d (G6PD deficient — give weekly 0.75 mg/kg × 8 wk under supervision; tafenoquine single-dose option — G6PD test required > 70% activity; chloroquine for blood-stage)
Pregnancy + lactation — same avoidance; partner / antenatal counsel; neonatal jaundice anticipation
COVID — methylene blue + hydroxychloroquine in G6PD caution
SSA + Asia SCALE-UP:
Universal newborn screen for haemoglobinopathies + G6PD where prevalent
Pre-marital + antenatal carrier screening + counselling
Hydroxyurea + transfusion + chelation programmes (chelation expensive — deferasirox biosimilar advocacy)
G6PD point-of-care test before tafenoquine + dapsone (TB + leprosy + dermatitis herpetiformis) + primaquine — increasing availability (CareStart, SD Biosensor)
Training paediatrics + haematology + primary care

references.label: WHO G6PD + malaria policy / tafenoquine guidance

title: Schistosomiasis — praziquantel MDA towards 2030 elimination
population: 240 million globally; 90% in sub-Saharan Africa (Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Egypt, Yemen, DRC); fresh-water snail intermediate; S. haematobium (urogenital), S. mansoni (intestinal), S. japonicum/mekongi/intercalatum.
presentation: ACUTE Katayama (3-8 wk post-exposure) — fever + urticaria + eosinophilia + cough + hepatosplenomegaly. CHRONIC — terminal haematuria (S. haematobium classic — schoolchildren); dysuria, frequency; bladder/ureteric/kidney fibrosis + hydronephrosis; bladder squamous cell carcinoma late; cervical schistosomiasis (women — abnormal smear, post-coital bleed, infertility); FGS (female genital schistosomiasis — IMPORTANT — increases HIV acquisition risk 3-4×). Intestinal — abdominal pain, blood/mucus diarrhoea, hepatic periportal fibrosis, portal HT, variceal bleed; pulmonary HT (S. mansoni eggs lodged); CNS rarely.
redFlags: Variceal haemorrhage from periportal fibrosis (Symmers' fibrosis)
FGS — HIV acquisition + infertility + advocacy + screening
Acute Katayama in traveller — eosinophilia + recent fresh-water
diagnostics: Urine — terminal microscopy ova ± concentration (S. haematobium) — peak shedding midday + after exercise
Stool ova + parasites (S. mansoni — Kato-Katz semi-quant standard for MDA monitoring)
Serology (ELISA) — useful in returning travellers (no eggs)
POC urine antigen CCA (circulating cathodic antigen) — S. mansoni — field-deployable
FBC eosinophilia, raised IgE; UEC + LFT + abdo US (hepatic fibrosis, hydronephrosis, bladder thickening)
Cervical exam + colposcopy if FGS suspected (sandy patches, rubbery polyps); HIV testing
Bladder cancer surveillance — chronic S. haematobium + haematuria — cystoscopy
management: WHO Roadmap 2030 + 2022 WHO Schistosomiasis Guideline:
TREATMENT — PRAZIQUANTEL 40 mg/kg PO single dose all species (60 mg/kg S. japonicum/mekongi divided 2-3 doses)
Repeat after 4-6 weeks in heavy infection or persistent symptoms (immature schistosomula not killed first dose)
Adverse: abdominal pain, dizziness, urticaria (common, mild, transient)
Pregnancy + lactation — SAFE — WHO 2006 reversed previous caution; treat pregnant + lactating
Paediatric — > 2 yr standard dose; under-2 limited data — paediatric formulation arpraziquantel (Pedriquantel — for under-6 + smaller children — WHO PQ 2024)
MASS DRUG ADMINISTRATION (MDA) — annual / biennial in endemic communities:
Targets school-age children (5-14 yr) primarily; preschoolers; adults in heavy transmission
WHO 2030 target: 75% MDA coverage in eligible communities
Kenya National Schistosomiasis Programme + Schools Health Programme
Integrated with deworming (albendazole/mebendazole for STH)
ACUTE KATAYAMA: praziquantel + STEROID pred 30-60 mg/d to suppress immune reaction; repeat PZQ 4-6 wk later (1st dose ineffective on schistosomula)
COMPLICATIONS:
Periportal fibrosis + portal HT — endoscopy + variceal band ligation + non-selective β-blocker; TIPS; transplant rare
Hydronephrosis — surgical intervention if obstructive
Bladder cancer — cystectomy + chemo per oncology
FGS — praziquantel does NOT reverse established lesions; advocacy + counsel + repeat PZQ + condom + HIV prevention/PrEP + fertility support
Neuroschistosomiasis — high-dose steroid + PZQ + surgical decompression if cord
Pulmonary HT — PAH specialist + sildenafil/bosentan
VECTOR CONTROL: snail elimination (molluscicides niclosamide — environmental issue); access to safe water + sanitation (WASH); behaviour change — avoid fresh-water contact in endemic areas
PREVENTION TRAVELLER: avoid fresh-water swimming/wading in endemic areas — Lake Victoria/Tana/Malawi — towel dry vigorously if exposed; serology 3 mo + treat empirically if exposure + symptoms
ELIMINATION 2030: Egypt + Morocco close; Kenya + most SSA target morbidity control → elimination; vaccine candidates in trials
SSA: Kenya — Bilharzia common Lake Victoria + Tana basin + coast + irrigated areas; school MDA + community awareness + WASH + healthcare access + FGS recognition (especially with high HIV).

title: Cutaneous leishmaniasis — local vs systemic per species and complexity
population: 0.7-1 million new cases/yr; Middle East (Afghanistan, Syria, Iran), Mediterranean, Central + South Asia, Africa, Latin America. Old World — L. major + L. tropica + L. aethiopica + L. infantum; New World — L. braziliensis (mucocutaneous risk), L. mexicana, L. amazonensis.
presentation: Skin lesion 2-6 wk post-sandfly bite — papule → nodule → ulcer with raised border + central crater (volcano sign) + 1-many lesions on exposed areas; usually painless. Heals over 2-15 mo with scar. Diffuse CL (L. aethiopica + L. amazonensis) — non-ulcerating widespread + immunocompromised. MUCOCUTANEOUS (espundia — L. braziliensis 1-5 yr after CL) — nasal + oral + laryngeal destruction.
redFlags: Mucocutaneous risk — L. braziliensis (New World) + L. aethiopica complex — ALL New World CL → consider systemic treatment + ENT followup
Facial / overlying joint lesions (functional + cosmetic) — favour systemic
Multiple > 4 lesions, large > 4 cm — favour systemic
diagnostics: Lesion smear (slit-skin or scraping border) — Giemsa staining for amastigotes
Lesion biopsy + culture (NNN medium) + PCR (species identification critical for treatment decision)
Montenegro skin test (historical)
PCR — species ID — crucial for selecting local vs systemic and predicting mucocutaneous risk
management: WHO 2022 Leishmaniasis Guidelines + PAHO + LeishGEN:
DECIDE LOCAL vs SYSTEMIC based on:
Species (L. braziliensis ALWAYS systemic — mucocutaneous risk)
Number + size + location (face / joints / multiple → systemic)
Patient (immunocompromised → systemic)
Cosmetic + functional concerns
LOCAL (single + small + away from joints + face + non-braziliensis):
Cryotherapy (liquid N2) — weekly × 3-6 wk
Thermotherapy (50°C × 30s — ThermoMed device) — single session — WHO suitable Old World
Intralesional antimony — meglumine antimoniate or SSG injected lesion + edges q3-7 d × 3-5
Paromomycin 15% + methylbenzethonium / urea topical ointment BD × 20 d
Topical imiquimod adjunct
Observation alone — many self-heal but scars
SYSTEMIC (large / multiple / face / joints / braziliensis / immunocomp):
Pentavalent antimony (SSG / meglumine antimoniate) 20 mg/kg/d IV/IM × 20 d (Old World) or × 28 d (New World)
Monitor — ECG, LFT, amylase, FBC; cardiac toxicity (QT, T wave)
Miltefosine 2.5 mg/kg/d × 28 d (oral; teratogenic; effective L. major / L. mexicana / L. donovani; less L. braziliensis)
Liposomal amphotericin B 3 mg/kg × 6 doses (immunocomp + pregnancy + refractory + Old World L. aethiopica + L. tropica)
Pentamidine — less common; L. guyanensis
Combination + sequential therapy emerging
MUCOCUTANEOUS (espundia):
Systemic — pentavalent antimony × 28-30 d OR LAmB OR amphotericin B deoxycholate OR miltefosine; longer + more aggressive
ENT specialist + reconstruction
DIFFUSE CL (immunocompromised, L. aethiopica/amazonensis):
Pentavalent antimony + interferon-γ; relapsing — long-term
PREGNANCY: LAmB preferred (avoid pentavalent + miltefosine); often defer if mild + non-braziliensis until post-partum
PAEDIATRIC: same regimens weight-based; cryotherapy + thermotherapy well tolerated
PREVENTION: insect repellent (DEET) + permethrin-treated clothing + bed nets + sandfly control + avoid dusk-dawn exposure endemic areas

SSA: Kenya — Old World L. tropica + L. aethiopica + L. major (highland and arid areas — Baringo, West Pokot, Turkana); MSF + DNDi programmes; biopsy + microscopy + PCR capacity scale-up; LAmB access for severe.

title: Dengue — recognise warning signs, capillary leak day 4-7, Qdenga vaccine
population: 390 million infections/yr; SE Asia + Pacific + Latin America + Africa expanding (Kenya — Mombasa + coastal + cross-border); Aedes aegypti/albopictus; 4 serotypes — second infection different serotype = higher severity (ADE).
presentation: Acute fever + headache + retro-orbital pain + myalgia + arthralgia + rash + leucopenia + thrombocytopenia. PHASES: 1) febrile day 1-3; 2) CRITICAL day 4-7 — defervescence + capillary leak + warning signs OR shock OR recovery; 3) recovery day 8+ with reabsorption + bradycardia.
redFlags: WARNING SIGNS day 4-7: abdominal pain + persistent vomiting + clinical fluid accumulation + mucosal bleed + lethargy/restlessness + hepatomegaly > 2 cm + rising Hct + falling platelets — ADMIT
Severe plasma leakage (shock — dengue shock syndrome, ARDS-like)
diagnostics: NS1 antigen day 1-5 — sensitive + specific early; rapid POC widely available
IgM (day 4-5 onward) ± IgG — paired serology
PCR (NS1 negative + suspicion); serotype identification
FBC — leucopenia + thrombocytopenia; HAEMATOCRIT serial (rise = plasma leak)
LFT (raised AST/ALT — myocarditis if very high), UEC, clotting
EXCLUDE — malaria smear + RDT (CO-INFECTION POSSIBLE), chikungunya (also Aedes), typhoid, leptospirosis, COVID-19 — all febrile zoonotic differentials
management: WHO 2009 + 2024 Dengue Guideline + CDC + Kenya MoH (post-2024 outbreak):
TRIAGE:
Group A — dengue without warning signs — outpatient + ORS + paracetamol + bed rest + AVOID ASA/NSAID (bleeding); return precautions DAY 4-7
Group B — warning signs OR comorbid/extreme age/pregnant — ADMIT for IV fluid + monitoring
Group C — severe dengue (shock + severe haemorrhage + severe organ) — ICU + resuscitation
FLUID MANAGEMENT — CRYSTALLOID (RL/NS) titrated to maintenance + replacement; avoid aggressive boluses unless shock — risk fluid overload during recovery (reabsorption phase day 8+)
Shock — initial 10-20 mL/kg over 1 h → reassess; second bolus if needed; colloid (5% albumin) if persistent shock + rising Hct
Recovery — STOP IV fluid + monitor (otherwise pulmonary oedema)
PLATELETS — TRANSFUSE ONLY for active major bleeding OR platelets < 10 + symptoms (NOT prophylactic) — recent IFEX-DENGUE Lancet 2017 — no benefit
FFP / cryoprecipitate / blood — for actual bleeding + coagulopathy
PARACETAMOL only for fever / pain; AVOID NSAID / ASA / IM injection
NO STEROIDS (no benefit in shock); no specific antiviral approved
MYOCARDITIS / ENCEPHALITIS / HEPATIC FAILURE — supportive + ICU
PREGNANCY: increased severe maternal + neonatal — admit + close monitor; vertical transmission near term
VACCINES:
DENGVAXIA (CYD-TDV) — restricted to seropositive 9-45 yr (severe disease in seronegatives — withdrawn many programmes)
QDENGA (TAK-003 — Takeda live attenuated) — TIDES trial 2022 + WHO SAGE 2024 — recommended endemic settings 6-16 yr, regardless of serostatus — broader use; emerging Kenya MoH consideration
TV003/TV005 NIH next-generation
PREVENTION:
Aedes vector control — eliminate breeding (containers, tyres, gutters), larvicide, insecticide adult
Personal — DEET repellent, long sleeves, screened windows, daytime biting (different from malaria)
Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes (World Mosquito Program) — Australia + Brazil + Indonesia + emerging — reduce transmission
OUTBREAK RESPONSE: surveillance + lab capacity + community engagement + integrated vector control + clinical management training

SSA: Kenya — Mombasa + coast + cross-border with Somalia + Tanzania — increasing burden (2024 outbreak); train HCWs on warning signs + fluid management + integrate with malaria + COVID + chikungunya capacity.

title: Lymphatic filariasis — IDA + DEC + ivermectin + albendazole; lymphoedema chronic care
population: 120 million infected; 25 countries endemic remaining (was 80); India + SE Asia + Africa + Pacific. Wuchereria bancrofti (90%) + Brugia malayi + timori. Mosquito vectors.
presentation: Acute — adenolymphangitis (ADL) + fever + lymphangitis + lymphadenitis. Chronic — LYMPHOEDEMA limb + HYDROCELE (men — major morbidity) + chyluria + tropical pulmonary eosinophilia. Microfilaraemia often asymptomatic.
redFlags: Severe lymphoedema with cellulitis / sepsis recurrent (acute attacks)
Genital lymphoedema / massive hydrocele — surgical + psychosocial impact
Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (cough + wheeze + nocturnal + IgE + eosinophilia)
Loa loa co-endemic Central Africa — DEC and ivermectin caution (encephalopathy risk in heavy microfilaraemia — pretest with mapping)
diagnostics: Night blood smear / membrane filtration for microfilariae (W. bancrofti — nocturnal periodicity 10pm-2am)
Filariasis Test Strip (FTS) — circulating filarial antigen W. bancrofti — programmatic + day-time
BmR1 IgG4 — Brugia
Ultrasound — adult worms in lymphatics (filaria dance sign in scrotal vessels) + hydrocele assessment
Loa loa co-endemic — Central Africa — eye worm/Calabar swelling + microfilariae before mass treatment with IVM/DEC (encephalopathy in heavy load)
management: WHO 2030 GPELF Roadmap + 2017 IDA + Triple Therapy:
MASS DRUG ADMINISTRATION (MDA) — annual community treatment 5+ years to interrupt transmission:
IDA TRIPLE THERAPY — IVERMECTIN 200 μg/kg + DEC 6 mg/kg + ALBENDAZOLE 400 mg single dose (where loiasis NOT co-endemic) — accelerates clearance — WHO 2017 game-changer
Loa loa co-endemic (Central Africa) — IDA + DEC CONTRAINDICATED (encephalopathy) — use IVERMECTIN + ALBENDAZOLE only; or doxycycline programmes (kill Wolbachia → kills adult worms)
Onchocerciasis co-endemic — IVERMECTIN + ALBENDAZOLE (no DEC — severe reaction to Onchocerca)
COVERAGE 65% effective threshold 5+ years → transmission interruption verified by survey
INDIVIDUAL TREATMENT:
DEC 6 mg/kg × 12 d (W. bancrofti / B. malayi) — kills microfilariae + adult worms
Doxycycline 200 mg/d × 4-6 wk (anti-Wolbachia — kills adult worm — sterilising; especially for established disease)
Ivermectin + albendazole — kills microfilariae (not adult)
MORBIDITY MANAGEMENT — equally important as MDA (WHO MMDP):

LYMPHOEDEMA: hygiene (daily wash with soap + dry + check for cuts + cellulitis treatment); skin care; emollients; elevation; gentle exercise; compression bandaging (mild); train community + patient self-care; treat acute attacks (ADL) with antibiotic + paracetamol + elevation
HYDROCELE: surgical excision (hydrocelectomy) — high-volume programme + train surgeons + integrated; significant QoL impact
Chyluria: dietary fat restriction + medium-chain triglycerides; persistent — sclerosing therapy + surgical
Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia: DEC × 21 d
VECTOR CONTROL: integrated mosquito control + bed nets
ELIMINATION as public health problem 2030 — many countries achieved (Sri Lanka, Egypt, China, Korea, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, Pacific island states); Africa — most progress + remaining work
SSA: Kenya — coastal + Lamu + Tana River — MDA + MMDP integrated; community hygiene + surgical access + integrate with other NTD MDA.

references.label: WHO 2030 GPELF Roadmap + IDA Triple Therapy 2017

title: Onchocerciasis — ivermectin MDA + moxidectin newer; prevention of blindness
population: 18 million infected; 99% Africa (savannah + forest); Yemen + Latin America historic. Onchocerca volvulus; Simulium black fly vector (riverine breeding).
presentation: Onchocercal skin disease — pruritus + onchodermatitis + leopard skin (depigmentation) + lichenification + nodules (subcutaneous adult worms). Eye — sclerosing keratitis + iritis + chorioretinitis + optic atrophy → BLINDNESS in highly endemic. CNS — Nodding syndrome + onchocerciasis-associated epilepsy emerging.
redFlags: Vision loss / corneal opacity / optic atrophy — refer ophth

Loa loa co-endemic (Cameroon, Gabon, CAR, DRC, Congo, Equatorial Guinea, S Nigeria, S Sudan) — TEST loiasis BEFORE ivermectin — heavy Loa microfilaraemia + IVM → encephalopathy + death (Mectizan Expert Committee)
Nodding syndrome (children, S Sudan + Uganda) — onchocerciasis-associated epilepsy
diagnostics: Skin snip — bloodless biopsy from iliac crest / scapula incubated in saline 24h — microfilariae emerge — microscopy
Mazzotti test (DEC) — historical + provocative — not used now (severe reaction)
Ov16 ELISA / RDT — serological — surveillance
PCR — pool screening + species
Slit lamp — microfilariae in anterior chamber
Loa loa microfilarial count (REQUIRED before ivermectin in co-endemic areas — > 30,000 mf/mL → encephalopathy risk)
management: WHO + APOC + Mectizan Donation Program:
MASS DRUG ADMINISTRATION (MDA):
IVERMECTIN 150 μg/kg single dose annual or BIANNUAL community treatment (CDTI — community-directed treatment with ivermectin)
Continue for ≥ 12-15 yr to interrupt transmission (adult worm lifespan 14 yr)
MOXIDECTIN single dose (FDA 2018) — superior microfilarial clearance + duration vs IVM — adult > 12 yr — emerging programme adjunct

LOA LOA co-endemic (Cameroon, Gabon, CAR, DRC, S Nigeria, S Sudan, Congo, Eq Guinea) — TEST Loa first; > 30,000 mf/mL — DO NOT GIVE IVM (encephalopathy + death); alternative — doxycycline programme + LoaScope individual screening
AVOID DEC for onchocerciasis (severe Mazzotti reaction)
ANTI-WOLBACHIA:
DOXYCYCLINE 100-200 mg/d × 4-6 wk — kills Wolbachia (endosymbiont) → kills adult worm → sterilises macrofilaricidally (IVM is only microfilaricidal)
Increasingly used for individual treatment + selected MDA (especially Loa co-endemic) — A-WOL + ANCHOR programmes
INDIVIDUAL TREATMENT:
Ivermectin 150 μg/kg q3-6 mo (multiple doses + better symptoms)
Doxycycline 4-6 wk for sterilisation
Surgical nodulectomy — selected (head/face risk eye)
Topical permethrin / antihistamine for itch
EYE: refer ophth; treat iritis; secondary infection
NODDING SYNDROME: antiepileptic + supportive + nutrition + psychosocial
VECTOR CONTROL: SIMULIUM black fly — riverine larviciding (historic OCP 1974-2002 — eliminated transmission in 11 West African countries — landmark)
ELIMINATION as public health problem — Latin America — Ecuador + Colombia + Mexico + Guatemala verified; Africa — challenging due to Loa + scale + transmission dynamics
SSA: Kenya — NOT considered endemic — but cross-border + research; ESPEN (Expanded Special Project for Elimination of NTDs in Africa) coordinates.

title: Human African trypanosomiasis — fexinidazole oral first-line (T.b. gambiense — Sleeping Sickness)
population: Historic outbreaks — recent dramatic decline; < 1000 cases/yr now (WHO elimination as public health problem 2020 achieved). T.b. gambiense (West/Central Africa — DRC, CAR, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Nigeria, Angola, Chad — 95%); T.b. rhodesiense (East/Southern Africa — Uganda, Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Kenya cross-border).
presentation: Stage 1 — chancre at bite + fever + headache + lymphadenopathy (Winterbottom's posterior cervical T.b. gambiense). Stage 2 (CNS) — sleep disorder + neurological — encephalopathic + apathy + psychiatric + death untreated.
redFlags: UNTREATED = 100% fatal — case finding + treatment is the public-health priority
T.b. rhodesiense = ACUTE + rapidly progressive (weeks-months) — myocarditis + acute encephalopathy
Encephalopathic reactions to old drugs (melarsoprol — historical — 5% mortality from treatment itself)
diagnostics: T.b. gambiense:
CATT (Card Agglutination Test for Trypanosomiasis) — screening
Lymph node aspirate / blood / chancre — wet prep + Giemsa — trypanosomes
mAECT (mini-anion exchange concentration) + capillary tube centrifugation — sensitivity
T.b. rhodesiense:
Blood smear (high parasitaemia) + thick + thin film
STAGING — LP — CSF WBC + trypanosomes — Stage 2 if WBC > 5/μL or trypanosomes present (T.b. gambiense)
Recent loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) field tests
management: WHO 2019 + 2024 HAT Guidelines + DNDi:
T.b. GAMBIENSE (95% of cases):
FEXINIDAZOLE — ORAL — REVOLUTIONARY (DNDi + Sanofi; WHO approved 2019; first all-oral HAT treatment):
Stage 1 + early stage 2 — 1800 mg OD × 4 d then 1200 mg OD × 6 d (adults > 35 kg)
Adolescents > 6 yr + > 20 kg — weight-adjusted
With food (improves absorption)
AVOIDS lumbar puncture for staging in most cases — simplifies massively in rural settings
NEW: ACOZIBOROLE single oral dose × 1 — trial NEJM 2022 — game-changer (under regulatory review)
Severe stage 2 (WBC > 100/μL or severely symptomatic) — nifurtimox-eflornithine combination therapy (NECT) — 10 d eflornithine IV q6h + nifurtimox PO; or fexinidazole
Pentamidine — historical Stage 1 only
Melarsoprol historical (5% encephalopathy + death) — no longer first-line
T.b. RHODESIENSE:
SURAMIN IV (haemolymphatic + stage 1)
MELARSOPROL (stage 2) — toxic but limited alternative
Trials underway for fexinidazole + acoziborole
FOLLOW-UP: clinical + LP at 6-12-18-24 mo to confirm cure (CSF normalises) — fexinidazole simplifies
PUBLIC HEALTH:
Active case detection (mobile teams + screening)
Tsetse fly vector control — traps + targets + insecticide-impregnated cloth (Trypa-NO model)
Reservoir — humans (gambiense) + cattle/game (rhodesiense)
WHO target — verify elimination of transmission 2030 (was 2020 — public health problem milestone achieved gambiense)
PREGNANCY: fexinidazole limited data — eflornithine + pentamidine selected
SSA: Kenya — cross-border with Uganda + Tanzania (rhodesiense); surveillance + tsetse control; cattle reservoir + integrated 'One Health' approach.

title: Chagas (American trypanosomiasis) — benznidazole/nifurtimox + cardiac follow-up + transfusion screening
population: 6-7 million infected; Latin America endemic (Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia, Mexico, Colombia); US + Europe + Asia diaspora (untreated chronic). Trypanosoma cruzi; triatomine kissing bug; congenital + blood-transfusion + oral (juice contamination) + organ transplant transmission.
presentation: ACUTE (rare diagnosed) — fever + Romaña's sign (unilateral eyelid swelling at bite + chagoma + lymph) + myocarditis + meningoencephalitis (severe). CHRONIC indeterminate — asymptomatic carrier 60-70%. Chronic CARDIAC (20-30% over decades) — DCM + arrhythmia + sudden death + thromboembolism. Chronic DIGESTIVE (10%) — megaoesophagus + megacolon (Brazil > Mexico).
redFlags: Stroke from cardioembolic (LV thrombus chronic CCM)
Reactivation in immunosuppression (HIV, post-transplant, oncology) — re-emerges with acute features + high mortality
Blood transfusion + organ donor screening essential
diagnostics: ACUTE: direct microscopy (high parasitaemia) — blood + buffy coat + microhaematocrit; PCR sensitive
CHRONIC: SEROLOGY — ELISA + immunofluorescence + agglutination — TWO positive different antigens for diagnosis confirmed
PCR — congenital + immunosuppressed + reactivation + post-treatment
Cardiac: ECG (RBBB + LAFB + ST/T changes + AV block + complex ventricular ectopy) + echo (DCM + apical aneurysm + LV thrombus); Holter; MRI cardiac
GI: barium / endoscopy — megaoesophagus + megacolon
Blood + organ donor universal screening endemic + non-endemic with diaspora
management: PAHO + WHO 2019 Chagas Guidelines + Argentinian + Brazilian:
ANTITRYPANOSOMAL — INDICATED for:
ALL acute infection
ALL congenital
ALL chronic up to age 18 (esp. children — high cure)
Adults < 50 yr without advanced cardiomyopathy — recommended (BENEFIT trial NEJM 2015 — no benefit in advanced CCM but recommended pre-fibrosis stages)
Reactivation
Women of childbearing age (prevent congenital — outside pregnancy)
DRUGS:
BENZNIDAZOLE 5-7 mg/kg/d (children up to 10) × 60 d — first-line
NIFURTIMOX 8-10 mg/kg/d × 60 d (or 60 wk in children) — alternative
Adverse — common — rash (benznidazole — sometimes severe), GI, peripheral neuropathy (nifurtimox)
Newer regimens — shorter course + intermittent under study (BENDITA trial — benznidazole 150 mg × 14 d non-inferior to 8-wk in some — emerging)
Posaconazole + fosravuconazole — disappointing trials
PREGNANCY: DO NOT TREAT (teratogenic) — treat after delivery; treat NEONATE within first year if congenital (high cure rate)
CARDIAC MANAGEMENT (chronic CCM):
HF treatment per HFrEF GDMT (β-blocker + ACE-i/ARB/ARNI + MRA + SGLT2i)
Pacemaker / ICD per indications (often need pacing for AV block; ICD for VT/VF)
Anticoagulate LV thrombus / AF
Cardiac transplant — last resort + post-transplant reactivation surveillance
DIGESTIVE: oesophageal dilatation / Heller + fundoplication; colon resection
ALL HIV + IMMUNOSUPPRESSED endemic — reactivation surveillance + suppressive therapy if needed
FAMILY SCREENING — congenital + sibling + mother + transfusion (chronic asymptomatic carrier)
PUBLIC HEALTH: vector control (insecticide) + housing improvement (no thatched roofs hiding triatomines) + blood/organ screening + congenital screening + travel education
SSA: not endemic — but diaspora screening + blood transfusion safety + awareness for Latin American travellers.

references.label: BENEFIT trial NEJM 2015 benznidazole chronic CCM

title: Leprosy (Hansen disease) — WHO MDT + single-dose rifampicin PEP + zero discrimination
population: 200,000 new cases/yr globally; India + Brazil + Indonesia + DRC + Nigeria + Bangladesh + Ethiopia + Mozambique. Mycobacterium leprae; close prolonged contact transmission; long incubation 5-20 yr.
presentation: Hypopigmented or erythematous anaesthetic skin patches + thickened nerves (great auricular, ulnar, median, common peroneal, posterior tibial) + sensory + motor deficit + nerve trunk pain. Multibacillary (BL/LL) — many lesions + nerve damage + symmetric; paucibacillary (TT/BT) — few lesions + asymmetric. REACTIONS — Type 1 (reversal) + Type 2 (ENL — erythema nodosum leprosum) + Lucio phenomenon.
redFlags: Nerve damage WITH deformity / dysfunction — physiotherapy + surgical referral
Eye involvement (lagophthalmos, corneal hypoaesthesia) — risk blindness
diagnostics: CLINICAL diagnosis — cardinal signs: (1) hypopigmented anaesthetic patch (2) thickened nerve (3) acid-fast bacilli (AFB) on slit-skin smear or biopsy
Slit-skin smear — earlobe + active lesions × 6 sites — Ziehl-Neelsen — bacterial index (BI 0-6+) + morphological index
Skin biopsy — Fite stain + histopathology + classification (Ridley-Jopling TT-BT-BB-BL-LL spectrum)
Nerve assessment — sensory testing (10g monofilament; voluntary muscle test); palpation thickened nerves
PCR — selected; LepraScan emerging
management: WHO MDT (Multidrug Therapy) — FREE in endemic countries:
PAUCIBACILLARY (1-5 skin lesions, AFB-negative) — 6 MONTHS:
Rifampicin 600 mg (450 if < 35 kg) ONCE MONTHLY supervised
Dapsone 100 mg (50 if < 35 kg) DAILY
+ Clofazimine added to all per WHO 2018 unified regimen
MULTIBACILLARY (> 5 lesions, AFB+ or LL/BL/BB) — 12 MONTHS (was 24):
Rifampicin 600 mg monthly supervised
Dapsone 100 mg daily
Clofazimine 300 mg monthly supervised + 50 mg daily (skin pigmentation common — counsel + temporary)
PAEDIATRIC: weight-adjusted; same regimens
PREGNANCY: same MDT — safe + treat per usual schedule
G6PD: test before dapsone (haemolysis risk); use alternative if deficient (clofazimine + rifampicin + minocycline)
ROM (rifampicin + ofloxacin + minocycline) single dose — emerging single-lesion paucibacillary alternative
REACTIONS — emergency:
TYPE 1 (REVERSAL) — increased lesion inflammation + neuritis (NEW NEURITIS = EMERGENCY — irreversible damage in days):
Prednisolone 30-60 mg/d taper over 3-6 mo (longer for neuritis)
Continue MDT
Splint affected nerves; physio
TYPE 2 (ENL — multibacillary patients) — tender red nodules + fever + arthritis + iritis + neuritis:
Prednisolone 30-40 mg taper
Thalidomide 100-400 mg/d (ENL — gold standard but TERATOGENIC — strict contraception + protocol; restricted access)
Clofazimine high-dose; pentoxifylline; methotrexate
Continue MDT
PREVENTION:
Contact tracing — household + close contacts

SINGLE-DOSE RIFAMPICIN PEP — 600 mg adults / 450 mg 25-34 kg / 300 mg 15-24 kg / 150 mg < 15 kg — for ALL contacts > 2 yr (WHO 2018 LPEP study + COLEP RCT 2008) — reduces leprosy in contacts 57% (NNT 26-32)
BCG offers some protection (booster in contacts emerging)
LepVax in trials
REHABILITATION + DISABILITY:
Eye care — lagophthalmos surgery + lubrication + lid closure
Hand + foot care — daily self-inspection + soak + oil + protective footwear + adapted tools
Reconstructive surgery (claw hand + foot drop + facial)
Mental health + stigma + livelihood support — Persons Affected by Leprosy advocacy + zero discrimination
Plantar ulcer management — rest + dressing + protected footwear
SSA: Kenya — endemic but low burden; integrate with skin services + train HCWs + zero discrimination + community awareness.

references.label: WHO 2018 + 2020 Leprosy Guidelines + Towards Zero Leprosy 2030
WHO LPEP single-dose rifampicin contacts study
COLEP trial single-dose rifampicin contacts BMJ 2008
Kenya Guidelines on Use of Antiretroviral Drugs for Treating and Preventing HIV Infection (NASCOP)

title: Trachoma — SAFE strategy + WHO 2030 elimination (azithromycin MDA)
population: Endemic in 42 countries; sub-Saharan Africa (Ethiopia + Mali + Niger + Uganda + Tanzania + Kenya pockets) + Yemen + Pacific. Chlamydia trachomatis serovars A-C; flies + close contact transmission; communities with limited water + sanitation.
presentation: Active disease — TF (follicular conjunctivitis) + TI (intense — eyelid swelling + papillae) — children; cumulative repeated infections → TS (cicatricial scarring) → TT (trichiasis — eyelashes inwards) → CO (corneal opacity + blindness). Trachoma was leading infectious cause of blindness.
redFlags: TRICHIASIS (TT) — surgical priority — eyelashes scraping cornea → blindness within years
Recurrent active TF/TI in MDA setting — adherence + transmission
diagnostics: CLINICAL grading WHO Simplified — TF / TI / TS / TT / CO at lid + cornea slit-lamp / loupe
Mass screening — community surveys at district level (Trachoma Action Plan)
PCR + serology — research + epidemiology + impact monitoring
management: WHO Alliance for Global Elimination of Trachoma by 2030 (GET2030) — SAFE STRATEGY:
S — SURGERY for TRICHIASIS:
Bilamellar tarsal rotation (BTR) procedure — community-based surgical campaigns + community ophthalmic clinical officers / trichiasis surgeons
Free + community-based + outreach for backlog cases
Recurrence 10-20% — monitor + repeat
A — ANTIBIOTIC — single-dose AZITHROMYCIN 20 mg/kg PO (max 1 g) annual MDA in districts with TF prevalence ≥ 5% in children:
Coverage > 80% × 3-5 years to interrupt transmission
Donated through ITI (International Trachoma Initiative) Pfizer Zithromax donation programme — 1 billion+ doses
Tetracycline 1% eye ointment BD × 6 wk alternative (limited use)
Treat household contacts
F — FACIAL CLEANLINESS:
Daily face-washing for children — reduces fly attraction + transmission
Community-led behaviour change
Soap + water access
E — ENVIRONMENTAL improvement:
Access to clean water + sanitation (WASH integration)
Latrines + waste management (reduces fly breeding)
Housing + animal management
PROGRESS:
Multiple countries eliminated as public health problem: Oman + Morocco + Mexico + Iran + Cambodia + China + Saudi Arabia + Iraq + Ghana + Gambia + Myanmar + Togo + Malawi + Vietnam + Nepal + others
Ethiopia — largest burden, intensive programme + progress
Kenya — endemic pockets in Turkana, West Pokot, Marsabit, Samburu, Baringo, Narok — programme active + nearing elimination thresholds in many districts
ELIMINATION THRESHOLDS:
TF < 5% in children aged 1-9 yr in each formerly endemic district
TT < 0.2% in adults ≥ 15 yr unknown to health system
Continued surveillance
SSA: Kenya — National Eye Health Plan + Ministry of Health + ITI + Sightsavers + Lions Clubs — surgery campaigns + MDA + WASH integration + community engagement.

title: MRSA bacteraemia + endocarditis — vancomycin / daptomycin source-control
population: Methicillin-resistant S. aureus — health-care + community + IVDU. Catheter + skin + bone + endovascular.
presentation: Persistent bacteraemia ± metastatic seeding (endocarditis, vertebral osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, psoas/epidural abscess, lung). Catheter-related; injection drug use right-sided endocarditis.
redFlags: Persistent bacteraemia > 7 d on appropriate therapy
Back pain / neurological deficit (epidural abscess + vertebral osteo)
Septic emboli (right-sided septic pulmonary, left-sided systemic)
diagnostics: ≥ 2 blood cultures pre-antibiotic (paired sets); REPEAT q48h until clear
TTE all MRSA bacteraemia; TOE if persistent / prosthetic / inadequate TTE / IE features
Source workup: vascular catheter, skin / soft tissue, bone (MRI), psoas, joint, vertebral
MIC: vancomycin (target < 2 mg/L), daptomycin baseline
Vancomycin AUC24/MIC 400-600 (preferred over trough alone — IDSA 2020); CK baseline + weekly (daptomycin)
management: IDSA 2011 MRSA + 2020 vancomycin therapeutic monitoring + 2023 ESC IE:
Source control FIRST — remove catheter / drain abscess / surgical debridement
VANCOMYCIN IV (loading 25-30 mg/kg, maintenance 15-20 mg/kg q8-12h) — TARGET AUC24/MIC 400-600 by Bayesian software or two-level pharmacokinetics; alternative trough 15-20 mg/L (less accurate)

DAPTOMYCIN 8-10 mg/kg IV OD if vancomycin MIC ≥ 2, hVISA/VISA, vancomycin AKI/allergy, persistent bacteraemia, IE (use ≥ 8 mg/kg for IE; ≥ 10 mg/kg for persistent); NOT for pneumonia (surfactant inactivates)
CEFTAROLINE 600 mg q8h IV — combination with vanco/dapto for persistent bacteraemia or salvage
LINEZOLID 600 mg q12h alternative; NOT for IE/bacteraemia first-line (bacteriostatic); reserve for refractory soft tissue/bone with bacteraemia
Combination therapy with rifampicin 300 mg q12h for prosthetic device / hardware infection (NOT routine for native bacteraemia)
DURATION: uncomplicated bacteraemia + cleared in 72h + no metastatic 14 d IV from first negative blood culture; complicated/metastatic/endocarditis 4-6 wk IV; vertebral osteomyelitis 6-8 wk
FOLLOW-UP cultures q48h; persistent > 7 d = complicated → search seed + escalate
Native MRSA IE: vancomycin OR daptomycin 6 wk; prosthetic — combination + surgical
Surgical IE referral: HF, perivalvular abscess, persistent bacteraemia, large vegetation > 10 mm + embolic, fungal, prosthetic
OPAT (outpatient parenteral antibiotic) for selected stable
Long-acting alternative: oritavancin / dalbavancin single/twice-weekly for selected uncomplicated SSTI bacteraemia
Decolonisation: mupirocin nasal + chlorhexidine wash — controversial routine; consider recurrent / outbreak
Avoid quinupristin-dalfopristin + cotrimoxazole monotherapy for IE
SSA: vancomycin + cloxacillin (MSSA) widely available; MRSA recognition + lab capacity essential; bed nets for resource-limited; daptomycin + ceftaroline access advocacy.

references.label: Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: ESBL-producing Enterobacterales — carbapenem for serious; ceftolozane/zoledronate cautions
population: ESBL Enterobacterales (E. coli, Klebsiella) — globally rising; high prevalence S Asia / SSA / Mediterranean. Healthcare + community (urinary + travel).
presentation: UTI (community most common), bacteraemia, intra-abdominal, hospital-acquired pneumonia. Bloodstream often urinary source.
redFlags: Septic shock + ESBL suspected — broad cover + carbapenem early
Pyelonephritis with ESBL — switch to active agent
diagnostics: Culture + sensitivity (ESBL phenotype by clavulanate inhibition; ESBL gene PCR research)
Urinalysis + urine culture
Blood cultures if febrile / severe
Imaging for source (US/CT abdo if intra-abdominal; CXR for pneumonia)
Risk factors: travel S Asia / Mediterranean, recent antibiotic, hospitalisation, catheter, recurrent UTI
management: IDSA AMR Guidance 2024 + ESCMID:
MILD-MODERATE UTI (uncomplicated cystitis):
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg QDS × 5 d (preferred — preserves carbapenem)
Fosfomycin 3 g single dose (multidose for males / complicated)
Pivmecillinam 400 mg TDS × 3-7 d (active where licensed)
Cotrimoxazole or fluoroquinolone IF susceptible (often not)
PYELONEPHRITIS / SEVERE / BACTERAEMIA:
CARBAPENEM first-line — ertapenem 1 g OD (good if no Pseudomonas/Acinetobacter) or meropenem 1-2 g q8h
Step-down to oral if susceptible: cotrim, ciprofloxacin (if susceptible), pivmecillinam, amox-clav (caution bacteraemia)
Aminoglycoside (amikacin 15-20 mg/kg OD or gentamicin) — combination salvage selected; monitor
INTRA-ABDOMINAL: carbapenem + source control (drainage); piperacillin-tazobactam INFERIOR to meropenem for ESBL bacteraemia (MERINO RCT JAMA 2018 — increased mortality with pip-taz)
BACTERAEMIC INFECTION: carbapenem definitive; transition oral selected once clinical improvement + clearance + source control + susceptibility documented
Ceftolozane-tazobactam + ceftazidime-avibactam — generally reserved for CRE / Pseudomonas — selective ESBL use
PREVENTION: hand hygiene + contact precautions + decolonisation (limited evidence) + antimicrobial stewardship + AWaRe (Watch carbapenem)
PROPHYLAXIS: recurrent UTI ESBL — nitrofurantoin / fosfomycin nightly; address contributing factors
SSA: ESBL widely prevalent; ertapenem + nitrofurantoin + fosfomycin essential AWaRe Watch; stewardship + lab capacity + IPC + KEML alignment.

references.label: MERINO RCT pip-taz vs meropenem ESBL bacteraemia JAMA 2018

title: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales — ceftazidime-avibactam / meropenem-vaborbactam by mechanism
population: CRE — emerging globally; KPC + NDM + OXA-48 + VIM/IMP enzymes; healthcare-associated; high mortality.
presentation: Bacteraemia, ventilator-associated pneumonia, intra-abdominal, urinary in critically ill / immunocompromised; often colonisation precedes infection.
redFlags: Septic shock — empirically cover CRE if local epidemiology + risk factors (travel, recent admission, prior CRE, transfer from endemic)
Persistent bacteraemia despite carbapenem — refer ID urgently
diagnostics: Culture + carbapenemase phenotype (CIM/mCIM) + genotype (KPC/NDM/OXA-48/VIM/IMP — informs treatment)
Rapid molecular tests (BioFire, GeneXpert) where available
Screen rectal swab (admission high-risk units)
Source identification + imaging
management: IDSA AMR 2024 + ESCMID:
TREAT BY MECHANISM (PCR identifies enzyme):
KPC (USA/Europe/Latin America): CEFTAZIDIME-AVIBACTAM 2.5 g q8h OR MEROPENEM-VABORBACTAM 4 g q8h OR IMIPENEM-RELEBACTAM
OXA-48 (Middle East / Mediterranean / Africa): CEFTAZIDIME-AVIBACTAM 2.5 g q8h preferred

NDM / VIM / IMP metallo-β-lactamases (S Asia / Middle East): CEFTAZIDIME-AVIBACTAM + AZTREONAM combination (aztreonam stable to MBL + avibactam protects aztreonam from ESBL/AmpC); OR CEFIDEROCOL 2 g q8h (siderophore cephalosporin — only approved single agent for MBL CRE — APEKS-NP/CREDIBLE-CR)
Activity uncertain — request ID + lab consultation + susceptibility panel

ALTERNATIVES / SALVAGE: polymyxin B / colistin (nephrotoxicity + neurotoxicity), tigecycline (NOT for bacteraemia — low serum), aminoglycoside (plazomicin where available, gentamicin/amikacin if susceptible), eravacycline, fosfomycin IV (urinary preferred)
DURATION: 7-14 d depending on source + clinical response; complicated/endovascular 4-6 wk
SOURCE CONTROL — drain abscess, remove catheter, control intra-abdominal — essential
ID consultation MANDATORY
DECOLONISATION: not generally recommended (no benefit + risk of resistance)
INFECTION CONTROL: contact precautions + cohort + dedicated equipment + active surveillance high-risk units + hand hygiene + environmental cleaning + antimicrobial stewardship
REPORTING: notifiable in many jurisdictions; report to national AMR surveillance (WHO GLASS)
SSA: emerging; lab capacity building essential (Kenya KEMRI surveillance); access to newer agents (ceftaz-avi, cefiderocol) limited — advocacy + ID/microbiology training.

title: Loiasis (Loa loa) — pre-screen microfilarial load before ivermectin to prevent encephalopathy
population: 12 million infected; Central + West Africa rainforest — Cameroon, Gabon, CAR, DRC, Congo, Equatorial Guinea, southern Nigeria, South Sudan. Chrysops deer-fly vector.
presentation: Calabar swellings (transient subcutaneous oedema), pruritus, conjunctival 'eye-worm' (adult migrating across conjunctiva — characteristic), urticaria; many asymptomatic carriers.
redFlags: Heavy microfilaraemia (> 30,000 mf/mL) + IVERMECTIN / DEC = ENCEPHALOPATHY + death — TEST FIRST before MDA in co-endemic areas (with onchocerciasis or LF)
diagnostics: Day-time blood smear (10am-2pm — diurnal periodicity opposite W. bancrofti) — microscopic microfilariae
Microfilarial count quantitative — ESSENTIAL before mass treatment (LoaScope point-of-care smartphone — Cameroon RCT)
Serology + PCR (research)
Adult worm — eye worm visualisation + surgical removal if subconjunctival
management: WHO Loiasis + APOC + LoaScope studies:
INDIVIDUAL treatment:
DEC 6 mg/kg/d × 21 d (escalate from low dose to avoid encephalopathy) — first-line for symptomatic + low microfilarial load
Pretreatment with antihistamine + steroid for symptomatic relief during microfilarial killing
IVERMECTIN 150 μg/kg single dose — reduces microfilaraemia but does NOT cure adult — CONTRAINDICATED in > 30,000 mf/mL (encephalopathy risk)
Albendazole 200 mg BD × 21 d — slow microfilarial reduction + macrofilaricidal — alternative for high microfilarial load (slow + safer)
Surgical removal of eye worm if subconjunctival under topical anaesthesia (forceps after slit-lamp)
PRE-MDA SCREENING (essential in co-endemic with oncho/LF):
LoaScope smartphone POC microfilarial count — < 20,000 mf/mL → IVM safe; 20,000-30,000 → caution; > 30,000 → DO NOT GIVE IVM (encephalopathy)
Alternative pathway in Loa-endemic: doxycycline 200 mg/d × 4-6 wk (anti-Wolbachia — works for oncho/LF without IVM/DEC risk)
Albendazole alone can pre-treat to reduce Loa microfilarial load before IVM (TEST-AND-NOT-TREAT or TEST-AND-DOSE strategies)
PREVENTION: insect repellent + long clothing + avoid forest day-time exposure
Encephalopathy treatment: high-dose IV steroid + supportive intensive care; consider IVIG + plasma exchange experimental
SSA: Loa loa is huge obstacle to onchocerciasis + LF elimination programmes in Central Africa — LoaScope deployment + alternative regimens essential.

title: Cystic echinococcosis — WHO-IWGE stage-based + albendazole + PAIR + surgery
population: E. granulosus — sheep + dog endemic (Mediterranean, Central Asia, North + East Africa, S America, Australia). E. multilocularis (alveolar — Europe, Russia, China, N America) — more aggressive, malignant-like.
presentation: Cystic — slow-growing liver (70%) > lung (20%) > brain/bone/other; often asymptomatic incidental imaging; pain, mass, rupture (anaphylaxis + dissemination), secondary infection, biliary obstruction. Alveolar — infiltrative liver mass, jaundice, hepatomegaly.
redFlags: Cyst rupture into biliary tree / peritoneum — anaphylaxis + dissemination — surgical emergency
Alveolar echinococcosis (E. multilocularis) — locally invasive, late metastases — manage like malignancy
diagnostics: Abdominal US + serial — WHO-IWGE staging: CE1 active unilocular / CE2 multivesicular / CE3a-b transitional / CE4 inactive / CE5 calcified
CT / MRI for complex + extra-hepatic + pre-op planning
Serology (ELISA + immunoblot) — positive cystic echinococcosis; less in lung; cross-reactivity (cysticercosis)
FBC eosinophilia + LFT
FNA / aspiration — only with antihelminthic cover (anaphylaxis risk)
management: WHO-IWGE Cystic Echinococcosis 2010 + 2017 + Brunetti Acta Tropica:
STAGE-BASED:
CE1 / CE3a (active small < 5 cm) — albendazole alone or PAIR + albendazole
CE1 / CE3a (large > 5 cm) — PAIR + albendazole OR surgery
CE2 / CE3b multivesicular — surgery (open or laparoscopic); PAIR not effective
CE4 / CE5 inactive — WATCH AND WAIT — no treatment; serial US
ALBENDAZOLE 10-15 mg/kg/d divided BD (max 800 mg/d adult, 400 BD; smaller children weight-based) × 3-6 mo (continuous OR cyclical 4 wk on / 2 wk off × 3-6 cycles); reassess imaging
Add praziquantel for daughter cysts / pre-op / post-spillage prophylaxis
Monitor LFT + FBC monthly (transaminitis + neutropenia)
Pre-op + intra-op albendazole (4 d before, 1 mo after) — reduce risk of recurrence
PAIR (Puncture-Aspiration-Injection-Reaspiration) for selected CE1/CE3a:
Trained centre + emergency anaesthesia + adrenaline for anaphylaxis ready
Aspirate cyst → inject scolicide (95% ethanol or hypertonic saline) wait 15-30 min → reaspirate
Albendazole cover before + 1 mo after
Catheterisation drainage modification for complex

SURGERY: cystectomy / pericystectomy / partial hepatectomy / lobectomy — bilateral lung — depending on anatomy + complications + recurrent; minimise spillage with hypertonic gauze + meticulous technique
BILIARY RUPTURE / OBSTRUCTION: ERCP + sphincterotomy + drainage; surgery
ANAPHYLAXIS during procedure: adrenaline IM + intensive care
PULMONARY: surgical resection preferred (lung less responsive to albendazole)
BONE: surgery + long-term albendazole; recurrent
ALVEOLAR (E. multilocularis): radical surgery if resectable (R0 like cancer) + long-term albendazole; many require lifelong; transplant selected
PREVENTION + One Health: dog deworming (praziquantel monthly endemic), pig/sheep slaughter hygiene, hand hygiene, vegetable washing, community education, prevent dog access to viscera
SSA: Kenya (Turkana) + East African endemic — surgical centres + community education + One Health.

title: Brucellosis — doxycycline + rifampicin/streptomycin × 6 wk; longer for focal
population: 500,000 cases/yr; Mediterranean + Middle East + Central Asia + Latin America + sub-Saharan Africa; unpasteurised dairy + occupational (vets, farmers, abattoir) + lab exposure.
presentation: Undulant fever + sweats + arthralgia + back pain + hepatosplenomegaly + lymphadenopathy. Chronic / relapsing. FOCAL — spondylitis (sacroiliitis), arthritis, orchitis/epididymitis, endocarditis (rare but fatal), neurobrucellosis, hepatic abscess.
redFlags: Endocarditis (rare but #1 mortality cause) — surgical + prolonged combination
diagnostics: Blood culture (special media — incubate 3-6 wk; PCR faster); bone marrow more sensitive but invasive
Serology — Rose Bengal (screen) + standard tube agglutination (SAT) + IgM/IgG ELISA + 2-mercaptoethanol
FBC pancytopenia, LFT raised, ESR/CRP elevated
Imaging — MRI spine (spondylitis), echo (endocarditis), US testes (orchitis)
LP for neurobrucellosis (CSF lymphocytic + raised protein + low glucose + culture/PCR)
Occupational + dietary history
management: WHO + IDSA + Ioannidou Lancet Infect Dis 2019:
UNCOMPLICATED ADULT:
DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg BD × 6 weeks + RIFAMPICIN 600-900 mg OD × 6 weeks (oral combination preferred WHO)
OR doxycycline 100 mg BD × 6 wk + STREPTOMYCIN 1 g IM OD × 14-21 d (or GENTAMICIN 5 mg/kg OD × 7-14 d) — often superior to oral combination (less relapse)
AVOID monotherapy (high relapse)
PAEDIATRIC < 8 yr (avoid doxy):
Cotrimoxazole + rifampicin × 6 wk (± gentamicin first week)
Doxycycline acceptable short course > 7 d if benefits outweigh (WHO update)
PREGNANCY:
Cotrimoxazole (after 1st trimester) + rifampicin × 6 wk; or rifampicin monotherapy 900 mg/d × 6 wk (less effective + higher relapse)
Avoid doxycycline + aminoglycoside
FOCAL (SPONDYLITIS / NEURO / ENDOCARDITIS):
TRIPLE THERAPY × 3-6 MONTHS minimum:
Doxycycline + rifampicin + streptomycin/gentamicin first 2-4 wk
Continue doxy + rifampicin to ≥ 12 wk (spondylitis ≥ 3 mo), ≥ 4-6 mo neurobrucellosis
Add cotrimoxazole for neurobrucellosis (CSF penetration)
ENDOCARDITIS: triple/quadruple therapy ≥ 3 mo + early valve surgery (better outcome)
Spondylitis: doxy + rifampicin + aminoglycoside; surgical drainage abscess; bracing + physio
Neurobrucellosis: doxy + rifampicin + cotrimoxazole ± ceftriaxone × 4-6 mo + steroid for vasculitis/cranial nerve
MONITORING: clinical + ESR + serology titres trend (slow normalisation 6-12 mo); LFT (rifampicin/doxy); CBC (cotrim, rifampicin)
RELAPSE 5-15% — same regimen + extended duration; consider focal source
PREVENTION: pasteurise dairy + boil milk + occupational PPE + animal vaccination (Rev-1 + S19); LAB EXPOSURE PEP — doxycycline + rifampicin × 3 wk + serology surveillance
SSA: Kenya — pastoralist communities + occupational + dairy; integrated with veterinary services (One Health) + animal vaccination + pasteurisation + community education.

title: Q fever — doxycycline acute; doxycycline + hydroxychloroquine ≥ 18 mo chronic endocarditis
population: Globally distributed (except NZ); occupational (vets, farmers, abattoir, lab); pregnancy + valvulopathy + immunocompromised increased risk chronic. Coxiella burnetii — small Gram-negative obligate intracellular; aerosol transmission.
presentation: ACUTE — fever + headache + atypical pneumonia + hepatitis + flu-like; 60% asymptomatic. CHRONIC (1-5% of acute, especially valvulopathy / vascular / immunocompromised / pregnant) — culture-negative endocarditis + vascular infection + osteomyelitis + post-Q fever fatigue syndrome.
redFlags: Culture-NEGATIVE endocarditis in valvulopath / prosthetic — Q fever (+ Bartonella + Tropheryma whipplei) — serology
Pregnant + acute Q fever — high risk congenital + chronic
diagnostics: Serology — indirect immunofluorescence (IFA) — phase I and phase II IgG/IgM antibodies
Acute: phase II IgG ≥ 1:200 + IgM ≥ 1:50 (or 4× rise paired)
Chronic: phase I IgG ≥ 1:1024 (or ≥ 1:800 some centres) — endocarditis / vascular
PCR blood + tissue early acute (before seroconversion)
Culture — BSL-3 (highly infectious)
Echo (TOE + TTE — culture-negative endocarditis), PET-CT (vascular + endocarditis)
FBC + LFT + CRP
management: CDC + ESC + European Q Fever Treatment 2017:
ACUTE Q FEVER:
DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg BD × 14 d (extend to 21 d if severe)
Pregnancy: COTRIMOXAZOLE 160/800 BD throughout pregnancy (until delivery) — reduces congenital + chronic risk
Children < 8 yr: cotrimoxazole or short doxycycline
CHRONIC Q FEVER (endocarditis / vascular / persistent focus):
DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg BD + HYDROXYCHLOROQUINE 200 mg TDS — for ≥ 18-24 MONTHS native valve, ≥ 24 MONTHS prosthetic
Monitor — HCQ ophthalmology baseline + 6 mo annually (retinopathy)
Phase I IgG titre serial — decreasing = response; ≥ 4-fold drop sustained = consider stopping after 18-24 mo
Surgical valve replacement for severe / refractory / structural complication
POST-Q FEVER FATIGUE: supportive + graded exercise + CBT + symptom management; no specific antibiotic
VACCINATION: Q-VAX (Australia — occupational; not widely available globally) — pre-vaccination skin + serology screening
PREVENTION: occupational PPE (P2 respirator), animal vaccination (limited), birthing fluid management (avoid attending livestock parturition), pasteurisation, environmental control
OUTBREAK: ID + public health + occupational + livestock investigation; serology screening at-risk + treat
PREGNANCY POST-OUTBREAK: serology screen + treat + follow paediatric (congenital risk)
REPORT — notifiable in many jurisdictions
SSA: Kenya — pastoralist + abattoir + livestock — integrated One Health surveillance.

Kenya National Guidelines for Cardiovascular Diseases Management, Ministry of Health

title: Lyme disease — doxycycline (most stages); IV ceftriaxone for severe neuro/cardiac
population: Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato (USA — B. burgdorferi; Europe — B. afzelii, B. garinii); Ixodes tick (deer / sheep); peak summer; northern hemisphere; not endemic SSA (sporadic).
presentation: EARLY LOCALISED (days-weeks) — ERYTHEMA MIGRANS (expanding annular rash > 5 cm, central clearing — diagnostic) ± flu-like. EARLY DISSEMINATED (weeks-months) — multiple EM + carditis (AV block) + neuritis (cranial — facial palsy; meningitis; radiculitis). LATE (months-years) — arthritis (oligoarticular knee), acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans (Europe), encephalopathy.
redFlags: AV block 2nd/3rd degree (Lyme carditis) — telemetry + IV antibiotic + temporary pacing if needed
Bilateral facial palsy = Lyme until proven otherwise (Borrelia + sarcoidosis + GBS)
Pregnant + active Lyme — treat (no doxy — use amox or cefuroxime)
Post-Lyme symptoms (PTLDS — not relieved by prolonged antibiotic — supportive)
diagnostics: EARLY LOCALISED erythema migrans — CLINICAL diagnosis; treat empirically + DO NOT need serology (sensitivity poor early)
Disseminated / late — TWO-TIER SEROLOGY (ELISA → if positive/equivocal → Western blot — IgM + IgG)
PCR — skin biopsy / synovial fluid / CSF (limited sensitivity)
LP for neuroborreliosis (CSF lymphocytic + raised protein + intrathecal antibody synthesis)
ECG ± telemetry / Holter for carditis (PR > 300 ms = high block risk)
MRI / synovial fluid for arthritis / encephalitis
management: IDSA/AAN/ACR 2020 Lyme Guideline + NICE NG95 2018 + ESCMID:
EARLY LOCALISED + DISSEMINATED MILD:
DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg BD × 10 d (early localised) or × 14 d (disseminated mild)
Alternative: amoxicillin 500 mg TDS or cefuroxime axetil 500 mg BD × 14 d
Pregnancy: AMOXICILLIN or cefuroxime × 14 d (no doxy)
Children: doxy now ACCEPTED short course < 21 d age ≥ 8 yr (IDSA 2020 update) or amoxicillin
LYME ARTHRITIS:
Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 28 d (or amoxicillin)
If incomplete response — repeat 28 d course OR IV ceftriaxone 2 g OD × 14-28 d
Refractory (post-antibiotic Lyme arthritis) — NSAID + DMARD; not antibiotic
LYME CARDITIS:
Hospitalise if 2nd/3rd-degree AV block, symptomatic, syncope, PR > 300 ms
IV ceftriaxone 2 g OD × 14-21 d, transition to oral doxy when stable + PR < 300 ms
Mild (1st-degree) outpatient oral doxy × 14-21 d
Temporary pacing if high-grade block; permanent rarely needed (recovers)
NEUROBORRELIOSIS (meningitis, radiculitis, encephalitis):
IV ceftriaxone 2 g OD × 14-28 d (severe / encephalitis 28 d)
Alternative: doxycycline 200 mg BD or 100 mg BD × 14-28 d (CSF penetration acceptable — Lancet trials)
Facial palsy isolated: oral doxy or amox × 14-21 d (palsy resolves over weeks regardless)
ACRODERMATITIS chronica atrophicans (Europe): doxy × 28 d

POST-TREATMENT LYME DISEASE SYNDROME (PTLDS): NO benefit from prolonged/repeated antibiotic (multiple RCTs — Klempner NEJM 2001) — supportive + graded exercise + symptom management + multidisciplinary
PROPHYLAXIS post-tick bite:
Single-dose doxy 200 mg if (a) adult or > 8 yr (b) tick attached ≥ 36 h (c) within 72 h of removal (d) endemic area
Otherwise watch + treat if EM develops
PREVENTION: avoid tick areas + DEET / permethrin clothing + tick check + prompt removal (fine forceps at skin) + tick-borne disease vaccine — VLA15 Pfizer-Valneva Phase 3 emerging
SSA: not generally endemic — return-from-travel symptoms; consider in differential — refer ID.

title: Long COVID / Post-acute COVID-19 syndrome — multisystem rehabilitation + symptom-based
population: 10-30% of acute COVID infections develop ≥ 1 persistent symptom > 4-12 weeks; female + older + severe acute + comorbid + vaccinated less. Hundreds of millions globally affected.
presentation: Persistent symptoms > 4 wk (subacute) or > 12 wk (long COVID / post-COVID condition) post-SARS-CoV-2: fatigue + post-exertional malaise + cognitive dysfunction ('brain fog') + dyspnoea + chest pain + palpitations / POTS + autonomic dysfunction + anosmia/dysgeusia + sleep disturbance + mood + arthralgia + GI + chronic urticaria + thrombosis risk early + paediatric MIS-C. WHO definition: symptoms > 3 mo post-infection lasting > 2 mo, not explained by alternative.
redFlags: Persistent dyspnoea — exclude pulmonary embolism (early period); chronic ILD / pulmonary fibrosis (HRCT)
Chest pain — exclude myocarditis (cardiac MRI), pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, ischaemia
POTS / autonomic dysfunction — tilt table + holter
Cognitive impairment — formal neuropsychology + neuroimaging if focal
MIS-C (multisystem inflammatory syndrome) — children + young adults — fever + multi-organ — IVIG + steroid + ICU
diagnostics: CLINICAL diagnosis (no specific test confirms)

Tailored workup per symptom: D-dimer + CT-PA if PE suspected; HRCT chest if persistent dyspnoea/cough/abnormal exam; PFT (DLCO often low); echo + ECG ± cardiac MRI for chest pain/dyspnoea/palpitations; tilt-table for POTS; thyroid + cortisol if fatigue; ferritin + Hb + B12/folate / vit D / autoimmune; neuropsychology if cognitive
Exclude alternatives — hypothyroid, anaemia, depression, OSA, postural hypotension, cardiac, ME/CFS
Validated tools: COVID-19 Yorkshire Rehab Scale (C19-YRS); EQ-5D; FACIT-Fatigue
management: NICE NG188 + WHO 2023 + CDC + various long COVID consortia (RECOVER, PHOSP-COVID):
MULTIDISCIPLINARY PHENOTYPE-BASED:
Holistic assessment + rehabilitation plan + GP + multidisciplinary clinic if available
PACING for post-exertional malaise — DO NOT push graded exercise if PEM (worsens — same caveat as ME/CFS); energy management
Symptom-targeted graded return to activity if no PEM
RESPIRATORY:
Pulmonary rehabilitation + breathing techniques (inspiratory muscle training)
Inhaled corticosteroid/bronchodilator if asthma-like / new airway
Anticoagulation if PE confirmed
ILD / fibrosis — pulm + transplant pathway if progressive
CARDIOVASCULAR:
Myocarditis — cardiology + exercise restriction 3-6 mo + serial imaging
POTS — increased salt + fluid + compression stockings + graded exercise (recumbent → upright) + β-blocker (low-dose propranolol/ivabradine) + midodrine + fludrocortisone
Pericarditis — NSAID + colchicine
NEURO + COGNITIVE:
Brain fog — cognitive rehab + sleep + treat sleep apnoea + mood + exercise as tolerated
Headache — standard migraine pathways
Anosmia — olfactory training + corticosteroid trial
Small fibre neuropathy — gabapentinoid + IVIG investigational
Stroke — secondary prevention per stroke guidelines
FATIGUE / PEM — pacing + energy management + sleep + mood + treat anaemia / endocrine; AVOID forced graded exercise if PEM
MENTAL HEALTH: CBT for adjustment / anxiety / depression; mindfulness; peer support; specialist if severe
GI / OTHER: probiotics evidence weak; H2 blocker / PPI for dyspepsia; standard pathways
VACCINATION: COVID-19 vaccine + boosters + may modestly improve long COVID symptoms; influenza + pneumococcal protect
ANTIVIRALS post-acute — no proven benefit (PAXLOVID for long COVID trials mostly negative; ongoing)
PAEDIATRIC LONG COVID: less common; supportive + school accommodations + reassurance + MIS-C surveillance
OCCUPATIONAL: workplace accommodations + phased return + disability assessment + employer engagement
RESEARCH ONGOING: low-dose naltrexone, IVIG, plasma exchange, anti-inflammatory, exercise tolerance — enrol in trials (RECOVER + PHOSP-COVID + others)
SSA: under-recognised + access to multidisciplinary care limited; integrate with chronic disease + mental health + rehab services; advocacy + research participation.

references.label: NICE NG188 Managing Long-term Effects of COVID-19 (updated)

title: Pre-travel consultation — vaccines + malaria prophylaxis + risk-tailored advice
population: All travellers to higher-risk regions; visiting friends and relatives (VFR) particularly under-served + higher disease burden; pregnant + immunocompromised + young + chronic conditions need specialist input.
presentation: Pre-departure ideally 4-8 weeks before travel; last-minute possible but reduces some vaccine schedule completeness.
redFlags: Imminent travel < 1 wk — accelerated schedules + counsel limitations
Pregnant + endemic area (Zika / malaria / dengue) — defer or rigorous prevention
Immunocompromised + LIVE vaccine contraindication (yellow fever, oral typhoid, MMR, varicella, BCG, oral polio)
Chronic disease decompensation risk at altitude / temperature
Sub-Saharan Africa / Amazon yellow fever endemic — IHR vaccination certificate
Pilgrimage (Hajj) — meningococcal ACWY mandatory + IHR certificate
diagnostics: Itinerary: countries + regions + duration + style (urban/rural/expedition) + activities (animal contact, freshwater, altitude, diving)
Patient: age + pregnancy + medical conditions + medications + immunosuppression + prior vaccines + allergies
Country-specific risk: WHO + CDC Yellow Book + UK NaTHNaC TravelHealthPro + Kenya MoH Travel Clinic
management: VACCINES — schedule + book early:
ROUTINE catch-up: MMR + Tdap + polio booster + varicella + HPV + influenza + COVID

YELLOW FEVER (single dose lifetime per WHO 2016; IHR certificate valid 10 days after) — required entry to / from many SSA + Amazonian countries; live — contraindicated < 9 mo (caution 9-12 mo), pregnant (unless high risk), severely immunocompromised, thymic disease, ≥ 60 yr (caution — YEL-AVD risk)
TYPHOID injectable (Vi polysaccharide) or oral live Ty21a × 3 doses (live — contraindicated immunocompromised); booster 3-5 yr
HEPATITIS A: 2 doses 6-12 mo apart (1st dose protective 2 wk pre-travel); combined Hep A/B if both needed
HEPATITIS B: at-risk (medical / sex / drugs / blood / > 6 mo travel); accelerated 0-7-21 day + 12 mo
MENINGOCOCCAL ACWY: HAJJ/UMRAH MANDATORY + meningitis belt SSA dry season + students/military; some countries B (UK, NL, SA) for outbreak
RABIES pre-exposure 3-dose IM (or 2-dose accelerated WHO 2018) for prolonged rural + animal contact + remote (post-exposure simpler)
JAPANESE ENCEPHALITIS: rural Asia + > 1 mo or high-risk activity
TICK-BORNE ENCEPHALITIS: central / eastern Europe + forest activity
CHOLERA: live oral Dukoral for outbreak / cholera-endemic / aid worker / Hajj
POLIO: WHO IHR certificate from endemic / outbreak countries (Pakistan, Afghanistan, others); single dose before departure
COVID + INFLUENZA seasonal
MALARIA CHEMOPROPHYLAXIS — by region risk + drug resistance + traveller:
ATOVAQUONE-PROGUANIL (Malarone) — well-tolerated, 1-2 d before to 7 d after; daily; child weight-based; costly
DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg OD — 1-2 d before to 4 wk after; cheap; photosensitivity + GI + avoid pregnancy + < 8 yr
MEFLOQUINE 250 mg weekly — 2-3 wk before to 4 wk after; neuropsych contraindication (depression, anxiety, epilepsy, arrhythmia); usable pregnancy
PRIMAQUINE OR TAFENOQUINE for terminal eradication + P. vivax-predominant areas (G6PD TEST required)
CHLOROQUINE only in chloroquine-sensitive (rare now — Caribbean, Central America)
Recent: TAFENOQUINE single-dose + weekly emerging
Bite-prevention: DEET 30-50% / picaridin / IR3535 + permethrin-treated clothing + bed nets + air-conditioned/screened accommodation
TRAVELLERS' DIARRHOEA:
Food/water hygiene; ORS pack
Self-treatment: loperamide + azithromycin 500 mg × 3 d (preferred Asia — high quinolone resistance) or ciprofloxacin (Africa/Americas — caution)
Rifaximin prophylaxis selected (avoid routine)
Rotavirus + cholera vaccines selected groups
ALTITUDE: acclimatise + 'climb high, sleep low'; acetazolamide 125 mg BD 24h before + 2 d at altitude; HAPE/HACE — descend + dexamethasone + nifedipine
VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM long-haul: hydration + movement + compression stockings if risk; aspirin / LMWH if high-risk

OTHER: sun protection, water safety, road traffic (#1 traveller mortality cause — TRAUMA), animal bites, sexual health (condoms + STI awareness + PrEP), mental health, medical insurance + evacuation cover, jet lag, motion sickness, contraception

SPECIAL: pregnant — defer non-essential travel to high-risk (Zika WHO list); paediatric — adjusted prevention; chronic disease — letter + medications + alert card; cruise + expedition + diving — specialist input

POST-TRAVEL: fever within 3 mo of returning endemic area = malaria until proven otherwise + thick film + RDT + workup; persistent diarrhoea / skin / respiratory / fever — pattern-based ID workup; schistosomiasis serology 3 mo post freshwater exposure; HIV/STI + sexual exposure
SSA: Kenya — referral travel clinics (Aga Khan, Nairobi Hospital) + KMTC training; cross-border travel; pilgrimage Hajj.

title: Renal replacement therapy — modality choice (HD vs PD vs transplant) + shared decision-making
population: End-stage kidney disease (eGFR < 15 or symptomatic / fluid overload / electrolyte refractory) — preparing for or starting RRT.
presentation: ESKD symptoms (uraemia, anorexia, fluid overload, acidosis, hyperkalaemia) approaching dialysis. Plan ahead from eGFR < 20-30.
redFlags: EMERGENCY dialysis indications: refractory hyperkalaemia, severe metabolic acidosis, refractory fluid overload + pulmonary oedema, uraemic encephalopathy or pericarditis, severe drug intoxication
VASCULAR ACCESS planning — AVF maturation 8-12 wk + avoid PICC/cannulae in non-dominant arm
Cognitive / functional / social factors affecting modality choice
Carers + home setup for home modalities
diagnostics: eGFR trajectory + symptom burden + fluid + electrolyte + comorbidity
Vascular mapping ultrasound for AVF planning
Hepatitis B/C + HIV screen pre-RRT + immunise HBV early
Cardiac assessment (CKD — high CV burden)
Functional / cognitive / social assessment for home modality + transplant suitability
management: KDIGO 2024 + ERA-EDTA + ISN + KDOQI:
PREDIALYSIS EDUCATION + SHARED DECISION (start eGFR ~20):
Modalities — haemodialysis (HD in-centre vs home), peritoneal dialysis (CAPD vs APD), transplantation (deceased vs living donor), conservative care
Patient values + lifestyle + comorbidities + access + social
TRANSPLANT — best outcomes when feasible (esp. pre-emptive from living donor):
Refer early eGFR ≈ 20 for assessment
Living donor preferred + better outcomes
ABO-incompatible + paired exchange programmes
Contraindications: active malignancy, untreated infection, severe comorbidity + frailty, non-adherence
HAEMODIALYSIS:
Vascular access: AVF (gold) > AV graft > tunnelled CVC (last) — Fistula First initiative
AVF needs 8-12 wk maturation + avoid PICC/forearm cannulation early CKD
4 h × 3/wk standard (in-centre or home); home / nocturnal / daily for better outcomes selected
Heparin / regional citrate anticoag; monitor adequacy Kt/V ≥ 1.2
PERITONEAL DIALYSIS:
Catheter inserted + 2 wk for healing; gentle initiation
CAPD 4 exchanges manual day + APD automated overnight
Suitable home / employment / preserving residual renal function / less cardiovascular swings / good first modality often
Peritonitis — empirical Gram + + Gram − coverage intraperitoneal (cefazolin + ceftazidime / gentamicin); catheter retain unless refractory
Exit-site infection — topical / oral abx
Encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis (EPS) — rare late
CONSERVATIVE / SUPPORTIVE CARE:
Active comprehensive management without dialysis — frail, high-comorbidity, patient preference
Symptom control + advance care planning + palliative care + shared with family
Survival can be comparable in some elderly + frail vs dialysis with less QoL burden
ANCILLARY:
Iron + ESA (erythropoiesis-stimulating agent) for anaemia — target Hb 100-115; check iron studies; HIF-PHi (roxadustat) oral alternative
Phosphate binders (calcium carbonate / sevelamer / lanthanum) + active vitamin D (alfacalcidol / paricalcitol) + cinacalcet for SHPT
BP target individualised < 140/90 (often)
CV RF management + statin (KDIGO 4D + SHARP)
Vaccinations: HBV (essential before HD), pneumococcal, influenza, COVID, zoster recombinant; avoid live on transplant
Nutrition: protein 1.0-1.2 g/kg HD/PD; sodium / potassium / phosphate management; dietitian
Psychosocial: dialysis depression high; screen + manage; peer support

SSA: Kenya — KRH transplant programme expanding; HD access growing (private + KNH); PD scale-up potential (lower infrastructure); transplant capacity advocacy + ETHICS + donor regulation; cost a major access barrier — NHIF coverage advocacy.

title: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) — modality + anticoagulation in ICU
population: Critically ill AKI with haemodynamic instability + multi-organ failure where intermittent HD poorly tolerated; sepsis + cardiogenic shock + post-operative + ARDS.
presentation: AKI Stage 3 / RRT indication in ICU patient hemodynamically unstable for IHD; or fluid + solute control needs.
redFlags: Refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, pulmonary oedema, uraemic complications
Tumour lysis / rhabdo / drug toxicity dialysable
Sepsis with cytokine storm + AKI — CRRT for fluid management (cytokine removal not proven)
diagnostics: AKI severity KDIGO 1-3 (creatinine, urine output)
Fluid balance + haemodynamics + electrolytes + acid-base
Catheter — ultrasound-guided internal jugular preferred > femoral > subclavian (avoid)
Anticoagulation choice: heparin contraindications, citrate eligibility (severe liver failure caution)
management: KDIGO 2012 AKI + 2024 update + Surviving Sepsis 2021:
INDICATIONS (RIFLE/AKIN/KDIGO):

EMERGENCY (AEIOU): Acidosis severe + refractory, Electrolyte K+ > 6.5 refractory, Intoxication (lithium / metformin / salicylate / methanol / ethylene glycol / theophylline / valproate), Overload refractory fluid, Uraemic encephalopathy / pericarditis / bleeding
Earlier initiation — STARRT-AKI NEJM 2020 — NO benefit + harm; wait for established indication
MODALITY:
CRRT for haemodynamic instability + multi-organ — CVVH (convection), CVVHD (diffusion), CVVHDF (mixed)
SLED (sustained low-efficiency dialysis 6-12 h) — middle ground; cost-effective
IHD if stable + access available
DOSE:
Effluent 20-25 mL/kg/h (ATN trial NEJM 2008 + RENAL NEJM 2009 — no benefit of higher 35 vs 20-25)
Prescription vs delivered — aim 20-25 delivered (often need higher prescribed due to interruptions)
ANTICOAGULATION:
REGIONAL CITRATE (RCA) PREFERRED (KDIGO 2024) — circuit citrate + calcium reinfusion patient; longer filter life + less bleeding than heparin
Citrate contraindicated severe liver failure / shock (citrate accumulation + metabolic acidosis + ionised hypocalcaemia — monitor ionised Ca + total Ca + total/ionised Ca ratio < 2.5)
Heparin (systemic or regional) — alternative; HIT precautions
No anticoag — bleeding patient; high filter loss
Argatroban / fondaparinux — HIT alternative
FLUID MANAGEMENT:
Net ultrafiltration based on haemodynamics + cumulative balance
Avoid rapid fluid shifts; integrate with vasopressor + sedation
RECOVERY phase — slow weaning + native renal function recovery
CATHETER:
Right IJ preferred + ultrasound; left IJ; femoral acceptable; AVOID subclavian (stenosis later AVF)
Confirm position CXR before use
Tunnelled if prolonged need (> 2-3 wk)
WEANING:
Spontaneous urine output > 500 mL/d off diuretic = good sign
Discontinue + monitor 24-48 h; restart if needed
DRUG DOSING:
Most antibiotics + sedatives need adjustment for clearance with CRRT — pharmacist + drug clearance per modality + flow
Vancomycin, aminoglycoside, beta-lactam therapeutic monitoring
COMPLICATIONS:
Hypothermia (warm dialysate / blood)
Electrolyte derangement (hypophosphataemia common — add to dialysate)
Catheter infection / dysfunction
Bleeding from anticoagulation
Air embolism + clotting + access alarms
RECOVERY OUTCOMES — significant proportion become dialysis-independent (varies by aetiology + comorbidity); reduced QoL + mortality + dialysis dependence with severe AKI
SSA: CRRT machines expanding tertiary ICUs (KNH, Aga Khan, MTRH); SLED + PD alternatives where CRRT unavailable; train ICU + nephrology + nursing.
