title: Gestational trophoblastic disease — molar pregnancy + GTN with chemotherapy
population: Hydatidiform mole 1/1000 pregnancies in West, higher in Asia (Philippines 1/100). GTN (gestational trophoblastic neoplasia) — 50% follow molar, 25% follow miscarriage, 25% follow term pregnancy. Extremely chemo-sensitive.
presentation: Molar pregnancy: vaginal bleeding + uterus larger than dates + hyperemesis + early pre-eclampsia (< 20 wk — classic) + theca-lutein cysts + hyperthyroidism (β-hCG cross-reacts TSH) + 'snowstorm' US appearance + very high β-hCG (> 100,000). GTN: persistent / rising β-hCG + post-evacuation; metastasis (lung, vagina, brain, liver) — haemoptysis, neuro, pulmonary nodules.
redFlags: Brain or liver metastases — high-risk metastatic GTN — urgent oncology
Acute respiratory failure from pulmonary metastases
Severe pre-eclampsia + eclampsia presenting before 20 weeks (rare; suspect mole)
Subsequent pregnancy too soon — affects β-hCG monitoring
diagnostics: Quantitative β-hCG (very high — > 100,000) + serial monitoring
Pelvic US (snowstorm — complete mole; partial mole — fetus + abnormal placenta)
Histopathology — complete mole (46XX paternal genome) vs partial mole (69 chromosomes, triploid) — IHC + ploidy
Pre-evacuation: FBC + UEC + LFT + TFT + coagulation + blood group + CXR (lung mets baseline)
If suspected GTN: WHO FIGO scoring — age + antecedent pregnancy + interval + β-hCG + tumour size + sites + number of mets + prior chemo; ≤ 6 low-risk, ≥ 7 high-risk
Staging CT chest + abdo + pelvis + MRI brain (high-risk) + LP if neuro symptoms
Cardiology + thyroid storm risk pre-evacuation if very high β-hCG
management: ESMO 2022 + RCOG + FIGO + ISSTD + Charing Cross:
MOLAR PREGNANCY:
Suction evacuation (NOT misoprostol — risk of trophoblast embolisation) at experienced centre + cross-match + IV access; uterotonic post-evacuation
Anti-D if Rh- (partial mole has fetal tissue)
Histopathology + ploidy + genetic confirmation
CONTRACEPTION mandatory while β-hCG monitored (combined oral preferred; IUD after β-hCG normalises — risk if mole present)
Avoid pregnancy 6 mo (complete) or 12 mo (partial / GTN) until β-hCG documented normal
REGISTER in national trophoblastic disease centre (UK: Charing Cross, Sheffield, Dundee; Kenya/SSA: KEMRI / KNH oncology referral)
FOLLOW-UP β-hCG:
Weekly until normal × 3, then monthly × 6-12 mo (complete mole) or 6 mo (partial)
Rising or plateau β-hCG → GTN suspected → treat
GTN (persistent / metastatic / choriocarcinoma):
WHO FIGO score determines regimen
LOW-RISK GTN (score ≤ 6):
Single-agent — methotrexate (MTX 0.4 mg/kg/d × 5 d q2 wk OR MTX 50 mg IM days 1,3,5,7 with folinic acid days 2,4,6,8)
Or actinomycin D (DACT) — alternative or salvage
Cure rate > 90%
HIGH-RISK GTN (score ≥ 7) or metastatic (lung > 3 cm, brain, liver):
EMA-CO (etoposide + MTX + DACT + cyclophosphamide + vincristine) combination chemo
Brain mets: high-dose MTX + intrathecal MTX + whole-brain RT or stereotactic
Liver mets: arterial embolisation + chemo
Cure rate 80-90%
Refractory: EMA-EP (replacing CO with etoposide+cisplatin); BEP; immunotherapy emerging
Hysterectomy — selected (perimenopausal + resistant local + life-threatening bleeding)
CHORIOCARCINOMA (post-term pregnancy / metastatic) — same EMA-CO + intensive
PSTT (placental site trophoblastic tumour) — chemo-resistant — hysterectomy + EMA-EP
PROGNOSIS — excellent if early recognition + specialist referral + adequate chemo + follow-up
SUBSEQUENT PREGNANCIES — usually normal; 1-2% recurrence; early US in next pregnancy + β-hCG post-delivery
PSYCHOSOCIAL: pregnancy loss + cancer diagnosis + chemo + fertility uncertainty — support + counselling
SSA: Kenya — refer KEMRI / KNH / Aga Khan oncology; methotrexate + DACT widely available; EMA-CO needs tertiary infusion centre; trophoblastic registry advocacy.

title: Adult SVT + WPW — vagal → adenosine → ablation; avoid AV-node blockers in pre-excited AF
population: SVT 2-3/1000 in adults; AVNRT (60%) > AVRT (incl. WPW, 30%) > atrial tachycardia (10%). WPW pre-excitation 1-3/1000; risk of sudden death from pre-excited AF.
presentation: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia 150-250 bpm + palpitations + chest discomfort + dizziness + dyspnoea + light-headedness + syncope. WPW: short PR + delta wave + wide QRS on resting ECG; AF + WPW = irregular wide-complex tachycardia ("AF with pre-excitation") — EMERGENCY.
redFlags: Pre-excited AF (irregular wide complex + WPW) — AV-node blockers (adenosine, β-blocker, CCB, digoxin) CONTRAINDICATED — facilitate accessory pathway conduction → VF — give procainamide or DC cardiovert
Sudden cardiac death risk in WPW (short refractory accessory pathway) — ablation indicated
diagnostics: 12-lead ECG during SVT + sinus (look for short PR + delta wave in WPW)
Telemetry for paroxysmal
Echo to exclude structural disease
Holter / loop recorder if paroxysmal + not captured
Electrophysiology study + induction of pre-excited AF + accessory pathway refractory period — risk stratify WPW (short < 250 ms = high risk)
Electrolytes, TSH, drugs/caffeine review
management: ESC 2019 + ACC/AHA/HRS 2015:
ACUTE TERMINATION (haemodynamically stable narrow-complex regular SVT):
VAGAL MANOEUVRES first — Valsalva (modified — supine + leg-raise — REVERT trial Lancet 2015, more effective than standard) or carotid sinus massage (auscultate first, avoid in elderly / bruit / TIA)
ADENOSINE 6 mg IV rapid bolus + 20 mL saline flush in large vein (antecubital); if no response 1-2 min later → 12 mg → 12 mg
Warn patient of brief chest discomfort + flushing + impending doom feeling
Caution asthma (theoretical) + transplanted heart (start 3 mg)
Verapamil 5-10 mg IV slow (avoid in WPW + HF + LV dysfunction); diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg IV; β-blocker (metoprolol 5 mg IV)
Synchronised DC CARDIOVERSION 50-100 J if haemodynamically unstable or drug-refractory
AF + WPW (PRE-EXCITED AF — IRREGULAR WIDE COMPLEX):
EMERGENCY — DC cardioversion synchronised 100-200 J first-line
Procainamide 10-15 mg/kg IV over 30 min — if stable + no IHD/HF
Ibutilide alternative
AVOID AV-node blockers (adenosine, β-blocker, CCB verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin, amiodarone IV — can accelerate accessory pathway in some, controversial) — facilitate accessory → VF
Anticoagulate per AF (CHADS-VASc) + plan electrophysiology + ABLATION
PROPHYLAXIS recurrent SVT:
CATHETER ABLATION first-line for symptomatic SVT + WPW + recurrent — > 95% success + curative; minimal complication
Drug therapy if ablation deferred / refused — β-blocker, CCB (verapamil), flecainide / propafenone (no IHD) for AVRT/AVNRT
ASYMPTOMATIC WPW:
Risk stratify with EPS — short refractory pathway < 250 ms in AF + multiple pathways + high-risk occupation (pilot / soldier) → ablation
Most asymptomatic + long refractory — observation
PREGNANCY + SVT:
Vagal + adenosine safe; β-blocker (metoprolol) if needed (avoid atenolol 1st trimester); flecainide alternative
Delay ablation until post-delivery if possible (radiation exposure)
EDUCATION: identify + train vagal manoeuvres self-administered; medic-alert; recognise + present to ED if symptomatic SVT/AF
SSA: vagal manoeuvres + adenosine + DC cardioversion widely available; catheter ablation tertiary (KNH + Aga Khan + few centres); EPS scale-up advocacy.

references.label: ACC/AHA/HRS 2015 SVT + 2024 AF Guideline (incl. pre-excited AF)

title: Prostatitis + epididymo-orchitis — STI vs uropathogen pathway
population: Prostatitis: 8% lifetime men; bacterial (5-10%) vs chronic non-bacterial pelvic pain syndrome (CPPS, 90%). Epididymo-orchitis: STI < 35 yr (chlamydia, gonorrhoea); uropathogen + BPH ≥ 35 yr.
presentation: Acute prostatitis: fever + chills + perineal/pelvic pain + dysuria + LUTS + acute retention; very tender boggy prostate (gentle PR ONLY — avoid vigorous — bacteraemia). Chronic bacterial: recurrent UTI + same organism + perineal pain weeks/months. CPPS: pain + LUTS without infection (NIH IIIa inflam vs IIIb non-inflam). Epididymo-orchitis: scrotal pain + swelling + erythema + warmth ± fever; Prehn's sign (relief on elevation — supports vs torsion).
redFlags: Acute scrotum + young man — EXCLUDE TESTICULAR TORSION (sudden onset + nausea + high-riding + absent cremasteric + sx < 6h = surgical emergency — Doppler if available, otherwise surgical exploration)
Septic prostatitis + bacteraemia + perineal abscess — emergency IV antibiotic + drainage
Acute urinary retention from inflammation — catheter (SUPRAPUBIC preferred — avoid urethral worsening + sepsis seeding)
Recurrent UTI + same organism in man — chronic bacterial prostatitis / urological referral
Sterile pyuria + epididymitis < 35 — STI screen + treat
diagnostics: Urinalysis + culture (mid-stream)
STI screen if epididymitis < 35 or risk factors — urethral / urine NAAT for chlamydia + gonorrhoea + HIV + syphilis (Kenya MoH/CDC syndromic + lab confirm)
Acute prostatitis: blood culture if septic; FBC + CRP + creatinine; PSA NOT measured acutely (elevated; recheck after 6-8 wk recovery)
Imaging: scrotal US Doppler if torsion suspected; transrectal US if abscess; CT/MRI selected
Mears-Stamey 4-glass test (chronic prostatitis classification)
management: EAU 2024 + NICE NG109 + CDC STI 2021 + AUA:
ACUTE BACTERIAL PROSTATITIS:
Empirical antibiotic — Gram-negative coverage:
Outpatient mild: ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD or co-trimoxazole 960 mg BD × 2-4 wk
Inpatient severe: gentamicin + ampicillin OR ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD then PO step-down ciprofloxacin
Duration 2-4 weeks (longer to prevent chronic + abscess)
ANALGESIA + ANTIPYRETIC + α-blocker (tamsulosin) for LUTS + suprapubic catheter if retention (avoid urethral)
Drain abscess + urology if prostatic abscess on imaging
CHRONIC BACTERIAL PROSTATITIS:
Fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin / levofloxacin) × 4-6 wk (good prostate penetration); cotrim alternative
Refractory: tetracycline / azithromycin (atypical); intraprostatic injection (research)
CHRONIC PROSTATITIS / CPPS:

UPOINT-based: Urinary (α-blocker), Psychosocial (CBT), Organ-specific (5α-RI, NSAID, pelvic-floor PT), Infection (trial antibiotic if Mears-Stamey suggests), Neurologic (gabapentin / amitriptyline), Tenderness (pelvic-floor PT)
Multidisciplinary
EPIDIDYMO-ORCHITIS:
< 35 yr OR high-risk STI: CEFTRIAXONE 500 mg IM single + DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg BD × 10-14 d (covers chlamydia + gonorrhoea)
+ Test of cure GC at 1 wk + chlamydia at 4 wk; contact tracing partners; HIV + syphilis screen; Kenya MoH algorithm
≥ 35 yr / no STI risk OR enteric organism: cipro 500 mg BD × 10-14 d or ofloxacin
Severe / sepsis: IV ceftriaxone + admit + urology
Bed rest + scrotal elevation + ice + analgesia + NSAID + ABSTAIN sex until partners treated
Surgical exploration if torsion uncertain
Mumps orchitis — supportive (most resolve)
TB epididymo-orchitis — chronic indurated mass — biopsy + TB workup + ATT
PREVENTION:
Safe sex + condoms
STI screen + partner notification + treat
PrEP for high-risk MSM
Vaccination — HPV + Hep B + meningococcal as indicated
Treat BPH / structural urological cause
FOLLOW-UP: PSA at 6-8 wk recovery if elevated initially; sexual function counselling; recurrence surveillance
SSA: STI antibiotics widely available + syndromic management Kenya NASCOP + partner notification; tertiary urology referral for chronic / refractory; TB awareness.

title: Primary sclerosing cholangitis — MRCP + colonoscopy + transplant pathway
population: 1-16/100k; male 2:1; peak 30-50; 75% co-existing IBD (usually UC). Increased risk cholangiocarcinoma + colorectal cancer + gallbladder cancer.
presentation: Often asymptomatic; raised ALP + GGT on routine labs; fatigue + pruritus + abdominal pain; jaundice + cholangitis (RUQ + fever + jaundice) later; cirrhosis + portal HT + variceal bleed + liver failure end-stage.
redFlags: DOMINANT STRICTURE — workup cholangiocarcinoma (10-15% lifetime risk — CA 19-9 + ERCP + brush cytology + FISH; sometimes MRCP follow-up)
Colorectal cancer — annual colonoscopy in UC-PSC + dye-spray / chromoendoscopy
End-stage liver disease — transplant evaluation (MELD-Na used; PSC-specific exception)
Gallbladder polyps / mass — cholecystectomy threshold low
diagnostics: MRCP — gold standard; multifocal strictures + dilatations + 'beaded' appearance intra + extrahepatic ducts
ERCP only if intervention needed (dominant stricture, brush cytology, stenting) — risk of cholangitis
LFT (cholestatic — ALP + GGT raised) + ALT/AST + bilirubin + albumin + INR + IgG4 (exclude IgG4-related cholangitis)
ANA + ANCA (especially p-ANCA) — positive in 70%
Antimitochondrial Ab — exclude PBC overlap (positive PBC → different pathway)
Liver biopsy — usually NOT needed; only small-duct PSC (normal MRCP) or overlap workup
COLONOSCOPY at diagnosis + annually (50-75% have IBD often subclinical)
CA 19-9 baseline + serial annual (cholangiocarcinoma surveillance)
Abdominal US + CT/MRI 6-12 monthly (HCC / cholangiocarcinoma / gallbladder)
Fibroscan / staging
management: AASLD 2010 + EASL 2022 + BSG:
NO disease-modifying therapy with proven survival benefit (URSO does NOT improve overall survival despite improving LFTs — meta-analyses)
Ursodeoxycholic acid 13-15 mg/kg/d (low-mid dose) — some clinicians use for symptom + LFT improvement; AVOID HIGH-DOSE > 28 mg/kg (Lindor NEJM 2009 — adverse outcomes)
Vedolizumab + investigational therapies (norUDCA, FXR agonists obeticholic acid + cilofexor, anti-LOXL2, anti-fibrotics, biologics) — research trials
DOMINANT STRICTURE — ERCP + balloon dilatation ± temporary stent + brush cytology + FISH; cholangiocarcinoma workup
CHOLANGITIS: ceftriaxone + metronidazole + biliary drainage urgent (ERCP / PTC / surgery)
PRURITUS:
Cholestyramine 4 g BD-QDS
Rifampicin 150-600 mg/d
Naltrexone / nalmefene
Sertraline / odevixibat (IBAT inhibitor — Bylvay FDA 2021 progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis; emerging PSC trials)
Phototherapy refractory
MAINTENANCE:
Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)
Bone health — DEXA + Ca + vitamin D + bisphosphonate if osteoporotic
Vaccinations (no live if cirrhotic / pre-transplant — pneumococcal + influenza + COVID + zoster recombinant + Hep A + Hep B)
Cardiovascular RF + statin (NOT contraindicated)
Manage IBD per gastroenterology
SURVEILLANCE:
Cholangiocarcinoma — annual CA 19-9 + MRI/MRCP
Colorectal cancer — annual colonoscopy + chromoendoscopy if UC-PSC (highest CRC risk)
Gallbladder cancer — annual US; cholecystectomy for any polyp regardless of size
HCC — 6-monthly US ± AFP
Osteoporosis — DEXA every 2-3 yr
Endoscopy variceal screen at cirrhosis + every 1-2 yr
TRANSPLANT:
Refer when MELD ≥ 15 or refractory pruritus / cholangitis / dominant strictures unresponsive / quality of life
PSC-specific MELD exception in many programmes
Recurrence post-transplant 20-30% — affects long-term outcome
Cholangiocarcinoma + transplant — Mayo protocol selected (chemo-radiation + transplant) for early hilar < 3 cm
PSYCHOSOCIAL: chronic + uncertain + cancer risk + transplant — counselling + peer support + IBD overlap
SSA: MRCP access tertiary; ERCP for dominant stricture; URSO + supportive widely available; transplant programmes emerging (Kenya KNH planning); awareness for cholangitis prompt treatment.

title: Primary biliary cholangitis — UDCA first-line, OCA / fibrate for non-responders
population: Female 9:1; peak 40-60; 35/100k; AMA-positive autoimmune cholestasis; family history common.
presentation: Often asymptomatic — raised ALP + GGT + AMA on screening. Fatigue (40-80%) + pruritus + sicca syndrome + dry eyes + jaundice late; portal HT + cirrhosis end-stage. Increased risk of osteoporosis + dyslipidaemia.
redFlags: Cirrhosis decompensation — ascites + variceal bleed + HE + transplant referral
AIH-PBC overlap (high ALT/AST + raised IgG + biopsy) — adds steroid + AZA
Pregnancy + PBC (cholestasis worsens 3rd trimester; UDCA safe; pruritus management)
diagnostics: ALP > 1.5× ULN + AMA-M2 positive (≥ 1:40) = diagnostic without biopsy in most
AMA-negative PBC (5-10%) — anti-sp100, anti-gp210, anti-PML (PBC-specific ANA) — biopsy + clinical
LFT cholestatic + bilirubin + albumin + INR + IgG + IgM
ANA + SMA + IgG (exclude AIH overlap)
Lipids (often elevated — usually not atherogenic)
TSH (autoimmune thyroid 20-25%)
DEXA + bone profile + vit D
US baseline + 6-monthly (HCC surveillance once cirrhotic)
Fibroscan / non-invasive fibrosis staging
Biopsy reserved — AMA-negative, AIH overlap suspected, drug-induced exclusion, atypical course
management: EASL 2017 + AASLD 2018 + 2023 updates:
FIRST-LINE: URSODEOXYCHOLIC ACID (URSO/UDCA) 13-15 mg/kg/d divided — improves LFTs + survival + reduces transplant need (POISE + multiple cohort studies)
Response assessment at 12 months: POISE-criteria + Paris-II + Toronto + GLOBE/UK-PBC risk scores
GOOD responder: ALP < 1.67× ULN + bilirubin normal at 12 mo — continue UDCA only — normal life expectancy approx
INADEQUATE responder ~ 25-40% — ADD second-line
SECOND-LINE (UDCA inadequate response):

OBETICHOLIC ACID (Ocaliva — FXR agonist) 5 mg OD titrate to 10 mg OD (FDA 2016, POISE NEJM 2016) — improves LFTs; SE pruritus (often dose-limiting); caution decompensated cirrhosis (REGENERATE-style warnings — recent label restrictions)
FIBRATES — bezafibrate 400 mg OD (BEZURSO NEJM 2018) or fenofibrate — improves LFTs + survival; off-label many countries; renal + muscle monitoring
Triple therapy emerging (UDCA + OCA + fibrate)
THIRD-LINE / refractory:
Seladelpar (PPARδ agonist) — RESPONSE trial Hepatology 2023 + FDA approval 2024
Elafibranor (PPARα/δ agonist) — ELATIVE NEJM 2023 + FDA 2024
Anti-IL-12/23 (ustekinumab) — research
Liver transplant — end-stage / refractory pruritus
PRURITUS:
Cholestyramine 4 g BD-QDS
Rifampicin 150-600 mg
Naltrexone / nalmefene
Sertraline
IBAT inhibitor — odevixibat / linerixibat (GLIMMER trial)
FATIGUE: rule out anaemia + hypothyroid + sleep apnoea + depression; modafinil selected
OSTEOPOROSIS: Ca + vitamin D + bisphosphonate / denosumab if FRAX-high
DYSLIPIDAEMIA: statin (not contraindicated; rarely causes flare)
AIH-PBC OVERLAP: add prednisolone + azathioprine to UDCA
PREGNANCY: UDCA SAFE throughout; cholestasis worsens 3rd trimester — manage pruritus + monitor fetal wellbeing + LFT; multidisciplinary
VACCINES: pneumococcal + influenza + COVID + Hep A + Hep B + zoster recombinant (no live if cirrhotic / immunosuppressed)
HCC surveillance once cirrhotic — 6-monthly US ± AFP
TRANSPLANT — MELD ≥ 15, refractory complications, severe pruritus, recurrent variceal bleed; PBC recurrence post-transplant 20-30% — affects long-term outcome
SSA: UDCA widely available + KEML; OCA + fibrate + newer agents access advocacy; transplant programmes emerging.

title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria — flow cytometry + complement inhibitor (eculizumab/ravulizumab)
population: Rare — 1-10/million; acquired PIGA mutation in haematopoietic stem cell → CD55 + CD59 GPI-anchor deficiency → complement-mediated haemolysis. Median age 30s-40s.
presentation: Intravascular haemolytic anaemia (Hb low, LDH high, indirect bilirubin, haemoglobinuria — classically morning urine) + pancytopenia (overlap with aplastic anaemia + MDS) + thrombosis (venous esp. hepatic — Budd-Chiari, cerebral, abdo) + abdominal pain + dysphagia + erectile dysfunction (NO-related smooth muscle).
redFlags: Acute thrombosis — Budd-Chiari + cerebral venous sinus + abdominal venous — leading mortality cause — anticoagulate + complement inhibition
Aplastic anaemia overlap with profound cytopenia + transfusion dependence
Meningococcal infection on complement inhibitor — vaccinate before + chemo-prophylaxis
Pregnancy + PNH — high thrombotic risk + management + delivery planning
diagnostics: FLOW CYTOMETRY — GPI-anchor (CD55 + CD59) deficient clone on RBC + granulocytes + monocytes; FLAER (fluorescein-labelled aerolysin) most sensitive — gold standard diagnosis
FBC (anaemia + neutropenia + thrombocytopenia variable); reticulocyte raised; LDH markedly raised; haptoglobin low; indirect bilirubin raised; urine haemosiderin
Coombs DAT NEGATIVE (distinguishes from AIHA)
Iron studies (chronic haemoglobinuria → iron deficiency)
UEC + LFT + coag; D-dimer for thrombosis
Bone marrow if cytopenias / AA overlap / MDS workup; cytogenetics
Imaging for thrombosis (Doppler, CT/MRI venous, MRCP for Budd-Chiari)
management: International PNH Working Group + IWG 2024 + AAWG:
COMPLEMENT INHIBITION first-line for classical PNH + symptomatic (haemolysis + thrombosis + transfusion-dependent):
ECULIZUMAB (Soliris) — C5 inhibitor IV q14 d — TRIUMPH + SHEPHERD NEJM 2004/2006 — landmark — reduces haemolysis + thrombosis + improves survival
RAVULIZUMAB (Ultomiris) — long-acting C5 inhibitor IV q8 wk — FDA 2018, ALXN1210 trials — non-inferior to eculizumab; better convenience
PEGCETACOPLAN (Empaveli) — C3 inhibitor SC twice weekly — FDA 2021 (PEGASUS NEJM 2021 — superior to eculizumab for haemoglobin + transfusion in suboptimal responders to anti-C5)
Iptacopan (Fabhalta — oral factor B inhibitor BID) — FDA 2023 (APPLY-PNH + APPOINT-PNH) — first ORAL treatment
Danicopan (factor D inhibitor) — add-on to anti-C5
Crovalimab (anti-C5 — long-acting subcutaneous) — emerging
MENINGOCOCCAL VACCINE — MenACWY + MenB at least 2 wk BEFORE complement inhibitor (and revaccinate per schedule) — MENINGOCOCCAL SEPSIS risk increased 1000× on anti-C5
Penicillin V prophylaxis 250 mg BD additional layer (some guidelines) for at least first 2 wk after vaccine + ongoing in some programmes
Medic-alert card + emergency antibiotic supply + fever education
Other vaccines: pneumococcal + Hib + influenza + COVID
FOLATE + IRON supplementation
ANTICOAGULATION:
For acute thrombosis — therapeutic LMWH → DOAC (apixaban / rivaroxaban) or warfarin INR 2-3
Prophylaxis if PNH clone > 50% + thrombosis history (not all asymptomatic on anti-C5)
Budd-Chiari — anticoagulant + TIPS / liver transplant
STEM CELL TRANSPLANT (allo-HSCT) — CURATIVE option:
Indications: aplastic anaemia / severe pancytopenia / MDS evolution / refractory PNH / pregnancy planning / cost-prohibitive lifelong therapy
Best with matched sibling donor
Multidisciplinary
TRANSFUSION + IRON CHELATION as needed
APLASTIC ANAEMIA overlap — immunosuppression (ATG + ciclosporin) + eltrombopag + transplant
MDS evolution — surveillance (cytogenetics); transplant
PREGNANCY:
High maternal + fetal risk + thrombosis
Continue eculizumab / ravulizumab throughout (safe + extensive data — Kelly NEJM 2015)
Prophylactic LMWH throughout pregnancy + 6 wk postpartum
Monitor closely + obstetric MDT
MONITORING: FBC + LDH + reticulocyte + flow cytometry clone size periodic; thrombosis surveillance + symptom enquiry
PSYCHOSOCIAL: rare + chronic + lifelong infusion + cost — peer support + counselling
SSA: ultra-rare; complement inhibitor access extremely limited + cost ($400-700k/yr in US) — advocacy + transplant access + clinical trial referral.

title: Hypertensive urgency vs emergency — end-organ damage flag, gradual vs rapid BP reduction
population: 1-3% of hypertensive patients yearly; majority hypertensive urgency (no acute end-organ damage); hypertensive emergency (with damage) is uncommon but life-threatening.
presentation: BP ≥ 180/120 mmHg. URGENCY: high BP without acute end-organ damage. EMERGENCY: severe HTN + acute target-organ injury — hypertensive encephalopathy, acute stroke, acute LV failure / pulmonary oedema, ACS, aortic dissection, AKI (creatinine rise + proteinuria + haematuria), retinopathy grade 3-4 (haemorrhage / exudate / papilloedema), eclampsia, pheo crisis.
redFlags: EMERGENCY end-organ — neuro (encephalopathy / stroke / haemorrhage), cardiac (ACS / LV failure / pulmonary oedema), AKI, aortic dissection (asymmetric pulse + radial-femoral delay + tearing pain), eclampsia — IMMEDIATE controlled BP lowering + cause-specific
Pseudohypertensive crisis — anxiety + non-adherence + pain — recheck after rest + treat trigger
Pheo crisis — use α-blocker FIRST never β-blocker monotherapy
Pregnancy + severe hypertension ≥ 160/110 — pre-eclampsia / eclampsia pathway
Stroke + thrombolysis BP > 185/110 — must reduce before tPA
diagnostics: Repeat BP after 15-30 min rest in seated quiet environment with appropriate cuff size
Check both arms + leg BP if suspected dissection (asymmetry > 20 mmHg systolic = consider)

Examine for end-organ damage: neuro (mental + focal + fundoscopy), cardiac (chest pain + ECG + troponin + CXR + echo), renal (urinalysis + UEC), aortic (asymmetric pulse + CT), pregnancy (urinalysis + PCR + FBC + LFT + reflexes)
Symptoms — headache + visual + chest pain + dyspnoea + neuro + abdominal pain + nausea
Medication history + adherence + new drugs (cocaine, sympathomimetic, MAOI + tyramine, sudden BP-med stop)
Pregnancy test in women of childbearing age
management: ESC 2024 + ACC/AHA 2017/2023 + NICE NG136 + JNC8:
FIRST — distinguish URGENCY vs EMERGENCY (end-organ damage determines pathway):
URGENCY (severe BP ≥ 180/120 NO acute organ damage):
NO need for IV / parenteral therapy — slow oral BP reduction over hours-days
GOAL: 20-25% reduction over 24-48 h to ≤ 160/100; THEN gradual toward 140/90 over days-weeks
AVOID short-acting nifedipine sublingual (sudden drops + ischaemic events — historic + abandoned)
Restart / adjust outpatient regimen: ACE-i / ARB / CCB / thiazide / β-blocker as appropriate
Identify + treat trigger — non-adherence + new med + pain + anxiety + alcohol + drugs
Outpatient with 24-48 h follow-up; ensure no end-organ before discharge
EMERGENCY (BP severe + acute end-organ):
ICU / HDU + arterial line + IV antihypertensive titration
GOAL: 25% reduction in MAP within 1 h (some specific scenarios faster); then to ~160/100 over 2-6 h; then gradual toward 140/90 over 24-48 h
AVOID rapid normalisation — cerebral / coronary / renal hypoperfusion
AGENT BY CAUSE (organ-specific):
HYPERTENSIVE ENCEPHALOPATHY / acute ischaemic stroke + tPA candidate (BP > 185/110): labetalol / nicardipine; AVOID nitroprusside (ICP rise)
Acute haemorrhagic stroke (SBP > 180 + ICH): nicardipine / labetalol → target SBP ~140 (INTERACT-3 / RIGHT-2 / ATACH-II)
ACS: nitroglycerin + β-blocker (labetalol / metoprolol)
Acute LV failure / pulmonary oedema: nitroglycerin + furosemide + nitroprusside or clevidipine
Aortic dissection: target SBP < 120 + HR < 60 within 5-10 min — esmolol / labetalol FIRST (β-blockade) then nicardipine or nitroprusside (avoid lone vasodilator — increases shear stress)
AKI: nicardipine / fenoldopam
Pheo crisis: PHENTOLAMINE (α-blocker) / sodium nitroprusside; NEVER β-blocker alone
Eclampsia / severe pre-eclampsia: LABETALOL / NIFEDIPINE (immediate-release IR — short-acting safe in pregnancy) + magnesium sulphate for seizure prevention
Cocaine / sympathomimetic crisis: BENZODIAZEPINE first (calms sympathetic) + phentolamine / nitroglycerin; AVOID β-blocker alone (unopposed α)
IV AGENTS COMMONLY USED:
Labetalol 10-20 mg IV bolus + infusion (mixed α/β — good first-line many emergencies)
Nicardipine 5 mg/h IV infusion titrate (CCB)
Clevidipine (short-acting CCB infusion)
Nitroglycerin infusion (cardiac contexts)
Nitroprusside (last resort + ICU + cyanide risk + short-term)
Esmolol (β-blocker — dissection + tachyarrhythmia)
Hydralazine IV (pregnancy)
POST-EMERGENCY — transition to oral after stabilisation; outpatient follow-up with comprehensive workup for secondary HTN (renovascular + endocrine + OSA)
WORKUP for secondary HTN if emergency in young / refractory: renal Doppler + renal artery + plasma metanephrines + aldosterone-renin ratio + TSH + cortisol + OSA screen
PRIMARY CARE follow-up: home BP monitoring + adherence + lifestyle (DASH + reduce Na + weight + exercise + alcohol + smoking) + medication reconciliation + identify barriers

SSA: oral antihypertensives (amlodipine + lisinopril + losartan + hydrochlorothiazide) widely available KEML; IV agents tertiary; magnesium for pregnancy emergency universally available + Kenya MoH protocol.
